rationale: Walls provide vertical support for the roof structure; roof cannot be installed without completed load-bearing walls.
Roof trusses or joists form the structural framework onto which the roof deck and covering are applied.
Roof decking (e.g., plywood sheathing) must be laid over trusses before final roof covering (shingles, membrane) can be applied.
While roof completion before cladding is preferred for weather protection and proper drainage detailing, it is not always physically mandatory.
Roof must be completed to provide a weather-tight enclosure before interior finishes (drywall, painting, flooring) can be installed to prevent water damage.
Walls require a stable load-bearing base; foundations and slabs provide the level surface and structural support needed for wall construction.
The framing (wood or metal studs) must be laid out and partially assembled or ready before the wall system (as a component) can be erected or installed.
Sheathing (plywood, OSB, or gypsum) is typically applied to the frame or is integral to the wall assembly installation process.
The roof structure and ceiling systems bear on top of walls; walls must be erected and braced before any roof framing or decking can be placed.
Interior finishing work like drywall installation, taping, and plastering requires the wall structure to be fully erected and stable before application.
The ground must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstacles, and graded to the proper elevation before excavation and foundation work can begin.
Soil bearing capacity and composition must be analyzed to determine the appropriate foundation type, depth, and reinforcement requirements.
Property boundaries and building footprint must be staked out precisely before excavation can proceed to ensure the foundation is placed correctly.
The foundation provides the load-bearing base upon which the structural frame is erected; framing cannot begin without a cured foundation in place.

Underslab plumbing pipes and drains are laid directly on or within the foundation slab/footing system before the slab is poured; however, rough-in plumbing must be installed after foundation walls/footings are in place but before the final slab pour.
Beams require stable support from completed foundations to bear structural loads safely.
Beams are typically placed on or between columns to transfer loads; columns must be in place to support the beams.
For cast-in-place concrete beams, formwork must be constructed to shape and support the wet concrete before beam casting.
Steel reinforcement must be positioned within the formwork before concrete is poured for the beam.
Beams provide primary support for floor or roof slabs; slabs are poured after beams are in place to ensure proper load transfer and structural continuity.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work above ceilings can begin after beams are installed to use beams for support and routing, though this is a soft preference as some work can be done in parallel.
Columns require a stable load-bearing base. Foundation or footings must be completed first to provide structural support and proper load transfer.
Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied within the column formwork before concrete is poured, as it cannot be inserted after the concrete has set.
Formwork (molds) must be erected and secured before pouring concrete to contain and shape the column.
Concrete must be poured and gain sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed without damaging the column.
Columns must be erected and cured to support vertical loads before beams and slabs that rest on them can be constructed.
The foundation provides a stable, level base that supports the slab. The slab cannot be poured until the foundation walls or footings are in place and cured.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and compacted before any concrete slab can be poured.
A compacted gravel or crushed stone layer is required beneath the slab for drainage and to prevent ground movement.
A vapor retarder (polyethylene sheet) must be placed over the subbase before pouring concrete to prevent moisture migration into the slab.
The slab serves as the ground floor platform upon which walls and vertical framing are erected.
While some under-slab utilities are laid before the pour, any post-pour MEP work in the slab area must wait until concrete has fully cured.
The rough opening (framed hole in the wall) must be prepared and sized correctly before a window can be installed, as the window needs a structurally sound and properly dimensioned opening.
Waterproof membrane and flashing must be applied around the rough opening before window placement to prevent moisture intrusion behind the window frame.
After the window is set in place, the gaps between the window frame and the rough opening can be insulated with spray foam or other insulation to provide thermal and air sealing.
Interior trim (casing, sill, stool) is attached to the window frame and wall; this cannot be properly installed until the window is securely in place.
Exterior siding or cladding around the window must be installed after the window is placed to properly overlap the window flange and ensure weathertightness.
The door frame provides the structural support and mounting surface for the door; without a properly installed frame, the door cannot be hung or fitted.
The rough opening (with correct dimensions, studs, and headers) must be built and ready before a door can be installed into the wall.
Load-bearing and non-load-bearing walls must be framed to create the opening and support structure where the door will be placed.
Handles, locks, hinges, and other hardware are mounted on the door and frame after the door is hung; installing hardware before the door is in place is not physically possible.

While painting can be done in any order, it is standard practice to finish wall surfaces and install trim around the door after the door is hung to achieve clean lines and proper fitting, though this is a workflow preference rather than a physical necessity.
The structural frame (steel or concrete) must be fully erected and stabilized to provide the load-bearing support and attachment points for the curtain wall system.
Floor slabs and slab edges must be completed to provide the horizontal support and anchorage for curtain wall panels and to establish floor-by-floor working platforms.
Building envelope waterproofing and air/vapor barriers must be applied to the slab edges and structural elements to prevent moisture intrusion before the curtain wall is sealed against them.

While interior work can begin in other areas, finishing walls directly behind curtain wall areas should wait until the curtain wall is installed and sealed to prevent water damage to interior finishes.
The curtain wall framing must be installed first so that glass panels (glazing) can be set into the frames and perimeter sealants can be applied to ensure weathertightness.
Stairs require a stable base; foundations must be completed to support the structural load of the staircase.
The main structural frame or floor slabs must be in place to define the vertical openings and support points where stairs will be anchored.
Stairs provide access between levels; wall finishing near stair openings is typically done after stairs are installed to ensure proper alignment and fit.
Handrails and balustrades are attached to the stair structure itself, so the stair must be in place first.
While not physically required, it is more efficient to install stairs before laying finished flooring on upper levels to avoid damage and ensure proper stair-to-floor transitions.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the proper depth and slope before ramp construction can begin, as the ramp requires a stable, prepared subgrade.
A compacted subbase or foundation layer (e.g., crushed stone or concrete base) must be placed to support the ramp structure and prevent settling or cracking.
The ramp structural form (e.g., formed concrete, asphalt base) must be completed before any final surface treatment like topping, sealcoating, or non-slip finish is applied.
Ramp must be fully constructed and cured (if concrete) before safety railings and handrails can be anchored or installed along its edges.

While the ramp must be structurally complete for final inspection and ADA compliance signage placement, some preliminary checks could occur during construction, making it a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
The ceiling is typically attached to or suspended from the structural framing or roof structure above. The structural frame must be in place to provide support for the ceiling system.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems that run above the ceiling (ductwork, wiring, piping) must be installed before the ceiling is closed in, otherwise access would be blocked and rework would be required.
Although walls can be finished before ceilings, it is common practice to complete ceiling work before final wall painting to avoid damaging finished wall surfaces during overhead work.

Ceiling work (e.g., drywall, acoustic tiles, painting overhead) generates debris and dust that would damage finished flooring. Flooring should be installed after ceiling completion to avoid contamination and damage.

successor: Final Electrical Fixture Installation (Lighting, Ceiling Fans)
rationale: Ceiling-mounted fixtures and devices are attached directly to the ceiling surface or grid; the ceiling must be in place to provide the mounting surface for these fixtures.
Concrete must be fully cured and dried before waterproofing membrane application to prevent moisture entrapment and ensure adhesion
Surface must be clean, dry, and free of debris, dust, oil, or protrusions to ensure proper bonding of waterproofing materials
Primer must be applied to the substrate prior to waterproofing membrane to enhance adhesion and seal porous surfaces
A protective screed or overlay must be applied over waterproofing to protect the membrane from mechanical damage during subsequent construction activities
Floor finishes such as tiles or coverings must be installed after waterproofing is complete to ensure the waterproofing layer remains intact and uninterrupted
Structural framing (columns, beams, slabs) must be completed to provide load-bearing support and floor attachment points for partition walls.
Rough-in services such as conduit, piping, and ductwork that run within or behind walls must be installed before partitions are closed up, otherwise costly demolition or rework would be required.
Partition walls require a finished floor surface or structural slab to anchor to; the floor must be poured and cured before wall layout and erection.
Partition framing must be complete before applying drywall, plasterboard, or plaster finishes to the wall surfaces.
Partition openings (door/window rough openings) must be framed before doors and windows can be installed and fixed into the partition.

While not physically mandatory, it is best practice to complete partition installation before installing final fixtures (switches, sockets, outlets) to avoid damage and enable precise placement against the finished wall surface.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable and safe working surface for formwork setup.
Excavation and foundation preparation (including footings and blinding concrete) must be completed so that formwork can be accurately placed and aligned on the prepared foundation.
In many construction sequences, reinforcement cages or rebar mats are placed first, then formwork is erected around them to encase the steel before concreting.
Formwork creates the mold that holds liquid concrete in place; concrete cannot be poured until the formwork is fully erected, aligned, braced, and secured.
After concrete is poured and gains sufficient strength, the formwork must be removed (struck); thus formwork installation is a prerequisite to the eventual striking process.
Concrete must be poured and placed into the formwork before the forms can be removed. The formwork holds the wet concrete in shape until it gains sufficient strength.
Concrete must undergo adequate curing and reach sufficient compressive strength before formwork can be safely stripped without damaging the structural element.
The formwork must first be installed and erected before it can be removed or struck. Striking is the dismantling and removal of previously installed formwork.

Once formwork is removed, any surface defects, tie holes, or imperfections in the concrete surface become visible and can be patched, ground, or finished. This is a soft preference as some finishing can be done during or alongside striking in some cases.
The exposed concrete surface must be inspected only after formwork is removed to verify quality, appearance, and structural integrity. Inspection cannot occur while forms are still in place.
Steel reinforcement bars must be positioned and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity; concrete cannot be poured over missing rebar.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and compacted before concrete can be placed, especially for footings or slabs.
After pouring, concrete must be left to cure and gain strength before any loads or further work can be applied; curing is the natural follow-up process.
Formwork cannot be removed until the poured concrete has sufficiently hardened and cured to support its own weight.

Concrete must be placed and finished before curing can begin, as curing is the process of maintaining moisture and temperature conditions to allow the concrete to properly hydrate and gain strength after it has been placed.

The concrete surface must be finished (screeded, floated, troweled) before curing starts, because curing involves applying moisture-retaining methods (like wet coverings or curing compounds) that should only be applied after final finishing is complete.
Formwork should remain in place during the curing period to support the concrete until it achieves sufficient strength; stripping too early can damage the green concrete.
Curing must be completed (i.e., the concrete has reached the specified maturity) before any coatings, sealers, or further surface preparation can be applied to the concrete surface.
The concrete must be properly cured to achieve its design strength before it can safely bear structural or service loads.
Concrete must be placed and spread into forms before any finishing operations (screeding, floating, troweling) can begin.
Concrete must be consolidated (vibrated) to remove voids and ensure proper compaction before finishing can take place.
Screeding is the initial strike-off operation to bring the concrete surface to proper grade and is required before final finishing operations.
Contraction/control joints are typically cut after finishing but before the concrete fully hardens, to control random cracking.
The structural frame (concrete/steel) must be in place to provide load-bearing support and attachment points for glazing systems.
The building must be watertight from above before installing glazing to prevent water damage to interior finishes and glazing components.
Interior finishes such as drywall, painting, and flooring must be protected from weather; glazing encloses the building envelope first.
HVAC system testing requires a sealed building envelope to accurately measure air pressure, temperature control, and system performance.
Glazing should be completed before final cleaning to avoid re-soiling surfaces, but this is a logical sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems must be fully installed before they can be tested and commissioned to verify they operate correctly.
The building structure must be substantially complete and enclosed before testing of internal systems can commence, as the systems require a protected environment.
Permanent electrical power supply must be connected to allow testing of all electrical systems, equipment, and controls during commissioning.
All systems must be tested, commissioned, and proven to work correctly before the building can be formally handed over to the client for practical completion.
Commissioning must be completed so that any defects identified during testing can be rectified and a final inspection carried out.
Surfaces must be clean, smooth, and free of debris or defects before paint can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and a uniform finish.
Primer must be applied and dried before painting to seal the surface, improve paint adhesion, and provide a uniform base color.
Plastering or drywall taping and mudding must be completed, sanded, and cured before painting to create a smooth substrate.
Fresh masonry or concrete must be fully cured (typically 28 days) before painting to prevent alkali attack on the paint and ensure proper bonding.
Caulking around windows, doors, and joints must be applied and cured before painting to seal gaps and prevent moisture ingress behind the paint film.

Final cleaning and touch-up work is typically performed after painting to remove paint splatters and correct any defects, though this is a preference for quality finish rather than a physical necessity.
Wall painting should be completed before installing finished flooring to avoid paint drips, dust, and debris damaging the new floor surface.

successor: Trim and Millwork Installation (if painting before install)
rationale: If painting is done before final trim installation, the trim work comes after; however this depends on the construction approach (paint before install or after install), so it is a soft preference.

successor: Final Fixture Installation (Lighting, Electrical Covers, Switches)
rationale: Final electrical fixtures, switch plates, and outlet covers should be installed after painting to avoid getting paint on them and to ensure a clean finish around the fixtures.
Formwork provides the mould and support structure into which reinforcement bars are placed; rebar cannot be fixed in position without the formwork in place first.
Reinforcement bars must be fully installed, tied, and positioned before concrete is poured so that the steel is embedded within the concrete to provide the required structural strength.
Inspection of rebar placement, spacing, cover, and tying must be completed after installation and before concrete pouring to ensure compliance with structural drawings and standards.
Rebar must be cut and bent to specified shapes and dimensions before it can be transported to the work area and fixed/installed in position.

While MEP embedment work can overlap, it is preferable to install major conduits and sleeves after rebar fixing so that the reinforcement is not obstructed, but some coordination can occur concurrently.
Masonry walls require a solid, level foundation to bear the load and prevent settlement cracks.
Bricklaying often starts from the finished floor level; the slab provides the base course support.
A damp-proof membrane must be placed at the base of masonry walls to prevent rising damp before bricks are laid.
Lintels are installed as the masonry reaches window/door head height to support the brickwork above the opening.
Roof trusses and rafters bear on the completed masonry walls; walls must be fully built and cured to support roof loads.
Plaster is applied onto masonry walls; bricks/blocks must be laid and mortar cured before plastering can adhere properly.
All conduits, pipes, back boxes, and wiring must be installed within walls before they are covered by plaster.
Windows and doors must be installed and sealed so that plaster can be finished neatly around frames and reveals.
Paint and wall finishes require a smooth, dried plaster surface as a substrate; plaster must cure before paint can be applied.

Skirting boards and finished floor levels are often installed after plastering to avoid damaging new plaster, but in some sequences flooring is laid first — this is a soft preference for quality and cleanliness.
Tile requires a clean, level, and cured substrate to adhere properly and prevent cracking. Concrete must be cured (typically 28 days) or subfloor must be prepared before tile can be installed.
In wet areas such as showers or bathrooms, waterproofing membrane must be applied and cured before tile installation to prevent water damage.
Electrical conduits, junction boxes, and plumbing rough-ins within walls or floors must be completed before tiling, as tile covers these areas and would need to be removed to access them later.
Grout is applied into the joints between installed tiles after the tiles are set and the thin-set mortar has cured. Grouting cannot occur before tiles are in place.

Baseboards and trim are typically installed after tile to overlap the tile edge for a clean finish. While it could be done before, post-tile installation is standard practice for aesthetics and to avoid damage.
Structural framing (walls, ceilings, roof structure) must be in place to provide support and attachment points for ductwork, and to define the spaces through which ducts will run.
Electrical rough-in must be completed first to avoid conflicts with ductwork placement and to ensure that ducts are not installed where electrical conduits or boxes need to go.
Plumbing pipes must be installed before ductwork to prevent clashes and to allow proper routing of both systems without interference.
Ductwork should be tested and sealed before insulation is applied around ducts to ensure accessibility for leak testing and to prevent insulating over unsealed joints.
Ductwork must be fully installed and inspected before drywall is closed in, as access to ducts is required for connections, sealing, and inspection before walls and ceilings are enclosed.
Pipework requires a stable, level base (the slab/foundation) to be laid on or embedded in before installation can begin.
Pipework often runs within walls, penetrates slabs, or is supported by structural elements, so the main structure must be in place first.
Underground drainage lines and external utility connections must be laid before internal pipework can connect to them.
Pipework must be installed and accessible for pressure testing and inspection before it can be covered by walls, ceilings, or insulation.
Internal finishing works (plasterboard, plaster, cladding) can only commence after pipework is installed, tested, and approved, as these finishes will conceal the pipes.
Structural framing (beams, columns, roof deck) must be in place to provide support and attachment points for overhead sprinkler piping and hangers.

Overhead electrical conduits, HVAC ducts, and mechanical systems should be roughed in before sprinkler piping so that sprinkler heads can be routed around or coordinated with these systems to avoid conflicts.
Sprinkler heads and piping are installed within the ceiling plenum before ceilings are closed in, as access to the plenum is required for sprinkler installation and testing.

Fire alarm devices (smoke detectors, pull stations) are often integrated with sprinkler system flow switches and tamper switches; while alarm wiring can begin earlier, final connection and commissioning typically follow sprinkler installation.

Sprinkler installation involves significant water-based testing (hydrostatic testing) which could damage finished surfaces; therefore, painting and flooring are completed after sprinkler testing is passed.

Structural framing provides the main support skeleton of the building, including walls, floors, and ceilings where electrical conduits, cables, and wiring trays will be routed and mounted. Without the structural framework in place, there is no substrate to attach electrical infrastructure.

While electrical wiring can technically begin before drywall is fully installed, in practice rough wiring is often run before interior wall finishes are closed up to allow access to stud cavities and ceiling plenums. However, some wiring can proceed concurrently, so this is more of a soft sequencing preference to minimize rework.

Trim-out activities such as installing outlets, switches, light fixtures, and faceplates can only begin after the in-wall and ceiling cabling and wiring runs have been pulled, terminated, and tested. The final connections depend on the rough wiring being complete.

successor: Wall and Ceiling Finish (Taping, Mudding, Painting)
rationale: Final finishing of walls and ceilings (drywall compound, sanding, painting) must occur after electrical rough-in is complete because the wiring and boxes are embedded within or mounted to the wall/ceiling assembly. Finishing over open cavities that still require electrical work would be damaged or would have to be redone.

In suspended ceiling systems, electrical cables, conduits, and junction boxes must be run in the ceiling plenum before the ceiling tiles or grid are permanently installed; otherwise access to run overhead wiring would be blocked or require removal of finished ceiling elements.
Drywall must be attached to the structural framing; without stud walls or furring strips in place, there is no substrate to fasten the drywall to.
Electrical cables, boxes, and conduits must be run inside the wall cavities before they are closed off by drywall; otherwise, walls would need to be cut open later.
Plumbing pipes and drain lines inside walls must be installed and pressure-tested before drywall conceals them.
Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning ducts that run through wall or ceiling cavities must be in place before drywall is hung to avoid costly rework.
Insulation must be placed inside wall and ceiling cavities before drywall is installed to ensure proper thermal and acoustic performance and to meet building code requirements.
Drywall panels must be installed and fastened to the framing before their joints can be taped and the seams finished with joint compound.
Corner beads (metal or vinyl) must be fastened to drywall corners to provide a straight edge and reinforcement before tape and compound can be applied over them.
Joint compound must be applied and allowed to dry (with tape embedded) before it can be sanded smooth and flush with the drywall surface.
Taped and jointed drywall surfaces must be completely smooth, dried, and sanded before primer and paint can be applied for a uniform finish.

While trim is often installed after taping for a cleaner look, some trades install trim first and tape afterward; however, the typical sequence has taping completed first to avoid damaging finished trim work with mudding and sanding activities.
Plumbing pipes must be installed in walls and ceilings before insulation, as insulation would obscure and prevent access to plumbing rough-in work.
HVAC ducts must be installed before insulation, as insulation is placed around and over ductwork and would need to be removed or disturbed if ducts were added later.
The vapor barrier (if separate from faced insulation) must be installed immediately after insulation to seal the thermal envelope, and prior to any interior finish work.
Floor screeding requires a stable, cured concrete base to adhere properly; pouring and curing the concrete slab must be completed first to provide a sound substrate.
If underfloor heating pipes or cables are to be embedded, they must be laid and pressure-tested before the screed is poured over them.
A damp proof membrane must be placed on the substrate before screeding to prevent moisture ingress into the screed from below.

successor: Floor Covering Installation (e.g., tiles, wood, vinyl)
rationale: Screed must be fully cured and dried before any finished floor covering can be installed on top to avoid cracking, moisture damage, or poor adhesion.
Skirting boards are typically installed after screeding to cover the expansion gap at the edge; however, this is a practical preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The structural framing (roof trusses, rafters, or decking) provides the necessary support structure for the roofing materials to be installed upon.
Roof sheathing (plywood or OSB panels) must be installed over the framing to create a solid base for the roofing underlayment and finish materials.
While not a strict physical requirement, installing roofing before wall cladding allows the roofing to overhang and integrate properly with the wall flashing, preventing water intrusion.
Roofing must be completed to ensure the building is weather-tight before interior finishes like drywall and ceiling tiles are installed, preventing water damage.
Although electrical wiring can be run before the roof is complete, completing the roof first protects the interior from weather and allows safer working conditions for electrical installation.

Rough framing creates the structural openings (rough openings) that windows and doors are installed into. Without the framed openings, there is no structural support or defined space to place windows and doors.

Exterior wall sheathing provides the backing and structural diaphragm for the walls. Windows and doors are typically installed after sheathing is in place to ensure proper alignment, weatherproofing, and structural continuity.

House wrap or weather-resistive barrier is installed before windows and doors to provide a continuous drainage plane and water barrier behind the window/door flanges, ensuring proper flashing integration and moisture management.

Windows and doors must be installed before interior drywall can be hung because drywall is fitted around window and door openings, and the installed frames provide the reference surfaces for taping, trimming, and finishing edges.

Exterior siding and trim work around windows and doors cannot be completed until the windows and doors are installed, as the trim must be fitted to the window/door frames and the siding must butt against the installed units for proper flashing and weather sealing.
The building structure, including lift shaft core walls and slabs, must be complete to provide the physical enclosure and support for lift installation.
The lift shaft (including walls, floor slabs, and pit) must be fully constructed to house the lift equipment and car.
The lift pit must be waterproofed to prevent water ingress that could damage lift equipment before installation commences.
Electrical rough-in for lift shaft lighting and power can only be completed after lift rails and equipment are in place to determine final positions.
The lift must be fully installed before it can be powered up, tested, and commissioned for safe operation.
Flooring, wall finishes, and ceiling works in lift lobbies are preferably done after lift installation to avoid damage, but can be sequenced otherwise with protection measures.
Structural work such as concrete slabs, staircases, and load-bearing walls must be completed to provide a stable base and framework for fixed seating installation.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work including underfloor conduits, drainage, and ventilation must be installed before fixed seating is placed, as access beneath seating areas becomes restricted afterward.
Wall framing, drywall, and associated finishes must be completed in seating areas, as seating installation would obstruct access to these wall surfaces.
Fixed seating must be installed before the final floor finish (e.g., carpet, tile) is laid around the seating supports, allowing flooring to be fitted tightly and neatly against the seat bases.

While some cabling can be roughed-in earlier, final connection of power outlets, lighting controls, or audiovisual equipment integrated with or near fixed seating is best done after installation to ensure precise placement and avoid damage to finishes.
Rough framing establishes the structural walls and partitions that cabinetry is attached to or fitted within; cabinets cannot be installed without framed walls.
Electrical wiring for outlets, switches, and appliance connections must be roughed in behind walls before millwork covers and encloses those areas.
Plumbing supply and drain lines for kitchen or bathroom cabinetry (e.g., sinks, dishwashers) must be roughed in before cabinets are installed to avoid rework.
Drywall must be installed, finished, and taped behind cabinets to provide a clean backing and fire-rated assembly; installing cabinets before drywall leads to gaps and code violations.
Floor underlayment or subfloor must be level and complete so that base cabinets sit squarely; installing cabinets before floor prep causes alignment issues.
Countertops are fabricated and installed directly on top of base cabinets; cabinets must be in place and leveled before countertops can be templated and set.
After cabinets are installed, electricians can mount outlet receptacles and switches on finished walls and install under-cabinet lighting that is attached to or wired through the cabinets.
Sink fixtures, faucets, and drain assemblies are connected after the cabinet that supports them is permanently in position.
Backsplash tile is installed against the wall above countertops; cabinets and countertops must be in place to define the backsplash boundary and ensure tile alignment.

While finish flooring (e.g., hardwood, tile) is often installed after cabinets for a cleaner edge, some installers prefer to set cabinets on top of finish flooring. This is a soft preference because either sequence is possible with proper detailing.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before excavation can begin; otherwise, obstructions would prevent access to the earth and grading work.
Property boundaries, building footprint, and finished floor elevations must be staked out by a surveyor so that excavation crews know exactly where and to what depth to dig.
Soil compaction, bearing capacity, and contamination levels must be assessed to determine if the ground is suitable for excavation and if special handling of contaminated material is required.
Existing underground utilities (gas, water, electric, telecom) must be located and marked to avoid accidental strikes during excavation, which could cause safety hazards and service disruptions.

Excavation creates the pit or trench at the required depth and dimensions for footings and foundations; foundation concrete cannot be placed until the earth has been removed to the proper elevation and the subgrade prepared.
Once earth is removed, the exposed sides of the excavation must be shored or the adjacent structures underpinned to prevent collapse and maintain stability during subsequent foundation work.

While often performed simultaneously, systematic dewatering may need to commence immediately after excavation reaches the water table to keep the work area dry; however, in dry conditions this is not required.
After bulk excavation is complete, the bottom of the excavation must be compacted and leveled to achieve the required bearing capacity before any structural fill or concrete is placed.
The trench must be excavated before it can be backfilled.
All pipes, conduits, or utilities must be placed in the trench before backfilling can begin.
Proper bedding material must be placed and leveled around installed pipes before backfilling.

predecessor: Inspection and Approval of Installed Utilities
rationale: Inspections must be completed and approved before covering utilities with backfill material.
Final surface layers such as pavement, sidewalks, or topsoil cannot be placed until backfilling and compaction are complete to avoid settlement issues.
Scaffolding requires stable, level ground to ensure structural integrity and safety; uneven ground would make scaffolding unsafe and unstable.
Completed foundations provide the necessary base and structural support for scaffolding to be erected alongside or against the building structure.
Scaffolding provides access and working platforms for masons to lay bricks or blocks at height; without scaffolding, masonry work at upper levels is impossible.
Workers need scaffolding as a stable platform to install external cladding, siding, or curtain walls on the building exterior.

While scaffolding provides convenient access for window/door installation at height, some installations can be done from inside or with other access equipment; however, scaffolding is strongly preferred for efficiency and safety.
Scaffolding often supports formwork for concrete structures; the concrete must reach sufficient strength before the forms and supporting scaffolding can be safely removed.

Scaffolding is typically erected to facilitate work on a structure; once the structural and exterior finishing work at height is complete, the scaffolding is no longer needed and can be dismantled. This is a logical/functional dependency rather than a strict physical one.
Dismantling scaffolding generates debris and frees up work areas, but cleaning can sometimes proceed in parallel. Typically dismantling precedes final clean-up for efficiency.
The site must be free of temporary works like scaffolding before a final inspection or handover can occur, as scaffolding obstructs views and access.

Scaffolding provides the access platform for work on the building exterior; thus, all façade work requiring that access must be completed before the scaffold is removed. If any finishing remains, it cannot be performed safely without the scaffold.
Site grading, soil compaction, and drainage preparation must be completed before landscaping can be installed to ensure stable ground conditions and proper water management.

The building structure including foundation, walls, and roof must be complete before building-integrated landscaping (e.g., green roofs, planter walls) can be installed, as the structure provides the physical support.
Waterproof membranes and drainage layers must be in place before planting to prevent water infiltration into the building structure and ensure proper drainage for plant health.
Underground utilities such as irrigation lines, drainage pipes, and lighting conduits must be roughed in before landscape finishes are applied to avoid re-excavation.

successor: Final Inspection & Commissioning of Landscape Systems
rationale: After landscaping installation, the irrigation, drainage, and plant health systems must be tested and commissioned to ensure they function correctly before project handover.
Walls provide the vertical support structure that the roof rests upon; roof cannot be installed without completed walls.
The floor slab provides a stable working platform and reference elevation for erecting walls and roof structure.
Roof sheathing is installed directly onto the roof framing members; the structural frame must be in place first.
Insulation is placed between or over the roof structural members after the frame is complete.
Waterproofing membrane is applied over the roof deck and sheathing, which require the roof structure to be fully erected.
Roof decking (typically plywood or OSB) must be installed on top of the roof trusses or rafters, which provide the structural support framework.
Wall sheathing is typically completed before roof decking to ensure the structural envelope is ready for roof loads, though in some sequences roof decking may begin after walls are framed.
Roof underlayment is installed directly on top of the roof decking to provide a water-resistant barrier before roofing final materials are applied.
Final roofing materials (shingles, metal panels, etc.) are installed over the roof decking and underlayment, requiring the decking to be complete.
While fascia and soffit can be installed alongside roof decking, it is typical to have the decking in place before finishing the roof edge trims for a clean integration.
The roof covering (e.g., shingles, tiles, metal panels) requires a complete structural roof frame or truss system to be in place as a substrate for attachment.
Roof decking (e.g., plywood or OSB) must be fastened to the roof trusses to provide a solid, continuous surface for the roof covering material to be applied.
A water-resistant or waterproof underlayment (e.g., felt paper, synthetic underlayment) must be installed over the roof deck before the final roof covering to provide an additional moisture barrier.
Gutters and downspouts are typically mounted onto the fascia or roof edge after the roof covering is complete to ensure proper water collection and integration with the finished roof system.

successor: Roof Flashing and Vent Installation (final trim)
rationale: Penetration flashings (e.g., around chimneys, vents) and ridge vents are integrated with the roof covering; some final flashing and vent components are installed as part of or after the roof covering to ensure weather-tightness.
Roof flashing is installed on top of the roof sheathing to seal joints and transitions; the sheathing provides the structural base needed for flashing attachment.
Roof underlayment (e.g., felt or synthetic membrane) must be laid over the sheathing before flashing can be installed, as flashing integrates with the underlayment to create a watertight seal.
Flashing must be in place before the final roofing material is applied because shingles or tiles are installed over and interlock with the flashing to shed water properly.
Gutters are installed after flashing because flashing integrates with the drip edge and roof edges, which are critical for directing water into gutters.
Flashing around the chimney base must be completed before any chimney cap or cricket is installed, as flashing seals the roof-chimney intersection.
Roof edge trim and fascia are installed onto the roof sheathing and decking, which must be in place to provide a nailing surface and structural support for the edge trim.
Roof underlayment (felt or synthetic) must be laid over the sheathing before edge trim is installed to ensure proper water shedding and to prevent moisture ingress behind the trim.
Gutters are mounted directly onto or below the fascia board; the fascia must be securely installed first to provide the attachment point and structural support for the gutter system.
Soffit panels typically fit into the bottom channel of the fascia, so the fascia must be installed before the soffit can be fitted and secured.

successor: Final Roofing Material (Shingles/Metal Panels) Installation at Edges
rationale: While edge trim is often installed before the final roofing material to provide a clean edge and drip edge function, some installations allow the trim to be installed after; however, it is a strong best practice to install edge trim first to ensure proper water drainage and a finished appearance.
The roof deck or structural sheathing must be in place to provide a surface for installing roof ventilation components such as soffit vents, ridge vents, or mechanical roof fans.
The waterproofing underlayment (felt or synthetic) must be laid over the roof deck before ventilation components are installed to ensure the building envelope is properly sealed against moisture.

Roof ventilation systems such as ridge vents or turbine vents are typically integrated with or covered by the final roofing material (shingles, tiles, metal panels) and cannot be properly installed after the roof covering is in place.

While attic insulation can technically be installed before roof ventilation, it is best practice to install ventilation first to ensure proper airflow paths (soffit baffles, ridge vents) are not blocked by loose insulation material.

Ceiling drywall is typically installed before roof ventilation work to provide access for attic-based ventilation components from below, though this is a soft preference as ventilation can also be installed from the rooftop.
The structural steel frame must be erected to provide the supporting structure onto which the rooflight/skylight will be mounted.
The roof decking must be installed to create the roof opening and substrate that the rooflight/skylight integrates into.
The waterproof membrane around the rough opening must be in place before the skylight is installed to ensure proper weather sealing and flashing integration.
Flashing is installed around the skylight to seal the gap between the skylight and the roof; the skylight must be in place first for flashing to be properly fitted.

The skylight must be installed before interior ceiling finishes (e.g., drywall, ceiling tiles) are completed, as the skylight frame and trim integrate with the ceiling plane and access may be needed from below.
Roof curbs and supports are typically mounted on the structural steel framing of a building. The steel structure must be in place to provide the load-bearing support needed for roof curbs.
The roof deck (typically metal decking or structural concrete) must be installed before roof curbs can be placed, as the curbs are mounted on and supported by the roof deck surface.

Roof curbs provide the raised platform and flashing base for roof penetrations; the roofing membrane is installed up to and over the curb flanges to maintain a watertight seal. The curbs must be in place first.
Roof-mounted HVAC equipment is set on and bolted to the roof curbs. The curbs must be installed and properly anchored to the structure before heavy mechanical units can be placed on them.

Counterflashing, reglets, and other sheet metal components are installed around roof curbs to seal the transition between the curb and roofing/equipment. The curb must be in place to receive these flashings.
The roof deck or structural substrate must be in place to provide a stable base for the parapet to be built upon and anchored to.
The roof structural framing must be complete to support the parapet wall, which is typically an extension of the roof structure or attached to it.

The parapet provides the upstand or vertical termination point for the roof membrane; waterproofing is typically lapped up the parapet wall and cannot be properly installed without the parapet in place.
Coping caps and metal flashings are installed on top of and around the parapet to protect it from water intrusion; they cannot be installed before the parapet is constructed.

While not always physically required, it is typical construction sequencing to complete the parapet before finalizing adjacent exterior cladding so that cladding can terminate properly against the parapet and ensure a clean weather-tight interface.
The roof access hatch requires a structurally complete roof opening with proper framing and decking to support and secure the hatch assembly.
The roof membrane must be installed after the access hatch is in place to properly flash and seal around the hatch curb, ensuring a watertight roof system.
The hatch installation must be completed before interior ceiling finishes are applied, as the hatch opening and framing must be accessible for installation and integration with the roof structure.
The roof hatch must be installed first so that any fixed ladders or stairs leading to it can be properly aligned and anchored to the hatch frame or surrounding structure.
Ideally insulation around the hatch area is placed before the hatch is installed to ensure a continuous thermal envelope, but it can be cut and fitted afterward if needed.
Snow guards/fences are mounted onto or through the finished roof decking and underlayment; the structural deck must be in place to provide a secure attachment substrate.
The underlayment (e.g., felt or synthetic membrane) is laid over the decking before snow guard installation to provide waterproofing; snow guards are installed on top of the underlayment.

Snow fences are typically installed concurrently with or integrated into the roof covering; however, if installed as a surface-mounted unit, they go on top of the finished roof covering. For integrated systems, the snow guard is placed during shingle installation, with shingles wrapping around or over the guard base.
The structural framing (walls, columns, beams) must be completed to provide the load-bearing support required for the roof system.
Wall sheathing provides lateral stability to the structure and ensures the walls are properly aligned before the roof is attached.

While not always strictly required, it is best practice to complete mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins in the walls before roofing to avoid having to work around overlapping trades and protect materials from weather.
Roof overhangs and flashing are installed first to protect the top edges of the siding; installing siding before roofing would leave it exposed to water damage.
The roof structure must be watertight before interior ceiling finishes are installed to prevent water damage to interior materials.
The roof deck or sheathing provides the structural base onto which waterproofing membranes are applied; the surface must be continuous and stable before any waterproofing layer can be installed.

Underlayment (e.g., felt paper or synthetic underlayment) is typically laid directly over the roof deck to provide a secondary moisture barrier and a smooth surface for the primary waterproofing membrane; waterproofing cannot be applied directly to an uncovered deck.
The roof framing, trusses, and slope must be fully erected and braced before any decking or waterproofing can commence, as there is no substrate without completed structural framing.
Flashing (at valleys, vents, chimneys, and edges) is installed after the main waterproofing membrane to cap and seal joints, ensuring water-tightness at transitions.

In warm-roof or inverted-roof assemblies, rigid insulation boards are placed on top of the waterproofing membrane; the membrane must be fully complete and leak-tested before being covered by insulation.
The roof deck (typically plywood or OSB sheathing) must be installed to provide a structural base for the insulation to be placed upon or between.
A waterproof underlayment (e.g., felt paper or synthetic membrane) must be laid over the roof deck before insulation to protect against moisture ingress from below.
The roof covering (finish material like shingles, tiles, or metal panels) must be installed after insulation to enclose and protect the insulation layer from weather exposure.

While ventilation can be partially pre-installed, final integration of ventilation components that interact with the insulation layer (e.g., baffles ensuring air channels remain clear) should follow insulation placement to guarantee proper airflow paths.

For cathedral or vaulted ceilings where insulation is installed from above, the interior ceiling finish (drywall/plaster) must be installed after insulation to enclose it. For attic installations, this may not apply as insulation sits above the ceiling.

Gutters and downpipes are mounted directly onto the roof edge/fascia, so the roof structure, underlayment, and roofing material must be in place to provide a surface for attachment and ensure proper water collection from the roof surface.
Gutters are typically fastened to the fascia board; therefore, fascia and soffit must be installed first to provide a secure mounting surface and proper alignment for the gutter system.

While gutters can be installed after wall finishing, installing gutters first can prevent damage to finished walls and allows for better integration. However, this is a soft preference as the order can be reversed with careful work sequencing.

Downpipes must be installed and connected to underground drainage or splash blocks before final grading and landscaping to ensure proper water drainage away from the foundation. Landscaping after gutter installation prevents rework and damage to finished landscaping.

Gutter and downpipe installation is often part of the waterproofing and drainage scope that must be completed and verified before final inspection, though some inspections can be phased. This is generally a soft preference based on local inspection requirements.
The roof structural frame must be erected to provide the supporting substrate and opening into which the skylight or rooflight unit is installed.
Roof decking or sheathing must be placed to create the completed roof surface, with the skylight opening cut out, before the skylight unit can be set and flashed in.
The weather-resistive barrier or underlayment must be installed around the opening to ensure water-tight integration with the skylight flashing system.
Skylight-specific flashings and counter-flashings must be installed immediately after the skylight unit is placed to seal the penetration against water ingress.
Final roofing materials (shingles, tiles, or membrane) are laid up to and over the skylight flange after the skylight and its flashings are in place to complete the waterproof envelope.
The roof trusses or roof structure must be in place to provide the framing onto which eaves and soffits are fixed.
The external walls need to be framed and stood to support the eaves line and provide the vertical reference for soffit attachment.
Eaves and soffits are installed before the main roof cladding to allow proper detailing at the eaves edge and to provide access for fixing the underside.
Gutters are fixed onto the fascia which is part of the eaves assembly, so eaves and soffits must be completed to provide the mounting surface for gutters.

While often sequenced after eaves installation for a neat finish and weatherproofing integration at the top of walls, this is a typical construction preference rather than an absolute physical necessity.
Load-bearing walls must be built on top of a properly constructed foundation to distribute the wall's vertical loads evenly into the ground and prevent settlement or structural failure.
The building site must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the required depth before any structural walls can be erected.
Load-bearing walls typically rest on the ground floor slab or floor structure; the floor must be in place to provide a stable base and to properly locate the wall.
The roof structure (rafters, trusses, or roof deck) bears directly on load-bearing walls; the walls must be fully erected, aligned, and braced before roof loads can be applied.
In multi-story construction, upper floor joists and beams bear on load-bearing walls below; the load-bearing walls must be installed and cured (if masonry) to support the next floor's loads.

Non-load-bearing walls do not support structural loads; the primary structural frame or load-bearing walls must be in place first so that the non-load-bearing walls can be properly aligned and attached without risk of structural instability.
Non-load-bearing walls are typically built on top of finished floor slabs. The slab must be poured and cured to provide a stable, level base for wall layout and erection.
While not always physically mandatory, it is a strong practical preference to run vertical MEP risers before enclosing the walls, to avoid costly rework and wall demolition later.
Wall finishing materials such as drywall, plaster, or cladding are applied directly to the installed non-load-bearing wall frame, so the wall structure must be complete first.
Electrical cables, outlet boxes, and plumbing pipes that run within the wall cavity must be installed after the wall frame is erected but before the wall is closed with finish materials.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before the retaining wall foundation can be excavated and wall constructed.
Soil bearing capacity and lateral earth pressures must be determined to properly design the retaining wall's dimensions, drainage, and reinforcement.
Any buried utilities in the wall alignment must be relocated prior to excavation and construction to avoid damage and safety hazards.
The retaining wall structure must be fully cured and achieve sufficient strength before backfill material can be placed behind it to avoid collapse or excessive lateral pressure.
Surface drainage systems (e.g., swales, catch basins) and finish grading adjacent to the wall can only be completed after the wall is in place to ensure proper water diversion and grade transitions.
The cavity wall must be built on a stable foundation; the foundation must first be completed to support the structural load of the wall.
The ground floor slab provides the base for the inner leaf of the cavity wall and must be in place before wall construction begins.
The damp proof course must be laid on the foundation or slab prior to the cavity wall to prevent moisture rising into the wall structure.
The wall plate and roof structure bear directly on the completed cavity wall; the wall must be fully built and cured to support the roof load.
Insulation is installed within the cavity after the wall is erected; the cavity must exist before it can be filled.
Shear walls require a stable load-bearing foundation to transfer lateral and vertical loads to the ground; without foundation, the wall has no structural support.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied before concrete is poured for the shear wall to achieve required structural strength.
Formwork must be erected to shape and contain the wet concrete until it cures and gains sufficient strength.
Shear walls provide lateral bracing and vertical support for floor slabs; slabs typically bear on or connect to the completed shear walls.
Freshly poured concrete requires a curing period to achieve design strength before any subsequent loads or formwork removal can occur.
Foundations must be excavated before any wall construction can begin, including party walls, as the wall requires a stable base.
Concrete foundations must be poured and cured before party wall construction can commence to provide structural support for the wall.
Party walls are load-bearing and support the roof structure, so they must be completed before roof installation begins.
Floor slabs on either side of a party wall often bear on or tie into the wall, requiring the wall to be in place first.

While not physically required, it is more efficient to finish the party wall (e.g., plastering, fireproofing) before adjacent interior wall finishes to avoid rework and ensure fire separation compliance.
Firewalls must be supported on a continuous foundation or slab to provide structural stability and fire resistance continuity from the ground up.
Firewalls are often erected after the structural frame to allow integration with the building's lateral load system, though some firewalls are self-supporting.
Firewalls must extend through the roof line to create a fire-resistant barrier; the roof structure is built after the firewall is in place to maintain continuity of the fire separation.

Fire-rated penetrations and firestop systems for mechanical, electrical, and plumbing lines through the firewall must be installed after the firewall is constructed to maintain its fire-resistance rating.
Interior finish work typically occurs after firewalls are in place to avoid damaging the fire-resistive assembly and to ensure proper fire ratings are achieved.
The veneer wall is a non-structural cladding that attaches to the structural wall framing; the structural support must be in place before the veneer can be applied.
A weather-resistant barrier must be installed behind the veneer to prevent moisture intrusion; the veneer cannot be installed without this underlying protection.
Veneer walls typically define the final exterior surface; windows and doors are often installed after the veneer is complete to ensure proper flashing and integration with the finished cladding.
Exterior trim elements such as corner beads, control joints, and decorative accents are applied after the veneer surface is installed to provide a clean finished appearance.
The veneer wall loads rest on the foundation or slab, so the foundation must be cured and ready to support the veneer before installation begins.
The foundation provides a level, stable base for wall framing. Walls cannot be safely or accurately framed without a completed foundation to anchor them to.
The floor slab (if present) must be in place before wall framing to provide the surface on which bottom plates rest and to ensure wall layout accuracy.
Roof framing rests on top of load-bearing walls. Walls must be framed, plumbed, and braced before roof trusses or rafters can be installed.
Structural sheathing (plywood/OSB) is attached directly to the wall frame. The frame must be complete to provide the nailing substrate for sheathing.
Window and door rough openings are created during framing. Windows and doors are installed after the frame is up and openings are formed.
Bearing walls require a stable, level foundation to distribute the vertical loads they carry. The foundation must be completed and cured before any load-bearing wall construction begins.
Bearing walls transfer loads to the foundation system. Concrete footings or slab edges that support the wall must be in place and cured before wall erection.
Floor joists, beams, or decking that bear on or are supported by the bearing wall cannot be installed until the wall is in place and properly anchored.
Roof trusses or rafters that bear on the bearing wall require the wall to be complete and braced to carry vertical and lateral roof loads.

While exterior sheathing can be installed after the wall frame is up, it is technically possible to delay until after all bearing walls are erected, but sequencing typically follows immediately for weather protection.
The wall structure must be built first to provide the framework within which a window opening can be created. Cutting an opening before the wall is erected would have no structural context.
The rough opening with properly sized headers, sills, and trimmers must be framed to define the precise dimensions and load-bearing support for the window unit before the window can be installed.

Flashing and weatherproofing at the rough opening sill and jambs must be applied before window installation to ensure water is directed away from the opening, preventing moisture intrusion behind the window frame.
The wall opening must exist before the window unit can be physically placed, shimmed, leveled, and fastened into the opening.
After the window is installed in the opening, gaps between the window frame and the rough opening must be sealed and insulated to prevent air and water infiltration.
Wall lintels are installed within or above wall openings (such as doors and windows). The wall framing must be erected first to create the opening that the lintel will span across.
Lintels support the load above openings in masonry or concrete walls; the wall must be built up to the lintel level before the lintel can be placed.

Lintels are load-bearing elements that transfer loads from the structure above (roof, upper floors) to the surrounding wall; the lintel must be in place and cured before any framing above it is installed.
Lintels form the top of wall openings; doors and windows are fitted into these openings after the lintel is installed and the opening is structurally complete.

While finishing can often proceed after lintel installation, in some sequences lintel placement may occur before final wall finishing to ensure a smooth transition between the lintel and surrounding wall surface.
Wall ties must be anchored into a stable foundation structure; without the foundation, there is no base to support or anchor the wall tie system.
Wall ties are embedded into or attached to the structural wall (e.g., brick veneer, blockwork, or stud framing), so the wall structure must be in place first.
Wall ties serve as the connection between the structural wall and the exterior cladding or veneer; cladding cannot be securely attached without wall ties being in place.

While wall ties are typically installed before cavity insulation, in some sequences insulation can be placed as the wall is built up; however, optimal practice is to install ties first to maintain cavity integrity.

Wall ties often penetrate the cavity and must be correctly positioned relative to the damp proof course to prevent moisture bridging; the DPC installation usually follows or is coordinated with wall tie placement.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil, and graded to proper elevations before any foundation work can begin to ensure a stable and level base.
Trenches or pits must be excavated to the required depth and width to accommodate the wall footings and foundation walls.
The bearing soil must be tested for adequate load-bearing capacity and compacted to prevent differential settlement under the foundation.
Foundation corners and wall lines must be staked out and verified by survey to ensure the footer/foundation wall is placed in the correct location and alignment.
After the foundation wall is cured and stable, drainage systems (perforated pipe, gravel, filter fabric) and waterproofing membranes can be applied to the exterior wall surface.
Backfill around the foundation can only proceed once the wall is fully cured and sufficiently strong to resist lateral earth pressures.
Interior floor slabs or framed floors rest on or are supported by the foundation walls, so walls must be complete before floor construction begins.
Underslab utilities must be roughed in after the foundation wall forms are set but before the slab is poured; the wall itself must be in place to define the building footprint.
Waterproofing is applied to the structural wall surface; the wall must be fully constructed and cured before waterproofing can be applied.
The wall surface must be cleaned of debris, dust, and laitance and any irregularities must be smoothed to ensure proper adhesion of waterproofing materials.
Some waterproofing systems require a primer coat for optimal bonding; this is a manufacturer-recommended step that could be skipped with alternative products but generally improves performance.
Backfilling must not occur until the waterproofing membrane is fully installed and cured to prevent damage to the waterproofing layer from soil and compaction equipment.

successor: Installation of Drainage Board / Protection Board
rationale: A protection or drainage board is typically placed over the waterproofing membrane to shield it from damage during backfill and to facilitate water drainage; this layer must be installed after waterproofing is complete.
Walls require a stable load-bearing foundation to transfer vertical loads to the ground; building walls without a foundation would cause settlement and structural failure.

predecessor: Slab on Grade / Ground Floor Slab
rationale: The ground floor slab provides a level working platform and base for wall layout; walls are typically built on or anchored to the slab.
Site must be cleared, graded, and excavated to the required level before any structural elements like walls can be erected.
Roof trusses or rafters bear directly onto wall top plates; walls must be fully erected, plumb, and braced to support roof loads.
Wall framing must be complete to provide the rough openings and structural support required for installing doors and windows.
Electrical wiring is run through wall cavities; walls must be framed and sheathed before electricians can install cables and outlet boxes within them.
Plumbing pipes for supply and drainage are installed inside wall cavities; walls must be built first to route pipes through stud spaces.
Insulation is placed between wall studs; the wall frame must be complete and enclosed (sheathing on exterior side) before insulation can be installed.
Drywall is fastened to wall studs; walls must be fully framed and all rough-in services completed before drywall can be applied.
Wall framing creates the structural cavity that holds insulation; insulation cannot be installed before the wall frame is in place.

Electrical wiring must be run through the wall cavities before insulation is blown or placed, otherwise the wiring would be inaccessible or would have to be installed on top of insulation, violating code.
Plumbing pipes within wall cavities must be installed before insulation fills the cavity, as adding pipes afterward would require removing insulation.
A vapor barrier or air-sealing membrane is placed over the insulation to control moisture diffusion; this cannot be applied until the insulation is in place.
Drywall (interior wall covering) encloses the wall cavity and must be installed after insulation is placed, as the insulation fills the cavity behind the drywall surface.
Wall cladding requires the structural frame to be in place as its substrate and load-bearing support.
Roof must be completed to provide weather protection during wall cladding installation and to ensure proper integration at the roof-wall interface.

A sheathing or substrate layer (e.g., plywood, gypsum board, or insulation board) must be installed prior to cladding to provide a flat, rigid surface and to meet fire/weather resistive barrier requirements.
Windows and doors are typically installed after wall cladding to ensure proper flashing, sealing, and integration with the finished cladding surface, preventing water intrusion.
Final exterior coatings, paints, or sealants must be applied after cladding is fully installed to protect the cladding material and achieve the desired aesthetic finish.
Wall framing provides the structural support and substrate onto which thermal break materials are installed. Without the framed wall in place, there is no surface to attach the thermal break.

Exterior wall sheathing is typically applied before thermal breaks to create a continuous substrate and structural diaphragm. Thermal break installation over sheathing ensures proper integration with the building envelope.

The thermal break creates a separation between the structural wall and the cladding system to reduce thermal bridging. Cladding must be installed after the thermal break is in place to maintain the continuous insulation layer.

Thermal breaks often integrate with or provide the substrate for air barrier systems. The air barrier must be applied after or in coordination with thermal breaks to ensure continuity and proper sealing.

Foundation walls must be complete and cured before any above-grade wall thermal break work begins, as the thermal break at the wall-to-foundation transition requires a stable base and is critical for preventing thermal bridging at this interface.
Wall framing must be complete to provide a structural surface for wall finishing materials such as drywall, plaster, or paneling to be attached.
Electrical wiring, outlets, and switch boxes must be installed within the wall cavities before they are enclosed by wall finishing materials.
Plumbing pipes, drains, and supply lines within walls must be installed and inspected before walls are closed up with finishing materials.
HVAC ductwork and vents within wall cavities must be placed and sealed before wall finishing is applied to avoid costly rework.
Insulation must be placed inside wall cavities for thermal and acoustic performance before the walls are enclosed with finishing materials.
Primer and paint are applied over the finished wall surface (drywall, plaster, etc.) after it has been installed, taped, and sanded smooth.
Tile installation requires a solid, flat finished wall surface as a substrate for adhesion and proper alignment.
Trim moldings and baseboards are installed after wall finishing to cover the gap between finished walls and floors, and to provide a clean aesthetic transition.
Cabinets are mounted onto finished walls to ensure proper fit, level mounting, and to avoid damaging unfinished surfaces.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to the required depth and level before strip footings can be formed, as footings are placed directly into the excavated trench.
The exact positions and alignment of the strip footings must be marked out on site before any concrete is poured, to ensure the footings follow the designed layout.
Strip footings provide the load-bearing base; formwork for ground beams or slabs is erected after footings are cast and cured to build upon the completed foundation.
Steel reinforcement for ground beams or foundation walls rests on or ties into the strip footing, so the footing must be in place first.
Strip footings support the walls and subsequent ground floor slab; the slab is poured after footings are complete and cured to transfer loads to the foundation.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to the required depth and dimensions before the isolated pad footing can be placed.
The bearing soil must be tested and compacted to proper bearing capacity to ensure the footing has adequate support.
The exact position and alignment of each pad footing must be marked out from reference points before excavation or pouring can begin.
A thin layer of lean concrete (blinding) is typically placed over the excavated soil to provide a clean, level working surface and prevent reinforcement from contacting soil directly.

successor: Reinforcement Steel Fixing for Pad Footing
rationale: Reinforcement bars must be placed and tied within the footing formwork before concrete is poured, so the rebar fixing occurs after the blinding but before concrete placement as part of the footing construction sequence.
Formwork is erected around the footing perimeter to contain the wet concrete during pouring and curing.
Concrete is poured into the formwork after reinforcement has been placed and inspected; the footing is then cured.
After the concrete has cured and formwork is stripped, excavated soil is backfilled and compacted around the completed footing.

successor: Ground Beam or Plinth Beam Construction
rationale: Ground beams spanning between isolated pad footings are cast after the footings are complete to tie them together and distribute loads.
Columns are erected directly on top of isolated pad footings, using starter bars cast into the footing, so column work begins after footing completion.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth and dimensions before the combined footing can be placed, as the footing is constructed within the excavated trench.

A lean concrete blinding layer must be poured and cured over the excavated base to provide a clean, level, and stable working surface before the reinforcement and main concrete of the combined footing can be placed.
The subgrade must be compacted and prepared to the required bearing capacity to ensure the footing has adequate support and to prevent differential settlement.

After the combined footing concrete has been placed and has achieved sufficient strength, the formwork can be stripped and proper curing must commence to ensure the concrete reaches its design strength.

Starter bars or dowels for columns or walls must be embedded into the combined footing during placement; once the footing has set and cured, vertical reinforcement can continue above the footing level.
Pile caps are structural elements that transfer loads from columns or walls to pile groups. Piles must be installed and cured before pile caps can be constructed on top of them.
The excavation for the pile cap must be completed to expose the pile heads and provide a working area before forming and pouring the pile cap concrete.
Pile heads must be trimmed or cut to the required design level and exposed reinforcement cleaned before they can be embedded into the pile cap.
After the pile cap concrete has cured and formwork removed, the excavated area around the cap can be backfilled to restore ground level and provide lateral support.

successor: Column / Wall Reinforcement Above Pile Cap
rationale: Pile cap provides the foundation base; starter bars are cast into the pile cap to continue vertical reinforcement for columns or walls above, which cannot proceed until the pile cap is in place.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the required depth before any foundation work can begin.
If the soil conditions are poor, ground improvement (e.g., compaction, stone columns) must be completed to achieve the necessary bearing capacity before placing the raft foundation.
The exact foundation layout must be surveyed and marked on site to guide excavation and formwork placement.
A layer of lean concrete (blinding) is typically poured over the excavated soil to provide a clean, level working surface and prevent contamination of the reinforcement before raft concreting.
If a waterproofing membrane is specified below the raft, it must be laid on the blinding concrete before reinforcement and pouring of the raft slab.
The raft foundation must be fully cured and achieve sufficient strength before vertical load-bearing elements like columns and shear walls can be constructed on top of it.
After the raft is cast and cured, the excavated areas around the foundation can be backfilled to prepare for subsequent ground floor works.

Services passing through or under the raft slab (e.g., drainage pipes, conduits) must be installed and inspected before the raft concrete is poured, but any above-slab service connections proceed after curing.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to the required depth and dimensions before the foundation wall can be constructed, as the wall is built within the excavated trench.
The subgrade soil must be tested for bearing capacity and properly compacted to provide a stable base before placing the foundation wall to prevent settlement or structural failure.
The concrete footings must be poured and cured to provide a load-bearing base upon which the foundation wall rests; the wall cannot be built without footings in place.
Damp-proofing and waterproofing materials are applied directly to the exterior surface of the finished foundation wall to prevent moisture ingress; the wall must exist first.
Backfill around the foundation can only be placed after the foundation wall is fully constructed and cured, as the wall must be in place to retain the soil.

successor: Slab on Grade / Ground Floor Slab
rationale: Interior floor slabs are typically poured after foundation walls are complete, as the walls define the perimeter and provide lateral support for the slab.
The superstructure framing (walls, columns, beams) is erected on top of or anchored to the foundation wall; the foundation must be complete to provide the load-bearing platform.
The site must be cleared and excavated to the required depth and grade before any grade beam can be formed or poured, as the grade beam rests on the excavated subgrade or pile caps.
Grade beams typically span between pile caps or foundation piers. The pile caps must be constructed first to provide support and reinforcement connection for the grade beam.
The subgrade beneath the grade beam must be properly compacted and prepared to provide uniform bearing support and prevent differential settlement.
Formwork must be erected and aligned to the correct dimensions and elevations before concrete for the grade beam can be placed.
Steel reinforcement must be tied and positioned within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity.
Concrete for the grade beam must be poured and cured to sufficient strength before backfilling can occur, as backfilling against uncured concrete could displace or damage the beam.

successor: Slab on Grade / Ground Floor Slab
rationale: Grade beams often serve as edge supports or integral parts of the slab system; the slab is poured after the grade beam has cured to ensure a monolithic or properly jointed connection.
Columns and walls typically bear on or are doweled into grade beams, so the grade beam must be complete and cured to transfer loads from the superstructure.

The construction site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before any foundation work can begin, as pier foundations require a clean and stable ground surface for layout and excavation.
