Soil bearing capacity and ground conditions must be assessed to determine the appropriate depth, diameter, and reinforcement requirements for pier foundations before construction starts.
The exact locations of each pier must be surveyed and marked on the ground based on structural drawings before excavation or drilling can commence.
Pier caps are structural elements that sit atop the pier foundations to distribute loads; they cannot be constructed until the piers are complete and have achieved sufficient strength.
Grade beams connect pier foundations to distribute lateral loads and support walls; they require finished pier foundations as their support points.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the correct elevation and slope before the slab can be poured, as the slab rests directly on the prepared subgrade.
A compacted granular fill or gravel sub-base layer must be placed and compacted to provide a stable, well-draining foundation before the concrete slab is poured.
A vapor retarder membrane must be laid over the prepared sub-base to prevent moisture migration from the ground into the concrete slab before the slab is poured.
All underground plumbing pipes, electrical conduits, and other utilities that will run beneath the slab must be installed and inspected before the concrete is poured.
Load-bearing walls and the superstructure are erected on top of the completed slab, which serves as the structural floor and foundation.

successor: Floor Finishing (e.g., Tiling, Polishing, Floor Coverings)
rationale: Any final floor finishes, coatings, or coverings applied to the slab surface cannot be installed until the slab concrete has fully cured and achieved sufficient strength.
Formwork provides the mold and structural support for concrete; reinforcement bars must be placed inside the formwork before concrete is poured.
Steel reinforcement bars must be cut, bent, and fabricated to the required shapes and sizes before they can be placed/installed in the formwork.
Concrete must be poured over the placed reinforcement to embed the steel and create reinforced concrete; reinforcement must be in position before concrete is placed.
Reinforcement bars must be positioned first, then tied/wired together and secured with spacers/chairs to maintain correct cover and spacing before concrete pouring.
Quality control inspection of placed reinforcement (checking bar sizes, spacing, cover, and tying) must occur before concrete is poured, as it becomes impossible to inspect afterward.
Vegetation, debris, and existing surface obstructions must be removed before excavation can begin to provide clear access and a safe working area for excavation equipment.
Accurate layout and staking of foundation corners, benchmarks, and excavation limits are required before digging to ensure the excavation is positioned correctly according to design drawings.
Geotechnical analysis of soil bearing capacity, groundwater conditions, and soil classification must be completed to determine excavation slopes, shoring needs, and dewatering requirements.
Existing underground utilities (water, gas, electric, telecom) must be located, marked, and if necessary rerouted to prevent damage, service disruptions, and safety hazards during excavation.

Required environmental permits (e.g., stormwater pollution prevention) must be obtained and erosion/sediment control measures (silt fences, sediment basins) installed before any earth-disturbing activities can legally commence.
After excavation to design depth, the exposed subgrade must be leveled, compacted, and proof-rolled to achieve the required bearing capacity before any subsequent foundation work.
If groundwater is encountered at excavation depth, dewatering systems (wellpoints, sump pumps) must be installed and operated to maintain dry conditions for foundation construction.
Concrete formwork and steel reinforcement for footings or mats can only be placed after excavation is complete and the subgrade has been prepared and inspected.
Final foundation concrete can only be poured after excavation, subgrade preparation, formwork, and reinforcement placement have all been completed.
Formwork (molds) must be erected and secured before concrete can be poured into them to give the concrete its intended shape and support.
Steel reinforcement bars must be placed and tied within the formwork before pouring concrete, as the rebar provides tensile strength and must be embedded in the concrete.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and prepared before any concrete foundation or slab can be poured to ensure proper bearing and stability.
Concrete must be poured and cured to sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed; premature removal can cause structural failure.
Waterproofing membranes or coatings must be applied only after concrete has fully cured, to ensure proper adhesion and effectiveness.
Waterproofing requires a clean, cured, and properly prepared concrete substrate. The slab must be fully cured and any defects repaired before waterproofing membrane can be applied.
The substrate must be thoroughly cleaned of dirt, debris, oil, and laitance. Any dust or contaminants will prevent proper adhesion of the waterproofing membrane.

Many waterproofing systems require a primer coat to ensure adhesion between the substrate and the waterproofing membrane. Primer must be applied and allowed to dry/cure per manufacturer specifications.
Waterproofing must be completed and cured before any finish flooring or tile is installed over it. Installing flooring before waterproofing would trap moisture and defeat the waterproofing purpose.
After waterproofing is applied and cured, a flood test or leak test must be conducted to verify the integrity of the waterproofing membrane before proceeding with further construction.
Trenches and excavations must be dug before drainage pipes can be laid in them.
The subgrade must be prepared, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable foundation for drainage pipes.
Rough grading establishes proper slopes so that drainage pipes can be installed with correct gravity flow gradients.
Drainage pipes must be installed and inspected before trenches can be backfilled around and above them.
Drainage pipes must be in place before they can be connected to the main sewer system or stormwater outfall.
Underground drainage must be completed before concrete is poured to avoid having to cut through or disturb the slab later.
While final grading can begin after drain installation, it is a soft preference as some landscaping can be done concurrently in different areas.
Regulatory approval of drainage plans and permits must be obtained before installation work commences.
The ground must be cleared and graded before helical piers can be installed, as debris or uneven terrain would prevent proper placement and alignment of the piers.
Soil conditions must be analyzed to determine required pier depth, size, and torque requirements before helical pier installation can proceed.
Foundation layout must be staked out on site to mark exact locations for each helical pier before installation begins.
Helical piers must be fully installed and load-tested before caps can be placed on top to transfer structural loads.
Grade beams connecting the piers require the helical piers to be in place as the load-bearing support elements before beam concrete can be poured.
The foundation must be poured and cured to provide a stable base to support and anchor the steel beam.
The steel beam provides the primary structural support; roof decking is placed on top of and supported by the steel beams.
Steel beams are typically connected to and supported by vertical columns; columns must be erected first to provide attachment points for beams.
Final welding and bolting of beam-to-column and beam-to-beam connections can only be performed after the steel beam is positioned and aligned in place.
The steel beam must be fabricated, inspected, and delivered to the construction site before it can be erected and installed.
Formwork creates the mold that shapes and supports the wet concrete until it cures. Without formwork in place, the concrete beam cannot be poured or take its required shape.
Steel reinforcing bars must be positioned and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide tensile strength to the beam. The rebar cage is embedded within the concrete.
After the concrete beam is poured, it must undergo a curing period to achieve sufficient strength before any loads are applied or formwork is removed.
The concrete beam must be poured and achieve initial set before the formwork can be safely removed. Formwork removal too early would cause the beam to collapse.
Beams provide horizontal support and load transfer for vertical elements above. Columns or walls that rest on or connect to the beam must wait until the beam is cast and cured.
Raw timber must be harvested from forests before it can be processed into beams.
Harvested timber must be milled, cut, and shaped into beams before installation.
Timber beams must be dried to the appropriate moisture content before installation to prevent warping and shrinkage.
Timber beams (as roof rafters or floor joists) must be in place before sheathing or decking can be applied on top.
After timber beams are installed, a structural inspection must be completed to verify load-bearing capacity and correct placement before proceeding with subsequent work.
The steel beam must be fabricated before it can be embedded in the composite beam assembly to form the structural core.
Formwork or molds must be set up to contain the concrete pour that forms the composite action with the steel beam.
Shear connectors (studs) must be welded onto the steel beam before concrete is cast to ensure composite action between steel and concrete.
After the concrete is placed around the steel beam, sufficient curing time is required for the concrete to achieve design strength before any loads are applied.
The composite beam must be fully installed and cured before the floor or roof deck can be placed on top of it to transfer loads.

The beam dimensions, prestressing requirements, reinforcement details, and connection details must be fully designed and approved before fabrication can begin to ensure structural integrity and compliance with specifications.

High-strength concrete, prestressing steel strands, mild reinforcement, and other materials must be sourced, tested, and approved before precast beam production can commence to meet quality and strength requirements.
The precast bed or mold must be cleaned, oiled, and set up with the correct camber and geometry before concrete placement and prestressing operations can begin.
After casting and initial set, the concrete must cure to sufficient strength before the prestressing force can be safely transferred from the jacking system to the concrete member.

Only after the prestress has been fully transferred and the concrete has reached its specified release strength can the beam be lifted from the bed, stored, and later transported to the construction site.
The precast beam must be delivered to the project site and staged before erection onto substructures can proceed.
Bridge piers, abutments, or supporting walls must be completed and cured to design strength before the precast prestressed beams can be lifted and placed onto their bearings.
The exact beam seat elevations, alignment, and bearing locations must be surveyed and marked prior to beam placement to ensure correct positioning.
A stable foundation is required to support the loads transferred through the lintel beam; without proper foundation preparation, the beam would have no structural base.

Lintel beams are typically installed above openings such as doors or windows in load-bearing walls; the supporting wall masonry must be built up to the level of the lintel before the beam can be placed.
The lintel beam acts as a structural support that bridges an opening; masonry or wall construction above the lintel cannot proceed until the lintel is in place to carry the load.

If the lintel is part of a load-bearing wall system supporting a roof or upper floor, those structural elements cannot be placed until the lintel is installed and cured to provide continuous load transfer.
While not physically required, it is standard construction practice to complete all structural elements including lintels before applying finishes to avoid damage and rework.
Tie beams connect columns and require columns to be already installed and stabilized to provide support and anchorage.
Foundations must be completed to support columns and the overall structural load before tie beams can be placed.
Tie beams provide lateral support and form part of the structural frame that must be in place before floor slabs are poured.
Tie beams serve as a horizontal structural element that walls above rest upon; masonry cannot proceed without the beam in place.
The tie beam must be installed (cast and cured) before its formwork can be stripped.
The ring beam / plinth beam rests directly on the foundation or footing; the foundation must be completed and cured to provide a stable load-bearing base for the beam.
Vertical column reinforcement bars must be erected and tied up to the plinth level before the ring beam can be cast, as the beam ties into and surrounds the columns at the plinth level.
The ground inside the foundation must be backfilled and compacted to the plinth level to provide a working platform and support for the ring beam formwork and concrete.
The ring beam / plinth beam acts as a leveling and load-distributing element; superstructure columns and walls rise from the plinth beam and cannot be built without the completed beam in place.
The ground floor slab is often cast after the plinth beam is complete, as the beam defines the perimeter and level for the slab pour, and the slab may tie into the beam.
The supporting structure must have reached sufficient strength before spandrel beam placement can occur, as the beam relies on the cured concrete for support.
Formwork must be built and aligned before concrete can be poured into it to form the spandrel beam.

predecessor: Steel Reinforcement Placement for Spandrel Beam
rationale: Rebar cage must be positioned and tied within the formwork prior to concrete placement for structural integrity.
Once the concrete for the spandrel beam is poured, it must undergo curing to achieve design strength before any loads are applied.
Spandrel beams provide the structural support and attachment points for exterior façade panels; panels cannot be installed until the beams are in place and cured.
Transfer beams require a stable foundation to support and distribute their substantial loads; without completed foundations, the transfer beam cannot be placed.
Transfer beams are supported by columns below them; the columns must be erected and cured before the transfer beam can be placed on top.
Temporary formwork and falsework must be built to support the wet concrete of the transfer beam during casting before the beam itself can be poured.
The steel reinforcement cage must be fabricated, positioned, and tied within the formwork before concrete can be placed for the transfer beam.

successor: Upper Floor/Wall Construction Above Transfer Beam
rationale: The transfer beam must be in place, cured, and have achieved sufficient strength before any structure above it can be built, as the transfer beam redistributes loads from upper stories.
The cantilever beam requires a stable support structure; the foundation must be complete to bear the load and provide anchorage for the cantilever.
Cantilever beams are typically supported by or monolithic with columns or piers; these vertical supports must be constructed first to provide the fixed connection point.
Formwork and falsework must be erected to shape the concrete and support the cantilever beam during casting and curing before the beam itself can be placed or poured.
Rebar or post-tensioning tendons must be positioned within the formwork to provide tensile strength before the concrete for the cantilever beam is poured.
Any deck, slab, or superstructure that is supported by the cantilever beam can only be placed after the cantilever beam has cured and achieved sufficient strength to carry the additional load.
Edge beams are typically structural components that require the main steel frame to be in place as a support structure.
If edge beams are concrete and cast in place, the supporting columns must be sufficiently cured to bear the load.
Edge beams often form the perimeter support for roof decking or floor slabs, which must be placed after the edge beam is secured.
Edge beams define the building perimeter and provide attachment points for facade and curtain wall systems.
Waterproofing at roof or balcony edges is applied over or after the edge beam is in place to ensure proper sealing.
Columns provide vertical support for beams; beam formwork cannot be installed until columns are poured and sufficiently cured to bear the load from beam shoring.

In monolithic construction, beam and slab formwork are often installed together; however, if slab formwork is erected first, it can serve as a working platform for beam side formwork, though this is a sequencing preference rather than a strict physical requirement.

Beam reinforcement must be placed inside the formwork; typically, bottom reinforcement is laid after the beam bottom form is in place, but the sequence can vary. In some methods, rebar cages are pre-assembled and lowered into formwork, requiring formwork to be partially installed first.
Concrete for beams cannot be poured until the formwork is fully erected, aligned, braced, and checked for dimensions and stability to contain the wet concrete.

In typical cast-in-situ construction, the beam bottom formwork is installed first, then rebar is placed, followed by beam side formwork. So formwork installation and rebar installation are interleaved, not strictly sequential.
Formwork provides the mold and support structure for the beam; reinforcement bars must be placed within the formwork before concrete is poured, so formwork must be complete.
Reinforcement bars must be fabricated (cut, bent, and tied) to the specified dimensions before they can be placed into the beam formwork.
If beam reinforcement needs to be anchored into or supported by columns, the columns' concrete should be poured first to provide a stable base or connection point.
Concrete for the beam cannot be poured until the reinforcement cage is fully placed, tied, and positioned within the formwork per the engineering design.
A structural inspection of the placed reinforcement (cover, spacing, ties, supports) must be completed and approved before concrete placement to ensure compliance with design specifications.
Steel reinforcement bars must be placed, tied, and inspected within the formwork to provide structural strength before concrete is poured.
Formwork alignment, dimensions, and reinforcement must be formally inspected and approved by the engineer/quality control to ensure compliance with design before pouring.
After concrete is poured, a controlled curing process must begin immediately to ensure proper hydration and strength development of the concrete.
Formwork cannot be removed until the poured concrete has gained sufficient strength (after initial curing) to be self-supporting.
The foundation must be fully poured, cured, and achieve sufficient strength to support the dead and live loads imposed by steel columns and beams before any steel erection begins.
Steel beams are typically connected to steel columns (or column splices) to form the frame; columns must be erected and bolted/temporarily braced before beams can be placed between them.
Anchor bolts embedded in the foundation must be accurately set and grouted to receive the base plates of steel columns, which in turn support the steel beams.
Metal decking (e.g., composite steel deck) is laid on top of and perpendicular to the steel beams to form the floor/work platform; beams must be in place to support the deck.

After beams are placed (usually bolted temporarily), final connections (welding, high-strength bolting, and permanent bracing) must be completed to stabilize the steel frame before releasing hoisting cables.
Steel columns must be erected and stabilized before any beam-to-column connections can be installed, as beams are connected to the columns at their joints.
Columns must be verified as plumb and properly aligned to ensure accurate fit-up and connection of beams to columns.
Steel decking is typically placed after beam-to-column connections are complete, as the beams must be installed and connected to support the decking.

After beam-to-column connections are installed (i.e., beams placed and connections bolted in snug-tight condition), the final tightening/torqueing of bolts must follow to achieve design connection strength.
If the connection requires welding, welding must be performed after the beam is positioned and the connection is installed, but before the full load is applied.
Fireproofing material must be applied to the steel beams after they have been erected and fixed in place, as the beams need to be in their final position to receive the coating.
The steel beam surface must be cleaned, primed, and free of debris, rust, or oil for the fireproofing material to properly adhere.
While ceiling installation can begin after fireproofing is complete to avoid damaging the fireproofing, it is a soft preference as some coordination may allow partial overlap.
Inspections typically occur after fireproofing is complete, but this is more of a procedural preference than a physical necessity.
Any final decorative or protective top coating on the beams must be applied after the fireproofing layer has cured and been inspected.
The steel beam must be fabricated and cut to length before cambering (pre-stressing or curving) can be applied.
Cambering must be completed before the beam is lifted and placed into its final position, as the cambered shape is needed for proper load distribution.
The required camber amount and method must be specified in the structural design before cambering can be performed on the beam.
Cambering must be completed before the beam is permanently welded or bolted to its supporting columns or girders.
Verifying steel grade and properties before cambering is a quality control preference to ensure the steel can withstand the cambering process without cracking or permanent deformation.
The embed plates are installed onto or within the structural steel beams; therefore, the beams must be in place first to serve as the mounting substrate for the embed plates.

predecessor: Concrete Column / Wall Pour (if beam bears on concrete)
rationale: When beams bear on concrete elements, the embed plates are cast into or attached to the cured concrete; the concrete supporting element must be completed and cured before the embed plates can be installed.

predecessor: Survey / Layout of Beam Centerline and Elevations
rationale: Accurate positioning of the embed plate depends on established beam centerlines and elevations; layout must be completed prior to placement to ensure embed plates are located correctly.
The embed plates serve as the interface for subsequent beam-to-beam or beam-to-column connections; final welding or bolting cannot proceed until the plates are installed and secured.
Fireproofing is applied to the completed beam and embed plate assembly; installation of the plates must be finished before the fireproofing coatings are applied to ensure full coverage and bond.
Structural columns require a stable foundation to transfer loads to the ground; columns cannot be erected without a completed foundation base.
Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied inside the formwork before concrete can be poured to encase the rebar.
The mold (formwork) that shapes the column must be erected and secured before concrete is poured into it.
Concrete must reach sufficient strength through curing before formwork can be safely removed without damaging the column.
Columns must be in place to support beams and slabs that connect to them; beams transfer loads to columns.
The foundation provides the structural base and load-bearing support needed to anchor the decorative column securely.
Decorative columns are typically cladding or aesthetic finishes applied around or onto structural columns, so the structural column must be in place first.
The floor slab provides the finished walking surface and base level from which the decorative column is installed and aligned.
Final finishing and plastering work on the decorative column can only commence after the column itself is erected and fixed in position.
Surface preparation, painting, and other cosmetic finishes applied to the decorative column must be done after the column is fully installed.
Steel columns require a stable and level foundation to bear the load; without proper foundation preparation (excavation, formwork, concrete curing), the column cannot be safely placed or aligned.
Anchor bolts must be embedded in the foundation to allow the steel column baseplate to be bolted down; columns cannot be erected without these bolts in place.
Steel beams and girders typically connect to columns to form the structural frame; the columns must be erected and plumbed before beams can be installed between them.
Temporary or permanent bracing (cross-bracing, moment connections) stabilizes the column; bracing is applied after the column is in place to resist lateral loads.

While cladding typically follows the steel frame, it is a soft preference as cladding could theoretically be installed in parallel with column erection if safe access is managed, but standard sequencing places cladding after columns to provide the building envelope.
Columns require a stable foundation to transfer loads; footings must be completed and cured before column formwork and reinforcement can be placed.
The steel reinforcement cage must be assembled and placed within the column formwork before concrete can be poured.
Formwork must be erected and braced to contain the wet concrete; pouring cannot occur without proper formwork in place.
Freshly poured concrete must undergo a curing period to achieve sufficient strength before any subsequent loads or further construction can be applied.
Column formwork can only be removed after the concrete has gained adequate strength; stripping too early can damage the column.
Columns provide vertical support for slabs and beams above; those upper structural elements cannot be placed until columns are poured, cured, and hardened.
Finishing work such as plastering or painting is typically done after curing and formwork removal, but could be deferred; it is a logical but not physically mandatory sequence.
Raw timber must be harvested and milled into dimensional lumber before a timber column can be fabricated.
The column must be cut, shaped, and fabricated before it can be erected or installed on site.
A concrete foundation or base must be in place to support and anchor the timber column before it can be erected.
Columns must be erected and secured before beams and girders can be placed on top of them to transfer loads.
Temporary or permanent bracing and connection details must be installed after the column is in position to ensure stability.
Composite columns require a stable foundation or footing to transfer loads to the ground. The foundation must be cured and ready before column erection begins.
Steel reinforcement cage or embedded steel section must be placed and tied before concrete is poured around it to form the composite column.
Formwork molds must be erected and secured to shape the concrete portion of the composite column before pouring.
After the composite column is cast (concrete poured), it must undergo a curing period to gain strength before any loads are applied.
Beams and slabs supported by the column cannot be constructed until the composite column is in place and sufficiently cured to carry the load.
A masonry column requires a stable, load-bearing foundation to support its weight and prevent settlement or structural failure.
Steel reinforcement (rebar) must be placed and tied within the column formwork before masonry work begins to provide tensile strength to the column.
Formwork or moulds must be erected to shape and contain the masonry materials (bricks, blocks, or stone) during construction of the column.
After the masonry column is built, proper curing time is required for mortar and grout to achieve sufficient strength before any loads are applied.
Beams or slabs supported by the column can only be constructed after the masonry column has been completed and cured to bear the structural load.
Waterproofing of the column surface is typically done after the column is complete to protect it from moisture, though it is a protective measure rather than a physical structural necessity.
The column base plate must be placed on a prepared, level foundation surface that has been excavated, compacted, and poured with concrete to provide structural support.
Anchor bolts must be embedded in the foundation concrete at precise locations before the column base plate can be positioned and bolted down.
The foundation concrete must be fully cured to sufficient strength to bear the load of the column and base plate before installation can proceed.
The column base plate must be in place and leveled before the steel column can be erected and welded or bolted to the base plate.
After the base plate is positioned and leveled, the gap between the base plate and foundation must be filled with non-shrink grout to ensure full bearing and load transfer.
Column formwork must be installed to create the mold for the column, and the column capital sits atop the column, so the column formwork must be in place first.
Reinforcement steel for the column must be placed and tied before the column capital is formed, as the capital connects to and rests on the column reinforcement.
The column must be poured and cured to provide structural support for the column capital, which is cast or placed on top of the column.
The column capital acts as a support or head for the slab formwork; slab formwork often rests on or is supported by the column capital, so the capital must be in place first.

While reinforcement for the capital would typically be placed before concrete pouring, the capital itself (as a structural element) must be formed before additional reinforcement for beams or slabs can be placed on top of it. This is a logical sequencing preference.
Fireproofing is applied to steel columns after they are erected; the structural steel must be in place before fireproofing can be applied.
Fireproofing material must be fully applied and cured before any cladding, architectural finishes, or coverings are installed over the column.
MEP rough-in work near columns can proceed more easily after fireproofing is complete to avoid damaging the fireproofing material.
Fireproofing is a base layer; any paint or final decorative coating must be applied after the fireproofing is cured and complete.
Reinforcement bars (rebar) must be placed and tied inside the column before formwork can be erected around them, as formwork encloses the reinforcement cage.
The exact position and alignment of the column must be marked on the slab/deck before formwork panels are placed, to ensure correct location.
If the column sits on a freshly poured slab, the slab concrete must have gained sufficient strength to support the formwork loads before erecting column forms.
Formwork must be fully assembled, aligned, braced, and checked before concrete can be placed into the column.
Stripping (removing) the formwork can only occur after the formwork has been installed and concrete has been poured and cured sufficiently. The formwork removal is inherently after installation.
Column formwork must be installed before placing the reinforcement cage inside the formwork, as the cage is lowered into the pre-assembled formwork shell.
The reinforcement cage must be fully placed and secured within the formwork before concrete can be poured, as concrete encases the reinforcement.
While stirrups are typically tied as part of assembling the cage itself, any final adjustments or additional ties can only be completed after the main cage is positioned.
The foundation or footing must be completed to provide a stable base and proper anchorage for the column reinforcement cage, which typically extends into the footing.
All longitudinal bars and stirrups must be cut, bent, and prepared to the specified dimensions before they can be assembled into the reinforcement cage.
Reinforcement steel must be in place within the column before the column sections can be spliced together, as the splice connects the reinforcing bars.
Formwork must be set up to hold and align the column segments before the splice can be executed.
The lower column segment must be supported by a completed foundation or pier before the splice to the upper segment can be performed.
After the column segments are spliced (mechanically connected or welded), concrete can be poured to encase the splice and complete the column.
Grouting of the splice connection (if applicable) must follow the physical splice to fill voids and ensure load transfer.
Columns require a stable foundation base to be erected upon; the foundation must be fully cured and ready to support the column loads before column erection can begin.

Vertical reinforcement bars (rebars) must be placed and tied within the foundation or column footings before the column formwork or precast column can be erected, as the rebars provide structural continuity.
The exact positions, grid lines, and elevations for each column must be marked and verified through surveying to ensure columns are placed at correct locations and alignments.
Beams and slabs are typically supported by columns; columns must be erected and secured before beams can be placed on top of or connected to the columns.

After erecting columns, their verticality (plumbness) and horizontal alignment must be checked and adjusted before proceeding with subsequent structural elements to ensure overall structural integrity and tolerances are met.
Formwork must be erected and secured before concrete can be poured to contain and shape the wet concrete.
Steel reinforcement cage must be placed and tied inside the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity.
Concrete must be poured and gain sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed without damaging the column.
Immediately after pouring, curing must begin to maintain moisture and temperature conditions for proper concrete hydration and strength gain.

successor: Vertical Structural Load Transfer (e.g., beams/slabs on columns)
rationale: Concrete must be poured and cured to design strength before the column can bear loads from beams, slabs, or other structural elements placed on top.
Fireproofing must be applied to steel columns after they are erected and in place; applying fireproofing before erection would damage the coating during handling and lifting.
The steel column surface must be clean, free of rust, mill scale, and debris, and any primer coatings must be properly cured before fireproofing materials can bond correctly.

predecessor: Welding & Bolting Completion of Column Connections
rationale: All welding, bolting, and connection work on the column must be finished because fireproofing would obstruct access to connections and heat from welding would damage fireproofing material.

Fireproofing must be completed before mechanical or HVAC work is installed adjacent to or penetrating through the column, as fireproofing provides the required fire-resistance rating and any subsequent work could damage or compromise the fireproofing integrity.

successor: Electrical Conduit & Cable Tray Installation on Columns
rationale: Electrical rough-in work that attaches to or runs along columns must occur after fireproofing is applied and cured, so that the fireproofing is not disturbed and the electrical components do not create thermal bridges that compromise fire resistance.
The column must be cast and the concrete must be allowed to cure sufficiently before inspection can be performed to verify structural integrity, alignment, and surface quality.

Formwork must be installed and secured before the concrete is poured and subsequently inspected; however, inspection of formwork alignment and rebar placement is typically done before pouring, so 'Column Inspection Activity' here refers to post-pour inspection.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied before concrete is poured; a pre-pour inspection of rebar is typically required prior to concreting, which precedes the post-concrete column inspection.
Inspection must confirm that the concrete has achieved sufficient strength before formwork can be safely stripped.
Inspection must be completed and any defects rectified before finishing works such as plastering or painting can commence on the column surface.
The structural columns must be erected and fully set in place before any cladding can be attached, as cladding is applied onto or around the structural column frame.

Any mechanical, electrical, or plumbing rough-in work that runs within or behind the column cladding must be completed and inspected before the cladding is installed, otherwise it would require removal of the installed cladding.
After cladding is installed, finishing work such as caulking, joint sealing, and aesthetic touch-ups must be performed to complete the weatherproofing and final appearance.
Inspection for quality, alignment, and compliance with specifications can only occur after the cladding installation is fully complete.

Scaffolding or temporary access platforms used during cladding installation must remain in place until installation is complete; removal only begins after all cladding work is finished to ensure safe access.
The floor slab requires a stable, load-bearing base from the completed foundation system to distribute loads evenly and prevent differential settlement.
The ground must be properly graded, leveled, and compacted before pouring the floor slab to ensure uniform support and avoid future cracking or subsidence.
A vapor barrier or damp-proof membrane must be laid over the prepared sub-base before the slab is poured to prevent moisture migration from the ground into the slab.
Steel reinforcement mesh or rebar must be positioned and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide tensile strength and control cracking.
Load-bearing walls, columns, and other vertical structural elements are typically erected on top of or anchored into the completed floor slab, requiring the slab to be cured first.
Walls must be built to support the roof slab; the roof slab rests directly on the walls.
Columns must be erected to provide vertical support and load transfer for the roof slab.
Formwork (shuttering) must be set up to provide the mold and temporary support for casting the concrete roof slab.

predecessor: Reinforcement Steel Fixing for Roof Slab
rationale: Steel reinforcement bars must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide tensile strength.
Waterproofing membrane/layer must be applied after the roof slab has cured to protect the slab from water ingress.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (e.g., conduit, drain pipes) is typically done after the slab is poured but can sometimes be embedded prior; post-pour installation is common and preferred for accuracy.
Ceiling finishes (plaster, paint, false ceiling) cannot begin until the roof slab is complete and adequately cured.
Any top-layer finishing (tiles, screed, or paver blocks) on the roof must follow after the structural slab is fully set and cured.
The ground must be excavated and cleared of debris, topsoil, and organic material before any concrete slab can be poured to ensure stable load-bearing conditions.
The subgrade must be properly compacted and graded to the required levels to provide a uniform, stable base that prevents differential settlement of the slab.

predecessor: Installation of Blinding Layer / Lean Concrete
rationale: A thin layer of lean concrete (blinding) is typically placed over the compacted soil to provide a clean, level working surface and protect the subgrade from weather before the main slab is poured.
A vapor barrier or damp-proof membrane must be laid over the blinding layer to prevent moisture migration from the ground into the concrete slab, which is essential before pouring the slab.
After the slab is poured, it must undergo a specified curing period to achieve sufficient strength and durability before any subsequent construction loads are applied.

successor: Vertical Reinforcement / Column Starter Bars Installation
rationale: Column starter bars and vertical reinforcement are set into the wet concrete of the slab or immediately after; the slab pour must be complete before these can be properly embedded and aligned.
Load-bearing walls require the foundation slab as a stable base; the slab must be fully cured and have achieved adequate strength before masonry or formwork for walls begins.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) services that are embedded in or run beneath the slab must be installed before the slab pour; however, above-slab MEP work and other services can only begin after the slab is complete and cured.

Slab edges and spandrel slabs are embedded into or bear on vertical structural elements (columns and walls). Therefore, the vertical supports must be erected first to provide a bearing surface and connection point.

Slab edges and spandrels form the perimeter closure of a floor slab. The main slab or deck must be placed first (or concurrently) so the edge formwork and reinforcement can be integrated with the slab system.
Reinforcement steel for the slab edge must be tied and positioned before concrete is placed for the spandrel or edge element.
After the slab edge concrete has cured sufficiently, the edge formwork can be stripped and removed to allow subsequent façade and waterproofing work.
The spandrel slab provides the structural perimeter edge to which curtain wall anchors and façade panels are attached. The slab edge must be complete and cured for proper load transfer and alignment.
Formwork provides the temporary mold and support structure required to shape and hold the wet concrete of the suspended slab until it cures and gains sufficient strength.
Steel reinforcement bars (rebar) must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide tensile strength to the suspended slab.
The suspended slab concrete must be poured and cured to achieve the required design strength before the supporting formwork and shoring can be safely removed.

Columns, walls, or other vertical structural elements on the next level cannot be constructed until the suspended slab (floor deck) below them is completed and provides the working platform and structural base.

Waterproofing is typically applied after the slab is cured, but it is a soft dependency as it depends on the design specification and project sequencing; some projects may waterproof at a different stage.
The structural frame (columns and beams) must be in place to provide bearing support for precast hollow-core slabs.
Grouting fills the keyways between adjacent slabs to ensure load transfer and diaphragm action.
A structural topping slab is typically placed over the hollow-core planks to create a composite structural diaphragm and level surface.
While some MEP work can proceed in parallel, final routing of conduits, ducts, and pipes above the slab is best performed after the slab is in place since the slab defines the ceiling plane.
Load-bearing and non-load-bearing partition walls are built on top of the finished slab; the slab must be in place and cured to provide the working surface and floor elevation reference.
Composite steel deck slabs require a supporting structural steel frame to be in place before decking can be installed, as the deck panels rest on and are welded to the steel beams.
The steel deck panels must be laid, fastened, and have shear studs welded before concrete can be poured to form the composite slab.
Steel reinforcing bars or welded wire mesh are placed on top of the deck after it is installed but before concrete pouring, as part of the composite slab construction sequence.
After concrete is poured onto the steel deck, a curing period must elapse before the slab can carry construction loads or have subsequent work performed on it.

predecessor: Shear Stud Welding to Steel Beams
rationale: Shear studs must be welded through the deck to the steel beams to achieve composite action; this is done as part of or immediately after deck installation and before concrete is placed.
Formwork provides the mold and support structure for the slab, so it must be installed before any reinforcement can be placed within the slab area.
The slab deck or soffit must be cleaned, leveled, and prepared as the working surface before placing reinforcement bars or mesh.
Vertical reinforcement from columns or walls that will be tied into the slab must be in place first to allow proper overlap and continuity of reinforcement.

While some conduits can be placed concurrently with rebar, final positioning of embedded electrical and plumbing services is typically done after the bottom reinforcement layer is placed and before the top layer, making it a soft sequential preference.
All reinforcement bars, mesh, and chairs must be fully placed, tied, and inspected before concrete can be poured to ensure structural integrity and code compliance.
The formwork provides the mold and temporary support structure needed to cast the post-tensioned slab. Without the formwork in place, the concrete cannot be placed and shaped.

Steel rebar reinforcement (including un-tensioned reinforcement) must be placed within the formwork before concrete is poured, as it provides structural reinforcement and anchors for the post-tensioning tendons.

The post-tensioning tendons (cables or strands encased in ducts) must be positioned within the formwork and tied to the reinforcement before the concrete is poured, so they become embedded in the slab.
After the concrete for the post-tensioned slab is poured, it must be allowed to cure and gain sufficient strength before tensioning forces can be applied to the tendons.

The concrete must reach its specified compressive strength (typically around 75% of design strength) before the post-tensioning tendons can be tensioned; otherwise, the concrete could crush or fail under the high compressive forces.
After the tendons have been tensioned and anchored, the ducts must be grouted to protect the tendons from corrosion and to bond them permanently to the concrete section.
The post-tensioned slab must be cast, cured, and tensioned before the formwork can be safely removed, as the slab requires its full post-tensioning force to be self-supporting.
Column and beam formwork must be installed first to create the supporting framework onto which slab formwork is placed.
Reinforcement in supporting elements (columns and beams) must be completed before slab formwork to ensure structural continuity and proper load transfer.
Slab formwork must be in place to provide a working platform and mold for placing and tying the slab reinforcement bars.
Formwork serves as the mold for the concrete; it must be fully installed, aligned, and secured before any concrete can be poured into the slab area.

While curing technically begins after pouring (which requires formwork), the formwork removal is often timed with curing completion; however, this is a soft constraint as curing duration can be adjusted based on formwork striking schedules.
Formwork must be installed and securely braced to create the mold that shapes and supports the wet concrete until it cures.
Steel reinforcement bars must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide tensile strength to the slab.
Any electrical conduits, plumbing pipes, or sleeves for future services must be positioned within the slab area before concrete is poured, as they cannot be placed afterward.
Freshly poured concrete must undergo a controlled curing process to achieve design strength and prevent cracking due to rapid moisture loss.
Formwork cannot be removed until the concrete has gained sufficient strength to support its own weight and any imposed loads; however this follows after pouring and initial curing.

Concrete must be poured and placed into the slab formwork before curing can begin, as curing is the process of maintaining adequate moisture and temperature conditions for freshly placed concrete to harden and gain strength.

The concrete slab surface must be finished (troweled, floated, and textured as required) before curing can start, because curing compounds or wet coverings are applied only after final finishing is complete.
Formwork must remain in place during the curing period to support the slab until the concrete reaches sufficient strength; stripping can only begin after curing is substantially complete.

Control joints and saw cuts should be made after the concrete has cured sufficiently to prevent raveling, but before full hardening; typically done after initial curing but while the slab is still gaining strength.

Waterproofing membranes, sealers, or coatings must only be applied after the concrete slab has fully cured to the specified moisture content and strength, ensuring proper adhesion and preventing coating failure.
Concrete must be poured and reach sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed; otherwise the slab may crack or collapse.
Concrete requires adequate curing time to achieve the necessary compressive strength to be self-supporting before forms are stripped.
Formwork must be installed and securely braced before concrete can be poured into it.
After formwork is removed, the exposed slab surfaces can be finished, patched, ground, or coated as required.
Formwork from the completed slab must be removed to allow vertical elements for the next floor level to be erected on the slab.

The formwork provides the mold and structural support for the wet concrete; reinforcement bars (rebar) must be placed inside the formwork before concrete pouring, making formwork installation a prerequisite.
Reinforcement steel must be fully placed, tied, and inspected before concrete can be poured; pouring concrete before reinforcement is complete would result in a structurally unsafe slab.
An inspection of the installed rebar (checking spacing, cover, tying, and bar sizes) is required before concrete placement to ensure compliance with structural drawings and codes.

While MEP conduits and sleeves can be placed alongside rebar installation, ideally rough-in should be completed before concrete pouring; however, some coordination can occur simultaneously, making this a soft preference rather than a strict hard constraint.
Edge forms and stop-ends define the slab perimeter and must be in place before reinforcement can be properly positioned and tied to the correct slab edges.
The slab formwork (shuttering) must be erected to provide the mold and support for the concrete slab before post-tensioning tendons can be placed and stressed.
Post-tensioning tendons (cables/strands) are placed within the slab reinforcement cage; general rebar and formwork must be in place before tendons are laid out and stressed.
The post-tensioning tendons must be placed and housed within ducts or sheathing before concrete is poured and tensioning can occur.
The concrete slab must be poured and sufficiently cured to achieve the required compressive strength before the post-tensioning tendons can be stressed and anchored.

Post-tensioning is itself the process of stressing the tendons after concrete curing, so the tensioning operation (stressing and anchoring) is the execution of post-tensioning, not a separate successor. However, after stressing, the ducts are grouted.
After post-tensioning tendons are stressed and anchored, the ducts must be grouted to protect tendons from corrosion and lock in the prestress force.
Formwork can only be removed after post-tensioning is completed and the slab is self-supporting under the induced prestress, ensuring structural safety.
Inspection and quality checks are typically performed after post-tensioning to verify tendon forces, slab camber, and grout integrity before proceeding with subsequent works.
Slab layout and marking must be completed first to indicate where cuts and cores should be placed, ensuring accuracy and alignment with structural and MEP drawings.

successor: Slab Edge Formwork / Recess Formwork Installation
rationale: Cutting and coring creates openings and edges; formwork for slab edges or recesses can only be installed after the slab surface has been prepared and openings defined.
After cutting or coring, core holes and cut edges need patching, grouting, or structural repair to restore integrity and finish.
Cored holes and cut openings must exist before mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in can pass through the slab.
The concrete slab must be poured and sufficiently cured to achieve adequate strength before any cutting or coring can be performed without damaging the slab.
The concrete slab must be poured and sufficiently cured (reaching initial set) before any finishing work can be performed on its surface; otherwise, finishing would damage the wet concrete.
Formwork must be in place and concrete poured within it before the slab surface can be finished; the surface finishing is performed on the freshly placed concrete within the forms.
Steel reinforcement must be positioned and tied before concrete is poured, which then precedes surface finishing; surface finishing cannot begin without the structural reinforcement being in place.

After surface finishing (screeding, floating, troweling) is complete, the slab must undergo its final curing process to achieve proper strength and durability; finishing must happen before extended curing begins.

While waterproofing typically follows surface finishing, it is a soft preference as some waterproofing systems can be applied to green concrete; however, best practice is to finish the surface first for proper adhesion and smoothness.
The rough opening must be framed in the wall structure to provide the physical space and support for installing the window frame.
Weather-resistant barrier (house wrap) must be installed behind the window area to seal the building envelope before the window frame is placed.
The window frame provides the structural casing and support needed to hold the glass panes; glass cannot be installed without the frame in place.
While it is physically possible to finish walls before windows, it is standard practice to install window frames first to avoid damaging finished surfaces and to allow proper fitting and sealing.
The rough opening must be framed in the wall before the window sash can be installed, as the sash requires a structurally prepared opening to fit into.
Flashing and weatherproofing around the rough opening must be applied before installing the window sash to ensure proper water drainage and prevent moisture intrusion.

Exterior trim (e.g., casing, brickmold) is typically installed around the window sash after it is placed to cover the gap between the sash and the rough opening for aesthetic and weatherproofing purposes.
Interior wall finishes around the window are applied after the sash is installed to create a seamless transition between the wall surface and the window frame.
Interior trim and casing are installed after the window sash is in place and interior wall finishing is complete, as the trim covers the junction between the sash/frame and the finished wall.
The window frame must be installed and secured in the wall opening before glazing (glass panes) can be placed, as the frame provides the structural support and containment for the glass.
The rough opening must be framed, weatherproofed, and properly sized before the window assembly (including glazing) can be installed.
The window glazing must be completed and sealed before interior wall finishes such as drywall and trim can be installed around the window, to ensure a weather-tight seal and proper alignment.
The window glazing must be in place before the exterior cladding and flashing can be installed around it, to integrate the window into the building envelope and prevent water intrusion.

While not physically required, it is preferred to complete window glazing before conducting building envelope air and water barrier testing, as windows are a critical point of leakage and should be fully installed for accurate test results.
The window frame must be installed first to provide a structural opening and support for the window sill to be fitted against.
The rough opening must be prepared and framed to the correct dimensions before the window sill can be placed and secured.
Weatherproofing or flashing must be applied around the window opening before installing the sill to ensure water-tightness and prevent moisture intrusion.
The window sill provides the bottom support ledge; window glass or glazing units are typically set onto or against the completed sill.
Although interior finishes can often proceed after the sill is in place to allow clean edges and trim, it is a soft preference as some finishing work could be done with the sill temporarily absent.
The rough opening (framed opening) must be prepared and sized correctly before the window head can be installed, as the window head sits at the top of the opening.
The window frame must be assembled before the window head can be attached or installed, as the head is the top horizontal member of the frame.
The window head provides the top structural support for the window; glass panes cannot be installed until the head is in place to create a complete frame.
Flashing and sealing around the window head is part of the weatherproofing process that occurs after the head is installed to prevent water ingress.
Interior trim around the window head is typically installed after the head is in place, though this is a sequential preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and cavity into which the window jamb is installed.
The window jamb forms the side frame that houses and supports the window sash; the sash cannot be installed until the jamb is in place.
Interior trim and casing are applied around the window jamb; the jamb must be installed first to provide a surface for the trim.
Weatherproofing and flashing are applied around the installed window jamb to seal against moisture ingress; the jamb must be in place to receive these materials.
Wall sheathing provides lateral rigidity and a backing surface; the window jamb is typically installed after sheathing is in place around the rough opening.
Weatherstripping is applied to the gaps around windows and doors; these must be installed first to provide the surfaces and gaps that weatherstripping seals.
Weatherstripping seals the interface between wall assemblies and openings; walls must be fully constructed and sided to provide proper backing and alignment.
Framing must be complete to define window and door openings; weatherstripping cannot be applied until rough openings exist.
While interior finishing often proceeds after weatherstripping to avoid damage, this is a soft preference; in some sequences interior finish can be done before final weatherstripping adjustment.

successor: Final commissioning and air leakage testing
rationale: Air leakage tests and building commissioning must be performed after weatherstripping is complete to verify the envelope is properly sealed.
The rough opening framing must be complete to provide the structural support and space for the window and its hardware to be installed.
The window frame must be set and secured in place before the window hardware (hinges, locks, handles, stays) can be attached to it.
The glass panes must be installed in the frame before the hardware (such as locks and handles) can be fitted, as the hardware often secures the glazing or operates in relation to it.
Final weatherstripping and sealing around the operable hardware elements must occur after the hardware is installed to ensure proper fit and airtight performance.
Testing the operation of windows (opening, closing, locking) can only be fully performed once all hardware is installed, to verify proper function and make any needed adjustments.
The window insect screen must be mounted onto or within the window frame; the frame provides the structural support and attachment points for the screen.
After the insect screen is installed, the window's opening and closing mechanisms must be tested to ensure the screen does not obstruct normal window operation.
The insect screen must be fully fabricated (cut to size, framed, mesh attached) before it can be physically installed on site.

While not a strict physical constraint, installing the insect screen before interior finishes like painting around the window allows for a cleaner appearance and avoids damaging finished surfaces during screen installation.
The rough opening must be prepared and the window frame installed before the insect screen can be fitted, as the screen attaches to the frame assembly.
Window grilles and mullions are attached to or sit within window/door frames; the frame must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the grille/mullion.
Window openings must be fully formed within the structural wall before window frames and their associated grilles/mullions can be installed.
Grilles and mullions form the supporting framework for glass panes; glass panels are set into the grille/mullion framework.
Interior trim and sealant work around windows is typically done after the grille/mullion system is in place to ensure proper fit and sealing, though some finishing can be done concurrently.
Weatherproofing membranes, sealants, and flashings around the window assembly are applied after the grille/mullion is installed to create a continuous weather barrier.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed and sized correctly before the casement window can be installed.
Proper weather barrier and flashing must be applied around the opening to prevent water intrusion before the window is set in place.
Exterior trim, casing, and siding around the window must be installed after the window is secured and properly flashed.
Interior drywall, casing, and finishes around the window opening can only be completed after the window unit is installed.
The crank mechanism, hinges, and locking hardware must be adjusted and tested after the window frame is securely installed in the opening.
The rough opening must be framed, weatherproofed, and sized correctly before any window unit can be installed; the window cannot be placed without a prepared opening.
Flashing and exterior weather barriers are applied after the window is set in the opening to ensure proper integration with the building envelope and prevent water intrusion.
Interior casing, stops, and operating sash components are installed after the window frame is secured in place to allow proper fit and operation.
Spray foam or other insulation around the window frame must be applied after the window is installed to seal gaps and ensure thermal efficiency.
Glass panes, balances, locks, and operating hardware are finalized after the window frame is securely mounted and aligned in the rough opening.
The sliding window must be installed into a prepared window frame; the frame provides the structural support and mounting surface for the window unit.
The rough opening must be framed, measured, and squared before any window can be placed to ensure proper fit and alignment.
Weatherproofing membranes and flashing must be applied around the rough opening prior to window installation to prevent water intrusion behind the window.
After the sliding window is placed and secured, the gaps around it must be sealed with insulation, caulking, and trim to ensure airtightness and weather resistance.
Interior drywall, trim, and paint around the window area should be completed after the window is installed to achieve a finished appearance and proper integration with the wall.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before an awning window can be installed, as the window unit requires a structurally sound and correctly sized opening.
Weatherproofing membranes and flashing around the rough opening must be applied before installing the window to ensure water tightness and prevent moisture intrusion behind the window frame.
Exterior trim, siding, and final cladding around the window can only be completed after the awning window is properly installed and secured in the opening.
Interior wall finishing such as drywall, casing, and paint around the window frame must wait until the window unit is fully installed to ensure proper fit and seamless integration.

Final adjustment, cranking mechanism testing, and sealing checks are best performed after installation, though could theoretically be done concurrently; however, practical sequencing requires the window to be in place first.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed, sized, and prepared before the fixed window can be installed into it.
The fixed window unit (frame and glass) must be fully assembled or manufactured before it can be placed into the rough opening.
Weather-resistant barrier and flashing must be applied to the rough opening before setting the window to ensure proper water drainage and sealing.
After the fixed window is set in place, the perimeter must be sealed with caulk and sealant to provide an airtight and watertight closure.

Interior casing and trim work around the window is typically done after the window is installed to cover gaps and provide a finished look; this is a logical sequence preference but not a strict physical necessity.
The exterior siding or cladding around the window must be completed after the window is installed to integrate the window into the building envelope and prevent water intrusion.
The skylight must be installed on a completed roof deck structure; the roof deck provides the structural support and opening for the skylight.
Roof framing defines the rough opening and structural support needed for skylight placement.
Flashing is installed around the skylight after it is placed to create a watertight seal and prevent leaks.
The interior ceiling finish around the skylight shaft can only be completed after the skylight is installed and the shaft is enclosed.
The final roofing material around the skylight is applied after the skylight and its flashing are in place to ensure proper integration and weatherproofing.
The foundation provides the load-bearing support for the bay window structure; without a stable foundation, the bay window cannot be safely installed.
Rough framing creates the structural opening and support framework into which the bay window is fitted; the bay window cannot be installed before the wall framing is complete.
Exterior sheathing provides the structural backing and weather-resistant layer around the bay window opening; the bay window assembly needs to be secured against the sheathed wall.
After the bay window is placed in the opening, flashing must be installed around its perimeter to seal against water intrusion; this cannot be done before the window is in position.
Interior drywall, trim, and finishing around the bay window can only be completed after the window unit is installed and secured in the opening.
Window frames require a structured rough opening framed by studs, headers, and sills to provide structural support and proper dimensions for installation.
Weather-resistant barriers (house wrap) are typically installed before windows to ensure proper integration with window flashing and prevent water intrusion.
Flashing, caulking, and sealant around the window frame must be applied after the window is placed and secured to ensure a watertight seal.
Drywall, casing, and interior trim around windows are installed after windows are in place to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance.
Exterior siding is installed after windows to allow proper integration with window flanges and flashing, ensuring a weathertight exterior envelope.
The window frame must be installed and securely fixed in the rough opening before any glazing (glass) can be placed. Glazing requires a stable, finished frame to sit within.
The rough opening in the wall must be prepared, squared, and weatherproofed before the window unit (frame and glazing) can be installed.
After the glazing is installed, the perimeter must be sealed with caulk, gaskets, or weatherstripping to prevent air and water infiltration.
Interior trim and drywall can only be finished around the window once the glazing is in place, but this is a soft preference as temporary covers could allow some overlap.
Exterior siding or cladding around the window must be completed after the window glazing is installed so that flashing and weatherproofing can integrate properly with the window unit.
Windows must be installed and secured in their frames before any weatherproofing (sealing, caulking, or weatherstripping) can be applied to the window perimeter.
The window frame must be cleaned, dried, and any old sealant removed so that new weatherproofing materials can properly adhere.
Exterior wall sheathing provides the structural backing around the window; weatherproofing seals the gap between the window frame and this sheathing.

Weatherproofing (e.g., flashing, caulk, weather barrier) must be applied around windows before exterior cladding (siding, brick, stucco) is installed, as the cladding covers and protects the weatherproofing layer.
Weatherproofing ensures no moisture intrusion around the window, which must be verified before interior finishes (drywall, trim, paint) are applied to avoid water damage behind walls.
Window hardware (hinges, handles, locks, operators) must be attached to installed and secured window frames; the frame must be in place before hardware can be mounted and commissioned.

Hardware such as locking mechanisms and operating hardware interfaces with the glazed window assembly; glass must be installed so that hardware can be properly aligned and tested for fit and operation.
Weather seals, gaskets, and exterior caulking are applied after hardware is commissioned to ensure the hardware operates correctly and seals are not damaged or misaligned during hardware adjustment.
Performance testing requires fully commissioned hardware so that windows can be properly closed, locked, and sealed to achieve accurate test results.
While interior finishes can proceed after hardware is commissioned to avoid damage or obstruction, this is a soft preference as finishes could be installed earlier if hardware is carefully protected.
The door frame must be installed and properly aligned before the door leaf can be hung, as the leaf is physically attached to the frame via hinges.
The rough opening in the wall must be prepared (sized, framed, and cleared) before the door frame can be installed.
The door leaf must be hung in the frame before locksets, handles, and other hardware can be fitted onto the leaf.
Final adjustments to door alignment, gap tolerances, and swing operation can only be performed after the leaf is installed in its frame.
The structural wall framing and sheathing must be completed before the rough opening can be cut or framed out for the door.
Door frames are installed within wall openings; the wall structure must be framed first to create the rough opening for the door frame.
The rough opening must be measured, cut, and prepared in the wall framing to the correct dimensions before the door frame can be placed and secured.
The door frame must be installed and secured in the opening before the door slab can be hung on the hinges attached to the frame.
The door frame provides the structural base onto which decorative trim and casing are fastened; trim cannot be installed without the frame in place.
Weatherstripping is applied around the perimeter of the installed door frame to seal gaps; the frame must be complete before sealing can be applied.
The door frame must be installed and secured in the rough opening before any door hardware (hinges, locks, handles) can be mounted, as the hardware attaches directly to the frame.

Rough electrical work (wiring for electric strikes, maglocks, or access control systems) must be completed before installing door hardware, as the hardware often integrates with these systems and wiring must be in place behind the frame.

Wall finishing around the door opening must be complete to avoid damaging finished surfaces when installing door hardware; hardware installation after painting prevents paint drips on hardware and allows for proper fitting of trim and casings.

Door hardware must be installed before the final adjustment, testing, and commissioning of door operation (checking latch alignment, closing speed, lock function) to ensure everything works correctly together.

While not physically required, it is preferable to install door hardware before interior signage and final trim work around the door to ensure proper alignment of signage with hardware (e.g., push/pull plates, keypad placement) and to avoid rework.
The rough opening for the door must be framed before the threshold can be installed, as the threshold sits within and is anchored to the framed opening.
The subfloor must be installed to provide a stable base and proper elevation for the door threshold to be set upon.
Door casing and trim are installed after the threshold because the threshold serves as the bottom reference point and the vertical jambs and trim rest on top of or alongside the threshold.
The door slab or door unit is installed after the threshold because the threshold provides the bottom seal and alignment surface that the door closes against.
Weatherproofing and sealing around the threshold is applied after installation to ensure a watertight seal between the threshold and the surrounding floor or walls.
The door sill must be installed into the rough opening, which must first be framed to provide the correct dimensions and structural support.
The door sill sits on top of the subfloor or floor structure, which must be completed first to provide a level and stable base.
The door frame is typically assembled on top of the door sill, so the sill must be in place first to anchor the jambs.
Weatherproofing and sealing around the door opening must be applied after the sill is installed to ensure a proper watertight seal at the bottom.
The threshold often sits on or integrates with the door sill, so the sill must be in place before the threshold can be installed.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and defined space for the transom panel to be installed.
Exterior sheathing and weather-resistant barrier must be in place to protect the building envelope before the transom panel opening is finished.
Interior trim and casing around the transom panel cannot be installed until the panel itself is securely in place.
Final sealing and caulking around the transom panel perimeter must occur after the panel is fully installed to ensure weathertightness.
While painting can be done after installation, some painters prefer to paint the frame before installing the transom panel for cleaner lines; however, touch-up painting always follows installation.
The door frame must be installed and properly secured before glazing can be added, as the glass panels are fitted into the frame.
The wall structure and rough opening for the door must be completed to provide the structural support and defined aperture into which the glazed door unit will be installed.
After the glass is set into the door, weatherstripping, sealants, and gaskets must be applied around the glazing to ensure water and air tightness.

Door hardware such as handles, hinges, and locks are typically installed after the glazing is complete to avoid damaging the glass during hardware fitting and to ensure proper alignment of hardware on the finished door assembly.

Interior trim, moldings, and aesthetic finishes around the door are preferably done after glazing to avoid damaging the glass during trim installation, though in some sequences finish work may precede glazing if the glass is protected.
The door stop must be installed onto or within the door frame, so the frame must be in place first.
If the door stop is surface-mounted to the wall or jamb, the wall/drywall must be finished before the stop can be attached.
The door stop creates the physical stop that limits the door's swing; the door must be hung after the stop is in place so it can close against the stop properly.
It is preferable to adjust the latch, strike plate, and hinges after the door stop is installed so everything aligns correctly, but this could be done beforehand with re-adjustment later.
If the door stop is floor-mounted (e.g., a rubber floor stop), the finished flooring should be in place. However, it is a soft preference as a stop could be installed on subfloor and later adjusted.
The door closer must be mounted on the door frame and door leaf, so the door frame must be installed first.
The door must be hung and operable before the door closer can be attached to regulate its motion.
After installing the door closer, the closing speed, latch action, and backcheck must be adjusted to ensure proper function.
The door closer must be installed before the final inspection can verify full door hardware operation, though inspection could technically be done in stages.

predecessor: Install door frame and rough opening preparation
rationale: The door frame and rough opening must be fully prepared and structurally ready before the automatic door operator can be mounted, as the operator is attached to the frame or header.

predecessor: Run electrical conduit and wiring to door location
rationale: Electrical power supply must be roughed in to the door location so the automatic door operator can be connected to power upon installation.

successor: Connect electrical supply and test door operator
rationale: The operator must be physically mounted before electrical connections can be made and functional testing can be performed.

successor: Install door sensors and safety devices
rationale: Safety sensors (motion sensors, presence sensors) are typically integrated with the operator after it is installed, as they connect to the operator's control board.

successor: Final commissioning and adjustment of door operation
rationale: Full commissioning including speed adjustment, force settings, and safety checks must occur after the operator and all associated components are installed.
The door frame must be installed and properly aligned to provide the structure into which the lockset is mounted.
The door must be hung on its hinges before the lockset can be fitted, as the lockset interacts with both the door edge and the frame strike plate.

successor: Door Painting/Finishing (after lockset removal or masking)
rationale: Typically painting is done before hardware installation to avoid getting paint on the lockset; if painting after, lockset must be removed or masked first.
The lockset must be fully installed to test door operation, latch engagement, and key/knob functionality.
