The lockset must be installed and functioning before the completed door assembly can be inspected and turned over to the building owner or tenant.

Door hinges must be attached to a structurally sound door frame that is already in place and properly aligned; the frame provides the structural support and precise positioning required for hinge placement.
Hinges must be installed on both the door frame and the door panel before the door can be hung; the hinges are the mechanical connection that allows the door to swing open and closed.

Door hardware such as locks and handles are typically mounted after the hinges are in place, as the door must be properly positioned and operable on its hinges for accurate alignment and functioning of the hardware.
The wall structure, including framing and sheathing, must be completed to provide the rough opening and structural support into which the door frame (and subsequently hinges) are installed.

After hinges are installed and the door is hung, alignment and adjustment of the door's swing, gaps, and fit must be performed to ensure proper operation; this step is dependent on the hinges being in place.
Kickplates are attached to the bottom of base cabinets; the cabinets must be installed first to provide the mounting surface and location for the kickplate.

Kickplates define the finished toe-kick zone; flooring is often installed up to the kickplate or the kickplate is installed after flooring to cover the expansion gap and provide a finished look, but typically the kickplate goes on after cabinets but may need to be coordinated with flooring order.
Door frame anchors are installed into the rough framing (studs and headers) of the wall opening; the rough framing must be complete to provide a structure to which the anchors are attached.
Door frame anchors secure the door frame to the rough opening; the anchors must be in place before the door frame can be properly mounted and fastened.
Once anchors are installed, the door frame can be positioned, shimmed, and leveled within the opening before final fastening.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and space for the door to be installed.
Wall sheathing provides structural backing and weather barrier around the door opening before installation.
The door must be hung and in place before the surrounding trim and casing can be installed around it.

It is typical to install the door before final painting and finishing the surrounding wall area, though painting can be done before installation in some cases with careful masking, making it a soft preference.
The door slab must be hung on the frame before hardware such as locks, latches, and handles can be installed.
If the door hardware includes electric strikes, magnetic locks, or access control wiring, the rough electrical must be completed first to provide power and connectivity.
Hardware must be installed before final inspection can verify that doors operate correctly, locks function, and access control systems are operational.
The door must be physically installed in its frame before weatherproofing materials (weatherstripping, seals, and gaskets) can be applied around its perimeter.

predecessor: Door Frame Preparation / Rough Opening Inspection
rationale: The door frame must be properly aligned, squared, and structurally sound before weatherproofing can be applied; any defects would compromise the seal.
Weatherproofing creates a barrier against moisture and drafts; interior trim and casing should be installed after weatherproofing to ensure a proper seal and prevent water damage behind finishes.

successor: Final Door Adjustment and Hardware Installation
rationale: While some hardware can be installed beforehand, final adjustments to hinges, locks, and handles are best done after weatherproofing to ensure the door closes properly against the new seals without binding.
Blower door or air leakage tests should be performed after weatherproofing is complete to accurately measure the effectiveness of the air seal around the door.
The door frame must be installed to provide the structural support and mounting surface for the door before commissioning can begin.
All door hardware (hinges, locks, closers, handles) must be procured and available on-site before commissioning can occur.
The rough opening must be properly framed, squared, and prepared with necessary shims and blocking before door installation and commissioning.
Door commissioning must be completed to verify proper function, fit, hardware operation, and code compliance before the final inspection and sign-off can occur.
While some finishing work may occur before, final paint touch-ups around the door are often done after commissioning to avoid damaging the finish during adjustment and testing.
The structural steel frame must be erected before the curtain wall frame can be installed, as the curtain wall attaches to and is supported by the building's structural frame.
Floor slabs must be in place to provide anchoring points and structural support for the curtain wall frame at each floor level.
The curtain wall frame must be fully erected before glass panels or glazing units can be installed, as the frame serves as the supporting structure for the glass.
Weather seals and gaskets must be applied after the frame is in place to ensure the curtain wall system is watertight and airtight.
Spandrel panels (opaque panels between vision glass) are installed after the curtain wall frame is complete, as they fit within the frame system.
The structural frame (slabs, columns, or perimeter beams) must be in place to provide the supporting structure for curtain wall glazing panels to be mounted onto.
Building envelope weatherproofing at the structural edges must be installed before glazing panels to prevent moisture intrusion behind the curtain wall system.
Once glazing panels are placed, perimeter seals, gaskets, and weatherstripping must be applied to ensure watertightness and air-tightness of the completed assembly.

successor: Interior Finishing Adjacent to Curtain Wall
rationale: Interior work such as drywall, painting, and ceiling installation near the curtain wall is typically done after glazing to avoid damaging finishes and allow proper alignment with the glazed assembly.
Permanent window cleaning anchors or rigging systems are generally installed after glazing panels are in place so that they can be properly aligned and safely tested on the completed façade surface.
The structural steel frame must be erected to provide the load-bearing support and attachment points for the curtain wall spandrel panels.
Floor slabs must be completed to define the floor-to-floor heights and provide the horizontal structural support and fire-stopping boundaries for spandrel panel installation.
The vertical mullions and horizontal transoms (the curtain wall framing system) must be in place to receive and secure the spandrel panels.
Spandrel panels (opaque panels between vision glass) are typically installed before the vision glass or operable windows to complete the building envelope from the structural infill areas outward.

Interior finishes adjacent to spandrel areas (backer rods, insulation, drywall) are typically completed after spandrel panels are in place to allow proper sealing and thermal continuity, though this is a logical sequence preference rather than a physical impossibility.
The curtain wall frame must be fully erected and structurally secured before any gaskets or glazing beads can be installed, as the gaskets and beads are seated into the frame's channels and recesses.
Glass panels must be placed into the curtain wall frame before the gaskets and glazing beads can be installed to secure and weather-seal the panels in place.
After gaskets and glazing beads are installed to hold the glass, sealant must be applied over and around them to complete the weatherproofing and prevent water infiltration.

successor: Curtain Wall Pressure Plate & Caps Installation
rationale: Pressure plates and caps are installed over the gaskets and glazing beads to provide final compression and a finished aesthetic appearance, so they must follow the gasket/bead installation.
Inspection for water-tightness and air infiltration testing can only be performed after gaskets and glazing beads are fully installed to ensure the entire assembly is sealed and ready for testing.
The structural frame must be in place to provide the load-bearing support and anchorage points for the curtain wall system, including its thermal break components.
Floor slabs must be completed to provide horizontal support and attachment points for the curtain wall mullions and thermal break assemblies at each floor level.

The thermal break (typically an insulated aluminum frame assembly with polyamide or other thermal isolation material) must be installed first before glass panels or infill panels can be placed into the frame.

The thermal break assembly forms part of the continuous insulation and air barrier; sealants and gaskets are applied after the thermal break is in place to ensure thermal continuity and weathertightness.

successor: Interior Finishing Adjacent to Curtain Wall
rationale: While not physically required, it is best practice to complete the thermal break and curtain wall frame before interior finishes such as drywall, insulation, and perimeter trim to avoid rework and ensure proper thermal performance at the perimeter edge.
The structural steel frame provides the primary support structure onto which curtain wall anchors and brackets are mounted. Without the completed steel frame, there is no substrate for the anchors.
Perimeter concrete slabs must be cured and in place to provide bearing surfaces and proper alignment reference points for curtain wall anchor installation at each floor level.
The anchors and brackets serve as the attachment points for the curtain wall framing system; mullions and transoms cannot be installed until their supporting brackets are in place and aligned.

Perimeter insulation and weather barriers must be detailed around and integrated with the anchor brackets. However, the brackets themselves must be installed first to define the plane and allow proper sealing transitions.
Glass panels and glazing units are mounted onto the curtain wall frame, which itself depends on anchors and brackets. The anchors must be secured before any frame or glass can be installed.
The structural steel frame must be complete to provide the load-bearing support and attachment points for the curtain wall system.
Floor slabs must be in place to provide working platforms and to define the vertical levels for curtain wall alignment and anchoring.
The curtain wall framing system (mullions and transoms) must be erected before glass or infill panels can be installed into the frame.

Interior partitions are often started after the curtain wall is sealed to avoid weather exposure and to allow for proper interface detailing, but this can be sequenced differently with adequate protection.
The structural steel frame provides the load-bearing support onto which the curtain wall system is anchored. The curtain wall cannot be installed without a completed structural frame to attach to.

Floor slabs provide lateral support and working platforms. Curtain wall installation typically proceeds floor-by-floor, requiring each floor slab to be cured and in place for safe access and to establish floor-to-floor dimensions.

Perimeter waterproofing at the slab edges and spandrel areas must be in place to prevent moisture intrusion after the curtain wall is installed. If not completed beforehand, water damage could occur behind the finished curtain wall.

Interior finishes near the curtain wall, such as drywall, insulation, and trim, should only commence after the curtain wall is installed and sealed to prevent weather damage to interior materials and to allow proper alignment between the wall system and interior partitions.

successor: Curtain Wall Glazing Air & Water Seal Testing
rationale: Air and water infiltration testing must occur after installation is complete to verify the performance of the installed curtain wall system before proceeding with adjacent finishing work.
The curtain wall framing and glazing panels must be installed first to provide the substrate onto which sealants and weatherproofing membranes are applied.
The main building structural frame must be complete to support the curtain wall system before sealing and weatherproofing can begin.
Perimeter firestopping at floor slabs must be installed prior to final weatherproofing seals to maintain fire-rated separations and ensure continuity of the building envelope.
Weatherproofing must be complete to prevent water intrusion that could damage interior finishes before they are installed.

successor: Building Air Barrier & Insulation Continuity Check
rationale: The sealing and weatherproofing forms part of the building envelope's air and moisture barrier; its completion allows for continuity testing and final verification of the thermal envelope.
The curtain wall system must be fully installed, including framing, glazing, and seals, before air leakage testing can be performed, as the test validates the integrity of the completed assembly.
All sealants and gaskets must be fully cured and in place to create a continuous air barrier; testing before sealant application would not reflect the final as-built condition.

If air leakage test results exceed acceptable thresholds, remediation such as re-sealing or gasket replacement may be required. This is a conditional (soft) follow-up triggered by test results, not a mandatory sequence for every project.
Air leakage testing must be completed and passed before enclosing the curtain wall from the interior side with drywall, ceilings, or other finishes, to allow access for repairs if leaks are detected.
The air leakage test is a key component of building envelope commissioning; the envelope cannot be signed off until testing confirms compliance with specified performance standards.

Stair flights must rest on and be supported by a structural floor slab or ground slab at their base. The floor slab provides the structural bearing surface for the stair flight's bottom landing or bottom step.

Stair flights are often supported by or anchored to adjacent structural walls (core walls, shear walls). These walls must be in place to provide lateral support and connection points for the stair flight.
Handrails are installed onto the completed stair flight structure. The stair flight must be fully constructed and set to provide the substrate for handrail brackets, posts, and fixings.

Final finishes such as tiling, carpeting, or painting on the stair treads and risers must occur after the structural stair flight is cast/assembled and cured. Finishing work proceeds on the completed substrate.

While some MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing) work can be done before stairs, lighting conduits, sprinkler lines, and electrical outlets serving the stairwell are typically roughed-in after the stair flight structure is in place to coordinate actual spatial routing.
The stair landing must be supported on a solid foundation or structural slab; foundation work must be completed before any vertical structural elements including stair components are installed.
The stair landing is typically cast or installed as part of or upon the floor slab or structural framing at the landing level, so the slab/framing must be in place first.
Stair flights (treads and risers) span between landings; the landing must be in place to provide the structural support and anchorage for the stair flight.
Handrails and guardrails at the landing area are anchored to the landing slab or structure; the landing must be complete to provide attachment points and proper alignment.

successor: Finishing Works (tiling, flooring, painting at landing)
rationale: Finishing work such as tiling or painting on the landing surface and walls typically follows structural completion; however, this is a soft preference because finishes can sometimes be applied concurrently if the landing is stable and clean.
Stair stringers provide the structural support and framework for the stair treads. Treads cannot be installed without the stringers in place to bear their weight.
Stair risers form the vertical back of each step, providing support and proper geometry for treads. Treads must be seated on risers.
The subfloor and underlying structure at the stair landing must be complete and level to provide a stable base for the bottom tread and overall stair assembly.
Handrails and guardrails are typically anchored to the treads or stringers after treads are in place. Installing rails first would block access for tread placement.

While it is physically possible to install carpet on treads later, it is standard sequencing to install finish flooring or carpet over treads after they are securely fastened to avoid damaging the tread surface during subsequent work.
Stair risers are vertical components that attach to the stair stringers; the stringers must be installed first to provide the structural framework and support for the risers.

predecessor: Stair Tread Installation (for closed riser stairs)
rationale: On closed-riser stairs, the tread is typically installed before the riser above it, as the riser sits on top of or behind the tread below; this ensures proper overlapping and structural continuity.

successor: Finish Flooring / Carpet Installation on Stairs
rationale: Finish floor coverings (carpet, tile, hardwood) are applied over the completed stair riser surfaces; the riser must be fully installed and secured before any finish material can be laid.

Handrails and balusters are often anchored to or aligned with the stair structure including risers; the risers must be in place to provide attachment points and to establish the final stair profile for railing layout.

Final painting, staining, or sealing of the stair riser must occur after the riser is installed; any adjacent finishing work (e.g., wall painting near stairs) also depends on the riser being in place to achieve clean transitions.
Stair stringers must be anchored to the floor structure; rough framing and floor sheathing provide the structural support required at the top and bottom of the stair run.
The stringers must be measured, marked, and cut to the correct rise/run geometry before they can be physically installed in the stairwell.
Treads and risers are fastened directly to the stringers; stringers must be in place to provide the supporting framework for the steps.

Handrails and guardrails are typically attached to the stringers or to brackets connected to the stringers; the stringers must be secured first to establish the stair geometry and structural anchorage.
Structural inspection of the stair assembly, including stringer attachment, must be completed before closing in finishes (drywall, trim) to verify code compliance and safety.
Stair nosing is typically installed onto finished concrete stairs; the concrete must be poured and fully cured to provide a solid, stable substrate for the nosing.

successor: Floor Covering / Tile Installation on Stairs
rationale: Stair nosing is often integrated with or installed before the adjacent floor finish (e.g., tiles, vinyl, carpet) so that the nosing acts as a finished edge and the flooring can be laid up to or over it.

Handrails and balustrades are typically installed after stair nosing is in place so that the nosing provides a definitive edge and finished surface for alignment and safety; however, this is a soft preference as they can be done concurrently with careful coordination.
The structural stair frame (stringers and rough treads) must be built before any finishes such as stair nosing can be applied.
Stair nosing should be completed before final inspections to ensure safety compliance and aesthetic finish, but this is a scheduling preference rather than a physical necessity.
Handrails are attached to the structural frame (e.g., stair stringers, balconies, or wall structures). The structural frame must be complete and stable to provide a secure mounting surface.
Handrails are installed along staircases or balcony edges. The concrete or structural slab must be poured and sufficiently cured to bear loads and anchors before handrail posts can be set.

predecessor: Rough-In of MEP Services (in adjacent walls/floors)
rationale: Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins behind walls or beneath floors near handrail attachment points must be completed before handrails are installed, to avoid interference or the need to remove handrails for access.

It is generally easier to tape, mud, and paint walls before handrails are mounted to avoid masking and obstruction; however, if handrails are installed first, temporary protection can be used, so this is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.

Floor finishes are typically installed after handrails to avoid damaging finished floors during handrail installation and to achieve a clean transition; however, handrails can be retrofitted over finished floors, making this a soft preference.
Guardrails and balustrades require a stable structural frame, floor slab, or supporting substrate to be in place so they can be anchored and secured properly.
Waterproofing membranes often need to be applied up to and integrated with balustrade base flashings, which requires the balustrade to be installed first.
While often installed after cladding for alignment, final aesthetic integration and sealing between cladding and balustrade typically occur after the balustrade is fixed.

successor: Final Coating / Paint Finish (on balustrade elements)
rationale: If the balustrade is to have a field-applied paint or protective coating, it must be installed first so that the coating can be applied to the in-place assembly.
Guardrails and balustrades serve as permanent safety barriers; they must be installed before work platforms and scaffolding at that location are dismantled to ensure fall protection.
Newel posts are structural components anchored to stair stringers or floor framing; the staircase structure must be framed and in place to provide a mounting surface for the newel post.
Newel posts typically bolt through the subfloor or are embedded into the floor structure; a solid subfloor must be installed to secure the newel post base.
Handrails attach directly to newel posts at landings and turns; the newel post must be fixed in place to serve as a secure anchor point for the handrail.

Balusters (spindles) are typically fitted between the stair tread/stringer and the handrail or are sometimes housed into the newel post; the newel post establishes the boundary and support points for the baluster run.

While the newel post itself can be pre-finished, final painting or staining of the assembled staircase system is often done after all components including newel posts are installed to ensure a uniform appearance; this is a soft preference for quality and aesthetics, not a physical necessity.
Balusters require a structural base (slab, stair tread, or masonry support) to anchor into; the supporting structure must be in place before balusters can be installed.

predecessor: Layout and Marking of Baluster Positions
rationale: Accurate layout lines and marked positions are needed to position each baluster correctly; this must be done before balusters are set.
Handrails are typically mounted onto or between balusters, so balusters must be securely in place to support the handrail.
Decorative caps or finials are placed on top of the balusters after the balusters themselves are fixed in position.
Balusters must be prefabricated, cut to proper length, and have any necessary holes or tenons prepared before they can be installed on site.
The spiral stair must be supported on a structurally sound base; the ground floor slab and foundation must be poured and cured before stair installation can begin.
The spiral stair typically connects multiple floors; the structural framing and floor openings must be in place to provide support and the correct opening dimensions for the stair.
The spiral stair structure must be erected first so that railings and balustrades can be attached to the stair stringers and treads for safety and code compliance.

It is easier to paint and finish walls before the stair is in place for better access, but the stair can be installed first and finishing done carefully around it; thus this is a soft preference for efficiency.

successor: Floor Covering (e.g., Carpet/Tile) on Adjacent Floors
rationale: Final floor coverings around the stair opening are best completed after the stair is installed to ensure a clean transition and fit, but in some sequences the flooring can be laid first; hence a soft preference.
The stair structure must be supported by a stable foundation or substructure that has already been completed to bear the load.

predecessor: Slab on Grade / Ground Floor Slab
rationale: The ground floor slab or landing area must be in place to provide a base and reference elevation for stair installation.
Load-bearing walls or columns framing the stairwell must be erected to define the stair opening and provide lateral support and attachment points.
MEP rough-in work such as conduit, piping, and junction boxes in the stairwell area must occur after the stair structure is in place to avoid rework and to coordinate routing around the stair.
Finish work such as painting, railing installation, and stair tread/riser finishes must follow structural stair completion to protect finished surfaces and ensure proper alignment.
Metal pan stairs require a supporting structural steel frame to be in place before they can be installed, as the pans attach directly to the steel stringers and supports.

predecessor: Concrete Slab / Deck Pouring (at stair openings)
rationale: Stair openings in floor slabs must be formed and poured so that the metal pan stairs can be positioned and anchored at each floor landing.

successor: Concrete Fill / Topping for Metal Pans
rationale: Metal pans are designed to receive a concrete fill or topping; the concrete cannot be placed until the metal pans are fully installed, shored, and aligned.
Handrails and guardrails are typically anchored to the metal pan stair structure or the concrete fill; they cannot be installed until the stair pans are in place and the concrete topping has cured.

Finish treads (e.g., terrazzo, tile, or applied abrasive strips) must be applied after the metal pans are installed and the concrete topping has been poured and cured, to avoid damaging the finish during stair installation.
Stairs must be supported by a structurally complete floor or concrete slab to bear load and provide a stable base.
The rough framing defines the vertical and lateral openings where stairs will be placed; stairs are typically installed after walls and structural supports are in place.
Drywall work around the stairwell must follow stair installation to achieve proper fit and finishing around the stringers and landings.
Handrails, balusters, and trim are installed after the stair structure is in place to ensure proper alignment and attachment.

successor: Flooring (finished floor on stairs and adjacent areas)
rationale: Finished flooring materials (e.g., hardwood, tile, carpet) are applied onto the stair structure after the rough stairs are installed.
The structural frame and core (including floor slabs and support beams) must be in place to provide the load-bearing structure onto which fire escape stairs are anchored and supported.

Fire escape stairs are often enclosed within rated shafts or walls; however, the stair itself is typically installed before the full enclosure to allow access for installation and welding. The enclosure walls come after.

The structural steel or metal components of the fire escape stair must be fireproofed (e.g., with spray-applied fire-resistive materials or intumescent coatings) after the stair framework is erected but before final finishes.
The base landing or bottom support of the fire escape stair requires a completed foundation or slab-on-grade to bear the load and provide a stable starting point for stair erection.
Handrails and guardrails are attached to the stair structure after the main stair stringers and treads are in place, as they are secondary safety components that depend on the stair geometry.
Handrails and guardrails require a structural substrate (stairs, landings, balconies, or raised floor edges) to anchor to. Framing must be complete to provide attachment points.
Guardrails on concrete decks or balconies need the concrete to be fully cured to embed anchors or brackets securely.
Steel guardrails often attach to steel beams/columns, which must be erected and stabilized before rail installation.
While not physically blocking drywall, installing rails first allows precise fit and avoids damaging finished finishes; it is a soft preference for quality and workflow.
Guardrails are a critical life-safety system; building occupancy permits and final inspections require rails to be installed and tested before the space is deemed safe for use.

The stair structure (e.g., concrete, wood framing, or metal stringers) must be fully installed and prepared before any finish is applied, as the finish cannot be adhered to an incomplete or unstable substrate.

Rough carpentry work such as installing stair stringers, risers, and treads structurally must be complete; finish materials (e.g., carpet, hardwood treads, or tile) require a stable, fully framed stair structure.
If the finish requires an underlayment (e.g., for tile, vinyl, or carpet), it must be installed first to provide a suitable base for the finish layer.
Handrails and guardrails are typically installed after stair finishes to avoid damaging the finish during rail installation and to allow precise alignment with the finished surface height.

While touch-up painting is often done after finishing stairs to correct any scuffs, this is a soft preference as the finishing sequence can vary; however, it is generally preferable to protect the finish by painting last.
A stable foundation is required to support the straight ramp structure.
Construction materials must be available on-site before ramp construction can begin.
The ground surface must be properly graded to the correct slope and elevation before the ramp can be built.
The ramp structure must be completed before applying any surface treatments or finishes.
Safety railings can only be installed after the ramp structure is in place to anchor them.

Fire caulking seals gaps around penetrations in fire-rated assemblies; the concrete slab must be in place and cured to provide a solid substrate for caulking around pipes, conduits, and other penetrations.
Fire caulking is applied at joints and penetrations through walls; walls must be erected to define the boundaries needing fire-stopping seals.
All pipes, conduits, ducts, and cables that penetrate stairwell fire-rated assemblies must be installed before fire caulk can be applied around them to maintain the fire-resistance rating.
Fire caulking must be completed before inspection and testing can verify that all penetrations are properly sealed and the assembly meets code-required fire-resistance ratings.
Fire caulking seals need to be fully installed, cured, and inspected before finishes are applied, as finishing over unsealed joints would conceal deficiencies and violate fire-code requirements.
A curved ramp requires a stable foundation to support its structure and distribute load, so foundation work must be completed before ramp construction can begin.

predecessor: Rebar Placement and Formwork for Ramp
rationale: Reinforcement steel and formwork must be installed prior to placing concrete for the curved ramp structure.
The ramp structure must be fully cured and in place before any surface finishing (e.g., topping, waterproofing, or coating) can be applied.
Safety railings can only be installed after the ramp structure is complete to ensure proper anchoring and alignment.
While it is typical to connect adjacent pavements after the ramp is built for smooth transitions, it is a logical preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to provide a stable foundation before the switchback ramp structure can be built.
The subgrade must be properly compacted to support the ramp without settling or shifting.
The structural ramp must be completed before the wearing surface (pavement or concrete) can be applied on top.
Guardrails and barriers are installed along the completed ramp edges for safety and cannot be placed until the ramp structure exists.
Drainage elements such as culverts or ditches along the ramp are typically installed after the ramp is formed, though some drainage may be pre-installed depending on design.
The helical ramp requires a stable structural foundation to support its load before construction can begin.
The helical ramp typically wraps around or connects to a central core or main structural frame, which must be erected first to provide anchorage and support points.
The ramp structure must be fully installed before any surface finishing, coating, or paving work can be applied to the ramp.
Safety railings along the helical ramp can only be installed after the ramp structure itself is in place to provide the mounting surface.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within or along the ramp area must follow the structural completion of the ramp to allow proper routing and embedment.
The ramp requires a stable load-bearing substructure (footings and foundations) to be in place before any ramp superstructure can be built.
The ramp typically bears on or ties into the ground slab; the slab must be cast and cured to provide a level working surface and structural support.
The ramp structure must be erected and stabilized before any final surface topping, screeding, or wear surface can be applied.

For safety, handrails are typically installed after the ramp structure is complete, though in some cases temporary rail sections may be added earlier for worker safety; not a hard physical constraint.
The ramp must be completely built to establish correct elevations and alignments before connecting adjacent stairs, landings, or walkways to ensure proper fit and continuity.
The ramp landing requires a stable and level base, which is provided by the completed foundation.
Ramp landing is typically cast as part of or on top of the slab on grade, requiring the slab to be placed first.
The ramp itself connects to the landing, so the landing must be in place to support and anchor the ramp structure.
Handrails for the ramp are typically anchored to or adjacent to the landing, requiring the landing to be completed first.
While waterproofing can be done at any time, it is preferable to seal the landing before heavy construction traffic to prevent damage.
The ramp handrail must be anchored to or installed on top of the finished ramp slab/base structure; the base must be hardened and in place before railing installation can begin.

Handrails are typically installed before final surface coatings or anti-slip treatments to avoid damaging the finished surface and to allow seamless integration of the railing bases with the final finish.
The handrail must be fully installed before it can be inspected and load-tested to verify compliance with safety codes.
While not physically required, it is good practice to complete handrail installation prior to final cleanup to avoid re-cleaning around the newly installed railings.

The ramp edge guard or curb is typically formed and placed after the main concrete curb and gutter are installed, as it abuts or sits atop the curb edge to provide a smooth transition and protect the ramp edge.

predecessor: Ramp Slab Placement / Concrete Ramp Pour
rationale: The ramp slab must be placed first to establish the ramp surface; the edge guard / curb is then installed along the ramp edge for containment and protection.
The edge guard defines the ramp boundary; adjacent sidewalk or walkway finishing can proceed up to and abutting the installed edge guard for a flush transition.

Handrails are often installed after the edge guard is in place so that the rail base or posts can be properly aligned with the curb edge, though this ordering is a preference for alignment accuracy rather than a strict necessity.
The subgrade and base course must be compacted and graded before any concrete curb or edge element is placed to ensure proper support and drainage.
The ramp slope transition must be built on a stable and level base, which requires the foundation or slab to be completed first to provide structural support.
The substrate or base layer of the ramp must be prepared and compacted before the slope transition element can be installed, ensuring proper drainage and stability.
The ramp slope transition structure must be in place before the final surface topping or wearing layer can be applied, as the topping is cast or placed over the transition.

While guardrails are typically installed after the ramp structure is complete for safety, this is a soft preference as handrails could potentially be installed concurrently in some staging approaches.
The ramp slope transition must be fully constructed before accessibility inspections can verify compliance with slope and transition requirements per building codes.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the required profile before trench excavation can begin, as the trench is cut into the graded earth.
The subbase layer provides the foundation and proper elevation for the drainage trench installation.
The trench must be excavated and prepared before drainage pipes can be placed and bedded inside the trench.
The drainage trench and its piping must be completed and backfilled before paving over the area to avoid rework and ensure proper drainage function.
After trench excavation and pipe installation, the trench must be backfilled and compacted to restore the ground surface for subsequent work.
The ramp structural concrete must be poured and sufficiently cured before any surface finish or tread can be applied to provide a stable, solid base.
The ramp substrate must be clean, level, and repaired prior to applying the surface finish/tread to ensure proper adhesion and a uniform final surface.
After applying the surface finish or tread material, a curing or protection period is required to allow the material to set, harden, and reach design strength before being subjected to traffic.
Handrails are often installed after surface finish to avoid damaging the fresh tread; however, some coordination may allow concurrent work if protection is provided.
Surface markings such as slip-resistant strips or directional arrows must be applied after the surface finish/tread is complete and cured to ensure they adhere properly.
The ground must be properly prepared, leveled, and excavated to the correct depth before the vehicle ramp can be constructed to ensure proper foundation and structural support.
A stable concrete foundation or compacted subbase must be in place to bear the load of the vehicle ramp and prevent settling or cracking.
The ramp structure must be fully installed before the final paving or surface coating is applied to create a smooth, continuous driving surface.
Safety barriers along the ramp edges can only be installed after the ramp itself is in place to ensure correct alignment and anchoring.
While drainage can be partially installed beforehand, final connection and grading at the ramp surface is best done after the ramp structure is complete to ensure proper water runoff.
The ground surface must be properly graded and compacted before ramp construction to ensure a stable base and proper drainage.
Any underground utilities (water, gas, electrical, drainage) that would intersect with the ramp area must be relocated or installed before the ramp is built to avoid later excavation and damage.
The curb and gutter along the roadway define the transition edge where the ramp meets the street; the ramp needs to tie into an existing curb line for ADA compliance and proper water flow.
The ramp at street level must be installed first so that the adjacent sidewalk can be graded and poured to meet the ramp's landing platform at the correct elevation and slope.

The truncated dome detectable warning surface is applied directly onto the ramp surface at the curb line; the ramp concrete must be in place and cured before the warning panels can be set or embedded.
The concrete slab and foundation must be in place to provide a stable, level base for mounting and anchoring the dock leveler equipment.
The site must be graded and prepared so that the dock area is at the correct elevation relative to the truck approach, ensuring proper alignment and drainage.
Electrical power and control wiring for the dock leveler's hydraulic or electric operation must be roughed in and stubbed up before the ramp/leveler is installed.
Bumpers and seals are positioned relative to the installed leveler and ramp to ensure proper truck access and weather sealing, so they must be installed after the leveler is in place.

successor: Final Paving / Asphalt of Dock Apron
rationale: The final paving surface of the dock apron should be completed after the dock leveler is installed to achieve a smooth transition and proper height match between the apron and the leveler plate.
A stable foundation or slab must be in place to support the wheelchair ramp structure.
The ground must be graded and drainage provisions installed to ensure water flows away from the ramp area, preventing erosion and ice buildup.
Handrails are attached to the ramp structure and must be installed after the ramp frame and surface are complete.
Non-slip coatings or finishes are applied to the completed ramp surface after all structural work is finished.
The top landing of the ramp must connect to an existing walkway or doorway threshold, which is adjusted or completed after the ramp structure is set.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the correct levels before any ramp structure can be built upon it.
Foundations or substructures that support the ramp must be completed before the ramp reinforcement/structure can be erected.
The structural reinforcement and framework of the ramp must be complete before the surface pavement or topping can be applied.
Waterproofing membranes are typically applied over the finished ramp structure surface to protect it from moisture intrusion.
Safety barriers and handrails are installed on or after the ramp structure is fully erected to provide edge protection.
Expansion joints must be installed after concrete has been poured and while it is still curing, as they are placed within the concrete slab to control cracking.
The base/sub-base for the ramp must be compacted and leveled before expansion joints can be positioned, as joints are part of the finished slab system.
Formwork must be in place to define the boundaries of the concrete pour before expansion joints can be laid out and secured within the slab.
After expansion joints are placed, the concrete must cure undisturbed to achieve design strength, with joints allowing for thermal movement during curing.
Surface finishing (troweling, brooming) occurs after the concrete has been placed and the expansion joints are installed; finishing must account for joint locations.
The ramp base must be fully constructed and stable before any lighting fixtures can be installed on or along the ramp structure.
Lighting fixtures and wiring must be installed before final surface finishing (e.g., coating, sealing) to avoid damaging completed finishes during electrical work.
Lighting installation must be complete before the ramp can be inspected and commissioned for safe use.
The ground must be cleared, graded, and compacted before any foundation work can begin to ensure stable bearing conditions.
Excavation to the required depth and dimensions is necessary to create space for the foundation and abutment construction.
Existing underground utilities must be identified, relocated, or protected before excavation and foundation work to avoid damage and safety hazards.
Foundation and abutment must be cured and achieve sufficient strength to support the ramp structural steel.
The abutment provides the end support for the ramp deck; deck construction cannot proceed until the abutment is in place.
Backfill operations behind the abutment can only commence after the abutment structure is complete and cured.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and compacted before a ramp can be installed to ensure a stable foundation and proper load distribution.
The ramp's supporting foundation or footings must be poured and cured before the ramp structure can be anchored to it.
The ramp structure must be fully installed and secured before applying anti-slip coatings, sealants, or surface treatments to ensure an even and durable finish.
Ramps must be fully in place before handrails or guardrails can be accurately measured, cut, and attached alongside the ramp edges for safety compliance.
The completed ramp installation must be inspected for compliance with accessibility codes (e.g., ADA) before the area can be opened for use.
The ramp surface and structural base must be fully completed and cured to provide a stable anchor point for handrail posts and brackets.
Handrails are typically mounted into or onto the finished concrete or deck surface; the concrete must be cured to sufficient strength to hold fasteners securely.
The underlying ramp structure (joists, decking, or slab) must be in place to provide the substrate for handrail attachment.
Handrails must be installed before safety inspectors can verify railing height, strength, and compliance with building codes.
While finish coating can be done before or after, it is preferred to apply final sealant after handrail installation to avoid damaging fresh coating during drilling/mounting.
A stable, compacted sub-base must be completed before surface finishing can begin to ensure proper support and prevent cracking or unevenness.
Concrete or structural surface must be poured, levelled, and sufficiently cured before finishing (e.g., troweling, brooming, or applying sealant) can take place.
Surface finishing must be completed before the curing or drying period begins, as finishing operations would damage the curing surface.
Finishing must be done before control joints are cut, as the finishing process would fill or damage pre-cut joints.
It is safer and more practical to install guardrails after the ramp surface is finished and clean, though some rail posts could be set beforehand as a soft preference.
The area must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil before any grading can commence to expose the native soil/subgrade and provide a clean working surface.
Accurate survey control points, slope stakes, and grade references must be established to guide the grading equipment to the correct alignment and elevations for the ramp slope.
Sediment barriers, silt fences, and drainage controls must be in place prior to grading to prevent soil erosion and runoff from the disturbed slope area.

Installing underdrains or French drains before grading, where required, ensures the slope's subsurface drainage system is integrated correctly; however, this may sometimes be done after rough grading.
After the slope is graded to the specified lines and grades, the fill/embankment layers must be tested for density and proof-rolled to verify stability before subsequent layers or paving can proceed.
The graded and compacted subgrade of the ramp slope provides the foundation for the aggregate base course; base material cannot be placed until grading is complete and accepted.
Grading the slope establishes the finished subgrade for curbing along the ramp edges; while formwork can start after grading, minor adjustments may occur simultaneously on integrated pours.
The ramp slope must be fully graded, compacted, and accepted before any paving can be placed on the ramp surface.

The suspended ceiling system is typically hung from the structural slab or roof deck above. The structural framing and slabs must be complete to provide the anchorage points and support structure for the ceiling grid.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (Mechanical Ductwork, Electrical Conduit, Plumbing Pipes)
rationale: All overhead MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing) rough-in work must be installed before the suspended ceiling is closed in, because once the ceiling grid and tiles are in place, accessing these systems becomes extremely difficult and costly.
Sprinkler piping and heads that penetrate the ceiling must be roughed in and tested prior to ceiling installation. The ceiling layout is often coordinated with sprinkler head locations.

While the ceiling grid and tiles form the finished surface, any painting or specialized finishing of the ceiling components must be done after installation. However, this is often a soft preference as some tiles come pre-finished.

Recessed and surface-mounted lighting fixtures are integrated into the suspended ceiling grid. The ceiling must be in place to support and align the lighting fixtures, and final electrical connections are completed after ceiling installation.

successor: Interior Partition / Wall Completion (to ceiling level)
rationale: Non-structural interior partitions often terminate at the underside of the suspended ceiling. The ceiling grid must be installed first so that the top track of the partitions can be anchored to the ceiling grid or so that partitions align properly with the ceiling layout.
The ceiling grid is typically suspended from the structural roof deck or floor slab above. The structural framing and deck must be complete to provide attachment points for hanger wires.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing - ducts, conduits, pipes) Above Ceiling
rationale: All mechanical ducts, electrical conduits, plumbing pipes, and other overhead utilities must be installed and inspected before the ceiling grid is hung, as the grid will conceal and restrict access to these systems.
Ceiling tiles are laid into or clipped onto the completed T-bar grid. The grid structure must be fully installed and leveled before tiles can be placed.

successor: Overhead MEP Finish Work (e.g., sprinkler heads, light fixtures, diffusers)
rationale: Once the grid is installed, sprinkler heads, lighting fixtures, and air diffusers can be mounted into or through the grid tiles. The grid provides the supporting framework for these ceiling-mounted components.

While final painting of walls is often done before ceiling tile installation to avoid overspray, the grid itself can be installed before wall painting. This is considered a soft preference as sequencing may vary based on project workflow.
Gypsum board ceiling must be attached to a structural framing or ceiling joists system. The structural support must be complete and in place before any gypsum board can be secured.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing - ducts, conduits, pipes) Above Ceiling
rationale: All wiring, ductwork, piping, and conduits that run above the ceiling must be installed and inspected before the gypsum board is placed, as the ceiling will conceal these elements and make later access difficult or destructive.
Thermal or acoustic insulation placed above the ceiling must be installed prior to enclosing the space with gypsum board.
After gypsum boards are screwed into place, the joints between panels must be taped, mudded, and sanded to create a smooth monolithic surface.

successor: Priming and Painting / Final Ceiling Finish
rationale: The gypsum board surface must be installed and finished (taped and sanded) before any primer or paint coats can be applied.
While trim can technically be installed before the ceiling finish, it is standard practice and preferred for a clean aesthetic to install trim after the gypsum board is in place.
A suspension system or furring channels must be installed first to provide the structural support for plaster application.
All electrical wiring, conduits, HVAC ducts, and plumbing lines that run above the ceiling must be roughed in before the ceiling is plastered, as they become inaccessible afterward.
Ceiling plastering should be completed before finish flooring is installed to prevent dust and debris from the plaster work from damaging the new floor surface.
Ceiling plaster must be fully cured before applying paint or final wall finishes to avoid cracks and ensure proper adhesion.
Light fixtures, speakers, smoke detectors, and other ceiling-mounted items are installed after the ceiling surface is finished to avoid damaging the plaster during installation.

predecessor: Install Suspension System (main T-profiles and wall angles)
rationale: The stretch ceiling membrane requires a perimeter track (wall angle) and main support profiles to be installed first, as the membrane attaches directly to these framing components.

predecessor: Rough Electrical and HVAC Work Above Ceiling
rationale: All wiring, ducts, and piping that will be hidden above the stretch ceiling must be completed before the ceiling membrane is installed, as access becomes extremely limited or impossible afterward.

successor: Install Lighting Fixtures and HVAC Diffusers
rationale: Stretch ceiling installation must be completed before any fixtures or diffusers are mounted, because these elements are integrated into or penetrate the stretched membrane and require the finished ceiling surface as a reference.

It is preferred to complete stretch ceiling installation before final wall painting to avoid damaging freshly painted surfaces during the ceiling work, though it is not physically impossible to reverse the order.
Metal ceiling panels are laid into or clipped onto a supporting grid or suspension system; the grid must be in place before panels can be installed.

predecessor: Complete rough-in of MEP services above ceiling
rationale: Electrical, HVAC, plumbing, and fire-protection rough-ins (conduit, ductwork, piping) running above the ceiling must be completed and inspected before ceiling panels are installed, as access above becomes very limited after the ceiling is closed.

Ceiling-mounted fixtures are typically installed after the metal ceiling panels are in place, as they cut into or are fitted within the panels, and the panels provide the finished surface and alignment references.

successor: Complete painting/finishing of walls (if walls run up to ceiling)
rationale: While painting can be done before ceiling installation, it is often preferred to install the ceiling after wall finishing to avoid damage to the panels from paint splatter or scaffolding movement; this is a soft preference for quality and workflow efficiency.

successor: Install floor finishes and final cleanup
rationale: Floor finishes and final cleaning are typically performed after ceiling installation to prevent dust and debris from falling onto finished floors from above; however, this is a soft preference for cleanliness rather than a hard physical constraint.
The ceiling framing (joists, rafters, or furring strips) must be complete to provide the structural support onto which wood ceiling panels are attached.
Electrical wiring, junction boxes, and conduit must be installed in the ceiling cavity before being enclosed by wood panels, as accessing them afterward would require removing panels.
Ductwork and HVAC components within the ceiling plenum must be installed before being covered by ceiling panels to avoid costly rework.
Any plumbing lines running through the ceiling must be roughed in and pressure-tested before the ceiling is enclosed with wood panels.

While some wood panels come pre-finished, if field finishing (staining, sealing, or painting) is required, it is typically done after installation; however this is a preference as pre-finished panels can skip this step.
Flooring is typically installed after ceiling panels to avoid damaging finished floors with debris, tools, and ladders during overhead ceiling work.
Recessed lighting fixtures and other ceiling-mounted electrical trim are installed after ceiling panels are in place, as the panels form the finished ceiling surface.
Structural framing and deck (roof/floor slab) must be in place to provide a substrate for hanging the acoustic ceiling grid.

Mechanical ducts, electrical conduits, plumbing pipes, and fire sprinkler lines that run above the ceiling must be installed and inspected before the ceiling grid and tiles are placed, as they would be inaccessible afterward.

successor: Final MEP Trim-Out and Fixture Installation
rationale: After ceiling tiles are installed, final electrical fixtures (lighting, speakers, smoke detectors), diffusers, and sprinkler heads must be fitted flush with the ceiling surface.

Typically walls are painted before the ceiling to avoid overspray on ceiling tiles, but some trades prefer to finish ceiling first to avoid damaging fresh paint — this is a soft preference based on sequencing logic.
Flooring is often installed after ceiling to prevent dust and debris from falling on finished floors, but this is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
The structural framing or roof deck must be in place to provide the supporting substrate onto which the ceiling soffit framing and boarding are fixed.

predecessor: Overhead MEP Rough-In (Ductwork, Piping, Electrical Conduit)
rationale: Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work above the ceiling must be completed before the soffit is enclosed, as access to overhead services becomes difficult or impossible after soffit installation.
The soffit structure provides the framework upon which ceiling boards (e.g., plasterboard, drywall) are fixed and finished.
Light fittings, switches, and outlets are typically mounted onto or within the finished soffit; the soffit must be in place to receive these components.

Painting and final decorative finishes are applied after the soffit and ceiling boarding are complete; however, this is a soft preference as some finishes could theoretically be applied in sections with careful sequencing.
Structural framing must be installed to provide the supporting framework from which the coffered ceiling grid is suspended.
MEP rough-in work must be completed above the ceiling before the coffered ceiling is installed, as access to the plenum space would be severely restricted or impossible afterward.
The coffered ceiling panels and trim must be fully installed before final painting, staining, or decorative finishes can be applied to the ceiling surface.
Coffered ceiling installation must precede installation of recessed or surface-mounted lighting fixtures that integrate with or mount to the coffered grid.

Coffered ceiling work is typically completed before final flooring to avoid damage to finished floors from scaffolding, tools, and debris associated with overhead work, though this is a practical sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
The tray ceiling structure must be framed as part of the overall ceiling framing before any tray ceiling components can be installed.
Electrical wiring for lighting fixtures and junction boxes within the tray ceiling must be roughed in before the ceiling finish materials are installed.
Ductwork and HVAC components that pass through the ceiling area must be installed before the tray ceiling is enclosed.
The tray ceiling structure and backing must be in place before drywall can be applied to the ceiling surface.
The tray ceiling must be fully installed and drywalled before any paint, texture, or decorative finishes can be applied.
Cove/cornice moulding is installed onto finished walls; wall framing must be complete to provide a mounting surface.
Moulding is applied onto finished plastered walls and ceiling junctions; plastering must be done before moulding can be fixed.
Cornice moulding bridges the wall-ceiling joint; ceiling must be installed and finished before cornice can be applied.
Cove/cornice moulding is typically painted or finished as part of the final decorative coat; painting must occur after moulding is installed and set.

While floor finishing is often done after moulding to avoid debris damaging the moulding, it is not a strict physical dependency; however, sequencing moulding before final flooring prevents dust and damage to the finished floor.
The vaulted ceiling must be supported by load-bearing walls or columns which rest on the foundation. Without completed walls, there is no structural support for the vault.

predecessor: Structural Framing (Ribbed Arches or Formwork Support)
rationale: Vaulted ceilings require either permanent ribbed arches or temporary formwork/falsework to shape and support the masonry or concrete during construction. This structural framework must be in place before the vault can be constructed.
The vaulted ceiling forms the structural top of the building enclosure; roof covering (tiles, shingles, membrane) must be applied after the vault is complete to protect it from weather.
Interior finishes such as plaster, paint, or decorative elements are applied only after the vault's structural shell is fully constructed and cured.

While it is physically possible to install wiring or ductwork after the vault is built, it is far more efficient and less disruptive to do so after the vault is complete to avoid interference with formwork and to allow proper routing along the curved surface.
The ceiling grid provides the structural support framework into which the access panel is mounted. Without the grid installed, there is no attachment point for the panel.

predecessor: Rough-in MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) services above ceiling
rationale: MEP rough-in work (ductwork, conduit, piping) must be completed in the plenum space before access panels are installed, otherwise access to complete those services would be blocked or severely restricted.

predecessor: Complete ceiling insulation and vapor barrier work
rationale: Insulation and vapor barriers in the ceiling cavity should be fully installed before placing access panels, as panels make subsequent access to those areas more difficult.
Access panels are typically installed flush with the finished ceiling surface. The panel frame must be in place before surrounding tiles or drywall can be trimmed and fitted around it.

While painting can be done around an installed panel, it is a soft preference to have the panel in place so that it can be painted or finished together with the surrounding ceiling for a uniform appearance.
Electrical wiring must be run to the fixture location in the ceiling before the fixture can be mounted and connected.
The ceiling structure (joists, furring, or grid) must be in place to provide a mounting surface for the light fixture.

predecessor: Ceiling Drywall or Ceiling Finish Installation
rationale: Finished ceiling surface (drywall, plaster, or drop ceiling tiles) must be installed before cutting openings or mounting fixtures to achieve a finished appearance and proper support.
After the fixture is physically mounted, final wiring connections, installation of bulbs, and trim/cover installation can be completed.

While it is common to paint ceilings before fixture installation for efficiency, if the ceiling is painted after the fixture is mounted, touch-up painting around the fixture may be needed to achieve a clean appearance.
Ceiling diffusers and grilles are mounted into or onto the ceiling grid; the grid must be in place to support and position the diffusers.
Ductwork must be installed and terminated at the diffuser locations before diffusers can be connected to the duct system.
Flexible or rigid duct connections must be run to the diffuser drop locations prior to mounting the diffuser/grille.
Diffusers and grilles must be installed before final ceiling finishing or painting to allow for proper sealing and a finished appearance around the edges.
Once all diffusers are installed, the HVAC system can be balanced and airflow measured at each diffuser to ensure design performance.

Rough-in electrical conduits, junction boxes, and low-voltage cabling must be installed before cable trays and conduits are placed in the ceiling plenum, as the tray supports and organizes these already-run cables.
The structural ceiling and overhead steel must be in place to provide support anchors and hangers for the cable tray and conduit systems.
While not a strict physical requirement, installing major HVAC ducts first reduces conflicts and allows cable trays to be routed around or below ductwork in the plenum, preventing spatial clashes.
Cable trays and conduits must be completely installed and approved before the suspended ceiling grid is closed in, as the ceiling tiles conceal and provide access to the plenum.
After all cable tray and conduit runs are placed, any penetrations through fire-rated assemblies must be sealed with firestop materials to maintain fire-resistance ratings.
The ceiling grid must be installed to provide the structural support and framework into which the fire/smoke damper is mounted and secured within the ceiling assembly.
The HVAC ductwork must be in place so that the fire/smoke damper can be installed at the duct penetration through the ceiling or fire-rated barrier.
The damper must be fully installed, tested, and approved before ceiling tiles are placed, as the damper needs to be accessible for inspection and the tiles would conceal the damper assembly.

Fire/smoke dampers are often integrated with the fire alarm system for automatic closure; therefore, they must be installed and connected before the fire alarm system can be fully tested for proper damper response.
Firestop sealant must be applied around the damper penetration after the damper is installed to maintain the fire-rated integrity of the ceiling assembly.
Ceiling clouds and baffles are typically suspended from the structural slab or roof deck above. Therefore, the structural framing and slab must be in place to provide the overhead attachment points.

predecessor: MEP rough-in (ductwork, piping, conduits) in ceiling plenum
rationale: Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing services that run above the ceiling must be installed and routed before the ceiling clouds/baffles are placed, because once the ceiling is installed, access to the plenum is restricted.

Ceiling clouds often incorporate or support integrated lighting fixtures; additionally, lighting is typically installed after the ceiling grid/clouds are in place so that fixtures can be properly aligned and secured.

successor: Fire alarm / sprinkler head trim-out and testing
rationale: Sprinkler heads and fire alarm devices that penetrate the ceiling must be trimmed and tested after the ceiling finish is installed to ensure correct positioning and sealing around penetrations.

successor: Final painting / touch-up of ceiling elements
rationale: While painting can be done after installation, it is a soft preference to sequence final touch-up painting after the clouds/baffles are hung to avoid damage and ensure a uniform finish.
Structural framing must be complete to provide support and attachment points for the metal linear ceiling system.
Overhead MEP rough-in work (ductwork, piping, conduit, wiring) must be installed above the ceiling before the metal linear ceiling is closed in, as access becomes difficult or impossible afterward.
Fire sprinkler piping and heads above the ceiling must be installed and tested before the ceiling is placed, since the ceiling will conceal these systems.
Recessed lighting fixtures are typically integrated into or mounted through the metal linear ceiling panels, so the ceiling grid must be in place to receive and align the fixtures.
Smoke detectors, speakers, occupancy sensors, and other ceiling-mounted devices must be installed after the ceiling is complete so they can be properly positioned and secured to the ceiling system.

predecessor: Structural Framing and Ceiling Grid Installation
rationale: The open-grid or egg-crate ceiling system is typically suspended from or attached to the structural ceiling framing. The structural support grid must be in place before the open-grid panels or egg-crate components can be installed.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing - ducts, conduits, pipes) Above Ceiling
rationale: Ductwork, conduit, piping, and other MEP services are typically routed above the suspended ceiling. These must be roughed-in before the ceiling grid is closed up, as accessing them afterward would require partial demolition of the ceiling.

predecessor: Fire Protection / Sprinkler System Installation (above ceiling)
rationale: Sprinkler piping and heads must be installed and tested before the open-grid ceiling is placed, as the ceiling system conceals these elements and access is limited afterward.
In open-grid ceilings, lighting fixtures are often integrated into or supported by the grid. The grid structure must be in place to mount and wire the lighting fixtures.

While not a strict physical requirement, it is preferable to complete the ceiling installation before applying final wall and trim finishes to avoid damage or soiling of finished surfaces during ceiling work.
The structural frame (including ceiling supports and joists) must be in place to provide a mounting surface for radiant ceiling panels.

predecessor: Overhead MEP Rough-In (Ductwork, Piping, Electrical Conduit)
rationale: Major overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before installing ceiling panels, as panels would block access to these systems.
The suspension grid or mounting system that supports the radiant panels must be installed first to provide the attachment structure.
Radiant panels must be installed before final ceiling finishes to allow integration and ensure a consistent finished appearance.

Radiant panels should be in place before system balancing and commissioning to accurately test and adjust the radiant heating/cooling performance, though it is a logical workflow preference rather than a strict physical necessity.

The structural framing (e.g., steel beams, concrete slab above) must be in place to provide a secure anchorage point for ceiling suspension hangers/wires. Without the structure above, there is nothing to attach the hangers to.

Suspension hangers/wires are the primary support for the ceiling grid system. The grid channels (main tees and cross tees) must be hung from the suspension wires, so the wires must be installed and anchored first.

While MEP rough-in (ductwork, piping, conduit) can technically be done before or concurrently with hanger installation, it is often more efficient to install hangers first to establish the ceiling plane elevation, then route MEP services around them. This is a soft preference for workflow coordination.

Major overhead MEP elements such as large ductwork, plumbing risers, and electrical conduits that occupy the plenum space above the ceiling must be installed before ceiling hangers so that hanger placement can work around these services and avoid conflicts. Additionally, if heavy MEP equipment is mounted to the structure, hangers cannot be installed until those loads are resolved.

Ceiling tiles or panels are the final finished surface that attach to the ceiling grid, which is itself supported by the suspension hangers/wires. The hangers must be in place to hold the grid, and the grid must be in place to receive the tiles.

predecessor: Installation of structural framing (studs, joists, or trusses)
rationale: Furring channels/hat channels are typically attached to structural framing (studs or joists) to create a gap for insulation or services. The structural framing must be in place to provide a mounting surface.
Furring channels provide the cavity space for insulation to be placed before the final finish surface is applied.

The furring channel/hat channel serves as a substrate or furring for attaching finish materials such as drywall, metal panels, or other cladding. The finish surface cannot be installed until the furring is in place.

predecessor: Rough-in of electrical, plumbing, and mechanical services (within wall cavities)
rationale: While not a strict physical necessity, it is preferred to complete rough-in services before furring to avoid interference and rework, since furring can obstruct access to wall cavities.

successor: Install vapor barrier / air barrier membrane
rationale: In exterior wall assemblies, the vapor or air barrier is often applied over the furring channels (or between furring and cladding) to control moisture and air infiltration. The furring provides a nailing surface and proper drainage cavity for the barrier.
The structural framing or roof deck must be in place before ceiling systems can be suspended or attached.
All ductwork, piping, conduit, and wiring that run above the ceiling must be installed before the ceiling is closed in.
Any insulation required above the ceiling plane must be placed before the ceiling material is installed.
The ceiling panels or drywall must be installed before surface finishing or painting can be applied.

successor: Final MEP Trim-Out and Fixture Installation
rationale: Ceiling-mounted light fixtures, sprinklers, diffusers, and other trim items are installed after the ceiling substrate is in place.
The ceiling grid must be supported by the structural framing above; structural work must be complete before any ceiling systems can be installed.
HVAC ducts, pipes, and conduits are typically installed in the plenum space above the ceiling grid before the grid is assembled, as the grid would block access to run these services.
Plumbing pipes and sprinkler lines running in the ceiling plenum must be installed before the ceiling grid is put in place, otherwise access would be severely restricted.

predecessor: Electrical Rough-In (Conduit and Cable Trays Above Ceiling)
rationale: Electrical conduits, cable trays, and junction boxes located above the ceiling must be roughed in prior to grid assembly to avoid having to work around or cut through the finished grid.
Sprinkler piping and heads in the ceiling plenum must be installed before the grid goes up, as the grid supports the ceiling tiles and blocks access to overhead systems.

Structural framing (e.g., ceiling joists, roof trusses) must be in place before ceiling plenum work can begin, as the plenum space is defined by the structural ceiling and the suspended ceiling system below.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing - ducts, conduits, pipes) Above Ceiling
rationale: All above-ceiling MEP rough-in work (ductwork, piping, conduit, cables) must be completed first so that the Ceiling Plenum Inspection can verify these installations are correct before enclosing them with the ceiling system.
Fire sprinkler piping and components installed in the plenum must be in place prior to inspection to ensure code compliance and proper coverage before ceiling installation.

The ceiling plenum must be inspected and all rough-in work verified/approved before the suspended ceiling grid is installed, as the grid encloses the plenum space and makes subsequent inspection difficult or impossible.
Ceiling tiles cannot be installed until the plenum inspection and rough-in is complete because the tiles are the final enclosure of the plenum space, blocking access to all above-ceiling systems.
Solid partitions (non-load-bearing walls) typically rest on the structural floor slab, which is part of the substructure. The floor/foundation must be complete to provide a stable base.
The structural frame (beams, columns, slabs) must be in place before solid partitions are built, as partitions are infill elements between the structural grid.
While not strictly required for ground-floor partitions, completing the roof/envelope before interior partitions prevents weather damage to finished wall materials.
Plaster and surface finishes cannot be applied until the partition substrate (brickwork, blockwork, or stud framing) is fully built and stable.
Electrical cables, switch boxes and outlets must be installed within or on the partition wall after the wall structure is complete but before final cladding/plaster.
Plumbing pipes within solid partitions must be run after the wall is built, as the partition itself conceals the pipework.
Door frames and window frames are installed into the openings left in the partition wall, requiring the wall structure to be complete first.
Wall tiling requires a solid substrate (the finished partition surface) to adhere to, so the partition must be complete before tiling can proceed.
Bottom track must be installed and anchored to the floor before studs can be placed, as studs slot into the bottom track.
Top track must be installed and anchored to the ceiling/overhead structure before studs can be placed, as studs slot into the top track.
Wiring and electrical boxes are installed within the stud cavity after the stud wall frame is erected.
Piping and plumbing fixtures within the wall are installed after the stud framing is complete.
Insulation is placed between studs after the frame is fully erected and before drywall is applied.
Structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide support and define the spatial boundaries for demountable partitions.
A finished floor surface is required as the base on which demountable partition tracks are fixed.

predecessor: Overhead MEP Rough-In (Ductwork, Cable Trays, Piping)
rationale: Overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in must be completed first so that demountable partitions can be aligned to ceiling grids and service zones without obstruction.
Demountable partitions form the substrate for wall-mounted MEP devices; switches, outlets, and diffusers are installed into or onto the completed partition surfaces.
Although demountable partitions often come pre-finished, any field-applied joint treatment, caulking, or touch-up painting should occur after all panels are in place for a uniform appearance.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide the load-bearing support and fixing points for glazed partition systems.
The floor slab must be finished and cured to provide a level base for the glazed partition bottom track/channel.
Ceiling grids are often installed before partitions so that partition heads can be fixed to the ceiling framework, though this can be sequenced differently depending on design.
Once glazed partitions are installed, electrical outlets and conduits integrated into or passing through the partition can be roughed in, though this may be done concurrently.
Floor finishes are typically applied after glazed partitions are erected, as partitions define room boundaries and the bottom track must be installed before final flooring goes down.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the folding partition can be installed, as the partition fits into the opening.
Folding partitions are typically hung from an overhead track or support structure that must be installed first to bear the weight of the partition system.
A bottom guide track or floor channel must be set in the floor slab/flooring before the partition panels can be positioned and aligned.
Acoustic seals, edge trims, and gaskets are installed after the partition panels are in place to ensure proper fit and sound isolation performance.
