The folding partition must be fully installed before it can be opened, closed, and adjusted for proper tracking, alignment, and operation.
The rough opening (frame, header, and jambs) must be fully prepared and structurally sound before the sliding partition can be fitted and installed.
The overhead support track and rail system must be anchored to the structure before the sliding partition panels can be hung or placed onto the track.
The bottom floor guide or channel must be set in place before the sliding partition panels can be positioned, as the panels align into both the top track and bottom guide simultaneously.
The sliding partition must be fully installed (panels hung, hardware attached) before it can be tested for smooth operation, alignment, and acoustic sealing adjustments.

The sliding partition floor guide/channel is typically installed before finish flooring, but final flooring work around the partition must occur after the partition is placed to ensure proper fit and transitions.
Acoustic partitions (walls) require a structural frame to be installed first, as the partition material is attached to or supported by the framing.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within walls must be completed before the acoustic partition is closed up, to avoid costly rework and ensure access.
Acoustic insulation (e.g., batts) is typically placed within the partition cavity after the partition framing and one side of the board are in place, but before the second side is fully closed.
Surface finishing such as joint taping, mudding, and painting must occur after the acoustic partition boards are installed to achieve the final finished appearance.
Doors and windows within an acoustic partition require the partition wall structure to be in place before they can be framed and fitted into their openings.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide the supporting framework to which fire-rated partitions are attached.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (Electrical, Plumbing, HVAC rough-in within zone)
rationale: Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the partition zone must be completed before the partition is installed, as the partition will cover and enclose these services, and access would require demolition afterwards.
Fire caulking and sealing of gaps, joints, and penetrations through the partition must follow immediately after partition installation to restore the fire-resistance rating.
The fire-rated partition boards must be installed first before any surface finishing (taping, mudding, plastering) can be applied to the faces of the partition.

successor: Final MEP Trim-Out (Electrical outlets, switches, diffusers)
rationale: Trim-out items such as electrical outlets, switches, and HVAC diffusers are installed into the finished partition after the partition boards are in place and finished.
Operable partitions require structural support from framed walls and ceiling headers to be in place before they can be mounted.
Most operable partitions are top-hung systems that require an overhead track or support beam capable of bearing the partition's weight.
Any wiring for motorized or power-operated partitions must be roughed in before the partition and its header are installed.
Operable partitions often have bottom guides or sweeps that interface with the finished floor; installing finish flooring after the partition allows proper alignment and clearance.

While it is preferable to paint after partition installation to touch up around the track, some painting can be done beforehand if carefully masked, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.

Toilet cubicle partitions are typically installed after floor finishes (tiles and waterproofing) are complete, as the partitions sit on top of the finished floor and any wet trades must be completed beforehand to avoid damage.

While some suspended ceilings are installed first, partitions can often be installed before or after; a common preference is to complete the ceiling first to avoid having to work around partitions, but this is not a strict physical necessity.

Cubicle partitions must be in place before toilets and other fixtures are installed within the cubicles, as the fixtures are physically enclosed by the partitions and would be difficult or impossible to position correctly otherwise.

successor: Door Hardware (locks, hinges, handles) installation on cubicle doors
rationale: The cubicle partitions and doors must be erected before the hardware can be fitted to the doors, as the hardware attaches directly to the partition components.

successor: Final Painting / Touch-up of walls adjacent to cubicles
rationale: It is a soft preference to complete painting before partitions to avoid masking and touch-up work, but in practice partitions are often installed and then walls are touched up around them.
Framing requires a stable, level base substrate to anchor bottom plates and provide structural support for the partition walls.

Any plumbing or electrical conduits that run beneath the slab must be installed before the slab is poured, which must be complete before framing begins; otherwise partition walls cannot be properly located or anchored.
Drywall installation requires the partition framing (studs, headers, blocking) to be fully erected and braced in order to have a surface to attach gypsum boards to.
Electrical wiring and outlet boxes are installed within the stud cavities after framing is complete, as the framing defines the wall thickness and cavity spaces.
Plumbing pipes that run inside partition walls must be installed after the stud walls are framed, as the pipes are placed within the wall cavities before being covered by sheathing.
Furring strips are typically attached to existing stud walls or masonry surfaces. The rough framing or stud walls must be fully erected to provide a substrate for the furring.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the partition must be completed before furring is installed, as furring covers these elements and access would be lost or require rework.
Furring creates the cavity depth needed to hold insulation; insulation is placed into the furred space before the final finish layer is applied.
Furring strips serve as the nailing or screwing substrate for drywall or other wall cladding; cladding cannot be attached until the furring is secured in place.
All finish work such as trim installation, painting, and wall coverings must occur after the furring and cladding are complete, as furring is a substrate layer that must be enclosed.
The partition walls must be installed first to provide the vertical structure that the head detail will interface with at the top.
The partition head detail forms the top connection between the partition wall and the overhead structure; ceiling work typically follows to enclose the head track and finish the transition.

While MEP rough-in can sometimes precede head detail installation, it is preferable to install the head detail first to establish precise partition locations and top-of-wall elevations for coordinating MEP penetrations and supports.
The base/skirting is installed on top of the finished floor slab or subfloor; the slab or foundation must be complete to provide a stable substrate.
The wall framing must be erected so that the skirting/base can be attached to the bottom of the wall assembly.
The subfloor or underlayment should be installed and leveled before skirting is placed to ensure proper fit and finish.

Typically, baseboards/skirting are installed after the finish flooring is laid so that the skirting covers the expansion gap; in some sequences skirting is installed first and flooring butts against it—this is a trade/soft preference depending on method.

Skirting/baseboards are usually painted or finished after installation, and the wall surfaces above the skirting are finished prior to or alongside skirting installation; however, final painting of the skirting itself follows its installation.
Partitions (walls) must be installed on a completed floor slab that provides a level, stable surface and structural support.
The building's structural frame (columns, beams, roof) must be in place before interior partitions are installed, as the partitions are non-load-bearing infill within the structural grid.

Overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work that runs above ceiling lines must be completed before partitions are erected, otherwise access for these horizontal runs becomes extremely difficult or impossible.
Electrical wiring, conduit, plumbing pipes, and data cables that run inside wall cavities can only be installed after the partition framing is in place, as they are placed within the stud cavities.
Door and window frames are installed within the partition wall openings; the partition framing must exist first to define the rough openings for these frames.
Fire stopping is applied to seal gaps and joints in installed partitions; the partition framing and sheathing must be in place before fire stopping can be applied.
Fire stopping seals penetrations made by MEP services through partitions; rough-in work must be completed so that all penetrations are present and can be sealed properly.
Fire stopping must be installed and inspected before finishing work covers the partition surfaces, ensuring all fire-rated seals are complete and accessible for inspection.
Fire stopping installation must be completed before the formal inspection can take place to verify compliance with fire safety codes.
Fire stopping at the top of partitions (head-of-wall joints) must be installed before ceilings are closed up, as these joints are critical for compartmentation and would be inaccessible afterward.
The acoustic sealing is applied to the completed partition frame structure; the frame must be in place to provide a substrate for the sealant and acoustic materials.
Acoustic sealing is typically applied at joints, edges, and penetrations after at least one layer of board is fixed, as the sealant fills gaps between boards and between board and frame.

Where double-layer boarding is specified, acoustic sealing between layers (e.g., acoustic sealant at perimeter and joints) must be applied before the second layer is fixed to ensure continuous airtightness.
Acoustic sealing around cutouts and penetrations must be completed before electrical fittings are installed to ensure the integrity of the acoustic barrier is not compromised.
Acoustic sealants and tapes are applied to joints and gaps before the final decorative finish; painting or wallpapering over sealed joints protects and conceals the acoustic treatment.
AHUs are heavy rooftop or mechanical room equipment that require the structural framework (steel beams, concrete slab) to be in place to support their weight.
AHUs must be installed under a completed roof or weathertight enclosure to prevent water damage to sensitive internal components (coils, filters, controls).
Power supply conduits, drain piping, and chilled/hot water piping connections must be roughed-in before the AHU is set in place so it can be connected immediately.
Supply and return ductwork must be physically mated to the AHU's plenums after the unit is set to ensure airtight connections and proper airflow.
Sensors, actuators, and controllers for the building automation system must be installed on the AHU after it is positioned, and they cannot be commissioned until the unit is in place.

predecessor: Install chilled water piping and connections
rationale: Chilled water supply and return piping must be roughed-in and terminated at the FCU location before the unit can be connected and installed.
Condensate drain piping must be in place to handle moisture removal from the FCU during operation.

predecessor: Complete ceiling grid and overhead rough-in
rationale: Overhead structural and MEP rough-ins must be completed before the FCU can be hoisted and positioned in the ceiling plenum.

successor: Connect electrical supply and controls to FCU
rationale: The FCU must be physically installed before electrical wiring, thermostat connections, and control cables can be terminated at the unit.
Supply and return ductwork must be connected after the FCU is set in place to ensure proper alignment and sealing.
All installation steps (piping, electrical, ductwork connections) must be complete before system startup, balancing, and commissioning can occur.
Ceiling tiles around the FCU access panels and grilles are installed after the unit and all connections are verified to allow for maintenance access.
VAV boxes are connected to the main supply ductwork; the ductwork must be in place to provide the physical connection point and support for the VAV box.
VAV boxes require power for actuators and controls; rough electrical wiring must be run to the VAV box location before the unit can be wired and commissioned.
While VAV boxes can be installed before the ceiling grid, it is preferable to have the ceiling grid in place as a reference for positioning diffusers and ensuring proper clearance.
The VAV box must be physically mounted before flexible duct connections can be made from the box to the diffusers or downstream ductwork.
The VAV box must be installed in its final position before the control contractor can terminate control wiring and calibrate the actuator and damper position sensors.
The boiler requires a level, reinforced concrete foundation or pad to support its weight and maintain proper alignment. Without a cured foundation, the boiler cannot be safely placed.

predecessor: Structural Steel Erection (if boiler room is part of superstructure)
rationale: The boiler room enclosure and overhead structural supports must be in place before the boiler can be craned or moved into its final position.
The boiler must be positioned and its flue outlet located before the chimney/flue system can be connected and aligned to the boiler.
Supply and return water piping must be connected to the boiler's nozzles after the boiler is set in place to ensure proper alignment and avoid stress on connections.
Fuel lines can only be run to and connected at the boiler burner after the boiler is in its final installed position to ensure safe, code-compliant connections.
The chiller unit requires a stable, level concrete foundation or ground preparation to support its weight and ensure proper operation.
Chillers are heavy mechanical components that must be set on a reinforced concrete equipment pad or structural steel frame designed for the load.
The chiller must be set in place before the chilled water supply and return pipes can be connected to its evaporator and condenser barrels.
The chiller must be physically installed so that electricians can terminate power cables at the chiller's starter panel or VFD.
For a water-cooled chiller, the condenser water piping from the cooling tower must be connected after the chiller is positioned.
Refrigerant can only be charged into the system after the chiller is installed and all piping connections are made and leak-tested.
Commissioning activities such as testing controls, checking refrigerant pressures, and verifying flow rates must follow complete installation.
The building cooling system cannot be operated until the chiller has been successfully started up, commissioned, and proven functional.
The heat pump requires a stable, level base (concrete slab or ground mount) to be installed upon. Without a completed foundation or slab, the heat pump unit cannot be properly placed or secured.

Dedicated electrical circuits, wiring, and disconnect switches must be run to the heat pump location before the unit can be connected and powered. The heat pump requires electrical supply for its compressor, fans, and controls.

The refrigerant line sets connecting the outdoor heat pump unit to the indoor air handler must be installed (or at least prepared/roughed-in) before final connection and charging of the heat pump system.
The ductwork must be attached and sealed to the heat pump's air handler after the unit is in its final position. The physical connection of ducts to the unit cannot occur until the unit is installed.

successor: Refrigerant Line Charging and System Testing
rationale: After the heat pump is physically installed and the refrigerant lines are connected, the system must be evacuated, charged with refrigerant, and leak-tested before it can be operated.
Structural framing must be in place to support ductwork hangers and provide the basic building envelope for routing ductwork.
Electrical and plumbing rough-ins that share ceiling space must be completed before ductwork to avoid conflicts and rework, as ducts are bulky and less flexible to route around other services.
Duct insulation is applied directly to the installed ductwork surface after ducts are hung and connected.
Ceiling grids are installed after ductwork is complete to enclose the ducts within the plenum space.
Ductwork must be installed to connect to HVAC equipment such as air handlers, fans, and VAV boxes for system completion.
Ductwork must be in place to ensure proper airflow distribution before thermostat/zone controller can accurately regulate temperature zones.
Power and control wiring must be run to thermostat and zone controller locations before these devices can be connected and energized.
The main HVAC equipment must be installed so the thermostat/zone controller can be wired to and communicate with the heating/cooling system.
The thermostat and zone controller must be installed and wired before the overall HVAC system can be tested and commissioned for proper operation.
Installing the thermostat after painting and finishing prevents damage to wall surfaces, though it is a soft preference for aesthetics rather than a physical necessity.

Diffusers, grilles, and registers are terminal devices that attach to the end of HVAC ductwork. The ductwork must be in place and terminated at the correct locations before the diffuser/grille/register can be installed and connected.
The ceiling, wall, or floor framing must be complete to define the openings and support structure where diffusers, grilles, and registers are mounted.
For ceiling-mounted diffusers, the ceiling grid or finished ceiling surface must be installed to provide the mounting surface and proper opening for the diffuser.
Air balancing and system commissioning require all terminal devices (diffusers, grilles, registers) to be installed and properly adjusted so airflow measurements and system tuning can be performed.
While it is common to install diffusers after painting is complete to avoid paint splatter, final touch-up painting around installed diffusers is a soft preference for aesthetic finish quality.
The expansion tank is part of the chilled water system and must be connected after the chiller plant is installed to ensure proper system integration and pressure management.
The expansion tank must be in place and secured before connecting the chilled water pipes to it, as it serves as a point of connection and pressure regulation in the piping system.
The expansion tank must be installed and connected before the overall chilled water system can be pressure-tested to verify integrity and proper operation under load.
If the expansion tank is to be supported by the building structure, structural steel should be in place first to provide a mounting point, though alternative supports may allow some flexibility.
Insulation of the expansion tank and its connecting pipes must occur after the tank is installed and all connections are made to ensure complete coverage and thermal performance.
BMS controller requires electrical power to operate; power supply must be installed and energized before the BMS controller can be powered on and commissioned.

BMS controller needs network connectivity (BACnet, Modbus, or IP cabling) to communicate with field devices and the central monitoring station; cabling must be run and terminated before controller installation.

predecessor: Mechanical HVAC Equipment Installation (AHUs, Chillers, Pumps)
rationale: BMS controller is designed to monitor and control HVAC equipment; those mechanical systems must be physically installed so the controller can be connected to sensors, actuators, and control points.

successor: BMS Field Device and Sensor Calibration
rationale: The BMS controller serves as the central processing unit that collects data from and sends commands to field devices; sensors and actuators can only be calibrated and validated once the controller is installed, powered, and communicating.

successor: BMS Software Configuration and User Interface Setup
rationale: The physical controller must be in place and operational before the control logic, schedules, alarms, and graphical user interfaces can be programmed and tested against the live hardware.
The pump requires a stable, level concrete base or foundation to sit on and be anchored to, preventing vibration and misalignment.
The pump must be connected to the hydronic piping system; rough-in piping needs to be in place to flange or thread the pump into the system.
Electrical supply conduits and wiring must be brought to the pump location to provide power for the motor.
The pump must be installed and connected before the entire hydronic system can be filled and pressure-tested for leaks.
Final electrical termination and commissioning of the pump motor can only occur after the pump is mechanically installed.
The condenser coil requires a stable, level foundation or pad to be installed upon, which must be prepared and cured before the coil can be placed.
Refrigerant piping connections must be roughed in and ready at the condenser location before the coil can be connected to the system.
The condenser coil must be in place before refrigerant lines can be physically connected to it.

successor: Brazing and Leak Testing of Refrigerant Circuit
rationale: The coil must be installed before brazing connections and performing leak tests on the completed refrigerant circuit.
The refrigerant system cannot be evacuated or charged until the condenser coil is installed and connected as part of the sealed circuit.
Cooling towers are heavy structures that require a properly constructed foundation or base slab to support their weight and ensure stability.
The cooling tower must be in place before condenser water supply and return piping can be connected to it.

successor: Cooling Tower Fan and Motor Installation
rationale: The cooling tower structure must be erected before fans, motors, and drives can be mounted on top of or within the tower.

successor: Cooling Tower Fill and Drift Eliminator Installation
rationale: The tower casing must be assembled before internal components like fill media and drift eliminators can be placed inside.
Cooling towers provide the heat rejection loop for chillers; the tower must be operational (or at least physically installed and piped) before chiller systems can be fully commissioned.
Air filters are typically installed within the HVAC ductwork system; ductwork must be in place to house and support the air filter.
Air filters must be installed before the HVAC system can be balanced and tested to ensure proper airflow and filtration performance.
Air filters must be in place to provide acceptable indoor air quality before occupants can safely occupy the building.
While not physically required, electrical rough-ins should precede filter installation to avoid contamination or damage to filters from electrical debris and dust.

successor: Final Commissioning of Air Handling Units
rationale: Commissioning requires all components including filters to be installed to verify system performance under design conditions.
Ductwork must be in place to provide the air pathway and mounting connection points for the humidifier/dehumidifier unit.
Power supply wiring and dedicated circuit must be run to the location before the unit can be connected and energized.
The humidifier/dehumidifier must be installed and connected before the overall HVAC system can be tested, balanced, and commissioned to ensure proper humidity control.
The unit must be mounted and in position before drain lines can be connected to carry away condensate.
The control device must be wired and configured after the humidifier/dehumidifier is installed to ensure proper communication and control logic.
Dampers are installed within or at connections of HVAC ductwork. Ductwork must be in place to provide the structural support and attachment points for the damper.
Fire dampers are often enclosed by fire-rated duct wrap or insulation. Wrapping over a properly installed damper ensures continuous fire protection coverage.
Dampers must be installed and in their default positions before air balancing and testing can verify system performance.
For fire/smoke dampers installed in fire-rated walls or floors, the opening (sleeve) must be framed and prepared in the barrier before the damper can be placed and secured.
After damper installation, gaps between the damper sleeve and the surrounding wall/floor opening must be sealed with firestop materials to maintain the fire rating of the barrier.
The structural frame (walls/roof) must be in place to provide an opening and mounting surface for the louver assembly.
The rough opening in the wall or roof must be cut, framed, and weatherproofed before the louver can be installed.
The louver must be installed first so that the ductwork can be physically mated to the back of the louver assembly.
After louver installation, flashing and sealants are applied around the perimeter to prevent water infiltration.
The louver must be in place to complete the air path before the HVAC system can be balanced and tested for airflow and pressure.

predecessor: Rough-in for ductwork and electrical connections
rationale: Ductwork rough-in and electrical conduit/wiring must be in place before the ERV/HRV unit can be physically mounted and connected.
The unit requires a structural base or support framing to be completed to safely bear the weight of the energy recovery ventilator.
The ERV/HRV unit must be set in place before supply and exhaust ducts can be connected and sealed to the unit's collars.
Power and control wiring connections to the ERV/HRV unit can only be made after the unit is physically installed.
Final testing, airflow balancing, and performance verification of the energy recovery wheel must occur after the unit is fully installed and all connections are made.
HVAC equipment (condensing units, air handlers, etc.) must be installed first so that refrigerant piping can be properly routed and connected between system components.
Structural framing, walls, and ceilings must be in place to provide support and pathways for refrigerant lines before piping installation can begin.
Electrical power and control wiring for HVAC equipment must be roughed in to ensure proper coordination with refrigerant line locations and to avoid conflicts.
Refrigerant piping must be fully installed, brazed, and leak-checked before the system can be evacuated and charged with refrigerant.
Refrigerant lines must be installed and pressure-tested before insulation can be applied to prevent moisture ingress and ensure thermal efficiency.

predecessor: Structural Steel and Roof Deck Installation
rationale: The roof structure must be complete to provide a stable mounting surface and structural support for the heavy RTU equipment.
The roof curb must be installed and properly sealed to the roof deck before the RTU can be set onto it, providing a weather-tight mounting base.
Roofing membranes and flashing around the curb area must be completed to prevent water intrusion before the RTU is placed.
Supply and return duct connections to the unit can only be made after the RTU is set in its final position on the roof curb.
Electrical wiring and disconnects for the RTU must be connected after the unit is placed and secured to avoid safety hazards and ensure proper alignment.
Refrigerant piping between the RTU and any remote air handlers or DX coils must be run and charged after the RTU is in its permanent location.
All mechanical, electrical, and control connections must be complete before the unit can be safely energized, tested, and commissioned.
Structural framing must be in place to support ductwork hangers, supports, and overhead runs before ductwork can be installed.
Overhead utilities and major piping must be routed first so that ductwork can be coordinated in the remaining ceiling space without conflicts.
Ductwork must be fully installed and tested before insulation can be applied to the duct surfaces.
Ductwork must be complete and sealed to enable air balancing, pressure testing, and commissioning of the HVAC system.
Ductwork must be installed and closed up before ceiling grids and finishes are placed, as the ductwork is concealed above the ceiling.
Ductwork must be installed first to provide the connection pathways for the air handling unit to distribute conditioned air throughout the building.

predecessor: Install chilled water piping and connections
rationale: Chilled water piping must be in place to supply cooling water to the air handling unit's cooling coil, enabling heat exchange.
Hot water piping must be installed to provide heating water to the air handling unit's heating coil for temperature control.
The structural framework and support platform must be complete to safely support the weight of the air handling unit.
Electrical power connections and control wiring can only be completed after the air handling unit is physically installed in its final position.
Supply and return diffusers are connected to the ductwork which connects to the AHU; the AHU must be installed first to ensure proper alignment and connection.

successor: Start-up and Testing of HVAC System
rationale: System start-up, balancing, and functional testing can only proceed once the air handling unit is fully installed and connected.

Ductwork must be installed before terminal units (FCU, VAV, VRF indoor units) because terminal units connect to and are supported by the ductwork system. The ductwork provides the air pathway and physical support structure for the terminal units.

Electrical conduits, wiring, refrigerant piping, condensate drain lines, and control wiring must be roughed-in to the terminal unit locations before the units themselves can be physically installed and connected.
Structural framing, ceiling grids, and overhead supports must be completed to provide mounting points and support for terminal units, which are often hung from the structure above.
After terminal units are installed in their final positions, control wiring, thermostats, sensors, and actuators can be connected to the units for proper operation and zone control.

Insulation of ductwork connections, refrigerant lines, and condensate drains at the terminal unit interfaces must be completed after the units are installed to ensure continuous thermal insulation coverage around all connections.

predecessor: Install Foundation & Pads for Chiller/Cooling Tower
rationale: The chiller and cooling tower require a stable, properly cured concrete foundation or pads to support their weight and maintain alignment, preventing structural failure or vibration issues.

predecessor: Rough-in Electrical Conduit & Wiring to Chiller Location
rationale: Electrical conduit and wiring must be routed to the chiller location before the unit is set in place, as it is difficult or impossible to run wiring underneath or behind the equipment once installed.

predecessor: Rough-in Piping for Chilled Water Supply/Return
rationale: Chilled water supply and return piping must be routed to the equipment location and stubbed up before the chiller is set, allowing direct connection to the unit's piping connections.

successor: Connect Chilled Water Piping to Chiller
rationale: Final piping connections require the chiller to be in its permanent position so that flanges, valves, and fittings can be aligned and secured to the unit's connections.
Electrical supply wiring must be terminated at the chiller's control panel and disconnect switch, which is only accessible after the chiller is installed and positioned.

System commissioning, including refrigerant charging, pump startup, and performance testing, can only occur after the chiller and cooling tower are physically installed and all connections are complete.

Internal cooling tower components such as fill media and fan assemblies are typically installed after the tower shell is set in place to avoid damage during rigging and to allow proper sequencing of assembly.
Boilers are heavy and require a stable, load-bearing concrete foundation or slab to be in place before installation can begin.
Electrical connections and plumbing rough-ins for the boiler room must be completed before the boiler and piping can be installed and connected.
After the boiler and hydronic piping are installed, the system must be pressure-tested and flushed to verify no leaks and remove debris before being placed into service.
Finishing work such as flooring is typically done after major mechanical equipment is installed to avoid damage to finished surfaces from heavy equipment and piping installation.

successor: Install Air Handling Units / HVAC Distribution
rationale: Hydronic piping supplies hot water or steam to HVAC distribution equipment (e.g., AHUs, radiators), so boiler and piping must be in place before these downstream components can be connected and tested.
Air balancing requires complete ductwork to be installed so that airflow measurements and adjustments can be made throughout the system.
The AHU must be fully installed and operational to provide the air that will be balanced and commissioned.
Variable air volume (VAV) boxes and other terminal units must be in place to allow for zone-level airflow balancing.

successor: Final Filter Installation / Clean Room Certification
rationale: In critical environments, final HEPA filters are installed and certified only after air balancing ensures the correct airflow direction and pressure differentials.
Commissioning and air balancing must be completed and verified before the building can be handed over for occupancy, as it confirms the HVAC system operates per design specifications.

Electrical power must be roughed in (conduits, cables, outlets) before controls and BMS (Building Management System) wiring can be run, as controls wiring often ties into power sources and electrical infrastructure.

Mechanical equipment such as air handling units (AHUs), pumps, and valves must be installed before control wiring can be connected to them, as the wiring terminates at sensors and actuators on the equipment.
All control wiring must be installed and terminated before the system can be powered up, tested, and commissioned for proper operation.
While not physically required, it is a soft preference to complete controls wiring above ceilings before ceiling grids and finishes are installed, to avoid costly rework or access issues.
Controls wiring must be complete before building systems startup and testing, as the BMS is needed to control and monitor the mechanical and electrical systems.
Duct insulation is applied after the ductwork framing and installation is complete, as insulation wraps around or adheres to the exterior of the duct surfaces.
The ductwork must be hung and properly supported before insulation can be applied, as insulation is installed onto the ducts after they are in their final position.
Ducts should be leak-tested before insulation to allow access for sealing leaks; insulation would conceal joints and make leak repairs difficult.
Vapor barriers or exterior jacketing are installed over the insulation to protect it and prevent moisture ingress.
Duct insulation must be completed before ceilings are enclosed or drywall is finished, as access to the ducts is needed for insulation installation and inspection.
Plumbing rough-in work (piping, drain lines, vent stacks, and water supply lines) must be completed before any fixtures can be installed, as fixtures connect to these embedded systems.
Floor-mounted fixtures (toilets, floor drains) require the structural floor slab to be poured and cured to provide a stable substrate and proper drain connections.
Wall and floor framing must be complete to provide support and enclosure for plumbing stub-outs and to allow access for fixture installation.
Fixtures such as bathtubs, shower pans, and wall-mounted lavatories must be installed before surrounding wall finishes are applied, as they are set into or against the framing and finishes.

While not strictly physically required, it is standard sequencing to install plumbing fixtures before final cabinetry and countertops to allow for precise alignment of supply lines, drain connections, and fixture cutouts; however, some installations can reverse this order with careful planning.
Structural framing and rough-in plumbing/electrical work must be completed before water heaters can be installed, as the water heater needs a designated space and connections.
Hot and cold water supply lines and drain lines must be roughed in before the water heater can be connected to the plumbing system.
Electrical wiring, conduit, and outlet for the water heater must be installed prior to setting the unit to allow for power connection.
Water heater installation must be completed before interior finishes are applied in the mechanical room to allow full access for installation and avoid damage to finished surfaces.
Water heaters must be operational before final connection and testing of plumbing fixtures (sinks, showers, etc.) to ensure hot water supply is available.
Pumps require a stable, level foundation to be installed upon, preventing misalignment and operational issues.
Inlet and outlet piping connections must be roughed-in to the pump location before the pump can be physically set and connected.
Power supply conduits and wiring must be run to the pump location to allow final electrical connections after pump installation.
Final piping connections to the pump flanges and alignment checks can only be done after the pump is set in place.
Electrical connections to the pump motor and subsequent testing require the pump to be installed and secured first.
The entire pumping system including the installed pump must be in place before flushing and pressure testing can be performed.
Valves must be installed after the piping system is in place because valves are components that connect to and control flow within pipes.
Pressure testing of the piping system can only be conducted after valves are installed to ensure the entire system including valves is sealed and can withstand operating pressures.
System flushing must occur after valve installation to remove debris and contaminants from the piping system including the valve internals before final commissioning.
Support structures, brackets, or foundation anchors for heavy or large valves must be in place before the valve itself can be mounted and secured.

Insulation is typically applied after valve installation to cover the pipe and valve body; however in some cases valves may be left uninsulated or insulation can be cut and fitted around valves later.

Piping systems (especially underground drainage, water supply, and conduit runs) must be laid within or beneath the foundation slab. The foundation and slab must be completed to provide the structural base and embedment for piping.

Vertical pipe risers, main distribution lines, and fire-protection piping are typically installed after the structural frame is erected, as they run within walls, columns, and ceiling voids of the superstructure.

successor: Wall and Ceiling Finishes (Drywall, Plaster, Cladding)
rationale: Piping and fittings must be installed, pressure-tested, and inspected inside wall/ceiling cavities before they are enclosed by finishes. Finishing over un-inspected piping would create costly rework and code violations.
Where pipes are embedded in floor screeds or laid beneath the finished floor, they must be fully installed, tested, and approved before the final floor finish is applied.
Plumbing fixtures connect directly to the piping outlets; the rough-in piping and fittings must be in place and terminated at the correct locations before fixtures can be mounted and connected.
Backflow prevention devices are typically installed on water service lines; the underground water main must be in place to provide the upstream water supply connection.
The interior water supply piping must be roughed-in to the point where the backflow preventer can be connected as part of the water distribution system.
After the backflow preventer is installed, the entire water supply line must be pressure-tested to verify there are no leaks and that the device functions correctly.
Backflow prevention must be in place before final fixture connections to ensure the water supply is protected from potential backflow contamination during fixture installation.
The backflow preventer must be installed and operational to pass code-required inspections and commissioning of the building's potable water system.
The site must be excavated and prepared before any underground plumbing rough-in work can begin, as plumbing lines are typically laid in trenches below the foundation.
Underground plumbing (drain, waste, vent pipes) must be placed and inspected before the concrete slab is poured, so the pipes are embedded within or beneath the foundation.
Interior plumbing rough-in for supply lines and waste pipes runs through wall cavities and floor joists; framing must be in place to provide the structural support and access routes for these pipes.
After all rough-in plumbing work is completed, a mandatory rough-in inspection must be performed by the building inspector before any walls or ceilings are closed up.

While electrical rough-in can technically proceed concurrently with plumbing rough-in, it is often sequenced after plumbing to avoid conflicts in wall cavities and to allow plumbers unobstructed access first.

Insulation cannot be installed until all rough-in plumbing, electrical, and mechanical work is complete, as these services run within the wall and ceiling cavities that will be filled with insulation.

Drywall cannot be hung until all rough-in work (plumbing, electrical, HVAC) and associated inspections are completed, because the walls must be open to allow installation and inspection of these systems.

Plumbing rough-in (running supply and drain lines through walls) must be completed before trim-out can begin, as trim-out involves installing fixtures, faucets, and connections that require the rough piping to already be in place and inspected.
Building code requires that all rough-in plumbing work be inspected and approved before it is concealed or before fixtures (trim-out) are installed, to ensure no rework of buried pipes is needed.
Insulation is typically installed before trim-out to provide access to wall cavities, though this is a soft preference as trim-out can technically proceed without insulation in place.

Trim-out installation (sink faucets, toilet connections, shower valves, etc.) must be complete before final wall finishes, tiling, and painting to avoid damage and ensure flush fit of trim pieces against finished walls.
After all trim-out fixtures are installed, a final plumbing inspection is required to verify functionality, leak-free operation, and code compliance before the building is occupied.
Water supply and drain pipes must be roughed in before the water heater can be connected to the plumbing system.

predecessor: Gas Line Rough-In (if gas water heater)
rationale: Gas supply piping must be installed and pressure-tested before connecting a gas water heater to ensure safety and code compliance.
Dedicated electrical circuit and wiring must be run to the water heater location before making final electrical connections.
Final connections (shut-off valves, T&P relief valve discharge piping, and water line hookups) can only be completed after the water heater is set in place.
Commissioning procedures (filling the tank, purging air, checking for leaks, igniting burner or energizing elements, and adjusting temperature) must occur after installation is physically complete.

All plumbing pipes, fittings, and fixtures must be fully installed in the rough-in stage before pressure testing can be performed. Testing a system before installation is complete is physically impossible.
All soldered, glued, threaded, or mechanical joints must be fully cured and connected before pressurization to avoid leaks and ensure the integrity of the test.
Pressure testing must be completed and witnessed before the inspecting authority can sign off on the rough-in plumbing work.
Pressure testing must be successfully completed and leaks resolved before walls and ceilings are closed up; otherwise, access to repair leaks would require costly demolition.

Final fixtures and trim should only be installed after the pressure test confirms the piping system is sound, to avoid damage to fixtures from test pressures or from having to disconnect them for access.
Conduits and cable trays provide the pathways for electrical cables that connect to the distribution board; without them, cables cannot be routed to the panelboard.
Branch circuit wiring must be pulled and routed to the panelboard location before the panelboard can be mounted and connections terminated.
The panelboard is typically mounted on or within a wall; the structural framing and sheathing must be in place to provide support and enclosure.

successor: Terminate and connect circuit breakers and wiring
rationale: After the panelboard enclosure is installed, electricians can install circuit breakers, terminate branch circuits, and make final connections inside the panel.

successor: Energize and test electrical distribution system
rationale: The panelboard must be fully installed and connected before the main power supply is turned on and system testing can be performed safely.

Cable trays and ladders are typically supported from the building structure (steel beams, columns, or concrete slabs). Structural steel must be in place to provide the mounting points and support framework before cable trays can be hung or installed.

Fire protection sprinkler piping is typically installed close to the structure above cable trays. If cable trays are installed first, they obstruct access and create safety hazards for fire protection installers. Fire protection piping must be completed overhead first to maintain clear working space and avoid interference.

Large HVAC ducts are typically routed above cable trays due to their size. Installing ducts first ensures that cable tray routes can be coordinated around existing ductwork, and avoids the need to cut or relocate cable trays later for duct access.
Cables must have a continuous supported pathway (tray or ladder) installed before they can be pulled, laid in, or terminated. The tray system provides the physical infrastructure for cable routing.

successor: Electrical Rough-In / Conduit Termination at Trays
rationale: Conduits entering cable trays (via connectors, bushings, or grounding) and final electrical connections to the tray system require the trays to be fully installed and secured first. The tray must be in its final position for conduit alignment and attachment.
Electrical panels must be installed before the main switchboard can be connected and energized.
Main switchboard must be in place to serve as the termination point for cable trays that feed from it.
The main switchboard requires a stable, level concrete foundation to be installed upon.
Branch circuits originate from the main switchboard, so the switchboard must be installed first to supply power downstream.
Commissioning activities including testing and energization can only proceed after the main switchboard is fully installed, connected, and terminated.
The Sub-Distribution Board receives its power feed from the Main Distribution Board; therefore, the MDB must be installed and energized first to supply power to the SDB.

predecessor: Run Main Feeder Cables from MDB to SDB location
rationale: Feeder cables that supply the SDB must be routed and terminated before the SDB enclosure can be mounted and connected.

successor: Run Branch Circuit Cables from SDB to downstream loads
rationale: Branch circuits supplying lights, power outlets, or equipment originate from the SDB; cable pulling and termination must follow SDB installation to ensure proper connections.
Energizing and testing the SDB, including checking insulation resistance, phase rotation, and protection device settings, can only occur after the board is fully installed and wired.

predecessor: Mount SDB Enclosure and Install Internal Busbars/Components
successor: Terminate Incoming and Outgoing Cables at SDB
rationale: Cable lugs must be fastened to busbars and circuit breakers inside the SDB; this work cannot be done until the enclosure is securely mounted and internal components are fitted.
The circuit breaker and fuse assembly must be mounted onto a structural mounting panel or backplate, which must be installed first to provide a stable mounting surface.
The main conduit and cable tray pathways need to be in place so that incoming and outgoing power cables can be routed to the breaker and fuse assembly location.
Bus bars that distribute power to multiple downstream breakers or loads must be connected to the main breaker/fuse assembly after it is securely installed and positioned.
Power cables from the source and to the loads must be terminated and lugged onto the breaker and fuse terminals, which can only be done after the assembly is in place.

Final labeling of each breaker and fuse (circuit identification) and closing of the panel cover must occur after the assembly is fully installed and wired to ensure correct identification and safe enclosure.
Electrical conduit and wiring must be in place to provide the necessary power supply and connectivity for the metering and monitoring equipment to function.
The metering and monitoring equipment must be physically installed and connected before it can be calibrated, configured, and tested to ensure accurate readings.
Mounting brackets, panels, and support structures must be securely installed to provide a stable platform for attaching the metering and monitoring equipment.
Metering devices must be connected to the electrical panels before the panels can be fully commissioned and energized for operational use.
The main electrical substation or distribution system must be installed to provide the primary power source that the metering equipment will monitor.
Concealed conduits must be embedded in walls/structures before outlet positions are available for switch/socket installation.
Walls must be plastered and finished to provide a flush mounting surface for switch and socket outlet boxes.
Cables must be pulled and routed to outlet positions before the switch/socket outlets can be wired and terminated.
Switch and socket faceplates are installed before final paint/decorative finishes to achieve a clean, flush appearance.
All outlets must be installed and connected before continuity, polarity, and insulation resistance tests can be performed.
Cable trays are typically supported by or attached to the building's structural steel framework. The steel structure must be in place to provide mounting points and support for cable tray systems.

Large mechanical ducts and HVAC equipment are bulkier and less flexible than cable trays. Installing cable trays before ducts could block access or require rework, so mechanical rough-in is typically completed first to establish spatial priority for larger services.
Cable trays often originate from or terminate in electrical rooms. The electrical room floors, walls, and main equipment pads must be prepared before tray installation can begin.
Cables are pulled through or laid into the cable trays after the trays are fully installed. The tray pathway must exist before any cable can be placed inside it.

Fire-stopping compounds are applied around cable trays where they pass through fire-rated walls and floors. The trays must be in final position before firestopping can be properly applied to seal the penetrations.
The ground must be excavated and trenches prepared before conduit can be placed into the trench.
Conduit must be laid and positioned before concrete encasement or backfilling the trench to cover and protect it.
Conduit must be fully installed and continuous before cables can be pulled through the conduit.
After installation, the conduit must be inspected and tested (e.g., mandrel testing) before being covered or used.
Although not always mandatory, a roughly graded and level site simplifies conduit layout and reduces installation issues.
Cables must have a physical pathway (conduits, trays, or ducts) installed before they can be pulled through or laid in.
Backboxes, junction boxes, and termination enclosures must be fixed in place before cables can be terminated into them.
Cables must be physically pulled and terminated before they can be electrically tested for continuity, insulation resistance, and correctness.
The cable ends must be pulled to the panel location and terminated before internal panel wiring and connections can be completed.

successor: Installation of Devices (Sockets, Switches, Light Fittings)
rationale: Final devices such as sockets, switches, and lighting fixtures can only be connected and installed after the cables supplying them have been pulled and terminated at the device location.
Conduits and wiring rough-in must be completed before the distribution board can be installed, as the board serves as the termination point for these circuits.
The main incoming supply and utility meter must be installed to provide power to the distribution board for testing and commissioning.
The earth/ground connection must be in place to safely bond the distribution board enclosure and provide a safe path for fault currents during commissioning.
Final circuit wiring from the distribution board to outlets, lights, and equipment can only commence after the board itself is installed and energized.
Full electrical testing (insulation resistance, polarity, RCD testing) of all circuits must follow board commissioning as the board is the central distribution point.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before earthing conductors, rods, and grids can be placed into the soil or foundation.
Earthing components (e.g., earth electrodes, grounding loops) are often embedded in or laid beneath foundations before concrete is poured or as part of the foundation stage.

successor: Main Electrical Cable Laying and Routing
rationale: The earthing grid and earth electrodes must be in place to provide a reference ground before main power cables are laid and connected to the system.
All electrical equipment must have its earthing connection made after the earthing system is installed to ensure proper bonding and safety grounding.

successor: Testing and Commissioning of Earthing System
rationale: The earthing system must be fully installed before it can be tested for resistance, continuity, and compliance with standards.
The HVAC unit must be physically installed and in place before electrical power connections can be made to it.
Conduit pathways must be run from the electrical panel to the HVAC unit location before final power wiring can be pulled and connected.
Power must be connected to the HVAC unit before it can be commissioned, started up, and tested for proper operation.

successor: Building Electrical Panel Energization (for HVAC circuit)
rationale: The branch circuit breaker for the HVAC unit can only be turned on and energized after the power connection to the unit is complete.
While controls can be wired earlier, verifying thermostat communication with the powered HVAC unit is best done after power is connected.
Structural steel must be in place to support the busway and bus duct hangers and supports.
Electrical rooms housing the switchgear and panelboards that connect to the busway must be built and enclosed before busway installation can begin.
While not strictly required, it is preferable to install cable trays before busway as they share overhead space and busway is more clearance-sensitive.
Busway sections must be fully installed and mechanically connected before electrical terminations to switchgear, panelboards, and downstream equipment can be made.
Firestopping and fireproofing at floor and wall penetrations can only be applied after the busway is installed through those openings.
The step-down transformer requires a stable, level foundation or plinth to be constructed and cured before the heavy transformer can be delivered and set in place.
The transformer must be physically delivered to the site and offloaded onto its foundation before installation activities can commence.
HV cables supplying the primary side of the step-down transformer cannot be terminated and connected until the transformer is installed and positioned.
LV cables from the secondary side of the step-down transformer to the main LV switchboard must be connected after the transformer is in place.
Commissioning activities such as oil filling, insulation resistance testing, and functional tests can only be performed after the transformer is fully installed and secured.
Cable trays and ladders provide the primary support structure upon which cable management accessories (such as cable ties, clamps, ducts, and raceways) are mounted and secured.
Conduits must be in place before cable management accessories like pull boxes, junction boxes, and fittings can be installed to connect and terminate the conduit runs.
The building's structural frame and steel supports must be complete to provide anchor points and mounting surfaces for cable management hardware.

Cable management accessories such as cable ties, clips, ducts, and raceways must be installed first to provide the pathways and securing mechanisms needed before cables can be pulled, laid, and fastened.
Cable management accessories must be in place to organize and route cables before technicians can perform terminations at panels, outlets, and equipment.
Conduits must be installed in their rough-in positions before on-site bending and fabrication can be performed to ensure proper fit, alignment, and routing around structural elements.
Bent and fabricated conduits must be in place and secured before wires or cables can be pulled through them; pulling cannot occur without a completed conduit pathway.
Final connections and terminations at junction boxes, panels, and devices require the conduit to be bent, fabricated, and positioned first to ensure proper alignment and fit.
Structural framing and any rough inspections must be completed to confirm that conduit pathways are clear and that bending/fabrication will not interfere with structural elements or require rework.
Bending, fabrication, and installation of conduits must be finished and inspected before walls and ceilings are closed to avoid costly rework and ensure accessibility for final connections.
Electrical conduits and wiring must be in place before switches and sockets can be connected to the electrical supply.
Walls must be plastered and finished before switches and sockets are mounted to ensure proper alignment, fit, and aesthetics.

predecessor: Back Box Embedding / Conduit Box Installation
rationale: The back boxes or conduit boxes into which switches and sockets are fixed must be installed and embedded in the wall beforehand.
Once switches and sockets are installed, the electrical circuits can be tested for continuity, insulation resistance, and proper operation.

Final painting and touch-up work around installed switches and sockets is typically done after installation to cover any gaps or marks, though this is a soft preference for aesthetic finish rather than a physical necessity.

Rough electrical wiring (running cables, installing junction boxes) must be completed before lighting fixtures can be connected, as the wiring provides the necessary power supply and termination points for the fixtures.

Ceilings and drywall must be finished and painted before lighting fixtures are installed, because fixtures mount to the finished ceiling surface and access to open ceiling cavities is no longer available after drywall is closed.
All overhead structural framing, steelwork or decking must be complete to provide a stable mounting surface and safe access for fixture installation.
Fixtures must be physically connected to the power source before they can be tested for proper operation, illumination levels, and control functionality.

While not a hard physical constraint, completing lighting fixture connection before final ceiling touch-ups is preferred to avoid needing to re-access ceilings for fixture installation after paint and finish work is complete.
All electrical systems must be installed before they can be tested and commissioned to ensure power supply is available for system testing.
Mechanical systems such as HVAC, plumbing, and fire protection must be fully installed before they can be functionally tested and commissioned.
Fire protection equipment must be in place before commissioning to allow for pressure testing, alarm testing, and verification of system functionality.
Building management systems, sensors, and controllers must be installed before they can be programmed, calibrated, and commissioned.
All systems must be tested and commissioned to verify they operate per design before the facility can be formally handed over to the client.
The fire suppression control panel requires electrical power to operate; electrical rough-in must be completed to provide power supply connections before the panel can be installed and connected.

The fire suppression control panel monitors and controls the suppression system; the piping network that delivers the suppression agent must be in place before the control panel can be wired and programmed to operate the system.
The control panel must be fully installed before the fire suppression system can be tested and commissioned, as the panel is the central control unit for system operation and alarm signaling.
The fire suppression control panel must be installed and connected before it can be integrated with the building fire alarm system for coordinated emergency response signaling.

Although final inspection occurs after installation, it is a procedural preference rather than a physical constraint, as the panel must be in place for inspectors to verify code compliance and proper operation.

Fire suppression piping is typically hung from or supported by the structural steel frame. The steel structure must be in place to provide support points and overhead anchorage for piping hangers and supports.

Major overhead utilities such as HVAC ducts and large electrical conduits are generally installed before fire suppression piping to avoid interference conflicts. Fire suppression piping often snakes around these larger utilities and must be installed after they are roughed-in to maintain required clearances and proper coverage.

Fire suppression sprinkler heads must protrude through the ceiling finish. Therefore the piping network including drops for sprinkler heads must be completed and pressure-tested before ceiling grids and tiles are installed.

successor: Wall and Partition Framing (if above-ceiling piping)
rationale: In areas where fire suppression piping runs within or above partitions, the piping must be installed and connected before walls are closed up with drywall to avoid costly rework and to allow access for inspection and testing.

Fire suppression system must be hydrostatically tested and verified leak-free before final flooring, painting, and other water-sensitive interior finishes are applied, to prevent water damage in case of a test failure.
Rough-in inspection of sprinkler piping must be approved before installing sprinkler heads to ensure piping is correctly positioned and compliant.
Sprinkler heads are typically installed after ceiling grid or finish work so they can be positioned flush with the finished ceiling surface.
The sprinkler system must have all heads installed before a full system pressure/flow test can be performed.
Sprinkler heads must be installed and in place before the final fire suppression system inspection and commissioning can occur.
The storage tank requires a level, load-bearing concrete foundation or base slab to support its weight and prevent settlement or tilting.
Drain, overflow, and fill piping connections must be installed and stubbed up through the slab before the tank is placed, as they run beneath or through the base.
Above-grade piping connections to the tank (e.g., fill line, agent supply line, vent, drain) can only be made after the tank is set in its final position.
Level sensors, pressure transmitters, and other instrumentation mounted on or inside the tank must be installed after the tank is positioned and secured.

If the tank requires insulation or heat tracing (e.g., for freeze protection), these are typically applied after the tank is set, though this may be considered a soft preference if wrapping could be done partially off-site.
The dry pipe valve must be connected to the piping system; the rough-in piping must be in place to provide the physical connection points for the valve.
The dry pipe valve is the interface between the water supply and the compressed air system; it must be installed before the air compressor can be connected to pressurize the system.

successor: Trim and accessories installation (e.g., gauges, drains, test valves)
rationale: Trim components such as pressure gauges, drain valves, and test valves are mounted directly on or adjacent to the dry pipe valve; the valve body must be in place to attach these accessories.
The dry pipe valve must be installed and closed to seal the system before air pressure testing can be performed to verify integrity of the piping and valve.

successor: Fire alarm and supervisory switch connection
rationale: Supervisory switches monitoring the dry pipe valve position and air pressure require the valve to be installed and trim completed to allow proper wiring and testing of alarm signals.
Flow switches are installed inline on piping systems; pipes must be in place to mount and connect the flow switch.
The flow switch must be physically installed before electrical connections (wiring, terminal connections) can be completed.
The flow switch is part of the sealed piping system; all components including the flow switch must be installed before pressure testing can verify system integrity.
The flow switch must be physically mounted and wired before it can be calibrated and functionally tested for proper flow detection.
All individual component testing including flow switch verification must be completed before the overall system can be commissioned and put into operation.
The tamper switch must have a secure mounting bracket installed before the switch itself can be placed, as the bracket provides the physical support and alignment for the switch.

predecessor: Run Conduit to Tamper Switch Location
rationale: Electrical conduit must be in place before installing the tamper switch so that wiring can be pulled through to the switch location without obstruction.
Wiring must be routed to the switch location prior to physically mounting the switch so connections can be made easily and without straining the conductors.
The tamper switch must be fully installed before it can be tested to verify proper operation and alarm triggering.

successor: Wire Tamper Switch into Alarm Circuit
rationale: The switch must be physically in place and connected to its wiring before it can be integrated into the broader alarm or monitoring circuit.
The zone valve must connect to the main fire suppression riser, which supplies the water or suppression agent to the zone.

successor: Fire Suppression Piping to Zone Layout and Connection
rationale: The zone valve controls flow to the zone's piping; downstream piping cannot be fully connected and tested until the valve is in place.
It is easier to install the valve before walls or enclosures are closed up, allowing access for connections and testing.

successor: Fire Suppression System Pressure Testing and Commissioning
rationale: The zone valve must be installed and operational before the overall system can be pressure-tested and commissioned for the zone.
The fire suppression system must be fully installed before it can be commissioned, as commissioning involves testing and verifying a completed installation.
Fire suppression systems often interface with fire alarm systems for detection and activation; the alarm system must be installed to allow integrated testing during commissioning.
Commissioning requires electrical power to operate pumps, control panels, valves, and testing equipment; power supply must be installed and energized.
Commissioning validates the system's readiness and corrects any deficiencies before formal acceptance testing by authorities or the client.
Regulatory and safety codes require the fire suppression system to be commissioned and verified operational before the building can be occupied.
Structural steel must be in place to provide support and hanging points for suppression piping before piping can be installed.
The concrete floors and slabs must be cured and completed to provide a stable base and accessible work area for pipe installation.
Piping must be fully installed before pressure testing can be performed to verify integrity.
The piping network must be complete before the overall fire suppression system can be commissioned and tested.
Insulation is typically applied after piping installation, but some sections may be insulated before installation as a soft preference depending on access.
Sprinkler piping must be installed and in place before sprinkler heads can be attached to the branch lines.
Sprinkler heads are typically installed after ceiling grid or framing is in place so that heads can be properly positioned and aligned with ceiling tiles or openings.
Ceiling tiles are installed after sprinkler heads to allow access for head positioning and to cut precise holes around each head for a finished appearance.
While not physically required, it is best practice to complete sprinkler head installation before full fire suppression system testing to ensure all components are in place.
Interior finishing such as painting is typically done after sprinkler head installation to avoid damaging finished surfaces and to allow for precise fit around heads.
Fire suppression piping must be installed before control wiring can be run, as the wiring connects to and controls the piping system components (valves, sensors, etc.).
The fire suppression control panel must be mounted and in place before wiring can be terminated and connected to it.
Conduit pathways and junction boxes must be installed to provide the physical raceway for the fire suppression control wiring.
All control wiring must be completed and connected before the fire suppression system can be tested and commissioned for proper operation.
Ceilings and wall finishes are typically installed after control wiring is complete to avoid damage and rework, though this is a sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
Piping must be installed before valves can be assembled onto the piping system, as valves are components that connect to the piping network.
Valve assembly must be complete before pressure testing can be performed to verify system integrity and leak-tightness.
Valves must be assembled before functional testing of the suppression system can verify correct valve operation.
All valve assembly work must be completed prior to system commissioning to ensure the system is fully installed and ready for operational verification.

The fire suppression system piping, nozzles, and storage tanks must be fully installed and pressure-tested before any agent can be charged into the system, as charging requires a complete, sealed system.

Detection and alarm systems must be operational and tested prior to charging the suppression agent to ensure that any accidental discharge during charging will trigger appropriate alarms and safety protocols.
Electrical connections to the suppression system control panels and release mechanisms must be completed and energized to allow for proper charging and system control.

successor: Final Fire Suppression System Testing and Acceptance
rationale: The system must be fully charged with the suppression agent before final acceptance testing can be performed, as the test verifies proper agent discharge, coverage, and system functionality under charged conditions.

successor: Ceiling and Finish Work in Protected Areas
rationale: While it is generally preferred to complete ceiling finishes after agent charging to avoid damaging finishes during the charging process, this is a soft preference as finishes could be installed before charging if proper protection measures are taken.

predecessor: Fire Pump Foundation / Base Slab Pour
rationale: The fire pump requires a stable concrete foundation or base slab to be cured and ready before the pump unit can be set in place.
Underground water supply piping to the fire pump suction must be in place before the pump can be connected.
The pump unit must be set and anchored before overhead and discharge piping can be connected to its flanges.
The pump must be physically in place before the motor controller and electrical conduits can be terminated and connected to the pump motor.
All piping connections to the fire pump must be complete and tight before pressure testing and flushing of the system can be performed.
The fire hydrant must be connected to an existing water main; the underground water main provides the water source and pressure required for the hydrant to function.
Excavation and trenching must be completed to expose the water main and create space for installing the hydrant lateral and connections.
Backfilling can only occur after the hydrant and its connections are fully installed and inspected to avoid burying unconnected or defective components.
Pressure testing and flushing of the hydrant assembly must be performed after connection to verify integrity, flow, and to remove debris from the system.
Surface restoration (e.g., paving, sidewalk repair) is typically done after hydrant installation to avoid rework, though in some sequences it could overlap if access is preserved.

predecessor: Install foundation bolts and anchor plates
rationale: Guide rails must be anchored to a stable foundation; foundation bolts and anchor plates provide the structural base for mounting the rail brackets.
The precise alignment path for the guide rails must be surveyed and marked beforehand to ensure correct positioning and level.
The elevator car frame rides along the guide rails; the rails must be in place before the car can be installed.
In many designs, the main guide rails define the vertical reference plane; counterweight rails are aligned relative to the main rails and installed after them.
Rail brackets secure the guide rails to the building structure; the rails must be positioned and temporarily held before brackets are permanently fastened.
The hoistway (elevator shaft) must be structurally complete to provide the physical enclosure and guide rails necessary for elevator car installation.
Guide rails must be installed and aligned in the hoistway before the elevator car can be placed, as the car's guide shoes run along these rails.
The machine room or overhead structure must be complete to house the hoisting machinery, governor, and sheaves that will lift and control the elevator car.
The structural elevator car frame must be installed first before interior finishing (walls, flooring, ceiling, lighting, handrails) can be applied.
The elevator car must be mechanically installed and connected to the hoisting system before load testing, safety device testing, and final commissioning can occur.
The traction/hydraulic system requires a stable, level foundation to be installed upon, as it involves heavy mechanical components that need structural support.
The steel frame or structural framework must be in place to support or house the traction/hydraulic system components before they can be installed.
Electrical connections to the traction/hydraulic system can only be made after the system's physical installation is complete, to avoid damage and ensure proper alignment.
Testing and commissioning of the overall system must occur after installation and connection of the traction/hydraulic system to verify performance and safety.
Hydraulic fluid piping can only be connected after the main traction/hydraulic system unit is in its final position to ensure accurate connection points and avoid leaks.

The elevator hoistway (shaft) must be physically constructed and enclosed before the machine/controller can be installed inside or adjacent to it, as the controller is mounted within or on the hoistway structure.
Guide rails must be installed in the hoistway before the machine/controller can be positioned, as the controller's operation depends on the car being guided within the completed rail system.
Electrical conduit, wiring, and power supply infrastructure must be roughed-in to the controller location before the controller unit itself can be mounted and connected.

successor: Elevator Car Controller / Drive Tuning & Testing
rationale: The machine/roomless controller must be physically installed, mounted, and wired before it can be powered up, tuned, programmed, and tested with the elevator car drive system.
The controller installation must be complete as it governs all car movements; the car installation proceeds afterward and relies on the controller for operational testing and leveling adjustments.
A stable foundation is required to bear the weight of the counterweight assembly before it can be installed.
The base frame provides the structural mounting point onto which the counterweight assembly is placed.
The counterweight must be in place to provide stability before the main load-bearing structure is erected.
Cables connect to the counterweight assembly; thus the assembly must be completed before cables can be routed and secured.
While load testing typically follows assembly, in some cases partial testing can begin once the counterweight is in place even before final assembly is fully torqued.
The elevator shaft must be fully constructed to provide the structural opening and framing into which landing doors are installed.
Guide rails must be in place to ensure proper alignment of the elevator car and door mechanisms before landing door frames are set.

predecessor: Rough Electrical and Wiring for Elevator Controls
rationale: Electrical rough-in for door operators, sensors, and control interfaces must be completed before landing door installation to allow connections behind the door frame.
Landing doors must be installed and aligned first to serve as the reference point for matching elevator car door operation at each floor.

successor: Floor Finishing and Wall Finishing at Elevator Landings
rationale: Landing door frames and doors must be in place before final floor and wall finishes are applied around the door openings to achieve clean transitions and proper tolerances.
Car doors must be assembled onto the body-in-white frame, so the body shell structure must be completed first to provide the mounting points and alignment references for the doors.
