The metal door panels must be stamped and formed before they can be assembled into complete door units with internal components.
The inner and outer door panels must be welded together to form the door frame structure before final door assembly can proceed.
Door hinges can only be installed onto the car body after the complete door assembly has been fitted and aligned to ensure proper fitment.
The fully assembled doors must be mounted on the car body before they go through the paint shop together to ensure color matching and uniform paint application.
While some interior trimming can proceed without doors, final trim installation on the door panels themselves requires the door assemblies to be complete and mounted for proper alignment and fit.
The mounting base or bracket for the governor must be installed and secured before the safety brake/governor assembly can be mounted onto it.
The machine room floor and anchor points must be prepared to support the governor assembly before installation can begin.
The governor rope must be connected to the governor sheave, so the governor assembly must be installed first to provide the anchoring point for the rope.
The safety gear linkage connects to the governor mechanism; the governor must be in place before the linkage rods and arms can be aligned and adjusted.

The governor rope must be installed and tensioned before the overspeed governor trip test and safety brake functional test can be performed, as the rope transmits motion to trigger the brake mechanism.
The hoistway must be prepared and clear of debris before traveling cables can be installed to ensure safe access and proper routing.
The elevator car must be assembled in place, as the traveling cable connects the car to the building electrical supply and control systems.
The elevator controller must be installed and positioned so that the traveling cable can be properly connected between the car and the controller.
Cable hangers and brackets must be installed after the traveling cable is positioned to secure and support the cable along its run.
Electrical termination of the traveling cable conductors and subsequent continuity/insulation testing can only be performed after the cable is physically installed.
Buffers (rubber or elastomeric bearing pads) are placed on top of the foundation or base slab to provide a resilient layer before track installation.
Buffers must be in place to provide the required support, vibration damping, and alignment foundation for the rail tracks.
Track fasteners (clips, bolts) attach the rail to the buffers/pads; thus buffers must be installed first.
Once buffers support the rails, continuous welded rail (CWR) installation and stress relief can proceed on the stable track structure.

predecessor: Concrete Plinth or Support Pedestal Construction
rationale: Buffers are often mounted on or bedded against concrete plinths/pedestals at rail ends or transitions; the plinth must be cured and ready before buffer placement.
The Car Operating Panel is mounted onto or integrated within the dashboard frame, so the dashboard frame must be in place first.
Electrical wiring and harnesses must be routed to the panel location before the operating panel is installed to allow proper connections.
The operating panel must be installed and connected before its functionality (buttons, displays, controls) can be tested as part of the electrical system.
While trim can be partially done before, final trim finishing around the panel is typically done after installation to ensure a seamless fit; this is a soft preference for aesthetic precision.
The operating panel includes HVAC controls, so its installation is required before the HVAC system can be fully integrated and tested from the user interface.
Electrical rough-in (conduit, wiring, back boxes) must be installed in the wall before hall call fixtures can be mounted and connected.
Walls must be finished, painted, and ready for final trim before surface-mounted or flush hall call stations can be installed.
The elevator hoistway and structure must be in place to define the locations where hall call fixtures will be mounted adjacent to each floor landing.
Hall call fixtures are typically installed and aligned with the landing door frame; final door trim and alignment may reference the already-placed call station.
Hall call fixtures must be physically installed and wired before the elevator control system can be tested for call registration and response functionality.
The foundation or mounting surface must be prepared and leveled before a position indicator can be installed to ensure proper alignment and accurate readings.
The structural framework must be in place to provide the mounting points and support structure needed for the position indicator.
The position indicator must be physically installed before the overall system can be calibrated, as calibration involves setting reference points based on the installed indicator.
Electrical wiring and connections to the position indicator can only be completed after the indicator is physically mounted in its final position.
The position indicator must be fully installed and connected before system commissioning can verify its functionality and accuracy.
The elevator shaft and hoistway must be structurally complete to provide the physical enclosure and support for elevator installation.
Floor slabs define the elevator shaft openings and provide the landing surfaces at each floor level; elevator rails and doors cannot be installed without completed floor slabs.
The elevator pit (bottom of the shaft) must be excavated, waterproofed, and concreted to provide the physical base for the elevator buffer and car.

The elevator cab, controller, and machinery require permanent power connections; however, temporary power may be used for initial testing, but final commissioning ties to the building's main electrical system.

While elevator operation does not strictly require finished lobbies, it is standard practice to complete elevator commissioning before finishing adjacent areas to avoid damage to finishes during elevator testing and adjustment.
Structural steel framing provides the main structural support and vertical load path for the building, and the hoistway must be built within or attached to the structural frame.
A stable foundation is required to support the hoistway structure and elevator loads; the hoistway cannot be built without a completed foundation.
Floor slab openings for the elevator hoistway must be formed or cut before the hoistway walls and guide rails can be installed through the building.
Elevator cars, counterweights, guide rails, and mechanical equipment can only be installed after the hoistway enclosure is complete and structurally ready.
Waterproofing and fireproofing coatings or boards are applied to the completed hoistway structure to meet building code requirements, and cannot be applied before the hoistway is built.
The foundation must be in place before any superstructure or truss assembly can begin, as trusses require a stable base load-bearing surface.
Vertical supports (columns or walls) must be erected first to provide the structural bearing points onto which trusses and balustrades are mounted.
Roof decking or sheathing is placed directly on top of the trusses; therefore trusses must be fully assembled and secured before decking can be installed.

While it is physically possible to run some MEP services before trusses, the optimal sequence is to complete the truss structure first so that routing paths are clearly defined and to avoid interference during assembly.
The truss/balustrade structural frame must be fully assembled to provide the mounting framework before infill elements like glass panels or balusters can be installed.
A stable, level foundation is required to support the Step Chain and Pallet System. The pallets and chains must be mounted on a prepared base to ensure alignment and load distribution.
The structural framework provides the mounting points and support structure necessary for installing the step chain and pallet components.
The step chain and pallets form the moving platform; the conveyor drive, sensors, and control systems must be installed and aligned after the chain and pallet assembly is in place.
Electrical connections for motors, sensors, and limit switches associated with the step chain and pallet system can only be run after the mechanical assembly is complete.
Functional testing, load testing, and commissioning of the step chain and pallet conveyor can only commence once the mechanical assembly and supporting systems are fully installed.
Fixed handrails must be installed first to establish the structural support and alignment baseline before moving handrails are added for transitional sections.
Structural framing must be complete to provide the primary support surfaces and attachment points for moving handrail components.
Moving handrails must be fully installed before system testing can verify smooth operation, clearance, and safety functionality.
Installation of moving handrails must be complete before safety certification inspections can assess compliance with building codes and operational safety standards.
Finishing work adjacent to moving handrails (e.g., paint, cladding) is preferably done after installation to avoid damage, but can be sequenced otherwise if necessary.
The handrail drive mechanism must be mounted on or within the escalator truss structure, which must first be in place to provide support and alignment.
The handrail drive mechanism powers and guides the handrail loop; the handrail cannot be installed and tensioned until its drive mechanism is in place.

While the drive mechanism for the handrail is typically synchronized with the step chain, it is possible to install step chains before the handrail drive is fully mounted, but best practice suggests completing the handrail drive first to ensure proper alignment and tensioning of the handrail relative to the steps.
The handrail drive motor requires electrical power and control connections to function; these must be run to the drive location before the mechanism can be operationally tested or commissioned.
The handrail drive must be fully installed and mechanically complete before the overall handrail system can be tested for speed synchronization, tension, and safety compliance.
A stable, level foundation and base must be prepared and cured before the heavy drive motor and gearbox assembly can be installed to ensure proper alignment and load distribution.
The mounting frame or skid that supports the motor and gearbox must be in place and secured before the motor and gearbox can be set onto it.
The drive motor and gearbox must be installed and bolted down before the coupling between the motor shaft and gearbox input shaft can be aligned and connected.
The gearbox must be in its final position before lubrication supply and return piping can be connected to its ports.
The drive motor must be physically installed before electrical cables, motor leads, and control wiring can be terminated at the motor junction box.
The drive shaft and sprockets must be mounted onto or within the assembled frame structure, so the frame must be completed first to provide a stable mounting platform.
The chain wraps around the sprockets on the drive shaft; sprockets must be in place before the chain can be fitted and tensioned.
The pedal crank connects to the drive shaft or front sprocket; the drive shaft and sprockets must be installed before the crank mechanism can be attached and aligned.

While brakes can technically be installed independently, it is preferable to have the drive train in place first to verify clearances and ensure brake components do not interfere with the rotating sprockets.
Bearings and bushings are required to support the drive shaft rotation; the shaft and sprockets can only be installed after these support components are fitted into their housings.
The foundation/basement provides the stable structural base on which the guide rails/track system is mounted and aligned.
The elevator shaft steel structure must be in place to provide the vertical framework for attaching and supporting the guide rails/track.
The guide rails/track must be installed and aligned before the elevator car can be assembled and placed onto the rails for movement.
Main guide rails/track installation serves as a reference for positioning counterweight guide rails to ensure parallel alignment and proper clearance.
Once the rails/track are installed, the brackets and fasteners must be checked and aligned to ensure secure attachment and proper rail positioning before loading.
The stair stringers provide the structural support framework for the staircase; newel posts must be anchored to or secured alongside the stringers.
Newel posts are typically installed on or adjacent to stair treads, so the treads must be in place to provide the landing surface and attachment point.
The subfloor must be prepared and leveled to provide a solid base for anchoring the newel post securely.
The handrail connects into or rests upon the newel post at the base (and often at intermediate points), so the newel must be fixed in place first to support the handrail.
Balusters typically fit between the handrail and the tread or newel base; the newel serves as an anchor or termination point for the baluster run and must be installed first.
The landing platform requires a stable foundation to support its structure and load.
The structural steel frame must be erected to provide the supporting framework onto which the landing platform is mounted.
Deck surfacing materials can only be applied after the landing platform structure is in place.
Safety barriers and handrails are installed after the platform is erected to provide edge protection and comply with safety regulations.
The comb plate is a component that attaches to or integrates with the steel frame structure; the frame must be erected first to provide the supporting structure for the comb plate.
The foundation must be poured and cured to provide a stable base for the steel frame and subsequently the comb plate assembly.
The comb plate serves as a formwork or shear connector element for the composite deck slab; the slab concrete cannot be poured until the comb plate is in place.
After the comb plate is installed and welded into position, the welds must be inspected to ensure structural integrity before any subsequent load is applied.
The comb plate component must be fabricated, cut, and delivered to site before it can be installed in the structure.
Skirt panels are typically installed after wall panels are in place because skirt panels fit at the base of walls, providing a finished transition between the wall and floor.

Floor finishing (tiles, wood, or other flooring) must be completed before skirt panels are installed because skirt panels sit on top of or against the finished floor surface to cover the expansion gap.

While painting can be done before skirt installation, typically wall finishing may touch up after skirt panels are installed to blend the joint, but this is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.

Furniture is typically placed after skirt panels are installed to avoid damaging both the furniture and the skirt panels, but this is a sequencing preference for protection rather than a physical necessity.
Any electrical outlets or data ports that will penetrate the skirt panel must have their rough-in wiring completed before the skirt panel is installed, so that cutouts can be made accurately.
Site preparation including foundation work and crane positioning must be completed before any truss stringer components can be lifted or positioned.
The main truss structure must be erected and stabilized to provide the primary frame onto which side beams (stringers) are attached.
Side beams (stringers) serve as the supporting framework for deck panels; deck panels cannot be installed until the stringers are securely in place.
Lateral cross bracing between stringers is typically installed after stringers are positioned to provide stability to the beam system.
Final connection welding and bolting of stringer-to-truss joints must be performed after the stringer components are placed and aligned.
The controller/panel must have a physical mounting surface or bracket secured to the wall or structure before it can be attached.
Conduits and cable trays must be in place to route wiring to and from the controller/panel location before the panel is mounted.
All field wiring and cable connections to the controller/panel can only be terminated after the panel is physically installed and secured.
The controller/panel must be installed and all connections made before it can be powered on and commissioned for testing.
Programming and configuration of the controller/panel require the unit to be installed and powered up to load firmware and set parameters.
The emergency stop switch must be electrically connected to the main control panel; therefore, the electrical panel must be installed and powered first to provide the necessary connection point.
After the emergency stop switch is installed, it must be verified that the switch functions correctly to cut power before any equipment power-on testing can be safely conducted.
Electrical conduits or cable trays that will carry wiring to the emergency stop switch must be installed first to allow proper routing of cables.
The emergency stop switch is a critical component of the safety system; commissioning and testing of the overall safety system can only proceed once the switch is physically installed and wired.
The emergency stop switch must be mounted on a secure bracket or support structure; therefore, the mounting hardware must be installed first to provide a stable base.

Safety sensors and switches require electrical power and wiring connections, so the electrical rough-in (wiring, conduit, and junction boxes) must be completed first to provide the necessary infrastructure.
Safety sensors and switches often need to be connected to control panels for monitoring and actuation; the control panels must be installed and operational beforehand.
After safety sensors and switches are installed, the overall system (including safety interlocks) must be commissioned and tested to verify proper functionality and compliance with safety standards.
Safety sensors and switches are critical for interlocking and emergency stop systems; they must be in place before the overall system safety verification can be performed.
Safety sensors and switches need to be mounted on structural elements (walls, frames, or equipment); the structural framing must be complete to provide secure mounting surfaces.

Step demarcation lighting is typically installed to illuminate specific features like stairs, ramps, or level changes. The striping and pavement marking must be completed first to define the boundaries and areas that require demarcation lighting, ensuring proper alignment and functionality.

Step demarcation lighting must be fully installed and operational before the final inspection and commissioning of the area can take place, as the lighting is a safety-critical component that needs to be verified.

The step or surface structure (concrete or asphalt base) must be fully installed and cured before step demarcation lighting can be mounted or embedded, providing a stable substrate for the lighting fixtures.

Electrical conduit and wiring rough-in must be completed prior to installing step demarcation lighting to provide power supply infrastructure, ensuring the lighting can be connected to the electrical system.

In some cases, final surfacing or sealcoating may be done after lighting installation to protect the area; however, this is a soft preference as it depends on the specific installation method and sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
The escalator truss must be supported by the building's structural steel frame. The steel frame provides the primary structural support and attachment points for the truss.
The escalator truss rests on or is anchored to the foundation slab and support beams. A completed base slab is required to provide the lower support and bearing surface.
The escalator truss is the structural framework that houses the step chain, tracks, and pallets. Steps and tracks cannot be installed until the truss is in place and secured.
The drive system (motor, gearbox, drive chain) is mounted on or within the truss assembly. The truss must be positioned before the drive components can be installed.
Balustrades and handrails are attached to the truss structure. The truss provides the mounting framework and must be fixed in position first.
The railing is fixed adjacent to the escalator and its positioning, alignment, and attachment points depend on the escalator being in place first.

predecessor: Structural Support Framework for Escalator Area
rationale: The railing requires a structural substrate or support framework to anchor to, which must be completed before railing installation.

successor: Final Finishing / Cladding Around Escalator Opening
rationale: Finishing work such as cladding, trim, or cosmetic covers around the escalator opening should follow railing installation to achieve a clean, integrated appearance and avoid rework.

successor: Safety Inspection and Handrail Load Testing
rationale: The railing must be installed before it can be inspected and load-tested for compliance with safety codes.
Floor finishing adjacent to the railing is typically done after railing installation to ensure a neat edge, though sequenced installation is possible with careful planning.

The escalator is a structural element that must be supported by the building's main structural frame; the frame must be in place to bear the load and provide the physical opening for the escalator shaft.
The shaft or opening through which the escalator truss will be placed must be fully constructed (including supporting steel, concrete pit, and walls) before the escalator can be installed.
The escalator unit must be physically in place before electricians can run wiring, connect motors, and install controls specific to that escalator.
Fireproofing material (e.g., intumescent coating or board) must be applied after the escalator truss and components are installed, as the fireproofing protects the installed structure.
The escalator truss and steps must be in place as the foundation before balustrades (side panels) and handrails can be mounted and aligned along the escalator.

The escalator structure must be physically installed and in place before any commissioning activities can begin, as commissioning requires power, control systems, and mechanical functionality testing of the installed equipment.
Electrical power supply connections to the escalator must be completed before commissioning can proceed, as commissioning involves testing electrical components, motors, and control systems.
All mechanical components (drive units, chains, steps, handrails) must be fully assembled and mechanically complete before commissioning can test safe and proper operation.

Commissioning must be successfully completed prior to formal handover and acceptance testing to verify that all systems operate correctly and meet performance specifications before the building owner accepts the escalator.

Commissioning must be finished before regulatory or third-party final inspection and certification can occur, as inspectors need to verify that the escalator operates safely and as designed under operational conditions.
Electrical wiring must be run to junction boxes before any lighting fixture can be connected to the power supply.
The ceiling or overhead mounting surface must be in place to provide a structural attachment point for the lighting fixture.
Switches and final trim plates are installed after the fixture is wired and mounted to ensure proper connections and alignment.
While not physically mandatory, it is preferred to perform final ceiling touch-ups after lighting installation to blend the fixture trim with the finished surface.
The fixture must be physically installed before it can be powered on and tested for correct operation.
Electrical wiring, junction boxes, and conduits must be installed in walls/ceilings before any light fixtures can be attached.
For ceiling-mounted lamps, the ceiling structure (drywall, drop ceiling grid, etc.) must be in place to provide a mounting surface.
For wall-mounted lamps/sconces, the wall surface (drywall, plaster, paneling) must be finished before fixtures can be mounted.
After the lamp/light source is mounted, trims, diffusers, and switches/controls are installed as final finishing steps.
While painting can sometimes be done before light installation, installing lamps first and then doing final touch-up painting around fixtures produces a cleaner finish.
The sub-ballast layer must be compacted and leveled before ballast can be placed, as it provides the structural foundation and drainage base for the ballast layer.
The protection layer (intermediate layer between sub-ballast and ballast) must be completed to ensure proper separation and filtration before ballast is laid.
The ballast layer must be placed and compacted to provide a stable, level bed before rails can be unloaded and distributed on the track.

After the initial ballast is dumped and driven, the ballast regulator shapes the ballast profile and the compactor consolidates it; these finishing operations logically follow the primary ballast placement.
Sleepers must be laid directly onto the prepared ballast bed, so ballast placement and tamping must precede sleeper positioning to ensure proper support and alignment.
Electrical wiring must be run to the switch box location before the switch can be installed and connected.
The electrical box housing the switch must be mounted in the wall before the switch device can be secured into it.
Wall framing provides the structural support for the switch box and must be completed before any electrical rough-in or box installation.
The switch must be wired and operational before the lighting fixture can be connected and tested for proper control.

Installing the switch first allows for neat cutouts and cover plate fitting, but finishing can be done around switches after installation if needed, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
Switch installation is part of the trim-out phase; devices must be installed before final testing of the lighting circuit can occur.
Electrical wiring must be run to the sensor location before the sensor can be physically installed and connected.
A junction box or mounting bracket must be in place to provide a secure attachment point and electrical connection for the occupancy sensor.
Surface finishing (drywall, paint, ceiling tiles) must be completed before installing the sensor so that the sensor mounts flush and finished surfaces are not damaged.
The sensor must be installed and wired before final connection of lighting fixtures that the sensor controls, as the sensor's control wiring feeds the lighting circuits.
After physical installation, the sensor must be powered on and its sensitivity, timeout, and coverage settings must be tested and calibrated to ensure proper operation.
Conduit and wiring must be run to the panel location before the panel can be installed, as the panel connects to these upstream electrical feeds.
The lighting control panel must be mounted and powered before lighting circuits can be terminated and connected to it.
The panel must be physically installed and energized before control programming and system commissioning can take place.
All lighting circuits and controls must be connected through the panel before final testing and inspection can verify proper operation.

predecessor: Structural Framing and Ceiling Grid Completion
rationale: The building structure and ceiling grid must be in place to support the panel mounting and provide clear access for installation.

Electrical rough-in work (conduit, junction boxes, and wiring pathways) must be completed before installing the daylight sensor/photocell to provide the necessary electrical infrastructure and connection points.
The ceiling grid must be in place to provide a mounting structure for the daylight sensor/photocell, as these sensors are typically mounted in or on the ceiling.

The daylight sensor/photocell must be installed first so that when lighting fixtures are connected, the sensor can be wired into the lighting control circuit to enable automatic dimming or switching based on ambient light levels.

The sensor must be physically installed before the lighting control system can be commissioned and calibrated, as commissioning involves testing sensor functionality and setting light level thresholds.

It is preferable to complete sensor installation before final ceiling finishes and trim work to avoid damage to finished surfaces during sensor mounting and wiring, though retrofit installation is possible.
Power supply wiring must be in place before exit signs can be connected and energized.
Exit signs are typically mounted to or suspended from the ceiling grid; the grid must be in place to provide mounting support.
Exit signs mounted on walls require finished wall surfaces and framing for proper attachment and alignment.
Exit signs must be physically installed before final connections are made and the system is tested for functionality.

successor: Fire alarm and life safety system commissioning
rationale: Exit signs are part of the egress and life safety systems; commissioning verifies proper operation and must occur after installation.

The building's substructure and foundation must be completed first to provide a stable base for installing the lightning conductor system, which typically connects to the building's grounding network embedded in the foundation.
The main structural frame must be erected before lightning conductor tracks (down conductors) can be installed along the building's vertical structure, as they are routed along columns or walls.
The roof structure and covering must be completed to allow installation of air termination (lightning rods) and conductor tracks on the highest points of the building.

The lightning protection system must be installed before general electrical rough-in to ensure bonding and equipotential connections between the lightning conductor and the building's electrical system are properly integrated.
The lightning conductor system must be fully installed before electrical testing and commissioning can verify continuity, resistance, and proper grounding of the lightning protection system.
The lighting diffuser or lens is typically installed into or onto the ceiling grid or support system, so the ceiling grid must be in place first.
The diffuser or lens is the final covering for a light fixture; the fixture housing must be mounted and wired before the diffuser can be snapped or screwed into place.
Electrical wiring to the light fixture must be completed and inspected before the diffuser/lens is installed, as the diffuser covers access to the fixture's internal components.
In a drop ceiling, ceiling tiles are often installed after diffusers/lenses because the diffusers are part of the ceiling plane and tiles are cut around or butted up to them.

Painting and finishing work should ideally be completed before installing diffusers to avoid dust and overspray, but if diffusers are already installed they must be protected; it's a soft preference to complete painting first.
The structural frame must be in place to provide support and attachment points for reflector, baffle, or louver components.
Reflectors and baffles often house or shield lighting fixtures; electrical wiring must be run after the supporting hardware is in place to ensure proper routing and clearance.
Reflectors, baffles, and louvers are typically installed as part of or in support of lighting fixtures; the fixture itself is placed after or concurrently with the reflector assembly.
A ceiling grid or overhead mounting system must be in place to suspend or secure reflectors, baffles, or louvers.

After installation of reflectors, baffles, or louvers, the system should be inspected and tested for alignment, light distribution, and performance, though this is a quality assurance preference rather than a physical necessity.
The conduit or tubing must be physically supported by the mounting bracket/hanger before it can be attached to it.
Wiring/cables are typically routed through or along the bracket after the bracket is fixed in place.
The position and location for the bracket must be marked and planned before the bracket can be physically mounted.
The structural surface (stud, joist, wall, ceiling) must be in place to provide an anchor for the bracket or hanger.
Any supported device, fixture, or equipment (e.g., light fixture, HVAC unit) must have the bracket installed first to rest upon or attach to it.
Conduit must be installed before junction boxes can be mounted, as the junction box connects to and is supported by the conduit system.

successor: Run Lighting Wiring Through Junction Box
rationale: Wiring must pass through the junction box, so the box must be mounted first to serve as the routing and connection point.
Light fixtures connect directly to the junction box for power supply and support, so the junction box must be in place first.
The lighting circuit rough-in (including breaker panel preparation and circuit routing) must be established before individual junction boxes are installed on that circuit.
The switch wiring typically passes through or is connected to a junction box; the box must be installed before switch wiring connections can be completed.
Conduits must be installed in walls, ceilings, or slabs before lighting circuit cables can be pulled through them.
Junction boxes, switch boxes, and outlet boxes must be mounted in place before lighting feeder cables can be terminated into them.
Lighting fixtures cannot be connected and installed until the lighting circuit feeder cables are in place and terminated at the junction boxes.
Switches and dimmers require the lighting feeder circuit to be run to their locations before they can be wired and installed.
The lighting feeder circuit must be completely installed before any continuity, insulation resistance, or operational testing can be performed.
Electrical rough-in (wiring, junction boxes, conduit) must be installed before lighting fixtures can be connected and mounted.

predecessor: Install Ceiling Grid / Drywall Ceiling Finish
rationale: The ceiling structure or finished ceiling surface must be in place to provide the mounting surface and support for lighting fixtures.
Fixtures must be physically installed before they can be energized, tested, and commissioned for proper operation.
It is a soft preference to install lighting after ceiling painting/trim work to avoid damage to finished surfaces, but it can be done in reverse order with careful protection.
Soft preference: lighting is typically done before finished flooring to avoid dropped fixtures or debris damaging floors, but not a physical necessity.
Lighting controls are typically mounted on or within the ceiling grid; the grid must be in place to provide structural support and a mounting surface for the lighting fixtures and controls.

Electrical conduits, wiring, and junction boxes must be roughed-in before lighting controls can be connected; the controls cannot be installed without the underlying electrical infrastructure in place.
Ceiling tiles are installed after lighting controls because the controls need to be accessible for wiring and adjustment; installing tiles first would block access to the controls above the ceiling.
The lighting controls must be fully installed before the lighting system can be tested and commissioned; testing validates that the controls function correctly.
Although lighting fixtures can sometimes be installed before controls, it is preferred to install controls first so that wiring connections to fixtures can be made efficiently and without rework.

Emergency lighting requires power supply from the building's electrical system; conduit and wiring must be installed to provide the electrical pathways and connections needed for the emergency lighting units.

predecessor: Install Emergency Lighting Power Supply / Battery Backup
rationale: Emergency lighting units require a dedicated power source or battery backup system; this power supply must be installed and connected before the lighting fixtures themselves can be mounted and wired.
Rough-in electrical work (including mounting boxes, pulling cables, and installing conduits) must be completed before final fixture installation, including emergency lighting, can proceed.
Emergency lighting must be fully installed and connected before testing and commissioning can verify proper operation, battery charge, illumination levels, and code compliance.
Ceiling finishes are typically installed after emergency lighting fixtures are mounted in or on the ceiling to avoid damage to finishes and allow proper fixture alignment and wiring connections.
All lighting fixtures must be physically installed before they can be tested and commissioned to ensure they are functional and properly connected.
Lighting control systems (dimmers, sensors, switches, control panels) must be installed before commissioning to verify proper operation and integration with fixtures.
Electrical wiring, conduits, and connections must be roughed-in and terminated before lighting can be powered and commissioned.
While finishing work can proceed alongside commissioning, any touch-ups or final adjustments to finishes may be delayed until after lighting is verified to avoid rework.
The lighting system must be fully commissioned, tested, and verified operational before the building or space can be turned over for occupancy and use.
Task lighting fixtures are typically mounted on or suspended from ceilings, so the ceiling structure must be in place to provide support and attachment points.
The electrical conduit, junction boxes, and wiring must be roughed in before task lighting fixtures can be connected and installed.
Task lighting fixtures must be installed before the ceiling is finished so that wiring connections are accessible and fixtures are integrated seamlessly.

successor: Lighting Fixture Trim and Diffuser Installation
rationale: The main fixture body must be mounted first, then trim pieces, lenses, or diffusers can be attached as final finishing.
Task lighting must be fully installed and connected before the building can be commissioned and tested for occupancy readiness.
Electrical power supply must be roughed in and available before any lighting fixtures can be installed and connected.
The structural supports, brackets, or mounting hardware for display/accent lighting must be in place before the lighting fixtures can be attached.
Drywall, plaster, paint, or other wall/ceiling finishes must be completed before installing accent lighting fixtures to avoid damage to finished surfaces.
All accent/display lighting must be installed and connected before the final electrical trim-out, switch installation, and system testing can be completed.
While accent lighting can be installed before final decorations, it's preferred to have lighting operational to highlight displays accurately, but not a hard structural dependency.
Electrical wiring and junction boxes must be installed and routed to the ceiling locations before recessed downlights can be physically mounted and connected.
The ceiling structure and finished drywall must be in place to provide the mounting surface and opening for the recessed light housing.
The main housing (can) must be installed in the ceiling first before the decorative trim ring and light bulb can be inserted and secured.
The downlight housing must be in place so that the ceiling can be painted around it and any gaps can be properly finished for a seamless appearance.

successor: Electrical Fixture Trim and Switch Plate Installation
rationale: Downlights must be installed and connected before final trim-out work and before switch plates can be installed to complete the circuit.

predecessor: Install ceiling electrical rough-in (junction boxes & wiring)
rationale: Power supply and junction boxes must be in place before surface-mount luminaires can be connected and mounted.
Surface-mount luminaires are attached to the finished ceiling surface; ceiling must be framed and boarded to provide a mounting substrate.
Luminaires must be mounted and wired before lamps can be inserted and the circuit tested for functionality.
It is preferable to complete painting before installing luminaires to avoid paint splatter on fixtures, but touch-up work after installation is possible if needed.
Lighting must be fully installed and operational before the space can be occupied or handed over to the client.

predecessor: Install ceiling electrical box and wiring
rationale: The pendant luminaire requires an electrical power source; the ceiling electrical box and wiring must be in place to provide electricity and a mounting point.
Ceiling finishing must be done before installing the pendant luminaire to avoid damaging finished surfaces and to ensure the luminaire sits flush against a finished ceiling.
The pendant luminaire must be physically installed before the lighting circuit can be energized and tested for proper operation.
All installed fixtures, including pendant luminaires, must be in place before the final inspection can verify compliance with specifications.
Aesthetic trim around the pendant base is typically installed after the luminaire is hung, though in some sequences it can be pre-fitted if access is available.
Electrical wiring and junction boxes must be installed and roughed-in within the wall before the sconce can be mounted and connected.
The wall structure must be framed to provide a mounting surface and cavity for the sconce electrical box and wiring.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and finished (mudded and sanded) around the electrical box so the sconce has a finished wall surface to mount against.
After the sconce is physically mounted and wired, final trim-out (e.g., bulbs, covers) and electrical testing/energizing can be performed.

While painting is typically done before fixture installation, any minor touch-up painting around the sconce after installation may be needed to achieve a flawless finish, but this is a soft preference.
Electrical supply cables and junction boxes must be installed in the ceiling before strip light fixtures can be mounted and connected.
Strip lights are typically suspended from or recessed into the ceiling grid; the grid structure must be in place to support the fixtures.
Fixtures must be physically mounted before final electrical connections can be made and the lighting circuit can be energized and tested.
Strip lights are often installed flush with or integrated into the ceiling finish; completing the ceiling finish after fixture installation ensures proper alignment and fit.

successor: Final commissioning and lighting control setup
rationale: While physically possible to configure controls earlier, best practice is to commission and program lighting controls after all fixtures are installed to ensure consistent performance.
The structural steel frame must be in place to provide mounting points and support for high-bay/low-bay luminaires, which are typically suspended from or attached to the steel structure.
Overhead cranes must be installed first because they occupy the same overhead space; luminaire installation after crane installation ensures safe access and avoids interference.
Electrical conduit and rough-in wiring must be run to the luminaire locations before the fixtures themselves can be installed and connected.
In areas with ceilings, luminaires should be installed before ceiling finish work to allow for proper positioning and electrical connections; however, in open high-bay structures this may not apply.

successor: Final commissioning and lighting control setup
rationale: Luminaires must be physically installed before they can be tested, commissioned, and integrated with lighting control systems.
The site must be graded, leveled, and cleared before any landscape lighting can be installed. Underground conduits and trenching for exterior lighting are part of site preparation.
Electrical conduits, junction boxes, and power supply lines for exterior lighting must be roughed in and buried underground before lighting fixtures can be connected and installed.
Concrete slabs, footings, and foundation walls must be completed because exterior lighting poles, bollards, or wall-mounted fixtures often attach to or are anchored in foundation elements.
Wall-mounted exterior light fixtures are installed after exterior wall finishes are complete to ensure proper sealing, weatherproofing, and aesthetic alignment with finished surfaces.

Final landscaping (topsoil, sod, plants, decorative stone) must be placed after exterior lighting and its wiring are fully installed to avoid disturbing or damaging underground cables and fixture bases.
Conduit and raceways must be installed to provide a physical pathway for pulling the lighting control bus and communication cables through walls, ceilings, and floors.
Ceiling grids must be in place to support and route the lighting control bus cables above the finished ceiling.
Lighting control bus cables must be run and terminated to each fixture location before the lighting fixtures can be connected to the control network.
The physical bus and communication cabling must be installed and terminated before the lighting control panel can be commissioned and programmed to communicate with connected devices.
The entire bus and communication cable infrastructure must be complete before end-to-end testing of lighting control signals and system commissioning can be performed.

successor: Control Panel / Fire Alarm Control Unit (FACU)
rationale: Conduits and electrical rough-in must be completed to provide the pathway and power feed for the FACU.

predecessor: Fire Alarm Device Installation (Detectors, Pull Stations, Notification Appliances)
successor: Control Panel / Fire Alarm Control Unit (FACU)
rationale: All field devices (smoke detectors, heat detectors, pull stations, horns, strobes) must be installed and wired back to the panel before the FACU can be fully connected and commissioned.

predecessor: Control Panel / Fire Alarm Control Unit (FACU)
successor: Fire Alarm System Programming and Configuration
rationale: The FACU must be physically installed and powered before programming, addressing, and system configuration can be performed.

predecessor: Control Panel / Fire Alarm Control Unit (FACU)
successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: All devices and the panel must be installed and programmed before end-to-end system testing, verification, and commissioning can occur.

predecessor: Control Panel / Fire Alarm Control Unit (FACU)
successor: Fire Alarm System Acceptance / AHJ Inspection
rationale: The fully installed, programmed, and tested FACU must be in place and operational before the Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ) can perform final inspection and acceptance.
Electrical wiring and boxes must be installed before smoke detectors can be connected and mounted.
Smoke detectors are typically mounted on ceilings, so the ceiling must be installed first to provide a mounting surface.
Smoke detectors are part of the final electrical trim-out, and all detectors must be installed and wired before final connections and cover plates are installed.

successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: All smoke detectors must be installed before the fire alarm system can be tested and commissioned to ensure proper operation.
While painting can be done carefully around detectors, it is preferable to complete painting before installing detectors to avoid overspray and contamination of the sensor.
The base must be physically mounted before the heat detector unit can be attached.

predecessor: Run Wiring for Fire Alarm System
rationale: Electrical wiring must be installed and terminated at the detector location before the heat detector can be connected and powered.
Conduit must be in place to protect and route wiring before the heat detector can be wired.
The heat detector must be fully installed before it can be functionally tested for proper operation.
All heat detectors must be installed as part of the fire alarm system before the overall system commissioning can proceed.

predecessor: Mount backbox / flush mounting plate for pull station
successor: Install Manual Pull Station (Manual Call Point)
rationale: The backbox or mounting plate must be securely installed to provide a stable base and electrical enclosure before the pull station unit can be attached.

predecessor: Run conduit and wiring to pull station location
successor: Install Manual Pull Station (Manual Call Point)
rationale: Electrical conduit and alarm circuit wiring must be routed to the location to allow connection of the pull station's internal contacts.

predecessor: Install Manual Pull Station (Manual Call Point)
successor: Connect pull station wiring to fire alarm control panel
rationale: After physical installation, the station must be electrically connected to the fire alarm system so it can signal an alarm when activated.

predecessor: Install Manual Pull Station (Manual Call Point)
successor: Test manual pull station activation and alarm response
rationale: Testing must occur after installation and wiring to verify that pulling the station triggers the correct alarm sequence.

predecessor: Install Manual Pull Station (Manual Call Point)
successor: Install protective cover or signage (if required)
rationale: Protective covers and signage are typically added after installation to prevent accidental activation and clearly mark the station, but this is a soft preference as they could be installed concurrently.
The back box or mounting plate must be securely installed before the notification appliance (strobe/horn/speaker) can be attached.

predecessor: Rough-in Electrical Conduit and Cabling to Appliance Location
rationale: Electrical power and fire alarm signaling cables must be pulled to the appliance location before the device can be connected and mounted.
The appliance must be physically installed and wired before it can be functionally tested for proper audio/visual output.
All notification appliances must be installed and connected before the overall fire alarm system can be commissioned and certified.

While it is preferable to install notification appliances before final finishes so they can be properly integrated, in some sequences the appliance can be retrofitted after finishes if trim rings are used.

The fire alarm bell/sounder is a field device that connects to and receives signals from the fire alarm control panel; the panel must be installed and operational to provide power and control signals to the sounder.
Electrical conduits and wiring pathways must be run to the bell/sounder location before the device can be physically mounted and connected.
The fire alarm bell/sounder is typically mounted on finished walls or ceilings; mounting before finishing would require removal or result in damage during finishing work.

successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: All fire alarm notification devices (bells/sounders) must be installed and connected before the overall system can be tested and commissioned for proper operation and audibility.
Fire alarm notification devices must be fully installed and operational before a building can receive final occupancy approval and be handed over for use, as they are critical life safety systems.
Electrical conduit and wiring must be run to the mounting location before the visual alarm/strobe device can be physically connected and installed.
The mounting bracket or backplate must be secured to the wall/ceiling before the strobe light unit can be attached to it.
It is preferred to complete surface finishing before installing the alarm device to avoid damage to the device or the need for masking/protection.

successor: Visual alarm system testing and commissioning
rationale: The strobe light must be physically installed before the alarm system can be tested to verify proper operation, strobe synchronization, and coverage.
If the strobe light is recessed into a ceiling tile, the tile should be installed after the device to allow proper alignment and fit.

successor: Addressable Device Module / Loop Interface Installation
rationale: The backbox or enclosure must be installed first to provide the physical mounting surface and containment for the Addressable Device Module / Loop Interface.

successor: Addressable Device Module / Loop Interface Installation
rationale: Cabling infrastructure (trays, conduits) must be in place to route the loop cables to the module location before the module can be connected.

predecessor: Addressable Device Module / Loop Interface Installation
successor: Loop Cable Termination and Continuity Testing
rationale: The module must be physically installed and ready before its loop cables can be terminated and tested for continuity.

predecessor: Addressable Device Module / Loop Interface Installation
rationale: The module must be installed and wired before it can be addressed and integrated into the fire alarm system during commissioning.

predecessor: Addressable Device Module / Loop Interface Installation
successor: Device Loop Power-Up and Functional Testing
rationale: Power cannot be applied and loop devices tested until the module is correctly installed and connections are verified.
The Conventional Detector Zone Module must be housed within an enclosure or cabinet; therefore the cabinet must be mounted first.

predecessor: Run fire alarm cabling to zone module location
rationale: Cables must be pulled and terminated at the module's location before the module can be connected and installed.

successor: Connect detection loop wiring to zone module terminals
rationale: The zone module must be physically installed and secured before its terminals can be wired to the detection loop devices.

successor: Configure zone addressing and sensitivity settings
rationale: Configuration and programming of the zone module can only occur after the module is installed and powered.

successor: Test zone continuity and end-of-line monitoring
rationale: Functional testing of the zone requires the module to be installed and all wiring connected.
Conduit and electrical pathways must be installed before backup battery units can be placed and connected to the building's electrical system.
Backup battery units must be installed and in place before final electrical connections, terminations, and trim-out can be completed.
A level, cured concrete pad or slab is required to support the weight of backup battery cabinets/power supply units.
Backup power systems must be physically installed before they can be commissioned, tested, and verified for proper operation.
Backup battery/power supply must be operational to support integrated life safety systems during testing and eventual occupancy.
Electrical rough-in wiring must be completed before the fire alarm control panel enclosure can be installed, as the conduit and wiring pathways need to be in place to feed into the enclosure.
The wall or structural surface where the enclosure will be mounted must be prepared (e.g., framing, drywall, or concrete finished) to provide a stable mounting surface.

successor: Fire Alarm Device Wiring and Termination
rationale: The control panel enclosure must be installed first to serve as the central hub for terminating all fire alarm device wiring (detectors, pull stations, horns/strobes, etc.).

The enclosure must be mounted and secured before installing the internal electronic components (motherboard, CPU, power supply, etc.) to protect them from dust and damage during preceding construction activities.

successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: The control panel enclosure and its internal components must be fully installed before the system can be powered up, programmed, and tested/commissioned.
The detector base requires a stable and level foundation to ensure proper alignment and structural integrity.
The detector must be mounted onto its base; the base must be secured first to provide a support structure.
Cables and wires are routed through or connected to the detector base before the main detector body is attached.
The installation area must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before placing the detector base.
After positioning the base, it must be anchored or bolted to the foundation to ensure stability before further assembly.
The annunciator panel requires a secure mounting surface; the backbox or mounting panel must be installed and ready before the annunciator unit can be attached.
Electrical conduit or cable pathways must be routed to the annunciator location before wiring can be pulled and terminated to the panel.

predecessor: Fire alarm system control panel installation and configuration
rationale: The remote annunciator communicates with the main fire alarm control panel (FACP); the FACP must be in place, programmed, and operational so the annunciator can be properly connected and tested.

predecessor: Annunciator Panel (Remote Annunciator) installation and wiring
rationale: The annunciator must be fully installed, wired, and terminated before the overall fire alarm system can be commissioned and functionally tested.

predecessor: Annunciator Panel (Remote Annunciator) installation and wiring
rationale: Final labeling of zones/indicators and close-out inspection are typically performed after the annunciator is installed; this is a soft preference because labeling could theoretically be done concurrently but is more accurately done after installation.
Duct smoke detectors are installed within HVAC ductwork; the ducts must be in place before the detectors can be mounted inside them.
Power and control wiring must be run to the detector location before the detector can be connected and terminated.
Duct smoke detectors must be installed and operational before the HVAC system can be balanced and tested to ensure they function properly under airflow conditions.
The duct smoke detector must be physically installed and wired before it can be integrated into the building's fire alarm system and undergo commissioning tests.
Duct smoke detectors installed within ductwork above ceilings must be in place before ceilings are closed to allow access for installation and inspection.
Power and communication wiring must be in place before the beam detector can be mounted and connected.
The beam detector's transmitter and receiver units require a stable mounting surface (e.g., ceiling or wall) to be installed and aligned.

successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: The beam detector must be installed and wired before the overall fire alarm system can be tested and commissioned.
After physical installation, the projected beam requires precise optical alignment and sensitivity calibration before it can be placed into service.
Rough-in electrical back boxes and conduit stubs must be in place at the planned beam detector locations prior to device installation.
Flame detectors require electrical power and signal wiring; conduit and cabling must be in place before the detector can be connected and mounted.
Flame detectors must be mounted on a secure bracket or base, which must be installed first to provide physical support.
After physical installation, the detector must be tested and calibrated to ensure proper sensitivity and coverage before being placed into service.
The flame detector must be installed and wired before it can be integrated into the larger fire alarm or safety system for commissioning.
Conduit and electrical wiring must be installed before ASD devices can be connected and powered.
ASD sampling points are typically mounted in or above ceiling tiles; the ceiling structure must be in place to support detector placement.
ASD units must be physically mounted before final electrical connections and terminations can be completed.

successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: ASD devices must be installed and wired before the overall fire alarm system can be commissioned, tested, and verified.
While ASD access panels are required, ceiling finishing is typically done after ASD installation to allow access for adjustments; this is a soft preference for construction sequencing efficiency.
Electrical power supply wiring must be run to the detector location before the detector can be connected and mounted.
The gas detector must be physically installed and wired before final termination and trim-out of electrical devices can be completed.
The detector must be installed before the commissioning team can test and calibrate the gas detection system.
A mounting bracket or junction box must be in place to support and house the wiring connections for the gas detector.
Conduit or cable tray must be installed to provide the pathway for electrical cables feeding the gas detector.
The control panel must be mounted to provide a stable surface and physical connection point for the interface relay/control module.
Control wiring must be run and terminated before the relay/control module can be connected to the control system.
The power supply must be installed and energized to provide the necessary electrical power for the relay/control module to operate.
The relay/control module must be installed and connected before the control system can be functionally tested.
The interface relay/control module must be fully installed and verified before the electrical system can be commissioned as a whole.
Electrical power and control wiring must be roughed in and conduits run to the door frame or ceiling location before the magnetic door holder can be physically installed and connected.
The door frame must be set and secured in place so the magnetic door holder can be mounted to the frame or adjacent wall/floor surface.
For ceiling-mounted magnetic door holders, the ceiling grid or structure must be in place to provide a mounting point and support for the device.
The magnetic door holder must be installed before the door is hung so that the door can be aligned with the magnet plate, and the strike or armature can be properly positioned on the door leaf.

successor: Fire Alarm / Life Safety System Integration & Testing
rationale: The magnetic door holder must be installed and wired so that the fire alarm system can control it (release on alarm), and subsequent integration testing verifies door release functionality.

successor: Fire Alarm System Ground Fault / Surge Protector
rationale: The fire alarm panel must be installed and operational before adding ground fault and surge protection devices, as these protect the panel and its circuits.

predecessor: Fire Alarm System Wiring and Cabling
successor: Fire Alarm System Ground Fault / Surge Protector
rationale: Wiring and cabling for the fire alarm system must be run to the panel location before the ground fault / surge protector can be connected to protect those circuits.

successor: Fire Alarm System Ground Fault / Surge Protector
rationale: Main electrical power must be available to the fire alarm panel area before installing a surge protector, as the surge protector is wired into the power feed.

predecessor: Fire Alarm System Ground Fault / Surge Protector
successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: Ground fault and surge protection devices must be installed and connected before the full system can be commissioned and tested, to ensure all devices are protected during testing.

predecessor: Fire Alarm System Ground Fault / Surge Protector
successor: Fire Alarm System Final Acceptance and Inspection
rationale: The surge protector and ground fault protection must be in place prior to final inspection to verify code compliance and proper operation of the fire alarm system.

predecessor: Installation of Fire Alarm System Devices and Panels
successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: All fire alarm components (detectors, panels, pull stations, horns, strobes) must be physically installed and wired before they can be tested or commissioned.

predecessor: Electrical Power Supply Connection to Fire Alarm Panel
successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: The fire alarm system requires electrical power to operate; the panel and devices must be energized before any testing can be performed.

predecessor: Cable Pulling and Termination for Fire Alarm System
successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: All signaling and control cables must be pulled, terminated, and continuity checked before the system can be functionally tested.

predecessor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
successor: Final Inspection and Handover of Fire Alarm System
rationale: Successful testing and commissioning must be completed and documented before the system is formally inspected and handed over to the client or authority having jurisdiction.

predecessor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
successor: Integration Testing with Other Building Systems (e.g., HVAC, Elevators, Suppression)
rationale: Fire alarm system must be verified as functioning correctly on its own before it can be used to trigger other building systems such as smoke control, elevator recall, or fire suppression activation.

successor: Installation of Fire Alarm Devices and Cabling
rationale: Electrical rough-in (conduits, backboxes, wiring paths) must be in place before fire alarm devices and cabling can be installed.

successor: Installation of Fire Alarm Devices and Cabling
rationale: Overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins must be completed to clear the ceiling space for fire alarm cable trays and device mounting.

predecessor: Installation of Fire Alarm Devices and Cabling
successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: Fire alarm devices and cabling must be physically installed before they can be tested, programmed, and commissioned as a functioning system.

predecessor: Installation of Fire Alarm Devices and Cabling
rationale: Fire alarm devices such as smoke detectors and sounders are typically mounted on or through ceilings; ceiling panels/finishes must go in after the devices and cabling are in place to avoid rework.

predecessor: Installation of Fire Alarm Devices and Cabling
rationale: Fire alarm cabling must be run and devices mounted before final terminations at the fire alarm control panel and final trim-out of the electrical system can be completed.

predecessor: Fire Alarm System Final Acceptance and Inspection
successor: Cable Pulling and Conduit Installation for Fire Alarm
rationale: The design and layout of the fire alarm system must be finalized and approved to determine the routing of conduits and cables before installation can commence.

successor: Cable Pulling and Conduit Installation for Fire Alarm
rationale: Structural work such as walls, ceilings, and floor slabs must be in place before conduits can be embedded, mounted, or routed through building cavities.

predecessor: Cable Pulling and Conduit Installation for Fire Alarm
successor: Fire Alarm Device Installation (Detectors, Horns, Strobes, Panels)
rationale: Conduits must be installed and cables pulled first to provide the pathways and wiring needed to connect and mount fire alarm devices.

predecessor: Cable Pulling and Conduit Installation for Fire Alarm
successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: All conduit and cabling work must be complete before the system can be energized, tested, and commissioned for proper functionality.

predecessor: Cable Pulling and Conduit Installation for Fire Alarm
rationale: Conduits and cables must be installed and inspected before walls and ceilings are closed up with drywall or finishes to avoid rework and ensure code compliance.

Electrical rough-in work (conduit, wiring, and junction boxes) must be completed before the security control panel can be installed, as the panel requires power and communication cabling to be in place.

The wall or column where the security control panel/annunciator is mounted must be framed and finished (or at least structurally ready) to provide a secure mounting surface before the panel can be attached.
The control panel must be installed and powered before field security devices (cameras, card readers, motion sensors) can be cabled back to it and terminated at the panel.
The panel hardware must be physically installed before any software programming, configuration, and system-level testing can begin.
All security system components must be installed and operational before the final inspection and commissioning of the security system can be completed.
The door contact sensor is typically mounted on or within the door frame; the frame must be installed first to provide the structural mounting surface.

The door contact sensor requires electrical wiring (or low-voltage cabling) to connect to the security/alarm panel; this wiring must be routed before the sensor can be physically connected and installed.
The security system panel must have the sensor physically connected before it can be programmed, tested, and integrated into the alarm system.
Installing trim and finishes after the sensor allows for clean integration and concealing of wiring, but this is a soft preference for aesthetic and ease-of-access reasons, not a physical necessity.
The door contact sensor consists of two parts (sensor on frame, magnet on door); the door must be hung to properly align and secure the magnet component on the door leaf.
Electrical wiring must be run to the sensor location before the sensor can be physically mounted and connected to power.
The sensor must be mounted onto a secured junction box that provides the electrical connection point.
The sensor is typically mounted on a wall or ceiling surface, so the structural framing must be in place to support it.
The sensor must be physically installed before the security system can be fully tested and commissioned to verify proper detection and signal transmission.

successor: Install trim and finishes (paint, ceiling tiles)
rationale: Finishing work should ideally be done after sensor installation to avoid damaging the sensor or obstructing its field of view, though some finishing may be done before with careful masking.
Glass break detectors require electrical power and/or signal wiring to function; wiring infrastructure must be in place before the detector can be connected and mounted.
The glass break detector must be physically secured to a properly installed bracket or electrical box for stable mounting and code compliance.

The glass break detector senses the acoustic signature of breaking glass; the glass it monitors must be installed and in place before the detector can be positioned and calibrated to the correct sensitivity.
System commissioning and testing (including functional alarm tests) can only proceed after all detection devices, including glass break detectors, are physically installed and connected.

While not physically required, it is preferable to install the detector after finishes to avoid dirt/debris damage, or before if surface-mounting on finished walls; typically a soft preference based on construction sequencing.
The electronic/magnetic lock must be mounted on or integrated into the door frame/door leaf, so the door must be installed first.
Electronic/magnetic locks require electrical power and control wiring; rough-in electrical work (conduit, wiring, junction boxes) must be completed before the lock can be connected and terminated.

Cabling for the access control system (e.g., reader cables, door position switch cables, request-to-exit device cables) must be run to the door location before the lock and associated devices are installed.
The lock must be physically installed and wired before the access control system can be tested, programmed, and commissioned to ensure proper lock/unlock functionality.

successor: Door Hardware Trim Adjustment & Final Finishing
rationale: After the electronic lock is installed, final adjustments to trim, strike plates, and alignment can be made, and any finishing work (paint, touch-ups) around the lock can be completed.
Power and data cables must be run through conduits to the card reader location before the reader can be physically mounted and connected.
The backbox or mounting plate must be secured to the wall or structure to provide a stable mounting surface for the card reader.
The door and frame must be in place so that the card reader can be positioned correctly relative to the door entry point.

successor: Wiring and Termination to Access Control Panel
rationale: After the reader is mounted, the signal and power wires must be terminated and connected to the access control panel for communication.
The card reader must be physically installed and wired before the access control system can be programmed to recognize it and test its functionality.
The biometric scanner requires a stable, clean mounting surface (wall, door frame, or kiosk) with pre-installed anchors to support the device securely.
Power wiring and conduit must be run to the scanner location before the unit can be physically connected and mounted.

predecessor: Network cabling and data drop installation
rationale: The scanner requires a network connection (Ethernet/Wi-Fi backbone) for communication with the access control system; cabling must be terminated before the device can be connected.
Physical installation must be completed before power can be applied and the device can be configured with firmware, network settings, and user enrollment.
The scanner must be physically in place and connected before system-level testing of door locks, authentication workflows, and alarm interfaces can proceed.
Power and control wiring must be run in the walls and ceiling before the exit device can be connected and installed.
The door frame must be in place to mount the exit device hardware onto the door and frame.
The door must be hung before the exit device (push bar, touchpad, or request-to-exit sensor) can be mounted on it.

successor: Fire Alarm / Life Safety System Integration & Testing
rationale: The exit device must be installed and wired before it can be tested as part of the integrated fire alarm and life safety system to ensure proper release and alarm signaling.
The request-to-exit device must be in place and connected before the full access control system can be programmed and commissioned to handle exit requests.
The security camera must be physically attached to a mounting bracket or junction box that is already securely installed to the wall or ceiling.
Power and data cables (e.g., Ethernet, coax, power lines) must be run and terminated at the camera location before the camera can be connected and mounted.
A dedicated power source or Power over Ethernet (PoE) switch must be installed and energized to provide electricity to the camera.
The camera must be physically installed before it can be powered on, configured, assigned an IP address, and integrated with the video management system (VMS).

successor: Cable Management and Cover Plate Installation
rationale: After the camera is mounted and connected, it is good practice to tidy and secure excess cables and attach trim rings or cover plates for aesthetics and protection.

successor: Digital Video Recorder (DVR) / Network Video Recorder (NVR)
rationale: DVR/NVR must be installed and operational before CCTV cameras can be connected and configured to record.

successor: Digital Video Recorder (DVR) / Network Video Recorder (NVR)
rationale: Network and power cabling to the DVR/NVR location must be run before the unit can be mounted, powered, and connected to the network.

successor: Digital Video Recorder (DVR) / Network Video Recorder (NVR)
rationale: Electrical power supply must be available at the installation location before the DVR/NVR can be powered on and commissioned.

predecessor: Digital Video Recorder (DVR) / Network Video Recorder (NVR)
rationale: The DVR/NVR must be installed, powered, and configured before the overall video surveillance system can be commissioned, tested, and calibrated.

predecessor: Digital Video Recorder (DVR) / Network Video Recorder (NVR)
rationale: The DVR/NVR hardware must be in place and operational before video management software can be installed, configured, and integrated with the recording hardware.
The site must be cleared and graded to establish the proper perimeter boundaries and ensure a stable foundation for fence posts and gate installation.
Underground utility lines must be identified and marked before digging fence post holes to avoid damaging existing utilities.

successor: Sensor Calibration and Security System Testing
rationale: The fence and gate with integrated sensors must be fully installed before the sensors can be calibrated and the security system tested.
Landscaping work such as planting and mulching is typically done after fencing is complete to avoid damaging the fence, though this is a soft preference for workflow efficiency.
Access control systems (card readers, keypads, intercoms) are mounted on or integrated with the gate, so the gate must be installed before access control hardware can be fitted and configured.
The electrical wiring and conduit must be run to the alarm button locations before the buttons themselves can be physically installed and connected.
The alarm buttons are typically mounted on walls, so the wall framing and sheathing must be in place to provide a mounting surface.

successor: Alarm system wiring and control panel connection
rationale: After the button is physically mounted, it must be wired into the alarm system's control panel and integrated into the overall security system.
The full alarm system including panic/duress buttons must be tested after installation to verify functionality, signal transmission, and proper response protocols.

While the button is typically installed after wall finishing for aesthetics, it can be roughed in beforehand; however, standard practice is to finish walls first to avoid damage to the button during finishing work.
Conduits and raceways must be installed in walls, ceilings, and floors before security cables can be pulled through them. This is a physical necessity for cable routing.
Power sources and electrical boxes need to be in place to supply power to security system components. Security cabling often runs alongside or near electrical wiring.

predecessor: Overhead and In-Wall Rough-In Work Completion
rationale: All ceiling, wall, and floor rough-in work (e.g., HVAC ductwork, plumbing, general electrical) should be completed before low-voltage security cabling is installed to avoid damage or interference.
Cables must be pulled and terminated at device locations before security devices (cameras, sensors, keypads, control panels) can be physically mounted and connected.
Cabling must be installed behind walls and in ceilings before those surfaces are enclosed with drywall and finished with paint. This avoids costly retrofitting and damage to finishes.

successor: Install Intrusion Detection Wiring and Sensors
