rationale: Electrical rough-in (conduit, junction boxes, and power supply wiring) must be completed before intrusion detection wiring can be run, as the detection system's wiring often shares pathways and needs power available at termination points.

predecessor: Complete Overhead MEP Rough-In (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing)
successor: Install Intrusion Detection Wiring and Sensors
rationale: All overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be complete so that the intrusion detection wiring can be installed without interference and without needing to work around or after overhead obstructions.

predecessor: Install Ceiling Grid and Above-Ceiling Infrastructure
successor: Install Intrusion Detection Wiring and Sensors
rationale: While wiring can sometimes be pulled before ceilings are fully closed, installing the ceiling grid first provides a stable platform and clear access pathways for sensor wiring; however, this is a soft preference as some installations run wiring before ceiling grid completion.

predecessor: Install Intrusion Detection Wiring and Sensors
rationale: Intrusion detection wiring and sensors must be placed within walls and ceilings before those surfaces are enclosed with drywall and finished; once finishes are applied, accessing and installing the wiring would require destructive rework.

predecessor: Install Intrusion Detection Wiring and Sensors
successor: Commission and Test Intrusion Detection System
rationale: The wiring and physical sensors must be fully installed before the system can be powered on, configured, and tested to verify proper operation and coverage.

successor: Install Access Control Hardware and Cabling
rationale: Access control hardware requires electrical power and conduit pathways; conduit and backboxes must be in place before access control devices and cabling can be installed.

successor: Install Access Control Hardware and Cabling
rationale: Rough-in inspections must be completed and approved before covering access control cabling with final connections and devices.

predecessor: Install Access Control Hardware and Cabling
successor: Install Access Control Panels and Controllers
rationale: Field devices (readers, locks, request-to-exit sensors) and their cabling must be installed first so they can be connected to the control panels and controllers.

predecessor: Install Access Control Hardware and Cabling
successor: Commission and Test Access Control System
rationale: All access control hardware and cabling must be physically installed before the system can be powered on, programmed, and tested for proper operation.

predecessor: Install Access Control Hardware and Cabling
successor: Install Finish Flooring and Wall Finishes
rationale: While not a physical necessity in all cases, it is a preferred sequencing to install access control hardware and cabling before final finishes to avoid damaging finished surfaces during installation.

successor: Install CCTV Cameras and Recording Equipment
rationale: Electrical rough-in (conduit, wiring, backboxes) must be in place before CCTV cameras and recording equipment can be mounted and connected to power and network cables.

successor: Install CCTV Cameras and Recording Equipment
rationale: Ceiling and wall finishes (drywall, painting, ceiling tiles) must be completed before camera mounting to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to ensure correct final placement.

predecessor: Complete Network Cabling and Structured Cabling
successor: Install CCTV Cameras and Recording Equipment
rationale: Network/data cabling (Cat6/coaxial) must be run and terminated before cameras can be connected to the network and the recording system.

predecessor: Install CCTV Cameras and Recording Equipment
rationale: The cameras and recording equipment must be physically installed before they can be powered on, configured, tested, and commissioned for operation.

predecessor: Install CCTV Cameras and Recording Equipment
rationale: All CCTV hardware must be installed before the final system-wide inspection and testing can be performed to verify functionality and coverage.

The physical security system infrastructure (e.g., foundations for perimeter barriers, secure walls, and mounting points for cameras/sensors) must be in place before the commission and program security system installation can begin.

The building or facility structure must be completed to provide the physical environment (walls, ceilings, secure rooms) where security system components such as access control panels, CCTV, and alarms will be installed.

Electrical power and low-voltage cabling (e.g., data, alarm, camera cables) must be roughed in to the designated locations before security system equipment can be mounted, connected, and commissioned.

After the security system is fully installed and commissioned, comprehensive final testing and acceptance procedures must be performed to verify all security functions operate correctly before facility occupancy.
The security system must be operational and commissioned to ensure the facility is secure before personnel and assets can be brought in for occupancy and normal operations.
The BMS controller and head-end server require electrical power to operate, so the electrical supply must be installed and energized before the controller can be started.
The BMS head-end server typically communicates over a building network (LAN/WAN); the network infrastructure must be in place to allow connectivity and data exchange.

successor: BMS Field Device Installation and Commissioning
rationale: The BMS controller/head-end server acts as the central supervisor; field devices (sensors, actuators, VAV boxes) must be connected to and configured through the controller, so the controller must be operational first.
The head-end server hosts the BMS software; system-wide configuration, programming, and graphics creation require the server to be installed and running before these tasks can begin.
Integration testing of the BMS with other building systems (HVAC, lighting, fire alarm) requires the central controller/head-end to be operational to serve as the integration platform.

predecessor: Electrical Room Preparation & Distribution Board Installation
rationale: Field controllers and PLCs require main power feeds from electrical distribution boards. The electrical room and distribution boards must be installed and energized before controllers can be powered up and commissioned.
Field controllers often communicate with a central control system. The control room/server room infrastructure (cabinets, racks, networking) must be ready to house or connect to the controllers.
Cable pathways (trays, conduits) must be installed before running control cables to and from field controllers to ensure proper cable management and routing.

successor: Field Device Installation & Termination (sensors, actuators, VFDs)
rationale: Field controllers send control signals to and receive feedback from field devices. Controllers must be installed, mounted, and powered before field device cables can be terminated and commissioned.

PLCs and field controllers are the execution platform for control logic. The hardware must be physically installed and operational before programming, testing, and commissioning of the control system can begin.

predecessor: Install electrical conduit and junction boxes
rationale: Sensors require electrical power and a physical mounting location; conduit and junction boxes must be in place to provide wiring pathways and mounting points.
Communication cables must be pulled to sensor locations before the sensors themselves can be physically installed and connected to the building automation system.
Many sensors are mounted inside or adjacent to ductwork to measure air conditions; ductwork must be installed first to provide mounting surfaces and ensure representative air sampling.

successor: Commission and calibrate building automation system
rationale: Sensors must be physically installed and connected before the automation system can be configured, commissioned, and calibrated to ensure accurate readings and proper control logic.

successor: Perform system integration testing and validation
rationale: Sensor data feeds are essential inputs for system-level testing; integration tests cannot be completed until all sensors are operational and reporting correctly to the central system.
Actuators must be mounted on valves, dampers, and relays, which must first be installed and in place before the actuator can be physically attached.
Damper actuators are mounted onto dampers within ductwork; the ductwork and dampers must be installed before actuators can be fitted.
Electrical conduit and control wiring pathways must be roughed in to the actuator locations so that power and signal connections can be made to the actuators upon installation.
Actuators must be physically installed and connected before the control system can be commissioned, calibrated, and tested for proper operation and stroke verification.
System balancing and airflow/water flow testing require actuators to be operational and responsive to control signals before final adjustments can be made.

predecessor: BMS Control Network Cabling & Bus Installation
successor: BMS Control Network Cabling & Bus Testing
rationale: Cabling must be physically installed and terminated before any testing or commissioning of the BMS control network can begin.
The control network cabling and bus backbone must be in place before BMS controllers can be connected and integrated into the network.
The physical site must be prepared (walls, conduits, cable trays, mounting surfaces) before the gateway hardware can be installed.

predecessor: Electrical rough-in and power supply installation
rationale: The gateway requires electrical power; power conduits, outlets, or dedicated circuits must be roughed in before the device can be connected and powered up.
Ethernet, BACnet MS/TP, LonWorks twisted pair, or Modbus RTU cabling must be pulled and terminated before the gateway can be physically connected to the networks it bridges.

The gateway must be installed, powered, and connected to the networks before field devices (sensors, actuators, controllers) on each protocol can be commissioned and tested for communication through the gateway.
The hardware must be physically in place and operational before engineers can configure point mappings, protocol translations, and network parameters on the gateway device.
Electrical wiring must be in place before metering hardware can be connected to the power supply and data networks.
Metering hardware requires connection to the main electrical panel to measure energy consumption.
The physical enclosure or meter socket must be mounted to house and secure the metering hardware before it can be installed.
The metering hardware must be physically installed before it can be programmed, configured, and calibrated for accurate readings.
Metering hardware must be in place and connected before it can be integrated with the building's energy management or building automation system.
Installation of the metering hardware must be complete before functional testing, verification of readings, and commissioning can be performed.

predecessor: Building Management System (BMS) Network Infrastructure Installation
rationale: The BMS network infrastructure (cabling, switches, and communication backbones) must be installed and operational to provide the physical and logical connectivity needed for the operator workstation to communicate with BMS controllers and field devices.

BMS controllers must be installed, powered, and configured to serve as the data acquisition and control endpoints before the operator workstation software can connect to them and function as a supervisory interface.

The BMS server hardware must be in place and running the core BMS server software to host the database, web services, and communication drivers that the operator workstation software depends upon to retrieve live data and issue commands.

System-level integration testing and commissioning activities require the operator workstation and its software to be fully installed and operational so that test engineers can monitor points, execute control sequences, and validate end-to-end functionality from the operator interface.

Operator training on the BMS is logically dependent on having the workstation software ready, but it is a soft preference because training can use a simulated or test environment if needed, and the training schedule is typically adjustable based on project milestones.
Electrical infrastructure must be in place to provide power and connectivity to the Alarm Annunciation Panel.
The alarm annunciation panel typically interfaces with the control system for receiving alarm signals, so the control system backbone must be installed first.

successor: Alarm Annunciation Panel Testing and Commissioning
rationale: The panel must be physically installed and wired before it can be powered on and tested for functionality.
End-to-end testing of alarm annunciation requires the panel to be fully installed and operational to verify correct signal routing and annunciation.
BMS controllers and sensors require power supply connections; electrical rough-in must be completed to provide necessary wiring and power sources for BMS equipment.
BMS sensors (temperature, humidity, pressure) and actuators are installed within or on HVAC ductwork; ducts must be in place before sensor placement and commissioning.
BMS controls and monitors mechanical plant equipment; all HVAC major equipment must be installed before BMS controllers can be wired, connected, and commissioned.
After BMS installation and initial commissioning, comprehensive functional testing of all connected systems and points must be performed before system handover to the client.

While BMS sensors and controllers should ideally be installed before ceiling closure for access, some BMS commissioning adjustments can occur after finishes; this is a soft preference to avoid rework.

Electrical rough-in (wiring, conduit, and power supply installation) must be completed before the Integrated Lighting Control Interface can be installed, as the interface requires power and pre-run control cables to function.

Lighting fixtures must be physically installed and connected before the control interface can be commissioned, since the interface controls these fixtures and needs to verify connectivity and addressing.

The Integrated Lighting Control Interface must be physically installed before software programming, system configuration, and commissioning can begin, as the programming depends on the presence of the installed hardware.

Calibration and testing of lighting zones (e.g., dimming levels, occupancy sensor integration) can only occur after the control interface is fully installed and powered, as it is the central hub for zone control.

Final inspection and acceptance testing of the lighting control system must occur after the Integrated Lighting Control Interface is installed and all subsystems are operational, to verify overall system performance and compliance.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical work for fire alarm system
successor: Integrated Fire Alarm / Life Safety Interface
rationale: Electrical rough-in, including conduit, wiring, and backboxes for fire alarm devices (smoke detectors, pull stations, horns/strobes), must be installed before the fire alarm interface components can be mounted and connected.

predecessor: Installation of fire alarm control panel (FACP) and power supply
successor: Integrated Fire Alarm / Life Safety Interface
rationale: The main fire alarm control panel and its dedicated power supply must be in place and operational to provide the central processing and power needed for the integrated life safety interface to function.

predecessor: Completion of vertical and horizontal cable tray/riser infrastructure
successor: Integrated Fire Alarm / Life Safety Interface
rationale: Cable trays, risers, and pathway infrastructure that carry fire alarm and life safety communication cables must be installed before the interface can be wired into the overall system.

predecessor: Installation of fire alarm initiating and notification devices
successor: Integrated Fire Alarm / Life Safety Interface
rationale: Individual field devices (smoke detectors, heat detectors, manual pull stations, horns, strobes) must be physically installed and terminated so the integrated interface can communicate with and supervise these devices.

predecessor: Integrated Fire Alarm / Life Safety Interface
successor: System-wide fire alarm testing and commissioning
rationale: The integrated interface must be fully installed and wired before the entire fire alarm system can be functionally tested and commissioned, as the interface serves as the central coordination point for all life safety subsystems.

predecessor: Integrated Fire Alarm / Life Safety Interface
successor: Integration with building management system (BMS) and elevator recall controls
rationale: The fire alarm interface must be operational before it can send signals to the BMS for smoke control, HVAC shutdown, and to elevator controllers for firefighter recall operation.

predecessor: Integrated Fire Alarm / Life Safety Interface
successor: Final inspection and approval by authority having jurisdiction (AHJ)
rationale: The integrated life safety interface must be fully installed, configured, and tested before the municipal fire marshal or other AHJ can perform the required final inspection and approve the system for occupancy.

predecessor: Integrated Fire Alarm / Life Safety Interface
successor: Ceiling and wall close-in and finish work
rationale: Once the fire alarm interface components, associated wiring, and devices are verified as operational, ceilings and walls can be closed in, as access to these components is no longer needed for rough-in adjustments.

Secondary structural framing (e.g., purlins, girts, joists) relies on the primary structural frame (columns, beams, girders) as its supporting structure and attachment points. The primary frame must be erected and stable before any secondary members can be installed.
The primary structural frame depends on completed foundations; since secondary framing attaches to the primary frame, foundations must be complete to support the entire structural steel system.

Roof decking, wall panels, and exterior cladding are typically fastened directly to secondary framing members (purlins, girts). The secondary frame must be in place to provide the support substrate for these enclosure elements.

While not a strict physical requirement, it is common practice to route conduits, piping, and ductwork through the building's structural framework after secondary framing is complete, as the secondary members define the final open spaces and support points. This is a soft preference as some rough-in can occur concurrently.

Secondary framing members such as bracing, bridging, and diaphragm connections complete the lateral stability system of the structure. The secondary elements must be installed and connected for the full structural stability to be achieved.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any structural framing can be erected to ensure a stable foundation and proper load distribution.
The foundation system (spread footings, mat foundations, or piles/caps) must be fully cured and load-bearing before the primary structural frame columns and beams can be anchored to them.
Underground plumbing, electrical conduits, and drainage lines must be installed beneath the slab before the structural frame is erected, as access is impossible once the frame and slab are in place.
The roof structure depends on the primary frame (columns and main beams) for vertical support; the frame must be complete to carry roof loads.
Intermediate floor slabs are supported by the primary structural frame beams and girders, so they cannot be placed until the supporting frame is erected.
Exterior walls are typically non-structural infill or cladding attached to the structural frame; the frame must first be in place to provide attachment points and lateral stability.
Elevator shafts are framed by the primary structure; elevator guide rails and cars cannot be installed until the structural frame enclosing the shaft is complete.

While some MEP work can begin in completed areas, full rough-in throughout a floor typically waits until the structural frame is erected to avoid rework and allow overhead routing through the structural bays.
The excavation must be completed to expose the foundation area and provide working space for making connections between foundation elements.
Concrete foundations must be poured and fully cured to achieve sufficient structural strength before any connections (e.g., anchor bolts, rebar splicing, or steel embedments) can be made.
Formwork must be in place and secured to define the shape of the foundation before connection components (like dowels or anchors) can be positioned accurately.
Foundation connections (e.g., base plates, anchor bolts, embedded plates) must be completed to provide the load-transfer interface before steel columns or beams can be erected.
While it is preferable to complete all connections before waterproofing to avoid disturbing the membrane, some connections may be done concurrently; this is a soft preference for sequencing.

Structural steel requires a stable, level foundation (concrete footings, piers, grade beams) to transfer loads to the ground. Steel columns and connections cannot be erected without completed foundations to anchor to.
Anchor bolts must be set into the foundation concrete at precise locations to receive the steel column base plates. The steel connections cannot be made without these embedments in place.
Roof decks and structural decking are typically placed directly on and supported by steel framing. The steel frame must be connected and stabilized before decking can be laid.
Exterior walls (brick, block, curtain wall) often bear on or are tied into the structural steel frame. The steel skeleton must be complete to provide support and attachment points for wall systems.

While some MEP work can begin before steel completion, major ductwork, piping, and conduit runs are typically suspended from or routed through the steel structure. Full steel erection allows optimal routing without rework, though limited MEP can proceed in parallel.
Composite decking requires a stable, level, and prepared subfloor or substructure (joists, bearers) to be installed upon. Installing decking without proper substructure would be structurally unsound.
The structural frame (joists, beams) must be completed to provide the support framework onto which composite decking boards are fastened.
Any waterproof membranes or flashing around the deck area must be installed before decking to prevent moisture damage to the substructure.

While composite decking often requires less finishing, any protective sealant or final cleaning should be applied after installation; however this is a preference for aesthetic protection rather than a physical necessity.
Railings and balustrades are typically anchored to or through the deck surface; the deck boards must be in place to properly locate and secure railing posts.
Trusses and space frames must be erected on a stable foundation or slab, which provides the load-bearing base and anchorage points.
Trusses and space frames typically bear on columns or beam supports, so the primary structural frame must be in place before roof or long-span trusses can be installed.
Roof decking and cladding are applied directly onto the trusses or space frames, which serve as the structural substrate.
Suspended ceilings are hung from or supported by the trusses/space frames, so the overhead structure must be complete first.

While overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in can technically begin after trusses are in place, it is a soft preference because some MEP work could be pre-installed or coordinated prior; however, best practice is to complete the frame before hanging heavy ductwork and conduits.
Steel columns and frames require stable, cured concrete foundations to bear loads and provide anchorage for bolting or welding.
Foundation concrete must achieve sufficient compressive strength (typically 75% of design strength) before steel erection to prevent structural failure or pull-out of anchor bolts.
The building site must be graded, compacted, and leveled to provide stable access for cranes and delivery trucks, and to ensure the steel structure is erected on a sound subgrade.
The steel frame must be erected and stabilized before roofing materials can be applied, as the roof decking and membrane rely on the steel purlins and rafters for support.
Wall panels, curtain walls, or brick veneer cannot be installed until the steel structural frame is in place to provide a supporting framework and attachment points.
The steel frame must be erected and positioned before the connections between members can be bolted and torqued.
Bolting and torquing of connections must be completed before the structural frame can be inspected for alignment and connection integrity.
The bolted connections must be fully torqued and secured before decking or cladding can be installed, as the structural frame must be stable.
If the design requires welding in addition to bolting, bolting and torquing should precede welding to avoid interference with bolt tensioning.

predecessor: Material and Bolt Delivery to Site
rationale: Bolts, washers, nuts, and torquing equipment must be delivered and available on site before bolting and torquing work can commence.
Materials must be cut, beveled, and prepared to the correct dimensions before welding can be performed.
Workpieces must be properly aligned and fitted together before welding can commence to ensure correct joint geometry.
Welding must be completed and inspected before any post-weld heat treatment can be applied.
Welding and inspection must be finished before surface cleaning and coating/painting can be applied to the welded area.
Welds must be completed and inspected before pressure or leak testing can be performed to verify weld integrity.

successor: Deck Installation and Shear Stud Welding Activity
rationale: Steel beams must be in place to provide the structural support framework onto which deck panels are installed and shear studs are welded.

predecessor: Deck Installation and Shear Stud Welding Activity
rationale: The metal deck and welded shear studs must be fully installed before concrete can be poured, as the deck serves as the formwork and the studs provide composite shear connection.

predecessor: Deck Installation and Shear Stud Welding Activity
rationale: Welded shear studs and deck panels must be in place prior to placing reinforcing steel (rebar) on top of the deck to ensure proper embedment and composite action.

predecessor: Layout and Marking of Stud Locations
successor: Deck Installation and Shear Stud Welding Activity
rationale: Stud locations need to be pre-marked on the steel beams or deck to guide accurate welding; this layout step precedes deck installation when studs are welded through the deck.

predecessor: Deck Installation and Shear Stud Welding Activity
rationale: While some rough-in work can be done concurrently, major above-deck MEP rough-in typically follows deck installation to avoid damaging the deck and to work on a stable platform.
Fireproofing is typically applied to structural steel members after they have been erected and the structural frame is stable. The steel must be in place to receive the fireproofing material.
The steel must be primed before fireproofing is applied to ensure proper adhesion and corrosion protection underneath the fireproofing layer.
Metal decking or floor slabs must be installed to provide working platforms and access for fireproofing crews, and to define the spaces where fireproofing is needed.

Fireproofing must be completed and cured before above-ceiling mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work and inspections can proceed, as fireproofing is a fire-resistance-rated assembly component.
Fireproofing should be fully cured before enclosing it with drywall or other finishes to allow for inspection and to prevent damage to the fireproofing material.

successor: Steel Frame Alignment and Plumb Checking Activity
rationale: Steel columns must be anchored to properly set and cured foundations before any frame alignment can begin, as the base supports are physically required to hold the steel structure.

predecessor: Steel Erection and Bolting (Main Columns and Beams)
successor: Steel Frame Alignment and Plumb Checking Activity
rationale: The steel frame must first be erected and bolted together before alignment and plumb checking can be performed, as there is no frame to align otherwise.

predecessor: Steel Frame Alignment and Plumb Checking Activity
rationale: Final bolt tightening should only occur after the frame is properly aligned and plumb to avoid locking in misalignments, which would compromise structural integrity.

predecessor: Steel Frame Alignment and Plumb Checking Activity
rationale: Permanent welding of structural connections must be performed only after the frame is aligned and plumb, because welding locks the geometry permanently and misalignments cannot be corrected afterward.

predecessor: Steel Frame Alignment and Plumb Checking Activity
rationale: Roof decking installation requires a properly aligned and plumb frame to ensure correct fit-up and load distribution, otherwise panels will not align correctly.
Electrical rough-in (wiring, conduit, junction boxes) must be completed before corridor lighting fixtures can be installed, as the fixtures need to connect to the electrical supply.
Corridor lighting fixtures are typically mounted to or recessed within the ceiling grid; thus the ceiling grid must be in place first to support the lighting.
Once corridor lighting fixtures are installed and wired, ceiling tiles or finish panels can be placed around them for a clean finished appearance.
Painting and final finishes can proceed after lighting is installed to avoid damaging new fixtures, though this is a soft preference as painting could be done earlier with fixture protection.
Lighting fixtures must be physically installed before they can be tested and commissioned to verify proper operation.
Power supply wiring must be completed before emergency exit signs can be connected and powered.
Emergency exit signs are typically mounted on ceilings or above doorways; the ceiling structure must be in place to support the sign mounting.
If wall-mounted, the walls must be framed, finished, and painted before exit signs can be affixed.
Exit signs must be installed and operational before the building can undergo final safety inspection and commissioning.
While not strictly required, exit signs are typically verified as part of overall life safety system testing; testing may be more efficient after signs are operational.
The rough opening must be framed, shimmed, and prepared to the correct dimensions before the fire door assembly can be hung and fitted.
The fire-rated door frame (including anchors and firestopping) must be installed and secured in the wall opening before the door leaf can be hung on the hinges.
Hardware such as closers, locks, latches, and panic devices are mounted onto the installed door leaf after it is hung in the frame.
Fire door inspection, labeling, and final commissioning for fire rating compliance must occur after the door assembly is fully installed and operational.
Handrails must be anchored to the wall structure, which requires the wall framing (studs) to be in place to provide a secure mounting surface.
Handrails are typically mounted on the finished wall surface; sheathing or drywall must be installed to provide the proper finished surface for handrail attachment.
While it is preferable to paint before installing handrails to avoid paint splatter on the rails, touch-up painting can be done after installation, making this a soft preference.
Handrails must be installed before final flooring to allow proper alignment and to avoid damaging newly installed flooring during handrail installation work.
Handrail installation must be complete before the final inspection to verify compliance with building codes for handrail height, strength, and continuity.

The corridor slab or deck must be poured and cured before any wall base can be installed, as the wall base sits on top of the slab/deck and requires a stable, cured horizontal surface for proper alignment and load distribution.

Wall framing (studs, tracks) must be erected before the wall base (bottom track or plate) can be permanently secured, as the base is part of the wall assembly and supports the vertical framing elements.
The wall base must be installed to provide the lower termination and attachment point for wall cladding materials (e.g., drywall, paneling, baseboards), which are applied after the base is in place.
Door frames in corridor walls require the wall base to be in place to establish the finished floor-to-wall transition and ensure proper alignment of door jambs with the base.

While some MEP rough-in (electrical, plumbing) occurs before wall base installation, final MEP trim-out and device mounting (outlets, switches, data ports) near the base should occur after the wall base is installed to achieve proper coverage and finished appearance.
The corridor soffit is typically supported by or attached to the corridor walls. Wall framing must be complete to provide a structural backing for the soffit.

predecessor: Corridor Ceiling Rough-In (MEP rough-in above ceiling)
rationale: Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work above the ceiling area must be completed before enclosing the soffit, as the soffit often hides or integrates with these systems.
The soffit structure/framing must be in place before any finishing materials (drywall, panels, paint) can be applied to it.
If lighting fixtures are to be mounted on or recessed into the soffit, the soffit must be installed first to provide the mounting surface or cavity.
While not physically required, it is a preferred sequence to install the soffit before flooring to avoid damaging finished flooring with scaffolding or dropped materials during soffit work.
The floor slab must be poured and cured before a floor drain can be installed, as the drain is embedded into the slab.
Waterproofing around the drain opening is typically completed prior to drain placement to ensure a watertight seal.
Floor drains must be positioned and fixed before the final floor finish or screed is applied to achieve proper slope and drainage.
Tiles or final floor finish are laid after drain installation to ensure proper integration and fall toward the drain.
The underground drainage pipework must be laid and connected before the floor drain body is installed.

Wall protection (e.g., corner guards, crash rails, handrails) must be installed after the wall framing is complete and the wall surface is finished, as the protection is mounted onto the finished wall surface.
Drywall must be installed and finished (taped, mudded, sanded) before wall protection can be applied, since protection products are attached to the finished drywall surface.
Paint or wall finish must be completed before installing wall protection, as protection is typically the final wall treatment to avoid damage during painting.

While wall protection can be installed before flooring, it is preferable to install flooring first to avoid damaging wall protection during floor installation work; however, this is a soft preference as the sequence can be reversed with careful work.

Wall protection must be installed before ceiling installation in corridors if ceiling elements (e.g., crown molding, ceiling tiles) overlap or interface with wall protection; otherwise, ceiling work may damage exposed walls.
Overhead electrical distribution must be installed before corridor signage to ensure power supply for illuminated signs and avoid rework when routing electrical conduits above corridors.
Ceiling grid must be in place to provide the structural support and mounting points for overhead corridor signage and to determine the final ceiling height for sign placement.
Corridor wall framing defines the physical boundaries and mounting surfaces for wall-mounted corridor signage.

successor: Final Finishing and Painting of Corridors
rationale: Signage must be installed before final painting and finishing so that any gaps around sign mounts can be sealed and painted over for a clean appearance.
Signage should be completed prior to occupancy inspections to ensure egress paths and room identification are clearly marked for code compliance and occupant safety.
The corridor access panel is mounted within or onto the corridor wall framing, so the framing must be in place to provide structural support.
Electrical cables and junction boxes that will be accessed via the panel must be installed and routed behind the panel location before the panel can be fitted.
The access panel must be installed and its trim/flange positioned before the final wall finishing is applied, so that finishes can be worked around the panel for a neat appearance.

While not a strict physical requirement, it is good practice to install the access panel before the ceiling to avoid working in a confined overhead space and to allow easy access for overhead connections.
Electrical conduits and wiring must be installed before smoke barriers are erected to avoid cutting through the barrier later.
HVAC ductwork penetrations through the smoke barrier must be planned and roughed-in before the barrier is fully installed to ensure proper fire/smoke dampers and sealing.

successor: Fire & Smoke Damper Installation at Barrier
rationale: Fire/smoke dampers at duct penetrations must be installed in coordination with the smoke barrier construction; the barrier provides the supporting frame.
All gaps and penetrations through the smoke barrier must be firestopped after the barrier is in place to maintain smoke-tight integrity.
Smoke barriers must extend from floor slab to underside of roof or deck; corridor ceilings are installed after the barrier is complete to maintain continuous smoke-tight construction.
The ceiling grid is typically supported by the walls or wall-mounted angles; wall framing must be complete to provide structural support and anchor points for the ceiling grid.
MEP rough-in work such as ductwork, conduit, and piping must be installed above the ceiling before the grid is hung; otherwise, access for installation is blocked by the finished ceiling.
Ceiling tiles are placed into the grid after the grid framework is fully installed and leveled, providing the support structure for the tiles.
Lighting fixtures are often integrated into or suspended from the ceiling grid; the grid must be in place to attach and align the fixtures.

While painting walls and ceiling can be done before the grid, it is often preferred to paint after the grid to avoid overspray and damage to the grid. However, painting can also occur before grid installation if the grid is protected; thus it is a soft preference.
The fire extinguisher cabinet is typically recessed into or mounted onto a finished wall. Wall framing and drywall must be completed to provide the structural support and cavity for the cabinet.
If the cabinet includes an alarm or light, rough-in wiring should be run before the cabinet is mounted to avoid rework.
The fire extinguisher must be placed inside the cabinet after the cabinet is securely installed and accessible.
Installation must be complete before final inspection is performed and signage (e.g., 'FIRE EXTINGUISHER' signs) is affixed above the cabinet.
Flooring and final finishes are preferably completed first to avoid damaging new finishes during cabinet installation, though this is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
Wall framing provides the structural support and enclosure against which base cabinets are mounted and secured.
Finished wall surfaces (e.g., drywall, plywood) must be in place before cabinets are attached to provide a flush mounting surface and meet fire/ building code requirements.
Base cabinets sit on the floor; a level, stable subfloor or underlayment is required for proper alignment and load distribution.
Countertops are fabricated and installed on top of the base cabinets after the cabinets are fixed in place and leveled.
Final connections for sinks, outlets, or fixtures within or above the cabinet occur after the cabinet body is installed.
The corridor bench must be anchored to or placed on a finished floor slab; the slab provides the structural base for the bench.
Wall finishing behind the bench should be completed before the bench is installed to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to allow proper alignment against the wall.
Installing the bench first allows floor finishing to be laid flush against the bench base for a clean finish, though floor can be completed before bench if bench is surface-mounted.
Lighting installation can proceed after bench placement to ensure adequate illumination of the seating area, but lighting is typically roughed-in before bench installation.
All concealed electrical outlets, conduits, or plumbing within the corridor walls must be roughed-in before the bench is installed, as the bench may obstruct access to walls.
The kickplate is installed at the base of walls along the corridor floor, so the flooring must be completed first to establish the finished floor level and provide a base for kickplate attachment.

Kickplates are typically mounted onto finished wall surfaces; wall finishing must be complete to provide a clean, finished surface for kickplate installation and to avoid damaging finished walls during kickplate work.

While not always required, kickplates are often installed before doors to allow unobstructed access to the full wall length for kickplate alignment and fastening; however, this is a soft preference as doors can also be installed first if coordination allows.
If a separate base molding or trim is used above the kickplate, the kickplate must be installed first as it serves as the lower element, with trim or base molding installed above it.
The structural frame or support system for the corridor must be in place to provide a mounting surface and structural support for the glazing panels.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the corridor must be completed before glazing is installed to avoid damage to finishes and allow access for MEP work.
After glazing panels are installed, sealing, caulking, and weatherproofing around the glazing must be applied to ensure water tightness and thermal performance.
While not a strict physical necessity, completing glazing before interior finishing avoids damage to finished surfaces and allows for clean transitions around windows and doors.
Glazing installation should be complete before final cleaning and handover to protect glass surfaces from construction dust and debris during subsequent finishing work.
The ceiling grid must be installed first to provide a structural support framework for the HVAC diffusers.
The main ductwork supplying air to the diffuser must be roughed in and accessible before the diffuser can be connected to it.
Ceiling tiles around the diffuser must be installed after the diffuser is in place to fit around it properly.
The diffuser must be physically installed before the HVAC system can be balanced and airflow tested at the diffuser.
While not physically required, finishing work is typically done after diffuser installation to avoid damage to the diffuser from paint or debris.

predecessor: Install electrical conduit and junction boxes
rationale: Smoke detectors require electrical wiring and junction boxes to be in place before the detector unit can be mounted and connected.
Corridor smoke detectors are typically mounted on or within the ceiling; the ceiling structure must be in place to provide a mounting surface.

successor: Complete fire alarm system wiring and termination
rationale: The smoke detector unit must be physically installed before final wiring connections and terminations to the fire alarm panel can be completed.
All smoke detectors must be installed before the system can be functionally tested and commissioned for operation.
It is generally preferred to complete detector installation before final ceiling finishing to avoid disturbing newly finished work, though access panels can allow later installation.
Electrical conduits for lighting and power must be routed along the corridor ceiling before sprinkler heads are installed to avoid interference and allow proper spacing between utilities.
The sprinkler branch lines and supply piping must be roughed in and pressure tested before the sprinkler heads themselves can be attached.

predecessor: Install corridor ceiling grid or framing
rationale: The ceiling suspension grid or framing must be in place to support and locate the sprinkler head positions precisely within the ceiling plane.
Sprinkler heads must be installed and properly positioned protruding through the ceiling plane before ceiling tiles can be fitted around them.

successor: Final fire alarm and sprinkler testing
rationale: All sprinkler heads must be in place before the system can be pressurized and tested for proper coverage and response.
Cable trays provide the physical pathway and support structure for cables to reach the junction box; the junction box cannot be positioned or connected without the tray infrastructure in place.
Conduits must be roughed in to provide the enclosed raceway for electrical cables to be pulled to the junction box location before the box can be mounted and terminated.
The junction box is typically mounted on or within corridor walls/partitions; the wall framing must be in place to provide a structural surface for box attachment.
Cables are pulled through trays and conduits to terminate inside the junction box; the box must be installed and open before cable pulling can commence.

successor: Corridor Junction Box Cover / Trim Out
rationale: The junction box interior must be fully wired, terminated, and inspected before the cover can be installed to enclose and protect connections.
The structural framing (walls, columns, ceiling) must be in place before any outlet boxes can be mounted or embedded within the corridor structure.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins (including conduit pathways) must be completed before data outlet wiring and installation can begin, as the outlet needs to connect to these systems.
Data outlet boxes and wiring must be installed before drywall is applied, so that the outlet can be properly set within the wall and the faceplate can be flush with the finished surface.
The physical outlet unit must be installed first before data cables can be terminated at the outlet and functional testing can be performed.
It is preferable to install data outlets before the ceiling is closed to allow easy access for wiring, though not a strict physical requirement if access panels exist.
Electrical wiring must be run through walls and conduit before outlets can be connected and installed.
Conduit provides the pathway for electrical cables; outlets cannot be mounted without conduit in place.
Outlet boxes are mounted to wall studs or framing, so walls must be framed first.
Outlet boxes and wiring must be in place before walls are closed up with drywall; however the outlet cover plate is installed after finishing.
Outlets must be installed and wired before they can be inspected for code compliance.
The cover plate is the final trim item and cannot be installed until the outlet device is mounted and wired.
The electrical system must be fully connected before power can be turned on and outlets tested for proper operation.
Wall painting must be completed before installing light switches to avoid paint splatters on the switch plates and to ensure a clean finish.
Electrical conduits must be run and in place within the walls before switches can be wired and mounted.
Switches must be installed and wired before light fixtures are connected, as the switch controls power to the fixtures.
Switch installation must be complete before electrical testing can verify switch functionality and circuit integrity.
The switch mechanism must be installed first so that the decorative cover plate can be attached over it for safety and aesthetics.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical wiring for thermostat location
rationale: Electrical wiring must be in place before the thermostat can be connected and mounted.
The thermostat must be physically installed before it can be wired and integrated into the HVAC control system.
The thermostat must be installed before the overall HVAC system can be tested and calibrated for proper operation.
The thermostat is typically mounted on or within the ceiling; ceiling must be in place to define the mounting surface and location.

successor: Install corridor wall finishing and painting
rationale: While thermostat is often installed before final painting for a clean aesthetic fit, it can also be installed after. It is a soft preference to avoid damaging finished surfaces.
The corner guard must be mounted onto finished surfaces; wall framing provides the structural substrate needed to attach the corner guard securely.
Corner guards are typically installed after drywall is hung and finished, as they protect the finished wall surface at corners.

While painting can be done before corner guard installation, it is common practice to install corner guards after painting to protect the corner guard from paint overspray, or before painting so the guard is painted over. This order is a preference, not a physical necessity.
Corner guards should be installed before final flooring to avoid the corner guard sitting on top of the finished floor, which can cause gaps or improper fit at the base of the wall.
Corner guards are a finish item that must be in place before final walkthrough and inspection to ensure the corridor is complete and protected.
Corridor expansion joints are installed within the corridor slab; the slab must be poured and partially cured before the joint can be placed.
After the expansion joint is installed, the surrounding joint gaps must be sealed and finished to ensure water tightness and movement tolerance.
Expansion joints are typically placed after the structural support system (formwork or steel) is erected and the slab is ready for pouring, to ensure correct alignment and anchorage.
Final floor finishes (tiles, coating, or topping) must be applied after expansion joint installation to properly terminate at or around the joint profile.
While MEP work can proceed in parallel in other areas, final adjustments to conduits or pipes crossing the joint must wait until the joint is installed to avoid conflicts with joint movement.
The stretcher cabinet needs to be mounted on or recessed into the corridor wall; the wall framing must be in place to provide structural support and attachment points.

Electrical wiring for lighting or outlets inside/around the cabinet and any plumbing connections (if the cabinet includes a sink or medical gas) must be roughed-in before the cabinet is installed, as access behind the wall will be closed off.
The cabinet must be installed before final wall finishing so that drywall can be cut and taped around the cabinet and paint can be applied seamlessly up to the cabinet edges.

It is preferable to install the cabinet before final flooring to avoid damaging finished floors with heavy cabinet placement, though flooring can technically be done first if the cabinet is carefully set.
It is preferable to have the cabinet in place before the ceiling is fully closed to allow for tighter fit and alignment, but ceiling work can proceed simultaneously or before if access is maintained.
The walls must be framed to provide structural support and define the corridor space before the soapstone sink can be installed against or within them.
Water supply lines and drain pipes must be roughed-in within the walls before the sink can be connected to the plumbing system.
The floor must be finished to provide a stable, level base for the sink base cabinet or vanity.
The soapstone sink and countertop must be installed before final sealing, polishing, or finishing can be applied to the stone surface.
The sink must be set in place before the faucet, drain assembly, and P-trap can be physically connected to the sink basin.
The door closer must be mounted on a properly installed door frame and door; the frame provides the structural support for the closer bracket.
The door closer attaches to the door leaf itself, so the door must be hung and aligned before the closer can be installed.
After the closer is installed, it must be adjusted for sweep speed, latch speed, and backcheck, and the door operation must be tested to ensure proper closing and compliance with fire/safety codes.
Door closer installation is typically completed before final inspections so that all door hardware can be verified together, though some inspection items may happen in parallel.

If corridor flooring (e.g., tile, carpet) is installed after the door closer, the closer may need to be adjusted or protected; typically flooring is completed before closer installation to avoid damage, so this ordering can be reversed depending on sequence.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed and sized correctly before the door frame can be fitted into it.
Wall framing must be complete to provide the structural support and opening for the corridor door frame.
The door frame must be securely installed and squared before the door leaf can be hung on hinges.
Architraves, casings, and trim around the door frame can only be applied after the frame itself is fixed in place.
Drywall taping, mudding, and finishing around the door opening must wait until the door frame is installed to achieve a clean junction.
The corridor threshold sits on top of the finished floor or subfloor, so the floor slab must be in place and properly prepared to support the threshold.
Thresholds are typically set between wall jambs; corridor walls must be framed to define the opening where the threshold will be installed.
The door must be hung after the threshold is in place because the threshold provides the bottom seat and alignment reference for the door frame and door.
The threshold defines the transition point; floor finishes on either side of the threshold are typically laid up to or against the threshold after it is installed.
Caulking and sealing around the threshold edges must be done after the threshold is fully set to ensure a watertight and finished transition.

predecessor: Layout and Mark Corridor Wall Locations
rationale: Corridor wall locations must be laid out and marked on the floor/deck before framing can begin to ensure walls are placed in the correct positions per the architectural plans.
Floor decking or underlayment must be installed to provide a stable working surface and proper base for corridor wall framing.

predecessor: Complete Rough-in for MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing) in Corridor Areas
rationale: Rough-in work for MEP systems within corridor ceiling and floor areas should be completed before walls are framed to avoid rework and access issues.
Wall framing must be complete before sheathing or drywall can be applied to the corridor walls.
Corridor wall framing must be in place before door frames can be installed and secured within the wall openings.
The ceiling grid provides the structural framework that supports the ceiling tiles, so the grid must be in place before tiles can be installed.
Lighting fixtures are typically mounted to or within the ceiling grid system, so the grid must be installed first.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (conduit, ductwork, piping) above the ceiling must be completed before the ceiling grid is installed, as the grid would block access to the overhead space.
Wall framing defines the corridor boundaries and provides support for the ceiling grid edges, so walls must be framed before the ceiling grid can be hung.
Building codes require inspection of all overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing work before it is concealed by the ceiling grid and tiles.
The subfloor must be clean, level, and dry before any floor finish can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and a smooth final surface.
Wall base or trim installation before flooring allows the floor finish to be run up to or slightly under the trim, creating a clean finished edge.

predecessor: Complete Rough-In of MEP Services in Corridor
rationale: Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before flooring to avoid damaging the finished floor during subsequent MEP work.
It is a soft preference to complete flooring before ceiling work to avoid debris falling onto a finished floor; however, protective coverings can allow reverse sequencing.
Soft preference to complete painting before flooring to prevent paint drips on the new floor; however, careful masking and sequencing can reverse this order.
Corridor ceiling must be in place to provide a mounting surface for light fixtures and to allow wiring to be run through ceiling cavities before lighting installation.
Electrical conduits, junction boxes, and wiring must be roughed in before light fixtures can be connected and mounted.
Framing must be complete to define the corridor space and provide support structures before any electrical or finishing work begins.
Lighting fixtures must be installed before applying final ceiling finishes to allow access for wiring connections and adjustments.
While flooring can technically be installed before lighting, it is preferred to complete overhead work first to avoid dust and debris damaging new flooring.
The door frame and rough opening must be prepared before the fire door assembly can be installed, as the door assembly fits into the prepared opening.
The corridor walls must be framed to define the doorway opening and provide structural support for the fire door assembly.
One side of the wall sheathing is typically installed before the door to allow proper alignment and fastening of the door frame.
The door assembly must be in place before the opposite side of drywall is installed, as the drywall butts against the door frame.
The fire door must be fully installed before it can be inspected and tested for proper fire rating compliance, closing, and latching operation.
Ceiling grid must be installed before wall protection to ensure overhead alignment and to avoid damaging wall panels when working overhead.
Flooring should be installed before wall protection to allow wall protection to be set at the correct height above finished floor and to prevent damage to flooring from wall protection installation.
Rough-in work in walls must be completed before covering walls with protection to avoid rework and damage to finished wall surfaces.
Wall-mounted fixtures should be installed after wall protection to allow secure mounting through or onto the protection surface without damaging it.
Final painting is typically done after wall protection to ensure a clean finish, though this can be considered a soft preference if protection is installed over already painted surfaces.
Corridor signage installation requires walls and ceilings to be closed after rough-in of MEP systems; rough-in work must be completed before signage can be securely mounted.
Signage is typically mounted on or suspended from finished ceilings; ceiling must be complete to provide proper attachment points and alignment.
Signage is affixed to finished walls; wall surfaces must be painted or otherwise finished to avoid damage and ensure proper adhesion/mounting.

successor: Final Punch List and Occupancy Inspection
rationale: Corridor signage is a life-safety and wayfinding requirement that must be in place before final inspections and occupancy can be approved.
While not a hard physical constraint, corridor signage is typically installed before furniture and interior fit-out so that wayfinding is clear during subsequent finishing activities.

predecessor: Install Corridor Smoke Control System Components
rationale: All smoke control system components (fans, dampers, ducts, controls) must be physically installed before commissioning can begin, as commissioning tests the installed system's functionality.

predecessor: Complete Electrical Rough-In for Smoke Control
rationale: Power must be supplied to smoke control equipment before it can be operated and tested during commissioning.

predecessor: Complete Fire Alarm System Installation and Testing
rationale: The fire alarm system provides the initiating signals for smoke control modes; it must be operational to test smoke control sequences.
Smoke control commissioning results must be verified before integrating into the overall building management/control system to ensure proper handshake and response sequences.

successor: Obtain Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ) Approval for Smoke Control
rationale: Commissioning tests must be complete and documented before the AHJ can review and approve the smoke control system for occupancy.
Handrails must be mounted on finished walls to ensure proper anchoring and alignment; installing before wall finishes are complete would require removal or damage to finishes.
Structural framing provides the load-bearing substrate that handrails are attached to; without completed framing, there is no stable structure to mount the handrail.
MEP rough-ins in the corridor walls and ceiling must be completed before handrail installation to avoid having to remove or work around the handrail for access.
Handrail installation can scuff or damage fresh paint; final painting and touch-up coats should be applied after handrails are installed to cover any marks and achieve a uniform finish.
Flooring installation (e.g., tile, vinyl, carpet) is typically completed after handrails to avoid damaging the new floor with scaffolding, tools, and heavy materials during handrail work.
Drywall must be installed and finished (taped, mudded, sanded) before painting can occur, as paint requires a smooth, prepared surface to adhere properly.
Primer must be applied before the final paint coat to ensure proper adhesion, uniform color, and to seal the surface.
It is generally preferred to complete ceiling installation and painting before painting walls to avoid overspray or drips damaging finished wall paint, though not a strict physical requirement.
Flooring installation should occur after wall painting to prevent paint drips, dust, and debris from damaging the new floor surface.
Baseboards and trim are typically installed after wall painting to ensure clean paint lines and to avoid painting around installed trim.
Landings are structural components that require a stable foundation or supporting structure to be in place before they can be installed.
Landings must be supported by vertical structural elements such as columns or walls, which need to be erected first.
Stair flights typically land on or are supported by landings, so the landing must be in place before stair flights can be installed.
Handrails are attached to or adjacent to landings, requiring the landing structure to be complete before handrail installation can proceed.
While finishing can be done after landing installation, it is a soft preference as finishing could theoretically be done prior if protected, but sequential finishing is typical for consistency.
Corridor walls must be framed to provide the structural support and cavity for access panels to be mounted and recessed into.

predecessor: Rough-in Electrical and Data Cabling in Corridor
rationale: Electrical and data cabling must be routed through the corridor ceiling/wall cavities before access panels are installed, as panels will cover and restrict access to these services.
Access panels are typically integrated into the ceiling system; the ceiling grid provides the framework into which access panels are placed.
Access panels must be installed before the ceiling is fully closed/boarded so that panels can be properly positioned and secured.

Access panels provide maintenance access to overhead services; lighting fixtures are typically installed after access panels are in place to allow for coordinated placement and electrical connections.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide the supporting structure onto which balustrades are mounted.
Balustrades are attached to staircases, balconies, or floor edges, so these structural elements must be built first.
Handrails are typically mounted on top of or integrated with the balustrade structure, requiring the balustrade to be in place first.
While painting can often be done before or after, it is common practice to complete balustrade installation before final finishing touches to avoid damage to finished paintwork during installation.
Balustrades serve as critical safety barriers; final inspection and handover of the building requires balustrades to be installed and tested for compliance with safety codes.
Nosing is typically installed on the edge of stair treads to provide a finished edge and improve safety. The tread (and riser) must be in place for the nosing to be attached to.
The nosing is often used at the edge of a finished floor where it meets a step or transition; the subfloor or underlayment must be prepared and leveled before nosing can be installed.

predecessor: Floor Covering Installation (e.g., carpet, tile, hardwood)
rationale: Nosing is usually the final trim piece that covers the edge of the floor covering where it meets a stair or transition; the floor covering must be laid before the nosing can cap and finish the edge.

If the nosing is wood and part of a sand-and-finish floor system, final sanding and finishing may occur after nosing is installed to blend the finish; but this is a sequencing preference rather than a hard physical constraint.

Handrails and balusters can be installed before or after nosing, but typically are installed after nosing to ensure proper alignment and fit at the stair edge; this is a soft preference for convenience and alignment.
Structural framing must be complete to provide support and openings for smoke vent installation.
The roof deck must be in place to provide a mounting surface for roof-mounted smoke vents.
Smoke vents are typically installed before the final roofing membrane to ensure proper flashing and waterproofing integration.

successor: Electrical Rough-In for Smoke Vent Controls
rationale: Smoke vent controls and wiring connections are typically run after the vent unit is physically installed.
Smoke vents must be installed and connected before the fire alarm system can be fully tested, as they are part of the smoke control system.
Stairwell walls require a stable base and are typically constructed on top of the foundation slab. The foundation must be poured and cured before wall construction can begin.
The stairwell walls provide vertical support for the framing and roof elements above. Structural walls must be in place before overhead framing can be installed.
Staircase stringers and treads are typically anchored to or supported by the stairwell walls. Walls must be built and cured before stairs can be installed.

MEP rough-in work in the stairwell is typically done after walls are erected to allow for routing and installation, though some pre-wall work may be possible; this is a strong preference for sequencing efficiency.
Wall finishes such as drywall, fireproofing, and paint are applied after the structural wall is complete. The wall substrate must exist before any finishing layers can be added.
The rough opening (framing, headers, and jambs) must be prepared and structurally sound before the stairwell door can be installed.
The walls surrounding the stairwell must be framed and in place to provide the structural support and opening for the door assembly.
For fire-rated stairwell doors, the opening and its framing must be inspected and approved before installing the fire-rated door assembly to meet code compliance.
Locks, handles, closers, panic bars, and hinges must be mounted on the installed door frame and leaf; the door must be in place before hardware can be fitted.
Fire-rated stairwell doors require perimeter intumescent seals and smoke gaskets, which must be applied after the door assembly is hung and closed properly to ensure a tight seal.
The stairwell must be fully constructed and structurally complete before fire barrier signage can be installed, as the signage is mounted on the walls/structures of the stairwell.
Fire barrier walls must be installed to provide the surface and location for the fire barrier signage to be affixed.
Fire safety inspections require that all fire barrier signage is in place to verify compliance with fire codes.
Fire barrier signage must be installed and verified before the building can be occupied, as it is a life-safety requirement.
Ideally, signage is completed before final commissioning walkthroughs to avoid rework, but commissioning can technically proceed with temporary signage if needed.
The foundation must be completed before stairwell construction can begin, as stairwells require a stable base and load-bearing support from the foundation structure.

predecessor: Slab on Grade / Ground Floor Slab
rationale: The ground floor slab must be poured and cured before stairwell walls and framing can be erected, as the stairwell sits on and is anchored to the slab.
The primary structural frame of the ground floor must be in place to provide lateral support and attachment points for the stairwell structure.
Interior walls that abut the stairwell cannot be framed until the stairwell structure itself is built, as they rely on the stairwell for alignment and support.
The stairwell enclosure (walls and structural opening) must be complete before the actual staircase components (treads, risers, handrails) can be installed within the shaft.

Firestopping requires the stairwell walls and floors to be framed, with all penetrations (electrical, plumbing, mechanical) roughed in, so that firestop materials can seal around those penetrations within the finished assembly.

Firestopping must be applied to all gaps and penetrations in the stairwell enclosure before enclosing them with gypsum board or final finishes; otherwise the fire-resistive seal would be inaccessible.
Firestopping seals joints between walls and floors; therefore the structural floor/slab must be in place so that the firestop material can be installed at the slab-to-wall interface.
Firestopping must be fully installed before the stairwell can be inspected for fire-resistance rating compliance and tested for smoke containment.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing penetrations through stairwell fire-rated walls must be in place so that firestop sealants and collars can be applied around the penetrating items to maintain the fire rating.
Heat exchangers, especially large industrial or rooftop units, require a stable, level foundation or concrete slab to bear their weight and ensure proper alignment.
The connecting piping (supply and return lines) must be routed to the heat exchanger location before setting the unit, as access for pipe connection may be blocked afterward.
Once the heat exchanger is set in place, the previously roughed-in piping can be connected to its nozzles and then insulated for thermal efficiency.

Control sensors (temperature, pressure), valve actuators, and any pumps associated with the heat exchanger require electrical power and control signals, which must be pulled and terminated after the unit is positioned.
After all piping and electrical connections are made, the system must be pressure-tested for leaks and commissioned to verify performance before being placed into service.
The stairwell must be physically enclosed with walls, floor slabs, and installed doors to contain the pressurized air; otherwise the pressure differential cannot be established or measured.
Supply and exhaust ductwork serving the stairwell pressurization fan must be installed and connected so that the fan can deliver the required airflow into the stairwell.
The pressurization fan (or fan system) must be physically mounted and electrically connected before it can be operated to achieve pressurization.

predecessor: Electrical Power Supply to Pressurization Fan
rationale: The fan requires permanent or temporary electrical power to run; testing cannot proceed without power to the fan motor.

predecessor: Fire Alarm System & Controls Integration (for fan start/stop)
rationale: The pressurization fan is typically controlled by the fire alarm system; the control interface must be functional to initiate the fan during the test sequence.
Pressurization test results inform the air-balancing process; while balancing can partially proceed beforehand, the final adjustments depend on verified pressure readings.

successor: Life Safety Systems Acceptance (Authority Having Jurisdiction sign-off)
rationale: Code compliance for stairwell pressurization must be tested and documented before the AHJ will approve the life safety systems and issue the certificate of occupancy.

successor: Installation of Stairwell Finishes (paint, flooring, signage)
rationale: While not physically required, it is typical to complete pressure testing before finishing work to avoid damage to finishes from test-induced airflows or corrective ductwork modifications.
A stable foundation slab must be prepared and cured before the circulation pump can be installed to ensure proper support and alignment.
The main piping network must be roughed-in to the pump location so the circulation pump can be connected to the supply and return lines.
The circulation pump must be installed before the system can be pressurized and tested for leaks, as the pump is a component of the closed-loop system.
The pump must be physically set in place before electrical connections (power supply, control cables, and sensors) can be made to it.
The pump must be fully installed and connected before the entire system can be flushed of debris and commissioned for operation.
The expansion vessel must be physically supported by a mounting bracket before it can be installed.
The pipe connections to the expansion vessel must be prepared and routed before the vessel can be connected to the system.
The expansion vessel must be installed and connected before the entire system can be pressure-tested to verify integrity.
Commissioning of the hot water or heating system requires the expansion vessel to be in place to manage thermal expansion pressures.
While insulation can be done partially before, final insulation around the vessel connection area is typically completed after the vessel is installed to ensure full coverage.
Pipework and plumbing rough-in must be completed before the hot water cylinder/calorifier can be installed, as the cylinder connects to the plumbing system for water supply and distribution.
The cylinder must be installed before it can be insulated to ensure thermal efficiency and prevent heat loss.
The hot water cylinder/calorifier must be in place before final connections to the heating system or boiler can be made to supply hot water.

successor: Commissioning and Testing of Hot Water System
rationale: The cylinder must be fully installed and connected before the entire hot water system can be commissioned and tested for functionality and safety.
Final connections and finishing of pipework around the cylinder can only be completed after the cylinder is mounted and positioned.
The cold water storage tank requires a stable, level foundation or base slab to bear its weight when filled with water. Without the foundation, the tank cannot be safely placed.
The tank is typically located within a plant room or roof area that must have its structural frame and basic enclosure completed to protect the tank and provide support before installation.
Inlet, outlet, overflow, and drainage pipework cannot be connected until the tank is physically installed and secured in its final position.

successor: Insulation of Cold Water Storage Tank
rationale: Thermal insulation must be applied after the tank is in place and all connections are made to ensure full coverage and proper sealing around penetrations.

successor: Water Filling / Commissioning of Cold Water System
rationale: The system can only be filled and commissioned once the tank is installed with all connections complete, to avoid damage and ensure safe operation.
The piping manifold requires a stable, level foundation or base structure to be installed first to support its weight and ensure proper alignment.
The structural frame must be in place to provide support points and attachment locations for the piping manifold within the overall structure.
The manifold must be physically installed and secured in its final position before any connecting pipes can be welded or joined to its ports.
After installation and all pipe connections are made, the manifold system must be pressure tested to verify integrity and leak-tightness before being put into service.
Insulation and cladding around the manifold area can proceed after the manifold is installed, though in some cases partial insulation may be done beforehand; this is a soft preference for completion.
Pipes must be installed and in place before valves can be assembled onto them, as valves are mounted directly onto pipe connections.
Flanges must be prepared and aligned to the pipe ends before valves can be bolted onto them during assembly.
Gaskets must be placed between flanges to ensure a proper seal before the valve is mounted and bolted into position.
Pressure testing of the assembled pipeline system must be done after the valve is installed to verify the integrity of all connections including the valve assembly.
Pipe insulation must be applied after valve assembly is complete, as the valve and connections need to be accessible for inspection and testing before being covered.

The switchgear panel must be installed within a dedicated electrical room that is enclosed, weatherproof, and secure. The room walls, floor, ceiling, and door must be completed before bringing in sensitive electrical equipment.
Cables can only be terminated and connected to the switchgear panel after it has been physically mounted, grounded, and secured in its final position.
The main distribution board relies on power from the switchgear panel; commissioning and energizing the MDB requires the switchgear to be fully installed and connected.
Conduits and cable trays leading to the switchgear location must be pre-installed to allow cable pulling and termination into the panel.
All electrical testing (insulation resistance, continuity, and functional tests) and final energization of the switchgear can only occur after the panel is fully installed and connected.
The VSD enclosure or cabinet must be physically installed and secured in place before the VSD unit itself can be mounted inside it.
The VSD is typically mounted within a motor control center (MCC) or control panel, so the panel infrastructure must be in place first.

predecessor: Electrical Cabling (Power Supply) to VSD Location
rationale: Power supply cables must be run to the VSD location to provide input power once the drive is installed.
