The VSD must be installed before output cables can be connected from the drive to the motor terminals.
Commissioning activities such as parameter configuration, motor data entry, and functional testing can only begin once the VSD hardware is physically installed and wired.
The drainage trench is formed within or on top of the structural slab; the slab must be poured and cured before trench excavation and forming can begin.
Waterproofing is typically applied to the structural slab prior to trench construction to ensure a continuous waterproof barrier beneath the trench.
The trench must be excavated before drainage pipes can be laid within it.
The trench structure must be complete before covers or gratings are placed on top to allow access and finishing.
The drainage trench should be installed and set before the final floor screed is applied to achieve proper floor levels and drainage falls.

The fire suppression system header is typically suspended from or supported by the building's structural steel framework. The structural steel must be erected first to provide the mounting points and support structure for the header pipes.

Fire suppression system mains and headers are often routed in the ceiling/roof space. The roof deck must be in place to allow for proper routing, support, and protection of the header from weather exposure during installation.
Branch lines in a fire sprinkler system run off the main header. The header must be installed first to serve as the supply distribution point from which branch lines can be extended.
Sprinkler heads are connected to the branch lines or directly to the header. The header piping network must be in place before individual sprinkler heads can be fitted and connected.
The entire fire suppression system, including the header, must be fully installed before hydrostatic pressure testing can be conducted to verify the integrity of the piping and joints.
The plant room must be structurally built (walls, slab, roof) to provide an enclosed space before any mechanical equipment can be installed.
Waterproofing must be completed to protect the room and its equipment from moisture ingress before installing sensitive mechanical equipment.
Electrical conduits, cabling, and power supply must be roughed-in to the fan location before the fan unit can be physically mounted and connected.
The fan unit must be installed and fixed in position before ductwork can be accurately connected to its inlet/outlet flanges.
The fan must be mounted and physically in place before final electrical connections (wiring, commissioning, testing) can be completed.
Acoustic louvers are typically mounted onto structural openings or frames; the steel framework must be in place to provide support and attachment points.
Acoustic louvers are integrated into exterior wall openings; the wall assembly must be built to define the rough opening.
The rough opening must be framed and sized correctly before the louver unit can be set and secured in place.
After the louver is installed, perimeter joints must be sealed and flashed to prevent air and water infiltration.

successor: Final Inspection and Commissioning of Façade Systems
rationale: Commissioning and inspection for acoustic performance, airtightness, and overall façade integrity must occur after the louver is fully installed and sealed.
The plant room floor slab must be cast and cured to provide a level substrate before any plinth or equipment base can be constructed on top.

predecessor: Plant Room Waterproofing / Damp Proof Membrane
rationale: Any waterproofing or damp-proof membrane on the plant room slab must be installed before plinth construction to ensure the base is protected from moisture ingress.
The equipment plinth must be fully constructed, cured and set before any heavy plant equipment can be positioned and mounted onto it.

successor: Plant Room Grouting / Levelling of Base
rationale: The plinth must be in place before grouting and fine levelling can be applied to ensure the equipment base is perfectly level and aligned.

successor: Plant Room Pipe / Duct Connections to Equipment
rationale: Pipe and duct connections to plant equipment require the equipment to be mounted on its plinth first so that connection points are fixed at the correct elevation and alignment.
Vibration isolators require a stable, level, and cured foundation or concrete slab to be placed on; the slab must be fully cured to bear the load and allow proper anchoring.
A dedicated equipment pad or housekeeping pad must be cast and cured first to provide a clean, level surface for mounting the vibration isolators.

successor: Mechanical Equipment Placement (e.g., chiller, pump, fan)
rationale: The vibration isolators must be installed and positioned on the foundation before the heavy mechanical equipment can be set onto them; the equipment rests directly on the isolators.
Once the vibration isolators are in place, the equipment placed on them must be aligned and leveled; the isolators' adjustment mechanisms are used after equipment placement.
Anchor bolts, sleeves, or embedments for the vibration isolators must be set into the concrete pour beforehand, as they cannot be installed after the concrete has fully cured.
A stable foundation is required to support the weight of the chimney and flue system before any connection work can begin.
The building structure must be erected to provide the vertical chase and support for the flue/chimney, and to define where the chimney penetrates the roof or wall.
The flue or chimney structure must be connected and in place before the lining or insulation can be installed inside it.
The chimney/flue must be installed and protruding through the roof before flashing and weatherproofing can be sealed around it to prevent water ingress.
The flue or chimney must be connected and ready before the fireplace or heating appliance can be installed and connected to the flue system.

successor: Fuel Oil / Gas Supply Line Termination
rationale: The fuel oil/gas supply line requires a stable and level base or support structure (such as concrete pads or steel supports) to be installed first, ensuring the line is properly anchored and protected from settlement or movement.

successor: Fuel Oil / Gas Supply Line Termination
rationale: Any underground piping or conduits for the fuel/gas supply must be laid and backfilled before the termination point is assembled, so that the line can be connected without re-excavation.

predecessor: Fuel Oil / Gas Supply Line Termination
rationale: The supply line termination (i.e., the connection fitting at the tank or equipment end) must be completed before the tank or vessel is set in place, to allow a direct leak-tight connection and avoid repositioning the heavy tank later.

predecessor: Fuel Oil / Gas Supply Line Termination
rationale: Final connection of the fuel line to the burner or appliance can only occur after the line termination is fully installed and secured, ensuring a safe and proper fuel supply path before commissioning.

predecessor: Fuel Oil / Gas Supply Line Termination
rationale: Pressure testing and purging of the fuel line must follow termination installation to verify integrity and remove any debris or air from the system before the line is placed into service.
Backflow preventers must connect to the main water supply line; the underground water main must be installed and pressurized first to provide the water source connection point.
The trench for the water line and the vault/pit where the backflow preventer will be housed must be excavated before the backflow preventer can be placed and connected.
A stable concrete base or vault is needed to support the backflow preventer and allow proper anchoring before the unit can be set in place.
The backflow preventer must be fully installed and connected to the water main before the system can be pressure-tested and flushed to verify integrity and clear debris.
Interior plumbing systems (e.g., building water supply risers) can only be connected to the water source after the backflow preventer is in place to protect against backflow contamination.

The water treatment and dosing system requires a stable foundation and structural support to be installed upon. The building structure must be completed to provide the necessary load-bearing capacity and weather protection before installing this equipment.
The main water supply lines, drainage pipes, and connection points must be roughed in before the water treatment and dosing equipment can be connected to the building's plumbing infrastructure.
Electrical conduits, wiring, and power supply connections need to be roughed in to provide power to the water treatment pumps, dosing controllers, and monitoring equipment.
The water treatment and dosing system must be fully installed before it can be tested, calibrated, and commissioned to ensure it operates correctly and meets water quality specifications.

Final plumbing connections to end-use fixtures (taps, equipment, etc.) must be made after the water treatment system is installed, treated water needs to be available from the treatment system before final distribution connections can be completed.
Plant room equipment (e.g., boilers, pumps, chillers) must be set in place before piping can be connected to them, as piping ties directly into equipment connections.
Structural elements such as floors, walls, and supports must be finished to provide a stable mounting surface and clear routing paths for piping installation.
Piping must be fully connected before pressure testing can be performed to verify integrity and leak-tightness of the completed system.
Insulation is typically applied after piping is installed, but some sections may be pre-insulated; however, complete connection is needed before final insulation wrap-up can proceed.
Commissioning and system startup require all piping connections to be complete so that fluids/gases can flow through the entire system under controlled conditions.
The plant room must be fully enclosed and weathertight before installing sensitive mechanical and electrical equipment to protect from weather damage and provide structural support.
A finished, cured floor slab is required to provide a stable, level base for mounting heavy plant equipment such as boilers, chillers, and pumps.
Electrical conduits, cabling, and sub-panels must be in place before connecting plant equipment to power sources.
Pipework, drains, and water supply lines must be roughed in to allow connection of plant equipment such as boilers, pumps, and water heaters.
All plant equipment must be physically installed before functional testing, calibration, and commissioning can occur to verify performance.

successor: Connect Plant Room to Building Services
rationale: Plant equipment must be in place and connected before it can supply heating, cooling, or ventilation to the rest of the building.
Insulation of pipes and ducts can proceed after equipment installation, though some pre-insulation of pre-fabricated sections may occur earlier as a soft preference.
Conduit and back boxes provide the physical pathway and mounting points for wiring and switches; wiring cannot be installed before these are in place.
Rough-in electrical work (including running cables and positioning boxes) must precede the installation of wiring and switchgear to ensure correct placement.

successor: Install Electrical Fixtures & Devices (switches, outlets, panels)
rationale: Switchgear and wiring must be in place before final fixtures like switches, outlets, and panel covers can be installed for safety and proper connection.
Testing and commissioning require the wiring and switchgear to be fully installed to verify electrical continuity, insulation resistance, and system functionality.
While it is preferred to complete electrical wiring before closing walls with drywall to avoid rework, it is not an absolute physical constraint; wiring can be retrofitted in some cases.
All plant room equipment (boilers, chillers, pumps, etc.) must be physically installed and connected before any commissioning activities can begin to verify their operation.

predecessor: Complete Electrical Connections to Plant Room
rationale: Electrical power and control wiring must be completed and tested for safety before energizing and commissioning plant room systems.

predecessor: Complete Plumbing/HVAC Pipework to Plant Room
rationale: All water, steam, refrigerant, and HVAC pipework connections must be installed and pressure-tested before plant room systems can be operated and commissioned.

The central plant room systems must be commissioned and operational before building-wide HVAC distribution can be tested, as the plant provides the conditioned air, chilled water, or heating to the entire building.

successor: Hand Over Plant Room to Operations
rationale: Formal handover of the plant room to the operations team can only occur after commissioning is complete and all systems are verified as functioning correctly.
Ground must be excavated and leveled before concrete bases/plinths can be poured.
Main building foundations and substructure must be completed to provide a stable substrate and to coordinate elevations for equipment plinths.
Underground pipes, conduits and utilities must be laid before pouring concrete bases to avoid later excavation through finished plinths.
Equipment can only be placed and aligned after the supporting bases and plinths have been cast and cured to required strength.
Grouting under equipment baseplates requires the plinth concrete to be fully cured and prepared first.
Pipe and vessel insulation cannot be applied until the supporting structures (supports and hangers) are in place, as insulation would interfere with or be damaged during support installation.
Pressure testing must be completed before insulation is applied so that leaks can be identified and repaired without removing and reinstalling insulation.
Weatherproofing or cladding is installed directly over insulation to protect it from environmental damage, so insulation must be in place first.

successor: Final Inspection & Testing of Insulated Systems
rationale: A final quality check of the insulated systems logically follows installation, but this is a soft preference as partial inspections could occur concurrently with other finishing work.
Surfaces must be clean, dry, and free of debris, rust, or coatings that could compromise insulation adhesion or performance before insulation material is applied.
The plant room must be structurally enclosed and weathertight before ventilation equipment can be installed to protect equipment from weather damage and provide a secure mounting environment.

predecessor: Complete Structural Waterproofing of Plant Room
rationale: Waterproofing must be finished to prevent water ingress that could damage ventilation equipment and electrical components during and after installation.
The ventilation system must be fully installed before it can be tested, balanced, and commissioned to verify airflow rates and system performance.

While some electrical rough-in can precede ventilation installation, final electrical connections to ventilation units are typically done after the mechanical equipment is in place to ensure correct conduit and wiring routing.
A finished, cured floor slab is required to provide a stable base for mounting ventilation equipment and to allow safe access for installation crews.
Hydronic piping must be installed before circuits can be tested and balanced, as the piping system forms the physical pathways for water flow that need to be measured and adjusted.
Pumps and valves must be in place to enable water circulation through the hydronic system, which is necessary for testing flow rates and balancing.
Terminal units must be installed to serve as endpoints in the hydronic system, as balancing requires measuring flow at all terminal devices.
Testing and balancing must be completed before full system commissioning, as balanced flow conditions are a prerequisite for evaluating overall system performance.

While insulation can often be partially installed earlier, final insulation work over valve stations and balancing components is best done after balancing is complete to allow access for adjustment and measurement.
The parking barrier must be mounted on a stable, level foundation. The base slab must be cured and load-bearing before installing the barrier.
If the parking barrier is powered (e.g., automatic rising bollard or barrier arm), electrical conduits and power supply lines must be laid in the ground before the barrier posts are set in concrete.
The barrier mounting posts or foundations are installed first, then the final paving or asphalt layer is laid up to and around the barrier to create a seamless finished surface.

successor: Electrical connection and testing of barrier mechanism
rationale: The physical barrier unit must be in place and anchored before electricians can connect power, wire control systems, and test the opening/closing or raising/lowering functions.

successor: Parking lot striping and signage installation
rationale: While it is operationally convenient to paint lane markings and install signs after the barrier is in place to ensure correct alignment, this is a soft preference as markings could theoretically be adjusted later.
Charging stations require a stable, level foundation (concrete pad or similar) and prepared site with proper drainage before installation can begin.
Charging stations require high-capacity electrical supply from transformers and switchgear. Power must be available at the site before connecting and commissioning the charging units.
Electrical conduits and trenches must be laid underground between the power source and the charging station locations before the stations can be physically installed and wired.
After the charging station units are physically mounted, the internal electrical connections and cable terminations can be completed to link them to the power supply.
Functional testing, software configuration, and safety verification of the charging stations can only proceed after the units are fully installed and electrically connected.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth before the car park slab can be poured or placed.
A compacted sub-base or hardcore layer is required to provide a stable, load-bearing foundation for the car park slab.
A damp proof membrane must be laid over the sub-base to prevent moisture rising into the slab.
After the slab is poured, it must undergo a curing period to achieve sufficient strength before any loads are applied.
Once the slab is cured, waterproofing and sealants can be applied to protect the concrete from water ingress and chemical damage.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared to ensure proper drainage and a stable base before installing a speed bump.
The road's structural base layers must be in place to support the speed bump and integrate it with the pavement structure.

predecessor: Asphalt or Concrete Pavement Laying (Main Road Surface)
rationale: Speed bumps are typically installed on top of or formed as part of the finished road surface, so the main pavement must be completed first.
Warning signs and pavement markings (e.g., white triangles, 'SPEED BUMP' text) must be applied after the speed bump is constructed to alert drivers accurately.
The road can only be opened to traffic after the speed bump is fully cured and installed to ensure safety and structural integrity.
Column formwork creates the concrete column shape; protection guards can only be installed after the column is formed and cured.
Concrete must be poured and fully cured to provide structural integrity before any protection guard can be mounted or attached.
Corner beads are typically installed after column protection guards for a cleaner finish, but this is a preferred sequence rather than a physical necessity.
The protection guard must be in place before final finishing work (e.g., painting, sealing) can be completed around the column base.
The ground must be graded and compacted before any bike rack can be installed to ensure a stable, level foundation and proper drainage.
A concrete pad or footing must be poured and cured before the bicycle rack can be bolted or anchored to it for structural stability.
Any underground utilities (electrical, water, drainage) in the area must be completed before installing a bike rack to avoid digging conflicts and rework.
It is often more efficient to complete paving after the rack is installed to ensure precise alignment and avoid damaging fresh pavement, but the rack can be installed on finished pavement if needed.
Landscaping, planting, and final site cleanup should occur after the rack is installed to avoid damaging plants and to allow access for installation equipment.
The car park surface (asphalt/concrete) must be completed and cured before any line markings or signage can be applied. Signage cannot be installed on an unfinished or unstable surface.
Lighting poles and overhead fixtures must be installed first to ensure signage placement does not conflict with light poles, and to allow proper visibility assessment of signage during installation.
All signage must be in place before the final inspection and handover of the car park, as signage is a critical safety and wayfinding element that must be verified by inspectors.

While signage can be installed concurrently with barrier/gate installation, it is preferable to have directional and regulatory signage in place first so that drivers can understand traffic flow before gates are operational.
Drainage channels and grates must be installed and covered before signage installation to avoid having to relocate signage due to drainage runoff patterns, and to ensure the ground is fully prepared.
The surface must be clean, dry, and free of debris before painted line markings can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and durability.
The pavement or concrete surface must be fully placed, cured, and finished before any line markings can be painted onto it.
The base structural layer of the roadway or parking area must be completed before the final surface and markings are applied.
While signs can be installed before paint, final sign placement is often coordinated with line markings to ensure consistency; typically markings are done first to guide sign positioning.

successor: Road / Parking Lot Opening to Traffic
rationale: The facility cannot be opened to vehicular traffic until all line markings are in place to provide clear guidance for drivers and ensure safety.
The mounting bracket must be securely installed before the camera can be attached to it.

predecessor: Run Power and Data Cables to Camera Location
rationale: Cables must be in place and terminated before the camera is connected to power and the network.

successor: Configure and Calibrate Parking Guidance Camera
rationale: The camera must be physically installed before it can be powered on, configured, and calibrated for use.

predecessor: Configure and Calibrate Parking Guidance Camera
rationale: The camera must be properly configured and calibrated before it can be tested as part of the overall parking guidance system.

successor: Connect Camera to Network and Power
rationale: Physical installation must be completed before electrical and network connections are made to the device.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared before a vehicle barrier can be installed to ensure a stable foundation and proper alignment.
Vehicle barriers often require anchored foundations or concrete bases to be set and cured before the barrier structure can be mounted or fixed in place.
Any underground electrical, hydraulics, or drainage lines for the barrier system must be laid before the barrier is installed to avoid excavation after placement.
Final paving or surface finishing around the barrier is typically completed after the barrier is in place to achieve a flush, continuous surface and proper transitions.
The barrier must be physically installed before its operation (opening, closing, security functions) can be tested and commissioned.
Formwork provides the mold and structural support needed to contain and shape the wet concrete during slab pouring; without formwork in place, the concrete cannot be properly contained or shaped.
Steel reinforcement bars must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure the slab has the required tensile strength and structural integrity.

Any embedded items such as conduits, sleeves, anchor bolts, or utilities must be positioned and secured within the formwork prior to pouring concrete, as they cannot be placed after the concrete is cast.

Freshly poured concrete must be screeded, floated, and troweled to achieve the desired surface finish and levelness; this finishing work must be performed while the concrete is still wet and workable, immediately after pouring.
After pouring and finishing, the concrete must undergo a controlled curing process to develop its design strength and durability; curing cannot begin until the concrete has been placed and finished.
Waterproofing must be applied to a fully cured concrete substrate to ensure proper adhesion and prevent moisture entrapment.
The substrate must be clean, dry, and free of debris, dust, or contaminants for the waterproofing membrane to bond correctly.
A primer must be applied and fully dried prior to waterproofing membrane installation to ensure proper adhesion as per manufacturer specifications.
After waterproofing is installed, a water test or flood test must be conducted to verify the integrity of the membrane before covering it.
A protective layer or screed must be placed over the waterproofing membrane to shield it from physical damage during subsequent construction activities.
The site must be cleared and excavated to the required depth and grade before drainage pipes can be laid, as drainage installation requires a prepared trench and stable subgrade.
Existing underground utilities must be identified and marked to avoid damaging them during drainage trench excavation and pipe installation.
Drainage pipes must be fully installed, jointed, and inspected before trenches can be backfilled and compacted to protect the pipes and ensure proper compaction around them.
Subsurface drainage must be operational before placing foundations or pavements to prevent water accumulation and ensure long-term structural stability.
Final grading and landscaping ideally follow drainage installation to ensure surface water flows correctly into drains, though some landscaping work may proceed concurrently in non-critical areas.

successor: Construction Activity - Marking and Signage Application
rationale: Surface preparation (cleaning, leveling, and priming) must be completed before any markings or signage are applied, as markings will not adhere properly to unclean or uneven surfaces.

predecessor: Construction Activity - Base Pavement / Flooring Installation
successor: Construction Activity - Marking and Signage Application
rationale: The base pavement or flooring layer must be installed and cured before markings are applied, as markings are placed on top of the finished surface.

predecessor: Construction Activity - Marking and Signage Application
successor: Construction Activity - Final Inspection and Quality Control
rationale: Markings and signage must be fully applied and dried before the final inspection can verify compliance with design specifications.

predecessor: Construction Activity - Marking and Signage Application
successor: Construction Activity - Site Handover / Opening to Traffic
rationale: All markings and signage must be in place to provide proper guidance and safety information before the site can be opened for use or traffic.

successor: Construction Activity - Marking and Signage Application
rationale: Underground utility installation and backfilling must be completed before surface markings are applied, as markings would be destroyed or covered during excavation work.
The site must be evaluated for suitability, electrical capacity, and physical layout before any construction begins to ensure the charging station can be properly installed.
Adequate electrical supply (e.g., transformer upgrades, conduit runs, panel upgrades) must be in place to support the charging station's power requirements before installation.
Required building permits, electrical permits, and regulatory approvals must be obtained prior to starting physical construction to comply with legal and safety requirements.
After the hardware is physically installed, the system must be connected to the grid and commissioned (tested, configured, and verified) before it can be put into service.
A formal inspection and operational testing must be conducted after installation is complete to ensure safety compliance and proper functionality before public use.
Control systems require electrical power to operate and be tested during commissioning. Electrical installation must be complete to provide power to control panels, sensors, and actuators.
Control systems monitor and control mechanical equipment such as HVAC, pumps, and fans. Mechanical installation must be in place before the control system can be commissioned.
The control system hardware (controllers, sensors, actuators, wiring) must be physically installed before it can be powered on, tested, and commissioned.
Commissioning validates individual control system components and basic functionality, which must pass before integrated system testing across multiple building systems can proceed.
Control system commissioning is a prerequisite for final building acceptance and handover, as the building's automated systems must be verified as operational before occupancy.
Ceiling must be in place to provide the structural support and mounting surface for light fixtures.
Electrical wiring, junction boxes, and conduit must be installed and roughed in before lighting fixtures can be connected and mounted.
Lighting fixtures must be installed first so that drywall and finishing work can be cut and fitted around the fixtures properly.

While painting can be done before or after lighting installation, it is typical to install lights after painting to avoid damaging fixtures; however, this is a soft preference as wiring can be left protruding.

successor: Construction Activity - Final Electrical Testing and Commissioning
rationale: Lighting fixtures must be physically installed before they can be connected to power and tested for proper operation.
Structural framing and enclosure must be complete to provide the physical support and enclosed spaces where fire systems (sprinklers, piping, detectors) will be installed.
Electrical rough-in and conduit pathways must be in place to supply power and control wiring for fire alarm panels, smoke detectors, and fire suppression system components.

predecessor: Overhead Mechanical Rough-In (HVAC ducts, plumbing mains)
rationale: Mechanical rough-in must be completed first to avoid interference conflicts and to allow fire sprinkler piping and detection devices to be routed around or coordinated with existing overhead utilities.

Fire system piping, sprinkler heads, detectors, and control panels must be fully installed, tested, and approved before walls and ceilings are enclosed to allow access for installation and inspection.

successor: Fire Suppression System Pressure Testing and Commissioning
rationale: The fire suppression system must be physically installed before it can be pressure-tested, inspected, and commissioned to verify it meets code and performance requirements.
Security system components (sensors, control panels, wiring) require electrical power and conduit paths that must be roughed-in before final installation can begin.

predecessor: Interior Wall Framing and Drywall Installation
rationale: Security system sensors and keypads are typically mounted on or within walls, requiring the wall framing and drywall to be in place before installation.
Security cameras and motion detectors are often mounted to the ceiling grid; the grid must be installed to provide attachment points and routing for cabling.

Security system components such as sensors and keypads are often installed before final painting so that any touch-ups around mounting points can be performed, though this is a preference, not a physical requirement.
The security system must be fully installed before it can be powered on, programmed, and tested for proper operation.
Structural framing (walls, ceilings, roof structure) must be in place before ductwork can be routed and supported, as ducts are typically hung from or installed within the structural framework.
The building must be enclosed (roof and walls complete) to protect ductwork materials and installation work from weather damage and to create a controlled environment for installation.
Floor slabs must be poured and cured to provide working surfaces and to establish floor-to-ceiling heights for vertical duct risers and floor-mounted equipment.
Fireproofing or fire-resistive wrap must be applied after ductwork is installed and inspected, as it coats the exterior of the installed ducts.

successor: Electrical and Low-Voltage Rough-In (in ceiling spaces)
rationale: While electrical work can partially precede ductwork, final routing of cables and conduits in crowded ceiling spaces is more efficiently done after ducts are in place to avoid conflicts, though this is a soft preference for coordination rather than a physical necessity.

predecessor: Construction Activity - Foundation and Base Preparation
successor: Construction Activity - Barrier and Guardrail Installation
rationale: A stable foundation and base surface is required before barriers and guardrails can be anchored, post-mounted, or bolted securely. Without the prepared base, the barrier system will lack structural integrity.

successor: Construction Activity - Barrier and Guardrail Installation
rationale: The main structural framework or substructure must be in place to provide attachment points and support for barriers and guardrails, especially for bridge or elevated deck applications.

predecessor: Construction Activity - Utility and Conduit Installation (Underground/Roadbase)
successor: Construction Activity - Barrier and Guardrail Installation
rationale: Underground utilities, conduits, and drainage must be installed prior to barrier installation to avoid excavation or disruption after barriers are fixed in place.

predecessor: Construction Activity - Barrier and Guardrail Installation
successor: Construction Activity - Paving and Surface Finishing
rationale: Barriers and guardrails delineate the final alignment; paving and surface finishing must be performed after installation to ensure flush transitions, proper drainage gradients, and to avoid damaging new barriers with paving equipment.

predecessor: Construction Activity - Barrier and Guardrail Installation
successor: Construction Activity - Final Inspection and Testing
rationale: Barrier and guardrail installation must be complete and cured (if applicable) before final safety inspections, impact testing, and acceptance testing can be conducted.
Cubicles need a flat, level finished floor surface to be installed upon; the floor slab and screed must be completed first.
If raised access flooring is specified, it must be fully installed and leveled before cubicles can be placed on top.

predecessor: Overhead MEP Rough-In (Ductwork, Cable Trays, Piping)
rationale: Overhead services such as electrical conduits, data cables, and HVAC ductwork must be roughed-in above the ceiling grid before cubicle walls are erected, as later access becomes restricted.
The suspended ceiling must be completed (or at least the grid installed) before cubicles are positioned, to ensure overhead clearances and lighting locations are fixed.

successor: Workstation electrical/data fit-out (floor boxes, power whips, data drops)
rationale: Cubicles must be in place so that in-floor or under-cubicle power and data connections can be routed to the correct locations within each workstation.
Cubicle partitions and work surfaces define the layout; loose furniture is placed after the cubicle framework is complete.
Soft preference: completing cubicles first avoids dust and paint splatter on finished workstations, though painting can be done before in some sequencing.
Office desks must be placed on a finished floor slab to provide a stable, level surface and to ensure proper alignment.
Interior walls define the office layout and spatial divisions; desks cannot be positioned accurately until walls are framed.
Electrical outlets, data cabling, and power points must be installed in the walls and floors before desk placement to avoid obstruction and rework.
Floor coverings must be laid before desks are placed to avoid moving heavy furniture over finished floors or having to work around desks.
Computers, monitors, phones, and related IT equipment are placed on and around desks after desks are installed in their final positions.
Although final cleaning typically occurs after all furniture is in place, this is a soft preference as cleaning can be done around desks if necessary.
Office chairs need a finished, level floor surface to roll and function properly without damaging the flooring material.
Chairs must be placed in the workspace before desks or workstations are fully configured, as desks are typically positioned after chairs to ensure proper ergonomic alignment and spacing.
Ceiling work (including lighting and overhead fixtures) should be completed before bringing in furniture like office chairs to avoid dust, debris, and damage from overhead work.
Painting should be finished before installing chairs to prevent paint splatter, dust, and fumes from damaging upholstery and to avoid moving furniture around wet walls.
While it is preferred to do final cleaning after chair installation to remove any packing debris, it is not a hard physical constraint as chairs can be moved for cleaning.
The conference table must be placed on a finished floor surface to ensure stability, level placement, and to avoid damage to both the floor and the table during installation.
Wall and ceiling finishing (painting, drywall, etc.) generates dust and debris that could damage the conference table surface; these messy tasks must be completed before bringing in the table.

Underfloor or in-wall electrical and data cabling that will serve the conference table area must be roughed in before the table is placed, as the table may obstruct access to floor/wall areas for this work.

Audio-visual equipment (monitors, presentation systems, cable management) is often integrated with or mounted on/through the conference table; the table must be in place to properly route cables and mount equipment.

Chairs and other furniture are positioned around the conference table; while it is a logical flow, the seating could theoretically be placed before the table in some layouts, making this a soft preference for workflow efficiency.
The reception desk must be placed on a finished, level floor surface. Foundation and concrete slab work must be completed to provide a stable base.
Electrical outlets, data ports, and cabling for the reception desk area need to be roughed-in behind the walls and floor before the desk is installed.
If the reception desk includes a sink or water feature, plumbing rough-ins must be completed before the desk is positioned and finished.
It is a soft preference to have walls painted before the desk is installed to avoid needing to paint around the desk, but the desk can be installed first and walls painted afterward with masking.
The reception desk must be in place before telephones, computers, and IT equipment can be installed on or connected to the desk.
Floor finishing is often done before the desk to avoid cutting around it, but the desk can be installed first and flooring later with careful trimming.

successor: Final electrical trim-out and outlet cover installation
rationale: Electrical trim-out can be done before or after the desk; it is a soft preference to complete after the desk so outlets align with desk placement.
The wall mounting structure must be securely attached to the wall before the presentation screen or whiteboard can be mounted onto it.

predecessor: Run electrical wiring to screen location
rationale: Electrical wiring must be roughed in and available at the mounting location before the screen can be plugged in or hardwired.
Walls should be finished and painted before mounting a screen or whiteboard to avoid damaging the finished surface or having to work around the installed component.
The screen must be physically installed in its final position before AV cables (HDMI, VGA, etc.) can be connected to it.
Testing and calibration of the screen can only be done after it is mounted and connected, but this is a soft preference as some basic tests could be done on the ground.

Storage cabinets and filing cabinets need a finished, level floor surface for proper installation and stability. Installing them before floor finishing would damage the floor or require moving the heavy cabinets.

Walls behind and around cabinets must be finished (painted, wallpapered, or paneled) before installing cabinets, as the cabinets will be placed against walls and cannot be easily moved later for finishing.

Electrical wiring, outlets, and switches for the area must be roughed in before cabinets are installed, as cabinets may cover wall areas where electrical work is needed, and access to walls is restricted once cabinets are in place.

It is typical to install baseboards and trim after cabinet installation so that trim can be cut to fit neatly around the cabinet bases, though this is a soft preference as trim can also be installed first with careful scribing.
After cabinets are installed, the space can be thoroughly cleaned and furniture/office equipment moved in, as cabinets are a major built-in component that should be in place before final occupancy.
Demountable partitions require a level finished floor surface for proper installation, alignment, and stability.
Demountable walls are typically installed after overhead structures are complete to allow full-height installation and avoid rework from overhead trades.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (Electrical, Plumbing, HVAC rough-in within zone)
rationale: Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work in the area must be done before demountable walls are placed, as the walls would block access to overhead and underfloor services.

successor: Final MEP trim-out and fit-out (sockets, switches, terminal units)
rationale: Demountable partitions accommodate integrated MEP services; electrical sockets, data outlets, and HVAC terminals are installed into or onto the wall after it is erected.

successor: Finishing works (painting, wall coverings, cabinetry installation)
rationale: Interior finishes and built-in furniture that abut or are installed on the partition walls can only proceed once the partition walls are in place and fixed.

Electrical wiring, ductwork, plumbing pipes, and other MEP services must be installed in the plenum space above the ceiling grid before the suspended ceiling is installed, as they would be inaccessible afterward.
The structural deck or slab above must be finished and cured so that ceiling hangers and anchors can be securely attached to it.
Spray-applied fireproofing on beams and deck must be installed before the ceiling is enclosed, because the ceiling would block access for fireproofing application.

successor: Ceiling tile installation and grid finishing
rationale: The suspended ceiling grid (main tees, cross tees, and hanger wires) must be fully installed and leveled before ceiling tiles or panels can be placed into the grid.

successor: Lighting Fixture Trim and Diffuser Installation
rationale: After the suspended ceiling grid is in place, lighting fixtures, air diffusers, and other ceiling-mounted devices can be fitted and trimmed out, as their placement depends on the ceiling grid layout.
The raised access floor system requires a stable, level concrete subfloor as its base. Without a properly finished concrete slab, the access floor pedestals cannot be installed securely.
All underfloor cables, conduits, and ductwork must be laid out before the raised floor panels are installed, as access beneath the floor becomes extremely limited once panels are placed.

successor: Final floor covering installation (carpet tiles, vinyl)
rationale: Finish floor materials such as carpet tiles or vinyl are laid directly on top of the raised access floor panels and cannot be installed until the access floor system is fully assembled and level.

successor: Interior fit-out and partition wall installation
rationale: Partition walls and interior finishes are built on top of the finished floor surface; erecting walls before the floor is complete would result in misalignments and rework.

successor: Final MEP trim-out and outlet installation
rationale: Floor-mounted power and data outlets are set into the access floor panels and require the raised floor grid to be in place for proper positioning and connection to underfloor services.
Ductwork must be in place to provide an air path and connection point for diffusers/grilles.
Diffusers and grilles mount into or align with ceiling or wall openings; the support structure must be installed first.
Diffusers/grilles are typically installed before ceiling finish is completed to ensure proper fit and sealing around openings.
Diffusers and grilles must be in place to measure and adjust airflow during balancing and commissioning.
Soft preference to install diffusers before final painting so paint can be touched up around the installed grille for a clean finish, though the grille can be masked if painted after.
Electrical wiring and junction boxes must be installed in the ceiling/floor slab before lighting fixtures can be connected and mounted.
Suspended ceiling grids (T-bar) must be in place to provide the support structure for recessed or surface-mounted lighting fixtures in offices.
Ductwork in the plenum space above the ceiling must be completed before lighting fixtures are installed to avoid interference and access issues.
Ceiling tiles must be installed after lighting fixtures are mounted and wired so that tiles can be cut to fit around fixtures and the fixtures can be properly positioned within the grid.
Wall switches, dimmers, and final connections to lighting circuits must be completed after fixtures are in place to verify proper operation and connectivity.

Structural steel provides the primary support framework and attachment points (via hangers, clamps, and brackets) for cable trays and conduits. Without the steel structure in place, there is no surface or framework to mount the trays and conduits.

Overhead plumbing and HVAC ductwork must be installed first to establish spatial routing. Cable trays are often routed around or below these larger mechanical systems, so knowing their final positions is essential to avoid clashes and ensure proper clearance.

Cables are pulled into and through the installed cable trays and conduits. The tray/conduit raceway system must be fully in place before any cables can be run, as it serves as the physical pathway and support for the cables.

successor: Fireproofing (on trays and conduits if required)
rationale: If fireproofing or firestopping is required at cable tray/ conduit penetrations through fire-rated walls or floors, the tray/conduit must be installed first so that the firestop sealant or wrap can be applied around it.

Cable trays and conduits run above ceilings and must be fully installed, inspected, and approved before ceiling finishes are closed up. Installing ceilings first would block access and require costly rework to install the raceway system.
Fire alarm devices require electrical power and communication wiring to be run in walls and ceilings before the devices can be connected and mounted.
Conduit must be in place to house and protect fire alarm cables before devices can be wired and installed.
Ceiling-mounted fire alarm devices (smoke detectors, sprinkler heads) require the ceiling grid or structure to be in place for proper mounting and positioning.

successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: All fire alarm devices must be physically installed and connected before the system can be powered on, tested, and commissioned for functionality.
Fire alarm devices are often installed in coordination with or slightly before ceiling and wall finishes to ensure proper fit and avoid rework, but finishing should not cover device access panels.
Electrical wiring must be run to the outlet location before the outlet can be installed and connected.
Outlet boxes are mounted in or on walls; drywall must be in place so that the outlet can be properly positioned and trimmed out.

It is easier to paint walls before installing outlets to avoid paint on the devices, but outlets are often installed after painting for a clean finish; this is a soft preference as either order can work with care.
The outlet device must be physically installed before the final electrical connections (wiring the receptacle, installing cover plates) and testing can be completed.
Data jacks must be installed in their boxes before network cables can be terminated to the jack and tested.
The structural frame and roof must be in place to provide the necessary support and weather protection before installing the curtain wall system.
Rough openings must be framed and blocking installed to provide a secure mounting surface for windows and curtain wall anchors.

successor: Window / curtain wall waterproofing & air sealing
rationale: Waterproofing and air sealing must be applied immediately after installing the curtain wall to prevent water and air infiltration.
Interior finishes like drywall should only be installed after windows/curtain walls are in place to avoid damage from weather exposure and to allow proper integration with window frames.
Exterior cladding systems often integrate with or abut the curtain wall, so the curtain wall must be installed first to establish the weathertight envelope and alignment.
Interior doors require framed openings with studs, headers, and rough openings to be in place before the door unit can be installed.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in must be completed within walls before doors are installed to avoid damaging the door units or blocking access.
While doors can be installed before or after drywall, it is often preferred to install doors after wall finishing to avoid damaging the door slab or frame during drywall work.
Flooring must be installed after doors so that the door bottom clearance can be set correctly relative to the finished floor height, and to prevent damage to flooring during door installation.

successor: Painting and finishing of door and frame
rationale: It is a soft preference to paint/finish doors after installation to ensure a uniform finish, though pre-finished doors may not require this.
Window blinds and shades are mounted onto or within the window frame, so the frame must be installed first to provide the structural support and attachment surface.
The glass panels must be in place before blinds or shades are installed, as blinds are mounted to the window frame/header and need the glass to be present for proper fit and alignment.
It is preferable to complete painting and wall finishing first to avoid getting paint or debris on the blinds/shades and to allow clean edges around the window trim.
While trim can be installed before blinds, it is often easier to install blinds after the window casing/trim is finished to ensure proper clearance and a finished appearance.
Blinds and shades should be installed before final cleaning to avoid dust and debris settling on them after installation, but they are sensitive and should be protected.
Partitions require a stable, level floor surface to be installed upon; the floor slab must be fully poured, leveled, and cured to support partition walls.

predecessor: Complete Overhead MEP Rough-In (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing)
rationale: Overhead ductwork, pipes, and conduit must be installed before partitions are erected, otherwise access for overhead work would be blocked by the walls.
Suspended ceiling grids are typically installed before partitions so that partitions can align with and support the ceiling grid, and to avoid cutting partitions for ceiling hangers.
Wiring and devices within partition walls can only be installed after the wall framing and sheathing are in place.
Painting and final finishing of partition surfaces must occur after the partitions are fully erected and secured.
Raised floor systems require a clean, level concrete substrate to ensure proper support and alignment of pedestals and floor panels.
Electrical conduits, data cables, and other underfloor utilities must be placed in or on the substrate before the raised floor system is installed, as they become inaccessible afterward.

successor: Floor tile/carpet installation on raised panels
rationale: The structural raised floor panels and pedestal grid must be fully installed before any final floor covering (e.g., carpet tiles, vinyl, or laminate) can be laid on top.
The raised floor plenum must be enclosed and sealed before the air distribution system can be balanced and tested for proper airflow.

While it is physically possible to place furniture before raised floors, it is standard practice to complete the raised floor system first to provide a stable, level surface and to allow for later reconfiguration of underfloor services.
The concrete slab must be fully cured to provide a stable, level surface for workstation assembly; otherwise, the workstations would be unstable and could shift.
The building must be enclosed to protect workstations and assembly personnel from weather, dust, and moisture during installation.

predecessor: Overhead electrical and data cabling installation
rationale: Overhead utilities must be run before workstations are placed underneath, as access above the workstations will be restricted once they are installed.
Workstations must be physically assembled and positioned before they can be connected to power and data networks.
It is practical to adjust chairs, monitor arms, and desk accessories after workstations are in place, though some ergonomic setup could theoretically occur concurrently.

The structural framing (walls, columns) and MEP rough-ins (ductwork, piping, conduit) must be completed before the ceiling grid is installed, as the ceiling system is suspended from the structural deck and must accommodate overhead services.

predecessor: Overhead MEP Rough-In (Ductwork, Piping, Electrical Conduit)
rationale: All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing services that run above the ceiling must be roughed-in, inspected, and pressure-tested before the ceiling grid is hung, as access to these systems becomes extremely difficult after the ceiling is closed.
Fireproofing of structural elements and any thermal/acoustic insulation above the ceiling plane must be installed before the ceiling grid and tiles are placed, as they conceal these materials.

successor: Final electrical and lighting fixture installation
rationale: Ceiling-mounted lighting fixtures, speakers, sprinkler heads, and HVAC diffusers are typically installed after or concurrently with the ceiling grid and tile installation, but the grid must be in place first to support and align these fixtures.

While painting can technically be done before the ceiling, it is preferable to complete ceiling installation first to avoid drips, overspray, and damage to finished wall surfaces from ceiling work above.
Conduits and pathways must be installed before cables can be pulled through them.
Cable trays and support pathways must be in place to route and support cables before cable pulling and termination.

predecessor: Electrical rough-in and outlet box installation
rationale: Outlet boxes must be installed and secured to provide a mounting point for data outlet faceplates and terminations.
Terminated cable ends must be completed before faceplates can be snapped onto outlet boxes.
Cables must be fully terminated at both ends before continuity, performance, and certification testing can be performed.
Conduits and junction boxes must be in place before fixtures can be mounted and wired.

predecessor: Overhead ceiling grid or mounting surface completion
rationale: Fixtures need a finished ceiling grid, suspended structure, or mounting surface to be physically attached.
Fixtures must be installed and wired before surrounding ceiling tiles are placed, to allow access for connections.

successor: Final electrical testing and building commissioning
rationale: Lighting fixtures must be installed, connected, and individually commissioned before the overall electrical system and building-wide commissioning tests can be conducted.

While finishing can proceed after lighting is installed, it is a soft preference because lighting may be needed for proper illumination during finishing work, but finishing can be done with temporary lighting if necessary.
Diffusers are attached to the ductwork system; ducts must be installed and sealed before diffusers can be mounted to ensure proper airflow and avoid leaks.
The main HVAC distribution network (ducts, pipes, and wiring) must be roughed-in before diffusers can be installed, as diffusers are terminal devices connected to this network.
Diffusers are typically mounted into ceiling tiles or the ceiling grid; the ceiling support structure must be in place to receive the diffusers.
Air balancing of diffusers is part of the overall HVAC system commissioning; balancing must be completed before the system's final performance testing and verification can be done.

Soft preference: Installing and balancing diffusers before final interior finishing avoids rework, but finishing could theoretically proceed concurrently; however it is best practice to complete diffuser work before ceilings are fully closed and painted.

Tiles must be laid and grouted before WC installation to ensure proper waterproofing, allow for correct positioning of the WC flange on top of finished floor tiles, and prevent damage to tiles by heavy fixtures.

predecessor: Rough-In Plumbing for Waste and Water Supply
rationale: The waste pipe (soil pipe), vent pipe, and water supply line must be roughed into the correct location behind the wall and in the floor before the WC can be physically connected and secured.
A stable, level subfloor (often with plywood or cement board) must be in place to support the toilet flange and the weight of the WC unit.

successor: Final Plumbing Connections and Fixture Trim-Out
rationale: After the WC is set in place over the wax ring and bolted to the flange, the final connections (water supply line to fill valve, toilet seat installation, and leak testing) must be completed.

Installing the WC early in finishing can allow paint and finishing work to proceed around it, but it is a soft preference as painting is often done before fixture installation to avoid overspray on fixtures.
The urinal requires a drain connection to the waste plumbing system, which must be roughed-in before the fixture can be mounted.
The urinal needs a water supply line (for flush valve or tank) that must be roughed-in before the fixture is attached.
The urinal is wall-mounted, so the wall framing and backing/support must be in place to bear the weight of the fixture.
Proper blocking between studs is required to securely anchor the urinal to the wall.
If the urinal uses an electronic flush valve, electrical rough-in should be completed before fixture installation to avoid retrofitting.
The flush valve and water supply connections are made after the urinal is mounted in place.
Privacy screens or partitions between urinals are typically installed after the urinals themselves are in place to ensure proper alignment.

While tile work often precedes fixture installation for a clean finish, in some sequences the urinal is mounted first and then the wall finish is applied around it; this is a soft preference depending on the construction method.
Grab bars must be mounted to wall studs or blocking within framed walls to provide structural support.
Reinforced backing or blocking must be installed inside the wall cavity at grab bar locations to anchor the bars securely.
If grab bars are installed in a tiled shower area, the waterproofing membrane and tile backer board must be in place before grab bars are mounted.
Grab bars that protrude through tile must be installed before final tile or grout work around the flange to achieve a waterproof seal.
It is a soft preference to verify grab bar compliance with accessibility codes after installation, though inspections can occur at various stages.
The water supply lines and drain/waste pipes must be installed and roughed-in within the wall before the sink and faucet can be physically connected and mounted.
The wall frame provides the structural backing for securing the sink bracket, faucet, and any wall-mounted lavatory components.
Drywall must be installed and finished to provide a clean surface against which the sink backsplash or rim will seal, and to conceal plumbing within the wall.
If the sink is an undermount or drop-in type, the sink must be installed first so the countertop can be fabricated and fitted around or over the sink rim.

It is common to install the faucet to the sink deck before mounting the sink, but this is a preference for ease of access rather than a hard physical constraint; the faucet can also be installed after the sink is in place.
Tile backsplash should be installed after the sink is in place so that tiles can be cut and fitted precisely around the sink rim and backsplash flange, ensuring a watertight seal.

Typically the vanity cabinet is installed first and the sink is placed on top, but some installations place the sink before the cabinet's final anchoring; this is more of a sequencing preference than a strict physical requirement.
Flooring is usually completed before the vanity and sink are installed to avoid damage, but the sink can be installed over finished flooring without a strict physical dependency.
Toilet paper dispensers are typically mounted on partition walls in toilet stalls; the partition walls must be installed first to provide a mounting surface.
Walls need to be finished (drywall, painting, or tiling) before mounting any fixtures to ensure a clean, finished appearance and proper adhesion/anchoring.

While the toilet paper dispenser could technically be installed after the toilet, it's more convenient to install it first to avoid working around the toilet fixture, but this is a soft preference, not a physical necessity.
The toilet paper dispenser must be installed before the final inspection to ensure all fixtures are in place and functional for occupancy.
Plumbing rough-in should be completed before wall finishes are applied, which is a prerequisite for the dispenser, but this is an indirect constraint.
The hand towel dispenser must be mounted to a wall or structural backing; wall framing and backing provide the necessary support surface for secure attachment.

predecessor: Complete rough-in plumbing (supply and drain lines)
rationale: Plumbing rough-in must be finished behind the wall before the dispenser is mounted, as the dispenser does not connect to plumbing but the adjacent sink area needs readiness; however, the dispenser installation typically occurs after walls are finished.

predecessor: Finish wall surface (drywall, tiling, or paint)
rationale: The dispenser is mounted on finished wall surfaces; installing before finishing would damage the wall or require removal for finishing work.

successor: Install paper towel refill / stock dispenser with towels
rationale: The dispenser must be physically mounted and secured before it can be stocked with towels for use.

successor: Complete final inspection and commissioning of restroom fixtures
rationale: All fixtures including the hand towel dispenser must be installed before the final inspection can verify completeness and functionality of the restroom.
Soap dispensers are typically mounted on or adjacent to lavatories/sinks; the lavatory must be in place to establish the location and mounting surface for the soap dispenser.
It is a common sequence preference to install the soap dispenser before mirrors to avoid damaging the mirror surface during dispenser installation, but it is not a physical necessity.
Plumbing rough-in (supply lines for water if applicable) must be completed before the soap dispenser is mounted and connected.
The soap dispenser must be physically mounted before final connections to supply lines can be made.
Wall surfaces must be finished before mounting the soap dispenser to ensure a clean, finished appearance and proper adhesion/mounting.
Waste receptacles placed on finished floors need a stable, cured floor surface for proper support and level positioning.

predecessor: Rough-In Plumbing for Waste and Water Supply
rationale: If the waste receptacle is a sink or floor drain type, the drain/waste piping must be roughed-in before the receptacle is set in place.
For wall-mounted waste receptacles, the wall structure must be framed and sheathed to provide attachment support.
It is preferable to install waste receptacles before finish flooring to coordinate cutouts and avoid damaging finished surfaces, but final flooring can be installed around a receptacle if needed.
Trim and millwork should be completed after waste receptacle installation to allow for precise fit and seamless integration around the receptacle.
Mirrors are typically mounted on finished walls; the wall surface must be completed (e.g., painted, tiled, or plastered) to provide a stable and clean substrate for mirror attachment.

It is easier and safer to install mirrors after flooring is in place to avoid damaging the floor or the mirror during installation, but this is a preference for logistics and safety rather than a physical necessity.

If electrical fixtures (e.g., lights above a bathroom mirror) or vanities are positioned relative to the mirror, the mirror must be installed first so that the fixtures can be aligned correctly and wiring can be routed around the mirror.
Touch-up painting around the mirror edges is easier after the mirror is installed to cover any gaps or marks, but this is a cosmetic preference.
If a decorative frame or trim is added around the mirror, it is typically installed after the mirror is in place for precise fit and alignment.
Baby changing station needs to be mounted on a wall, so wall framing must be complete to provide structural support.
If the baby changing station is located near a sink or plumbing fixture, rough-in plumbing must be completed before final fixture installation.
Any electrical wiring for lighting near the changing station area must be roughed in before wall finishes and station mounting.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and finished before mounting the baby changing station to provide a clean finished wall surface.
Baby changing station must be installed and secured before the final building inspection can verify proper safety and accessibility compliance.
The shower stall must be placed on a solid, waterproofed floor to prevent water damage and structural issues.
Drain and supply lines must be roughed into the floor/wall before the shower pan or stall base is set in place.
The shower stall base or pan must be installed first so that surrounding wall framing and cement board can overlap the base flange for proper waterproofing.
The shower stall enclosure must be in place before mounting trim and fixtures that seal against the stall walls.
Tile work on shower walls must begin after the shower pan is set to ensure proper overlap and waterproof transition between wall and base.

successor: Install Toilet Exhaust Fan / Ventilation Grille
rationale: Electrical power supply wiring must be roughed in and available before the exhaust fan unit can be connected and installed.

predecessor: Install Toilet Exhaust Fan / Ventilation Grille
rationale: The exhaust fan housing or grille must be physically mounted before the ductwork can be attached and sealed to its discharge collar.

predecessor: Install Toilet Exhaust Fan / Ventilation Grille
successor: Install Ceiling Finish / Drywall Around Grille
rationale: The grille or fan housing must be in place so that ceiling material can be cut and finished neatly around it, ensuring a proper fit and seal.

predecessor: Install Toilet Exhaust Fan / Ventilation Grille
rationale: If the fan penetrates a fire-rated assembly, damper testing should follow installation, though scheduling may be flexible depending on inspection sequence.

successor: Install Toilet Exhaust Fan / Ventilation Grille
rationale: The duct chase or shaft must be framed and accessible before the fan/grille can be positioned and secured in its intended location.
Floor drains require connection to the plumbing waste pipe system, which must be roughed-in before the drain body can be positioned and connected.
The concrete slab or subfloor must be prepared (excavated, gravel bed placed, vapor barrier laid) before the floor drain can be set at the correct elevation and embedded.
The floor drain body must be installed and secured in place before the concrete slab is poured around it to ensure proper embedment and a watertight seal.
After the floor drain is installed, waterproofing membrane is applied around the drain flange and integrated with the drain to prevent leaks at the penetration point.
Floor finishing (tiling, epoxy, etc.) must be completed after the drain is installed so that the finish can be sloped toward the drain and the drain grate set flush with the finished floor level.
Restroom signage indicating restroom locations depends on knowing where restrooms are finalized, which requires rough-in plumbing to be complete.
Restroom signage must be mounted on walls; wall framing must be complete to provide a structure for mounting signs.
Signs are typically mounted on finished drywall surfaces; drywall must be installed and finished before signage can be attached.
Painting should be completed before installing signage to avoid needing to paint around signs and to ensure a clean finished appearance.
Restroom signage is required for building occupancy and code compliance; the final inspection and occupancy phase cannot be completed until proper restroom signage is installed.
The structural framing for the toilet partitions must be in place to provide the support structure and anchorage points for the partition system.
Plumbing rough-ins (waste, water supply lines) must be installed in the walls and floor before partitions are placed, as access behind or under the partitions would be blocked after installation.

predecessor: Complete rough-in electrical for toilet area
rationale: Electrical conduit, junction boxes, and wiring within walls must be roughed in before partitions are installed, as they would be inaccessible afterward.

predecessor: Install floor finish (tile, sheet vinyl, etc.) in toilet area
rationale: Floor finishes need to be completed beneath the partitions so that partitions sit on top of the finished flooring, allowing for proper fit, seal, and a finished appearance.
Toilet fixtures must be installed after partitions are in place because the partitions define the stall layout and provide the mounting/attachment points for the toilets.
Rough-in plumbing (drain, waste, vent pipes) must be installed in walls and floors before sanitary fixtures (toilets, sinks, basins) can be set and connected to those pipes.
Hot and cold water supply lines must be run to fixture locations before fixtures can be connected to the water supply.
Tile backing, waterproofing membranes, and finished wall/floor surfaces in wet areas must be completed before sanitary fixtures are mounted to avoid damaging finishes or requiring rework.
Sanitary fixtures must be installed and connected before trims (escutcheons, toilet paper holders, grab bars, soap dispensers) can be fitted around or onto them.
Fixture installation must be complete before final connection of supply lines, operation testing, and leak checks can be performed on the assembled system.

successor: Install Waterproof Membrane and Tile Finishes
rationale: The underlayment provides a weather-resistant barrier and a smooth substrate that is necessary before installing the waterproof membrane and tile finishes.

successor: Install Waterproof Membrane and Tile Finishes
rationale: All rough-in work for electrical outlets, plumbing pipes, and drains must be completed behind the wall and floor surfaces before tiling, as accessing these systems after tile installation would require destructive removal.

predecessor: Install Waterproof Membrane and Tile Finishes
rationale: Wall and floor finishes (tile, membrane) must be fully installed before fixtures (toilets, sinks, faucets, showerheads, towel bars) and trim can be mounted, as these items are set onto or through the finished tiled surfaces.

predecessor: Install Waterproof Membrane and Tile Finishes
rationale: Tile grouting and sealing can only occur after the tiles and waterproof membrane are fully installed in place.

predecessor: Install Waterproof Membrane and Tile Finishes
rationale: While tile installation is near the end of interior finishes, the final inspection is typically performed after all finishes including tile are complete, but this is a soft ordering preference as inspections could theoretically occur in phases.
The ventilation system must be physically installed before it can be commissioned and tested for proper operation.
Electrical power supply must be roughed-in and connected to the ventilation unit before commissioning can verify its operation.
All ductwork connecting the ventilation fan to the outside must be installed before the system can be commissioned to ensure airflow path exists.
Ceiling installation often integrates the ventilation fan mounting and grille; commissioning requires the system to be in its final installed configuration.
Commissioning of ventilation must be completed and verified before the restroom can be finalized, closed up, and made ready for occupancy use.
Structural steel framing must be complete before any ceiling work can begin, as the ceiling systems are supported by or attached to the structural frame.
All mechanical ducts, electrical conduits, and plumbing pipes that will run above the ceiling must be installed before the ceiling is closed in, to avoid costly rework and access issues.
Fire sprinkler piping and heads above the ceiling must be installed and tested before ceiling installation, as they are concealed above the ceiling plane.
Ceiling work should be completed before flooring to prevent damage to finished floors from scaffolding, debris, or dropped tools during overhead work.
Ceiling grid or drywall must be in place before final installation and trimming of recessed lighting fixtures that mount into the ceiling.

Lobby wall finishes (painting, drywall, paneling) must be completed to provide a finished mounting surface for lobby signs. Installing signage before walls are finished would require removal or damage to signs.
Ceiling work must be complete before hanging signs, especially suspended or ceiling-mounted signage, to avoid overhead conflicts and ensure safe installation.
Flooring must be finished to provide stable access and staging for sign installation, and to avoid damaging finished floors with heavy equipment during sign mounting.
Electrical conduit, junction boxes, and wiring for illuminated signs must be roughed-in before the actual sign is installed and connected.
It is preferable to install signage before furniture to coordinate layout and avoid moving furniture, but furniture could be placed first if carefully managed.
The ceiling grid provides the structural support and mounting framework for HVAC diffusers; diffusers cannot be installed without the grid in place.
Ductwork must be run to the diffuser locations to supply conditioned air; diffusers connect directly to duct terminals and cannot function without ductwork.
Ceiling tiles are installed around or after diffusers are positioned; diffusers must be in place so that tiles can be cut and fitted properly around them.
Air balancing adjusts airflow at each diffuser; diffusers must be installed and fully connected before airflow measurements and adjustments can be performed.

While diffusers are often installed after painting to avoid overspray, in some sequences diffusers may be installed before final touch-up painting; this is typically a soft preference to protect finishes rather than a physical necessity.

predecessor: Lobby Slab on Grade / Floor Slab Placement
rationale: Partition walls must be built on top of a finished floor slab to provide a stable, level base. The floor slab must be placed and cured before any walls can be erected.
Underslab plumbing, electrical conduits, and other underground MEP work must be completed before the slab is poured; after the slab is in place, partition walls can be laid out and built on top.
Electrical wiring, outlets, switches, data cabling, and plumbing pipes that run inside wall cavities can only be installed after the wall framing is complete and stud cavities are accessible.
Gypsum board or other wall sheathing cannot be applied until the partition wall framing is fully erected, braced, and inspected; the wall structure must exist before it can be covered.

successor: Lobby Ceiling Grid / Suspended Ceiling Installation
rationale: While ceiling work can theoretically proceed in parallel, it is standard practice to complete partition walls first so that the ceiling grid can be tied into wall angles and so that wall top tracks are fully installed before ceiling layout is finalized.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to receive the door assembly; the door cannot be installed without an adequate opening.
The door frame must be set, leveled, and secured before hanging the door assembly to ensure proper fit and alignment.
Door hardware such as handles, locks, and door closers must be installed after the door is hung to ensure correct positioning and function.
Weatherstripping and seals are applied after the door is assembled and hung to create a proper seal around the closed door.
Final adjustments, alignment checks, and operational testing can only be performed after the door assembly is complete.
The turnstile must be mounted on a finished floor surface to ensure proper alignment, anchorage, and level operation.

predecessor: Rough-in Electrical Conduit and Wiring at Lobby
rationale: Electrical power and data cabling must be run to the turnstile location before the unit can be physically installed and connected.

successor: Test and Commission Turnstile Access Control
rationale: The turnstile hardware must be installed and powered before its access control functions can be tested and calibrated.

It is preferable to complete the security turnstile installation before installing nearby signs and wall finishes to avoid damage or rework, but this is a soft sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.

Ceiling and lighting work overhead should ideally be completed first to minimize dust and debris falling on the turnstile equipment, but the turnstile could technically be installed before ceiling completion if protected.
