Flooring must be installed before the back wall is erected to avoid damaging finished flooring with heavy wall materials and to ensure proper alignment.
Electrical rough-in wiring and outlets must be run in the wall cavity before the wall is closed up with the back wall paneling/sheets.
Final electrical trim-out (switches, outlets, and fixtures) can only be installed after the back wall is fully built and finished.
The reception desk is typically anchored to or placed against the back wall, so the wall must be complete before desk installation.

While painting is often done after wall erection, it could be done earlier if the wall is pre-finished; however, it is standard sequencing to paint after the wall is in place to achieve a seamless finish on site.

The subfloor must be clean, level, and properly prepared (e.g., moisture barrier applied, underlayment installed) before any flooring material can be installed, otherwise the flooring will not adhere or will fail prematurely.

All rough-in mechanical, electrical, and plumbing work within or beneath the lobby floor must be completed and inspected before flooring is installed, as accessing these systems afterward would require destroying the finished floor.

It is generally preferable to complete overhead work (ceilings, overhead conduits, lighting) before flooring to avoid debris, dust, and drips damaging the new floor surface, though this is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
Wall base, baseboards, and trim are installed after flooring to cover the expansion gap at the floor-wall junction and to sit on top of the finished floor for a clean appearance.

All heavy furniture, fixtures, equipment, and final decorative elements should only be brought into the lobby after the flooring is fully installed and cured/protected, to prevent damage to the floor surface.
The reception desk must be placed on a finished, level floor surface. Installing the desk before floor finishes would damage the flooring or require reinstallation.
Wall finishing work generates dust and debris that would soil a newly installed reception desk. Walls should be painted and finished before installing the desk.
The reception desk often incorporates power outlets, data ports, and cable management. Rough-in wiring must be completed and routed to the desk location before the desk is installed.

successor: Connect Electrical and Data Outlets at Desk
rationale: Final electrical and data connections to the built-in outlets of the reception desk can only be made after the desk is physically in place and secured.

successor: Install Decorative Front Panels/Cladding on Desk
rationale: While decorative panels can often be installed beforehand, it is easier and more efficient to install them after the desk frame is in position to ensure proper alignment and avoid damage during placement.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (conduit, wiring, pipes) must be completed before the ceiling is installed, as these systems are housed above the ceiling and would be inaccessible afterward.
The ceiling grid or suspension system (e.g., T-bar grid for drop ceilings or furring channels for drywall) must be in place to support the ceiling panels or finish material.

predecessor: Complete Lobby Wall Framing and Drywall
rationale: Wall framing and drywall should be completed before ceiling installation to allow for proper integration of wall-to-ceiling joints, and to avoid damaging finished walls when working overhead.

Flooring is typically installed after ceiling work to prevent dust, debris, and dropped materials from damaging the finished floor surface; this is a soft preference for schedule optimization rather than a hard physical constraint.
Recessed or surface-mounted lighting fixtures are often integrated into or supported by the ceiling, and must be installed after the ceiling material is in place for proper alignment and connection.
All rough-in work for electrical, data, and other services must be completed before installing lighting fixtures, as lighting installation covers walls and ceilings.
Lighting fixtures must be physically installed before they can be tested for functionality and safety.
Lighting fixtures are typically recessed or mounted to the ceiling structure, so they must be installed before the final ceiling finishes (e.g., drywall, ceiling tiles) are applied to avoid rework.
While not physically required, it is preferred to complete lighting installation before flooring to avoid damaging finished floors with ladders, tools, or dropped fixtures.
The structural framing, slab, and overhead supports must be in place to provide a safe mounting surface for lighting fixtures.
Lobby rough-in work (electrical, data, plumbing, and framing) must be completed before doors can be installed, as the door frames need to be set into finished rough openings.
Flooring or subfloor must be in place to establish the correct finished floor height for door installation, ensuring proper door clearance and threshold alignment.

predecessor: Complete Overhead/ Ceiling Work in Lobby
rationale: Overhead ceiling work (e.g., drywall, grid, lighting) should be complete to avoid damage to doors and to allow access for large door components before ceilings are closed in.
Door frames and doors must be installed before adjacent wall cladding, casing, and trim can be applied flush against the door frame.
Lobby doors must be hung and aligned before locks, closers, handles, electronic strikes, and access control devices can be mounted and adjusted on the doors.
Flooring must be fully installed and finished before signage is placed to avoid damage to signage during flooring work and to ensure accurate positioning relative to finished floor levels.
Ceiling work (lighting, ceiling tiles, or soffits) must be finished to allow overhead signage to be mounted securely and to ensure clearance and alignment with finished ceiling heights.
Wall surfaces must be finished and painted before signage is mounted, as signage installation after painting avoids the need to work around signage or risk damaging it during wall finishing.
Signage installation generates debris, dust, and protective film removal; final cleaning should occur after all signage is in place to ensure a spotless finish.

Signage installation is typically one of the last finish activities; final inspections and punch list walkthroughs are best scheduled after signage is installed so it can be evaluated as part of the complete lobby.
The structural steel frame must be erected to provide the primary support structure onto which the atrium roof/glazed canopy is installed.
The perimeter walls of the atrium must be completed to provide the supporting framework and sealing surfaces for the glazed canopy.
Completing adjacent roof areas first is a soft preference to ensure weather-tight coordination and to avoid sequencing conflicts with crane access and material staging.

Interior ceiling finishes and lighting installation below the atrium canopy must occur after the glazed canopy is in place to protect the interior from weather and to allow for proper alignment with the overhead structure.
Atrium floor finishes and waterproofing work should proceed after the canopy is installed to prevent water damage to finished flooring and to ensure the space is weather-enclosed.

The structural steel frame must be in place to provide the load-bearing support and attachment points for the curtain wall system. Without the structural frame, the glazed wall has no structural backing to be mounted onto.

The main building enclosure and waterproofing must be completed to ensure a watertight seal where the curtain wall interfaces with the adjacent building structure, preventing moisture intrusion at connections and transitions.

Interior finishes such as drywall, painting, and flooring in the atrium area should be installed after the curtain wall is in place to avoid damage from glazing installation work and to allow for proper sealing and trim work at the wall interfaces.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the atrium zone is sequenced after curtain wall installation to coordinate penetrations, supports, and routing around the glazed wall system, and to prevent damage to the glazing during MEP work.

HVAC system balancing and commissioning is preferably performed after the curtain wall is fully installed as the glazed wall significantly affects the thermal envelope and airflow dynamics of the atrium space, but some preliminary balancing could occur beforehand.
The atrium structural frame requires a properly prepared and excavated foundation area to support its load, making site preparation a physical prerequisite.
The structural frame columns and beams must be anchored to completed foundations or pile caps to transfer loads to the ground.
The roof structure and glazing panels need the completed structural frame as their supporting substructure before installation can begin.
Intermediate floor slabs or decks within the atrium require the primary structural frame to be in place to support their loads.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work typically follows the structural frame since conduits, ducts, and pipes are often run through or hung from the structural elements.

successor: Atrium Floor Slab Openings / Balcony Edges
rationale: The atrium floor slab openings and balcony edges depend on the primary steel frame being in place to provide structural support and define the geometry of the atrium space.

predecessor: Atrium Floor Slab Concrete Pour & Cure
successor: Atrium Floor Slab Openings / Balcony Edges
rationale: The slab must be poured and cured before openings can be cut or balcony edge formwork/railings can be installed, as the slab provides the base material for these features.

successor: Atrium Floor Slab Openings / Balcony Edges
rationale: Any MEP penetrations or sleeve placements through the slab must be coordinated and roughed-in prior to finishing slab openings and balcony edge details.

predecessor: Atrium Floor Slab Openings / Balcony Edges
rationale: Balcony edge framing and slab openings must be complete to provide a secure substrate for mounting glass balustrades and guardrails along the atrium edges.

predecessor: Atrium Floor Slab Openings / Balcony Edges
rationale: Slab openings define the atrium's vertical shaft geometry; the skylight or glazed roof enclosure is installed after the openings are framed and the balcony edges are finished to ensure proper alignment and weather sealing.
The structural steel frame must be erected to provide the primary support structure to which the atrium railing/balustrade will be attached.
The floor slab or deck must be in place to provide the walking surface and base anchorage point for the railing/balustrade installation.

predecessor: Atrium Glazing and Curtain Wall Installation
rationale: The atrium glazing system must be installed first as the railing/balustrade is often designed to integrate with or abut the glass curtain wall, and the glazing defines the atrium enclosure perimeter.

successor: Interior Finishes (Painting / Wall Coverings) at Atrium Areas
rationale: The railing/balustrade must be fully installed before adjacent wall finishes are applied, to avoid damaging finished surfaces during railing installation and to allow proper sealing at the interface.
The railing/balustrade must be installed and tested before the final safety inspection can verify guardrail compliance and before the area can be handed over for occupancy.

predecessor: Foundation & Structural Steel Erection for Atrium
rationale: The structural framework and support points for the atrium must be in place to provide the anchor points and structural support for the skywalk/bridge installation.

predecessor: Atrium Glazing and Curtain Wall Installation
rationale: The glass enclosure or curtain wall of the atrium is typically installed before the bridge to allow the bridge to be suspended or anchored to the glazing frame, and to protect the bridge installation from weather.
The structural bridge must be in place before interior finishes such as flooring, handrails, and lighting can be applied to the bridge surface.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems serving the bridge (e.g., lighting, ventilation) require the bridge structure to be in place for routing and installation.
Structural load testing and safety inspections of the skywalk must occur after the bridge is fully installed to verify structural integrity before occupancy.
The sun control / shading devices are typically mounted to or supported by the atrium roof structure, so the roof structure must be in place first.

predecessor: Atrium Glazing and Curtain Wall Installation
rationale: Exterior shading devices are often installed after or integrated with the glazing system, as the glass curtain wall provides the mounting surface or backing for the shading elements.

While not physically required, it is preferable to complete exterior shading before interior finishes to avoid damage to finished surfaces during shading installation and to coordinate with natural lighting design.

successor: Atrium MEP Rough-In (electrical for shading controls)
rationale: If the shading devices are motorized or automated, electrical rough-in for controls and power must be coordinated, but the shading devices themselves must be installed before final connections and trim-out.
Commissioning and testing of automated sun control / shading devices can only occur after the devices are fully installed and connected.
The structural framing and roof of the atrium must be in place to provide weather protection and structural support before interior landscaping and planters can be installed.

predecessor: Atrium Glazing and Curtain Wall Installation
rationale: The glass curtain wall must be installed to enclose the atrium space and create a weathertight envelope before interior landscaping work can commence.
The floor slab and waterproofing membrane must be completed to provide a stable, watertight base for planter construction and to prevent moisture damage to the structure.
Landscaping and planters must be fully installed with plants in place before the irrigation system can be tested and commissioned to ensure proper water delivery to all planted areas.

While landscaping is typically done before final architectural trim and railings to avoid damage to finishes, this is a soft preference as the finishes can be installed first if protection measures are taken.
The water feature requires a structural slab base and waterproofing membrane to contain water and prevent leakage into lower levels.
Plumbing supply lines, pump connections, and drainage pipes must be installed in the slab before the water feature shell or basin is constructed.
Conduit and junction boxes for the water pump, lighting, and control systems need to be run and embedded before the feature is built over them.
Once the water feature basin, shell, and finishes are complete, the assembly must be waterproofed and tested for leaks before it can be filled with water.
Finishes such as tile, stone cladding, or paint on walls immediately surrounding the water feature are best done after the feature is installed to ensure clean transitions and avoid damage.
Ceiling structure must be in place to provide mounting surfaces for overhead signage and wayfinding elements in the atrium.
Floor-mounted signage, directional markers, and floor-based wayfinding elements require finished floor surfaces for proper installation and alignment.
Wall-mounted signage and wayfinding panels require completed wall surfaces to ensure proper adhesion, alignment, and aesthetic integration.
Signage installation must be complete before final cleaning and punch list walkthrough to avoid damage to newly installed signs and to allow inspection of all signage elements.
Wayfinding signage must be fully installed and verified before occupants and visitors begin using the atrium, to ensure clear navigation from day one.
The structural steel frame must be fully erected and stabilized to provide the supporting framework onto which atrium glazing panels are mounted.
The roof structure over the atrium must be in place to allow top-supported glazing systems and to provide overhead weather protection during glazing work.

successor: Interior Finishing & MEP Rough-In Within Atrium
rationale: Glazing must be installed to enclose the atrium space and provide weathertightness before interior finishes, drywall, and mechanical/electrical/plumbing rough-in work can proceed inside the conditioned atrium area.
The glazing system must be fully installed to allow for water infiltration and air leakage testing of the curtainwall and window assemblies.
Once glazing is complete, scaffolding used for access can be dismantled, though this is a soft preference as scaffolding can be partially removed earlier if other sequencing allows.
The atrium must be fully constructed and enclosed before smoke control testing can begin, as the system relies on the physical structure to contain and manage smoke flow.
All smoke control equipment (fans, dampers, ductwork, controls) must be installed before testing can verify their operation.
Power supply and control wiring to smoke control equipment must be energized and commissioned to enable equipment operation during testing.

predecessor: Complete Fire Alarm System Installation and Testing
rationale: The fire alarm system must be operational since smoke control testing may be initiated by or integrated with the fire alarm system for sequencing and verification.
Smoke control system testing must be successfully completed and accepted before final building commissioning and handover can occur, as it is a life safety system critical for occupancy.
The atrium structure requires a stable foundation to bear its load; foundation works must be completed before any structural erection above ground.
A prepared ground slab provides the base for atrium structure erection and must be finished beforehand.
The structural frame of the atrium must be in place before roof and glazing installation can proceed.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the atrium space requires the structural frame to be erected for access and routing.
While interior finishes can technically begin after structure is up, it is a soft preference to sequence them after MEP rough-in to avoid rework.
A structurally complete and level floor slab is required to support the weight of auditorium seating and to provide a stable mounting base.
Electrical conduits and floor outlets must be installed before seating is placed, as they will be inaccessible once the seating rows are fixed in place.
HVAC supply/return ducts running beneath the seating area must be completed and tested before seating installation seals access.
Carpet or floor finishing in aisles and adjacent areas can only be completed after seating is installed, as the seating defines the precise layout and avoids damage to finished flooring.

Seating installation should precede final acoustical panel adjustments to ensure clear sightlines and sound paths, though this is a soft preference for optimal acoustics rather than a physical necessity.
Acoustic panels require a stable wall structure. Wall framing must be complete to provide the substrate for panel attachment.

Electrical wiring, outlets, switches, plumbing, and HVAC ducts must be roughed in within the wall before acoustic panels are installed, as accessing these systems after panel installation would require damaging or removing the panels.
Acoustic insulation within wall cavities should be placed before acoustic panels are mounted to achieve proper sound attenuation performance.

predecessor: Gypsum Board / Drywall Installation and Finishing
rationale: Acoustic wall panels are typically installed over finished drywall surfaces. Drywall must be hung, taped, mudded, and sanded smooth to provide a clean substrate for panel adhesive or mounting hardware.
Any painting, caulking, or trim work around the acoustic panels should be completed after installation to ensure clean edges and proper finish integration.
Acoustic panels are typically one of the last finishes installed before a space is occupied to avoid damage from other trades and to ensure acoustic performance is not compromised by dust or debris.

MEP rough-in work (ductwork, piping, conduit, and wiring) must be completed within the ceiling plenum before ceiling tiles or acoustic panels are installed, as accessing these systems after ceiling installation would require removing or damaging the finished ceiling.
The structural ceiling grid, joists, or suspension framework must be in place to provide the supporting structure from which acoustic ceiling components are hung or attached.

Spray-applied fireproofing or intumescent coatings on overhead steel must be completed before enclosing these elements with acoustic ceiling tiles, as the fireproofing application is a messy process that would damage finished ceiling surfaces.

While not a strict physical requirement, it is a soft preference to complete wall painting and finish work before ceiling installation to avoid paint splatter or damage to the finished acoustic ceiling surfaces.

Hard physical constraint: Ceiling installation is typically completed before final flooring to prevent dust, debris, and dropped materials from damaging newly installed flooring surfaces, and to allow overhead work without requiring floor protection.
A level, structurally sound subfloor must exist before a raked (sloped) floor structure can be built upon it, as the raked floor requires a stable base to achieve the required slope.
The primary structural supports (beams, joists, or trusses) that will carry the raked floor must be in place before the raked floor decking or slab can be installed.

successor: Floor Covering Installation (e.g., carpet, tile, hardwood)
rationale: The raked floor substrate must be fully complete and structurally sound before any finish floor coverings can be applied.
Fixed seating is anchored to the raked floor; therefore the raked floor must be fully constructed to provide the correct slope and structural support for chair installation.

While it is physically possible to route services after the floor is built, it is far more efficient and less destructive to install underfloor conduits and drainage before the raked floor structure is closed in.
The rough opening framing must be constructed before doors can be installed, as the doors need a framed opening to fit into.
The door frame (jambs, head, sill) must be installed before hanging the door leaves, as the doors are mounted onto the frame.
Floor finishing is typically completed before door installation to avoid damaging new floors with door installation debris, though it is a scheduling preference rather than a physical necessity.
Door hardware (handles, locks, hinges, closers) must be installed after the doors are hung, as hardware is mounted onto the installed door leaf.

Painting and wall finishing around the door opening is often done after door installation so that the door trim and casing can be painted seamlessly, though this can be sequenced differently with careful masking.

Structural framing provides the primary structural support and framework onto which handrails and guardrails are attached. Without the structural framing in place, there is no substrate to mount the handrails.
The deck or floor slab must be completed to provide the walking surface adjacent to handrails and guardrails, and to establish the finished floor level that determines the required guardrail height.

Stair stringers, treads, and risers must be installed before handrails can be mounted alongside stairs, as the handrail geometry follows the stair slope and the handrail posts attach to the stair structure.

Handrails and guardrails are critical life-safety components; building and safety inspectors must verify their proper installation (height, load resistance, baluster spacing) before the structure can receive a final occupancy approval.

It is preferable to install handrails before finishing adjacent wall surfaces so that any patching or touch-up around rail brackets can be completed seamlessly, though this is a scheduling preference rather than a physical necessity.
Window frames must be installed and fully secured before any curtain or drapery hardware can be mounted to the frame or surrounding wall.
Walls around windows must be finished and painted before installing curtain rods or brackets, as painting after installation would be difficult and could damage the curtains.
Any electrical outlets, switches, or wiring near the window area must be completed before curtains are installed to avoid obstructing access and to prevent safety hazards.

Once blackout curtains are installed, interior decoration and furniture placement can proceed with the final lighting conditions established, though this is a soft preference for workflow convenience.

Curtains and drapes should be hung before final cleaning and floor finishing to prevent dust and debris from settling on the fabric, and to allow cleaning crews to work around the finished window treatments.
Acoustic panels are typically mounted onto wall frames; the framing provides the structural support needed to attach the panels securely.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the walls must be completed before acoustic panels are installed, as the panels would block access to wall cavities.
Acoustic insulation within wall cavities must be in place before panels are fixed, as the panels enclose the wall assembly and prevent later access.
Acoustic panels are often the final surface treatment; painting and other finishing work should be done after panels are installed to achieve a clean, integrated finish.
While not physically required, it is standard practice to complete acoustic panel installation before final inspections to verify acoustic performance and overall room readiness.
The concrete slab or foundation must be poured and cured to provide a stable, level base for seating installation; seating cannot be placed on unfinished ground.
Structural supports (e.g., steel risers or concrete tiers) that hold the seating rows must be erected before seats can be attached or mounted.
Underfloor electrical conduits, junction boxes, or power outlets for seat-mounted devices (e.g., lighting, charging ports) must be in place before seating covers them.

While floor finishes near seating can be completed beforehand, final perimeter flooring or carpet is often installed after seating to avoid damage and ensure a tight fit; this is a soft preference for finish quality.
Final paint touch-ups are preferably done after seating installation to repair any scuffs or marks from the installation process, but it is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
The foundation must be completed and cured before stage construction begins to provide a stable base and load-bearing support for the stage structure.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and graded to ensure a proper working surface and correct drainage before stage construction can commence.

Underground and rough-in utility lines such as electrical conduit and plumbing must be installed before the stage is built to avoid the need for disruptive excavation or rework after the stage structure is in place.
The structural framing and core of the stage must be fully erected and secured before any finishing work such as flooring, painting, or surface coatings can be applied.

successor: Installation of Stage Lighting and AV Equipment
rationale: The physical stage structure must be in place before mounting overhead rigging, lighting trusses, and audiovisual equipment that attach to or integrate with the stage framework.
AV system commissioning requires power and data connectivity; rough-in wiring must be installed and terminated before AV equipment can be powered on and tested.

predecessor: Install Ceiling Grid and Above-Ceiling Infrastructure
rationale: AV components such as projectors, speakers, and sensors are typically mounted in or suspended from the ceiling grid; the grid must be in place to support these devices before commissioning.

Commissioning verifies that all AV components are operational; acoustical tuning and calibration of the sound system can only be performed once the system is verified to be powered and functioning correctly.
End-user training on AV system operation should occur after the system has been commissioned and verified to be fully functional, ensuring trainees learn on a properly working system.

successor: Punch List Completion and Final Inspection
rationale: While commissioning is typically completed before final inspections, some inspectors may accept commissioning results submitted alongside punch list items; however, it is strongly preferred to finalize commissioning before the final walkthrough to avoid rework.
Floor finishing (tile, marble, or carpet) must be completed before seating can be installed, as seating must rest on a finished floor surface to ensure stability and avoid damaging the flooring.

Wall finishing (painting, paneling, or cladding) must be completed before seating is brought in to prevent dust, debris, or paint splatter from damaging the seating and to allow unobstructed access for wall work.
Overhead lighting fixtures must be installed before seating is placed, as scaffolding or lifts needed for lighting work would be obstructed by installed seating.

While decorative elements like artwork, plants, or signage can be placed after seating, it is a soft preference to arrange them after seating is in place to ensure proper spatial coordination and visual balance.

Final cleaning and polishing of the lobby must occur after seating installation because seating installation introduces dust, packaging debris, and requires movement of materials that would soil a previously cleaned space.
The reception partition structure requires a stable and level base, which is provided by the completed ground slab or subfloor.
Electrical outlets, data ports, and wiring for the reception desk area must be routed within the partition walls before they are enclosed.
The reception desk is typically placed against or integrated with the partition, so the partition structure must be in place first.
The partition framing must be completed before applying any wall finish materials such as plasterboard, cladding, or paint.
Ceiling grid or panels are typically installed after partitions are in place, as partitions help define the ceiling layout and support.
The structural framing must be in place to provide a supporting structure for the reception back wall.
Electrical wiring and outlets need to be run within the wall cavity before the wall is closed up with the back wall finish.
Any plumbing lines that run through the wall must be installed before the wall surface is applied.
The back wall must be fully installed before surface finishes (drywall, taping, painting) can be applied to it.
The back wall provides the anchor and reference surface for the reception desk, so the wall must be complete before the desk is attached or positioned.
The site must be properly graded and prepared before any permanent signage can be installed to ensure a stable foundation and proper alignment.
The concrete foundation or footings for the welcome sign must be poured and cured before the sign structure can be erected.
If the welcome sign requires electrical power for lighting, underground conduits and electrical lines must be routed and connected before the sign is installed.
Landscaping, planting, and decorative finishing around the welcome sign area must be done after the sign is in place to achieve proper layout and avoid damaging the sign.
The welcome sign must be fully installed before final inspections can verify its compliance with design specifications, codes, and site requirements.
The ceiling structure requires the load-bearing walls to be framed and stable before ceiling joists or ceiling boards can be installed.
Wiring, conduits, and junction boxes for lighting and power must be run within the ceiling cavity before the ceiling is closed in with boards or panels.
Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning ducts must be suspended from the structure and routed through the ceiling space before the ceiling finish is applied.
Recessed and surface-mounted light fixtures are typically installed into or onto the completed ceiling surface; the ceiling must be in place to mount and wire the fixtures.

Although painting can sometimes be done before the ceiling, it is common practice to finish the ceiling first to avoid damaging freshly painted walls when working overhead; this is a soft preference for workflow efficiency.
The rough opening (framing and header) must be built and sized correctly before the door assembly can be installed into the opening.
The subfloor or finished floor must be in place to provide a stable base and proper threshold support for the entry door assembly.
The wall framing, including studs and rough sill, must be completed to define the doorway opening before the door can be hung.
After the door is installed, weatherproofing materials such as flashing, caulking, and weatherstripping must be applied around the door frame to prevent water intrusion.

Interior trim around the door is typically installed after the door is hung and aligned, though this is a soft preference because trimming could theoretically be done before, but standard construction sequence places it after for proper fit and alignment.
Data cabling must be installed to the back boxes before outlets can be fitted and terminated.
Power cabling must be run to the outlet locations before the outlets can be connected and installed.

predecessor: Reception Wall Framing & Back Box Installation
rationale: Wall framing and mounting of electrical/data back boxes must be completed to provide a fixed mounting surface and enclosure for the outlets.

successor: Reception Outlet Cover Plate Installation / Trim-Out
rationale: Outlet cover plates and final trim cannot be installed until the outlets themselves are fixed and wired.
Once outlets are wired and mounted, the final wall finish (plasterboard, paint/trim) can be completed around them for a neat appearance.
The reception area must be structurally complete (walls, ceiling, floors in place) before fire safety equipment like smoke detectors, fire alarms, and extinguishers can be mounted and installed.
Electrical wiring for fire alarm systems, smoke detectors, and emergency lighting must be roughed in before the fire safety devices can be connected and made operational.

successor: Reception Fire Alarm System Testing & Commissioning
rationale: All fire safety equipment (detectors, alarms, extinguishers, sprinkler heads) must be installed before the fire alarm system can be tested and commissioned to ensure it operates correctly.

While it is possible to install ceilings after fire safety equipment, it is preferred to install ceiling-mounted fire devices (sprinklers, smoke detectors) before the ceiling finish so wiring and mountings can be concealed and adjusted easily.
Fire safety equipment should generally be in place before final interior finishes and decoration to avoid damage to decorative elements during subsequent installation work.
The ceiling grid must be installed to provide the structural support and mounting surface for recessed or surface-mounted reception lighting fixtures.
Electrical rough-in (conduit, junction boxes, and wiring runs) must be completed before any lighting fixtures can be connected to the power supply.
Drywall finishing and painting of the ceiling must be finished to avoid damage to finished surfaces and so that lighting trim rings can sit flush against the finished surface.
Light switches and dimmers must be installed after the lighting fixtures are in place so that the switch wiring can be connected directly to the fixtures and control functionality can be verified.
All lighting fixtures must be physically installed before the commissioning process can test each fixture, verify illumination levels, and adjust controls for proper operation.
A stable, cured concrete floor slab is required as the structural base to support the lobby seating. Without the finished floor slab, seating cannot be properly anchored or placed.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be completed before seating installation, as seating would obstruct access to walls and floors for MEP work.
Wall finishing (painting, cladding) must be done before seating is brought in, as the seating would block access to wall surfaces and risk damage to finished walls.
Floor finishes must be installed before seating placement to avoid having to move heavy seating later and to ensure finishes extend fully beneath the seating.

successor: Final Lobby Cleaning and Punch List
rationale: After seating is installed, final cleaning can occur around and under the seats, and any touch-up work can be completed, though this is a soft preference for a clean finish rather than a physical necessity.
Permanent built-in or heavy lobby seating must be installed first before other loose furniture, rugs, and decorative items are placed, to establish the layout and avoid rearranging later.

predecessor: Prepare Kiosk Location (rough-in electrical and data)
rationale: The kiosk requires power and network connectivity; rough-in electrical and data cabling must be completed before the kiosk can be physically installed and connected.

predecessor: Complete Flooring and Wall Finishes at Kiosk Area
rationale: Flooring and wall finishing must be done so the kiosk is placed on a finished surface and aligned properly without requiring rework or damage to finishes.
The kiosk hardware must be physically in place and powered on before software configuration, network setup, and user acceptance testing can be performed.

successor: Train Front Desk Staff on Kiosk Operation
rationale: Training is typically done after installation so staff can learn on the actual installed unit, but it is a soft preference as training could theoretically occur on a mock unit elsewhere.
The kiosk must be fully installed and operational before the final inspection and project sign-off can occur.
The reception area must have its wall, ceiling, and floor finishes completed before signage can be mounted, as signage is typically attached to finished surfaces.

Electrical rough-in (wiring, conduit, boxes) behind the reception wall must be completed before signage is installed, as signage often requires backlighting or power and wiring cannot be accessed after wall finishes are covered by signage.

It is preferable to install signage before placing the reception desk and furniture to allow clear access to the wall and to ensure the signage is properly positioned as a focal point, though furniture could be moved if needed.
Reception signage installation must be complete before the final inspection and punch list walkthrough, as the signage is considered a completed element that inspectors will verify.
Walls must be painted and fully prepared before signage installation because signage is mounted on the wall surface. Installing signage before painting would require removal and reinstallation.
Countertops must be supported by base cabinets, which provide the structural foundation for the countertop surface.
A subtop or plywood layer is often required as a base for countertop material, especially for laminate, solid surface, or stone countertops.
The countertop must be installed before the backsplash can be fully completed, as the backsplash sits on top of and abuts the countertop surface.
Sinks are typically mounted into the countertop cutout, so the countertop must be in place before the sink can be installed.
Drop-in cooktops and ranges are installed into countertop cutouts, requiring the countertop to be present first.
The backsplash tile is installed against the wall above the countertop, using the countertop surface as a reference line and support.
Base cabinets require a level, stable floor surface to be installed upon; the floor slab or subfloor must be completed first.
Electrical outlets in walls behind base cabinets must be roughed in before cabinets are installed, as accessing walls after installation is difficult.
Plumbing lines for sinks or appliances that will be within base cabinets must be roughed in before cabinet installation.
Countertops are physically installed on top of base cabinets; cabinets must be in place and leveled to support the countertop.

While not a strict physical requirement, installing base cabinets first allows proper alignment and spacing with wall cabinets for a cohesive fit; it is standard practice but could theoretically be done in reverse order if careful.
Electrical wiring must be roughed in before wall cabinets are installed to avoid having to remove cabinets for electrical work.
Plumbing rough-ins (such as for sinks) must be completed behind the walls before cabinets are mounted.
The walls must be framed and standing to provide the structural support for mounting wall cabinets.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and finished before cabinets are mounted to ensure a clean wall surface and proper fit.
Wall cabinets are installed before countertops to allow proper alignment and support, as countertops often sit atop or adjacent to base and wall cabinets.
It is preferable but not strictly required to install wall cabinets before installing light fixtures or outlets in the cabinet area to avoid rework.
Water supply lines must be roughed in before the sink and faucet can be connected to the water supply.
Drain waste vent piping must be in place for the sink drain to connect to.
The supporting cabinet or vanity must be framed and installed to provide a structural mounting surface for the sink.
The P-trap and final drain connections are made directly to the sink drain outlet after the sink is mounted.
Water supply valves and faucet operation can only be tested after the faucet is installed on the sink and supply lines are connected.
Electrical wiring must be completed to provide power to the microwave unit.
The built-in microwave is typically installed into a cabinet opening; cabinets must be in place first.
Walls behind and around the microwave area must be finished before the microwave is mounted to avoid damage and ensure a clean installation.

In some designs, the countertop may be installed before the microwave; however, if the microwave is installed above the counter, it's often easier to install the countertop first to avoid damaging the microwave, but this is a soft preference.
Trim around the microwave cabinet is installed after the microwave unit is placed to conceal gaps and create a finished look.
Flooring must be installed before heavy appliances are placed on top, as it's nearly impossible to install flooring under an already-placed built-in refrigerator.
Built-in refrigerators are often designed to fit between or under cabinets; cabinets provide the enclosure and dimensions for the fridge compartment.
A dedicated electrical outlet or hardwired connection must be in place to power the refrigerator before it can be installed and connected.
If the refrigerator has an ice maker or water dispenser, a water supply line must be roughed in before the fridge is positioned.
For under-counter fridge models, the countertop is installed after the fridge is in place to ensure proper fit and alignment above the appliance.
While backsplash can be installed around the fridge, it's easier to tile the backsplash first. However, the backsplash is done after countertops which are after the fridge, so it's a soft constraint.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical and plumbing for kitchen
rationale: Electrical supply (power) and plumbing (water supply and drain) must be roughed in behind the dishwasher location before the unit can be installed and connected.
The dishwasher sits on the finished floor; flooring must be installed first so the unit can be properly positioned and leveled.
An under-counter dishwasher is typically installed beneath a countertop and adjacent to base cabinets; the cabinetry framework must be in place to secure and house the dishwasher.

While the dishwasher can often be slid in before the countertop is fully installed, it is generally easier to install the countertop after the dishwasher to ensure proper fit and clearance; however this is a soft preference as the countertop can be installed first with the dishwasher fitted underneath.

successor: Final plumbing and electrical connections to dishwasher
rationale: The physical unit must be in place before the supply lines, drain hose, and electrical connection can be made to the dishwasher itself.
Backsplash is typically installed after the dishwasher is in place to provide a clean finished edge around the appliance, though it could be done before with careful planning.
The overhead microwave/exhaust hood is typically mounted under upper cabinets or requires the cabinet structure above for support and proper alignment.
Electrical power must be roughed in and available at the location before the microwave can be wired and installed.
The exhaust ductwork must be in place to connect to the microwave's vent outlet; the microwave cannot be installed and then have ductwork added behind it.
While not physically mandatory, it is a soft preference to have the microwave installed first so that any gaps around the unit can be properly finished and painted for a clean appearance.
The microwave must be physically mounted before the final electrical connection (hardwiring or plugging in) and trim plate installation can be completed.
The backsplash is installed over finished wall surfaces; drywall must be complete, smooth, and primed before tile/adhesive can be applied.
The backsplash typically abuts the countertop and is set on top of it; the countertop must be in place to establish the lower edge alignment and support.
Upper and base cabinets define the field for the backsplash; the backsplash is installed between countertops and upper cabinets, so cabinets must be hung first.
Grout and caulk are applied after tile is set and the adhesive has cured; they fill joints and seal edges against countertops and cabinets.
Electrical outlet boxes are roughed in before tile, but the cover plates and any decorative trim must be installed after the tile is cut around boxes and set.
Electrical power supply must be roughed in before undercabinet lighting fixtures can be connected and installed.
Cabinets must be mounted in place first so that undercabinet lighting can be properly positioned and attached underneath them.
Walls behind and above cabinets must be finished before lighting fixtures are installed to avoid damage to fixtures and allow for proper wall finishing.
Installing countertops after undercabinet lighting allows for precise alignment of lighting with the countertop edge, though countertops can sometimes be installed first with careful planning.

Undercabinet lighting installation is part of the electrical trim-out phase, and other final electrical connections (switches, outlets) should be completed after the lighting is in place to ensure all circuits are fully connected and tested together.
Electrical wiring must be run and terminated in the ceiling junction box before a light fixture can be attached and connected.
The ceiling structural framing must be in place to support the junction box and fixture mounting.
The electrical junction box must be securely mounted to the ceiling framing before the light fixture can be attached to it.
Drywall must be installed and finished around the junction box opening before the fixture can be mounted to the finished ceiling surface.
It is preferable to paint the ceiling before installing fixtures to avoid paint marks on the fixture, though the fixture can be installed first and painted around.
The fixture must be installed before the electrical system can be fully tested, powered on, and commissioned for operation.
Flooring must be installed before counter/bar seating to ensure a level surface and to avoid damage to the flooring during heavy counter installation.
Walls must be framed and finished before installing counter/bar seating to allow for proper anchoring and alignment with wall surfaces.
Electrical outlets and wiring must be roughed-in behind the counter area before the counter/bar seating is installed to allow access for wiring.
Plumbing supply and drain lines for any sink or wet bar must be roughed-in before counter/bar seating is installed to avoid rework.
Counter/bar seating must be installed before final trim, baseboards, and touch-up painting can be completed around the bar area.
The wall must be framed to provide a structural surface for mounting the upper shelf or open shelving unit.
Electrical wiring behind the wall must be completed before shelving is installed to avoid obstruction and ensure accessibility for inspections.
Shelving installation should be completed before final wall painting or finishing to allow for touch-ups and seamless integration of shelving brackets and supports.
While not physically required, installing upper shelving before the countertop allows easier access and avoids interference during placement of the countertop.
Shelving must be in place before final electrical trim-out to ensure outlet and switch placement coordinates correctly with the shelving layout.

predecessor: Flooring installation (tile, vinyl, hardwood, or laminate)
rationale: The kickplate/toe-kick sits at the bottom of base cabinets and rests on or directly above the finished flooring. The floor must be installed first to establish the finished floor height, so the kickplate can be cut to the correct height and fitted properly.

The kickplate/toe-kick is attached to the bottom front of base cabinets. The cabinets themselves must first be installed, leveled, and anchored to the wall/floor before the kickplate can be fastened to them.

Countertops are installed on top of the base cabinets with the toe-kick already in place. The countertop installers need the full cabinet assembly (including the toe-kick) to be complete to take accurate measurements and fit the countertop correctly.

successor: Base cabinet door and drawer installation
rationale: While doors and drawers can technically be hung before the kickplate, installing the toe-kick first allows for proper alignment and clearance adjustments at the bottom, making it a preferred sequence to avoid later re-adjustments.

The subfloor must be level and prepared before the finished flooring is installed, which in turn is required before the kickplate. Any unevenness in the subfloor will affect the finished floor and consequently the fit and appearance of the toe-kick.
The garbage/recycling pull-out cabinet frame needs to be built into the rough framing structure before the pull-out mechanism can be installed.
Any electrical outlets or wiring in the cabinet area must be roughed in before the pull-out is installed to avoid interference.
The pull-out base cabinet must be fully installed and positioned before countertops are fabricated and installed over it.
The garbage pull-out is typically located in a base cabinet adjacent to or under the sink area, so the cabinet pull-out must be in place before the sink is installed.
The pull-out mechanism and cabinet must be installed before final door fronts, drawer fronts, and trim hardware can be attached.

The pop-up outlet strip is installed into/through the countertop surface, so the countertop must be fabricated, cut, and installed first to provide the physical substrate and opening for the outlet strip.
Electrical wiring must be run to the location of the pop-up outlet before the unit can be connected and installed, as the wiring needs to be available behind or under the countertop for termination.

After the pop-up outlet strip is physically mounted in the countertop, the final electrical connections (terminating wires, installing cover plates, testing) must be completed to energize the device and finish the installation.

It is good practice to seal around the pop-up unit where it penetrates the countertop to prevent moisture infiltration, but this is a quality/finish step rather than a strict physical necessity for installation.

Pop-up outlets are typically installed on the countertop surface, so adjacent vertical elements like backsplash or upper cabinets may be installed before or after; however, installing backsplash after may allow for cleaner integration, but this is not a hard physical constraint.
Electrical rough-in (wiring, outlets, switch boxes) must be completed before cabinets are installed, as walls need to be open for wiring and cabinets would block access to electrical work.
Plumbing rough-in (water lines, drain lines) must be completed before cabinet installation, as cabinets would obstruct access to plumbing in walls and floors.

predecessor: Complete Wall Finishing (Drywall, Taping, Mudding, Priming)
rationale: Walls must be finished with drywall and priming before cabinets are installed, as cabinets are mounted directly onto finished walls and wall finishing creates dust that would damage cabinetry.

In many construction sequences, cabinetry is installed before finish flooring to allow cabinets to sit on the subfloor, making future replacement easier without disturbing flooring, though this can vary by preference.
Appliances (sink, stove, dishwasher) depend on countertops and cabinetry being in place for proper fitment and connection to countertop cutouts and cabinet openings.
Backsplash tile is installed after countertops are set, as the countertop provides the bottom edge reference line for backsplash installation.
Ceiling work (texture, painting) should be completed before cabinets to avoid dust and debris falling on finished cabinets, though it is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
Plumbing rough-in work (running pipes, drain lines, and vent stacks within walls and floors) must be completed before fixtures can be installed, as the fixtures connect to these concealed pipes.

predecessor: Install Underground Drainage & Water Supply Lines
rationale: Underground drainage and water supply lines must be in place and tested before above-ground fixtures are installed to ensure proper connections and flow.
Wall and floor framing must be complete to provide structural support and mounting surfaces for plumbing fixtures such as toilets, sinks, and tubs.

successor: Connect Fixtures to Supply & Drain Lines
rationale: After fixtures are set in place, final connections to water supply and drain lines can be made to complete the plumbing system.

successor: Install Wall and Floor Finishes (Tiling, Drywall)
rationale: While fixtures can be installed before final finishes, it is preferred to complete wall and floor finishes around the fixtures for a cleaner appearance, though fixtures are often temporarily installed for rough-in testing and then removed or protected.
Rough-in work (plumbing, electrical, HVAC) must be completed before appliances can be installed, as appliances connect to these systems and rough-in provides the necessary hookups and clearances.
Flooring must be installed before placing heavy appliances to avoid damaging the subfloor and to ensure appliances sit on the finished surface at the correct height.
While not always strictly required, it is strongly preferred to finish walls before installing appliances to avoid dust, debris, and paint damage to the appliances.
The subfloor must be clean, level, and dry before any floor finish can be installed to ensure proper adhesion and a smooth final surface.
Underlayment (e.g., moisture barrier, soundproofing, or cushion) must be laid down before the finished flooring material to provide necessary protection and support.
Baseboards and trim are typically installed after the floor finish to cover the expansion gap at the perimeter and to sit on top of the finished flooring for a clean appearance.

In standard construction sequence, flooring should be installed before cabinets or fixed furniture to allow the flooring to run continuously underneath, providing a cleaner look and avoiding transition strips.

Wall cabinets are typically installed before backsplash because the backsplash tile needs to fit snugly against the bottom edge of the cabinets. Installing cabinets after would risk damaging the tile or creating gaps.
Electrical wiring for outlets and switches behind the backsplash area must be roughed-in before tiling so that outlet boxes can be properly positioned and cut around.
The wall surface must be fully finished (drywall installed, taped, mudded, and primed) before backsplash tile can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and a flat substrate.

After backsplash tile is installed and grouted, outlet covers and decorative trim pieces are installed to cover the cutouts and finish the appearance. Installing these before tiling would be impossible or require removal.
Electrical wiring for ceiling fixtures must be in place before ceiling installation to avoid retrofitting and safety hazards.
HVAC ducts must be installed above the ceiling before the ceiling is closed up to ensure proper airflow and accessibility.
Structural framing must be complete to provide support for ceiling grids and attachment points for lighting fixtures.
Ceiling work should be completed before flooring to prevent debris and dust from damaging new flooring materials.
Ceiling installation must precede final wall finishing to allow for seamless integration of ceiling edges with wall surfaces.
Drywall must be installed, taped, mudded, and sanded before any trim can be applied, as trim is installed over finished drywall surfaces.
Wall painting must be completed before final trim installation, as trim is typically installed after painting to allow for clean paint edges and to avoid painting over trim.
Base trim and other floor-related trim must be installed before finished flooring, as flooring is often run up to or under the trim, and trim covers floor expansion gaps.
Completing trim and hardware installation allows for the final clean-up and punch list walkthrough, as all finish work should be in place before final inspection and cleaning.
Cabinets must be installed before trim and hardware such as drawer pulls and knobs are attached, as these are mounted directly onto cabinet fronts.
The floor slab must be constructed and cured to provide a stable, level surface for installing meeting room chairs.
Wall framing defines the meeting room boundaries and ensures the room dimensions are correct before placing chairs.
Electrical outlets and wiring for the meeting room must be roughed in behind walls and under floor before chairs are placed, to avoid obstruction and rework.
If chair installation occurs before final floor finishing, chairs may need to be moved or protected; this is a soft preference based on protecting finishes.
Chairs must be installed and positioned before the room can be furnished with other furniture and made ready for occupancy.
The display screen must be mounted on or attached to a wall surface; therefore, the wall must be constructed and finished before screen installation can begin.
Power outlets and data cabling for the display screen must be roughed in behind the wall or in the ceiling before the screen is mounted, as accessing these after installation is difficult.
The display screen must be physically installed before audio-visual equipment (e.g., cables, media players, control systems) can be connected to it and the entire system tested.

While the screen can be installed before final trim, it is often preferred to complete painting and trim around the screen area first to avoid damage to the screen; however, this is a soft preference, not a physical necessity.

If the display screen is ceiling-mounted or requires ceiling support for cabling, the ceiling structure should be in place; however, for wall-mounted screens this is not a hard constraint, only a preference for clean cable routing.
The video conferencing camera needs a secure mounting bracket or wall plate to be installed first, as the camera attaches directly to this hardware.
Power, HDMI, and USB cables must be routed and terminated at the camera location before the camera can be connected, as the camera requires power and data connectivity to function.
Network cabling (Ethernet) and switch configuration must be completed to provide IP connectivity if the camera is a network-based (PoE) model.
After physical installation, the camera must be configured (resolution, framing, autofocus, white balance) and tested for proper operation before it can be used in live calls.

It is a soft preference to install the display monitor before or after the camera; however, if the camera is placed above or beside the monitor, positioning alignment is easier if both are installed concurrently or the monitor is installed first.
Wall framing provides the structural support surface onto which the whiteboard/marker board will be mounted.
Drywall or wall sheathing must be in place to provide a smooth, finished surface before mounting the whiteboard.
Wall painting and finishing must be completed prior to mounting the whiteboard to avoid paint splatter and damage to the board.
Trim work such as baseboards or chair rails can be installed after the whiteboard for a cleaner finish, though this is a preference (the board could be installed after trim if carefully fitted).
The whiteboard must be securely mounted before the room is used or furniture is placed to avoid damage, dust, or rework.

The Room Scheduling Panel requires network connectivity to communicate with the scheduling system, so basic network cabling and infrastructure must be in place before the panel can be installed and configured.
The Room Scheduling Panel is typically mounted on a wall or door frame, so the structural support or backing must be prepared before the panel can be physically attached.
The panel requires power, so electrical wiring must be run to the installation location before connecting the device.
The physical panel must be mounted and connected before software configuration, network registration, and end-to-end testing of the scheduling display can be performed.

While not physically required, it is operationally preferable to install and program the scheduling panel before finalizing room signage so that room numbers and names can be confirmed and matched between physical signs and the digital system.
The ceiling grid and support system must be in place to provide structural support for mounting the projector.

predecessor: Run electrical wiring and install power outlet
rationale: Electrical power supply must be available at the mounting location to power the projector.

predecessor: Run AV/data cabling (HDMI, VGA, control cables)
rationale: Audio/visual and control cables must be routed to the projector location before the unit is mounted, as access is difficult afterward.
The projector must be physically mounted before electrical and AV connections can be completed and tested.
While the screen can technically be installed independently, aligning it with the mounted projector ensures proper image projection and is best done after the projector is in place.
System configuration and programming require the projector to be installed, connected, and operational to verify settings.
Electrical power and control wiring must be run to the projection screen location before the screen can be physically installed and connected.
The ceiling structure and grid must be in place to provide support and mounting points for the projection screen, which is typically suspended from or attached to the ceiling.
The projection screen must be installed before the projector can be properly positioned and aligned to ensure the projected image fits correctly on the screen surface.
The screen must be in place and fully installed for technicians to calibrate the audio-visual system, including focusing, keystone correction, and color balancing against the screen surface.

While not physically required, it is preferable to complete wall finishing and painting before installing the projection screen to avoid damaging the screen surface with paint splatters or dust from finishing work.
The walls and supporting structure must be framed and in place before the built-in cabinet can be attached and secured.
Wiring for outlets, lighting, or media connections behind or within the cabinet must be run before the cabinet is installed, as it will cover and block access to those areas.

While the cabinet can be painted or finished separately, it is often preferred (soft) to paint or finish the walls behind before installation to avoid having to cut in around the cabinet. However, this is not a hard physical constraint.

The cabinet may be installed over finished flooring or the flooring may be installed up to the cabinet. In many built-in scenarios, flooring is done first and the cabinet sits on top (preferred), but physically the cabinet can be installed first and flooring trimmed around it.
If the credenza includes a countertop or solid surface top, the cabinet base must be fully installed and leveled before the countertop can be fabricated or placed on top.
The window frame and rough opening must be fully constructed and prepared to provide a stable mounting surface and proper dimensions for the blinds and shades to be installed.
Windows must be installed before any interior window treatments like blinds or shades can be mounted onto or adjacent to the window assemblies.

predecessor: Electrical Rough-In / Wiring for Motorized Shades
rationale: For motorized shades, electrical wiring and low-voltage control cables must be run within the walls or ceiling before the shades are physically installed, as the wiring needs to be concealed and terminated at the shade location.

While it is often more convenient to install blinds before final trim to allow for adjustments, it is a soft preference because trim can be installed around the blinds or the blinds can be surface-mounted after trim is complete.

Blinds and shades are typically among the final installed components before occupancy since they are delicate, need to be free of dust and debris from other construction activities, and are part of the final finishing of the interior space.
Floor boxes and power outlets are typically embedded in or mounted on concrete slabs. The slab must be poured and cured to provide a stable substrate for installing the floor box.
Electrical conduits or raceways that feed power to the floor box must be roughed in before the floor box can be connected and set in place.
Branch circuit wiring to the floor box location must be pulled and terminated before the floor box can be fully installed and connected.
Floor boxes must be set to the correct height before final floor finishes are applied so that the box cover is flush with the finished floor surface.

successor: Final Electrical Trim Out / Device Cover Installation
rationale: The floor box body must be installed and wired before its trim plate, cover, and receptacle devices are attached in the final trim-out phase.
Ductwork must be installed first to provide the physical air pathways that zone dampers control. The damper is installed within or at the branch of the ductwork.

predecessor: HVAC Main Distribution Piping / Refrigerant Lines
rationale: Main HVAC distribution systems (piping and refrigerant lines) need to be in place so that the zone-level components can be connected to them and function properly.
Electrical wiring and low-voltage control wiring must be roughed in to provide power and control signals for the zone damper actuator and thermostat.
Zone dampers and thermostats must be installed before the HVAC system can be balanced and tested, as they are active control devices that regulate airflow in each zone.
The thermostat must be physically mounted and wired before calibration, programming, and commissioning of zone control sequences can occur.
The door frame rough opening must be prepared and framed to the correct dimensions before the door unit can be installed.
Load-bearing and non-load-bearing walls must be framed to create the doorway opening before the door can be hung.
The door unit must be hung and secured in the opening before trim and casing can be applied around it.
The door slab must be hung and properly aligned before the privacy lock mechanism can be fitted to ensure correct alignment of latch and strike plate.
While it is typical to paint or finish the door after installation, some prefer pre-finishing; however, final touch-ups and painting are generally done after the door is hung.
Acoustic treatment panels or materials are typically mounted onto or within wall cavities, so the wall framing must be in place to provide structural support.
Electrical wiring must be routed within walls before acoustic treatments are installed, as accessing wiring after treatment would require removal of acoustic materials.
HVAC ducts must be in place before acoustic insulation and treatments are added, to avoid having to cut through or remove acoustic materials for duct installation.
Thermal/acoustic insulation within wall cavities should be installed before the final acoustic treatment layers (e.g., panels, bass traps) are applied.
Acoustic panels and treatments are typically finished surfaces that must be in place before final painting, touch-ups, and aesthetic finishing of the space can be completed.

While flooring can sometimes be installed before acoustic treatment, it is generally preferred to complete acoustic ceiling and wall treatments first to avoid damaging newly installed floors with scaffolding or equipment.
The acoustic treatment must be fully installed before room calibration, acoustic testing, and soundproofing verification can be performed.
Power and data cabling must be run and terminated in the rack location before the AV rack can be installed and connected.
AV rack equipment must be installed and mounted before cables can be terminated and tested at the rack end.
Commissioning and full system testing requires all rack-mounted equipment to be installed and operational first.
Although not strictly required, completing ceiling work before rack installation avoids dust and debris contamination of sensitive AV equipment.
All AV equipment (displays, speakers, microphones, projectors, control systems) must be physically installed and wired before the system can be powered on and commissioned.
Room finishes such as ceiling tiles, wall paint, and flooring must be completed to provide a clean environment before installing and commissioning sensitive AV equipment.

predecessor: Complete Electrical Rough-In and Power Availability
rationale: Power outlets, circuits, and electrical infrastructure must be complete and live to supply power to AV equipment during commissioning.

successor: Room AV Acceptance Testing and Handover
rationale: Commissioning (testing, calibration, and programming of the AV system) must be successfully completed before the room can undergo formal acceptance testing and be handed over to the client.
The AV system must be fully commissioned and verified operational before the room can be occupied and used for its intended functions (meetings, presentations, etc.).
The floor must be leveled, sealed, and load-bearing capacity verified before installing heavy server racks to ensure stability and safety.
Overhead cable trays and ladder racks should be installed before server racks to allow easy routing of cables from above into the racks without obstruction.
Raised floor tiles and support structure must be in place to provide a stable platform for rack placement and to allow underfloor cooling and cabling.
Servers, switches, and other IT equipment can only be mounted inside racks after the racks themselves are securely positioned and leveled.
Cables are routed to and terminated at the patch panels and equipment within the racks, so the racks must be in place first.

successor: Power Distribution Unit (PDU) Installation in Racks
rationale: Vertical or horizontal PDUs are mounted inside the racks; the racks must be installed and secured before PDUs can be placed.
CFD analysis and airflow balancing depend on the exact rack layout and position to ensure hot/cold aisle containment works properly.
PDU must be connected to a main electrical panel or switchboard for primary power input; the panel must be installed and energized first.
The PDU is a heavy floor-mounted unit that requires a level, load-bearing concrete surface or raised floor before placement.
Cable trays and conduits feeding power to/from the PDU should be installed before the PDU is set in place to allow efficient cable pulling and termination.
Final connection of branch circuits, load cabling, and testing of PDU outputs can only occur after the PDU unit is physically installed and secured.

successor: Server Rack / IT Equipment Power On
rationale: IT equipment in server racks requires power from the PDU; the PDU must be installed, cabled, and tested before rack equipment can be energized.
Structural steel and roof trusses provide the primary support framework from which overhead cable trays and ladder racks are suspended or mounted.
Large-diameter overhead pipes and plumbing runs are typically installed before cable trays to avoid clashes and allow cable trays to route around or below fixed piping.
Cable trays and ladder racks must be fully installed and secured before any cables can be pulled, laid, or terminated within them.

successor: Overhead Electrical Conduit & Cable Tray Final Routing
rationale: Final routing adjustments for smaller conduits may be sequenced after main cable trays to coordinate pathways, though some parallel installation is possible with coordination.

successor: Fireproofing & Firestopping at Cable Tray Penetrations
rationale: Firestopping around cable tray penetrations through floors and walls can only be applied after the cable tray is in its final position.
The grounding electrode system provides the reference ground potential; the busbar must connect to this system to establish proper grounding.
The busbar is typically mounted on walls or within electrical rooms that are built after the foundation and slab are complete.
Conduits and raceways must be in place so they can be terminated and bonded to the busbar.

successor: Connect Equipment Grounding Conductors to Busbar
rationale: Equipment grounding conductors from branch circuits and feeders terminate at the busbar and cannot be connected until the busbar is installed.

successor: Terminate Bonding Jumpers for Metallic Systems
rationale: Bonding jumpers for metallic piping, ductwork, and structural steel must connect to the installed busbar to ensure equipotential bonding.

successor: Install Patch Panel & Fiber Optic Termination Enclosure
rationale: The Patch Panel & Fiber Optic Termination Enclosure is typically mounted into or onto a back-mount enclosure or rack; the enclosure or rack must be in place first to provide structural support.

predecessor: Run & Secure Conduit/Cable Tray to Enclosure Location
successor: Install Patch Panel & Fiber Optic Termination Enclosure
rationale: Conduit or cable tray pathways must be installed and terminated at the enclosure location before the enclosure is mounted, so that cables can enter the enclosure cleanly and be properly secured.

predecessor: Install Patch Panel & Fiber Optic Termination Enclosure
successor: Pull & Route Fiber Optic Cables to Enclosure
rationale: Fiber optic cables must be pulled into and through the enclosure after it is mounted; the enclosure provides the terminus point and cable management features needed to organize and protect the fibers.

predecessor: Install Patch Panel & Fiber Optic Termination Enclosure
successor: Terminate Fiber Optic Connectors on Patch Panel
rationale: Fiber optic termination (splicing or connectorizing) is performed on the patch panel or termination enclosure itself; the enclosure must be installed and fixed in position before technicians can safely terminate fibers.

predecessor: Install Patch Panel & Fiber Optic Termination Enclosure
rationale: Optical testing of the installed fiber links requires the patch panel and termination enclosure to be in place so that test equipment can connect to the terminated patch panel ports.

The vibration isolation base must be installed on a properly prepared, clean, and fully cured concrete slab to ensure a stable and level substrate, preventing cracking or uneven loading of the isolation system.

predecessor: Rough Electrical / Mechanical Rough-Ins Below Slab
rationale: Any underground conduits, plumbing, or mechanical lines that pass beneath the slab must be completed and inspected before the slab is poured and the isolation base is installed, as retrofitting would require demolition.

The subfloor framing or structural underlayment sits directly on top of the vibration isolation base; the isolation base must be fully placed and adjusted before any framing or sheathing is attached above it.
Load-bearing and non-load-bearing walls are typically erected on top of the completed subfloor system, including the vibration isolation layer, to ensure the entire structure is isolated from below.

While the flooring finish must go after the isolation base and subfloor are complete, it is a soft preference because the base itself is the structural/acoustic layer; finishing can be scheduled flexibly but follows logically for protection.

predecessor: Pour and Cure Concrete Floor Slab
rationale: The raised access flooring system requires a level, cured concrete subfloor to bear the weight of the pedestals and panels. Installing on a wet or uncured slab would cause instability and structural failure.
The building structure must be complete to provide the enclosed space and support for the floor system. Access flooring cannot be installed in an open, unenclosed structure.

All conduit, piping, and cabling that runs beneath the raised floor must be placed in the slab or on the subfloor before the pedestals and panels are installed, as access to the subfloor will be blocked once the raised floor is in place.

Once the raised floor panels are installed, they provide a clean, elevated platform for routing data, power, and communication cables above or within the floor cavity, and for installing floor boxes and grommets.

Interior walls and partition systems are typically built on top of the finished raised floor to ensure proper alignment, leveling, and to allow for floor-mounted anchorages. Building walls before the floor would create uneven transitions and installation difficulties.

predecessor: Prepare Equipment Pad / Foundation for CRAC/CRAH Unit
rationale: The CRAC/CRAH unit must be placed on a level, structurally sound foundation or equipment pad to ensure proper alignment, vibration control, and load distribution. Without the pad/foundation in place, the unit cannot be installed.

successor: Connect Refrigerant / Chilled Water Piping to CRAC/CRAH Unit
rationale: The piping connections to the unit can only be made once the unit is physically set in its final position and the ducting is roughed in. Pipe routing and connection points depend on the exact location and orientation of the installed unit.

successor: Connect Electrical Power and Control Wiring to CRAC/CRAH Unit
