rationale: Electrical connections to the unit require the unit to be in its final installed position. Wiring cannot be terminated until the unit is physically placed and secured.

While the CRAC/CRAH unit ducting should ideally connect to overhead distribution ductwork, some sequencing flexibility exists if temporary or alternate duct paths are used. However, for a complete functional system, ceiling-level ductwork is needed after the unit's ducting is installed.

predecessor: Floor Slab / Structural Steel Complete in Equipment Area
rationale: The structural floor or steel framing must be complete and capable of supporting the heavy CRAC/CRAH unit weight before the unit can be delivered and set in place.
Electrical rough-in must be complete to provide the necessary conduit, wiring, and infrastructure for connecting the UPS and battery bank.

predecessor: Pour and Cure Concrete Floor Slab
rationale: A cured concrete floor slab is required to provide a stable, level, and load-bearing surface for the heavy UPS equipment and battery racks.
HVAC system must be roughed in to ensure adequate cooling and ventilation for heat-generating UPS and battery equipment before installation.

successor: Complete UPS and Battery Bank Termination and Testing
rationale: The UPS and battery bank must be physically installed before electrical terminations can be made and system commissioning and load bank testing can be performed.

successor: Complete Fire Alarm and Suppression System Installation
rationale: While fire suppression can be partly installed earlier, final integration with the energized UPS room requires the UPS equipment to be in place. This is a soft preference to sequence after installation for coordination.

successor: Install Server Racks and Cable Management
rationale: Power and data cabling must be run to rack locations before racks can be positioned and secured, otherwise the racks would block access to floor boxes or wall penetrations.

successor: Install Server Racks and Cable Management
rationale: In raised-floor data centers, the floor tiles and cable trays beneath must be fully installed before racks are placed, because racks sit on or are bolted to the raised floor and cables route underneath.

predecessor: Complete Overhead Cable Trays and Ladder Rack
successor: Install Server Racks and Cable Management
rationale: Overhead cable management pathways must be in place before racks are installed so that network cables can be routed from the trays directly into the racks.

predecessor: Install Server Racks and Cable Management
successor: Mount and Cable IT Equipment (Servers, Switches, Patch Panels)
rationale: Server racks and cable management arms/panels must be in place and secure before any IT hardware is mounted, as the racks provide the physical structure and grounding for equipment installation.

predecessor: Install Server Racks and Cable Management
rationale: Cable management systems (horizontal and vertical managers, D-rings, cable ladders) must be installed first so that structured cabling can be dressed, bundled, and terminated neatly within those pathways.
The clean-agent system requires the fixed piping network to be in place before nozzles, tanks, and detection components can be installed.

predecessor: Run Electrical Conduit and Cabling for Fire Alarm System
rationale: Electrical power and control wiring for the suppression system's release panel and detectors must be pre-installed to allow connections.

predecessor: Complete ceiling grid and overhead rough-in
rationale: Clean-agent nozzles are often mounted in or above ceilings; ceiling grid and rough-in work must be done to provide mounting and access.
Ceiling tiles must be installed after the suppression nozzles and detection devices are in place to avoid damage and ensure proper alignment.

successor: Commission and Test Fire Suppression System
rationale: System commissioning and testing logically occur only after the complete installation of all suppression system components.

predecessor: Install Environmental and Access Control Systems
successor: Commission Environmental and Access Control Systems
rationale: Environmental and access control systems must be fully installed and in place before they can be commissioned, as commissioning involves testing and verifying the functionality of already-installed systems.

successor: Commission Environmental and Access Control Systems
rationale: Electrical power and mechanical infrastructure must be roughed in and available to power the environmental and access control systems for commissioning testing.

predecessor: Commission Environmental and Access Control Systems
rationale: Commissioning of these critical building systems is a prerequisite for substantial completion inspections, as inspectors need to verify that all environmental and access systems function correctly.

predecessor: Commission Environmental and Access Control Systems
successor: Commission Other Building Systems (e.g., Fire/Life Safety)
rationale: While environmental and access control systems can be commissioned independently, coordinating with other system commissioning helps ensure integrated system performance, though it is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before formwork can be erected, as the formwork needs a stable, prepared base to sit on and to define the correct shape and elevation of the concrete element.

Rebar cages or reinforcing steel mats must be placed within the formwork volume before the formwork panels are fully closed and secured, as the reinforcement provides structural integrity to the concrete and cannot be added after the forms are in place.
Formwork creates the mold that shapes and contains the wet concrete; therefore, the formwork must be fully erected, aligned, and braced before any concrete is poured into it.
The formwork panels, ties, and bracing must be designed, fabricated, and delivered to site before erection can commence; without the engineered components, the physical formwork cannot be assembled.
Rebar must be cut, bent, and fabricated to the required shapes and sizes before it can be placed in the formwork.
Formwork must be erected to create the mold into which concrete will be poured; rebar is placed inside the formwork before concrete is poured.
Rebar must be fully placed, tied, and inspected within the formwork before concrete can be poured to ensure proper reinforcement.
After rebar placement, an inspection must be conducted to verify correct positioning, spacing, tying, and coverage before concrete placement is permitted.
If post-tensioning tendons are used, they are typically installed after the rebar cage is in place but before concrete pouring, though this depends on the specific post-tensioning system design.
Rebar must be placed and tied within the slab formwork before concrete is poured, as the reinforcement provides structural integrity and cannot be added after the concrete has set.
Formwork (molds) must be constructed and secured to define the shape, edges, and thickness of the concrete slab before any concrete can be placed.
The ground or base layer beneath the slab must be excavated, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable, uniform support surface; pouring on unprepared subgrade leads to cracking and settlement.
A vapor retarder is laid over the prepared subgrade to prevent moisture migration from the ground into the concrete slab; this must be in place before pouring.
After the concrete is poured and finished, a curing period is required for the slab to gain strength and dry to specified moisture levels before any subsequent work can be performed on or above it.
Formwork must be installed to create the mold and support structure before concrete can be poured to form the beam.
Steel rebar must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide tensile strength for the reinforced concrete beam.
After concrete is poured into the beam formwork, it must undergo a curing period to gain sufficient strength before any loads are applied.
The concrete beam must be poured and allowed to cure to sufficient strength before the formwork can be safely removed.
Concrete beams must be completed and cured to support the transfer of loads from vertical structural elements that will bear on or connect to the beams above.
Concrete walls require a stable foundation to bear their load; footings must be completed and cured before wall construction begins.
Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity.
Formwork (molds) must be assembled and braced to contain and shape the wet concrete during pouring and curing.
Waterproofing membranes or coatings are applied to the cured concrete wall surface to prevent moisture intrusion.
Backfilling against a concrete wall can only occur after the concrete has sufficiently cured and gained strength to resist lateral earth pressures.
Formwork provides the mold that shapes and supports the wet concrete until it cures, so it must be installed and secured before concrete is poured.
Steel reinforcement bars must be placed and tied within the formwork prior to concrete pouring to provide tensile strength to the column.
The column's loads must be transferred to a prepared foundation; the column rebar typically extends into the footing, which must be cast first.
The concrete must reach sufficient initial strength (curing) before the formwork can be safely removed without damaging the column.
Curing (keeping concrete moist and at proper temperature) begins immediately after pouring; finishing work like patching or smoothing can only proceed after the concrete has set.

successor: Vertical Structural Load Transfer (e.g., beams/slabs on columns)
rationale: Beams and slabs that bear on the column require the column to be fully cured and load-bearing before their own construction or loading can commence.

Waterproofing or protective coatings are typically applied after the concrete has fully cured; this is a recommended sequence for adhesion but not a strict physical necessity (could be done later if access allows).
Concrete stairs require a stable load-bearing base; the foundation/footing must be in place to support the stair structure.
Railings are attached to or anchored into the concrete stair structure, which must first be cured and hardened.
If stairs are in contact with soil or a lower level, waterproofing must be applied before pouring concrete to prevent moisture damage.
Formwork defines the shape of the concrete stair; the concrete cannot be poured without the formwork in place.
Finishing operations (troweling, grinding, sealing) must occur after the concrete has been placed and initially set but before full cure.
The ground must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and topsoil, and excavated to the required depth before any concrete can be poured to form the foundation.
The soil must be tested for bearing capacity and properly compacted to ensure it can support the foundation load; pouring concrete on unprepared soil would lead to settlement and structural failure.
Formwork (molds) must be constructed and in place to shape and contain the wet concrete until it cures and gains sufficient strength.
Steel reinforcement bars must be positioned and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide tensile strength and structural integrity to the foundation.
After the concrete is poured, it must be allowed to cure (harden) for a specified period before formwork can be stripped away and subsequent loads can be applied.
Waterproofing membranes or coatings are applied to the cured foundation surface to prevent moisture ingress before backfilling or further construction proceeds.
The excavated areas around the foundation can only be backfilled after the concrete has fully cured and waterproofing has been applied to protect the foundation.
The load-bearing walls, columns, or framing of the building must be erected on top of the completed foundation, as the foundation provides the stable base for all above-grade structural elements.
Formwork (molds) must be erected and braced to contain and shape the wet concrete before pouring can begin.
Reinforcing steel bars (rebar) must be positioned, tied, and inspected within the formwork to provide tensile strength before concrete is placed.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and compacted to the required subgrade to provide a stable foundation for casting concrete.
Freshly placed concrete must undergo a controlled curing period (maintaining moisture and temperature) to achieve design strength and durability before any loads are applied.
Concrete must reach sufficient initial strength (set and harden) before formwork can be safely removed without damaging the structural element.
The ground must be excavated and foundation prepared before any concrete joints can be installed, as the joint rests on or is cast within the prepared foundation/sub-base.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied before concrete joints are formed, as the joint material or joint former is positioned within the reinforcement cage.
Formwork must be erected to define the concrete slab or wall geometry before the joint can be located and installed at the correct position within the pour.
The joint material (e.g., expansion joint filler, waterstop, or joint former) must be in place before concrete is poured around it, so that the joint is properly embedded and functional.

After the concrete joint is installed and concrete has been placed and partially cured, the joint groove must be cleaned, sealed, and finished to ensure proper movement accommodation and waterproofing.
Precast concrete elements require a stable and level foundation to be placed upon. The foundation must be fully cured and ready to support the loads from precast components.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and compacted before any foundations or precast elements can be installed.

Drainage pipes, electrical conduits, and other underground services must be laid before precast elements are placed, as access to the ground surface becomes restricted once precast members are installed.
Temporary bracing, grouting of connections, and completion of the structural framing system must follow immediately after precast elements are erected to ensure stability.
Roofing and upper floor slabs are typically installed after the precast wall and column elements are in place, as they bear on or connect to these vertical elements.
Final finishing operations such as floating and troweling must be completed before curing starts, as curing should begin after finishing is done and the concrete has begun to harden.
Surface preparation for waterproofing, sealants, or other coatings must wait until the specified curing period is complete and the concrete has dried to the required moisture content.
Structural loads (equipment, construction traffic, or additional construction elements) should not be applied until concrete has reached its design strength through proper curing.
Concrete must be placed and poured before its surface can be finished; finishing is performed on freshly placed concrete while it is still workable.
Screeding levels and strikes off the concrete to the correct grade, which must be done prior to final finishing operations such as floating or troweling.
Surface finishing (floating, troweling, brooming) must be completed before the curing process begins, as curing is the controlled maintenance of moisture and temperature after finishing is done.
Control joints or saw cuts are typically made after the concrete surface has been finished and has gained sufficient strength to prevent raveling, but before shrinkage cracking occurs.

successor: Application of Floor Hardener or Sealer
rationale: Hardeners, sealers, or surface treatments are applied only after the concrete surface has been properly finished and has cured sufficiently to accept the coating.
The excavation and footing area must be prepared, cleared, and leveled before any concrete anchor or embedment can be placed into the ground or foundation.
Reinforcement steel (rebar) must be positioned and tied in the footing or slab area before anchor bolts or embedment plates are set, so they can be properly integrated into the reinforcing cage.
Anchors and embedments must be positioned, leveled, and secured in place before concrete is poured so that they become permanently embedded in the cured concrete.
Concrete must be poured and given sufficient time to cure (gain strength) before forms can be stripped and before any load can be applied to the anchors.
After concrete has cured and forms are removed, the exposed anchor bolts or embedment plates are ready to receive and connect the steel columns or structural frame elements.
The structural concrete slab must be fully cured and provide a stable base before any topping or screed can be applied.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied before pouring the concrete topping to ensure structural integrity.
If the topping is over a waterproofed area (e.g., balcony, wet room), the waterproofing membrane must be installed first to protect against moisture ingress.
The topping/screed must be fully cured and dry before any final floor finishes can be applied, otherwise the finish will not adhere properly.
While partitions can sometimes be installed before the topping, it is generally preferred to complete the topping first to achieve a level substrate and avoid having to work around existing walls.
The timber frame must be erected on a complete and cured foundation system to provide a stable, level bearing surface and to anchor the posts/base connections.
All underground plumbing, electrical conduits, and utilities beneath the slab must be installed and inspected before the slab is poured and the frame erected, as access is impossible afterward.

predecessor: Slab on Grade / Ground Floor Slab
rationale: The ground floor slab provides the working platform and base for erecting the timber frame; posts and beams bear on the slab or on embedded connections in the foundation.
The roof structure (rafters, purlins, or roof trusses) bears directly upon the timber frame beams and posts; the frame must be complete to support the roof load.
Wall and roof sheathing is installed on the timber frame to enclose the structure; the frame must be fully erected to provide the substrate for sheathing attachment.
Roofing membranes and weatherproofing materials are applied over the roof deck/sheathing, which depends on the timber frame being complete to support the roof structure.

If SIPs are used as the enclosure system, they are typically installed directly onto the timber frame, but in some sequences SIPs can be installed as the frame is raised (panelized approach), so this is a strong preference but not an absolute physical constraint.
Steel frame provides the primary structural support and attachment points for the timber truss system. The steel structure must be in place to carry the loads from the timber trusses.
Bearing walls are required to support the ends of the timber trusses. Trusses cannot be installed without completed bearing walls to rest upon.
Roof sheathing (plywood/OSB) is fastened directly to the top chord of the timber trusses. Trusses must be fully erected and braced before sheathing can be applied.

While insulation typically follows truss completion, some insulation can be installed beforehand. However, complete truss installation is preferred before full insulation to avoid material conflicts and ensure proper cavity filling.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the roof/attic space requires the truss structure to be in place to run ductwork, wiring, and piping through the truss cavities and to attach hangers/supports.

successor: Light Timber Framing (Stud Walls, Joists, Rafters)
rationale: The ground floor or slab provides the base platform upon which the timber stud walls and framing are erected. Without a level and cured floor structure, the wall frames cannot be safely or accurately installed.

successor: Light Timber Framing (Stud Walls, Joists, Rafters)
rationale: If it is a suspended timber floor, the subfloor structure (bearers and joists) must be installed first to provide the working platform and supporting structure for the wall frames above.

predecessor: Damp Proof Course (DPC) / Termite Protection Installation
successor: Light Timber Framing (Stud Walls, Joists, Rafters)
rationale: Damp proof courses and termite barriers must be placed between the foundation/concrete and the timber frame to protect the timber from moisture and insect attack before the timber elements are installed.

predecessor: Light Timber Framing (Stud Walls, Joists, Rafters)
rationale: The wall frames must be erected and braced to support the roof structure. Roof trusses or rafters bear directly onto the top plates of the wall frames.

predecessor: Light Timber Framing (Stud Walls, Joists, Rafters)
rationale: Structural bracing (e.g., plywood or diagonal strapping) is typically installed after the frame is erected to provide lateral stability, though some bracing may be integrated with the frame itself.

predecessor: Light Timber Framing (Stud Walls, Joists, Rafters)
rationale: External cladding, weatherboards, or structural sheathing boards are fixed to the outside of the timber frame after it is erected to provide the building envelope.

predecessor: Light Timber Framing (Stud Walls, Joists, Rafters)
rationale: While some services can be run through the frame after it is erected, rough-in work is traditionally done after framing to allow access through stud cavities. However, some pre-wiring may occur before closed-in stages; this is a soft preference/sequence.

predecessor: Light Timber Framing (Stud Walls, Joists, Rafters)
rationale: Insulation batts or boards are placed between studs and joists after the frame is erected and before internal lining is fixed.

predecessor: Light Timber Framing (Stud Walls, Joists, Rafters)
rationale: Internal linings (e.g., plasterboard/gypsum board) are fixed directly to the timber studs and joists, so the framing must be fully erected and inspected first.

predecessor: Wall Framing and Rough Opening Preparation
rationale: The rough openings in walls must be framed and prepared before timber door and window frames can be installed, as the frames are fitted into these openings.
Load-bearing walls must be constructed to provide structural support and define the openings before timber frames can be set in place.

successor: Door and Window Installation (Hanging Doors / Glazing)
rationale: The timber frames must be installed first to provide the structural surround into which doors are hung and window sashes or glazing units are fitted.
Timber frames are installed before internal wall finishes so that the plaster or drywall can abut neatly against the frames, ensuring a clean finish.
Priming and painting of timber frames is often done after installation to protect the wood, though pre-finished frames may reverse this; typically a soft preference for sequencing.

Electrical wiring, outlets, and switches must be roughed-in behind wall and ceiling surfaces before timber paneling and moldings are installed, as timber finishes would cover and block access to these services.
Plumbing pipes and drains behind walls must be installed before timber paneling is fixed in place, as the paneling would prevent access to plumbing rough-ins.
HVAC ductwork and vent runs in walls and ceilings must be completed before timber finishes enclose these spaces.

predecessor: Interior Framing & Sheathing (Stud Walls, Ceiling Joists)
rationale: Timber paneling and trims are attached to the interior framing or sheathing, so the structural frame must be in place first to provide a mounting surface.
Insulation must be placed within wall cavities before they are sealed by timber paneling, otherwise the insulation would be inaccessible.

successor: Interior Painting & Wall Finishing (Paint, Wallpaper, Plaster)
rationale: Timber trims, moldings, and paneling must be installed before adjacent wall surfaces are painted or finished, because the timber elements define the edges and must be completed first to allow clean paint lines and seamless finishing.

While often baseboard trims are installed before flooring, there are soft preferences either way; typically timber trims and moldings (especially baseboards) are installed before final flooring to allow a clean interface, but this can vary by trade preference.
The structural frame must be complete to provide the supporting structure for timber stairs and railings installation.
Floor slabs or decking need to be in place to define the levels between which stairs connect.
Walls provide attachment points for stair stringers, railings, and handrails.
Stairs and railings must be installed before final wall finishes so that joints between stairs and walls can be properly trimmed and finished.
Stairs must be installed before applying any stair coverings or floor finishes that abut the stairs.
The heavy timber members must be fully installed and in place before fireproofing or encapsulation can be applied to them. Fireproofing cannot be applied to timber that hasn't been erected yet.

Adjacent structural steel and metal deck that may intersect or be integrated with heavy timber elements must be installed before encapsulation can be applied, as the fireproofing system often wraps or interfaces with both materials.

predecessor: Rough Mechanical / Electrical / Plumbing (MEP) Rough-In in Vicinity
rationale: Any MEP rough-in that will run through or behind the timber fireproofing/encapsulation must be completed first, so that encapsulation can be applied continuously without subsequent openings or penetrations that would compromise the fire-resistance rating.

Interior finishes, cladding, or drywall that conceal or abut encapsulated timber must be installed after the fireproofing/encapsulation is complete, so that the fire-resistive assembly is fully in place before finishing work covers it.

While not strictly a physical constraint, it is standard practice and code-required that fireproofing/encapsulation be completed and inspected before final fire-rating closeout inspections can be performed to verify compliance.
The timber-concrete composite system relies on the primary structural steel frame for support and load transfer, so the steel frame must be erected first.
Lateral stability and vertical load paths from the composite system often depend on concrete cores or shear walls being completed first.
The composite floor system forms the structural substrate; waterproofing and screeding are applied on top of the finished structural deck.
Partition walls are built on top of the finished floor system, so the composite slab must be in place before interior framing can begin.
MEP services are typically installed after the structural slab is complete, running below or embedded within the composite system.
Structural timber requires a level, stable, and load-bearing foundation to transfer loads safely to the ground; without completed foundations, timber framing cannot be properly anchored or supported.

The ground floor slab or substructure provides the base surface upon which timber walls and frames are erected; timber must be installed on a completed substrate to ensure dimensional stability and moisture protection.
Timber wall frames and columns must be in place to support roof trusses, rafters, and roof decking; the roof structure relies on completed vertical load-bearing timber elements.
Permanent bracing, diaphragms, and shear walls are installed after the main timber frame is erected to provide lateral stability and wind load resistance to the structure.

While some services can be chased into timber framing, it is generally preferred to install rough-in conduits, pipes, and ducts after the timber frame is in place to avoid rework and to coordinate with framing penetrations.
The structural framing (floor joists, beams, or subfloor) must be in place to provide the load-bearing support for the timber decking or flooring to be installed upon.
The subfloor surface must be leveled, cleaned, and prepared (including any necessary underlayment or moisture barrier) to ensure a stable and even base for the timber flooring.

All rough-in services (plumbing pipes, electrical conduits, HVAC ducts) that run beneath or within the floor assembly must be completed before flooring is installed, as accessing them afterwards would require removal of the finished flooring.

Flooring is typically installed before final wall finishes and painting to allow flooring materials to be laid seamlessly up to the walls and to prevent damage to finished wall surfaces during flooring installation.

While often preferred after flooring to avoid scratching new cabinets, in some sequences cabinetry is installed first and flooring is cut around it; however, installing flooring first provides a cleaner finish and easier future replacement.
The structural frame (steel or timber) must be erected and stable to provide a mounting surface and support for the timber cladding system.
A weather-resistant barrier (building wrap or membrane) must be installed over the sheathing before cladding to protect the structure from moisture infiltration.
Exterior sheathing (e.g., plywood or OSB) must be fixed to the frame to provide a rigid substrate and nailable surface for the cladding attachment.
While windows/doors can be installed before cladding, it is preferable to install them after cladding to allow proper flashing integration and weather sealing at the cladding-to-opening junctions.
The timber cladding must be fully installed to allow application of protective finish, stain, or paint to the entire cladding surface for weather protection and aesthetics.
Rough framing provides the structural support and backing surfaces onto which timber joinery and millwork elements (such as cabinets, trims, and moldings) are installed.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before millwork installation to avoid covering unfinished services and to allow for proper routing of wiring, pipes, and ducts within or behind joinery.

predecessor: Interior Wall Sheathing / Drywall (at least first fix)
rationale: Interior wall surfaces (e.g., drywall or plasterboard) need to be installed and finished prior to fitting millwork so that joinery has a flat, true backing and can be properly secured and trimmed.

Millwork such as baseboards, shoe moldings, and cabinetry is typically installed before finished flooring is laid, as the flooring is then cut and fitted around the millwork for a clean, finished appearance.

While final painting and touch-up often follow millwork installation to blend and seal around joinery, this is a soft preference because millwork can also be pre-finished and installed after painting if careful sequencing is managed.
Raw timber must be harvested and milled into usable lumber before any treatment or coating can be applied to the wood surfaces.
Timber must be dried to the appropriate moisture content before treatment and coating; applying coatings to wet or green timber会导致 trapping moisture and subsequent decay or coating failure.
After coating is applied, the timber needs adequate curing or drying time for the coating to harden and bond properly before further handling or installation.
Treated and coated timber components must be fully finished before they are installed or fixed into the building structure, as installation may obstruct access for coating and treatment application.

successor: Final Finishing and Inspection of Timber Elements
rationale: The coating and treatment process is part of the finishing work; after completion, final inspection of the timber elements for quality and appearance can be conducted.

Timber connection hardware (such as brackets, bolts, screws, and plates) must be installed after the timber frame members are erected because the hardware physically connects the frame components together. The frame must be in place to know exact positioning and fit.
Load testing can only occur after all connection hardware is installed and tightened, as the hardware provides the structural integrity needed to bear loads.

Building enclosure or cladding systems are installed after the timber connections are complete, as the hardware often protrudes or must be accessible for tightening and inspection before being covered.
Anchor bolts and foundation connections must be set in the concrete foundation before timber connection hardware can be attached to them, as the hardware connects timber members to the foundation.
Timber members must be cut, drilled, and fabricated to accept connection hardware (e.g., pre-drilled holes for bolts) before the hardware can be installed on site.
Structural steel columns require a stable load-bearing foundation to transfer their loads to the ground. The foundation must be completed and cured before any steel columns can be erected.

predecessor: Anchor Bolt Installation and Concrete Curing
rationale: Anchor bolts must be embedded and set in the foundation concrete, and the concrete must achieve sufficient strength to hold the bolts, before steel column base plates can be bolted down.
The building site must be excavated and graded to design elevations to provide a level working surface and proper embedment for column foundations.
Steel beams and girders span between columns and require the columns to be erected, plumbed, and temporarily braced to provide the vertical supports they connect to.
Roof steel trusses or rafters must be supported by the column tops; columns must be in place before any roof-level steel can be installed.
Steel beams require support from foundations and columns to transfer loads to the ground; the supporting structure must be in place before beams can be erected.
Steel beams must be fabricated, delivered, and inspected on site before erection can begin.
The site must be graded, cleared, and surveyed for accurate placement of foundations and columns that support the steel beams.
Metal decking and concrete slabs are placed on top of or between steel beams; beams must be in place to support the decking.
Final connection work (welding, bolting, moment connections) between beams and columns can only be completed after beams are positioned and aligned.
Fireproofing spray or intumescent coatings are applied to steel beams after they are erected and connections are completed.
Overhead MEP runs are often hung from or routed through steel beam bays; it is more efficient to do this after beams are in place, but some pre-assembly is possible.
Steel trusses require stable and level foundation support to bear their load; without completed foundations, trusses cannot be safely placed.
Steel trusses are typically mounted onto columns or vertical supports; these structural supports must be in place before truss installation.
If concrete foundations or columns are used, they must be fully cured to achieve required strength before accepting truss loads.
Roof decking or sheathing is placed directly on top of the steel trusses; trusses must be fully installed and secured to provide the supporting framework.

MEP rough-in work in the ceiling space (ductwork, piping, electrical conduits) is typically done after trusses are in place to utilize the overhead space, though some work can be staged concurrently in certain designs.
Steel girders require a stable, load-bearing foundation to support their weight and the loads they transfer. The foundation must be fully cured and ready before girder placement.
Steel girders span between columns and rest on column connections or cap plates. Columns must be erected, plumbed, and bolted/welded in place before girders can be installed.
The site must be cleared, graded, and surveyed for precise girder placement coordinates and elevations before any steel erection begins.
Metal decking or concrete formwork is placed on top of the steel girders to form the floor or roof system. Girders must be in position to support the decking.
After girders are set between columns, the beam-to-column and beam-to-beam connections must be permanently welded or bolted to ensure structural continuity and stability.
The ground must be excavated to expose the foundation area where steel base plates will be placed and anchored.
Concrete footings or foundation piers must be poured and cured to provide a stable, level bearing surface for steel base plates to be bolted or anchored onto.
Anchor bolts must be embedded in the concrete foundation (or set in place before pouring) so that the steel base plates can be aligned, placed over them, and secured with nuts.
Steel base plates must be installed and leveled first to provide a mounting surface onto which steel columns are welded or bolted.

Base plates are typically set on leveling nuts/shim stacks first; then after columns are erected and plumbed, high-strength grout is pumped underneath to fill any gaps between the plate and the foundation for full bearing.
Steel connections and fasteners cannot be installed until the main steel structural members (columns, beams, girders) are erected and positioned in place, as connections join these members together.
Steel columns must be anchored to foundations via base plates and anchor bolts before the column-to-beam connections can be completed, ensuring structural stability.

All bolted and welded connections must be completed before inspection and non-destructive testing (e.g., ultrasonic testing of welds, torque checks on bolts) can be performed to verify connection integrity.
Metal deck panels are typically fastened to the steel frame; the connecting bolts and welds securing the frame must be finished before deck panels can be safely placed and attached.
Fireproofing spray-applied materials are applied after all steel connections are complete, as the connections must be exposed for inspection and then covered by the fireproofing system.

The composite steel decking is typically installed on top of and supported by the structural steel frame. The steel beams and columns must be erected first to provide the structural support framework for the decking panels.

The composite steel decking serves as both a working platform and formwork for the concrete slab. Concrete must be poured over the decking to form the composite floor slab, and cannot be placed until the metal deck is installed and fastened.
Shear studs are welded through the decking to the steel beams to create composite action. This must be done before the concrete pour, but after the decking is placed and secured to the steel frame.

While some services can be run after decking is installed, it is preferable to complete rough-in work below the deck from the floor below before the deck is fully closed in, to avoid access difficulties later.
Safety edge protection (guardrails, netting) must be installed immediately after the deck is laid to protect workers from falls during subsequent work on the elevated deck surface.

Steel shear studs are typically welded through the steel deck to the supporting beams below. The steel deck must be installed first to provide the surface through which the studs are welded and to ensure proper composite action between the steel beam and the concrete slab.
Shear studs are welded directly to the top flange of steel beams. The steel beams must be erected and in place before shear studs can be installed onto them.

Shear studs are designed to be embedded in the concrete slab to create composite action between the steel beam and the concrete. The concrete slab placement must occur after the studs are installed so the studs become fully encased in concrete.
After shear studs are welded, they must be tested (e.g., bend testing or torque testing) to verify weld quality and integrity before being covered by concrete.
In many composite deck designs, shear studs are installed before the reinforcement mesh or rebar is placed, as the studs protrude through the deck and the reinforcement is laid around or over them.
Structural steel columns and frames require stable foundation systems (footings, piers, or pile caps) to transfer loads to the ground; steel cannot be erected on unprepared ground.

predecessor: Concrete Slab on Grade / Mud Slab
rationale: A concrete slab or mud slab provides a level, stable working surface for cranes and staging equipment needed to lift and assemble steel members.
Anchor bolts must be embedded, aligned, and fully cured in the foundation before steel base plates can be grouted and bolted down.
The site must be graded and drained to prevent standing water or soft soils that could compromise crane stability and steel placement safety.
Metal deck panels are laid directly on and welded to the structural steel framing; the steel frame must be in place to support the deck.

successor: Steel Girder and Beam Connection Detailing
rationale: Final bolting/welding of connections, stiffeners, and moment connections can only be completed once steel members are erected, plumbed, and aligned.
Fireproofing is applied to the exposed steel surfaces after the steel frame is complete and inspected; it cannot precede erection.
Cladding panels (metal, insulated, etc.) are attached to the structural steel frame (girts, purlins); the steel frame must be erected first.
Elevator guide rails and escalator trusses are supported by the structural steel frame; installation cannot begin until the steel is erected.
Overhead ductwork, conduit, piping, and cable trays are suspended from or penetrate the steel structure; they require the steel frame to be in place for routing and support.
Steel members must be erected and aligned in their correct positions before any welding or bolting can be performed to join them permanently.
Welds and bolted connections must be completed before they can be inspected and tested for quality and structural integrity.
Fireproofing materials are applied over the steel structure after all welding and bolting are finished, as the application would interfere with welding/bolting work or be damaged by it.
Building envelope or cladding panels are installed after the steel framework is fully welded/bolted and stable, as they attach to or are supported by the steel frame.
Final painting or protective coating of steel connections is performed after welding and bolting are complete, because coating before would be damaged by the welding heat or cover connection points.
Steel columns require a solid foundation and base plates to be installed first to provide structural support and load distribution before erecting steel members.
Accurate surveying and layout marking is required to ensure columns are placed at correct positions and alignment before steel erection begins.
Anchor bolts must be embedded in the foundation to secure steel column base plates before columns can be erected and bolted down.
The roof structure (roof trusses, purlins, decking) depends on the steel frame being erected as the primary load-bearing support system.
Metal decking and floor slabs (for multi-story buildings) require the steel beams to be in place as the supporting framework before concrete can be poured.

Steel fireproofing materials (such as sprayed fire-resistive materials or intumescent coatings) are applied directly to structural steel members. The steel must first be erected, aligned, and connected before fireproofing can be applied.
Steel surfaces must be cleaned and primed (if required by specifications) to ensure proper adhesion of fireproofing materials. Contaminants, rust, and mill scale must be removed prior to application.

All steel connections (bolts and welds) must be completed and inspected before fireproofing is applied, as fireproofing would conceal these connections and make post-application inspection impossible without costly removal.

While fireproofing is typically completed before MEP rough-in to avoid damaging fireproofing during installation of conduits, ducts, and piping, this is a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint — MEP work can sometimes proceed with protective measures if necessary.
Fireproofing on overhead steel must be completed before ceilings are enclosed, as once ceilings are installed, the fireproofing becomes inaccessible for application and inspection.
Steel shop drawings can only be produced after the structural steel detailing and 3D modeling is complete, as these drawings are derived from the model and detailing information.

The steel materials must be ordered and mill release obtained before shop drawings can be finalized, reviewed, and staged, because the drawings must reflect the actual ordered sections, grades, and availability.

Steel fabrication and cutting cannot commence until the shop drawings have been reviewed, approved, and staged for release, as the fabrication process directly depends on the approved shop drawing dimensions, connections, and piece marks.

Steel erection on site cannot begin until shop drawings are reviewed and staged because the erection sequence, connection details, and piece identification all come from the approved shop drawing package.
The steel stair structure and railings typically bear on or connect to the main structural steel frame. The frame must be erected first to provide the supporting structure for the stairs.
Landings and intermediate floor levels where stairs terminate must be poured and cured to provide a stable base for stair installation and anchorage.

While not physically mandatory, it is a practical sequencing preference to have the stairs in place before running conduit, piping, or ductwork in the stair enclosure areas to avoid interference and rework.
Fireproofing spray-applied to steel and drywall installation around stair enclosures must occur after the steel stairs and railings are in place, as they enclose and cover the installed components.
The steel stair stringers and main structural supports must be installed first to serve as the substrate for mounting handrails, guardrails, and any decorative railing infill.
Steel canopies and their supports require solid concrete foundations/footings to be cast and cured to bear the structural load and provide anchorage.
Any underground pipes, conduits, or drainage must be installed and backfilled before erecting canopy supports to avoid excavation conflicts and rework.
The structural steel frame must be erected and stabilized before any roofing sheets, cladding, or finishing materials can be applied to the canopy.
Electrical conduit runs and junction boxes for canopy lighting are typically attached to or routed through the steel structure after it is in place.
While it is preferable to apply protective coatings after erection to avoid damage during lifting, some coatings may be applied off-site, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.

The embedded steel anchor systems must be placed into wet concrete or set into properly cured concrete. If using cast-in-place anchors, the concrete must be poured and at least partially set before the anchor systems are embedded. If using drilled-in anchors, the concrete must be fully cured to provide sufficient structural strength for drilling and anchoring.

Steel columns or structural steel members depend on the embedded anchor bolts and plates for alignment, load transfer, and structural connection. The anchor systems must be in place, correctly positioned, and cured before any steel can be erected on them.

After steel columns are erected on the embedded anchor systems, the gap between the base plate and the foundation must be filled with grout to ensure uniform load transfer and to protect the anchor bolts.

predecessor: Layout and Survey of Anchor Locations
rationale: Precise surveying and layout of bolt hole patterns, elevations, and grid lines is required before setting the embedded steel anchor systems to ensure structural alignment and compliance with design drawings.

successor: Tensioning and Torque Testing of Anchor Bolts
rationale: Once the grout has cured and the steel structure is in place, the anchor bolts must be tensioned or torqued to specified values to ensure the connection meets design load requirements.
The frame and gasket system must be in place to receive and support the IGU within the window or curtain wall assembly.
The glazing pocket or frame rebate must be clean and free of debris to ensure proper seating and sealing of the IGU.
Setting blocks must be positioned at the bottom of the frame to support the weight of the IGU and prevent glass-to-metal contact.
Glazing beads or stops are installed after the IGU is placed in the frame to retain the unit in position.
Exterior and interior sealants or weatherstripping are applied after IGU placement to create an airtight and watertight seal around the unit.
The glass balustrade requires a stable structural frame to which it can be anchored; without the main building structure in place, there is no support for the balustrade system.
Glass balustrades are typically mounted onto finished floor slabs or decks; the floor surface must be cast, cured, and prepared to receive the base shoe or channel for the glass panels.

If the balustrade is on an exposed balcony or rooftop, waterproofing must be completed before the base channel is installed to avoid trapping moisture and to maintain the integrity of the waterproof layer.

The top rail or handrail is mechanically fixed onto the top edge of the glass panels after the glass is securely in place; installing the handrail first would block access to the glass panel alignment.
Silicone sealant and weatherproof caulking must be applied after the glass panels are positioned and clamped, to seal gaps between glass, frames, and adjacent finishes.
Structural framing provides the supporting framework onto which glass partitions are mounted. The glass panels cannot be installed without the structural frame in place.
The floor slab provides the base surface for the glass partition tracks and bottom channels. Glass partitions require a finished floor surface for proper alignment and anchoring.
The ceiling structure provides attachment points for top channels or suspension systems that hold glass partitions in place, especially for floor-to-ceiling installations.

While some cabling can be done before partitions, running data and electrical lines after glass partitions are installed is more difficult and may require drilling through glass or working around frameless panels, so it is preferred to complete rough-in first.

Glass partitions define room boundaries, so final interior finishes like painting and flooring are best completed after partitions are installed to ensure clean edges, transition strips, and seamless finishing around the glass panels.
The rough opening (door frame) must be framed, sized, and prepared before the glass door unit can be installed into it.
Load-bearing walls and structural framing must be completed to provide a stable opening for the glass door system.
The floor must be leveled and the subfloor prepared to ensure the glass door sits correctly and operates smoothly without binding or gaps.
Once the glass door is installed, all perimeter joints must be sealed and weatherproofed to prevent air and water infiltration.
Interior finishes around the door frame should be completed after the door is installed to ensure proper fit and clean transitions.
The glass canopy is supported by the structural steel frame, so the steel frame must be erected first to provide the structural support system.
The glazing system components (mullions, framing, sealants) must be prepared and installed before the glass panels can be placed into the canopy frame.
Weatherproofing sealants must be applied after glass panels are installed to ensure watertightness and proper sealing of joints.
While not physically required, it is preferable to complete the canopy first to protect interior finishing work from weather exposure during construction.
The glass canopy installation must be complete before performing final structural and water-tightness inspections and testing procedures.
The structural steel frame must be in place to provide the supporting framework onto which glass floor panels are mounted.
Support brackets, sub-framing, or aluminum framing must be installed to create the load-bearing perimeter and intermediate supports for the glass panels.
Joint sealants and waterproofing must be applied after the glass panels are placed to ensure watertightness and protect the underlying structure.

successor: Safety Glass Film or Coating Application
rationale: Although often pre-applied, final safety coatings or anti-slip films may be applied after installation for protection during construction, but this can also be done prior to installation as a soft preference.
Once installed, the glass floor panels must be inspected and load-tested to verify structural integrity and safety compliance before the area is opened to traffic.
The structural frame (steel or aluminum curbing/curb frame) must be installed to provide the support structure onto which the glass skylight is mounted.
The roof deck or sheathing must be completed to create the opening and substrate for the skylight curb and flashing.
Roof underlayment and flashing base must be installed prior to the skylight to prevent moisture ingress behind the unit.
After the skylight unit is set in place, the step flashing and counter-flashing are installed around the perimeter to seal the interface between the skylight and the roof.
It is a soft preference to complete the skylight before interior ceiling finishing to avoid damaging finished paint/trim when installing the skylight, though not physically required.
The structural frame (e.g., concrete or steel framework) must be complete to provide the supporting structure onto which glass panels or curtain walls are mounted.
Window/door rough openings must be framed, squared, and properly sized to receive glass units; glass cannot be installed into unprepared openings.
Waterproof membranes and flashings around openings must be in place before glass is installed to ensure a watertight seal and prevent moisture intrusion behind the glass.
Glass and windows are typically installed before interior finishes to avoid damage to finished walls from handling large glass panels, though not a strict physical necessity in all cases.
Once glass is installed, sealants and weatherproofing compounds must be applied and allowed to cure to ensure a watertight and airtight seal before any adjacent work proceeds.
The glazing frame must be installed to provide a structural substrate for the sealant to adhere to and to create the gap that needs sealing.
Glass panels must be placed into the frame before sealant can be applied to secure and weatherproof the edges.
All surfaces where sealant will be applied must be clean, dry, and free of dust, oil, or debris to ensure proper adhesion.
Once applied, the sealant must be left to cure undisturbed to achieve its full strength and weathertightness before any further work can proceed.
After sealant application, water testing or inspection is typically performed to verify weathertightness, though this is a quality control step rather than a strict physical prerequisite.
Glass sheets must be delivered and stored on-site before they can be cut and prepared.
The workspace and cutting area must be set up and organized before glass cutting activities can commence.
Window and curtain wall openings must be framed and ready to receive glass; final measurements depend on as-built opening dimensions.
Glass must be cut to size and prepared before it can be installed into the prepared openings.

successor: Tempering or Heat Treatment (if done on-site)
rationale: If tempering is performed on-site, glass must first be cut to the required dimensions before undergoing heat treatment.
The structural steel frame must be in place to provide the primary support structure onto which the glass balustrade can be mounted and anchored.
The concrete slab (typically at floor edges or balconies) must be poured and fully cured to provide a solid base for fixing the glass balustrade base shoes or brackets.
Waterproofing must be completed before balustrade installation to ensure that the fixings through the waterproofing layer can be properly detailed and sealed to maintain weathertightness.
The glass panels must be erected and secured first so that the handrail can be fixed onto the top of the glass panels or onto the supporting posts.

After the balustrade framework and glass panels are assembled, the final sealant joints and gaskets between glass panels and frames must be applied to ensure weathertightness and structural integrity.
The structural steel frame provides the primary load-bearing support and mounting points for the curtain wall system; without the erected frame, there is no structure to attach the glass panels to.
Floor slabs must be completed to provide working platforms, anchor points, and to transfer wind loads and dead loads from the curtain wall into the building structure.
Embedded anchors, brackets, and embeds must be cast into the structure or bolted to the frame before curtain wall mullions and transoms can be attached.

successor: Interior Drywall & Finishing (adjacent to curtain wall)
rationale: Interior finishes such as drywall, insulation, and sealants around curtain wall perimeters cannot be completed until the curtain wall is installed and watertight; otherwise, moisture damage and access issues would occur.
Final weatherproofing sealants, gaskets, and glazing infill panels must be installed after the curtain wall frame is in place to ensure a continuous water and air barrier.
SIPs panels require a level, structurally sound foundation (slab or basement walls) to bear the load and provide a base for wall and roof panels.
All below-grade plumbing, electrical conduits, and ground preparations must be completed before the floor SIPs are placed, as access is impossible afterward.
The SIP roof panels must be installed before weatherproofing membranes and roofing can be applied to seal the structure.
With the SIP envelope in place, chases and service cavities become accessible for running electrical wiring, plumbing lines, and ductwork through the pre-cut channels in the panels.
The structural SIP panels define the rough openings for windows and doors; these openings must exist before window and door frames can be set and flashed.
Air sealing is applied to the exterior sheathing and framing connections; rough framing must be complete to provide a substrate for air sealing materials.
The roof deck must be installed before air sealing can be applied at the attic floor or roof plane to create a continuous air barrier.
Exterior wall sheathing provides the surface on which air sealing details (e.g., caulking, gaskets, tapes) are applied at joints and penetrations.

Air sealing must be completed before insulation is installed because insulation cannot properly stop air leakage, and sealing behind insulation would be inaccessible or ineffective once insulation is in place.
Air sealing of the interior air barrier (e.g., at top plates, rim joists, and penetrations) must be completed before drywall is hung, as drywall encloses these areas and makes them inaccessible.
The ground must be excavated and leveled to create a proper foundation bed before ICFs can be placed, as ICF walls require a stable, prepared base.
A concrete foundation footing or slab must be poured and fully cured before ICF blocks can be stacked on top, as the ICFs need a solid, level structural base to bear the load.
Plumbing, electrical conduit, and other underground utilities must be laid beneath the foundation before ICF walls are erected, as access would be impossible after the walls and slab are in place.
ICF blocks must be fully assembled, braced, and aligned before concrete is poured into the forms, as the ICFs serve as the permanent formwork that shapes and insulates the concrete wall.
After the ICF walls are erected and the concrete core is cured, openings for windows, doors, and utility chases can be cut or framed, as attempting this before ICF placement would be impossible.

The thermal break component typically sits between the foundation/substructure and the superstructure to prevent thermal bridging; thus, the foundation must be completed before installing the thermal break.
Thermal breaks are placed between the foundation and the superstructure to interrupt heat flow; the superstructure cannot be built on top until the thermal break is installed.
If the thermal break is part of a perimeter insulation system, the floor slab is poured after the thermal break material is positioned to ensure continuous insulation.
It is good practice to complete thermal bridging details at transitions before cladding, but it is not a strict prerequisite if other detailing is used.
Interior finishes can proceed after thermal breaks are in place to avoid rework, but sequencing can vary depending on construction methods.
Wall framing must be in place to create the cavities that will receive blown-in insulation.
Electrical wiring must be run through wall cavities before they are filled with insulation, as adding wiring after insulation is extremely difficult and would disturb the insulation.
Plumbing pipes must be installed within walls before insulation is blown in, since access to wall cavities becomes blocked once filled.
HVAC ducts must be installed in cavities before they are filled with insulation to ensure proper routing and access.
A vapor barrier (if required by design) must be installed on the warm side of the wall before insulation is blown in to prevent moisture accumulation.
Blown-in insulation must be completed before drywall is installed, as drywall encloses the wall cavities and permanently seals in the insulation.
All interior finishes (paint, trim, etc.) occur after drywall, which itself requires completed insulation in the walls.

successor: Final electrical and lighting fixture installation
rationale: Electrical boxes and fixtures are typically installed after insulation is complete to ensure they are not buried or obstructed by loose-fill insulation.
The ground must be excavated and shaped to the required profiles before any drainage or protection layers can be installed on the prepared surface.
A leveled and stable subgrade or blinding concrete layer is required as a base to install the drainage composite and protection board.

The drainage composite/protection board serves as a protective layer; the waterproofing membrane is typically placed on top of or after the protection board to ensure the membrane is not damaged by backfill or construction activities.
The drainage composite and protection board must be fully installed to protect the waterproofing and structure before backfill material is placed against the wall.

Surface landscaping and final grading can commence after the below-grade drainage system and protection board are in place, though this is a logistical preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
Flashing is installed on top of the roof deck; the deck must be in place to provide a substrate for the flashing.

predecessor: Underlayment (Roof Felt / Ice & Water Shield) Installation
rationale: Underlayment is typically applied before flashing to provide a water-resistant barrier; flashing is then integrated over or into the underlayment.

successor: Roof Shingles / Tiles / Final Roofing Material Installation
rationale: Flashing is installed around penetrations and edges before the final roofing material is placed, as shingles/tiles overlap the flashing for proper water shedding.
Counter-flashing is often built into or behind wall cladding to create a weather-tight seal; cladding must follow to cover and secure the flashing.

successor: Roof Penetration Seal / Pipe Boot Installation
rationale: While flashings around penetrations are often installed before pipe boots, some sealants or boots can be applied after; however, it is strongly preferred to flash first so the boot covers the flashing top.
The substrate must be clean, dry, and free of debris to ensure proper adhesion of the torch-on bitumen membrane.
A primer is typically required to be applied and cured on the substrate before torching on the bitumen membrane to enhance adhesion.
The structural roof deck or substrate (e.g., plywood, concrete, or insulation boards) must be fully installed and secured before any waterproofing membrane can be applied.
Immediately after torching, the bitumen membrane must be rolled and embedded into the molten bitumen to ensure a fully bonded, void-free layer.

A reflective or protective top coating is often applied after the torch-on membrane has cooled to improve UV resistance and durability, though it is a design preference rather than a structural requirement.
A smooth, clean, and dry substrate is essential for proper membrane adhesion and to prevent punctures or uneven application. Membrane cannot be laid directly on unprepared ground.
Primer must be applied to the prepared substrate to improve bonding of the membrane. The primer needs to cure before membrane installation.

In some waterproofing systems (e.g., green roofs, inverted roofs), a drainage layer may be placed above the membrane. However, in conventional systems, the membrane goes first; this ordering depends on system design.

A protection layer (e.g., geotextile, sand, or cement screed) must be placed immediately over the installed membrane to shield it from UV degradation, mechanical damage during subsequent trades, and foot traffic.

successor: Waterproofing Integrity Testing (Flood Test / Electronic Leak Detection)
rationale: After membrane installation but before covering with subsequent layers, the waterproofing must be tested for leaks and defects to ensure the integrity of the system.
For below-grade waterproofing, backfilling can only proceed after the membrane is fully installed, inspected, and protected to avoid damaging the waterproofing layer.
Any final wearing surface (e.g., tiles, pavers, asphalt, or topping slab) must be laid after the membrane and its protection layer are in place to avoid compromising waterproofing.
The membrane must be installed and placed in position before lap joints can be formed and seamed together.
Membrane panels must be cut and trimmed to the correct dimensions and overlap alignment before the lap joints can be seamed.
The substrate or underlying surface must be clean, dry, and properly prepared before membrane placement and seaming to ensure adhesion and joint integrity.
After seams are formed, they must be inspected and tested (e.g., peel test, air pressure test) to verify watertightness and structural integrity before subsequent work.
Edge terminations and flashings at perimeters, penetrations, and details are installed after the main membrane field seams are completed to cover and seal all transitions.
The main membrane body must be laid and in place before the edges can be terminated and detailed, as edge detailing seals the margins of the installed membrane.
A clean, properly prepared substrate is required before any membrane work, including edge detailing, to ensure proper adhesion and sealing at the terminations.
Edge detailing creates the termination points that receive flashings and counter flashings, which must be installed after the membrane edges are secured and sealed.
Edge detailing completes the membrane enclosure; water testing and inspection should be performed after detailing is finished to verify the integrity of the terminations.

While protective cover or ballast is typically installed after edge detailing to avoid damaging the finished edges, it is possible to place ballast concurrently in some systems, making this a soft preference for sequencing.
The brick wall requires a solid, level foundation to bear its load; without a cured foundation, the wall would lack structural support and could settle unevenly or collapse.
Concrete must reach sufficient strength (typically 7+ days of curing) before the weight of brickwork can be applied; premature loading can crack or fail the foundation.
Waterproofing membranes are applied to the completed brick surface; the wall must be fully assembled and stable before weatherproofing can be installed effectively.
Roof trusses typically bear on top of the wall structure; the load-bearing brick walls must be complete to support the roof framing.
While electrical conduit can be chased into brickwork later, it is far more efficient and cleaner to run wiring and install boxes after the wall is built, avoiding excessive drilling or cutting.
Brick veneer requires a structural backing (typically wood or steel framing with exterior sheathing) to support its weight and provide a nailing surface for ties.
A weather-resistant barrier (WRB) must be installed behind brick veneer to prevent moisture intrusion into the wall assembly.
Brick veneer requires a properly cured foundation or concrete ledge (often a brick shelf on the foundation wall) to support the dead load of the masonry.
Flashing and weep screeds at the base of the brick veneer must be integrated during and after the first course of brick to direct moisture outward.

successor: Window/Door Installation (if brick opening trim is required)
rationale: In some sequences, windows/doors are installed after brick veneer to allow proper flashing integration and brick trim detailing, though often windows are installed before brick and trimmed afterward.
A stable foundation is required to support the load of the brick arch structure.
The brick arch must be built upon or between already-erected supporting walls that carry its lateral thrust.
The arch must be completed before roof structures that bear on or are supported by the arch can be installed.
While interior finishing above the arch can technically begin after the arch is set, it is a soft preference because the arch completion provides a stable reference point for finishing work.
A stable foundation must be excavated and prepared to support the weight of the brick pillar/pier before masonry work can begin.
Concrete foundations must be poured and cured to provide a solid load-bearing base for the brick pillar/pier structure.
Beams and joists require completed brick pillars/piers as vertical support elements before they can be placed and connected.
Lintels spanning between brick pillars/piers rely on the pillars being in place to provide bearing support at each end.
While roof framing can proceed once pillars are complete to transfer loads, temporary shoring could allow some roof work; however, full load transfer typically requires completed pillars.
The subgrade must be properly graded and compacted to provide a stable, uniform base before any brick paving can be laid to prevent differential settlement and uneven surfaces.
A granular base course (e.g., crushed stone or gravel) must be placed and compacted over the subgrade to provide drainage support and a stable platform for the brick floor.
A leveling layer of sand (or mortar bed) must be spread and screeded to the correct thickness and grade immediately before bricks are laid to ensure proper alignment, level, and support.
After bricks are laid, joints must be filled with sand or fine aggregate and compacted (using a plate compactor) to lock the bricks in place and provide lateral stability.

Applying a surface sealant or curing compound is typically done after all bricks are laid and joints are filled; this is a soft preference based on design specifications for protection and durability.
Brick cavity walls require a solid foundation to bear their weight and provide stability; without a completed foundation, the wall cannot be properly supported.
A damp proof course must be laid on the foundation before brickwork begins to prevent rising damp from migrating up the wall structure.
While often done concurrently, completing the ground slab before cavity wall construction helps with staging and bracing support, though it is not always physically mandatory.
The load-bearing cavity walls must be fully constructed and cured to support roof trusses or rafters, which rest directly on the wall plates.
Cavity insulation is installed after the walls are built and cleaned out; it is blown or placed into the cavity space, which requires the full wall height to be in place.
A stable foundation is required to support the structural load of the brick corbelling.
Corbelling involves projecting bricks outward from a completed wall surface, so the base wall must be fully constructed and cured first.
Properly mixed mortar is needed to bond the corbelled bricks together and to the existing wall.
After corbelling bricks are placed, the mortar must cure and gain strength before further loads are applied.

successor: Structural Load Application (e.g., roof or upper floor support)
rationale: The corbelled brick projection must be fully completed and set before it can safely carry any additional structural loads from above.

Brick coping is typically installed as a cap or top covering on masonry walls, parapets, or freestanding walls. The wall structure must be fully constructed and cured before the coping is applied to provide structural support and a stable base.

Waterproofing or a vapor barrier is often applied to the top of the wall before installing brick coping to prevent moisture penetration into the wall assembly. Installing coping before waterproofing would trap moisture and lead to deterioration.

After brick coping units are set in place, the mortar joints must be tooled, pointed, and allowed to cure properly to achieve full strength and weather resistance before any further work can proceed on adjacent finishes.

Cap flashing or counterflashing is often installed over or integrated with brick coping to shed water away from the wall. This must be done after the coping is set so the flashing can be properly fitted and secured to the coping's top or reglet.

While not a strict physical dependency, it is more efficient and safer to complete brick coping installation from scaffolding before dismantling it, avoiding the need to re-erect scaffolding for a small finishing task.
Brickwork requires a solid, level foundation or floor slab to build upon; without a properly prepared base, the brickwork would lack structural support and alignment.
A damp proof course must be laid on the foundation before brickwork begins to prevent moisture rising through the walls; this is a critical moisture control layer.
The foundation/slab concrete must be sufficiently cured to gain strength before bearing the load of brickwork walls.
Lintels are placed over door and window openings as brickwork reaches those heights; the brickwork must be built up to the required level first.
Load-bearing brickwork walls must be completed to their full height to provide support for roof trusses, rafters, and roofing materials.
Brick lintels are installed within masonry walls to span openings; the wall must be built up to the lintel height before the lintel can be placed and supported.
For cast-in-situ reinforced brick lintels, temporary formwork must be erected to support the wet concrete and brickwork until the lintel gains sufficient strength.
Reinforcing bars (rebar) must be positioned and tied within the lintel formwork before concrete or brick-laying can proceed to provide tensile strength.
The lintel creates the structural opening; door or window frames are installed within the rough opening after the lintel is cured and load-bearing.
Masonry above the opening (such as continued walling or arches) rests on the lintel, so the lintel must be fully set and cured before any load is applied from above.
Brick joint pointing involves finishing the mortar joints between bricks, which can only be done after the bricks have been laid and the main mortar has been placed.
The pointing mortar must be prepared before it can be applied to the joints.
After pointing is applied, the mortar must be allowed to cure and harden before any subsequent work that could disturb it.
Pointing completes the brickwork surface; plastering or wall finishing should follow pointing to avoid damaging the finished joints.
Damp proof course installation is often done at a certain level in brickwork; while pointing should generally precede final waterproofing details, it is not always a strict physical constraint.
Bricks must be fully installed and mortar must be set before any cleaning or chemical washing can begin.
Mortar joints need adequate curing time to harden sufficiently to withstand the pressure and chemicals used during brick cleaning without being damaged.
Sealants and waterproofing coatings require a clean, residue-free brick surface to adhere properly; cleaning must be done before any sealing application.
Inspections are preferably done after cleaning to assess the final appearance and condition of the brickwork without dirt or efflorescence obscuring the view.
Scaffolding provides safe access for workers to reach and clean upper brick surfaces; must be in place before cleaning activities can commence at height.
The brick wall must first be constructed (laid) before damp-proofing can be applied, as the damp-proof course (DPC) is installed within or onto the completed brickwork structure.
Foundations must be finished and cured to provide a stable base before the damp-proof course is installed at the required level above ground.
The mortar in the brick wall must have achieved sufficient initial set and strength to support the installation of the damp-proof membrane or course without displacement.
Backfilling must occur after damp-proofing is installed and protected, to avoid damaging the DPC and to ensure the damp-proof membrane forms a continuous barrier against ground moisture.
Internal plastering and rendering should follow damp-proofing to prevent moisture ingress from being trapped behind finishes and to allow the DPC to function as designed.

successor: Brick Tying and Wall Starter Installation
rationale: The foundation must be poured and fully cured to provide a stable, load-bearing base for brick walls and wall starters. Without a cured foundation, the brickwork cannot be properly anchored and would lack structural support.

successor: Brick Tying and Wall Starter Installation
rationale: The concrete slab must be in place and cured before wall starters (metal tracks or channels) can be embedded or fastened to it. The slab provides the substrate onto which wall starters are anchored.

successor: Brick Tying and Wall Starter Installation
rationale: Excavation and grading must be completed to establish proper elevations and drainage before any foundation or slab work, which in turn supports brick tying and wall starter installation.

predecessor: Brick Tying and Wall Starter Installation
rationale: Wall starters serve as the bottom anchoring point for brick courses. Brick laying must begin after wall starters are installed because the starter tracks guide and support the first row of bricks.

predecessor: Brick Tying and Wall Starter Installation
rationale: Wall ties and starters must be in place before reinforcement (e.g., rebar or ladder wire) can be integrated into the brick wall assembly, as the ties anchor the reinforcement to the structure.
Brickwork must be fully laid and constructed before curing can begin, as curing is the process of maintaining moisture and protecting freshly laid brickwork to achieve proper strength development.
