Mortar must be mixed and applied during brick laying; curing can only start once the mortar joints are finished and initial setting has commenced.
Plastering or rendering on brickwork surfaces should only commence after the brickwork has been properly cured and has gained sufficient strength, otherwise cracking and adhesion failure may occur.
Final pointing or joint tooling work on brickwork is typically done after initial curing to ensure the mortar has hardened enough to hold the finish without being disturbed.
Waterproofing treatments are applied after the brickwork is cured and stable, as applying them before curing is complete can trap moisture and prevent proper hydration of the mortar.

The brick masonry must be laid up to the point where the expansion joint is required before the joint can be installed. Typically, the first few courses of brickwork are built, then the expansion joint material (e.g., compressible filler, sealant) is placed at the designated locations before continuing with the remaining brick courses.

Once the expansion joint material (backer rod, sealant, or compressible filler) is placed in the joint gap, the remaining brick courses above can be laid. The joint installation must be complete to ensure the brickwork above does not bridge the joint and compromise its ability to accommodate thermal and moisture movement.

The structural frame or supporting elements (e.g., concrete slab, steel beams) that the brickwork bears upon must be in place and cured/set before expansion joints are installed in the brick veneer or masonry, as the brickwork depends on the substructure for alignment and load transfer.

After the expansion joint filler and backer rod are installed, a weatherproof sealant (e.g., silicone or polyurethane) is typically applied over the joint to prevent water ingress. This sealant application cannot be done before the joint is formed.

The foundation or subgrade upon which the brickwork rests must be properly prepared, leveled, and cured. Expansion joints in brickwork are often aligned with structural expansion joints in the foundation; thus the foundation must be ready prior to brickwork and its joints.
The CMU wall construction requires a stable, level foundation and footings to bear the load and provide a solid base for block laying.
Vertical reinforcement dowels from the foundation must be in place before starting CMU layout so blocks can be threaded over the rebar for structural continuity.
Proper site grading and drainage should be established before wall construction to prevent water accumulation around the base during and after construction.
Grouting and placing horizontal reinforcement in the CMU cores can only occur after the blocks are laid and aligned to the required height.
Waterproofing coatings or membranes are applied to the completed CMU wall surface and cannot be done until the masonry is fully erected and cured.
Solid CMU walls require a stable, level foundation to bear the load and prevent settlement cracks.
The ground must be properly excavated and graded to the correct elevations before any masonry work begins.
Underground plumbing, electrical conduit, and drainage lines must be installed and inspected before the slab or CMU stem walls are placed.
The structural CMU wall must be fully erected and cured before any exterior veneer or cladding can be applied to it.
CMU load-bearing walls must be complete to support roof trusses, beams, or rafters.
Core-filling/grouting of CMU cells and subsequent inspection must occur after the CMU is laid but before concealing finishes.
In-wall conduit, boxes, and piping within CMU cores or chases can only be placed after the wall is erected.
Lightweight CMU walls require a solid, level foundation or slab to bear on, as the masonry units cannot be placed on prepared earth or unstable surfaces.
Underground utilities and conduits that will run beneath or through the CMU walls must be installed prior to laying block to avoid cutting or coring cured masonry.
Vertical and horizontal reinforcing dowels must be set and anchored in the foundation before CMU placement begins so that the reinforcement can be lapped and grouted within the block cores.
Grouting (where required) must wait until the CMU walls are laid and cured sufficiently to contain the fluid grout; the block itself forms the formwork for the grout.
Bond beams and lintels are installed after the CMU is laid to the required height, as these elements sit atop or within the block courses to provide lateral and door/window header support.
Split-Face CMU walls require a level, cured concrete foundation or slab to bear upon, providing a stable base and proper load distribution.
Underground or under-slab rough-in utilities must be placed before CMU walls are erected, as access below the slab is impossible once walls and slab are complete.
Proper grading and drainage must be established before wall construction to ensure water is directed away from foundation and wall bases.
After CMU placement, mortar joints must cure and waterproofing (or damp-proofing) must be applied to the exterior face before backfilling to prevent moisture ingress.

While some conduits can be chased or core-drilled later, it is far more efficient to embed conduit and boxes in the CMU cores or between wythes during construction; this is a strong practice preference rather than an absolute physical constraint.
Load-bearing CMU walls must be fully cured and grouted (if reinforced) to support roof or upper floor framing loads.
Finishing work is sequential after CMU is complete, but some finish work may proceed in parallel in other areas; this is a logical sequencing preference for clean transitions.

The concrete masonry units must be manufactured, cured, and fully hardened before they can be subjected to grinding and polishing operations. Polishing green (uncured) concrete will not achieve the desired finish and can damage the block.

The CMU blocks must first be laid and installed as part of the wall assembly before their face can be ground and polished in place. Grinding/polishing is a finishing operation applied to the already-installed wall surface.
The mortar joints between CMU blocks must be sufficiently cured to prevent displacement or damage when grinding and polishing equipment vibrates the wall surface.
After grinding and polishing, the surface must be cleaned of all slurry and dust, and a protective sealer or finish should be applied to preserve the polished appearance and prevent staining.
The ground and polished finish must be completed before a final quality inspection can verify gloss level, uniformity, and absence of surface defects.

Structural steel framing and metal decking provide the primary structural support and floor/roof diaphragm. Glazed/faced CMU walls are typically non-structural infill or veneer that require the structural frame to be in place to bear upon or tie into.
Concealed MEP services that run within or behind CMU walls must be roughed-in before the CMU is installed, as the masonry would cover and block access to these systems.
Glazed/faced CMU walls require a level concrete bearing surface (slab on grade, footing, or structural slab) to be cast and cured before masonry can be laid on top.

After CMU blocks are laid, vertical and horizontal reinforcing bars must be placed and grout pumped into the cores before the wall is complete; this grouting operation is a direct follow-on to the block installation.

successor: Final MEP trim-out and device installation
rationale: After CMU walls are fully installed and cured, wall-mounted electrical devices, plumbing fixtures, and trim-out work can be accurately positioned and secured to the finished masonry surface.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the proper elevation and slope before any wall construction can begin, as the wall footing requires a prepared, stable subgrade.
Subdrainage systems behind the retaining wall must be placed before wall construction to ensure proper water management and prevent hydrostatic pressure buildup.
Backfill material behind the completed CMU wall can only be placed and compacted after the wall is built and the mortar/core has achieved sufficient strength to resist lateral earth pressure.
Waterproofing coatings are applied to the exterior face of the completed CMU wall after it is fully erected, as the coating requires a clean, cured surface.
Coping or cap stones are installed as the final top course element only after all CMU courses below are completed and the wall is fully stable.
AAC blocks require a properly prepared and leveled foundation or structural frame to bear upon, as they cannot be installed on uneven or unprepared ground.
In framed structures, the load-bearing frame (steel or RC columns and beams) must be erected first so that AAC blocks can be infilled between the structural members as non-load-bearing partitions.
AAC blocks are highly absorbent and susceptible to moisture damage; a damp-proof course must be applied at plinth level before AAC block laying to prevent capillary rise of moisture.
Plaster and surface finishes cannot be applied until AAC block walls are fully erected, cured, and stable to provide a proper substrate for adhesion.
Chasing/grooving for electrical conduits and plumbing pipes in AAC walls must be done after the blocks are laid and the mortar has set, as the conduits are embedded into the completed wall surface.

CMU bond beam blocks are installed as part of the CMU wall system at the top of walls or at intermediate levels; the regular CMU wall courses must be laid before the bond beam block course can be placed.
Reinforcing steel bars must be placed in the bond beam cavity before the bond beam blocks are laid, as the blocks encase the rebar.
After bond beam blocks are installed, the continuous cavity must be filled with grout to create a reinforced horizontal structural element.
Inspection of the reinforcement and block placement must occur after bond beam blocks are laid, typically before grouting.

successor: Top Plate or Roof Framing Installation
rationale: The bond beam provides a level, reinforced bearing surface at the top of CMU walls; roof or floor framing above rests on the completed bond beam.
The CMU lintel block sits on top of the CMU wall; the wall must be built first to provide support for the lintel block.
The lintel block must be in place before reinforcement (rebar) can be placed within the block's channel to form the structural lintel beam.
The lintel block must be installed and reinforced before grout can be poured into the block cores to create a solid structural lintel.
CMU courses above the lintel (e.g., at window or door openings) can only be laid after the lintel block is in place to span the opening and support the masonry above.
CMU corner blocks must be laid on top of a cured concrete foundation or slab to provide a stable, level base for masonry walls.
The exact location of walls and corners must be marked on the slab before placing the first corner block to ensure correct alignment and dimensions.
A damp-proof course must be installed on the foundation before masonry work begins to prevent moisture wicking into the CMU walls.
Corner blocks establish the alignment and plumbness for the entire wall; all subsequent CMU courses are laid by stringing lines from the corner blocks.
Vertical reinforcement and grout are placed after corner blocks and initial wall courses are laid, as the blocks form the permanent formwork for the reinforced core.

Horizontal joint reinforcement is embedded within the mortar joints of masonry walls, so the masonry wall construction must be in progress (or completed) to provide the substrate for reinforcement installation.
A mortar bed must be laid first so that the horizontal joint reinforcement can be placed within the fresh mortar before the next course of masonry units is laid.
After placing the horizontal joint reinforcement, the next layer of mortar must be applied over it to embed the reinforcement and continue the masonry wall construction.
The reinforcement must be placed in the mortar joint before the next course of masonry units (bricks/blocks) is laid on top, as the reinforcement is intended to be embedded between courses.
CMU block walls require a stable, level foundation or slab to bear upon; the foundation must be poured and cured before any masonry units can be laid.
The positions of block walls must be marked on the foundation or slab to guide the first course of CMU placement.

Reinforcing bars are placed as the CMU wall is built up; however, vertical reinforcement in cores and horizontal joint reinforcement are installed concurrently or after blocks are laid to the appropriate height.
Grout is pumped into hollow cores only after the CMU blocks have been laid and the reinforcement is in place; the blocks serve as the formwork for the grout.
Bond beams are constructed as part of the CMU wall assembly at specified courses; the stretcher blocks must be laid up to the bond beam elevation before the bond beam can be formed and reinforced.

Horizontal rebar must be placed and tied before vertical rebar can be installed in CMU walls, as the vertical bars typically thread through the horizontal reinforcement cage and must be placed after horizontal bars are in position.
CMU blocks must be laid first, as vertical rebar is placed into the hollow cores of the CMU blocks after the masonry is built up to a certain height.
Vertical rebar must be installed in the CMU cores before grout is pumped into the cells to encase and bond the rebar to the masonry.
Vertical rebar placement must be completed and inspected before grouting operations begin, as per code requirements for reinforcement in masonry.

successor: CMU Control Joint / Expansion Joint Material
rationale: Control joints in CMU walls must be installed as the wall is being constructed, after the CMU units are laid but before the wall is fully completed, to accommodate movement and prevent cracking.

predecessor: CMU Control Joint / Expansion Joint Material
rationale: Sealant must be applied over the control joint material after it is placed to complete the weatherproofing and accommodate movement.

predecessor: CMU Control Joint / Expansion Joint Material
rationale: While some reinforcement may be continuous, control joint installation typically interrupts reinforcement; grouting and reinforcement should be coordinated around control joints, but this is often a design preference rather than a strict physical constraint.

CMU block walls must be laid at least to the first course or base level before wall ties or anchors can be installed, as the ties connect the CMU wall to adjacent structural elements (e.g., brick veneer, backup walls).

Wall ties/anchors are often embedded into the CMU wall during or immediately after block placement, and reinforcement (rebar) must be placed after ties are positioned to ensure proper anchorage and embedment within the grout cells.
Grouting must occur after ties/anchors are installed because the ties need to be set in place and secured before grout is poured into the CMU cells to lock them in position.

Wall ties for cavity walls or anchored veneers must be installed in the CMU backup wall before the brick veneer is laid, as the ties extend from the CMU into the brick wythe to structurally connect the two.
Wall anchors must be fully embedded and cured before any exterior cladding or finish is applied to ensure a secure connection and load transfer path.

The CMU (concrete masonry unit) walls must be installed before washout access and cleanout can occur, as the cleanout process removes debris and excess mortar from the wall cavities after the CMU walls are in place.

successor: Concrete Fill / Grouting of CMU Cells
rationale: Washout access and cleanout of CMU walls must be completed before concrete fill or grouting of the CMU cells, because cleanout holes allow debris removal from the bottom of cells and must be sealed/patched after cleaning but prior to pouring grout or concrete fill.
Cleanout must be completed prior to inspection to ensure the wall cavities are clear of debris and ready for grouting, allowing inspectors to verify proper conditions.

While reinforcement is typically placed before cleanout, cleanout access may still allow some adjustment; however, best practice is to place reinforcement before final cleanout to avoid disturbing the rebar.
After cleanout is performed, the cleanout access holes in the CMU walls must be sealed or patched with masonry materials to restore the wall integrity before any subsequent finishing work.
The foundation or slab must be fully cured and ready before any masonry work can begin, as CMU walls are built directly on top of the foundation.
Rough grading must be completed to provide a stable and level working surface for masonry installation.
All underground plumbing, electrical conduits, and other utilities must be installed and inspected before the slab is poured and masonry walls are erected.
Load-bearing masonry walls must be completed and achieve sufficient strength before roof framing can be placed on top of them.
Masonry walls must be in place before wall rough-ins can be performed, as electrical, plumbing, and mechanical rough-ins require access to the completed wall cavities.
CMU blocks must be erected and stacked in place before any grouting or core-filling can occur, as the grout fills the hollow cores of the already-placed masonry units.
Vertical and horizontal reinforcement bars must be positioned within the CMU block cores before grouting, so that the grout encases the rebar, creating structural continuity.
After grouting, the grout must be allowed to cure and gain sufficient strength before any further loading or subsequent construction activities proceed.
While inspections can technically occur after grouting is complete, they are a soft preference to verify grout integrity and compliance before covering or proceeding with finishes.

Waterproofing is often applied after grouting is finished and the wall is fully assembled, but in some sequences it can overlap; however, for quality and continuity, grouting is typically completed first.
The wall layout and marking must be completed first to define the exact locations and alignments where the rebar will be placed within the CMU walls.
The foundation or slab must be fully cured and ready to accept CMU walls before any rebar placement and tying can begin on top of it.
Rebar materials must be delivered to site and inspected for compliance before they can be placed and tied within the CMU walls.
Rebar must be placed and tied in position before CMU blocks can be laid around the reinforcement, as the rebar is embedded within the hollow cores of the blocks.
Rebar placement and tying must be completed and approved by inspection before the masonry work proceeds above, to ensure reinforcement meets specifications.
Control joints can only be cut after the CMU wall has been built and mortar has cured sufficiently to allow cutting without damaging the wall.
Mortar must be adequately cured to provide sufficient strength for the block to be cut without dislodging units or causing cracks.
Sealant or caulking for control joints can only be applied after the joints have been cut/routed to create the proper gap and profile.
Cutting control joints generates dust and debris that must be cleaned from the wall surface before finishing or coating work begins.
Control joint installation should be completed before final wall inspection so that joint placement and spacing can be verified per specifications.
The scaffolding structure must be erected and stable before any material hoisting can occur on it, as hoisting requires the scaffold to be in place to support loads.
CMU blocks and other materials must be delivered and staged at the site before they can be hoisted onto the scaffolding for use.
CMU blocks must be hoisted to the working level on the scaffolding before masons can begin laying the blocks and constructing the walls.
Hoisting operations place dynamic and static loads on the scaffold; after hoisting is complete, the scaffold must be inspected to verify it remains safe for continued work.
All material hoisting and masonry work must be complete before scaffolding can be dismantled, as the scaffold is needed to support ongoing work at height.
CMU walls must be fully erected, cured, and stable before any waterproofing or dampproofing coating can be applied to their surface.
The CMU surface must be cleaned of dirt, dust, mortar splatter, and laitance, and any surface defects repaired to ensure proper adhesion of waterproofing/dampproofing materials.
Waterproofing/dampproofing must be fully applied, cured, and inspected before backfill operations begin, to protect the waterproofing membrane from damage and ensure it is fully functional.

successor: Dampproofing Membrane Protection Board / Rigid Insulation Installation
rationale: Protection boards or rigid insulation are installed directly over the cured waterproofing membrane to shield it from damage during backfilling, requiring the waterproofing to be completed first.

Weep holes at the base of the wall are often required to be installed after or coordinated with dampproofing to ensure proper drainage above the waterproofing level, though this may be a design preference rather than physical impossibility.
The wall layout must be marked and positioned before anchoring can begin, as anchoring requires the exact intersection points to be identified and prepared.
The foundation or slab must be cured and ready to receive anchor dowels or reinforcing bars before the intersecting wall anchoring can be installed.
Anchoring of intersecting walls must be completed before grouting and reinforcement placement, as the anchor bars or ties need to be embedded within the grouted cores.
Intersecting wall anchors must be installed at the proper course before continuing with upper courses, as the anchors tie the intersecting walls together at specified lift heights.
CMU walls require a level, cured concrete foundation or slab to bear upon and to provide a stable base for load distribution and anchorage.
Utilities that run beneath the slab must be installed and inspected before the slab is poured and before CMU walls are erected, as access becomes impossible afterward.
Once CMU walls are laid, vertical chases and embedded conduits/pipe sleeves must be installed within the wall cavities before they are closed up.
Load-bearing CMU walls must be fully cured to support the steel beams or floor joists that bear on or are anchored to the masonry.
Waterproofing membranes and coatings are applied to the exterior face of CMU walls after the mortar has cured, to protect the interior from moisture intrusion.
The rebar cage sits on or within the foundation/footing and requires a stable base to be placed upon.
Formwork must be erected before rebar placement, as the rebar cage is positioned inside the formwork to ensure proper cover and geometry.
Concrete must be poured around the rebar cage while the cage is in position; the cage provides reinforcement and cannot be placed after concrete hardens.
Concrete must be placed over the rebar cage and allowed to cure before formwork can be safely removed; stripping too early would compromise structural integrity.
Individual rebar pieces must be cut, bent, and shaped before they can be assembled and tied into the cage structure.
Rebar must be placed and positioned in the forms before splices can be made between adjacent bars.
Rebar must be cut to length and bent to required shapes before the ends can be lapped or mechanically coupled.
All rebar splices must be completed and inspected before concrete is placed to ensure proper reinforcement continuity.
Spliced connections should be inspected before final tie-off and concrete pour to verify splice integrity.
Formwork is typically erected before rebar placement and splicing, though some splicing can occur on the ground prior to placement.
Rebar must be cut and bent to the required shapes and sizes before it can be placed and fixed in position.
Formwork provides the mold and support structure into which rebar is placed; rebar cannot be positioned without the formwork in place.
This ordering is incorrect as stated; actually Rebar Placing & Fixing must precede Concrete Pouring.
Rebar must be fully placed, tied, and fixed into position before concrete is poured to embed the reinforcement within the concrete element.

Formwork cannot be stripped until after concrete is poured and cured; however, since rebar placement precedes concrete pouring, rebar fixing must be complete before formwork stripping indirectly via concrete placement.
If post-tensioning tendons are used, rebar must be placed first before post-tensioning ducts and tendons are installed and stressed.
Formwork must be in place to provide the mold and support structure before placing reinforcement mesh within the slab or wall.
Welded wire fabric must be positioned and tied in place before concrete is poured so that the mesh becomes embedded within the concrete for tensile reinforcement.
Typically mesh is placed after main rebar if they overlap, but if mesh is used as primary reinforcement it can be placed first; this is a soft preference based on design sequence.
The ground or base must be properly compacted and leveled before placing mesh for slabs-on-grade to ensure uniform support.
After mesh placement, an inspection of laps, cover, and tie spacing must be completed before concrete pour to verify structural compliance.
Rebar must be in place before ties can be wrapped around or tied to the rebar cage to secure the reinforcement.
Ties must be completed and inspected before formwork is placed around the rebar cage, as the formwork would block access to install ties.
Ties must be fully installed to secure the rebar cage before concrete is poured; pouring prematurely would lack proper reinforcement confinement.
In some methods, forms are partially erected first as a guide, but typically ties are done before enclosing formwork; this is a soft preference depending on the construction approach.
Stirrups are placed around the main longitudinal reinforcement bars to provide shear resistance. Main bars must be in position first so that stirrups can be correctly positioned and tied around them.
Formwork provides the mold and support structure. Stirrups are placed inside the formwork after the bottom form is in place, allowing proper positioning within the member cross-section.
In beams, stirrups must be installed before top reinforcement bars can be placed, as the top bars sit within the stirrup cages.
All reinforcement including stirrups must be fully placed, tied, and inspected before concrete is poured to encase the reinforcement.
Cover blocks are placed after stirrups are in position to maintain proper concrete cover between the stirrups and the formwork.
Formwork provides the mold and containment for concrete; spiral reinforcement ties must be placed inside the formwork before concrete is poured.
The main longitudinal reinforcing bars must be erected first, as spiral ties are wrapped around and tied to these vertical bars.
Spiral ties must be fully in place, tied, and positioned before concrete is poured so they become embedded and provide confinement to the core.
Concrete pouring must occur before curing; since spiral reinforcement is a prerequisite to pouring, it is also a prerequisite to the curing phase.
After all reinforcement (including spiral ties) is installed, an inspection must be performed to verify correct spacing, diameter, cover, and tying before concrete is placed.
Dowels must be embedded into freshly poured concrete while it is still wet/plastic to ensure proper bonding and anchorage between concrete pours.
Formwork defines the edge of the concrete pour into which dowels will be placed, and provides a mold to hold the concrete in place while dowels are inserted.
After dowels are placed and the concrete is poured, the concrete must cure undisturbed to develop the strength needed to anchor the dowels.
Dowels protruding from the first pour act as load-transfer devices; the adjacent slab or element is poured after the dowels are in place so that the dowels bond with both concrete sections.
After dowels are installed and both adjacent concrete sections are poured and cured, joints around dowels are sealed to prevent debris ingress and allow controlled movement.
Rebar materials must be procured and delivered to the site before on-site bending and cutting can begin, as the raw rebar stock is required for the bending and cutting operations.
Delivered rebar must be properly stored and inventoried before being retrieved for bending and cutting to ensure organized material handling and traceability.
Bent and cut rebar pieces must be prepared before they can be assembled and tied into rebar cages or mats.
Individual bent and cut rebar pieces or pre-assembled cages are needed before rebar can be placed into formwork and fixed in position.
Bending and cutting must be completed before the bent/cut rebar can be inspected for compliance with bending schedules, dimensional tolerances, and quality standards.

Post-installed rebar anchoring involves drilling into and bonding rebar into hardened concrete. The concrete must be placed, set, and cured to sufficient strength to support the mechanical and chemical anchorage without cracking or failing.

Formwork defines the geometry of the concrete element into which rebar will be post-installed. The formwork must be in place before concrete placement, which must then be cured before post-installed anchoring can occur.

For post-installed dowels into grade beams or foundations, the subgrade must be prepared and any cast-in reinforcement placed prior to concrete pour, which then hardens to receive the post-installed anchors.

successor: Vertical Reinforcement Tying and Formwork for Next Lift
rationale: Post-installed rebar anchors serve as starter bars for the next concrete lift. Once the anchors are installed and the adhesive has cured, vertical reinforcement can be tied to them and formwork set for the subsequent pour.

The post-installed rebar provides the connection between existing hardened concrete and new concrete. The new concrete must be placed after the rebar anchors are fully installed and the bonding adhesive has cured to design strength.
Rebar cage fabrication must be completed before mechanical connectors are installed because the couplers are used to join reinforcing bars, requiring the rebar to already be in place.
Formwork provides the mold and support structure; mechanical couplers for reinforcement are placed within or against the formwork before concrete is poured.
Mechanical couplers must be fully installed and secured within the rebar system before concrete is poured, as they will be embedded in the concrete and cannot be accessed afterward.
If post-tensioning is used, the mechanical couplers joining the reinforcement must be in place before tensioning forces are applied to the tendons.
After mechanical couplers are installed, the full reinforcement assembly including couplers must be inspected for proper alignment, torque, and compliance before proceeding to concrete placement.
Cover blocks (spacers) are placed onto the rebar framework to maintain the correct concrete cover. Therefore, the rebar must already be installed before spacers can be attached or positioned.

Cover blocks ensure that the rebar is held at the correct distance from the formwork during concrete pouring. Once spacers are in place, concrete can be poured; pouring must not happen before spacers are positioned, or the rebar cover will be incorrect.
Rebar chairs are placed on top of the bottom layer of reinforcing steel to support the top layer; therefore, the bottom rebar must be cut, bent, and placed first.
Rebar chairs rest on the bottom reinforcement mat to elevate the top mat; the bottom mat must be in position before chairs can be installed.
Rebar chairs provide the support and spacing for the top layer of reinforcing steel; the top mat cannot be placed until the chairs are positioned.
Both top and bottom reinforcement mats, including the chairs that separate them, must be fully in place and inspected before concrete can be poured over the rebar cage.
The complete reinforcement assembly including chairs must be inspected for proper spacing, cover, and stability before concrete placement is permitted.
Formwork provides the mold and support structure into which reinforcement bars are placed; reinforcement cannot be installed without the formwork in place.
Stirrups (shear reinforcement) are typically placed first to form the cage framework, then main longitudinal bars are threaded through and tied to the stirrups.
Concrete must be poured over the tied reinforcement cage; the main longitudinal bars must be fully in position and tied before concrete placement to ensure proper embedment and structural behavior.

If post-tensioning is used, the main longitudinal bars (or tendons) must be placed before the tensioning operation can commence; this is a hard constraint only if post-tensioning is part of the design.

In beams with both tension and compression reinforcement, the tension bars are typically placed first at the bottom, followed by compression bars at the top; however this order can vary and is a preference for work sequencing rather than a physical necessity.
Formwork provides the mold into which concrete is poured; compression reinforcement (rebar) must be placed inside the formwork before concrete is poured.
In reinforced concrete elements, tension reinforcement is typically placed first to establish the structural cage, followed by compression reinforcement bars.
Compression reinforcement must be fully installed and tied in place before concrete is poured so that the rebar becomes embedded within the concrete element.
Post-tensioning tendons must be placed after the compression reinforcement cage is assembled and before concrete pouring; the compression rebar cage provides the framework.

Temperature and shrinkage reinforcement must be placed within the concrete slab to control cracking, but it is typically placed after the initial concrete pour while the concrete is still plastic to ensure proper embedment and positioning.

Temperature and shrinkage reinforcement must be properly embedded in the concrete before finishing operations such as floating, troweling, and curing can commence, as the reinforcement controls cracking during the curing process.

The primary structural reinforcement (bottom mat) must be placed and tied first to establish the structural grid, after which the temperature and shrinkage reinforcement (top mat or additional layer) can be positioned above it using support chairs.
Formwork must be erected and secured to contain the concrete before any reinforcement, including temperature and shrinkage reinforcement, can be placed within the slab area.

In post-tensioned slabs, temperature and shrinkage reinforcement may need to be placed before post-tensioning tendons; however, in some sequences tendons are placed first. This is a soft preference as sequencing can vary by design.
Structural framing (e.g., stud walls, metal or wood studs) must be installed first to provide the support framework onto which gypsum boards are attached.
Electrical wiring, outlets, and switch boxes must be placed within the wall cavities before the gypsum boards are installed, as access is impossible after boarding.
Plumbing pipes and fittings within walls must be installed and pressure-tested before covering with gypsum board, as access would require destructive removal.
Joint compound (mud), tape, and finishing coats are applied directly over the installed gypsum boards to create a smooth surface; this cannot begin until boards are hung.
Paint, wallpaper, or other wall finishes are applied only after gypsum boards are installed and the taping/mudding is cured, as the board face is the substrate for these finishes.
Gypsum board soffit requires a supporting frame structure to be in place before boards can be attached.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the soffit area must be completed before enclosing with gypsum board, as access would be impossible or require destructive removal afterward.
Support brackets or hangers for the soffit framing must be installed before the gypsum board can be applied to the soffit frame.
After the gypsum board soffit is installed, the joints and fastener heads must be taped, mudded, and finished to create a smooth surface.
Paint application requires a finished gypsum board surface; painting cannot begin until the soffit is installed and taped/finished.

The metal stud framing provides the structural support framework onto which the gypsum board bulkhead is attached. Without the underlying metal studs, there is no substrate to secure the gypsum boards.

Electrical cables and boxes must be installed within the bulkhead cavity before it is enclosed with gypsum board, as accessing wiring after board installation would require cutting into the finished surface.
HVAC ducts that pass through or are concealed by the bulkhead must be fully installed and tested before the gypsum board encloses the space, since the boards permanently seal off access.
Once the gypsum boards are installed as the bulkhead, the joints between boards must be taped, mudded, and sanded to create a smooth, continuous surface ready for priming and painting.
The finished gypsum board surface requires primer and paint for protection and cosmetic finish; painting cannot logically commence until the board installation and joint finishing are complete.
Chase walls are framed with metal studs and tracks before any gypsum board can be applied. The structural framing must be complete to provide a substrate for the board.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (Plumbing, Electrical, HVAC within chase)
rationale: All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing lines that run inside the chase wall cavity must be installed and inspected before enclosing them with gypsum board. Boarding over un-inspected utilities would violate code and require costly demolition.

successor: Finishing / Taping and Mudding of Gypsum Board
rationale: Once the gypsum board is installed, the joints, fasteners, and corners must be taped and finished before any painting or final wall covering can be applied.

While it is possible to install some trim before boarding, best practice sequencing installs gypsum board first so that trim can be fitted tightly against the finished plane of the wall. This is a soft preference for quality and finish appearance.
Taped and finished gypsum board surfaces must be fully cured and ready before paint can be applied. Painting before finishing is complete would result in poor adhesion and an unacceptable finish.

Gypsum board furring/liner systems are typically attached to or supported by the structural framing (studs, tracks, or concrete/masonry walls). The structural framing must be in place to provide a substrate for furring channel attachment.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins (conduit, piping, ductwork, and wiring) within walls and ceilings must be completed before enclosing them with gypsum board furring/liner systems, as access to these systems after installation would require demolition.

Any insulation that will be enclosed behind the gypsum board furring/liner system must be placed before the gypsum board is installed, since the furring/liner system will permanently cover and conceal the cavity.

Once the gypsum board furring/liner panels are installed, the joints and fasteners must be taped and finished with joint compound to create a smooth, uniform surface ready for painting or final wall covering.

successor: Final Painting or Wall Finish Application
rationale: The gypsum board furring/liner system provides the substrate for paint, texture, tile, or other final wall finishes. These finishes cannot be applied until the gypsum board is installed and the joint compound has dried and been sanded.
Steel stud framing provides the structural support framework onto which gypsum shaft wall boards are attached; the boards cannot be assembled without the studs in place.

predecessor: Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP) Rough-In for Shaft Areas
rationale: MEP rough-in work within shafts must be completed before enclosing the shaft with gypsum boards, as access would be blocked and rework costly after wall assembly.
Firestopping around penetrations in the shaft area should be installed prior to board assembly to ensure continuous fire protection and code compliance.

successor: Joint and Seam Taping (Shaft Wall Finishing)
rationale: After the shaft wall boards are assembled, the joints and seams between boards must be taped and finished to provide fire-rated integrity and smooth surfaces.

successor: Shaft Wall Door and Frame Installation
rationale: Door frames and doors for shaft wall access points are installed after the shaft wall boards are in place to ensure proper alignment and fit within the completed wall assembly.

Gypsum board corner beads are typically installed over gypsum boards which are attached to metal studs or framing. The framing must be complete to provide a substrate for the gypsum boards and corner beads.

Corner beads are applied to the external corners of gypsum board assemblies after the boards themselves have been hung and attached to the framing. The gypsum board provides the surface onto which the corner bead is fastened.

Corner beads must be installed prior to applying joint compound (mud) and tape because the bead serves as a reinforcement and guide for the compound at corners. The compound is applied over and around the bead to create smooth corners.
After corner beads are embedded in joint compound, the compound must be sanded smooth before painting or texturing. The bead provides a rigid edge for finishing.
All drywall finishing, including corner bead installation and joint compound application, must be completed and sanded smooth before primer and paint are applied to achieve a uniform finish.

Gypsum board trim/accessories (such as corner beads, edge trims, and joint compounds) must be applied after the gypsum boards themselves are installed, as they are used to finish and protect the board edges and joints.

Trim and accessories (e.g., corner beads, L-beads) must be fixed in place before taping and joint compound finishing can be applied, as the trim serves as a guide and reinforcement for the finishing layers.
All trim and accessory surfaces must be fully installed, taped, and finished before any primer or paint is applied to ensure a smooth, uniform surface for coating.
The structural framing (studs, tracks) must be in place to support the gypsum boards and their associated trim; however, the trim itself is applied after the boards are hung.

It is preferable to complete all trim and finishing work before the final drywall inspection so the inspection can assess the completed surface, but inspections could theoretically occur earlier if needed.
Drywall is attached to wall and ceiling framing studs/joists; without the frame in place, there is no structural substrate to fasten the drywall to.
Electrical cables and boxes must be installed inside the wall cavities before they are enclosed by drywall, as access is impossible after the drywall is hung.
Plumbing pipes and drain lines within walls must be installed and pressure-tested before enclosing them with drywall.
Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning ducts and vents within wall/ceiling cavities must be installed before the drywall seals them off.
Insulation (batts, rolls, or spray foam) must be placed in wall and ceiling cavities before drywall is installed to close off the spaces.
The joints between drywall sheets, screw dimples, and corners must be taped and covered with joint compound after the boards are hung; finishing cannot begin on bare framing.
Paint cannot be applied directly to bare drywall or unfinished joints; the drywall joints must first be taped, mudded, and sanded smooth before the surface can be primed and painted.

While trim is typically installed after drywall is finished, it is a soft preference because trim can technically be installed after drywall hanging but before finishing in some sequences, though standard practice places it after finishing.
Drywall sheets must be installed, screwed, and secured to the studs/framing before any taping, mudding, or finishing can begin; the taping covers the joints between installed sheets.

All electrical wiring, outlet boxes, plumbing pipes, and HVAC ductwork within walls must be installed and inspected before drywall is closed up; finishing cannot start without the substrate being complete.
Insulation in wall cavities must be placed before drywall is hung and finished; the taping and mudding process seals the finished wall surface.
Taping, mudding, sanding, and finishing must be fully complete and the joints smooth before any primer, paint, or texture can be applied to the wall surface.
Finished drywall provides the flat, flush surface against which trim and casing are installed; trim is typically nailed to the studs through or against the finished drywall.
Drywall boards must be installed, fastened, and taped before sanding can begin, as sanding is performed on the joint compound applied over taped joints.

predecessor: Drywall Taping and Joint Compound Application (First Coat)
rationale: The first coat of joint compound over tape and fastener dimples must be applied and dried before sanding to achieve a smooth, level surface.
Sanded drywall surfaces must be clean and dust-free before primer can adhere properly; painting cannot proceed until sanding is complete.
Any decorative or spray texture must be applied after sanding is finished, as sanding would remove or damage applied texture.
While cleaning can partially overlap, thorough dust cleanup after sanding is strongly recommended before finishing trades begin to prevent contamination of surfaces.
Drywall sheets must be installed and fastened to the framing before any trim or accessories (like corner beads, edge trims, or joint compounds) can be applied to them.
The taping, mudding, and initial sanding of drywall joints must be completed so that trim accessories like corner beads and L-trim can be embedded and finished flush with the drywall surface.
All drywall trim, corner beads, and accessories must be installed and smoothly finished before paint primer and paint can be applied, as paint will not properly adhere to unfinished trim gaps.
After trim and accessories are installed, any excess joint compound must be sanded smooth to ensure a uniform surface before finishing coats.
The mortar bed must be applied onto a prepared, clean, and structurally sound subfloor (such as a concrete slab) to ensure proper bonding and level surface.
The mortar bed serves as the substrate for tile or stone; it must be cured and firm before tiles are set into it.
After placement, the mortar bed requires time to cure and harden before any subsequent loads or installations can proceed.
While the mortar bed provides a level surface, final floor level inspection is a soft preference after mortar bed completion to verify tolerances before tiling.
In wet areas (e.g., showers), a waterproofing membrane must be installed before the mortar bed to prevent moisture damage to the substrate.
Mortar is applied between bricks or blocks during the laying process; the bricks/blocks must be positioned first to create the joint space.
The mortar must be mixed to the correct consistency before it can be applied to form joints between masonry units.
After the mortar joint is formed and has begun to set, tooling or raking of the joint (to create a concave or weather-struck profile) must follow to ensure proper compaction and weather resistance.
Fresh mortar joints must be allowed to cure and gain strength before any further loading or subsequent work is applied to the wall.

If joints are defective or incomplete, pointing (filling and finishing) follows after the initial joint is formed, though this is a remedial preference rather than a strict physical necessity in all cases.
Cement, sand, water, and admixtures must be delivered to the site before mixing can begin.
Materials need to be properly stored (e.g., cement kept dry) and moved to the mixing area prior to use.
Fresh mortar must be available to lay bricks or blocks; mortar sets over time so it must be used shortly after mixing.
Mortar (or plaster mix) is required as the base material for plastering or rendering walls.
Pointing uses mortar to finish joints after brickwork is laid, but can be done with a separate batch; however, it typically follows mixing.

Pointing (repointing or new pointing of masonry) requires access to the brickwork or stonework at height, which is provided by scaffolding. Without scaffolding, workers cannot safely or effectively reach the joints to apply pointing mortar.

Pointing is the finishing of mortar joints in masonry. The brick or stone units must be laid and the initial bedding mortar must be in place (and often partially set or raked out) before pointing mortar can be applied to the face joints.
Before fresh pointing mortar can be applied, the existing mortar in the joints must be raked out to a sufficient depth (typically 15-20mm) to provide a clean, sound key for the new pointing material.
Excess pointing mortar and smears must be cleaned off the masonry face after pointing is complete but before the mortar fully hardens, to avoid staining the brick or stone surface.

Pointing is typically one of the final finishing operations on masonry. A quality inspection of the completed pointing work is logically done after pointing is finished to check weathertightness and appearance.
Mortar must be mixed to the correct consistency and proportions before it can be applied to surfaces.
The substrate must be clean, level, and properly prepared (e.g., dampened) to ensure mortar adhesion; applying mortar to unprepared surfaces leads to failure.
Scaffolding must be erected and layout lines marked so that mortar can be applied at the correct positions and heights.
Fresh mortar is spread as a bed for bricks/blocks to be placed into; placement must occur before mortar sets.
While some pointing is done after initial set, the main joint finishing and tooling occurs after mortar has been applied and bricks placed, when mortar is partially set but still workable.

Mortar curing can only begin after bricks or blocks have been laid and the fresh mortar joints are in place, as the curing process hardens and develops strength in the mortar that holds the masonry units together.
Fresh mortar must be mixed and applied to the masonry before the curing process can commence; curing refers to the chemical hydration process that occurs after the mortar is placed.

Any additional pointing or tooling of mortar joints should be completed before full curing, but if curing has progressed too far, pointing may become difficult; this is a soft preference for timing rather than a strict physical impossibility.

Mortar must be fully cured (typically 7–28 days) before any waterproofing membrane or sealant is applied, because applying sealants over uncured mortar can trap moisture, prevent further curing, and cause adhesion failure or efflorescence.
Plaster or render applied to masonry walls requires that the underlying mortar joints have fully cured to provide a stable, non-shrinking substrate; otherwise cracking and debonding can occur.
The surface must be clean, dry, and free of dust, oil, or debris to ensure proper adhesion and a durable bond. Adhesive will not bond effectively to dirty or unprepared surfaces.
Some adhesives and sealants require a primer to be applied first to improve bonding, especially on porous or difficult surfaces. Primer must be allowed to cure before adhesive application.
The substrates or components to be bonded must be properly positioned, aligned, and fitted before adhesive is applied, as the adhesive will set and lock the components in place.
After adhesive/sealant is applied, the joint or seam must be closed and pressure applied to spread the adhesive evenly and ensure full contact between the bonded surfaces.

Once applied, the adhesive or sealant requires a specified curing or drying period to reach its designed strength and performance characteristics before any subsequent loads or finishing work can be applied.
Sealant must first be applied before it can cure and be finished.
Curing must be complete before inspection can take place to verify the finished sealant meets specifications.
Sealant must be fully cured before water testing to ensure watertight integrity without damaging the uncured sealant.
The substrate must be properly cleaned and primed prior to sealant application and cure to ensure proper adhesion.
Tooling and finishing of the sealant must occur immediately after application and before the curing process begins, as curing changes the sealant's workability.
Surfaces must be properly prepared and cleaned before masking so that masking tape and protective materials adhere properly and contaminants are not trapped underneath.
Any surface repairs (filling holes, sanding, etc.) must be completed before masking to ensure the repair area is fully prepared and not accidentally covered by protective materials.

Masking and protecting adjacent surfaces must be completed before primer application to ensure that primer is only applied to the intended surfaces and adjacent areas are shielded from overspray or drips.

Masking and protecting must be finished before painting begins so that paint is confined to the target surface and adjacent surfaces, fixtures, and hardware are protected from paint splatter and overspray.
Texture coating application requires precise masking of adjacent surfaces to prevent texture material from adhering to areas that should remain smooth or have a different finish.
The roof deck provides the structural substrate to which edge metal and fascia flashing are fastened; without a completed deck, there is no surface to attach the flashing.

Edge metal and fascia flashing typically overlap the underlayment to provide a watertight seal; the underlayment must be in place before flashing is installed to ensure proper drainage and weatherproofing.

Edge metal and fascia flashing act as a termination bar that the roofing material laps over or abuts against; the flashing must be in place to provide a clean edge and prevent water intrusion at the perimeter.

Gutters are typically hung on or below the fascia/flashing; the fascia flashing provides the attachment point and finished surface for gutter hangers, so it must be complete before gutters are installed.
The roof drain assembly must be installed on a complete roof deck/sheathing surface to provide proper structural support and a continuous substrate for the flashing and drain components.
Underlayment provides a water-resistive barrier beneath the drain flashing; the drain and flashing must integrate with the underlayment to ensure proper drainage and prevent leaks.
The roof drain and flashing must be in place before the main roofing membrane is applied so that the membrane can be lapped over and sealed to the drain flange, creating a watertight connection.
In typical built-up or membrane roof systems, insulation boards are installed around and over the drain sump after the drain flashing is set, ensuring proper thermal continuity and drainage slope.

successor: Roof Drain Connection to Downspout / Plumbing
rationale: The internal drain body and outlet must be connected to the vertical plumbing stack once the roof drain assembly is secured, establishing the path for water to exit the building.
The roof deck provides the structural surface onto which the pipe penetration boot/flashing is mounted; without a completed roof deck, there is no substrate to attach the flashing.
The underlayment creates the waterproof membrane layer that the pipe flashing integrates with; flashing must be installed over the underlayment to maintain a continuous water barrier.
The pipe must be in place and protruding through the roof before the boot/flashing can be fitted around it and sealed.
The boot/flashing must be installed first so that the finished roofing material can be lapped over or sealed against the flashing to ensure a watertight transition.
After the boot/flashing is in place, sealant is applied at the joints and edges to complete the waterproofing; this cannot be done before the flashing is installed.
The expansion joint cover is installed on top of the finished roof deck; the deck must be in place to provide a substrate for the cover assembly.
Insulation is typically placed before the expansion joint cover to ensure thermal continuity and a proper base for the cover flashing.
The waterproof membrane must be installed and properly flashed around the expansion joint before the cover can be placed to maintain watertight integrity.
The expansion joint cover is part of the completed roofing system; acceptance testing (e.g., flood test, inspection) must occur after all components including the cover are installed.
Adjacent wall cladding or parapet caps often abut or overlap the expansion joint cover; the cover must be in place to properly sequence the flashing and trim.

Membrane installation requires a clean, smooth, and properly prepared substrate surface to ensure proper adhesion and waterproofing performance. Any debris, dust, or unevenness would compromise the membrane's effectiveness.

Any embedded plumbing or electrical conduits that will pass through or under the membrane must be roughed in before the membrane is installed, as the membrane would be compromised if punctured or cut after installation.
After membrane installation, the waterproof membrane must be tested for leaks before any subsequent work is done, to verify the integrity of the installation.
If the membrane is a below-slab waterproofing system, the concrete slab or screed can only be poured after the membrane is fully installed to protect and cover it.
Finish flooring such as tiles can only be installed after the waterproof membrane is in place and tested, as the membrane provides the necessary waterproof barrier beneath the finished surface.
The substrate must be clean, dry, and free of debris before membrane sheets can be seamed or welded together to ensure proper adhesion and weld quality.
Membrane panels must be unrolled, laid out, and positioned in their correct locations before the seams between adjacent sheets can be seamed or welded together.
Welded seams must be inspected for continuity, strength, and defects immediately after welding is completed to ensure waterproof integrity before proceeding with further work.
Full membrane sheets must be seamed together into a continuous liner before the perimeter edges can be terminated and anchored at penetrations, curbs, and flashings.
All membrane seams must be fully welded and completed before flood testing or leak testing can be conducted to verify the waterproofing integrity of the entire membrane system.
The membrane must be placed and positioned before its edges can be terminated and secured.
Edge termination must be completed before final weatherproofing and sealants are applied to ensure watertight sealing at the edges.
Edge securing must be finished before the completed membrane installation (including terminations) can be inspected.
The substrate must be properly prepared (cleaned, smoothed, primed) before any membrane work including edge termination can be performed.
Edge securing must be complete before any protective layers or overburden are placed over the membrane system.
The waterproofing membrane must be fully installed before it can be tested for water tightness.
The installed membrane must be allowed to cure and set properly before flood testing to avoid damage to the uncured membrane.
If the water/flood test reveals leaks or failures, drainage or membrane repairs must be performed before proceeding.
Water/flood testing must pass before any concrete topping or slab is poured over the membrane, as the membrane must be verified watertight first.
Final finishes over the membrane require a successful water test to ensure no hidden water leakage will damage the finished surfaces.
The perimeter frame material (e.g., aluminum tracks, furring channels, suspension components) must be procured and delivered to site before the frame can be installed.
A completed ceiling grid or supporting substrate (e.g., suspended T-grid, drywall backing) is required to provide the structural base to which the perimeter frame is attached.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the ceiling plenum must be completed before the frame is installed, as the frame would block access to these services.
The perimeter frame (e.g., wall angles, edge trim) must be fully installed and leveled before the acoustic panels themselves can be seated or inserted into the frame.

While not a hard physical constraint, it is best practice to apply acoustic sealant at frame edges after the frame is in place and before panels are fully locked in, to ensure airtight acoustic performance.
Acoustic panel mounting brackets must be attached to the wall framing; the framing provides the structural support needed to securely fasten the brackets.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the wall cavities must be completed before mounting brackets are installed to avoid interference and to allow access for MEP installations.
The mounting brackets serve as the supporting structure to which the acoustic panels are attached; panels cannot be installed until their brackets are in place.
After brackets are mounted, they must be checked and aligned to ensure panels will hang straight and level; this quality check logically follows bracket installation.

Before acoustic brackets can be mounted, the wall surface should be finished (drywall installed, taped, and mudded) to provide a clean, plumb substrate for bracket attachment and to avoid damaging finished surfaces later.
The suspension cables for acoustic panels must be attached to the ceiling structure or grid above; thus the ceiling grid or overhead support structure must be in place before cables can be installed.
The structural ceiling (e.g., concrete slab) must be completed to provide anchorage points for suspension cables.
Suspension cables must be installed and secured first so that acoustic panels can be hung or attached to them.
After cables are hung, they must be tensioned and adjusted to the correct level before panels are mounted.

It is generally preferred to complete MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) rough-in work above the ceiling before suspension cables are installed, but if scheduling requires, some MEP work could be done after cables are placed with extra care; this is a soft preference to avoid interference.
Perforated acoustic panels are typically mounted onto a supporting frame or stud wall. The frame must be fully installed, leveled, and structurally sound before panels can be attached.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work behind the wall must be completed before acoustic panels are installed, as the panels will conceal and block access to these services.
Acoustic insulation (e.g., fiberglass or mineral wool) is often placed in the wall cavity behind perforated panels to enhance sound absorption. This must be installed before the panels are placed.

successor: Final Finishing / Painting of Panels (if factory-unfinished)
rationale: While panels may come pre-finished, if on-site painting or sealing is required, it must occur after installation. This is often a soft preference or scheduling preference rather than a hard physical constraint, as panels can theoretically be painted before mounting.
Trim, baseboards, and molding are typically installed after wall paneling is in place to create clean finished edges and cover panel edges/gaps.

Acoustic baffles are typically suspended from or mounted to a ceiling grid or overhead structure. The ceiling grid must be installed first to provide the structural support and attachment points for the baffles.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (ductwork, conduit, piping) in the ceiling plenum must be completed before acoustic baffles are installed, as the baffles would obstruct access to these systems.
Any overhead structural elements, fireproofing, or primary steel/truss work must be completed before acoustic baffles are hung, as the baffles would interfere with access and create safety hazards.

Lighting fixtures are often integrated into or positioned relative to acoustic baffle layouts. Baffles must be in place to coordinate lighting positions, and to avoid damaging baffles during fixture installation.

While not a hard physical constraint, it is preferred to complete acoustic baffle installation before final ceiling and wall touch-ups to avoid damaging finished surfaces when handling and positioning baffles.
Acoustic cloud panels are suspended from or attached to a ceiling grid or suspension system; the grid must be in place to provide structural support for the panels.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in above the ceiling must be completed before enclosing the ceiling space with a grid and acoustic panels.

Lighting fixtures are often integrated into or positioned relative to acoustic cloud panels; while co-ordination is needed, it is sometimes possible to install lighting first with careful planning, so this is a soft preference to avoid rework.

successor: Install fire alarm / sprinkler devices in ceiling
rationale: Fire safety devices must be positioned with clear access and proper coverage; acoustic panels should not obstruct them, so these devices must be installed after or concurrent with panel placement to ensure correct positioning.

It is preferable to finish painting and ceiling surface work before installing acoustic panels to avoid damaging finished panels with paint splatter or dust; this is a soft preference for quality control.

successor: Install acoustic ceiling tile grid system
rationale: All MEP services running above the ceiling must be installed and inspected before the ceiling grid is hung, as they become inaccessible once the ceiling is closed.
Ducts and pipes must be in place and pressure-tested before ceiling installation because access for repairs or testing would require ceiling removal.

predecessor: Install acoustic ceiling tile grid system (main tees and cross tees)
successor: Place acoustic ceiling tiles into grid
rationale: The suspension grid must be fully installed and leveled before tiles can be placed; tiles rest directly in the grid channels.

predecessor: Complete above-ceiling electrical and low-voltage wiring
rationale: All wiring, junction boxes, and devices above the ceiling (e.g., speakers, smoke detectors) must be roughed in and connected prior to tile installation to avoid removing tiles for access.

successor: Perform final interior painting and wall finishing
rationale: Ceiling installation should precede painting to prevent overspray on finished walls and to allow a clean paint line where ceiling meets wall, though some projects paint before ceiling installation.
Acoustic panels are typically installed onto or within a ceiling grid system; the grid must be in place to provide the structural support and attachment points for the panels.
If the acoustic panels themselves require painting or any surface finishing, that work can only begin after the panels are installed in place.
Many lighting fixtures are installed within or adjacent to acoustic ceilings; the panels must be in place to properly align and secure the lighting fixtures within the ceiling grid.
It is preferable to install acoustic panels before final cleanup activities to avoid damage, but this is a soft preference as panels can be protected or cleaned afterwards if necessary.
Bass traps are installed within a room; the room's structural surfaces must exist before acoustic treatment can be mounted or placed.
Bass traps modify the low-frequency response of the room; final acoustic calibration should measure and adjust frequencies with all treatments already in place.
It is often preferable to install bass traps in corners first, then apply trim around them for a finished look, but this is an aesthetic preference, not physically required.

predecessor: Structural Framing and Ceiling Grid Installation
rationale: Acoustic panels are typically mounted onto or within a structural ceiling grid or framing system. The grid must be fully installed and stable before layout and marking can begin to ensure accurate positioning and support.

Ductwork, conduit, piping, and electrical boxes that will penetrate or be concealed above the ceiling must be roughed in first. Marking panel layouts around these elements requires knowing their final positions.
The layout and marking step establishes reference lines and locations for each panel. Panels cannot be installed until these markings are complete, as they guide exact placement.

successor: Cutting and Trimming of Acoustic Panels
rationale: Layout markings indicate where full panels go and where perimeter cuts or penetrations for lights/sprinklers are needed. Cutting must follow the marked layout to achieve proper fit.

While not a hard physical constraint, it is best practice to complete panel layout and marking before trimming out lights and sprinkler heads so that these elements align precisely with the panel grid.
The ceiling grid framework provides the structural support system needed to mount and secure acoustic sound diffuser panels in place.

predecessor: Complete rough-in of MEP services (electrical, HVAC, plumbing)
rationale: MEP rough-in work must be finished before installing diffuser panels because accessing utilities above the ceiling would be difficult or impossible after panels are mounted.
Acoustic diffuser panels are typically installed after painting is complete to avoid damaging the panels with paint overspray, and because the panels themselves are a finished surface.

While lighting can be installed before or after diffuser panels, it is generally preferred to install panels first to avoid damaging delicate lighting fixtures during panel handling, though the order can be reversed if needed.
Acoustic testing must occur after the diffuser panels are fully installed to measure and verify the actual acoustic performance of the completed assembly.

Tile flooring requires a clean, level, and structurally sound subfloor surface. Any subfloor repair, leveling, or underlayment installation must be completed before tiling can begin to ensure proper adhesion and prevent cracking.
Fresh concrete slabs must be fully cured (typically 28 days) before tile installation to prevent moisture damage and ensure the substrate is stable.
In bathrooms, showers, or other wet areas, waterproofing membranes must be applied to the substrate before tiling to prevent water damage and mold behind the tile.
Grouting can only be applied after tiles are firmly set in place with thinset mortar. The mortar must cure sufficiently before grout is applied to fill joints.

While baseboards can be installed before tiling, it is a strong preference to install them after so the tile can be laid flush to the walls and baseboards cover any uneven tile edges for a finished look.

A level, clean, and dry subfloor (e.g., concrete slab or plywood underlayment) must be prepared before any plank flooring can be installed to ensure proper adhesion, stability, and to prevent future squeaking or warping.
A moisture barrier or vapor retarder must be laid down prior to plank flooring (especially on concrete subfloors) to protect the planks from moisture damage and mold growth.

Plank flooring materials must be acclimated to the room's temperature and humidity for the recommended period (typically 48-72 hours) before installation to minimize expansion/contraction after installation.
Baseboards and quarter-round moldings are installed after plank flooring to cover the expansion gap around the perimeter and provide a finished appearance.

Typically walls are painted before flooring installation to avoid paint drips on new flooring, though this is a soft preference; some contractors prefer painting after flooring to touch up any scuffs.
Sheet flooring requires a smooth, clean, dry, and level subfloor. Any unevenness, debris, or moisture can cause the flooring to bubble, telegraph imperfections, or fail prematurely.
Underlayment provides a cushioning and moisture barrier layer that must be placed before the sheet flooring to ensure comfort, sound reduction, and protection against subfloor irregularities.

Any electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, or HVAC ductwork running beneath the floor must be installed before flooring is laid, as accessing them afterward would require cutting or removing the sheet flooring.
Wall base (baseboard) or cove base is installed after sheet flooring so that it overlaps the flooring edge, providing a finished appearance and covering the expansion gap.

While some builders prefer to install cabinets before flooring to save material, the best practice for sheet flooring is to install it first so cabinets sit on top of the finished floor, preventing moisture wicking and allowing easier future replacement. This is a soft preference as the order can be reversed.
Resinous flooring requires a clean, dry, fully cured concrete substrate to achieve proper adhesion and prevent moisture-related failures.

predecessor: Rough-in Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP) Services
rationale: All embedded conduits, pipes, and underfloor services must be installed before the flooring system is applied, as accessing them afterward would require cutting and damaging the seamless finish.

predecessor: Interior Wall and Partition Construction (including drywall/plaster)
rationale: Walls and partitions should be erected before flooring to allow the resinous material to be applied in a continuous manner up to the wall edges, and to avoid damage to finished walls during floor installation.

successor: Final Interior Finishes (painting, wall coverings, trim)
rationale: Although not a physical necessity, scheduling painting and wall finishes after resinous flooring prevents drips, spills, or scaffolding from damaging the pristine floor surface.
Heavy equipment, machinery, and permanent fixtures must be placed after the flooring is fully cured to avoid indentation, cracking, or contamination of the resinous surface during placement.
Carpet must be installed on a clean, level, and dry subfloor. Any debris, moisture, or unevenness will compromise carpet adhesion and longevity.
Carpet padding must be laid down before carpet to provide cushioning, sound absorption, and a proper base for the carpet to be stretched and secured over.
Painting, drywall finishing, and other wall work should be completed before carpet installation to avoid paint drips, dust, and debris falling onto the new carpet.
Baseboards or quarter-round trim are typically installed after carpet to cover the carpet edges at the wall, providing a finished look and securing the carpet perimeter.

While furniture can theoretically be moved in before carpet (with protection), it is standard practice to install carpet first to prevent damage, allow proper stretching, and avoid having to work around furniture.

A smooth, clean, and level subfloor (e.g., concrete slab or plywood underlayment) must be prepared and cured before wood strip flooring can be installed to ensure proper adhesion, stability, and to prevent moisture issues.

A moisture barrier (e.g., 6-mil polyethylene or specialized underlayment) must be placed over the subfloor to protect the wood flooring from ground moisture or concrete slab moisture before installation.
Baseboards and shoe moldings are installed after the wood strip flooring is laid and acclimated, as they cover the expansion gap at the perimeter and must sit atop the finished flooring.
If unfinished wood strip flooring is installed, sanding and application of stain/sealer/finish coats must occur after installation to achieve a smooth, protected surface.

While painting can be done before flooring, it is a soft preference to complete final wall finishes after flooring to avoid drips or damage to the new floor; however, taping and protective covering can allow painting first.
A clean, level, and properly prepared subfloor is essential for terrazzo installation to ensure proper adhesion and prevent cracking or unevenness.

predecessor: Rough-In Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP) Work
rationale: All underground conduits, pipes, and rough-in work must be completed before terrazzo is poured to avoid cutting into or damaging the finished floor.
A vapor barrier must be installed beneath the terrazzo to prevent moisture migration from the subfloor, which could cause delamination or staining.
After the terrazzo mix is poured and cured, it must be ground down and polished to achieve the final smooth, glossy finish.

It is preferred to complete terrazzo flooring before applying wall finishes to avoid damaging walls during the grinding and polishing process, though it is not a physical impossibility to reverse the order.
Subfloor must be clean, dry, level, and structurally sound before underlayment can be installed to ensure proper adhesion and prevent future damage.
Underlayment provides a smooth, stable base and moisture/vapor barrier that is required before final floor covering (e.g., tile, hardwood, laminate, vinyl) can be installed.
Moisture content must be verified to be within acceptable range before underlayment installation to prevent mold, mildew, and adhesive failure.

While baseboards are typically installed after flooring is complete, underlayment alone does not dictate this order; final floor covering is the trigger. This is a soft preference for sequential workflow.
Underlayment materials often require a period of acclimation to room temperature and humidity before installation to prevent expansion/contraction issues.
The subfloor must be smooth, clean, and level before any floor finish (e.g., tile, hardwood, vinyl, carpet) can be installed; otherwise the finish will be uneven, crack, or fail to adhere properly.
Underlayment (e.g., moisture barrier, soundproofing, or decoupling membrane) must be placed before the finished flooring to protect the finish from moisture and subfloor imperfections.

predecessor: Rough-In Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP) Work
rationale: All rough-in wiring, piping, and ductwork in or below the floor slab must be completed before final flooring is installed, as accessing them afterward would require tearing up the finished floor.
Baseboards and trim are installed on top of or against the finished floor; installing them first would leave a gap between the trim and the flooring.

While paint can be applied before flooring, it is often preferred to install flooring first so that paint drips and overspray land on the subfloor rather than the new finished floor; however, this is a soft preference as careful masking can reverse the order.

The concrete subfloor must be fully cured and properly prepared (clean, dry, and level) before grinding and polishing can begin, as grinding on uncured or unprepared concrete will damage the equipment and produce poor results.
