The concrete slab must be poured and initially finished before any grinding/polishing can take place, as grinding is a surface refinement process that requires the base concrete to be in place.
If a vapor barrier is required under the concrete slab, it must be installed prior to pouring and subsequently before grinding, to prevent moisture issues that would ruin the polished surface.
After grinding and polishing the concrete to the desired finish, a sealer or protective coating must be applied; the surface must be clean and polished first for the coating to adhere properly.

Once floor grinding and polishing is complete, the area can be thoroughly cleaned and readied for occupancy; the polished floor is the finished surface and should not be subjected to further construction traffic.
The concrete slab must be fully cured (typically 28 days) before any sealing or coating can be applied, otherwise moisture trapped within the slab will cause coating delamination and failure.
The substrate must be mechanically prepared (ground, shot-blasted, or scarified) to remove laitance, contaminants, and to create a proper mechanical profile for coating adhesion.
All cracks, spalls, and control joints must be repaired and filled prior to coating application, as the coating will not bridge active cracks and will telegraph defects.
The sealer/coating acts as a primer or base layer; any subsequent floor coverings (tile, VCT, polished topping) must be applied over the properly sealed and coated substrate.

It is standard practice to allow the coating to fully cure (per manufacturer specifications) before placing furniture or heavy equipment on the floor to avoid indentation or damage; however, this is a soft preference since some light loads may be permissible.

The subfloor must be clean, level, and structurally sound before any floor base or transition strip can be installed. Installing these components on an unprepared subfloor would result in improper fit, instability, and potential damage.
Underlayment (e.g., moisture barrier, soundproofing, or padding) must be placed before the floor base and transition strips to provide the necessary foundation and protection for the flooring system.

The main flooring material (e.g., tile, hardwood, laminate, carpet) must be installed first, as floor base and transition strips serve as finishing elements that cover edges, joints, and transitions between different flooring surfaces.

Transition strips are typically installed at floor level, and baseboards are installed above them to create a clean finished look. The transition strip sits flush with the flooring while the baseboard covers the gap between the floor and the wall.

While some finishing touches can be done beforehand, applying final sealants or touch-up paint near transitions is often done after installation to ensure a seamless, professional appearance, though this is a workmanship preference rather than a strict physical requirement.
A smooth, cured concrete slab is the necessary structural substrate for slip-resistant flooring; flooring cannot be applied to uncured or unformed concrete.
A moisture barrier or underlayment must be placed before the finished flooring to protect against moisture damage and to ensure proper bonding or adhesion.
The subfloor must be level and smooth before applying slip-resistant flooring to prevent uneven surfaces, poor adhesion, and tripping hazards.
Wall base or cove base trim is installed after the flooring is in place to cover the expansion gap at the perimeter and create a clean finished edge.
For tile or sheet flooring systems that require grouting or surface sealing, these finishing steps can only be performed after the flooring material is fully installed and set.
It is a soft preference to place heavy equipment after flooring to avoid damaging the new surface, though temporary protection could allow some overlap.
The final cleaning and project walkthrough must follow flooring completion to ensure the surface is unmarred and ready for inspection/occupancy.

Electrical conduits, junction boxes, and grounding systems must be installed in the subfloor before the conductive flooring is placed, as the flooring system often incorporates grounding elements that connect to these rough-ins.
A smooth, clean, and properly prepared subfloor is required for the conductive flooring material to bond correctly and maintain its electrical continuity properties.

Overhead work such as ductwork, piping, and ceiling electrical rough-ins should be completed before flooring installation to prevent debris from damaging the conductive flooring surface and to avoid rework requiring access to the finished floor.
Wall base or cove base is installed after the conductive flooring is laid and cured, to cover the expansion gap at the perimeter and to provide a clean transition between the floor and the wall.

After the conductive flooring is installed, the grounding strips or conductive adhesive must be connected to the building's grounding electrode system and continuity/resistance tests performed to verify the floor meets antistatic specifications.
Sport flooring requires a stable, level, and clean subfloor surface to ensure proper adhesion, structural integrity, and uniform playing surface.
A moisture barrier must be installed prior to sport flooring to prevent moisture migration from the subfloor that could damage the flooring material, cause warping, or promote mold growth.
The underlayment (e.g., foam, rubber, or engineered subfloor system) provides shock absorption, acoustic insulation, and a smooth base and must be installed before the sport flooring.
Game lines and markings for sports courts must be applied or painted after the sport flooring is fully installed and cured to ensure accurate placement and adhesion.

Wall base and trim are typically installed after sport flooring to cover the expansion gap at the perimeter and provide a finished appearance, though in some sequences trim can be installed concurrently.
Site excavation must be completed to expose the below-grade surfaces (foundation walls and slab) that require waterproofing application.

The foundation drainage system (e.g., perimeter drains, sump pump) is typically installed before or concurrently with waterproofing, but the waterproofing membrane must be applied to clean, prepared surfaces before final drainage backfill.

Concrete foundation walls and slabs must be fully cured (typically 7–14 days) before waterproofing is applied to ensure proper adhesion and prevent trapped moisture from causing blistering or delamination.
A protection board or drainage mat is installed directly over the cured waterproofing membrane to shield it from damage during backfilling and to provide a drainage path for groundwater.
Backfilling against below-grade walls can only proceed after waterproofing and any protective layers are fully installed and cured, to avoid damaging the waterproofing system.
The above-grade walls must be constructed and cured before waterproofing can be applied to their exterior surfaces.
Roof or deck waterproofing is typically installed before above-grade wall waterproofing to ensure continuous water shedding from top down.
Waterproofing must be fully installed and tested before the final exterior cladding or finish is applied to protect the waterproofing layer.
Waterproofing around openings is typically completed before windows and doors are installed to ensure proper flashing and sealing integration.
For above-grade walls that interface with grade, waterproofing must be completed and cured before backfill is placed against the wall.
The roof deck or structural framing provides the physical substrate on which waterproofing membranes are applied; without a complete and stable roof deck, waterproofing cannot be installed.
A smooth, clean, and properly prepared substrate (e.g., plywood, concrete deck, or insulation board) is essential for waterproofing membranes to adhere correctly and perform effectively.

predecessor: Roof Drainage Installation (e.g., drains, gutters, downspouts)
rationale: Roof drains and drainage components are typically set into the deck or substrate before waterproofing is applied so that the membrane can be flashed and sealed around them for watertight integrity.

While some insulation can be placed above or below the waterproofing depending on system design, in many conventional flat roof assemblies the waterproofing layer is applied first to protect the structure, and insulation is installed above it; however this ordering can vary by design.

successor: Final Roof Covering / Wearing Surface (e.g., gravel, pavers, membrane coating)
rationale: The waterproofing membrane must be fully installed, cured, and water-tested before any final protective layer or wearing surface is placed over it to avoid damaging the membrane and to ensure leak-free performance.
All drain and water supply pipes must be installed and roughed-in before waterproofing is applied, as the waterproof membrane must be integrated around pipe penetrations and the floor waste.
Wall framing provides the structural support onto which waterproofing membranes and backing boards are fixed; waterproofing cannot be applied to an open stud wall without substrate.
The floor substrate (concrete slab or structural floor) must be poured, cured, and cleaned prior to waterproofing to ensure a sound, debris-free surface for membrane adhesion.
Waterproofing must be fully cured and tested before tiling commences, as tiles are laid directly on top of the waterproof membrane in wet areas.
After the waterproof membrane is cured, drain grates and floor waste trims can be installed flush with the finished tile height, completing the waterproofing system at penetrations.
The structural deck or slab provides the physical base onto which the waterproofing membrane is applied; without it, there is no surface to waterproof.
Roof drains and drainage outlets must be in place prior to waterproofing to ensure proper integration and flashing details around drains.
After the waterproofing layer is applied, it must be inspected and tested (e.g., flood testing) to verify integrity before it is covered by subsequent layers.
Root barrier is installed directly above the waterproofing membrane to protect it from root penetration; waterproofing must be in place first.
The drainage layer and geotextile filter fabric are placed over the waterproofed surface (and root barrier) to manage water flow; waterproofing must be complete beforehand.
The concrete balcony/terrace slab must be fully cast, cured, and structurally sound before waterproofing can be applied, as waterproofing membranes require a stable, clean substrate.
The concrete surface must be cleaned of debris, dust, and laitance, and any cracks or defects repaired to ensure proper adhesion of the waterproofing membrane.

predecessor: Parapet / Upstand Wall Construction (Masonry or Concrete)
rationale: Parapet walls and upstands must be built before waterproofing can be installed, as the membrane typically extends up these vertical surfaces to create a continuous watertight seal.
Floor drains, scuppers, and drainage piping must be positioned and fixed before waterproofing, so the membrane can be dressed into the drain outlets to prevent leaks.
Finish floor coverings (tiles, timber decking, or paving stones) must be laid after waterproofing is fully cured and tested, to protect the waterproof membrane and avoid puncturing it.
A protective layer (e.g., geotextile, mortar screed) is placed immediately over the cured waterproofing membrane to shield it during subsequent construction activities.

While balustrades can be installed before waterproofing (if post-mounted through the slab), post-installation is preferred to avoid penetrating the newly installed waterproof membrane; if base-plate mounted on top of the finished surface, they can be installed after.
After waterproofing is fully cured, a water test (flood or hose test) must be conducted to verify the membrane is watertight before covering it with tiles or paving.
The substrate must be clean, dry, and free of debris, dust, oil, or curing compounds to ensure proper adhesion of the liquid-applied membrane.
Cracks, joints, and surface irregularities must be repaired and a primer applied where required to create a sound, uniform surface for membrane application.

predecessor: Installation of Drainage and Flashing Details
rationale: Drainage pipes, scuppers, flashings, and metal edge details must be installed first so the liquid membrane can be seamlessly integrated and lapped over these components.
A protective layer or insulation board must be installed over the cured membrane to shield it from UV degradation, physical damage during backfilling, or subsequent construction traffic.

Backfilling against foundation walls or placing the wearing course (e.g., concrete slab or asphalt) over the membrane can only proceed after the membrane has fully cured to avoid puncture or displacement.

Sheet membrane waterproofing requires a smooth, clean, dry, and cured concrete or cementitious substrate to properly bond and adhere. The slab must be prepared, patched, and free of debris, laitance, and moisture before membrane application.
Many sheet membrane systems require a primer to be applied to the prepared substrate to ensure proper adhesion of the membrane. The primer must be fully cured before the sheet membrane is installed.

A protection board or drainage layer must be installed over the sheet membrane immediately after application to shield it from UV exposure, mechanical damage during backfilling or subsequent construction, and to ensure its long-term integrity.
Backfilling against waterproofed walls can only commence after the sheet membrane is fully installed, inspected, and protected (with protection board), to avoid damaging the membrane.

For horizontal applications (e.g., plaza decks, balconies, wet areas), all subsequent flooring finishes or toppings must be placed after the sheet membrane is installed and leak-tested to ensure a watertight seal before covering.
Bentonite clay waterproofing panels or sheets require a clean, smooth, and properly cured concrete substrate to adhere correctly and activate the swelling properties of the bentonite.
Waterstops at construction joints must be installed prior to bentonite waterproofing to ensure a continuous, integrated waterproofing system.
Protection boards or drainage panels must be placed immediately after bentonite waterproofing to shield the bentonite layer from damage during backfilling and to allow proper water drainage.
After bentonite waterproofing is applied and protected, subsequent concrete placement (e.g., slabs, walls) or backfilling can proceed without damaging the waterproofing membrane.
Backfilling against the foundation wall must only occur after the bentonite waterproofing and its protective board are fully installed to prevent puncturing or displacing the bentonite layer.

The substrate (concrete or masonry) must be clean, free of dust, oil, loose particles, and laitance, and must be properly wetted/saturated to ensure adhesion and penetration of the cementitious coating.

Fresh concrete or mortar must be fully cured (typically 7-28 days) before applying cementitious waterproofing, as the coating will not bond properly to uncured concrete and moisture movement can cause delamination.
After application, cementitious waterproofing requires a moist curing period (typically 2-3 days) to allow proper hydration and development of its waterproofing properties.
Finish materials such as tiles, paint, or render must not be applied until the cementitious waterproofing coating has fully cured (typically 3-7 days) to avoid damaging the waterproof membrane.
Backfill against waterproofed foundation walls must wait until the cementitious coating is fully cured (minimum 3-7 days) to prevent physical damage to the waterproofing layer.
Waterstops need to be embedded into fresh concrete joints; the concrete slab must be poured first to create the joint where waterstops are placed.
Waterstops must be installed in the construction joint before the joint can be sealed and finished.
Waterstops need to be in place and the concrete cured before backfilling against the structure to ensure waterproofing integrity.
Formwork must be set up to define the concrete joint location where waterstops will be positioned.
Reinforcement steel must be placed before waterstops can be positioned within the joint area.
Structural walls must be completed before drainage boards and membranes can be installed against them, as the membranes are applied directly to the structural wall surface.
Primary waterproofing (e.g. tanking or membrane on the substrate) must be in place before cavity drain membranes are installed, as the cavity drain system is a secondary line of defense.
Cavity drain membranes on walls must be installed before the floor slab is poured, so that the membrane can be properly lapped and connected to the floor drainage system.
Cavity drain membranes should be fully installed before internal partitions are built, to ensure continuous drainage paths and to avoid damaging the membrane during partition work.

All drainage board and membrane installation must be complete before plastering or internal finishing begins, as these finishes would obstruct access to the drainage system and must not cover the membrane surface.
Flashing is typically installed over sheathing to provide a weather-resistant barrier; sheathing must be in place to support and secure the flashing.
Flashing must be installed before windows and doors to create a proper water seal; windows/doors are set into the flashed opening to prevent moisture intrusion.
Siding is installed over flashing to overlap and shed water away; flashing must be in place first to direct water outward over the siding.
Roof flashing is installed on top of the roof deck; the deck provides the structural substrate for flashing application at roof penetrations and edges.
Flashing is installed before the final roofing material (shingles, membrane) to integrate into the roofing system and prevent leaks at joints and transitions.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth before dampproofing can be applied to foundation walls.
Dampproofing is applied directly to the exterior surface of foundation walls, so the foundation must first be constructed and cured.
Concrete must be fully cured before dampproofing materials can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and prevent moisture trapping.
Backfilling against foundation walls can only occur after dampproofing has been applied to protect the walls from ground moisture.
It is preferred to install dampproofing before exterior insulation to protect the insulation from ground moisture, though some systems combine both.

The protection board is installed directly over the waterproofing membrane to shield it from damage during subsequent construction. The membrane must first be fully installed and cured before the protection board can be placed on top.
The substrate (typically concrete slab or wall) must be prepared, cleaned, and primed before the waterproofing membrane can be applied, and consequently before the protection board is installed.
Primer must be applied to the substrate to ensure proper adhesion of the waterproofing membrane, which must be in place before the protection board is installed.

The protection board acts as a cushion and barrier between the waterproofing membrane and the backfill material. Backfilling cannot commence until the protection board is in place to prevent damage to the membrane.

successor: Concrete Slab Pouring (for slab-on-grade or deck)
rationale: When a concrete topping slab or wear course is poured over a waterproofed deck or slab, the protection board must first be installed over the membrane to protect it from the weight and abrasion of the wet concrete and reinforcement installation.

Formwork ties and hardware are installed into or onto the formwork panels/framework to secure them; the formwork structure must first be in place before ties and hardware can be positioned and tightened.

Formwork ties and hardware must be fully installed and tightened to hold the formwork in place and withstand the pressure of wet concrete; concrete cannot be poured until the formwork is secured with all ties and hardware.

Ties and hardware are often used to pull formwork into alignment and hold bracing; proper alignment and bracing adjustments follow the installation of ties to ensure the formwork is plumb, level, and stable.
The release agent must be applied to the formwork surface after the forms are installed and cleaned, to ensure proper coating before concrete placement.
Forms must be cleaned of debris, dirt, and old concrete residue before applying release agent, as the agent will not adhere properly to dirty surfaces.
Release agent must be applied and allowed to dry/cure before concrete is placed against the formwork to prevent concrete from bonding to the forms.

While rebar is often installed after release agent application to avoid damaging the coating, in some sequences rebar can be placed first; however, applying release agent before rebar placement helps ensure the form face is fully coated.
Inspection of the formwork, including verification that release agent has been uniformly applied, must occur before concrete pouring can proceed.

Concrete must be poured and placed into the formwork and allowed to cure sufficiently before the formwork can be stripped. The formwork supports the wet concrete until it gains enough strength to be self-supporting.

A minimum curing period is required for the concrete to achieve sufficient strength to support its own weight and any imposed loads before the formwork is removed. Stripping too early can cause structural failure or surface defects.
The formwork must first be erected, installed, aligned, and secured before it can be stripped. Formwork Stripping & Removal is the reverse/deconstruction process of the assembly.
After formwork is removed, it is common to perform patching, grinding, and finishing work on the exposed concrete surfaces to repair any tie-hole marks, honeycombing, or surface imperfections.

For post-tensioned concrete structures, stressing operations can only begin after the formwork has been stripped to allow access to the tendon anchorage zones and to avoid restraining the stressing forces.
Formwork must be stripped from the hardened concrete before it can be cleaned and refurbished. The formwork cannot be cleaned while still in place holding wet concrete.
Formwork must first be removed (stripped) from the cured concrete structure before it can be transported to the cleaning area and undergo cleaning and refurbishment.
Cleaned and refurbished formwork panels must be ready and available before they can be reassembled and re-erected for the next concrete pour cycle.
After cleaning and refurbishment, formwork may be stored for future use; this is a logistical preference for organization and protection rather than a strict physical necessity.
Formwork should be inspected for damage and残留 concrete before cleaning to identify which panels need repair or refurbishment, ensuring the cleaning process addresses all defects.
Formwork must be erected and installed before it can be aligned and surveyed, as alignment is a quality-check step performed on the installed formwork.

Reinforcement placement typically occurs after formwork installation but before final alignment verification, as the alignment check ensures both formwork and rebar are correctly positioned before concrete pour.
Alignment and survey must be completed and verified before concrete is poured; pouring without alignment verification risks structural defects and non-compliance.
Survey data from the alignment check is required for the formal inspection and sign-off process before the pour can proceed.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the proper elevation and bearing capacity before any foundation or ICF walls can be installed.
ICF walls require a properly cured concrete footing (or slab-on-grade) to bear upon and to anchor the ICF blocks/panels.
All buried plumbing, electrical conduits, and drainage lines must be installed and inspected before placing ICF walls or pouring slabs, as accessing them afterward would require breaking concrete.
The ICF forms must be fully assembled, braced, and aligned before concrete can be pumped into the forms to create the structural wall.

successor: Rough-in Electrical & Plumbing in ICF Walls
rationale: Conduits, outlet boxes, and plumbing sleeves must be embedded or routed through the ICF foam before concrete is poured; once concrete hardens, no changes can be made inside the wall core.
Stay-in-place formwork must be installed on a stable, completed foundation or pile cap to provide a level and structurally sound base for the formwork system.
Reinforcement steel must be placed in the correct position before the stay-in-place formwork is installed, as the formwork will enclose the rebar and access becomes restricted.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the required levels and dimensions before formwork can be positioned and aligned.
Stay-in-place formwork serves as the mold and containment system for fresh concrete; concrete cannot be poured until the formwork is fully installed, aligned, braced, and inspected.

In some designs, waterproofing membranes are applied over the exterior face of stay-in-place formwork after installation but before backfilling; however, this is a design-dependent preference rather than a hard physical constraint.

Formwork safety netting and guardrails must be installed after the formwork structure is in place, as the netting and guardrails are attached to or supported by the formwork system to provide fall protection for workers operating on or around the formwork deck.

Concrete pouring and curing must be completed before formwork safety netting and guardrails are removed or dismantled, as the netting and guardrails serve as fall protection during concrete placement and finishing operations on the elevated formwork deck.

Formwork safety netting and guardrails must be removed prior to or during formwork stripping and dismantling to allow access to the formwork components for disassembly, and to avoid hazards associated with dismantling the fall protection system while working at height.

After safety netting and guardrails are in place on the formwork deck, subsequent vertical element construction (such as columns and walls on the same level) can proceed safely, though the ordering is a soft preference as other sequencing may be possible depending on the specific construction method.

Scaffolding must be erected before formwork safety netting and guardrails can be installed, as the scaffolding provides a working platform and anchor points for workers to safely install the netting and guardrails around the formwork perimeter.
Concrete must be poured and allowed to cure sufficiently before formwork can be removed (struck). The concrete needs to gain adequate strength to be self-supporting.
The concrete must undergo a specified curing period to achieve the required compressive strength before the formwork can be safely removed without damaging the concrete structure.
After formwork is struck, any surface defects (e.g., honeycombing or tie holes) can be repaired and finished. This is a logical sequence but not a strict physical necessity.
Waterproofing membranes or external cladding can only be applied after the formwork has been removed to access the concrete surface.

The next stage of construction (e.g., propping or pouring of the floor above) often requires the formwork below to be struck to free up space and support systems. However, in some cases reshoring is needed before full loading.
Concrete must be poured and allowed to achieve sufficient strength before formwork can be stripped, otherwise the concrete would not be self-supporting and could collapse or be damaged.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied before the formwork is erected and subsequently removed, as it is embedded in the concrete.
Formwork must first be assembled and installed around the reinforcement before concrete is placed; removal is the final step after curing.
After formwork is stripped, the exposed concrete surfaces can be finished, patched, or have curing compounds applied.
Once formwork is removed, the vertical concrete element (e.g., column or wall) can be visually inspected and tested (e.g., rebound hammer, ultrasound) for quality assurance.
Concrete must be poured and gain sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed; otherwise the slab would collapse.
Concrete must cure to reach the required minimum compressive strength (typically 70-100% of design strength) before formwork striking to prevent structural failure or excessive deflection.
Formwork must be stripped before any finishing work (screeding, tiling, or floor coverings) can be applied to the slab surface.
Striking of slab formwork is required before constructing vertical elements on top of the slab (e.g., walls/columns on the next floor) can begin.

In multi-storey construction, backpropping is often installed after formwork striking to support the cured slab while construction continues above. This is a soft preference where scheduling may allow alternative support systems.

successor: Formwork Cleaning and Preparation for Reuse
rationale: Formwork cannot be stripped and cleaned until the concrete has been poured and sufficiently cured to maintain structural integrity and surface quality.

successor: Formwork Cleaning and Preparation for Reuse
rationale: The formwork must be physically removed from the cured concrete element before it can be cleaned, inspected, and prepared for reuse in the next pour.

predecessor: Formwork Cleaning and Preparation for Reuse
rationale: Cleaned and prepared formwork panels must be reassembled and re-erected for the next concrete pour; this cannot begin until cleaning and preparation are complete to avoid contamination or misalignment.

predecessor: Formwork Cleaning and Preparation for Reuse
rationale: After cleaning, a form release agent is applied to the prepared formwork surfaces to prevent concrete adhesion; this step logically follows cleaning.
Slipforms cannot be struck (removed) until the concrete placed into them has gained sufficient strength to be self-supporting, otherwise the concrete would collapse or deform.
A minimum curing period is required for the concrete to achieve the necessary early strength before the forms are removed; premature striking could damage the structural integrity.
Surface finishing and remedial work (e.g., patching tie holes, grinding joints) can only be performed after the slipforms have been struck and the concrete face is exposed.
Final survey checks for plumbness and alignment of the newly formed wall/shaft section can only be carried out once the forms have been removed and the structure is visible and accessible.

successor: Lifting/Jacking of Slipforms to Next Level
rationale: The striking operation releases the slipforms from the poured concrete section, allowing the formwork to be lifted or jacked upward to commence the next lift cycle.
Concrete must be placed and reach sufficient strength before formwork can be struck and temporary propping installed to support the structural element.
Formwork must be in place and concrete cast within it before striking can occur; temporary propping is part of the striking process itself.
Temporary props are typically installed before or simultaneously with the removal of main formwork to safely support the concrete element during and after striking.
While not a strict physical necessity, finishing work is typically performed after propping is in place to ensure the structure is stable and accessible for finishing operations.

successor: Progressive Dismantling / Removal of Temporary Propping
rationale: Temporary propping must be installed first to support the structure; only after the concrete has gained full design strength can the temporary props be progressively removed in a controlled sequence.
Striking tools and equipment must be manufactured, procured, or fabricated before they can be used in construction activities.
Striking tools such as hammers, picks, and mallets are required to break ground, drive stakes, or loosen soil during excavation.
Hammers and mallets are needed to assemble and secure formwork panels, nails, and bracing before concrete pouring.
Striking tools such as hammers are used to position and adjust rebar, and to secure tying wire during reinforcement installation.
Brick hammers and masonry tools are essential for cutting, shaping, and placing bricks or blocks in wall construction.
Concrete must be poured and allowed to reach sufficient initial set strength before edge formwork can be safely removed; otherwise the concrete would not hold its shape and could slump or collapse.
The edge formwork must first be installed and secured in place before it can be struck (removed). This is the logical prerequisite for the striking activity.

A minimum curing period (typically 24-48 hours depending on weather and concrete mix) is required after pouring before formwork can be stripped to ensure the concrete has achieved adequate strength to be self-supporting.

After formwork is struck, the exposed concrete edges typically require inspection for defects and finishing work such as patching bolt holes or grinding imperfections. This is a soft preference as finishing could theoretically be postponed but is best done promptly.

Edge formwork must be removed from the slab edge before vertical elements (columns, walls, or next-floor formwork) can be erected on top of or adjacent to that slab, as the formwork occupies the space and interfaces needed for subsequent construction.
Concrete must be adequately cured before formwork can be struck (removed); striking too early can cause structural damage or failure.
Formwork must be removed (struck) before an inspection can be conducted on the exposed concrete surface.
Any defects identified during inspection must be rectified before further works can proceed; inspection identifies issues that need repair.
Quality control inspection must verify the struck concrete surface before finishing works (e.g., patching, grinding, coating) can be applied.
Inspection must confirm concrete has achieved sufficient strength before the structure can be loaded with subsequent construction loads.
Formwork must be in place to provide the mold and support structure for the reinforcement bars before they can be placed and tied.
Shoring and falsework must be erected to support the formwork and the weight of wet concrete, which is necessary before rebar can be placed.
A clean, level working surface (such as a blinding concrete layer or mud mat) must be prepared to allow accurate placement of rebar and maintain cover requirements.
Rebar and reinforcement must be fully placed, tied, and inspected before concrete can be poured to ensure the reinforcement is properly embedded and positioned within the concrete member.

In post-tensioned structures, ducts and tendons are often installed within or after reinforcement placement; however, tensioning occurs after concrete cures. This is a soft preference as some post-tensioning ducts may be placed concurrently with rebar.

Soil investigation provides data on exposure conditions and sulfate/chloride levels in the ground, which determines the required cement type, water-cement ratio, and admixture selection for the concrete mix design.
Structural design specifies required concrete grade (compressive strength), exposure class, and member dimensions, all of which dictate the target mix proportions and aggregate sizes for batching.
The actual physical properties (specific gravity, gradation, moisture content, strength) of available cement, aggregates, and admixtures must be known before trial mixes can be designed and batched.
The batched concrete mix must be prepared and delivered before it can be placed into formwork; fresh concrete has a limited workability window and cannot be poured without a prepared mix.

successor: Quality Control Sampling & Testing (Slump, Compressive Strength Cubes)
rationale: Samples for quality control tests such as slump and compressive strength can only be taken from the batched concrete during or immediately after batching/pouring.
Concrete must be mixed and batched before it can be transported to the construction site; the material does not exist in a usable form until mixing is complete.
Concrete must be delivered to the point of placement before it can be poured; transport is the physical link between batching and pouring.
Formwork must be in place and ready to receive concrete before concrete is delivered; otherwise delivered concrete would have no containment and would be wasted.
Steel reinforcement must be positioned within the formwork before concrete is delivered; once concrete is placed, inserting rebar is impossible.
Concrete must be delivered, placed, and finished before the curing process can begin; curing starts after the concrete has been placed and initial set occurs.
Formwork must be installed and secured to provide the mold into which concrete is pumped; without formwork, the concrete has no containment structure.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is pumped to ensure structural integrity.
The concrete mix must be designed, tested, and approved to ensure proper pumpability, strength, and workability.
The concrete pump, boom, and delivery pipelines must be positioned and assembled before pumping can commence.
Freshly pumped concrete must be screeded, leveled, and finished immediately after placement before it begins to set.
Proper curing must begin after concrete placement and finishing to ensure adequate hydration and strength development.
Formwork can only be removed after the concrete has gained sufficient strength through curing, which follows pumping.
Formwork provides the mould into which concrete is placed; concrete cannot be poured without the formwork being in place to contain and shape it.

Reinforcement steel must be tied and positioned within the formwork before concrete is placed, as the concrete encases the rebar to create reinforced concrete; rebar cannot be added after concrete is poured.
The ground or base surface must be properly graded, leveled, and compacted to provide uniform support for the concrete slab, preventing differential settlement or failure.
Freshly placed concrete must be screeded and leveled immediately after placement to achieve the required surface profile and elevation before it begins to set.
Concrete must be placed and spread before curing can begin; curing is the process of maintaining moisture and temperature conditions to allow hydration and strength gain in the placed concrete.
Formwork must be installed, aligned, and secured before concrete can be poured and compacted, as the formwork provides the mold that shapes and contains the fresh concrete during compaction.

Steel reinforcement must be correctly positioned and tied before concrete is placed and compacted; compaction consolidates concrete around the rebar, and the rebar cannot be placed after concrete is poured.
Concrete must be poured/pumped into the formwork before compaction can begin; compaction is the process of consolidating freshly placed concrete to remove air voids.

Surface finishing operations such as screeding and floating must follow compaction because the concrete needs to be properly consolidated first to achieve a uniform surface; disturbing the concrete after finishing would ruin the surface.
Curing can only begin after compaction and finishing are complete, as curing involves maintaining moisture and temperature conditions to allow the now-consolidated concrete to gain strength.
Concrete must be poured and placed before it can be screeded and leveled; screeding is the process of striking off excess concrete to bring the top surface to the correct grade.
Formwork must be in place to contain the poured concrete and define its edges before screeding and leveling can be performed.
Reinforcement steel must be positioned and tied prior to concrete pouring and subsequent screeding to ensure structural integrity.
Screeding and leveling must be completed to achieve a uniform surface before finishing operations like floating and troweling can begin.
The concrete surface must be screeded and leveled to the proper grade before the curing process can commence to prevent premature drying and ensure proper strength development.
Concrete must be poured and placed into forms before any troweling or finishing operations can begin, as troweling is performed on freshly placed concrete.
After pouring, concrete must be spread and leveled (screeded) to the correct grade before troweling and finishing can commence.
Troweling and finishing must be completed before the curing process begins, as curing involves maintaining moisture and temperature conditions after the final finish has been applied.
Control/contraction joints are typically cut after the concrete has been finished and has gained sufficient initial strength, but before curing is fully complete, to control cracking.
While not a strict physical necessity, applying surface protection or sealers is typically done after finishing is complete to protect the finished surface and is a logical sequencing preference.
Concrete must be poured and partially set before joints can be cut or formed in it.
Concrete needs to reach sufficient initial strength (typically after initial set) to hold the joint profile without crumbling or deformation during cutting.
Joints must be formed/cut and cleaned before any sealant or filler material can be applied into the joint gap.
Jointing operations (cutting or tooling) should be completed before the final curing process to ensure cracks form at intended joint locations.

In some cases, certain surface finishes are applied after jointing to ensure a clean edge; however, this depends on the specific finishing method and may be a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
Concrete must be poured and achieve sufficient initial set before formwork can be safely removed to avoid deformation or collapse of the structural element.

Concrete must cure to a minimum required strength (typically 24-72 hours depending on mix design and ambient conditions) before forms are stripped, to ensure the concrete can support its own weight and avoid structural damage.
Formwork stripping exposes concrete surfaces; any defects, honeycombing, or tie-hole repairs must be completed before final surface finishing or plastering can commence.
Formwork must be stripped and the concrete surface repaired and prepared before applying waterproofing membranes to below-grade walls or slabs.

Stripping formwork is a prerequisite before conducting load tests on the structural element, though this is a sequential preference rather than a strict physical necessity if partial loading is designed.
Excavation must be completed to expose the foundation area where anchor bolts and embeds will be placed.
Formwork must be set before anchor bolts and embeds can be positioned and secured within the formwork for concrete pour.
Rebar cage must be in place so that anchor bolts and embeds can be tied or positioned relative to the reinforcement before concrete is poured.
Anchor bolts and embeds must be set in their final positions before concrete is poured so they become embedded and fixed in place.
Survey verification of bolt locations is ideally done after placement but before pour to ensure alignment; however it could also be done concurrently. This is a soft preference for quality control.
Formwork must be installed and secured to define the concrete pour area before a pour stop or bulkhead can be placed.
Reinforcing steel must be in place before the bulkhead is installed, as the bulkhead often intersects or abuts rebar and must be positioned accordingly.
The pour stop/bulkhead defines the boundary of the concrete placement; concrete cannot be poured until the bulkhead is installed to contain it.
Finishing operations occur after concrete is placed, which requires the bulkhead to be in place to define the pour edge.
Forms adjacent to the pour stop can only be stripped after the concrete has been placed and cured, which requires the bulkhead to have been installed first.
Concrete must be batched and mixed before samples can be taken for testing (slump, compressive strength, etc.). Testing cannot occur without a concrete batch to sample.
Concrete testing (e.g., slump test, temperature test) is typically performed on fresh concrete during or immediately after placement to ensure it meets specifications before it cures.

Concrete must be tested and approved (e.g., slump and compressive strength tests) before the curing process officially begins, as curing follows placement and finishing only after quality control acceptance.
Formwork can only be stripped after concrete has achieved sufficient strength, which is confirmed through concrete testing (e.g., cylinder compressive strength tests).
Surface finishing and any necessary repairs follow quality control inspection and testing to identify defects or non-conformances that need rectification.
Wet curing must begin after concrete has been poured and placed, as curing is the process of maintaining moisture and temperature conditions to allow the concrete to hydrate and gain strength.
Surface finishing operations (troweling, floating, brooming) must be completed before wet curing begins, as curing is initiated after the final finishing is done.
Wet curing should start after the concrete has reached its final set (initial hardening), typically a few hours after pouring, to avoid damaging the freshly placed concrete surface.
Formwork removal can only begin after adequate curing has taken place to ensure the concrete has developed sufficient strength to support itself and resist damage during form stripping.

Curing must be complete before any further surface treatments (waterproofing, tiling, coatings) or subsequent construction activities can commence, as these require the concrete to be fully cured and dry.
Steam curing is applied to concrete after it has been poured and placed into forms; the concrete must be in place before curing can begin.
Formwork must be erected to hold the wet concrete in place before pouring and subsequent steam curing can proceed.
Surface finishing operations (troweling, floating) must be completed before steam curing begins to seal and smooth the concrete surface.
Steam curing accelerates concrete strength gain; forms can only be safely removed after the concrete has achieved sufficient strength through the curing process.
Standard quality control tests on cured concrete are performed after the steam curing cycle is complete to verify that specified strength has been achieved.

Internal curing involves introducing water-absorbent materials (like lightweight aggregates or superabsorbent polymers) into the concrete mix. Therefore, concrete must first be placed so that the internal curing agents are distributed within the fresh concrete.

Internal curing agents (e.g., pre-wetted lightweight aggregate or SAP) must be incorporated during the batching/mixing stage. The concrete mix must be designed and batched with these agents before placement and subsequent internal curing can occur.

After concrete placement and during internal curing, the concrete surface may need to be finished. However, finishing can proceed in parallel or shortly after placement; internal curing is an ongoing process that occurs within the concrete, so it does not strictly block finishing, but ideally initial finishing is completed soon after placement while the concrete is still workable.

Internal curing can supplement or reduce the need for external curing. External curing methods like wet burlap or curing compounds are typically applied after finishing and initial set, which can overlap with or follow internal curing. It is not a strict prerequisite but is often done concurrently or subsequently.

The concrete must achieve sufficient strength through proper curing (including internal curing) before formwork can be safely removed. Internal curing supports strength development, so formwork stripping must wait until curing has progressed adequately.
Curing can only begin after concrete has been poured and placed, as curing is the process of maintaining moisture and temperature conditions for freshly placed concrete to gain strength.
Final finishing operations such as troweling must be completed before curing begins, as curing compounds or wet covers are applied after finishing is done.
Formwork should remain in place during the curing period to support the concrete until it reaches sufficient strength; stripping can only commence after adequate curing is achieved.

Although it is preferable to allow full curing before applying waterproofing membranes, some systems allow early application; however, best practice recommends completing the initial curing period to avoid surface damage and ensure adhesion.

Strength testing is performed after or during the curing period to verify that the concrete has achieved its design strength before proceeding with subsequent construction activities such as loading or post-tensioning.
Concrete must be poured and in place before curing temperature control can begin, as curing is the process that occurs after concrete placement.
Formwork must be installed to contain the concrete during pouring and initial curing before temperature control measures are applied.

Temperature control during curing ensures concrete gains sufficient strength; formwork should remain in place during the curing period and only be removed after adequate curing (including temperature control) is completed.

Surface finishing operations (e.g., grinding, coating application) should only commence after the concrete has properly cured under controlled temperature conditions to achieve required surface hardness and durability.

While strength testing typically occurs after a certain curing period, it is a soft preference that temperature control be fully complete before testing; some tests may be conducted during the curing process to monitor progress.
Concrete must be poured before it can be finished. The slab finishing process (screeding, floating, troweling) can only begin after the concrete has been placed and initially leveled.

Freshly poured concrete must undergo initial setting (hardening) to a point where it can support the weight of workers and finishing equipment without marring the surface. Finishing too early would damage the slab.

After finishing operations (floating, troweling, brooming) are complete, the slab must undergo final curing to achieve design strength and durability. Finishing must be completed before covering with wet burlap, curing compounds, or moisture barriers for the curing phase.

Control joints or sawcuts must be performed after the finishing is complete and the concrete has hardened sufficiently to prevent raveling, but before uncontrolled shrinkage cracking occurs. Finishing must be done first to achieve the final surface profile.

Ideally, no loads should be applied to the slab until finishing is fully complete and curing is well-advanced. However, light construction traffic may be permitted after finishing with protection; this is a soft constraint based on scheduling preferences rather than a physical impossibility.
Concrete walls must be poured and fully cured before any finishing work can begin, as finishing involves surface treatment (smoothing, patching, coating) that requires a stable, hardened substrate.
The forms holding the wet concrete must be removed to expose the concrete surface before finishing operations such as patching, grinding, or applying coatings can be performed.

Any embedded items (electrical conduits, plumbing sleeves) must be installed prior to finishing because finishing seals and levels the surface, making post-finishing embedment impossible without damaging the finish.
Waterproofing membranes or coatings must be applied to a smooth, finished concrete surface to ensure proper adhesion and uniform coverage; rough or unfinished walls can cause delamination.
Paint, sealers, or decorative coatings require a properly finished surface (free of honeycombs, voids, and sharp projections) for adequate adhesion and an acceptable aesthetic result.
Concrete surface sealing can only be applied after the concrete has been poured, finished, and sufficiently cured to provide a stable surface for the sealant to bond properly.
The concrete surface must be properly finished and textured before sealing, as sealant applied to an unfinished surface will trap imperfections and compromise the final appearance and performance.
Concrete must undergo initial curing to reach adequate strength and dryness; sealing too early can trap moisture, prevent proper curing, and cause sealant failure or delamination.

successor: Floor Covering Installation (e.g., tiles, carpet, epoxy coating)
rationale: Sealant must be fully applied and cured before any floor coverings are installed, to protect the concrete and ensure proper adhesion of subsequent flooring layers.

While it is standard practice to inspect sealed surfaces after completion, the ordering is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity, as inspection could theoretically be performed before sealing in some cases.

Fresh concrete must be poured, finished, and fully cured before any staining or dyeing can be applied, as the chemical bonding and penetration of the stain/dye require a stable, clean concrete surface.

The concrete surface must be thoroughly cleaned, degreased, and possibly etched or mechanically abraded to remove contaminants, laitance, and previous coatings so that the stain/dye can properly absorb and react with the concrete.

All cracks, holes, and surface defects must be repaired and patched beforehand, as stains and dyes will accentuate imperfections and repairs cannot be performed after staining without visible discoloration.

After staining/dyeing, a protective sealer or topcoat must be applied to lock in the color, protect the surface from wear and moisture, and enhance the final appearance; staining must be fully dry before sealing.

Any additional finishing steps such as waxing, buffing, or polishing to achieve the desired sheen level should occur after staining/dyeing is complete, though this is a preference based on desired aesthetic outcome rather than a physical necessity.
Concrete must be poured and cured before it can be polished. Polishing requires the concrete slab to be fully set and sufficiently hard.
Freshly poured concrete must undergo sufficient curing (typically 7–28 days depending on mix and conditions) to reach the necessary hardness for grinding and polishing without damaging the surface.
Moisture content must be verified to be within acceptable limits before polishing begins, as excessive moisture can cause coating adhesion failures and surface defects.
Polishing opens the concrete pores and achieves the desired gloss level; sealers, densifiers, or coatings must be applied after polishing is complete to protect the finished surface.
Once polished, the floor must be protected from construction debris, foot traffic, and subsequent trades to preserve the finish until project completion.
Concrete must be placed and spread before it can be troweled; troweling finishes the surface after placement.
Screeding levels the concrete to grade and removes excess before troweling can begin.
Bull floating embeds aggregate and smooths the surface, preparing it for initial troweling passes.
Troweling produces the final finished surface; curing must begin after the finishing operation is complete to prevent moisture loss and allow hydration.
Curing compound should be applied after final troweling to seal the surface and retain moisture for hydration.
Concrete must be poured and placed before any finishing work can begin, as the broom finish texturing is applied to the freshly placed concrete surface while it is still in its plastic state.
The concrete must be screeded and leveled to achieve a uniform surface before the broom finish can be applied to create the textured pattern.

Bullfloating or darbying is required to smooth and flatten the surface and bring fines to the top before brooming, as the broom finish is applied immediately after these operations while the concrete is still workable.

successor: Concrete Curing (Wet Curing or Curing Compound)
rationale: After the broom finish is applied, the concrete must be allowed to set and then curing must begin to ensure proper hydration and strength development; the broom finish texturing must be completed before curing starts.

While joint cutting can technically be done after broom finishing, in practice it is often timed to occur after the finish is complete but before the concrete fully hardens; the broom finish should be applied first to avoid damaging the textured surface during sawing operations.
Concrete must be poured and placed before joint finishing can begin, as joints are created in the fresh or hardening concrete after placement.
The concrete surface must be screeded and roughly leveled before joint finishing (cutting or tooling joints) to ensure a flat, uniform surface for joint creation.
Concrete must reach its initial set (or appropriate stiffness) before joint finishing can be performed; otherwise the joints will not hold their shape or the concrete will be too fluid.
Joint finishing must be completed before curing begins, as curing compounds or water curing should be applied after joints are formed to ensure proper curing without damaging the fresh joints.
Final surface finishing texturing (e.g., brooming or troweling) must follow joint finishing to avoid disturbing or damaging the freshly formed joints.

Exposed aggregate finish is applied to freshly placed concrete before it fully sets. The concrete must be poured, screeded, and floated first to create the surface that will receive the aggregate exposure treatment.
Formwork must be in place to contain and shape the concrete before it is poured and subsequently treated with exposed aggregate finish.
After the aggregate is exposed (by washing, brushing, or using a retarder), the concrete must cure properly to develop strength and durability before any loads are applied.
Sealers are applied after the concrete has cured and the aggregate surface is fully exposed and clean, to protect the finish and enhance appearance.
After the aggregate is exposed and the concrete has set, loose debris, slurry, and residue must be cleaned from the surface before any subsequent finishes or coatings are applied.
Concrete must be placed and poured into the formwork before any finishing work, including formliner finishing, can begin on the surface.
Formwork with attached formliners must be installed before concrete is placed; the formliner finish is achieved during or after concrete placement against the formliner surface.
The formliner material must be attached to the formwork before concrete is poured to impart the desired pattern/texture onto the concrete surface.
The formliner finish must be completed (concrete cured enough to retain the pattern) before formwork and formliners can be safely stripped without damaging the finished surface.
After the formliner finish is complete and forms are stripped, the concrete surface can be inspected for quality and defects in the patterned finish.
The damaged concrete surface must be cleaned, free of loose debris, oil, grease, and contaminants to ensure proper bonding of the repair material.
Assessment of concrete condition (e.g., delamination, spalling, chloride content) must be completed to determine the extent and location of areas requiring repair.
Unsound or deteriorated concrete must be removed (chipped/hammered) down to sound substrate before patching can be applied.
After placing the repair patching material, proper curing (moisture retention, temperature control) must be performed to achieve design strength and durability.
Repaired areas typically need to cure and dry before any protective coating, sealant, or architectural finish is applied, though this may be a preference depending on specifications.
Concrete must be fully poured, set, and cured before blast cleaning can begin, as blast cleaning removes surface contaminants and prepares the cured concrete surface.
The concrete surface must be inspected for defects and readiness prior to blast cleaning to ensure the substrate is suitable for the cleaning process.
Blast cleaning prepares the concrete surface by removing laitance, dirt, and contaminants, which is necessary before applying any primer, sealer, or coating to ensure proper adhesion.
After blast cleaning exposes the true concrete surface, any cracks, spalls, or defects become visible and must be repaired before final finishing or coating.
A final inspection after blast cleaning ensures the surface is properly prepared to specification, though this is a quality control preference rather than a physical construction necessity.
Curing can only begin after concrete has been poured and is in place, as curing is the process of maintaining moisture and temperature conditions for freshly placed concrete to develop strength.

Final finishing operations (troweling, brooming, etc.) must be completed before curing compounds are applied or wet curing begins, as finishing alters the surface which would be disturbed by premature curing.
Forms must be in place to contain the concrete during placement and initial curing; however, formwork can sometimes be removed after initial set, depending on the curing method.

While some formwork can be stripped after concrete reaches sufficient strength (which depends on proper curing), it's generally a soft preference to complete at least initial curing before stripping forms to avoid damage to the green concrete.

Curing must be completed (typically 7-14 days for standard concrete) before any subsequent surface treatments, coatings, or coverings are applied, as the concrete needs to reach adequate strength and the curing process must not be interrupted.
The structural frame or window opening must be installed to provide a stable support structure before the glazing frame can be fitted.
The rough opening must be prepared, including proper sizing, leveling, and weatherproofing, to receive the glazing frame.
The glazing frame must be installed and secured in place before glass panels or glazing units can be set into the frame.
The glazing frame must be in place before sealants and gaskets can be applied to ensure weathertight installation.
Interior and exterior trim and finish work around the window typically follows glazing frame installation, though some finishes could theoretically be done concurrently.
The glazing panel (glass unit) must be installed into a prepared frame or curtain wall system; the structural frame or supporting mullions must be in place to receive the glazing.
After the glazing panel is positioned in its frame, sealants and gaskets are applied around the perimeter to provide weather-tightness and secure the panel.

Interior finishes near windows (e.g., drywall, trim) are often completed after glazing to avoid damage and to ensure proper integration with the installed window units, though this sequencing can sometimes be adjusted.
The rough opening in the wall or curtain wall grid must be prepared, measured, and cleared of debris before the glazing panel can be lifted and installed.
Performance testing for water penetration and air leakage must occur after all glazing panels are installed and sealed to verify the envelope integrity.
The glazing gasket is typically installed after the glazing panel is in place, as the gasket seals around the panel edges.
The frame (e.g., curtain wall frame or window frame) must be installed before the glazing gasket, as the gasket is fitted into the frame's channels or recesses.

While sealant can be applied before gasket installation in some sequences, it is preferable to install the gasket first to ensure proper compression and sealing performance before final weatherproofing.
Interior trim pieces (such as cover caps or decorative covers) covering the gasket area must be installed after the gasket is in place, as they conceal and protect the gasket.
The gasket must be installed before performing water penetration and air infiltration tests, as the gasket provides the primary seal that is being tested.

The glazing spacer bar is placed between glass panes in an insulating glass unit (IGU). The glass panes must first be cut and prepared to the correct size before the spacer bar can be positioned along the edges.

The spacer bar typically contains a desiccant to absorb moisture within the IGU. The desiccant must be filled into the hollow spacer bar profile before the bar is placed onto the glass, otherwise it cannot be inserted later.

Once the spacer bar is positioned on the glass, a primary sealant (e.g., polyisobutylene/PIB) is applied to the sides of the spacer bar to bond it to the glass and create the initial gas/moisture seal.
The spacer bar is placed on the first glass pane; the second glass pane is then pressed onto the opposite side of the spacer bar to form the complete insulating glass unit.

After the IGU is assembled with the spacer bar between the panes, a secondary structural sealant (e.g., silicone) is applied and must cure to provide edge strength and full encapsulation of the spacer bar assembly.
The window or door frame must be installed and structurally ready to receive the IGU, as the IGU is mounted into the frame.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed, sized, and prepared to the correct dimensions before the frame (and subsequently the IGU) can be installed.
Flashing and weatherproofing around the frame opening must be applied before installing the IGU to prevent water infiltration behind or around the glazing unit.
The IGU must be placed into the frame before the glazing beads or stops can be installed to secure the unit in place.
The IGU must be positioned and secured before the final perimeter sealant or caulking is applied to ensure an airtight and watertight seal around the glazing unit.
Glass panels must be cut to the required dimensions before they can be laminated, as lamination requires precise sizing and alignment of glass layers.
Glass surfaces must be thoroughly cleaned and prepared to ensure proper adhesion of the interlayer (typically PVB or EVA) during the lamination process.
The interlayer material (such as PVB or EVA film) must be cut, conditioned, and ready for placement between glass panels before the lamination process can begin.
After lamination, the finished laminated glass must undergo quality inspection (e.g., checking for bubbles, delamination, edge quality, and optical clarity) to ensure it meets specifications.
Laminated glass panels must be fully fabricated and cured before they can be installed into window frames, curtain walls, or structural glazing systems.
Glass must be cut to the required dimensions before it can undergo the tempering process, as tempering is performed on finished-sized pieces.
Glass edges must be ground and polished before tempering because the tempering process heat-treats the glass and any edge work after tempering would risk shattering the glass.
Any holes, cutouts, or notches must be made before tempering, as the glass cannot be drilled or cut after the tempering process without causing fracture.
Tempered glass must be fully processed before it can be installed into window frames, doors, or curtain wall systems.
Tempered glazing must be completed before final quality checks (e.g., surface flatness, edge quality, and fragmentation tests) can be performed to verify it meets safety standards.
The window frame must be installed to provide the structural support and mounting location for the Low-E coated glass units.
After the glazing is installed, the gaps around the glass must be sealed and weatherstripped to ensure thermal performance and prevent air leakage.
Interior trim work around windows can only be completed once the glazing units are in place.
Exterior weatherproofing elements such as flashing and cladding around window openings must be installed after the glazing is set to ensure proper integration and water tightness.
The rough opening must be properly framed, squared, and prepared to receive the window frame and glazing assembly.
The window frame must be installed and structurally ready before the tinted glazing can be fitted into it.
The structural wall and window openings must be completed so that the window frame and glazing have a surface to be installed into.
The tinted glazing must be in place before weatherproofing seals and caulking can be applied around the glass edges to ensure a watertight installation.
It is preferable to complete the glazing before finishing interior walls around windows to avoid damage to finished surfaces during glass installation, though not physically required.
The window or curtain wall frame must be installed first to provide a structural mounting surface for the reflective glass panels.
After the reflective glass is placed into the frame, sealants and weatherproofing must be applied around the edges to prevent water infiltration and ensure thermal performance.

Interior work such as drywall and trim near windows is typically done after glazing to avoid damaging finished surfaces during glass installation, though this is a construction sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
The building's primary structural frame and any supporting mullions or sub-frames must be erected to carry the weight and wind loads of the reflective glazing system.
Air and water infiltration testing of the completed building envelope must occur after all glazing is installed to validate the performance of the installed reflective glass system.
The self-cleaning glazing panels must be installed within a supporting frame that holds them in place; the frame structure must be completed first to provide the mounting surface.
The window or curtain wall frame must be properly sealed and prepared before glazing is inserted to ensure weather-tightness and prevent moisture ingress.
Once the self-cleaning glazing panels are placed, perimeter sealants and gaskets must be applied around the panels to secure them and make the assembly watertight.

After installation, the self-cleaning coating should be gently cleaned and protected from construction debris to maintain its photocatalytic properties; this is a soft preference as it protects performance but is not structurally required.
Interior wall and ceiling finishes near the glazed areas are typically done after glazing to avoid damaging the glass or coating; this is a preferred sequencing to protect the installed glazing.
The frame or curtain wall system must be installed and the rough opening prepared before electrochromic glazing units can be placed and secured.
Structural supports (mullions, anchors) must be in place to carry the weight of the electrochromic glass panels.
Wiring and low-voltage conduits for powering and controlling the electrochromic tinting must be run to the glazing locations before the glass is installed.
After the electrochromic units are set in the frame, perimeter seals, gaskets, and weatherproofing can be applied to ensure building envelope integrity.
The electrochromic glass must be physically installed before control wiring can be connected to each unit and the tinting system can be commissioned and tested.
The window frame or structural support system must be in place before thermochromic glazing units can be installed, as the glazing is mounted into the prepared frame.
Any electrical connections, sensors, or control systems for smart or thermochromic glass typically require rough-in wiring before the glazing panels are installed.
While not a strict physical necessity, it is standard practice to complete glazing before interior finishing to avoid damaging finished surfaces during glass installation.

successor: Building Envelope Air and Water Sealing
rationale: The thermochromic glazing units must be installed to complete the building envelope before final air and water sealing can be applied around the perimeter of the installed glazing.

successor: Commissioning and Calibration of Smart Glazing Controls
rationale: The glazing panels must be physically installed before the thermochromic control system can be calibrated, tested, and commissioned for operation.
The supporting frame must be installed before fire-rated glazing can be placed, as the glazing units are mounted into the prepared frame openings.
After fire-rated glazing is installed, the perimeter must be sealed with fire-rated sealants and firestopping materials to maintain the fire-resistance rating of the assembly.
Inspection and any required fire-testing of the installed glazing should occur after installation to verify proper fit, labeling, and fire-resistance performance.
The rough opening must be prepared, cleaned, and sized correctly before fire-rated glazing units can be installed into the frame.

Surrounding finish work such as drywall finishing or trim installation is typically done after glazing is in place to achieve a clean final appearance, though it is a soft preference as sequencing can vary.

predecessor: Rough Framing for Curtain Wall / Storefront / Window Openings
rationale: The structural framing must be in place to receive and support the heavy bullet-resistant glazing units.

predecessor: Masonry / Concrete Wall Construction (if glazing is set in a wall)
rationale: The surrounding wall structure must be built to provide the rough opening and anchorage for the glazing frames.
Glazing may need to be seated in frames; however, if the frame is pre-installed the glass goes into the frame after framing is complete.
Perimeter seals and weatherproofing must be applied after the glazing panels are in place to prevent water/air infiltration.

successor: Interior Finishes (drywall, trim) around glazed openings
rationale: Interior finishes adjacent to the glazing are typically completed after the glazing is installed to allow for proper fit and finishing.
Structural framing provides the load-bearing support and frame into which decorative glazing panels are installed; glazing cannot proceed without the structural framework in place.
Rough openings must be framed, measured, and prepared to receive glazing units before decorative glass can be installed.
Weatherproofing membranes behind or around openings must be applied prior to glazing to ensure the building envelope is protected from moisture intrusion.
It is preferable to complete glazing before interior finishes to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to allow for proper sealing around windows, though it is not always a strict physical necessity.
After decorative glazing is placed, final sealants and gaskets must be applied to complete the watertight and airtight installation; this is a physical requirement of the assembly.
The structural frame (including floor slabs and edge beams) must be complete to provide the supporting framework onto which spandrel glazing panels are installed.
Rough openings in the building facade must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before spandrel glazing units can be fitted.
Waterproof membrane and air barrier systems must be applied around the openings to prevent moisture ingress; spandrel glazing is installed over or against these layers.
Interior drywall, trim, and sealant work adjacent to spandrel panels cannot be completed until the glazing is in place to provide the finished boundary.
Final exterior sealants, gaskets, and pressure caps on the curtain wall system are applied after spandrel glazing panels are installed to ensure a weathertight seal.
The structural frame must be complete to provide the support framework onto which glazing panels are installed.
Roof must be waterproofed to prevent water damage to interior spaces and ensure weather-tight conditions before installing glazing.
Glazing must be installed to seal the building envelope before applying interior finishes that could be damaged by weather or moisture.
Glazing installation is a critical component of completing the building envelope, and must be finished before the envelope can be considered weather-tight.
It is generally preferred to complete glazing before MEP rough-in adjacent to glazed areas to avoid damaging finished glazing, though it is not a physical impossibility to do otherwise.
Glazing (glass panels) must be installed before gaskets can be applied to seal and secure them in place.
The window or curtain wall frame must be in place to provide the structure into which glazing and gaskets are set.
Gaskets must be positioned around the glazing before final waterproofing sealants or weatherproofing membranes are applied over them to ensure a complete seal.
While interior finishes can often proceed after glazing and gasketing are complete, this is a soft preference since interior work might be done in parallel with careful sequencing.

successor: Pressure Testing / Air Infiltration Testing Activity
rationale: Gaskets must be fully installed to create the seal required for accurate pressure and air infiltration testing of the facade system.
Glazing sealant is applied to seal the edges of installed glazing units. The glass or glazing panels must be physically in place before sealant can be applied around their perimeter.
The frame or substrate must be cleaned, primed, and prepared to ensure proper adhesion of the sealant. Applying sealant to a dirty or unprepared surface would compromise the seal.
After sealant is applied, it requires a specified curing or drying time before it can be exposed to weather, stress, or subsequent work such as pressure testing or cleaning.
Sealant must be fully applied and cured before water or air infiltration testing can be performed on the glazing system to verify the integrity of the seal.

successor: Final Cleaning / Finishing of Glazed Areas
rationale: It is preferable to complete sealant application before final cleaning to avoid smearing fresh sealant or trapping dirt behind the sealant bead, but cleaning can be done afterwards in some sequences.
Glazing panels must be delivered and stored on-site before they can be handled and lifted into position.
Panels must be inspected for damage and prepared (e.g., cleaned, fitted with lifting attachments) before being lifted.
Lifting equipment such as cranes or vacuum lifters must be positioned, rigged, and tested before lifting operations can commence.
The supporting structural frame or curtain wall substrate must be in place to receive the glazing panels.
After lifting, panels must be precisely positioned, aligned, and temporarily fixed prior to final glazing installation.
Glass panels must be manufactured, cured, and delivered to site before any quality control checks on the glazing can be performed; the physical panels must exist to be inspected.
The glazing units must be fully installed (set into frames, gaskets applied, sealants cured) before quality control testing can verify correct placement, seal integrity, and performance.
