Sealants and gaskets require specified curing time before water-tightness tests or air-infiltration tests can be meaningfully performed; testing too early would give false results.
Formal sign-off and handover of the glazing system to the client/architect can only occur after all quality control and testing has been successfully completed and documented.
The surface must be cleaned, sanded, and primed before paint can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and a smooth finish.
Areas not to be painted must be masked off with tape and protective covers before rolling paint to avoid unwanted paint marks.
Paint must be properly mixed, thinned if necessary, and poured into trays before roller application can begin.
The applied paint must be allowed to dry and cure after roller application before any subsequent coats or finishing work can be performed.
While a second coat is dependent on the first coat being applied first, it is a soft preference because the need for a second coat depends on coverage requirements, not a physical impossibility.
The surface must be cleaned, sanded, and primed before paint can be applied, otherwise the paint will not adhere properly.
Areas not to be painted must be masked off with tape and protective covering before brush application to prevent paint from getting on unwanted surfaces.
Paint must be stirred, thinned if necessary, and poured into trays before brush application to ensure correct consistency and color.
Applied paint requires adequate drying and curing time before any subsequent coats or handling.
While a second coat typically follows the first, it is a soft preference as a single coat may be sufficient depending on coverage requirements.
The surface must be clean, dry, and free of contaminants, rust, or old paint to ensure proper adhesion of the new spray paint coating.
Areas not intended to be painted must be masked off with tape and protective covers to prevent overspray and ensure clean edges.
A primer coat must be applied and allowed to cure before the topcoat spray paint is applied, as primer ensures better adhesion, corrosion resistance, and uniform finish.
After spray painting, the applied coating must be allowed to dry and cure properly before any subsequent handling, recoating, or exposure to service conditions.
The painted surface must be fully applied before a quality inspection can assess film thickness, uniformity, color accuracy, and defect detection.
Structural framing (walls, floors, ceilings) must be in place before surface preparation begins because surface preparation involves treating the finished surfaces of these structural elements.

All rough-in work for electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, and HVAC ducts must be completed within walls and ceilings before surfaces are prepared, as opening up finished surfaces to add these would damage the prepared surfaces.
Surfaces must be properly prepared (cleaned, patched, sanded) before any primer or paint can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and a smooth finish.
Wall surfaces must be smooth, clean, and properly prepared before wallpaper can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and a bubble-free finish.
Wall and floor surfaces must be clean, level, and properly prepared before tile can be installed to ensure proper adhesion and a flat finished surface.
Walls must be plastered and smoothed before painting to ensure proper paint adhesion and a smooth finish.
A primer coat must be applied before the final paint to seal the surface and ensure uniform paint absorption.
Painting should be completed before floor finishing to avoid paint drips, splatters, and dust settling on newly finished floors.
Final painting should be done before installing light switches, sockets, and fixtures to prevent damage to paint and allow clean edges around fixtures.

Once painting is complete, final cleaning and touch-up work typically follows to address any minor imperfections, though this is a practical sequencing preference rather than a strict physical necessity.

Wall framing must be completed before ceiling painting because the ceiling is typically supported by the wall structure, and painting the ceiling before walls are framed would leave unfinished joints and edges.
Electrical wiring and boxes in the ceiling must be installed before painting, as painting over or having to cut into a finished painted ceiling to run wires would damage the finish.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and mudded (finished) before painting can occur, as paint is applied to the finished drywall surface.
A primer coat must be applied before the final paint coat to ensure proper adhesion, coverage, and a uniform finish.
It is a soft preference to install flooring after ceiling painting to avoid dripping paint on new floors, but flooring can be installed first if properly protected.
It is a soft preference to paint ceilings before walls to allow for overspray and drips from ceiling work to be covered by wall painting, but it is not a physical necessity.
Drywall must be installed and finished before trim and millwork painting can begin because trim is installed over finished drywall, and drywall dust from sanding would damage fresh paint.
Wall and ceiling priming should be completed before trim painting to avoid overspray and drips on freshly painted trim, and to allow for cleaner cut-in lines.

Trim and millwork must be physically installed (nailed, glued, or fastened in place) before they can be painted, as painting loose or uninstalled pieces would be impractical and may cause damage during installation.

While trim is often painted before final wall coats for cleaner cut-in lines, this is a preference rather than a hard constraint — some painters prefer to paint walls first. Sequence depends on technique.
Flooring installation should follow trim painting because paint drips, spills, and sanding dust from the painting process would damage finished flooring surfaces.
Paint must be fully applied and cured before inspection can occur; inspection cannot start on unpainted surfaces.
Surfaces must be properly prepared and primed before paint is applied, which is then inspected. Without proper preparation, paint adhesion and finish quality cannot be evaluated.
Any touch-up painting must be completed before final cleaning to avoid re-soiling freshly touched-up areas and to ensure all paint debris is cleaned.
Inspection and touch-up work requires access; dismantling scaffolding prematurely would prevent inspectors from reaching all painted surfaces.
The paint inspection and any necessary touch-ups must be completed and approved before the project or area can be signed off as complete and handed over.
Power, water, network connectivity, and HVAC systems must be operational before any computer systems can be safely powered on and initialized.
All physical hardware (servers, switches, storage arrays) must be physically installed, cabled, and secured in racks before system boot and initialization can occur.
All data cables (Ethernet, fiber channel, SAS) and power cables must be properly connected between components before any system can be powered on and initialized.
The hardware must be powered on and BIOS/UEFI initialized before any operating system can be installed or configured on the system.
Basic system boot and network interface initialization must be complete before network settings can be configured and connectivity testing can be performed.
Pre-functional checklists verify that all equipment, systems, and components are installed and ready for startup before functional testing can proceed.
All mechanical and electrical equipment must be physically installed and connected before it can be functionally tested to verify performance.
Building control systems, sensors, actuators, and DDC controllers must be installed and wired to allow functional testing of system response and sequences of operation.
Individual system functional performance must be verified before integrated multi-system testing can occur to ensure each component operates correctly on its own.
Functional performance testing must demonstrate that all systems meet design specifications and code requirements before the building can be accepted and occupied.
All individual system components must be physically installed and in place before integrated systems testing can begin, as testing requires the complete assembly of all subsystems.
Electrical wiring and connections must be completed to provide power necessary for testing integrated systems.
Mechanical components such as HVAC, piping, and ductwork must be installed before integrated testing can verify system interactions.
Building management and control systems must be wired and configured to allow automated testing of integrated responses.
Integrated systems testing must be successfully completed before formal commissioning and handover to the client, as commissioning validates that all systems work together as designed.
Control systems require electrical power and wiring infrastructure to be in place before they can be calibrated.
All sensors, actuators, and field devices must be physically installed before the control system can be calibrated to read and control them properly.
The control panels, PLCs, DCS cabinets, and all associated wiring must be completed before calibration can commence.
All control loops must be calibrated before the overall system integration tests can verify correct end-to-end operation.
Calibration ensures control loops function correctly, which is a prerequisite for safe plant commissioning and startup activities.

Rough-in inspections must be completed to verify that all mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems are properly installed and ready before air and water balancing can begin to ensure the systems are functional and code-compliant.
Complete ductwork must be installed and sealed before air balancing can be performed to measure and adjust airflow through the distribution system.
All water piping, hydronic piping, and connections must be fully installed before water balancing can be performed to verify proper flow rates and pressure.
All HVAC equipment (air handlers, chillers, boilers, pumps, VAV boxes) must be installed and operational before balancing can test and adjust system performance.

Air and water balancing must be completed before final commissioning because balancing ensures that all HVAC systems are operating at design specifications, which is a prerequisite for comprehensive system performance verification and acceptance testing.

The sequence of operations cannot be verified until all control system components (sensors, actuators, controllers, and field devices) are physically installed, wired, and configured. Verification requires the actual control logic to be executable on the installed hardware.

HVAC equipment (air handling units, chillers, boilers, VAV boxes, dampers, and valves) must be installed and fully commissioned before the sequence of operations can be verified, since the control sequences operate these mechanical systems.
The control logic and programming for the building automation system must be loaded and operational before the sequence of operations can be tested and verified against design intent.

predecessor: Electrical Power and Lighting System Installation
rationale: Reliable electrical power must be available and lighting control systems must be installed to verify the sequence of operations for lighting control, demand response, and power monitoring sequences.

The sequence of operations must be verified and confirmed correct before proceeding to formal acceptance testing, as acceptance testing validates that all systems operate according to the approved sequence of operations.

Building cannot be occupied or handed over to the owner until the sequence of operations has been verified, ensuring all building systems respond correctly to occupancy schedules, alarms, and operational modes.
Fire alarm system must be physically installed before it can be tested.
Notification devices must be mounted and wired before testing their functionality.
The control panel must be installed and programmed to send test signals to notification appliances.

predecessor: Backup Battery and Power Supply Installation
rationale: Backup power must be operational to test alarm functionality under normal and emergency power conditions.
Alarm and notification testing must be successfully completed before the system can be formally commissioned and accepted by the client or authority having jurisdiction.
Testing must be complete and passed before the building can be occupied or handed over to the owner.

successor: Safety and Life Safety System Testing
rationale: Fire alarm devices, panels, and detectors must be physically installed before they can be tested for functionality and compliance.

successor: Safety and Life Safety System Testing
rationale: Sprinkler heads, piping, and valves must be in place before flow testing and pressure testing can be performed.

successor: Safety and Life Safety System Testing
rationale: Emergency lights, exit signs, and battery backup units must be installed prior to testing illumination levels and battery duration.

successor: Safety and Life Safety System Testing
rationale: Smoke dampers, fans, and ductwork for smoke control must be installed before operational testing of the smoke management system.

predecessor: Safety and Life Safety System Testing
rationale: All life safety systems must be tested and verified operational before the building can be formally commissioned for occupancy.

predecessor: Safety and Life Safety System Testing
rationale: Authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) typically requires proof of successful life safety system testing before issuing a certificate of occupancy.

predecessor: Safety and Life Safety System Testing
rationale: While testing may be done before full closeout, completing punch list items related to safety systems is often sequenced after testing to incorporate any identified corrections.
Electrical rough-in work including conduit, wiring, and panel installation must be complete before commissioning can test and verify the electrical system.
Commissioning must be complete and systems verified to be functional before the building can be occupied and final inspections signed off.
Fire alarm systems are powered and integrated with the electrical system; they must be installed to allow integrated system testing during commissioning.
Commissioning verifies individual electrical components, which must be complete before full building systems integration testing (e.g., BMS, HVAC interface) can proceed.
Main electrical distribution equipment such as transformers and switchgear must be installed and energized before commissioning can verify performance and safety.

Ductwork must be physically installed and in place before the HVAC system can be commissioned, as commissioning involves testing airflow, balancing, and verifying system performance through the ducts.

predecessor: HVAC Equipment Installation (Chillers, Boilers, AHUs, RTUs)
rationale: All major HVAC equipment must be fully installed and connected before commissioning can verify their operation, control sequences, and performance.

predecessor: Electrical Rough-In and Power Supply to HVAC Equipment
rationale: Commissioning requires powering up and testing all HVAC components; electrical connections and power supply must be complete and energized.

predecessor: Building Management System (BMS) / DDC Controls Installation
rationale: Controls and sensors must be installed and wired to allow commissioning to test control sequences, setpoints, and system responses.
Commissioning must be completed and signed off to certify that the HVAC system operates correctly, safely, and efficiently before the building can be handed over to the owner or occupied.

Plumbing and piping rough-in (installation of pipes, fittings, and fixtures within walls/floors) must be physically completed before testing can commence, as testing requires a complete closed system to pressurize and check for leaks.
Underground and under-slab drain, waste, vent, and water supply lines must be installed and backfilled before above-ground rough-in and subsequent system testing can occur.

Testing must be successfully completed before enclosing walls and ceilings with drywall, as access to pipes and joints is needed for leak inspection and repairs. Once tested and approved, the system can be covered.

Plumbing fixtures and trim items should only be installed after the piping system has been pressure-tested and proven leak-free, to avoid damage to finished fixtures and to ensure system integrity before final connections.

Final connections to appliances (water heaters, dishwashers, washing machines) and permanent service connections should be made only after the rough-in system has passed pressure and leakage tests, ensuring no leaks behind finished walls.

The building enclosure (roof, walls, windows, doors, and air/water barriers) must be fully installed before commissioning can begin, as commissioning tests the performance and integrity of the installed enclosure system.
Structural framing must be complete to provide the supporting framework for the enclosure elements that will be commissioned.
Air and water barriers are critical components of the enclosure system and must be installed before commissioning tests for air leakage and water penetration can be performed.

Interior finishes such as drywall, paint, and flooring should not be installed until enclosure commissioning is complete, because commissioning may involve water testing, air pressure tests, or access to the enclosure that could damage finished interiors.

Enclosure commissioning (including air leakage testing) must be completed before HVAC balancing and commissioning, as the building envelope's airtightness directly affects HVAC system performance, pressure relationships, and airflow measurements.
Lighting fixtures and electrical components must be physically installed before they can be commissioned and tested.
All lighting fixtures, ballasts, and controls must be in place before commissioning can verify their proper operation.
Photosensors, dimming controls, and automated shading devices must be installed to be tested during commissioning.
The BAS or lighting control network must be operational to allow commissioning of integrated lighting control sequences.
Commissioning may require access to wiring and control devices above ceilings; finishing work should follow after commissioning verifies all systems are functional.
Commissioning confirms lighting systems meet design intent and code requirements before the building is occupied and handed over to the owner.
While commissioning typically feeds into final inspections, some inspection items may proceed in parallel; however, full system verification should precede final sign-off.
Conduit, wiring, and junction boxes must be roughed in before lighting fixtures can be connected and commissioned.
Structural construction must be complete to verify that the built structure conforms to design specifications and safety standards before documentation can be prepared.
Material test results (e.g., concrete compressive strength, steel tensile tests) must be available to include in verification documentation.
Site inspections must be completed to document compliance findings and any non-conformances in the verification report.
Verification documentation and reports must be finalized and approved before the project can be handed over to the client or operator.
Verification reports serve as the basis for the certifying authority or engineer to grant final approval and sign-off on the completed works.
Seasonal performance testing requires the HVAC system to be fully installed to evaluate its performance under actual seasonal conditions.
The building envelope must be complete (walls, roof, windows sealed) to create controlled conditions for testing heating/cooling loads and air leakage.
Full electrical power supply and controls must be operational to run HVAC equipment and monitoring systems during seasonal testing.
The results of seasonal performance testing inform adjustments needed for final balancing of airflow, water flow, and refrigerant charge.
Seasonal performance testing results may be required as part of documentation for building permit sign-off, confirming systems operate efficiently before occupancy.
All systems must be fully installed and commissioned before training can begin, as trainees need to work with operational systems that are fully functional and tested.
Systems must pass all quality assurance and testing protocols prior to training to ensure trainees are learning correct procedures on verified equipment.
Operating manuals, maintenance guides, and training materials must be prepared and available before training sessions can commence.
Project closeout and formal acceptance by the client can only occur after training is complete and the facility has been formally handed over to the operations team.
The facility can only begin full operation and maintenance activities after the operations staff have been trained and formal handover has taken place.
Retro-commissioning is applied to existing buildings that have not previously been commissioned; thus the initial commissioning (or lack thereof) is the baseline state before retro-commissioning.
An energy audit or preliminary assessment identifies system deficiencies and performance gaps that retro-commissioning will address.
After retro-commissioning activities (investigation, testing, and adjustments), the building systems are optimized and retuned for improved performance.
Ongoing monitoring-based commissioning often follows retro-commissioning to verify that performance improvements persist over time.
A post-occupancy evaluation may be conducted after retro-commissioning to assess occupant comfort and energy performance outcomes.
The equipment or system must be fully assembled in the factory before it can undergo witness testing to verify its functionality and compliance.
Preparation activities such as setting up test equipment, connecting power sources, and configuring instrumentation must be completed before witness testing can commence.
The equipment can only be packed and shipped after it has successfully passed witness testing to ensure that only compliant equipment is dispatched.
Witness testing must be completed before the equipment is delivered to the site and installed, as the testing validates that the equipment is ready for field deployment.
All components and materials used in the equipment must be inspected and approved prior to assembly and testing to ensure quality and safety standards are met before witness testing.
Components and equipment must be physically installed before their installation can be witnessed or inspected at hold points.
Welds must be completed before they can be inspected at designated witness or hold points.
Preparation and setup for pressure testing must be completed before the test itself can be witnessed as a hold point.
Materials must be received and verified before any installation work that will be subject to witness/hold point inspections can commence.
Witness and hold point inspections of the installation and preparation work must be completed and signed off before pressure testing can proceed.
Inspection hold points must be cleared before subsequent installation activities (e.g., further piping, insulation, or covering of inspected work) can begin, as per quality control procedures.

Data collection systems (sensors, data loggers, monitoring equipment) must be installed and operational before any trend logging and data analysis can begin, as they provide the raw data needed for analysis.
The building systems (HVAC, electrical, plumbing) must be commissioned and in normal operation before meaningful trend data can be collected and analyzed.
The BMS or building automation system must be installed, configured, and connected to the relevant sensors and equipment to enable automated trend logging and data capture.
Analysis of trend data identifies performance gaps and inefficiencies, which then inform targeted optimization efforts - though this is a soft preference as some tuning may proceed in parallel.
Accurate energy audits and reporting rely on trend data analysis to quantify energy consumption patterns and identify savings opportunities; the analysis must be completed first.
The ground or foundation surface must be excavated, leveled, and prepared before placing rebar supports/chairs to ensure stable placement and correct positioning.
Formwork defines the shape and boundaries of the concrete pour; rebar supports/chairs are placed within or on top of the formwork to hold reinforcement at the correct cover depth.
A blinding layer of lean concrete provides a clean, level working surface that prevents rebar chairs from sinking into soft soil and ensures consistent rebar coverage.
Rebar supports/chairs must be positioned first to hold the reinforcement bars at the correct elevation and cover; the rebar is then laid on and tied to the chairs.
All rebar, including supports/chairs, must be fully placed, tied, and inspected before concrete can be poured, as the chairs become embedded and support the reinforcement during the pour.
Rebar must be cut and bent to the required lengths and shapes before mechanical splices can be installed on the rebar ends.
Rebar sections must be placed in position before the couplers can connect them together at the splice locations.
Mechanical splices and couplers must be fully installed and torqued before concrete is poured to ensure the rebar continuity is established within the structural element.
If post-tensioning follows rebar installation, mechanical splices should be completed to ensure reinforcement continuity before stressing tendons, though scheduling may allow overlap in some cases.
Mechanical splice couplers must be visually inspected and sometimes torque-tested before concrete placement to verify proper installation.
Reinforcement spacers are placed between or around reinforcement bars to maintain proper cover and spacing; therefore the reinforcement bars must first be positioned.
Formwork provides the mold and boundary within which reinforcement and spacers are placed; spacers are often attached or set against the formwork to ensure correct concrete cover.

Spacers ensure the reinforcement is held at the correct position and cover depth during concrete placement; concrete must be poured after spacers are in place to lock the reinforcement in the designed location.
After spacers are positioned, the reinforcement bars are tied together and to the spacers to secure the cage assembly before concrete pouring.
Formwork must be in place to provide the mold and working platform before shear reinforcement (stirrups/links) can be placed inside the beam or column formwork.
Main longitudinal reinforcing bars must be positioned first because shear stirrups/links are typically placed around and tied to the longitudinal bars to form the reinforcement cage.

Concrete cannot be poured until all shear reinforcement (stirrups/links) is fully placed, tied, and inspected, as the reinforcement must be encased in concrete to form the composite structural element.
After shear reinforcement placement, an inspection is required to verify spacing, alignment, cover, and tying before concrete placement is permitted.

Starter bars/dowel bars must be embedded into the freshly placed concrete of the foundation or footing to ensure proper anchorage and structural continuity between the foundation and the vertical wall/column elements.
The main reinforcement cage in the foundation/footing must be in place so that starter bars can be tied and lapped with the foundation rebar before concrete is poured.
Accurate layout and positioning of the foundation/footing geometry must be completed so that starter bars are placed at the correct locations and spacing as per structural drawings.
Starter bars projecting from the foundation must be in position before formwork can be erected around them, as the dowels protrude into the wall/column formwork space.
Starter bars/dowel bars serve as the reinforcement connection between the foundation and the wall/column; the wall/column concrete cannot be poured until these dowels are in place and properly tied.
Tendons/strands must be installed and placed in their ducts before they can be tensioned. Tensioning cannot begin without the tendons being physically in place.
The concrete surrounding the tendons must reach sufficient compressive strength before tensioning can occur, otherwise the concrete would crush or fail under the prestressing forces.
Ducts or conduits must be placed in the formwork before tendons can be threaded through them, as they provide the void path for the strands.
After tensioning, the ducts must be grouted to bond the tendons to the concrete and protect them from corrosion. This can only be done once the tendons are tensioned and anchored.
Once tensioning reaches the required force, the anchorage devices (wedges, plates) must be set to lock in the tension. This follows immediately after the tensioning operation.
Structural detailing and modeling must be completed to determine the exact rebar sizes, shapes, and placement requirements before a bending schedule or drawing schedule can be prepared.
Rebar must be procured and available on site or in the fabrication yard before bending can commence according to the schedule.
Rebar must be bent and scheduled according to drawings before it can be placed and tied in formwork or on the construction site.
In many sequences, formwork is installed after or in coordination with rebar placement, and the bending/drawing schedule must be complete to guide rebar installation before formwork is fully closed.

Concrete can only be poured after rebar has been bent, delivered, and placed according to the schedule and drawings; the bending schedule is a prerequisite to the entire rebar installation and concrete placement workflow.
The column position must be marked on site to provide the exact location and alignment for placing the reinforcement cage.
The reinforcement bars must be cut, bent, and fabricated to the required dimensions before they can be assembled and fixed into position.
Column formwork (shuttering) can only be erected around the reinforcement cage after the cage is fully assembled, tied, and in place.
Concrete cannot be poured until the reinforcement cage is fixed in position because the concrete must encase the steel reinforcement.
While MEP sleeves can often be placed concurrently, it is best practice to position conduits and sleeves within or alongside the cage before formwork is closed, to avoid coring later.
The formwork for the beam must be in place before reinforcement can be fixed, as the reinforcement bars need to be placed and tied within the formwork mould.
Bottom reinforcement must be placed first to form the base layer before additional reinforcement (stirrups, side bars, top bars) can be fixed and tied.
After the main beam reinforcement cage (including stirrups) is fixed and tied, the side and top longitudinal bars can be placed and secured.
Concrete pouring must occur only after all reinforcement is fully fixed, tied, inspected, and approved, as the reinforcement must be embedded within the concrete.
Cover blocks for maintaining concrete cover to reinforcement are placed after the reinforcement cage is fixed, to ensure proper spacing between rebar and formwork.
Formwork provides the mould and support structure for the slab; reinforcement bars cannot be placed in position until the formwork is erected and secured.
Main structural reinforcement for beams and columns must be in place before slab reinforcement is laid, as slab bars typically extend into and integrate with beam/column cages.

successor: Electrical and Plumbing Conduit Installation in Slab
rationale: Conduits and embedded services are placed on top of or within the bottom reinforcement mat; however, this is often done concurrently after bottom reinforcement is fixed, but before the top reinforcement. Typically conduits are laid after the bottom reinforcement is completed.
Concrete cannot be poured until all reinforcement steel is completely fixed, tied, and inspected to ensure structural integrity and cover requirements.
For slabs with top and bottom reinforcement mats, the bottom reinforcement is fixed first, then spacers/chairs are placed, followed by the top layer of reinforcement.
All reinforcement materials (rebar, mesh, ties) must be cut, bent, and prepared before they can be fixed in place on the wall.
Formwork for the wall must be erected first to provide a framework and support for placing and tying reinforcement bars in the correct position within the wall.

predecessor: Wall Surface Preparation / Concrete Substrate Preparation
rationale: The base wall surface or concrete substrate must be clean, roughened, and free of debris to ensure proper bonding and alignment of the fixed reinforcement.
Reinforcement must be fully fixed, tied, and positioned before concrete is poured; otherwise the reinforcement would not be embedded correctly within the wall structure.
After fixing the reinforcement, an inspection must be conducted (often by an engineer) to verify correct spacing, cover, and tying before concrete placement is allowed.
Excavation must be completed to expose the ground and create space for foundation work before reinforcement can be fixed in place.
A layer of lean concrete (blinding) is typically poured over the excavated base to provide a clean, level working surface before reinforcement bars are placed.
Reinforcement must be fixed and positioned correctly before formwork is installed around it, as the formwork encloses the reinforcement cage.
Concrete cannot be poured until the reinforcement steel is fully fixed, tied, and inspected, as the reinforcement must be embedded within the concrete.
While inspection often occurs concurrently or immediately after fixing, formally the reinforcement must be fixed before it can be inspected and approved by the engineer.
Tendons and ducts must be installed and placed within the concrete formwork before stressing can begin, as the tendons are the elements being tensioned.
Concrete must be poured and cured to sufficient strength (typically 75-100% of design strength) to withstand the compressive stresses induced by post-tensioning before stressing can commence.
Formwork must be in place to contain the concrete during pouring and curing, providing the structural mold before post-tensioning stressing can occur.
Reinforcing steel (rebar) must be placed and tied prior to stressing to provide the required reinforcement within the concrete member.
Grouting the tendon ducts must follow immediately after stressing and anchoring to protect the tendons from corrosion and to bond them to the surrounding concrete.

Formwork can only be removed after post-tensioning is complete and the concrete has been placed under compression, as the structure gains sufficient strength from the post-tensioning to be self-supporting.
If temporary stressing is used, detensioning or release of stressing force must occur after anchoring is complete and the structure is ready.
Cover blocks are placed on top of the tied rebar mesh to maintain proper concrete cover. Rebar must be fully installed and tied before cover blocks can be positioned.
Cover blocks ensure the rebar is positioned at the correct depth within the concrete element. Concrete cannot be poured until cover blocks are installed to guarantee the required cover thickness.
Curing follows pouring which follows cover block installation. This is an indirect soft constraint since curing is a later stage.
Formwork defines the outer boundary of the concrete element; cover blocks are placed within the formwork against the forms to provide proper cover. Formwork must be in place first.

successor: Inspection / Approval of Reinforcement and Cover Blocks
rationale: Although inspection typically happens after both rebar and cover blocks are placed, it is a quality assurance step that can also be done concurrently. This is a soft preference for sequential order.
Rebar must be fabricated, cut, and bent to the specified lengths and shapes before it can be placed, tied, and lapped in the formwork.
Formwork must be erected and braced to provide the mold and support structure before rebar can be placed and tied within it.
Rebar must be tied and lapped in position before spacers and chairs can be installed to ensure proper concrete cover and bar positioning.
All rebar tying, lapping, and positioning must be completed and inspected before concrete can be poured, as concrete embeds the rebar permanently.
Rebar tying and lapping must be finished before post-tensioning tendons are placed and stressed, as the rebar cage provides the structural framework.

Surface must be clean, free of rust, mill scale, dirt, grease, and other contaminants for coating to adhere properly. Coating applied over contaminated surfaces will fail prematurely through delamination or disbondment.
An angular surface profile (anchor pattern) must be created by abrasive blasting to provide mechanical keying for the coating system. Without adequate profile, coating adhesion will be insufficient.

Steel members must be erected and assembled into their final position before final coating application to avoid damage to the coating during handling, welding, and bolting operations. Field touch-up is minimized by coating after erection.

After coating application, inspection must be performed to verify dry film thickness (DFT), detect pinholes/holidays, and ensure continuity of the coating system before the structure is put into service.

The applied coating must be allowed to cure (dry, polymerize, or cross-link) fully before the coated surface is subjected to service conditions, handling, or subsequent trades to prevent coating damage and ensure specified performance.
Rebar must be fabricated, cut, and bent to the specified shapes and dimensions before they can be inspected for compliance with engineering drawings.
All reinforcement bars must be placed, positioned, and tied in their final locations before inspection can verify correct spacing, cover, and alignment.
Formwork must be erected to define the concrete element geometry; inspection of reinforcement within the formwork is required before concrete is placed.
Concrete can only be poured after reinforcement has been inspected and approved; pouring over uninspected rebar risks structural non-compliance that cannot be corrected after concrete hardens.

If inspection reveals issues with rebar position relative to formwork, adjustments to formwork may be needed, but normally formwork is finalized before inspection; this is a soft constraint as it may not always be required.
Bond patterns are applied to the superstructure masonry; foundations must be completed first to provide a stable base for wall construction.
Bond patterns (the arrangement of bricks/stones) are created during the laying of masonry units with mortar; thus mortar must be prepared before bonding can commence.
Reinforcement (e.g., steel bars or mesh) is typically placed within or after the masonry bond pattern is laid, as the pattern defines the positioning.
Exterior or interior plaster/rendering is applied over the completed masonry bond pattern to finish the wall surface.

While a damp-proof course is often inserted during early brickwork, final bond completion above the DPC level must occur before upper wall finishing; this is generally a hard constraint in practice, but soft if considered as a preference for scheduling.
The foundation must be completed and cured to provide a stable, level base to support the weight of the reinforced masonry walls.
Steel reinforcement bars must be placed and tied in the forms or block cores before masonry units are laid and grouted, as the rebar is embedded within the masonry.
For cast-in-place reinforced masonry, formwork must be erected to shape and contain the concrete or grout before the masonry work begins.
After reinforced masonry is placed, sufficient curing time is required for the grout or concrete to achieve design strength before any loads are applied or subsequent work proceeds.
Waterproofing is typically applied after the reinforced masonry is complete and cured, though it is a soft preference because in some designs it can be integrated during construction.
Masonry veneer is a non-structural cladding that must be applied over the completed structural frame and sheathing to provide a stable backing surface.
A weather-resistive barrier must be installed behind the masonry veneer to protect the sheathing from moisture penetration.
Masonry veneer requires a structural support ledge or footing at the base to bear the weight of the veneer; the foundation must be complete before veneer can start.
Flashing and weep holes are integrated into the masonry veneer as it is laid up to direct moisture out; they must be placed during veneer installation.
While masonry veneer often rises around roughed-in openings, installing windows/doors after avoids damage; however, some sequencing allows windows first with careful detailing.
The building envelope must be closed by the masonry veneer before interior finishes are applied to protect them from weather and moisture.
Masonry veneer forms the outermost finished surface; any exterior finish or insulation applied over it must be installed after the veneer is complete.
Stone masonry requires a stable, level foundation to bear the weight of the stone structure; without proper foundation preparation the masonry would settle unevenly and crack.
Stones must be quarried, cut, and shaped to the required dimensions before masons can lay them in place.
Fresh mortar must be prepared and available on-site for binding stones during the masonry process.
Scaffolding provides the working platform for masons to reach higher elevations safely during stone placement.
Pointing (finishing mortar joints) must be done after stones are laid and the initial mortar has partially set, to ensure clean, weather-tight joints.
While reinforcement can be embedded during masonry, final reinforcement and grouting typically occur after masonry walls are erected to ensure structural integrity.
Waterproofing treatments are best applied after the stone wall is complete and cured, though it could be applied during construction as a soft preference.
Final cleaning, dust removal, and protective sealant application must follow stone masonry completion to avoid damaging fresh mortar and stone surfaces.

Movement joints in concrete slabs (e.g., saw-cut control joints) must be installed after the concrete slab has been placed and finished, because the joints are typically cut or formed into the hardened or semi-hardened substrate to control cracking.
For tile/flooring movement joints, the substrate or underlayment must be fully prepared and cured so that the joint material can be properly applied over a stable base.

Movement joints (e.g., expansion joints, isolation joints) must be in place before the final flooring or tile is installed, as the joints provide the necessary space for thermal and moisture expansion.
Sealants and finish compounds are applied after movement joints are formed or cut, to ensure the joint is properly shaped and prepared for sealing.
In concrete work, reinforcement must be placed before movement joints are formed, because the joint location often relates to the reinforcement layout and must be positioned accordingly.

Lintels and arches span openings in masonry walls; the supporting wall on both sides of the opening must be built up to the level of the lintel/arch springing point before the lintel or arch can be installed or constructed.
Arches require temporary formwork or centering to support the voussoirs during construction until the keystone is placed and the arch becomes self-supporting.

The masonry above a lintel or arch rests on it; the lintel/arch must be complete and cured (for concrete lintels) or fully set (for masonry arches with keystone in place) before the wall above can be built.

The temporary centering supporting an arch during construction can only be removed after the arch is complete (keystone placed) and the mortar has gained sufficient strength to allow the arch to be self-supporting.

While frames can sometimes be installed beforehand, it is typical and practical to install window and door frames after lintels/arches are in place to ensure the opening is fully formed and protected from weather. This is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
The ground must be stable, level, and cleared before scaffolding can be safely erected. Uneven or unprepared ground poses a serious safety risk for scaffold stability.
Foundations must be completed and cured to provide a stable base for scaffolding, especially where scaffolds are supported on or adjacent to the building structure.
Scaffolding provides the necessary elevated working platform and access for workers to safely erect structural steel, concrete columns, or load-bearing walls.
Scaffolding is required to provide safe access for masons to lay bricks or blocks at height and to store materials at working level.
Workers need scaffolding platforms to access the building exterior for installing cladding panels, curtain walls, insulation, and finishing materials safely.
Scaffolding must be in place to provide safe access for workers to reach all masonry surfaces for cleaning and repointing.
Cleaning and repointing must be completed before any waterproofing or sealant is applied, as the sealant would trap dirt and prevent proper bonding if applied over uncleaned or damaged mortar.
A final quality inspection of the cleaned and pointed masonry should logically follow the completion of the work to verify standards are met.
If masonry is to be painted, cleaning and pointing must be finished first to ensure a clean, sound substrate for paint adhesion.

Any structural repairs (e.g., crack stitching, replacement of damaged stones) must be completed before cleaning and pointing, as cleaning could disturb fresh repairs and pointing would need to integrate with repaired areas.
The subgrade must be properly prepared and compacted to provide a stable, level base for brick paving. Laying pavers on unprepared ground would lead to uneven settling and failure.
A compacted aggregate base course is required to distribute loads and provide drainage support before brick pavers can be installed.
Edge restraints (such as concrete curbs or metal edging) must be in place before pavers are laid to contain the pavers and prevent lateral movement.
After brick pavers are laid, joint sand must be swept into the gaps between pavers and compacted to lock the pavers in position and stabilize the surface.
Once pavers are installed, final compaction with a plate compactor and optional sealing must be performed to ensure the pavers are fully seated and the surface is finished.

The building's substructure and foundations must be in place before damp-proof courses (DPCs) can be installed, as DPCs are laid at a specific level within or above the foundation walls to prevent moisture rising from the ground.
DPCs are typically installed within or above the masonry or concrete foundation walls; the foundation structure must be complete to provide the base on which the DPC is laid.
Walls above the DPC level cannot be built before the DPC is in place, as the DPC acts as a horizontal barrier against rising damp and must be continuous within the wall construction sequence.
Ground floors are often constructed after DPCs to ensure that the damp-proof membrane connects properly with the DPC, preventing moisture ingress at floor-wall junctions.

Internal plastering and finishes should ideally be applied after DPC installation to avoid trapping moisture behind finishes, though this is a best-practice sequencing rather than a strict physical impossibility.
Masonry must be built and installed before it can be inspected and tested — inspection is performed on the completed or partially completed masonry work.
Inspection and testing identifies any defects or non-conformances in the masonry; corrections can only proceed after issues are identified.
Formal approval or acceptance of masonry work is contingent upon successful inspection and testing results.

Follow-on finishing trades such as plastering or rendering typically wait for inspection approval to avoid covering uncertified work, though this may be a contractual preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
Structural elements like retaining walls or foundations require passing masonry inspection before backfilling or applying design loads to ensure structural integrity.
The structural framing must be in place to provide a surface for plaster molding. Molding cannot be applied to open or unfinished walls and ceilings.
Drywall provides the finished substrate on which decorative plaster molding is applied. Molding cannot be installed over bare studs or open walls.

Walls and ceilings must be primed and base-coated before decorative molding is applied, as the molding integrates with the finished wall surface and attempting to paint behind installed molding is impractical.

The decorative molding itself must be painted or finished after installation. Final finish coats should be applied over the molding to ensure a seamless, uniform appearance with the surrounding surfaces.

In crown molding and base molding scenarios, flooring is typically installed after molding to allow molding to overlap flooring edges cleanly, but this can be a soft preference if installers are careful with sequencing and protection.
Plaster keys are formed when plaster is applied to and squeezed through the gaps between laths; the lath substrate must be installed first to provide the surface and gaps for key formation.

The plaster key is the mechanical bond formed when the first coat (scratch coat) of plaster is applied; the key itself is created during that application, and then the scratch coat sets and cures before subsequent coats.
The brown coat (second coat) is applied over the cured scratch coat, which relies on the keys for adhesion; thus the key formation (during scratch coat) must precede the brown coat.
The final finish coat is applied after the brown coat, which in turn depends on the scratch coat and its keys; the key formation is a prerequisite for all subsequent plaster layers.
Plaster beads/trims are installed on framed walls to serve as screeds and corner protection; framing must be complete to provide a substrate.
Plaster beads are typically attached over sheathing or backing boards (e.g., drywall or cement board) before plaster is applied.
Plaster beads and trims serve as guides and edge protection for plaster; they must be installed before plaster is applied.
Once beads are in place, corner finishing and taping can proceed to blend the bead with the plaster surface.

Plaster can only be applied onto a stable, load-bearing substrate. The masonry or concrete wall must be fully constructed and cured before any plasterwork substrate (e.g., rendering, lathing) can be prepared on its surface.
The building must be enclosed by a completed roof structure to protect the plaster substrate from rain and weather exposure during preparation and curing.
Window and door frames must be installed and fixed in place so that the plaster substrate can be worked around openings, properly finished at reveals, and integrated with the frames.
The substrate (e.g., scratch coat, metal lath, or backing board) must be fully prepared, clean, and dry before any subsequent plaster coats can be applied over it.

While substrate preparation does not physically block inspections, it is common practice to complete and sign off rough-in inspections for services embedded in walls before covering them with plaster substrate, to avoid costly rework. However, this is a procedural preference rather than a physical necessity if inspection access is maintained.
The surface must be clean, dampened, and properly prepared (e.g., metal lath or masonry substrate) for the scratch coat to bond effectively.
Metal or wire lath must be installed as a base for the scratch coat to adhere to; the scratch coat is applied directly onto the lath.
Weep screed must be installed at the bottom of wall assemblies to allow moisture drainage before any stucco coat is applied.
A weather-resistive barrier must be installed behind the lath to provide moisture protection before the scratch coat is applied.
The scratch coat must cure and harden for at least 24-48 hours before any subsequent coat (brown coat or finish coat) can be applied.
The brown coat (second coat of stucco) can only be applied after the scratch coat has set sufficiently to provide a sound base.
Scaffolding must be in place to provide access to walls for plastering work.
Walls must be clean and joints raked out to ensure proper adhesion of the brown coat.
DPC must be installed to prevent moisture rising into the plaster.
Masonry must be complete and cured before applying render or plaster base coats.
The brown coat (scratch/undercoat) must be applied and sufficiently set before the final finishing coat can be applied.
The brown coat requires adequate curing time before any subsequent coats or finishes are applied to prevent cracking.
Tiling typically follows plastering, but this is a soft preference as tiles can be installed over properly prepared brown coat if scheduling requires.
The scratch coat provides the base surface for the float coat; it must be applied and set first so the float coat has a rough key to bond to.
Metal lath must be attached to the substrate to provide the mechanical key for plaster coats; without lath, the plaster has no structural support.
The scratch coat must cure sufficiently before applying the float coat to prevent cracking, delamination, or moisture entrapment.
After the float coat is set to the right firmness, the final troweling and finishing can be performed to create a smooth, hard surface.

While it is standard to paint after plaster is fully dry, it could be considered a soft preference because the paint can be applied once the plaster is dry enough; however, structurally it must be done after plaster to avoid sealing in moisture.
Surfaces must be clean, dry, and free of dust/debris to ensure proper plaster adhesion.
A scratch coat (brown coat) must be applied and cured to provide a mechanical key for the finish plaster coat.
Metal lath or wire mesh must be securely fastened to the substrate to serve as a reinforcement base for plaster applications.
Freshly sprayed plaster must be allowed to cure and dry properly before any subsequent finishing work can proceed.
Final surface texturing, painting, or decorative finishes cannot be applied until the spray-applied plaster base coat has fully set and dried.
Plaster must first be applied to the surface before it can begin curing and drying. The curing/drying process only starts after the plaster has been placed.
The plaster must be fully cured and dried before any inspection or quality checking can take place, as assessing the finish requires the material to have set and hardened.
Sanding or smoothing the plaster surface can only be performed after the plaster has completely cured and dried, otherwise the material would be too soft and would be damaged.
Paint or wall coverings can only be applied to a fully cured and dried plaster surface to ensure proper adhesion and avoid moisture entrapment or defects.

While it is strongly preferred to let plaster cure fully before any decorative preparation, minor surface prep might sometimes begin slightly before complete drying in some methodologies, making this a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
Framing provides the structural support and substrate (studs, lath, or backing) onto which plaster is applied or patched; without framing in place, plaster has no surface to adhere to.
Electrical wiring and boxes must be installed within walls before plaster is applied or repaired, as plastering conceals these elements and access after plastering would require destructive removal.
Plumbing pipes and fittings within walls must be installed and pressure-tested before plaster/patching closes them in; otherwise, leaks or repairs would damage finished plaster.
HVAC ducts and vents within wall/ceiling cavities must be installed before plaster is applied, as they are concealed within the same substrate.
Insulation must be placed within wall/ceiling cavities before plaster or patching closes them off; plaster repairs typically seal the cavity permanently.
Fresh plaster and patching compound must be fully cured and sound before primer/sealer can be applied; primer seals the porous plaster and provides a uniform surface for paint.
Paint cannot be applied over damaged or unfinished plaster; plaster repair/patching must be completed, dried, and sometimes sanded smooth before the final paint finish is applied.
Wallpaper requires a smooth, clean, and sound substrate; any plaster damage or holes must be repaired and smoothed before wallpaper can be applied.
If tiling over plaster surfaces, the plaster must be sound and level; however in wet areas tile backer board typically precedes finish tiling, but the plaster substrate must be repaired first.

It is preferable to complete plaster repairs before installing baseboard and trim so that repairs extend fully to the floor/wall junction and trim covers the repaired edge neatly; but order can sometimes be reversed if repairs are limited to higher wall areas.
The insulation board must be securely installed and fixed to the substrate before plaster can be applied over it; plastering over an uninstalled or loose board is physically impossible.

predecessor: Apply Base Coat to Insulation Board
rationale: A base coat (or primer/scratch coat) is typically required on insulation board to create a bonding surface for the final plaster layer; applying finish plaster directly onto raw insulation board would result in poor adhesion.
Fiberglass mesh is often embedded into the base coat on insulation board to provide crack resistance and structural integrity; this mesh must be in place before the final plaster layer is applied.
The plaster layer must be fully set and cured before any decorative finish, paint, or render coat can be applied over it; painting over uncured plaster would ruin the finish.
Once plastering is complete, the surface must be allowed to cure and then be inspected for defects (cracking, unevenness) before any further work such as tiling or painting proceeds.
Venetian plaster requires a smooth, stable substrate. Drywall must be installed, taped, and finished (mudded and sanded) to provide a proper base for the plaster to adhere.

A primer or sealer must be applied to the drywall surface before Venetian plaster to ensure uniform absorption and adhesion, and to prevent the drywall from sucking moisture out of the plaster prematurely.
After application, Venetian plaster requires a controlled curing and drying period before any subsequent finishes can be applied or the surface can be handled.

Venetian plaster is typically polished or burnished and may have a protective wax or sealant applied. This final finishing step can only begin after the plaster has been fully applied and initially dried.

While not a hard constraint, it is standard practice to complete Venetian plaster before applying final paint or wallpaper to adjacent wall surfaces to avoid damaging the plaster finish or causing overspray/contamination.

Sgraffito is a decorative technique applied onto a final plaster finish layer; a sound, cured base plaster coat (the 'finish coat' or 'arriccio') must be completed and set before the sgraffito layers can be applied.
The scratch coat provides the mechanical key for subsequent plaster layers; it must be applied and partially cured before the finish coat and then the sgraffito layers can follow.
Sgraffito work on walls and ceilings requires stable access; scaffolding must be erected before plasterers can reach the working surface to apply and carve the sgraffito layers.
Freshly carved sgraffito plaster is fragile and must be allowed to cure and harden without disturbance before any subsequent finishes or cleaning can occur.

Although sgraffito is typically the final decorative finish, adjacent non-plaster detailing or painting work is often scheduled after sgraffito completion to avoid dust or overspray damaging the carved plaster.
Stucco requires a solid substrate (sheathing) to adhere to; framing and sheathing provide the structural backing and nailing base for the metal lath or stucco mesh.
A weather-resistant barrier (e.g., building paper or house wrap) must be installed over the sheathing before stucco to prevent moisture infiltration into the wall assembly.
Metal lath or wire mesh must be fastened to the sheathing to serve as a mechanical key for the stucco layers to bond properly.

Windows and doors are typically installed after rough openings are framed and sheathed, but stucco application around openings is done after window/door frames are in place to create proper flashing and sealing; however, if stucco is applied first, windows/doors would lack a properly finished and weather-sealed opening. In typical sequencing, windows/doors are installed before stucco is applied around them, so stucco is the successor.
Stucco must be allowed to cure properly before any subsequent coatings, sealants, or finishes are applied to prevent cracking and ensure strength development.
The base coat of plaster provides the structural foundation and surface for the skim coat to adhere to; without it, skimming cannot be applied.
Screeding (leveling the base coat) ensures a flat and even substrate; skimming requires a smooth, level surface to achieve a fine finish.
The base coat must be sufficiently dry and cured before skimming to prevent cracking, moisture entrapment, or delamination of the skim layer.
Skimming applies the final thin layer of plaster; once set, sanding and finishing are required to achieve a smooth, paint-ready surface.
The skim coat must be fully dried and finished before any paint or decorative coating can be applied to the wall surface.
The tile substrate (e.g., concrete slab, plywood underlayment) must be in place before any preparatory work like cleaning, leveling, or priming can be performed on it.
All rough framing, wall structures, and subfloor systems need to be complete so that the substrate surfaces are accessible and stable for preparation.
Plumbing pipes, drain lines, and other rough-ins that will be embedded in or pass through the substrate must be installed before substrate preparation to avoid rework or damage.
The substrate must be properly prepared (cleaned, leveled, primed, moisture-tested) before tile can be set with mortar or adhesive to ensure proper adhesion and long-term performance.
In wet areas, waterproofing membranes are applied directly onto the prepared substrate; substrate preparation must be complete to ensure the membrane bonds correctly and provides a watertight seal.

The subfloor must be clean, level, dry, and structurally sound before thin-set mortar can be applied. Any debris, moisture, or unevenness will compromise the bond of the thin-set mortar to the substrate.

If the substrate is a newly poured concrete slab, it must be fully cured (typically 28 days) before applying thin-set mortar. Applying mortar over uncured concrete can lead to moisture issues and poor adhesion.

Some substrates require a primer to be applied and fully dried before thin-set mortar. The primer improves adhesion and seals the substrate; skipping this step or applying mortar before the primer dries will result in bond failure.

Thin-set mortar acts as the bonding adhesive for tiles. Tiles must be embedded into the wet thin-set mortar before it skins over or dries. If the mortar dries first, the tiles will not adhere properly.

After tile installation into the thin-set mortar, the mortar must be allowed to cure (typically 24-48 hours) before any grouting or foot traffic occurs. Disturbing the uncured mortar will dislodge tiles and compromise the installation.

The subfloor must be clean, level, dry, and structurally sound before any tile layout and cutting can begin. Laying tiles on an unprepared subfloor would result in uneven tiles, cracking, and adhesive failure.

A moisture barrier or waterproofing membrane must be installed prior to tile layout to protect the subfloor and tile adhesive from moisture damage, especially in wet areas like bathrooms and kitchens.

Tiles must be laid out and cut to size before adhesive is applied to ensure proper fit, pattern alignment, and to minimize waste. Cutting tiles after adhesive placement would be impractical and messy.
Grouting can only begin after tiles have been laid out, cut, and set in adhesive. Grout fills the joints between placed tiles, so the tile layout must be complete first.
Accurate measurements and marking of reference lines on the subfloor must be completed before tile layout and cutting to ensure tiles are aligned properly and cuts are made to the correct dimensions.
The surface (subfloor or wall) must be clean, level, dry, and structurally sound before any tiles can be set, otherwise tiles will crack or loosen.
In wet areas (bathrooms, showers), waterproofing membrane must be fully cured before tiling to prevent moisture damage behind tiles.
Plumbing and electrical rough-ins must be inspected and approved before tiling covers them up, avoiding costly rework.
Grout cannot be applied until all tiles are firmly set in the thinset/mortar bed; grouting fills the joints between already-placed tiles.
Sealer is typically applied after tiles and grout have cured; however some natural stone tiles require sealing before grouting. In the standard sequence, sealing follows tile placement.
Grout is used to bond and protect post-tensioning tendons; tendons must be installed and stressed before grouting can fill the ducts.
Grout is injected into ducts that house the tendons; ducts must be in place before grout can be applied.
Tendons must first be tensioned/stressed to the required force, and then grout is applied to lock in the prestress and protect against corrosion.
After grout is applied, it must be allowed to cure and gain strength before any subsequent loads or construction activities can proceed.

In post-tensioned concrete, grout application completes the tendon encapsulation; however formwork removal is typically dictated by concrete strength rather than grouting, so this is a soft preference for sequencing.
Expansion joints are installed within or between tile fields. The tile substrate and tile setting must be in place before the expansion joint material can be installed.
Expansion joints must be installed and fully set before grout or sealant is applied, so that the joint is properly formed and the sealant bonds correctly to the joint sides.
The substrate must be clean, level, and cured before any tile work including expansion joints begins, to ensure proper adhesion and joint performance.
It is preferable to complete expansion joint installation before final cleaning to avoid damaging the joint or introducing debris into the joint cavity.
Expansion joints must be fully cured and set before allowing foot or vehicular traffic to prevent displacement or deformation of the joint material.
Subfloor must be properly prepared (cleaned, leveled, and moisture-barrier installed) before tile base and transitions can be installed to ensure proper adhesion and a level finished surface.
The main tile flooring must be fully installed, set, and grouted before tile baseboards and transition strips can be placed, as transitions bridge the finished floor to adjacent surfaces.
Underlayment or backer board must be laid and secured prior to tile base installation to provide a stable substrate and the correct finished floor height for transitions.
Once base and transitions are installed, final cleaning, grout sealing, and floor protection can be applied; however this is a soft preference as cleaning can be done before if needed.
Tile base and transitions must be installed before wall base or shoe molding is added, because the wall trim typically sits atop or abuts the tile base.
Tile backer board must be installed over structural framing; there is no substrate to attach to without completed framing.
Exterior sheathing (e.g., plywood or OSB) provides a flat, rigid substrate for the backer board to be fastened to.
Plumbing pipes and shower valves must be installed within the wall before the backer board is placed, as accessing them after would require destructive removal of the board.
Electrical wiring, boxes, and any in-wall fixtures must be roughed in before backer board installation to avoid cutting or removing the board later.
Liquid or sheet waterproofing membranes must be applied over the backer board surface (especially in wet areas like showers) to create a watertight assembly before tiling.
Backer board provides the rigid, cementitious substrate required for bonding tile; tile cannot be installed directly on framing or drywall in wet areas.
Grout fills joints between tiles after they are set on the backer board; grouting is the final step after tile placement.

The substrate (concrete slab, plywood, or existing underlayment) must be clean, dry, smooth, and structurally sound before any waterproofing membrane can be applied. Debris, dust, or uneven surfaces would compromise membrane adhesion and integrity.

Any necessary slope towards drains or self-leveling compounds must be completed prior to waterproofing, as the membrane must be applied over a properly sloped and cured substrate to ensure drainage and prevent ponding.
Substrate cracks and joints must be filled or bridged with appropriate crack isolation materials before waterproofing, otherwise membrane may tear or fail at those locations.

successor: Tile Installation (Thin-set Mortar Application & Tile Setting)
rationale: The waterproof membrane must be fully cured and continuous before tile is installed over it. Tile cannot be set directly onto an unfinished or uncured membrane, as the mortar needs a stable, waterproofed base and the membrane must be intact to provide the waterproof barrier.
A flood test (typically 24-48 hour water test) is performed after membrane cure to verify no leaks exist. This test must be completed before tile installation to allow access for repairs if needed.

Grouting is the final step in the tile assembly and only occurs after the tile is set upon the waterproofed substrate. However, the membrane must be in place first to protect the substrate from grout moisture and to ensure the waterproofing system is continuous beneath the tile.

Tile trim and edge profiles are installed as part of the tiling process, and the substrate must be properly prepared (clean, level, and ready for tile installation) before any trim or edge profiles can be placed.

Edge profiles and trims (such as schluter strips or corner beads) are typically installed before or during tile setting to create finished edges and transitions; tiles are then placed up to or over the profiles.
Grouting can only occur after tiles and any edge trim profiles are fully installed in place, as the grout fills the joints between tiles and along trim edges.
Waterproofing membranes and underlayments must be installed over the substrate before any tile work including trim profiles begins, to ensure proper moisture protection beneath the tiled surface.
Final cleaning and finishing touches are typically done after all trim and tile installation is complete to avoid damaging the profiles during other finishing work.
Tile spacers and leveling systems can only be placed after tiles have been set into the adhesive/mortar, as they are used to create consistent gaps and level the tiles during the setting process.
The adhesive must be allowed to cure undisturbed; spacers and leveling systems must be removed or adjusted before final curing is complete to avoid locking them into the set mortar.
Grouting can only begin after tiles are properly spaced, leveled, and the adhesive has set; grout fills the uniform gaps created by spacers.
The substrate must be clean, level, and prepared before tiles are laid and spacers are used; otherwise, the spacers and leveling system cannot function correctly and tile alignment will be poor.
After spacers and leveling systems are removed, final cleaning and finishing of the tile surface can be performed more easily, though this can also be done concurrently in some cases.

successor: Heated Floor System Integration for Tile
rationale: Electrical rough-in (wiring, thermostat cables, junction boxes) must be installed before the heated floor system is laid, as the heating cables or mats are connected to the electrical supply and need power availability.

successor: Heated Floor System Integration for Tile
rationale: The subfloor must be clean, level, and structurally sound before installing heating mats or cables to ensure even heat distribution and prevent damage to the heating elements.

successor: Heated Floor System Integration for Tile
rationale: A vapor barrier should be placed beneath the heating system to protect against moisture migration from the subfloor, which could damage the electrical components or compromise the tile installation.

predecessor: Heated Floor System Integration for Tile
successor: Thin-set Mortar / Self-Leveling Underlayment Over Heating Elements
rationale: After the heating cables or mats are laid and secured, a thin-set mortar or self-leveling compound must be applied to encapsulate the heating elements before tile can be installed on top.

predecessor: Heated Floor System Integration for Tile
rationale: Tile must be installed over the completed and tested heated floor system (with the encapsulating mortar cured) to permanently cover and protect the heating elements.

successor: Tile Sealer and Grout Sealer Application
rationale: Tile sealer and grout sealer can only be applied after tiles and grout have been fully installed and cured. The sealer is applied to the finished tile and grout surfaces to protect them.

predecessor: Tile Sealer and Grout Sealer Application
rationale: After applying the sealer, sufficient drying and curing time is required for the sealer to bond and cure properly before any further work or traffic occurs on the surface.

predecessor: Tile Sealer and Grout Sealer Application
successor: Final Cleaning and Inspection of Tiled Surfaces
rationale: It is preferred to complete sealing before final cleaning and inspection to ensure the sealed surface is clean and ready for final review, but not a strict physical necessity.

successor: Tile Sealer and Grout Sealer Application
rationale: Tiles and grout must be thoroughly cleaned and free of dust, debris, and contaminants before sealer application to ensure proper adhesion and an even finish.

predecessor: Tile Sealer and Grout Sealer Application
rationale: The sealed surface must not be used or trafficked until the sealer has fully cured to avoid damaging the sealant film and compromising protection.
The AHU must be set on its foundation or base before ductwork can be connected, as the ductwork attaches to the unit's casing and requires the unit to be in its final fixed position.

The AHU casing, including coils, filters, and fans, must be fully assembled and installed in its permanent location so that the ductwork connection points (flanges, collars) are accessible and properly aligned.

Any structural supports, curbs, or roof penetrations for supply/return/exhaust ductwork must be in place before ductwork is routed and connected to the AHU, to ensure safe and code-compliant support pathways.

Duct insulation and vapor barriers are applied after the ductwork is fully connected to the AHU to ensure continuous coverage over all joints and connections, preventing condensation and thermal bridging.
The ductwork must be fully connected to the AHU before the system can be started, airflow can be measured, and dampers can be balanced to achieve design air distribution throughout the building.
Structural steel must be in place to support ductwork hangers and supports before ductwork can be installed.
Electrical conduits and junction boxes must be roughed in before ductwork to avoid conflicts and ensure proper clearances above ceilings.
Plumbing pipes and drainage must be roughed in before ductwork to prevent cross-trade interference and allow proper routing.
Duct insulation cannot be applied until the bare ductwork is fully installed, hung, and connected to avoid trapping moisture and ensure complete coverage.

successor: Start-up and Testing of HVAC System
rationale: Supply ductwork must be fully installed and sealed before the HVAC system can be started up and tested to ensure balanced airflow and prevent air loss.
Rough-in inspection must be completed before enclosing ductwork to ensure all mechanical systems are properly installed and meet code requirements before they are concealed behind finished surfaces.
Return ductwork must be installed first so that insulation can be applied to the exterior of the installed ducts for thermal efficiency and condensation control.
Return ductwork must be fully installed and secured before drywall is hung, as the ducts run within wall and ceiling cavities that will be enclosed by drywall.
Return ductwork must be fully installed and connected before the HVAC system can be balanced to ensure proper airflow and pressure throughout the system.
Structural framing must be complete to provide the support framework and chases through which return ductwork is routed and hung.
Structural steel framework must be in place to provide support and hanging points for exhaust ductwork.
Utility rough-ins must be completed to avoid interference and to allow coordination of duct routing with other building services.
Dedicated overhead supports, hangers, and seismic bracing must be installed before ductwork can be hung and secured.
Ductwork must be fully installed, leak-tested, and approved before insulation can be applied to the duct surfaces.
Exhaust ductwork must be in place so that fire dampers can be installed at duct penetrations through fire-rated walls and then tested for proper operation.
All overhead ductwork must be completed and pressure-tested before ceilings are enclosed to allow access for adjustments and inspections.
Structural steel framing must be in place to provide support and hanging points for ductwork, including fresh air intake ducts.
The roof deck must be completed to provide the penetration point and weatherproof collar for the fresh air intake hood and ductwork that passes through the roof.
Insulation must be applied after the fresh air intake ductwork is installed to ensure full coverage around the duct exterior for thermal and condensation control.
The fresh air intake ductwork must be in place before it can be connected to the air handling unit's outside air intake section.
Ductwork must be fully installed and sealed before airflow testing and balancing can be performed to measure and adjust fresh air intake rates.

predecessor: HVAC Design and Duct Routing Layout
