rationale: The duct layout and sizing must be designed and approved before any duct can be fabricated and installed, to ensure correct routing, airflow, and coordination with other building systems.
Structural supports, hangers, and the building frame must be in place to provide attachment points for ductwork before ducts can be hung and secured.
Insulation must be applied to the exterior of installed ductwork to prevent condensation and thermal loss; this cannot be done until the duct is in place.

successor: Duct Leakage Testing and Air Balancing
rationale: Pressure testing and air balancing to verify duct integrity and proper airflow distribution can only be performed after the duct system is fully installed and sealed.
Final enclosure of ceilings and walls with drywall or panels must occur after duct installation to allow access for duct hanging, connections, and testing.

predecessor: HVAC Ductwork Layout Planning and Approval
rationale: The layout and routing of spiral round ducts must be planned and approved before installation to ensure proper coordination with other building systems and structural elements.
Structural framing (beams, columns, roof structure) must be in place to provide support and attachment points for hanging spiral round ducts.

predecessor: Overhead MEP Rough-in (Electrical, Plumbing, Fire Protection)
rationale: Other overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins should be completed first to avoid conflicts and allow for proper routing of spiral round ducts in the available ceiling space.
Insulation must be applied after the spiral round duct is installed in its final position to ensure full coverage and proper thermal performance.
Air balancing and system testing can only begin after spiral round ducts are fully installed, connected, and sealed to measure correct airflow and system performance.
Flexible duct installation must occur after the HVAC rough-in inspection to ensure the ductwork meets code requirements before being covered or connected.
Flexible ducts are installed after wall and ceiling framing and drywall are complete to allow proper routing and support within the building cavities.

successor: Connect duct to HVAC equipment and diffusers
rationale: Flexible duct must first be positioned and secured in place before making final connections to air handling units, plenums, and room diffusers.
After flexible duct is installed, all joints and connections must be sealed with mastic or tape and insulated to prevent air leakage and thermal loss.
System balancing and airflow testing can only be performed after all flexible ducts are installed, connected, and sealed to measure actual performance.

Ductwork hangers and supports are typically anchored to the building's structural steel or concrete framing. Without the primary structural elements in place, there is no surface to attach hangers and supports.

General overhead MEP rough-in work, including larger piping and conduit runs, must be completed first to establish the overhead zone layout. Duct hanger locations must be coordinated around these existing elements.
Duct sections cannot be placed and connected until the supporting hangers and brackets are installed and secured. The hangers provide the immediate structural support for the ductwork.

While duct insulation can be applied after ducts are hung, it is preferred that the support system is fully in place before insulation work begins so that insulation can be continuous around the duct without gaps at hanger locations.
Fire and smoke dampers are installed within the ductwork system. The ductwork must be supported before heavy dampers are fitted, and damper installation follows duct placement.
Volume control dampers are installed within ductwork systems; the ductwork must be in place to provide the physical location and support for the damper.
Dampers must be installed and sealed before duct leakage testing can be performed to ensure the system is airtight and the damper operates correctly within the sealed duct.
HVAC balancing adjusts airflow using the volume control dampers; therefore dampers must be installed and operable before balancing can take place.
If the volume control damper is combined with a fire damper, testing of fire dampers typically follows installation but is a separate operation that could be done concurrently in some sequences.
Overhead supports and structural framing must be in place to hang and secure ductwork and associated dampers.
The motorized fire damper is installed within the HVAC ductwork. Ductwork must be in place to provide the structural framework and location for the damper.

Fire dampers are installed where ductwork penetrates fire-rated barriers. The fire-rated wall, floor, or partition must be built first so the damper can be properly mounted and sealed within the rated assembly.

Motorized fire dampers require electrical power connections for their actuator motor. The electrical rough-in (conduit, junction box, wiring) must be completed before the damper can be wired and tested.
The damper must be fully installed before it can be tested for closure, airflow leakage, and actuator operation as part of commissioning.

Insulation and finishing of ductwork in the damper vicinity should occur after damper installation to ensure the damper is accessible for adjustment and testing, and to avoid covering or obstructing the damper before it is verified.
Smoke dampers are installed within HVAC ductwork; ducts must be in place to provide the structural support and mounting surface for the damper.
Smoke dampers are mounted at fire/smoke barrier penetrations; the wall or floor assembly must be constructed first to define the penetration opening.
Duct leakage testing must include installed dampers; dampers must be in place and closed to verify system integrity.

successor: Fire Alarm / Smoke Detection System Testing
rationale: Smoke dampers are typically tied to fire alarm and smoke detection systems for automatic closure; the damper must be installed before testing these control and actuation interfaces.
Access to overhead smoke dampers for installation, adjustment, and inspection must occur before ceilings are enclosed to allow proper clearance and future maintenance access.
Backdraft dampers are installed within HVAC ductwork; the duct system must be in place before dampers can be mounted inside it.

successor: Duct Leakage Testing and Air Balancing
rationale: Dampers must be installed before the duct system is tested and balanced to ensure they are properly incorporated and functioning in the airflow control.
Damper installation is a prerequisite for commissioning because the system must be fully assembled with dampers in place before performance verification and inspection.
The duct-mounted access door must be fabricated and assembled as part of the ductwork before it can be installed.
Duct insulation is applied after the access door is installed so that the door is accessible and properly integrated into the insulated duct envelope.
Balancing and commissioning typically occur after installation of all duct components including access doors to ensure proper airflow and system performance.

predecessor: Duct Layout and Routing Plan Approval
rationale: The duct routing and layout must be approved before duct takeoff fittings can be positioned, as the takeoff connects to the main duct run and must align with the approved layout.
The main duct run must be installed first because the duct takeoff fitting is a branch connection that attaches to the main duct; it cannot be installed without the main duct in place.
Structural elements such as ceilings, walls, and framing must be roughed in to provide the support and clear space for installing duct takeoff fittings.
Branch ducts connect to the duct takeoff fitting; the takeoff serves as the transition point from the main duct, so it must be installed before branch ductwork can be attached.
All duct connections including takeoff fittings must be installed and sealed before final insulation can be applied over the joints and connections.
The duct elbow's position and orientation must be determined by the overall duct layout and routing plan before installation can begin.
The physical duct elbow component must be procured and delivered to the site before it can be installed.
Structural supports and hangers for the duct system must be in place to secure the duct elbow during installation.
The duct elbow must be installed as part of the complete duct run before the entire duct system can be pressure-tested for leaks and integrity.
The duct elbow must be installed first so that insulation can be applied around its exterior surfaces for thermal and condensation control.
The duct layout and routing must be designed first to determine where transitions and reducers are needed for changes in duct dimensions.
Structural framing and rough-in work must be completed to provide the support framework and clear openings through which duct transitions and reducers can be installed.
The transition/reducer piece must be in place before adjacent duct sections can be connected and sealed to it.
Insulation is applied after the duct component is installed to ensure complete coverage and thermal protection of the transition/reducer.
The transition/reducer must be installed and sealed before the system can be tested for proper airflow and pressure balancing.
Duct silencers are installed inline within the main ductwork runs. The main supply and return duct trunks must be in place before silencers can be positioned and connected.

predecessor: HVAC Rough-In / Ductwork Layout and Support Framing
rationale: Support framing, hangers, and structural rough-in for ductwork must be installed prior to placing heavy silencer units to provide proper structural support.

successor: HVAC Ductwork Final Connections and Sealing
rationale: After the silencer is installed, final duct connections (upstream and downstream) must be made and all joints sealed to ensure airtight system performance.
The silencer is a component of the air distribution path; system balancing and airflow testing can only be performed once all inline components including silencers are fully installed.
Verification that the silencer meets noise reduction specifications is best performed after installation, but this is a quality assurance step rather than a hard physical dependency.
Ducts must be installed and in place before any sealing can be applied to joints, seams, or connections.
Duct insulation must be installed after sealing is complete, as sealing the joints first ensures airtightness; insulating over unsealed ducts would trap leaks and reduce efficiency.

Pressure testing identifies leaks which are then sealed; however, in typical sequences, sealing is done before final pressure testing. If reordering, initial rough testing may precede sealing, but the final air leakage test must be done after sealing is complete.
System balancing and commissioning should only be performed after ducts are sealed to ensure accurate airflow measurements and proper system performance.

successor: Concealment of Ductwork (e.g., ceiling closure, drywall)
rationale: Ducts must be sealed before they are enclosed behind walls, ceilings, or other finishes, as access to joints is required for proper sealing and subsequent inspection.
Ductwork must be fully installed, assembled, and sealed before pressure testing can be performed to verify system integrity and air-tightness.
Insulation must not be applied until pressure testing is complete, as insulation would conceal leaks and make testing impossible or inaccurate.
If testing reveals leaks, remediation sealing work follows immediately after testing, though this is a conditional soft dependency based on test results.
System air balancing and final commissioning require verified ductwork integrity confirmed by successful pressure testing before proceeding with airflow adjustments.
Ceilings, drywall, or other enclosures must not be closed/installed until ductwork pressure testing is complete, as access is required to locate and repair any air leaks discovered during testing.
Structural framing must be in place to provide support and attachment points for ductwork hangers and supports.
Structural inspections must be passed before commencing ductwork installation to ensure the building structure is safe and ready for MEP rough-in.
The HVAC design and ductwork layout drawings must be finalized and approved to provide the necessary dimensions, routing, and specifications for installation.
Ductwork must be fully installed and connected before insulation can be applied to prevent moisture issues and ensure complete coverage.
Ductwork must be in place before ceiling grids are installed, as ducts are concealed above the ceiling and would be inaccessible afterward.
Diffusers and grilles are the terminal devices that connect to ductwork; ductwork must be installed and in place before diffusers and grilles can be attached to the duct openings.
Diffusers and grilles are typically mounted into or supported by the ceiling grid system; the ceiling grid must be installed to provide a mounting surface and proper alignment.

All diffusers and grilles must be installed before the HVAC system can be balanced and commissioned, as balancing requires adjusting dampers at each terminal device and measuring airflow through the installed diffusers/grilles.
Ceiling tiles are installed around diffusers and grilles; diffusers and grilles must be in place first so that ceiling tiles can be cut and fitted to accommodate them.
Installing diffusers and grilles before final painting or finishing allows for any touch-up work around the diffuser frame and avoids damaging freshly painted surfaces during installation.
The reheat coil is mounted within the ductwork, so the duct sections where the coil will be installed must be in place first.
Duct supports and structural framing must be in place to bear the weight of the duct-mounted reheat coil.

successor: Ductwork pressure testing and leak check
rationale: The reheat coil penetrates the duct wall; after installation the duct section must be sealed and tested for leaks before system commissioning.

successor: HVAC control wiring and thermostat connection
rationale: The reheat coil's actuator and valve must be electrically connected and controlled after the coil is physically mounted in the duct.

successor: Pipe connection to hot water/chilled water supply
rationale: The coil's hydronic piping connections must be made after the coil is secured in place, and these connections must precede final system filling and balancing.
The duct-mounted humidifier is physically installed into the HVAC ductwork. The ductwork must be in place to provide the mounting location and air path for the humidifier.
The humidifier must be installed before the HVAC system can be fully balanced and tested, as the humidifier affects air flow and system performance.
A duct-mounted humidifier typically requires an electrical power supply for its controls, solenoid valve, and fan. Electrical rough-in (wiring, outlet) must be completed to provide power to the unit.

successor: Duct Insulation (if required around humidifier section)
rationale: While not always required, insulating the duct section around the humidifier after installation is a best practice to prevent condensation and heat loss. It is a soft preference as it depends on climate zone and design specs.

The humidifier requires a connection to a water supply line (typically from the nearest plumbing riser or cold water line). The water supply rough-in must be completed before the humidifier can be connected and operated.
Electrical power and control wiring must be roughed-in to the VAV box location before the duct connection is made to ensure accessibility for wiring terminations and to avoid rework.
The main supply duct trunk must be installed and in place so that the VAV box can be physically connected to the duct system.
The VAV box itself must be hung and secured in its final position before duct connections can be made to its inlet and outlet collars.
All duct connections to the VAV box must be completed before insulation can be applied or the duct system can be pressure-tested for leaks.
The duct connection must be completed before final wiring and control devices (actuators, sensors) are connected to the VAV box, to avoid damage during duct work.
Electrical rough-in must be completed to provide power and control wiring connections for the plenum box before it can be installed.
The plenum box connects to the HVAC ductwork system, so the main duct runs must be in place before the plenum box can be integrated.
While not strictly required, installing the ceiling grid first provides support and reference for positioning the plenum box within the ceiling space.
The plenum box must be physically installed and secured before ductwork can be connected to it.
Plenum box installation must be complete and tested before ceiling tiles are installed, as the plenum box is located above the ceiling and access is needed for connections and adjustments.

Structural framing and roof decking must be in place before kitchen exhaust ducts can be routed through the roof and ceiling spaces, as the ductwork requires structural support and penetration locations.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical and plumbing for kitchen
rationale: Rough electrical and plumbing work in the kitchen area should be completed before installing exhaust ducts to avoid conflicts and ensure adequate clearance for the duct route.
The duct must be installed first so that the exhaust fan and hood can be connected directly to the ductwork.
Fireproofing and insulation wrap are applied to the installed duct to meet fire code requirements; the duct must be in position before these finishes can be applied.
Ceiling drywall and finishes are installed after the exhaust ductwork is in place, as the duct is concealed within the ceiling plenum.
The exhaust duct requires structural supports (hangers, brackets, or trapezes) to be in place before the ductwork can be suspended and secured.
The building must be weather-tight (roof, walls, glazing) before installing ductwork to prevent moisture ingress and damage to the duct material.

predecessor: Rough-In Electrical and Conduit Work (Overhead Zone)
rationale: Working above ceiling in the same overhead zone is more efficient if electrical rough-ins are completed first to avoid conflicts and rework, though not physically mandated.
The exhaust duct system must be fully installed and sealed before pressure/leakage tests can be performed to verify system integrity.
Insulation and fireproofing wraps are applied to the completed ductwork; they cannot be installed until the ducts are in their final position.
Ductwork must be in place and tested before ceilings are closed in, to allow access for adjustments and verification.

successor: Laboratory Fume Hood Connection and Commissioning
rationale: The main exhaust duct trunk must be available before individual fume hood branch connections can be made and the system commissioned.
Pipework routing often requires structural steel supports and hangers to be in place before pipes can be installed and secured.
Foundations must be completed to provide stable base support for pipe racks, equipment, and underground piping systems before routing can begin.
Underground drainage and below-ground pipework must be completed before above-ground pipework routing to avoid excavation conflicts and ensure proper connection sequencing.
Insulation can only be applied after the pipework is fully routed, installed, and pressure-tested to ensure complete coverage and integrity.
Final connections to mechanical equipment such as pumps, chillers, and boilers require the pipework to be routed and aligned first before making fixed connections.

Pipework supports and hangers are typically attached to the steel structure (columns, beams, or roof trusses). The steel frame must be erected and stabilized before any supports can be installed onto it.
Pipework is laid onto and secured to the installed supports and hangers. The supports must be in place to hold the pipes before the pipes can be run.
Where pipe supports are floor-mounted or cast into concrete, the concrete slab or foundation must be poured and cured to provide a stable base for support installation.
Once pipes are hung on their supports, subsequent work such as insulation application and pressure testing of the pipework system can proceed.
Coordination of overhead MEP services (ductwork, cable trays, lighting) should be resolved before installing pipe hangers to avoid spatial conflicts and rework.
Pipework must be physically installed and positioned before joints and connections can be made.
Pipe ends must be aligned, cleaned, and prepared (e.g., beveling, deburring) to ensure proper joint fit and weld/connection quality.

successor: Pipework Pressure Testing and Leak Testing
rationale: Joints and connections must be completed before pressure/leak testing can be performed to verify integrity.
Insulation and protective coatings should be applied only after all joints and connections are completed and verified, to avoid covering incomplete joints.
The complete pipework system must be jointed and connected before flushing and cleaning to remove debris and verify system continuity.
Pipework must be fully installed (including all pipes, fittings, hangers, and supports) before any testing or commissioning can take place, as testing validates the integrity of the installed system.
All welded joints and mechanical connections must be completed before pressure testing can be performed, as the test verifies the strength and leak-tightness of these joints.

Pressure testing is a core component of pipework commissioning; it must be conducted before system flushing, chemical cleaning, or final commissioning checks to verify the system can safely hold operating pressure.
After pressure testing confirms integrity, the pipework must be flushed and chemically cleaned to remove debris, weld slag, and contaminants before the system is placed into service.
Testing and commissioning is a prerequisite to formally handing over the pipework system for operational use, as it certifies that the system meets design specifications and safety requirements.
The main pipework must be installed before valves and fittings can be attached to it, as valves and fittings are components that connect into or onto the pipework system.
Valves and fittings must be in place and properly installed before the pipework system can be pressure tested to ensure the entire system, including all connections, is leak-tight.
Insulation is typically applied after valves and fittings are installed, as these components need to be accessible for adjustment and the insulation must be fitted around them.
Supports and hangers must be in place to hold the pipework securely before valves and fittings (which add weight and stress) are installed onto the pipework system.
Once all valves and fittings are installed, the complete pipework system can be flushed and cleaned to remove any debris or contaminants before final commissioning.
Pipework must be installed before creating penetrations and applying firestopping around the pipes.
The structural elements (walls, floors, slabs) must be in place so that penetrations can be cut or formed through them for pipework passage.
Firestopping must be completed before enclosing walls or floors with finishes to ensure firestopping is properly installed and inspected.
Firestopping must be fully in place before fire safety inspections can verify compartmentation integrity.

successor: Pressure Testing of Pipework (if required after firestopping sealant cure)
rationale: Some pipework pressure tests should occur after firestopping sealants have fully cured to avoid disturbing the seals, though this depends on project specifications.
Pipework must be physically installed and assembled before it can be identified and labeled, as labels are affixed to the installed pipes.
Pressure testing verifies the integrity of pipework and is typically completed before labeling to avoid damage to labels during testing or rework if pipes fail the test.
Pipework must be cleaned and flushed of debris before labeling, as labeling after cleaning ensures labels are not damaged or dislodged during cleaning operations.
Labels must be applied before insulation covers the pipework, as insulation would hide and prevent access to the labels if installed first.
Proper identification and labeling of pipework is required before system commissioning can proceed, as operators and testers need to identify pipes correctly during commissioning activities.
Pipework must be physically installed in place before corrosion protection (such as coating, wrapping, or painting) can be applied to it.
Surfaces must be cleaned and prepared (e.g., abrasive blasting, degreasing) to ensure proper adhesion of corrosion protection coatings.
Pressure testing must be completed before applying corrosion protection, as any leaks or defects discovered after coating would require costly removal and reapplication of the protection system.
Corrosion protection (e.g., anti-corrosion coating) must be fully applied and cured before insulation is installed over the pipework.
For buried pipework, corrosion protection must be completed and cured before backfilling to avoid damaging the protective coating.

Cable trays and ladder racks are typically mounted on structural steel members, walls, or overhead supports. The structural framework must be in place to provide the physical mounting points and support for the cable tray system.

Large mechanical ducts, pipes, and plumbing lines that occupy overhead space must be installed first so that cable trays can be routed around them with proper clearances, avoiding clashes and ensuring adequate separation.
Overhead conduit runs should be installed before cable trays to prevent interference and to allow cable trays to be positioned without conflicts, maintaining required bending radii and access space.

Cable trays and ladder racks serve as the physical support pathway for cables. The tray system must be fully installed, secured, and inspected before any cables can be laid, pulled, or secured within them.

After cable trays are installed and before cables are pulled, firestop systems at tray penetrations through fire-rated walls and floors must be installed to maintain fire-resistance ratings, though final firestopping around cables occurs after cable installation.
Underground conduit or rough-in work must be placed before overhead or wall conduit systems are installed to ensure proper foundation and below-grade paths are established.
Conduits are typically run within or along structural elements; the structural frame must be in place to provide support and embedment points for conduit routing.
Conduits must be fully installed, connected, and inspected before wires or cables are pulled through them, as the conduit serves as the protective raceway.
Conduit must terminate into boxes and enclosures before devices (outlets, switches, panels) can be mounted and connected.

While firestopping can begin after conduit is installed, it is a soft preference because some firestopping can be done concurrently; however, final sealing around conduit penetrations occurs after conduit placement.
Cable trunking and raceways are typically mounted on or supported by structural steel or metal decking, so the steel structure must be in place before cable support systems can be installed.

predecessor: Overhead Mechanical Services Installation (HVAC ducts, pipes)
rationale: Large mechanical services are installed first to allow cable trunking to be routed around them; installing trunking earlier would obstruct access for mechanical runs.
Underfloor or embedded raceways require the concrete slab to be poured and cured before raceway installation can commence or before trunking can be fixed to the slab.
Cables are laid into or pulled through trunking and raceways after the containment systems are fully installed and secured.
Junction boxes and outlet boxes are often mounted on or aligned with trunking runs; trunking must be in place to position and support these boxes.
Structural steel provides the primary support framework onto which cable baskets and mesh systems are mounted. The steel structure must be in place before cable trays can be securely attached.

Large HVAC ducts must be installed first as they occupy significant overhead space and are typically routed above cable trays. Installing cable baskets before ductwork would create conflicts and require rework.

Major piping systems (sprinkler mains, plumbing risers) should be installed before cable trays since pipes are larger, less flexible to route around obstacles, and often must maintain specific slopes.

Cable baskets and mesh systems serve as the support pathway for low voltage cables. The tray system must be fully installed and secured before any cables can be laid into or pulled through the baskets.
Power cables are often routed within or alongside cable tray systems. The tray infrastructure must be in place to support and contain the electrical conductors before cables can be run.

Cable trays and ladders provide the primary support and routing pathway for cables. Cable glands and entry fittings are installed at the termination points of these cable routes, so the support structure must be in place first.

Cable glands are fitted onto the cables themselves after they have been pulled into position, securing them at entry points to equipment or enclosures. The cables must be in place before the glands can be installed.

Cable glands secure the cable at the entry point to equipment. After the gland is installed and tightened, the cable cores inside the equipment can be terminated and connected to terminals. Termination cannot occur before the gland is fixed.

Glands are installed into gland plates or entry plates which are then mounted onto enclosures. The gland installation into the plate must precede the final mounting of the plate assembly onto the enclosure.

successor: Earthing and Bonding of Cable Screens/Armour
rationale: Earthing connections for cable screens or armour are typically made at the gland, using earthing rings or tags integrated with the gland assembly. The gland must be fitted first to establish the earthing path.
Cables must be pulled through installed conduits or laid in cable trays; conduits and trays provide the physical pathway for cables.
Cable trays and ladders must be in place to support and route cables before cable pulling can commence.
Cables are terminated at electrical panels and switchgear; these enclosures must be installed and positioned before cable pulling and termination.
Cables must first be pulled and laid into position before they can be terminated (stripped, connected, and lugged) at equipment and panels.
Cables must be installed and terminated before electrical testing (e.g., insulation resistance, continuity) can be performed to verify integrity.
Cables must be physically laid and routed into position before their ends can be terminated and connected to equipment or panels.
Cables need to be pulled and tensioned to the correct length and position before the excess can be cut and terminations applied.
Cable support systems (trays, ladders, conduits) must be installed first to provide the pathway and support for cables before their ends are terminated.
Terminations and connections must be completed before electrical testing (e.g., insulation resistance, continuity, hi-pot testing) can be performed to verify the integrity of the connections.
Power cannot be applied to the circuit until all cable terminations and connections are properly completed and verified to avoid electrical hazards and equipment damage.
Cables must be physically laid and installed before they can be tested and commissioned, as testing requires the cable to be in its final position and connected.
Cable ends must be terminated and connected to equipment or panels before testing can be performed to verify continuity and insulation integrity.
Support systems such as trays, ladders, and conduits must be installed first to provide the physical pathway for cable laying.
Cables must be tested and commissioned to confirm they are safe and functional before the system is energized and placed into service.

Although testing is typically completed before final labeling and documentation, some minor labeling adjustments may be done concurrently; however best practice is to finalize testing before completing documentation to capture actual test results.
Cable trays and ladders provide the physical support infrastructure for cables; cables cannot be dressed and managed until the support pathways are installed.
Cables must first be pulled into position before they can be dressed, tied, and managed within the trays or ladders.
Cables must be dressed and properly positioned before termination to ensure correct cable routing, service loops, and accessibility for connections.
Cables need to be dressed and secured before testing to ensure test results reflect the final installed configuration and to avoid movement during tests.
While labeling can begin during dressing, final permanent labels are best applied after dressing to ensure labels align correctly with the dressed cable routes.
The sprinkler control valve must be connected to the main sprinkler piping system; therefore, the main piping must be installed first.
Main piping pressure testing must be completed before installing the control valve to avoid damaging the valve during testing.

successor: Connect Branch Lines to Control Valve
rationale: Branch lines (zone piping) connect downstream of the control valve; the valve must be in place before branch connections can be made.

successor: Install Flow Switches and Alarm Devices
rationale: Flow switches and alarm devices are typically installed downstream of the control valve and require the valve to be in position to define the zone boundaries.

successor: Flush and Hydrostatically Test Sprinkler System
rationale: System flushing and hydrostatic testing occur after the valve is installed to verify the entire system, including the valve assembly, is leak-free and operational.

predecessor: Cable Pathway Installation (e.g., Cable Tray, Conduit, Ladder Rack)
rationale: The firestop sealant or device must be applied around cables and the pathway system (cable trays, conduits, etc.). The pathway structure must be physically in place so that the firestop material can be properly installed at the penetration points through fire-rated walls, floors, or partitions.

Firestop systems are installed at penetrations through fire-rated barriers. The barriers (e.g., drywall, concrete walls, floors) must be built and cured before any penetration firestop work can be performed.

After firestop installation is complete, it must be inspected and tested to verify compliance with fire-resistance ratings, listing requirements, and building codes before the penetrations can be enclosed or concealed.

Cables must be installed and terminated after firestop systems are in place if the firestop is designed for the specific cable fill. Alternatively, if the pathway is a cable tray, the firestop is often installed after cables are laid. However, in strict sequence planning, firestop installation around cable bundles must occur after cables are pulled through the penetration. The more common sequence is: pathway installed -> cables pulled -> firestop applied. But if we consider the firestop itself, cables must be present so that the sealant can be packed around them. Thus, cable pulling should precede firestop application.

Coordination of all mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins must be completed and approved to ensure that firestop locations align with all penetrations and that no conflicts exist before firestop material is applied.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical and fire alarm wiring
rationale: Electrical power and fire alarm connections must be roughed in before the pump can be installed and wired.
The fire sprinkler pump requires connection to a water supply source; underground water mains must be in place before the pump can be connected.

successor: Fire sprinkler pump testing and commissioning
rationale: The pump must be physically installed before it can be tested, started, and commissioned.

successor: Above-ground sprinkler piping connection to pump
rationale: Above-ground sprinkler risers and branch piping connect to the pump discharge; the pump must be set before these connections are made.

successor: Fire pump controller installation and programming
rationale: The pump controller is typically mounted and wired after the pump is installed, as it must be physically and electrically connected to the pump unit.
The underground water main must be installed to provide the water source and pressure required for the sprinkler water supply connection.
Site excavation and grading must be completed to expose the underground utilities and provide access for connecting the sprinkler water supply.
The main water supply connection must be established before branch piping for the sprinkler system can be installed, as it provides the source of water.
The water supply connection must be complete before the sprinkler system can be pressure tested, as the test requires water from the supply line.
The exterior water supply connection must be established before interior fire protection rough-in work can proceed, as it provides the water feed for the interior system.
Flow switch must be installed on the sprinkler piping; piping must be in place first.

successor: Electrical wiring and connection to fire alarm panel
rationale: Flow switch must be physically installed before electricians can wire it to the fire alarm system.
Flow switch must be installed to participate in system pressure testing.

successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: Flow switch must be wired and operational before overall fire alarm testing can proceed.
While not physically mandatory, it is preferred to install and test the flow switch before enclosing it in ceilings to avoid costly rework.
The sprinkler riser must connect to the building's main water supply line, which is part of rough-in plumbing. The water supply piping must be in place before the riser can be installed.
The riser typically sits on or connects to piping embedded in the slab, so underslab plumbing work must be completed first.
The riser is typically mounted to or supported by structural walls or columns; framing must be in place to provide support and clearance.
Branch lines that feed individual sprinkler heads connect to and are fed from the riser; the riser must be installed first to serve as the distribution manifold.
Sprinkler heads are installed on branch lines that connect to the riser; the riser must be in place to pressurize and test the system before final head installation.

Sprinkler piping must be installed first because the tamper switch is mounted on the sprinkler riser or branch pipe to monitor valve position; the physical pipe infrastructure must be in place to attach the switch.
The tamper switch must be installed before pressure testing so that the switch can be verified as properly sealed and its electrical components are not damaged during the test.

successor: Electrical Conduit and Wiring to Fire Alarm Panel
rationale: The tamper switch must be physically mounted and its terminal connections completed before the conduit and wiring can be connected from the switch to the fire alarm control panel.

successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: The tamper switch must be installed and wired before the fire alarm system can be commissioned and tested, as the switch provides a critical input signal indicating valve position.
The sprinkler piping rough-in work including riser installation must be completed before the tamper switch can be mounted, as the switch attaches directly to the pipe or valve assembly.
The sprinkler drain valve requires connection to the sprinkler system piping; rough-in plumbing must be completed to provide the pipe connection point for the valve.
The drain valve must be installed before the system can be pressure-tested to ensure the valve is in place and sealed to hold pressure during testing.
Insulation work is typically done after valve installation to avoid interfering with the valve fitting and to allow access for adjustments.
While not strictly physically required, having the full sprinkler system (including drain valves) operational is preferred before integrated system testing to avoid draining issues during testing.

The drain valve must be installed and operational before final inspection and commissioning of the sprinkler system can be completed, as it is a required component for system functionality and code compliance.
Sprinkler pipe hangers and supports are typically attached to the structural steel or concrete deck above, so the structural framing must be in place to provide a mounting surface.

Hangers and supports must be installed before the sprinkler pipes themselves are run; however, other overhead trades may need to coordinate locations, but the hanger installation generally follows structural completion.

successor: Sprinkler Piping and Main Line Installation
rationale: Hangers and supports must be in place before any sprinkler piping can be secured to them; the pipe cannot be hung without the hangers first being installed.

successor: Fire Sprinkler Head and Branch Line Installation
rationale: Branch lines and sprinkler heads depend on the main piping and hangers being in place, as the support system must be complete before lateral runs and heads are positioned.

Sprinkler escutcheons are decorative trim plates that mount around sprinkler heads where they penetrate ceilings or walls. The sprinkler piping and branch lines must be installed first to provide the water supply infrastructure, and sprinkler heads must be connected to the piping system before escutcheons can be fitted around them.

The escutcheon plate fits around the sprinkler head where it protrudes through the finished ceiling or wall surface. The sprinkler head must be installed and in its final position before the escutcheon can be placed around it.

Escutcheon plates are typically installed after ceiling finish work is complete, as they serve as the trim piece that covers the gap between the sprinkler head and the finished ceiling surface. However, if escutcheons are considered part of the final trim, they are installed after painting but before final inspection.
All sprinkler components including escutcheons must be fully installed before the fire protection system can be tested and commissioned to ensure a complete and code-compliant system.

The ceiling support structure (grid, furring, or framing) must be in place to define the ceiling plane through which sprinkler heads and their escutcheons will protrude. Without the ceiling substrate, there is no surface against which the escutcheon can mount.

The sprinkler head guard is a protective cage or shield that is mounted around or over a sprinkler head. The sprinkler pipes and the sprinkler head itself must be installed first so that the guard can be properly positioned and attached.
The sprinkler head guard is designed to protect the sprinkler head. The head must be installed before the guard can be placed over or around it.

The sprinkler head guard must be installed before the ceiling finish (e.g., drywall, ceiling tiles) is completed, as the guard may need to be positioned relative to the ceiling plane and the finished ceiling would block access.
The sprinkler head guard should be installed before the final painting or finishing of the ceiling area to ensure the guard is properly integrated and finished around it.
While the sprinkler system can be tested without the guard in place, it is preferable to install the guard before final inspection to ensure the entire assembly is verified as complete and compliant.

predecessor: Structural Framing and Ceiling Grid Installation
rationale: Sprinkler pipes and heads are typically mounted to or suspended from the structural ceiling grid. The framing and grid must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the sprinkler system.
The water supply lines and connections for the fire sprinkler system need to be roughed in before sprinkler piping and heads can be installed and connected to the water source.

Electrical wiring for flow switches, tamper switches, and monitoring devices is often run concurrently but should ideally be roughed in to allow integration with the sprinkler system during installation.

Sprinkler heads must be installed and tested before the ceiling is enclosed with drywall, as the heads need to be positioned precisely and any leaks or issues must be resolved before access is sealed off.
It is preferable to complete sprinkler testing before painting and final finishes to avoid water damage or rework if leaks are discovered during testing.
Corner beads are installed over drywall edges to reinforce and protect corners; drywall must be in place first.
Corner beads are embedded in joint compound to create smooth finished corners; taping and mudding covers and blends the bead into the wall surface.
Framing provides the structural support for drywall; corner beads have no substrate until drywall is hung on framed walls.
Metal stud framing requires a stable, level concrete slab or foundation to anchor the bottom track (runner) and provide a solid base for vertical stud installation.
The precise layout lines for walls, partitions, door openings, and corners must be marked on the slab before metal studs can be placed, ensuring accurate alignment.
Electrical conduits and wiring are run through stud cavities after framing is complete; attempting to install them before walls are framed is not possible as there is no structure to attach to.
Plumbing lines within partition walls must be installed after the metal stud framework is erected so that pipes can be properly supported and run through stud penetrations.
Drywall sheets are screwed directly onto metal stud flanges; stud framing must be fully complete, aligned, and braced to provide the substrate for drywall attachment.
Drywall sheets are attached to wall and ceiling framing (studs, joists, and tracks). Without completed framing, there is no structural surface to mount the drywall onto.
Electrical wiring, outlet boxes, and switch boxes must be installed within the walls before drywall is placed, as they are concealed behind the drywall surface.
Plumbing pipes, drain lines, and vent stacks that run inside walls must be installed and inspected before the walls are enclosed with drywall.
Ductwork, air handler units, and ventilation components that run through wall or ceiling cavities must be in place before drywall covers them.
Drywall panels must first be measured, cut, and fitted to wall/ceiling dimensions before they can be permanently screwed or nailed into place on the framing.
Panels must be fabricated, cut, prepared and delivered to the installation location before they can be hung and fastened in place.
The primary structural steel frame must be erected to provide the supporting framework onto which panels will be hung and fastened.
Panels must first be hung and fastened securely before weatherproofing seals and joint sealants can be applied between panels.
Panels are initially hung and fastened temporarily, then final alignment, leveling, and adjustment must follow to ensure proper fit and tolerances.

Interior finishes such as drywall, insulation, or cladding typically begin after exterior panels are installed to protect interior spaces, though some interior work may proceed in parallel in different zones.
Drywall panels must be fully installed and fastened to the studs before taping and bedding can begin, as the tape is applied over the seams between adjacent drywall panels.
Taping and bedding (applying joint compound and tape to seams) must be completed and allowed to dry before sanding can smooth the compound.
The joint compound from taping and bedding must be fully dried and sanded before any primer or paint can be applied to the walls.
Taping and bedding is typically performed after or concurrently with corner bead installation; the corner bead must be embedded in joint compound, which is part of the taping and bedding process.
Taping and bedding creates a smooth base over drywall joints; texture (e.g., knockdown, orange peel) is applied after the compound is dry and sanded.
Drywall must be installed and secured to the framing before joint compound (mud) can be applied to the seams and screw heads.
Joint tape must be embedded in the first layer of mud to reinforce seams before additional coats of mud can be applied and finished smooth.
After the final coat of mud is applied and dried, sanding is required to smooth the surface before priming and painting.
The mudded and finished drywall surface must be smooth, dry, and free of dust (after sanding) before primer and paint can be applied.

While trim is often installed after mudding to allow for seamless caulking between trim and finished drywall, some trades install trim before final mudding to hide gaps; however, the preferred sequence is to finish drywall first for a cleaner look.
Rough framing must be complete to provide the structural surfaces (walls, ceilings) that require sanding and preparation before finishing.
Drywall must be installed and joints taped before sanding can smooth the taping compound and prepare surfaces for painting or finishing.
Joint compound (mud) must be applied over drywall tape and screw indentations before sanding can level and smooth these areas.
Surfaces must be sanded smooth and cleaned of dust before primer can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and a uniform finish.
Sanding and surface preparation must be fully complete before any paint coatings are applied to achieve a smooth, defect-free painted surface.

predecessor: Overhead Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP) Rough-In
rationale: All mechanical ducts, electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, and fire sprinkler lines that run above the ceiling must be completely installed and inspected before enclosing them behind drywall. This is a hard constraint because it would require costly demolition to access these systems after drywall is installed.

predecessor: Ceiling Grid / Suspended Ceiling Framework (if applicable)
rationale: Any ceiling grid supports, furring channels, or direct-attach clips must be in place to provide the substrate onto which the drywall is screwed or nailed. This is a physical prerequisite for installing the drywall itself.
All drywall panels must be hung before the joints can be taped, mudded, and sanded. Taping and finishing cannot begin until the entire ceiling surface is enclosed with drywall.

successor: Wall Drywall Installation (if sequence requires ceiling-first approach)
rationale: On many commercial sites, ceiling drywall is hung before wall drywall to allow the ceiling panels to bear on the wall top track and to avoid damaging finished wall surfaces. This is a soft preference because some crews reverse the order or work concurrently.

The ceiling must be fully drywalled, taped, and sanded before primer and paint can be applied. This is a hard physical constraint as paint cannot adhere properly to unfinished joints or bare substrate without prior preparation.
Drywall boards must be installed and fastened to the framing before any texture can be applied to the surface.
The joints and fastener heads must be taped and covered with joint compound (first coat) before texture application to create a smooth base.
The dried joint compound must be sanded smooth before texture is applied, otherwise imperfections will telegraph through the texture.
Texture must be applied and allowed to dry/cure before primer or paint can be applied to the textured surface.

successor: Final Trim and Door Installation (if subsequent to texture)
rationale: While not physically required, it is preferred to complete texture before installing finish trim and doors to prevent texture overspray from damaging them, though trim can be installed before texture if properly masked.
All MEP penetrations (pipes, ducts, conduits) must be installed before fire-caulking can seal the gaps around them through fire-rated walls and floors.

predecessor: Fire-Rated Wall and Floor Assembly Construction
rationale: Fire-rated walls, floors, and partitions must be built and in place so that the penetrations through them exist and can be sealed with firestop materials.
Fire-caulking must be completed before the inspection authority can verify that all penetrations are properly sealed and compliant with fire codes.
Fire-caulking around penetrations must be applied to the exposed substrate; applying interior finishes before caulking would cover the gaps and prevent proper sealing and inspection.
Fire-caulking around penetrations in fire-rated ceilings must be completed before ceilings are enclosed, as access to the penetrations is required for application and inspection.
Trim and reveal are installed around window and door frames to cover gaps and provide a finished look; windows and doors must be in place first so trim can be fitted to the actual openings.
Trim and reveals are typically installed against finished drywall; the drywall must be hung, taped, and mudded before trim can be nailed or adhered to the walls.
Rough-in work within walls must be completed before enclosing walls with trim; trim would otherwise block access to wiring, outlets, or plumbing.

Trim and reveals are often painted or stained as part of the finishing process; however, in typical sequences, wall painting is done before trim installation (to avoid getting paint on trim), or trim is painted separately. More critically, final touch-up painting and caulking around trim occurs after installation, and floor finishing often follows trim.

Flooring (especially hardwood, tile, or laminate) is typically installed after baseboard trim is in place, or baseboards are installed after flooring. In standard construction, base trim (baseboards) is often installed before final flooring to allow flooring to butt against the trim, but if the trim is installed after flooring, it covers the expansion gap. The more common sequence is flooring is installed, then baseboard trim covers the edges. However, to avoid confusion: in many residential builds, trim (including baseboards) is installed before final flooring to create a clean transition, requiring flooring to be cut around it. A widely accepted sequence is: rough flooring subfloor -> trim installation -> finished flooring. Given this common approach, flooring follows trim.

predecessor: Rough-in of Electrical and Mechanical Services
successor: Install Metal Furring and Resilient Channels
rationale: Electrical wiring, outlet boxes, conduit, and mechanical ductwork must be roughed-in within the wall/ceiling cavities before furring channels are installed, as the channels will enclose these services and make access difficult or impossible.

predecessor: Install Metal Furring and Resilient Channels
rationale: Metal furring and resilient channels form the supporting framework to which gypsum boards are attached. The channels must be securely fastened and leveled before any board installation can commence.

successor: Install Metal Furring and Resilient Channels
rationale: The primary structural frame (steel studs, joists, or concrete substrate) must be fully erected and stable to provide a mounting surface or supporting structure for the furring and resilient channels.

predecessor: Install Metal Furring and Resilient Channels
rationale: Firestopping, acoustical sealants, and final wall/ceiling finishes at penetration points are typically applied after the channel framework is in place but before/during drywall installation to ensure continuity of sound and fire barriers.

successor: Install Metal Furring and Resilient Channels
rationale: Plumbing pipes and fixtures that run within framed wall cavities must be installed and pressure-tested prior to enclosing them with furring channels, to allow for inspection and prevent future demolition.
Access panels and hatches are typically installed into wall or ceiling framing. The framing must be complete to provide a structure for mounting the access panels.

Electrical wiring, junction boxes, and conduit that require future access must be roughed-in before access panels are installed, so the panels can be positioned to provide correct access to these elements.
Plumbing pipes, valves, and connections that need maintenance access must be in place before access panels and hatches are installed, to ensure proper alignment for future service access.
HVAC ducts, dampers, and equipment requiring inspection or maintenance access must be installed before access panels are positioned, to ensure the panels align correctly with service points.
Access panels and hatches must be installed before drywall is finished around them, so the panels can be properly framed, set, and trimmed to be flush with the finished wall or ceiling surface.

Drywall joint compound (mud) is applied over the joints, screw heads, and seams between drywall panels. Therefore, all drywall panels must be fully hung and secured before any joint compound can be applied.

predecessor: Drywall Taping and Joint Compound Application (First Coat)
rationale: Each coat of joint compound must dry completely before the next coat is applied. However, the question asks about the activity as a whole; for the entire Drywall Joint Compound Application process, all preceding structural and drywall hanging work must be complete.
Once the final coat of joint compound is applied and dried, it must be sanded smooth to prepare the surface for priming and painting.
The joint compound must be applied, dried, and sanded before primer can be painted onto the drywall surface to seal the paper and compound.
All joint compound finishing and sanding work must be complete before any paint or decorative wall finish is applied.
Tape must be applied to clean surfaces for proper adhesion; dirt or moisture prevents bonding.
The tape must be selected and cut to appropriate lengths before it can be embedded into the joint compound.
A bed layer of joint compound must be applied to the joint before tape can be embedded into it.
The embedded tape must be in place and set before a second coat of joint compound can be applied over it.
After tape embedding, the compound must be allowed to dry and cure before further finishing coats can be applied.
Corner beads are installed over drywall panels to protect and reinforce corners; drywall must be hung first to provide the surface for bead attachment.
Drywall panels must be securely fastened to studs before corner beads can be applied, otherwise the beads would be installed on unstable panels.
Corner beads provide a straight edge for mudding/taping; taping over the beads embeds them into the joint compound and finishes the corner.
Joint compound (mud) is applied over corner beads to create a smooth, seamless finish; the beads must be in place before finishing coats can be applied.
After mudding over corner beads, sanding is required to smooth the dried compound; sanding cannot occur before beads and mud are applied.
The ground must be excavated to remove topsoil and organic material before it can be flattened and skimmed to create a level surface.
Vegetation, debris, and existing structures must be cleared from the site before flattening and skimming can be performed.
The surface must be flattened and skimmed to a uniform level before compaction can begin to ensure even density and stability.
After the area is flattened and skimmed, the sub-base layer can be prepared and laid on the leveled surface.

Internal corners cannot be finished until the adjacent wall surfaces have been plastered or rendered, as corner finishing typically involves applying joint compound, tape, or corner beads over the plastered surfaces.
The wall surfaces must be properly prepared (cleaned, primed, and any imperfections filled) before corner finishing can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and a smooth finish.
Drywall sheets must be installed and fixed before corner beading and jointing can be carried out at the internal corners.

Painting or final decorative coatings must be applied after internal corner finishing is complete, as the corner finish (compound, tape, beads) needs to be fully set, dried, and sanded before paint can be applied over it.

While final inspection typically occurs after finishing work, some inspection of corner quality may occur concurrently with other finishing trades; however, formal snagging is more efficient after all corner finishing is complete.

predecessor: Wood or surface preparation (e.g., planing, filling, priming)
rationale: The surface must be prepared with planing, filling of holes/gaps, or primer application before sanding, as sanding is meant to smooth the prepared surface, not remove large imperfections or uncured materials.
The material must first be cut or shaped to its approximate dimensions; sanding refines and finishes the shape, so rough cutting must precede sanding.

successor: Staining, painting, or final finish application
rationale: Sanding creates a smooth, clean surface necessary for stain, paint, or clear coat to adhere properly and achieve a uniform finish; applying finish before sanding would trap dust and roughness under the coating.

Sanding generates dust and material debris that would contaminate joints, adhesives, and adjacent surfaces; therefore, sanding should be completed before final assembly and installation to ensure cleanliness and proper fit.
Sanding produces fine dust that must be removed (via vacuuming, tack cloth, or damp wiping) before any finishing coat or adhesive is applied to prevent contamination and poor adhesion.
Fasteners are used to connect steel members; the steel frame must be erected first so that fastener locations are established and accessible.
Steel members must be properly aligned and plumbed before fasteners can be installed to ensure correct fit-up and structural integrity.
Fasteners must first be spotted (placed and snug-tightened) before final torquing or tensioning can be performed.
In hybrid connections, fastener spotting is often done before welding to temporarily hold members in place, though sequencing can vary by design.
Inspection of bolted connections can only occur after fasteners have been spotted and tightened to the required specification.
Electrical wiring must be roughed in within wall cavities before drywall patching seals the walls closed, as access would be lost.
Plumbing rough-in work inside walls must be completed before drywall patching covers and seals the wall cavities.
There must be a framed wall structure in place before pre-finished drywall panels can be cut and patched into position.
After pre-finished panels are patched in, the joints and seams between them need to be taped and mudded to create a smooth, continuous surface.
Pre-finished drywall patching must be complete (including joint finishing) before primer and paint can be applied over the entire wall surface.
Surface must be clean, dry, and smooth for texture to adhere properly; texture cannot be applied over dust, debris, or uneven surfaces.
Primer provides a sealed, uniform base that ensures proper texture adhesion and prevents the substrate from absorbing moisture unevenly from the texture material.
Drywall must be hung, taped, and the joints mudded and sanded smooth before any texture is applied; texture cannot cover unfinished drywall joints.
Paint must be applied over the cured texture to seal and protect it; painting cannot occur before texture is applied and dried.
It is a soft preference to install trim and hardware after texture to avoid damaging the freshly textured surface during installation work.
Drywall primer cannot be applied until the drywall boards are fully installed, fastened, and the joint compound/tape is applied and dried.
All joint compound must be applied and fully cured/sanded before primer is applied to ensure a smooth, uniform surface.
Sanding of dried joint compound must be completed and dust cleaned/vacuumed before priming to avoid dust contamination and ensure proper adhesion.
Primer must be fully dry before finish paint coats are applied, as primer provides a sealed, uniform base for topcoat adhesion and color consistency.

In some sequences, primer is applied before texture; however, some texture types are applied directly to bare drywall and then primed/painted after. This is a soft preference depending on the specified finish schedule.
Structural framing (studs, joists, rafters) must be in place to provide the structural support and nailable surface onto which insulated sheathing panels are attached.

An air barrier or house wrap is typically applied directly to the structural framing before insulated sheathing to prevent air infiltration and protect the building envelope; insulated sheathing goes over this layer.

Insulated sheathing must be installed up to the rough openings before windows and doors can be fitted, as the sheathing defines the opening edges and provides the continuous insulation layer around openings.
Exterior cladding (siding, brick, stucco) is applied over the insulated sheathing, which serves as the substrate and insulation layer beneath the final exterior finish.

While rough-ins often occur before sheathing is fully closed in, any exterior wall penetrations for electrical or plumbing that need to pass through the sheathing are best completed after sheathing is installed so that holes can be accurately drilled through the completed assembly.
The steel structural frame provides the primary support and attachment points for insulated metal panels. Panels cannot be installed until the structural frame is fully erected and stable.

The roof structure provides overhead protection and a complete building envelope. Wall panels should generally be installed after the roof structure is in place to ensure proper weatherproofing sequencing.
Insulated metal panels form the building envelope. Openings for windows and doors must be framed out or cut after the panels are installed to ensure proper alignment and fit within the panel system.
All panel joints, edges, and penetrations must be sealed after panel installation to ensure the building envelope is weather-tight and to prevent moisture intrusion.

Interior finishes such as drywall, insulation (if separate), and interior wall coverings must occur after the exterior envelope (insulated metal panels) is in place to protect interior spaces from weather during construction.
The structural frame and exterior sheathing must be in place to provide a substrate for the vapor retarder/air barrier to be applied against.
The building must be enclosed and weathertight (roof on, windows/doors installed) to protect the vapor barrier from moisture and weather damage before installation.
It is common practice to complete exterior wall prep work before installing the air barrier so that the barrier is applied to a clean, unobstructed surface.
The vapor retarder/air barrier must be in place before interior insulation is installed, as it acts as a control layer to prevent moisture migration into the wall cavity.
The air/vapor barrier must be fully installed and sealed before interior finishes are applied to ensure continuity and effectiveness of the barrier layer.
Structural framing and enclosure must be completed before insulation can be installed, as insulation is typically placed within or against the structural frame and enclosed spaces.
Roofing and waterproofing systems must be in place to protect insulation from moisture and weather exposure before installation.
Electrical wiring, conduit, and mechanical ductwork must be roughed in before insulation is installed, as insulation would otherwise obstruct access to these systems.
Insulation must be fully installed and secured before interior wall finishes such as drywall or panels can be applied over it.
Fireproofing and final sealing treatments often go over or adjacent to insulation, requiring the insulation to be in place first.
Air leaks must be sealed before insulation is installed; otherwise, insulation will be displaced by airflow and its thermal performance will be compromised.
All electrical cables, junction boxes, and fixtures must be installed and inspected before insulation is blown in, as accessing them afterward would require removing insulation.
HVAC ducts and vents must be fully installed and sealed before insulation is added, since insulation will cover and conceal them, making later installation difficult and inefficient.
Soffit vent baffles must be in place to maintain proper attic ventilation channels; without them, blown-in insulation would block airflow at the eaves, leading to moisture and mold issues.

successor: Attic Insulation Inspection and Final Close-Out
rationale: Insulation must be installed and levelled before any final attic inspections or close-out activities can be performed, as inspectors need to verify the insulation depth and coverage.

Spray-applied insulation requires an enclosed cavity or substrate (walls, ceilings, floors) to be in place. The structural framing and sheathing create the backing surface and cavities that the insulation is sprayed onto or into.

Wiring, outlet boxes, and plumbing pipes must be installed within the wall cavities before insulation is sprayed, as the insulation would otherwise cover and block access for these rough-in installations.

Air sealing (caulking, sealing gaps) and weather barriers (house wrap) should be completed prior to insulation to ensure the building envelope is sealed, preventing air leakage that would compromise insulation performance.

Once spray foam or cellulose insulation is installed, it must be covered by drywall or other interior finish materials for fire safety (thermal barrier requirement per building codes) and to protect the insulation from damage.

After insulation is in place and before walls are enclosed, final rough-in inspections and trim-out work (e.g., pulling wires through, mounting devices) occurs, but this is typically sequenced after insulation but before drywall.
The cavity wall must be structurally built before insulation can be installed within the cavity.
Wall ties are typically installed during brickwork, but if they haven't been, insulation must go in before or around them.
Insulation must be installed before cavity closers (such as at windows/doors) are fitted to ensure continuous thermal barrier.
Insulation installation must precede internal wall finishes to enclose and protect the insulation within the cavity.
While outer leaf finishing can be done later, it is preferable after insulation to seal the cavity and prevent moisture ingress.
Excavation must be completed to expose foundation walls and provide working space for insulation application.
Foundation walls and slabs must be cast and cured before insulation can be applied to them.
Waterproofing membranes must be applied to the foundation before insulation is placed over them to protect the waterproofing and ensure proper drainage.
Insulation must be fully installed and secured before backfill material is placed against the foundation to protect the insulation and prevent damage.

Soft preference: Sometimes drainage board or perimeter drains are installed concurrently or after insulation, but ideally insulation should be placed first to protect the waterproofing layer before drain installation.
Unbonded screed requires a clean, cured concrete slab substrate to be placed upon; the slab must be fully set and able to support the screed layer without bonding.

The concrete slab must undergo sufficient curing (typically 7–28 days) to reach adequate strength and dryness before unbonded screed can be applied, otherwise moisture or shrinkage could compromise the screed.
A damp proof membrane must be laid over the concrete slab before unbonded screed is poured, to prevent moisture migration from the slab into the screed and to ensure the 'unbonded' condition.
Unbonded screed must be fully cured and dried before any final floor finishes (e.g., tiles, wood, vinyl) can be installed, to provide a stable, flat base and avoid damage to the finish.
If underfloor heating pipes are embedded in or beneath the unbonded screed, the screed must be fully cured before the system is pressure-tested and commissioned, to prevent cracking or pipe movement.

Bonded screed must be applied to a properly prepared and cured concrete substrate to ensure adequate bond strength. The concrete slab needs to be clean, roughened, and sufficiently cured (typically minimum 28 days) before the bonded screed can be applied, otherwise the screed will not adhere properly.

successor: Floor Covering Installation (e.g., tiles, wood, vinyl)
rationale: The bonded screed must be fully cured and dried (typically 3-7 days minimum depending on thickness and conditions) before any floor covering can be installed on top. Installing floor finishes prematurely can trap moisture, cause debonding, or lead to screed failure.

Skirting boards and trim should be installed after the bonded screed is complete and finished to the correct level, as the screed determines the final floor height and provides the surface against which skirting is fitted.

Where required, a damp proof membrane must be installed beneath the concrete slab or within the floor build-up before bonded screed is applied, to prevent rising damp that could damage the screed and floor finishes.

If underfloor heating is present, the heating pipes must be laid, tested under pressure, and confirmed leak-free before the bonded screed is poured over them. The screed then encapsulates and protects the pipes while providing thermal mass.
The subfloor must be clean, level, and structurally sound before screed can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and even thickness.
Thermal insulation boards must be laid beneath the screed to prevent heat loss downwards, which must be done before the screed is poured.
The heating pipes or cables must be laid out and fixed in position on top of the insulation before the screed is poured to encase them.
After the screed is poured, it must be left to cure and dry for a specified period before any further work can proceed on top of it.

successor: Floor Covering Installation (e.g., tiles, wood, vinyl)
rationale: Final floor finishes can only be installed after the screed has fully cured and dried to prevent cracking, moisture entrapment, or adhesion failure.
The subfloor must be properly cleaned, primed, and prepared before a floating screed can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and level surface.

predecessor: Moisture Barrier / Damp Proof Membrane Installation
rationale: A damp proof membrane must be laid down prior to the floating screed to prevent moisture migration from the substrate into the screed layer.
Perimeter edge insulation strips must be placed around walls before screeding to allow for thermal expansion and acoustic decoupling of the floating screed.
If underfloor heating is included, all heating pipes or panels must be laid and pressure-tested before the floating screed is poured over them.
The floating screed must be fully cured and dried before any final floor coverings can be installed on top of it.
Skirting boards should ideally be installed after the screed is complete and the edge insulation is trimmed, though in some sequences skirting is fitted earlier and the screed is poured up to it.
Final painting is typically done after screeding to avoid dust and debris contaminating wet paint, but this is a preference for cleanliness rather than a physical necessity.
The base screed bed or substrate must be prepared, cleaned, and leveled before any reinforcement mesh can be placed onto it.
The underlying concrete or screed layer must be poured and sufficiently set to provide a stable base for the reinforcement mesh to be positioned.
The reinforcement mesh must be fully placed and tied in position before the final screed topping is poured over it to embed the mesh within the layer.
Individual mesh sheets or rolls must be laid out first so that adjacent sheets can then be tied together at overlaps to ensure continuous reinforcement.
The mesh must be positioned at the correct height (using spacers/chairs) before it can be considered fully installed for the screed pour.

Expansion/contraction joints must be installed while the concrete is still fresh/plastic, either before final set or immediately after pouring, to create deliberate weak planes that control cracking. The joint installation (tooling or saw-cutting timing) is critically dependent on the concrete placement.
The subgrade must be properly compacted and graded before concrete is poured and joints are installed, as the joint pattern and location depend on a stable, level base.
Formwork defines the slab geometry and edges; joint locations are often marked on or aligned with the formwork, so forms must be in place before joint installation.

After joint installation (especially saw-cut joints), the concrete must be allowed to cure properly. Joint installation must be completed before the final curing process can proceed without interruption.

After joints are formed/cut and the concrete has sufficiently cured, the joints are typically cleaned and sealed with filler material. Sealing cannot occur until the joint itself is fully installed and the concrete is ready.
The screed surface must be installed, finished, and sufficiently cured before applying hardener and dust-proofer, as the chemical treatment bonds to and penetrates the screed substrate.
The surface must be clean, dry, and free of debris, dust, oil, or laitance to ensure proper adhesion and penetration of the hardener/dust-proofer.
A minimum initial curing period (typically 7-28 days depending on specifications) is required to allow the screed to achieve sufficient strength and dryness before chemical treatment.
After application, the hardener and dust-proofer must be allowed to dry and cure for a specified period before any subsequent activities can take place on or over the surface.

successor: Floor Covering Installation (e.g., tiles, epoxy, paint, or sealant)
rationale: While it is physically possible to install floor coverings after the hardener has cured, this is typically preferred rather than mandatory; some specifications require the hardener as a final surface treatment with no further covering.
The screed must be installed, spread, and leveled before it can begin the curing process. Curing starts immediately after the screed has been placed and finished.
Final finishing operations such as trowelling and surface preparation must be completed before curing begins, as curing involves moisture retention and protection of the finished surface.

successor: Floor Covering Installation (e.g., tiles, wood, vinyl)
rationale: The screed must be fully cured to achieve sufficient strength and dryness before any floor finishes or coverings can be installed on top, otherwise the covering may fail or moisture damage may occur.
