During the curing period the screed is vulnerable to damage; only after sufficient curing has occurred can the surface withstand foot traffic or construction load without being damaged.

If underfloor heating is embedded in the screed, it is preferable to allow the screed to cure fully before applying heat for commissioning to avoid rapid drying, shrinkage, and cracking. However, some controlled early heating may be used in certain systems.
The screed must be installed and fully cured before moisture testing can be performed, as the test measures moisture content within the cured screed.
The screed requires a specified curing/drying period (typically 1 day per mm of thickness) before moisture levels stabilize enough for accurate testing.

Moisture testing must be completed and results verified to be within acceptable limits before any moisture-sensitive floor coverings (e.g., vinyl, timber, carpet, tiles) can be installed, to prevent adhesion failure or moisture damage.

While moisture testing is ideally done before final floor leveling or self-levelling compound application to avoid trapping moisture, this is a soft preference as some preparatory work can commence in parallel if moisture levels are already known to be acceptable.
Roof deck requires structural framing (beams, joists, trusses) as a supporting substrate before it can be installed.
Load-bearing and exterior walls must be erected to support the roof structure before roof deck installation.
Insulation is placed directly atop or beneath the roof deck; the deck provides the base for insulation installation.
The waterproof membrane is applied over the roof deck to protect the building from water intrusion.

While some top-floor MEP work can precede decking, running ductwork and conduits above the ceiling is often easier after the deck is in place, but this is a soft preference based on construction sequencing efficiency.
Roof sheathing provides the structural base and flat surface onto which edge flashing and trim are fastened. Without the sheathing, there is no substrate to attach the flashing to.
Underlayment (e.g., felt or synthetic) is laid over the sheathing to provide a water-resistant barrier, and edge flashing must overlap the underlayment to properly shed water away from the roof edge.
Edge flashing (drip edge) is installed at the eaves and rakes before the primary roofing material so that the first course of shingles or panels can overlap the flashing, creating a watertight seal.
Fascia boards and soffit are typically installed after edge flashing/trim to allow the flashing to extend over or behind the fascia, ensuring proper water drainage and a finished appearance.
Penetration flashing must be installed over a completed roof deck or substrate that provides the structural base and support for the flashing components.
The underlayment provides a secondary waterproofing layer beneath the flashing; penetration flashing is integrated with the underlayment for proper water shedding.
The actual penetration (pipe, vent, duct, skylight curb, etc.) must be in place so the flashing can be fitted and sealed around it.
Flashing is installed first to create the waterproof transition; the main roof membrane or shingles are then lapped over the flashing's top edge to shed water away.
Counterflashing is installed over the base flashing to cover its top edge and seal it against the vertical penetration surface, completing the weatherproof assembly.

Expansion joints are typically installed after the concrete or structural substrate has been placed and cured, as they bridge gaps between structural sections to accommodate thermal and volumetric movements.
The expansion joint assembly requires the formwork and reinforcing steel to be in place so the joint can be properly positioned at the specified construction gap or control joint location.
Waterproofing is applied over and around the expansion joint assembly to ensure the joint remains watertight; the joint must be installed first so the membrane can be properly lapped and sealed.

successor: Deck Paving or Wearing Surface Placement
rationale: The wearing surface (asphalt or concrete overlay) is placed after the expansion joint is installed so the joint is embedded or abutted correctly, preventing damage during paving operations.
Sealant is applied into the joint cavity after the assembly is installed to prevent debris ingress and provide a weathertight seal; the joint must be in place before sealant can be applied.
Roof curbs are typically installed on top of structural steel framing that supports the roof; the steel structure must be in place to provide support for the roof curb.
The roof curb sits on and is anchored to the roof deck; therefore the roof deck must be completed before the roof curb can be installed.
Roof curbs are installed before the final roofing membrane so that the membrane can be properly flashed and sealed around the curb to ensure watertightness.
HVAC units and rooftop equipment are typically mounted on top of roof curbs, which serve as the structural support and transition piece; the curb must be in place before the equipment can be set.
Flashing around the roof curb is installed after the curb is in place to create a weatherproof seal at the penetration point.
The roof walkway pads must be installed on top of a completed roof deck to provide a stable and waterproof surface for walking.
Roof insulation is typically placed beneath the roof membrane and walkway pads to provide thermal protection; walkway pads go over the insulation and membrane system.
The waterproof membrane must be fully installed and cured before walkway pads are placed to ensure the roof is watertight and protected from damage during pad installation.
Perimeter flashings and edge trims are typically installed after walkway pads are laid to cover and seal the edges of the pad system against water infiltration.

It is preferable to install walkway pads before heavy roof equipment to protect the roof membrane and provide stable access paths, though equipment could be installed first if walkway routes are carefully coordinated.
The roof structure must be framed and in place to provide the structural support and opening for the skylight or roof window to be installed.
Roof decking must be completed to create the substrate into which the skylight opening is cut and the skylight is mounted.
The waterproof membrane must be laid over the roof deck before the skylight is installed to ensure proper integration of the skylight flashing with the roof's water barrier.
The skylight itself must be positioned and secured before the flashing can be fitted around its perimeter to seal against water ingress.
The final roof covering (e.g., shingles, tiles) that abuts the skylight must be installed after the skylight and its flashing are in place to create a weathertight finish.
The roof hatch must be installed on top of the roof deck or sheathing, which provides the structural base for mounting.
The roof frame must be built to support the roof structure and provide the rough opening for the roof hatch.
Flashing around the roof hatch must be installed after the hatch is in place to seal the gap and prevent water infiltration.
Insulation around the hatch perimeter is installed after the hatch is set to ensure a continuous thermal envelope.
The roof waterproofing membrane must be applied up to and around the installed hatch to maintain a watertight roof system.
The roof deck provides the structural base upon which insulation is fastened; without a completed deck, there is no surface to attach the insulation.
The roof structural framing (trusses or rafters) must be in place and stable to support the roof deck and subsequently the insulation system.

While often recommended to install underlayment before insulation for moisture protection, in some systems insulation is applied directly to the deck and underlayment follows; this is a typical sequencing preference but not always a physical necessity.
A vapor barrier is typically installed over the insulation to control moisture diffusion; the insulation must be in place first to serve as the substrate for the vapor barrier.
The final roof covering is installed over the insulation system; the insulation must be securely fastened before the weatherproof covering is applied.

The substrate (e.g., geomembrane liner or roofing underlayment) must be clean, smooth, and properly prepared before any membrane material can be laid out and seamed. Debris or uneven surfaces would compromise weld integrity.
Membrane panels must first be unrolled and positioned in their final location before adjacent panels can be seamed or welded together.
Welded seams must be allowed to cool and set before being tested (e.g., via air channel pressure testing, vacuum box, or peel/shear tests) to ensure a watertight bond.
Ballast, batten bars, or termination bars are installed after seaming is complete to avoid interfering with the welding process and to ensure continuous seam integrity.

While site restoration typically follows membrane installation, this is often a soft preference rather than a hard constraint — restoration could theoretically begin in areas not dependent on the membrane work, but for quality and sequence efficiency it is best deferred until all membrane welding is complete.
The membrane must be fully installed and laid in place before its edges can be terminated and secured. Termination and edge details finish the membrane system.
The substrate must be clean, dry, and properly prepared before the membrane is laid and its edges secured to ensure proper adhesion and long-term performance.
Flashing is installed over and around terminated membrane edges to seal and protect the termination points from water ingress.
All membrane terminations and edge securements must be completed and inspected before water testing can proceed to verify the integrity of the waterproofing system.
Edge terminations need to be secured before protective cover boards or insulation layers are placed over the membrane to avoid damaging the termination details.
Roof flashing is installed directly onto the roof sheathing (deck). The sheathing provides the structural base that flashing is fastened to, so it must be in place first.

Roof underlayment (e.g., felt or synthetic membrane) is applied over the sheathing before flashing is installed, as flashing typically integrates with or sits on top of the underlayment to provide proper water shedding.

Flashing is installed at roof penetrations, valleys, and edges before the primary roofing material (shingles, tiles, or metal panels) is laid, so that the roofing material overlaps and seals over the flashing for weatherproofing.
Drip edge flashing (a type of roof flashing) must be installed before gutters, as the gutter system is mounted after or over the drip edge to ensure proper water runoff into the gutters.
Roof drains must be installed on top of the completed roof deck/sheathing so they can be properly integrated into the structure.
The roof drain must be in place before the waterproofing membrane is installed so the membrane can be properly flashed and sealed around the drain flange.
Insulation is placed around and over the drain assembly, requiring the drain to be secure first.
The structural roof framing must be complete to support the deck and drains before drain installation can begin.
After the drains are installed, the connected piping must be tested for leaks before being concealed.
The roof deck or structural sheathing must be in place to provide a surface for the insulation to be installed upon.
The roof framing (trusses/rafters) must be fully erected and secured before insulation can be placed between or over them.
A weather-resistant barrier (e.g., felt paper or synthetic underlayment) should be installed to protect the insulation from moisture ingress.
Final roofing materials (shingles, tiles, or metal panels) must be installed after insulation to protect it from weather and UV exposure.
The interior ceiling finish (drywall/plaster) cannot be installed until the insulation is in place, as insulation is placed within the roof/ceiling cavity before enclosing it.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared (with proper dimensions, headers, and sills) before any window frame can be installed, as the frame physically sits within the opening.

Weather-resistant barrier or building wrap must be installed around the rough opening before the window frame is placed to ensure proper flashing integration and moisture management behind and around the frame.
Flashing, caulking, and sealant work around the window must be applied after the frame is in place to create a watertight seal between the frame and the rough opening.
Interior wall finishes like drywall or plaster are installed after the window frame is in place so they can be cut and finished neatly around the frame and incorporate the window reveal.
The wall sheathing or masonry substrate must be completed to provide a structural surface to which the window sill can be anchored and sealed against weather penetration.
After the sill is installed, the joints around it must be sealed with caulk or weatherproofing material to prevent water ingress and air leakage.

Interior finishes such as drywall or window trim are typically installed after the sill is in place to create a clean, finished appearance. This is a soft preference because the sill can be installed after rough interior work in some sequences, but standard practice places interior finishing after sill installation for aesthetics and fit.
The window unit must be installed and secured in the rough opening before casing and trim can be applied around it, as the casing covers the gap between the window frame and the wall.
The rough opening framing must be complete and properly sized to accept the window, and the wall surface (e.g., sheathing) must be in place for the casing to be fastened against.

Exterior waterproofing, flashing, and weather-resistant barrier around the window must be installed prior to interior casing/trim to prevent water intrusion that would be hidden or obstructed by the trim.

While casing can technically be installed before finished painting, it is standard practice to complete wall finishing first so that the casing sits flush against the finished surface and paint lines are clean. This is a soft preference for quality and finish.

After casing and trim are installed, they are typically painted or stained. This is a preference (soft) because pre-finished trim could be installed after painting, but field finishing is normally done after installation.

Flooring (especially hardwood or tile) is often installed after window trim so that the casing sits over or abuts the finished floor cleanly, avoiding gaps. This is a soft preference as it can be done in reverse with careful detailing.
Weatherstripping is applied around installed window frames to seal gaps; windows must be in place before weatherstripping can be applied.
Weatherstripping should be completed before interior wall finishing to ensure a clean seal around the window; this is a preferred sequence but not absolutely physically required.
Weatherstripping is typically installed before interior trim/casing to create a proper seal; the trim covers and protects the weatherstripping edges.
Exterior cladding is installed before interior weatherstripping to ensure the window is properly integrated into the building envelope from the outside.
Weatherstripping is often installed before painting to avoid paint bridging the seal, but painting could be done first with careful masking; thus it is a soft preference.
Window hardware such as hinges, locks, and handles must be attached to the window frame. The frame must be installed and secured in the wall opening before any hardware can be mounted onto it.
Hardware components like locks, latches, and handles are typically installed on or around the glass panels. The glazing must be completed first so the hardware can be properly aligned and fastened.
Weatherstripping and final seals are applied after all hardware is mounted to ensure proper fit around hardware components and to avoid interference with moving parts.
Functional testing of the window (opening, closing, locking) can only be performed after all hardware is installed to verify proper operation and adjust if necessary.

successor: Interior Trim and Finish Work around Window
rationale: Interior finishing around the window (such as casing, trim, and drywall finishing) should be done after all hardware is installed and tested to allow access for adjustments and to ensure a clean final appearance.
Door frames must be installed within the rough opening created by wall framing; there is no structural support for the door frame without the surrounding wall studs being in place.
A level and stable subfloor is required as the base upon which the door frame sits; installing the frame before the subfloor is level would result in misalignment and operational issues.
The door frame (jambs, threshold, and header) must be securely installed and squared before the door slab can be hinged to it; hanging a door requires a properly positioned frame.
Drywall is installed up to and around the door frame, and the frame provides the reference edge for taping and finishing; drywall cannot be properly completed without the door frame in place.
The door frame must be installed and structurally secure before the door leaf (the door itself) can be hung on its hinges, as the hinges are attached to the frame.
The door leaf must be hung in place before locks, latches, and handles can be installed, as these components need to align with the door and the frame.
The door leaf must be hung before final adjustments (e.g., hinge tightening, gap alignment) can be performed to ensure proper operation.

While painting can sometimes be done before hanging, typically the door leaf is hung first to ensure fit and then removed or masked for finishing; however, this is often a preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The door leaf must be cut, planed, and prepared to fit the specific door opening before it can be hung on its hinges.

Wall surfaces must be finished and smooth before door casings and architraves are installed, as architraves cover the gap between the door frame and the finished wall. Installing them before plastering would leave gaps or require the architraves to be removed and reinstalled.

The door frame must be in place and properly aligned before the casing/architrave trim can be installed around it, as the architrave is fixed to the frame and covers the junction between frame and wall.
Subfloor or rough flooring must be laid to establish the finished floor level, which determines the proper height and positioning of the door casing at the bottom of the opening.

All electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, and HVAC ducts that run within or near walls must be roughed-in before architraves are installed, to avoid damaging the finished trim if wall access is later required.

Architraves are typically installed before final painting and decorating so that paint can be applied to the architraves and the paint film can seal the joint between the architrave and the wall for a clean finish.

The door frame provides the structural support and mounting surface for weatherstripping and threshold components; without a properly installed frame, there is nothing to attach the weatherstripping or threshold to.

The door must be hung and properly aligned within the frame before weatherstripping can be applied, as the gap tolerances between the door and frame determine the correct placement and compression of weatherstripping.

Weatherstripping and threshold are installed at the perimeter of the door opening; interior trim and casing are applied over these assemblies, so the weatherproofing must be in place first to avoid having to remove trim later.

The weatherstripping and threshold define the final closed position and gap of the door, which is critical for properly aligning the strike plate and latch; hardware installation should follow weatherstripping to ensure correct fit.
After weatherstripping and threshold are installed, the door must be adjusted for proper compression, seal, and operation; final adjustments cannot be done before sealing components are in place.
The rough opening must be framed, sized, and prepared (including header, sill, and jack studs) before the window frame can be installed into the wall opening.
The weather-resistant barrier (e.g., house wrap) must be applied to the sheathing before window installation to ensure proper flashing integration and moisture management around the window opening.
The window frame must be securely installed, leveled, and flashed before the glass panes or sash are placed into the frame to avoid damage and ensure proper fit.
The window frame must be in place before applying final flashing tape, sealants, and trim around the frame to create a watertight seal.
Interior wall finishing around the window, including drywall and casing trim, can only begin after the window frame is installed and secured.
The window or door frame must be installed first to provide a stable structural opening into which the glazing or glass panel can be fitted and sealed.
The rough opening in the wall structure must be framed and prepared to receive the window unit before glazing can be installed.
Weatherproofing, flashing, and moisture barriers around the rough opening must be applied before window installation to prevent water infiltration behind the glazing.

successor: Interior Trim and Finish Work around Window
rationale: After the glass panel is installed, interior trim, casing, and drywall finishing around the window can be completed to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance.
The final exterior sealant and caulking around the glazing perimeter must be applied after the glass panel is in place to ensure a watertight and airtight seal.
The door frame provides the structural support and hinge mounting surface; the door leaf cannot be hung without a frame in place.
Walls must be framed to define the rough opening dimensions for the door.
Hardware such as hinges and locks must be mounted onto the door leaf/slab after it is positioned in the frame.
While finishing can be done off-site or before hanging, final touch-up painting or staining is typically done after installation to ensure color matching and coverage of nail holes or adjustments.

Window units must be installed and properly secured within the rough opening before casing and trim can be applied around them. Trim is fitted against the window frame, so the window must be in place first.
Rough opening framing for windows must be complete and inspected to ensure correct size, level, and plumb before any window installation and subsequent casing can proceed.
Weather-resistant barriers and proper flashing around window openings must be installed before casing and trim to prevent moisture intrusion behind the trim.

While not strictly required in all cases, interior wall finish is typically completed before installing casing so that the casing covers the gap between the window frame and drywall, providing a finished look. However, some sequences install casing before drywall, so this is a soft preference.
Casing and trim are typically installed before painting so that paint can be applied over the trim and any nail holes can be filled and painted, allowing for a seamless finish between walls and trim.

While casing can be installed before flooring, it is often preferred to install flooring first so that casing sits on top of finished flooring, avoiding gaps. However, this sequence can vary, making this a soft preference.

Window and door trim work can be done concurrently or in any order, but some crews prefer to complete all casing work in a room at the same time for consistency. No physical constraint necessitates a specific order.

The door casing (architrave) is installed around the door frame to cover the gap between the frame and the wall. The door frame must first be securely in place before the architrave can be fixed around it.
Architrave is installed against finished wall surfaces (plastered/rendered walls) to create a clean trim. Plastering must be completed so the architrave sits flush against the finished wall surface.
All rough-in work (electrical cables, plumbing pipes) within walls must be completed before architraves are installed, as once architraves and casings are in place, wall access becomes restricted.
The architrave forms the finished trim around the door opening. The door leaf is typically hung after the casing is installed to ensure proper alignment and clearance between the door and the casing.

While architraves are typically installed before skirting boards for a cleaner junction (skirting butts against the architrave), it is possible to reverse this order with careful cutting; thus it is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
The glazing bead must be installed onto the window or door frame; the frame provides the structural support and mounting surface for the bead.
The glazing bead is used to secure the glass or infill panel into the frame; the glass/panel must be in place before the bead can be installed to hold it.
After the glazing bead is installed, sealant or caulking is applied around the bead to ensure weathertightness and prevent water infiltration.

Interior trim and finishing work (such as painting or drywall finishing) typically occurs after bead installation to achieve a clean aesthetic, though this is a soft preference based on work sequencing.
The complete assembly including the glazing bead must be in place before the final inspection of the window/door system can be performed.
Window screens are installed into the window frame; the frame must be in place to provide the structural support and attachment points for the screen.
The window glass or sash must be installed before the screen so that the screen can be properly fitted and secured to the existing window assembly.

Although trim can often be installed before or after screens, it is typically easier to install trim work after screens are in place to avoid damaging the screen material during trim carpentry; this is a soft preference.

Final painting or touch-up work is typically done after screen installation to avoid paint splatter on the screen mesh, but screens can also be installed after painting if care is taken — this is a soft preference.
Window screens are part of the fenestration system; the building enclosure and weatherization inspection cannot be finalized until all windows, including screens, are properly installed.
The glass pane must be set into the window frame before the screen is installed, as the screen is typically placed on the exterior side of the glass or within the same frame assembly.
Window screens are often installed before final exterior finishes (like siding or trim), as the screen frame may need to be integrated or flashed into the exterior envelope.
While interior trim can technically be done before screens, installing screens first allows for easier access and adjustment from the exterior without risk of damaging interior finishes.
Window screens must be in place before final inspection and occupancy to meet building code requirements for insect screening, ventilation safety, and fall protection where applicable.
Door hardware (hinges, locks, closers, handles) must be physically installed before adjustment and testing can occur, as there is no hardware to adjust without prior installation.
The door frame and door leaf must be in place and hung before any operating hardware can be fitted, adjusted, or tested for proper function.
Adjustment and testing of door operating hardware must be completed and verified before the final inspection and sign-off of the door assembly can take place.

Commissioning of all architectural hardware (including electronic access, automatic operators, etc.) requires that the basic door hardware has first been adjusted and tested for correct mechanical operation.
While punch list items typically follow adjustment and testing, some minor adjustments may be revisited during snagging, making this a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
Windows must be physically installed in their frames before any hardware (handles, locks, hinges, stays) can be adjusted and tested for proper operation.
The window frame and sash must be in place and secured to provide the mounting surfaces and proper alignment for operating hardware components.
After hardware is adjusted and windows are verified to open, close, and lock correctly, the final seals and weatherstripping can be installed without risk of damage from subsequent adjustment work.

Interior and exterior window trim is typically installed after hardware adjustment is complete to avoid interference with hardware access and to ensure proper fit around operating components, though some trim work may proceed in parallel.
Window hardware function and operation must be verified and adjusted before final inspection sign-off to ensure all windows operate as intended per specifications.
The door frame must be in place to provide a structure around which flashing can be applied and sealed.
The rough opening must be properly framed, cleaned, and prepared before flashing can be installed to ensure proper water management.
The weather-resistive barrier (house wrap) must be installed prior to door flashing so that the flashing can integrate with and overlap the barrier for continuous water shedding.
Flashing must be installed first to provide a watertight seal around the opening before the door unit is hung and secured.
Exterior cladding is installed after flashing so that the siding can overlap the flashing flanges, creating a continuous weatherproof exterior.
The rough opening must be properly framed, sheathed, and prepared before window flashing can be applied to seal the opening against moisture.
The building must be dried-in (roof and wall sheathing in place) to provide a stable surface for flashing tape and membrane application around the window opening.

Flashing must be installed at the sill, jambs, and head of the rough opening before the window unit is placed so that the flashing wraps under and integrates with the window frame for proper water drainage.

Flashing must be completed and integrated with the window before siding, brick, or other cladding is applied over the flange to ensure the weather-resistant barrier is continuous and prevents water intrusion.

While interior work can begin in other areas concurrently, finishing around the window interior (e.g., drywall, trim) typically follows window installation and flashing to allow for proper sealing and air barrier continuity.
The door must be installed and in place before a kick plate can be attached to it, as the kick plate is mounted onto the door surface.
Installing kick plates after final painting avoids damaging the finish, but touch-ups can be done after installation if needed.
The kick plate must be fully installed before the final inspection of the door assembly can take place.
While kick plates are typically installed after other hardware to avoid interference, this is often a soft preference to allow easier access for aligning hardware.
Flooring is usually completed before kick plate installation to ensure proper clearance, but kick plates can be adjusted afterward if needed.
Kick plates are typically installed at the base of walls, so the wall framing must be in place to provide a mounting surface.
Kick plates are often attached to finished wall surfaces; drywall provides the finished surface needed for proper kick plate attachment.
Kick plates sit at the junction of the wall and floor, so the finished floor surface must be installed first to ensure proper alignment and fit.
Kick plates are protective finish elements that must be in place before final quality control inspection of the completed space.
Kick plates protect walls from damage during use; they must be installed before the space is occupied to ensure wall protection.
The door frame must be installed first to provide the structural support and rough opening into which the vision panel or door lite will be fitted.
The rough opening must be properly framed, sized, and prepared before the vision panel/door lite can be placed and secured.
After the vision panel or door lite is installed, glazing compounds and sealants must be applied to ensure weather-tightness and proper sealing around the lite.

Interior trim and finish work around the door lite can begin after installation, though it is a soft preference since some finishing could be done concurrently or out of order without structural risk.
The vision panel/door lite must be fully installed before final hardware (e.g., locks, handles, hinges) is mounted on the door to avoid damaging the lite during hardware installation.

successor: Door Viewing Port / Vision Panel Installation
rationale: The door viewing port or vision panel must be installed into an already-installed door frame, as the frame provides the structural support and proper alignment for the door leaf that will contain the vision panel.

successor: Door Viewing Port / Vision Panel Installation
rationale: The door leaf must be fabricated, cut to size, and prepared with the necessary cutout before the vision panel or viewing port can be installed into it.

predecessor: Door Viewing Port / Vision Panel Installation
rationale: The vision panel must be installed into the door leaf before the door is hung on its hinges, as it is much more difficult and risky to install the glass panel after the door is already mounted.

predecessor: Door Viewing Port / Vision Panel Installation
rationale: While hardware can be installed concurrently, it is generally preferred to install the vision panel before final hardware fitting to avoid glass damage from tool impacts during hardware installation.

predecessor: Wall Framing and Rough Opening Preparation
successor: Door Viewing Port / Vision Panel Installation
rationale: The wall framing and rough opening for the door must be complete to allow the door frame to be installed, which is a prerequisite for the vision panel installation.
The wall framing must be in place to provide structural support and a mounting surface for the sliding door track system.
The rough opening for the sliding door must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the track can be installed.
The track and hardware must be securely mounted before the door panels can be hung on the track.
The track and hardware must be fully installed to allow for proper alignment, adjustment, and testing of the sliding door operation.
While the track must be in place before trim is installed around the door opening, this is a soft preference as trim could potentially be adjusted after track installation depending on the design.
Electrical power supply and wiring conduits must be roughed-in to the door frame/location before the automatic door operator can be connected and installed.
The door frame must be installed and properly anchored to support the automatic door operator mechanism and hardware.
The header or overhead support structure must be in place to mount the automatic door operator, especially for sliding or swinging automatic doors.
The door operator mechanism must be mounted and aligned before hanging the door leaf so that the door can be properly attached to the operator arm or drive system.
After the operator is physically installed, final electrical connections and system testing/commissioning can be performed.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and space needed to install the sliding door track and hardware.
A properly sized and installed header above the door opening is required to carry the load and provide a mounting surface for the sliding door track.
The track and hardware must be installed first so the door panels can be hung and attached to the rolling mechanisms.
After the track and hardware are in place, the door must be adjusted and aligned to ensure smooth operation within the track system.

While trim can be partially installed beforehand, final casing and finishing around the sliding door area are typically done after the track and hardware are in place to ensure proper fit and appearance.
The rough opening (framed and sized) must be complete before installing the folding door system, as the door system is fitted into the opening.
Ideally floor finishes are installed before folding doors so the door tracks and bottom guides can be set to the finished floor height, though in some sequences it can be done after.
Once the folding door system is physically installed, the hardware must be adjusted and the doors tested for smooth operation and proper alignment.
Finish trim and casings around the door frame are typically installed after the door system is in place to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance.
Wall finishing is often done before or after door installation depending on preference; if done after, care must be taken to protect the door system from paint and debris.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the bay/bow window assembly can be installed.
The weather-resistive barrier (house wrap or building paper) must be applied to the exterior wall before installing the window to ensure proper water management and drainage.
Bay and bow windows are heavy and require adequate structural support, including a properly sized header and sometimes a support bracket or knee brace, installed before the window unit is placed.
After the window assembly is set into the rough opening, flashing tape and sealant must be applied around the perimeter to prevent water infiltration.
Interior casing and trim around the window are installed after the window unit is fully secured and weather-sealed.
Exterior siding or finish materials are installed up to the window frame after the window is in place and flashed.
The window opening control device must be mounted on or within the window frame structure, so the frame must be installed first to provide a physical mounting surface.
The window opening control device is typically integrated with the window assembly; the window must be in place before the control device can be installed.
If the window opening control device is electrically powered, rough-in electrical wiring must be completed before device installation to provide power connections.
Final finishing and trim around the window must be completed after the control device is installed to properly integrate and conceal device components.

successor: Window Control System Commissioning and Testing
rationale: The control device must be physically installed before the system can be commissioned, tested, and calibrated to ensure proper operation.
The window opening restrictor must be mounted onto an installed window frame or sash. The frame must be in place to provide the physical anchorage surface for the restrictor bracket.
The window restrictor attaches to the window sash, which must first have its glass panes installed. The restrictor's fixing points and alignment depend on the finished sash assembly.
After the restrictor is fitted, a safety inspection must verify that the restrictor limits opening to the required gap (typically 100mm or less for child safety) and that it functions correctly.

Once the restrictor is installed, the window's operation including opening, closing, and restrictor engagement should be tested to ensure smooth function and that the restrictor does not impede normal operation.
Acoustic seals must be applied to fully installed and fixed door/window frames. The sealant or weatherstripping cannot be properly installed on a frame that is not yet in place.
Acoustic seals around glass panels require the glass to be set in the frame first, as the seal is applied between the glass and the frame.
The rough opening must be properly framed, leveled, and prepared before the door/window unit is installed and acoustic seals are applied.
Interior finishes such as drywall and paint must be applied after acoustic seals are installed to avoid damaging the seals or covering them with paint/mud.

successor: Final Door/Window Adjustment and Hardware Installation
rationale: After acoustic seals are in place, final adjustments to door/window fit and installation of handles, locks, and other hardware should be done to ensure proper compression of the seals.
The rough opening must be framed to the correct dimensions to accommodate the fire-rated door assembly.
The supporting walls must be framed and sheathed to provide structural support and fire-rated barrier continuity for the door frame.
Fire-rated gap sealing (intumescent caulking) around the door frame must be applied after the door frame is installed to maintain fire-resistance rating.
Inspection and testing (e.g., closing, latching, smoke seal checks) can only occur after the door assembly is fully installed.
The structural frame (walls, floors, ceilings) must be in place to provide the supporting opening and framework into which fire-rated glazing assemblies are installed.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins within walls that contain fire-rated glazing must be completed before sealing the wall assembly with glazing to avoid rework and maintain the fire-resistance rating continuity.

Fire-rated glazing must be installed before surrounding finishes are applied so that the glazing assembly's perimeter seals and firestop systems are fully integrated into the wall assembly without being obscured or damaged by finish work.

After glazing installation, the firestop sealant and perimeter seals around the glazing frame must be inspected to verify code compliance and fire-resistance integrity before enclosing or covering these critical seals.

successor: Final Testing and Commissioning of Fire/Smoke Barriers
rationale: Fire-rated glazing systems are integral components of passive fire protection; therefore, final commissioning of fire and smoke barriers must occur after all glazing is fully installed and sealed to ensure the system performs as designed under fire conditions.
The intumescent seal must be applied to the door frame or frame assembly; the frame must be in place first.
Typically the intumescent seal is installed on the frame before the door leaf is hung, though some seals are applied to the door edge; in standard sequence, frame seals precede leaf hanging.
The door and frame surfaces must be clean, free of debris, and properly prepared (cut, routed, or rebated) to accept the intumescent seal.
Intumescent seals are typically installed in the frame rebate before the door leaf is hung; the seal would be damaged or inaccessible if the leaf were already in place.
The intumescent seals must be fully installed before the fire door assembly can be inspected, tested, or certified for fire resistance compliance.
The door must be hung in the frame so that the door stop can be positioned correctly to limit the door's swing and prevent over-travel.
While not strictly required, it is preferable to have wall finishes complete before installing door stops to avoid damage to the finished surfaces or the stops themselves.

successor: Final Door Adjustment and Hardware Installation
rationale: Door stops must be installed before final adjustments are made to the door and before installing hardware such as door handles and locksets, as the stop's position affects the door's final resting position.
The lift shaft provides the physical enclosure and guide rail structure that the lift car operates within; without the shaft being constructed, the lift car cannot be installed.
Guide rails must be in place and aligned before the lift car can be mounted, as the car's guide shoes or rollers run along these rails for vertical movement.

successor: Lift Car Wiring and Electrical Connection
rationale: The lift car must be physically installed before electrical wiring, control cables, and power connections can be run to it.
The counterweight is typically installed after or concurrently with the lift car as part of the hoistway balancing system, but the car must be positioned first for proper rope alignment.
Lift car doors are mounted onto the car itself; the car must be in place before its doors can be fitted and aligned with the landing doors.
The lift shaft must be constructed to provide the physical space and structure within which the guide rails will be installed.
The guide rails must be in place to guide the lift car; the lift car cannot be installed before the rails are fixed.
Counterweight guide rails (often part of the same guide rail system) must be installed before the counterweight can be placed.
Structural steelwork and embedded brackets/fixings in the lift shaft must be installed to provide anchoring points for the guide rails.

While not strictly a physical necessity, it is standard practice to install guide rails before landing doors to allow access and alignment of door machinery relative to the car position defined by the rails.
The lift guide rails provide the vertical track within which the counterweight travels. The counterweight cannot be installed without guide rails in place to guide its movement.
The physical counterweight assembly must be delivered to the construction site before it can be lifted and installed into the shaft.
The lift shaft enclosure must be structurally complete to provide a safe and enclosed space for counterweight installation, preventing fall hazards and ensuring structural support.
Lift cables must be connected between the lift car and the counterweight. The counterweight must be in position before cables can be properly routed and tensioned between the two.
The counterweight is an essential component of the lift balance system. Testing and commissioning can only proceed once the counterweight is installed to balance the lift car.

predecessor: Lift Installation (Machine Room, Guide Rails, Car)
rationale: The lift machine room equipment, guide rails, and car must be installed before hoisting ropes/belts can be rigged, as the ropes connect the car and counterweight via the machine room sheaves and require the guide system to be in place for proper alignment.

Hoisting ropes/belts are the load-bearing connection between the lift car, counterweight, and drive machine; commissioning (load testing, brake testing, travel calibration) cannot proceed without the ropes/belts installed and tensioned.

Although landing doors can be physically installed beforehand, final door adjustment and clearance setting rely on the car position relative to landings, which is affected by rope stretch and tensioning; therefore it is good practice to refine door settings after rope installation.
The lift shaft (hoistway) must be fully constructed to provide the structural enclosure and support for the traction machine installation.
The machine room (or machine space) must be prepared, with structural floor/base, walls, and access provisions, to accommodate and support the traction machine.

successor: Lift Traction Machine Alignment and Levelling
rationale: The traction machine must first be installed into its designated position before it can be precisely aligned and levelled.
The traction machine (sheave/drum) must be in place and secured before hoisting ropes or cables can be routed over the traction sheave and connected to the car and counterweight.
Electrical and control connections from the controller/drive to the traction machine motor can only be made after the machine is physically installed and positioned.
The lift controller requires a dedicated electrical supply and proper grounding from the electrical room before it can be safely powered and operated.
The lift controller needs a main power feed to be routed to its cabinet location before it can be connected and energized.
The physical mounting structure or cabinet frame must be in place to securely house the lift controller.
After the controller is physically mounted, wiring connections to the lift motor, sensors, and call buttons can be made.
The controller must be physically installed and wired before it can be programmed, tested, and commissioned for operation.
The lift shaft must be structurally complete to provide a frame and opening for the landing doors to be installed into.
The door frames must be installed and aligned before the landing doors themselves can be hung or fitted.

successor: Lift Landing Door Finishing and Cladding
rationale: Final finishes such as painting, cladding, or trim around the doors can only be applied after the doors are in place and adjusted.
Lift landing doors must be operational before the lift car can be tested for proper floor-level alignment and door interlock functionality during commissioning.
Safety tests including door interlocks, closing force, and emergency release mechanisms cannot be performed until the landing doors are fully installed.
The lift car must be installed before the car doors can be fitted, as the doors are physically attached to the lift car structure.
The car frame provides the structural support and mounting points for the doors; doors cannot be installed without the frame in place.
Door interlocks and safety systems can only be tested after the doors are installed and operational.
While interior finishing can often proceed concurrently, complete installation of doors is preferable before final interior trim work to avoid damage and ensure alignment.
Full lift commissioning and operational testing requires the car doors to be installed and functional to verify safe operation.

Lift buffers are typically installed within the lift shaft, which is part of the building's concrete core. The core must be constructed first to provide the structural enclosure and support for the buffer installation.
The lift shaft must be prepared, cleaned, and checked for plumbness and dimensions before buffers can be positioned and fixed at the base of the shaft.

Lift buffers are safety devices installed at the bottom of the lift shaft to arrest a descending car in an overspeed event. The lift car must be installed after the buffers are in place to ensure proper alignment and safety compliance.

Buffer installation is often coordinated with guide rail installation, but rails may be partially installed before buffers. However, final buffer positioning should precede final rail alignment to ensure correct clearances are maintained.
The lift safety gear must be installed after the lift system itself is in place, as safety gear components mount to and interface with the lift structure.
Load testing can only be performed after safety gear (e.g., overspeed governor, safety brakes) is installed to ensure the lift can be safely stopped in an emergency during testing.
The lift shaft or hoistway must be fully constructed to provide the mounting surfaces and clearances required for installation of lift safety gear components.
Commissioning and final certification of the lift system requires all safety gear to be installed and functional before the lift can be put into service.
The building's structural frame must be complete to support the lift shaft and enable safe installation of safety-critical lift components.
The overhead beam must have vertical supports (columns and brackets) installed to provide a resting place and structural anchorage before the beam can be lifted into position.
A crane is required to hoist the overhead beam; the crane must be set up and ready on site before lifting operations can commence.
The beam must be inspected, cleaned, and fitted with lifting slings/chokers before it can be lifted safely.

successor: Secure and Bolt Beam to Columns
rationale: After the beam is lifted into position, it must be bolted and secured to the supporting columns to ensure structural stability before releasing crane load.
The overhead beam must be in place before any crane rails can be mounted onto it for overhead crane operation.
The lift shaft must be structurally complete to provide the vertical pathway and support for the traveling cable installation.
The lift car must be assembled in place as the traveling cable connects to the lift car and provides power/signal transmission.
Electrical supply and control wiring must be routed to the lift shaft and machine room before the traveling cable can be connected.
The traveling cable must be installed and positioned before it can be terminated at both ends (car and controller) and electrically tested.
All lift cabling including the traveling cable must be fully installed and connected before the lift can be commissioned, tested for operation, and adjusted.
The lift shaft must be structurally complete to provide a mounting surface and proper alignment for call buttons and indicators at each landing.

predecessor: Electrical Conduit Installation to Lift Landings
rationale: Power and control wiring must be available at each landing position before call buttons and indicators can be connected and function.
Landing doors and frames define the exact location and mounting surface for call button stations adjacent to the doors.

successor: Lift Control System Integration and Testing
rationale: Call buttons and indicators must be physically installed and wired before the overall lift control system can be fully integrated, programmed, and tested for correct response to landing calls.
While finishing can be done before or after, it is preferable to install call buttons first so that finishing works can neatly trim around the installed units, avoiding damage to finished surfaces.

predecessor: Foundation and base preparation for lift equipment
rationale: The hydraulic lift power unit requires a stable, level foundation to support its weight and maintain alignment with the hydraulic cylinders and piping. The foundation must be cured and properly prepared before the power unit can be set in place.

predecessor: Hydraulic piping and tubing rough-in to power unit location
rationale: Hydraulic supply and return lines must be routed to the power unit location and left with termination points ready before the unit can be positioned and connected, as access to run piping behind or under the unit is impractical after placement.

predecessor: Electrical conduit and wiring rough-in to power unit location
rationale: Power supply conduits and control wiring must be brought to the power unit location and terminated at the disconnect or junction box prior to setting the unit, as the electrical connections are integral to the power unit startup and cannot be completed afterwards without obstruction.

successor: Hydraulic cylinder and hose connection to power unit
rationale: The power unit must be positioned, leveled, and anchored before the main hydraulic hoses or rigid piping can be connected between the power unit's manifold and the lift cylinders, ensuring correct alignment and avoiding stress on fittings.

successor: Hydraulic fluid filling and system commissioning
rationale: The power unit must be fully installed, with all mechanical and electrical connections made, before the hydraulic reservoir can be filled with fluid and the system can be pressurized, tested, and commissioned for operation.

successor: Hydraulic Lift Ram and Cylinder Installation
rationale: The hydraulic lift ram and cylinder require a stable, level foundation and base slab to support the load and ensure precise alignment.

predecessor: Hydraulic Lift Ram and Cylinder Installation
rationale: The ram and cylinder must be physically installed and anchored before hydraulic lines can be connected to them.

predecessor: Hydraulic Lift Ram and Cylinder Installation
successor: Lift Platform or Carriage Assembly Installation
rationale: The lift ram and cylinder provide the lifting force; the platform or carriage that moves must be attached to or guided by the cylinder after it is in place.

predecessor: Hydraulic Lift Ram and Cylinder Installation
successor: Electrical Control and Safety System Commissioning
rationale: While electronics can be partially pre-wired, full commissioning of controls and safety interlocks depends on the cylinder's physical position and stroke limits being verified.

successor: Hydraulic Lift Ram and Cylinder Installation
rationale: The structural frame that houses or supports the lift cylinder must be erected to provide attachment points and alignment for the cylinder.
The lift shaft requires a stable load-bearing foundation to transfer its vertical loads safely to the ground. Without completed foundation works, the lift shaft structure would have no base support.
The lift shaft typically extends down to the lowest basement level. Excavation must be completed to expose and prepare the area where the lift shaft pit and base will be constructed.
The lift shaft rises from the ground slab or raft foundation which forms the working platform and structural base for the shaft walls.
The physical lift shaft structure (walls, openings, and pit) must be fully constructed before lift rails, cabling, guide rails, and mechanical equipment can be installed inside the shaft.

The lift shaft often acts as a lateral stability core for the building. Adjacent floor slabs and beams typically bear onto or connect into the lift shaft walls, requiring the shaft to be completed first to provide vertical and lateral support.

The lift shaft must be structurally complete and enclosed to provide the physical vertical space and support structure for installing the guide rails. Without a finished shaft, the rails cannot be anchored or aligned.
The pit base at the bottom of the lift shaft must be constructed and cured to provide the bottom support point and anchoring for the guide rails. Rails need a firm base to rest on.

The guide rails define the vertical path for the lift car; the car assembly (including guide shoes) must run on these installed rails. Therefore, rails must be fixed in place before the car can be installed.
It is preferable to install guide rails before lift door frames to ensure precise alignment of door openings relative to the rail positions, though some overlap is possible on site.
The counterweight also travels on its own set of guide rails or within the same shaft, and its installation depends on the guide rails being in place to guide the counterweight frame.

The lift machine room and shaft must be fully constructed and structurally complete before lift machine installation can commence, as the machine needs to be placed in the machine room and connected to the shaft.
Lift guide rails must be installed in the shaft before the lift machine can be installed, as the machine drives the system that interacts with the rails.
Electrical conduits and power supply rough-in work must be completed to provide the necessary electrical connections for the lift machine.
The lift machine must be installed and operational before the lift car can be installed, as the machine provides the hoisting mechanism needed to position and support the car.
The lift machine must be in place before hoisting cables/ropes can be connected, as the cables are attached to the machine's drive sheave.
The lift pit at the bottom of the shaft must be excavated, concreted, and waterproofed to provide a stable base and buffer zone before any lift car assembly can commence.

successor: Lift Door Installation and Sill Setting
rationale: Lift landing doors and sills must be installed after the lift car is in place to ensure correct alignment and clearance between the car and each floor landing.
Electrical connections to the lift car (such as lighting, control signals, and door mechanisms) require the car to be physically installed before final wiring and termination can be completed.
The counterweight assembly typically needs to be supported by the building's steel structure or framework, which must be erected first to provide structural support and attachment points.
The lift shaft (elevator hoistway) must be constructed before the counterweight can be assembled inside it, as the counterweight operates within the shaft space.
Counterweight assembly must be in place to guide and align the installation of lift rails that the counterweight will travel along.
The counterweight must be assembled and secured before lift cables (hoist ropes) can be attached to it as part of the elevator system.
The counterweight assembly is typically installed before the lift car, as the counterweight is needed to balance the system during car installation and rope attachment.

The hoisting ropes must be delivered to site and inspected for damage, quality, and correct specifications before any rigging work can begin. Rigging with uninspected or unsuitable ropes would be unsafe and non-compliant.

The lift car (or its partial structure) must be assembled and positioned within the shaft so that the hoisting ropes can be connected to the car's rope hitch or suspension points. Rigging ropes before the car is in place would leave them unconnected at one end.

The counterweight frame must be installed in the shaft so the hoisting ropes can be attached to the counterweight hitch on the opposite side of the sheave. Without the counterweight in place, the rope rigging cannot be completed.
After the ropes are rigged around the sheave and attached to both the car and counterweight, they must be tensioned and equalized to ensure even load distribution and proper lift operation.

successor: Lift Governor and Overspeed Governor Rope Installation
rationale: The hoisting ropes must be rigged before installing the governor rope because the governor rope routing is closely related to the hoisting rope positions on the sheave and the car/counterweight attachment points, and the overspeed governor mechanism depends on the hoisting ropes being in place for correct alignment.
The lift shaft must be fully constructed to provide the structural opening and frame for landing door installation.
Guide rails must be installed first to ensure proper alignment of the lift car and landing doors.
Landing doors must be installed before the lift car can be assembled and tested for safe operation.
Landing doors are critical safety components that must be in place before the lift system can be commissioned and tested for safe passenger use.

predecessor: Structural Floor Slab Completion at Each Landing
rationale: The floor slabs at each landing level must be completed to provide a stable and level working platform for door installation.
The lift shaft must be fully constructed to provide the physical enclosure and mounting surfaces for electrical conduits, junction boxes, and wiring within the shaft.

predecessor: Lift Equipment and Machine Room Installation
rationale: The lift machine room equipment (controller, drive, power supply) must be installed before wiring can be connected from the machine room to the shaft and car.
The main electrical supply must be available at the lift machine room to provide power for the lift controller, drive, and control wiring terminations.
The control wiring and electrical connections must be completed before the lift car is installed to allow for wiring of car controllers, call buttons, indicators, and safety circuits.
All electrical and control wiring must be complete and terminated before power can be applied and the lift system can be tested for correct operation and safety compliance.
The lift controller cannot be programmed or tested until all electrical wiring (power supply, control cables, sensors) is installed, as the controller needs to be connected to the system to function.

Mechanical components such as the lift car, guide rails, and counterweight must be installed before the controller can be programmed and tested, as the controller interacts with these mechanical elements.
After the lift controller is programmed and tested individually, the full lift system must be integrated and tested to verify that all components work together correctly.
The lift controller must be fully programmed and tested before the lift can be commissioned and handed over to the client.
Safety certification can only be carried out after the controller has been programmed and tested to ensure all safety functions operate correctly.
The lift and its mechanical components must be physically installed before safety devices (e.g., overspeed governors, safety gears, limit switches) can be mounted, wired, and commissioned.
A permanent electrical power supply must be available to power the lift controller and safety circuits, as commissioning of safety devices requires functional testing with live power.
Safety devices (e.g., brakes, overspeed governors, safety gears) must be commissioned and verified operational before the lift can undergo full load testing under rated capacity.
Final handover and issue of an operation permit or certificate of compliance require that all safety devices have been successfully commissioned and tested.
The lift pit must be excavated to the required depth before construction and waterproofing can begin, as the pit structure is built within the excavated void.

The lift pit typically forms part of the substructure and must be constructed on top of or within the foundation system; adequate ground support (e.g., piles or foundation slab) must be in place before the pit structure is built.

The physical lift pit must be constructed and waterproofed before lift equipment (guide rails, buffers, car sling) can be installed inside the pit, as the pit provides the structural enclosure and dry environment required for mechanical installation.

successor: Ground Slab / Basement Slab Pour (at lift pit area)
rationale: The lift pit is usually constructed as part of or before the final basement slab; the slab may be poured after pit walls are formed, or the pit waterproofing must be completed before the slab is cast to ensure a continuous waterproof membrane.
Once the lift pit is waterproofed, surrounding backfill and continuation of the external waterproofing membrane can proceed to protect the pit from groundwater ingress.

predecessor: Lift Shaft Construction / Core Wall Construction
successor: Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) Shielding for Lift Shaft
rationale: The physical lift shaft structure (walls, slabs) must be in place before any shielding material can be applied or installed onto the shaft surfaces.

successor: Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) Shielding for Lift Shaft
rationale: Waterproofing must be completed to protect the EMI shielding materials from moisture damage and to ensure a dry substrate for shielding installation.

predecessor: Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) Shielding for Lift Shaft
rationale: EMI shielding (e.g., copper tape, conductive mesh) is applied to the shaft interior surfaces; lift rails are then installed over or after the shielding to avoid damaging the shielding during rail placement.

predecessor: Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) Shielding for Lift Shaft
successor: Electrical Cabling and Wiring in Lift Shaft
rationale: Cables and wiring should be pulled after shielding is in place so that shielding can be properly grounded and to prevent cables from interfering with the shielding continuity.

predecessor: Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) Shielding for Lift Shaft
rationale: While lift car installation can theoretically begin before shielding completion, it is strongly preferred to complete EMI shielding first to avoid rework and to ensure electromagnetic compatibility during testing.
The emergency phone/intercom requires electrical power to operate, so the lift's electrical supply must be installed and energized before the phone/intercom can function.

predecessor: Lift Shaft and Car Wiring Installation
rationale: Communication wiring connecting the lift car to the control room or building management system must be run through the shaft and car before the emergency phone/intercom can be connected and tested.

predecessor: Lift Car Body and Interior Installation
rationale: The emergency phone/intercom unit is mounted within the lift car interior; the car body and interior panels must be in place to provide a mounting surface for the device.
The emergency phone/intercom must be installed and connected before the overall lift commissioning and testing phase, which includes verifying that emergency communication systems function correctly.
Safety inspection must verify that emergency communication devices are operational; therefore the phone/intercom must be installed and working prior to formal safety inspection.
The auditorium tiered seating requires a stable, level structural slab or foundation base to be constructed first, as the seating tiers are built upon this substrate.

Primary structural steel or concrete framing that supports the building envelope and/or overhead structure must be erected before installing tiered seating, as the seating is often anchored to or supported by the building frame.

predecessor: Rough-In MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing) Below Slab
rationale: Any under-slab conduits, drainage pipes, or electrical rough-ins that will be beneath the tiered seating area must be installed before the seating tiers are constructed, to avoid costly rework or demolition.
The physical tiered platforms (concrete or structural bleachers) must be fully constructed and cured before seats or chairs can be bolted or anchored to them.
The tiered seating structure must be complete before applying final flooring finishes (e.g., carpet, rubber treads) and installing safety railings or guardrails on the tiers.

While acoustic treatments and wall finishes around the seating area can often proceed concurrently, it is preferable to complete the tiered structure first so that acoustic panels and wall finishes align properly with the seating levels.

Bleacher and grandstand seating require a stable, level, and structurally sound base. The concrete slab or foundation must be poured and cured to support the seating loads and provide anchorage points.

For bleachers or grandstands that are supported by a structural steel frame, the steel framework must be erected and stabilized before seating components are attached or installed to ensure structural integrity.
Handrails and guardrails are safety-critical components that are installed after seating is in place to ensure proper alignment with aisles and seating rows, providing occupant fall protection.
The completed seating installation must be inspected and certified for load capacity, proper attachment, and compliance with building codes before the venue can be opened to the public.

While finishing work can be done after seating is installed, it is a soft preference to allow touch-ups without risk of damaging new seating - often scheduled after installation to complete aesthetic work.
Fixed bench seating requires a stable, level base. The foundation or slab must be poured and cured before benches can be securely anchored.

While benches could be installed after floor finishing, installing them before final floor work allows seamless integration and avoids damaging finished floors during bench installation. This is a practical sequencing preference.
Wall cladding or skirting around bench areas can be finished after bench installation for a neat trim, but it is not a physical necessity.
Any electrical conduit or outlets designated for the bench area must be roughed-in before the bench is installed, as the bench structure would block access to walls and floors.
The bench structural frame must be fully installed before any cushions or upholstered seating elements can be attached.
Seat tracks must be installed first to provide the anchoring mechanism for fixed individual seats.
Floor deck provides the structural surface that seat tracks are mounted onto and that supports the seat loads.

predecessor: Complete Cabin Interior Finishing (Walls, Ceiling, Flooring)
rationale: While seats can be installed before full interior finishing, it is preferred to complete wall and ceiling panels to avoid damage to finished surfaces during seat installation.
Seat belts are directly attached to the fixed seat frame or structure; the seat must be in place before restraint systems can be mounted.

successor: Passenger Comfort Testing (Seat Fit & Layout Verification)
rationale: Seats must be installed before ergonomic testing and layout verification can be performed to ensure proper spacing and comfort.
The reception desk must be anchored to a finished, level floor slab or subfloor to ensure stability and proper alignment.
Electrical outlets, data ports, and conduit for the reception desk must be roughed-in within the floor or wall before the desk is installed, as later access would require demolition.
The reception desk is often built against or integrated with a wall; the wall must be framed, boarded, and finished before the desk can be secured in place.
The base cabinets and structure of the reception desk must be installed first so that the countertop can be fitted, sealed, and finished on top of them.
While overhead lighting can be installed independently, it is preferable to coordinate fixture positioning with the finished desk location to ensure proper illumination and aesthetic alignment.
Fixed booth seating requires a level, stable floor surface for installation and anchoring.
If booth seating includes integrated power outlets or lighting, electrical rough-in must be completed before the booths are installed and block access.

Booth seating is heavy and fixed; floor finishing should ideally be done before installation to avoid cutting around the booths, but if booths go in first, the finished floor must be protected. Typically the booth goes on top of finished flooring.
It is easier to paint and finish walls behind booths before they are installed, but touch-ups can be done after.
Booth installation generates debris; final cleaning should occur after all furniture including booth seating is in place.
The stadium structure foundation must be completed before any seating installation can begin, as seats need a stable structural base to be mounted onto.
The concrete terraces or bleachers that support the seats must be cast and cured before seat brackets can be anchored and seats installed.
Mounting brackets or rails must be installed and secured to the concrete structure before individual seats with armrests can be attached to them.
The seat with armrest structure must be fully installed before any upholstery or padding is applied to the armrests, as the padding material is added on top of the rigid armrest.
Seat numbering is typically done after installation for accurate row/seat identification, though it could theoretically be done beforehand, making it a soft preference.
The concrete slab must be fully cured to provide a stable surface for anchoring the seat system.
Seats cannot be installed until their anchoring system is in place and secured.
Torque verification must be performed after the anchoring system is installed to ensure proper tightening.
Underfloor conduits must be routed before anchoring is placed to avoid interference with anchor bolts or brackets.
The floor must be level and waterproofed to ensure proper alignment and durability of the anchoring system.
Seats must be physically installed before seat numbering or row marker plates can be applied, as the markers are affixed to or associated with the installed seats/rows.
Row layout and marking on the floor/structure must be completed first to define where rows are located, so that row marker plates can be placed at the correct positions.

successor: Final Inspection / Quality Check of Seating
rationale: Row marker plates and seat numbering must be in place before final inspection can verify correct labeling and seating alignment.

It is preferable (soft preference) that seat/row numbering is complete before installing directional signage so that signage can reference accurate row/seat numbers, but it is not physically required.
Floor or base surfaces must be prepared and finished before row marker plates (often floor-mounted or wall-mounted) can be installed securely.
A stable foundation and level site must be prepared before any seating structure can be installed to ensure structural integrity and safety.
The building's structural framing that defines the waiting area enclosure must be in place so that the built-in seating can be anchored to the walls and floor.

Any electrical outlets, USB charging ports, or data cabling intended to be integrated into or behind the seating must be roughed in before the seating is permanently installed, as accessing these after installation would require removal.

Flooring around and up to the built-in seating should be completed after the seating is installed to achieve tight, seamless transitions and avoid cutting flooring materials to fit around the seating base.

While painting can be done before installation, final touch-up painting and wall finishing around the seating area is best performed after installation to cover any gaps, marks, or patching needed from the installation process.
Concrete must be fully cured and dry to provide adequate strength and stability for anchoring bolts; otherwise bolts may not hold securely.
Seats must be anchored and bolted into place before they can be leveled and aligned for proper positioning.
Safety inspections (e.g., torque checks, pull tests) can only be performed after all bolts are anchored and secured.
Final assembly and finishing work such as attaching armrests or upholstery typically follows bolting, though some finishing could be done concurrently in certain sequences.
Fixed seating requires a level, cured concrete slab or finished floor surface to anchor the seating supports and ensure structural stability.
The building structure must be complete to provide the necessary support and enclosure for fixed seating installation.
Electrical conduits and junction boxes for seat lighting, power outlets, or accessibility systems must be installed before fixed seating covers floor areas and walls.
Fixed seating is typically installed after subfloor is ready but before final floor finishes (e.g., carpet, tile) to allow seamless finishing around seating bases.
While painting can often be done before or after seating installation, performing wall finishing after seating avoids damage to walls from seating installation activities.
The foundation and substructure must be completed first to provide a stable load-bearing base for the tiered riser/stadia structure.
The main structural frame must be in place to support the tiered riser elements, especially for elevated stadia.
Seats and chairs are fixed onto the completed riser terracing; the structural tiers must be fully constructed before seating can be installed.
Handrails and guardrails are typically mounted onto the finished riser edges and cannot be installed until the concrete/steel tiers are in place.

While lighting masts can be erected independently, precise aiming and final adjustment of stadium lights often depends on the completed rake and geometry of the risers to ensure proper illumination of all seating tiers.
The concrete structure (e.g., stadium seating bowl) must be fully cast and cured before survey markings can be applied, as the layout depends on the final as-built concrete surface geometry.
The seating surfaces (risers/floor) need to be finished and leveled so that accurate survey reference points can be established for seat row and column markings.
