The survey markings define precisely where each seat or seat bracket will be anchored; seats cannot be installed before the layout is marked out.
While not physically required, marking seat layout first helps coordinate railing positions so they align with seat rows, avoiding conflicts or rework.
Soft preference: concession fit-out can technically proceed in parallel, but completing seat layout marking first helps ensure overall venue zoning is coherent.
The seat frame and structure must be fully assembled before upholstery can be installed, as the upholstery is applied over the frame.
Cushions and padding must be in place on the seat structure before the final upholstery covering is applied.
Once the upholstery is complete, the completed seat can be integrated into the vehicle or final assembly.
To avoid damaging the fresh upholstery, trim and detail work is typically performed after upholstery installation; however, this is a soft preference as it can be sequenced differently with care.
The completed upholstered seat must be inspected for quality, fit, and finish before it is delivered or accepted.
Seating areas require a finished structural floor slab to be in place before seating can be installed and anchored.
Underfloor electrical outlets, data ports, and raceways for accessible seating positions must be roughed-in before seating is placed over them.
Seating installation can damage finished flooring; thus flooring is typically completed after seating is installed, or seating is installed before final floor covering to allow adjustments.
The accessible seating must be fully installed to verify compliance with ADA/accessibility codes before the space can be certified.
While seating is typically installed before final furnishing and occupancy, it is a logical workflow preference rather than a strict physical necessity.

predecessor: Install underfloor or raised floor system for accessible wiring
rationale: The Integrated Power/Data Grommet is typically placed into a cutout in the finished floor surface; the underfloor or raised floor system must be complete to provide the cavity for routing cables and to support the grommet housing.

predecessor: Run power and data cabling to grommet location
rationale: The grommet serves as a pass-through for power and data cables; those cables must be staged or pulled to the location before the grommet is seated so they can be fed through the opening.

successor: Connect power and data cables to floor outlets or junction boxes
rationale: After the grommet is installed, the previously staged cables are terminated into receptacles or connectors that sit within or below the grommet assembly.

successor: Install finish floor surface (e.g., carpet, tile, vinyl)
rationale: The grommet can be set before or after floor finishing; installing before the finish floor allows the grommet flange to be trimmed flush, but is not a hard physical constraint.

successor: Commission and test power/ data outlets at grommet
rationale: Final electrical and data testing cannot be performed until the grommet is in place and all connections are made through it.
Structural framing and sheathing must be complete to provide the supporting walls and enclosure for cabinet installation.
Rough-in electrical wiring and plumbing lines must be run within walls before cabinets are installed, as cabinets would block access to these utilities.
Cabinets must be permanently installed and leveled first to serve as the supporting base for countertops.
While often done after cabinets to save material and cost, it is a soft preference as cabinets can be installed over subfloor and finish flooring installed around them.
Final hardware (handles, pulls, hinges) and trim (crown molding, toe kicks) must be installed after cabinets are fully set in place to ensure proper alignment and fit.
Wall framing provides the structural support and backing needed to securely mount kitchen wall cabinets.
Electrical wires for lighting and outlets must be roughed in behind the walls before cabinets are installed, as cabinets would block access to wall cavities.
Any plumbing vents or lines running through walls must be roughed in before cabinets are mounted, as they would be inaccessible afterwards.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and finished (mudded and sanded) on the walls where cabinets will be mounted, as cabinets are attached to finished walls.
Wall cabinets must be installed first so that countertops can be fitted precisely between or below them, ensuring proper alignment and clearance.
Base cabinets must sit on a finished, level floor to ensure proper alignment, stability, and to prevent damage to the cabinets or flooring during installation.
Rough-in electrical wiring and plumbing pipes must be run behind the cabinet walls before cabinets are installed, as they would be inaccessible afterward.
Walls must be framed and drywalled (at least behind cabinet areas) so cabinets have a solid surface to mount to; bare studs are not an acceptable finished backing.
Countertops are fabricated and installed directly on top of base cabinets after the cabinets are leveled and secured in place.

While base cabinets are typically installed before wall cabinets to provide a working platform and ensure alignment, some crews install wall cabinets first; this is a soft preference based on workflow convenience.
Sinks drop into countertops or cabinet cutouts, and dishwashers/ovens slide into base cabinet openings, so base cabinets must be in place first.
Backsplash is typically installed after base cabinets and countertops to achieve clean seams, but it is a soft preference as it could theoretically be done before (though not recommended).

Electrical wiring and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before installing cabinets, as cabinets would block access to walls and make rough-in work difficult or impossible without damaging the cabinets.
Walls must be framed and drywall installed to provide a finished surface against which cabinets can be securely mounted.
Tall/utility cabinets support countertops; countertops must be installed after cabinets are in place to ensure proper alignment, support, and fit.
Cabinets are often installed before finished flooring to avoid damaging the floor; however, this is sometimes a soft preference as flooring could be installed first and cabinets placed on top.
Cabinets are typically installed before final painting and trim to allow for precise fit and touch-ups, though painting can be done in stages making this a soft preference.

Plumbing rough-in must be completed before vanity cabinets are installed because the plumbing pipes and drain lines need to be in place behind the vanity, and once the cabinet is installed, access to the wall for plumbing work becomes extremely difficult or impossible without removing the cabinet.
The wall structure must be framed and sheathed to provide a stable mounting surface for the vanity cabinet. The cabinet attaches directly to the wall framing, so this must be complete.

Wall finishes such as drywall or tile backing must be installed before the vanity cabinet is placed, as the cabinet will cover portions of the wall and finishing behind it later would require removal of the cabinet.

The vanity cabinet must be securely in place before the countertop can be installed, as the countertop rests directly on top of the cabinet and must be cut and fitted to match the cabinet's dimensions and layout.
The sink typically drops into the countertop or mounts to the vanity cabinet structure. The cabinet must be installed first to provide support and enclosure for the sink and its plumbing connections.
Medicine cabinets are typically recessed into or mounted on walls, so wall framing must be complete to provide the structural support and cavity for installation.
Electrical wiring for medicine cabinet lighting or outlets must be roughed in before the cabinet is installed, as access behind the cabinet is restricted after placement.
Medicine cabinets are typically mounted onto finished drywall or recessed into a drywalled opening, so drywall must be installed and finished before the cabinet can be properly secured.
While medicine cabinets are often installed before vanities to avoid working over finished surfaces, this is a soft preference; the vanity can be installed first if care is taken.
Medicine cabinets often incorporate mirrors or are placed adjacent to mirrors; preference is to install the cabinet first to align mirror placement, but it's not physically required.
Closet systems are installed against finished walls. Drywall, taping, and texturing must be complete to provide a smooth, finished surface for mounting closet components.

Flooring should be installed before closet systems to ensure the closet organizers sit on top of the finished floor, allowing proper height measurement and avoiding the need to cut around or work beneath closet components.
Ceiling work can cause dust and debris that would contaminate finished closet organizers. Ceiling finishing should be done prior to avoid damaging or soiling installed closet systems.

Any electrical wiring, outlets, or lighting fixtures in the closet area must be roughed in and installed before closet systems are mounted, as closet components may block access to walls and ceilings for electrical work.

While not a strict physical necessity, final touch-up painting and trim work are typically done after closet installation to cover any minor damage or gaps that occur during the mounting process, yielding a cleaner finished appearance.
The entertainment center cabinetry is typically built into or attached to the wall structure, requiring framed walls to provide the necessary support and mounting surface.

Electrical wiring for outlets, lighting, and entertainment system connections must be run within the walls before cabinetry is installed, as the cabinets will cover and block access to the wall cavities.
Flooring should be installed before built-in cabinetry to ensure proper clearance, avoid damaging the flooring, and allow the cabinets to sit on the finished floor surface.
If the entertainment center includes a counter or shelf surface, the cabinet boxes must be fully installed and leveled before countertop materials can be measured, cut, and placed on top.
Installing cabinetry may scuff or damage surrounding wall finishes, so final touch-up painting and trim work is typically performed after cabinet installation for a clean, finished appearance.
Flooring must be installed before built-in bookcases because the bookcases often rest on the finished floor, and installing flooring after would require removing or cutting around the bookcases.
Wall framing provides the structural support and backing onto which built-in bookcases are attached or secured.
Drywall and finishing must be completed before built-in installation so that the bookcases can sit flush against finished walls, and to avoid damage to finished surfaces during installation.
Trim and baseboards should be installed after the bookcases so that they can be cut to fit neatly around the built-in unit, providing a clean finished look.

It is often easier to paint the wall behind and around the bookcase before installation (touch-ups after), but if the bookcase is painted/finished as part of the trim, final painting may follow; this is a soft preference for sequencing efficiency.

Electrical outlets, data ports, and wiring for the desk area must be roughed in before the desk is built, as the desk structure would block access to walls and make retrofitting electrical work difficult and destructive.

predecessor: Drywall and taping/finishing in home office
rationale: Drywall must be installed, taped, and finished before the built-in desk is constructed, because the desk will be attached to and abut the finished walls; installing drywall after the desk would be impossible in the covered areas.

predecessor: Prime and paint home office walls
rationale: Wall painting should be completed before the built-in desk is installed, as the desk will sit flush against the walls and cannot easily be moved; painting behind the desk after installation would be impractical.
Baseboard and trim around the desk area must be installed after the desk is in place so that the trim butts neatly against the desk legs or cabinets, creating a finished appearance.

successor: Install desk lighting and receptacles (finish electrical)
rationale: Final electrical connections for under-cabinet lighting, desk-level outlets, and data jacks must be completed after the desk is built, because the fixtures are mounted to or integrated within the desk structure itself.
Electrical wiring must be roughed in behind walls before cabinetry is installed, as cabinets would block access to wall cavities.
If the mudroom includes a sink or laundry area, plumbing rough-ins must be completed behind walls before cabinetry installation.
Cabinetry requires finished wall framing to anchor cabinets securely.
Drywall must be installed and finished behind cabinetry before cabinets are mounted, as it is impractical to finish drywall around installed cabinets.
Walls behind cabinets should be painted before cabinets are installed, as they cannot be easily painted afterward.
Ideally flooring is installed before cabinets for a clean look, but cabinets can be installed first and flooring butted up against them; considered a soft preference for better finish quality.
Countertops must be templated and installed on top of the base cabinets after cabinets are securely in place.
Electrical trim-out such as installing outlets and switches on finished walls should happen after cabinetry is installed to ensure proper alignment.

successor: Interior Trim and Millwork (crown molding, baseboards)
rationale: Trim work around cabinets must be installed after cabinets are in place to create seamless transitions and proper fit.
Windows must be installed and sealed before window seats are built to ensure proper fit, clearance, and to avoid damaging the seats during window installation.
The wall framing and rough opening for the window must be completed to provide the structural support and cavity for the built-in window seat.
Any electrical wiring for outlets or lighting near the window seat area must be roughed in before the seat structure is built, as it would be inaccessible or require demolition later.
After the window seat structure is built and secured, trim work such as baseboards, window casings, and seat edge trim can be installed to cover gaps and create a finished appearance.
The window seat must be fully constructed before painting, staining, or applying any final finishes to the seat surface and surrounding trim.
The reception desks require a finished floor slab as a base support before installation can begin.
Structural framework defines the lobby space and provides overhead support before desk installation.
Electrical and data cabling must be roughed-in behind walls and floors before desks are placed and connected.
Walls define the lobby layout and create the recess or backdrop for the reception desk placement.
Desks must be installed before final floor finishes and painting around them to achieve a clean, professional appearance.

successor: Data and IT System Installation (Computers, Screens, Phones)
rationale: IT equipment is placed on or within the desks after the desks are physically installed and secured.
Signage is typically mounted after desks are in place to ensure correct alignment and positioning, though it could be done concurrently.
All reception area components including desks must be fully installed before the final inspection and handover can occur.
The banquette seating rests on the finished floor; the subfloor must be level, stable, and properly prepared before constructing the seating base to ensure structural integrity and alignment.

Back walls for banquette seating need to be framed, and any electrical outlets, data cabling, or plumbing for nearby areas must be roughed in before the banquette is built, as the seating would block access to wall cavities afterwards.

Floor finishes are typically installed after the banquette base is constructed, particularly if the banquette sits on top of the subfloor; finishing materials can be brought up to the edge of the banquette for a clean, finished look.
Wall finishing above and around the banquette area is done after the banquette frame is in place, allowing a seamless transition between the seating and the finished wall surface.
The companion dining table or surface adjacent to the banquette must be positioned and installed after the banquette is fully built to ensure proper spacing, alignment, and clearances for seating.

predecessor: Rough-in Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP) Services
rationale: MEP rough-ins (electrical, plumbing, gas, data lines) must be completed behind walls and below slabs before casework is installed, as casework would block access to these services.
Flooring must be fully installed and cured before casework is placed on top; otherwise, casework would need to be removed or worked around for floor installation.
Casework is anchored to wall framing/drywall; walls must be in place to support and align the casework.
Base cabinets and casework frames must be set and leveled before countertops and sinks can be installed on top of them.

successor: Final MEP Trim-Out (Fixtures, Outlets, Gas Valves)
rationale: Final connection of plumbing fixtures, electrical outlets, and gas valves to casework-mounted equipment can only be done after the casework is in its final position.
Trim and moldings are typically attached to framed walls, so the rough framing and backing must be complete before trim can be installed.
All wiring, plumbing, ductwork, and insulation within walls must be completed and inspected before covering them with trim and moldings.
Trim and moldings are installed over finished drywall; drywall must be hung, taped, mudded, sanded, and primed before trim can be applied.
While baseboards and casings can be painted separately, it is often preferred to paint walls first so that wall paint can lap slightly behind trim, though some trades paint trim after installation.
Door casing trim must be installed before doors and hardware are hung so that the casing frames the opening and provides the proper reveal for the door.

Baseboards and shoe moldings are typically installed before finished flooring (e.g., hardwood, tile, carpet) so that flooring can be run up to the trim, or in some methods, the flooring is installed first and baseboard over it; but standard sequencing has trim before final flooring to allow for scribing and gap coverage.
Crown moldings and soffit trims are often done before cabinets to ensure a seamless fit, though this depends on design. Typically, cabinets are set first, then crown molding is scribed to them.
Cabinets must be installed and leveled first because countertops are set directly on top of cabinet boxes to form the finished surface.
The subfloor must be complete and level to provide a stable base for cabinets which in turn support countertops.
Plumbing supply and drain lines must be roughed-in within walls before countertops are installed, as countertops may cover or be cut for sink openings.
Sinks are typically dropped into or mounted under the countertop cutout after the countertop is set in place.
Drop-in cooktops and similar appliances are installed into the countertop cutout after the countertop is fixed in position.
Cabinet boxes and doors must be fully installed and mounted before hardware (handles, knobs, pulls, hinges, locks) can be attached to them.
After hardware is installed, final adjustments to door alignment and drawer slide tension can be made to ensure proper operation with the hardware in place.
Hardware such as knobs and pulls cannot be installed until the doors and drawer fronts they attach to are already mounted on the cabinets.
Once hardware is installed, subsequent finishing/protection steps are needed to prevent paint or stain from getting on the hardware, or hardware must be installed after painting to avoid damage.
The cabinet boxes must be assembled, leveled, and secured in place before any hardware can be installed on the cabinet fronts.
Cabinet filler pieces and shims are installed to fill gaps and level cabinets after the main cabinet boxes have been set in place. This ensures proper alignment and fit.

Countertops are installed on top of finished, leveled cabinets. Fillers and shims must be in place to ensure the cabinets are stable, level, and properly aligned before countertops are fabricated and installed.
Door and drawer fronts are installed after filler strips and shimming are complete, as fillers affect the final alignment and reveal gaps that doors and drawers must fit against.
Flooring (especially under cabinets) should be installed before final cabinet adjustments and filler installation to ensure proper clearance and finished floor height considerations.
While filler installation can be done before or after wall finishing, it is preferred to have walls painted or finished first to avoid damaging finished walls when working with filler pieces.
The wall surface must be smooth, clean, and finished before tile or backsplash material can be properly adhered.
After backsplash tiles are installed, holes can be cut precisely for outlets, and outlet covers or trim plates can be mounted flush to the tile surface.
Final caulking along the top edge (between backsplash and cabinets) and side edges must be done after the backsplash is fully set and grouted to seal gaps and provide a finished look.
Cabinets must be installed first to provide the physical mounting surface and define the under-cabinet area where the lighting will be attached.
Electrical wiring and junction boxes must be run to the under-cabinet locations before the lighting fixtures can be connected and mounted.
Walls must be finished with drywall and painted before under-cabinet lighting is installed, as the lighting fixtures will be mounted against the finished wall surface.
Under-cabinet lighting is typically installed before countertops to allow access to the underside of cabinets for wiring and fixture mounting without obstruction from countertops.

The backsplash is installed after the under-cabinet lighting to allow the backsplash material (e.g., tile) to be fitted neatly up to the underside of the cabinets and around the lighting fixtures or wiring.
Electrical wiring and outlet installation must be complete before appliances can be connected to power sources.
Plumbing supply lines and drain pipes must be in place before water-using appliances (dishwasher, washing machine, etc.) can be installed and connected.
Flooring must be laid before heavy appliances are moved into position to avoid damaging unfinished floors.
Built-in appliances (dishwasher, range, refrigerator) must be installed before cabinets can be finally adjusted and trimmed around them.
Appliances must be physically positioned and connected to rough wiring before final electrical trim-out and breaker connections can be completed.
Custom paneled appliance fronts are attached to the cabinet boxes that house the appliances, so the cabinet boxes must be installed first to provide the structural support and attachment points.
The appliances (dishwasher, refrigerator, etc.) must be in place so that the custom paneled fronts can be accurately fitted and attached to them.

Ideally, custom paneled appliance fronts are installed before countertops to avoid damaging the countertops during panel fitting, but this is a soft preference as countertops can be installed after with careful handling.

Custom paneled fronts are often considered part of the finish work and are typically completed before final trim carpentry to ensure a cohesive look, but some trim can be adjusted after panel installation.
Toe kicks are typically attached to the bottom of base cabinets; base cabinets must be installed first to provide a mounting surface and proper alignment.
The subfloor must be leveled and prepared before toe kicks can be attached, as toe kicks sit on or near the finished floor surface and require a stable substrate.
While not always physically required, installing flooring before toe kicks allows for proper height alignment and a cleaner finished appearance without having to cut toe kicks to fit over flooring.
Toe kicks form the finished base of the cabinet assembly; doors and drawers are installed after the cabinet body and toe kick are fully set and aligned.
Decorative trim and molding often abut or sit atop the toe kick, so the toe kick must be in place to serve as a reference and attachment point.
Drawers and doors must be fitted to an assembled and installed cabinet frame, as they attach to the cabinet carcass.
Handles and hardware are mounted onto the fitted and adjusted doors and drawers, so fitting must be completed first.
After fitting, a final alignment check ensures all doors and drawers open/close properly; this is a quality control step that could theoretically be done concurrently but is best performed afterward.
Slides and hinges must be installed on the cabinet and on the drawer/door components before those components can be fitted and adjusted into their final positions.
It is preferable that painting or finishing of doors/drawers be completed before fitting to avoid damaging finished surfaces during adjustment, though not a strict physical necessity.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, structures, and debris before any earthmoving can commence to ensure a safe and unobstructed working area.
Accurate site levels, boundaries, and excavation depths must be established by survey prior to excavation to ensure correct positioning and depths.
While not physically essential, having temporary site offices, welfare facilities, and utility connections in place improves productivity and compliance before excavation begins.
Bulk removal of topsoil and general overburden must be completed before precise trench and foundation excavations can be performed to the required formation levels.
After bulk excavation reaches design levels, the exposed subgrade must be compacted and/or treated to achieve the required bearing capacity before subsequent construction.
The ground surface must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before any excavation can begin, as obstructions would prevent access and safe operation of excavation equipment.

The exact trench alignment, width, depth, and grade must be staked out and marked based on engineering drawings before excavation, to ensure the trench is dug in the correct location and to the required specifications.
All existing underground utilities (gas, water, electric, telecom) must be identified and marked to avoid accidental strikes during excavation, which is a critical safety requirement.
Once the trench is excavated, shoring systems (trench boxes, hydraulic supports, or sloping) must be installed to protect workers from cave-ins before anyone can enter the trench.
After excavation to the required depth, the trench bottom must be prepared with a bedding layer (e.g., sand or gravel) to provide a stable, uniform base for pipe or conduit installation.
The trench must be fully excavated to the required depth and dimensions before any pipes or conduits can be laid in it, as the excavation creates the physical space needed for installation.

The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before excavation can begin, otherwise excavation equipment cannot access the work area and loose debris would contaminate the excavation.
The exact location, boundaries, and depths of the pit must be surveyed and staked out before excavation begins to ensure the excavation is in the correct position and to the required dimensions.
All existing underground utilities (gas, water, electric, telecom) must be located and marked prior to excavation to avoid utility strikes, service disruptions, and safety hazards.

While some preliminary soil testing can be done earlier, detailed in-situ soil testing and groundwater level assessment at the open pit face is best performed after excavation begins to evaluate actual conditions for shoring and foundation design.

Once the pit is excavated to the required depth, shoring, bracing, and ground support systems must be installed to protect the excavation walls from collapse before any workers enter the pit for subsequent activities.
The pit excavation must be completed and the bearing surface prepared before any foundation concrete can be poured, as the foundation sits at the bottom of the excavated pit.
If groundwater is encountered during excavation, dewatering systems (sump pumps, wellpoints) must be installed after excavation to keep the pit dry for subsequent foundation works.

Site mobilization, including setting up site offices, storage areas, and access roads, must be completed before topsoil stripping begins to ensure equipment and personnel are available for the stripping operation.
Trees, shrubs, and other vegetation must be cleared from the site before topsoil can be stripped, as vegetation obstructs the stripping equipment and would mix organic material with the soil.

Topsoil must be removed to expose the underlying subgrade material before bulk earthworks (cut and fill operations) can commence, as the organic-rich topsoil is unsuitable for structural fill and compaction.

Stripping the topsoil exposes the subgrade, allowing for the installation of subsoil drainage systems (e.g., French drains, perforated pipes) to control groundwater and surface water during subsequent earthworks.
The stripped topsoil must be stockpiled in designated areas immediately after stripping to preserve it for later landscaping and restoration work, preventing loss and contamination.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, structures, and debris before any excavation can begin to provide unobstructed access for excavators and ensure safe working conditions.
Soil borings, bearing capacity tests, and groundwater analysis must be completed to determine excavation methods, slope stability requirements, and dewatering needs before bulk earthmoving commences.
The excavation footprint, cut/fill lines, and building corners must be staked and verified by a surveyor to ensure the excavation is performed to the correct location, dimensions, and elevations.
Existing underground utilities (gas, water, electric, telecom) must be located, marked, and either capped or relocated before excavation to prevent service strikes, injuries, and service outages.
Silt fencing, sediment basins, and other BMPs must be installed prior to earth disturbance to comply with environmental regulations and prevent off-site sedimentation.
Protected trees must be fenced at the drip line and any required environmental permits or mitigation measures must be in place before soil disturbance begins.
Grading permits, excavation permits, and environmental clearance must be obtained from authorities before any earthmoving activities can lawfully proceed.
Once mass excavation is complete to subgrade level, the exposed soil must be proof-rolled and compacted to verify bearing capacity and prepare a stable working surface for foundation construction.

Concrete foundations (spread footings, mat slabs, or pile caps) cannot be placed until the excavation has been completed to the design subgrade elevation and the bearing surface has been approved by the geotechnical engineer.
If groundwater is encountered during excavation, dewatering wells or sump pumps must be installed and operated continuously to keep the excavation dry for subsequent foundation work.
Below-grade waterproofing membranes and drainage boards cannot be applied to foundation walls until the surrounding excavation is complete and the wall surfaces are exposed and accessible.
Site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil to expose the rock surface before excavation can begin.
Accurate survey marks and staking are required to delineate exact excavation boundaries and depths before rock removal starts.
Borehole data and rock classification must be completed to determine excavation method (blasting, ripping, or breaking) and safety requirements.
Rock must be fully excavated to required depth and grade before foundation elements (footings, pads) can be placed on competent bearing material.
Excavated voids must be created before any backfill material can be placed and compacted to specified densities.

The site must be cleared of existing structures, vegetation, and debris before unsuitable material removal can begin, as clearing provides access to the ground surface and identifies the areas requiring material replacement.
Surveying is required to mark the exact boundaries and depths of excavation for unsuitable material removal, ensuring the correct areas are excavated and replaced according to design specifications.

After removing unsuitable material and placing replacement fill, compaction testing and proof rolling must be performed to verify that the replaced material meets density and load-bearing requirements before proceeding with further construction.

Foundations cannot be constructed on unsuitable or uncompacted ground; the removal and replacement of poor material with engineered fill is a prerequisite to providing a stable subgrade for foundation construction.

While underground utilities are typically installed after ground improvement, in some sequences shallow utilities could be installed concurrently with careful coordination; however, it is strongly preferred to complete material replacement first to avoid disturbing newly placed fill.

Site mobilization including setting up equipment, access roads, and temporary facilities must be completed before dewatering can commence, as dewatering requires operational setup and logistical support.
Vegetation, debris, and topsoil must be removed to access the ground surface for installing dewatering wells, pumps, and drainage systems.
Accurate site surveying is required to mark the locations for dewatering wells, sumps, and trenching to ensure effective groundwater control.
Dewatering must lower the groundwater table before excavation begins to prevent water inflow into the excavation pit, ensure stability, and provide safe dry working conditions.
Groundwater must be controlled and lowered before trenching operations to prevent trench collapse, water accumulation, and to maintain a stable working environment.
The area must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before excavation can begin to provide unobstructed access for earthmoving equipment and to ensure safe working conditions.
Erosion and sediment control measures (e.g., silt fences, sedimentation basins) must be installed prior to any earth disturbance to prevent runoff and comply with environmental regulations.
The excavation must be completed, including proper sloping and benching for safety, before the foundation subgrade can be trimmed, leveled, and compacted to design elevations.
Excavated trenches and pits must be ready before placing underground pipes, conduits, or drainage systems to avoid re-excavation and ensure proper bedding depth.
Excavation and benching must be fully completed before any backfill operations can commence, as backfill material is placed against or over the excavated/excavated-bench areas after the work is done.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, structures, and obstructions before excavation can begin to provide unobstructed access to the working area.
While not strictly physically required, establishing temporary access roads facilitates the movement of excavation equipment and haul trucks to and from the excavation zone, improving efficiency.

Surveying and marking of the excavation boundaries, slope gradients, and cut/fill lines must be completed to guide the excavation equipment and ensure the embankment is excavated to the correct geometry.
After excavation, the exposed subgrade and embankment surfaces must be compacted and graded to achieve the required density and surface tolerances before subsequent layers are placed.
Drainage systems such as subdrains, weepholes, or berm drains are installed after excavation to manage water flow and prevent erosion or saturation of the newly formed slopes.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, structures, and debris before excavation can begin to provide unobstructed access and safe working conditions for utility trenching.

Survey stakes and markings identifying utility routes, depths, and existing underground services must be in place before excavation to ensure accurate digging and avoid damaging existing infrastructure.
Silt fences, sediment basins, and other erosion controls must be installed before soil disturbance from excavation begins to comply with environmental regulations and prevent runoff.
The trench must be excavated and prepared before any pipes, conduits, or duct banks can be placed in the trench.
Excavation must be completed (or at least initiated) before trench shoring, shielding, or benching can be installed to protect workers from cave-ins as required by safety regulations.
Fill material must first be placed and spread to the required layer thickness before compaction testing can be performed to verify density.

The fill material must be conditioned to the optimal moisture content before compaction, as moisture significantly affects achievable density. Testing can then verify compaction at the correct moisture level.
Compaction testing (e.g., nuclear density gauge or sand cone) must confirm that the current lift meets specified density requirements before the next lift of fill material can be placed on top.

While testing is typically required for formal acceptance, some project workflows may allow conditional continuation if test results are pending, though strict quality control programs require passing results before sign-off.
If compaction test results fall below specified density requirements, corrective actions such as additional moisture conditioning and recompaction must be performed before subsequent work proceeds.
Spoil (excavated material) is generated by excavation and earthworks activities; therefore, excavation must occur first to produce the material that needs to be managed and hauled away.
Spoil must be removed or managed before final grading can be performed, as excess material would interfere with achieving the designed grade and surface levels.
Spoil material must be cleared from the building footprint before foundation excavation and construction can commence, to provide a clear and stable working area.

Soil backfilling can only begin after foundation construction is complete, as backfill material is placed around and against the finished foundation walls/structure to provide lateral support and protect the foundation.

All underground utilities (drainage, water supply, electrical conduits) must be installed and inspected before backfilling, as they are placed below grade and would be inaccessible after soil is backfilled.

Waterproofing membranes and damp-proofing coatings must be applied to foundation walls before backfilling to protect the structure from moisture intrusion, as these are applied to the exterior side of walls.
After backfill soil is placed, compaction testing must be performed to verify that the fill material meets specified density requirements, ensuring ground stability and preventing future settlement.

While final grading and landscaping typically follow backfilling to achieve proper site drainage and aesthetics, some preliminary grading could theoretically occur before full backfill completion, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
Compaction can only begin after the material (soil, aggregate, or asphalt) has been spread and placed at the required thickness. The material must be in place before it can be compacted.
For soil or granular materials, the moisture content must be adjusted to near optimum levels before compaction begins, as proper moisture is essential for achieving target density during compaction.

After compaction is complete, the final surface elevation and smoothness are typically checked with a straightedge or profilograph to verify it meets specifications, though this is often a quality control step rather than a strict physical dependency.

Subsequent layers (lifts) of material can only be placed after the current lift has been compacted to the required density, as placing additional material on uncompacted ground would lead to settlement and structural failure.

Field density tests (such as nuclear gauge or sand cone tests) must be performed after compaction is complete to verify that the required compaction percentage has been achieved before proceeding to the next construction phase.
The trench must be excavated first to create the void that will later be backfilled.
All pipes, conduits, or utilities placed in the trench must be installed and inspected before the trench can be backfilled.
Inspections and pressure/leak tests of installed utilities must be completed and approved before backfilling to avoid burying unverified work.
The trench must be backfilled and compacted before the surface layer (e.g., asphalt, concrete, or topsoil) can be restored or paved over.
Backfilling must be completed before compaction tests (e.g., Proctor density tests) can be performed on the fill material to verify it meets specification.
Foundation backfilling cannot commence until the foundation concrete has been poured, cured, and gained sufficient strength to withstand lateral earth pressures.

Waterproofing membranes or coatings must be applied to the exterior of foundation walls before backfilling to protect against moisture ingress; backfilling would otherwise damage or bury the unprotected wall.
Perimeter drainage systems (e.g., perforated pipes, gravel layers) must be installed against the foundation before backfill material is placed to ensure proper groundwater management.
Rough grading and final site shaping around the building typically follow backfilling, as the backfill provides the base material to bring surrounding ground up to final elevations.

While some underground utilities are laid before backfill, final connections and trench backfill compaction around utility lines often occur after or concurrently with general foundation backfilling to avoid re-excavation. This is a practical sequencing preference rather than an absolute physical requirement.
The retaining wall must be fully constructed, cured, and have achieved sufficient strength before backfilling can begin; otherwise the backfill pressure could damage or collapse the unfinished wall.
Weep holes, drainage pipes, and filter fabric must be installed behind the wall before backfill is placed to ensure proper drainage and prevent hydrostatic pressure buildup against the wall.
After backfilling behind the retaining wall, the surface must be graded and compacted to match design elevations and ensure proper drainage away from the wall.
Landscaping (sodding, seeding, planting) above and around the retained area typically follows backfill, though it is a soft preference as some landscaping could be done concurrently.

Any utilities (drainage, electrical, water lines) that pass through the backfill zone must be installed after backfill is placed and compacted to correct elevation, or alternatively before backfill — but if placed after, the backfill must be complete to support the utility bedding.
The asphalt mix must be designed and approved to define properties like aggregate gradation and binder content, which determine the required lift thickness for compaction and performance.
The underlying base or sub-base layer must be prepared, compacted, and leveled before placing the asphalt lift to ensure proper support and thickness uniformity.
A tack coat must be applied to the existing surface to ensure bonding between layers before the new asphalt lift is placed and its thickness controlled.
Lift thickness must be established and controlled during paving before compaction rolling can begin, as the rolling process compresses the layer to achieve the specified density.

While final surface finish inspection typically occurs after compaction, verifying lift thickness before compaction allows for adjustments; however, the inspection is a soft preference order as some thickness checks can occur simultaneously with later activities.
Raw materials must be harvested or collected before their moisture content can be measured and optimized.
The initial moisture level must be known before any optimization (drying or conditioning) can be performed.
After moisture is optimized to the target range, the material must be tested to verify it meets quality specifications.
Materials should be at the correct moisture content before being packaged or placed into long-term storage to prevent spoilage or degradation.
Many downstream manufacturing or construction processes require material to be at a specified moisture content before processing to achieve desired dimensional stability and performance.
The soil or fill material must first be placed and spread in lifts before compaction testing can be performed to verify density.
The material must be at or near the optimum moisture content before compaction occurs; compaction testing verifies the achieved density after moisture conditioning.
Compaction testing results must be reviewed and approved before the fill layer can be accepted for subsequent construction activities.
The current lift must pass compaction testing before the next lift of material can be placed on top to ensure structural integrity.
The underlying subgrade must be properly prepared and compacted before compaction testing on the overlying fill layer can be meaningfully conducted.
Proof rolling is performed on exposed subgrade to detect soft spots; therefore all vegetation, topsoil, and debris must be removed first.
The subgrade must be graded to near-final grade and shaped before proof rolling can be conducted to test its bearing capacity.
Proof rolling identifies soft or unstable areas that must be excavated and replaced; therefore remediation can only begin after the test results are known.
The subgrade must be accepted (via proof rolling) before any base course material can be placed on top of it.
Final subgrade acceptance through proof rolling must precede formal compaction testing sign-off for the subgrade layer.
Backfill material must be placed before compaction equipment can operate on it.
The compaction equipment must be set up and ready before compaction operations can begin.
Compaction must be completed before quality testing of the compacted backfill can be performed.
The current layer must be compacted before the next layer of backfill can be placed on top.
Scaffold tubes require a stable and level base to be erected safely; ground preparation or foundation work must be completed first.
Scaffold tubes must be delivered and stored on-site before they can be assembled or erected into scaffolding structures.
Scaffold tubes are the primary structural components needed to assemble and erect scaffolding systems.
Scaffold tubes must be installed and assembled before the scaffolding can be inspected and load-tested for safety compliance.
Scaffold tubes form the structural framework upon which working platforms, planks, and decks are placed.
Scaffold tubes must be delivered and laid out on site before couplers/fittings can be attached to connect the tubes together.

Couplers and fittings are used to join scaffold tubes into the structural framework; thus they must be installed as part of the assembly process, but the assembly cannot proceed without the couplers being ready and applied.
The scaffold structure must be fully erected (including all couplers/fittings secured) before inspection and load testing can take place to verify structural integrity.
The scaffold design and layout must be completed to determine the required positions, lengths, and quantities of scaffold boards/planks before they can be installed.
A stable base (base plates, sole boards) must be set and leveled to provide a safe foundation before scaffold boards/planks are laid.
The vertical standards (uprights) must be erected first to support the ledgers and transoms upon which scaffold boards/planks rest.
Ledgers (horizontal tubes along scaffold length) and transoms (across the width) must be in place to create the supporting framework on which scaffold boards/planks are laid.
Guardrails and toe boards provide edge protection for workers; they must be installed immediately after scaffold boards/planks are placed to ensure a safe working platform.
The ground surface must be leveled and compacted to provide a stable, load-bearing foundation for base plates; otherwise plates may sink or tilt.
Exact positions for each base plate must be marked out according to the scaffold design layout before plates can be placed.
Once base plates are positioned on the ground, they must be leveled and grouted to ensure a uniform bearing surface before any vertical scaffold components are erected.
Vertical scaffold standards (poles) are inserted into or mounted onto the base plates; the plates must be in place first to support and anchor the vertical members.

If timber sole plates are used under base plates for load distribution, they are typically placed before the base plates; however, in some sequences base plates are placed directly and sole timbers can be retrofitted as a soft preference for extra stability.
Scaffold standards (vertical posts) must be erected first to provide the vertical structural support onto which ledgers (horizontal members) are attached.
Ledgers are the primary horizontal longitudinal members; transoms (transverse members) are placed on top of or between ledgers to complete the scaffold framework.
Ledgers support the scaffold boards or decking planks; boarding cannot be safely laid until the ledger framework is in place.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and compacted before placing sole plates/timbers to provide a stable, even foundation for the scaffold.
The scaffold footprint must be measured and marked so sole plates/timbers can be accurately positioned to align with the scaffold standards.
Sole plates/timbers provide the load-distributing base onto which base jacks or adjustable base plates are placed.
Standards rest on the sole plates (via base jacks), so the sole plates must be in position first to support the vertical load of the scaffold structure.

While ledgers are installed much later in the sequence after standards are erected, the sole plates are a prerequisite foundation layer; however, this is an indirect dependency—the more direct successor is the standards/base jacks.

Scaffold standards (vertical posts) must be erected first to provide the vertical structure onto which transoms (horizontal members) are fixed. Transoms cannot be placed without the standards in position as they rely on the standards for support and connection.

Ledgers (horizontal longitudinal members) are typically installed before transoms in most scaffold systems, as transoms often rest upon or connect to ledgers between the standards. The ledgers provide the spanning support for transom placement.

Scaffold transoms support the decking planks or battens that form the working platform. The transoms must be in place to provide the cross-supports onto which decking is laid. Without transoms, there is no structural base for the decking boards.

While some diagonal bracing can be installed before transoms, the complete bracing system may require transoms to be in place for cross-bracing connections. This is a soft preference as bracing order may vary by scaffold design.

Handrails are typically installed after the working platform (decking on transoms) is completed, as the platform provides a safe standing area for fitting handrails. However, in some sequences handrails can be partially pre-assembled, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
The ground must be compacted and level before any scaffold standard (upright) is placed, to ensure stability and load distribution, preventing uneven settlement or collapse.
Base plates or sole boards must be positioned under each standard to distribute the load and provide a firm footing; standards are then erected onto these base plates.
Ledgers connect standards horizontally to form the scaffold frame; they cannot be installed until the vertical standards are in place and secured.

Diagonal bracing is added to stabilize the scaffold structure after the standards and ledgers form the primary framework, but bracing depends on the standards being erected first to provide anchor points.
Decking or working platforms are placed on top of the ledger and standard framework; standards must be erected to support the ledgers which in turn support the decking.

Scaffold toe boards are installed along the edges of the scaffold platform after the scaffold framing and platform decking are in place, as they attach to the platform edge to prevent tools and materials from falling.

Toe boards are installed before (or concurrently with) handrails since they form part of the guardrail system; building codes typically require the guardrail system including toe boards to be complete before the scaffold is used.
The scaffold must be fully assembled with all components (including toe boards) in place before a formal inspection and tagging can occur to certify the scaffold safe for use.
Toe boards are a safety-critical component; the scaffold cannot be used for work until the entire guardrail system including toe boards is installed to prevent falls of materials and personnel.
The scaffold base and frame must be erected first to provide the structure onto which guardrails are installed. Guardrails cannot be attached without the supporting frame in place.

Work platforms (planks/decks) must be laid before guardrails are installed so that workers have a safe standing surface from which to install the guardrails, and because guardrails are typically positioned at the edges of the decked platform.
Guardrails must be fully installed before the scaffold can be formally inspected and tagged for use, as guardrails are a critical safety component that must be verified during inspection.
Guardrails must be in place before installing access gates or ladder hatches, as these access features integrate with and are cut into the guardrail system.
While materials can be loaded earlier via crane, it is safer and standard practice to install guardrails first to provide fall protection before workers carry materials onto the platform.
The scaffold base/foundation must be set up first to provide a stable platform before bracing can be installed.
Vertical standards (uprights) must be erected before diagonal/lateral bracing can be connected to them to provide stability.
Ledgers (horizontal members) must be in place as connection points for diagonal/lateral bracing.
Bracing must be installed to stabilize the scaffold frame before any working platforms or decks are laid.
Bracing must be in place before the scaffold can be inspected and load-tested, as bracing is essential for structural integrity.
The foundation or base of the scaffold must be prepared and leveled before ladders or stair towers can be installed, as they require a stable and secure base to be anchored to.
The lower scaffold frames must be erected first to provide the structure onto which ladders or stair towers are attached or integrated.
Ladders and stair towers provide the means of access to upper scaffold levels; platforms at those levels can only be installed after access routes are in place for workers to safely reach them.

Guardrails and toprails at ladder or stair tower entry/exit points can only be installed after the ladders/stair towers are in place, as they must integrate with the access points for safety compliance.

While safety inspection typically occurs after all scaffold components are installed, it is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint because inspection could theoretically be done in stages. However, best practice holds that ladders/stair towers should be in place so that inspectors can verify all access and egress points.
The scaffold base and framework must be erected first so that there is a structure available to which ties/anchors can be attached for stability.
Ties/anchors must be installed to secure the scaffold before it can be safely loaded or used by workers and materials.
Scaffold ties must be in place so that the inspection can verify the scaffold is properly secured before sign-off.

Dismantling can only begin after all ties/anchors are removed or released; however a safer sequencing is that ties are removed as part of dismantling, so logically the scaffold must be fully tied before any dismantling occurs.
The scaffold structure must be fully erected to provide a supporting frame before sheeting or netting can be applied.
Sheeting and netting must be installed before the scaffold can be formally inspected and certified for use, as the complete scaffold system includes coverings.
Sheeting and netting must be removed prior to dismantling the scaffold structure, as the scaffold frame cannot be safely taken down with coverings still attached.

successor: Work on Scaffold (e.g., masonry, painting, cladding)
rationale: Sheeting/netting provides containment, weather protection, and safety screening; trades working on the scaffold require these protections in place before commencing their activities.
The sheeting/netting must be removed before any netting removal or stripping process begins, as it is the outermost layer of the scaffold covering system.
The fan/shield deck is an extension or attachment to the main scaffold structure; the main scaffold must be erected first to provide a stable support framework.
Fan/shield decks impose lateral loads; anchors and tie-ins must be secured to the building/structure to ensure the deck is safely restrained.
The fan/shield deck must be fully installed before it can be inspected and load-tested to verify it meets safety and design requirements.

The fan/shield deck serves as a protective catch platform or working platform; overhead work on the façade above can only commence once the deck is in place to catch debris and provide fall protection.
Dismantling logically follows installation, but this is a project sequence preference rather than a physical necessity; the deck must be removed in sequence after its use is complete.
The scaffold hoist bracket must be attached to the structural steel frame or concrete structure; the frame must be in place to provide a mounting surface and load path for the bracket.

successor: Hoist motor and platform assembly installation
rationale: The hoist bracket serves as the support anchor for the hoist motor and platform; the hoist equipment cannot be placed until its mounting bracket is securely fixed.
The scaffold hoist bracket supports the hoisting mechanism that raises and lowers the scaffold platform; thus the bracket must be installed before the platform can be erected and used.

successor: Load testing and safety inspection of hoist system
rationale: The hoist system including the bracket must be fully installed before load testing can be performed to verify structural integrity and safety compliance.
If the bracket bears on a concrete slab or foundation, that substrate must be cured and ready to receive the bracket anchorage; a weak or incomplete foundation would compromise bracket stability.
The ground or working area must be cleared, leveled, and stable before scaffolding can be safely erected. Uneven ground or debris creates instability and safety hazards.
For scaffolding erected on new construction, the concrete foundation or slab must be fully cured and load-bearing before scaffold base plates and frames are placed to ensure structural support.
Scaffolding provides the elevated working platform and access needed to safely erect formwork for concrete structures such as columns, walls, and slabs.
Masons require scaffolding to reach upper levels safely while laying brick or block; scaffold must be in place before masonry work can commence at height.
Steel erectors use scaffolding as temporary access and tie-off platforms for bolting and welding connections; scaffold installation must precede steel erection at those work locations.
Scaffold must be fully erected/installed before it can be inspected and certified for safety compliance.
All scaffold components and materials must be delivered to site before erection can occur, which is a prerequisite to inspection.

successor: Work on Scaffold (e.g., masonry, painting, cladding)
rationale: Workers can only access and use the scaffold for construction tasks after it has been inspected and certified as safe.
The inspection results must be documented and the scaffold tagged (e.g., green tag for safe, red tag for unsafe) immediately after inspection to communicate status to workers.
Any alterations to the scaffold after initial certification require re-inspection before use, but if modification is planned it occurs after the initial certification cycle is complete.
Scaffolding supports structural loads during construction. The structure must be self-supporting (fully cured or erected) before the scaffold is removed, otherwise the structure could collapse.

predecessor: Final Finishing Work (e.g., cladding, painting, rendering)
rationale: Scaffold provides access for workers to complete external finishes. All such work must be finished before striking the scaffold, as dismantling removes the access platform and would make rework extremely difficult and costly.

Dismantling the scaffold generates debris (pipes, fittings, boards) that must be cleared from the work area. Site clearance cannot logically begin before the scaffold is removed, as the scaffold itself occupies the space.
The building must be fully accessible and unobstructed for a final quality inspection and client handover. Scaffold removal is a prerequisite to present the completed structure.

External ground works and landscaping around the building footprint can only proceed once the scaffold has been dismantled, as the scaffold structure and its base plates occupy the ground area and restrict access.
The scaffold must be fully erected and assembled before its loading capacity can be checked, as the capacity check evaluates the assembled structure's load-bearing capability.
All scaffold materials and components must be delivered and inspected for quality and compliance before the scaffold is built and its capacity can be verified.
The ground or foundation supporting the scaffold must be properly prepared (leveled, compacted) prior to erection and subsequent capacity testing to ensure stability.
Workers and materials can only be allowed onto the scaffold for construction activities after the platform's load capacity has been verified as safe and compliant with regulations.
If formal load testing or third-party certification is required, the initial capacity check is typically performed first, followed by more formal load testing for official approval.
The structural steel frame must be erected before edge protection can be installed, as edge protection is attached to or supported by the steel structure to provide fall protection for workers.
Concrete decks must be poured and cured to provide a stable work surface before edge protection can be fixed around the perimeter.
Edge protection must be in place before roof work commences to ensure worker safety at heights during roofing and waterproofing activities.
Edge protection must be installed along the building perimeter before façade or cladding work begins, as workers need fall protection while working near the edge.

While scaffolding is typically erected first to provide access, edge protection may sometimes be installed independently; however, sequencing scaffolding before edge protection is a soft preference for safer access.
The scaffold structure must be erected first to provide the framework onto which ties are installed; ties connect the scaffold to the building and cannot be placed without an existing scaffold.
Ties provide lateral stability and structural integrity; the scaffold cannot be safely loaded or used until ties are installed to prevent collapse or excessive movement.
Scaffold ties must be in place before a formal inspection can certify the scaffold as safe and ready for use, as ties are a critical safety component.
Scaffold ties typically anchor into the building's structural facade or walls; these must be constructed or present at the tie locations to provide a secure anchorage point.

Ties must be removed only after the scaffold is no longer in use and before dismantling; however, the tie removal itself is part of the dismantling sequence, so ties being installed is a prerequisite to eventual dismantling.

Safety nets are typically attached to a scaffold structure or building frame. Scaffolding must be erected first to provide an anchor point for net installation, or alternatively the structural frame must be in place to support net attachments.

Safety nets are installed around the perimeter of the building's structural frame to catch falling debris or workers. The main structural elements (columns, beams, slabs) must be erected before nets can be attached to them.
Safety nets serve as fall protection during exterior work. Cladding, curtain wall, or facade installation must be performed after safety nets are in place to protect workers from falls.
Roofing activities present high fall risks. Safety nets should be installed at lower levels before roof work commences to catch any falling workers or materials.
Window installation at elevated floors creates fall hazards. Safety nets must be in place beneath the work area before window installation begins on upper stories.
The ground and work area must be cleared and levelled before erecting scaffolding to ensure stable footing and safety.
Scaffolding often needs to be erected on or around completed foundations before proceeding with vertical construction.
Scaffolding provides the elevated platform and access required for masons to safely lay bricks or blocks at height.
Scaffolding supports workers and materials during the assembly of structural steel elements at height.
External cladding and façade systems require scaffolding for safe access to the building envelope.
Couplers and clamps are used to connect scaffold tubes/pipes. The tubes must be in place before couplers can attach to them.
The scaffold structure must be erected from the base upward; couplers are installed as part of the scaffold assembly after the base is prepared and the first tubes are placed.
Planks/decking are placed on top of the scaffold frame that is held together by couplers and clamps; the structural connections must be complete before walking surfaces can be installed.
Handrails and toeboards are attached to the scaffold frame using couplers and clamps as connection points; the main structural connections must be secured before safety components are added.
Bracing elements are connected to the scaffold frame via couplers/clamps at tube intersections; the primary tube-to-coupler connections must be established before diagonal bracing can be installed.
The ground or surface must be prepared, leveled, and compacted before placing base plates to ensure stable load distribution and prevent scaffold tipping or uneven settlement.
The scaffold configuration, dimensions, and load requirements must be determined first so that base plates of the correct type and positioning can be installed according to the engineered plan.
Vertical scaffold standards/legs are placed directly onto or into the base plates and adjustable jacks; the base plates must be in position and leveled to provide a secure footing for the uprights.
Once the base plates and jacks are positioned, they must be adjusted and leveled (using the screw jacks) to compensate for ground irregularities before erecting further scaffold components.

Base plates form the foundation; longitudinal and transverse bracing, as well as ledger beams, are installed subsequently to stabilize the scaffold structure once vertical posts are erected on the base plates.
Scaffold standards (vertical posts) must be erected first to provide the vertical structural support onto which ledgers and transoms are attached to form the scaffold framework.
Ledgers and transoms form the horizontal framework that must be in place before diagonal bracing can be installed to stabilize the scaffold structure.
Ledgers and transoms create the horizontal support structure upon which scaffold planks or decking are laid to form the working platform.
Guardrails are typically attached to the standards and ledgers; the ledger framework must be complete to provide the attachment points for guardrail systems.
Adequate foundation and base plates (sole plates) must be prepared and standards placed on them before ledgers and transoms can be connected, ensuring stability and load distribution.
The scaffold structure must be erected before guardrails and toe boards can be installed, as they are safety components attached to the erected scaffold frame.
Guardrails and toe boards must be in place before the scaffold can be formally inspected and tagged as safe for use, as they are critical safety elements required for compliance.
Workers can only access and use the scaffold platform after guardrails and toe boards are installed to prevent falls and falling object hazards.
While materials can sometimes be loaded before guardrails are fully installed, it is strongly preferred to have toe boards in place first to prevent materials from falling off the edge.
The scaffold structure must be erected first to provide the framework to which ladders and stairs are attached, ensuring stable access between levels.
Ladders and stairs must be installed before the scaffold can be fully inspected and certified for safe worker access and egress.
Safe access via ladders or stairs is required before workers can start using the scaffold for their tasks.
The scaffold base must be installed and stable before bracing can be attached, as bracing connects to the base structure to provide lateral stability.
Vertical posts must be erected first so that diagonal and cross braces can be connected between them to form a rigid frame.
Bracing must be in place to ensure the scaffold frame is stable and safe before workers can access the platforms to install decking.
Bracing provides essential structural rigidity; thus, it must be installed before the scaffold can be load-tested and inspected for safety compliance.
The scaffold structure must be fully erected to provide a stable framework onto which debris netting and fans can be securely attached.
Debris netting and fans must be installed before any work begins at higher levels to catch falling debris, protect workers below, and comply with safety regulations.
Debris netting/fans must be in place before demolition starts to contain debris and prevent materials from falling onto lower levels or public areas.

Debris netting and fans may need to be removed prior to or during scaffold dismantling to allow access to scaffold connections and to avoid entanglement, though in some sequences nets are taken down first then scaffold is struck.

The scaffold hoist or gin wheel must be mounted to a fully erected and stable scaffold structure. The scaffold provides the physical support and anchorage points required for the hoist/wheel, so scaffolding must be built first.

The gin wheel / scaffold hoist is used to lift materials (bricks, blocks, mortar, tools) to higher working levels. Therefore, the hoist must be installed and secured before any material hoisting can take place.

Once scaffolding and hoists are in place, masons can use the hoist to lift bricks and mortar to upper levels. Upper-level masonry work depends on the material lifting capability provided by the gin wheel.
Materials to be hoisted should be staged near the hoist location to maximize efficiency. While not physically mandatory, it is a strong operational preference to minimize double-handling and delays.
The hoist is removed only after all material lifting needs have been fulfilled for the project phase. Dismantling the hoist too early would prevent further material handling at height.
Scaffold components must be delivered and unloaded to the site before they can be inventoried and segregated for use.
Components must be inventoried and segregated by type, size, and condition before they can be retrieved and used for scaffold assembly and erection.
Segregated components must be inspected and quality-checked before being certified for use in the scaffold structure.

A detailed structural assessment must be completed before dismantling begins to identify load-bearing elements, connections, and potential collapse risks. Reverse sequence dismantling requires understanding the original construction sequence and current structural condition to plan the safe reversal of assembly steps.
Asbestos, lead paint, and other hazardous materials must be identified and removed before dismantling to protect workers from exposure during the physical dismantling process.

A detailed engineered plan specifying the exact reverse sequence of dismantling steps, lift points, temporary supports, and load paths must be prepared and approved before any dismantling work can commence.

predecessor: Installation of Temporary Bracing and Supports
rationale: Temporary shoring, bracing, and propping must be installed to maintain structural stability as load-bearing elements are removed during the reverse sequence dismantling process.

Following the systematic dismantling in reverse sequence, the resulting debris, dismantled components, and waste materials must be removed and the site cleared for subsequent works or site restoration.
Proper grading and drainage must be established to direct stormwater flow into the bioretention planter and ensure it functions correctly.
The planter basin must be excavated to the required depth and dimensions before the bioretention planter structure can be constructed.
Underdrain pipes and gravel layers must be installed at the base of the excavation before layering soil media and planting materials.
Vegetation is planted into the prepared bioretention soil media after the planter structure and soil layers are in place.
The bioretention planter must be complete before final connections to stormwater pipes or curb inlets are made to ensure proper inflow and outflow alignment.
The subgrade must be properly graded and compacted before placing the drainage layer to ensure proper water flow and prevent settling or damage to the drainage system.
Any underground utilities (plumbing, electrical conduits) that run beneath the slab must be installed before the drainage layer is placed to avoid having to excavate through the drainage material.
A vapor barrier or geomembrane is typically laid over the prepared subgrade and under the drainage layer to prevent moisture migration from the soil into the drainage system.
The drainage layer (e.g., gravel or drainage board) must be in place to provide a stable, well-drained base before concrete slab or footings are poured on top.
While reinforcement is often placed directly on the drainage layer, the drainage layer should be completed first to provide a clean, level working surface for placing rebar or welded wire mesh.
Root barrier must be installed before vegetation mat to prevent roots from penetrating the roof structure.
Drainage layer must be in place before vegetation mat to ensure proper water drainage and prevent waterlogging of the vegetation.
Growing medium/substrate must be spread and leveled before vegetation mat is laid to provide a stable rooting base.
If drip irrigation is laid on top of the mat, it may be installed after; however irrigation is often installed before the mat. This is a soft preference depending on design.

successor: Final Inspection and Maintenance Access Setup
rationale: Once vegetation mat is placed, final touches such as setting up walkways or inspection paths and performing final quality checks can occur.
The substrate must be clean, dry, smooth, and free of debris, dust, or contaminants to ensure proper adhesion of the waterproofing membrane.
The concrete or structural substrate must be fully cured (typically 28 days) to achieve sufficient strength and prevent moisture entrapment or membrane damage from ongoing shrinkage.
A primer must be applied and fully dried before membrane installation to promote bond strength and seal porous surfaces.
A protection board or drainage mat must be placed over the cured membrane to shield it from mechanical damage during subsequent construction activities.
Backfilling against foundation walls can only commence after the waterproofing membrane is fully installed, inspected, and protected to avoid damaging the waterproofing layer.
The waterproofing membrane must be installed first to provide a watertight surface that protects the structure before the drainage layer is placed on top.
The filter fabric or geotextile is placed over the drainage layer to prevent soil and fines from clogging the drainage medium, so it must be installed after the drainage layer.
Backfill material is placed after the drainage layer and filter fabric are in place to protect the drainage system and provide lateral support to the foundation.
The subgrade must be excavated, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable and properly sloped base before the drainage layer can be installed.

Drainage pipes or French drains are typically embedded within or laid directly beneath the drainage layer to collect and convey water, so the drainage layer provides the surrounding medium for the pipes.
The area must be properly graded and prepared to ensure proper drainage and a stable base before placing growing medium.
A drainage layer (e.g., gravel or drainage mat) must be installed beneath the growing medium to prevent waterlogging and ensure proper drainage.
Waterproofing must be applied to protect the underlying structure from moisture damage before the growing medium is placed.
A root barrier must be in place to prevent roots from penetrating and damaging the waterproofing membrane or structure below.
Plants must be installed after the growing medium is in place, as the growing medium provides the rooting substrate for vegetation.
The site must be graded and rough-graded to the proper elevations before planting can begin, as planting requires a stable, prepared soil base.
Soils must be tested, tilled, and amended with compost or nutrients to support healthy plant growth before vegetation is planted.
Underground drainage pipes and irrigation lines must be installed prior to planting to avoid disturbing roots and soil after vegetation is in place.

successor: Mulching and Erosion Control Blanket Installation
rationale: Mulch and erosion control blankets are applied immediately after planting to retain soil moisture, suppress weeds, and protect seeds/seedlings from erosion.
Regular watering, weeding, and monitoring (the establishment phase) can only begin once vegetation is in the ground to ensure proper root development and survival.
Rough grading establishes the basic slope and drainage patterns for the site, ensuring water flows away from the foundation before underground irrigation pipes are laid.
