Underground utilities (water, sewer, gas, electric) must be installed first to avoid conflicts and interference with irrigation trenching and piping.
Soil must be cleared of rocks, debris, and organic matter and properly leveled to provide a stable trench bed for irrigation pipes and prevent future damage.
Trenches must be excavated to the required depth and width before irrigation lines can be laid into them.
Trenches cannot be backfilled until irrigation lines have been placed, connected, and tested to ensure proper function and no leaks.
Irrigation lines must be installed before they can be pressure-tested to verify system integrity and detect leaks.
Sprinkler heads and control valves attach directly to the irrigation lines and therefore can only be installed after the main lines are in place.
Fine grading and final site leveling must occur after irrigation lines are buried to avoid damaging or disturbing the newly installed pipes.
Turf installation (sodding or seeding) must follow irrigation line installation so that the system is operational and can water the new turf immediately.
The roof deck or substrate provides the structural base upon which the protection layer is installed; without it, the protection layer has nothing to be placed on.

The waterproofing membrane must be in place before the protection layer to prevent moisture damage; the protection layer is typically installed directly over the waterproofing to shield it during subsequent green roof construction.
The root barrier is placed beneath the protection layer to prevent plant roots from penetrating the waterproofing and structure; therefore it must be installed first.
The protection layer safeguards the waterproofing and root barrier; the drainage layer is placed on top of the protection layer to manage water flow, so it must follow.
The growing medium is placed on top of the protection and drainage layers; the protection layer must be complete first to prevent damage from the weight and installation of soil.
The planter retaining edge requires a stable, cured foundation or base slab to bear its weight and provide a level surface for construction.
The retaining edge must be fully constructed and cured before soil and landscaping materials can be placed against it to avoid structural damage and ensure proper containment.
Waterproofing must be applied after the retaining edge is built to seal joints and protect the structure from moisture intrusion from the retained soil.
Adjacent paving or decking should be installed after the planter edge to achieve a clean transition and avoid damaging finished surfaces.
Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied prior to forming and pouring the concrete retaining edge to provide structural integrity.
Separation walls require a stable, level base. The foundation slab must be poured and cured to provide the necessary structural support before any wall assembly can begin.
The floor platform or framing provides the substrate onto which the separation wall is mounted. Wall assembly cannot proceed without the floor structure in place.
Any plumbing, electrical, or mechanical lines running beneath the wall's footprint must be installed before the wall is built, as access would be blocked by the wall assembly.
The separation wall structure (studs/framing) must be fully assembled to provide the framework onto which drywall can be attached.
Wiring, outlets, and switches within the separation wall can only be installed after the wall framing is complete, as the electrical components are mounted within the wall cavity.

The rough opening (door frame or window frame) must be fully prepared, framed, and sized correctly before the threshold can be installed, as the threshold sits within and is anchored to the rough opening.
The subfloor or finished floor base beneath the threshold must be level, clean, and structurally sound before the threshold is placed to ensure proper support and sealing.
The threshold must be installed first as the door or window leaf is typically set onto the threshold, which provides the bottom seal and structural support for the door/window assembly.
Weatherproofing sealant, gaskets, and flashing around the threshold must be applied after the threshold is securely placed to prevent water infiltration and air leakage.

Finish flooring (tile, hardwood, etc.) adjacent to the threshold is typically completed after threshold installation to achieve a clean transition, though some sequences may allow pre-finishing with careful coordination.

The independent region demising walls (such as fire-rated separations, tenant separation walls) cannot be constructed until the primary vertical structural elements (columns, core walls) are in place to provide support and define the grid.
Demising walls typically bear on or attach to floor slabs; the slab must be poured and cured before walls can be installed.
Once demising walls define the boundaries of each independent region (tenant space), mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work can be distributed per region without crossing partitions.
Finish work is performed within each bounded region after demising walls are complete; finishing before walls are in place would result in rework or damage.
Firestopping at joints and penetrations through demising walls must be applied after the walls are installed to maintain fire-resistance ratings between independent regions.
The subfloor must be properly prepared (cleaned, leveled, and dried) before any floor finish can be installed; otherwise the finish will not adhere or will fail prematurely.
Underlayment (such as moisture barrier, soundproofing, or padding) must be placed over the subfloor before the final floor finish is installed to ensure proper performance and longevity.

All rough-in work for MEP systems that run beneath or through the floor must be completed before the floor finish is installed, as it would be extremely difficult and destructive to access these after the floor is finished.
Baseboards and trim are typically installed after the floor finish to cover the expansion gap at the wall and to sit on top of the finished floor for a clean, professional appearance.

While painting is often done before floor finishing to protect the floor from drips, many trades prefer to install flooring after painting to avoid damaging freshly painted walls with floor installation equipment; this is a soft preference depending on the project sequence.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before the Town Hall building can be constructed on the site.
Concrete foundations must be poured and fully cured to provide a stable load-bearing base for the Town Hall structure.
Underground utilities and rough-in connections must be installed before the Town Hall slab and superstructure to avoid costly retrofitting.
The building shell and structural elements must be completed before interior finishing work like drywall, flooring, and painting can begin.
The Town Hall building must be fully constructed before the final municipal inspection and occupancy permit can be issued.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any foundation work for the parking structure can begin.
Concrete footings, slab-on-grade, or other foundational elements must be poured and cured before the parking structure's vertical construction can start.
Drainage, water, electrical conduits, and other utilities that run beneath the parking structure must be installed before the slab or structure is built over them.

When a parking structure is integrated with or adjacent to the main building, the parking structure often serves as a stabilizing element or access route; the main building's lower levels or core may require the parking structure to be complete for crane access, material staging, or structural tie-in.

Drive lanes, sidewalks, and landscaping around the parking structure are typically finished after the structure is complete to avoid damage from ongoing construction traffic and to allow final grading and connections.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared to provide a stable, level foundation for the entry gate structure and its supporting posts/footings.
Concrete footings or a foundation base for the gate posts must be poured and cured before the gate structure can be erected and anchored securely.
Any underground electrical conduit for gate operators, intercom systems, or lighting must be laid before the gate posts and concrete work are completed to avoid costly rework.
The gate structure defines the opening alignment and width; adjacent fence panels must tie into the gate posts for a continuous, secure perimeter.
The physical gate frame and panels must be in place before motors, sensors, and control systems can be mounted and aligned to operate the gate.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any foundation or wall construction can begin to ensure proper load-bearing and alignment.
Property boundaries and wall alignment must be staked out by surveyors before excavation or wall construction can start to ensure the wall follows the correct property lines.
Soil bearing capacity and ground conditions must be assessed to design the wall foundation appropriately; construction cannot proceed without this data.
Backfill material can only be placed against the wall after the wall structure (and its curing) is complete, otherwise the wall would be unstable or damaged.
Permanent perimeter walls often serve as the final security boundary; temporary fencing may be removed and permanent security systems installed only after the wall structure is finished.
While landscaping can often be done after walls are built, it is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint, as some planting could theoretically be done concurrently.

Utilities that run along or cross the wall line should be installed before the wall is built (not after), so this relationship is reversed: utilities must precede the wall. Listed here as a note that wall completion blocks future utility access.
The subgrade must be excavated, graded, and compacted to the required lines and levels before curb and gutter forms can be set and concrete poured.
A stable granular base or aggregate base course is typically required beneath curbs and gutters to provide uniform support and proper drainage.
Underground drainage pipes, catch basins, and inlet connections must be installed before curb and gutter construction to allow proper water flow connections.
Curbs and gutters define the edge of the roadway and act as a form/constraint for adjacent asphalt or concrete paving; paving butts against the completed curb and gutter.
Although final grading and landscaping typically follow curb installation to achieve finished elevations, it is a soft preference as small adjustments can sometimes be made concurrently.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before grading can begin, as earthwork requires an unobstructed surface to shape and level.
Survey stakes and grade markers are needed to guide the earthmoving equipment to cut and fill to the correct elevations and slopes.
After grading and earthwork, the compacted fill must be tested to verify it meets density specifications before further construction proceeds.
The overall site pad must be brought to rough grade first, so that precise foundation excavations can be laid out and dug to the correct depths.

Utilities such as water, sewer, storm drainage, and electrical conduit are typically installed after rough grading to avoid disturbing the finished earthwork and to maintain proper trench elevation control.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before any roadway construction can begin, as these obstructions would prevent proper grading and earthwork.

Proper grading, compaction, and stabilization of the subgrade is essential before constructing the roadway layers above, as the subgrade provides the foundational support for the entire pavement structure.

Underground utilities (water, sewer, gas, electric, telecommunications) must be installed or relocated beneath the roadway footprint prior to pavement construction to avoid cutting into the newly constructed roadway later.

Subsurface drainage systems, culverts, and stormwater management infrastructure must be placed before the roadway layers are built to ensure proper water management and prevent future pavement damage from water accumulation.

Pavement markings, lane stripes, and road signs can only be applied after the roadway surface (asphalt or concrete) has been completed and cured, as markings require a clean, finished surface for proper adhesion and visibility.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil before any trenching can begin to provide unobstructed access for excavation equipment and to establish proper surface grades.
Erosion and sediment control measures (such as silt fences, check dams, and sediment basins) must be in place before trenching to prevent sediment runoff into waterways during excavation activities.
The utility alignments, trench locations, depths, and grades must be surveyed and staked out prior to excavation to ensure utilities are installed in the correct positions and at proper elevations.

After utility pipes, conduits, or cables are placed in the trench, backfilling and compaction must follow to protect the utilities and restore the trench to the required density for subsequent construction layers.
Once the utility lines are installed in the trench, they must be connected to the main systems and pressure-tested or inspected for leaks and proper function before the trench is fully closed.
Electrical conduits must be placed in the ground before light poles can be installed and wired.
Underground ductbanks for power cables must be laid before lighting fixtures can be connected to the power supply.

predecessor: Foundation / Base Preparation for Light Poles
rationale: Concrete footings or bases for light poles must be poured and cured before poles can be mounted.
Street lights should be installed before final paving to avoid damaging newly paved surfaces and to ensure proper alignment with finished grade.
After physical installation, lights must be tested and commissioned to verify functionality and compliance with specifications.
The site must be properly graded and prepared before any landscaping or hardscaping can begin, as uneven ground would prevent proper installation of patios, walkways, and plantings.
All underground utilities (water, sewer, gas, electrical, irrigation lines) must be installed before hardscaping and landscaping to avoid digging up finished surfaces.
Building foundations and concrete slabs must be completed and cured before adjacent landscaping and hardscaping can be installed around the structure.
Exterior finishes and siding must be complete before final grading and landscaping to prevent damage to finished walls and allow for proper drainage installation.
Landscaping and hardscaping are among the final site activities; once complete, the project can proceed to final inspection and closeout.
The ground must be leveled, excavated, and properly compacted before any plaza construction can begin to ensure a stable foundation.
Underground utilities must be laid before the plaza surface is constructed to avoid digging up finished work.
A reinforced concrete base or foundation slab is required as the structural platform upon which plaza features like paving, planters, and structures are built.
Trees, shrubs, grass, and decorative plants should be installed after hardscape elements (paving, walls, benches) are completed to avoid damage from construction equipment.

While it is preferable to install fixed amenities after the plaza surface is complete to ensure proper alignment and avoid rework, some elements could theoretically be installed concurrently with surface work.
The site must be cleared and leveled to provide a stable and unobstructed foundation area for constructing the boundary wall.
The exact property lines and wall alignment must be surveyed and marked before wall construction begins to ensure the wall is built on the correct boundary.
Soil bearing capacity and ground conditions must be assessed to design appropriate foundation depth and type for the wall.
The boundary wall is typically erected early to secure the construction site, define the working area, and prevent unauthorized access before main building works commence.

While landscaping can theoretically proceed alongside wall construction, it is more efficient to complete the wall first so that landscaping around the perimeter is not disturbed or damaged by ongoing wall work.
The exterior wall requires a completed foundation to provide structural support and load-bearing capacity before wall construction can begin.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide the supporting structure onto which the exterior wall panels can be attached or built.
Exterior wall openings must be framed and completed before windows and doors can be installed into those openings.
The base exterior wall structure must be completed before waterproofing membranes and final cladding finishes can be applied to its surface.
Exterior wall construction seals the building envelope, which is a prerequisite for starting interior finishing works that require weather-protected conditions.
The structural frame (columns, beams, and trusses) must be erected to provide the load-bearing support structure onto which the roof assembly is installed.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the roof cavity must be completed before the roof is enclosed, as access would be restricted or impossible after roof assembly.

successor: Finger Wing Roof Insulation and Waterproofing
rationale: The roof assembly (decking, sheathing, and underlayment) must be installed first to provide a substrate for insulation and waterproof membrane application.
The roof structure must be closed in to create a weathertight envelope before interior ceiling work such as drywall installation and finishing can proceed.

While roof assembly typically precedes facade cladding to ensure weathertight closure from top down, sequencing can vary based on design; this is a strong preference rather than an absolute physical necessity.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the correct depth before any foundation work can begin to ensure stable load-bearing conditions.
Proper soil compaction and installation of drainage systems must be completed prior to pouring or placing the foundation to prevent soil settlement and water damage.
The main building's foundation must be completed first to provide structural reference points, alignment, and load transfer continuity for the attached finger wing foundation.
The foundation must be fully cured and structurally complete before ground slabs are poured and waterproofing membranes are applied to avoid cracking and moisture ingress.
Vertical structural elements require a cured, leveled foundation to anchor into; the foundation provides the load-bearing base for the superstructure.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical and medical gas lines
rationale: Headwalls contain electrical outlets, medical gas outlets, and nurse call connections that require behind-wall rough-in before the headwall unit can be installed and connected.

predecessor: Rough-in plumbing for sinks and fixtures
rationale: Patient room headwalls often integrate with sink and handwashing station plumbing; rough-in piping must be in the wall before headwall placement.

predecessor: Wall framing and drywall (behind headwall area)
rationale: The headwall assembly mounts onto finished wall framing and backing; the wall structure must be ready to receive and support the headwall unit.

successor: Install patient bed and medical equipment
rationale: Patient beds, monitors, and medical equipment connect to headwall services; the headwall must be installed first to provide power, gases, and data connections.

While headwall installation can occur before final finishes, it is preferable to complete flooring and painting after headwall placement to achieve clean transitions and avoid damage to finishes during installation.
The structural steel frame must be erected and stabilized to provide a supporting framework onto which the glazing system can be mounted and attached.
The roof deck must be completed overhead to provide weather protection and a top bearing point for the curtain wall or glazing system before installing glass panels below.
The glazing system must be fully sealed and watertight before interior finishes such as drywall, painting, and flooring are installed to prevent moisture damage to finished surfaces.
The glazing envelope must be complete to properly seal the building before HVAC systems can be tested and balanced for pressurization and thermal performance.
The glazing system must be installed and tested for air/water infiltration before the building can be fully commissioned and handed over to the client.
The foundation slab provides the load-bearing base upon which the finger wing structure is built; without a solid foundation, the structure cannot be supported.
Underground utilities (drainage, electrical conduits, water pipes) must be placed before the finger wing structure is built to avoid excavation and disruption after construction.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied within the foundation before the concrete is poured and before any superstructure elements like the finger wing can be erected.
The roof structure depends on the finger wing's walls and supporting frame being in place to provide the load-bearing supports for roof installation.

successor: Rough-In Electrical and Plumbing in Finger Wing
rationale: Vertical and horizontal rough-in work for MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) systems within the finger wing requires the wall and floor structure to be framed and enclosed before services can be routed.
Structural foundations must be in place before any MEP rough-in work can begin, as the building structure provides the supporting substrate for MEP systems.
Wall, floor, and ceiling framing must be completed to provide the cavities and pathways for running MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing) conduit, piping, and wiring.
MEP rough-in must be completed and inspected before insulation is installed, as insulation would conceal and block access to MEP lines.
All MEP rough-in work (conduit, piping, wiring, ductwork) must be complete before drywall is hung, as drywall permanently encloses wall cavities and prevents access.
Rough-in must be finished before final connections, device installation, and trim-out can proceed, as the rough-in provides the backbone systems for final connections.

predecessor: Complete Structural Steel Frame for Finger Wing
rationale: The exterior cladding requires the structural steel frame to be in place to provide a substrate for attachment and load-bearing support.

predecessor: Complete Roof Structure for Finger Wing
rationale: Roof structure must be completed to provide weather protection and top-of-wall connections before vertical cladding installation begins.

successor: Install Windows and Doors in Finger Wing
rationale: Windows and doors are typically installed after rough openings are created in the completed cladding system to ensure proper flashing and waterproofing integration.

successor: Complete Interior Finishes in Finger Wing
rationale: Exterior cladding must be installed to create a weathertight envelope before interior finishes can proceed without risk of water damage.

successor: Install Exterior Insulation and Weather Barrier
rationale: Weather barrier and insulation are typically installed as part of or just after the cladding system to ensure continuous thermal and moisture protection of the building envelope.
Rough-in work such as electrical, plumbing, and framing must be completed before headwall panels can be installed, as the panels cover and conceal these utilities.
Ceiling installation must be completed before headwall panels are installed because headwall panels typically align with and extend up to the ceiling grid.
Headwall panels must be securely installed before any head-mounted service fixtures (medical gas outlets, electrical receptacles, nurse call devices) can be mounted onto them.
Headwall panels are installed prior to final wall finishing so that the panels are properly integrated into the wall assembly and any gaps or seams can be sealed and finished.
Trim pieces, end caps, and cosmetic accessories are installed after the main headwall panel body is in place to complete the installation.
The nurse call system must be physically installed before it can be commissioned and tested for proper operation.

predecessor: Run Conduit and Cable for Nurse Call System
rationale: All electrical conduit and cabling infrastructure must be in place and connected before the system can be powered on and commissioned.
Cable terminations must be completed at both ends to establish electrical connectivity before commissioning can verify system functionality.

successor: Train Staff on Nurse Call System
rationale: Staff training on the nurse call system cannot occur until the system has been fully commissioned, tested, and confirmed operational.

successor: Hand Over Nurse Call System to Owner
rationale: System handover to the owner/client requires that commissioning has been completed and the system has been verified as functioning correctly.
The growing media bed requires a stable, graded subgrade surface to ensure proper drainage and uniform depth, so site grading must be completed first.
Underdrain collection pipes and drainage gravel must be installed below the growing media to collect and convey excess water; placing the media before drainage would prevent proper installation.
Plants require the growing media as their rooting substrate; they cannot be planted until the media bed is in place.

successor: Mulching and Erosion Control Blanket Installation
rationale: While it is common practice to apply mulch after media placement to protect the surface, in some sequences mulch might be placed concurrently; however, standard practice places mulch after media to avoid mixing.
Irrigation can be tested before media placement, but final tuning and operation testing is typically done after the media bed is in place to simulate actual field conditions.
The vertical growing rack requires a level, structurally sound base to bear its load and prevent tipping or uneven settlement.
Floor drainage must be in place before racks are installed to avoid having to move or work around heavy racks later, and to ensure water management for hydroponic systems.

predecessor: Main Water Supply and Drainage Rough-In
rationale: Water supply and drainage lines serving the rack area must be roughed-in before racks are positioned, as access to floor and wall connections will be blocked.

successor: Hydroponic Plumbing and Drip Line Connection
rationale: Plumbing lines, drip trays, and irrigation tubing can only be attached to the rack after the rack is fully assembled and anchored in its final position.
Grow lights are mounted onto or above the rack structure; the rack must be in place to set correct light heights and spacing relative to tray levels.
The structural frame must be in place to provide mounting points and physical support for the nutrient delivery manifold component.
Incoming supply lines and fluid routing infrastructure must be established so the manifold can be connected to the nutrient source.

successor: Distribution Line Connection to Grow Sites
rationale: The manifold serves as the central distribution hub; individual grow-site lines cannot be connected until the manifold is installed and its output ports are accessible.
Pressure testing and flow calibration of the nutrient delivery system require the manifold to be in place and fully connected to verify performance under operational conditions.
Automated flow control valves, sensors, and the control system interface must be integrated after the manifold is physically installed to ensure proper alignment and connectivity.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before installing any trellis system to ensure stable footing, proper alignment, and consistent post placement.
Soil preparation and raised bed formation should be completed before installing trellis posts to avoid disrupting the amended soil or damaging root zones of planted crops.
Concrete footings or driven post anchors for the trellis uprights must be set and cured before the trellis framework can be assembled atop them.
The trellis structure must be fully erected and stable before climbing or vining crops are planted or trained onto it, as the plants require the support structure from the outset.

While irrigation can be installed before or concurrently, it is often more efficient to install drip lines after the trellis is in place so that lines can be run along trellis wires and positioned accurately relative to crop rows; however, this is a soft preference as pre-trellis irrigation is also possible.
The ground must be excavated and leveled to proper grade before gravel or sloped drainage layers can be installed, as the drainage system rests directly on the prepared subgrade.
The soil subgrade must be compacted to provide a stable base that prevents uneven settlement of the gravel drainage layer.
Foundation walls or perimeter footings should be in place to define the area boundaries before interior floor drainage gravel is placed, ensuring proper containment and slope alignment.
The gravel drainage layer or sloped fill provides a smooth, stable bed upon which the vapor barrier (polyethylene sheeting) is laid to prevent moisture migration through the slab.
The drainage layer and any sloped fill must be fully placed and compacted before the concrete slab is poured, as the slab is cast directly on top of the prepared drainage base.
The unit must have a stable, level foundation base before it can be installed.
The building frame must be in place to support and enclose the air circulation unit.
Power supply must be available to connect and operate the unit.
The unit must be installed first to allow ducts to be connected to its ports.
Final electrical connections to the unit's control panel can only be made after the unit is fixed in position.
Commissioning requires the unit to be fully installed, connected, and ready for operation.
It is preferable to install the unit before finishing work to allow access for adjustments, though finishing could be done around the unit if needed.
The structural steel frame provides the load-bearing support and attachment points for the curtain wall system. The curtain wall cannot be installed without a stable structural frame in place.
Floor slabs provide the intermediate support and anchorage levels for curtain wall panels. The curtain wall must span between floor levels which must already be in place.
The roof structure provides the top anchorage and completes the building envelope frame. Curtain walls typically require top support and need the roof diaphragm to be stable.

The curtain wall forms the exterior envelope; interior finishes adjacent to the curtain wall must wait until the wall system is in place to avoid weather damage to interior materials and to allow for proper sealing and flashing details.
The curtain wall framing must be fully erected before individual window units or glazing infill panels are installed within the curtain wall grid system.
Site grading establishes the required slopes and drainage patterns; piping must be laid in prepared trenches after rough grading is complete to ensure proper flow and avoid rework.
Other underground utilities must be in place first to avoid conflicts and to coordinate trench depths and horizontal separations as required by code.
Piping must be inspected and approved before trenches can be backfilled; backfill immediately after pipe installation prevents damage and supports subsequent surface work.
Drainage and irrigation lines must be in place before pouring slabs or walkways to avoid cutting into hardened concrete for later pipe installation.
Irrigation piping and drainage outlets must be fully installed and tested before topsoil placement, seeding, or sodding to prevent disturbance of finished landscape.
The concrete floor slab provides a stable, level base for mounting and anchoring the growing racks and trellis supports. Without the slab in place, the racks cannot be securely installed.

Electrical rough-in must be completed before rack installation so that wiring can be run behind or beneath the racks without obstruction, and to avoid having to dismantle racks later for electrical access.
Plumbing rough-in for irrigation/drainage lines should be installed before racks are placed, as the racks would obstruct access to walls and floors for pipe installation.
Irrigation lines are typically mounted onto or routed along the growing racks and trellis supports. The support structure must exist first to attach the irrigation system.
Plants or grow media are placed into or onto the racks and trellis system. The racks must be installed and stable before any planting or media filling occurs.

All environmental control system components (HVAC units, sensors, controllers, ductwork, etc.) must be physically installed before the commissioning process can begin, as commissioning involves testing and verifying the functionality of installed equipment.

predecessor: Complete Electrical Connections for Environmental Control System
rationale: Electrical power supply and control wiring must be completed to provide power and enable communication between system components before commissioning tests can be performed.

predecessor: Complete Environmental Control System Piping and Ductwork
rationale: All piping for refrigerants, chilled water, or hot water, as well as ductwork for air distribution, must be fully installed and leak-tested before the system can be commissioned and balanced.

Commissioning must be completed first to verify that all components are operating correctly and to establish baseline performance data before formal validation and performance verification can proceed.

successor: Hand Over Environmental Control System to Operations
rationale: The system must be fully commissioned, tested, and verified before it can be formally handed over to facility operations and maintenance teams for ongoing management.
Hydroponic plumbing and manifolds must be embedded in or placed on the concrete slab before finishing, so the slab must be poured first to provide the structural base.
Benches and growing systems are positioned over or connected to the plumbing manifolds, so the plumbing must be in place first to support these systems.
Irrigation controls and sensors interface directly with the plumbing manifolds; the plumbing must be installed before these control systems can be wired and configured.
Pressure testing must occur after installation to verify the integrity of the plumbing and manifold connections before commissioning the system.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and compacted before any pathway construction can begin to ensure a stable base.
A proper sub-base of compacted aggregate is required to provide drainage and structural support for the pathway surface.
Any underground pipes, conduits, or cables must be laid before paving to avoid cutting into or undermining the finished pathway.
It is easier and more efficient to install pathways first and then plant adjacent landscaping around them, though this is a soft preference as planting could be done beforehand with care.

successor: Installation of Pathway Furniture and Lighting
rationale: Benches, bollards, trash receptacles, and light poles must be anchored after the pathway surface is complete to ensure proper alignment and secure fastening.
Street signage posts and foundations must be installed into the completed road base and pavement structure to ensure stable support.
Final site grading must be completed to establish proper elevations and sightlines before signage placement.
All underground electrical conduits and utility lines must be in place to avoid conflicts with signage foundation digging.
Signage placement determines lane configurations and turning movements, which must be finalized before road markings are applied.
Soft preference to complete signage first so that landscaping can be designed around and not obscure sign visibility.
The subgrade must be properly graded and compacted to provide a stable base for the street curbs and edges. Without proper preparation, the curbs would lack support and could settle unevenly.
Underground utilities beneath the roadway must be installed before curbs are placed, as the curbs define the edge of the pavement. Digging after curb installation would damage the finished curbs.
The road base course provides the foundation that the curbs will sit on or abut against. The base must be in place to establish the correct elevation for curbs.
Curbs are installed first to act as forms/containment for the asphalt paving. The paving is laid up against the finished curbs, which define the edge of the paved surface.
Sidewalks often abut street curbs and must tie into them at proper grade. The curb edge establishes the boundary that sidewalks are poured or placed against.
The site must be properly graded and leveled before installing built-in street furniture to ensure a stable foundation and proper drainage.
Underground utilities such as water, gas, electricity, and drainage must be installed before street furniture to avoid digging up or damaging completed furniture.
The pedestrian pavement or hardscape surface must be in place to provide the finished base onto which built-in street furniture is anchored or integrated.

Landscaping and planting around built-in street furniture should be done after installation to avoid damage to plants during furniture installation and to ensure proper alignment of planting beds with the furniture.

While coordination is needed, electrical fixtures can be installed concurrently or after; however, finishing the street furniture first allows for precise placement of lighting to complement seating or other built-in elements.
The ground must be leveled, cleared, and compacted before any bridge or crosswalk foundations can be laid.
Bridge abutments, piers, or crosswalk supports require deep foundations or piles to be installed first to bear the structural load.
Any underground or overhead utilities interfering with the bridge/crosswalk alignment must be relocated before construction begins to avoid damage and ensure safety.
The structural connections (bridge beams, crosswalk supports) must be in place before the walking/driving surface can be poured or paved over them.
Safety railings and barriers are mounted onto the completed bridge/crosswalk structure; they cannot be installed before the main structural connections exist.
A stable foundation or substructure is required to support the canopy/covering structure before it can be erected.
The primary structural frame that will support the canopy must be in place before the canopy covering can be attached.
Canopy lighting or electrical fixtures are typically mounted onto or integrated with the canopy structure after it is installed.
Final aesthetic finishes or cladding around the canopy edges are applied after the primary canopy structure is in place.
The canopy provides weather protection, so paving or flooring beneath it is often completed after overhead covering is installed to keep the work area dry.

Street trees are typically planted in tree pits or tree beds within or adjacent to planting beds; their root systems and canopy shade influence the layout, soil volume, and plant selection for the surrounding planting beds. Trees must be installed first to avoid disturbing root zones.

The sidewalk and curb framework define the physical boundaries of street planting beds. The structural subbase and paving must be completed to establish the exact location, grade, and curb cuts/edges that contain the planting bed soil.

predecessor: Underground Utility Installation (water, sewer, electrical, gas)
rationale: All major underground utilities must be installed and backfilled before planting beds are created to avoid excavation damage to plant roots and to ensure utility corridors are not obstructed by deep planting.

successor: Irrigation System Installation for Planting Beds
rationale: Once the planting beds are excavated, edged, and filled with soil, the irrigation system (drip lines, emitters, or sprinklers) is laid directly within the bed medium before or concurrently with planting to ensure proper water distribution.

successor: Planting of Shrubs, Perennials, and Groundcover in Beds
rationale: The prepared planting bed (excavated, edged, soil amended) must be ready before any herbaceous or woody plants (shrubs, perennials, groundcovers) are installed into the bed soil.
The street columns must have their structural foundation installed and fully cured before cladding can be applied, as the cladding relies on the column being securely anchored.
The bare structural steel or concrete columns must be erected and in place before any cladding panels or finishes can be attached to them.
While lighting can be installed after cladding, it is a soft preference because integrated lighting fixtures are often mounted onto or through the cladding surface for a finished appearance.

Any final painting or protective coating around the column base and cladding joints must be done after the cladding is fully installed to ensure a seamless finish and avoid damage to the cladding material.

Sidewalk or paving work around the column base should follow cladding installation to achieve proper alignment, cover the column base correctly, and prevent damage to the cladding from paving equipment.
The structural slab or roof deck must be in place before any soffit treatment can be applied to the underside of the street ceiling.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work running overhead must be completed before soffit/ceiling finishes are installed to avoid rework or damage to the finished surface.
Soffit/ceiling surface preparation and finish must be complete before light fixtures can be mounted to or recessed into the ceiling.

While painting typically follows surface treatment, integrated finishes may be applied simultaneously; however, final paint/coating is best applied after soffit treatment is fully installed to ensure a uniform appearance.
Signage mounted to or suspended from the soffit should be installed after the soffit is finished to ensure proper anchoring and alignment.
The road base and sub-base must be compacted to provide a stable, level foundation before installing street furniture like benches, bollards, and bins.
Kerbs define the edge of the roadway and pedestrian zones; street furniture must be positioned relative to these boundaries.
Footpaths and paved surfaces must be completed before installing furniture to ensure correct alignment and avoid rework or damage to new paving.

predecessor: Underground Utility Installation (e.g., drainage, water, electrical conduits)
rationale: Underground services must be laid before street furniture is installed to avoid digging up or moving furniture to access utilities.
While landscaping can often be done concurrently, it is preferable to install furniture first to avoid damage to newly planted areas and to coordinate final planting around furniture locations.

The subgrade (earth base) must be properly graded, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable foundation before any paving layer can be applied. Without a prepared subgrade, the pavement will settle unevenly and fail.

A crushed stone or gravel base course must be laid and compacted on top of the subgrade to provide drainage support and a load-bearing platform for the final paving surface. Paving directly on subgrade without a base course would lead to poor performance and cracking.

predecessor: Installation of Underground Utilities (water, sewer, storm drains, gas, electric)
rationale: All underground utility lines and conduits must be placed and backfilled in trenches before paving, because once the pavement is laid, accessing underground utilities would require cutting and removing the pavement. It is physically and economically required to complete all below-grade work first.

While curbs and gutters are often installed before paving to act as forms for the pavement edge, in some sequences paving may be done first and curbs added after. This is a soft preference depending on the construction method; it is not a physical necessity in all cases.

successor: Application of Pavement Markings (Striping and Signage)
rationale: Road markings, lane striping, and signage must be applied after the fresh pavement surface is laid and fully cured. Painting on unpaved or uncured surfaces is impossible, and markings would be destroyed if placed before paving.

Street lighting poles can be installed either before or after paving, but typically they are set after paving to ensure proper alignment and to avoid damaging the new surface during pole installation. This is a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
Street signs must be mounted on or adjacent to completed road surfaces; pavement provides the structural base and reference alignment for sign placement.
Lighting poles often share foundations or proximity with signage; installing lighting first avoids rework and ensures signs are visible once installed.
Underground utilities must be laid before digging post holes for signs to avoid damage to utilities and ensure proper depth clearances.
Signage confirms street names and regulatory information needed to accurately place lane markings, stop bars, and crosswalks in correct positions.

successor: Final Road Opening / Traffic Flow Activation
rationale: Street signs are essential wayfinding and regulatory elements; traffic cannot be safely opened to the public without proper signage in place.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared to ensure proper drainage and a stable base for planting trees and shrubs.
Underground utilities (water, gas, electric, telecom) must be installed before planting to avoid digging up newly planted areas and to ensure utility access without damaging root systems.
Curbs and sidewalks define the planting strip boundaries and protect the planting area from vehicle traffic; they must be in place before street trees and plants are installed.
Planting must precede hardscape finishing to avoid soil compaction and damage to finished surfaces during planting operations.
The timber verandah structure requires a stable, level foundation or floor system to be built upon; the concrete slab or floor must be completed first to provide the base.
The verandah is typically attached to or supported by the main building's structural framing, so the wall/column framing must be in place first.
The verandah roof often ties into the main roof structure; the main roof framing must be complete to allow weatherproof connection.
The timber verandah frame/structural support must be erected before the roof cladding can be installed over it.
The verandah structural frame and joists must be in place before the finished decking or flooring boards can be laid.

The roof structure must be framed to provide the structural support needed for the wide eave overhang, as the overhang extends beyond the exterior walls and depends on the roof framing for its attachment and load path.
Wall sheathing must be installed before the eave overhang so that the overhang framing can be securely attached to the wall assembly and provide a continuous air and weather barrier.
Roof decking must be in place as the overhang typically integrates with the roof edge, and the decking provides the base onto which the overhang's soffit and underside finishes can be attached.
The wide eave overhang structure must be built first to create the framework onto which soffit panels and fascia trim can be attached for finishing and weather protection.
Gutters are mounted along the edge of the eave overhang; the overhang structure must be complete to provide a secure mounting surface for gutter attachment and proper water runoff alignment.
The corrugated metal roof requires the structural steel frame (roof trusses, purlins, etc.) to be in place to provide the load-bearing support and attachment surface for the metal roof panels.
A solid roof deck (e.g., plywood, OSB, or metal deck) must be installed to provide a continuous substrate for the corrugated metal roof panels to be fastened to.
Roof underlayment (felt paper or synthetic membrane) must be laid down over the roof deck to provide a moisture barrier before the corrugated metal panels are installed.
Ridge caps, eaves, rakes, and other roof flashings and trims are installed after the main corrugated metal roof panels are in place to seal edges and transitions.
Gutters and downspouts are typically installed after the roof is complete to collect and divert rainwater from the finished roof surface.
Fence posts require a stable foundation (e.g., concrete footings) to support the picket fence structure.
The ground must be graded and leveled before installing fence posts to ensure proper alignment and drainage.
Underground utilities (gas, water, electric) must be located and marked before digging post holes to prevent damage and ensure safety.
Gates are typically hung on fence posts, so the fence structure must be in place to support gate hardware.

successor: Landscaping and planting along fence line
rationale: It is easier to plant shrubs, flowers, or install edging after the fence is built so that the fence line is clearly established and to avoid damaging new plants during construction.
The ground must be excavated and leveled to provide a stable, prepared base for the foundation wall.
Trenches must be dug to the required depth and width to accommodate the stone foundation wall's footing.

predecessor: Footing installation (e.g., concrete or stone footing)
rationale: A load-bearing footing is required beneath the stone foundation wall to distribute the weight evenly and prevent settling.
Waterproofing applications are applied directly onto the completed stone foundation wall to protect against moisture ingress.
Backfill soil against the foundation wall can only be placed after the wall is fully constructed and cured to avoid displacement.
The ground floor structure rests on or abuts the foundation wall, so the wall must be complete before floor construction begins.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and legally approved for market use before any stall can be set up.
Basic utility infrastructure (water supply, electrical hookups) must be installed at the stall location before the stall can operate.
The physical base, framing, or modular structure of the stall must be erected before it can be fitted out and opened for business.
Interior shelving, countertops, and display fixtures can only be installed after the stall structure is in place.
Produce, goods, and vendor equipment cannot be moved in until the stall is fully constructed and enclosed.
A stable foundation must be prepared and cured before a silo can be erected to support its weight and contents.
Proper site grading and drainage must be completed to prevent water accumulation around the silo base, which could compromise structural integrity.
Concrete foundation must be poured and fully cured to sufficient strength before the silo structure can be erected on it.
The silo components must be positioned before they can be welded or assembled into a complete structure.
The silo walls/body must be erected before the roof can be placed on top.
Interior lining or protective coatings are applied after the silo structure is fully erected to ensure complete coverage.
Material handling equipment can only be connected to the silo after the silo is in its final position.
Electrical connections for level sensors, aeration fans, and controls require the silo to be in place for routing and termination.
Leak testing and commissioning can only occur once the silo is fully assembled and sealed.
Street lamp poles require a stable concrete foundation to be set into; the foundation must be excavated and poured first to provide structural support.
Power supply cables to the street lamp must be run through underground conduits before the lamp pole is erected, as the conduit must connect to the lamp's base.
Once the street lamp is physically installed, electrical wiring must be connected to the power source and the lamp must be tested to ensure proper operation.
It is preferable to finish the surrounding pavement after lamp installation to avoid damaging new pavement during pole placement and to allow precise alignment of the lamp base.
Final grading, landscaping, and decorative elements around the base of the street lamp are typically completed after installation to achieve a clean aesthetic finish.

The boardwalk requires a stable and level foundation or substructure (e.g., piles, sleepers, or concrete footings) to be installed first, as the boardwalk decking and supports are built upon this base. Without a proper foundation, the boardwalk would lack structural support.
The ground area where the boardwalk will be placed must be cleared, leveled, and graded to ensure proper drainage and a stable base before boardwalk construction can commence.

Handrails and guardrails are typically installed after the boardwalk deck surface is completed, as they need to be anchored to the finished deck structure and require the walking surface to be in place for proper alignment and safety.

Applying protective sealants, stains, or anti-slip coatings to the boardwalk surface is usually done after the boardwalk structure is fully assembled, but this could be considered a soft preference if some sealing is done pre-assembly. Typically, final finishing is done post-installation for even coverage.

Landscaping work around the boardwalk (e.g., planting, mulching, or placing adjacent pavers) is typically performed after the boardwalk structure is complete to avoid damaging the boardwalk during landscaping activities and to allow precise grading up to the boardwalk edges.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any wall foundation can be laid.
A stable foundation (e.g., concrete strip or trench footing) must be in place before the wall structure can be built upon it.
The wall structure must be complete before gates can be hung or installed within the wall openings.
While landscaping can begin after the wall is built for a tidy finish, it is a soft preference as some planting could be done prior if carefully planned.

successor: Plot layout and internal pathway marking within cemetery
rationale: The boundary wall defines the cemetery perimeter, so internal layout and pathways should be delineated after the enclosure is established.
The ground must be leveled and prepared before any dock construction can begin to ensure proper drainage and structural stability.
A concrete foundation or slab is required to support the loading dock structure and withstand heavy truck loads.
Underground conduits and pipes for dock levelers, lights, and communication systems must be laid before the slab is poured.
The dock structure must be complete before mechanical dock levelers can be mounted and anchored to the concrete.
The dock opening frame must be in place before sectional overhead doors can be installed and aligned.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any foundation work can begin to ensure a stable base.
Underground utilities (water, sewer, electrical) must be trenched and rough-in completed before pouring foundation to avoid later excavation under the foundation.
The foundation must be fully cured and load-bearing before any superstructure framing can be erected on top of it.

Plumbing pipes laid within the foundation slab must be installed after the foundation forms are in place but before the slab is poured; however, for the overall ordering the foundation base preparation precedes under-slab rough-in.
The foundation walls and footings must be completed and cured before the ground floor slab can be poured to ensure structural continuity.
The structural frame requires a stable, level foundation to bear the load and ensure structural integrity.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and excavated for foundations before any structural frame can be erected.
The concrete slab or footings must be cured and set before the structural frame can be anchored to them.
The roof structure relies on the frame for support; the frame must be in place to bear roof loads.
Wall cladding attaches to the structural frame; the frame must be erected first to provide the mounting surface.
A structural roof frame (rafters, battens, or purlins) must be erected first to provide the underlying support and slope onto which thatch is laid and tied.
Load-bearing walls must reach their full height (top plate) to carry the roof load and provide the perimeter anchor points for the thatch.
Any chimney stack that penetrates the roof must be built up to at least roof level before thatching, so the thatch can be waterproofed and flashed around it.
The roof covering must be in place to protect the interior from weather before any ceiling boarding, loft insulation, or interior finish work is done.
The main thatch body is laid first; the ridge (top) capping – often a decorative or waterproofing finish – is applied after the field of the roof is fully thatched.
The roof structure (rafters, trusses, decking) must be built to provide the structural support and substrate for the roof tiles to be fixed onto.
A waterproof underlayment must be laid over the roof deck before tiles are installed to provide secondary weather protection and a smooth base for tiling.
Battens (or counter-battens) are fixed to the roof structure to provide the nailing or hanging points for clay or slate tiles at the correct gauge.
The main field tiles must be laid first so that the ridge and hip capping tiles can overlap and seal the junctions at the top and hips of the roof.

While gutters can often be installed before tiling, it is preferable to complete the tiling first so that the lowest course of tiles overhangs correctly into the gutter, ensuring proper water shedding.
Timber cladding is an exterior finish that requires a complete structural frame to attach to, as the cladding system is mounted on the building's structural framework.
A weather-resistant barrier must be installed over the sheathing before timber cladding to protect the building envelope from moisture ingress.
Insulation is placed within the wall cavity behind the cladding and must be installed before the cladding covers it.
Windows and doors are typically installed after cladding to ensure proper flashing integration and weather sealing at the interface between cladding and openings.
The building envelope must be closed and weathertight (including cladding) before interior finishes are applied, to prevent moisture damage to interior materials.
The masonry wall requires a solid, level foundation to bear the load of the wall and ensure structural stability. Without a completed foundation, the wall cannot be properly supported.
If the masonry wall is built on a ground floor slab, the slab must be poured and cured first to provide a stable base for the wall.
Any vertical reinforcement bars that tie the masonry wall into the foundation must be placed and secured before masonry work begins.
Load-bearing lintels over doors and windows must be set in place as the masonry reaches the appropriate height, integrated within the masonry work itself.
The masonry wall must be completed to its full height to provide bearing support for roof trusses or upper floor beams.
Plastering or pointing cannot be applied until the masonry is fully laid, cured, and stable to ensure proper adhesion and finish quality.
While chases can be cut into masonry, it is preferable to complete masonry work first to avoid damage, though some rough-in can occur concurrently with careful coordination.
Window and door frames must be installed after the masonry wall is built, as the wall defines the openings and provides the structural frame for fitting.
Rough framing (walls, roof structure) must be complete to provide the structural openings and support for window and door installation.
Wall sheathing provides the backing and weather-resistant barrier necessary before windows and doors can be properly installed and sealed.
Windows and doors must be installed and framed in before interior wall finishing can begin, as the rough openings need to be enclosed and trimmed first.
Windows and doors are installed before the final exterior siding to allow proper flashing, sealing, and integration of the units into the building envelope.
The window and door units must be set and secured in the openings before interior trim, casing, and molding can be installed around them.
The structural framing and exterior sheathing must be in place to define the chimney chase and load-bearing support for the fireplace and stove.
The chimney or flue pipe path must be constructed before the stove/fireplace is set, as the unit connects directly to the flue system.
Non-combustible board, hearth pad, and clearance barriers must be in place before the appliance is installed to meet fire safety codes.
The stove/fireplace is heavy and must be set before finished flooring is laid around it; flooring cannot be installed underneath a masonry or heavy stove base.
Finishing walls and ceilings after stove installation avoids soot damage to finished surfaces, though it is a preference rather than a structural necessity.
The substructure and foundation must be completed before floor construction can begin, as the floor slab and flooring materials need a stable, load-bearing base to be placed upon.
The ground floor slab or base layer must be poured and cured before any finish flooring or floor assembly can be installed on top of it.
Walls are typically built on top of or anchored into the completed floor structure, so the floor must be finished before wall framing or masonry can proceed.
Final floor finishes such as tiling, screeding, or floor coverings can only be applied after the structural floor construction is complete.
While some underfloor MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) services can be installed before the floor, final connections and above-floor installations typically follow floor completion.
Vegetation and topsoil must be removed to expose a stable subgrade before constructing any hardstanding or track base.
Soil bearing capacity and ground conditions must be known to determine the required thickness and composition of the hardstanding/track sub-base.
A properly graded and compacted sub-base (e.g., Type 1 aggregate) must be laid and compacted to provide a stable load-bearing layer before the final track/hardstanding surface is placed.

successor: Final Surface Course (e.g., concrete, asphalt or gravel binder)
rationale: The final wearing surface is typically placed after the base layer of the track/hardstanding is complete; however, if the hardstanding itself IS the final surface, subsequent finishing or curing activities follow.

successor: Drainage Installation (e.g., road gullies, filter drains)
rationale: Drainage can be installed after the hardstanding to capture surface runoff, but ideally drainage is coordinated before or during construction; post-construction drainage is less efficient but possible.
The area must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before fencing lines can be accurately pegged and posts installed.
Boundary lines and fence alignments must be surveyed and pegged to ensure the fence is placed on the correct boundary and at the correct levels.
Gates are hung on and integrated into the completed fence line; the fence structure must exist to support the gate hinges and latch posts.
Final grading, topsoil placement, and seeding/planting near fence lines are typically done after fencing to avoid machinery damaging the newly installed fence.
Hedging plants are installed after the fence is erected so the fence can serve as a support and protection for the young hedge.

Mobilization of equipment, personnel, and temporary facilities must be completed before any site preparation work can begin, as it provides the necessary resources and setup for preparation activities.
Legal ownership or access rights and required environmental/construction permits must be secured before any physical site disturbance or preparation work can commence.
Site boundaries, topographical data, and layout stakes must be established first to guide clearing, grubbing, and grading operations accurately.
Site preparation (clearing, grubbing, rough grading, and compaction) must be completed to provide a stable and cleared work area before foundation excavation can proceed.
Prepared and graded site is required before trenching and laying of underground utilities (water, sewer, electrical conduits) can begin, ensuring proper subgrade conditions.
The ground must be cleared, excavated to a stable base, and leveled before any stone wall construction can begin to ensure structural stability and proper foundation.
A trench must be dug to accommodate the base stones (footings) of the dry stone wall, providing a stable foundation below the frost line.
Stones must be quarried, collected, sorted by size and shape, and delivered to the site before wall construction can commence.
Agravel drainage layer or French drain must be installed behind or beneath the wall base to prevent water buildup and frost heave, which could destabilize the dry stone structure.
The main body of the dry stone wall must be completed to the desired height before the top course of coping stones or capstones is placed to finish and protect the wall.
After the dry stone wall is built, any space behind retaining walls must be backfilled with drainage aggregate and compacted to provide lateral support.

Seeding or planting vegetation along the wall or aesthetic inspection is typically done after completion, though this is a soft preference as some planting can be done concurrently in non-structural areas.
A level, stable foundation with proper damp-proofing is physically required to support and anchor the timber frame structure.
The site must be cleared and levelled before any foundation or structural work can commence to provide a safe and stable working area.
Concrete foundations must be poured and fully cured to achieve sufficient strength to bear the load of the timber frame and anchor it securely.
A damp proof course must be installed on top of the foundation to prevent moisture rising into the timber frame, which would cause rot and structural failure.

predecessor: Setting Out and Marking Anchor Bolt Positions
rationale: Anchor bolt positions must be precisely set out and installed in the foundation to align with the timber frame's base plate for correct assembly.
The timber frame provides the primary vertical support and load-bearing structure; the roof cannot be installed until the walls and frame are erected and braced.
Sheathing boards and weather-resistant barriers are applied directly onto the timber frame to provide lateral stability and weather protection, and cannot logically precede the frame.
Window and door openings are formed within the timber frame structure; frames and glazing cannot be installed until the surrounding structural frame is in place.
First-fix services (cabling, conduit, pipework) are routed through the timber frame walls and cavities, requiring the frame to be erected before these services can be run.
Insulation is placed within the timber frame cavities; therefore the frame structure must be complete before insulation can be fitted.
Thatching is installed on top of the roof structure; roof framing or trusses must be completed to provide the structural support for the thatch.
A solid roof deck or batten system is often required as a substrate for thatch attachment, and this must be installed before thatching begins.
A waterproof membrane or underlayment is typically placed beneath the thatch to protect the structure from moisture, and must be installed prior to the thatch layer.
The ridge capping (e.g., decorative ridge pieces, saddle details) is installed after the main thatch layer is complete to seal and finish the roof peak.
Interior ceiling work can technically proceed after the roof is thatched to keep the interior dry, though it is a soft preference as interior work could be sequenced differently in dry conditions.
Lime plaster is applied directly onto masonry substrates (brick or block walls); the structural walls must be fully constructed and stable before plastering can commence.
The building must be watertight (roof and windows installed) before applying lime plaster, as lime plaster is vulnerable to rain and frost during curing and requires a dry environment.
Any conduit, pipework, or chases that need to be buried in the wall must be installed prior to plastering, otherwise the plaster would have to be cut or broken out later.

Lime plaster must be fully cured and dry before applying decorative finishes; this is a physical constraint (moisture would ruin paint) but the curing time is a waiting period rather than an irreversible dependency.
Skirtings and architraves are typically fixed after plastering so that the plaster can be finished neatly up to the joinery, but this is a preferred sequence rather than a strict physical necessity.

A level, clean, and properly prepared subfloor (e.g., concrete slab or screed) is physically required to provide a stable base for stone tiles; laying stone on an uneven or unprepared surface would cause cracking and failure.

Any underfloor plumbing, electrical conduits, or radiant heating pipes must be installed and tested before the stone floor is laid, as accessing them afterward would require breaking and removing the finished stone.
A moisture barrier or waterproof membrane must be placed beneath stone flooring to prevent moisture migration from the subfloor, which can damage the stone and adhesive over time.
Grout can only be applied after stone tiles are firmly set in place and the adhesive has cured; sealing must follow grouting to protect the stone surface.
Baseboards or skirting boards are typically installed after the stone floor is laid so that they sit on top of the finished flooring, providing a clean transition and covering expansion gaps.
The bulletin board or display system must be mounted on a finished wall surface. Wall finishing and painting must be completed first to provide a clean, stable mounting surface.
If the bulletin board includes any lighting (e.g., integrated display lighting), electrical rough-in must be completed and wiring run behind the wall before the board is installed.

While the bulletin board can be installed independently, coordination with other signage placement (e.g., directory signs, directional signs) is preferred to ensure consistent visual alignment and avoid rework.
The bulletin board is a finish item that should be installed before final cleaning to avoid dust and debris settling on the board surface and display area.
Signage and graphics require a clean, smooth, and primed surface for proper adhesion and longevity. Without surface preparation, the graphics may not adhere correctly or could be damaged.
The base paint or coating must be applied and fully cured before signage and graphics can be installed on top, as graphics are typically the final decorative layer.
If a clear protective topcoat or sealant is specified to protect the graphics, it must be applied after the signage and graphics are installed to safeguard them from wear and environmental damage.

The final inspection and touch-up phase typically occurs after all decorative finishes including signage and graphics are in place, so any damage or misalignment can be identified and corrected. This is a soft preference as inspection could theoretically occur in stages.
The wall substrate (framing and drywall) must be fully installed and finished before any surface-mounted signage or graphics can be applied.
The Integrated Performance Platform must be mounted on a stable structural base; the foundation and framework provide the physical support needed to install the platform.
The platform requires power and network connectivity to function; electrical and data cabling must be run before the platform can be connected and commissioned.
Once installed, the platform's sensors and monitoring tools need calibration and testing to ensure accurate data collection; this is a logical sequence but could theoretically be done concurrently.
The platform must be fully installed before being integrated into the broader building management system and undergoing end-to-end testing.
The platform must be operational before the building can be handed over to occupants, as it is a key component for monitoring building performance.
Storage cubbies require stable structural walls or framing to be mounted against or recessed into; rough carpentry must be complete to provide the support structure.
Any electrical wiring that will run behind or through the cubby area must be roughed in before the cubbies are installed to avoid costly rework and ensure code compliance.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and finished behind and around the cubby location before cubbies are mounted, as the cubbies would block access to the wall surface.

Flooring (especially tile, hardwood, or LVT) should be installed after cubbies to allow the flooring to run continuously under the cubbies, or at minimum to avoid damaging the cubbies during flooring work.

While painting can be done before cubby installation, final touch-up painting around the cubbies is best performed after cubbies are in place to ensure a seamless finish and cover any damage or gaps at the edges.

predecessor: Completion of Floor Finishes & Surface Preparation
rationale: Floor finishes (tile, carpet, etc.) must be complete before wayfinding signage is installed on walls and floors to ensure accurate placement and avoid damage to finished surfaces.
Wall signage requires finished wall surfaces (painted or clad) for proper mounting; installing signage before painting would require removal or protection and risk damage.
Overhead suspended signage and directional indicators require completed ceiling grids and MEP rough-in to verify clearances and mounting points without interference.
Wayfinding signage is part of the final fit-out completion; commissioning and final inspections should occur after all signage is installed to verify correct placement, legibility, and compliance.
Signage and wayfinding systems must be fully installed to guide occupants and visitors upon move-in; occupancy without wayfinding would cause confusion and safety issues.
The ground must be prepared and leveled before any partition assemblies can be constructed to ensure a stable and level foundation.
Foundations must be completed to provide the structural base upon which partition assemblies will be erected.
The main structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place before partition walls can be constructed, as partitions are installed within the framed structure.
Partition assemblies must be built first to define room layouts and provide cavities for running electrical conduits and plumbing pipes within the walls.
Partition installation must be completed before surface finishes such as plastering, painting, and flooring can be applied to the walls and rooms.

successor: Installation of Integrated Display & Mounting Systems
rationale: Electrical power, data cabling, and structural mounting points must be roughed-in and available before display systems can be physically installed and connected.

successor: Installation of Integrated Display & Mounting Systems
rationale: Display mounts are often suspended from or anchored to ceiling structures; the ceiling grid and support framework must be fully installed to provide secure attachment points.

successor: Installation of Integrated Display & Mounting Systems
rationale: Wall-mounted displays require finished walls for proper anchoring and aesthetic integration; rough framing and drywall must be complete before mounting brackets can be secured.

predecessor: Installation of Integrated Display & Mounting Systems
rationale: Integrated displays must be physically installed and powered before they can be calibrated, configured, and commissioned as part of the overall audiovisual system.

predecessor: Installation of Integrated Display & Mounting Systems
rationale: While displays are often installed before final cosmetic finishes, it is a soft preference to sequence painting and trim after installation to avoid damaging newly installed displays from paint, dust, or debris.

The floor surface must be properly prepared, leveled, and cleared of debris before any anchoring grid installation can begin, as uneven surfaces would prevent proper alignment and secure fastening of the anchor grid system.

The concrete slab must be poured and fully cured to achieve sufficient load-bearing capacity before anchor bolts or grid elements can be embedded or fastened into it, otherwise the concrete would not hold the anchors securely.

predecessor: Layout and Marking of Anchor Points
rationale: The precise locations for anchor points and grid lines must be surveyed and marked on the slab before installation begins, as the grid must align with structural drawings and equipment placement requirements.

Heavy equipment or machinery that requires anchoring to the floor must be installed only after the anchoring grid is in place, as the grid provides the structural tie-down points needed to secure the equipment safely.

While the anchoring grid should ideally be installed before final floor finishing to embed grid components flush with the surface, this is a soft preference because post-installation surface patching is possible, though it may compromise aesthetics and smoothness.
The acoustic separation systems must be physically installed before they can be commissioned, as commissioning involves testing and verifying the performance of already-installed systems.
A pre-commissioning inspection must be completed to verify that the installation meets design specifications and is ready for commissioning tests.
The commissioning of acoustic systems must be completed and verified before the building can be handed over or occupied, to ensure that acoustic performance requirements are met.
Commissioning must be completed before final acoustic testing and certification can take place, as commissioning results inform the final performance validation.

Any remedial acoustic works identified during commissioning can only be undertaken after commissioning identifies the issues, though this is a logical sequence rather than a strict physical constraint.
The floor slab must be installed and cured to provide a stable, level surface for placing the touchdown desk cluster.
The structural frame (columns, beams) must be in place to define the building zone and provide support before installing interior components like desk clusters.
Electrical and data cabling rough-in must be completed in the floor/ceiling zone to enable connections to the desk cluster's power and data outlets.
