While it's typical to complete flooring before final fixtures, screens can be installed over finished or unfinished floors; however, finishing flooring after avoids potential damage to the screen.
Plumbing rough-in must be completed before signage installation as signage indicates the location of a completed restroom facility.

predecessor: Wall Framing and Finishing for Men's Restroom
rationale: Walls must be framed, finished, and painted before signage can be mounted on them.
Paint and wall finish work must be complete before mounting signage to avoid damage or rework.
Signage is typically required for code compliance before a building can receive occupancy clearance.
Restroom signage must be in place for proper wayfinding and accessibility compliance before the building is open for use.
Restroom signage must be mounted on completed walls; walls must exist before signage can be attached.
The space must be verified as the women's restroom with all fixtures in place before signage is installed, ensuring the correct room is labeled.
While not physically required, it is preferable to have lighting operational so the signage placement can be seen and aligned properly.
Signage must be installed before the final inspection so that the inspector can verify the room is properly labeled and compliant with accessibility codes.
Restroom signage must be in place before the building can be occupied to ensure occupants and visitors can correctly identify restroom locations.
Signage must be mounted on finished walls; the wall structure must exist before signage can be installed.
Restrooms and their partitions must be in place so that the signage indicates the correct room designation.
Plumbing rough-in and fixture installation define the restroom's function and location, which must be confirmed before permanent signage is affixed.
Lighting must be operational to ensure the signage is visible; electrical work behind the wall where signage is mounted should be completed first.
Plumbing pipes and drains for toilets, sinks, and urinals must be installed within wall and floor cavities before restroom walls, fixtures, and finishes are placed.
Electrical wiring, conduit, and outlet boxes for lighting, exhaust fans, and hand dryers must be roughed in before wall coverings and fixture installation can commence.
Floor and wall waterproofing membranes in toilet and shower areas must be applied prior to tile, flooring, and fixture installation to prevent water damage.
Toilets, urinals, sinks, and faucets are installed after restroom framing, wall finishes, and rough-in are complete to avoid damage and allow proper alignment.
Final paint, trim, and finishing work is performed after all major construction and fixture installation is done to protect surfaces from damage during preceding work.

The building must be structurally complete and enclosed (roof, exterior walls, windows/doors installed) before any interior fit-out work can begin, to protect materials and provide a weathertight environment.

All MEP rough-in work (conduit, wiring, ductwork, plumbing drainage and supply lines) must be installed inside walls and ceilings before lockers, partitions, and finishes are installed, otherwise walls would need to be torn open later.
The floor slab must be poured, cured, and properly leveled/prepared before installing locker room flooring (tile, epoxy, or other finished surfaces) and placing heavy lockers.
After lockers, partitions, benches, and millwork are installed, final touch-up painting, trim work, and wall finishes can be completed without damaging newly installed elements.

Plumbing fixture trim-out (shower heads, faucets, sinks) must follow the locker room fit-out because shower partitions, grab bars, and locker placement determine final fixture positioning and connections.
Excavation must be completed to expose the ground surface and create space for foundation and core wall construction.
Core walls require a stable foundation (mat foundation or footings) to transfer vertical loads to the ground. The core wall cannot be erected without a completed foundation system.
Floor slabs often bear on or are structurally connected to the core wall. The core must be in place to support the slabs and provide lateral stability.
Elevator shafts are typically housed within the core wall. The core structure must be complete before elevator rails and cabs can be installed.
Staircases within the core require the core walls to be erected to define the stair enclosure and provide structural support for the stair flights and landings.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the correct bearing capacity before any structural element like a shear core can be constructed.
The shear core must be erected on a properly cast foundation slab that can transfer its immense vertical loads and overturning moments to the ground.
The shear core concrete must be placed and achieve sufficient initial set before formwork can be safely removed.
Floor slabs typically bear onto or tie into the shear core; the core must be in place to provide lateral support and bearing for the slab edges.
After the core walls are cast, vertical post-tensioning or additional reinforcing cage extensions can be installed to complete the core's structural capacity.
The core foundation or base slab must be completed first to provide a stable structural base for the core floor slab to be poured or placed upon.
Reinforcement steel and rebar for the core must be installed and tied before the concrete for the core floor slab can be poured.
Vertical reinforcement extending from the core walls or lift shaft must be in place so that it can be integrated with the core floor slab reinforcement.
Formwork and shuttering must be installed and aligned to the correct level before concrete for the core floor slab can be poured.
The core floor slab must be cured and hardened before formwork for the next level of core walls can be erected and concrete poured on top of it.

Rebar (reinforcement steel) must be in place within the core wall before formwork is installed, as the formwork is erected around the rebar cage to shape the concrete pour. Installing formwork first would make rebar placement impossible or require costly rework.

Inspection and approval of the installed rebar must be completed before formwork installation to ensure compliance with structural drawings and quality standards; once formwork is closed, inspection access is no longer possible.
Formwork must be fully erected, aligned, and secured before concrete can be poured into the core wall; the formwork acts as the mold that shapes and supports the wet concrete.

After installation, the formwork panels must be checked and adjusted for vertical alignment (plumbness) and proper positioning before concrete placement to ensure the core wall meets dimensional and structural tolerances.
After formwork is installed, embedded sleeves, conduits, or plumbing penetrations that pass through the core wall can be positioned precisely within the formwork boundaries before the concrete pour.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the proper depth and dimensions before any foundation work can begin.
Property lines, foundation footprint, and elevation benchmarks must be accurately marked and surveyed before excavation or foundation pouring.
Soil bearing capacity and ground conditions must be analyzed to determine foundation type, depth, and reinforcement requirements before constructing the foundation.
Underground plumbing, electrical conduits, and drainage pipes that pass beneath the foundation must be installed before the foundation slab or footings are poured.
The foundation must be fully cured and load-bearing before any vertical structural elements (columns, walls, beams) can be erected on top of it.
Foundation walls and slab must be in place before waterproofing membranes, sealants, and drainage boards can be applied to the exterior surfaces.
The foundation must be completed, waterproofed, and cured before soil can be compacted back around the foundation walls.
The foundation footings and stem walls must be in place before interior floor slabs can be poured and tied into the foundation system.
Formwork must be erected before reinforcement can be placed, as reinforcement needs to be positioned within the formwork cavity for proper concrete cover and alignment.
Reinforcement must be fully placed, tied, and inspected before concrete can be poured, as the steel reinforcing bars are embedded within the concrete to provide tensile strength.
After reinforcement is placed, formwork panels on the opposite side must be closed and all reinforcement inspected before concrete placement.

MEP sleeve placement can be done concurrently with or after reinforcement placement, but is a soft preference since sleeves are typically positioned within the reinforcement cage before final concrete pour.
Layout and marking of wall centerlines, boundaries, and rebar locations must be completed first to guide accurate placement of reinforcement bars.
Formwork must be erected and aligned before concrete can be poured into it to define the shape and position of the core walls.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured, as the rebar provides structural strength and must be embedded within the cured concrete.
Any mechanical, electrical, or plumbing sleeves, conduits, and embedded elements must be positioned within the formwork prior to pouring, as they cannot be installed after concrete has set.
The poured concrete must reach sufficient strength through curing before formwork can be safely removed without damaging the structural core.
Post-tensioning of core tendons can only commence after the concrete has cured to the required compressive strength to withstand the tensioning forces.

Core and shell must be structurally complete (foundations, structural frame, and exterior enclosure) before MEP rough-in can begin, as the building structure provides the physical substrate for routing MEP systems.
The structural slab or deck must be in place to provide the surface and embed points for conduit, piping, and ductwork rough-in within the core zones.
MEP rough-in embedded in slabs (conduit, sleeves, penetrations) must be completed and inspected before concrete placement encases them.
MEP rough-in in core walls, shafts, and ceilings must be fully installed, tested, and approved before they are enclosed by drywall, ceilings, or fire-rated assemblies.
Rough-in work must be complete before applying final finishes to avoid damage to finishes and to allow access for MEP installations.

Fire-stopping seals around MEP penetrations through fire-rated assemblies; MEP rough-in (pipes, ducts, conduits) must be installed first so that fire-stop materials can be properly applied around all penetrations.
Fire-stopping must be completed and inspected before enclosing assemblies with final finishes; covering fire-stopping before inspection would violate code and conceal potential defects.
Fire-stopping is applied within and through fire-rated assemblies (walls, floors) which must be framed first to provide the substrate where fire-stop materials are installed.

successor: Fire Protection System Activation / Final Inspection
rationale: Building code and life safety compliance requires fire-stopping to be fully in place and verified before the fire protection system is deemed operational and the final inspection occurs.
Fire-stopping must be installed before the formal close-in inspection that verifies all fire-rated penetrations are properly sealed prior to concealing them behind finishes.
The Density Ring Boundary must be installed on a stable foundation to ensure structural integrity and proper alignment.
The site must be cleared and leveled before any structural components like the Density Ring Boundary can be placed.
The boundary structure must be in place to contain and define the area for the density ring filling material.
Compaction testing of the density ring material can only be performed after the boundary is installed and the ring is filled.
Surface finishing typically follows boundary installation for aesthetic purposes, though in some sequences finishing could be done concurrently.
The ring transition threshold must be installed on a stable foundation; the ring foundation must be completed first to provide structural support.
The transition threshold forms the base from which the ring wall rises; wall construction cannot begin until the threshold is in place.
Sealing at the threshold joints must occur after the threshold is fully installed to ensure watertight integrity.
The base must be leveled and prepared before the ring transition threshold can be positioned and secured.
Steel reinforcement bars are placed atop the transition threshold to ensure structural continuity, so the threshold must be installed first.
Fixed Density Ring Seating must be installed on a stable, level foundation or base slab to ensure structural integrity and proper alignment.
Handrails and barriers are safety features that must be installed after seating is in place to ensure correct positioning relative to the seating rows.
Seat numbering and signage must be applied after seating is fully installed to ensure accurate identification of each seat location.
Final cleaning and inspection must occur after seating is installed to verify proper installation, cleanliness, and readiness for use.
The structural framing (e.g., columns, beams, or bleacher support structure) must be erected first to provide the supporting framework onto which the ring seating is anchored.
The concrete floor slab must be fully cured and finished to provide a stable, level surface for installing the density ring floor markings.
The floor must be cleaned, ground, and prepared to ensure proper adhesion of the density ring markings to the substrate.
Any underfloor utilities must be completed before floor markings are installed, as markings would be damaged or obscured if utilities were installed afterward.
A protective clear coating or sealant may be applied over the markings to prevent wear; this is a preference to extend marking durability rather than a strict physical requirement.
Density ring markings define controlled areas for equipment placement (e.g., cleanroom zones); equipment and workstation layout cannot begin until zone boundaries are permanently marked on the floor.
A stable foundation or base slab must be in place to support the ring partitions and ensure proper alignment before erection begins.
The exact positions for the ring partitions must be marked on the foundation to guide placement and ensure correct geometry.
Ring beams typically sit atop or connect the ring partitions, so the partitions must be erected first to provide support.
Ring partitions form the formwork or structural core for the ring walls; concrete placement requires partitions to be in place.
The roof structure often bears on the ring partitions or walls, so partitions must be erected to provide vertical support.
The elevated walkway requires a stable foundation and support structure (columns or beams) to bear its load before it can be installed.
The walkway structure must be in place before the walking surface (decking, paving, or grating) can be installed on top of it.
Handrails and guardrails are safety barriers that attach to the walkway structure, so the walkway must be erected first to provide the mounting surface.
While lighting can be installed after the walkway is complete for ease of access, it is a soft preference as some lighting could be pre-mounted on adjacent structures before walkway placement.
Applying protective coatings after installation is preferred to cover connections and welds, but components could be pre-coated before assembly.
The colonnade must be supported on a solid foundation to bear its structural load; without a completed foundation, the colonnade cannot be erected.
Column bases or pedestals must be in place before the colonnade columns can be positioned and aligned on top of them.
The entablature (horizontal beam structure) rests directly on top of the colonnade's columns; it cannot be placed until the columns are fully erected and stabilized.
The roof or ceiling structure is typically supported by the entablature which sits on the colonnade; thus the colonnade must be complete before roof framing can begin.

While decorative elements like a frieze are usually added after the colonnade is erected, in some cases they could be pre-assembled on ground, making this a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
The structural steel frame provides the primary support structure for the promenade canopy. The canopy cannot be installed until its supporting steel framework is in place and secured.
Foundations are required to support the columns and structural frame that will carry the promenade canopy. Without completed foundations, the canopy structure has no load-bearing base.

Lighting fixtures integrated into or mounted on the canopy require the canopy structure to be in place before electrical conduit, junction boxes, and wiring can be installed within or along the canopy.
The canopy frame must be erected before any glazing panels, roofing sheets, or cladding materials can be fixed to it, as these are applied onto the completed structural framework.
Waterproof membranes, sealants, and final architectural finishes are applied after the canopy structure is fully assembled to ensure continuity and proper sealing of all joints.
The built-in planter requires a stable, level base. Foundation or slab work must be completed first to provide the structural support for the planter.
If the built-in planter includes drainage or irrigation lines, rough-in plumbing must be installed before the planter is constructed, as the planter structure would cover or encase these pipes.
The built-in planter is typically a fixed structural element that should be installed prior to finish flooring, so that flooring can be cut and fit neatly around the planter base.
It is easier to paint or finish walls behind and around the planter after it is installed, but this is a practical sequencing preference rather than a strict physical impossibility to do otherwise.
The planter structure must be complete and cured (if concrete/masonry) before soil and plants are added, to avoid damaging the unfinished structure.
Railing must be anchored to a completed structural deck or subfloor surface to provide proper support and stability.
The main structural frame must be in place to provide attachment points for railing posts and supports.
Railings along staircases must be installed before final stair construction to ensure proper alignment and safe access during remaining work.
Railings serve as safety barriers and must be in place before the area can be officially inspected and approved for occupancy or further work.

Railings are typically among the last structural elements; interior finishes like drywall and painting can proceed after railings are installed, though this order can be flexible depending on access needs.
A stable foundation is physically required to support the column before it can be erected.
Reinforcing steel must be placed and tied in the foundation to connect with the column reinforcement before the column can be set.
The footing concrete must be poured and cured to sufficient strength to anchor the column before erection can begin.
Columns provide vertical support for beams; beams cannot be placed until columns are erected and secured.
Temporary or permanent bracing must follow immediately after column erection to ensure stability against lateral loads.
The ground must be properly graded, compacted, and prepared before any paving or decking can be installed to ensure a stable base.
Foundations and slabs provide the structural base or edge restraints that paving or decking often abuts against or is supported by.
All underground pipes, conduits, and drainage must be laid and inspected before paving is placed, to avoid digging up finished paving for utility connections.

While fencing can often be installed before or after paving, it is typically preferred to install paving first so that fence posts can be set on or against the finished paved surface for better alignment and drainage.

Hard landscaping (paving/decking) should be completed before soft landscaping (planting, turf, topsoil) to prevent soil and debris from staining or damaging the finished paved surface and to allow for clean edge detailing.
The canopy structure must be supported by the building's primary structural steel frame, which provides the load-bearing connections and attachment points for the canopy system.
The roof deck provides the base working surface and waterproofing layer upon which or adjacent to which the canopy is typically mounted and sealed.
The structural support framework of the canopy must be fully installed and secured before glass panels, cladding, or infill materials can be placed onto the canopy frame.
Waterproofing membranes and flashing details around the canopy can only be properly installed after the canopy structure is in place to ensure continuous sealing against moisture intrusion.

successor: Exterior Finishing & Cladding Adjacent to Canopy
rationale: While not physically required, it is standard sequencing to complete canopy installation before installing adjacent exterior wall finishes to allow for proper integration, alignment, and clean detailing at the interface.
The shopping street floor requires stable load-bearing support from the building's foundation and substructure before slab and flooring work can commence.
The structural frame must be in place to provide vertical and lateral support for the shopping street floor slab and to define the floor's structural boundaries.
Interior walls, partitions, and finishes for the shopping street level depend on the completed floor slab to build upon.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work at the shopping street level must follow the floor slab installation as conduits and pipes are embedded or laid on the slab.

While the structural slab must be complete for finishing work, some sequential dependencies can be adjusted through scheduling; however, it is strongly preferred to complete the slab before applying final paving and finishes.
The Shopping Street Wall requires a stable foundation to support its weight and maintain structural integrity.
The ground must be graded and leveled before wall construction to ensure proper alignment and drainage around the wall base.
Street paving adjacent to the wall must be done after the wall is in place to ensure proper interface and joint detailing between the wall and the paved surface.
Storefronts and shopfitting along the shopping street must be installed after the wall is complete to allow for proper anchoring and integration with the wall structure.
While street lighting and utilities can technically begin before the wall is finished, coordinating them after wall completion allows for better alignment and fewer rework issues.
The structural steel frame must be erected to provide support for the ceiling structure before ceiling installation can begin.
Mechanical ducts, electrical conduits, and plumbing lines that will run above the ceiling must be installed before the ceiling is enclosed.
The ceiling substrate must be fully installed before any finishing work such as painting, texturing, or applying cladding can be applied.
Recessed or surface-mounted lighting fixtures in the shopping street ceiling require the ceiling structure to be in place for attachment and wiring.
While not physically mandatory, completing the ceiling before internal finishes and tenant fit-out reduces rework and allows a clean, sequential workflow.

The rough opening must be framed and prepared (including header, sill, and jambs) before the storefront glazing system can be installed, as the glazing units require a structurally sound and dimensionally accurate frame to be set into.

Air and water barrier membranes, flashing, and sealants around the rough opening must be applied prior to installing the storefront glazing to ensure a continuous weatherproof seal behind the glazing system.
Any structural steel supports, lintels, or deflection channels needed to carry the weight of the glazing system must be installed and cured before the storefront glazing can be mounted.

successor: Interior Finishes (Drywall / Ceilings Adjacent to Glazing)
rationale: Interior finishes that abut or are sealed against the storefront glazing frames should be completed after the glazing is installed to allow for proper trim, caulking, and integration of the interior finish with the glazing system.
Final exterior sealants, glazing bead installation, and weather performance testing can only be performed after the glazing units and frames are fully in place and aligned.
The site must be properly graded and prepared to provide a stable, level foundation for installing public art or feature displays, especially for large sculptures or installations.
Concrete footings, pads, or structural foundations required to anchor heavy art pieces or display features must be poured and cured before the art can be installed.

If the public art requires lighting, water features, or power connections, underground conduits and utility rough-ins must be completed before the art is placed to avoid digging around or disturbing the installation.

Final landscaping, planting, paving, and hardscape elements around the art display should be completed after installation to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to ensure proper alignment and integration with the art piece.

While final cleanup could technically be done simultaneously, it is preferable to complete the art installation first so that cleanup does not need to be repeated if debris or construction dust settles on the art piece.
The foundation must be prepared and cured before any vertical structural elements like columns can be erected to provide a stable base.
Underground utilities (drainage, water, electrical conduits) must be laid before column placement to avoid excavation and disruption after columns are in place.
Columns must be erected first to support the overhead canopy or roof structure of the shopping street.
The structural column must be in place before cladding, plastering, or decorative finishes can be applied to it.
Columns define the structural bays and boundaries; shopfronts and partitions are installed between or against the columns after they are in position.
The rough opening must be framed, sized, and prepared to accept the door unit before installation can begin.
Door handle, lock, hinges, and other hardware can only be installed after the door itself is mounted and aligned in the opening.
Weather seals and perimeter caulking must be applied after the door is installed to ensure proper fit and sealing around the frame.
Interior casing and trim around the door can only be installed after the door unit is securely in place to achieve proper alignment and finish.
While flooring can be installed before or after depending on design, it is often preferred to install flooring after the door to allow for precise cuts and transitions at the door threshold.
The ground must be properly excavated, leveled, and prepared before any floor construction can begin to ensure a stable foundation.
A load-bearing foundation or sub-base (e.g., compacted aggregate, concrete slab) must be in place to support the shopping street floor structure.
Any underground pipes, conduits, or drainage systems running beneath the shopping street floor must be laid and inspected before the floor is poured or constructed, to avoid costly rework.
Final surface finishes such as tiling, polishing, coating, or paving can only be applied after the structural floor slab or base layer is fully constructed and cured.
Permanent shopfronts, retail kiosks, and display units should be installed on a completed and stable floor surface to ensure proper alignment and safety.
The rough opening must be framed, weatherproofed, and properly sized before any glazing or storefront framing can be installed.
Structural supports such as steel lintels or headers above openings must be in place to bear the load before storefront framing and glass are installed.
Building envelope waterproofing and air barriers must be applied to the rough opening to prevent moisture intrusion before the storefront system is placed.
While interior finishes can proceed concurrently in other areas, completing glazing first prevents damage to finished surfaces from glass handling and allows for a cleaner seal at the interface.
The storefront frame and glass panels must be fully installed before the exterior perimeter sealant and caulking can be applied to complete the weather seal.
The structural framework (columns, beams, load-bearing walls) must be in place before ceiling installation can begin, as the ceiling is supported by and attached to the structural frame.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (ductwork, piping, conduits, wiring) must be completed before ceiling installation because these components are typically run above the ceiling and would be inaccessible once the ceiling is closed.

successor: Shopping Street Ceiling Finishing and Painting
rationale: The ceiling panels or material must be installed first before any finishing work such as painting, texturing, or applying decorative coatings can be performed on the ceiling surface.
Ceiling installation must be completed before recessed or surface-mounted lighting fixtures can be installed, as the ceiling provides the mounting surface and support for these fixtures.

While it is possible to install flooring before ceiling work, it is generally preferred to complete ceiling installation first to avoid dust, debris, and potential damage to finished flooring from overhead work.
Structural framing must be completed to provide the physical substrate and access for rough-in installation of MEP systems (conduits, piping, ductwork) within walls, floors, and ceilings.

MEP rough-in must be completed and inspected before walls and ceilings are enclosed with insulation and drywall, otherwise subsequent access for connections and repairs would require destructive demolition.

Rough-in work (conduit, pipe, duct runs behind walls) must precede trim-out activities (installing fixtures, outlets, switches, registers, and final connections) to ensure all distribution systems are in place before final devices are attached.

successor: Shopping Street Lighting and Signage Commissioning
rationale: Electrical rough-in work (conduit, wiring, junction boxes) must be completed before lighting and signage can be commissioned, as commissioning requires live power and functional electrical connections.

predecessor: Shopping Street Lighting and Signage Commissioning
successor: Shopping Street Final Inspection and Handover
rationale: Commissioning of lighting and signage systems must be successfully completed and verified before the final inspection and handover of the shopping street can take place.

predecessor: Shopping Street Lighting and Signage Commissioning
rationale: Full operational testing of the shopping street environment (including nighttime ambiance, signage visibility) requires that lighting and signage commissioning is complete to ensure all systems are functional.

predecessor: Shopping Street Lighting and Signage Commissioning
rationale: While commissioning should ideally be finished before punch list items are closed out, some minor adjustments to lighting or signage may occur concurrently or after punch list work, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
A stable, compacted subgrade is physically required before any floor finishing can be applied to prevent uneven settlement and cracking.
All underground utilities (drainage, water, electrical conduits) must be installed and covered before the finished floor is laid, otherwise the floor would have to be broken up to access them.
The structural concrete slab must be poured and fully cured to sufficient strength before any floor finishing (e.g., tiles, paving, or screed) can be applied to avoid cracking and adhesion failure.
Floor finishing provides the final walking surface; installing benches, planters, bins, and landscaping elements must be done after the finished floor is complete to avoid damaging the new surface.

Canopy columns and footings should ideally be installed before final floor finishing, but if post-installed, the canopy erection must follow floor finishing to avoid heavy equipment traffic damaging the finished surface.
The structural frame and building enclosure must be complete to provide support and a weather-tight shell before storefront installation can begin.
Electrical rough-ins for storefront lighting, signage, and automatic doors need to be in place before commissioning the storefront systems.
The storefront and entry systems must be fully commissioned and sealed to create a secure, conditioned environment before interior finishing work begins.
Storefront commissioning ensures the mounting surfaces and electrical provisions are verified before permanent signage and branding elements are installed.

successor: Final Inspections and Certificate of Occupancy
rationale: Commissioned storefronts and entry systems must pass functional testing as a prerequisite for final building inspections and occupancy approval.
A stable concrete foundation or slab is required to support the stage structure and equipment loads.
The ground must be leveled and prepared before the stage can be positioned and anchored.
Underground or hidden power conduits and wiring must be laid before the stage is built over those areas.
Speakers, subwoofers, and audio equipment are mounted on or integrated with the stage structure after it is erected.
Stage lighting trusses, fixtures, and control systems are installed after the stage platform is in place.
The disco ball hoist must be attached to a structurally sound ceiling support; the support structure must be installed first to bear the weight.

predecessor: Run electrical wiring to hoist location
rationale: The hoist requires electrical power to operate; wiring must be in place before the hoist can be connected and powered.
The hoist mechanism must be installed and operational before the disco ball can be securely attached to it.

successor: Test hoist operation and lighting alignment
rationale: Testing the hoist's lifting/lowering function and aligning lighting with the ball can only occur after the hoist is fully installed.
While not physically required, it is preferable to finish ceiling work before installing the hoist to avoid damage or rework; however, some finishing may be done after if needed.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical and plumbing for bar area
rationale: Electrical outlets, lighting wiring, and plumbing for a bar sink must be roughed in behind the walls before the bar counter structure is built, as access to these services would be impossible after the bar counter framing is in place.

Flooring should be installed before the bar counter is built because the bar counter sits on top of the finished floor, and installing flooring around a built-in bar counter is difficult and results in an unprofessional finish.
The bar counter base (cabinetry/framing) must be fully built and secured before the countertop can be measured, cut, and installed on top of it.

The bar counter provides a level reference and support for backsplash tile installation; backsplash is installed after the counter is in place to create a clean seam between the countertop and the backsplash.

successor: Final painting and trim work around bar
rationale: While painting can be done before the bar counter is built, final touch-up painting and trim work around the bar is typically done after the bar is installed to cover any gaps and achieve a clean finish; however this is a construction sequencing preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
Wall framing provides the structural backing surface needed to securely mount bottle display racking.
Electrical wiring must be run behind the walls before racking is installed to avoid having to remove or work around the racking later.
Bottles cannot be placed on the racking until the racking structure is fully installed and secure.
While decorative lighting can be installed before or after, installing after avoids damaging the racking during lighting work.
Drywall finishing and painting must be completed before racking installation to prevent paint splatter and dust from contaminating the racking surface.

Banquette seating is typically installed on top of finished flooring. The floor must be complete to provide a stable, level base and to avoid damage to both the seating and the flooring during installation.

predecessor: Wall Finishing (including paint, wallpaper, or paneling)
rationale: Banquette seating is often placed against walls. Wall finishes must be completed first to avoid the need to work around or behind the installed seating, and to prevent damage to finished walls during installation.

predecessor: Electrical Rough-In (for outlets near banquette area)
rationale: Any electrical outlets, data ports, or lighting connections planned behind or adjacent to the banquette must be roughed in and wired before the seating is installed, as access will be blocked afterward.
Setting dining tables adjacent to banquettes is more efficient after the banquette is in place, as the seating defines the layout and spacing, making it easier to align tables properly.

successor: Final Decorative Trim and Cushion Installation
rationale: The banquette frame must be installed first before final trim pieces and cushions/ upholstery can be fitted and secured in place.
The turnstile/cover charge station requires a level, stable concrete base to support its weight and ensure proper alignment and operation.

predecessor: Run underground electrical conduit to turnstile location
rationale: Power supply to the turnstile must be roughed in underground before the station is placed, as the unit needs electrical connections that terminate at its base.

predecessor: Run data/network cabling to turnstile location
rationale: Network and payment-processing data cables must be installed and terminated at the turnstile location before the unit is physically installed.

successor: Commission and test turnstile access control system
rationale: The turnstile must be physically installed and connected before the access control software, payment system, and mechanical operation can be tested and commissioned.

successor: Install adjacent queue railings and barriers
rationale: Queue management barriers that channel patrons to the turnstile are ideally installed after the turnstile is in place so they can be aligned precisely with the entry point, though they could be roughed in beforehand if dimensions are known.
The stage riser framework must be anchored to a solid, level foundation or base slab to ensure structural stability and load distribution.
Floor decking sheets or panels are placed on top of and fastened to the riser framework to create the finished walking surface.
Edge trims and nosings are installed after the riser structure is in place to cover exposed edges and provide a finished, safe transition between riser levels.

While electrical rough-in can begin after the riser is built to access the cavity below, it is a soft preference because some cabling could be laid before the riser is fully enclosed if planned carefully.
The installation area must be surveyed and leveled, and any sub-base adjustments must be completed before the riser framework is erected to ensure the entire stage is plumb and level.
Electrical wiring, conduit, and power outlets must be in place before sound system components can be connected and powered.
Overhead speakers and mounting hardware are typically suspended from or attached to the ceiling grid; the grid must be installed to support speaker placement.
In-wall speaker wiring, wall-mounted control panels, and equipment racks require finished wall surfaces for secure mounting and concealment of cables.
While acoustic panels can sometimes be installed concurrently, optimal acoustic tuning and placement of panels are best done after the sound system is in place to calibrate the room response.
All sound system hardware must be physically installed and wired before the system can be powered on, configured, tuned, and tested for proper operation.

Lighting trusses must be rigged from the overhead steel structure; therefore the steel frame must be fully erected and stabilized to provide attachment points and load-bearing capacity before any rigging can begin.

Electrical conduits, junction boxes, and power drops serving the lighting positions must be installed before rigging trusses, as trusses will obstruct or complicate access to ceiling/overhead electrical work.
Lighting fixtures must be mounted to or hung from the trusses; therefore the trusses must first be rigged and secured in place before any fixtures can be attached.

While it is possible to run cables before trusses are rigged, it is much more efficient and safer to pull lighting control and power cables across or along the trusses after they are installed to avoid cable entanglement and rework.
Rigging trusses at height requires safe working platforms, lifts, or scaffolding to be in place for workers to access rigging points and handle truss sections.
The bar counter must be built on top of the finished floor surface to ensure proper leveling, stability, and alignment with the floor finish.
Bar counter installation requires completed wall surfaces for proper anchoring, backing support, and finishing against the walls.
Plumbing supply lines and drain pipes for the bar sink must be roughed-in within the walls and floor before the bar counter structure is built over them.
Electrical wiring for outlets, lighting, and equipment at the bar area must be completed in walls and floors before the bar counter encloses these services.
The bar counter base structure (cabinetry and framing) must be fully constructed before the final bar top surface (e.g., granite, wood, or quartz) can be measured, cut, and installed.
The bar counter must be built and in place before under-counter fixtures like the bar sink, glass washer, or tap system can be physically mounted and connected.
The bar counter must be installed so that plumbers can complete the final connections of faucets, traps, and supply lines to the fixtures mounted in/on the bar.
Bar counter must be in place before electricians can install receptacles, switches, and lighting fixtures on or above the bar surface.

Although the backsplash can technically be installed after the counter is complete, it is a soft preference because some backsplash work could be done concurrently; however, best practice is to complete countertops first to achieve a clean seamless joint between counter and backsplash.

A level, stable, and properly cured concrete slab or subfloor is required as the base for installing the dance floor system. Building the dance floor on an unprepared or uneven substrate would result in instability and structural failure.

Any electrical conduit, junction boxes, or wiring that runs beneath the dance floor area must be installed and inspected before the dance floor is built, as access will be permanently blocked once the floor is installed.
The dance floor must be fully assembled and secured before the final surface finishing (sanding, sealing, or polishing) can be performed to achieve a smooth, uniform surface.

While walls can be built after the floor, it is often a soft preference to complete the dance floor first to avoid damaging finished walls during floor installation and to allow for precise layout against wall lines.

The dance floor must be completed before applying final paint and decorative finishes to adjacent walls and ceilings, as floor installation activities (sanding, dust generation, material movement) would damage freshly applied finishes.
Interchange enclosure requires a stable foundation to support its structural load and ensure proper alignment of interconnected components.
Underground utilities (power, data, drainage) must be installed before the enclosure is placed to allow access for connections and avoid re-excavation.
The base slab provides the mounting surface and waterproofing layer upon which the interchange enclosure sits.
Internal equipment (shelving, cabling, termination panels) can only be installed after the enclosure is in place and weather-tight.
Cables entering the enclosure must be terminated and tested after the enclosure is secured and entry points are sealed.
Structural framing must be complete to provide support and enclosures for HVAC equipment and ductwork routing.
Electrical rough-in must be finished to provide power connections for HVAC equipment and control systems before commissioning.
Plumbing rough-in must be complete to supply water for HVAC systems (e.g., cooling towers, boilers, condensate drains) before commissioning.
All HVAC equipment must be physically installed before it can be tested, balanced, and commissioned.
Ductwork must be installed and sealed before the system can be commissioned to ensure proper airflow and pressure testing.
HVAC commissioning must be complete to verify proper operation before enclosing systems behind ceilings, walls, and finishes.
While final programming of building management systems can overlap, full commissioning data informs optimal control sequences and setpoints.
Commissioning verifies HVAC systems meet code and performance requirements, which is a prerequisite for occupancy inspection and permitting.
The interchange seating must be installed within the completed station structure, requiring excavation and structural works to be finished first.
Interchange seating is typically mounted on or anchored to platform slabs, which must be cast and cured before seating installation.
Passenger information displays are often integrated into or positioned above interchange seating areas, so seating must be in place to determine final positioning.
While seating can be installed before final finishes, it is generally preferred to complete cladding and painting first to avoid damage to the seating.
The fare control gates must be installed on a finished, level concourse floor surface to ensure proper anchoring, alignment, and stability.

predecessor: Concrete Encasement for Conduit/Slab Conduit Installation
rationale: Electrical and data conduits required for fare control gate power and communication must be embedded in the slab or run through the concrete encasement before the gates can be installed and connected.
Power cables, network/data cables, and control wiring must be pulled to the gate locations before the gates can be physically placed and terminated.
The gates must be physically installed, wired, and terminated before they can be powered on, tested for functionality, and commissioned.

successor: Station Finishes (Flooring, Ceiling, Wall Cladding) Completion
rationale: It is preferable to complete surrounding architectural finishes after gate installation to avoid damage to the gates from finishing work, but this is a soft preference as finishes could be completed first with careful protection.
Electrical power and conduit must be roughed in before fare control equipment can be installed, as fare gates and vending machines require electrical connections.
The floor slab must be completed to provide a stable, level surface for mounting fare control equipment.
Fare control equipment must be physically installed before it can be tested and commissioned for operation.
While final finishes can be completed after installation, it is preferable to delay sensitive equipment installation until after dirty finishing work to avoid dust and damage.
Anchor bolts and embedded metal plates must be set into the concrete to provide mounting points for fare control equipment.

predecessor: Civil Works & Excavation for Interchange Area
rationale: The ground must be prepared, excavated, and leveled before any enclosure structure can be installed. Civil works ensure a stable foundation and proper site conditions for enclosure placement.
The enclosure structure requires a solid foundation or base slab to be cast and cured prior to installation to support its weight and maintain structural integrity.
Underground utilities, conduits, or duct banks that will interface with the enclosure must be laid and positioned before installation to avoid rework and ensure proper alignment.
The enclosure must be installed and secure before any internal equipment, cabinets, or panels are mounted inside it, as the enclosure provides the structural support and weather protection.
The enclosure must be installed and fixed in place before cables are pulled into it and terminated, as cables enter through enclosure penetrations and need a stable structure for routing.
Rough-in framing and MEP rough-ins define the wall cavities and mounting surfaces where signage will be attached; these must be completed before signage installation can begin.
Signage is typically mounted on finished walls; drywall must be installed, taped, mudded, and sanded smooth before signage can be affixed to the wall surface.
Signage is applied over finished painted surfaces; painting and wall finishing must be completed prior to installing signs to avoid damage to the paint and to ensure proper adhesion.
Flooring installation must be complete because some wayfinding signage (e.g., floor-mounted signs, directional arrows) is installed on or adjacent to finished flooring surfaces.
Suspended or ceiling-mounted signage requires the ceiling grid and ceiling finishes to be in place for proper attachment and alignment.
Structural elements like slabs and columns must be in place before any internal fit-out can commence, as they provide the load-bearing framework and floor surface for seating and waiting areas.
Electrical conduits, plumbing pipes, and other MEP rough-in works must be installed within walls and floor slabs before enclosing them with seating area finishes, to avoid costly rework.

Fire sprinkler heads, smoke detectors, and alarm devices must be installed in the ceiling and walls prior to final ceiling and wall finishes in the seating/waiting area, as they are safety-critical systems that would be impeded by completed finishes.

Seating fixtures and waiting area joinery must be installed before applying final paint coats and floor coverings, to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to allow for proper alignment and trimming around installed elements.

Loose furniture, chairs, tables, and signage can only be brought in after the fixed seating and waiting area fit-out is complete, as the area needs to be ready to receive and arrange the furniture without interfering with ongoing construction activities.
The passenger information system must be physically installed before it can be commissioned and tested for proper operation.

predecessor: Cable Pulling and Termination - Passenger Information System
rationale: All necessary cabling and terminations for the passenger information system must be completed to provide power and data connectivity before commissioning can begin.

The backbone control system or central control infrastructure must be installed and operational to enable communication with and centralized control of the passenger information system during commissioning.

successor: System Integration Testing - Passenger Information System
rationale: Commissioning verifies basic functionality of the passenger information system, which must be completed before it can be integrated and tested with other systems (e.g., SCADA, signaling).
The passenger information system must be commissioned and verified as fully operational before it can be placed into trial operation or revenue service for passengers.
Structural framing (walls, columns, slabs) must be in place to define the building's primary structural grid and support the partitions that subdivide dwelling units.
Electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, and HVAC ductwork must be run within the structural bays before partitions are built, as enclosing walls would otherwise require costly cutting and rework.
Partitions define room boundaries and support surfaces for finishes; drywall, paint, and flooring cannot be applied until the partition framework is complete.
Doors and windows are installed into framed openings within the partitions; hence the partition framing must be complete before these elements can be fitted.

While rough-ins are done before partitions, final outlet installations, switch plates, and fixture trim-outs can proceed after partitions are enclosed; this is a logical sequence preference but some trim work could theoretically occur before full partition completion.

The main incoming supply cable must be installed to provide the electrical connection point that the household meter will measure. Without the supply cable in place, there is no physical electrical feed to connect the meter to.
The meter must be connected to the distribution board to route metered power to the household circuits. The distribution board provides the termination point for the meter's output side.
The physical meter enclosure or box must be securely mounted and wired to accept the metering device. The meter is installed into this enclosure.
The metering installation must be complete before the system can be energized and tested for correct operation, accuracy of readings, and safety compliance.

The meter must be installed and connected in line before the switchboard can be energized, as the meter is a critical series component in the supply path that must be in place to safely distribute power.
The structural frame (columns, slabs, and core walls) must be in place to provide the vertical shaft and support brackets for the rubbish chute.
Rubbish chutes typically run within or adjacent to the building's service core; core walls must be built to define the chute enclosure.
Each floor slab provides the opening and structural support for the chute pipe and hopper access doors at that level.
Once the chute pipe is installed through floor openings, fire-resistant sealants and collars must be applied around penetrations to maintain fire compartmentation.
The chute pipe must be in position before hopper intake doors are fitted and finished flush with the wall on each floor.
Plumbing risers must be embedded in or penetrate through the slab/foundation; the slab must be poured and cured before risers can be installed.
Underground drain, waste, and vent lines as well as water supply stub-ups must be in place and inspected before risers can be connected to them above the slab.
Risers must be in place before walls and shafts are framed and enclosed around them to allow access for connections and inspection.
Once risers penetrate floor slabs, firestopping materials must be applied around the penetrations to maintain fire-resistance ratings.
Branch lines to individual fixtures (sinks, toilets, etc.) connect off the vertical risers; the risers must be installed first to serve as the supply and drain distribution backbone.
The Central Mailbox Array requires a stable, level foundation slab to be fully cured before the heavy mailbox array structure can be safely mounted and anchored.

Electrical and data cables for the mailboxes (lighting, electronic lock systems, parcel notification) must be run through underground conduits before the mailbox array is placed, as access to those conduits would be blocked afterward.

Once the mailbox array is physically installed and secured, each individual mailbox unit can be numbered, labeled, and assigned to residents, which cannot logically be completed prior to installation.

The electrical supply to the array (lighting, electronic access, parcel lockers) can only be connected and tested after the array is in its final position, as wires must be terminated at the array connection points.

successor: Mailbox Key Handover and Resident Access Setup
rationale: While physically possible to prepare keys earlier, it is standard practice to complete key handover only after the mailbox array is fully installed and operational to avoid misplacement or confusion.
The door frame must be installed within the rough opening created by the wall framing; without the framed opening, the door unit has no structural support or place to be installed.
The rough opening must be verified for correct dimensions, plumbness, and levelness before installing the door unit to ensure proper fit and function.
Weatherproofing and flashing must be applied after the door unit is in place to seal the perimeter against water infiltration.
Interior trim and casing are installed after the door unit is set, as the casing covers the gap between the door frame and the finished wall.
Exterior siding is installed up to and around the door frame after the door assembly is in place to create a continuous weather-tight exterior envelope.
The public entrance structure requires a stable foundation to bear its load and ensure structural integrity.
The building's structural frame must be in place to support the entrance canopy, walls, and overhead elements.
Underground or in-wall utility rough-ins for lighting, door access controls, and drainage must be completed before enclosing the entrance area.
Once the entrance is structurally complete, interior finishing such as flooring, wall cladding, and ceiling work can proceed in the lobby or entrance hall.
The entrance opening must be framed and roughed-in before installing exterior cladding, curtain walls, or glass storefront systems around the entrance.

predecessor: Install electrical conduits and wiring to reception area
rationale: Electrical power must be available for lighting, computers, and equipment at the reception desk before the desk can be installed and operational.

predecessor: Complete flooring and wall finishes in reception area
rationale: Flooring and wall finishes need to be completed before fixed furniture such as the reception desk is installed to avoid damage and ensure proper alignment.

predecessor: Rough-in plumbing for any sink/water at reception
rationale: If the reception desk includes a sink or water feature, plumbing rough-in must be done before the desk is built over or around those connections.

successor: Install IT network and data outlets at reception desk
rationale: Network cabling and data outlets can be terminated and tested at the desk location only after the desk structure is in place and final positions are known.

successor: Install signage and branding elements at reception
rationale: Signage and branding are typically mounted to or above the reception desk, so the desk must be installed first to establish the correct position and height.
Electrical power and cabling infrastructure must be in place before access control system components (controllers, magnetic locks, card readers) can be installed and wired.
Doors and door frames must be installed to provide the physical mounting surface for magnetic locks, electric strikes, and door position sensors.
Network/data cabling (CAT6/fiber) must be run to control panel locations and reader locations before access controllers and network-enabled devices can be connected.
All hardware (controllers, readers, locks) must be physically installed and wired before the system can be powered on, programmed with user credentials, and tested for functionality.
While not a hard physical constraint, it is a workflow preference to install wall-mounted readers and trim plates after painting is complete to avoid damage and keep finishes clean.
The reception desk must be built on a completed, level floor surface. Concrete slab or finished subfloor must be cured and ready before any permanent desk structure is erected.
Electrical conduits, data cabling, and power outlets for the reception desk area must be roughed in within the floor or walls before the desk is built over or against them.
The desk frame and core must be fully constructed before applying any final surfaces, countertops, paint, or decorative veneers.
Final installation of power outlets, data ports, and lighting fixtures on/within the reception desk can only occur after the desk structure is in place.

While often completed after desk construction to avoid damage, flooring can technically be installed first if carefully protected; however, sequencing desk first avoids cutting flooring materials around the desk base.
The ground must be cleared and graded before any road construction can begin to ensure a stable subgrade and proper alignment.
Access roads must be in place to allow construction vehicles and material delivery to reach villa plots within the cluster.
Utility trenches and services are typically laid along or under access roads, and road completion allows coordinated utility installation alongside or after road construction.
The building must be weather-tight and enclosed before installing public signage to protect signage materials from weather damage and ensure proper mounting surfaces are available.
Interior walls must be finished (drywall, painting) before signage can be mounted, as signage is typically affixed to finished wall surfaces.
Electrical wiring for illuminated signage must be roughed-in and available at sign locations before signage can be installed and connected.
Flooring is typically installed before signage to avoid damage to new floors from ladders and equipment used during sign installation, though signage could technically be installed first if careful.
Public signage must be fully installed before final inspections can verify that all required safety and directional signage is in place and compliant with codes.
The site must be cleared, graded, and leveled before trenching can begin to ensure a stable work surface and proper alignment.
Existing underground utilities must be identified and marked to avoid damaging them during excavation of the common trench.
Soil conditions and bearing capacity must be assessed to determine appropriate trench depth, shoring requirements, and bedding materials.
The trench provides the excavated pathway into which utility pipes, conduits, and ducts are placed; they cannot be installed until the trench is opened.
After utilities are laid in the trench, the excavated material must be backfilled and compacted to restore ground stability and surface conditions.
A stable foundation or base layer must be prepared before installing the pedestrian walkway to ensure structural integrity and proper load distribution.
Proper site grading and drainage systems must be completed before walkway installation to prevent water accumulation and ensure long-term stability.
Any underground utilities, conduits, or cables that need to run beneath the walkway must be installed prior to walkway construction to avoid costly rework.
Landscaping, sodding, and final surface finishes adjacent to the walkway can only be completed after the walkway is installed to align properly with the walkway edges.
Safety handrails or barriers alongside the walkway are typically installed after the walkway surface is complete, though they could be installed concurrently in some cases.
The gateway structure requires a stable, level foundation and prepared ground before it can be installed or assembled.

Electrical, data, and control cabling conduits must be laid in the ground before gateway installation, as the gateway needs underground connections and trenching cannot be done after the gateway is in place.
Physical connection of power and control cables to the gateway components can only be performed after the gateway structure is installed and secured.
Hardware installation must be completed before any software configuration, control system programming, or network integration can begin on the gateway.
Functional testing, safety checks, and commissioning activities require the gateway to be fully installed and connected before they can proceed.
The site must be cleared, levelled, and graded before any boundary wall/fence can be erected, as uneven terrain or debris would prevent proper footing and alignment of the wall or fence posts.

Any underground utilities or drainage pipes that need to pass under the boundary line must be installed before the wall/fence foundation is laid, to avoid later digging through or undermining the structure.
Accurate boundary line survey and pegging must be completed first to define the exact alignment where the wall/fence will be constructed, ensuring it stays within property limits.
The boundary wall/fence defines the physical perimeter of the cluster; internal roads and pavements are laid out within that boundary and their alignment references the established boundary line.

While not strictly required in all sequences, it is prudent to establish the site perimeter first to control access, secure the site, and clearly demarcate the construction zone before commencing building foundations.
The mailbox kiosk must be mounted on a finished, level concrete slab or foundation to ensure stability and proper anchoring.
Electrical and data conduits must be run to the kiosk location before the kiosk is placed, as the kiosk requires power and possibly network connectivity.
The physical kiosk structure must be installed and accessible before individual mailbox compartments can be assigned, labeled, or keyed to residents.
Power connections to the kiosk (lighting, electronic lock, parcel locker) can only be completed after the kiosk is in its final position.
While the kiosk should be installed before final grading/paving to avoid rework, if necessary the surrounding work could be done first and patched later, making this a soft preference for sequencing.
Construction site must be mobilized with equipment, trailers, and utilities established before any earthwork operations can commence.
All vegetation, debris, and existing structures must be cleared from the site before grading and earthwork can begin to ensure a clear working area.
Erosion control measures (silt fences, sediment basins, etc.) must be in place before earthwork begins to comply with environmental regulations and prevent sediment runoff.
Accurate survey control points, boundary staking, and grading plans must be established to guide earthwork operations to the correct elevations and alignments.
Rough grading must be completed before trenching for underground utilities can proceed, as utility lines are placed at specified depths below finished grade.
Earthwork compaction and fill placement must be completed before soil compaction tests can be performed to verify that subgrade meets specification requirements.
Overall site grading must be completed to establish the building pad elevation before individual foundation excavations can be accurately located and dug.
Site grading establishes the subgrade profile for access roads and parking areas, which must be completed before road base materials can be placed and compacted.
The site must be properly graded and prepared to provide a stable working surface and clear area for trenching and utility rough-in work.
Existing underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid conflicts and damage when excavating for new utility rough-ins.
In some cases, utility rough-ins that penetrate slabs must be coordinated with or completed before slab placement; however, this is project-specific and not always a hard constraint.
After utility pipes, conduits, and sleeves are installed and inspected, trenches must be backfilled and compacted to restore the surface and support subsequent work.
The rough-in stubs must be in place before final connections can be made to main utility lines or building systems.

The site must be cleared of obstacles, vegetation, and existing structures before any new road and walkway construction can begin, as debris and uneven ground would prevent proper grading and foundation work.
The terrain must be graded to the required levels and slopes before roads and walkways can be constructed, as the road base and pavement depend on a properly prepared subgrade.
Water, sewer, drainage, electrical, and communication utilities must be laid beneath the road and walkway alignments before paving occurs, to avoid cutting into or damaging finished surfaces later.
Roads and walkways provide the necessary access routes for construction vehicles and equipment to reach building sites, which is required before foundation work can commence.

Final landscaping, planting, and surface finishes should be performed after roads and walkways are completed to ensure that construction traffic does not damage newly planted areas and that all hardscape elements are in place before soft landscaping is finished.

Site preparation including grading, drainage, and soil conditioning must be completed before any landscaping or planting can begin, as the ground needs to be properly shaped and prepared for vegetation.
Underground utilities such as water, drainage, and irrigation pipes must be laid before landscaping to avoid disturbing newly planted areas and to ensure irrigation systems are operational.
Major building construction should be completed to prevent heavy equipment and material storage from damaging newly landscaped and planted areas.
Hardscape elements such as walkways, retaining walls, and paved surfaces should be installed before planting to avoid trampling vegetation and to define the layout of planted areas.
Landscaping and planting are typically among the final finishing activities; once completed, the site can be cleaned up and prepared for handover or occupancy.
The water main must be installed first to provide a pressurized water supply source for the fire hydrant assembly to connect to.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth and dimensions to accommodate the hydrant assembly and its connections before installation can begin.
A stable, compacted bedding or gravel base must be prepared to support the hydrant assembly and ensure proper drainage and structural stability.
Backfilling can only commence after the hydrant assembly is properly installed and secured in position to avoid disturbing or damaging the assembly.
Pressure testing must be performed after assembly to verify the integrity of connections and ensure the hydrant meets required performance standards before being placed into service.
The front façade cladding and finishing elements require the building's structural frame to be in place to provide support and attachment points.
Foundations must be completed to provide a stable base for the building structure, which the front façade is part of or attached to.
Weather barriers and waterproofing membranes must be installed behind the façade to protect the building envelope from moisture intrusion.
Windows and doors are typically installed after the façade structure is in place to ensure proper sealing, flashing, and integration with the cladding system.

While interior work can technically begin before the façade is fully complete, it is more efficient and protects interior finishes if the building envelope (including the front façade) is closed in first.
The rear façade must be supported on stable foundations; without completed foundation works, the façade structure cannot be safely erected.
The rear façade is typically attached to or supported by the building's structural frame, which must be in place before façade installation can begin.
Windows and doors are installed into the façade openings; the façade structure must be complete to receive these elements.
Waterproof membranes and final cladding are applied onto the completed rear façade surface to ensure weathertightness.
Scaffolding erected for façade work can only be safely removed after the rear façade installation and finishing are fully complete.
The stoep/front steps require a stable and level foundation or footings to support their structure and prevent settling or cracking.
The front steps typically abut the ground floor slab, so the slab must be poured/cast first to establish the finished floor level from which the steps descend.
The front door threshold and frame sit on or above the finished stoep/step level; the steps provide the finished grade and access platform before the door is installed.
A canopy or roof over the stoep must be supported by posts or walls that are founded on the completed stoep structure, or the steps provide the base access before overhead covering is installed.
Handrails and balustrades for the front steps are fixed to the finished step structure; they cannot be installed until the steps themselves are complete.
The party wall parapet sits atop the party wall structure; the wall must be built to its full height before the parapet can be constructed.
Coping stones or capping are placed on top of the parapet to protect it from weather; the parapet must be complete before the coping can be installed.
Flashing is typically installed after the parapet is built to seal the junction between the parapet and roof or wall.
Scaffolding may remain in place until parapet work is finished, but dismantling is a soft preference dependent on schedule and safety logistics.
While logically the roof structure near the party wall may be completed beforehand to provide access, this is often a construction sequence preference rather than a strict physical constraint.
The structural frame must be erected to provide the supporting structure upon which the roof assembly is installed.
The roof deck must be installed as the substrate for the roofing membrane and insulation layers.
The common roof assembly (including substrate and insulation) must be completed before the waterproofing membrane can be applied.
Roof drains and scuppers are typically installed after or integrated with the roof assembly to ensure proper drainage on the finished surface.
Ceiling finishes below the roof are installed after the roof assembly is complete to avoid weather damage and allow overhead work.
The structural framing (floors, walls, roof) must be in place to provide support and enclosure before interior stairs can be installed.
The ground floor slab or foundation must be completed to provide a stable base for the stair structure to rest upon.
Stairs must be installed before wall and ceiling finishes can be completed around the stair opening to allow for proper taping, mudding, and painting without damaging finished surfaces.
The stair structure must be in place before upper-level floor finishes are laid, as stairs provide access and define the floor levels.
The stair stringers and treads must be completed to provide the structure onto which handrails and balusters are mounted.
A stable foundation must be prepared before any structural addition can be built upon it. The rear addition's footing and slab need to be in place before framing begins.
The existing rear wall must be removed or opened up to allow the new addition to connect structurally and seamlessly to the existing building.
Underground or in-slab utility lines (drainage, water supply, electrical conduit) must be roughed in before the slab or foundation is poured for the rear addition.
The structural framing and decking of the rear addition must be completed before the roofing membrane, shingles, or tiles can be installed over the addition.
The shell (walls, floor, roof) of the rear addition must be enclosed and weathertight before interior work such as drywall, flooring, and trim can proceed.
The cornice is mounted on top of the walls, so the wall structure must be completed first to provide a supporting surface.
The cornice typically connects to and integrates with the roof edge, so roof decking or sheathing should be in place to properly align and secure the cornice.
Roof flashing and trim often overlap or abut the cornice; the cornice must be installed first to provide a proper edge for flashing details.
While painting can be done after cornice installation for a uniform finish, it is a soft preference since some painting could be done beforehand if sections are pre-finished.
Gutters are typically attached to or below the cornice/fascia, so the cornice must be in place to provide a mounting surface for gutters.

successor: Row House Construction - Party Wall Erection
rationale: The ground must be excavated and leveled before any foundation or wall work can begin, ensuring stable load-bearing conditions for the party wall.

successor: Row House Construction - Party Wall Erection
rationale: The concrete foundation must be fully poured and cured to provide a solid base upon which the party wall can be erected, preventing differential settlement and structural failure.

predecessor: Row House Construction - Party Wall Erection
rationale: The party wall must be erected first to serve as a vertical support and boundary before the ground floor slab can be poured or installed adjacent to it.

predecessor: Row House Construction - Party Wall Erection
rationale: The party wall provides lateral support and a bearing surface for roof trusses or rafters, so it must be completed before roof framing can begin.

predecessor: Row House Construction - Party Wall Erection
successor: Electrical and Plumbing Rough-In (Party Wall Side)
rationale: While the wall structure must be in place, utilities can be routed later; however, it is a soft preference to rough-in services after the wall is up to avoid rework if wall positioning changes during construction.

predecessor: Row House Construction - Structural Frame Erection
rationale: The structural frame (load-bearing walls, columns, slabs) must be fully erected and stable before façade panels or cladding can be mounted onto the building structure.

predecessor: Row House Construction - Roof Structure Completion
rationale: The roof structure must be in place to provide weather protection and a stable top anchorage point, ensuring safe and sequential installation of façade elements from top to bottom.
Foundations and below-grade waterproofing must be completed to provide a level, dry base and to prevent moisture ingress that could damage façade materials.

successor: Row House Construction - Window & Door Installation
rationale: Façade panels and cladding must be installed first to define the building envelope openings; windows and doors are then fitted into these prepared rough openings for proper sealing and alignment.
The façade substrate must be fully installed and cured before any external paint, coating, or sealant can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and uniform finish.

successor: Row House Construction - Roofing Over Multiple Units
rationale: The roof structure must be supported by the building's structural frame, so framing must be completed before roofing can begin.

predecessor: Row House Construction - Wall Sheathing and Weatherproofing
successor: Row House Construction - Roofing Over Multiple Units
rationale: Wall sheathing provides lateral stability and weatherproofing continuity with the roof; exterior walls must be sheathed before roofing installation to ensure proper integration.

predecessor: Row House Construction - Roofing Over Multiple Units
successor: Row House Construction - Rough-In Electrical and Plumbing
rationale: Roofing must be complete to make the building watertight before interior rough-in work begins, protecting electrical and plumbing materials from water damage.

predecessor: Row House Construction - Roofing Over Multiple Units
