successor: Row House Construction - Exterior Masonry and Cladding
rationale: The roof edge flashing and overhang details must be installed before final exterior cladding to ensure proper weather sealing and finish integration.

predecessor: Row House Construction - Roofing Over Multiple Units
successor: Row House Construction - Interior Drywall Installation
rationale: Roofing must be completed to create a watertight and weather-sealed building envelope before interior finishes such as drywall can be installed, preventing moisture damage.

The foundation must be completed before unit partitioning can begin because partition walls require a stable and level base to be built upon, and the foundation defines the structural footprint and load-bearing capacity for the entire row house structure.

The main structural frame (columns, beams, and roof structure) must be erected before unit partitioning can start, as partition walls are non-load-bearing infill walls that fit within the established structural grid and cannot be properly aligned without the frame in place.

Unit partitioning must be completed before mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) rough-in work begins because partition walls define the room layouts and enclose the spaces where conduits, pipes, and wiring will be run; MEP rough-in requires access to the framed wall cavities.

successor: Row House Construction - Interior Drywall Installation
rationale: Unit partitioning must be finished before drywall can be installed, as the partition framing provides the substrate onto which drywall sheets are attached; drywall cannot be hung without the underlying stud walls in place.

While unit partitioning is typically completed before floor finishing to avoid damage to finished floors from construction debris and tools during wall framing, this is a soft preference as some projects may sequence floor work earlier if using protective coverings.
The foundation must be completed to provide a stable base for the stair structure.
The main structural framework (floors, walls, and supporting beams) must be in place to define the openings and landings where stairs will be installed.
Floor slabs must be poured and cured to provide the supporting surfaces from which stairs rise or descend.

Stairs must be installed before adjacent wall finishes can be completed, as stair installation may damage finished walls; however, this is a soft preference as sequencing can sometimes be reversed with protection measures in place.

Stair structure must be in place to serve as the mounting surface for handrails and guardrails, which are safety-critical components typically installed immediately after the stair stringers and treads.
The structural frame must be in place to provide load-bearing support for terrace and balcony elements such as slabs, cantilevers, and edge beams.
Rough floor slabs need to be poured at the same level as terrace slabs to provide a continuous structural base before balcony elements are formed or installed.
Waterproofing must be applied after balcony and terrace structures are complete to seal joints, cracks, and surfaces against water ingress.
Balustrades and railings are typically anchored into the finished balcony slab or edge beam, so the structural elements must be complete first.

While it is strongly preferred to install floor finishes after the structural balcony is complete, in some sequences finishes can be done concurrently; however, structural completion is generally required to avoid damage to finishes.
Entry doors require framed rough openings within load-bearing walls to be installed. Without the wall framing, there is no structural support or defined opening for the door frame.
The rough opening must be prepared with proper headers, king studs, and jack studs to provide the correct dimensions and load-bearing support for the entry door frame.

The building should be weathertight (roof sheathing and underlayment in place) before installing entry doors to prevent water damage to the door and frame, and to allow proper sealing against the elements.

Entry doors must be installed and weather-sealed before interior finishes are applied, so that the interior environment is protected from weather and the door casing can be properly integrated with finished walls.

It is preferable to install entry doors before adjacent flooring so that the door can be properly fitted and the threshold can be coordinated with the finished floor height, but in some sequences flooring may be installed first with careful planning.

Electrical wiring, outlets, switches, and plumbing rough-ins (water supply and drainage) must be installed and inspected before any cabinetry is fitted, as walls and floors need to be open for access.

Flooring must be laid and finished before built-in cabinets are installed because cabinets sit on top of the finished floor, and installing flooring after cabinetry would be impossible underneath fixed units.
Walls must be plastered, sanded, and painted before built-in units are installed, otherwise access for finishing behind and around cabinets would be blocked.

Kitchen benchtop (stone/laminate) and splashback tiles cannot be installed until base cabinets are in place because the countertop is fabricated to the exact cabinet layout and must be fitted directly onto the carcasses.

Built-in ovens, cooktops, rangehoods, dishwashers, and refrigerators cannot be installed until the cabinetry is in position, as the appliances are fitted into or onto the cabinets, and their pre-wiring/plumbing connections rely on the final cabinet positions.

Plumbing rough-in (drainage and water supply lines) must be installed within walls and floors before bathroom fit-out can commence, as the built-in components (cabinetry, vanity, toilet) cover and connect to these services.
Electrical wiring, outlet boxes, and lighting points must be run through wall cavities before built-in fit-out, as electrical fixtures will be integrated with vanity cabinets and mirrors.
Waterproofing of shower and bathroom floor areas must be completed and tested before installing built-in joinery and fixtures, to prevent water damage behind fixed elements.
Built-in cabinetry and vanities provide the structural support and connection points for installing sanitary fixtures such as basins and toilets.
While substrate preparation may occur before, the final wall tiling and finishing must be completed after built-in fit-out so that tiles abut neatly against installed cabinets and fixtures.

A thorough site survey and assessment must be completed before adapting a sloping site to understand the topography, soil conditions, drainage patterns, and existing vegetation, which are critical for designing the adaptation strategy.
Geotechnical investigation is required to determine soil bearing capacity, slope stability, and potential erosion risks before any earthworks or grading can be performed on the sloping site.
The sloping site must be graded, cut, and filled to create a level building platform before foundation excavation can commence, as foundations require stable, level ground.
Retaining walls are built to stabilize the slope after site grading and earthworks are completed, providing long-term slope stability before other structures are built.
Proper drainage systems (e.g., French drains, surface drainage) must be installed after reshaping the slope to manage water runoff and prevent erosion or water accumulation around the building.
The subgrade must be properly graded, compacted, and leveled to provide a stable and uniform bearing surface for the slab on grade, preventing differential settlement and structural failure.
All below-slab utilities such as plumbing, electrical conduits, and drainage pipes must be installed and pressure-tested before the slab is poured, as access is impossible afterward.
A vapor retarder or moisture barrier must be placed over the prepared subgrade and under the slab to prevent moisture migration from the ground into the concrete.
After the slab is poured and finished, it must undergo a specified curing period to achieve design strength before any loads or subsequent construction activities are applied.

The slab on grade provides the finished floor substrate and a stable work platform; vertical structural elements that bear on or rise from the slab must be constructed after the slab is in place and cured.
The roof terrace must be supported by the completed structural frame of the building to ensure load-bearing capacity and structural integrity.
A waterproof membrane must be installed beneath the roof terrace to prevent water infiltration and protect the structure below before terrace finishes are applied.
Safety railings and barriers must be installed after the terrace structure is in place to define the perimeter and ensure worker and occupant safety.
Final floor finishes such as tiles or paving stones must be laid after the terrace substructure and waterproofing are complete to avoid damaging finished surfaces.
Landscaping and planting can proceed after the terrace assembly is complete, but it is a soft preference as some planting could theoretically be done concurrently in designated areas.

The superstructure (columns, beams, slabs, walls) must be supported on a completed foundation system (footings, pile caps, raft foundations) that transfers loads to the ground. Erection cannot begin without a stable base.

The ground floor slab or at least a working platform/ blinding concrete is typically required before erecting the first lift of columns or walls to provide a level, stable working surface and to integrate with the foundation.
The roof structure (trusses, roof slab, steel frame) depends on the completed vertical support elements (columns, walls, beams) of the superstructure to bear its loads.
Cladding panels, curtain walls, or brick veneer are attached to or supported by the structural frame (beams, columns, slabs) of the superstructure, which must be erected first.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the superstructure (e.g., conduits in slabs, ducts through beams, risers in shafts) follows the erection of structural elements, as these services are embedded in or routed through the frame.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil, and graded to proper elevation before any foundation work can begin. Foundations require a stable, prepared subgrade.
Soil bearing capacity, groundwater levels, and soil composition must be assessed to design the appropriate foundation type and depth before construction can proceed.
The exact building footprint, corners, and foundation lines must be staked out on-site to guide excavation and formwork placement.

Underground utility lines (water, sewer, electrical conduits) that pass under the foundation slab must be laid and inspected before concrete is poured, to avoid cutting or compromising the foundation later.

Excavation to required depths for footings and foundation walls must be completed, with trenches dug for strip footings, to expose the bearing soil layer before forming and pouring foundation elements.
Foundation walls must be fully cured and complete before waterproofing membranes or coatings can be applied to the exterior surfaces.
Backfill against foundation walls can only proceed after the foundation concrete has cured sufficiently (typically 7 days) to withstand lateral earth pressures without cracking or displacing.
Interior floor slabs that bear on the foundation walls or grade beams require the perimeter foundation to be in place to contain and support the slab edges.

The superstructure columns, beams, and walls rely on the foundation for load transfer. Anchor bolts and base plates must be set in the foundation concrete before any structural framing can be erected.

Rough-in plumbing drains, vapor barriers, and reinforcing steel (rebar/mesh) are placed after excavation but before concrete pouring of the foundation slab, making them dependent on the foundation phase sequence.
Structural framing (walls, floors, ceilings) must be in place before MEP rough-in can begin, as MEP systems are installed within the building's structural cavities.
Concrete slabs must be cured and poured before MEP rough-in can start, as underground conduits, floor drains, and slab penetrations need to be embedded in or pass through the slab.
The building must be enclosed (roof, windows, exterior walls) to protect MEP rough-in work from weather damage and to create a secure environment for electrical, plumbing, and HVAC installations.

successor: Wall/ Ceiling Insulation and Drywall Installation
rationale: MEP rough-in (pipes, ducts, conduit, wiring) must be fully installed and inspected before walls and ceilings are closed up with insulation and drywall, as these systems would be inaccessible after closure.

Rough-in work (behind walls) must be completed before final trim-out activities such as installing outlets, switches, light fixtures, plumbing fixtures, and HVAC registers, as these devices connect to the rough-in infrastructure.
The structural frame (columns, beams, roof deck) must be in place to provide a supporting substrate for the roofing system.
Roof sheathing or decking provides the necessary base surface onto which underlayment and roofing materials are applied.
Roof overhangs and flashing are installed first to shed water away from walls; cladding is then installed up to the roofing to ensure proper weather sealing.
While not always a hard physical constraint, it is strongly preferred to have the building 'dried in' (roof complete) before starting moisture-sensitive interior work to prevent weather damage.
Roof-mounted HVAC equipment should be placed on a completed roof to ensure proper curbs, flashing, and waterproofing around penetrations are in place.
The structural steel frame must be erected to provide the load-bearing skeleton against which the exterior enclosure (curtain wall, cladding, etc.) is attached and supported.
The foundation and ground floor slab must be completed to provide a stable base and anchoring points for the exterior wall system.
The roof deck is typically installed before exterior enclosure so that the building's top structure is in place, providing a working platform and enabling the enclosure to tie into the roof assembly.
The building must be enclosed (dried-in) before mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work begins inside, to protect materials and equipment from weather exposure.
Interior wall framing and drywall installation should follow enclosure completion to ensure the interior environment is weathertight and to prevent moisture damage to gypsum board and insulation.
Grab bars must be attached to structural wall framing to provide adequate support and load-bearing capacity.
Gypsum board (drywall) must be installed and finished before grab bars can be mounted to provide a finished surface and proper backing.
In wet areas such as showers, tile backer board and tile must be installed before grab bars can be securely mounted to the substrate.
Waterproofing membrane must be applied behind grab bar mounting locations in wet areas to prevent moisture intrusion and structural damage.
After grab bars are installed, any exposed screw heads, gaps, or wall damage around mounting flanges should be touched up with paint for a finished appearance.
Grab bar installation must be complete before final accessibility compliance inspection can verify proper placement, height, and load capacity.
A stable, level foundation and concrete slab must be in place to support the door frame and ensure proper threshold alignment for accessibility compliance.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed to the correct dimensions before the door unit can be installed.
The door frame and casing must be installed before drywall finishing and painting can be completed around the opening to achieve a clean, finished look.
The door installation must be complete before inspectors can verify clear width, threshold height, hardware operability, and other ADA/senior accessibility requirements.
The door must be installed prior to final flooring so that flooring can be run up to the threshold without gaps or interference, maintaining a smooth transition for wheelchair and walker access.
Plumbing rough-in (water supply and drain lines) must be installed in the walls and floor before any bathroom fixtures can be mounted or connected to the plumbing system.
Tiling around fixtures like grab bars, shower seats, and raised toilets requires the fixtures to be securely in place to ensure proper alignment and waterproofing integration.
Electrical rough-in for lighting, exhaust fans, and any heated components must be completed before fixtures that may cover or block access to junction boxes and wiring.

successor: Senior Bathroom Final Trim and Accessories
rationale: Fixtures such as grab bars, non-slip shower base, and comfort-height toilet must be installed first so that final trim items (towel bars, soap dispensers, mirrors) can be placed at proper heights relative to the fixtures.
The fixture set must be fully installed and functional before the accessibility compliance inspection can verify clearances, grab-bar load capacity, and other ADA/senior safety requirements.
The overbed table's frame must be fully assembled before installation can proceed.
It is convenient but not strictly required to install the overbed table before assembling the bed, as the table can be positioned afterward.
The tabletop must be manufactured and finished before it can be mounted onto the overbed table frame.
The overbed table installation must be complete before the final quality inspection of the room or unit.
The floor surface must be fully finished and stable before placing the bed base to ensure level placement and prevent damage to flooring materials.
Wall finishes and painting should be completed before moving in large furniture items to avoid paint splatter, dust, or damage to the bed base.
Electrical outlets and switches for bed-side equipment must be roughed-in before the bed base is positioned, as the bed may block access to walls for later electrical work.
Bedside furniture is typically placed after the bed base is in position to ensure proper alignment and spacing around the bed.
Final cleaning is preferably done after all furniture including the bed base is in place, though this is a soft preference as cleaning can be performed around furniture.

The handrail is an interior finishing component of the corridor, so the main structural and shell components (walls, ceiling, floor) must be in place to provide a mounting surface and enclosure before handrail installation can begin.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work inside the corridor walls/ceilings must be completed before handrails are installed, since handrails would obstruct access and could be damaged by subsequent MEP work.

Handrails are typically installed after wall preparation but before final painting and finishing, as the handrail mounting areas need to be painted around or the handrail itself may be a finished element that could get damaged if painting occurs afterward.
It is a soft preference to install handrails before flooring to avoid damaging finished flooring during handrail installation work, but it is not a physical impossibility to reverse the order.
Handrails are a safety-critical component (required for accessibility), so they must be fully installed and secured before final inspection and occupancy of the corridor.
The raised toilet must be installed on a prepared, level subfloor or floor slab to ensure proper structural support and alignment of the toilet pan and plumbing connections.
Drainage pipes and water supply lines must be roughed in and terminated at the correct locations before the toilet can be positioned and connected.
Once the raised toilet is installed, adjacent wall surfaces, including tiles and waterproofing, can be finished up to the toilet fixture to create a clean, sealed interface and prevent water damage.
Grab bars for senior accessibility should be installed after the toilet is in place so that their position and height can be accurately set relative to the final toilet location.

successor: Final Plumbing Connection and Flush Testing
rationale: The final connection of the water supply and flush mechanism testing can only be performed after the toilet is physically installed and secured in position.

successor: Senior Window / Low Sill Window Installation
rationale: The rough opening must be framed, sized, and prepared before the window can be installed into it.

successor: Senior Window / Low Sill Window Installation
rationale: Weather-resistant barrier and flashing must be applied around the opening to prevent moisture intrusion before the window is set in place.

predecessor: Senior Window / Low Sill Window Installation
rationale: Interior and exterior trim and casing cannot be installed until the window unit itself is properly positioned, leveled, and fastened.

predecessor: Senior Window / Low Sill Window Installation
rationale: Spray foam or other insulation sealing around the window frame can only be applied after the window is secured in the opening.

predecessor: Senior Window / Low Sill Window Installation
rationale: Interior wall finishes around the window area cannot be completed until the window is installed and sealed in place.

The building's physical layout, floor plan, exit locations, and hallway widths must be designed before an egress plan for seniors can be developed, as the plan depends on the specific spatial configuration.

predecessor: Fire Safety and Alarm System Design
rationale: The location of fire alarms, emergency lighting, and notification systems must be determined before planning how seniors will be alerted and evacuated.

predecessor: Regulatory Code Review (Building and Fire Codes)
rationale: Applicable building and fire codes (e.g., for senior care facilities) must be reviewed first to ensure the egress plan complies with all legal requirements for accessible means of egress.

successor: Evacuation Drill and Training Program Development
rationale: The egress plan must be finalized before training materials and drill procedures can be created, as the drills will follow the specific routes and procedures defined in the plan.

The egress plan determines the designated evacuation routes and assembly points, so signage (including directional signs, exit signs, and accessible route markers) must be installed based on the approved plan.
The signage must be installed on completed walls and surfaces; construction and finishing work must be done first to provide a stable surface.
Signage installation requires clean, painted walls. Painting and wall finishing must be completed before signs can be mounted.
While not physically blocking, ceiling work is typically completed prior to signage to avoid dust/debris damaging new signs, though this is a soft preference.
It is preferable to install signage before moving furniture and equipment to avoid obstacles and potential damage, though furniture can be placed around signs if needed.
Signage must be installed before the room can be formally inspected and handed over, as signage is a required deliverable for occupancy.

Accessibility fixtures (e.g., grab bars, accessible toilets, sinks) require rough-in plumbing, electrical, and framing to be in place so that support blocking, water supply lines, drain lines, and electrical connections are ready before fixtures can be mounted.

predecessor: Wall and Floor Finish Work (Tile, Drywall, Waterproofing)
rationale: Wall and floor finishes must be completed before accessibility fixtures are installed to avoid damaging finished surfaces and to allow proper sealing around fixtures for waterproofing and accessibility compliance.
Once accessibility fixtures are installed, final trim work (e.g., escutcheon plates, caulking, covers) and finishing touches can be applied to seal and complete the installation.

successor: Final Inspection and Accessibility Compliance Testing
rationale: Installation of accessibility fixtures must be complete before the final inspection and compliance testing can be performed to verify that all fixtures meet ADA and local accessibility code requirements.
The building or space cannot be occupied or handed over until all accessibility fixtures are installed, ensuring the facility is fully accessible and code-compliant for occupants.

predecessor: Rough-in Electrical & Data Cabling for Nurse Call System
rationale: The physical conduit, cables, and backboxes for the nurse call system must be installed in walls and ceilings during rough-in before any final wiring and commissioning can begin.

predecessor: Ceiling & Wall Board Installation (or completion of accessible spaces)
rationale: Wiring and device terminations require finished surfaces (or at least open accessible ceilings/walls) so that cables can be pulled to final device locations and secured properly.

successor: Nurse Call System Device Installation & Testing
rationale: After wiring is complete and the system is commissioned (powered up and configured), individual nurse call devices such as pull cords, bed stations, and corridor lights can be installed and functionally tested.

successor: Final Integration with Building Management System / Nurse Call Headend
rationale: Commissioning verifies the wiring backbone and basic system functionality, which is a prerequisite for integrating the nurse call system with the central headend server and building management or nurse call software.
Raw lumber must be harvested and milled into usable timber before any woodworking can begin on the table.
The specific timber pieces must be selected and graded for quality before being cut and assembled into the table.
Green lumber must be dried (air-dried or kiln-dried) to the proper moisture content to prevent warping, cracking, or structural failure after assembly.
The assembled table must be fully constructed before sanding and applying sealants/finishes to its surfaces.
The completed table must undergo inspection and testing for stability, weight capacity, and craftsmanship before being approved for use or delivery.
The seating bench requires a stable, level foundation or concrete pad to rest on; the foundation must be cured and ready before the bench can be placed.

After the bench is installed, the seat surface may need final sealing, staining, or protective coating to withstand weather; this finishing work can only be done once the bench is in its permanent position.
The surrounding ground must be properly graded and drainage established before placing the bench to prevent water pooling or erosion around the base.

It is easier to install landscaping, mulch, and plants around the bench after the bench is in place, but landscaping could also be done beforehand with temporary protection; thus this is a soft preference for sequencing.
If the bench is mounted on a concrete pad, the concrete must be fully cured (typically 7 days) before bearing the weight of the bench to avoid cracking or settlement.
Wall framing provides the structural support and backing into which built-in cubbies are installed; cubbies cannot be built without framed walls.
Electrical wiring for outlets or lighting within or near the cubbies must be run in the walls before the cubbies are installed to avoid having to cut into or remove the cubbies later.
Drywall must be hung, taped, and finished behind and around the cubby area so that the cubbies can be mounted cleanly without damaging finished surfaces or requiring rework.
Baseboards, crown molding, and other trim around the cubbies must be installed after the cubbies are in place to ensure proper fit and seamless transitions.

Paint or stain on the cubbies themselves can be applied after installation, and final touch-up painting of adjacent walls should be done after cubbies are mounted to cover any gaps or marks from installation.
Electrical and data cabling must be completed before the whiteboard wall is installed, as the wall covers the stud cavity where wiring is routed.
The wall framing must be complete to provide structural support for mounting the whiteboard wall surface.
Insulation must be placed in the wall cavity before the whiteboard surface is installed, as the wall finish encloses the cavity.
It is preferable but not physically required to complete painting and trim after the whiteboard wall is installed to avoid damaging the wall surface during painting.
The room cannot be occupied or furnished until the whiteboard wall is fully installed, as it is a permanent wall finish.
The soft seating cluster must be placed on finished flooring to ensure a level, clean, and stable surface for furniture placement.
The room or area must be fully enclosed with walls and ceiling completed before installing soft seating, to protect furniture from dust, debris, and construction damage.
Electrical outlets and wiring must be installed in the walls/floor before placing seating, as access to walls behind the seating area will be blocked once furniture is arranged.
Soft seating is one of the last finish items; after placement, only final cleaning and inspection remain to avoid soiling or damaging the upholstery.
Decorative items, throw pillows, and signage can be added after seating is in place, but this is a soft preference as some accessories might be placed concurrently if carefully managed.
The wall must be framed to create the recess cavity before the vending machine recess component can be installed.
Electrical wiring and outlet boxes should be roughed in after the recess is in place to ensure proper positioning and connection for the vending machine.
The vending machine recess must be installed and secured in the framing before drywall can be applied around the recess opening.
The recess cavity must be fully built out (framed, wired, finished) before the actual vending machine unit can be placed into the recess.
Although not a strict physical dependency, completing floor finishing before installing the recess can prevent damage to the finished floor from construction debris.
Plumbing supply and drain lines must be roughed into the walls and floor before the sink cabinet and countertop can be installed, as the sink needs to connect to these lines.
Electrical wiring for outlets, switches, or under-cabinet lighting must be run in the walls before the countertop and backsplash are installed, to avoid surface-mounted conduit.
Walls must be framed, insulated, and drywalled (at least to the point where backing and blocking are in place) to provide a finished surface to mount the counter and sink cabinet against.
Flooring should be installed before base cabinets and countertops to allow the flooring to run under the cabinet toe-kick area, preventing a visible gap and ensuring a clean finished look.
After the sink and counter are set in place, the plumber can connect the faucet, trap, and supply lines, and verify the drain works.
Once the countertop is installed, any backsplash tiles or sealing work can proceed, as the counter provides a horizontal reference surface and must be in place before backsplash is applied.

Typically painting and trim finishing can be done after counter installation, but this is a soft preference since some crews prefer to paint walls before counters to avoid drips on the new countertop.
Walls must be finished before mounting a coat rack or wardrobe to prevent damage to finished surfaces and ensure proper alignment.
Flooring must be completed so the wardrobe or coat rack sits on the final floor surface, avoiding height/level issues or damage to new flooring.
Any nearby electrical outlets or switches behind or beside the wardrobe area must be roughed in before the unit is placed, as access will be blocked.
After installing a wardrobe, any gaps between the unit and walls/ceiling may need caulking and touch-up paint for a finished appearance.
The coat rack or wardrobe must be in place before occupants can use it for storing coats, bags, and other items.
Message boards/notice boards are typically mounted on walls, so the wall framing (and usually the finished wall surface) must be in place to provide a mounting surface.

It is preferable to install the message board before final painting or finishing so the board can be painted around or the wall finish can be applied up to the board edge for a clean look, though this is a soft preference rather than a hard physical requirement.
If the message board requires lighting above it or is placed where electrical boxes need to be routed around, completing electrical rough-in first avoids conflicts, though this is a soft preference.
It is often practical to install the message board before adjacent trim (e.g., baseboards, chair rails) so that the trim can be cut and fitted neatly around the board edges.
Casework requires finished wall surfaces to attach to and for proper fit verification.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins behind walls must be completed before casework installation to avoid rework and permit access.
Flooring should be installed before base cabinets so cabinets sit on finished flooring and to prevent damage to flooring from cabinet installation.
Ceiling work and overhead lighting are typically completed before casework to avoid dust/debris falling on finished cabinets, but this can be swapped if necessary.
Countertops and sinks are installed on top of base cabinets after casework is in place and secured.

successor: Complete Final Plumbing and Appliance Connections
rationale: Plumbing fixtures (sinks, dishwashers) and appliances are connected after casework and countertops are installed.
Touch-up painting is often done after casework installation to cover any damage or gaps, though it is a soft preference as painting can also be completed before.
Electrical and plumbing rough-in work must be completed behind walls and in floors before built-in seating is installed, as the seating would block access to these systems.

Flooring (e.g., tile, hardwood, or finished concrete) should be installed before built-in seating so that the seating sits on top of the finished floor and does not need to be moved or cut around later.

Wall finishing, including drywall, taping, mudding, and painting, must be completed before built-in seating is installed because the seating will be attached to or flush against the walls, making post-installation finishing impossible or very difficult.
While some trim work can be done concurrently, final trim pieces that abut or cap the built-in seating should be installed after the seating is in place for a seamless finish.
If the built-in seating includes integrated electrical outlets or switches, these can only be finished and trimmed out after the seating structure is fully installed.

predecessor: Complete Rough-in Wiring for Breakout Spaces
successor: Install AV Equipment in Breakout Spaces
rationale: Power and low-voltage cabling must be run in walls, ceilings, and floors before any AV equipment can be connected or mounted.

predecessor: Finish Ceiling Installation in Breakout Spaces
successor: Install AV Equipment in Breakout Spaces
rationale: Projectors, ceiling-mounted speakers, and wiring access require the ceiling grid to be complete and stable before mounting AV equipment overhead.

predecessor: Complete Wall Finishes and Painting in Breakout Spaces
successor: Install AV Equipment in Breakout Spaces
rationale: Wall-mounted displays, screens, and speakers must be installed after final painting and finishes to avoid damage from painting and dust during finishing work.

predecessor: Install AV Equipment in Breakout Spaces
successor: Configure and Test AV System in Breakout Spaces
rationale: All AV hardware must be physically installed and connected before system configuration, software setup, signal testing, and calibration can be performed.

predecessor: Install AV Equipment in Breakout Spaces
successor: Complete Room Fit-Out and Furniture Installation
rationale: While furniture can often be placed before AV is installed, it is preferable to install and test AV equipment before final furniture placement to avoid obstructing access to wall ports, cable pathways, and equipment racks.
Acoustic panels are typically mounted onto or within a ceiling grid system; the grid must be in place to provide structural support for the panels.
Electrical wiring, junction boxes, and lighting fixtures must be installed before ceiling panels are placed, as accessing them afterwards would require removing panels.
HVAC ducts and diffusers are installed in the ceiling plenum; these must be in place before acoustic panels cover access to the plenum space.
While not physically required, painting and wall finishing is typically done before acoustic panels are installed to avoid damaging the panels with paint splatter and dust.
Flooring installation generates dust and heavy foot traffic; acoustic panels are usually installed first to protect the finished flooring from debris and damage.
The ventilation system must be fully installed before it can be commissioned and tested for proper operation.
Electrical power supply must be roughed-in and available to operate ventilation equipment during commissioning.
All ductwork must be installed and sealed before the ventilation system can be balanced and commissioned.
While finishes can be done before, it is preferable to complete ventilation commissioning first to avoid rework if adjustments to the system are needed.
Ventilation system commissioning and verification of proper air changes and exhaust must be complete before the space can be certified as safe for occupancy.

Electrical and data cabling must be run to the phone booth location before the enclosure is installed, as the enclosure will cover wall/floor surfaces and make wiring access difficult or impossible after installation.
The physical enclosure must be in place before mounting internal components like the telephone handset, keypad, and any connected devices inside the booth.
Once the enclosure is installed and equipment mounted, final power and data connections can be terminated and the phone system tested for functionality.
Floor and wall finishes (tile, paint, wall covering) should be completed before installing the enclosure to avoid damaging finished surfaces or having to work around the installed booth.

Sealing edges and touching up paint or trim around the installed enclosure is a final cosmetic step, but could technically be done later; however, best practice is to finish immediately after installation to ensure a clean appearance.
Formwork must be in place to support the concrete pour and shaping of the Ribbon Slab.
Steel reinforcement bars must be positioned within the formwork before concrete is poured to achieve structural strength.
After pouring the Ribbon Slab, sufficient curing time is required for the concrete to reach design strength before any loads are applied.
Formwork can only be removed after the Ribbon Slab concrete has cured enough to be self-supporting.

successor: Vertical Structure Construction Above Ribbon Slab
rationale: Upper level walls and columns require the Ribbon Slab as their structural base or floor platform.

The structural steel frame provides the primary load-bearing support and mounting surface for the ribbon glazing system. The glazing cannot be installed until the supporting structure is in place and stable.
Floor slabs must be completed to provide working platform access and to establish the vertical floor-to-floor heights that the ribbon glazing spans between.
Interior wall finishes adjacent to the glazing system must follow after glazing installation to ensure proper sealing, trim work, and to avoid damaging finished surfaces during glazing installation.
Weatherproofing sealants and gaskets are applied to the perimeter of the ribbon glazing system after it is installed to create a watertight and airtight envelope.
Commissioning of the building envelope, including air and water leakage testing, can only proceed once the ribbon glazing system is fully installed and sealed.

The ribbon canopy is a lightweight tensile or fabric structure that attaches to the main structural steel frame. The steel frame must be fully erected and stabilized to provide the support structure for the canopy.
Concrete foundations, ground anchors, or base plates that will secure the canopy's support posts or tensioning cables must be poured and cured before the canopy structure can be installed.
The ribbon canopy provides weather protection overhead; installing glazing or cladding systems beneath it must wait until the canopy is in place to avoid weather damage to the finishes.

successor: Electrical and Lighting Installation on Canopy
rationale: Integrated lighting fixtures, cables, and other electrical components are mounted onto or within the canopy structure; the canopy must be in place before these fit-out details can be installed.

successor: Waterproofing and Sealant Detailing at Canopy Interfaces
rationale: Sealing the connections between the canopy and the main building envelope requires the canopy to be fully installed so that joints can be properly sealed to prevent leaks.

Ribbon soffit is typically a secondary steel or architectural component that attaches to or spans between primary structural steel members. The structural steel frame must be erected to provide the supporting structure and attachment points for the ribbon soffit.

The ribbon soffit is often located at the eave or fascia transition between the roof and wall. The roof deck must be in place to establish the roof plane and provide the reference for the soffit alignment and attachment.

Ribbon soffit forms the underside of the roof overhang/eave. Exterior wall cladding or siding abuts the soffit from below; therefore the soffit must be installed first to provide the finished edge and weather seal at the wall-to-roof transition.

The fascia board or trim is installed along the outer edge of the eave, covering the ends of the rafters/trusses and the edge of the soffit. The ribbon soffit must be in place to receive the fascia, which caps and finishes the eave assembly.

Gutters are typically mounted to the fascia or directly to the soffit edge. While the soffit should ideally be complete before gutter installation to ensure proper alignment and attachment, this is a soft preference as gutters can sometimes be retrofitted or adjusted after soffit completion.
The structural frame provides the primary support and attachment points for the ribbon balustrade. The balustrade cannot be installed until the structural frame is in place to anchor it.
The floor slab provides the walking surface from which the balustrade is installed. It must be poured and sufficiently cured to support loads and provide a stable work platform.

While interior finishes can proceed in parallel, having the balustrade installed first provides edge protection for workers and prevents damage to finished surfaces during balustrade installation. This is a safety-driven soft preference.

Scaffolding used for installation of the balustrade or adjacent work must remain in place until the balustrade is fully installed and providing fall protection. Dismantling scaffolding before guardrails are in place creates a safety hazard.
The balustrade is a critical life-safety component and must be fully installed and inspected before the building can be handed over or occupied.
The surface or deck where the ribbon expansion joint will be placed must be clean, level, and structurally sound before the joint can be installed.

successor: Surrounding Finish Application (e.g., flooring, paving, or topping)
rationale: The expansion joint must be in place before the adjacent finish materials are installed, as the joint accommodates movement between these finished surfaces.
The structural frame or slab must be fully erected and cured to allow proper placement and alignment of the ribbon expansion joint across the intended gap.

While sealants and waterproofing are often applied after joint installation to ensure a watertight seal, this can sometimes be done concurrently; however, best practice is to complete the joint first.
The designated expansion gap must be cut or formed to the correct width and depth before the ribbon expansion joint can be fitted into it.
Formwork must be erected and secured to provide the mould and support structure for the wet concrete before any slab pouring can take place.
Reinforcement bars (rebar) must be tied and positioned within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure the slab achieves its required structural strength.
Any electrical conduits, plumbing pipes, or other embedded services that will run through the slab must be placed and inspected before concrete pouring, as they cannot be installed afterward.
Immediately after pouring, the concrete must be leveled, finished, and then allowed to cure properly to gain strength before any subsequent construction loads are applied.
The poured concrete slab must harden and reach sufficient strength before the supporting formwork and shoring can be safely removed to avoid structural failure or collapse.
The steel frame provides the structural support and attachment points for the ribbon glazing system. Glazing cannot be installed without a completed frame to mount onto.
Blocking, shims, and rough openings must be prepared within the frame to receive and secure the glazing units. Installation requires properly sized and prepared openings.
Air and water barriers around the rough openings need to be installed prior to glazing to ensure a continuous seal behind the ribbon glazing system once it is placed.
Interior perimeter sealants, trim, and finish work around the glazing can only be applied after the glazing units are securely installed in their final position.
Pressure plates and aesthetic caps that secure and finish the exterior of the ribbon glazing system are installed after the glazing units themselves are placed in the frame openings.
The ribbon steel frame requires stable, level foundations and anchor bolts to be set and cured before the steel structure can be erected on top.
Accurate site layout and column centerline marking are necessary before steel columns can be placed to ensure correct positioning and alignment.
The steel frame provides the primary structural support and attachment points for roof decking; the roof cannot be installed until the frame is erected and stable.
Permanent lateral bracing and wind columns stabilize the frame; they must follow erection but should be completed before cladding to ensure structural integrity under load.
Exterior cladding panels attach to or are supported by the steel frame; the frame must be fully erected and braced before cladding can be applied.
Ribbon cladding panels are attached to the structural steel frame; the frame must be erected and stable to provide the supporting structure for cladding.
The roof structure must be in place to provide weather protection and a stable top connection point for ribbon cladding installation from top-down.
Ribbon cladding forms the outer envelope; windows and doors are typically installed after the cladding openings are established to ensure proper fit and waterproofing integration.

Internal finishes should be applied after the external cladding is fixed to prevent weather damage to interior materials and to allow for proper sealing of the building envelope before internal work commences.
Scaffolding used for cladding installation must remain in place until cladding fixing is complete; dismantling can only occur after all cladding panels are securely fixed.
All ribbon lighting fixtures must be physically installed (roughed-in) before commissioning can begin to test their functionality.

predecessor: Ribbon Lighting Power Wiring and Conduit Installation
rationale: Power supply wiring and conduit must be completed to provide electrical power to the ribbon lighting fixtures before they can be tested and commissioned.

predecessor: Ribbon Integrated Lighting Controls and Sensor Installation
rationale: Control systems, dimmers, and occupancy/light sensors must be installed before commissioning can verify integrated lighting control functionality.

successor: Ribbon Lighting Final Adjustment and Occupancy Tuning
rationale: After commissioning verifies all systems are operational, final fine-tuning of light levels, sensor sensitivity, and zone settings can be performed based on commissioning results.

successor: Ribbon Lighting Punch List and Close-Out
rationale: Commissioning must be completed and signed off before final inspection, punch list resolution, and project close-out activities for the ribbon lighting system can occur.
The structural wall framing must be installed before the exhibition display wall can be attached or built onto the framework.
Electrical wiring, outlets, and data/AV cabling for displays must be roughed in within the wall cavity before the display wall surface is closed up.
The display wall must be fully constructed before final surface finishing, painting, or wallcovering can be applied.
Exhibit panels, shelves, brackets, or hanging systems can only be mounted after the display wall structure is complete and stable.

While some accent lighting can be installed before the wall is finished, final display lighting aiming and positioning is optimally done after the wall is built to ensure correct illumination of exhibits.
The kiosk requires a stable, level base. Foundation work must be completed before any superstructure or kiosk installation can begin.
The building's main structural frame must be erected to define the lobby or entrance area where the kiosk will be placed, and to provide overhead protection.
The kiosk requires electrical power for lighting, screens, and devices; rough-in electrical (conduit, wiring) must be completed before kiosk installation.
The kiosk requires network/data connectivity for digital displays and information systems; data cabling must be run before the kiosk is placed and connected.
While painting and finishing can be completed around the kiosk, it is preferable to install the kiosk first to align final finishes and trim work precisely to the kiosk's position.

Flooring around the kiosk should be installed after the kiosk is placed to ensure proper alignment, cutouts, and seamless integration; however the kiosk could be placed on finished flooring as a soft preference.
The kiosk's electronic and interactive systems can only be tested and commissioned after the physical kiosk unit is fully installed and connected to power and data.
The rough framing or substructure for the window seat area (floor, wall backing) must be built before the fixed banquette frame can be installed.
The subfloor must be finished and level to provide a stable base for the fixed banquette.
Any electrical rough-in (outlets, lighting near the window seat) must be completed before the banquette frame encloses the wall area.

Finish flooring should be installed after the banquette is built so that the flooring butts neatly against the fixed base, or the banquette sits on top of finished flooring depending on design; typical sequence has flooring installed first but in many cases the banquette frame is installed over subfloor and flooring is trimmed around it, however if the banquette is site-built, finish flooring often goes after to allow clean transitions.
The fixed banquette frame and structure must be fully built and stable before custom cushions or upholstery can be measured, fabricated, and installed.
The display bracket or mounting frame must be securely attached to the wall or stand before the touchscreen display can be physically installed onto it.

predecessor: Run electrical wiring to display location
rationale: Power cables and any data cables (HDMI, USB, network) must be routed to the mounting location before the display is mounted, as access to the back of the unit will be restricted after installation.

Any wall finishing, painting, or surface treatment near the mounting area should be completed before installing the display to avoid dust, debris, or paint damage to the sensitive touchscreen surface.

Power, video, and network connections to the display and the initial functional testing (touch calibration, screen alignment, software setup) can only occur after the display is physically mounted and secured.

The interactive software, user interface, and content management system must be installed and configured on the connected computer or the display's built-in system after the display hardware is operational and tested.
The meeting pod must be placed on a finished, load-bearing floor slab to provide a stable, level surface.
Structural walls define the room boundaries and support the overhead structure; the pod cannot be positioned until the enclosing walls are framed.
Power, data, and lighting conduit must be run to the pod location before the pod is set in place to avoid costly rework.
While finishing can be done around the pod, it is more efficient to complete painting and trim before installing the pod to avoid damage and touch-ups.
The pod must be physically installed before audio-visual and IT equipment inside the pod can be connected and tested.
Display rails require a finished wall surface for proper mounting and alignment; installing rails on unfinished walls would result in misalignment and structural issues.
Structural framing provides the load-bearing support needed to anchor display rails securely; without framing, the rails cannot be safely attached.
Electrical wiring for integrated displays must be run within walls before rails are installed to avoid rework and ensure power/data connectivity is accessible behind the rails.
Display screens and equipment are mounted onto the installed rails; the rails must be in place first as they serve as the anchoring system.
Cables from displays are routed through or along the rails after installation; the rail system must be in place to guide and conceal cabling properly.

predecessor: Completion of Concrete Slab / Floor Base
rationale: Fixed seating rows require a stable, cured concrete slab or finished floor base to be installed upon. The floor must be fully set and leveled before seating can be anchored.

predecessor: Rough-In of Electrical and Data Conduit (under floor)
rationale: Any underfloor electrical, data, or grounding conduits that feed seating areas must be roughed in before the seating is installed, as the seating structure will cover and block access to the floor.

successor: Final Floor Finishing (e.g., Epoxy, Polishing, or Sealing)
rationale: While some floor finishing can be done before seating, final touch-ups or sealing around seat pedestals is often performed after seating installation to ensure a seamless finish. This is a soft preference for aesthetic quality.
Seat numbering or labeling plates must be installed after the fixed seating rows are fully in place to ensure correct alignment and spacing of numbers.
Once fixed seating rows are installed, a final safety inspection and load testing must be performed to verify structural stability and compliance with building codes before the venue can be occupied.
Public gallery seating must be installed on a finished structural floor slab that can bear the load and provide a stable base.
Guardrails and handrails are installed after seating to ensure proper alignment and safe clearance for the seated public areas.

successor: Final Finishing & Painting of Gallery Area
rationale: It is preferable to complete painting and finishing after seating installation to avoid damage to installed seats and to achieve a uniform finish around fixed seating.

predecessor: Rough-in Electrical & Data Cabling for Gallery
rationale: Underfloor electrical and data cabling must be installed before fixed seating is placed, as seats may cover floor access points and block subsequent cabling work.
The physical anchoring and bolting of seating units to the floor is the final step of the seating installation itself, completing attachment after positioning.

predecessor: Installation of AV Distribution System Components
rationale: All AV distribution components like amplifiers, switchers, splitters, and cabling must be physically installed before they can be powered on and tested during commissioning.

predecessor: Cable Pulling and Termination for AV System
rationale: Cables must be run, terminated, and continuity-tested before commissioning can verify signal routing and performance.

predecessor: Electrical Power Connection to AV Equipment
rationale: AV equipment requires permanent electrical power supply to be connected and energized before commissioning can test functionality.

predecessor: AV Rack Assembly and Equipment Mounting
rationale: Racks must be assembled and equipment securely mounted before commissioning can begin.
Basic control system programming must be loaded onto controllers to enable testing of AV distribution functions during commissioning.
After commissioning confirms basic functionality, fine-tuning of audio levels, video settings, and equalization can be performed.

successor: User Training for AV System Operation
rationale: Training users on the AV distribution system is logically done after the system has been verified to work correctly during commissioning.
The project cannot be handed over to the client until the AV distribution system has been commissioned and verified operational.
The bench and witness stand require a level, stable floor surface. Foundation and slab work must be completed first to provide the structural base.
Rough-in work for electrical outlets, data ports, and HVAC must be completed in the vicinity before installing the fixed bench and witness stand to avoid rework or damage.

successor: Installation of Judge's Bench Power/Data Cabling and Microphone Systems
rationale: Integrated power, data, and audio systems are installed into or onto the bench and stand after they are in place.

While some finishing can be done concurrently, it is generally preferable to complete paint and wall finishes before installing the bench to avoid damage; however, the bench installation often happens after rough finishes but before final touch-ups.

successor: Final Inspection and Commissioning of Courtroom
rationale: The bench and witness stand must be fully installed and secured before the final inspection and commissioning of the courtroom can be completed.
A stable foundation and prepared site must exist before constructing the counter area to ensure structural integrity and proper anchoring of the counter fixtures.
Electrical outlets, data ports, and utility connections must be roughed in behind the walls before the counter and service area can be enclosed and finished.
If the counter includes a sink or water fixture, rough-in plumbing must be completed before the counter cabinetry and tops are installed.
The counter installation must be completed before final wall finishing, painting, and trim work can be applied around it to achieve a clean, professional appearance.

successor: Installation of Service Windows and Security Glass
rationale: The counter structure must be in place before service windows, transaction drawers, and security glazing can be mounted and sealed to the counter surface.
Structural framing provides the physical support surfaces (walls, columns) where signage and directories are mounted; they cannot be installed before there is a structure to attach them to.
Exterior signage and directory boards are mounted on finished exterior walls; wall finishes must be complete to provide a proper mounting surface and to ensure accurate placement.

predecessor: Town Hall Interior Wall Finishes (including drywall, painting)
rationale: Interior directory signs are mounted on finished interior walls; painting and surface preparation must be done before installing signage to avoid damage and ensure proper adhesion.

successor: Town Hall Final Inspection and Commissioning
rationale: Signage and directories must be fully installed before final inspections can verify wayfinding compliance, building identification, and accessibility requirements.
Building occupants and visitors rely on signage and directories for navigation; the building cannot be handed over for occupancy until wayfinding elements are in place.
The floor slab must be fully cured and finished to provide a stable, level surface for seating installation.
Wall finishes (plastering, painting, wall coverings) should be completed before seating is installed to avoid damage to finished walls and to allow unrestricted access.

predecessor: Complete Ceiling Installation in Council Chamber
rationale: The ceiling and any overhead services (lighting, speakers, HVAC diffusers) must be installed before seating to prevent debris falling onto or damaging the seats.

successor: Final Inspection and Commissioning of Council Chamber
rationale: Seating must be fully installed and secured before the chamber can be inspected and commissioned for occupancy.

successor: Install Audio-Visual Equipment in Council Chamber
rationale: While AV equipment can technically be installed before seating, it is preferable to install seating first to establish sightlines and seating layout, then position AV equipment accordingly.
The reception and service counters need to be placed on a finished, level floor surface to ensure stability and proper alignment.

Electrical and data cabling for service counter equipment (computers, phones, POS systems) must be roughed-in within walls and floors before counters are installed, as access behind/under counters is highly restricted afterward.
If the reception counter includes a sink or water supply, plumbing rough-in must be completed before counter installation to allow proper connection.
The countertop and surface finishes (e.g., laminate, stone, or solid surface) are installed directly on top of the base cabinetry or counter structure, so the base counters must be in place first.

successor: Connect Electrical and Data Devices at Counter
rationale: Power outlets, data ports, and service equipment (e.g., monitors, card readers) are mounted into or onto the counter structure, requiring the counters to be installed first.
Electrical outlets, conduit, and junction boxes must be roughed-in before furnishings are installed, as walls and floors will be covered or obstructed by fixed cabinetry, benches, and millwork.
Ductwork, vents, and HVAC registers need to be installed before furnishings to ensure proper airflow and that furniture placement does not obstruct mechanical components.
Any plumbing rough-ins (e.g., for sinks in the bench area or jury room connections) must be completed before built-in furnishings are placed to avoid rework.
Data, audio-visual, and low-voltage cabling for the judge's bench, clerk station, witness stand, and jury box must be run before installing those fixed furnishings.
Flooring and wall finishes should be installed first to avoid damage to furnishings and to allow proper fit and alignment of fixed furniture against finished surfaces.

successor: Install Courtroom Audio-Visual and Sound System Equipment
rationale: Fixed furnishings like the bench, jury box, and witness stand must be in place before AV equipment, microphones, speakers, and monitors can be mounted on or integrated with them.

Final touch-up painting and caulking around built-in furnishings is typically done after installation to cover any gaps or scuffs, though this is more of a sequencing preference than a physical necessity.

If indirect or cove lighting is integrated into the bench or cabinetry, lighting installation may follow furnishings; however, in many cases overhead lighting is done first, so this is a soft sequencing preference.
Audio-visual equipment must be physically installed before it can be commissioned, tested, and verified for proper operation.
IT network infrastructure (cabling, switches, routers) must be in place to provide connectivity for AV and IT systems before commissioning can begin.
Power supply and electrical connections must be completed to provide necessary electricity for AV and IT equipment to be tested and commissioned.

successor: User Training for AV System Operation
rationale: Systems must be commissioned and verified as functional before end-user training can commence, though training could theoretically begin with partial commissioning.
All AV and IT systems must be fully commissioned and accepted before the building can be formally handed over to the client for occupancy.
Security and access control systems require power and low-voltage wiring connections, which must be roughed in before the security devices can be installed and connected.
Security systems (cameras, card readers, door controllers) need network/data cabling infrastructure in place before the security components can be physically mounted and terminated.
Walls must be finished, painted, and trim installed before mounting security devices like card readers, keypads, and sensors to ensure a clean installation and avoid damage to finishes.
The security and access control hardware must be physically installed before the system can be powered up, configured, programmed, and tested for proper operation.
Security system installation must be complete before the final project inspection and building handover, as operational security is typically a requirement for occupancy and closeout.
The porch entry requires a stable foundation to support its structural load, so foundation work must be completed first.
The porch entry often attaches to the main building's structural frame, which must be in place to provide support and proper alignment.
The porch entry structure must be in place before roofing can be installed over it, as the roof depends on the porch framing for support.

While finishing work typically follows structural installation, some finishing can proceed concurrently; however, it is preferable to complete the porch entry structure before adding trim and aesthetic finishes to ensure proper fit and weatherproofing.

Proper grading and drainage around the porch area is preferable before construction to prevent water issues, but some grading work can be completed after the porch is installed; this is a soft preference for optimal water management.
Modular partitions require a level, cured floor slab for proper anchoring, alignment, and load distribution.
Floor outlets, data ports, and underfloor conduit must be installed before partition placement to avoid cutting into or relocating finished partitions.
Ductwork, sprinkler lines, and overhead conduits that run above the partition must be in place to coordinate partition height and top track attachment without interference.
Paint and wall finishes cannot be applied until partition surfaces are fully installed, aligned, and ready for treatment.
Wall-mounted outlets, switches, and data jacks are installed into the finished partition panels after they are in place.
Display casework requires stable structural walls and framing to be in place for proper attachment and support.
Electrical and data cabling for lighting, displays, and interactive elements must be roughed in behind walls before casework is installed to avoid rework and accessibility issues.
Flooring or finished subfloor must be complete under the casework footprint, as casework is typically installed on top of finished flooring to avoid cutting or fitting around it later.
Casework installation can damage surrounding wall finishes; final painting and touch-ups should be performed after casework is set in place.

successor: Installation of Display Items and Artifacts
rationale: While display items can theoretically be placed at any time, it is standard practice to install the empty casework first to protect valuable contents and ensure proper fit.
The seating structure requires a stable, level floor base to ensure proper load distribution and alignment

predecessor: Rough electrical rough-in for alcove lighting and outlets
rationale: Electrical wiring and boxes must be installed behind or beneath the built-in seating before the seating structure is built over them
The seating structure defines the edge condition for flooring; flooring should be installed up to or under the seating base after the seating frame is in place

successor: Finish painting and wallcovering in alcove
rationale: While painting can be done before seating installation, it is easier to touch up walls after seating is installed to avoid damage to finished surfaces
The structural seating frame and any substrate must be fully constructed before upholstery and cushions can be applied or placed
The kiosk requires a stable, level base; site preparation and foundation work must be completed first to provide a proper mounting surface and structural support.
The kiosk requires electrical power and data connectivity; underground conduit and wiring must be installed before the kiosk can be placed and connected.
The kiosk must be physically installed and anchored before final electrical connections can be made to power it up.
Data cables to the kiosk can only be terminated and tested after the kiosk is in its final position.
The hardware must be installed and powered before the kiosk's software interface and resource management system can be commissioned and configured.
The shop stall/kiosk requires a stable load-bearing floor slab or foundation base to be constructed first, as it will sit directly on the slab.
The primary structural frame must be erected before the kiosk walls and roof can be formed, as the kiosk is typically enclosed within or supported by the main structure.
Concealed electrical conduits, data cables, and water supply/drainage pipes must be roughed in before internal walls and finishes of the kiosk are installed, to avoid rework.
The kiosk's internal partition walls and surfaces need to be fully erected before plastering, tiling, or painting can commence.
The structural opening and framing of the kiosk must be complete to allow precise fitting of glass panels, display windows, and doors.
While it is strongly preferred to fit out the interior after the kiosk shell is complete, some loose furnishings could technically be brought in earlier, making this a soft constraint.
The floor slab or base must be prepared and leveled before installing market counters and display shelving to ensure a stable, level foundation and proper alignment.

Rough electrical wiring and conduit installation must be completed before installing counters and shelving so that electrical outlets and lighting can be integrated into the fixtures without later rework.
Any plumbing rough-in for sinks or water lines in market areas must be completed before counter installation to avoid needing to cut through or move finished fixtures.
Once counters and shelving are installed, finishing touches such as trim, edge detailing, and decorative elements can be applied to integrate the fixtures seamlessly with the surrounding space.
The counters and shelves must be fully installed and stable before products can be placed on them for display and retail use.
Rough-in wiring (conduit, boxes, and cabling) must be installed before sub-metering equipment can be mounted and connected to the electrical supply.
The main electrical distribution panel must be in place to provide the upstream power feed that the sub-meter will measure from.
Sub-metering equipment must be installed and wired before final trim-out, device installation, and testing of the stall's electrical circuits can proceed.
Commissioning and verification of meter readings can only begin once the sub-metering hardware is fully installed and connected.
The sub-meter must be installed and operational before the stall's electrical system can receive final inspection approval and be energized.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared before any seating or rest area structures can be installed to ensure a stable, level foundation.
A concrete base or foundation pad must be poured and cured before installing seating fixtures, benches, tables, or rest area shelters to provide structural support.
Underground electrical conduits for lighting and/or plumbing pipes for drinking fountains must be laid before the rest area surface is finished to avoid later excavation.
Seating and rest area structures must be in place before final landscaping, sod, shrubs, and trees are planted around them to avoid damaging new plants during installation.
Adjacent walkways and paved paths should be completed after the seating/rest area is installed to ensure proper alignment, transitions, and seamless integration with the rest area.
The structural frame must be in place to provide mounting points and support for the security shutter system.
Electrical wiring and conduit for shutter motor controls and power supply must be installed before the shutter assembly can be connected and tested.
Security shutters must be installed before final interior finishes to avoid damaging finished surfaces during shutter installation and to allow proper sealing around shutter tracks.
Shutters must be in place and operational before signage is installed to coordinate mounting locations and ensure clearances for shutter operation.
Shutters must be fully installed to undergo operational testing, safety checks, and integration with security and access control systems.
A stable foundation or base floor must be completed before partitions can be installed to ensure proper alignment, anchoring, and structural stability.
Electrical and data cabling within walls or partitions must be run before the partitions are closed up or installed to avoid costly rework and accessibility issues.
Final electrical outlets, switches, and data ports on the partitions can only be installed after the partitions are in place to ensure correct positioning and wiring connections.
Final painting, sealing, or surface finishing of partitions must be done after installation to achieve a uniform, clean appearance without damaging surrounding work.
Assigning stall numbers and directional signage is easier once the partitions define the individual spaces, though it could theoretically be done simultaneously if needed.
Market counters and shelving require a finished, level floor slab as a stable base for installation and anchoring.
Electrical outlets and wiring for market counters (e.g., for refrigerated cases or registers) must be roughed-in behind walls and floors before counters and shelving are placed.
Plumbing lines for sinks or drainage in market counters must be roughed-in before the counters are installed to allow proper connections.
Walls need to be framed and finished so that shelving units can be securely mounted to the wall structure.
Counter and shelving installation should occur before final flooring is laid to avoid damaging finished flooring during heavy installation work and to allow adjustments.
Market signage requires a completed structural frame to attach to, ensuring stability and proper mounting.
Electrical rough-in must be completed to provide power connections for illuminated signage before installation.
Exterior wall cladding provides the finished surface onto which market signage is mounted.
Signage installation could interfere with interior finishing work if done simultaneously, but is not a strict physical dependency; sequencing is preferred for workflow efficiency.
Market signage must be fully installed and operational before the final project inspection can verify all scope items are complete.
Trenches must be excavated and prepared before any plumbing pipes can be laid in them.
Plumbing and drainage pipes must be installed and inspected before trenches can be backfilled.
Underslab plumbing and drainage must be in place before the concrete floor slab is poured.
Market-area underground plumbing must be installed before connecting to above-grade rough-in plumbing within the building.
Where trench space is shared, coordinating conduits and plumbing is preferred; however, sequencing can be adjusted so this is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
The ventilation hoods must be physically installed before they can be commissioned (tested, balanced, and verified for proper operation).
Commissioning ensures the ventilation hoods meet safety and performance standards before the market space becomes operational and occupied.
The ductwork and exhaust system must be fully installed and connected to the hoods so that airflow testing and balancing can be performed during commissioning.
Commissioning is a prerequisite step that must be completed before the overall system can pass final inspection and receive sign-off.
Electrical power must be supplied to the ventilation hoods so that fans, controls, and lights can be tested during the commissioning process.
The exam table must be placed on a stable, level floor. Foundation and flooring must be completed first to provide a load-bearing surface.
If the exam table has electrical components (lights, outlets, power adjustment), rough-in electrical work must be completed before the table is positioned to avoid rework.
Once the exam table is in place, final connections to power outlets, lighting, or adjustable mechanisms can be completed and tested.
The exam table serves as a foundational piece; other medical equipment (e.g., examination lights, procedural carts) is positioned and calibrated after the table is installed.
While not physically required, installing the exam table after wall and ceiling finishing prevents dust, debris, and paint from contaminating or damaging the table surface.
The reception desk/counter must be built on a finished, stable floor surface. The slab-on-grade provides the structural base and finished flooring substrate required before the desk can be installed.

Power outlets, data/network cabling, and any plumbing connections that serve the reception desk must be roughed-in beneath the floor before the desk is placed, as access below becomes impossible once the counter is installed.
Any walls behind or adjacent to the reception desk must be framed, insulated, and closed with drywall before the desk is installed to avoid rework or damage to the finished counter.
The main desk body and base must be in place before the final countertop surface, laminate, stone, or solid-surface finish can be installed on top.

While overhead lighting can be installed before the desk, final positioning and aiming of pendant or task lights above the counter is best done after the desk is in place to ensure proper alignment with the work surface. This is a preference for quality rather than a physical constraint.
The structural wall framing must be in place to provide a substrate and support for the lead-lined panels or sheets to be attached.

Electrical wiring, conduit, outlet boxes, and plumbing lines that will run within the wall cavity must be installed before the lead lining is placed, as accessing them afterward would require damaging or removing the lead shielding.

The lead-lined assembly must be fully installed before the final wall finish (e.g., drywall, paneling) can be applied over or adjacent to it, as the lead layer serves as the radiation shielding substrate.
The lead lining must be completely installed so that continuity testing and radiation shielding verification can be performed to ensure no gaps or breaches exist.
Completion of the lead-lined wall assembly is a prerequisite for the final inspection and commissioning of radiation-controlled areas.
