The handwashing station must be placed on a level, stable, and cured floor slab or foundation to ensure proper drainage and structural support. Installing it before the floor is prepared would result in instability and drainage issues.

Water supply lines and waste drain connections must be roughed in and stubbed up before the handwashing station can be connected. The station cannot be installed without existing supply and drain piping in place.
If the handwashing station is wall-mounted, the wall framing must be completed and the backing supports installed to securely anchor the station. Installation on unfinished framing is not possible.

It is preferred (but not physically required) to install finishing materials like tile or backsplash around the station after it is mounted, so that finishes can be cut precisely around the fixture. However, finishing can also be done first and the station installed over it.

After the handwashing station is physically mounted and positioned, the final connections to water supply lines and drain pipes must be made, and the unit must be tested for leaks and proper operation before it can be used.
Electrical wiring and outlets must be roughed in behind the walls before cabinetry is installed, as cabinets would block access to walls.
Plumbing supply and drain lines for sinks in exam rooms must be roughed in before cabinets are placed, as cabinetry would obstruct wall and floor access for plumbing.

predecessor: Wall Framing and Drywall for Exam Rooms
rationale: Walls must be framed, insulated, and drywalled before cabinets can be securely mounted and properly aligned against finished wall surfaces.
Cabinets must be installed and leveled first to provide the base and support structure for countertops to be placed on top.
Sinks are typically drop-in or under-mount fixtures that require the cabinet and countertop to be in place before the sink can be set and connected.
A stable, level foundation and prepared site are required to support the weight and ensure proper operation of the vaccine refrigerator.
Dedicated electrical supply lines, outlets, and grounding must be in place before the refrigerator can be connected and powered up.
If the refrigerator uses a remote condensing unit, refrigerant lines must be run and pressure-tested before the unit can be placed and connected.
The refrigerator must be installed and operational before temperature sensors and monitoring probes can be placed inside to verify proper temperature performance.
Vaccines can only be placed into the refrigerator after it has been installed, stabilized, and verified to maintain the required temperature range (2–8°C).
The ceiling pendant/boom must be physically attached to the structural ceiling; thus the ceiling structure must be complete to provide the mounting surface and support.

predecessor: Overhead MEP Rough-In (Electrical, Medical Gas, Data Cabling)
rationale: The pendant/boom requires overhead utility connections (power, medical gases, data) to be roughed-in before the unit is hung and connected.

successor: Final Connection and Testing of Medical Equipment on Pendant
rationale: Medical devices (monitors, ventilators, infusion pumps) can only be mounted and connected after the pendant/boom itself is securely installed and stable.

Although the pendant protrudes through the ceiling, finishing the ceiling around the penetration is typically done after the pendant is hung to ensure a clean fit and seal; this is a logical sequence preference but the ceiling can be partially finished beforehand.

All pendant-mounted equipment must be in place and connected before the room can be commissioned (functional testing) and final clean-up performed, as the pendant is a key functional element of the patient care space.
The seating benches require a stable, level surface for installation. The concrete slab or foundation must be poured and cured before bench footings or anchors can be set.
If the benches are attached to a wall or structural framing, that framing must be in place to provide the attachment surface and alignment references.
Benches define the final finished floor boundary; finishing materials such as tile or polished concrete should be installed up to the bench base for a clean seam and to avoid damaging the bench.
It is more efficient to paint or finish the wall behind the bench before the bench is installed, but if necessary touch-ups can be done afterward; this is a soft preference to avoid difficult access.
Any electrical outlets or data ports planned adjacent to or within the bench structure must have rough-in wiring completed before bench installation to avoid rework.
The curtain track is typically mounted to or suspended from the ceiling grid structure, so the ceiling grid must be in place to provide the structural support for the track.
Mechanical ducts, electrical conduit, and other overhead utilities must be installed before curtain tracks to avoid conflicts and ensure the track has a clear path for installation.
The curtain track must be fully installed and secured before curtains can be hung from it.
It is preferable to complete painting and finishing before installing curtain tracks to achieve a clean finish, but touch-ups can be done after installation if needed.

Load-bearing party walls require a stable foundation to transfer their vertical loads to the ground. Without completed foundations, the walls would have no structural support and would settle or collapse.
The ground floor slab or substructure provides the base surface upon which the load-bearing party walls are erected and helps distribute the wall loads.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the required depth before any structural wall construction can commence.
Floor joists and upper floor structures typically bear onto or are supported by the load-bearing party walls. The walls must be in place and cured to carry the floor loads.
The roof structure, including trusses or rafters, often bears directly onto load-bearing party walls. The walls must be complete to provide vertical support for the roof.

The lattice screen facade is a non-structural cladding element that must be attached to the completed structural frame. The building structure must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the facade system.
The lattice screen facade elements must be fully installed before weatherproofing sealants and joint treatments can be applied to ensure a continuous building envelope and prevent water infiltration.
The facade must be enclosed before interior finishes (drywall, painting, flooring) are completed to protect interior materials from weather exposure and to establish a conditioned environment.

Access scaffolding used for facade installation must remain in place until the lattice screen panels are fully installed and secured. Scaffolding can only be removed after facade completion for safety and access reasons.
The lattice screen panels and components must be fabricated, delivered, and staged on site before installation can commence.

The ground must be excavated and foundation footings prepared before any concrete frame can be erected, as the frame requires a stable, load-bearing base to transfer its weight and loads into the ground.

Steel reinforcement bars must be placed and tied within the formwork prior to concrete pouring, as the rebar provides the tensile strength necessary for the reinforced concrete frame to carry structural loads.
Formwork (molds) for columns, beams, and slabs must be erected and secured before concrete can be poured, as the forms define the shape and dimensions of the concrete frame elements.
The roof structure (whether concrete roof slab or steel roof trusses) depends on the completed vertical columns and horizontal beams of the concrete frame to provide support and bearing points.
Exterior walls and cladding systems are attached to or supported by the concrete frame; the structural frame must be complete to provide the supporting framework for the building envelope.

While some MEP rough-in can begin after the frame is erected, it is possible to start limited MEP work earlier. However, full MEP distribution through walls and ceilings depends on the completed frame for routing and support.
The planter bench needs a stable, level foundation to sit on, so site preparation (clearing, grading, and concrete footings) must be completed first.
If the planter bench includes integrated irrigation, supply and drain lines must be roughed in before the bench is placed to avoid later excavation or demolition.
The planter bench must be fully constructed and in its final position before soil and plants are added to avoid damage to the structure and to ensure proper containment.

successor: Final Landscape Finishing and Hardscape Adjacent Work
rationale: It is preferred but not strictly required to complete the bench before finishing surrounding hardscapes (e.g., paving stones, edging) to allow precise alignment and clean transitions.
Any protective sealants, waterproofing, or decorative coatings must be applied after the bench is fully assembled and installed to ensure even coverage and adherence.

The rammed earth infill panels require the structural frame (e.g., steel or timber) to be in place first, as they are placed between the frame members and rely on the frame for support and containment.
A raised plinth or foundation is needed to protect the rammed earth from moisture wicking and to provide a level base for the infill panels to rest upon.
After compaction, rammed earth panels must be left to cure and dry to achieve their full strength and durability before any further loads or finishes are applied.

Surface protection such as sealant, lime plaster, or render must be applied only after the rammed earth panel is fully compacted and sufficiently cured to avoid trapping moisture or damaging the surface.

While it is possible to chase conduits into rammed earth after completion, embedding services before compaction is challenging; typically rough-in work occurs after panel completion but is a soft preference as it depends on design integration and can be done differently.
The foundation must be completed to provide a stable load-bearing base for the frame and slabs.

predecessor: Placement of Reinforcement Steel for Foundations
rationale: Reinforcement steel in foundations must be placed and set before the superstructure frame can be erected.
The structural frame and slabs must be in place to support the walls and provide the structural skeleton before infill walls can be built.
The roof structure (trusses, decking) typically rests on the top slab or frame, requiring the frame and slabs to be completed first.
While plumbing can be started before slabs are poured (embedding pipes), generally the slab must be cast to allow vertical pipe risers and drainage to be installed through the floors.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and compacted before lattice screens can be installed to ensure a stable foundation and proper alignment.
Lattice screens are typically anchored to a concrete footing or foundation structure, which must be poured and cured before screen installation can begin.
If the lattice screens require a supporting metal or timber frame, that frame must be erected first to provide the attachment points for the screens.
Any final trim, molding, or capping pieces around the edges of the lattice screens must be installed after the screens themselves are in place to cover gaps and ensure a finished appearance.

Landscaping, planting vines, or placing decorative elements around the lattice screens is typically done after installation to avoid damage to the screens during landscaping work, though it is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
Trenches and excavations must be dug before rainwater pipes and tanks can be placed underground.
A stable concrete base or foundation is required to support the weight of a rainwater storage tank before it can be installed.
Rainwater downpipes and gutter connections must be tied into the system after the tank and primary pipework are in place.
Trenches around pipes and tanks should be backfilled only after the rainwater system installation is complete and tested.
Final connections from the rainwater system to the building's internal plumbing or irrigation network must happen after the system is installed.
The ventilation shafts must be fully constructed before they can be commissioned, as commissioning requires the physical structure to be complete and ready for testing.
Electrical systems (fans, motors, controls, lighting) must be installed and terminated before commissioning can test the shaft's ventilation functionality.
Mechanical equipment such as fans, dampers, and louvers must be installed before the system can be commissioned and tested for airflow performance.
Commissioning of individual ventilation shafts must be completed before the entire tunnel ventilation system can be integrated and tested as a whole.
Ventilation shafts must be commissioned and proven operational before the tunnel can be handed over for operational use or occupied for normal service.
The subgrade must be excavated, graded, and compacted to the required lines and levels before concrete curb can be placed, as the curb relies on a stable, prepared base for support and alignment.
Forms or slipform molds must be set to the correct alignment, grade, and cross-section before concrete can be poured; without forms the curb shape cannot be maintained.
Backfill against the curb sides can only be placed and compacted after the concrete has achieved sufficient initial set and strength to resist displacement from compaction forces.

Curing processes (e.g., wet curing, application of curing compound) and cutting of contraction/expansion joints must occur after the concrete has been placed and finished, as these steps preserve moisture and control cracking in the hardened curb.
Asphalt or adjacent paving can only be placed up to the curb after the curb concrete has cured sufficiently, ensuring the curb serves as a permanent, rigid edge guide for the paving operation.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable foundation for the gutter to be placed on.
The road base layers must be compacted to final level so the gutter can be cast against them at the correct road edge elevation.
The gutter defines the edge alignment and level for the road pavement, so paving follows gutter construction to abut neatly against it.
The asphalt layer is placed after the gutter is formed to ensure a clean joint and proper drainage flow into the gutter.
Gutter outlets must be cast in place and fully cured before connecting drainage pipes to ensure water-tight joints.
Traffic signage must be installed on completed road surfaces; paving must be finished to provide stable foundation and proper placement locations for signs.
Road base must be prepared before final surfacing, which itself must precede signage installation.
Underground electrical conduits for illuminated signs must be installed before sign posts are erected.
It is preferable but not strictly required to install signs before painting road markings so that signage placement can inform marking layout for consistency.
All traffic signs must be in place before a road is opened to public traffic to ensure driver guidance, warning, and regulation compliance.
Road pavement marking requires a stable, clean, and prepared road surface. The road base must be compacted and properly graded before any markings can be applied.
The final asphalt or concrete surface layer must be laid and cured before markings are applied, as markings adhere directly to the finished pavement surface.
Freshly laid asphalt or concrete must be fully cured and completely dry to ensure proper adhesion and durability of pavement markings.
Road markings must be fully applied and dried before the road is opened to traffic to ensure driver guidance, lane delineation, and safety.
After markings are applied, inspection and quality checks for proper alignment, thickness, reflectivity, and compliance with standards must be completed before final acceptance.

The drainage inlet must be installed on a compacted and graded road base or subgrade to ensure proper elevation, slope, and structural support. The base must be prepared first to achieve the required drainage flow path.
A pit or trench must be excavated to the correct depth and dimensions at the planned inlet location before the inlet unit (e.g., precast concrete box or catch basin) can be placed.

successor: Connection to Drainage Pipe / Outlet Main
rationale: The inlet structure must be set in place first so that the connecting drainage pipes can be aligned and joined to the inlet's outlet opening.
The inlet must be installed and secured before backfill material can be placed and compacted around its sides to provide lateral support and prevent shifting.
The inlet frame and grate must be set to the final pavement grade before the surrounding asphalt or concrete pavement is placed, so that the top of the inlet is flush with the finished road surface.
The concrete foundation must be excavated, formed, and cured to provide a stable base for the lighting pole before the pole can be erected and anchored.
Electrical conduits and cables must be laid in the ground before the pole is placed, so that cables can be fed up through the pole base and connected to the luminaire.
The lighting pole must be securely installed and upright before electrical wiring can be connected and the lighting system tested for functionality.
The pole shaft must be erected first so that the luminaire head, arm, or bracket can be attached at the correct height and orientation.
While not physically required, it is preferable to complete pole installation before final paving and landscaping around the base to avoid rework or damage to finished surfaces.
All vegetation, debris, and existing structures must be removed from the road alignment before subgrade preparation can begin to provide a clean working surface.
The road centerline, levels, and boundaries must be accurately surveyed and pegged out to guide the excavation and fill operations during subgrade preparation.
After preparing and shaping the subgrade, compaction and bearing capacity tests must be performed to verify that the subgrade meets specification before placing the pavement layers.
The prepared subgrade forms the foundation for the road pavement; the sub-base cannot be placed until the subgrade has been shaped, compacted, and approved.
Subgrade drains, edge drains, and cross-drains at subgrade level must be installed after subgrade preparation to ensure proper drainage of the pavement structure.
The subgrade must be properly graded, compacted, and approved before road base can be placed; otherwise the base will lack structural support and settle unevenly.
Vegetation, topsoil, and debris must be removed from the road footprint before any base material can be installed.
Subsurface drainage and cross-drainage structures must be in place before the base is laid to prevent water from undermining the base layer.

Any underground utilities (water, sewer, gas, electrical conduits) that cross the roadway must be relocated or buried before the road base is placed to avoid future excavation through the finished base.
A prime coat is applied directly onto the compacted road base to seal and bind the surface before the asphalt or pavement layers are placed.
The road base provides the load-bearing foundation; the asphalt or concrete surface course can only be placed after the base is compacted and cured to the required density.
Curbs and gutters are typically formed against or on top of the finished road base to define the roadway edges and manage stormwater runoff.
Shoulders are built adjacent to the roadway and depend on the base course being in place to match the cross-section and drainage profile.
The base or subgrade must be properly graded, compacted, and prepared to provide a stable foundation before asphalt can be applied.
A granular base course (e.g., aggregate base) must be placed and compacted to support the asphalt layer and distribute loads.
Underground utilities and drainage systems must be installed and covered before paving to avoid cutting or disturbing the finished asphalt surface.
Curbs and gutters define the pavement edges and grade, and must be in place so that asphalt can be laid flush against them for a smooth transition.
Traffic markings, lane lines, and symbols must be applied after the asphalt is laid and fully compacted to ensure visibility and durability.
Freshly laid asphalt must cool and cure to reach its final strength and stability before allowing traffic or subsequent surface treatments.

While not a strict physical necessity for the next construction step, inspection and testing (e.g., density, smoothness) logically occur after paving is complete to verify compliance with specifications before project closeout.
The area must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before any curb and gutter forms can be laid out and installed.
The site must be rough-graded to approximate final elevations to provide a stable, properly sloped subgrade for the curb and gutter alignment.
The subgrade beneath the curb and gutter must be compacted to the required density to prevent settlement and ensure long-term stability of the concrete.
Freshly placed concrete must be allowed to cure and gain sufficient strength before any loads are applied or subsequent work proceeds.
The road surface must be prepared and compacted before signage posts can be securely anchored or footings excavated.
Signs are installed on or adjacent to the finished road surface; pavement markings and sign placement reference the final surface elevation and alignment.
Pavement markings (lane lines, arrows, stop bars) must align with installed signs; signs define the regulatory and warning context for markings.

successor: Final Road Opening / Traffic Flow Activation
rationale: Signage providing regulatory, warning, and guidance information must be in place before the road is opened to public traffic to ensure safety and legal compliance.
While inspection can partially occur before signs are installed, a final check of signage placement, visibility, and compliance is typically done after installation and before road opening.
Road markings must be applied onto a finished, stable, and properly leveled asphalt or concrete surface. Applying markings before paving would result in the markings being buried or destroyed.
The surface must be free of dust, dirt, debris, and moisture to ensure proper adhesion and durability of road marking paint or thermoplastic material.

Road markings define lane usage and traffic rules; installing signs referring to lane-specific rules (e.g., turn-only lanes, pedestrian crossings) must occur after markings are in place to ensure proper alignment and consistency.
While lighting can be installed concurrently or before, final adjustments to lighting aiming and testing for nighttime visibility of markings is optimally done after markings are applied.

Road markings are essential safety elements that guide drivers and pedestrians; the road cannot be opened to public traffic until all permanent lane markings, edge lines, and crosswalks are clearly applied.
The road surface must be properly graded, leveled, and compacted before a speed bump can be installed to ensure proper adhesion, alignment, and structural integrity.
The final road surface (asphalt or concrete) must be laid and cured before a speed bump is constructed on top of it, as the speed bump is built upon the finished pavement.
Temporary traffic control measures (signs, cones, barricades) must be in place before construction begins to ensure worker safety and proper traffic management.
Underground utilities must be located and marked before any excavation or construction to avoid damaging gas, water, electrical, or communication lines.

Warning signs (e.g., 'Speed Hump Ahead') and pavement markings (e.g., chevrons, crosswalk lines) must be applied after the speed bump is constructed, as their placement depends on the exact location and dimensions of the finished bump.

After installation, the speed bump material (asphalt or concrete) must cure and a final inspection must be conducted to verify compliance with specifications and safety standards before the road is reopened to traffic.
Temporary traffic control devices can only be removed after the speed bump installation is complete and the area is safe for normal traffic flow.
The T-junction wall intersection requires a stable base or foundation to be in place before walls can be formed and intersect.
Steel reinforcement must be installed and tied at the wall intersection location before concrete can be poured to form the structural T-junction.
Wall formwork must be erected and aligned to create the T-shaped intersection geometry before concrete is placed.
After the T-junction concrete is poured and has achieved sufficient initial set, formwork can be stripped and curing can begin.
Waterproofing and surface finishing cannot be applied until the T-junction wall intersection is fully constructed and cured.
The door frame must be installed and secured before the T-Junction door can be assembled and fitted into the opening.
Handles, hinges, locks and other hardware can only be installed after the door assembly is in place.
Weatherstripping and finishing trim around the door require the assembled door to be in its final position to ensure proper fit and seal.
The door assembly must be complete before functional testing and quality inspection can be performed.

predecessor: Wall Framing and Rough Opening Preparation
rationale: The wall must be framed and the rough opening prepared to the correct dimensions before the T-Junction door assembly can be installed.
T-Junction corner guards are installed at the intersection where drywall meets, serving as protective edge trim. Drywall must be fully installed and finished before corner guards can be applied.
Corner beads provide the structural base at drywall corners. T-junction corner guards are typically installed over or after corner beads to reinforce the junction where three drywall edges meet.
Corner guards must be in place before joint compound is applied so that the compound can be smoothed over the guard to create a seamless finish.
After corner guards are installed and mudded in, sanding and finishing work must follow to achieve a smooth surface ready for painting.

Priming and painting typically occur after corner guard installation and finishing to protect and beautify the drywall assembly. While the guard itself doesn't physically require painting before use, the standard finishing sequence places painting after guards are embedded in joint compound.
The ceiling grid provides the structural framework onto which T-junction ceiling transitions are mounted; grid must be in place to support the transition component.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work above the ceiling must be completed before installing ceiling transitions to avoid rework and access issues.
T-junction transitions form part of the ceiling support structure; ceiling tiles are placed into the grid after transition components are installed.
The transition component must be in place before final finishing and painting of the ceiling surface can be completed around the junction.
Lighting fixtures are typically installed after ceiling grid and transitions are complete to allow proper alignment; however, in some cases fixtures can be integrated beforehand.
The subfloor must be level, clean, and structurally sound to provide a proper base for the T-junction floor transition piece.
The primary flooring on both sides of the T-junction must be installed before the transition piece can be placed to bridge the gap between them.

The T-junction transition is installed between two flooring sections; the first section is complete, then the transition is installed, and then the second flooring section can be installed abutting the transition. Alternatively, both flooring sections may be complete and the transition is installed last. In either case the transition must be in place before the final finishing/trimming of the interface.
Trim and molding work can proceed after the transition is in place for a clean finished appearance, though this is a soft preference for aesthetic sequencing.
Inspecting the completed floor including transitions should be done after the transition is installed, but this is a procedural preference rather than a physical necessity.
The T-junction signage must be placed on a completed road pavement surface to ensure stable installation and proper visibility for drivers.
Road markings at the T-junction should be completed before signage is installed to ensure signage placement aligns correctly with marked lanes and turning paths.
Signage indicating the T-junction layout must be in place before traffic lights are installed to ensure drivers are warned of the junction configuration.
It is preferable to install signage before junction lighting to avoid obstruction during lighting pole placement, though not physically mandatory.
All junction signage must be installed and verified before the road is opened to traffic to ensure driver safety and regulatory compliance.
The handrail must be fabricated and assembled before the T-junction termination can be applied, as the termination is a finishing detail on the assembled handrail.
The T-junction termination must be completed before the handrail is installed and fixed in place, as the termination detail is part of the handrail fabrication process.

predecessor: Welding or Joining of Handrail Sections
rationale: The handrail sections must be welded or joined together to form the continuous handrail before the T-junction termination detail can be executed.

predecessor: Measurement and Layout of Handrail Path
rationale: Accurate measurement and layout of the handrail path is required to ensure the T-junction termination aligns correctly with the handrail run.
The T-junction termination must be completed before final surface finishing and polishing, as the termination joint needs to be blended and finished as part of the overall handrail surface treatment.
The wall layout and marking must be completed first to establish the exact position and dimensions where the T-junction wall will intersect with the existing wall, ensuring proper alignment and fit.
The bottom plate must be installed and anchored to the floor to provide a base for the T-junction wall framing, as the studs and other framing elements attach to it.
Wall sheathing cannot be installed until the T-junction wall framing is complete, as the sheathing attaches directly to the framed studs and structure of the wall.

Electrical rough-in work such as running wires through studs is typically done after wall framing is complete but could theoretically be done concurrently; however, it is standard practice and more efficient to frame first to have open access to all cavities.

The straight wall sections that the T-junction will intersect with must be framed first so that the T-junction wall can be tied into the existing wall structure at the correct location and with proper connection details.

Drywall boards must be installed and hung before any finishing work (taping, mudding, or sanding) can begin at the T-junction. The T-junction is where two drywall panels meet at a perpendicular joint, and finishing requires access to the bare board edges and seams.

T-junction finishing involves applying joint compound (mud) and tape over the T-joint seam. This must be completed and allowed to dry before the entire drywall surface can be sanded smooth and prepared for priming/painting.

All drywall finishing, including T-junction treatment, must be fully complete and cured before primer and paint can be applied, otherwise the finished joints will be visible and the paint finish will be compromised.
Corner beads are installed onto drywall corners and edges; the drywall boards must be in place to provide a substrate for the bead.
The bead must be cut to the correct length and prepared (e.g., notching for the T-junction) before it can be positioned and fastened at the T-junction corner.

successor: Taping and Joint Compound Application (First Coat)
rationale: Corner beads must be installed and secured before joint compound (mud) can be applied to embed the bead and blend it into the drywall surface.

successor: Corner Bead Fastening and Alignment Check
rationale: After positioning the T-junction bead, it must be fastened (e.g., with nails, screws, or adhesive) and checked for plumb and alignment before the mudding process begins.

The site must be excavated and graded to the proper elevations and slopes before bioretention cells can be installed, as the cells are placed within the excavated areas and rely on the correct drainage grades.
Any existing underground utilities in the bioretention footprint must be relocated or protected prior to excavation and installation of the bioretention cell to avoid damage and safety hazards.
Erosion and sediment control measures (silt fence, inlet protection, etc.) must be in place before disturbing soils for bioretention cell construction to prevent sediment runoff.
The bioretention cell structure (soil media, underdrains, stone layers) must be completed before planting vegetation, as plants are installed into the prepared soil media of the completed cell.
Bioretention cell construction should be complete prior to final landscaping and site stabilization to ensure the drainage functionality is intact, though some landscaping can occur in parallel.
The site must be graded and rough-graded to final elevations before trenching for tree systems, as the trenches need to follow the established surface grades and drainage patterns.

Main underground utilities (water mains, storm drains, electrical conduits) must be installed first to avoid conflicts with tree root zones and to ensure trench locations do not interfere with utility corridors.

The trenched system (including structural soil cells, aeration/irrigation components, and gravel base) must be fully constructed before any trees are planted or soil media is placed into the trenches.
Tree trench systems are installed beneath the finished hardscape; sidewalks and plaza paving are placed on top of the trench system after it is completed and compacted.
After trench systems are in place, final surface finishes (topsoil, mulch, turf, or permeable pavers) can be applied to restore the site surface over the trench.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the proper elevation and slope before any curb structure can be formed and poured, ensuring a stable and correctly graded foundation.

Existing utilities (storm drains, catch basins, water lines) often lie beneath the sidewalk and curb area and must be relocated or protected before constructing the bump-out to avoid conflicts and damage.
The curb extension defines the new edge of the roadway; adjacent sidewalk and pavement surfaces are then poured or paved up to the newly installed curb.
Landscaping, planters, and streetscape elements (e.g., trees, soil, pavers) within the bump-out area can only be installed after the concrete curb structure is complete and cured.
Work zone traffic control, lane closures, and barricades must be in place before any construction activities in the roadway begin to ensure worker and public safety.
Tree pits must be excavated and prepared with soil substrate before canopy elements (such as tree stakes, guards, or irrigation systems) can be installed around the tree.
Underground utilities (water, gas, electric) must be located and protected to avoid conflicts before tree planting and canopy support installation can proceed.
Tree canopy elements (stakes, guards, grates, irrigation) must be installed before final hardscape finishes to allow for proper integration, compaction, and seamless paving around tree pits.
While not strictly required, it is preferable to complete canopy element installation before final grading and landscaping to avoid rework and ensure consistent soil levels.
The site must be excavated and graded to the proper elevation and slope before rain garden planters can be installed, as they need a stable, prepared base with appropriate drainage.
Inlet and overflow pipes that direct stormwater to and from the rain garden must be in place before the planter structure and planting medium are installed.
The planter structure must be fully assembled and placed before any vegetation can be planted and mulch applied within it.
Surrounding landscaping such as sod, edging, or decorative stone is typically completed after the rain garden planters are in place to ensure a clean finish.
Any irrigation lines feeding the rain garden planters must be tested only after the planters are fully installed to verify proper coverage and drainage.

predecessor: Green Street Pavement and Base Installation
successor: Green Street Signage and Interpretive Elements
rationale: Signage and interpretive elements are typically installed after the main pavement and base of the green street are completed, as they are surface-mounted or post-installed features that require stable finished ground.

predecessor: Green Street Planting and Soil Preparation
successor: Green Street Signage and Interpretive Elements
rationale: Planting and soil work must be completed before signage installation to avoid damage to signs from heavy equipment, soil disturbance, or rework needed for planting access.

predecessor: Green Street Signage and Interpretive Elements
successor: Green Street Final Inspection and Punch List
rationale: Signage and interpretive elements are finishing features that must be in place before the final project inspection and punch list walkthrough can be completed.

predecessor: Green Street Signage and Interpretive Elements
successor: Green Street Public Opening or Community Unveiling
rationale: Interpretive elements and signage are typically installed prior to a public opening or community unveiling event so that the public can read and enjoy them from day one.

successor: Construct Green Street Excavation and Grading
rationale: General site preparation, including clearing vegetation, debris removal, and establishing access routes, must be completed before any excavation and grading work can begin to ensure a safe and clear work area.

successor: Construct Green Street Excavation and Grading
rationale: Traffic control measures must be in place before excavation and grading on a green street to protect workers and the public from construction traffic hazards.

successor: Construct Green Street Excavation and Grading
rationale: All underground utilities must be located and marked prior to excavation to prevent utility strikes, service disruptions, and safety incidents.

predecessor: Construct Green Street Excavation and Grading
rationale: Excavation and grading must be completed to design grades before subgrade preparation and compaction can proceed, as subgrade work requires a stable, properly graded surface.

predecessor: Construct Green Street Excavation and Grading
rationale: Drainage systems and underdrains are typically installed after rough grading is complete to ensure proper drainage layout and grades are established.
The subgrade must be excavated and prepared to the required depth and slope before permeable pavement can be installed to ensure proper base support and drainage.
Geotextile fabric must be placed over the prepared subgrade to separate subgrade soils from the aggregate base, preventing soil migration and maintaining pavement structural integrity.
The crushed stone aggregate base (typically 4-6 inches deep) must be placed, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable, permeable foundation before the permeable pavement surface is installed.
Some permeable paver systems may require a surface sealant or joint stabilization treatment after installation; this is a manufacturer recommendation rather than a physical necessity for all systems.

The permeable pavement surface must be completed before adjacent landscaping, topsoil placement, and final grading can be finished to avoid debris contamination of the pavement system and ensure proper drainage transitions.

successor: Install Bioretention Soil Media and Plantings
rationale: The bioretention area must be excavated to the proper depth and shape before any soil media can be placed into it.

successor: Install Bioretention Soil Media and Plantings
rationale: The underdrain piping and gravel layer must be installed at the bottom of the bioretention basin to provide drainage before the soil filter media is placed on top.

successor: Install Bioretention Soil Media and Plantings
rationale: Geotextile fabric must be placed between the gravel drainage layer and the soil media layer to prevent soil migration into the drainage stone.

predecessor: Install Bioretention Soil Media and Plantings
rationale: Mulch is applied as a top dressing over the installed soil media and around plantings to retain moisture and suppress weeds.

predecessor: Install Bioretention Soil Media and Plantings
successor: Install Curb Cuts or Inflow Structures
rationale: Curb cuts and inflow structures that direct stormwater into the bioretention area must be installed after the soil media and plantings are in place to ensure proper grading and finished elevation alignment.

successor: Install Subsurface Drainage and Overflow Systems
rationale: The ground must be excavated and prepared to the required levels and grades before subsurface drainage pipes and overflow systems can be laid in the trenches.

predecessor: Install Subsurface Drainage and Overflow Systems
rationale: Backfilling of trenches over drainage pipes can only occur after the subsurface drainage and overflow systems are fully installed and inspected.

predecessor: Install Subsurface Drainage and Overflow Systems
successor: Pour Concrete Slab or Base Course
rationale: Concrete slabs or base courses placed over drainage areas require the subsurface drainage system to be in place first to ensure proper water management beneath the structure.

predecessor: Install Subsurface Drainage and Overflow Systems
successor: Install Above-Grade Drainage Components (e.g., gutters, downspouts)
rationale: Overflow systems connected to subsurface drainage must be tied into the underground network, requiring the subsurface system to be installed first to establish connection points.

successor: Install Subsurface Drainage and Overflow Systems
rationale: Final grading and shaping of the site establishes drainage slopes and elevations needed to position subsurface drainage pipes at the correct invert levels for proper water flow.

successor: Install Curb and Curb Extension Structures
rationale: The subgrade must be properly graded and compacted to provide a stable, uniform foundation for curb and curb extension structures. Installing curbs on unprepared or uneven subgrade would lead to settlement, cracking, and misalignment.

predecessor: Install Storm Drainage and Underground Utilities
successor: Install Curb and Curb Extension Structures
rationale: Underground drainage pipes, conduits, and utility lines must be installed and backfilled before curb construction to avoid digging through newly placed curb structures and to ensure proper drainage alignment with curb inlets.

predecessor: Install Curb and Curb Extension Structures
rationale: Curbs define the lateral boundary and grade for pavement sections; asphalt or concrete base and wearing courses are placed after curbs are installed to abut against the curb face and achieve proper edge support and drainage slope.

predecessor: Install Curb and Curb Extension Structures
rationale: Sidewalks typically tie into or abut curb extensions (bulb-outs) and pedestrian ramps at intersection corners; the curb structures must be in place to establish the correct elevation and alignment for adjacent sidewalk pours.

predecessor: Install Curb and Curb Extension Structures
rationale: Curb extensions often contain landscaped areas, planters, or streetscape elements; final grading, planting, and decorative finishes in these zones must follow curb installation to avoid damaging the new curb work and to ensure proper soil retention behind the curb face.
Vegetation, trees, stumps, and organic debris must be removed from the roadway footprint before any earthwork or base preparation can begin, as organic material cannot support pavement loads.
The native subgrade soil must be graded, shaped, and compacted to specified density before placing base materials, to provide a stable foundation and prevent differential settlement.

successor: Base Course Paving (Asphalt or Aggregate Base)
rationale: The prepared base layer (e.g., crushed aggregate) must be in place and compacted before any asphalt or surface pavement layer can be laid, as the base provides structural support and drainage for the wearing course.

Curbs and gutters should be installed after base preparation but before final paving, as they define the pavement edge and grade, and their presence helps contain and shape the subsequent paving layers.

Underground drainage structures and pipes are best placed after subgrade preparation and base layering but before final surface paving, so that drainage is functional before the finished surface is applied.

The subgrade must be properly graded, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable foundation for the paving layers; without a prepared subgrade, the pavement will lack structural support and will fail.
The aggregate base course must be placed and compacted over the subgrade to distribute traffic loads and provide drainage; paving cannot be laid directly on subgrade without this structural layer.
All underground utilities and drainage systems must be installed and tested before paving, because cutting into newly paved roadways to access utilities is costly and compromises pavement integrity.

Road markings must be applied on a finished, stable surface. Asphalt paving or the final base course must be completed and cured before markings can be applied to ensure adhesion and a smooth, level substrate.
The road surface must be thoroughly cleaned of debris, dust, dirt, and moisture prior to marking application. Contaminants will prevent proper adhesion of paint or thermoplastic markings.

Road markings provide essential traffic guidance and safety information. The road cannot be opened to traffic until markings are fully applied and dried/cured to ensure driver safety and regulatory compliance.
Completed road markings must be inspected for accuracy, reflectivity, dimensions, and placement before the project can receive final approval and sign-off.
While traffic signs can be installed before markings, it is preferable to apply markings first to ensure proper alignment and positioning of signs relative to the marked lanes and symbols.
The ground must be cleared, rough-graded, and compacted before curbs can be formed and poured to ensure a stable, level subgrade.
The subgrade must be properly prepared, graded to correct elevations, and compacted to support the curb and gutter forms and concrete.
Underground utilities must be placed in the road corridor before curbs are installed to avoid trenching through or damaging finished curb and gutter.
Curbs define the lateral boundary of the roadway; pavement is placed up against the finished curb, so the curb must be in place first.
Sidewalks and driveway aprons typically abut or tie into the curb and gutter, requiring the curb to be set first for proper alignment and elevation.

Traffic signs must be mounted on or beside a finished road surface; the pavement provides the stable base and proper elevation for sign placement and ensures signs are positioned at correct heights relative to the final road level.

Road markings and traffic signs must be coordinated for consistency; signs should be installed after markings are laid so that sign placement aligns with lane delineations, stop lines, and other pavement markings.

Traffic signs are essential safety devices that must be in place before a road is opened to public traffic; without proper signage, drivers lack critical regulatory, warning, and guidance information, creating a safety hazard.

While not physically required, it is preferable to install signs before lighting to avoid conflicts with light pole placement and ensure signs are visible under the lighting design; however, lighting can be installed concurrently or after if coordinated.
The ground or roadside area where sign posts are set must be graded and compacted to provide a stable foundation; installing signs before grading may result in unstable or unevenly placed posts.

Guardrails are typically anchored into the roadway base or adjacent ground; the road surface course must be completed to establish final grades and alignment for proper guardrail placement and height.
The subgrade and base layers must be compacted and finished to provide a stable foundation for the guardrail posts or barrier footings.

Drainage systems must be installed before barriers so that barrier placement does not interfere with drainage paths and so that subsurface water management is in place before posts are driven or foundations poured.
Road markings (edge lines, shoulder markings) are often laid after barriers are installed, because the barrier defines the precise edge of the drivable surface and marking machines need clear access.

Signage (e.g., barrier warning signs, reflectors) is typically placed after barriers are erected to ensure correct positioning, but this is a logical construction sequence preference rather than a strict physical impossibility.
The ground must be graded and leveled to the proper profile before a speed bump/table can be formed, ensuring a smooth transition and proper cross-slope drainage.
The subgrade soil must be compacted to the required density to provide a stable foundation for the speed bump/table structure and prevent differential settlement.
All underground utilities (water, sewer, electrical, communications) must be installed and backfilled prior to constructing the speed bump/table to avoid excavation through the finished structure.

Warning markings (chevrons, word messages, edge lines) and reflective markers must be applied after the speed bump/table is fully cured to ensure proper adhesion and alignment with the finished surface.

Advance warning signs (e.g., 'Speed Hump Ahead') and advisory speed limit signs must be installed after the speed bump/table is constructed so that sign placement accurately reflects the final location.
A stable foundation is physically required to support the structural load of the entry portal before it can be erected.
The ground must be properly graded and leveled to provide a stable base for the entry portal foundation and structure.
The portal structure must be in place before electrical lines and fixtures can be run through and attached to it.
Security cameras, intercoms, and access control hardware must be mounted on the completed portal structure.
Landscaping around the entry is best completed after the portal is installed to avoid rework, though it could be done beforehand with care.
The gateway canopy requires structural support from columns and a foundation to bear its load. Without these structural elements in place, the canopy cannot be safely installed or supported.

Electrical wiring and lighting fixtures for the canopy must be installed after the canopy structure is in place to ensure proper routing of conduits and attachment of light fixtures to the canopy frame.
The structural frame of the canopy must be erected before cladding materials (such as metal panels, glass, or roofing) can be applied to complete the aesthetic and weatherproof finish.

Signage is typically mounted after the canopy is complete to ensure proper attachment points and alignment, though in some cases signage could be pre-fabricated and installed simultaneously with cladding.
The installation area must be cleared, leveled, and excavated for foundations before any canopy components can be delivered or erected on site.
The ground must be leveled and prepared before installing the pylon foundation to ensure structural stability.
The concrete foundation for the pylon must be poured and cured to provide a stable base before the pylon structure can be erected.
Electrical conduits and wiring for the pylon's lighting must be installed in the ground before the pylon is placed to avoid re-excavation and damage.
Final landscaping around the pylon should be completed after installation to avoid disturbing finished soil and planting work during pylon erection.
Once the pylon is installed, electrical connections can be made from the utility supply to the pylon's lighting and signage components, followed by testing.
The gate leaves require a stable foundation to be mounted on; foundation preparation including concrete curing must be completed before installation can begin.
Gate leaves are hinged or attached to gate posts; therefore the posts must be erected and secured before hanging the leaves.
Hardware such as hinges, locks, handles, and automation components are mounted onto the installed gate leaves, so installation of leaves must precede hardware fitting.
Alignment, swing testing, and clearance checks can only be performed after the gate leaves are physically installed in their final position.
While it is preferable to apply final paint or protective coatings after installation to cover any installation scratches, some pre-coating may be done off-site, making this a soft preference.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before pouring the foundation to ensure structural stability.
Soil bearing capacity must be assessed to design the foundation correctly before any foundation work begins.

predecessor: Underground Utility Installation (e.g., drainage, water, electrical conduits)
rationale: Underground utilities must be laid in the excavated area before the foundation is poured to avoid later digging and structural damage.
The foundation must be fully cured and achieve required strength before any floor slab or superstructure work can proceed.
Vertical structural elements rely on the foundation for load transfer; they cannot commence until the foundation is set and load-bearing ready.
The gateway intercom station requires a stable and level foundation for mounting; site preparation including concrete pad or footing must be completed first.
Power and data cabling must be run through conduits to the intercom station location before the unit can be physically installed and connected.
The intercom hardware must be physically mounted and wired before firmware configuration, network setup, and access control programming can be performed.
Power connections to the station must be completed and verified only after the unit is properly mounted and all wiring terminations are secure.
End-to-end audio, video, and access control functionality can only be tested after the station is installed, configured, and energized.
The site must be cleared and graded before the perimeter fence can be laid out and erected, as the fence line needs a stable, unobstructed surface for surveying and installation.
Underground utilities (water, sewer, electrical conduits) that cross the fence line must be installed before the fence is built to avoid digging up or compromising the fence foundation later.
The perimeter fence establishes the site security boundary and access control, which is required before interior excavation work can commence safely.
The fence structure must be in place before security elements (gates, sensors, cameras) are mounted on or integrated with it.
The fence must be fully installed before final grading and landscaping around the perimeter can be completed, as the fence defines the property boundary and grade transitions.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to receive the bollard foundations before any bollard installation can begin.
Concrete footings or foundations must be poured and cured to provide a stable anchoring base for the bollards.
Any electrical conduits, data cables, or drainage pipes that will pass beneath the bollard locations must be installed and backfilled before bollard placement to avoid excavation after installation.
The bollards must be set and aligned before the surrounding pavement, asphalt, or concrete finish is poured to achieve a flush, neat interface.
Signage indicating the presence of bollards and any required road markings are typically applied after the bollards are in place to ensure correct positioning and visibility.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and compacted before any foundation work can begin to ensure a stable base and proper load-bearing capacity.
Accurate surveying and staking of the gateway location must be completed to mark exact foundation positions and ensure correct alignment with design plans.
Trenches or pits must be excavated to the required depth and dimensions before foundation materials (e.g., concrete, rebar) can be placed.
Existing underground utilities must be identified and marked to avoid damage during excavation and foundation installation, ensuring safety and regulatory compliance.
Freshly placed concrete foundations require a specified curing period to achieve design strength before any structural loads can be applied.
The gateway columns or structural frame can only be erected after the foundations are fully installed, cured, and have reached sufficient strength to support them.
Gate posts and concrete foundations must be fully cured and in place to provide structural support for hanging gate leaves.
The site must be graded and prepared to ensure proper alignment, clearance, and operation of gate leaves.
Underground conduits for gate operators, sensors, and intercoms must be installed before gates to avoid excavation after gate installation.
Gate operator arms, motors, and sensors must be mounted onto or aligned with the installed gate leaves and hinges.
While not physically mandatory, finishing pavement after gate installation avoids damage to new paving from heavy equipment and allows precise swing clearance adjustments.
Access control systems require electrical power to function; power distribution must be installed and energized before security devices can be tested and commissioned.
Access control panels, card readers, and security cameras require network connectivity for communication with the central control system; structured cabling must be in place first.
Conduit, backboxes, and mounting provisions for security devices must be roughed-in within walls and ceilings before final device installation and trim-out.
All security hardware (controllers, readers, sensors, cameras) must be physically installed and wired before system-level programming, configuration, and end-to-end testing can be performed.

While security device installation is often done after rough-in but before final finishes to avoid damage, in some sequences it is a soft preference to complete security trim after painting and flooring to protect devices from construction debris.
The canopy requires a stable concrete foundation to support its structural load; the foundation must be cured and ready before canopy installation can begin.
Signage is typically mounted onto or below the canopy structure; the canopy must be in place to provide the supporting framework for signs and lighting fixtures.

successor: Connect Electrical Supply to Gateway Lighting
rationale: The lighting fixtures must be physically installed before electrical connections can be made to them; wiring and final electrical hookup follow fixture placement.
The canopy and lighting installation must be complete and in place before the final inspection and commissioning can verify the work.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and graded to provide a safe and stable work area for canopy installation and to ensure proper drainage around the structure.
A stable foundation or mounting surface must be in place before the gateway signage can be installed to ensure structural integrity and proper alignment.
The signage materials and components must be physically present on site before installation work can begin.
Regulatory approvals and permits must be secured prior to installation to comply with local codes and avoid legal/construction delays.
The installed signage must be inspected for quality, safety, and compliance after installation is complete.

successor: Conduct Signage Lighting and Electrical Connection
rationale: If the gateway signage includes illuminated elements, electrical connections and lighting fixtures can only be connected and tested after the signage structure is securely mounted.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and compacted before any road crossing base can be installed to ensure proper foundation and load-bearing capacity.
All existing underground utilities must be identified and marked to avoid conflicts and damage during excavation for the road crossing base.
Trenching or excavation to the required depth and width must be completed before the base material (e.g., crushed stone, concrete) can be placed.
Base layer must be in place before drainage pipes or culverts are installed within the crossing to ensure proper support and alignment.

successor: Paving or Surface Paving of Road
rationale: The base provides the structural foundation; the asphalt or concrete wearing course cannot be laid until the base is compacted and cured.
After the base is constructed, surrounding areas can be backfilled and compacted to restore grade and support adjacent structures.
The ground must be properly prepared, graded, and compacted before any pavement can be laid to ensure a stable base.
Any underground utility conduits or drainage pipes crossing beneath the road must be installed before the pavement is placed to avoid later excavation and pavement damage.
The granular sub-base and base layers must be compacted to specification before the final pavement surface can be constructed, providing the structural support.
Road markings and signage are applied onto the finished pavement surface; they cannot be installed before the pavement is complete.
Curb and gutter work typically follows pavement placement to ensure proper alignment and drainage interface with the pavement edge.
Bollards are typically installed on or into the road surface/pavement, so the road base, sub-base, and pavement layer must be completed first to provide a stable foundation.

Bollards define the crossing area and traffic control points; road markings (e.g., zebra crossings, stop lines) and signage must be aligned with the bollard locations, so bollards must be in place first.

Any underground cables or ducts (e.g., for lighting, electrical supply to illuminated bollards, or drainage) must be laid and backfilled before bollard foundations are excavated and set to avoid conflicts and rework.
Kerbs define the edge of the carriageway and pedestrian crossing points; bollard positions are often referenced to kerb lines, so kerbs and adjacent footpaths should be completed first.

successor: Traffic management and road opening to traffic
rationale: Bollards are safety and traffic-calming devices that must be fully installed and secured before the road is opened to vehicular or pedestrian traffic to ensure safe operation.
The foundation and base layer of the road must be prepared before any signage can be installed to ensure stability and proper placement.
The road surface must be fully paved before painting road markings and installing signage, as signage placement depends on the final road surface level and layout.
Road crossing signage indicating pedestrian crossing areas should be installed before or concurrently with crosswalk markings to clearly designate crossing locations for road marking crews.
Pedestrian crossing signage is typically installed before traffic signals at crossings to provide advance warning to drivers and establish the crossing zone.
All crossing signage must be fully installed and verified before the road is opened to traffic to ensure pedestrian safety from day one of operation.
The road surface must be properly prepared and compacted before any markings can be applied to ensure a stable and even substrate for the paint or thermoplastic material.
The final asphalt or road surface layer must be laid and fully cured before markings are applied, as markings cannot be placed on unfinished or unpaved surfaces.

While ideal to align signals with crossing locations, signals can be installed before markings in many cases; however, marking positions help determine optimal signal pole placement for pedestrian crossings.
The road cannot be opened to public traffic until all safety markings, including pedestrian crossings, are clearly visible and in place to guide drivers and ensure pedestrian safety.
Pedestrian signals and crossing controls should be operational only after the crossing markings are fully applied so that pedestrians have clearly designated crossing areas.
A stable, compacted road base must be constructed before the ramp can be formed and poured over it; otherwise the ramp would lack structural support.
Any underground utilities (drainage, conduits) crossing the road must be installed and backfilled before the ramp is built to avoid cutting into or disturbing the completed ramp.
The ramp forms the transition from the road surface to the pedestrian walkway; the final pavement or asphalt layer is placed after the ramp is fully cured and integrated with the road base.
Tactile warning pavers (detectable warning surfaces) are installed on top of the ramp surface to provide accessibility cues for visually impaired pedestrians.

Guardrails or curbs adjacent to the ramp are typically installed after the ramp is in place to ensure proper alignment and slope, though in some sequences they could be placed concurrently as a soft preference.
The road base must be compacted and prepared to provide a stable foundation before installing the kerb.
Drainage pipes and systems must be in place before kerb construction to ensure proper water flow and prevent undermining of the kerb structure.
The kerb defines the edge of the road crossing and must be installed first so that paving can be laid up to it, ensuring a clean interface and proper alignment.
Kerb installation must be completed before line marking and signage for the pedestrian crossing can be applied, as the kerb establishes the crossing location and geometry.
Tactile ground surface indicators (e.g., blister paving for visually impaired pedestrians) at crossing points must be laid after the kerb is in place to ensure proper alignment with the kerb edge.
A stable, compacted subgrade is required to support the traffic calming device foundation and prevent differential settlement.
The base course provides the structural layer upon which the traffic calming device is placed, ensuring proper load distribution.
The underlying pavement must be in place so that the traffic calming device can be integrated into the road surface and achieve proper height/grade transitions.

successor: Road Surface Finishing / Wearing Course (Top Layer)
rationale: After installing the traffic calming device, the final wearing course or surface finish is applied to seamlessly blend the device with the surrounding road surface and ensure smooth transitions.
Warning signs, speed limit markings, and pavement markings indicating the traffic calming device must be applied after the device is physically in place to ensure accurate positioning and visibility.
The ground must be prepared, leveled, and graded before a road crossing barrier can be installed to ensure proper foundation and alignment.
Underground utilities must be surveyed, marked, and if necessary relocated before excavation for barrier foundations to avoid damage and ensure safety.
The barrier must be in place before the final road surface is paved around it to achieve a seamless integration and proper edge finishing.
Barrier installation must precede signage and road marking placement so that warning signs and reflective markings can be accurately positioned relative to the installed barrier.
A safety inspection and functional testing of the barrier (e.g., gate operation, locking mechanisms, warning lights) can only occur after the barrier is fully installed.
The ground must be cleared, excavated, and prepared before any foundation work can begin to ensure stable bearing conditions.
Knowledge of soil bearing capacity, groundwater conditions, and subsurface stratigraphy is required to design and construct the foundation appropriately.

The foundation provides the load-bearing base for the road crossing structure (e.g., bridge abutments, culvert supports, or pipe supports) and must be in place before any superstructure elements are erected.
Buried pipes or conduits at the crossing depend on the foundation being complete to ensure correct alignment and support.
Backfill operations around the crossing structure can only proceed once the foundation is in place and has achieved sufficient strength.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before any installation work can begin to provide clear access and a safe working area for crossing installation.
The trench across the road must be excavated before any pipes, conduits, or duct banks can be installed within the crossing.
Existing underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid damage during excavation and installation of the road crossing.
After the crossing pipes or conduits are installed, the trench must be backfilled and compacted to restore the roadbed and pavement support.
The road surface (asphalt or concrete) must be restored after the crossing installation and backfilling to reinstate the roadway for traffic.
The ground must be cleared and graded to provide a stable, accessible work area and expose the trenching path before any drainage pipes can be installed across the road.
The road subgrade must be compacted to the required density to prevent differential settlement before trenching and installing drainage structures beneath the road crossing.
Existing underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid damaging them during trenching for the drainage crossing.
Traffic control measures (lane closures, detours, signage) must be in place before any road crossing work begins to ensure worker and public safety.
The road surface must be restored and repaved only after the drainage pipes and structures are fully installed, backfilled, and compacted beneath the crossing.

successor: Road Crossing Drainage Installation Inspection and Testing
rationale: The installed drainage must be inspected and tested (e.g., for proper flow and watertightness) before the trench is completely backfilled and the road surface is restored.
Shoulder and embankment works adjacent to the crossing can only proceed after drainage installation to ensure proper integration and outfall for the drainage system.
The foundation or base where signage posts are installed must be prepared and cured before signage mounting to ensure structural stability.
Signposts (vertical posts or poles) must be installed before signage panels can be mounted onto them.
Paving or asphalt laying at the crossing area must be completed before signage mounting, as signage placement often marks the final surface level and prevents damage to fresh pavement.
Signage must be mounted and in place before the final inspection and approval of the road crossing can occur, as signage visibility and correctness are key inspection criteria.

While signage mounting can precede or follow markings, typically signage is mounted first to guide the exact placement of pavement markings relative to signs, though this is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
The road surface must be properly prepared and compacted before any markings can be applied to ensure adhesion and durability of the markings.
The final road surface (asphalt or concrete) must be laid and cured before markings can be applied, as markings are placed on top of the finished surface.
While signs can technically be installed before markings, it is preferable to complete markings first so that sign placement can align accurately with marked crossing locations.
The road cannot be opened to public traffic until all pavement markings, including crossing markings, are complete to ensure driver guidance and pedestrian safety.
Markings must be applied before the final inspection can verify that all road features, including crossings, meet specification and safety standards.
Ducts must be in place to house and protect the electrical cables that will power the road crossing lighting.
Electrical cables must be pulled through the installed ducts before lighting fixtures can be connected and energized.

predecessor: Footing / Foundation Construction for Lighting Poles
rationale: Concrete footings or foundations must be poured and cured to provide a stable base for mounting lighting poles.

Lighting fixtures are typically mounted on poles, so the lighting installation (fixture mounting and wiring) must be completed before or simultaneously with pole erection, though functionally lighting installation includes pole erection.
After lighting fixtures are installed and wired, they must be connected to the power supply and tested for proper operation.
Typically lighting is installed before final paving to avoid damaging new pavement, but this is a soft preference for scheduling efficiency and quality.
The ground must be excavated and trenches prepared to create space for embedding bollard foundations and conduit runs.
All existing underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid damage during excavation and bollard installation.
Concrete footings or foundations for the bollards must be poured and fully cured to provide a stable base for mounting.
Final paving or restoration of the road surface around the bollards must be completed after installation to ensure a flush, finished appearance.
Permanent traffic signs and markings indicating the presence of the bollards should be installed after the bollards are in place, though temporary controls may already be active.
Final site cleanup and inspection for compliance with specifications can only proceed after all bollards are installed and secured.

The raised walk decking requires a stable foundation or substructure (such as piles, footings, or support posts) to bear its load. Without this substructure in place, the decking cannot be safely installed.
The ground beneath and around the raised walk must be properly graded and drainage measures installed to prevent water accumulation, erosion, or instability under the deck structure.

Any underground or sub-deck utilities (electrical conduit, lighting, water lines, drainage pipes) must be installed before the decking is built above them to avoid costly rework or inaccessible buried services.

The deck surface finishing (such as applying sealant, stain, anti-slip coating, or membrane) must occur after the decking structure is fully assembled and secured to ensure complete coverage and protection.

Handrails and guardrails are mounted onto or adjacent to the finished deck surface; the decking must be in place to provide the structural attachment points and to establish finished walking surface elevations for proper rail height compliance.
A stable, level ground surface must be prepared before any substructure framing can be installed, as the support frame requires a compacted subgrade or foundation to bear loads.
Any underground utilities that will run beneath the raised walk must be trenched and installed before the support frame is erected, otherwise access would be blocked by the completed structure.

predecessor: Concrete Footings / Foundation Piers (for support posts)
rationale: Footings or piers must be cast and cured to provide load-bearing points for the support frame posts; the frame cannot be installed onto uncured or nonexistent foundations.

successor: Raised Walk Decking / Floor Surface Installation
rationale: The structural support frame must be fully erected and stable before decking boards or walking surface panels can be laid on top of it.
Safety handrails are attached to the support frame or deck structure; the frame must be in place to serve as the anchoring substrate for railing posts.
The raised walk surface (concrete slab) must be poured and cured to provide a stable base for installing handrails and guardrails.
The structural frame supporting the raised walk must be erected before handrails can be attached to it.
The walking surface must be completed so that handrail posts can be anchored and guardrail infill can be installed at the correct height relative to the finished floor.

While lighting can be roughed-in earlier, final fixture installation is often done after handrails to avoid damage and to coordinate mounting heights, though this is a practical preference rather than a physical necessity.
Final touch-up painting or coating of the handrails and surrounding areas must be performed after installation to cover weld marks, scratches, and fastener heads, protecting the metal from corrosion.
The balustrade must be anchored to the raised walk decking or substrate; the walking surface must be installed first to provide a stable base for balustrade posts and fixings.
The primary structural frame (beams, joists) of the raised walk must be in place to support the decking and subsequently the balustrade, ensuring load paths are established.
While often integrated, if handrails are separate components they are typically fitted after or concurrently with balustrade infill; this is a soft preference for logical sequence.

successor: Final Inspection / Safety Check of Raised Walk
rationale: The balustrade is a critical safety element; its completion is required before the walkway can be certified for use and undergo final safety inspection.
Foundations must be cured and load-bearing before any superstructure including the balustrade is installed, to ensure structural stability and compliance with building codes.
The ground must be prepared and excavated to the proper grade before any raised walk or stair/step structures can be built on it.
A stable foundation or compacted sub-base is required to support the raised walk or stair/step structure and prevent settlement or shifting.
Any underground utilities (drainage, electrical, etc.) that will pass beneath or adjacent to the walk/stair must be installed before the structure is built to avoid expensive rework.
Handrails and guardrails are safety features that must be installed after the stair/step structure is in place so they can be properly anchored and aligned with the treads and landings.
Final surface treatments (e.g., non-slip coatings, sealants, or paint) should be applied after the walk/stair structure is fully installed to ensure even coverage and protection of all surfaces.
The ground surface must be graded and leveled to the correct elevations before constructing any walk or ramp structure to ensure proper drainage and stable foundation.
A concrete footing or foundation must be poured and cured to support the raised walk ramp structure before the ramp itself can be installed.
