Any underground electrical, plumbing, or drainage utilities that will run beneath the ramp area must be installed and backfilled before the ramp is constructed to avoid costly rework.
Handrails must be mounted onto the completed ramp structure; the ramp must be structurally complete to serve as the anchoring base for handrail posts.

Applying a non-slip surface coating or sealant is typically done after the ramp structure is complete, though it is a finishing step that could be delayed if weather conditions are unfavorable; it is a best practice but not a hard structural dependency.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared to provide a stable, level base for the raised walk foundation, ensuring proper drainage and load-bearing capacity.
Any underground utilities (e.g., drainage, conduit) that will pass beneath the raised walk must be installed before the foundation/footing is poured to avoid digging up completed work.
The foundation/footing must be fully cured and load-bearing before any above-grade framing or structural elements are erected on top of it.
The structural support system (framing) must be built atop the foundation before the final walking surface can be installed; however, the foundation/footing is the necessary first step.
After the foundation/footing is placed, adequate curing time is required before any loads can be applied to ensure the concrete reaches sufficient strength.
The subgrade must be properly prepared and compacted to provide a stable, uniform base before any raised walk components (including expansion joints) can be installed.
Formwork defines the shape and boundaries of the raised walk slab; expansion joints are placed within or between slabs, so the formwork must be in place first.

predecessor: Rebar / Reinforcement Placement for Raised Walk
rationale: Steel reinforcement must be positioned within the slab before expansion joint material is installed, as the joint material may need to be placed around or between reinforcement elements.

successor: Concrete Pour for Raised Walk Slab
rationale: The expansion joint material must be in its final position before concrete is poured, so that the joint is properly embedded and can function correctly to accommodate thermal expansion.

successor: Joint Sealing / Finishing of Expansion Joint
rationale: After the concrete is poured and cured around the expansion joint, the top of the joint may need to be sealed or finished with sealant; this can only be done after the joint is installed and concrete has set.
The ground must be properly graded and cleared to provide a stable, level base for the raised walk deck structure.
Concrete footings or piers must be cured and in place to support the vertical posts and structural framework of the raised walk deck.
Any electrical conduits, plumbing, or drainage lines that will run beneath the deck must be installed before the deck structure covers the area, to avoid rework or access issues.
Once the raised walk deck is fully installed, the deck surface must be finished, stained, or sealed to protect it from weather and foot traffic.
Handrails and guardrails are mounted to the deck structure and must be installed after the deck framing and decking are in place to ensure proper alignment and secure attachment.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared to provide a stable, level foundation for the raised walk substructure.
Any underground utilities (drainage, electrical, water lines) beneath the walkway must be installed before the substructure is erected to avoid conflicts and the need for rework.
Concrete footings or pier foundations must be poured and cured to specified strength before the substructure framing can be erected on top of them.
The substructure (beams, joists, supports) must be fully erected and secured before the decking or floor surface can be installed on top.
Safety railings are typically attached to or supported by the substructure, which must be in place before railings can be mounted.

The raised walk structure (deck, platform, or walkway surface) must be fully built and stable before railing can be attached to it, as the railing relies on the walk structure for support and anchorage.
The load-bearing frame of the raised walk must be in place to provide a secure mounting surface for railing posts and brackets.

It is often easier to install railing before final decking boards or treads are placed, allowing better access to post bases and fasteners, but this is a soft sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
Railing must be fully installed before safety inspections and load testing can verify that the guardrails meet code requirements for fall protection.
Final finishing coats and cap installation typically occur after railing is erected, but this is a logical work sequence preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before installing any foundation or structure for the bicycle shelter.
A concrete foundation or slab must be cured and ready to support the shelter's structural columns or mounting points before erection can begin.
Any underground electrical, drainage, or data conduits serving the shelter area must be installed prior to placing the foundation and shelter to avoid rework.
Bicycle racks are typically installed under or adjacent to the shelter; the shelter roof/structure provides protection and defines the rack layout area.
Lighting fixtures mounted on or under the canopy require the shelter structure to be in place for conduit routing and fixture attachment.
The ground surface must be properly graded and compacted before installing any permanent structure like a bicycle repair station to ensure a stable foundation.
A concrete pad or foundation must be poured and fully cured before the bicycle repair station can be securely anchored and mounted.
Any underground electrical conduit, water lines, or drainage pipes needed for the repair station area must be installed before the foundation is laid and the station is placed.
The repair station should be installed first so that surrounding pavement or pathways can be finished flush against its base for proper drainage and a clean finished appearance.

Signage directing users to the bicycle repair station is typically installed after the station is in place to ensure accurate positioning, though this is a soft preference as signage could be installed simultaneously.
The bike path surface and base must be fully prepared and in place before signage can be installed, as signs are anchored into or adjacent to the completed path.
Paving must be completed to provide a stable surface for sign post installation and to ensure proper placement along the finished path.
Signage should be installed before final line markings are applied to avoid marking over sign post locations and ensure coordinated placement of signs and pavement markings.

It is preferred that signage is in place prior to the final inspection so the inspector can verify correct sign placement and visibility, but inspection could theoretically occur first and signage added after.

The subgrade must be properly graded, compacted, and prepared to provide a stable, uniform foundation before any curb or edge restraint is placed. Installing curb on unprepared subgrade would lead to settlement, misalignment, and failure.

The aggregate base course must be placed and compacted to the proper thickness and profile before curb installation, as the curb/edge restraint sits on or against the base layer and defines the lateral boundary of the paved surface.

The curb or edge restraint must be installed first to act as a form, containment edge, and lateral support for the asphalt paving. Paving cannot be placed without the edge restraint defining the boundary and preventing pavement edge raveling.

After the curb is set and aligned, the bike path surface (asphalt or concrete) is placed and finished up to the edge restraint. The curb serves as a screed guide and provides a clean transition edge for finishing operations.

Any subsurface drainage infrastructure (catch basins, drain pipes, or underdrains) near the bike path must be installed before the curb/edge restraint is placed, so that drainage features integrate properly with the path edge without requiring later disturbance of the completed curb.
The ground must be properly graded and compacted to provide a stable and level base for installing bollards.
A compacted aggregate subbase layer is required beneath the bollard footing to ensure proper load distribution and drainage.
Bollards are typically set into concrete footings; the concrete must be poured and sufficiently cured before the bollard can be mounted or installed.

successor: Asphalt or Paving of Bike Path Surface
rationale: Bollards are usually installed before the final paving layer so that the paving can be finished flush around the base of the bollard, ensuring a clean interface and preventing tripping hazards.
It is preferable to install bollards before applying surface markings so that markings can be laid around the bollard, but this is a soft preference as markings can be touched up after installation.

The concrete path foundation must be fully cured and completed before lighting installation begins, as lighting posts/fixtures need to be anchored into the concrete or positioned along the finished path surface.
Underground electrical conduits and wiring must be laid and routed before lighting poles or fixtures are installed, to ensure power is available and to avoid digging up finished surfaces.

The final surface layer (e.g., asphalt or seal coating) should be applied after lighting installation to avoid damage to the new surface during trenching or pole installation, and to ensure a seamless finish around fixtures.
The lighting system must be fully installed before the path can be commissioned, inspected, and tested for compliance with safety and illumination standards.
Landscaping and final clean-up are typically performed after lighting installation to avoid damaging newly planted vegetation or finished grading during the lighting work.
The ground must be properly excavated, leveled, and compacted before installing the bicycle wash station to ensure a stable foundation and proper drainage.
A concrete pad or reinforced foundation must be poured and cured before the bicycle wash station can be anchored and installed on a solid, level surface.
Underground water supply lines and drainage pipes must be laid and connected to the main systems before the wash station equipment can be attached to them.
The wash station structure must be fully installed before electrical work (e.g., lighting, pressure washer outlets) can be safely connected and completed.
The wash station must be fully assembled and connected to utilities before it can be tested for leaks, pressure, and operational functionality.
A stable, level surface (e.g., concrete pad or paved area) must be prepared before racks can be anchored/secured.
If racks are installed before final surfacing, the surfacing work may damage or obstruct the racks; typically racks are installed after final paving is complete.
Any underground electrical, water, or drainage work beneath the rack area must be completed to avoid digging up a finished rack installation.
If racks are bolted into concrete, the concrete must be cured and ready for anchoring before rack installation.
It is common to install racks before surrounding landscaping (e.g., sod, shrubs) to avoid heavy equipment damaging new plantings.
The subgrade must be properly graded, compacted, and prepared to provide a stable foundation before any pavement can be laid.
A granular base course (e.g., crushed stone or aggregate) must be placed and compacted over the subgrade to provide structural support and drainage before the surface pavement is constructed.

It is often easier to install edge restraints or curbs before paving to contain the pavement material, though some methods allow placement after. This is a soft preference in certain construction sequences.
Pavement must be fully placed, compacted, and cured (if asphalt or concrete) before lane markings, symbols, and signage are applied onto the surface.

Lighting poles and conduit are typically installed after the pavement is complete to avoid damaging new pavement or interfering with paving operations. However, underground conduit could be installed before paving as a soft preference depending on design.
The site must be graded and cleared to provide a level, stable surface for the bike shelter foundation.
Concrete footings or a slab foundation must be poured and cured before the shelter structure can be anchored to them.
Any underground electrical, water, or drainage lines serving the shelter area must be installed before the shelter is placed to avoid digging under the completed structure.
Painting or applying final finishes is typically done after the shelter is erected for convenience, though it could be done prior; this is a soft sequencing preference.
Bike racks are placed under or adjacent to the shelter, so the shelter canopy must be in place first to define the protected area and avoid rework.
Landscaping, paving, or concrete work around the shelter base should be completed after the shelter is installed to ensure proper fit and finish against the structure.
The bike path surface must be prepared and compacted before signage can be installed to ensure proper footing and alignment of sign posts.
Signage installation (e.g., post-mounted signs) requires the paved surface to be complete so that posts can be set correctly and pavement marking locations are finalized.
All signage must be in place before the final inspection can verify that signage meets regulatory and design requirements.
Safety signage (directional signs, warning signs, rules-of-the-road signs) must be installed before the path can be opened for public use to ensure user safety and regulatory compliance.
The subgrade/base must be compacted and ready before bollard installation so that bollard foundations can be properly set.
Concrete must be placed and cured (or asphalt laid) for the bike path surface before bollards can be anchored into the path.
Surveying and marking exact positions must be completed prior to drilling or setting bollard foundations to ensure proper alignment and spacing.
Bollards must be physically installed before any finishing treatments like reflective markings can be applied on them.
Safety barriers (bollards) must be in place before the path is opened to cyclists and pedestrians to prevent vehicular access.
The subgrade must be prepared and compacted to ensure a stable foundation before any lighting infrastructure (conduits, poles) is installed.
Underground conduits and wiring for the lighting system must be laid in the trench before the lighting fixtures are installed to provide electrical connectivity.
After all lighting fixtures are physically installed, the system must be tested and commissioned to ensure proper operation, electrical safety, and illumination levels.
Lighting poles and fixtures should be installed before final paving to avoid damaging the finished pavement surface during pole installation and trenching work.
It is preferable to install lighting before path signage and lane markings so that workers can see the path clearly during final marking installation, though not a strict physical necessity.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and foundation prepared before any built-in seating components can be installed to ensure structural stability.
The primary structural elements (walls, columns, or support beams) that the child-scale seating attaches to or integrates with must be erected first.

Any electrical outlets, lighting, or plumbing near the seating area should be roughed-in before the seating is built to avoid rework, though this is a coordination preference rather than a strict physical requirement.
The seating structure must be in place so that flooring materials (e.g., tiles, wood, or carpet) can be cut and fitted precisely around the base of the seating.
The seating installation must be complete before painters apply final coats to walls and trim around the seating area to ensure a seamless finish.
The counter/desk must be placed on a stable, level floor surface, which requires the floor slab to be installed first to provide proper support and anchoring.
The counter/desk is typically mounted to or supported by wall framing, so walls must be framed in place before the counter/desk can be secured.

Any sink or water supply plumbing that will serve the counter/desk area must be roughed-in behind the walls and through the floor before the counter/desk is installed, as access would be blocked afterward.

After the structural installation of the counter/desk unit, the final surface finishing (e.g., laminating, sealing, or painting) must be applied to protect the surface and achieve the desired appearance.

Electrical outlets near the counter/desk area are ideally placed after the counter is installed to ensure proper height alignment, though this could be done before if measurements are known precisely.

predecessor: Framing of wall where shelving will be installed
rationale: The built-in shelving needs to be mounted to or recessed into the wall frame; the framing must be complete to provide structural support.
If the shelving unit has integrated lighting, electrical rough-in must be completed before installing the shelving to avoid rewiring after installation.

If shelving is recessed, drywall work around the niche must be done after shelving is in place for proper edges; if surface-mounted, shelving is installed after drywall. Typically built-ins are set before finish work or after, depending on design. For flush built-ins, shelving goes in after rough framing but before drywall to create a seamless look.

Built-in shelving is usually installed before flooring so that the shelving sits on the subfloor and flooring butts up to it, or vice versa depending on design. This is a preference to avoid cutting flooring around the shelving base.
The shelving must be installed before final painting or staining of the trim and shelving surfaces can be completed for a finished appearance.
The door frame must be installed to provide the structural support and mounting surface for child-height door hardware such as handles and locks.
Walls and door openings must be fully framed and finished before any door hardware can be attached to them.
The door itself must be hung in the frame before child-height handles, knobs, or latches can be installed on it.
After installing child-height hardware, the door must be adjusted and tested to ensure the hardware operates correctly at the lower height.
While hardware can be installed after trim, it is often preferred to install hardware after trim work is complete to avoid damaging the hardware during trim installation.
The guardrail/barrier system requires a solid, level concrete foundation or slab to anchor and support the posts and structure securely.
Wall or structural framing must be in place to provide attachment points and backing for barrier systems that adjoin or integrate with walls.
Barrier systems define the protected edge; finished flooring is installed up to the barrier to ensure proper fit, height, and safety compliance.
The barrier must be fully installed before safety inspections can verify its compliance with child safety codes and building regulations.
While finishes can be done before the barrier, it is more efficient to install the barrier first to avoid damage to finished surfaces during drilling and mounting.
The structural wall framing must be completed before any partition walls can be installed, as partitions are non-load-bearing infill between structural elements.
Electrical and data cabling must be roughed-in before partition closure, as running wiring after the partition is built would require cutting into finished surfaces.
Any plumbing lines that run within or behind the partition walls must be installed before the partition is closed up, to avoid costly rework.
Gypsum board (drywall) is applied directly over the partition framing after the partition structure is complete and all rough-ins are inspected.
Door frames require the partition wall to be in place as the supporting structure for attachment and alignment.
The subfloor must be clean, level, and dry before any flooring material can be installed to ensure proper adhesion and a smooth finished surface.
Underlayment or padding is required beneath child-safe flooring (e.g., foam padding under carpet or vinyl) for cushioning, soundproofing, and moisture protection.
Rough-in work for electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, and HVAC must be completed before flooring is installed to avoid damaging finished flooring during subsequent work.
Baseboards and trim are installed after flooring is laid so that the flooring can extend beneath the trim for a clean, finished look and to hide expansion gaps.
While painting can be done before or after flooring, it is often preferred to complete final painting after flooring to avoid drips and spills on the new floor surface.
Shelving must be installed before it can be stocked with materials.

predecessor: Pour and Cure Concrete Floor Slab
rationale: A stable, cured floor slab is required to anchor and support low-level shelving; installation on uncured concrete would compromise stability.
Wall framing and drywall must be completed so that shelving can be anchored to finished walls and final room dimensions are known.
Electrical wiring must be roughed in before shelving is installed; otherwise, wires behind shelving become inaccessible and create safety hazards.
The glazing frame must be in place to provide a secure mounting structure for the safety glass panels.
The wall or structural opening must be prepared and ready before fitting any glazing.
Sealant must be applied to the edges of the installed safety glazing to ensure water tightness and weatherproofing.
Trim or beading is fitted after the glass is in place to secure and finish the edges.
A safety inspection of the installed glazing is recommended after completion to verify compliance with safety standards.

Framing walls and running rough-in plumbing/electrical must be finished so that the backing, support structure, and utility connections are in place for securely mounting child-height fixtures (e.g., sinks, toilets, drinking fountains).

Walls must be finished and painted (or otherwise surfaced) before fixtures are installed to avoid damage to the finished wall surface and to ensure proper sealing and mounting against a completed surface.

Flooring must be completed so that fixtures (especially floor-mounted toilets or sinks) are installed on top of the finished floor at the correct height reference, and to prevent damage to the flooring during fixture installation.

successor: Final Plumbing & Electrical Trim-Out and Connection
rationale: After fixtures are physically mounted, the final connections for supply lines, drains, and any electrical components must be made to complete the installation and make the fixtures operational.

successor: Commissioning and Testing of Child-Height Fixtures
rationale: Once fixtures are installed and connected, they must be tested for proper operation (water flow, drainage, electrical function) to verify they meet code and perform correctly for child users.
The door frame and rough opening must be framed before any door hardware including child-height hardware can be mounted.
The door itself must be hung in the frame before child-height door hardware (e.g., handles, locks, hinges at lower height) can be mounted onto it.
After mounting the child-height hardware, the door must be tested and adjusted to ensure proper operation of the child-height handles and locks.
It is a soft preference to inspect child-height hardware after installation to verify safety and compliance before occupancy.

predecessor: Install Posts or Supports for Guardrails
rationale: The guardrails require posts or supports to be anchored in place before the railing sections can be attached.
Guardrails are typically installed onto a completed structural frame (deck, balcony, or stair edge) to provide the supporting substrate.

successor: Perform Safety Inspection / Load Testing of Guardrails
rationale: After installation, guardrails must be inspected and tested to verify they meet safety codes and child-safe spacing requirements before the area is put into use.

successor: Apply Finish or Sealant to Guardrails (if required)
rationale: Finishing (painting, staining, sealing) can be done after installation for aesthetic or weather protection, but this is a soft preference as it does not affect structural/physical ordering.

successor: Proceed with Adjacent Flooring or Decking Finishes
rationale: Guardrails are often installed before adjacent finish work to avoid damage, but this is a logical workflow preference rather than a strict physical necessity.

successor: Install Acoustic Treatment in Children's Zones
rationale: Structural framing and enclosure must be finished to provide the wall and ceiling cavities where acoustic treatment materials (baffles, panels, insulation) will be installed.

predecessor: Complete rough-in of MEP services (electrical, HVAC, plumbing)
successor: Install Acoustic Treatment in Children's Zones
rationale: Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before acoustic treatments are installed to avoid damaging finished acoustic surfaces and to allow access for ductwork, conduits, and piping within wall/ceiling spaces.

predecessor: Install Acoustic Treatment in Children's Zones
rationale: Acoustic treatments such as insulation batts and resilient channels are typically installed within wall and ceiling assemblies before the final cladding (drywall, paneling) is applied.

predecessor: Install Acoustic Treatment in Children's Zones
rationale: It is generally preferable to install acoustic wall/ceiling treatments before final flooring to avoid damaging finished floors during overhead work and to allow for seamless integration of wall-base details.

predecessor: Install Acoustic Treatment in Children's Zones
rationale: Acoustic panels and treatments are often painted or finished as part of the final finishing work; painting should occur after installation to ensure a uniform appearance, though this is a sequencing preference rather than a strict physical requirement.
The child-scale seating must be built on top of a completed subfloor to provide a stable, level base and proper structural support.
The seating may integrate with or be attached to wall framing, so walls must be framed first to establish the spatial envelope and support structure.
Any electrical outlets, switches, or plumbing lines near the seating area must be roughed in before the built-in seating is constructed, to avoid the need for later demolition or difficult retrofits.

Finished flooring should be installed up to or around the base of the built-in seating for a clean, finished appearance and to avoid cutting flooring materials around an already-installed seating structure.

Finishing walls after the seating is built allows for seamless caulking and painting where the seating meets the walls, though it is a soft preference as it could be done before if careful masking is employed.
Corner guards must be installed on finished walls; painting or wall finishing must be complete to provide a clean surface for adhesive or mechanical attachment of corner guards.
Drywall must be in place as the substrate for wall finishing and subsequent corner guard attachment.
Soft preference: touch-ups may be done after guard installation to cover any damage, but not strictly required.
Corner guards typically extend to the floor line; flooring should be installed after to ensure clean alignment and avoid damaging guards during floor work.
The floor must be prepared, leveled, and finished before partitions are installed to ensure stability and proper alignment of the partitions.

predecessor: Complete Structural Framing and Wall Rough-Ins
rationale: All structural framing, electrical, plumbing, and other rough-in work must be completed before partitions are installed to avoid needing to cut through or relocate the partitions later.

successor: Apply Child-Safe Finishes and Edge Protectors
rationale: Child-safe finishes, corner guards, and edge protectors must be applied after the partitions are in place to cover all exposed edges and surfaces.
Door hardware, handles, and child-height accessories are mounted onto the partitions after they are fully installed.

Painting and decorative treatments can be completed before or after partition installation, but it is generally more efficient to paint before installing partitions to avoid overspray or damage; however, touch-ups are often needed afterward.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any structure or enclosure can be erected on the site.
A stable foundation or base is required to anchor the carnival structure/enclosure securely.
The main load-bearing framework (poles, beams, trusses) must be assembled before the enclosure elements (walls, roofs, tarps) can be attached.
The enclosure shell must be complete before interior decorations, lighting, flooring, and thematic elements can be installed inside.
The structure must be fully assembled before safety inspections and load testing can be conducted to ensure it meets regulatory standards.

Wall framing and electrical rough-in (including running wiring to outlet locations) must be completed before child-safe outlet boxes and receptacles can be installed, as the outlets need to be mounted into the framed wall cavities and connected to the branch circuit wiring.

Child-safe outlet boxes must be installed and properly secured in the wall framing before wall finishing materials (e.g., drywall) are applied, because the outlet boxes need to be flush with the finished wall surface and the drywall must be cut around the boxes.

successor: Outlet Trim and Cover Plate Installation
rationale: The child-safe outlet receptacle must be wired and installed into the outlet box before the tamper-resistant cover plates or safety caps can be attached, as the cover plates mount directly over the installed receptacles.

predecessor: Electrical Panel and Circuit Breaker Installation
rationale: The electrical panel with appropriate arc-fault circuit-interrupter (AFCI) and ground-fault circuit-interrupter (GFCI) breakers must be installed and wired to the outlet branch circuits before power can be connected to the child-safe outlets, ensuring overcurrent protection is in place.

All child-safe outlets must be fully installed before the final electrical safety inspection can be conducted, as the inspector must verify that tamper-resistant shutters, grounding, and GFCI/AFCI protection are correctly implemented.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable foundation for the stage structure.
The concrete base or deck foundation must be poured and cured before the stage platform can be assembled or installed on top.
Underground electrical conduit for stage lighting and sound equipment must be laid before the platform is built over it, to avoid later trenching.
The stage platform must be complete to provide a working surface and anchor points for erecting the overhead canopy and rigging equipment.
Speakers, lighting fixtures, and AV equipment are placed on and around the completed stage; the platform must exist first to support these installations.
A stable foundation and prepared site are physically required before the kiosk structure can be erected.
Underground conduit and rough electrical/data lines must be installed before the kiosk is placed and finished.
Final wiring, outlets, switches, and light fixtures can only be installed after the kiosk structure is in place.
Interior walls, counters, flooring, and paint must follow the structural installation of the kiosk.
Point-of-sale hardware, ticket printers, and computer systems require the completed booth/kiosk for secure mounting and power integration.
A stable foundation and leveled site must be prepared before building any structure including a concession stand.
Water supply and drainage lines must be roughed in before the concession counter and sink fixtures can be installed.
Electrical wiring and outlet boxes must be run to the concession area before the counter, equipment (e.g., refrigerator, cash register), and lighting can be connected and finalized.
The concession stand base/frame must be in place before countertops and sinks can be mounted on top of it.
Cooking equipment, refrigeration units, and point-of-sale systems are installed after the concession counter structure is complete to ensure proper fit and support.
The ground must be leveled, obstacles removed, and the booth location marked before any structure can be erected.
A stable base or foundation (e.g., concrete slab, deck platform, or compacted pad) is required to support the booth frame and prevent shifting or sinking.
Lumber, fasteners, panels, and hardware must be on-site before assembly of the booth structure can begin.
Electrical lines for lighting, scoring displays, or game mechanisms are typically run through or along the frame after the booth structure is erected.
Targets, throw lines, ball returns, and other interactive game components are mounted onto or within the completed booth frame.
Applying paint, banners, and decorations is easier and yields a cleaner finish once the structural frame is complete, though some decoration could theoretically be done beforehand.
The ground must be cleared, graded, and compacted before any foundation work can begin to ensure a stable base for the ride foundation.

Underground utility conduits and rough-in connections must be placed in the ground before the foundation is poured, so that services can be routed to the ride without cutting through the cured concrete later.
The foundation and anchor bolts must be fully cured and structurally ready before the ride's steel superstructure can be erected and bolted down to them.
The ride's electrical and control systems are typically mounted on or near the foundation; the foundation must be in place to provide a secure mounting surface for control cabinets and raceways.

Surrounding concrete work such as final grade slabs, pedestrian pathways, and decorative finishes around the ride area must be completed after the main foundation is set and stable to avoid damaging the primary structural base.
The structural frame (e.g., steel or aluminum framing) must be erected first to provide a stable support structure onto which the carnival enclosure curtain/partition can be mounted or attached.
The floor or deck surface must be completed and prepared (cleaned, leveled, and finished) to serve as the base for the curtain/partition and to ensure proper sealing and anchoring at the bottom edge.

The overhead or canopy structure (e.g., roof, top rail, or overhead track system) must be installed first to provide the top attachment points or tracks from which the curtain/partition is suspended or guided.

successor: Interior Fit-Out and Decoration of Enclosed Space
rationale: Once the curtain/partition is in place, it defines the enclosed space, allowing subsequent interior fit-out activities (e.g., lighting, flooring, decorative elements) to proceed within the defined area without interference from open sides.

successor: MEP Rough-In and Final Connections Within Enclosure
rationale: While MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) rough-in can partially be done before the curtain is installed, final connections, outlet placement, and commissioning within the enclosure are best performed after the partition is in place to ensure accurate positioning relative to the finished walls.
The ground must be prepared and leveled before installing barricades or queue rails to ensure they can be securely placed and remain stable.
If the barricade system requires permanent posts or embedded bases, concrete footings must be poured and cured first to provide a solid anchor for the railing.
Once barricades and rails are in place, the queue pathway is defined, allowing for accurate placement of signage, lane markings, and crowd direction indicators along the established route.
Barricades and queue rails must be installed before the event or attraction opens to the public to ensure safe crowd control and orderly queuing from the start of operations.
Barricades and rails must be in place and secured so that safety inspections can verify their stability, proper placement, and compliance with crowd management standards before public use.
The ground must be properly graded, compacted, and leveled before any flooring or decking can be installed to ensure a stable, level surface and prevent future settlement or unevenness.

predecessor: Installation of Underground Utilities (water, sewer, storm drains, gas, electric)
rationale: Underground utility lines must be placed before decking is installed because tearing up finished flooring to access underground services would be destructive and costly.
If a concrete slab or structural foundation is required for the carnival area, it must be poured and cured before decking materials are installed on top.
Rides and heavy attractions require a stable, finished flooring surface for safe installation and anchoring; the decking provides the load-bearing platform.
Booths and vendor stands are typically placed on top of the finished flooring/decking, so the decking must be complete before these structures are assembled.
A level, cleared, and stable ground surface is physically required before any tent or pavilion can be erected to ensure structural stability and safety.

predecessor: Delivery of Tent/Pavilion Materials to Site
rationale: The tent fabric, poles, frames, stakes, and all hardware must be physically present on site before assembly can commence.

predecessor: Layout and Marking of Footprint (Staking Plan)
rationale: The exact perimeter and anchor-point locations must be marked on the ground to guide the erection process and ensure the tent fits the allocated space.

successor: Install Interior Flooring or Ground Cover
rationale: Flooring or ground cover is laid inside the structure after the frame and canopy are up, as it would be in the way or get damaged if installed before the tent is erected.

successor: Install Lighting and Electrical Systems Inside Tent
rationale: Electrical wiring, lighting fixtures, and power distribution are installed after the structure is up since they are suspended from or run along the frame, and would be impossible or unsafe to install beforehand.

predecessor: Install Site Lighting / General Area Lighting
rationale: General site lighting provides the necessary ambient illumination and power infrastructure for safe and effective installation of specialized carnival lighting. It must be in place before carnival lighting work begins.
Electrical rough-ins (conduit, wiring, junction boxes) must be completed to provide power sources for carnival lighting fixtures before they can be installed.
The carnival lighting system must be fully installed before it can be tested, commissioned, and verified for proper operation and safety compliance.

While some theming can proceed in parallel, installing carnival lighting first allows lighting effects to be coordinated with decorative elements for best visual impact; this is a soft preference for aesthetic sequencing.
All installations including carnival lighting must be complete before the final inspection and approval can be conducted for the area.
The sound system layout and equipment placement must be designed before installation can begin to ensure proper coverage and equipment selection.
All speakers, amplifiers, mixers, cables, and related equipment must be purchased and delivered to the site before installation can commence.
The site must have power supply, mounting structures, and weather protection in place before sound system components can be installed.

successor: Test and Calibrate Carnival Sound System
rationale: Sound system testing, tuning, and calibration can only be performed after all components are installed and wired.

successor: Conduct Carnival Sound Check and Rehearsals
rationale: Sound checks and rehearsal sessions require the installed sound system to be operational before performers and technicians can use it.
The foundation area must be prepared (cleared, leveled, compacted) to provide a stable base before any platform construction can begin.
Concrete footings or piers must be poured and cured to support the stage platform structure; building the platform on unprepared ground would be unstable.
All necessary lumber, decking, fasteners, and hardware must be on-site before platform assembly can commence.
The stage platform must be fully constructed to provide a working surface and structural base for erecting the roof or canopy supports.
Lighting fixtures and rigging are mounted on or above the completed stage platform, which must be structurally ready to bear loads.
The ticket booth/kiosk must be physically fabricated and assembled before it can be installed on-site.
A level concrete pad or foundation must be poured and cured to provide a stable base for installing the kiosk.

predecessor: Run Electrical Conduit / Wiring to Kiosk Location
rationale: Underground or in-slab electrical conduits must be in place before the kiosk is set, so that power can be connected to the unit.

predecessor: Run Data / Network Cabling to Kiosk Location
rationale: Network and communication cables must be laid to the kiosk location before the unit is installed to enable connectivity.

successor: Connect Electrical & Data Services to Kiosk
rationale: After the kiosk is physically placed, electricians and technicians can terminate wiring and connect power and data services to the unit.
The kiosk must be installed and connected before it can be powered on, tested, and commissioned for use.
While signage can be installed before the kiosk, it is typically mounted after the kiosk is in place to ensure proper alignment and positioning.

Utility rough-ins (plumbing for sinks/ice machines, electrical for fryers/refrigeration, and mechanical ventilation for cooking equipment) must be in place before final equipment can be connected and installed.

predecessor: Pour and Cure Concrete Floor Slab
rationale: A finished, cured concrete floor is required to provide a stable, level base for heavy kitchen equipment such as fryers, grills, and refrigeration units.
Wall finishes (tile, FRP panels, paint) and ceiling finishes must be completed to meet health code requirements and avoid damaging finished surfaces during equipment installation.
After concession equipment is set in its final position, electricians and plumbers can make the final connections (hardwiring, gas lines, drain hookups) that require exact equipment placement.
All food service equipment must be fully installed, operational, and properly connected before the health department can inspect for code compliance and issue a food service permit.
The layout and location of game booths must be determined before they can be physically set up in the correct positions.
All game booth components, prizes, decorations, and play equipment must be on-site before assembly and setup can begin.
The ground or floor area where booths will be placed must be cleared, leveled, and ready to support the structures.
Games must be fully assembled and booths arranged before they can be tested for proper operation, safety, and fairness.
Staff scheduling can begin before booths are up, but final assignment to specific booths requires knowing which booths are operational and where they are located.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any foundation work can begin to ensure a stable and properly graded surface for concrete pouring and anchor installation.
Accurate survey staking and layout marking is required to position the ride anchors and foundations at the correct coordinates, elevations, and orientation per engineering drawings.
Any underground or overhead utilities in the anchor/foundation footprint must be relocated or protected before excavation and concrete work to avoid damage and ensure safety.
Soil bearing capacity and geotechnical data must be obtained to design the proper foundation dimensions, reinforcement, and anchor embedment depths.
The ride anchors and concrete foundations must be fully cured and achieve specified strength before the steel structure and ride components can be erected and bolted down to them.
After the anchor/foundation concrete is poured, it must undergo a specified curing period and strength testing before any loads can be applied from the ride structure.
The installation area must be cleared of debris, obstructions, and hazards before barricades and queue systems can be set up to ensure a safe and stable installation.
Any necessary permits for temporary structures or traffic/pedestrian management must be obtained before installing barricades or queue barriers.
The planned layout and ground markings for the queue paths and barricade positions must be established first to guide correct placement.
Barricades and queue systems must be in place to control access, crowd flow, and safety before the main event or construction operation can begin.
After barricades are installed, a safety inspection must verify their stability, correct positioning, and compliance before the area is opened for use.
All carnival utility systems (power, water, lighting) must be fully installed and connected before they can be tested, inspected, and commissioned for safe operation.
Utilities must be commissioned and verified as operational and safe before the carnival can open to the public for use.
Formal commissioning of utilities is a prerequisite for commencing full carnival operations, ensuring all systems are functioning correctly.
The structural frame and load-bearing walls must be in place to support the sound-attenuating partition system before it can be installed.
Any wiring, conduits, or piping that will run within or behind the partition must be roughed in before the partition is closed up, otherwise it would require destructive rework.
Switches, outlets, and other finish electrical components mounted on or through the partition can only be installed after the partition framing and sheathing are complete.
Final paint or wall finish cannot be applied until the partition surface is fully installed and prepared.

While acoustic caulking and sealing can begin immediately after the partition is built, formal sound attenuation testing is a soft preference that should follow completion, as it is for quality assurance rather than a physical necessity for subsequent trades.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the acoustic door assembly can be installed, as the door unit requires a structurally sound and properly sized opening.

Acoustic seals (perimeter gaskets, drop seals, and threshold seals) must be installed around the door after the door assembly is in place to ensure the airtight acoustic seal required for sound attenuation.
Hardware such as hinges, locks, handles, and closers must be fitted after the door assembly is hung and aligned to ensure proper operation and fit.
The final floor finish (or at least the subfloor level) should be completed before installing the acoustic door to establish the correct undercut clearance and threshold height for the acoustic seal.

Acoustic performance testing can only be conducted after the door assembly, seals, and hardware are fully installed; however, this is a verification activity rather than a physical construction dependency.
The seating nook requires a stable, level base; the foundation and floor slab must be finished to support the structure.
The nook is often built into or against walls, so wall framing must be complete to define the space and provide attachment points.
Electrical outlets, lighting, or data cabling intended to serve the nook area must be roughed in before the nook is enclosed or built.
Drywall and paint work around or adjacent to the nook should follow its installation to achieve a seamless finished appearance.
Flooring (e.g., tile, hardwood, carpet) around and up to the nook base must be installed after the nook is in place to ensure proper fit and transitions.
The area must be identified and assessed as a designated quiet zone before signage can be installed, as signage indicates an established quiet zone.
Signage design must be completed and approved before fabrication and installation can begin.
Physical signs must be fabricated before they can be installed in the quiet zone area.
Signage must be in place and visible before quiet zone rules can be formally enforced, as patrons need visual notification of the quiet zone.
Installation of signage must be complete before a final inspection can verify proper placement and compliance with quiet zone requirements.
The reception counter must be mounted on a finished, cured concrete slab to provide a stable, level foundation.

predecessor: Complete rough-in electrical for reception area
rationale: Electrical wiring, outlets, and data cabling for the counter's computer, phone, and lighting must be installed behind walls and floors before the counter is placed to avoid costly rework.

Flooring materials such as tile, carpet, or vinyl should be laid up to and around the counter base for a seamless finish; installing flooring first would trap the counter in place and complicate future removal.
The countertop is mounted directly on the base cabinet or frame of the reception counter, so the base must be in place first.

successor: Install signage and wayfinding elements above counter
rationale: Signage is typically mounted above or behind the counter for visibility, but it can be installed concurrently or even slightly before as a soft preference for aesthetic alignment.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) rough-in work (conduit, piping, wiring) must be completed before installing acoustic partitions, as these services are installed within wall cavities and would be inaccessible or require rework if partitions are installed first.
The floor slab or deck must be finished, cured, and clean to provide a stable base for acoustic partition tracks and bottom plates to be anchored securely.
Overhead ceiling grids or furring that will support the top of acoustic partitions must be installed first so the partition top track can be securely attached to the structure above.
Acoustic sealants (caulking at joints, perimeter gaps, and penetrations) are applied after partition installation to ensure airtightness and maximize sound transmission class (STC) ratings.

Final surface finishing such as drywall taping, mudding, and painting must occur after the acoustic partition framework is erected and enclosed, as the partitions form the substrate for these finishes.
The structural frame and roof deck must be in place to provide a substrate for suspending the acoustic ceiling grid and tiles.
All ductwork, conduit, piping, and wiring that will run above the ceiling must be installed before the ceiling grid is hung, otherwise access would be blocked.
Fire sprinkler mains and branch lines must be installed above the ceiling prior to enclosing the space with the acoustic ceiling.

While the ceiling tiles are typically pre-finished, any painting of the grid or perimeter trim is best done after installation. This is a soft preference as it can be done concurrently or pre-finished.
Typically flooring installation follows ceiling installation to avoid damaging finished floors with scaffolding and dropped debris, but it is a soft preference as some trades sequence otherwise.

The subfloor must be clean, dry, level, and properly prepared (e.g., patched, smoothed, primed) before any soft flooring (e.g., carpet, vinyl, linoleum, cork) can be installed; otherwise, the flooring will not adhere properly or will telegraph imperfections.
Structural framing, sheathing, and load-bearing walls must be complete so the building envelope is stable and the subfloor deck is fully supported before finishing flooring is laid.

All rough-in work for plumbing, electrical, and HVAC that runs below the floor or within walls must be completed before installing soft flooring, because accessing these systems afterward would require tearing up the finished floor.

Baseboards and shoe moldings are installed on top of the finished flooring to cover the expansion gap and provide a clean transition; the flooring must be in place first so trim can sit flush against it.

While painting can be done before flooring, it is often preferred to complete painting first to avoid drips and overspray on the new floor. However, this is a soft preference — if the floor is carefully protected, painting can occur afterward.
The acoustic glazing units must be installed into a pre-existing window frame that supports and seals the glass assembly.
The rough opening in the wall or facade must be ready and properly sized before the acoustic glazing assembly can be placed.
After the glazing unit is assembled and positioned, sealants must be applied to ensure acoustic insulation and weatherproofing.
Final acoustic testing can only be performed after the glazing assembly is fully installed to verify sound transmission class ratings.
Interior trim and finishing elements around the glazing can only be installed once the acoustic glass assembly is securely in place.
The floor slab must be in place to provide a solid substrate for acoustic sealant application, ensuring proper adhesion and acoustic separation between spaces.
Wall framing creates the cavities and surfaces where acoustic sealant will be applied along the base of walls and at joints; sealant cannot be applied before the wall structure exists.
One side of the wall assembly is typically installed first, and acoustic sealant is applied at the perimeter joints and penetrations before the second side is closed up.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins must be completed so that acoustic sealant can be applied around all penetrations and openings to ensure an airtight acoustic barrier before the wall is closed.

After acoustic sealant is applied at joints, perimeters, and around penetrations, the remaining drywall side can be installed to complete the assembly, trapping the sealant in place for acoustic isolation.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared to ensure proper drainage and a stable base before constructing the accessible ramp to prevent settling or structural issues.
The ramp requires a solid foundation or slab to anchor into; the base must cure before ramp construction to maintain structural integrity.
Any underground utilities (drainage, electrical conduits) must be installed and covered before building the ramp above them to avoid excavation after ramp completion.
The ramp structure must be fully installed before applying non-slip surface coatings, texture finishes, or sealants to ensure proper adhesion and coverage.
Handrails and guardrails are mounted onto or adjacent to the completed ramp structure; the ramp must be in place to serve as the reference for rail alignment and attachment points.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the door assembly can be installed.
The door frame (jambs, head, and sill) must be installed and secured before the door assembly can be hung or mounted.
Finished flooring must be in place to establish the correct threshold height and under-door clearance required for accessibility compliance.
The threshold must be installed after the door is hung to ensure proper alignment and weather sealing relative to the door bottom.
Door hardware such as handles, locks, closers, and automatic openers must be installed after the door is hung and aligned to ensure correct fit and operation.
The rough opening for the window must be framed and prepared before the accessible window unit can be installed.
The accessible window must be installed and secured before exterior sealing and waterproofing can be applied around it.
Interior trim, casing, and drywall finishing around the window can only be completed after the window unit is fully installed.
The accessible window hardware, crank mechanisms, and ease-of-operation testing must occur after the window is installed and sealed.
Load-bearing wall framing must be complete to provide the structural opening and support needed for the accessible window unit.
Signage must be mounted on finished wall surfaces; installing signage before wall finishes are complete would require removal or damage during finishing work.
Accessible signage (e.g., floor-level wayfinding, tactile indicators) must be placed on completed flooring to ensure correct placement and adherence.
Illuminated or powered signage requires electrical supply and conduit that must be roughed-in before signage can be installed and connected.
Overhead signage may be suspended from ceilings; while not always required, installing after ceiling completion avoids rework.
Accessible signage must be fully installed and verified before building inspection to confirm compliance with accessibility codes (e.g., ADA).
Signage must be in place before occupants or visitors can use the building, as wayfinding and accessible egress signage are required for safe occupancy.
Final paint touch-ups may be scheduled after signage to avoid paint splatter on newly installed signs, though this is a quality preference rather than a physical necessity.

successor: Fire Alarm and Safety System Testing
rationale: Signage indicating fire safety equipment (e.g., fire extinguisher signs, exit signs) should ideally be verified before final system testing, but testing can proceed without signage in place.
The floor must be finished and level before installing an accessible counter to ensure proper height and stability for accessibility compliance.
Electrical outlets and wiring for under-counter areas must be roughed in before counter installation to avoid having to cut into or work around the counter.
Plumbing supply and drain lines for sinks (if incorporated) must be roughed in before the counter is installed.
Walls must be framed, drywalled, and finished to provide a solid backing surface for mounting the counter and to establish the correct wall height references.
The base cabinet or support structure for the accessible counter must be in place first before any countertop or work surface finish layer is applied.
The counter surface must be installed before the sink and faucet can be mounted into or onto the counter.
Installing outlets, switches, or GFCI receptacles on or above the counter is easier and safer after the counter is in place, though rough wiring must precede counter installation.
Grab bars must be securely anchored to wall studs or blocking within the wall framing, which must be installed first.
The wall surface material (e.g., cement board, tile backer) must be in place to provide a substrate for grab bar mounting.
Waterproofing must be completed before grab bar installation to ensure the wall assembly is moisture-protected.
If grab bars are installed over tile, the tile surface must be finished and cured before drilling and mounting grab bars.
The drinking fountain requires water supply and drain connections that must be roughed in before the fixture can be installed.
The drinking fountain is typically mounted on a wall, so wall framing must be in place to provide structural support.
Wall finishes must be completed behind and around the mounting area so the fountain can be properly sealed and finished against the wall.
While the fountain can be installed after rough flooring, final floor finishes near the unit are best done after installation to ensure a tight fit and proper ADA clearance.
After the fountain is installed, the final plumbing connections, fixture trim, and water pressure/leak testing can be completed.

Tactile warning surfaces must be embedded in or placed adjacent to concrete curbs and gutters at pedestrian crossings; the concrete structure must be formed and cured first to provide a stable substrate.
The base course, grading, and compaction of the pedestrian pathway must be completed to ensure proper drainage and a level surface before placing tactile warning surfaces.
Tactile warning surfaces are typically cast into or applied on top of ADA-compliant curb ramps; the ramp concrete must be poured, screeeded, and finished to receive the tactile surface.
Once the tactile warning surface is placed, surrounding concrete or paving must be finished, jointed, and cured to integrate the warning surface seamlessly and prevent displacement.

successor: Final Inspection and ADA Compliance Verification
rationale: Tactile warning surfaces are a critical accessibility feature; their installation must be completed before final walkthroughs to verify compliance with ADA and local accessibility standards.
Electrical rough-in wiring must be installed in walls before switches and outlets can be placed and connected to the wiring system.

Switches and outlets are typically mounted on or within finished wall surfaces; however, the boxes are installed before drywall and the devices are trimmed out after. Strictly, the box is installed before wall finish, and the switch/outlet device is installed after wall finish and painting. For the device itself, wall finish must be complete before final trim installation.
Switches and outlets must be fully installed and connected before electrical system testing can verify correct operation, polarity, and grounding.
The electrical boxes and conduit runs that house the switch/outlet wiring must be positioned in the framing before the device itself can be mounted and wired.
Cover plates are installed over the switch/outlet device after the device is securely mounted and wired, completing the finished appearance and providing safety.
Wall framing must be in place to provide structural support for electrical boxes and to define the locations where switches and outlets are installed.

While it is common practice to paint walls before installing switch/outlet devices to avoid paint on the devices, it is a soft preference; devices can be installed before painting if carefully masked.

Power and data cabling must be run through conduit and terminated at the intercom location before the intercom device can be installed, as the intercom requires electrical power and network connectivity.
The intercom unit mounts onto or into the finished wall surface; framing and drywall must be complete to provide a stable mounting surface and proper backing support.
The intercom hardware must be physically installed and wired before it can be powered on and programmed with access credentials, door release schedules, and audio/video settings.

Trim-out of switches, outlets, and device faceplates, as well as functional testing of the entry system, must occur after the intercom is mounted and connected to ensure all components are operational and visually finished.

predecessor: Concrete Slab or Foundation Work (for gate/post-mounted units)
rationale: If the intercom is mounted on a pedestal, gate post, or wall at a building entrance, the concrete foundation or supporting structure must be cured and ready to receive the mounting hardware.
Fixed seating edges typically require a stable concrete slab or structural floor to be in place to anchor or support the seating edge system.
Steel framing establishes the primary structural grid and support points for seating tiers, and must be completed before fixed seating edge components can be installed.
Fixed seating edges form the front boundary of each seating row; seats and backrests are installed after the edge profiles are in place to ensure proper alignment and attachment.
Handrails and guardrails along seating rows typically rely on the fixed seating edge as a reference or attachment point for consistent positioning.
The bollard foundation must be installed and cured before the integrated lighting bollard can be mounted on it.
Electrical conduits must be laid in the ground before bollard installation to allow power supply to the integrated lighting.
The site surface must be graded and prepared to the final elevation before bollards are installed to ensure proper alignment and height.
Landscape finishing such as paving, planting, or decorative surfacing around the bollard must be done after the bollard is installed to avoid damage and ensure a clean finish.
The electrical supply cables must be connected and the integrated lighting system tested after the bollard is physically installed in its final position.
The tree pit excavation must be completed to create the void space before the tree pit structure and grating can be installed.
The subgrade must be properly prepared and compacted to provide a stable base for the tree pit structure.
The tree pit structure and grating must be installed first to provide the containment and support system before the tree can be planted within it.
The tree pit with grating must be fully installed before surrounding paving or hardscape is laid to ensure proper alignment and edge detailing around the grating.
Underground utilities in the vicinity of the tree pit must be located and, if necessary, relocated before excavation and installation of the tree pit to avoid damage and ensure safety.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded before any public square elements (paving, planting, furnishings) can be installed.
All underground utilities (drainage, electrical conduits, water lines) must be laid and backfilled before the square surface is constructed to avoid costly rework.
The load-bearing base layers (crushed stone, concrete slab) must be completed to provide a stable substrate for paving and hardscape elements of the public square.
Major square installation (paving, infrastructure) must be complete before final surface finishes, joint sealing, and detail work can be applied without damage.

While some planting can occur after square installation, it is a soft preference because trees and shrubs are typically installed after hardscape to avoid soil compaction and damage from construction equipment.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the correct depth, shape, and compaction to accommodate the basin structure before any basin installation can begin.
A stable concrete base or foundation slab is required to support the weight of the water feature basin and prevent differential settlement.
Drain lines, water supply pipes, and any electrical conduits for pumps must be laid and stubbed up before the basin is placed, as they will run beneath or into the basin.
The basin shell must be fully assembled and structurally complete before waterproof membranes or liners can be applied to seal the basin.
The basin must be in place and secured so that pump suction lines, return lines, and overflow pipes can be connected to the basin's pre-formed inlets/outlets.

Bicycle rack anchorage requires a solid, level foundation (concrete slab or paved surface) to which the anchor bolts can be securely fastened. The slab or paving must be cured and fully set before anchorage installation.
The ground must be graded and prepared to the correct elevation and drainage profile before the foundation or slab for the bicycle rack is placed, ensuring the rack is level and properly positioned.

Any underground utilities (electrical, water, drainage) in the vicinity must be roughed in and inspected before pouring concrete or paving to avoid cutting into the finished surface for utility access.

successor: Bicycle Rack Installation (Mounting Rack to Anchors)
rationale: The anchor bolts or embedded anchors must be set and cured in the foundation before the bicycle rack itself can be bolted or mounted onto them.

successor: Final Paving or Surface Finish (if applicable)
rationale: If anchor bolts are installed before the final surface finish is applied (e.g., in a staged pour), the anchorage should be completed first so that the final surface can be finished neatly around the rack base for a clean appearance.
The ground must be leveled and prepared before any structure, including a trash receptacle enclosure, can be built upon it.
A concrete pad or foundation is needed to provide a stable base for the trash receptacle enclosure.
The enclosure should be in place before final landscaping and grading around the structure to ensure proper integration.
The trash enclosure must be built before it can be used to contain debris during final site clean-up.
Any underground drainage or utility lines that might run under the enclosure area must be installed before the slab and enclosure are placed.
Wall surfaces must be built and accessible before signage mounting points can be established.
Electrical conduit and wiring for illuminated signage must be installed before signage foundations are finalized.
Concrete floor slabs must be poured and cured to provide a stable mounting substrate for freestanding or wall-based signage foundations.
The signage foundation must be in place and ready before the actual signage panels or letters can be mounted and finished.
It is preferable to paint walls after signage foundations are installed to avoid damage or rework, but it is not a physical necessity.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil before any sub-base preparation can begin, as the sub-base needs to be placed on a clean, stable surface.
The precise layout and boundaries of the square must be marked out before sub-base work starts to ensure correct positioning and dimensions.
Any existing underground utilities within the square area must be relocated or protected before sub-base preparation to avoid damage and ensure safety.
After the sub-base material is placed and prepared, compaction testing must be performed to verify it meets density and strength specifications before proceeding to the next layer.
The prepared sub-base provides a stable foundation; the base course layer cannot be installed until the sub-base preparation is complete and approved.
The ground must be prepared, cleared, and leveled before any structure can be erected to ensure a stable and level foundation for the pergola or trellis.
Concrete footings or foundation piers must be poured and fully cured before the pergola/trellis posts can be anchored to them, providing structural stability.
Any underground utilities (electric, irrigation, gas) must be located and routed away from footing locations before digging to avoid damage and ensure safety.

successor: Climbing Plant Installation or Vine Training
rationale: While planting can occur before or after, training climbing vines onto the trellis/pergola structure is most effective once the structure is complete to provide immediate support.

successor: Electrical Wiring for Lighting or Fans
rationale: Any electrical components such as overhead lighting, ceiling fans, or outlet installations must be done after the structure is erected to run wiring through the beams and rafters properly.
Attaching shade cloths, retractable awnings, or permanent roof panels is typically done after the pergola frame is complete to fit the covering to the exact dimensions.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to provide a stable, level foundation for the pedestal before it can be installed.
A concrete footing or foundation slab must be poured and cured to anchor the pedestal securely and prevent settling or tilting.
Any electrical conduit, drainage, or other underground utilities serving the art pedestal must be installed before the pedestal is placed to avoid rework or damage.
The pedestal serves as the structural base for the artwork; the art piece cannot be mounted or placed until its pedestal is fully installed and stable.

While not strictly physically required, finishing work such as planting, mulching, or paving around the pedestal is best performed after the pedestal is in place to achieve a seamless aesthetic and avoid damage to finished landscaping.
The ramp structure requires a stable load-bearing foundation and concrete slab to anchor and support the ramp system.
The ground must be graded and drainage systems installed to ensure proper water runoff away from the ramp, preventing erosion and water pooling.
Any underground electrical conduits for lighting or drainage pipes beneath the ramp area must be installed before the ramp is built over them.

successor: Ramp Surface Finishing and Non-Slip Coating
rationale: The structural ramp must be fully constructed and cured before applying surface treatments, coatings, or non-slip textures.
Handrails and guardrails are attached to the completed ramp structure; the ramp framework must be in place to serve as the mounting surface.
The site must be graded and excavated to the correct elevations and locations before stormwater planters can be installed, as the planter needs a prepared subgrade and proper drainage connections.

Any underground utilities (drainage pipes, water supply lines) that connect to or pass beneath the stormwater planter must be installed first to avoid disturbing the planter structure after it is built.
The stormwater planter structure (concrete or masonry walls, liner, drainage layer) must be fully constructed before engineered soil media and mulch can be placed within it.
Plants (trees, shrubs, grasses) must be installed after the planter structure is complete and soil media is in place, as the planter provides the containment and growing environment.

While it is physically possible to install adjacent hardscape after the planter, it is preferred to finish the planter first so that final grading and hardscape edges can be flush with the planter walls for a clean finish.
Staircases are typically integrated with the structural frame of the building. The floor slabs, beams, and load-bearing walls must be in place to support and anchor the staircase.

Staircases must be installed before final interior finishes such as flooring and wall cladding around the staircase area can be completed, as the staircase defines the final floor levels and wall interfaces.
Building safety inspections require the staircase (including its structural integrity, dimensions, and clearances) to be fully in place before certifying that means of egress meet code requirements.

The catwalk is a structural component that must be supported by the building's main structure. Foundation and substructure work provide the load-bearing base upon which the catwalk structure will be mounted or attached.

Catwalks are typically suspended from or supported by the main structural frame of the building (e.g., steel beams or concrete structure). The main frame must be in place to provide anchor points and structural support for the catwalk.

If the catwalk is located in the ceiling/roof area (e.g., for access to lighting, HVAC, or maintenance), the roof structure must be completed to define the space and provide overhead support or suspension points for the catwalk.

Catwalks provide access platforms for installing and maintaining overhead building services. The catwalk must be in place before workers can safely install lighting fixtures, HVAC ducts, sprinkler systems, or other overhead equipment from the catwalk access points.

Catwalks are structural access components that need to be installed before ceiling finishes are applied, as the catwalk may be concealed above or integrated with the ceiling system. Finishing works after catwalk installation allow for proper integration and aesthetic treatment around the catwalk structure.
The guardrail/parapet is typically installed on top of the bridge deck or slab; the deck must be in place to provide the mounting surface.
Reinforcement steel for the deck and often for the parapet itself must be placed before concrete parapet forms and concrete are placed.
Formwork must be erected and aligned before concrete for a cast-in-place parapet can be poured.
Waterproofing is often applied after parapets are in place to seal the interface between deck and parapet, but it is a soft preference as sequence could vary.
Guardrail/parapet provides the structural base onto which metal bridge railings or handrails are mounted.
Fall arrest anchors must be attached to stable structural elements (steel beams, concrete slabs) that are already erected and load-bearing.
Workers performing roof installation require fall arrest anchors to be in place for tie-off safety before accessing elevated roof areas.
Exterior cladding work at heights requires fall protection; anchors must be installed and certified before workers can tie off.

While not physically mandatory, it is strongly preferred that fall arrest anchors are installed before overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in to provide fall protection for workers on elevated platforms or lifts.
The specific locations, load ratings, and types of anchors must be designed and approved by a qualified engineer prior to installation to ensure compliance with safety standards.
The structural steel frame must be in place to provide the load-bearing support and attachment points for the high-level glazing system.
The roof structure must be complete to define the top boundary of the glazing and to provide weather protection for the glazing installation work below.
High-level glazing must be installed and sealed before internal finishes can commence to ensure the building envelope is weathertight and to prevent damage to interior finishes.
Glazing must be in place to allow for accurate positioning and integration of mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems that interface with or are located adjacent to the glazed areas.
The high-level glazing panels must be installed before the final sealing and water testing of the façade can be performed to verify weathertightness.

The elevated walkway or platform must be in place before guardrails can be installed, as guardrails are attached to the walkway structure and provide fall protection for workers accessing the completed platform.
The primary structural supports for the elevated area must be erected before guardrails can be mounted, as guardrails rely on the main structure for anchorage and stability.

predecessor: Complete Concrete/Masonry Work on Elevated Slab
rationale: The elevated slab or deck surface must be fully cured and finished to provide a stable base for guardrail posts and to ensure proper alignment and anchoring.
Guardrails must be fully installed and secured before fall protection systems can be tested and inspected to verify compliance with safety standards.

successor: Begin Work on Elevated Finishes/Railing Adjacent Work
rationale: While guardrails provide safety for subsequent finishing work on elevated surfaces, this is a soft preference because some finishing work could potentially be performed with alternative fall protection measures in place before guardrails are installed.
The fall protection plan must be developed to determine the type, location, and quantity of anchors needed before installation can proceed.
Fall protection anchors are typically attached to structural steel or concrete substrates; these supporting structures must be in place and cured before anchors can be installed.
After anchors are installed, they must be pull-tested and inspected to verify load capacity and correct installation before they can be used for worker safety.
