successor: Begin Work at Height (e.g., Roofing, Steel Erection, or Window Installation)
rationale: Fall protection anchors must be installed and certified before workers can tie off to them while performing elevated work tasks.
Once anchors are installed and tested, the entire fall protection system should be certified and tagged before being placed into service.
The balcony/deck requires a stable foundation to support its structural load; the foundation must be fully cured and load-bearing before any deck construction begins.
The balcony/deck is typically attached to or supported by the main building frame; the main structural frame must be in place to provide attachment points and load paths.
Floor joists form the underlying support structure for the deck surface; they must be installed before decking boards or balcony flooring can be laid.
Safety railings and balustrades are mounted onto or anchored to the completed deck structure; the deck platform must be fully built to provide a secure base for railing installation.
Waterproofing membranes and sealants are applied to the finished deck surface to protect against moisture damage; this treatment must be done after the deck structure is complete.
The structural frame must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the elevated glazing system.
The roof structure must be completed to provide overhead protection and support for curtain wall or glazing anchorage at the top of the elevation.
Glazing installation must be complete before sealants and waterproofing can be applied to the perimeter joints to ensure a continuous weather-tight seal.
Interior finishes such as drywall and trim near glazed areas are best performed after glazing to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to allow proper fit around the installed windows.
Elevated glazing should be installed and sealed before final cleaning and commissioning of the building envelope to prevent contamination and allow for inspection of weather-tightness.

The elevator/lift system must be fully installed, including all mechanical, electrical, and control components, before commissioning can begin. Commissioning involves testing and verifying the installed system's functionality.
Electrical power supply and connections to the elevator control panel, motor, and safety systems must be completed before the system can be energized and commissioned.

predecessor: Install Elevator Controller and Control Wiring
rationale: The elevator controller, all control wiring, and communication systems must be in place and terminated before commissioning can proceed, as the controller governs all elevator operations and safety functions.

The elevator must be commissioned (tested and verified) by a qualified elevator contractor before the local authority can inspect and issue an operating permit or certificate of occupancy for the elevator.

Commissioning ensures the elevator operates safely and correctly. The elevator cannot be opened for public or building occupant use until commissioning tests are successfully completed and any deficiencies are resolved.
The stage platform requires a stable and level foundation to be built upon; without proper foundation work, the platform would lack structural support and could settle unevenly.
The steel framing provides the primary structural support system that the stage platform deck will be mounted on or integrated with.
The stage flooring (finish surface) can only be installed after the underlying platform substructure/deck is in place.
Overhead stage lighting rigs and equipment are typically suspended from or supported by the stage platform structure, requiring the platform to be complete before rigging installation.
Safety railings around the stage edges are typically installed after the platform is built, though this could be considered a soft preference if temporary edge protection is used.
Structural wall framing must be completed before mirror wall system installation because mirrors require a stable, load-bearing substrate to attach to.
A solid sheathing or backing surface (e.g., plywood or drywall) must be in place to provide a flat, secure mounting surface for the mirror panels.
Electrical, plumbing, or other mechanical rough-ins within the wall cavity must be completed before mirror installation, as mirrors conceal the wall and prevent future access without removal.
Edge sealing, caulking, or protective coating application for the mirror system must occur after mirrors are installed to ensure complete coverage and water-tightness.

successor: Adjacent Finish Work (e.g., trim, lighting fixtures)
rationale: Trim installation, mirror-mounted lighting, or adjacent wall finishes must follow mirror installation to avoid damaging mirrors during subsequent construction work and to ensure proper alignment.
Ballet barres are typically mounted on walls, so wall framing must be complete to provide structural support for the barre brackets.
Proper wall backing (e.g., plywood or blocking between studs) must be installed to securely anchor the ballet barre brackets.
While the barre can be installed before final floor finishing, it is preferred to complete floor finishing first to avoid damaging the barre during floor work or having to work around the barre.
It is preferable to complete final painting and touch-ups after barre installation to address any marks or damage around the mounted brackets.
The wall framing provides the structural substrate onto which sound-absorbing panels are mounted or attached; panels cannot be installed on an open wall.
Wiring, outlets, switches, and pipes must be run inside the wall cavity before the wall surface is enclosed with panels; otherwise, retrofitting would require removing installed panels.
Acoustic or thermal insulation placed within wall cavities must be installed before panels are attached, as panels cover and seal the wall surface, preventing access to the cavity.

successor: Final Finishing and Painting of Panels
rationale: Once the panels are mounted in place, any final surface treatments, joint sealing, painting, or coating on the panel faces can be applied to complete the aesthetic finish.

Although trim can be installed before panels in some cases, typically baseboards, corner beads, and molding are fitted after panel installation to create clean transitions; this is a soft preference as order can be swapped with careful detailing.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical wiring for sound system
rationale: Electrical wiring must be installed behind walls before cabinetry is built, as sound system components require power and signal connections that would be inaccessible after cabinetry is in place.
Walls behind and around the sound system cabinetry must be finished before cabinets are installed, as the cabinetry will be mounted against or built into finished walls.
Flooring should be completed before heavy cabinetry is placed on top, to avoid damaging the floor and to ensure the cabinets sit level on the finished surface.

successor: Equipment rack installation and component mounting
rationale: Sound system components (amplifiers, processors, etc.) are mounted into the cabinetry after the cabinets are built and secured in place.
Speakers are installed into or onto the cabinetry after the cabinets are constructed, as the cabinetry provides the mounting structure and enclosure for the speakers.
A level, cured concrete slab is required as the structural base for the subfloor assembly; the subfloor cannot be installed on uncured or unprepared concrete.
A vapor barrier and/or sound-dampening underlayment must be placed on the concrete slab before subfloor assembly to prevent moisture damage and provide acoustic isolation.

predecessor: Floor Joist or Sleeper Layout (if raised)
rationale: If the subfloor is a raised sleeper system, the sleepers or joists must be positioned and fastened before the subfloor panels are installed on top.
After the subfloor panels are assembled and fastened, the surface must be sanded and leveled to eliminate any irregularities before the finished dance floor surface is installed.
The final dance floor surface (e.g., hardwood strips, sprung floor overlay, or vinyl) can only be installed after the subfloor substrate is fully assembled and secured.
Floor receptacle boxes are typically embedded in or mounted on the concrete floor slab; the slab must be poured and cured to provide the substrate for box placement.
Power and data conduits must be run in the slab or underfloor before boxes are set, so that the conduits terminate properly into the boxes.
Floor coverings (tile, carpet, etc.) are installed after boxes are placed and adjusted to finished floor height, so that the covering can be cut neatly around the box.
After boxes are secured, the wiring can be pulled from the panel or junction boxes to terminate at the receptacle boxes.
The final cover plates and trim rings for floor boxes are installed after wiring is complete and after the floor covering is finished, but the box body must be in place first.
The subfloor must be level, clean, and dry before installing a dance floor to ensure proper adhesion and a stable, even surface.
Underlayment (such as plywood or specialized padding) must be laid down first to provide a smooth base and protect the dance floor from moisture or unevenness.
While not strictly required, it is preferable to complete rough electrical work for any in-floor lighting or sound systems before installing the dance floor to avoid damaging the finished surface.
Baseboards or wall trim should be installed after the dance floor to cover the expansion gap and create a clean finished edge.
Any final sealing, sanding, or protective coating must be applied after the dance floor boards or panels are fully installed.
Wall framing provides the structural support onto which the mirror wall is mounted; without framing, there is no stable surface for installation.
Electrical wiring and outlet boxes must be installed behind or within the wall before the mirror is placed, as accessing them afterward would require removing the mirror.
Sheathing or backer board provides the finished surface onto which the mirror is adhered or fastened; the mirror cannot be installed over open studs.
Any trim, edge caps, or decorative moldings around the mirror can only be applied after the mirror itself is securely installed in place.
Final inspection of the mirror installation and cleaning of the mirror surface typically occur after the mirror is installed, but this is a procedural preference rather than a physical necessity.
The structural steel framework must be in place to provide the supporting structure from which the lighting grid can be suspended or rigged.
The roof must be installed to protect the lighting grid and rigging equipment from weather exposure before installation begins.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing runs that need to be routed above the lighting grid must be completed before the grid is installed, as the grid would block access to the overhead space.
The lighting grid (trusses, battens, or supports) must be rigged and secured before any lighting fixtures can be mounted or attached to it.

While often done concurrently, if AV equipment is to be hung from the same grid structure, the grid must be fully rigged and load-tested first before suspending AV equipment, though this could be a shared activity.
Ballet barres are typically mounted onto finished drywall surfaces; installing before drywall would leave the barre improperly mounted or require rework.
The dance floor surface must be complete to establish final finished floor elevation, ensuring the barre is mounted at the correct height relative to the floor.
Mirrors are typically installed after barres so that the barre does not obstruct mirror placement and to avoid damaging mirrors when mounting the barre brackets.
While baseboards can technically be installed before barres, it is preferred to install barres first to avoid cutting baseboards around barre brackets, creating a cleaner finish.
The ground must be excavated and properly graded to create a stable, level base for the swimming pool structure before any pool construction can begin.
A reinforced concrete foundation or slab is required to support the pool shell and prevent settling or cracking; this must be completed before pool installation.
Plumbing lines for circulation, filtration, and drainage as well as electrical conduits for pumps and lighting must be laid beneath the pool area before the pool shell is placed.
The pool structure must be fully constructed and stable before surrounding decking, coping, and paving can be installed around its perimeter.

successor: Pool Filling and Water Balance Testing
rationale: The pool must be structurally complete and watertight before it can be filled with water and chemically balanced for use.
The pool structure must be excavated and formed before any electrical components like lighting can be installed.
The concrete or vinyl pool shell must be in place to provide a mounting surface and conduit pathways for pool lighting fixtures.
Dedicated electrical circuits, conduits, and junction boxes must be run to the pool area before pool lighting fixtures can be wired and installed.
Pool lighting fixtures must be installed and their niches sealed before the final plaster or aggregate finish is applied to the pool surface.
Pool lighting fixtures must be fully installed and sealed before the pool is filled with water to test for leaks and ensure proper operation.
While deck installation can proceed concurrently in some cases, completing pool lighting first allows for easier access to fixture housings and conduit connections before the deck surface is poured.
The pool must be excavated and the pool structure formed before the pool cover system can be installed, as the cover system mounts to the pool structure.
The pool shell (concrete/gunite or vinyl liner) must be completed to provide a structural mounting surface for the pool cover tracks and mechanisms.
Pool coping is typically required before cover track installation, as the cover tracks are often integrated with or mounted onto the coping.
Decking around the pool should be finished after the cover system is installed so that the cover tracks can be properly integrated and the deck can be poured or laid flush against the track system.
While not a hard physical constraint, it is preferable to complete the cover system before final landscaping to avoid damage to finished landscaping during cover installation.
The pool shell (gunite/shotcrete or vinyl liner wall) must be fully cured and structurally complete before coping stones can be installed around the pool perimeter.
Waterproof membranes and waterline tiles must be installed on the pool wall before coping is placed, as coping overhangs and finishes the top edge.
Coping forms the transition edge between the pool wall and the surrounding deck; concrete or paver decks are poured against the installed coping to create a clean joint.
Coping must be fully set and sealed before the pool can be filled with water to prevent water leakage behind the coping stones and to ensure a finished appearance.
After coping stones are placed and anchored, expansion joints and stone-to-stone gaps must be sealed and caulked to prevent water infiltration and frost damage.
The pool stairs and ladders must be anchored into or attached to the pool shell or structural walls, so the pool structure must be complete first.
Stairs and ladders are typically installed before the final plaster or interior finish to allow proper embedding and seamless integration with the pool surface.
Stairs and ladders must be fully installed and secured before the pool is filled with water to ensure safety and structural integrity.
The water feature requires a structural base or foundation to support its weight and provide a stable mounting surface.
Underground or in-slab plumbing lines for water supply, recirculation, and drainage must be installed before the water feature is placed on top.

Electrical conduit and wiring for the water pump, lighting, and control systems must be roughed in before the feature is installed, as access to run these lines after placement is extremely difficult.

successor: Finish grading and landscaping around water feature
rationale: Final grading, soil placement, and planting around the feature must wait until the water feature is in its final position to ensure proper drainage and aesthetic integration.
Final sealing of plumbing connections, pump housing, and basin joints must be performed after the feature is installed to ensure a watertight system.
The ground must be graded and rough earth contours established before excavating and forming the artificial stream channel bed and banks.
Any existing buried utilities crossing the proposed channel alignment must be relocated or protected before excavation to avoid damage and ensure safety.
The channel must be fully excavated and shaped before any impermeable liner (e.g., clay, geomembrane) can be placed to prevent water loss.
Channel shaping must be complete before placing erosion-resistant stone or concrete lining along the banks and bed.
The channel profile must be fully formed before constructing internal hydraulic structures such as weirs, grade-control structures, or pools.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth and shape before any concrete work can begin for the pool shell.
A compacted base or sub-base (e.g., gravel layer and reinforcement) must be prepared to provide a stable foundation for the concrete shell.
Steel reinforcement bars or mesh must be placed and tied in position before concrete is poured to provide structural integrity to the shell.
All underground pool plumbing lines (suction, return, drains) must be laid and pressure-tested before the concrete shell is poured, as they will be embedded within or beneath the shell.
After the concrete shell is poured, a minimum curing time is physically required for the concrete to gain sufficient strength before any subsequent work (e.g., waterproofing, tiling) can proceed.

predecessor: Pool Shell Concrete Pouring and Curing
rationale: The pool shell must be fully poured and cured to provide a stable, crack-free substrate for waterproofing; applying waterproofing before the concrete has cured can lead to adhesion failure and cracking.
The concrete surface must be cleaned of debris, dust, and laitance, and any rough spots smoothed out to ensure proper bonding of the waterproofing membrane.
Waterproofing must be fully applied and cured before any finishing materials (tiles, plaster, or pebblecrete) are installed to prevent moisture migration and substrate damage.

While it is advisable to complete waterproofing before installing water features to avoid damaging the membrane, some plumbing rough-ins can be coordinated; this is a soft preference for scheduling simplicity.
Backfilling and deck construction must only occur after waterproofing is complete and cured to protect the waterproofing layer from damage during earthworks and concrete pours.
The pool shell must be fully constructed and waterproofed before any mechanical systems can be installed inside or around it.
Mechanical plumbing, fittings, and equipment niches must be installed prior to final waterproofing and tiling to ensure proper integration and sealing.
All mechanical equipment (pumps, filters, heaters, chlorinators) must be fully installed before the system can be tested and commissioned for operation.
While mechanical systems should ideally be installed before decking to avoid rework, in some cases deck construction can proceed simultaneously if access points and service hatches are planned.
Electrical conduits, subpanels, and wiring for pool pumps, heaters, and lighting must be roughed in before mechanical equipment is installed and connected.

The pool tile and coping must be installed on a stable, cured gunite shell. The gunite must be fully cured to provide structural support and a proper bonding surface, and all rough-in work for plumbing, electrical, and drainage must be completed before the finish surfaces can be applied.

The coping is installed at the intersection of the pool shell and the surrounding deck. The subgrade and any structural support for the deck must be prepared so the coping can be properly set and anchored.

The tile and coping form the finished waterline and edge of the pool. The interior plaster or pebble finish is applied after the tile is set, working from the tile line downward. This sequence ensures a clean, watertight seal between the tile and the plaster finish.

The coping serves as the edge detail between the pool and the deck. The deck surface (pavers, concrete, or other material) is installed after the coping is in place, abutting against the coping to create a finished transition. Installing the deck first would make proper coping installation difficult or impossible.

Once tile, coping, and interior finish are installed, the pool is typically filled with water to begin the curing process for plaster and to test the tile/coping seals. Filling cannot occur until the tile and coping are fully installed and sealed.
The pool structure (shell, walls, and floor) must be fully constructed and cured before any lighting fixtures can be mounted or embedded into the pool surface.
Electrical conduits, junction boxes, and wiring pathways must be installed before pool lighting fixtures can be connected and placed.
Pool lights are typically installed before the final interior finish is applied, as the light niches and housings need to be embedded behind or flush with the finished surface.
Lighting fixtures must be installed, secured, and sealed prior to filling the pool with water to ensure waterproof integrity and safe electrical operation.
After physical installation of light fixtures, final wiring connections to the power source and safety inspections must be completed to verify code compliance.

The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before any stream bed or liner work can begin to provide a clean, stable working surface and to prevent damage to the liner from sharp objects or roots.

Proper excavation to design depth and grading of the stream channel must be completed prior to liner installation to ensure the liner is placed on a correctly shaped and compacted subgrade that meets design specifications.
The liner must be laid and positioned in the excavated stream bed before it can be anchored at the edges and seams can be welded or sealed to adjacent liner panels.

Protective cover material (e.g., soil, gravel, riprap) must be placed over the installed liner to protect it from UV degradation, mechanical damage, and hydraulic forces; this cannot be done until the liner is fully constructed and inspected.
Water can only be introduced into the constructed stream bed after the liner is fully installed, anchored, and covered to prevent liner floatation, undercutting, or displacement during flow testing.
The structural deck framing must be completed before any deck finish materials (such as waterproofing, tiles, or timber decking) can be installed, as the finish relies on the structural substrate.
Waterproofing must be applied to the deck substrate before final finishes are laid to protect the structure from moisture ingress.
Adjacent walls or balustrade structures should be constructed beforehand to allow seamless integration of the deck finish with surrounding elements.
Deck finishing surfaces must be completed before railings and balustrades are installed to ensure proper alignment and secure fixing into the finished surface.
While not a hard physical constraint, it is good practice to complete deck finishes before placing furniture or landscaping elements to avoid damage to the finish surface.
The pool cover track is mounted onto the finished pool shell structure; the shell must exist before the track can be installed.
The cover track is typically embedded into or mounted onto the pool deck surface; the deck area must be prepared and ready for track anchoring.
The track must be fully installed and secured before the pool cover itself can be attached and operated.
It is a soft preference to complete track installation before finishing work to avoid damaging new finishes, but finishing can theoretically be done around the track if needed.

The pool structure must be fully constructed, including the shell, lining, and all structural components, before any start-up and commissioning activities can begin to ensure water containment and structural integrity.

predecessor: Pool Plumbing and Circulation System Installation
rationale: All plumbing, piping, pumps, filters, and circulation equipment must be installed and connected before the pool can be filled and commissioned, as these systems are essential for water treatment and circulation.

predecessor: Pool Electrical and Control System Installation
rationale: Electrical wiring, control panels, timers, sensors, and automation systems must be installed and connected prior to start-up to enable operation of pumps, heaters, lighting, and other equipment during commissioning.
After the pool is filled and circulation systems are started during commissioning, the water chemistry must be tested, treated, and balanced to ensure safe and clear water quality for use.

successor: Pool Safety and Accessibility Features Inspection
rationale: While some safety features may be installed prior to start-up, a final inspection and testing of safety equipment such as covers, alarms, fencing, and accessibility features is typically performed after commissioning is complete to ensure everything operates correctly under normal conditions.
The infant warmer provides necessary thermal regulation and a stable platform for resuscitation procedures; the resuscitation station must be set up on or adjacent to the warmer.

The designated delivery/resuscitation room must be prepared with electrical outlets, medical gas lines (oxygen/air), and proper lighting before the resuscitation station equipment can be installed and connected.

predecessor: Medical Gas System Installation and Testing
rationale: Oxygen and compressed air supply lines must be installed, tested, and verified to be operational before connecting the newborn resuscitation station's gas-powered equipment (e.g., T-piece resuscitator, blender).

successor: Functional Testing and Calibration of Resuscitation Devices
rationale: Only after the station is fully assembled and connected can the resuscitation devices (e.g., self-inflating bag, T-piece resuscitator, oxygen blender, suction apparatus) be functionally tested and calibrated for safe use.

Although training can partially be done in advance, hands-on simulation drills using the actual installed equipment should occur after the station is complete to ensure staff familiarity with the specific setup, device locations, and workflow.
Water supply rough-in must be completed before the birth bed/obstetric table can be installed, as the bed requires nearby water connections for cleaning and potential medical procedures.
Drainage rough-in must be complete before the obstetric table is placed, as the area needs proper drainage for cleaning and waste disposal.
Electrical rough-in for medical-grade outlets and connections must be completed before the birth bed is installed, as the table requires power for adjustability and medical equipment.
Medical-grade flooring must be installed before placing the heavy obstetric table, as the floor needs to be fully finished and sealed underneath the bed for infection control and stability.

successor: Final Medical Equipment Calibration and Testing
rationale: The birth bed/obstetric table must be installed and positioned before final calibration and testing of its mechanical and electrical functions can occur.
Electrical power supply and conduit pathways must be roughed-in before overhead surgical lights can be wired and mounted.

predecessor: Structural Framing and Ceiling Grid Installation
rationale: The ceiling structure must be in place to provide support points for mounting overhead surgical lights.
HVAC diffusers must be positioned in the ceiling layout before lights to avoid spatial conflicts and ensure proper airflow around lights.
Ceiling finish work (drywall, painting) should be completed after lights are installed to avoid damaging finished surfaces during light mounting and electrical connections.

successor: Surgical room equipment commissioning and testing
rationale: The surgical lights must be fully installed before the integrated commissioning of all operating room systems can be performed.

predecessor: Mount wall bracket or support structure
rationale: The radiant heater must be securely mounted on a wall bracket or support structure before it can be installed.
The heater must be physically mounted in place before electrical connections can be made to it.

successor: Test and calibrate Baby Warming Radiant Heater
rationale: Electrical power must be connected before the heater can be functionally tested and calibrated.

successor: Place baby warming bed or station beneath heater
rationale: The radiant heater location must be established before the warming bed/station can be positioned correctly underneath it.

predecessor: Complete overhead ceiling or wall mounting preparation
rationale: The mounting surface (ceiling or wall) must be prepared and structurally ready before the heater unit can be attached.
The headwall system must be mounted onto the wall structure; wall framing provides the structural support needed for installation.
Electrical wiring and conduit must be run within the wall cavity before the headwall is installed to avoid surface-mounted conduits and to comply with code.
Medical gas supply lines (oxygen, vacuum, air) must be run and pressure-tested inside the wall before the headwall unit is mounted and connected.
Finishing work such as trim, escutcheon plates, and sealing around the headwall must be completed after the headwall unit is securely installed.

successor: Gas Outlet Connection and Certification Testing
rationale: Final connection of medical gas outlets to the headwall and subsequent certification/verification testing (purity, pressure, flow) can only be performed after the headwall is fully installed.
Structural framing and backing/blocking must be installed in the wall cavity before the bassinet station can be securely mounted or recessed.
Any electrical outlets, lighting, or plumbing connections needed for the bassinet station area must be roughed-in before the unit is installed to avoid rework.
The bassinet station must be positioned and secured before drywall is installed so that the drywall can be cut and finished neatly around the built-in unit.
Final trim, casing, and millwork around the built-in bassinet area should be installed after the unit is in place to ensure a flush, finished appearance.
While painting could technically be done before installation, it is standard practice to paint after installation to avoid touching up cut edges and to achieve a seamless finish around the built-in.
The birth registration counter needs a stable, level floor foundation before it can be installed or constructed.
Any water supply or drainage lines needed at the counter area must be roughed in before the counter is built and finished.
Electrical wiring, outlets, and data lines for the counter's computer equipment and lighting must be run before the counter is enclosed and finished.
The counter structure must be in place before the final countertop surface and finishing materials can be applied.

successor: Birth Registration System Installation and Testing
rationale: Computers, printers, and registration software can only be installed after the counter structure is built and ready to receive equipment.

predecessor: Rough-in plumbing for placenta disposal chute
rationale: The rough-in plumbing (drainage and vent piping) must be in place before the chute itself can be installed, as the chute connects into the plumbing system.

successor: Connect chute to plumbing and seal
rationale: The chute must be physically installed before its final connections to the plumbing drain and vent lines can be made, as well as before sealing around the chute penetrations.

successor: Finish wall and ceiling surrounding chute
rationale: Wall and ceiling finishes (e.g., drywall, tile) around the chute must be completed after the chute is in place to allow proper fit and sealing around the penetration.
The structural framing must be complete and the rough opening prepared (sized and reinforced) to accommodate the chute before the chute can be set into place.
After installation, the chute must be inspected and tested to verify proper function, sealing, and compliance with healthcare facility requirements before being put into service.
Wall finishes must be completed before installing fixed cabinetry and counters to avoid damaging finished walls and to ensure proper fit and alignment.
Flooring must be installed before fixed cabinetry to ensure cabinetry sits on top of finished flooring for proper elevation and to avoid having to cut around cabinetry later.
Plumbing rough-in for sinks and fixtures must be completed before cabinetry and counters are installed, as the cabinetry will conceal and need to accommodate these connections.
Electrical rough-in for outlets, switches, and potential under-cabinet lighting must be completed before cabinetry is installed, as wiring needs to be placed within walls that will be covered.
Countertop appliances (e.g., soap dispensers, bottle warmers) must be installed after counters are in place, as they sit on or are mounted through the counter surface.
Plumbing fixture trim-out (faucets, sink fittings) must occur after cabinetry and counters are installed, as these fixtures mount directly to the countertop and sink basin.

predecessor: Complete Rough-In for Medical Gas and Electrical
rationale: Medical gas piping, electrical conduit, and data cabling must be roughed-in within the wall cavity before the headwall assembly can be mounted and connected.
The wall must be framed, sheathed, and finished to provide a structural surface for securely mounting the headwall assembly.

successor: Connect Medical Gas Outlets and Electrical Devices to Headwall
rationale: The headwall assembly must be physically installed and anchored before final connections of medical gas outlets, electrical receptacles, and data ports can be made to the assembly.

successor: Test Medical Gas and Electrical Systems
rationale: The headwall must be installed and all connections completed before system testing, certification, and commissioning can be performed.

successor: Install Ceiling and Floor Finishes Adjacent to Headwall
rationale: While it is preferable to install finishes after the headwall to allow for fit and sealing, it is a soft preference because finishes can be cut and trimmed around the headwall if needed.
Overhead lift tracks require structural support (e.g., ceiling joists, steel beams) to be in place to safely anchor the track system.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in above the ceiling must be completed before lift track installation to avoid conflicts and rework, as lift tracks occupy overhead space.
The lift track must be installed before the ceiling grid and finish ceiling are closed in, as the track is mounted to the structure above the ceiling.
The track provides the physical rail system; lift motor, trolley, and control systems can only be mounted and connected after the track is securely in place.

successor: Final Electrical Connection and Testing for Lift System
rationale: Electrical power and control wiring for the lift can only be terminated and tested after the lift motor and track system are fully installed.
The birthing pool shell must be physically installed in place before its plumbing can be commissioned, as the plumbing connections are made to the installed pool.

predecessor: Run Hot and Cold Water Supply Lines to Birthing Pool Location
rationale: Water supply lines must be run to the pool location before the plumbing system can be commissioned and tested.

predecessor: Install Birthing Pool Drainage and Overflow Pipework
rationale: Drainage and overflow pipework must be installed before commissioning to allow complete testing of both supply and drainage systems.
Regulatory rough-in inspections must be passed before commissioning and final connection of plumbing fixtures.

successor: Test Birthing Pool Water Quality and Temperature Control
rationale: Water quality testing and temperature control verification can only occur after the plumbing system is fully commissioned and operational.
Electrical power infrastructure must be in place before infant security system wiring can be connected and powered.
The central control panel for the security system must be installed first so that wiring can be routed and terminated to it.
Rough electrical and low-voltage work must pass inspection before finishing wiring to ensure safety and code compliance.
Wiring must be in place before sensors, cameras, and other security devices can be connected and mounted.
All wiring must be completed before the full system can be tested for functionality and continuity.
The desk must be installed on a stable, level surface; foundation work provides the necessary structural base.
The room or designated area where the desk will be permanently located must be built and enclosed before the fixed desk can be installed.
Proper lighting and power outlets near the registration area are required before the desk is fixed in place to avoid rework or unsafe conditions.
The registration desk must be in its final position before computers, printers, and network cabling are installed and connected.
Installing signage above or on the desk is typically done after the desk is fixed, though it could be done concurrently; it is a soft preference for logical workflow.

successor: Install Birth Unit Nurse Call Stations
rationale: Conduit and cable trays must be in place to route the low-voltage cabling for nurse call system wiring before installing the call stations.

successor: Install Birth Unit Nurse Call Stations
rationale: Electrical rough-in (backboxes, wiring, and power) must be completed to provide power and connectivity for the nurse call stations.

predecessor: Install Birth Unit Nurse Call Stations
successor: Connect and Test Nurse Call System
rationale: The physical nurse call stations must be installed before they can be wired, terminated, and tested for functionality.

predecessor: Install Birth Unit Nurse Call Stations
successor: Mount and Install Patient Room Equipment
rationale: Nurse call stations are often integrated with or mounted adjacent to other patient room equipment; the call station must be in place first to coordinate placement and wiring.

predecessor: Install Birth Unit Nurse Call Stations
rationale: While it is preferable to complete ceiling finish work after installing overhead nurse call devices to avoid rework, it is not physically impossible to sequence otherwise with careful access planning.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical and plumbing services in birthing suite ceiling
successor: Birthing Suite Ceiling-Mount IV Track System
rationale: The IV track must be installed after electrical and plumbing rough-ins are complete to avoid conflicts and ensure proper routing of infrastructure above the ceiling.

successor: Birthing Suite Ceiling-Mount IV Track System
rationale: The ceiling-mount IV track requires a completed ceiling grid or structural support system to anchor to before it can be mounted.

predecessor: Birthing Suite Ceiling-Mount IV Track System
rationale: The IV track must be mounted in the ceiling void before ceiling tiles are installed or the ceiling surface is finished, as the track is recessed or mounted above the finished ceiling.

predecessor: Birthing Suite Ceiling-Mount IV Track System
successor: Install medical gas and vacuum systems in birthing suite
rationale: It is preferable to complete the IV track first to avoid interference, though medical gas lines can be routed around the track if needed.

predecessor: Birthing Suite Ceiling-Mount IV Track System
successor: Commission and test IV track functionality
rationale: The IV track must be fully installed before it can be tested and commissioned for use.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to the required depth and dimensions before the foundation can be laid.
If the soil is unstable, it must be stabilized or compacted to ensure it can support the foundation load before pouring concrete or placing foundation elements.
The exact position, alignment, and levels must be marked out on site before foundation construction begins to ensure correct placement.
Waterproofing membranes and coatings can only be applied after the foundation concrete has cured and the surface is prepared.
The columns, walls, and load-bearing elements of the building superstructure require the completed foundation to transfer loads to the ground.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any wall foundations can be laid.
Trenches or foundation pits must be dug before the wall base or footing can be constructed.
The load-bearing footing or foundation must be set and cured before the wall structure can be built upon it.
The sacred enclosure wall defines the sacred perimeter; inner temple buildings are typically built after the enclosure is established to respect the sacred boundary and construction sequence.
The wall structure must be complete before gates or entranceways are installed within the wall openings.
A stable foundation is physically required to support the altar platform, otherwise the platform would lack structural support and could collapse or shift.
The ground must be leveled before constructing the altar platform to ensure the platform is even and structurally sound.
The altar platform serves as the base upon which the altar itself is placed, so the platform must be completed before the altar can be installed.

While staircases can be installed concurrently or after, it is preferable to complete the platform first so that staircase alignment and connection to the platform can be properly measured and executed.
Railings need to be anchored to the platform structure itself, so the platform must be fully constructed before railings can be securely installed around its perimeter.
The location for the Sacred Boundary Marker must be determined and surveyed before the marker can be placed or installed.
A stable base or footing must be prepared before the boundary marker can be erected or set in place.
The boundary marker defines the sacred perimeter, so fencing or enclosure work must follow its placement to align with the marked boundary.
The physical marker must be in place before the ritual consecration can be performed upon it.
The marker must be carved, inscribed, and prepared off-site or on-site before it can be installed at its final location.
The votive offering niche is typically carved into or built into a wall, so the wall structure must first be constructed to provide the surface and support for the niche.
The foundation or base structure must be prepared to support the wall into which the niche is integrated, ensuring stability.
Any decorative elements such as painting, carving details, or ornamental framing within the niche can only be applied after the niche structure itself is complete.
Votive offerings or sacred objects can only be placed into the niche after the niche has been fully constructed and finished.

If the niche is in an exterior wall, a roof or canopy overhead may preferably be completed after the niche to avoid damage during construction, though some construction sequences might build the roof first.
Legal and regulatory approval for the excavation site must be obtained before any ground disturbance can begin.
Pre-excavation survey is required to identify any sensitive cultural or archaeological resources before disturbing the ground.
Existing underground utilities must be located and relocated to prevent damage and ensure worker safety during excavation.
Vegetation, debris, and surface obstacles must be removed to provide clear access for excavation equipment.
Excavation creates the void and prepared subgrade necessary before concrete foundations can be poured.
The excavated subgrade must be tested and stabilized to ensure it meets load-bearing requirements before any further construction can occur.
Excavation provides open access for installing underground drainage systems, which must be placed before backfilling or above-grade work.
The site must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and existing structures before ground compaction and grading can begin, as any obstructions would prevent uniform compaction and proper grading.
Soil composition, bearing capacity, and moisture content must be assessed first to determine the required compaction specifications and methods for grading.
Survey stakes and grade markers must be set to establish proper elevation targets, slopes, and boundaries before compaction and grading work can proceed accurately.
The ground must be properly compacted and graded to a stable, level surface before any foundation excavation can begin, as unstable ground would compromise excavation safety and accuracy.
Final grade levels must be established before trenching for underground utilities, otherwise utility depths and cover requirements cannot be properly maintained relative to finished grade.
The temple building must be physically complete before any consecration preparation activities can commence, as there is no structure to consecrate otherwise.
The altar is a central element of the consecration ceremony and must be built and in place before preparation for the ceremony can begin.
The site must be ritually purified before consecration preparations can take place, as the consecration requires a clean and sanctified space.
All preparations such as gathering offerings, preparing ritual items, and organizing participants must be completed before the actual consecration ceremony can be performed.
The temple cannot be officially opened or dedicated to the public until after the consecration ceremony has been fully prepared and conducted.
A stable foundation must be prepared and cured before any sacred stone can be laid to ensure structural integrity and prevent settling or shifting.
The construction site must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and obstacles, and properly excavated to the required depth before the sacred stone placement can occur.

A ritual purification of the site is traditionally performed before laying a sacred stone to sanctify the ground, though this is a soft cultural preference rather than a physical construction constraint.
Walls or superstructures that incorporate the sacred stone as a cornerstone or base element cannot begin until the sacred stone is firmly positioned and set in place.
Formal dedication ceremonies for the structure typically occur after the sacred stone is laid, but this is a ceremonial preference rather than a physical construction necessity.
The foundation works must be completed before railings and balustrades can be installed, as the railings need a stable structural base to be fixed onto.
Concrete substrate must be cured and ready before metalwork/railing installation can commence.
Railings and balustrades must be installed before final floor finishes can be applied, as access for finishing trades is restricted once railings are in place.
It is preferable to complete painting and decorating after railings are installed to avoid damage to finished paintwork, though not physically mandatory.
Structural steelwork must be erected to provide the supporting framework onto which railings and balustrades are fixed.
The kneeling rail brackets must be installed to the wall or frame first, as the kneeling rail itself is mounted onto these brackets.
The wall structure must be framed in place to provide a surface to mount the kneeling rail brackets and support the rail.

Flooring should ideally be installed before kneeling rail to ensure proper height alignment and to avoid damaging new flooring when installing the rail, though it's not a strict physical requirement in all cases.
The kneeling rail often serves as a structural support or reference point for installing adjacent grab bars in accessible shower or bath configurations.

Shower wall panels are typically installed after the kneeling rail, as the rail penetrates or interfaces with the wall panels, requiring the rail to be in place first for proper sealing and alignment.
The ground must be prepared and foundations laid before any signage or inscription can be installed on the holy ground.
The structural elements that will support or frame the signage/inscription area must be completed before the signage can be mounted.
Signage and inscriptions are typically applied to finished surfaces; rough or unfinished surfaces would prevent proper installation or inscription work.
The signage and inscription must be in place before the final unveiling or inspection of the completed holy ground area.
It is preferable to complete signage first so that landscaping around it can be done cleanly, but landscaping could technically proceed in parallel if needed.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the required depth before any water feature can be constructed to ensure proper foundation and drainage.
A stable, waterproof foundation (e.g., concrete basin or liner) must be installed before constructing the sacred water feature to prevent water leakage and structural failure.
Pipes, pumps, drainage lines, and any recirculation systems must be laid and connected before the water feature is fully assembled to avoid having to tear apart finished work.
The structural shell of the water feature must be complete before applying decorative finishes, waterproof sealants, or tilework to the interior surfaces.

While landscaping can be done in parallel, it is preferred to complete the water feature first so that surrounding paths, plants, and decorative elements can be aligned precisely around the completed feature without risk of damage.
A stable foundation is required before any fixed seating can be installed to ensure structural integrity and level placement.
The floor slab must be poured and cured to provide the structural base onto which the fixed sacred seating is anchored.
Fixed seating must be fully installed before final interior finishes (painting, wall coverings) to avoid damage to finished surfaces during seating installation.

While preferred to run wiring after seating layout is known, it is technically possible to do electrical work before seating installation; however, having seating fixed allows precise placement of outlets and lighting relative to seating rows.
Fixed seating must be completely installed and secured before the final inspection can verify all components meet safety and occupancy requirements.
Site must be graded and leveled before installing site furnishings like benches, bike racks, and trash receptacles to ensure stable placement and proper drainage.
All underground utilities (water, sewer, electrical, gas) must be installed before site furnishing to avoid digging up or damaging finished site elements.
Walkways, plazas, and paved surfaces must be completed before placing site furnishings such as benches, tables, and trash cans onto those finished surfaces.

While site furnishings are typically installed before final planting to avoid damaging new plants, this is a soft preference as some landscaping can be done concurrently if protective measures are taken.
All site furnishings must be in place before the final inspection can verify that the site is complete and ready for occupancy or public use.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before fence posts can be set and fence lines established for proper alignment and stability.
Property lines and fence locations must be surveyed and staked to ensure the fence is built on the correct boundary and within legal limits.
All buried utilities (gas, water, electric, telecom) must be located and marked before digging post holes to avoid damaging underground infrastructure.
Landscaping such as planting, sodding, or mulching near the fence line is often completed after the fence is installed to avoid damage to new plants and to work around the final fence position.
The fence and gate installation must be fully complete before a final inspection can verify compliance with building codes, setback requirements, and property line regulations.
Signage must be mounted on finished surfaces such as walls, ceilings, and floors, so these finishes need to be completed first to provide the structural backing and aesthetic base.
Many signs require electrical connections for illumination or digital displays; electrical rough-in (wiring and conduits) must be in place before signage installation.
Signage is typically applied after painting is complete to avoid paint overspray, damage to signs, and to ensure the background color/finish is final.
Wayfinding and signage must be installed and verified before the building can be inspected for code compliance and occupancy, as egress and directional signage are life-safety requirements.
While occupants can technically move in before all signage is up, having wayfinding signage in place greatly improves safety, navigation, and user experience; it is a strong preference.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the proper elevation and slope before the fountain foundation and base can be installed.
Water supply lines, recirculation piping, drainage, and electrical conduits for pumps must be laid underground before the fountain structure is built over them.
A structural concrete pad or foundation must be poured and cured to support the weight of the fountain basin, pump equipment, and water.
The fountain basin and structure must be in place before surrounding paving, tiles, or hardscape are laid to ensure proper integration, waterproofing, and alignment.

Planting beds around the fountain are typically completed after the fountain is installed to avoid soil and debris contamination of the water feature, though it is a soft preference as some planting could be done concurrently with careful protection.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any outdoor lighting fixtures can be installed, as lighting posts, bases, or conduit trenches require stable, prepared ground.
Power supply conduits and wiring must be run underground to the lighting locations before fixtures can be mounted and connected.
Concrete pads or bases for light poles and bollards must be poured and cured before the lighting fixtures can be anchored and installed.

While not a strict physical necessity, completing outdoor lighting before final landscaping allows lights to be positioned and wires buried before sod, plants, or decorative ground cover are placed, avoiding rework.
Outdoor lighting must be fully installed and operational before the site can be commissioned and final electrical inspections conducted to verify proper function and safety.
Exterior stairs and ramps require a stable load-bearing foundation to support their structure and transfer loads to the ground.
Exterior stairs and ramps typically land on or abut against the slab-on-grade, requiring the slab to be in place to establish finished floor elevations and landing points.
Handrails and guardrails are mounted directly onto stair and ramp structures; the supporting structure must be complete before railings can be installed.
Soffit and fascia work under stair landings or ramp overhangs is often sequenced after the stair/ramp structure is in place, though in some designs it could be done concurrently.
Where stairs or ramps terminate at walkways or plazas, the adjacent paving is typically placed after the stair/ramp to achieve a clean joint and proper drainage transition.

The subgrade must be properly graded, compacted, and stabilized to provide a uniform and load-bearing foundation for the paving layer. Without adequate subgrade preparation, paving will crack, settle unevenly, or fail prematurely.

A granular or stone base course must be placed and compacted over the subgrade to provide drainage, distribute loads, and create a level surface for paving. Paving directly on unprepared subgrade would lack structural support.

Subsurface drainage pipes, catch basins, and French drains must be installed before paving since they are buried beneath the pavement. Retrofitting drainage after paving would require cutting and removing the pavement.

All underground utilities (water, sewer, electrical, gas, telecom conduits) must be trenched, laid, and backfilled before paving. Paving over unfinished utility work would require later demolition of the pavement to access utilities.

While curbs can be placed before or after paving, it is common practice to install curbs first as a form and edge restraint for paving. However, in some sequences curb installation can follow paving — this is a soft preference depending on construction method.

Paint striping, lane markings, and traffic markings can only be applied after the paving surface is fully compacted, cured (if asphalt or concrete), and clean. Marking before paving would be destroyed during paving operations.

Landscaping, topsoiling, and seeding adjacent to paved areas are typically performed after paving to avoid tracking mud and debris onto the fresh pavement. This is a soft preference for quality and cleanliness rather than a structural requirement.
The ground must be graded to the proper contours and slopes before any sod or seed is placed, ensuring proper drainage and a stable base for turf establishment.
A layer of quality topsoil must be spread over the graded subgrade to provide a fertile growing medium for grass seed or sod roots.
The surface must be fine-graded to remove large clods, stones, and debris, creating a smooth, uniform seedbed for optimal seed-to-soil contact or sod installation.

If an irrigation system is installed, it must be tested and operational before seeding or sodding to provide immediate watering; however, if seeding, the irrigation test can occur just after seeding to water it in. Alternatively, if hydroseeding is used, it may be combined.

Mulch or erosion control blankets are often applied immediately after seeding to protect seeds from erosion and retain moisture, but this is a soft preference as some methods do not require separate mulching.
Typically, large trees and shrubs are planted before sodding to avoid damaging the new turf with heavy equipment, but smaller plantings may occur after; this is a soft sequencing preference.
The planting area must be cleared of debris, existing vegetation, and obstructions before any new trees or shrubs can be planted.
The site must be brought to its approximate finished grade levels to establish proper drainage and soil conditions before planting begins.
All buried utilities (water, gas, electric, drainage, irrigation lines) must be installed before planting to avoid digging up and damaging new plantings.
Fine grading around planted areas is often completed after planting to ensure proper soil coverage and aesthetic finish around the root balls.
Trees and shrubs must be planted first so that lawn areas can be seeded or sodded around them without disturbing the newly planted stock.
Major hardscape surfaces like paved walkways and patios are typically installed after planting to avoid heavy equipment compaction and damage to root zones.
Trees and shrubs must be in place so that the irrigation system can be designed and adjusted to provide proper coverage to the planted areas.
Mulch is applied after planting to retain moisture, regulate soil temperature, and suppress weeds around the newly planted trees and shrubs.
The site must be properly graded and rough earthwork completed to provide a stable, level foundation for installing furnishings like benches, bike racks, and planters.
Underground utilities (water, electrical, drainage) must be installed before surface furnishings are placed to avoid digging up or moving completed furnishings for utility access.
Concrete pads, sidewalks, and paved areas must be completed first so that site furnishings (benches, tables, bollards) can be anchored or mounted onto finished hard surfaces.
Furnishings such as planters and edging should be in place before final planting to avoid damage to new vegetation from installation equipment and foot traffic.

While final cleanup typically occurs after all installations are complete to avoid re-soiling areas, it is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity as minor cleaning around furnishings could be done concurrently.
The ground must be leveled and prepared before any play structure components can be installed to ensure a stable foundation.
Concrete footings or anchor points must be set and cured before the climbing wall structure can be securely mounted.

successor: Safety Surfacing Installation (e.g., rubber mulch, poured-in-place rubber)
rationale: The climbing wall structure must be in place before safety surfacing is installed around and beneath it to ensure proper fit and coverage of the fall zone.
The climbing wall must be fully assembled before a final safety inspection can be performed to verify structural integrity and compliance with safety standards.
Landscaping around the play area is typically done after the structure is installed to avoid damage to plants and to allow precise placement of decorative elements.

predecessor: Structural framing and floor slab installation
rationale: The slide structure requires a completed building frame and floor slab to anchor and support it properly.

predecessor: Rough-in of electrical and mechanical systems
rationale: Overhead and wall-mounted utilities must be in place before the slide is installed to avoid conflicts and difficult access later.
The slide base and support columns must be installed before final floor finishes are applied to ensure proper integration and avoid damaging finished surfaces.

successor: Final wall and ceiling finishes (drywall, painting)
rationale: The slide is a large, volumetric component that is easier to install before enclosing walls and ceilings are fully finished, allowing access for rigging and fastening.
Safety surfacing around the slide exit and entry points must be installed after the slide is in place to ensure proper fit and seamless transition.
The ball pit enclosure must be installed on a prepared, level, and stable floor surface to ensure structural integrity and safety.
The bottom frame or base structure of the ball pit enclosure must be assembled first to define the perimeter and provide a foundation for the walls.
Safety padding is applied over the enclosure walls/frame after assembly to cover hard surfaces and prevent injury.
The enclosure must be fully constructed and secured before plastic balls are added, otherwise balls would spill out.
The completed enclosure must be inspected for stability, sharp edges, and proper assembly before opening for use.
The ground must be excavated and leveled to the required depth and dimensions before the foam blocks can be placed, as the pit forms the structural base.
Perimeter drains or drainage layers must be installed before foam block placement to ensure proper water management beneath the structure.
A compacted gravel or crushed stone base layer must be laid and leveled to provide a stable, well-draining substrate for the foam blocks.
The foam blocks must be fully placed and arranged in the pit before concrete can be poured over them, as the blocks serve as a void-forming or insulating formwork for the slab.
Once the foam block pit is complete, conduits and pipes must be run through or around the blocks before the final slab is poured, and this rough-in is impossible without the blocks in place.
The sensory play wall panel must be mounted onto a framed wall structure; the framing provides the structural support needed to attach the panel securely.
Any electrical wiring for lighting or interactive elements within or near the sensory panel must be roughed in behind the wall before the panel is installed to avoid rework or damage.
The wall surface must be finished with drywall and properly painted or prepared before the sensory play wall panel can be attached to ensure a smooth, clean mounting surface.

Flooring should be installed after the wall panel to prevent damage to the flooring material during panel installation and to allow the panel to be mounted at the correct height relative to the finished floor.
Any final electrical connections powering the sensory panel's interactive elements (lights, sound modules) must be completed after the panel is securely mounted to ensure safe and proper integration.
The support column must be installed first before padding can be applied to it, as padding wraps around the installed column.
Padding on the support columns must be in place before attaching platforms, as platforms may need to interface with or be positioned relative to the padded columns.
It is good practice to complete padding installation before the final safety inspection so that all protective components are in place for evaluation.
The indoor playground structure requires a level, stable, and properly prepared floor slab to ensure safe installation and structural integrity.
Safety surfacing (e.g., rubber mats, foam tiles) must be installed after the playground structure is in place to ensure proper fit around support posts and equipment.
While not physically required, it is preferred to complete the playground installation before final lighting adjustments to avoid damaging fixtures with tall equipment.
The building's structural framing must be complete to provide adequate overhead clearance and anchoring points before installing the playground structure.
Finishing work is typically done after the playground is installed to avoid damaging finished surfaces during equipment assembly and to allow precise placement of wall graphics and safety signage.
The ground must be properly graded and leveled before any anchoring system can be installed to ensure stable footing and correct alignment of play equipment.
Excavation for the anchorage points (concrete footings or ground sockets) must be completed before the anchoring system components can be placed and secured.
All underground utilities must be located and marked prior to excavation for anchors to prevent damage to gas, electric, water, or data lines during digging.
The anchoring system (e.g., ground sleeves, concrete anchors, or auger anchors) must be set and cured before the play equipment structure can be mounted, bolted, or attached to it.

While loose-fill surfacing can be placed after anchoring, installing the anchoring system first prevents disturbing the finished surface. However, some engineered surfaces may be installed before anchors if planned, so this is a soft preference for construction sequencing efficiency.
The gate requires a stable, level foundation to be properly anchored and aligned.
The entry gate provides a defined opening and access point; walls or enclosures are built to align with the gate frame.

successor: Child-Scale Entry Gate Finishing & Hardware Adjustment
rationale: Final adjustments, painting, and hardware installation (handles, latches) can only be done after the gate is mounted and fitted.
Proper grading ensures water does not pool at the gate base, but minor drainage work can be done concurrently or after if needed.
Pathways and landscaping are best completed after the gate is in place to ensure proper alignment with the entrance.
The soft play shape set must be installed on a finished floor surface; the floor slab must be completed to provide a stable base.
Any electrical conduit or outlets within or near the soft play area need to be roughed in before the play structure is installed to avoid interference.
The built-in soft play shape set is typically installed before the final finish flooring is laid around it, allowing the flooring to be fitted seamlessly against the structure.
It is preferable to complete wall finishes after the play shape set is in place so that edges and transitions are neatly aligned, though not a physical necessity.
Once the soft play shape set is fully installed and secured, a final safety inspection must be conducted before the area is opened for use.
The structural framing (walls, ceiling) must be in place to provide a substrate for acoustic panels and treatments.
Wiring for lighting, speakers, and outlets must be installed within walls/ceiling before covering them with acoustic materials.
HVAC ducts and vents must be run through the structure before acoustic treatments are applied, to avoid blocking access.
Any plumbing lines in walls or ceilings must be completed before acoustic treatment is installed over them.
Acoustic treatment is often the final surface layer; painting and final finishes should be done after installation to avoid damaging the acoustic materials.
Acoustic wall treatments are typically installed before flooring to prevent damage to finished floors from scaffolding/ladders, though it can be done after with careful protection.
Trim pieces (baseboards, moldings) are usually installed after acoustic panels to create clean edges and cover gaps between panels and flooring.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before anchors can be installed to ensure a stable foundation and proper alignment of the play structure.
Holes or trenches must be excavated to the specified depth and dimensions to accommodate the anchor footings or concrete piers before the anchors can be placed.

predecessor: Installation of Underground Utilities (water, sewer, storm drains, gas, electric)
rationale: Any underground electrical, drainage, or irrigation lines must be installed and inspected before anchor installation to avoid conflicts and ensure safety per code requirements.

successor: Pouring of Concrete for Anchor Footings
rationale: Anchors must be positioned and secured in the excavated holes before concrete is poured to embed them properly within the footing.
The anchors must be fully installed, cured (if concrete is used), and inspected before the play structure posts and framework can be bolted or attached to them.
The ground must be properly graded and leveled to provide a stable base for the soft fall flooring.
The sub-base must be compacted to prevent settling and uneven surfaces under the soft fall material.
Soft fall flooring must be installed first so play equipment can be anchored securely through or onto the finished surface, and to ensure the correct fall height protection is in place.
Typically the flooring installation is among the final finishing works, so cleaning and handover follows as a soft preference in the overall schedule.
Subsurface drainage must be in place before soft fall flooring is laid to prevent water accumulation and damage to the flooring material.

successor: Assembly and Erection of Indoor Play Structure
rationale: The indoor play structure requires a solid, level, and load-bearing foundation to be safely anchored and erected upon, ensuring structural stability and compliance with safety standards.

successor: Assembly and Erection of Indoor Play Structure
rationale: The building must be enclosed (roof, walls) to protect the play structure from weather during assembly and to provide the necessary overhead clearance and structural support points.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (Electrical, Mechanical, Plumbing) in Play Area
successor: Assembly and Erection of Indoor Play Structure
rationale: Underfloor and overhead MEP services (conduit, ductwork, piping) must be installed before the play structure footprint is occupied, as later access would require dismantling the structure.

predecessor: Assembly and Erection of Indoor Play Structure
successor: Finish Flooring Installation in Play Zone
rationale: The play structure must be in its final position before the surrounding finish flooring (e.g., rubber safety surfacing, tiles) can be laid tightly against and around the structure's base.

predecessor: Assembly and Erection of Indoor Play Structure
rationale: Safety padding, netting, and protective covers are fitted onto and around the assembled structure after erection to ensure full coverage and proper attachment.

successor: Integration of Interactive Digital Wall System
rationale: Power and data cabling must be run within walls before the digital wall system can be connected and integrated.

successor: Integration of Interactive Digital Wall System
rationale: The wall structure must be built and ready to receive the digital wall system components before integration can begin.

predecessor: Integration of Interactive Digital Wall System
rationale: The digital wall hardware must be physically installed and integrated before it can be calibrated and software can be configured to operate it.

predecessor: Integration of Interactive Digital Wall System
rationale: The digital wall system must be installed before surrounding finishes, trim, and cosmetic work can be completed around it.

predecessor: Integration of Interactive Digital Wall System
rationale: The integrated system must be fully in place before end-user testing and acceptance procedures can commence.
The Public Outdoor Room Floor/Deck requires a structural slab or deck substrate to be built first, as it serves as the load-bearing base upon which the outdoor room floor/deck surface is applied.
Waterproofing must be completed before installing the outdoor room floor/deck to protect the underlying structure from moisture intrusion, especially for exposed outdoor environments.
Any drainage, irrigation, or plumbing lines that run under the deck/floor area must be roughed in before the finished floor is installed to avoid future demolition.
If the outdoor room has walls or railings, the floor/deck provides the working platform and base for wall framing, so the deck must be completed first.
The floor/deck provides the stable surface for erecting scaffolding and supporting roof structure work above, so it must be complete before roof installation begins.
The roof/canopy requires the underlying structure and support framing to be in place to bear its weight and provide attachment points.
Ceiling or soffit finishes are typically installed after the roof/canopy structure is complete, as they are attached to or suspended from the roof framing.
Lighting fixtures mounted on or under the canopy require the roof/canopy structure to be in place for attachment and wiring routing.
Weatherproofing and waterproofing layers are applied after the roof/canopy deck or structure is installed to ensure continuous protection.
The foundation and substructure must be completed to provide a stable base for the vertical supports that hold up the roof/canopy.
The enclosure walls must be built on a stable foundation or slab, so foundation work must be completed first to provide the structural base.
Any plumbing, drainage, or electrical conduits that run beneath the slab must be installed before the slab is poured and the walls are erected, or costly rework would be required.

successor: Roof / Ceiling Structure Over Public Outdoor Room
rationale: The roof or ceiling framing depends on the enclosure walls for vertical support and bearing, so the walls must be complete before roof installation.
Rough openings for windows and doors are created within the walls; fenestration products can only be installed after the wall framing is in place.
Finishing work such as plastering, cladding, or painting must occur after the wall structure is fully erected to provide a substrate for the finishes.
The site must be graded and prepared to establish the correct elevations and drainage before any seating structures can be installed.

predecessor: Foundation / Slab Work for Outdoor Room
rationale: The concrete slab or foundation base of the outdoor room must be poured and cured to provide a stable mounting surface for integrated seating elements.
Any electrical, lighting, or drainage utilities serving the seating area must be roughed in below grade before seating is installed to avoid rework.

successor: Finish Surfacing / Decking of Outdoor Room
rationale: Integrated seating units are typically set in place before the final surface finish (e.g., decking, tile, or polished concrete) is applied around them to achieve flush, seamless transitions.
While seating can be installed before final landscaping, it is often preferred to complete planting after seating to avoid soil compaction and damage to new plants from construction equipment.

predecessor: Public Outdoor Room Concrete Slab and Floor Finishes
successor: Public Outdoor Room Power and Data Outlets
rationale: The concrete slab or base floor must be in place to provide a mounting surface for power and data outlet boxes and to embed any required conduits before outlets can be installed.

predecessor: Public Outdoor Room Rough Electrical and Data Rough-In
successor: Public Outdoor Room Power and Data Outlets
rationale: Conduits, junction boxes, and wiring must be roughed in and run to the outlet locations before the final outlet devices can be connected and trimmed out.

predecessor: Public Outdoor Room Power and Data Outlets
successor: Public Outdoor Room Wall and Ceiling Finishes (if any)
rationale: Outlet faceplates and final connections should be completed before or concurrent with final finishes to allow for flush installation and proper sealing around openings.

predecessor: Public Outdoor Room Power and Data Outlets
successor: Public Outdoor Room Testing and Commissioning of Electrical Systems
rationale: All outlets must be physically installed and connected before electrical testing, continuity checks, and commissioning can verify proper operation and safety.

predecessor: Public Outdoor Room Power and Data Outlets
successor: Public Outdoor Room Furniture and Equipment Installation
rationale: It is preferable but not strictly required to have power and data outlets operational before placing furniture and equipment that will use them, to avoid disrupting finished furnishings.
The structural frame (columns, beams, roof slab) must be in place to provide anchorage and support for mounting shading devices such as louvres, pergolas or tensioned fabric canopies.
Shading structures are typically installed before final floor finishes and paving to avoid damage to the finished surface and to allow access for lifting equipment and installation work.
Shading devices must be in place before running conduit, wiring and installing light fixtures that will be attached to or integrated with the shading structure.

It is preferable to complete heavy installation of overhead shading prior to planting and soft landscaping to avoid damage to plants and irrigation, though this is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
Any overhead MEP services (drainage, electrical conduits, HVAC ducts) that may be concealed above or integrated with the shading structure must be roughed in before the shading devices are installed.

successor: Public Outdoor Room Planting and Planters
rationale: The planting and planters require a stable, level base such as a concrete slab or foundation to sit on. Without the slab/foundation in place, the planters cannot be installed.

successor: Public Outdoor Room Planting and Planters
