rationale: Proper drainage must be installed before planting to ensure excess water can drain away from planters and soil, preventing waterlogging and structural damage.

successor: Public Outdoor Room Planting and Planters
rationale: The overall outdoor room structure (walls, roof, or pergola) must be erected first so that the planting and planters are placed within the completed spatial envelope.
The wind screens require a stable structural base or foundation to be installed upon; without completed structural support, the wind screens cannot be securely anchored.
While it is preferable to apply finishes after installation to avoid damage, this is a soft preference as some finishing could theoretically be done prior to installation.

Wind screens define the outdoor room boundary; seating placement is logically after the screens define the space, but this is a soft preference as seating could be installed concurrently or prior in some cases.
Floor paving or decking is typically completed after wind screens to ensure proper alignment, but this is a soft preference as the order could be reversed.
Any underground utilities or footings needed for the wind screen support structure must be excavated and routed before the above-ground screen elements can be installed.

successor: Public Outdoor Room Signage and Wayfinding
rationale: The outdoor room structure (walls, floor, landscaping) must be physically built before signage and wayfinding elements can be installed on or within that space.

successor: Public Outdoor Room Signage and Wayfinding
rationale: Concrete pads, pathways, and foundations for signage posts must be poured and cured before mounting any signage or wayfinding elements.

successor: Public Outdoor Room Signage and Wayfinding
rationale: Final grading, planting, and paving must be completed so signage locations are finalized and not disturbed by subsequent landscape work.

predecessor: Public Outdoor Room Signage and Wayfinding
rationale: Signage and wayfinding must be installed and complete before the overall project can receive final inspection and occupancy approval.

predecessor: Public Outdoor Room Signage and Wayfinding
rationale: While signage can be installed before furniture and activation elements, it is preferable to have wayfinding in place to guide placement of amenities, but it's not a physical necessity.
The ground surface must be properly graded and drained before installing fixed outdoor furniture to ensure stable placement and prevent water pooling around bases.

predecessor: Concrete Slab or Paver Base Installation
rationale: Fixed outdoor furniture such as benches, tables, or bike racks typically require a concrete footing, slab, or paved base to be installed first for structural support and anchorage.
Any underground electrical, water, or data lines serving the area must be laid before furniture installation to avoid digging up or removing fixed furniture later.

Surfaces around the furniture (e.g., concrete staining, sealing, or paver joint sanding) should be completed after furniture is installed to ensure seamless finishing and avoid damaging sealed surfaces during furniture placement.
While plants and sod can be installed before furniture, it is preferable to install fixed furniture first to avoid damaging new landscaping during heavy equipment or installation activities.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before any earthmoving or grading can commence, as obstructions would prevent proper subgrade preparation.
Topsoil must be stripped and stockpiled prior to earthworks because organic-rich topsoil cannot support structural loads and must be removed to expose the competent subgrade material below.
Accurate survey control points, levels, and alignment markers must be established before earthmoving begins to ensure the subgrade is prepared to the correct grades, levels, and dimensions.

After earthworks and subgrade preparation are complete, the compacted subgrade must be tested for density, moisture content, and bearing capacity to verify it meets specification before subsequent layers are placed.
The sub-base layer (e.g., crushed stone or granular fill) can only be placed after the prepared subgrade is complete, tested, and approved, as the sub-base relies on the subgrade for uniform support.
The structural frame requires a stable load-bearing foundation to transfer loads safely to the ground; erecting the frame before foundations are complete would lack structural support.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and compacted to provide a safe and stable working platform for crane mobilization and frame assembly.

Underground pipes, conduits, and drainage must be placed before the structural frame is erected because access for trenching and backfilling is severely restricted once columns and beams are in place.
Roof panels and exterior cladding require the structural frame to be in place as a supporting substrate for attachment and load transfer.

The erected frame must be surveyed and verified for plumb, level, and alignment before any permanent connections or subsequent building systems (MEP, finishes) are installed, to ensure structural integrity and dimensional compliance.
Structural framing must be complete to provide a stable support structure for enclosure and screen systems to attach to.
Roofing should be installed first to protect interior spaces and provide a weather-tight condition before enclosing walls and screens are installed.
MEP rough-in work behind walls and within building cavities must be completed before enclosure systems are installed to avoid rework and provide access.
Enclosure and screens must be in place to create a conditioned, enclosed environment before interior finish work begins to protect materials and ensure proper conditions.
Enclosure systems are typically installed prior to or concurrently with windows/glazing to ensure proper integration and weather sealing of the building envelope.

Flooring must be installed before built-in seating and furniture because built-in items are typically anchored to or placed on top of the finished floor. Installing flooring after would require removing or working around the built-in furniture.

predecessor: Wall Finishing (including paint, wallpaper, or paneling)
rationale: Wall finishes must be completed before installing built-in seating and furniture that abut walls, as the walls would otherwise be inaccessible behind the built-in units for painting, wallpapering, or paneling.

Electrical wiring for outlets, lighting, or any powered features in or near built-in seating must be roughed in before the furniture is installed, as the built-in structures would block access to wall cavities and wiring paths.

Interior trim and molding that meets or abuts built-in furniture should be installed after the built-in units are in place to ensure proper fit, seamless transitions, and to cover any gaps between the furniture and walls or floors.

successor: Final electrical and lighting fixture installation
rationale: While not a strict physical necessity, it is preferable to install final light fixtures and electrical cover plates after built-in furniture is in place so that lighting can be positioned relative to the seating layout and to avoid damage to fixtures during furniture installation.

Structural framing (columns, beams, slabs) must be complete before MEP rough-in can begin, as MEP systems are installed within and through the structural frame, and there is no structure to attach MEP components to until framing is in place.
The building must be enclosed (roof and walls) to protect MEP rough-in work from weather damage and to provide a dry environment for installing electrical, plumbing, and HVAC systems.

MEP rough-in (electrical wiring, conduit, plumbing pipes, ductwork in walls/ceilings) must be completed and inspected before walls and ceilings are closed up with drywall or plaster, as access to these systems would otherwise be blocked.

While insulation can sometimes be installed concurrently in some areas, typically the MEP rough-in is completed first so that insulation can be fitted around the installed pipes, ducts, and wiring without obstruction.

Final interior finishes such as flooring, trim, and painting must occur after MEP rough-in and fit-out because the rough-in work involves heavy materials, tools, and access to wall cavities that would damage finished surfaces.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared before planters can be constructed to ensure proper drainage, level surfaces, and stable foundation for the planter structures.
Any necessary concrete footings or foundation slabs for planters must be poured and cured before planter walls or structures are built on top.
Underground utilities (water, drainage, electrical) must be installed before planter construction to avoid digging up or damaging completed planters.
Planters must be built and plants placed before irrigation lines can be run to and within the planters and drip emitters positioned correctly around plants.
Mulch, decorative stone, and final landscape finishes are applied after planting is complete to cover soil, retain moisture, and provide a clean finished appearance.
Legal and regulatory requirements mandate that the burial plot location must be formally designated and permits obtained before any ground disturbance can occur.
The exact grave dimensions and boundaries must be surveyed and marked on the ground to ensure the excavation is dug in the correct location and to the right dimensions.
A grave liner or burial vault can only be placed into the grave hole after the excavation is complete and the hole is ready to receive it.
The casket cannot be lowered into the ground until the grave has been fully excavated to the required depth.
Backfilling the excavated soil into the grave can only occur after the excavation, burial, and any associated ceremonies are complete.
The excavation and grading must be completed to create the open grave space before the grave liner or vault can be placed into the ground.
A level base of crushed stone or sand is typically required beneath the vault to ensure proper support and prevent settling before installing the vault.
The grave liner or vault must be installed first to provide the containment structure before the casket can be lowered into it.
The vault lid or cover can only be placed after the vault base is in position and the casket has been placed inside the vault.
Backfilling of the grave can only commence after the vault with its lid is fully installed and sealed in place.
A stable foundation or base must be prepared and set before the headstone/stele can be installed, as the headstone requires a solid, level footing to remain upright and secure.
The grave must be excavated and the burial completed before the headstone/stele is placed, as the headstone marks the grave location.
The headstone or stele must be carved, inscribed, and fabricated before it can be transported and installed at the grave site.
Final landscaping, grass seeding, and site beautification around the grave are typically done after the headstone is in place so that the monument is not disturbed.
Any formal unveiling ceremony for the headstone must take place after the headstone is fully installed and in position.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth and dimensions before the grave base or foundation can be installed, as the foundation sits directly on the prepared subgrade.
The grave base provides the stable structural platform upon which the burial vault or crypt is placed; the vault cannot be installed without a completed foundation underneath.
The grave liner (if used) is typically set onto the prepared grave base/foundation to ensure proper alignment and support.
The headstone or footstone is anchored to or placed upon the completed grave base/foundation; the foundation must be set and cured before the monument can be installed.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and compacted before placing any curb or edging to ensure a stable, level base and prevent settlement or shifting.
The grave pit must be dug before the curb/edging is installed, as the curb defines the perimeter around the grave opening and the excavation must be complete to establish the correct boundaries.
The curb or edging forms the base perimeter structure upon which coping stones or cap pieces are placed, so the curb must be fully set and cured before caps are installed on top.
The curb/edging defines the grave boundary and must be in place before soil is backfilled around the grave area to retain the soil and maintain a clean edge.

While not physically mandatory, it is standard practice to install the curb/edging first to establish the grave plot boundary and provide a reference line for positioning the headstone or monument squarely within the plot.

The grave cover or lawn slab must be installed on a stable, level foundation or base. Without proper base preparation (compacted earth, gravel, or concrete foundation), the slab would not be properly supported and could crack or shift.
The grave must be excavated and the burial completed before a grave cover or lawn slab can be placed, as the slab sits above the burial site.
The interment of the deceased must occur before the grave cover/lawn slab is installed, as the slab permanently seals or marks the grave after burial.
Lawn slabs are designed to be flush with the surrounding ground, so sod or topsoil must be placed around or over the slab after it is set to integrate it with the lawn surface.

While inscriptions are typically done after installation to ensure correct positioning, some slabs may be pre-engraved. However, it is a strong preference to engrave after installation to avoid damage during handling and to align properly on site.
The grave must first be excavated to create the void space that will later be backfilled and compacted. Without prior excavation, there is nothing to backfill.
The burial container or coffin must be placed into the grave before backfilling can occur, as backfill material goes around and on top of the container.
The interment ceremony and lowering of the remains into the grave must be completed before the grave is backfilled, as backfilling would obstruct the ceremony and access to the grave.

Final landscaping, turf laying, and surface restoration can only begin after the grave has been backfilled and compacted to a stable level, as the surface needs to be at final grade for finishing works.
The headstone or memorial marker is typically installed only after backfill and compaction is complete so that the ground is stable and at the correct grade to support the monument.

The site survey establishes property boundaries, control points, and reference elevations that define where plot markers must be placed; without survey stakes and baseline layout, markers cannot be accurately positioned.
Vegetation, debris, and obstructions must be removed before installing plot markers to ensure clear access, unobstructed line-of-sight for surveying, and stable ground for marker placement.
Plot markers physically delineate the exact locations and boundaries for excavation work; digging cannot proceed until the layout is clearly marked on the ground.
Markers indicate where footings and foundations are to be poured; foundation work requires the marked layout to ensure correct positioning, alignment, and dimensions.
Underground utility runs must follow the marked plot layout to avoid encroaching on building footprints or easements; markers guide the trenching and pipe/cable placement.
The mausoleum walls require a stable foundation to bear their weight and prevent settling or cracking.
The walls must be erected to provide vertical support for the roof or deck structure above.
Interior finishes such as flooring, wall cladding, or crypt installation can only proceed after the structural walls are in place.
The load-bearing wall core must be built first before the decorative exterior stone veneer or cladding is applied.
Rough openings for doors and windows are formed within the wall, and frames/doors/windows are installed after the wall is complete.
The cenotaph requires a stable base; foundation must be completed before the cenotaph structure can be erected.
Inscriptions, carvings, and surface finishes must be applied after the cenotaph is fully erected and stable.
Landscaping around the cenotaph is typically done after the structure is in place to avoid damage and ensure proper alignment, though it is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the correct depth, shape, and compaction before the basin structure can be constructed.
A stable foundation or sub-base layer (e.g., compacted gravel or concrete base) is required to support the basin before its walls or lining can be placed.
The basin structure must be fully formed before waterproof membranes or liners are applied to ensure watertight integrity.
Pipes and fittings for filling and draining the basin can only be connected after the basin structure is in place and stable.
Aesthetic finishing and planting around the basin is typically done after the basin is complete, but this is a soft preference as some landscaping could theoretically be done concurrently.
The sump requires a prepared and excavated pit or trench at the correct depth and location before the sump structure can be installed.
The sump is typically integrated into the slab or foundation waterproofing system, so the waterproof membrane must be laid prior to sump installation to ensure a continuous watertight barrier.
The sump acts as the lowest collection point; the main water feature liner and internal waterproofing layers must connect to and overlap the sump to create a sealed basin.

successor: Still Water Feature Plumbing & Pump Connection
rationale: The sump houses or connects to the pump suction and drainage pipework; plumbing connections can only be made once the sump unit is in its final position.
After the sump is placed and connected, the area around it must be backfilled and the surrounding slab concrete poured to encase and secure the sump.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to proper grade and bearing capacity before any foundation or wall construction can begin.

predecessor: Foundation Pile Driving / Deep Foundation Installation
rationale: Deep foundation elements such as piles or secant piles must be installed to support the containment wall before the wall itself can be constructed.
Waterproofing membranes or coatings are applied to the completed containment wall surface to ensure watertightness, which can only be done after the wall is fully cured and in place.
Backfill against the containment wall can only be placed after the wall has achieved sufficient strength to resist lateral earth pressures.
Interior structural elements that tie into or bear on the containment wall require the wall to be complete and cured before connections or pours can proceed.
The overflow weir is part of the still water intake system and must be built after the intake structure to ensure proper water level control and flow regulation.
A stable foundation is required before constructing the overflow weir to ensure structural integrity and prevent settlement issues.

successor: Still Water Channel / Conveyance System Construction
rationale: The overflow weir must be in place before the conveyance channels can be aligned and constructed, as the weir sets the water elevation and flow control point for downstream channels.
Gates and mechanical components can only be installed after the weir structure itself is complete, as they are mounted onto or within the weir.
Hydraulic testing requires the overflow weir to be fully constructed to verify design water levels, overflow capacity, and system balance.

predecessor: Install Still Water Level Sensor System
successor: Connect Still Water Level Sensor to Monitoring System
rationale: The sensor system must be physically installed in its designated location before any electrical or data connections can be made to the monitoring system.

successor: Install Still Water Level Sensor System
rationale: A stable foundation or mounting bracket/structure must be in place to securely hold the still water level sensor, ensuring accurate readings and preventing movement or misalignment.

predecessor: Install Still Water Level Sensor System
rationale: The sensor must be installed and physically positioned before calibration can be performed, as calibration requires the sensor to be in its final operating location and orientation.

predecessor: Install Still Water Level Sensor System
successor: Commission / Test Still Water Level Monitoring
rationale: The sensor system must be fully installed, connected, and calibrated before the overall monitoring system can be commissioned and tested for proper operation.

predecessor: Run Conduit / Cabling to Sensor Location
successor: Install Still Water Level Sensor System
rationale: Electrical conduit and signal cabling must be routed to the sensor location prior to sensor installation so that connections can be made immediately upon mounting the sensor.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before any structural slab can be poured to provide a stable, uniform subgrade.
A compacted sub-base or blinding layer is required to support the slab formwork and reinforcement, preventing differential settlement.
Any drainage pipes or underdrain systems beneath the slab must be laid and tested before the slab is cast to avoid cutting into the hardened slab later.
The structural slab serves as the foundation base; basin walls must be built on top of the cured slab to ensure proper load transfer and waterproofing continuity.
Waterproofing is typically applied over the cured structural slab before wall construction to create a continuous water barrier at the base joint.
Structural works must be complete to provide a clean, enclosed environment for still water cleaning and commissioning, preventing contamination and ensuring safe access.
Mechanical rough-ins must be installed before still water systems can be cleaned and commissioned, as the piping and equipment need to be in place for the cleaning process.
Electrical rough-in work must be completed to provide power for pumps, monitoring equipment, and controls used during still water commissioning.

Still water systems must be cleaned and commissioned before final finishes and clean room certification to ensure water quality meets specifications and systems are operational for certification testing.

Commissioning of still water systems must precede formal qualification and validation activities (IQ/OQ/PQ) to confirm the system operates correctly and produces water meeting required purity standards.
The concrete basin surface must be properly prepared (cleaned, repaired, dried) to ensure proper adhesion of the waterproofing membrane.
The waterproofing membrane must be allowed to cure and dry completely before any subsequent work can proceed, as per manufacturer specifications.
Backfilling can only commence after waterproofing is fully applied and cured to prevent damage to the membrane.
Plumbing penetrations and connections must be made after waterproofing to ensure watertight seals through the membrane.
Applying protective coatings, tiles, or finishes over the waterproofing is typically done after application, but may vary depending on system design.
Site grading and preparation must be completed to establish proper drainage slopes and subgrade conditions before rough-in drainage work can begin for the still water feature.
Excavation must be completed to create the required space and foundation for the water feature before the drainage rough-in piping can be installed.
It is preferable but not strictly required that basic utility rough-ins for water supply and electrical be completed first, as drainage work often coordinates with these utilities to avoid conflicts.
The drainage rough-in system must be installed before the shell or waterproofing layer of the water feature is placed, as the drainage connects beneath or through the waterproofing membrane.
Drainage piping must be roughed in and inspected prior to pouring concrete or installing the permanent structural base, as the pipes will be embedded in or pass through the substructure.
Spectator seating and bleachers require a stable, level base. The foundation or slab on grade provides the structural support necessary to anchor the seating system safely.

predecessor: Structural Steel Framework (if supported by frame)
rationale: If the bleachers are mounted on or supported by a structural steel frame, the steel framework must be erected first to provide the support structure for the seating.

predecessor: Underfloor / In-slab Utilities (e.g., drainage, electrical conduits)
rationale: Any utilities running beneath the seating area must be installed and inspected before the seating structure is placed, to avoid costly rework or access issues.
Handrails and guardrails are typically attached to or integrated with the seating structure, so the seating must be in place to install safety barriers correctly.

successor: Final Finishing / Painting of Seating Area
rationale: While not physically required, final finishing work such as painting or applying sealants is more efficient and cleaner after the seating is installed, as a soft preference for workflow.

Sports flooring requires a smooth, level, cured concrete slab or subfloor as a stable base. The subfloor must be clean, dry, and free of debris before any sports flooring (e.g., rubber tiles, vinyl, wood) can be installed.
A moisture barrier must be placed on the concrete slab to prevent moisture migration from damaging the sports flooring system above.
If the sports flooring system includes a shock-absorbing underlayment or foam pad (e.g., for gymnasium use), it must be laid down before the final sports surface layer.
Wall base and baseboards are installed after the sports flooring is complete to cover the expansion gap around the perimeter and provide a finished look.
Line marking and game court layouts (e.g., basketball court lines, volleyball boundaries) must be applied on top of the finished sports flooring surface.
Court markings must be applied to a finished, smooth concrete slab or base surface; markings cannot be applied before the slab is installed and cured.
The surface must be properly prepared, ground, and leveled to ensure markings adhere correctly and provide accurate court dimensions.
Color coatings (e.g., acrylic resurfacer or color layers) must be applied and fully dried before line markings are painted on top.
Court lines define the precise locations for net posts, goal anchors, and other equipment; installation must follow marking layout.
The court lines and markings must be complete before a final inspection can verify compliance with regulation dimensions and specifications.
The concrete foundation must be fully cured to provide a stable and level base for mounting the basketball hoop pole or base plate.
The installation area must be cleared, leveled, and marked to ensure the hoop is positioned correctly according to court dimensions and safety clearances.
The main hoop pole/frame must be assembled and anchored before the backboard and rim components can be mounted onto it.
The rim must be fully installed and secured before the net can be attached to the rim hooks.

While the hoop can be installed before the final court surface, it is preferable to complete the court surface first to avoid damaging the fresh surface during hoop assembly and to ensure proper alignment markings.
The volleyball net system requires a stable and level surface for its posts. Foundation and slab work must be completed first to provide the proper mounting base and ensure structural stability.
The net system must be installed before final court surface markings can be applied, as the net post positions define the centerline and court boundaries for accurate marking.
The net system must be fully installed and tensioned before a final inspection and play testing can be conducted to verify proper height, tension, and safety.
The badminton posts require a stable, level base to be anchored or placed on; concrete slab or foundation must be cured and ready before posts can be installed.
Once the posts and net are in place, the court boundary lines can be accurately marked around and relative to the net position.
The net cannot be tensioned and adjusted until the posts are securely installed and upright.
It is preferable but not physically mandatory to install the net system before surrounding fencing to avoid damaging the net during fencing work.
Lighting is ideally adjusted after net installation to ensure the net and court are properly illuminated without shadows, but posts can be installed before or after lighting.
The futsal goal must be installed on a stable, level field base. Without proper ground preparation (clearing, leveling, and base compaction), the goal cannot be securely anchored.
The goal frame must first be assembled and installed in its final position before nets can be attached to the goal posts and backstays.
The exact position of the goal defines the goal area and penalty area markings. Court line markings around the goal must reference the installed goal location for accuracy.

successor: Safety Padding Installation on Goal Posts
rationale: Safety padding wraps around the goal posts and must be applied after the goals are fully assembled and positioned to ensure proper fit and coverage.
Anchoring points (e.g., ground sockets, concrete footings, or weighted base plates) must be prepared in the correct positions before the goal frame can be secured to them.
The climbing wall structure requires the wall framing to be in place as a support structure before climbing panels can be attached.
A level concrete foundation or slab is required to support the wall framing and climbing structure, ensuring stability and load distribution.
Climbing holds must be bolted onto the climbing wall surface after the wall panels are fully secured and in place.
Safety matting is installed after the climbing wall is complete so that the fall zone directly beneath the wall can be properly measured and padded.
Route setting (placing colored holds in specific patterns) can only begin once the wall structure and all holds are installed, as routes are defined on the completed surface.
Power conduits and electrical infrastructure must be run to the scoreboard location before the scoreboard unit can be physically installed and connected.
The structural brackets, anchors, or support framework must be secured to the wall, ceiling, or structure before the scoreboard can be mounted.
After the scoreboard is physically mounted, final electrical connections, wiring terminations, and power-up testing can be completed.
The scoreboard must be installed and connected before it can be powered on, programmed, and tested for proper operation.
Data and control cables (e.g., for remote control or content updates) must be connected after the unit is mounted in its final position.

predecessor: Floor Slab / Concrete Foundation Pour & Cure
rationale: Gym equipment mounts and floor anchors must be set into or bolted onto a finished, cured concrete floor. The concrete slab must be poured and fully cured to provide adequate structural strength for the anchors.

Any electrical conduit or wiring that will run beneath the floor slab or near anchor points must be roughed in before the floor is finished and anchors are placed, to avoid cutting into the slab later.
The fixed anchor points and floor mounts must be secured in place before the actual gym equipment (e.g., squat racks, cable machines, benches) can be installed and bolted down to them.

successor: Final Flooring Finish (Epoxy / Rubber Flooring Installation)
rationale: It is preferable to install anchor bolts and mounts before applying final floor coatings or rubber flooring, so that the anchors are properly aligned and the flooring can be cut/sealed around them for a clean finish.
Once heavy equipment is anchored, the room layout is fixed, allowing wall padding and mirrors to be positioned accurately without risk of damage from moving equipment into place.
Wall framing provides the structural substrate to which padded wall protection panels are attached; the padded panels cannot be installed without a framed wall surface.

Electrical wiring and outlet/switch boxes must be roughed in behind the padded wall protection before panels are permanently installed, as accessing wiring after padding is installed would require destructive removal.
Padded wall protection is typically applied over finished drywall or sheathing which provides a smooth, clean surface for adhesion or mechanical fastening of padding material.

The underlying wall surface should be primed and painted (or otherwise finished) before padding is installed, because the padding covers the wall and the finish cannot be applied later without removing the padding.
Baseboards and trim are typically installed after padded wall protection to cover the bottom edge of the padding and create a finished transition between the padded wall and the floor.
The court surface must be properly prepared (cleaned, leveled, and primed) before markings can be applied to ensure adhesion and durability of the paint.
The main court surface material (asphalt, concrete, acrylic, etc.) must be fully installed and cured before any line markings are painted on top.
Markings must be fully applied and dried before applying a protective sealant or top coat over the entire court surface to avoid smudging or damaging the lines.
Court line markings serve as positioning references for installing fixed equipment such as net posts, basketball hoops, and other fixtures, ensuring proper alignment and regulation dimensions.
All court markings must be completed and verified for accuracy and compliance before the project can undergo final inspection and sign-off.
Sports flooring requires a smooth, clean, dry, and properly cured substrate. Any moisture or unevenness in the subfloor will cause adhesion failure, buckling, or damage to the sports flooring system.

Most sports flooring systems (especially floating or glue-down systems) require a specific underlayment or shock-absorbing pad to be installed first to provide proper performance, impact absorption, and to meet manufacturer specifications.
A moisture barrier must be placed between the concrete subfloor and the sports flooring to prevent moisture migration that could delaminate or warp the flooring system.

Wall base (rubber or vinyl cove base) must be installed after the sports flooring is laid so that it overlaps and seals the edge of the flooring, providing a finished look and preventing dirt ingress.

successor: Court Line Marking / Game Line Painting
rationale: Game lines and court markings must be applied on top of the finished sports flooring surface. They cannot be installed before the flooring itself is in place.
Fixed equipment requires a stable, level foundation for support and alignment, which must be completed prior to equipment placement.
Structural steel framework must be in place to provide overhead crane access, support beams, and building envelope before large fixed equipment can be brought in and positioned.
The building must be enclosed to protect sensitive fixed equipment from weather damage, dust, and moisture during installation.
Piping, ductwork, and utility connections must be made to the equipment after it is set in its final position and anchored.
Electrical power cables, control wiring, and instrumentation must be connected to the equipment only after it is installed and secured in place.
Final precision alignment, leveling, and grouting of the equipment base must occur after the equipment is set in its designated position.

Thermal insulation and protective lagging on equipment are typically applied after installation, but in some cases pre-insulated equipment may be delivered, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
The seating system must be erected on a stable, level foundation. Without a completed foundation, the structural integrity and alignment of the seating cannot be assured.
The seating system is typically supported by or anchored to the main structural steel frame. The steel frame must be in place before seating brackets, supports, or terraces can be installed.
For concrete-tiered stadiums, the concrete slab or terracing that forms the seating bowl must be poured and cured before seating systems (e.g., seats, rails) can be installed on top.
Safety barriers and handrails are often integrated with or mounted to the seating structure. Once seats are erected, barriers can be properly aligned and installed for crowd safety.

successor: Final Finishing / Painting of Seating Area
rationale: While finishing work could theoretically be done before seating is installed, it is more efficient to erect the seating system first and then apply final touch-ups, especially near seat fixings, to avoid damaging finishes during seat installation.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any foundation work can begin.
The soil must be excavated to the required depth and dimensions before concrete or foundation materials can be placed.
Underground utilities must be identified and marked to avoid damage during excavation and foundation work.
After the foundation concrete is poured, it must be allowed to cure and gain sufficient strength before any loads are applied.
The play structure equipment can only be installed on top of a completed, cured foundation that provides a stable base.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the appropriate depth and dimensions before any pool basin structure can be built or installed.
The pool basin shell must be fully constructed (whether concrete, vinyl, or fiberglass) before any plumbing connections, drains, and return lines can be installed within the basin walls and floor.
After the basin structure is complete, waterproof membranes, plaster, tiles, or other interior surface finishes must be applied to seal and protect the basin.
Pool lights are typically embedded in the basin walls, so the basin must be constructed before conduit and light niches can be set into the walls.

While the deck can be poured after the basin is finished to allow a clean interface, it is technically possible to sequence deck work concurrently or even before, though standard practice places it after to ensure proper coping installation.
The slide unit components must be manufactured and fabricated before they can be assembled or installed on site.
The foundation or base structure must be prepared and cured to support the slide unit before installation can begin.
The main structural framework that supports or houses the slide unit must be erected before the slide unit can be mounted or positioned.
Electrical wiring and connections for any powered slide features (e.g., lighting, sensors) must follow after the slide unit is physically installed in place.
Safety inspections, load testing, and operational checks of the slide unit must occur after installation to verify structural integrity and safe operation.
Climbing wall panels must be anchored to a structurally sound foundation or slab; the mounting surface must be level and cured before panel installation.
If the climbing wall is attached to a structural wall, the wall framing and sheathing must be complete to provide a secure mounting substrate.
Any conduit, wiring, or plumbing that will run behind the climbing wall must be roughed-in before the panels are installed, as the panels will block access.
Climbing holds and t-nuts must be mounted onto the installed panels; the panels must be fixed in place before holds can be attached.
If painting or finishing is desired on the wall behind the climbing panel, it is easier to apply before the panel is installed, but this is a soft preference as it can be touched up later.
The swing frame assembly must be supported on the installed columns and require the foundation to be fully cured before any steel erection can commence.
The swing frame provides the structural backbone; swing mechanisms (hinges/pivots) can only be attached after the frame itself is assembled in place.
The swing frame forms the primary load-bearing structure; decking or floor planks are placed onto the completed frame.
Handrails and safety barriers are attached to the completed swing frame to ensure worker safety during subsequent work.

predecessor: Welding & Bolting Inspection of Swing Frame
rationale: While inspection typically follows assembly, this is a quality assurance step that could theoretically be done concurrently; but best practice requires inspection before load is applied.
The ground and area where the zip line will be installed must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to ensure a stable foundation for support structures.
Concrete footings or foundations for zip line support towers must be poured and cured before tower installation and cable anchoring can begin.
The support towers, platforms, and anchor points must be erected and secured before the zip line cable and trolley system can be installed.
Braking systems, emergency stop mechanisms, and safety nets must be installed and tested only after the zip line cable and trolley are in place to ensure proper integration.
Structural and operational inspections along with load testing must be performed after the zip line is fully installed to verify safety and functionality before public use.
The net climber structure requires a stable foundation to be installed first to provide structural support and anchoring.
The net climber's supporting frame or structure must be assembled and in place before the net components can be attached or installed.
Safety padding around the net climber must be installed after the net climber is in place to ensure proper fit and coverage of the structure.
A final safety and quality inspection of the net climber can only be completed once the entire structure is fully installed.
A stable foundation must be installed before the balance beam can be placed to ensure structural stability and safety.
The support structure (uprights or pillars) must be erected before the balance beam can be mounted on top of them.
The balance beam must be fully installed in place before safety padding and mats can be positioned around it for gymnast protection.
The balance beam installation must be complete before final inspection and load testing can be conducted to verify safety and compliance.
Accessories like springboards are typically positioned after the beam is installed, though they could theoretically be placed beforehand if space allows.
Bridge foundations must be constructed and cured before any bridge deck or play surface can be installed.
The main structural elements of the bridge (beams, arches, or trusses) must be in place to support the deck where bridge playing occurs.
The walking/playing surface must be fully installed before any play activity can safely take place on the bridge.
Safety railings or guardrails must be installed to prevent players from falling off the bridge during play.
The bridge must be played on (used) before a final inspection can verify it is safe and functional for ongoing use.
The ground area must be cleared and leveled before installing the tire swing support structure to ensure a stable and safe foundation.
The holes for the support posts must be excavated before the posts can be set in concrete.
Concrete must be poured and cured to secure the support posts in the ground before any swinging load can be applied.
The support beam or A-frame structure must be fully erected and stable before the tire/rope assembly can be hung from it.
The completed support structure must be in place before a safety inspection can check the integrity of the entire swing assembly.
A stable foundation and prepared ground are physically required before installing the spinner roundabout structure to ensure stability and safety.
The roundabout must be physically installed before electrical connections can be made to power any interactive or lighting features.
Safety surfacing (e.g., rubber mulch or pour-in-place rubber) must be installed after the roundabout is in place to ensure proper coverage and transition around the equipment.
All equipment must be fully installed before final safety inspections and functional testing can be conducted.
Landscaping, edging, and aesthetic finishes are typically done after equipment installation to avoid damage, but could theoretically be done concurrently with careful planning.
Raw materials (e.g., spring steel or composite) must be selected and procured before the spring rocker component can be fabricated.
The spring rocker must be fully fabricated (shaped, cut, formed) before surface treatments like coating or polishing can be applied.
Surface finishing must be completed before the spring rocker is installed into the final assembly to avoid damage to the finish or contamination.
The supporting frame or chassis must be prepared and ready before the spring rocker component can be mounted or assembled onto it.
The spring rocker must be installed in its final position before load testing can verify its performance and structural integrity under operational conditions.
The ground area must be excavated and leveled before constructing the sand play basin to ensure proper foundation and drainage.
Subsurface drainage must be installed before the sand basin is built to prevent water accumulation and ensure proper drainage of the sand play area.
The sand basin body must be formed and prepared before retaining walls or borders can be built around it to contain the sand.
The empty basin structure must be completed before sand is poured and filled into the basin.

Surrounding safety surfacing (e.g., rubber tiles or mats) around the sand play area is typically installed after the basin is complete to create a seamless transition, though some coordination may allow concurrent work.
The ground must be excavated and leveled to provide a stable foundation for the water play feature structure and its plumbing.
Water supply lines, drainage pipes, and electrical conduits must be installed underground before the water play feature can be built above them.
A concrete foundation must be poured and cured to provide a solid, level base for anchoring the water play feature equipment.
Once the water play feature is installed, final plumbing hookups, sealants, and waterproof membrane application must be completed to ensure leak-free operation.
Pumps, control panels, and lighting fixtures for the water play feature can only be wired and connected after the feature itself is securely in place.
The water play feature must be fully installed before water flow, pressure, and safety testing can be performed to verify proper operation.
The ground must be leveled and cleared before installing a fence to ensure proper alignment, stability, and safety of the fence posts and gate.
The playground base (e.g., poured rubber, sand, or mulch area boundaries) must be prepared first so that the fence line can be accurately positioned around the play area perimeter.
The fence and gate should be installed first to secure the construction site and prevent unauthorized access before heavy equipment is brought in and installed.
Though not physically required, it is preferable to install the fence before final surfacing to avoid damaging newly laid safety surfaces with fence installation equipment and materials.

Landscaping and finishing touches around the playground perimeter should follow fence installation to ensure landscaping is aligned with the fence line and not disturbed by post-hole digging or fence construction.
The shade structure requires a stable foundation to be built upon; without proper foundation work, the structure cannot be securely erected.

Typically electrical rough-in for lighting or fans integrated into the shade structure can begin after the structure frame is up, though it's a soft preference as some electrical could be pre-installed.
Landscaping under and around the shade structure must be done after the structure is complete to avoid damage to plants and to ensure proper grading and placement relative to the structure.
The seating wall requires a stable foundation to bear its load and prevent settlement or cracking.
Reinforcement steel must be placed before concrete is poured for the seating wall to ensure structural integrity.
Formwork molds must be erected and aligned before concrete placement to shape the seating wall.
After the seating wall concrete is poured, adequate curing time is required for the concrete to achieve its design strength.
Backfilling against the seating wall can only proceed after the wall concrete has sufficiently cured to withstand lateral earth pressures.
Signage posts require a stable foundation or base to be securely mounted, so any foundation or ground preparation must be completed first.
Signage often references specific equipment and must be positioned accurately relative to the installed equipment; equipment must be in place to determine correct signage placement and content.
Signage posts are typically installed within or adjacent to safety surfacing areas; the surfacing must be completed to properly set sign posts at the correct height and location.
Regulatory and safety signage must be in place before the playground can be inspected and approved for public use.
Signage providing rules, safety information, and age/use restrictions must be displayed before children and the public are allowed to use the playground.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and compacted before softfall surfacing can be applied to ensure a stable base.
A proper sub-base (e.g., crushed rock or concrete slab) must be in place to provide drainage and structural support for the softfall surface.
Edge restraints or borders (timber, concrete, or metal edging) must be installed to contain the softfall material and define the pour area.
Freshly installed rubber softfall surfacing must be allowed to cure and dry undisturbed before any foot traffic or equipment is placed on it.

Softfall surfacing is typically laid after equipment foundations are set but before final equipment assembly, or installed as a continuous pour; in either case, the surfacing must be complete and cured before placing the final playground equipment or allowing use.
The ground must be properly leveled, cleared of debris, and graded to provide a stable and safe foundation before play equipment can be anchored.
Concrete footings or anchor blocks must be poured and cured to provide structural hold for the play equipment anchors; anchoring into uncured or non-existent concrete is structurally unsound.
Underground utilities must be identified and marked before any digging or anchoring to avoid striking gas lines, water pipes, or electrical conduits.

Impact-absorbing surfacing (e.g., rubber mulch, poured-in-place rubber, engineered wood fiber) must be installed after the equipment is anchored so that it can be placed flush around the anchored posts and base plates.

Full assembly of the play structure and safety inspection must follow anchoring, because the equipment must be securely fixed to the ground before final assembly steps and before inspectors can verify stability.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before safety zones can be surveyed and marked out on the ground.
Accurate site surveying and staking of boundaries must be completed to define the reference points and limits within which safety zones will be marked.

Construction trailers, storage areas, and access roads/parking must be positioned first so that the safety zone markings can delineate restricted areas, walkways, and hazard perimeters around these established facilities.

Excavation work must not commence until the designated safety zones (e.g., exclusion zones around equipment, marked trench edges) are clearly marked to prevent accidents and ensure worker awareness of hazards.

While some material laydown can occur beforehand, designating specific safe storage zones marked on the ground should ideally be completed before major material deliveries to ensure materials are placed in correct, safe locations.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before any fencing can be installed to ensure proper alignment, stability, and consistent fence post foundations.
Property lines and fence alignments must be surveyed and staked out before fence posts are set to ensure the fence is built on the correct boundary and within legal limits.
All buried utilities (gas, water, electric, communication lines) must be located and marked prior to digging post holes to avoid utility strikes, safety hazards, and legal violations.
Final landscaping, topsoil placement, seeding, and sodding should be completed after the fence is installed to avoid damage to landscaping materials and to allow proper grading up to the fence line.

While the fence does not strictly need to be complete before a final inspection, it is standard practice to have all fencing installed before the final walkthrough to verify compliance with specifications and address any deficiencies.
The animal door must be installed within an existing wall or door structure. The wall framing or door must be in place to provide the structural support and opening for the animal door unit.

After the animal door is installed, any surrounding finishing work (trim, sealing, siding, drywall patching) must be completed to ensure proper weatherproofing and aesthetic integration with the wall.
A properly sized and framed rough opening must be cut and prepared in the wall or door before the animal door unit can be inserted and secured.
A stable concrete foundation must be cured and ready before any animal habitat fixtures can be installed to ensure structural support and level placement.
The ground must be properly graded and drainage systems must be in place before installing habitat fixtures to prevent water pooling and flooding around animal enclosures.
Underground water lines, electrical conduits, and drainage pipes must be roughed in before habitat fixtures are placed to avoid excavation and disruption after fixtures are installed.
All physical habitat fixtures (shelters, feeding stations, water troughs, enrichment structures) must be fully installed and secured before animals can be safely introduced to the habitat.

Final landscaping and thematic elements are typically installed after habitat fixtures are in place to work around the fixed structures, though some planting could theoretically be done beforehand with careful planning.
The ground must be leveled, cleared of debris, and properly graded before any building foundation or enclosure structure can be erected.
The concrete foundation, footings, and slab must be poured and fully cured to provide a stable load-bearing base for the animal enclosure walls, posts, and flooring.
Underground water lines, electrical conduit, and drainage pipes must be installed before the enclosure floor and walls are built to avoid costly rework and trenching through finished structures.
The primary enclosure structure must be completed to define the perimeter before adding external fencing, gates, locks, and security systems that attach to or surround the enclosure.
The structural shell, walls, flooring, and roof of the enclosure must be finished before installing interior elements like shelters, feeding stations, climbing structures, and water features.
The interior partition walls are built on top of the concrete slab. The slab must be cast and cured to provide a stable base for wall construction.
All underslab drainage and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before interior walls are built, as walls would block access to the slab area for plumbing installation.
Electrical wiring within walls requires the wall framing to be in place so cables can be run through stud cavities and junction boxes can be mounted.
Plumbing pipes for water supply and drainage within walls require the wall framing to be in place for pipe routing and support.
Insulation is placed within wall cavities after the wall framing is complete, before drywall is installed.
Window frames and rough openings must be framed in the walls before windows can be installed.
The roof structure must be in place to provide weather protection before installing windows to avoid water damage.
Windows must be installed and flashed before exterior siding can be applied around them to ensure proper weatherproofing.
Windows must be installed and sealed before interior wall finishing (drywall, trim) can be completed around window openings.
The window units must be in place before interior and exterior trim and casing can be installed around them.
Interior doors must be installed after flooring is complete to ensure proper clearance and fit at the bottom of the door.
Drywall finishing and painting must be completed before door installation to avoid damaging finished doors and to ensure proper trim work around the door frame.

predecessor: Family Room Rough Framing and Door Opening Preparation
rationale: The rough opening for the door must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the interior door unit can be installed.

successor: Family Room Door Trim and Casing Installation
rationale: Door trim and casing cannot be installed until the interior door is hung and in place, as the casing is applied around the door frame.

successor: Family Room Final Electrical and Switch Plate Installation
rationale: While electrical trim can often be done beforehand, it is preferred to install switch plates and outlet covers after doors are in place to coordinate final wall finishes and avoid damage.
The floor must be installed first to provide a stable, level base for the built-in family seating structure.
Wall framing provides the structural anchorage and backing needed to securely attach built-in seating against walls.
Any electrical outlets, lighting or wiring behind or within the built-in seating area must be roughed in before the seating structure is built over them.
The seat cushions are placed onto the completed built-in seating frame or platform after the structure is fully built.

It is preferable to finish painting and wall treatments after the seating is installed so that any gaps or seams between the seating and the wall can be properly caulked and painted for a seamless finish.
Wall framing provides the structural support and cavity within which built-in shelving can be anchored and secured.
Drywall must be installed and finished to create a clean wall surface before built-in shelving can be attached or trimmed against it.
Flooring must be installed before built-in shelving so that the shelving sits on top of the finished floor, avoiding gaps or the need to cut shelving later.
Built-in shelving must be installed before final painting so that the shelving unit can be caulked, trimmed, and painted seamlessly with the surrounding walls.

While electrical trim-out can partially proceed before shelving, any outlets or switches located within or adjacent to the shelving must be trimmed out after installation to ensure proper alignment and cover plate fit.
Subfloor must be level and prepared before installing fixed cabinetry to ensure cabinets sit flush and stable.
Electrical wiring and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before cabinetry to avoid having to run wires/pipes behind or through the cabinets after installation.
Walls must be finished (framed, drywalled, and taped/mudded) before cabinet installation to provide a clean mounting surface and proper wall attachment.
Countertops are installed on top of and supported by the base cabinets; cabinets must be fixed in place first to provide the substrate.
Fixed cabinetry must be in place before drop-in sinks, cooktops, dishwashers, and other built-in appliances can be installed into their designated cabinet cutouts.
Wall framing provides the structural support necessary for attaching the vanity securely to the wall.
Plumbing rough-in for water supply and drainage must be completed before the vanity is installed, as the vanity may cover access points and needs to align with pre-existing pipe locations.
The vanity cabinet must be fixed in place before the countertop can be measured, cut, and installed on top of it.
The vanity cabinet must be installed first to provide the supporting structure for the sink to be mounted in or on the countertop.

While the mirror is typically placed above the vanity and can be installed after the vanity is fixed, this is a soft preference as the mirror could theoretically be installed earlier if wall access is coordinated.
Wall framing must be complete to provide the structural support and mounting surface for window coverings.
Windows must be installed first so that window coverings can be properly measured, fitted, and mounted to the window frames.
Electrical wiring and outlets near windows must be roughed in before coverings are installed to avoid interference and rework.
Interior walls must be finished and painted before mounting window coverings to ensure a clean, finished appearance.
The foundation and slab must be completed to provide a stable base for interior construction, including flooring, walls, and finishes.
Rough framing establishes the structural walls, ceiling, and roof structure, which are necessary before interior work such as drywall, insulation, and finishes can begin.
The roof and exterior weatherproofing must be in place to protect the interior space from water damage and weather exposure during interior finishing.
Electrical wiring, outlets, switches, and any plumbing rough-ins must be installed within walls and ceilings before they are closed up with drywall and finishes.
Paint, trim work, baseboards, and final decorative elements can only be applied after the main interior construction (drywall, flooring, etc.) of the family room is complete.
The subfloor must be properly prepared (cleaned, leveled, and any underlayment installed) before flooring can be laid, otherwise the flooring will not be stable or level.
All rough-in inspections for electrical, plumbing, and HVAC must be completed and approved before flooring installation to avoid having to tear up or damage the finished floor for access.

Drywall installation, taping, mudding, and painting should be completed before flooring to prevent dust, debris, and paint drips from damaging the new floor, and to avoid the need for scaffolding on the finished surface.
Baseboards and trim are installed after flooring so they sit on top of the finished floor, covering the expansion gap at the walls and providing a clean finish.

While touch-up painting can be done before flooring, it is often preferred to complete flooring first so that painters do not drip paint on the new floor, though this is a soft preference rather than a strict physical requirement.
Structural integrity and waterproofing must be completed before internal fit-out works can commence to ensure the building envelope is watertight and structurally sound.
All concealed plumbing, electrical wiring, and ductwork for the kitchen and bathroom must be installed behind walls and floors before fit-out finishes are applied.
Kitchen cabinetry, countertops, bathroom fixtures, and tiling must be fully installed before final painting and touch-up finishes can be applied to avoid damage.
Flooring in kitchen and bathroom areas should be installed after fit-out to allow for precise cutting around cabinets and fixtures.
Custom joinery such as vanity units and cabinets for kitchen and bathroom must be installed before any wall or floor finishing details.
Paint cannot be applied until drywall is installed, taped, mudded, and sanded to provide a smooth, clean surface for painting.
Primer must be applied before final paint coats to ensure proper adhesion and uniform color coverage.
Painting should be completed before flooring installation to avoid paint drips and spills on the new floor surface.
While often trim is installed before painting, if painting is done first, trim can be installed afterward to allow for precise caulking and touch-up painting on the trim.
Painting and finishing work generates dust and debris, so final cleaning should occur after all painting is complete.

Structural framing (walls, floors, ceilings) must be in place to provide the cavities and support structures for MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing) rough-in installations such as conduit, piping, and ductwork.
The building must be dried-in (roof and basic enclosure) to protect MEP rough-in materials and workers from weather damage during installation.
MEP rough-in (electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, HVAC ducts) must be installed and inspected before insulation can be placed, as insulation will cover and conceal these MEP elements.
All MEP rough-in work must be completed and approved prior to closing up walls with drywall, as it would be impossible or extremely costly to access and modify MEP systems after drywall is installed.
Foundation and slab (including any under-slab plumbing) must be completed before above-floor MEP rough-in can begin, as the rough-in builds upon the structural base and floor systems.

Load-bearing walls require a stable and level foundation to transfer vertical loads safely to the ground. Without completed foundations, the walls would have no structural support and would settle or fail.
Site must be excavated and prepared before any structural work, including load-bearing walls, can begin to ensure proper ground conditions and access.

Underground drainage and utility pipes that pass beneath the footprint of load-bearing walls must be installed before the walls are built, as it is impractical or impossible to run them underneath after the walls are in place.
Upper floors and slabs rely on load-bearing walls for vertical support. The walls must be completed and cured to carry the loads from floors above.
The roof structure transfers its weight onto load-bearing walls. Roof framing, trusses, or rafters cannot be installed until the supporting walls are in place and structurally sound.
Rough framing creates the structural openings in walls that are needed to install doors and windows. Without framed openings, there is no structure to mount the doors and windows into.

Sheathing provides the exterior wall surface and weather barrier. Door and window openings are typically cut through the sheathing, and the sheathing must be in place to provide structural support around the openings.
House wrap or weather-resistant barrier should be installed before windows and doors so that the flashing can be properly integrated with the barrier, ensuring a watertight seal around openings.

Doors and windows must be installed before interior wall finishes like drywall are applied, because the drywall needs to be cut and finished around the installed door and window frames, and the frames provide the reference for the finished opening.

Exterior siding is installed after windows and doors so that the siding can be cut to fit tightly around the installed window and door frames, and flashing can be properly integrated to prevent water intrusion.
The foundation must be completed before any floor structure can be built, as the floor structure requires a stable, load-bearing base to transfer loads safely to the ground.
Underground or in-slab utility lines (e.g., plumbing drains, electrical conduits) must be laid and inspected before pouring or installing the floor slab to avoid costly retrofitting.
Walls are typically built on top of or anchored into the completed floor structure to ensure proper load transfer and alignment.

While some MEP rough-in can begin prior to the floor structure, above-floor routing, risers, and vertical chases are most efficiently installed after the floor deck provides access and working platforms.
Interior finish work such as flooring installation, ceiling framing, and drywall requires the structural floor to be complete to serve as a stable substrate and to define floor-to-floor heights.
Structural framing (columns, beams, slabs) must be complete to provide the load-bearing framework and floor plates that support and define the space where internal partition walls are installed.
MEP rough-in work (conduit, piping, wiring) within walls must be installed before the partition walls are closed up, otherwise walls would need to be demolished later to access utilities.
Partition walls must be fully erected to provide the substrate for wall finishes such as plaster, drywall taping, and mudding.
Partition walls define openings where door and window frames are set; frames are installed into the wall framing after walls are built.
Final wall finishes like paint or wallpaper are applied after the partition walls are completed and any surface preparation (taping, mudding) is done.
The structural framing and rough openings must be completed before windows can be installed, as windows require a defined framed opening to be placed into.
Weather-resistant barriers and building wraps are typically installed prior to window installation to ensure proper flashing integration and moisture management around openings.
Windows must be installed and sealed before interior wall finishes are applied, so that finishes can be trimmed neatly against window frames and to prevent weather damage to interior materials.
Windows are typically installed before the final exterior cladding or siding so that the cladding can be detailed to overlap and seal against the window flanges, ensuring proper weatherproofing.

Interior window trim and casing are installed after windows are in place to cover gaps and provide a finished aesthetic, though this is a soft preference as it could theoretically be sequenced differently with temporary coverings.
External doors require structural wall openings framed to precise dimensions before the door unit can be fitted and secured.
The rough opening must be prepared with proper header, jack studs, and sill to accommodate the door frame.
Weather barriers or house wrap must be applied to the wall sheathing before installing exterior doors to ensure continuous water management around the opening.
Interior and exterior trim/casing cannot be installed until the door unit is properly set, shimmed, and fastened in the opening.
Door locks, handles, hinges, and other hardware must be installed after the door is hung and aligned.
Exterior siding must abut or overlap the door frame; the door must be in place to establish the proper flashing and integration details.
It is preferable but not strictly necessary to install doors before finishing interior walls, as doors can be protected during finishing work.
Internal doors require framed openings to be installed into; walls must be framed to provide the structural support and rough opening dimensions for door frames.
Doors need a finished floor surface or subfloor to be installed against; without a stable walking surface, door frames cannot be properly positioned and shimmed.
While doors can be painted before installation or after, painting after installation allows for a seamless finish; however it's a soft preference as pre-finished doors can also be installed.
Final flooring is typically installed after doors to ensure the flooring runs up to the door frame cleanly and doors are hung at the correct final floor height.
Rough-in work for electrical, plumbing, and mechanical systems must be completed before interior doors are hung, as access to wall cavities is needed for routing wires and pipes.
Sanitary fixtures (toilets, sinks, urinals) must connect to water supply and drainage pipes. The rough-in plumbing must be installed in walls and floors before fixtures can be mounted and connected.

predecessor: Waterproofing & Backing Board Installation (in wet areas)
rationale: Wet areas such as bathrooms and toilets require waterproofing membranes and appropriate backing boards (e.g., cement board) behind tiles before sanitary fixtures can be installed to protect the structure from moisture damage.

Wall and floor finishes, especially tiling around showers and toilets, must be completed before sanitary fixtures are mounted to ensure proper alignment, sealing, and a finished appearance without damaging the fixtures.
After sanitary fixtures are set in place, final plumbing connections (supply lines, P-traps, and waste connections) can be completed to make the fixtures operational.
Sanitary fixtures must be fully installed before the plumbing system can be tested for leaks, proper drainage, and water pressure compliance during the final inspection phase.
Water supply and drainage pipes must be installed behind walls before kitchen cabinets and fittings can be mounted against them.
Electrical wiring, outlets, and switch boxes must be in place behind walls before kitchen fittings are installed to avoid rework and safety issues.
Flooring should be laid before base cabinets and kitchen islands are placed on top to ensure a finished, level surface and avoid having to cut around cabinetry.
Walls must be plastered and painted before cabinets and fittings are installed to avoid damaging finished surfaces and to allow for precise fitting.
Base cabinets must be installed and leveled first to provide a stable support structure for countertops to be placed on top.
Kitchen cabinets and housings must be in place before built-in appliances (oven, dishwasher, refrigerator) can be slid into their designated slots.
The sink cabinet must be installed before the sink can be mounted and connected to the plumbing rough-in.
Wall framing must be complete to provide the structural support and enclosure for built-in wardrobes to be installed against or within.
Wall surfaces must be finished (e.g., plasterboard installed, taped, and jointed) before wardrobes are built in, to ensure a clean finished appearance and proper fit.
Floor finishing (or at least subfloor/underlayment) should be complete so that wardrobes are built on a level, finished surface and to avoid damaging flooring materials afterward.
Built-in wardrobes are often painted or stained; however, if they are pre-finished, final wall painting can be done before installation—this is a soft preference to avoid touch-ups.
Any integrated wardrobe lighting or power outlets must be wired and connected after the wardrobe structure is in place to ensure correct positioning and safe installation.
The ground must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil, and excavated to the required depth before any slab can be poured, as the slab requires a prepared, stable subgrade.
A compacted sub-base (e.g., hardcore or crushed stone) must be laid and levelled to provide a stable, load-bearing platform for the concrete slab, preventing uneven settlement.
A damp-proof membrane must be placed over the prepared sub-base to prevent moisture rising from the ground into the concrete slab, which can cause damp issues and floor damage.
Freshly poured concrete must undergo a controlled curing period to achieve sufficient strength and durability before any subsequent loads or finishes are applied.
The ground slab acts as the structural base and working platform for erecting walls, columns, and other superstructure elements; these cannot be built until the slab is in place and cured.
Wall framing requires a stable, level base (foundation or slab) to anchor and support the walls. Without the foundation, walls have no structural support or attachment point.
For multi-story buildings, the floor platform must be complete to provide the working surface and structural base upon which walls are erected.
Any utilities that run through or under the slab must be installed before walls are framed, as they are inaccessible once the slab and framing are in place.
Roof structure depends on walls to provide vertical support and load transfer. Roof trusses/rafters bear on top plates of wall framing.
Wall sheathing (plywood/OSB) is applied directly to the exterior of the wall frame for lateral bracing. The frame must be erected first to provide the structural skeleton.
Rough openings for windows and doors are created by the wall framing. Windows and doors are installed into these framed openings.
Electrical wiring is run through stud cavities after the wall frame is erected and before drywall installation.
Plumbing pipes for sinks, showers, etc. are routed through wall cavities after framing is complete.
Insulation is placed between studs in the wall cavities after framing and rough-ins, but before drywall.
Roof trusses require a bearing surface; the top plates of the wall framing provide the support and anchor point for trusses. Without top plates, there is no structure to mount the trusses on.
Wall sheathing stiffens the wall assembly and is typically completed before trusses are set to ensure the walls can withstand the lateral loads imposed during roof installation.
Roof sheathing (plywood/OSB) is applied directly onto the installed trusses to form the roof deck; trusses must be in place to serve as the substrate for sheathing.
Temporary and permanent bracing, as well as hurricane/seismic tie-downs, are installed immediately after trusses are set to stabilize the roof structure and prevent collapse during construction.
Waterproof underlayment is applied over the roof sheathing that is installed on top of the trusses; the truss system must be complete before any roofing membrane can be laid.
The ceiling grid must be installed before plasterboard can be fixed to it, as plasterboard sheets are mounted onto the grid framework.
Stud wall framing provides the structural support onto which plasterboard sheets are screwed or nailed; plasterboard cannot be fixed without the framing in place.

Electrical, plumbing, and mechanical rough-in work must be completed before plasterboard is installed, as accessing these services after plasterboard is fixed would require cutting into and damaging the finished boards.
Plasterboard sheets must be fixed in place before the joints between them can be taped and joint compound applied; jointing cannot begin without fixed boards.
Paint and decorative finishes can only be applied after plasterboard fixing, jointing, and finishing are complete, as the plasterboard surface must be prepared and smooth before painting.
Foundation walls and slab must be poured and cured before plumbing lines (underground or in slab) can be installed.
Underground drain, waste, and vent (DWV) lines and water supply lines must be laid and inspected before the slab is poured and above-ground rough-in begins.

predecessor: Pour and Cure Concrete Floor Slab
rationale: The slab must be fully cured before plumbing rough-in work can proceed within the building's framed walls and floors.
Plumbing rough-in (pipes, vents, drains run through walls and floors) must be completed and inspected before the framing inspection can close, as the plumbing is concealed within the framing.

While plumbing and electrical rough-ins can often proceed in parallel, it is a common soft preference to complete plumbing first to avoid conflicts in wall cavities and to allow a single inspection pass for both MEP trades.
Structural framing (walls, floors, ceilings) must be in place before electrical rough-in can begin, as electrical wiring, boxes, and conduits are installed within the structural cavities.
