The building must be weathertight (roof and basic enclosure) before electrical rough-in to protect wiring and components from water damage.
Electrical wiring and boxes must be installed before insulation can be placed, as insulation goes over and around the rough electrical work.
All electrical wiring, outlet boxes, and switch boxes must be in place and inspected before walls are closed up with drywall.
While often done in parallel, plumbing rough-in is typically sequenced after or concurrently with electrical rough-in to coordinate chases and avoid conflicts in wall cavities.

The structural frame (beams, columns, and slabs) must be in place before staircase installation can begin, as staircases are typically supported by the structural frame and require the building's primary load-bearing structure to be complete.
Floor slabs at each level must be poured and cured to provide the landing surfaces and support points for staircase installation.

Staircase installation must be complete before interior finishing works (plastering, painting, flooring) can proceed on the staircase area, as these finishes are applied to the installed staircase structure.
Handrails and balustrades are typically installed after the staircase structure is in place, as they attach directly to the staircase stringers or steps.
The staircase must be fully constructed before vertical circulation paths (including fire escape routes) can be commissioned and certified for use by building occupants.
The subfloor must be clean, level, dry, and structurally sound before any flooring material can be installed to ensure proper adhesion and a level finished surface.
If flooring is installed over a concrete slab, the concrete must be fully cured (typically 28+ days) to prevent moisture issues that could damage the flooring.
Moisture barriers, vapor retarders, or acoustic underlayment must be placed before the final flooring to protect it from moisture and provide sound insulation.
It is a common sequencing preference to install flooring after painting to avoid paint drips on new flooring, but painting can also be done first if flooring is properly protected.
In most sequences, flooring is installed before cabinets so that the flooring runs continuously under the cabinets, allowing for easier replacement and eliminating the need for separate floor pieces.
Rough-in plumbing (water supply and drainage pipes) must be installed in walls and floors before sanitary fixtures (toilets, sinks, etc.) can be mounted and connected to the plumbing system.
Waterproofing of wet areas (bathrooms, toilets) must be completed before installing fixtures to ensure the substrate is protected against moisture damage.

Tile work should be completed before installing fixtures such as toilets and vanities, so that tiles run behind/underneath the fixtures for a clean, finished appearance and proper waterproofing continuity.
After the fixtures are physically mounted in place, the final plumbing connections (supply lines, drain traps, shut-off valves) can be made to complete the installation.

While not a hard physical constraint, it is preferred to complete painting and final finishes after fixture installation so that any damage or marks around the fixtures during installation can be touched up in a single coat.
Electrical wiring must be roughed in behind the walls before cabinets are installed, as cabinets would block access to the walls.
Plumbing rough-ins for sinks and dishwashers must be completed behind walls and under floors before cabinets are placed, as cabinets would obstruct access.
Walls must be framed and drywall installed (at least in the rough) to provide a finished surface for cabinets to be attached and to ensure proper fit.

Flooring should be installed before cabinets to ensure cabinets sit level on the final floor surface; installing cabinets before flooring can lead to height misalignment and difficulty replacing flooring later.
Countertops are fabricated and installed directly on top of the base cabinets, so the cabinets must be fully installed and leveled first.
Built-in appliances (e.g., range, dishwasher) are often installed after cabinets because cabinets define the openings and support for these appliances.
Backsplash is installed above countertops and against walls; cabinets must be in place to define the boundaries where backsplash ends.
Electrical power supply and wiring must be roughed in before HVAC equipment can be connected and powered.
Plumbing lines for condensate drainage and water supply (e.g., for hydronic systems) must be roughed in before equipment installation.
Building structure (walls, roof, floor slabs) must be complete to provide support and enclosure for heavy HVAC units and ductwork penetrations.
Main HVAC units (air handlers, condensing units, etc.) must be set in place before ducts can be connected to them.

successor: Refrigerant Line Charging and System Testing
rationale: Refrigerant piping connections can only be made and tested after the condensing unit and evaporator coil are installed.
Final power connections, control wiring, and system commissioning can only proceed once the equipment is physically in place.
Electrical wiring and junction boxes must be installed in the ceiling before lighting fixtures can be connected and mounted.
The ceiling surface must be finished (drywall installed) so that holes can be cut for recessed lights and mounting brackets can be secured.
While not strictly required, it is a strong soft preference to paint and finish the ceiling before installing fixtures to avoid paint drips and the need to mask or remove fixtures.

successor: Lighting Fixture Trim and Bulb Installation
rationale: The main housing/fixture must be mounted and wired first before trim rings, covers, and light bulbs can be installed.
All lighting fixtures must be physically installed before the electrical system can be energized and tested for proper operation.

Paint can only be applied to smooth, finished wall surfaces. Plastering and drywall taping/mudding must be complete and dried before painting can begin, otherwise paint will not adhere properly and surface defects will show through.
A primer or undercoat must be applied before the final decorative paint coats to ensure proper adhesion, uniform color, and to seal the surface. Skipping this step compromises paint finish quality.

While painting can technically be done before hard flooring, it is standard practice to paint first to avoid damaging new flooring with paint drips, dust, and scaffolding. However, this is a soft preference in some cases where flooring is installed early.
After painting and decorating is complete, a final clean is needed to remove paint splatters, dust from sanding, and masking materials. Touch-ups may also be required before handover.

Typically painting is done before installing finished trim, cabinets, and doors so that walls can be painted without masking expensive millwork. However, in some sequences, trim is installed first and painted later; this is a soft preference.
The site must be cleared, graded, and leveled before any underground septic or sewer systems can be installed to ensure proper drainage and accessibility.
Foundation excavation is needed to expose the building's underground drain lines and set the elevation reference for connecting sewer pipes from the building to the septic tank or municipal sewer.
Trenches and excavations for septic/sewer lines must be backfilled and compacted after installation to provide proper support and prevent settling.
All underground sewer and septic connections must be completed and inspected before they are covered or concealed by subsequent work.
Connection of sewer drains from the building to the septic tank or main sewer line must be completed before pouring the ground floor slab, as these pipes run beneath the slab.
Plumbing supply and drain lines must be roughed in before the hot water system can be connected to the building's water supply and distribution network.
Electrical wiring and dedicated circuit must be in place to provide power to an electric hot water system before it can be installed and energized.
Gas supply piping must be run to the water heater location before a gas-fired hot water system can be connected and tested.
The hot water heater must be installed before final connections to fixtures (sinks, showers, etc.) can be completed and the system can be fully tested for operation.

successor: Insulation of Hot Water Pipes (if applicable)
rationale: While pipe insulation can be done in stages, it is typically completed after the water heater is in place to ensure all pipe runs from the heater are properly covered for energy efficiency.
Exterior walls require a stable base; the foundation must be completed to support the load of the walls and provide a level surface for construction.
Floor framing provides the platform on which exterior walls are erected; walls cannot be safely built without a completed floor deck to work from.
The roof structure relies on exterior walls as load-bearing supports; walls must be in place and properly braced before roof framing can begin.
Sheathing and weather-resistive barriers are installed directly onto the exterior wall frame after walls are erected and braced.
Windows and doors are installed into rough openings framed within the exterior walls; the wall framing must be complete to define these openings.

predecessor: Slab on Grade / Ground Floor Slab
rationale: Interior partition walls must be built on top of a finished floor slab to provide a stable, level base and proper load distribution.
The main structural frame must be erected before interior partition walls are installed, as partitions are typically non-load-bearing infill within the structural grid.

predecessor: Rough-In MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing) Below Slab
rationale: Underslab MEP rough-ins (conduits, drains, pipes) must be placed before wall construction to avoid cutting into the slab or walls later.
Wall finishes cannot be applied until the partition walls are fully erected, framed, and secured in place.

successor: Overhead MEP Rough-In (Ductwork, Piping, Electrical Conduit)
rationale: Overhead MEP rough-in can proceed after walls are framed, as wall-mounted equipment and vertical risers depend on wall locations.
Door and window frames are installed within the partition wall openings once the wall framing is complete.
Window rough openings must be framed and prepared in the wall structure before windows can be installed.
Weather-resistant barrier (house wrap) must be applied around rough openings to prevent moisture intrusion before window installation.
Wall sheathing (plywood/OSB) provides structural rigidity and must be installed before windows can be mounted.
Windows must be installed and sealed before interior drywall and finishes can be applied around the window openings.
Windows must be installed first so that exterior siding can be flashed and sealed tightly against the window frames.
Windows must be in place before interior trim, casing, and sill work can be completed around them.
Insulation around window frames can only be installed after windows are set and sealed in the rough openings.
Rough framing (walls, studs, headers) must be complete to provide the structural openings and support for door frames.
The roof must be in place to provide weather protection before installing interior and exterior doors, preventing water damage.
Rough-in electrical wiring and plumbing must be completed inside walls before doors are hung, as access to wall cavities is needed.
Doors must be hung before drywall can be installed around door openings, as drywall butts against door frames and jambs.
Doors must be installed before finished flooring to ensure proper clearance at the bottom of the door and to allow flooring to be laid up to the door casing.
Wall framing provides the structural support and backing needed to securely attach kitchen cabinets to the walls.
Electrical wiring must be run in the walls before cabinets are installed, as cabinets would block access to the walls.
Plumbing pipes for sink supply and drainage must be roughed in behind the walls before cabinets are placed against them.

Drywall must be installed and finished (taped, mudded, sanded, primed) before cabinets are mounted, as cabinets will cover the walls and finishing drywall around installed cabinets is extremely difficult.

Installing flooring before cabinets is a soft preference — it allows cabinets to sit on top of finished flooring for a cleaner look and easier future floor replacement, but cabinets can also be installed over subfloor with flooring fitted around them.
Countertops must be fabricated and installed on top of the base cabinets after cabinets are leveled and secured in place.
Sinks, cooktops, and other built-in appliances are installed into or onto the cabinets and countertops after cabinets are in place.
Backsplash tiles are installed against the wall above the countertop, and the countertop is installed on top of the cabinets, so cabinets must be in place first.
Crown molding, light rail molding, and toe kick trim are added to the cabinets as finishing touches after the cabinet boxes are installed.
Plumbing rough-in (pipes, drains, vents) must be installed inside walls and floors before fixtures like toilets, sinks, and showers can be attached to them.
Electrical wiring for lighting, exhaust fans, and outlets must be run and boxes installed before fixtures that require power or illumination can be placed.
Wall framing provides the structural support for mounting fixtures such as vanity cabinets, toilets, and grab bars.
Walls must be closed in and finished (drywall, waterproofing, tile backer) before fixtures are installed to avoid damage and ensure proper sealing.
Floor substrate and waterproof membrane must be in place before installing floor-mounted fixtures like toilets and vanities to ensure structural integrity and moisture protection.
While exhaust fans and lights are often installed after fixtures are set to avoid damage, this is a soft preference as they can be installed concurrently or earlier.
Painting and final trim work should be completed after fixture installation to allow for touch-ups around installed items and to achieve a clean finish.
A stable foundation is required to support the weight of the fireplace and chimney structure.
The fireplace is typically installed after the surrounding wall framing is complete, as it is a structural element that integrates with the wall framework.
The chimney flue must be in place before the fireplace is fully installed, as the fireplace connects directly to the flue for smoke exhaust.
Decorative mantel and surround work is typically done after the fireplace unit is in place, but this is a logical sequence preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
Flooring is often installed after the fireplace to ensure a clean finish around the hearth base and to avoid damage to flooring during fireplace installation.
Formwork provides the mold into which concrete is poured; without formwork in place, concrete cannot be contained and shaped properly.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide structural tensile strength.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable foundation before any concrete can be placed.
After placement, concrete must undergo a controlled curing period to achieve design strength and durability; curing cannot begin until concrete is in place.
Formwork must remain in place until the concrete has gained sufficient strength to support itself; stripping can only occur after concrete placement and initial curing.
The foundation must be fully cured and load-bearing to support the structural framing system.
The slab provides a stable working platform and base for framing walls and columns.
The site must be cleared, graded, and leveled before any structural work can commence.
The roof structure (trusses, rafters) depends on the erected frame for support and attachment.
Sheathing panels (plywood/OSB) are fastened directly to the completed framing for lateral bracing and enclosure.
Structural framing (walls, columns, beams) must be complete to provide the load-bearing support for the roof structure
Exterior wall sheathing is typically installed before roofing to provide lateral bracing and a complete building envelope; roof trusses/rafters bear on top of wall plates
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins that will run through the roof or attic space must be positioned before roof decking is fully installed
Flashing, drip edges, and trim details are installed after the primary roof membrane to seal edges and transitions
Roof overhangs and eaves are completed before final siding install under the eaves to ensure proper weatherproofing sequencing
Trim and millwork are attached to framed walls and openings; rough framing must be complete to provide the structural substrate for trim installation.
Trim (baseboards, casing, crown molding) is installed over finished drywall; drywall must be hung, taped, and mudded before trim can be applied.
Typically walls are painted or at least primed before trim installation to avoid painting around trim; however, this is a sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.

Trim and millwork are often painted after installation; while some pre-priming may occur, the final paint coats on trim are applied after installation. This is a soft preference as trim can be painted off-site.

Baseboards and shoe molding are installed after the subfloor is in place but typically before final flooring to allow the flooring to be installed against the trim; however, in some sequences flooring is installed first and baseboards on top. The hard constraint is that trim must be complete before final finish flooring installation that butts up to it.
Electrical wiring must be run inside walls before drywall is installed; otherwise, walls would need to be opened up to access and run wiring, causing rework and damage.
Plumbing pipes (supply, drain, waste, vent) must be placed inside wall cavities before drywall encloses them; installation after drywall would require cutting into finished walls.
HVAC ducts, vents, and returns must be installed within wall and ceiling cavities before they are sealed with drywall.
Framing must be inspected and approved to ensure structural integrity and proper alignment before drywall covers the framing.
All rough-in MEP work must pass inspection before being concealed behind drywall; failing inspection after covering would require costly demolition.
Insulation batts or spray foam must be placed in wall cavities for thermal and acoustic performance before drywall seals the cavities.
Drywall boards must be hung and fastened before joints can be taped, mudded, and sanded.
Paint requires a finished drywall surface; taping and finishing must come first, but painting cannot begin until drywall is installed.
Baseboards, casings, and crown molding are installed over finished drywall surfaces; attempting before drywall would leave gaps and lack of backing.

While flooring is often installed after drywall to avoid dust and debris settling on finished floors, some sequences install drywall after rough flooring; generally hard preference for drywall first to avoid damage to flooring from mudding/sanding.
Structural framing must be complete to provide the supporting structure and load-bearing capacity for built-in seating elements.
The floor substrate must be prepared and leveled to provide a stable base for the built-in seating installation.
Any electrical wiring for outlets or lighting near the seating area must be roughed in before the seating is built in place, as access behind or under the seating would be blocked.
Finish flooring should be installed after the built-in seating framework is in place to allow flooring to be run up to or slightly under the seating for a clean finished appearance.

Final painting and finishing of surrounding walls and trim should occur after built-in seating installation to ensure seamless integration and to avoid damaging finished surfaces during seating installation.

All rough-in work for electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, and HVAC ducts must be completed and inspected before any final fixtures (light fixtures, faucets, vents) can be installed, as the rough infrastructure is concealed behind walls and ceilings.

Drywall must be hung, taped, mudded, and finished (including sanding and priming) before final fixtures are installed to avoid damage to fixtures from drywall dust and to allow proper mounting on finished surfaces.

Flooring (tile, hardwood, carpet, etc.) must be fully installed before installing final fixtures such as toilets, vanity bases, and floor-mounted electrical outlets to ensure fixtures sit correctly on the finished floor surface.

All painting, wallcovering, and decorative wall finishes must be completed before final fixtures are mounted, as fixtures would obstruct access to walls for painting and could be damaged by paint splatter.

Final fixture installation (lights, switches, outlets, plumbing fixtures) must precede the installation of final trim items like switch plates, outlet covers, escutcheon plates, and decorative trims that cover fixture mounting points.

All final fixtures must be installed before the final building inspections and testing can be performed, as inspectors need to verify that all fixtures are properly installed, functional, and code-compliant.

Final fixture installation is typically completed before the project closeout and punch list walkthrough, though some fixtures could theoretically be installed later as a soft preference for scheduling convenience.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to the required depth and level before any foundation work can commence, as the micro-foundation is installed directly into the excavated earth.

If the soil requires stabilization (e.g., compaction, grouting, or replacement), this must be completed prior to pouring the micro-foundation and floor slab to ensure adequate bearing capacity and prevent differential settlement.

Underground drainage pipes, water supply lines, and electrical conduits that will run beneath the floor slab must be laid and tested before the slab is poured, to avoid later excavation through the finished concrete.
Formwork defining the shape of the micro-foundation and floor slab, along with steel reinforcement (rebar or mesh), must be placed and inspected before concrete can be poured.

After the concrete slab is poured, it must undergo sufficient curing time and receive waterproofing treatment before any subsequent construction loads or finishes are applied, to achieve design strength and moisture protection.
The structural framing (e.g., steel or concrete frame) must be erected first to provide the load-bearing support and attachment surface for the exterior wall system.
The building foundation or ground floor slab must be completed to provide a stable base and anchorage point for the exterior wall panels.

Any electrical conduits, outlet boxes, plumbing lines, or other MEP rough-ins that will be embedded within or pass through the exterior wall cavity must be installed before the wall system is closed up, to avoid costly rework.
The exterior wall panels provide the structural openings and rough openings into which windows and doors are set; the wall system must be in place to receive and support these fenestration elements.
After the wall panels are installed, joints, seams, and penetrations must be sealed with weatherproofing membranes or sealants to ensure the building envelope is watertight and airtight.

The exterior wall system must be fully installed and closed to the outside before interior finishing work can begin, as interior finishes rely on the exterior wall as a backing and to protect them from weather damage.
The structural frame (beams, columns, trusses) must be in place to provide load-bearing support for the compact roof system.
A structural roof deck (e.g., metal deck, concrete slab) must be installed to provide the base substrate upon which the compact roof assembly is built.
Vapor retarder must be placed directly on the roof deck before the insulation and membrane layers to prevent moisture migration into the roof assembly.
Roof drains, scuppers, and gutters must be positioned and flashed in coordination with the completed compact roof membrane to ensure proper water evacuation.
HVAC units, solar panels, or other rooftop equipment must be placed after the compact roof assembly is completed to avoid damaging the waterproofing membrane and insulation layers.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed, sized, and prepared before the door unit can be installed, as the door frame requires a structurally sound and correctly dimensioned opening.
Exterior walls must be framed and sheathed to provide the structural support and mounting surface for the door frame and assembly.
The subfloor or rough floor must be in place to establish the finished floor height, threshold elevation, and provide a stable working platform for door installation.
Weather sealing, flashing, and exterior trim work around the door frame must follow door installation to ensure proper integration and water tightness.
Interior wall finishing around the door opening should be completed after the door and frame are installed to allow for proper casing installation, taping, and seamless paint lines.
Final floor coverings (tile, hardwood, etc.) should be installed after the door is hung to achieve precise fit at the threshold and to avoid damaging finished flooring during door installation.

The window rough opening (stud framing, header, sill) must be built to the correct dimensions before the window unit can be installed; the window cannot be placed without a structurally prepared opening.
The window unit must be fabricated, delivered, and on-site before the installation activity can commence.

predecessor: Weatherproof Membrane / Flashing Installation (at rough opening)
rationale: Weatherproofing and flashing must be applied around the rough opening before the window is set to prevent water intrusion behind the unit once installed.

successor: Window Trim / Casing and Siding Integration
rationale: Interior and exterior trim, casing, and siding must abut or overlap the installed window frame; these finishes cannot be completed until the window is in place.
Drywall around the window opening is typically installed and taped after the window is set to ensure a clean, finished edge against the window frame.
A stable, level foundation is physically required before the micro-kitchen block can be placed and secured.
Plumbing supply/drain lines and electrical conduit must be roughed-in behind the wall before the micro-kitchen block is fastened in position.
Once the micro-kitchen block is in its final position, the previously roughed-in utilities can be connected to the block's fixtures.
Countertops and trim are fitted after the block is set to ensure proper alignment and a finished appearance.
Backsplash and wall finishes are applied after the block is permanently in place to create seamless edges and proper sealing.
The structural frame must be completed to provide support and enclosure for the bathroom pod.
Main MEP risers and distribution lines must be in place so that the bathroom pod can connect to building services.
The floor slab or deck must be finished and load-bearing ready to support the bathroom pod.
The pod must be set in place before its plumbing, electrical, and ventilation connections can be finalized.
Adjacent finishes can be sequenced after pod placement to avoid damage and allow for precise alignment, though it's a soft preference rather than a strict physical constraint.
The main structural frame must be in place to provide a stable load-bearing support for the sleeping/living platform.
If internal walls define the compartment, they need to be framed before the platform can be securely mounted within that space.
The platform must be finished and in position before the mattress/cushion can be placed onto it.

successor: Mount Storage Drawers / Cabinetry Below Platform
rationale: Storage units that slide or fit under the platform require the platform to be installed first to define the available space and attachment points.

successor: Install Overhead Shelving / Lighting Above Platform
rationale: While not physically required, it is preferable to install the platform first so that overhead items can be positioned at the correct height relative to the sleeping surface.

The integrated storage system requires a level, structurally sound concrete floor slab to bear its weight and provide a stable base for precise alignment of storage racks and automated retrieval equipment.

The storage system components (especially electronics, drives, and stored materials) must be protected from weather exposure; the building envelope must be watertight and climate-controlled before installation begins.

The integrated storage system requires dedicated power connections for its control systems, conveyors, and automated retrieval units; main electrical panels and conduit runs must be in place before final connection and commissioning.

The storage system hardware must be physically installed and anchored before its control software, warehouse management system interface, and automated retrieval logic can be tested and integrated with the facility's IT network.

End-to-end testing of storage, retrieval, and inventory tracking workflows can only commence once the physical system is fully installed, as it requires actual operation of all mechanical and electronic components under load.

predecessor: Rough-in Plumbing for Hot Water Supply
rationale: Hot water supply piping must be roughed in to the location where the point-of-use water heater will be installed, so that the unit can be connected to the water supply.
Electrical power supply wiring must be run to the installation location before the water heater can be wired and energized.

successor: Connect Hot Water Supply Lines to Fixtures
rationale: The point-of-use water heater must be installed and connected before final hot water supply lines can be run from the heater to downstream fixtures (e.g., sink, shower).
Trim-out of fixtures that rely on hot water from the point-of-use heater must occur after the heater is operational to verify hot water delivery.

successor: Insulation of Hot Water Pipes (if applicable)
rationale: Insulating hot water pipes from the heater to fixtures can be done after the heater is connected, though it could also be done beforehand; it is preferrable to insulate after connection to ensure full coverage.

The electrical rough-in, which includes running conduits, cables, and installing junction boxes, must be completed before the Distribution Board & Meter can be installed, as the board serves as the central termination point for these incoming and outgoing circuits.

The building must be weathertight and the main structural walls (where the board is mounted) must be in place before installing the electrical distribution board and meter to protect equipment from weather damage and provide a stable mounting surface.

All final circuit connections (light switches, outlets, fixtures, appliances) terminate at the distribution board; therefore the board must be installed and energized before trim-out devices can be connected and tested.

The utility meter is physically mounted on or adjacent to the distribution board, and the utility company requires the board to be installed and inspected before they will set the meter and energize the service.

All downstream circuits and devices must be connected to the distribution board before comprehensive testing (insulation resistance, polarity, load balancing) can be performed on the complete electrical installation.
Lighting fixtures are typically mounted on or recessed into ceilings, so the ceiling structure must be in place before fixtures can be installed.
Electrical cables, junction boxes, and wiring for light locations must be run and terminated before fixtures can be connected.
If recessed lighting is installed, finishing work around the fixtures (mudding, taping, painting) should be done after the fixtures are in place to ensure a clean finished look.
It is common practice to install fixtures before finished flooring to avoid damage to flooring from ladders or dropped tools, but this is a soft preference rather than a strict physical constraint.

successor: Final Electrical Trim-out / Switch Plate Installation
rationale: Switches and dimmers controlling the fixtures must be installed after the fixtures themselves are connected and tested to ensure proper circuit completion.
The building foundation and slab must be in place before rainwater downpipes and greywater diversion pipes can be installed, as these pipes are embedded in or routed beneath/through the slab.
Roof gutters must be installed to collect rainwater before downpipes can be connected to them for water conveyance to the diversion system.
External wall surfaces must be complete to allow downpipes to be mounted and secured against the walls, and to provide the necessary structure for pipe routing.

It is preferable to complete grading and landscaping after the diversion system is installed to avoid disturbing or covering underground pipes, but this is a soft preference as some landscaping can proceed in parallel.
The diversion system, including downpipes and greywater connections, must be fully installed before the rough-in inspection can be conducted to verify compliance with plumbing codes.
Electrical wiring infrastructure and conduit must be installed in walls, ceilings, and floors before fire alarm devices (detectors, alarms, panels) can be mounted and connected.
Ceiling grids and wall framing must be in place to provide the structural mounting surface for fire alarm devices such as smoke detectors, heat detectors, and manual pull stations.

successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: All fire detection and alarm devices must be installed and wired before the entire fire alarm system can be tested, programmed, and commissioned for functionality.
While not physically mandatory, installing fire alarm devices before ceiling finishes are closed avoids costly retrofitting and damage to finished surfaces if devices need to be recessed or adjusted.
Fire detection and alarm devices must be fully installed and operational before the building can pass final fire safety inspection and be granted occupancy.

Site surveys and geotechnical investigations must be completed before excavation to understand soil conditions, identify underground utilities, and determine the excavation methodology required for safe and compliant earthworks.
Any existing structures, pavements, or obstacles on the site must be demolished and cleared before excavation can commence to provide a clear and safe work area for earthmoving equipment.
Regulatory permits and approvals from local authorities must be secured before any earth disturbance or excavation begins to comply with legal and environmental requirements.

Excavation to the required depth and grade must be completed before foundation construction can start, as the foundation concrete is placed directly onto the prepared subgrade or engineered fill within the excavated area.

Excavation opens up trenches and pits that allow for the installation of underground drainage pipes, water lines, and sewer connections; these utilities are typically laid in the excavated ground before backfilling and foundation work proceeds.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the required depth and dimensions before any foundation work can begin, as the foundation requires a prepared and stable subgrade.
Soil bearing capacity must be verified and the subgrade properly compacted to ensure it can support the foundation load without settlement or failure.
Underground plumbing, electrical conduits, and drainage lines must be laid and inspected before the slab is poured, as they will be embedded within or beneath the concrete.
The concrete foundation and slab must be fully cured and achieve sufficient strength before any above-grade structural framing can be erected on top of it.
Waterproofing membranes and drainage boards are typically applied to the exterior of foundation walls after the concrete has cured, and these systems protect the foundation from moisture intrusion.
The foundation and slab must be fully cured and structurally ready before any framing or wall erection can begin, as framing loads require a stable base.
Site must be cleared, excavated, and leveled before foundation work and subsequent framing can proceed.
Underground plumbing, electrical conduits, and drainage must be installed before slab pouring and framing to avoid rework and structural damage.
Roof trusses and roofing materials depend on the walls and framing being in place to provide the supporting structure.
Rough-in of electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, and HVAC ducts typically occurs after walls are framed so that services can be run through the wall cavities before drywall installation.
Structural framing provides the load-bearing skeleton and roof deck surface that the roofing system is installed onto; without the frame in place, there is no structural support for the roof.
Roof sheathing or decking (e.g., plywood or OSB) must be installed over the framing to create a solid substrate for underlayment and roofing materials.
Any electrical, HVAC, or plumbing work that runs through the roof or attic space must be roughed in before the roof is closed up, otherwise access would be impossible without removing roofing.
The roof must be watertight before interior ceiling finishes (drywall, paint) are installed; otherwise water damage would ruin the finishes.
While siding can sometimes be installed in parallel, it is standard practice to complete roofing first to prevent water running down behind incomplete siding and causing moisture issues.
Structural framing (walls, roof, floor) must be complete to provide the rough openings and structural support needed for window and door installation.
Electrical wiring and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before windows and doors are installed to avoid interference and to allow easy access for routing services through wall cavities.
Exterior sheathing, house wrap, and weather-resistive barriers must be in place before window and door installation to ensure proper flashing integration and weather sealing.
Windows and doors must be installed before drywall can be applied so that drywall can be fitted and finished around the window and door frames, providing a clean interior finish.
Exterior siding and cladding must be installed after windows and doors to allow proper flashing, trim installation, and weather sealing around the openings.
Structural framing, roof, and exterior enclosure must be complete to provide a weather-tight envelope before MEP rough-in work begins, protecting materials and equipment from weather damage.
Floor slabs and decks must be poured and cured to provide the structural substrate for mounting MEP equipment and running conduit, piping, and ductwork.
MEP rough-in (piping, ducts, conduit, wiring) must be installed in walls, ceilings, and floors before insulation can be placed around or over them.
All MEP rough-in work within wall cavities and ceiling spaces must be completed and inspected before closing them up with drywall or ceiling boards.

While finishing can technically begin in areas not affected by MEP, it is standard practice to complete MEP rough-in first to avoid damaging finished surfaces when accessing walls or ceilings for late MEP changes.

MEP rough-in work (electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, HVAC ducts) must be installed within wall/ceiling cavities before they are closed off by interior linings such as drywall or plaster. Otherwise, costly rework or demolition would be required.
Interior wall framing, studs, and structural supports must be fully erected and inspected before any lining or finish material (e.g., drywall, paneling) can be applied to them.

Thermal and acoustic insulation must be placed inside wall and ceiling cavities before they are sealed by interior linings; otherwise, insulation cannot be added without removing the finished surface.
Interior linings (e.g., drywall, plasterboard) must be installed and finished (taped, jointed, sanded) to provide a smooth substrate before paint or decorative coatings can be applied.
Wall linings and finishes are typically completed before flooring is installed to avoid damaging finished floors and to allow baseboard or trim installation that sits atop the flooring.
The HVAC system must be fully installed before it can be commissioned, as commissioning verifies proper operation of installed equipment.
The water heater must be physically installed and connected before commissioning can test its functionality and performance.
Ductwork must be installed and tested for airtightness before the HVAC system can be commissioned to ensure proper airflow and system performance.
Electrical connections and power supply must be completed to provide power for the HVAC and water heater systems during commissioning.
Plumbing supply and drain lines must be installed to allow the water heater to operate and be tested during commissioning.
Commissioning ensures HVAC systems are balanced and functioning, which is preferable before final enclosure sealing to allow access for adjustments, but is a soft preference.
Commissioning must be completed before final interior finishes (ceilings, drywall, paint) because commissioning may require access to mechanical spaces and could cause dust or damage.
The HVAC and water heater systems must be commissioned and verified as operational before integrating them into the building management system (BMS) for centralized control.

successor: Final Inspections and Certificate of Occupancy
rationale: Commissioning is a prerequisite for final inspection and certificate of occupancy, as authorities require verified operation of mechanical systems before occupancy is granted.

Structural shell, exterior cladding, roofing, and rough-in utilities (plumbing, electrical, HVAC rough-ins) must be completed before interior fit-out can commence, as fit-out requires enclosed, weathertight spaces with pre-installed utility stubs.
Subfloor leveling and underlayment must be finished before installing kitchen cabinets, bathroom vanities, and finishes to ensure stable, level base and prevent damage to flooring.
Water supply pipes, drain/waste/vent lines must be roughed-in and pressure tested before connecting fixtures, sinks, toilets, and showers during fit-out.
Electrical cables, switch boxes, outlet boxes, and lighting junction boxes must be installed and wired in walls/ceilings before fitting cabinets, splashbacks, and ceiling finishes.
Internal partition walls must be framed and lined with plasterboard/drywall (at least the first fix) before kitchen cabinetry and bathroom fixtures can be installed against finished walls.
After fit-out of cabinets and fixtures, waterproofing membranes to wet areas must be inspected and approved before proceeding to final tiling and finishing.
After cabinets and vanities are installed, plumbers can connect supply lines, faucets, traps, and trim out fixtures (toilets, sinks, showerheads) that are mounted to the units.
After cabinetry and fit-out is complete, electricians can install final switches, outlets, light fixtures, range hoods, and connect appliances (oven, dishwasher) in their designated spaces.
Final paint touch-ups, caulking, and protective trim work around installed kitchen/bathroom units must be performed after fit-out to seal joints and achieve finished appearance.
Tiling of bathroom walls and floors (and kitchen splashbacks) must occur after cabinetry and fixtures are installed so that tiles abut neatly against installed units and waterproofing is continuous.
Structural framing and enclosure must be completed to provide the physical substrate (walls, ceilings, floors) for mounting electrical conduits, junction boxes, and wiring pathways.
Plumbing rough-in (pipes, drains) must be completed before electrical work to avoid conflicts in wall/ceiling cavities and to coordinate vertical chases.
HVAC ductwork and equipment installation must be completed before electrical work to prevent spatial conflicts and to ensure electrical runs can be routed around ducts.
Electrical wiring and boxes must be in place before insulation is installed to ensure proper coverage and to avoid needing to disturb insulation for later wiring.
All electrical cables, outlets, switches, and junction boxes must be roughed in and inspected before walls are closed with drywall.
All rough carpentry, framing, and structural work must be completed before final finishes are applied, as finishing covers and seals the interior surfaces.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and mudded before final finishing and sealants can be applied to create smooth, finished walls.
Electrical wiring, boxes, and rough-in work must be completed before walls are sealed and finished, to avoid cutting into finished surfaces.
Plumbing pipes and rough-in work must be completed before final finishes and sealants are applied, as access to walls is needed during rough-in.
HVAC ductwork and rough-in must be completed before sealing walls and applying final finishes to ensure all mechanical systems are in place.
Final finishing and sealants prepare the surfaces; painting and wallcovering follow as the final decorative layer over finished surfaces.
Flooring installation should occur after final finishing and sealants to avoid damaging finished floors during wall and ceiling finishing work.
Final trim, baseboards, and millwork are installed after wall finishing and sealants to ensure clean edges and proper fit against finished surfaces.
Cabinets are installed after final wall finishes and sealants to ensure walls are fully prepared and to avoid damaging finished cabinets during wall finishing.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the required depths before any structural framing can begin, as the framing system relies on a stable, prepared foundation substrate.
Foundations (footings, piers, or slabs) must be poured and fully cured to provide a load-bearing base for structural columns, beams, and walls to be erected upon.
Plumbing, electrical conduits, and drainage lines running beneath the slab or within footings must be placed and inspected before framing, as they would be inaccessible after the structure is built.
Exterior wall panels, siding, or curtain walls require the structural frame to be fully erected to provide attachment points and structural support before they can be installed.
The foundation and slab must be completed before interior walls can be erected, as interior walls require a stable, level base surface for load distribution and structural integrity.
Exterior walls and roofing must be in place to provide structural enclosure and weather protection before interior wall framing can proceed safely.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins are installed within the interior wall cavities and must run after the walls are framed but before they are closed up with drywall.
Insulation is placed inside interior wall cavities after framing is complete and before drywall is applied.
Drywall is fastened directly to the interior wall framing; therefore, the interior wall studs and structure must be fully erected and inspected before drywall can be hung.
The fireplace and chimney require a solid foundation to support their weight and structural loads.
The chimney must be integrated with the wall and roof framing for structural support and proper roof penetration.
Roof flashing around the chimney must be installed after the chimney is completed to ensure a watertight seal.
Fireplace surround and chimney chase must be built before drywall is installed around it for proper integration and finishing.
While flooring can often be installed before or after, it is preferable to install flooring after the fireplace hearth is set to allow for precise cuts and a finished look.
Flooring must be installed before kitchen cabinets to ensure cabinets sit on a level surface and to avoid damaging finished floors during cabinet installation.
Electrical wiring and rough-ins for kitchen appliances and lighting must be completed before cabinets are installed, as cabinets will cover walls and restrict access.
Plumbing rough-ins (water supply and drain lines for sinks and dishwasher) must be completed before cabinets are installed since cabinets will block access to walls and floor areas.
Countertops are installed directly on top of base cabinets; cabinets must be fully installed and leveled before countertops can be fabricated and placed.
Sinks, cooktops, and built-in appliances are typically installed after cabinetry is in place, as they are mounted into or adjacent to the cabinets.
Plumbing rough-in (pipes, drains, vent lines) must be installed in walls and floors before fixtures (sinks, toilets, tubs) can be attached and connected to the supply and waste lines.
Electrical wiring, boxes, and switch/dummy-out locations must be roughed in before light fixtures, exhaust fans, or outlet covers can be installed and connected.
Waterproof membrane or backer board must be installed and sealed before fixtures like tubs, showers, and toilets are placed to protect the structure from moisture damage.

It is often preferred to install finish flooring (tile, vinyl) before permanent fixtures so the flooring runs continuously under the fixtures, but in some trades the fixtures go first; soft preference to avoid cutting around fixtures.
The vanity top and sink fixture are typically set in place before the mirror and cabinet doors are installed, as the vanity must be fixed to the wall and plumbed first.
Guttering and downpipes are installed to collect and channel rainwater from the roof. The roof covering must be completed first to define the roof edges and drainage points.
Downpipes are fixed to external walls, so they should be installed before final wall cladding or rendering to allow proper integration and waterproofing behind the pipework.
Downpipes connect to the underground drainage system; the above-ground guttering and downpipes must be in place before final connection to the stormwater drainage system can be completed.
Roof framing provides the structural support required for gutter fascia boards and the roof edge where gutters are mounted.
Gutters are typically attached to fascia boards along the roof edge, so fascia installation must be completed before gutters can be securely fixed.
The ground must be properly graded and compacted before any paving or walkway installation to ensure proper drainage and a stable base.
Underground utility lines must be laid before pouring concrete or laying pavers to avoid digging up finished surfaces for utility connections.
Foundation work and associated drainage around the building must be completed before driveway/walkway installation to ensure proper tie-in and avoid conflicts.
Driveways and walkways provide access and define edges for final landscaping, topsoil placement, seeding/sodding, and decorative planting.
While not strictly necessary, it is preferred to complete driveway and walkway installation before exterior finishes to avoid damaging finished walls with paving equipment and materials.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before fence or wall foundations can be laid to ensure proper alignment and stability.
Property boundaries must be accurately surveyed and staked to ensure the fence/wall is built on the correct property line and within legal setbacks.
Any underground utilities (water, gas, electric, data lines) that will cross the fence line must be installed first to avoid digging after the wall/fence is built.
Gates must be hung on and anchored to the completed fence or wall structure for proper alignment and support.
Final landscaping and planting adjacent to the fence line is typically done after the wall is complete to avoid damage to plants during construction and to allow accurate grading up to the wall.
Final grading and drainage swales are often completed after the perimeter wall to direct water away from the structure properly.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and prepared before any deck or patio structure can be built on it.
Concrete footings or foundation piers must be poured and cured to support the deck structure or patio slab.
Any underground drainage, irrigation, or plumbing lines that will run beneath the deck/patio area must be installed before the surface is covered.
Railings are attached to the deck structure or patio edge and cannot be installed until the deck/patio framework or slab is complete.
Any electrical conduits for outdoor lighting, outlets, or fixtures that are embedded in or mounted on the deck/patio must be installed after the deck/patio structure is in place.
Structural framing and rough carpentry must be completed to provide the supporting framework and enclosed spaces through which HVAC ducts can be routed and equipment mounted.
Roof must be in place to protect HVAC rooftop units and ductwork penetrations from weather damage and to provide a weathertight enclosure before ductwork installation begins.
Exterior walls need to be enclosed to protect interior spaces and ductwork from weather, and to provide the structural backing for wall-mounted duct runs.
HVAC ductwork occupies ceiling and wall cavities; plumbing rough-in should follow to avoid conflicts with ducts and to allow coordinated routing of pipes around installed ductwork.

Electrical wiring and boxes must be routed around and after HVAC ductwork is in place to avoid conflicts and to ensure proper clearances between electrical components and ductwork as required by code.
Drywall and ceiling finishes must be installed after HVAC ductwork and equipment are fully in place to allow for duct concealment, access for connections, and to avoid rework.
Terminal device installation (registers, grilles, thermostats) and system balancing/commissioning can only occur after the main ductwork and equipment are installed and connected.
Plasterboard/drywall is fixed directly to the structural framing (studs and joists). The framing must be fully erected, braced, and approved to provide a stable substrate for the plasterboard sheets.
All electrical cables, outlet boxes, and switch boxes must be installed within the wall cavities before the plasterboard is fixed, as access is impossible once the boards are in place.

Plumbing pipes, fittings, and drainage lines running inside walls and ceilings must be installed and pressure-tested before being enclosed by plasterboard. Any leaks would cause severe damage if detected after boarding.
Heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning ductwork and piping must be routed and installed within ceiling and wall cavities before they are enclosed by plasterboard.

Thermal and acoustic insulation batts are placed within wall and ceiling cavities behind the plasterboard. Insulation must be fully installed prior to boarding to allow access and ensure complete coverage.

Once plasterboard sheets are fixed to the framing, the joints between boards (taping, joint compound application, sanding) must be completed to create a smooth, continuous surface ready for painting or finishing.

successor: Door and Window Frame Installation (if not pre-fitted)
rationale: While door and window frames can be installed before boarding in many cases, some sequences install them after boarding to achieve precise alignment with the finished plasterboard thickness. This is a soft sequencing preference depending on the construction method.

All painting, wallpapering, or other wall finishes are applied over the finished, jointed, and sanded plasterboard surface and cannot begin until the plasterboard installation and jointing is complete.

Plumbing and electrical rough-ins (pipes, wiring, outlets) must be completed and inspected before any cabinetry, fixtures, or finishes are installed to avoid damaging completed work and to meet building codes.

Floor screeding and waterproofing in wet areas must be completed and cured before kitchen cabinets, bathroom vanities, and flooring finishes are installed, as these surfaces need a stable, watertight base.
Wall surfaces must be plastered and waterproofed in wet zones before installing splashbacks, tiling, or mounting cabinets, as these processes would be impossible or damaging to do after fit-out.

Final connection of plumbing fixtures (taps, toilets, sinks) and electrical fittings (light switches, power points, appliances) must occur after cabinets and fixtures are installed so that connections align correctly and are accessible.

While painting can be done before fit-out, final touch-ups and finishing coats are typically done after cabinetry and tiling to ensure clean edges and a polished appearance; this is a soft preference for quality rather than a strict physical necessity.

The structural framing and sheathing (e.g., OSB or plywood) provide the substrate and structural backing onto which cladding and siding are attached. Without this framework, there is nothing to secure the siding to.

Roofing must be completed to provide weather protection for the building envelope and to avoid water damage to unfinished walls. Installing siding before roofing creates a risk of water intrusion at the top edge of the walls.
Windows and doors must be installed and properly flashed before siding is applied, so that the siding can be integrated with window/door flashing details to ensure a watertight seal around openings.

Exterior trim, soffits, and fascia are typically installed after or concurrently with siding to cover edges and provide a finished appearance, but the main siding panels must be in place to establish the final wall plane.

While some siding materials come pre-finished, painting or staining is typically done after siding installation to protect the material and achieve the desired aesthetic. This is a logical sequence but not a strict physical constraint if using factory-finished products.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil before paving can begin, as paving requires a clean, stable subgrade.
Excavation to achieve proper grades and sub-base depths must be completed before paving to ensure correct drainage and structural support.
All underground utility lines and drainage pipes that cross under the driveway or path must be installed and inspected before paving to avoid future digging and damage to the paved surface.
A compacted granular base or sub-base layer must be placed and compacted prior to paving to provide a stable foundation and prevent settling or cracking.
It is preferable to complete paving before final landscaping and topsoiling adjacent to the paved surface to avoid soiling or damaging the fresh pavement and to achieve a clean edge.

The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil, and rough grading completed to expose the actual ground levels and boundaries before any boundary walls or fences can be accurately positioned and constructed.
Accurate survey and setting out of the property boundary lines, pegs, and profiles must be completed first to ensure the fence or wall is built on the correct legal boundary and alignment.

Boundary walls/fences establish the secure perimeter and defined site boundary, which is necessary to control site access, prevent trespassing, and demarcate the construction zone before main building works commence.

While fencing can precede site facilities, it is a soft preference because temporary facilities like site offices and storage can technically be installed simultaneously or even first; however, a secured perimeter is typically preferred to protect those facilities from theft.

Underground drainage pipes, utility ducts, and service connections that cross the boundary line must be laid before the fence/wall foundation is built above them, to avoid having to excavate through or under the completed wall later.
Internal wall surfaces must be smooth, filled, and primed before painting can be applied; painting over unprepared walls results in poor adhesion and finish.
Ceilings must be installed, taped, and jointed before painting begins, as painting ceilings is typically done first and requires a finished surface.
Doors and window frames need to be fitted and hung before final painting and decorating can take place, to allow for painting of frames and surrounding trim.
Electrical outlet boxes and switch boxes must be installed and their faceplates fitted before painting; painting is the final finishing step after all rough-in work.
Painting and decorating should be completed before final flooring (carpet, tile, hardwood) is laid to prevent paint drips, dust, and debris from damaging the new floor surface.
Skirting boards and trim are typically installed after painting to ensure a clean paint line and to avoid paint overspray on the trim; they can be painted separately before fixing.
Painting and decorating is one of the last finishing trades; all paintwork must be complete and dried before the final clean and handover of the building.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (wiring, pipes, ducts) must be completed and inspected before installing final fixtures like outlets, switches, faucets, and trim to avoid damage, rework, or code violations.

Drywall must be hung, taped, mudded, and sanded before installing trim such as baseboards, door casings, and window trim; fixtures would be obstructed or damaged if installed prior to drywall completion.
Final paint coats must be applied before installing trim and fixtures to ensure clean edges, avoid paint drips on finished fixtures, and allow seamless caulking between walls and trim.

Flooring (tile, hardwood, carpet, etc.) must be installed before baseboard trim and floor-mounted fixtures are placed, as trim sits atop the finished flooring and floor-mounted fixtures (e.g., toilets, floor registers) require the finished floor height for proper alignment.

All fixtures and trim must be fully installed before the final clean-up and punch-list walkthrough can occur, as debris from installation would soil cleaned areas and trim/fixture adjustments may generate dust and waste requiring cleaning.
The partition must be installed on a level, cured floor slab or subfloor to provide a stable base and proper load distribution.

predecessor: Rough Electrical Routing to Partition Location
rationale: Electrical supply lines for outlets/switches within the partition must be roughed in before the partition frame is erected to avoid later core drilling or surface-mounted conduit.
Final wiring, outlet installation, and switch plates cannot be installed until the partition framing and drywall are in place to conceal the wiring.
Painting and final surface finishing must occur after the partition is fully erected and boarded to achieve a uniform finish without damaging adjacent areas.
Any cabinetry, workbenches, or shelving that attach to the partition require the partition to be structurally complete to serve as a mounting surface.
The workshop bench requires a stable, level foundation slab to be in place before it can be installed or positioned.
The building's main structural frame must be erected to provide the enclosed space and support structure for the workshop bench.
Workshop bench must be installed before any mounted equipment, tools, or workstation accessories can be fitted onto or organized around it.
Utility lines for power, compressed air, or data must be connected after the bench is in its final position to ensure proper alignment and safe routing.

successor: Final Quality Inspection of Workshop Area
rationale: The bench must be installed and all equipment placed before the final inspection of the workshop area can be completed.
The modular desk system requires a level and stable floor surface for proper assembly and alignment. Installing desks on an uneven floor would cause structural instability and misalignment.

Electrical wiring for power outlets, data ports, and cable management must be roughed-in before desk installation because the desks often integrate with or cover floor/under-desk power and data connections.

Overhead ceiling installation, lighting fixtures, and HVAC ductwork should be completed before placing modular desks to avoid dust/debris falling on finished furniture, and to prevent the need for moving desks to access overhead systems.
Once desks are positioned and assembled, final connections of power outlets, data ports, and cable management systems can be made to ensure proper fit and integration with the desk layout.

Touch-up painting and final wall finishing are often done after furniture is installed to address any damage from moving desks, though this is a soft preference as it could be done before with careful protection.
The integrated tool storage wall is built into the wall framing, so the framing must be in place to support the storage components.
Electrical wiring for lighting or outlets in the tool storage wall must be installed before the storage system is mounted to avoid rework.
Drywall must be completed and finished before mounting the integrated tool storage wall to ensure a clean finished surface behind the storage system.
Tools and equipment can only be placed into the storage system after the wall unit is fully installed and secured.
The storage wall should be in place before final inspection to verify that all components are properly installed and functional.

The desk base must be placed on a finished, level floor surface to ensure stability and proper alignment. Installing flooring first prevents the need to work around the desk base and ensures a clean, even surface for mounting.

Any underfloor electrical conduits, data cabling, or power outlets that will serve the desk must be roughed-in before the desk base is permanently installed, as the base would block access to the floor area underneath.
The adjustable base must be anchored and fully assembled in place before the desktop can be mounted on top of it, as the base provides the structural support and lifting mechanism for the desk.

Power and control cables for the height-adjustment mechanism must be connected and routed after the base is installed, but these connections are typically integrated with the desk assembly before full furniture placement.

It is preferable (soft constraint) to complete all major workstation assembly including the desk base before moving in chairs, monitors, and personal items to avoid damage and congestion, though occupancy could technically begin with the base installed even if some accessories are missing.

The self-governing booking display must know who the customer is before it can show personalized booking options. Customer authentication (login, profile retrieval) provides the necessary user context and permissions for the booking display to function.

The booking display must have up-to-date information on room availability, rates, and inventory to present accurate options. Without synchronized inventory data, the display cannot show correct booking choices.
The availability engine that checks date ranges, occupancy, and blackout periods must be operational before the display can render available time slots to the user.

The user must first select and review their booking via the self-governing display before the system can process payment and issue a confirmation. The booking display is the user interface through which selections are made.

Once the booking display captures the user's chosen options and the booking is confirmed, the reservation record must be saved to the database and notification (e.g., email/SMS) sent to the customer. The display generates the data that feeds into record-keeping.

predecessor: Complete Structural Framing and Wall Rough-Ins
rationale: Structural framing and wall rough-ins (studs, backing) must be in place to provide a substrate for mounting the self-governing partition system.

predecessor: Complete MEP rough-in (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) within partition zones
rationale: All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work behind or within the partition cavity must be completed before installing the partition system, as access will be restricted once the system is in place.
Self-governing partitions often require the partition tracks to be installed before finished flooring to allow the flooring material to be run up to or under the partition track.
The partition system typically connects to the overhead structure; ceiling grid installation should follow partition installation so that the ceiling aligns properly with the partition head track.

successor: Final MEP trim-out and device installation
rationale: After the partition system is in place, electrical outlets, switches, data jacks, and other devices can be installed into the finished partition surface.
The workbench array must be fully fabricated and assembled in the factory before it can be transported to the site and installed in its final location.
A level, structurally sound foundation or support base must be ready to receive and anchor the workbench array, ensuring stability and alignment.

Electrical power and data network cabling must be run to the workbench location before the bench is set in place, as access behind or under the bench is extremely difficult or impossible after installation.
Final electrical, data, and any plumbing connections to the installed workbench can only be made after the bench is physically in position.
The main workbench frame and integrated array must be installed first so that worktop surfaces, countertops, or finishing layers can be fitted onto the structure.
The busway must be physically installed before it can be commissioned, as commissioning involves testing and energizing an already-installed system.
The busway must be commissioned (tested and certified) before downstream zone-level distribution can be energized, to ensure safety and operational readiness.
Loads can only be connected to the busway after it has been commissioned to avoid damage to equipment and ensure electrical safety.
Rough-in work including conduit, wiring, and mounting must be finished before commissioning can proceed to verify proper installation.
Commissioning produces the test results and documentation needed for the final electrical inspection sign-off.
The digital booking interface must be mounted on the digital kiosk hardware; the kiosk structure and mounting brackets must be installed first.

predecessor: Run Power and Data Cables to Kiosk Location
rationale: Power and network connectivity must be available at the mounting location before the booking interface device can be mounted and connected.
Although the software can be configured in parallel or after mounting, it is preferable to have the backend ready before mounting so that the interface can be tested immediately upon installation.

successor: Connect and Test Digital Booking Interface
rationale: The interface must be physically mounted before it can be connected to power/data and functionally tested.
Calibration of the touchscreen and display adjustments can only be performed after the unit is mounted in its final position.

predecessor: Structural Framing and Ceiling Grid Installation
rationale: The cassette unit is typically installed into a suspended ceiling grid or structural ceiling, which must be in place first to support the unit.

predecessor: Main HVAC ductwork and refrigerant piping rough-in
rationale: Supply and return air ducts as well as refrigerant lines must be run to the unit location before the cassette can be connected.
Power supply cables and thermostat/control wiring must be brought to the unit location for final connection.

successor: Condensate drain piping connection and testing
rationale: The unit must be hung and leveled before the condensate drain line can be properly connected and slope-checked.
Final ceiling finish work and trim must be done after the cassette is positioned to ensure proper fit and aesthetic integration.
The shaft must be excavated before the compact ventilation shaft structure can be installed or assembled.
A stable foundation or base slab is required to support the compact ventilation shaft unit.
The ventilation shaft structure must be in place before fans, ducts, and other ventilation equipment can be mounted inside it.
Power and control cabling for the ventilation system can only be run after the shaft assembly is complete, as routing depends on the shaft's final position and layout.
Waterproofing membrane application and backfilling around the shaft can only be performed once the shaft structure is fully erected and sealed.
The chassis frame must be fabricated first to provide the structural base onto which all utility components are mounted.
The suspension system must be assembled and attached to the chassis frame before the combined utility chassis can be considered complete, as it is an integral structural component.
The engine, transmission, and drivetrain components must be installed onto the chassis before the utility chassis is finalized, as they are mounted directly to the frame.
The body shell can only be mounted onto the chassis after the combined utility chassis (frame, suspension, powertrain) is fully assembled and ready to accept the body.
Major electrical harness routing and component mounting depend on the chassis structure being in place, so electrical integration must follow chassis completion.
The subfloor must be properly prepared and leveled before the floor gully can be installed to ensure proper drainage and stability.
The floor gully must be installed first so that waterproofing membrane can be properly integrated and sealed around the gully outlet.
The gully must be in place and its height set before screeding or tiling the floor to achieve correct fall and drainage slope towards the gully.
The drainage pipe network must be roughed in and the waste pipe connection point prepared before the floor gully can be connected to the drainage system.
While plumbing fixtures can often be connected later, connecting them after gully installation ensures proper drainage alignment and avoids rework.
A level, load-bearing foundation or floor slab is required to support the modular service chassis and ensure proper alignment and stability.
Electrical rough-ins including conduit, wiring, and junction boxes must be in place before the service chassis can be connected to power and control systems.
Plumbing rough-ins such as supply lines and drain pipes need to be installed before the service chassis can be connected to the building's water and waste systems.
The chassis must be securely installed before any modular service components (e.g., electrical panels, plumbing manifolds, data distribution units) can be mounted and connected within it.
While firestopping can be done after chassis installation, it is a soft preference to coordinate sealing around chassis penetrations immediately to maintain fire rating integrity.
The roof curb provides the structural base and support platform onto which the HVAC unit is mounted; the curb must be installed first to ensure proper support and alignment.
The roof deck must be fully constructed and waterproofed before mounting heavy rooftop equipment to prevent water infiltration and structural damage.

predecessor: Run Electrical Conduit to Unit Location
rationale: Electrical conduit must be stubbed out at the unit location before the HVAC unit is placed, because accessing the area after the unit is mounted is difficult and may require unsafe or complex work.
Refrigerant piping connects to the mounted unit; the unit must be in its final position before lines can be measured, cut, and brazed to its service ports.
Final power and control wiring from the electrical panel and thermostat must be landed at the unit's electrical compartment after the unit is securely mounted and accessible.
Conduit supports (hangers, trays, brackets) must be in place to physically hold and secure the conduit network before the conduit runs can be installed.
If conduit is run underground, trenches must be excavated and prepared before conduit can be laid in the ground.
Rough-in electrical work (panel locations, junction boxes, pull boxes) defines the endpoints and routing paths that the conduit network must connect to.
Conduit must be fully installed and continuous before any cables or wires can be pulled through it.
Firestopping and sealing of conduit penetrations can only be applied after the conduit runs are fully in place at the penetration points.
Electrical power and data cabling must be roughed in to the data closet location before the closet components (racks, patch panels, switches) can be installed and connected.

predecessor: Complete Interior Wall Framing and Drywall
rationale: The walls that define the data closet enclosure must be framed and finished before installing any closet infrastructure to provide a clean, enclosed space.
Data closet components (patch panels, switches) must be installed first so that the horizontal cabling can be terminated into the patch panels and tested for continuity.
Network equipment (switches, routers) in the data closet must be physically installed before they can be powered on, configured, and commissioned as part of the active network.

successor: Install Ceiling and Floor Finishes in Closet Area
rationale: While finishes can be installed after the closet is in place, it is a soft preference to complete them first to avoid dust and damage to sensitive equipment; however, the closet can be functional before final finishes.
The shower pan/liner must be installed before the direct drain can be connected, as the drain flange is integrated into or penetrates the pan/liner assembly.
The rough-in drain position and pipe stub must be set and properly located before making the final connection to the direct-drain system.
The drain connection must be complete before leak testing can be performed to verify watertight integrity.

successor: Install Finished Floor / Tile Over Pan
rationale: The direct-drain connection and any required drain grate/strainer must be installed before the finished floor or tile work is applied over the shower pan.
The direct-drain connection must be completed and verified prior to backfilling or enclosing the drain piping within walls/floors.
Simplified services must be fully installed and connected before they can be commissioned, as commissioning validates proper installation and functionality.
Power supply must be roughed in and available to simplified services equipment before commissioning can verify electrical connectivity and operation.
Data and communication cabling must be terminated and tested prior to commissioning to ensure network connectivity is ready for system validation.
Commissioning must confirm that simplified services are functioning correctly before end users can perform acceptance testing on the operational system.
Commissioning must be completed and signed off before the system can be formally handed over to the operations team for ongoing management and use.
The bridge or skywalk requires a stable foundation or substructure to bear its load; without completed foundations, the bridge structure cannot be safely erected.
