Bridge spans and skywalks are supported by piers or columns; these vertical supports must be in place before the deck or walkway structure can be installed.
If the bridge or skywalk is steel-framed, the primary steel members (girders, trusses) must be erected prior to placing the bridge deck or skywalk components.
The bridge or skywalk structure must be in place before the deck slab is poured or placed on top of it to form the walking or driving surface.
Waterproofing membranes are applied to the completed bridge or skywalk deck to protect it from moisture; this cannot occur until the deck structure is installed.
The rough opening (door frame walls and header) must be framed and finished to the correct dimensions before the automatic sliding door unit can be set in place.
The finished floor surface under the sliding door track must be completed to provide a level, stable base for the bottom track or sill.
Conduit and wiring for the automatic door operator, sensors, and control box must be roughed-in before the door unit is installed so connections can be made.
Once the door panels, track, and motor are physically installed, the automatic operator must be programmed and sensors calibrated for proper operation.

It is easier to finish drywall, paint, and trim around the door frame after the sliding door unit is in place to ensure tight fit; however this is a soft preference as finishing could be done prior with careful planning.
Wayfinding signage is typically mounted on finished walls and surfaces; wall finishes must be complete to provide a clean, stable substrate for sign installation.
Many wayfinding signs (e.g., suspended directional signs) are attached to or below ceilings; ceilings must be in place to support overhead signage.
Floor-mounted or wall-base signs require completed flooring for proper alignment and installation; flooring also defines final floor levels for sign placement.

Wayfinding signage must be installed before final inspections and commissioning to ensure all egress paths, room identification, and directional information are in place for safety and functionality verification.
Occupants and visitors rely on wayfinding signage to navigate the building; signage must be fully installed for safe and efficient building use during occupancy.

Interior glazing and partition systems are typically installed within or against framed wall openings. The rough framing must be complete to provide the structural support and defined openings for the glazing.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within walls must be completed before interior glazing is installed, as glazing encloses wall cavities and access would be blocked.
Interior glazing and partition installation must precede final interior finishes because glazing work can be messy (sealants, gaskets, adjustments) and finishes would be damaged if installed earlier.

While some flooring can be installed before partitions, it is generally preferred to complete glazed partitions first so that flooring can be run continuously up to or under the partition base, avoiding cut pieces and achieving a cleaner aesthetic.
The structural slab or subfloor must be in place and cured to provide a level, stable base for the partition walls and glazing systems to be anchored to.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide the supporting structure to which handrails and guardrails are attached.
Handrails and guardrails are typically anchored into concrete slabs, decks, or stair landings, which must be poured and sufficiently cured to bear the loads and accept anchors.
Stair stringers, treads and riser rough framing must be built before guardrails and handrails can be installed along the stair edges.
While it is common to install handrails before final trim to allow for adjustments, some trim work can be done concurrently; this is a soft preference for sequencing the finishing trades.
Handrails and guardrails are a critical life-safety component; final inspection for fall protection cannot be completed until they are installed.
The fire door frame must be installed and secured in the wall opening before the fire door can be hung, as the door hinges attach directly to the frame.
The surrounding wall structure (stud framing, drywall) must be completed to provide the correct rough opening and fire-rated assembly into which the fire door frame is set.
Hardware such as hinges, locks, closers, and panic bars are mounted onto the door itself and frame; the door must be hung first before these components can be properly fitted and adjusted.
The fire door must be fully installed and operational before a certified inspector can verify its compliance with fire ratings, clearances, self-closing function, and labeling requirements.

While painting and finishing can be done after installation, it is a soft preference to install the door first so that the fit, gaps, and operation can be verified before final surface finishes are applied to avoid damaging the finish during installation adjustments.

The raised floor system requires a level, structurally sound base slab to bear the load of the pedestals and panels. Without the structural slab in place, there is no substrate to support the raised floor.

All cables, conduit, pipes, and ducts that will run beneath the raised floor must be installed before the floor panels are placed, because access to the subfloor space is extremely limited or impossible after the panels are installed.

successor: Floor Covering / Finish Application (e.g. Carpet Tiles, Vinyl)
rationale: The finish flooring material is laid directly on top of the raised floor panels; the panels must be in place and leveled before the finish layer can be applied.

successor: Overfloor Equipment & Wall Installation (e.g. Server Racks, Partitions)
rationale: Typically, walls and heavy equipment are built after the raised floor to avoid damaging the finish floor and to allow precise layout based on the finished floor grid; however, in some phased build-outs, equipment placement can occur concurrently.

successor: Final Firestopping & Penetration Sealing at Floor
rationale: Firestopping around cable penetrations through the raised floor or slab must be completed after the floor panels are installed and all underfloor services are in place, to ensure fire-rated compartmentalization.
Ducts must be installed first to provide the physical pathway (conduit, raceway, or chase) through which connections (cables, pipes, or wires) will be run.
Foundations provide the stable base for the structure; connections (e.g., to utility lines, grounding systems) cannot be installed until the foundation is in place and cured.
The structural frame (walls, floors, ceilings) must be erected to define the routing paths and support points for connection installations such as electrical, plumbing, and data cables.
All connections (electrical, plumbing, data) must be fully installed before testing can begin to verify continuity, pressure integrity, and system functionality.
Connections must be installed and inspected before being enclosed behind insulation and drywall to ensure accessibility for inspection and to avoid costly rework.
The elevator shaft and hoistway must be structurally complete before elevator rails and cars can be installed.
The physical shaft enclosure must exist to provide the vertical pathway and support points for elevator guide rails and equipment.
The machine room (or overhead machinery space) must be constructed and waterproofed to house the elevator hoist motor, controller, and sheaves.

successor: Elevator Cab Finishing and Interior Fit-Out
rationale: The elevator car structure must be installed and operational before interior finishes, handrails, mirrors, and flooring can be applied.
While electrical connections follow elevator placement, some pre-wiring can often precede installation; hence this is a soft preference for safety and coordination.
The complete elevator assembly must be physically in place and mechanically connected before safety tests, load testing, and commissioning can begin.
A stable structural substrate (e.g., slab-on-grade or structural floor) must be in place to support the dead and live loads of built-in seating.
Built-in seating is typically anchored to or abuts structural walls and framing; these must be erected to define the spatial enclosure and provide attachment points.

Any embedded conduits, floor drains, or power/data boxes that pass beneath the seating area must be installed before the seating is built because it would be impossible or destructive to access them afterward.

Floor finishes are typically laid after fixed seating is installed because the seating acts as a built-in element that defines the finished floor perimeter; trying to finish the floor first would result in damage or misalignment when the seating is anchored.

While wall paint can be touched up after seating installation, it is more efficient to complete final wall finishes before seating to avoid awkward cutting-in. This is a soft preference for sequence efficiency, not a physical necessity.
The workbench requires a stable, level foundation to ensure structural integrity and proper functioning during use.
The supporting frame must be constructed before the workbench top and components can be mounted onto it.
All wood or workbench materials must be cut, shaped, and prepared to the correct dimensions before assembly can begin.
Tool racks and storage compartments are typically mounted onto or alongside the workbench after the bench itself is assembled and positioned.
Final sanding, sealing, or coating of the workbench surface must be done after the bench is fully assembled to ensure an even and durable finish.
The completed workbench must be inspected for stability, alignment, and safety before it can be approved for apprentice use.

predecessor: Design and engineering of Master Demonstration Bench
rationale: The design and engineering phase must be completed before fabrication begins to ensure correct specifications, dimensions, and material requirements are established.
All individual components and parts must be fabricated before they can be assembled into the complete bench.

successor: Installation and commissioning of Master Demonstration Bench
rationale: The bench must be fully assembled before it can be installed in its final location and commissioned for operation.

successor: Functional testing and validation of Master Demonstration Bench
rationale: Testing can only be performed after the bench is properly installed and all connections are made.

successor: Operator training on Master Demonstration Bench
rationale: While training ideally follows validation, it is a soft preference as some familiarization could occur earlier, but full training is best after the bench is validated and ready for operation.
The display rack requires a structural frame to be built first to provide support and mounting surface for the rack.
The display rack must be fully assembled before it can be mounted and secured to the wall or support structure.
Items cannot be placed on the display rack until the rack itself is fully constructed and installed.
A stable foundation or base floor must be prepared before shelving units can be installed, as shelves require a level and load-bearing surface for safe assembly and loading.
Shelving units must be fully assembled and secured in place before any materials or supplies can be placed onto them; otherwise, loading an incomplete shelf is unsafe and impractical.
While labeling can be done concurrently, it is more efficient and systematic to first erect the shelving and then apply location labels to each shelf section for clear material organization.

predecessor: Layout Marking and Floor Plan Verification
rationale: The exact positions where shelving units will be placed must be marked on the floor and verified against the layout plan before installation begins, to ensure correct spacing and access aisles.

Forklifts, pallet jacks, or other material handling equipment can be brought in before shelving is complete, but final positioning and tuning of equipment aisles is best done after shelving is installed to ensure clearance.
A stable foundation is required to support the safety equipment locker before it can be installed.
The structural frame must be in place to provide attachment points and enclosure for the safety equipment locker.
The locker must be physically installed before it can be stocked with safety equipment and inspected.
It is preferable but not physically required to install the locker before placing safety signage indicating its location.
If the locker requires electrical connections (e.g., for lighting or alarm systems), the electrical rough-in must be completed beforehand.
The mechanical core (structural framework) must be fully erected and stable before any workstation installation can occur, as it provides the physical support and enclosed space for the workstations.
Electrical conduit, wiring, and outlet boxes must be installed in the walls/floors before workstations are placed to avoid having to move or work around installed furnishings.
Workstations must be physically installed and positioned before final electrical and data connections can be made to them.

successor: Perform Final Quality Inspection of Apprentice Area
rationale: The workstation installation must be complete before a final quality inspection of the apprentice area can be conducted to verify all work meets specifications.
Though not strictly required, completing flooring and painting before installing workstations prevents damage to new finishes and avoids the need to work around workstations during finishing.
A stable, level foundation and prepared site are physically required before any installation work for the demonstration area can begin.
Underground and in-wall utility rough-ins must be completed before the demonstration area is installed to avoid rework and access issues.
The demonstration area must be fully installed before its systems (audio/visual, lighting, interactive displays) can be connected and functionally tested.
Final finishing work (painting, trim, signage) and commissioning of the space must follow installation to avoid damage during the installation process.

It is strongly preferred that the demonstration area is fully installed before the client walkthrough so they can see the complete setup, though walkthrough could theoretically occur earlier in stages.
The area must be cleared, leveled, and ready before tool storage (cabinets, racks, pegboards) can be installed.
Electrical outlets and lighting for the storage area need to be roughed in before fixed storage units are placed, to avoid rework.
Any plumbing for wash sinks or utility areas near tool storage must be roughed in before permanent storage is installed.
Flooring (concrete, tile, or epoxy) should be finished before heavy storage systems are placed, as moving them later is impractical.
Tools can only be placed into storage racks, cabinets, and drawers after the storage system itself is fully installed and secured.
The floor area must be prepared and leveled to provide a stable, even surface for installing shelving and waste stations, ensuring safety and structural integrity.
Rough-in electrical and plumbing work must be completed before installing shelving and waste stations to avoid obstructions and allow easy access for utility connections.
Shelving must be installed before materials can be placed on them; waste stations must be in place before waste disposal operations begin.

successor: Set Up Waste Segregation & Disposal Protocols
rationale: While waste stations must be physically present to implement segregation, the protocols could theoretically be defined earlier, but practical sequencing places protocol setup after installation.
Floor finishes should be completed before heavy shelving and waste stations are installed to prevent damage to finished surfaces and allow seamless installation.
Flooring must be installed before any seating can be placed to provide a stable, finished surface and prevent damage to flooring materials.
Wall finishing must be completed before seating installation to avoid dust, debris, or paint splatter damaging the seating and to allow access to walls without moving furniture.
Electrical outlets and related rough-ins for device charging (common in teen lounges) must be installed before seating is positioned to ensure access for wiring and avoid blocking outlets.
Seating placement is typically one of the final furnishing steps; after seating is installed, final cleaning and inspection can proceed without risk of disturbing the seating.
Soft preference: decorative accessories like throw pillows, signage, or small tables are often added after seating is in place to coordinate layout, but could be placed simultaneously if desired.
Study workstations must be installed on a finished, cured floor slab to ensure a level and stable foundation.
Electrical outlets, data ports, and cabling for study workstations must be roughed-in before the workstation units are placed to allow proper connection and avoid rework.
Room partitions defining the study area must be framed and drywalled before workstations can be positioned and anchored correctly.
While touch-up painting can be done after workstation installation, completing final painting before installation avoids overspray and damage to workstations.

Overhead task lighting or localized lighting for each workstation may need to be positioned relative to the installed desks; however, rough-in electrical must precede. Final fixture trim can happen after workstations are in place to align correctly.
The display and presentation wall requires a structural framework to be built first, as it needs to be mounted on or integrated into the wall framing for support.
Electrical wiring for lighting, screens, or interactive displays must be run within the wall cavity before the display wall is fully finished and installed.
The display wall should be installed before finish flooring to allow for proper base trim and flooring transitions against the wall.
After the display wall structure is in place, final painting, wallpaper, or surface treatments can be applied for a seamless finish.
Mounting screens, projectors, or presentation equipment onto the display wall requires the wall to be fully constructed and structurally ready to support the load.

Plumbing rough-in for the kitchenette sink and drainage must be installed inside walls and floors before the kitchenette cabinetry and countertops can be installed, as pipes need to run behind and beneath these finishes.
Electrical wiring and outlet boxes for the kitchenette's microwave, refrigerator, and countertop outlets must be roughed-in within the walls before the kitchenette can be enclosed and finished.
The subfloor must be level and prepared to receive the final flooring material that will go under the kitchenette cabinetry and appliances.
The base cabinetry of the snack bar/kitchenette must be installed first so that the countertop can be measured, cut, and placed on top of the cabinets.
The sink must be set into the countertop of the kitchenette before the faucet and supply lines can be connected to it.
The cabinetry and designated alcoves of the kitchenette must be fully built before the appliances can be slid into place and connected.
The kitchenette base and countertop must be in place so that the backsplash tile can be installed to meet the countertop surface and seal the wall-to-counter joint.

predecessor: Complete Teen Lounge Rough-In Work (Electrical, Plumbing, HVAC)
rationale: All rough-in electrical, plumbing, and HVAC work must be completed before built-in seating can be installed, as the seating would block access to walls, floors, and ceilings where these systems terminate.
Flooring must be installed underneath the built-in seating because the seating is fixed in place and cannot be moved later to install flooring.

Wall finishes behind and adjacent to built-in seating must be completed before the seating is installed, as the seating will be attached to or flush against the walls and would block access for finishing.

It is a soft preference to install overhead and accent lighting after seating is in place so that lighting positions can be fine-tuned relative to the seating layout, though fixtures could theoretically be installed earlier if exact positions are predetermined.

successor: Perform Teen Lounge Final Punch-List & Occupancy Clean
rationale: Built-in seating installation must be complete before final cleaning and punch-list walkthrough, as the seating is a fixed finish that would be damaged or soiled if cleaning occurred beforehand, and all final touch-up work must be done with seating in place.
Power and low-voltage electrical rough-in (conduit, wiring, outlets) must be installed before media and AV equipment can be connected and powered.
Ceilings and walls must be enclosed and finished to provide mounting surfaces and concealed pathways for AV cables, speakers, and projectors.

predecessor: Complete Rough-in for Low Voltage Cabling
rationale: Low voltage cabling (data, audio, video, control) must be run and terminated prior to connecting AV equipment to ensure signal paths are in place.
Media and AV installation is typically completed before final trim, paint touch-ups, and finishing to avoid damage to sensitive electronics from dust and debris.
After installation, the AV systems must be powered on, configured, and tested to verify proper operation before project closeout.

Kitchenette units require a flat, level, and stable surface to be installed upon; any subfloor preparation (screeding, leveling compound, waterproofing) must be completed before placing the cabinetry.
Water supply lines and drain/waste pipes for the kitchenette sink must be roughed-in and pressure-tested before the fit-out can enclose walls and install fixtures.
Electrical outlets, switches, and wiring for appliances (e.g., fridge, microwave, under-cabinet lighting) must be run and terminated in junction boxes before cabinetry and countertops are installed.
The kitchenette base cabinet and countertop must be in place before the sink can be seated and the tap and trap connected to the rough-in supplies.
Built-in appliances require the surrounding cabinetry and allocated niches to be fully installed before they can be slid into position, secured, and connected.
The kickplate panel is typically installed against a finished wall surface, so the wall must be constructed first.
The kickplate panel sits on or near the finished floor, so the floor must be prepared and leveled before installation.
While base trim often meets the kickplate, some installers may do base trim first; however, typically kickplate is installed before base trim to allow a clean overlap or seamless transition.
If the kickplate panel extends to the floor, final floor finishing (e.g., sealing, carpet) can be done after the kickplate is in place to create a clean edge.
The display window sill is typically mounted onto or anchored into the structural wall; the wall must be built and cured before the sill can be attached.
The window frame defines the opening and provides the recess/support for the sill; the sill is installed after or simultaneously with the frame.
The sill provides the bottom support and drainage plane for the window glass; glass panels are set onto the finished sill.

successor: Interior Finishing (e.g., drywall, plaster around sill)
rationale: While interior finishing can technically proceed after sill installation, it is a logical soft preference to avoid damaging finished surfaces or having to redo work around the sill area.
The sill must be in place before the exterior weatherproofing sealant and cladding are applied around it to ensure a watertight assembly.
The building's structural frame and shell must be complete to provide a stable mounting surface and structural support for the canopy/awning attachment.
The roof waterproofing must be installed before the canopy/awning to ensure no water ingress behind the awning mounting points and to avoid compromising the roof membrane.
Exterior wall finishes must be completed so that the canopy/awning can be properly flashed and sealed against the finished wall surface, ensuring weatherproofing.
If signage is to be mounted on or below the canopy/awning, it is typically installed after the canopy is in place to ensure proper alignment and integration.
The structural steel frame must be in place to provide a mounting surface and support for the signage mounting frame.
The concrete slab or foundation must be cured and ready to provide a stable base for anchoring the signage mounting frame.
Electrical conduit and wiring for illuminated signage should be roughed in before the mounting frame is installed to avoid rework or difficult access.
The mounting frame must be securely installed and leveled before the actual signage panels or letters can be attached to it.
The mounting frame must be in place before electricians can make final connections to power the signage lighting components mounted on the frame.
The rough opening for the storefront must be prepared and framed before the bulkhead can be installed, as the bulkhead sits within or attaches to the framed opening.
Structural supports such as steel lintels above the storefront opening must be in place before the bulkhead is installed to provide load-bearing support.
The bulkhead forms the base or sill area of the storefront; glass panels and windows are installed on top of or within the bulkhead frame.
Finish cladding materials (e.g., masonry, metal panels) around the bulkhead area must be installed after the bulkhead is in place to ensure proper fit and weatherproofing.
Base flashing and waterproofing membranes must be installed before the bulkhead to prevent moisture intrusion at the sill transition.
The display plinth requires a stable, level floor surface to be installed upon. The floor slab must be fully cured and load-bearing before the plinth can be positioned.
Any plumbing lines that need to run beneath or around the plinth area must be completed before the plinth is installed, as the plinth will cover or block access to those areas.

Electrical conduits, outlets, or wiring serving the display plinth (e.g., for lighting or power) must be roughed in before the plinth is placed, as access to wall/floor cavities will be restricted afterward.
The artifact, sculpture, or exhibit item cannot be placed on the plinth until the plinth itself is fully constructed, installed, and stable.

While final flooring can often be installed first with the plinth on top, it is a soft preference to finish flooring around the plinth after installation to ensure a clean, seamless edge and avoid damaging the plinth during floor work.
The roller shutter requires a stable, level structural slab or floor to mount the bottom track and support the weight of the shutter assembly.
The side channels, jambs, and lintel/head bracket for the roller shutter must be anchored into the finished walls or columns surrounding the opening.
The roller shutter hood/barrel assembly is mounted to the overhead lintel or soffit, which must be fully cured and capable of bearing the load.
The motor conduit and junction box must be wired to the shutter location after the shutter is physically installed to ensure proper alignment and connection.
Installing the shutter first allows precise trimming and painting of the surrounding frame without damaging the shutter finish; however, painting could also be done prior with careful masking.
The lighting trough is typically mounted onto or supported by the steel cage framework, so the cage must be installed first to provide structural support.
Electrical conduits and wiring to supply power to the lighting trough must be roughed in before the trough can be physically installed and connected.
The lighting trough is often positioned above or around the glazing area; installing it before the glass allows access for fixing and avoids damage to the glass panels.
The trough structure must be in place before lights can be mounted inside it and final electrical connections made.
Soft preference: finishing the ceiling lining after the trough avoids rework around the trough area, but the trough could be retrofitted if necessary.
The structural frame or shell of the building must be in place to provide the supporting structure onto which the shopfront glazing system can be fixed and sealed.
Rough openings and window sills must be prepared and set to the correct dimensions so that the shopfront glazing units can be installed accurately and securely.
Waterproof membranes and flashings around the shopfront opening must be in place before glazing to prevent moisture ingress behind the glass and framing.
After the glazing units are installed, sealants (e.g., silicone) and finishing trim pieces must be applied around the perimeter to weatherproof the installation and provide a clean appearance.

While interior finishing can proceed in parallel, it is preferred to complete glazing first to prevent dust and debris from construction work settling on the interior side of the glass, reducing cleaning effort.
The rough openings must be framed and prepared before storefront framing can be assembled in place, as the storefront framing sits within the prepared opening.
Storefront framing materials (aluminum extrusions, glass, etc.) must be on-site before assembly can begin.
The storefront framing must be fully assembled and erected to provide the structural support and frame into which glazing and glass panels are installed.
Weatherproofing sealants and gaskets are applied to the assembled framing to ensure airtight and watertight performance; the framing must be in place first.
Doors and operating hardware are installed into or onto the completed storefront frame assembly.
The door frame and rough opening must be fully constructed and prepared before any hardware can be installed on the door.
The door slab itself must be hung in the frame before hardware such as locks, handles, hinges, and strike plates can be attached to it.
Weatherstripping and seals are applied around the closed door; the door hardware (including latch and strike plate) must be in place to ensure proper alignment and sealing.
The door hardware must be fully installed before functional testing of the lock, latch, handle, and overall door operation can be performed.
Touch-up painting or finishing around the hardware is often done after installation to cover any scratches or marks; this is a soft preference as it could also be done before if care is taken.
The shutter box or frame must be installed first to provide the structural housing and alignment reference for the track system.
The track must be in place to guide and support the shutter curtain or blade assembly during installation.
The opening must be prepared, cleaned, and dimensionally correct before the track can be fitted.
The track must be completely installed before operational testing of the shutter can be performed.
The control mechanism connects to the shutter assembly which rides in the track, so the track must be installed first.
The bulkhead structure must be physically installed before any waterproofing can be applied to its junctions.
Junction surfaces must be cleaned, dried, and primed to ensure proper adhesion of waterproofing materials.
The junction waterproofing must be completed before the main waterproofing membrane is applied over the junction area to ensure continuous sealing.
Junction waterproofing must be fully cured and sealed before pressure testing can validate its integrity.
The waterproofed junction must be inspected and approved before covering it with backfill or encasement concrete.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before fencing can be installed to ensure proper fence alignment, footing stability, and consistent elevation along the perimeter.
Property boundary lines must be precisely surveyed and staked to ensure the fence is erected within legal property limits and to avoid encroachment.
Underground utilities (gas, water, electric, telecom) must be located and marked before digging fence post holes to prevent utility strikes, service disruptions, and safety hazards.
The perimeter fence line must be complete before installing main access gates, as gates are integrated into and supported by the fence structure.

Security cameras and alarm sensors are typically mounted on or along the perimeter fence, so the fence structure must be in place first; however, some pre-wiring can be done in parallel, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
Window guards must be mounted onto or within the window frame, so the frame must be fully installed and structurally ready to receive the guards.
Accurate measurements of window openings are required before custom or standard guards can be ordered, fabricated, or installed.

Window guards must be fitted and secured in place before any final trim, molding, or finish work is applied around the window, as the guards may need to be sandwiched between the frame and finish materials.

While guards can be painted over later, it is preferable to complete wall and window surround painting first to avoid overspray and ensure a clean finish; this is a soft preference for work sequencing.

The installation of child-safe window guards is a critical safety element; a final inspection must verify proper installation, secure fastening, and compliance with safety codes before the building is occupied.
Wall and ceiling finishes must be completed before child-height fixtures and fittings can be installed, as these fixtures typically attach to finished walls (e.g., shelves, hooks, coat rails).
Flooring should be installed first to establish finished floor levels and to avoid damaging new flooring with fixture installation work.

predecessor: Base Building Services (Electrical and Plumbing Rough-In)
rationale: Electrical outlets, plumbing connections, and other rough-in services behind walls must be in place before fixtures (e.g., child-height sinks, drinking fountains) are mounted.
After installing fixtures, final painting and touch-ups around the installed items are typically performed to achieve a clean finish, though this is a soft preference for sequencing.
All child-height fixtures and fittings must be completely installed before the space can be occupied and used by children, as these are essential functional elements.
The crib or cot anchoring system must be fastened to a stable, finished floor surface to ensure secure attachment and structural integrity.
If the crib anchors to the wall, walls must be fully framed and finished to provide a solid backing for anchoring brackets or hardware.
The mattress or crib bed can only be placed after the crib structure is securely anchored in position.
Safety padding around the crib is best installed after anchoring to ensure proper fit and alignment, though it could be done concurrently if needed.
The final inspection and safety verification of the crib installation must occur after the unit is fully anchored in place.

The subfloor must be clean, dry, level, and structurally sound before any flooring material can be installed. Any debris, moisture, or unevenness would compromise the adhesion and long-term performance of the non-slip flooring.
A moisture barrier must be laid down before flooring to prevent ground moisture or slab moisture from migrating up and causing the flooring to delaminate, bubble, or develop mold underneath.

An appropriate underlayment (e.g., foam, cork, or rubber underlay) must be installed prior to the final flooring to provide cushioning, sound insulation, and a smooth surface for the non-slip flooring system.
The building must be enclosed (roof on, walls up, windows in) before flooring is installed to protect the flooring material from weather damage, dust, and moisture during construction.

While not a hard physical constraint, it is common practice to install flooring before baseboards, trim, and wall painting to allow for cleaner edges and to avoid damaging finished walls. However, some trades may prefer painting first to avoid drips on new flooring.

Heavy fixtures, cabinets, and built-in furniture should be installed after the flooring is complete to avoid damaging the floor surface while moving heavy items and to ensure that the flooring runs continuously under these elements for a finished look and proper sealing.
The child-guard railing must be installed on or alongside the staircase structure; the staircase must first be built to provide a mounting surface and structural support for the railing.
Guard rails for balconies or decks require the underlying floor framing and deck structure to be in place so that posts and railing can be securely anchored.

predecessor: Wall Framing (where railing attaches to wall)
rationale: If the child-guard railing is wall-mounted, the wall framing must be complete to provide a solid substrate for attachment brackets.

It is preferred to install drywall before installing handrails/guardrails so that the railing brackets can be installed flush against the finished wall surface without later rework; however, some projects install railing first and then finish around it.
The guard railing must be fully installed before the final building inspection or safety sign-off can be completed, as the railing is a critical life-safety element.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared to provide a stable, level base before safety surfacing can be installed.
Concrete footings or foundations for play structures must be set and fully cured before safety surfacing is applied around them.
Subsurface drainage must be in place to prevent water accumulation beneath the safety surface, which could cause degradation or failure.
Play equipment should be installed on top of or anchored through the safety surfacing to ensure proper integration and fall-height coverage.
While safety surfacing is typically completed before final landscaping and fencing to avoid damage to finished surfaces, some border work can precede surfacing.
Wardrobe and closet units require finished wall framing to provide structural support and attachment surfaces.
Electrical wiring for lighting or outlets within wardrobes/closets must be installed before enclosing the space with built-in units.
Any plumbing lines that may run through or behind closet areas must be completed before permanent built-in units are installed.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and finished behind and around the wardrobe area before built-in units are placed, as the units would block access to walls.
Flooring (tile, hardwood, laminate, or carpet) should be installed before wardrobes/closets are placed to avoid cutting around the units and to ensure a clean, finished look.
Walls behind and around the wardrobe must be painted or finished before installation, as the built-in units will be difficult to move or remove later for painting.

successor: Final electrical and lighting fixture installation
rationale: Interior closet lighting fixtures or electrical outlets within the built-in units must be installed after the wardrobes are in place to ensure proper alignment and connection.
Baseboards and trim around closet openings are typically installed after the built-in units to create a seamless finished edge, though this is a quality preference rather than a structural necessity.

successor: Final Flooring Touch-Up and Transition Strips
rationale: Any transition strips or floor finishing details adjacent to the closet area are best completed after the wardrobe is installed for a precise fit, but this is a cosmetic preference.

Display fixtures must be placed on finished floors and against finished walls to ensure proper alignment, stability, and aesthetics. Installing them before interior finishes would result in damage or misalignment.
Power outlets and data connections need to be in place behind or near display fixture locations so that fixtures can be connected and powered without requiring later wall cutting or rewiring.
Products cannot be placed on shelves, racks, or hooks until the display fixtures themselves are fully installed, secured, and ready to bear weight.
Overhead signs, shelf talkers, and promotional displays attach to or are mounted on the fixture framework; thus the base fixtures must be in place first.
It is preferred to clean and buff floors before bringing in fixtures to avoid trapping dust and debris under the fixture bases, though fixtures can be moved temporarily for spot cleaning if needed.
The checkout counter must be placed on a finished, level floor slab to ensure stability and proper installation.
Electrical wiring and outlets must be roughed in before the checkout counter is installed so that power can be connected to the register and payment terminal.
Network and POS data cables must be run to the checkout location before the counter is placed, as access to run cabling after installation would be extremely difficult.
The POS system and cash register must be placed on top of the installed checkout counter, so the counter must be in place first.
Signage above or on the checkout counter is typically installed after the counter is in place, but this is a soft preference as signage could be added at any time.
Partition walls require a finished structural floor to bear their load and provide a stable base for construction.
Electrical wiring within partition walls must be installed after walls are framed but before they are closed up.
Plumbing lines running inside partition walls need to be installed after the wall framing is complete.
Drywall or cladding is applied to the partition wall framing after the wall structure is erected.
Partition walls are typically built after the overhead structure and ceiling are in place, as walls must align with ceiling grids and overhead structural supports.

Structural steel framing provides the primary support structure onto which signage mounting brackets and systems are attached. Without the steel frame in place, there is no substrate to mount the signage system.

Exterior wall cladding (e.g., curtain wall, brick veneer, or metal panels) must be completed to provide the finished façade surface through or onto which signage is mounted. Mounting signage before cladding would require rework or damage to the system.

Electrical conduits, junction boxes, and wiring for illuminated signage must be roughed-in behind the wall or within the ceiling before the signage mounting hardware is installed, as access to these elements is restricted once the signage is mounted.

The physical mounting system must be in place to support the sign panels and provide a pathway for electrical connections. Only after the mounting system is secured can electricians connect the sign wiring and test illumination.

successor: Final Sign Panel Attachment and Alignment
rationale: The mounting system (rails, brackets, standoffs) must be installed and leveled first before the actual sign face panels or letters can be attached and aligned to ensure proper fit and appearance.

Electrical outlets, switches, and plumbing rough-ins must be installed within the fitting room walls before the wall enclosure is completed, as these services are hidden within the walls and cannot be accessed after enclosure.
The wall framing for the fitting room must be erected to provide the structural support onto which the enclosure (drywall, panels, etc.) is attached.
The enclosure surfaces must be complete before final finishes like paint or wallpaper can be applied to them.

successor: Fitting Room Fixtures Installation (Mirrors, Benches, Hooks)
rationale: Mirrors, benches, and clothing hooks must be mounted onto the finished walls/enclosure, requiring the enclosure to be complete for secure attachment.
The door frame and trim for the fitting room are installed after the wall enclosure is complete to ensure proper fit and alignment.
The floor mat recess must be formed or cut into the concrete slab; therefore the slab must first be poured and cured.
Any below-slab waterproofing or vapor barrier must be in place before the recess is constructed to prevent moisture ingress.
Any drainage, conduits, or electrical rough-ins that pass beneath the entry mat area must be completed before the recess is formed/finished.
The recess frame or formed opening must be in place so that adjacent floor finishes (tiles,石材, etc.) can be laid up to its edges.
The recess must be fully constructed and cured before the mat or insert can be placed into it.
The rough electrical work, including running conduit and wiring from the main panel to the subpanel location, must be completed before the subpanel can be installed and connected.
The subpanel must be installed and energized before individual circuits in the shop (outlets, lighting, equipment connections) can be trimmed out and terminated.
The subpanel rough-in must be in place before insulation and drywall are installed, as the subpanel and its wiring need to be embedded within or pass through walls that are then closed up.
While equipment can be placed before power is available, final connection and commissioning of shop equipment requires an energized subpanel; this is a soft preference for sequencing efficiency.
The main service panel must be installed and live to feed the subpanel; the subpanel derives its power from the main panel via a dedicated feeder circuit.
Ductwork must be installed to provide the air distribution path that the terminal unit connects to.
Zone terminal units (e.g., VAV boxes) are often installed above ceilings; the ceiling grid provides support and access.
Electrical power and controls wiring must be roughed in to power and control the terminal unit's actuators and reheat components.
Terminal units are part of the duct system; pressure testing must include the connected terminal units to verify system integrity.
Air balancing and commissioning require all terminal units to be installed and operational to measure and adjust airflow at each zone.
The door structure must be in place before hardware such as hinges, handles, locks, and closers can be mounted onto it.
Once hardware is installed, the door must be tested and adjusted for proper alignment, latch operation, and security before the space is finished.

While hardware installation ideally occurs after painting to avoid damage, sometimes hardware is installed before final touch-ups; this is a soft preference to protect hardware finish and ensure clean paint lines.
The subfloor must be properly prepared, cleaned, and leveled before any flooring material can be installed to ensure adhesion, stability, and a smooth finished surface.
Underlayment or subfloor materials (e.g., plywood, cement board, moisture barrier) must be in place to provide a suitable base for the retail flooring system.
All rough-in work for electrical conduit, plumbing pipes, and other in-floor utilities must be completed before flooring installation to avoid cutting or damaging the finished floor later.
Wall base, cove base, or transition strips must be installed after the flooring is laid to cover the expansion gap and provide a finished transition between floor and wall.

Permanent floor-mounted retail fixtures, shelving, and display racks should only be installed after flooring is complete to avoid damaging the flooring material and to ensure proper fit and alignment.

The structural steel frame provides the primary load-bearing support and the structural opening into which the shop front glazing system is installed. Without the frame, there is nothing to fix the glazing to.
Masonry work around the shop front opening must be completed to define the rough opening dimensions and provide structural support/reference edges for the glazing frame installation.
The glazing panels must be installed and fixed in place before perimeter waterproofing and sealants can be applied to ensure a weathertight seal between the glazing frame and the building structure.

Internal finishes such as plasterboard lining, painting, or trim installation around the shop front opening should follow glazing installation to achieve a neat finished appearance and avoid damage to finishes.

While signage installation can technically be done before glazing, it is preferable to install the glazing first to allow safe access and to ensure the shop front is weathertight before costly signage elements are mounted above or on the glazing.
The electrical system must be fully installed before it can be commissioned, as commissioning is the process of testing and verifying a completed installation.
Commissioning must be completed and approved before the system can be energized to ensure safety and proper operation.
Production equipment requires commissioned and operational electrical power before it can be started and tested.

predecessor: Complete Interior Wall Framing and Drywall
rationale: Display fixtures need to be mounted on finished walls; interior framing and drywall must be completed to provide a solid mounting surface.
Electrical wiring for lighting or power to displays must be roughed-in before fixtures are mounted, as running wires behind the fixtures later would be difficult or impossible.

While not physically required, flooring is typically completed before heavy fixtures are mounted to avoid damaging finished floors and to allow precise fixture positioning relative to the floor level.
Merchandise cannot be placed on display shelves until the shelves are securely mounted and stable.
Final painting and touch-ups are often performed after mounting to cover any marks, screw holes, or gaps created during fixture installation, though painting could be done earlier if careful.
A stable, level floor must be in place to support the checkout counter structure and ensure proper installation and anchoring.

predecessor: Install Electrical Rough-In at Checkout Area
rationale: Electrical wiring and outlet boxes must be roughed in before the counter is installed, as the counter will cover or sit over these utilities.
The checkout counter provides the physical platform and mounting surface for POS terminals, scanners, and registers.

successor: Install Cash Register and Payment Terminals
rationale: Cash registers and payment terminals must be placed on or integrated into the completed checkout counter.

successor: Run Final Electrical and Data Cabling to Checkout
rationale: While cabling can be pre-run in conduits, final connections and terminations are easier and cleaner after the counter is in its permanent position.
The cafe service counter must be placed on a finished floor slab to provide a level and stable base.
Plumbing supply and drain lines must be roughed in before the counter structure is built over them.
Electrical conduit and junction boxes for under-counter equipment and outlets must be installed before the counter framework encloses them.
The counter base and cabinetry must be fully assembled and in place before the finished countertop can be mounted on top.
Sinks and other fixtures are mounted into or onto the counter structure, requiring the counter to be built first.
The structural slab (e.g., concrete deck) must be poured, cured, and properly leveled to provide a stable substrate for outdoor terrace flooring installation.
A waterproofing membrane must be installed over the structural slab to prevent moisture penetration; terrace flooring is laid on top of this membrane.
Drainage channels and drains must be placed and connected before flooring to ensure proper water runoff away from the finished surface.
Railings are typically anchored after the finished flooring is in place to achieve correct height alignment and secure base fixing.

While furniture can theoretically be placed before flooring is complete, it is a soft preference to place furniture only after flooring is finished to avoid damaging the new surface and to ensure a clean, professional result.
The building shell (walls, roof, and structural frame) must be completed to provide the structural opening and support for installing the cafe storefront system.
Rough framing defines the window and door openings that the storefront system will be installed into, and provides the structural substrate for mounting.
Interior finishes around the storefront (such as drywall trim, window sills, and interior framing) cannot be completed until the storefront system is installed and sealed.
Exterior cladding and weatherproofing details around the storefront must be installed after the storefront system is in place to ensure proper flashing, sealing, and integration.

While it is possible to install flooring before the storefront, doing so after the storefront avoids potential damage to flooring material from storefront installation work and allows for proper alignment at the storefront threshold.
Ductwork provides the pathway for air to be exhausted, so it must be in place before the hood can be connected and installed.
The ventilation hood requires electrical power for fans and lights, so wiring must be run to the installation location before the hood can be wired and mounted.
The hood must be mounted and positioned first so that ceiling finishes (drywall, tiles) can be trimmed and fitted tightly around the hood and duct connection.

successor: Install kitchen exhaust fan and terminate duct to exterior
rationale: The hood serves as the collection point; the exhaust fan and exterior termination must be connected to the duct riser from the hood, and this connection is made after the hood is in place.
The hood must be fully installed, connected to ductwork and power, before the entire ventilation system can be tested for airflow, noise, and performance.

The roof structure provides the primary overhead support and attachment points for awnings or canopies. The awning/canopy must be anchored to or supported by the roof framing, so the roof structure must be complete before awning installation can begin.

Awnings and canopies are often attached to exterior walls for support and anchoring. The wall framing must be in place to provide a structural connection point for the awning/canopy brackets and supports.

While not a strict physical necessity, installing exterior finishes like siding or cladding is more efficient and less prone to damage if done after the awning/canopy is in place, as the canopy provides weather protection during finishing work.

Exterior light fixtures that are mounted on or beneath the awning/canopy structure require the canopy frame to be installed first to provide the mounting surface and to allow for proper routing of electrical conduits.

For freestanding canopy structures, the foundation or concrete slab must be poured and cured to provide a stable base for erecting the canopy columns and supports. Without a stable foundation, the canopy structure cannot be safely erected.
Power supply and data cabling must be run to the display location before the digital display unit can be connected and mounted.
The physical mounting frame or bracket must be securely attached to the wall or ceiling to provide a secure anchor point for the display.
Final power and data connections to the display unit are made after the display is physically installed in its final position.
The digital display hardware must be in place and powered on before menu content, pricing, and scheduling software can be configured and tested on the unit.
The display should be fully installed and operational before the overall system is inspected and signed off, though inspection could theoretically be done in stages.
Electrical and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before walk-in cooler installation to ensure power and drainage connections are available at the correct locations.
A level, cured concrete slab or structural floor must be in place to support the weight of the walk-in cooler and its refrigeration equipment.

predecessor: Framing and drywall for cafe area
rationale: Wall framing and drywall must be complete to define the cooler's enclosure and allow for proper sealing and fitment of the cooler panels.

successor: Walk-in cooler refrigerant piping and refrigeration system startup
rationale: The cooler must be fully assembled and in place before refrigerant lines can be connected and the refrigeration system can be charged and started up.
While shelving can technically be installed during cooler assembly, it is far more efficient and safe to install shelving after the cooler structure is fully erected to avoid interference and damage.
Electrical rough-in must be completed before millwork installation to allow for wiring to be run behind walls and millwork, and to avoid damaging finished millwork with electrical work.
Plumbing rough-in must be completed before millwork installation to ensure pipes are in place behind walls and under counters, preventing damage to installed millwork.
Ceiling finishing (drywall, paint) should be completed before millwork installation to avoid damaging millwork with ceiling work and to allow for proper alignment.
Millwork (cabinetry) must be installed first to provide the supporting base for countertops to be placed on top.

While flooring can sometimes be installed before millwork, typically millwork is set on the subfloor and finished flooring is installed after or flush with the millwork toe-kick for a clean appearance.
The wall or structural opening must be prepared (framed, rough opening sized) before the storefront assembly can be installed.
Structural header or lintel above the storefront opening must be in place to support loads before installing the storefront frame.
Electrical wiring for lighting and power near the storefront area must be roughed in before the storefront is installed, as access behind the wall will be restricted.
The storefront frame must be installed first to provide the supporting structure before glass panels or glazing can be fitted into the frame.
Weatherproofing and sealant application around the storefront perimeter must occur after the storefront is fully installed to ensure a continuous water and air barrier.
Foodservice equipment requires connection to water supply and drainage systems, which must be roughed in before equipment can be installed and connected.
Foodservice equipment requires electrical power connections, so electrical conduits and wiring must be roughed in before equipment installation.
Kitchen ventilation hoods, exhaust systems, and HVAC ductwork must be roughed in before foodservice equipment is placed to avoid rework and clearance issues.
Final plumbing connections (supply lines, drains, gas lines) to foodservice equipment can only be made after the equipment is positioned in its final location.
Final electrical connections to foodservice equipment require the equipment to be in place so that wiring can be terminated correctly at each appliance.
Awning/canopy typically attaches to or is supported by the roof structure, so roof sheathing (or decking) must be in place to provide a nailing/support surface and structural integrity.
The building's rough framing, including wall and roof framing, must be complete to provide the structural support framework to which the awning/canopy is attached.
While not always required, it is common to install awnings/canopies before final siding/cladding so that flashing and weatherproofing can be integrated properly behind or beneath the cladding.
Exterior trim and finish details around the awning/canopy mounting points are often completed after the awning is installed to ensure proper fit and seal.

If the awning/canopy is installed over a door or window, interior finishes in that area may be protected by having the exterior covering in place first, though this is a soft preference for sequencing.
The checkout counter must be placed on a level, finished floor surface to ensure stability and proper alignment.
Electrical wiring and outlets for the checkout counter (e.g., for POS systems, scanners, and lighting) must be run in the walls/floor before the counter is installed.
The physical checkout counter structure must be in place before point-of-sale terminals, scanners, and registers can be mounted and connected.
Signage above or on the checkout counter is typically installed after the counter is assembled, though it could be done in parallel if preferred.
All built-in electrical components of the checkout counter (lights, power outlets) must be fully assembled before final connections to the building supply and testing can be performed.

All rough-in work for electrical and plumbing must be completed before flooring is installed, as these services typically run beneath the floor subfloor or within walls that abut the floor. Installing flooring over unfinished rough-ins would require destructive removal later.

The structural subfloor or concrete slab must be fully cured and prepared before any finish flooring can be installed. Installing finish flooring on an unprepared or uncured slab would result in adhesion failure, moisture damage, and an unstable surface.

Heavy kitchen equipment should be placed on the finished flooring to ensure proper weight distribution, alignment, and to prevent damage to the subfloor. Installing equipment before flooring would require later lifting or shimming.
Base cabinets and countertops are typically installed on top of finished flooring to achieve proper height, a seamless appearance, and to protect the floor edges from moisture and wear.

successor: Final Painting and Wall Finishes (Base Level)
rationale: While walls are typically painted before flooring to avoid drips, the final base trim and touch-up painting at the wall-floor interface must be done after flooring is installed for a clean, finished look. This is a soft preference as the order can vary with careful masking.

The shelving/racking system requires a level, load-bearing floor slab or finished subfloor to bear the concentrated loads. Installing racking before the floor is finished would result in instability and inability to meet structural load requirements.

Racking systems are often anchored to or braced against structural columns. The building's primary structural frame must be in place to provide lateral support and anchorage points for the shelving system.

Overhead fire sprinklers, lighting, and HVAC ductwork must be roughed-in before tall racking is installed because racking blocks overhead access. Installing utilities afterward would be extremely difficult or impossible with racking in place.
In-rack sprinkler heads and detection are installed after the racking framework is erected because their exact placement depends on the rack configuration and shelf levels.

successor: Final Floor Finishing / Sealing (in racked aisles)
rationale: Floor sealing or coating in rack aisles may be preferred after racking to protect the finish during installation, but it is not physically mandatory if the floor is already sealed before rack installation.
Cooler display cases require a level, stable, and load-bearing floor slab to be installed first, as the units are heavy and need a solid foundation to sit on.
Electrical conduits, wiring, and outlets must be roughed in before cooler display cases can be installed, as the coolers need electrical connections that are run beneath or behind the units.

Plumbing drain lines and refrigerant supply lines must be roughed in beneath the slab or within walls before cooler display cases are set in place, as the units require connection to refrigeration and drainage systems.
After cooler display cases are physically positioned, the final electrical connections (hardwiring, plugging in) can be made to power the units.
The refrigeration lines can only be connected and the system charged/commissioned after the cooler display cases are in their final installed location.
Raw materials such as wood, metal, or plastic must be procured before fabrication of shelving can begin.
Design specifications must be finalized before production to ensure correct dimensions and materials.
The shelving must be produced before it can be installed at the intended location.
Basic production (cutting, assembly) must be completed before applying paint or final finishes.
Shelving must be fully produced before it can undergo quality control inspection.

predecessor: Install floor slab and structural support
rationale: Freezer display cases are heavy and require a level, structurally sound floor slab to bear their weight and prevent settling or damage.
Freezer cases require dedicated electrical supply lines for lighting, compressors, and controls; these must be roughed in before the cases are positioned.
Refrigerant lines must be installed and pressure-tested in the ceiling/walls before connecting to the case, as the case needs to be in its final location for final connections.
Defrost drain lines and plumbing connections must be roughed in to the correct location under the slab before freezer cases are set in place.
Shelving and product merchandising can only be added after the freezer case body is installed and stable, though this is a soft preference for logistics sequencing.
The installed cases must be connected, tested, and verified operational before the store can open; this ordering is physically required for a functioning system.
The ground must be leveled and prepared before installing the shopping cart corral to ensure a stable and level foundation.
A concrete pad is typically required as the base for the shopping cart corral to provide a stable, durable surface that can withstand heavy cart traffic.
Parking lot lines and markings should be applied after the corral is installed so that the striping can accurately reflect the corral's final position and avoid painting over the installation area.

While ideally the corral is installed after the final pavement layer, in some sequences the corral base is installed first and the final asphalt is laid around it; this is a soft preference for ensuring a neat finish.
Landscaping and curbs near the corral are best done after installation to avoid damage to plants or hardscaping during corral assembly, but it is not a strict physical requirement.
The bulk food bins need to be placed into or integrated with the storage containers, so the containers must be installed first.
A level, finished floor surface is needed to support the bulk food bins and allow for proper placement and stability.

successor: Stock Bulk Food Bins with Product
rationale: The bins must be physically installed and ready before they can be filled with bulk food products.
While labeling can be prepared in advance, final placement and attachment of labels is easier after bins are installed to ensure correct positioning.
Electrical work in the vicinity must be completed before installing bins to avoid interference and allow access to wiring and outlets.
The deli service counter requires a finished floor slab as a load-bearing base before installation can begin.
Plumbing connections for sinks and drainage at the deli counter must be roughed in before the counter framework is installed.
Electrical wiring for outlets, lighting, and equipment at the deli counter must be completed before the counter is built over the walls and floors.
The deli service counter base and framework must be in place before the countertop surface can be installed on top.
Sinks and other plumbing fixtures at the deli counter can only be connected once the counter structure is installed and secured.
Shelving must be placed on a finished, level floor surface to ensure stability and proper load distribution.
Walls define the perimeter and support structure for shelving attachment; shelving cannot be installed before walls are in place.

predecessor: Complete Rough Electrical Work in Dry Storage
rationale: Electrical wiring behind walls must be completed before shelving is installed to avoid blocking access to outlets and conduits.
Shelving must be fully installed, secured, and load-tested before any materials or goods can be placed on it.
Lighting fixtures can be installed after shelving is in place to ensure optimal positioning relative to shelf layout, though pre-wiring must be done before.

A level, structurally sound concrete slab foundation is required to support the cold storage room walls, flooring insulation, and heavy refrigeration equipment. Building the cold storage room without a completed foundation would result in structural instability.

predecessor: Main Building Structural Framing and Enclosure
rationale: The cold storage room is typically built within the main building envelope. The main structure's walls, roof, and weatherproofing must be completed to protect the cold storage room construction from weather elements and to provide the structural shell to which cold room panels are attached.

Any plumbing lines that need to run beneath or near the cold storage floor area must be installed before the insulated cold room floor and vapor barrier are placed, as accessing these utilities after cold room construction would require destructive demolition of the insulated envelope.

The refrigeration evaporators, condensing units, and refrigerant piping must be installed only after the cold storage room's insulated panels, vapor barrier, and structural shell are fully constructed, as the refrigeration system is mounted to and contained within the completed cold room envelope.

successor: Cold Storage Room Interior Finishing and Shelving
rationale: Interior racking, shelving, and any internal fit-out must be installed after the cold room panels, floor, and ceiling are fully in place. The structure must be complete before any interior storage systems can be attached or positioned.

The checkout run (a retail checkout counter system) requires a stable, level concrete floor foundation to be poured and cured before installation can begin, as it supports the weight of the equipment and must be structurally sound.

Power outlets, data cabling, and conduit for the checkout system's POS terminals, scanners, and payment devices must be roughed-in to the wall and floor locations before the checkout units can be installed and connected.

Once the checkout run units are physically installed in place, the final electrical connections, network hookups, and system testing/commissioning can be performed to verify all POS equipment functions correctly.

Installing the checkout run base cabinets first allows the finished flooring to be laid flush up to the units for a clean, professional appearance; however, flooring could be installed before if the units are later set on top, making this a soft preference for quality.

Completing ceiling grids, lighting, and painting before installing checkout runs avoids dust and debris settling on the new equipment and reduces risk of damage; however, it is possible to work around with protective covering, making this a soft preference.
Shelving must be erected on a finished, stable, and cured floor slab to ensure proper load distribution, level alignment, and structural safety.
The precise floor layout, aisle widths, and shelving positions must be marked out to guide accurate placement and alignment of shelving units.
Overhead ductwork, piping, conduit, and fire sprinkler mains must be installed before tall shelving is erected, as the shelving obstructs overhead access and may interfere with MEP routes.
Products can only be stocked on shelves after the shelving structure is fully erected, leveled, and secured.

While POS counters are typically installed independently, finishing shelving first allows a smoother workflow and avoids congestion in the retail area; a soft preference for sequential rather than parallel work.
The floor area must be prepared, leveled, and finished before refrigerated cases can be positioned and installed to ensure stability and proper alignment.
Refrigeration supply and return lines must be installed and pressure-tested before connecting to the refrigerated cases to ensure leak-free operation.
Electrical power supply conduits, wiring, and outlets must be roughed-in to allow connection of the refrigerated cases to power for commissioning and operation.
Refrigerated cases must be fully commissioned (temperature verified, alarms tested, and stable operation confirmed) before perishable products are stocked to maintain cold chain integrity.

Commissioning includes initial temperature pull-down and stabilization; final temperature validation across all zones must follow after the cases are fully operational and loaded to confirm compliance.
The structural steel framework must be in place to provide a mounting surface and support structure for the signage band and canopy.
The roof deck must be completed to establish the top-of-building elevation and perimeter conditions that the canopy and signage band interface with.
Exterior wall sheathing provides the backing surface for the signage band to be mounted against and ensures weathertight integration.
The signage band and canopy are typically installed first as the base layer, with final façade cladding or finishes installed around them to achieve a clean, integrated appearance.
Signage band installation must precede electrical rough-in for sign lighting to allow conduit and junction boxes to be positioned correctly relative to the installed band.
Electrical power must be roughed-in and available at equipment locations before deli/bakery equipment can be connected and installed.
Water supply and drainage piping must be roughed-in to serve deli/bakery equipment such as sinks, ice machines, and dishwashers before those units can be set in place.

Finished flooring must be installed before heavy equipment is placed, as setting equipment first would make flooring installation underneath impossible or require costly temporary relocation of equipment.

Wall finishes, especially splashback and wall protection behind cooking and washing areas, need to be completed before equipment is positioned against walls, as access behind the equipment would be blocked.
All equipment must be physically installed, connected, and in place before it can be commissioned, tested, and started up for operation.
The health department or internal sanitary inspection requires all equipment to be installed and functional before inspecting food-safety compliance of the deli/bakery area.

While some shelving can be installed independently, the primary deli display cases and bakery merchandising units should be placed before secondary shelving and merchandising fixtures are arranged around them to optimize layout and spacing.
Menu boards and signage are typically installed after equipment is in place to ensure proper alignment and visibility relative to the deli counters and bakery display cases.
The bar counter must be installed on top of the finished floor; the floor provides a level base for the counter structure.
Walls need to be completed before the bar counter can be anchored and positioned against them, and for any wall-mounted plumbing/electrical to be roughed in.
Supply and drain lines for the bar sink and taps must be roughed in within the floor/walls before the counter is installed, otherwise retrofitting would require demolition.
Electrical wiring for bar outlets, lighting, and tap cooling must be roughed in before the bar counter is placed to avoid costly rework.

successor: Beer Hall Bar Top Finishing & Sealing
rationale: Once the bar counter structure is in place, the top surface can be finished, sealed, and detailed without risk of damaging surrounding surfaces.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and compacted before benches can be placed to ensure stability and level seating.

predecessor: Concrete Slab or Paver Base Installation
rationale: A stable, load-bearing base (concrete pad, pavers, or crushed stone) must be in place to support the benches and prevent sinking or shifting.
Any underground electrical, water, or data lines in the seating area must be installed before benches are placed to avoid digging up or moving finished benches.

successor: Landscaping and Finishing Touches (e.g., mulch, plants, path edging)
rationale: Benches are installed first so that surrounding landscaping and decorative finishes can be placed around them without damaging the benches.
The benches must be fully installed and secured before the area can be inspected and opened for public use to ensure safety compliance.

predecessor: Pour and Cure Concrete Floor Slab
rationale: The stage/band platform requires a level and cured concrete floor substrate to be built upon, ensuring structural stability.

predecessor: Beer Hall Stage / Band Platform Framing
rationale: The structural frame of the stage must be erected before decking or surface material can be applied.
Electrical outlets and wiring for band equipment must be installed after the stage platform is in place to properly locate outlets on/within the stage.
Safety railings around the stage can only be installed once the stage platform is fully constructed.
Lighting fixtures for the stage must be mounted after the stage is complete to ensure correct positioning and attachment.
The steel frame of the building must be erected first to provide the structural support onto which the glazed frontage framing can be attached.
The floor slab or deck at the frontage location must be completed to provide a base for erecting the steel framing and glass panels.

predecessor: Waterproofing and Weatherproof Membrane at Interface
rationale: Weatherproofing at the perimeter must be in place before installing the glazed frontage to ensure a watertight seal and prevent moisture ingress behind the frame.
The steel framing structure for the frontage must be fully erected before glass or glazing panels can be installed into the frame.

Interior drywall, painting, and finishes adjacent to the frontage are typically done after the glazed frontage is installed to allow for proper sealing and trim work, though some prep work could theoretically proceed in parallel.
The bar counter base must be installed first to establish the location and mounting surface where the drainage trench will be positioned along the bar counter.
The trench must be excavated and formed before drainage pipes can be laid and connected to the trench outlet.
The drainage trench must be installed before the surrounding floor finishing is applied, as the trench is integrated into the floor surface and would be covered or obstructed by later flooring work.

The drainage trench must be completed before the bar counter top surface is installed, as the trench is part of the underlying base and drainage infrastructure that the counter top will sit above or adjacent to.
While water supply is typically roughed in before drainage trenches, this is a soft preference as drainage can be installed concurrently or before water supply in some sequencing.

successor: Install Industrial Ceiling Mounted Extract Hood
rationale: The extract hood must be mounted to and supported by the ceiling structure, which must be in place first.

predecessor: Run electrical conduit and wiring to hood location
successor: Install Industrial Ceiling Mounted Extract Hood
rationale: Power supply cabling must reach the installation point before the hood can be connected.

predecessor: Install ductwork from hood to exterior or ventilation system
successor: Install Industrial Ceiling Mounted Extract Hood
rationale: The duct connections must be in place so the hood can be directly attached to them at installation.

predecessor: Install Industrial Ceiling Mounted Extract Hood
