successor: Connect electrical supply to hood and test
rationale: The hood must be physically mounted before final electrical connections and commissioning can be performed.

predecessor: Install Industrial Ceiling Mounted Extract Hood
successor: Install ceiling finishing (tiles, panels) around hood
rationale: The hood must be in position so that ceiling finishes can be cut and fitted neatly around it.
Formwork must be erected to provide the mold and support structure before concrete can be placed for the floor slab.
Steel reinforcing bars (rebar) must be positioned and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to create the reinforced slab.
Electrical conduits, plumbing sleeves, and other embedded items must be placed within the slab area before concrete pouring to ensure they are encased in the slab.
After the concrete slab is poured, it must undergo a controlled curing period to achieve design strength before any loads are applied.
The concrete slab must gain sufficient strength (after curing) before the supporting formwork can be safely removed.
The layout and marking of the bar counter position must be completed before the framework can be installed to ensure proper positioning and alignment.
The subfloor or base surface must be prepared, leveled, and finished before installing the bar counter framework to provide a stable and even foundation.
The countertop cannot be installed until the supporting framework is fully in place and secured, as the framework provides the structural support for the top surface.
The front paneling and kickplate are typically attached to the framework after it is erected to cover the structure and provide a finished appearance.

successor: Install Plumbing and Electrical for Bar
rationale: Plumbing (e.g., sink supply/drain lines) and electrical (e.g., outlets, lighting) rough-in work for the bar area can only be properly routed through or along the framework after the framework is in place.

predecessor: Install Rough-in Plumbing for Draft Beer System
rationale: The rough-in plumbing (supply and waste lines, chiller loop connections) must be in place before the final beer pipework is installed, as the pipework connects to these rough-in points.

predecessor: Complete Overhead Structural Work / Ceiling Grid
rationale: Draft beer lines often run overhead through ceiling spaces or above ceilings; the ceiling grid or overhead structure must be complete to provide support and access for routing beer lines.

successor: Pressure Test & Sanitize Draft Beer Lines
rationale: After the pipework is installed, it must be pressure tested to check for leaks and sanitized before any beer is run through the system.

successor: Connect Beer Tap Towers / Dispense Heads
rationale: The beer tap towers and dispense heads at the point of service connect to the end of the draft beer pipework, so the pipework must be installed first.

successor: Install Walk-in Cooler / Keg Storage Room
rationale: The beer lines run from the keg storage area (walk-in cooler) to the point of service; the pipework installation must precede or occur concurrently with cooler installation, but logically the pipework routing must be established before the cooler is fully enclosed and finalized.
The subfloor must be properly prepared (clean, dry, level, and free of debris) before any floor finish can be installed to ensure proper adhesion and a smooth finished surface.
A moisture barrier must be installed prior to the floor finish to prevent moisture migration from the concrete slab which could cause delamination or failure of the floor finish.

All overhead and in-wall rough-in work such as MEP rough-ins must be completed before floor finishing to avoid damage to the new floor and to allow access for trades that could scratch or stain the flooring.
Baseboards and trim should be installed after the floor finish so that they sit on top of the finished flooring, providing a clean appearance and covering the expansion gap at the edges.
The floor finish must be fully installed, cured, and protected before the space can be turned over for occupancy or final walkthroughs to prevent damage to the new flooring.
The beer dispensing system must be physically installed and connected before it can be commissioned, tested, and verified for operation.
Electrical power supply connections must be completed to provide power for the beer dispensing system during commissioning.
Water and drainage plumbing connections must be in place to support cleaning and operation of the dispensing system during commissioning.
A level, stable, and prepared subfloor or base surface is physically required before any fixed seating can be anchored or installed securely.
Any electrical, data, or other utility rough-ins for the seating area must be completed before fixed seating is installed to avoid the need to move or work around the seating later.
Fixed seating must be in place before final flooring, tile, or other finishes are installed around its base to ensure a tight, finished edge and avoid cutting materials around the seating.

successor: Install Communal Tables (if fixed and adjoining)
rationale: If fixed tables are attached to or positioned adjacent to fixed communal seating, the seating must be anchored first so that the tables can be correctly aligned and secured to the seating or the floor relative to the seating.

Acoustical wall panels require a completed wall framework and rough-in (studs, electrical, plumbing) to have a stable substrate for attachment and to avoid damaging finished panels during subsequent rough-in work.
A finished drywall or backing surface is needed as a base for mounting acoustical panels; panels cannot be installed directly on open studs.

Overhead ceiling installation, ductwork, and sprinklers should be finished before wall panel installation to prevent damage to the panels from overhead work and to allow proper ceiling-to-wall transitions.
Acoustical panels are typically installed before final painting so that paint edges can be cut in neatly against the panels, and to avoid paint overspray or damage to finished panels.
Baseboards and finished flooring are installed after wall panels to allow proper fit and to avoid damaging the panels during flooring installation.

predecessor: Rough Door Frame Installation & Wall Framing
rationale: The door frame and wall opening must be structurally complete before the door assembly can be installed.
All necessary electrical wiring for electronic locks, card readers, and door sensors must be in place before the door and lock system is mounted.
Door installation must be complete before finish work around the door frame can be performed to ensure clean edges and proper fit.

successor: Lock Programming & Access Control System Integration
rationale: The physical lock hardware must be installed before it can be programmed and integrated into the building's access control system.
While inspection typically follows installation, it is a soft preference because some inspections could theoretically be performed concurrently or in a different order if needed.
Ductwork must be installed before terminal units can be connected to the duct system.

predecessor: Install guestroom above-ceiling piping and valves
rationale: Chilled water or hot water piping must be in place to connect to the terminal unit.

predecessor: Complete guestroom ceiling grid and above-ceiling rough-in
rationale: Above-ceiling rough-in work should be finished before terminal units are installed to avoid congestion and rework.
Terminal unit must be physically in place before final duct connections can be made.
The terminal unit must be installed so that control wiring and sensors can be properly connected to it.

successor: Install guestroom ceiling tiles in terminal unit area
rationale: Ceiling tile installation near the unit should wait until the unit is installed to allow access for connections and testing.
The wardrobe structure requires wall framing as a backing surface and to define the alcove or recess where the wardrobe will be installed.
Electrical wiring for any lighting or outlets inside or near the wardrobe must be completed before the wardrobe is built, as access to wall cavities will be blocked afterwards.
Wall and ceiling surfaces must be finished before installing the wardrobe to ensure a clean fit and avoid damage to finished surfaces.
Floor covering (tiles, timber, carpet) should be laid before the wardrobe is installed so that the wardrobe sits on top of the finished floor and the floor doesn't need to be cut around it.
While painting can be done beforehand, final touch-up painting around the wardrobe edges is easier after installation to blend the wardrobe trim with the wall finish.
The window frame must be installed first to provide the structural opening and support for the window assembly to be mounted into.
Sealing and weatherproofing can only be applied after the window assembly is fully installed and positioned correctly in the frame.
Interior wall finishing such as drywall and painting should be completed before window assembly to avoid damaging the window with dust, paint, and debris.

successor: Window Trim and Interior Sill Installation
rationale: Trim and interior sill work must follow window assembly since they are fitted against the installed window unit.
The rough opening must be framed, squared, and prepared to the correct dimensions before any window assembly can be installed.
Electrical rough-in wiring must be completed before lighting fixtures can be installed, as the wiring provides the necessary electrical connections and junction boxes that the fixtures attach to.
The ceiling grid or framing must be in place to support and receive lighting fixtures, especially for recessed or grid-mounted fixtures.
Final ceiling finishing and patching around installed fixtures requires the fixtures to be in place so that gaps can be properly sealed and finished.
Switches and final trim-out work (cover plates, connections) are done after fixtures are installed to complete the circuit and ensure proper functionality.
While painting can be done before or after, it is typical to install fixtures after painting to avoid damage, but this is more of a soft preference than a physical necessity.
A level, stable subfloor is physically required to support the bed base and headboard installation; otherwise, the bed cannot be properly anchored or aligned.
Electrical outlets, lighting, and data cables must be roughed-in behind the headboard wall area before the headboard is installed, as access would be blocked afterward.
The wall to which the headboard attaches must be framed and finished (drywall) to provide a solid mounting surface.

successor: Headboard Wall Outlet / Switch Plate Installation
rationale: Though not physically mandatory, it is standard practice to install outlet and switch plates after the headboard is in place to ensure proper alignment and fit with the headboard.
The bed base must be assembled and in position before the mattress and box spring can be placed on top; physically, the mattress cannot be set down before its supporting base exists.
The lobby floor slab must be poured and cured before any seating components can be placed or installed on the floor surface.
Wall framing defines the spatial boundaries and layout of the lobby, which is necessary to position the seating group accurately within the space.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be completed before installing seating to avoid interference and rework.

Floor finishing around and under seating should generally be completed after the seating group is placed to ensure proper alignment and fit, though in some sequences seating is placed on finished floors; this depends on whether seating is fixed or modular.
While painting could be done before seating installation, completing wall finishes after seating helps avoid damage to walls from furniture moving and ensures a clean finish.
The building must be fully enclosed with walls and roof before exterior signage can be mounted, as signage attaches to the finished building exterior surface.
Exterior wall finishes (cladding, paint, masonry) must be completed to provide a finished surface for mounting signage.
Scaffolding and exterior access equipment must be removed so that signage can be installed on clear, accessible building faces.
It is preferable to complete landscaping and site cleanup after signage installation to avoid damage to new plantings and to coordinate the overall site appearance.
Exterior signage must be in place prior to final inspection and building commissioning to verify compliance with approved plans, code requirements, and tenant identification.
A stable foundation is required to support the canopy structure and transfer loads to the ground.
The canopy/porte-cochère typically attaches to or is supported by the main building's structural steel frame, so the primary steel must be in place first.
The ground surface under the porte-cochère must be finished (slab or paving) before the canopy is installed, as it provides the working platform and ensures proper clearance.
Once the canopy structure is in place, its roof membrane and waterproofing layer can be applied to protect the structure and the area below from water ingress.

Lighting fixtures are typically mounted to or suspended from the canopy; however, wiring can sometimes be pre-run, making this a soft preference for scheduling efficiency rather than a hard constraint.
The ground must be properly graded and compacted to provide a stable, even sub-base before any pavement layers can be placed.
A compacted aggregate base course must be laid and compacted to distribute loads and prevent settling before the asphalt or concrete pavement surface is applied.

All underground utilities, drainage pipes, conduits, and catch basins must be installed and backfilled beneath the parking area before pavement is placed to avoid cutting or patching the finished surface.
Paint striping, handicap symbol markings, and directional arrows can only be applied after the asphalt or concrete pavement surface has been fully placed, cured, and cleaned.
While curbs are often placed before pavement in a monolithic pour, if curbs are pre-cast or slip-formed, they can be installed after paving; however, soft preference is to have curbs in place first.
The structural frame (steel, concrete, or load-bearing walls) must be complete to provide a stable supporting structure onto which the exterior wall cladding can be attached.
The roof structure is typically erected before wall cladding to provide overhead protection and to allow for proper detailing of the cladding-to-roof interface and flashings.
Cladding is installed first, and windows/doors are then fitted into prepared openings within the cladding system, with flashings and sealants applied after.
Final exterior paint or protective coating is applied after the cladding is fully installed to protect the cladding material and provide a uniform finish.
Soft preference: Scaffolding can be partially removed during cladding work, but full dismantling typically occurs after cladding is complete for safe access; not a strict physical dependency.
Electrical rough-in must be completed before HVAC units are installed to ensure power supply is available and to avoid rework or damage to installed units.
Plumbing rough-in for condensate drains and refrigerant lines must be in place before HVAC units are installed.
Ductwork must be connected and sealed to the HVAC units after they are installed to ensure proper airflow and system performance.
Final electrical connections and system commissioning can only occur after the HVAC units are physically installed.
Ceiling installation must follow HVAC unit installation to allow access for unit placement, duct connections, and testing before the ceiling is closed.
Rough-in plumbing (water supply lines, drain/waste/vent pipes) must be installed within walls and floors before fixtures such as toilets, sinks, showers, and bathtubs can be attached and connected.
Subflooring and waterproof membrane must be in place to support fixtures and prevent water damage before setting tubs, shower bases, and toilets.

predecessor: Complete Rough Electrical & HVAC in Guestrooms
rationale: Rough electrical wiring and HVAC ductwork within walls should be completed before plumbing fixtures are installed, as access to wall cavities is needed and to avoid damaging finished fixtures.

successor: Install Guestroom Bathroom Wall & Floor Tile
rationale: Plumbing fixtures (toilets, sinks, tubs) must be set in place before tile work can be fitted around them, ensuring proper alignment, trim, and sealing at fixture edges.
Vanities and cabinetry are installed after plumbing fixtures so that sink bowls and countertops can be precisely positioned and connected to supply and drain lines.

predecessor: Install Rough-in for Electrical and Plumbing
rationale: Fire sprinkler pipes and electrical conduits often share ceiling spaces; rough-in work must be completed first to avoid conflicts and allow sprinkler pipes to be installed without obstruction.

successor: Pressure Test and Flush Sprinkler Pipes
rationale: After installation, the system must be pressure-tested and flushed to verify integrity and remove debris before any further finishing work or activation.

successor: Connect Sprinkler System to Fire Alarm and Monitoring
rationale: Flow switches and tamper switches are installed as part of the sprinkler system; connecting them to the fire alarm panel is a logical next step to enable monitoring and automatic response.
Structural framing (walls, floors, roof) must be in place to support sprinkler pipe hangers and provide mounting points before sprinkler installation can begin.

Interior doors require framed openings in walls. Rough framing defines the door openings, and drywall finishes the wall surfaces around the frames. Doors cannot be installed without framed and finished wall openings.
Doors need a finished floor height to set the correct clearance and threshold height. Installing doors before flooring can result in incorrect door fit, binding, or improper clearances.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before doors are installed because access to wall cavities and ceilings is needed for running wires, pipes, and ducts. Once doors are hung, access may be restricted and finished doors could be damaged by subsequent trade work.
In commercial construction, ceiling grid installation often precedes door installation to avoid damaging doors during overhead work. This is a soft preference as sequencing can vary by project.

Finish flooring is typically installed after doors are hung so that flooring runs up to and under the door frame (or door bottom), providing a clean finished appearance and proper clearance. Installing finish flooring first may result in damage to flooring during door installation.
Door casing/trim is installed around the door frame after the door is hung. Baseboards are installed after doors as well, running up to the door casing for a clean finish.

Doors and door frames are typically painted or finished after installation. Additionally, final painting of walls and trim occurs after doors are installed to ensure a seamless finish and to avoid paint damage during door hanging.
Structural walls and framing must be in place to provide a support substrate for millwork and casework installation.

Electrical wiring, outlets, plumbing stub-outs, and ductwork must be roughed in before millwork is installed to avoid cutting into or blocking finished woodwork, and to allow proper fit around services.
Drywall provides the finished wall surface that millwork and casework are mounted against or attached to; millwork cannot be installed before wall surfaces are complete.
Base cabinets and casework typically sit on the finished floor; flooring must be installed first to establish the correct elevation and avoid damaging the millwork during flooring work.
Countertops are templated and installed directly onto base cabinets/casework; the supporting millwork must be in place and level before countertops can be fabricated and set.

Final painting and trim touch-up is easier and produces a cleaner result after millwork is installed, though it could be done before with careful masking; this is a soft preference for quality and efficiency.
Cabinet and millwork hardware is mounted directly onto the installed millwork pieces; the millwork must be in place first to properly align and attach hardware.
Trim electrical work can be sequenced after millwork to ensure precise placement of outlet covers and switches relative to casework; however, it is not a strict physical necessity.
All fire alarm system components (detectors, control panels, notification devices, wiring) must be physically installed before the system can be commissioned and tested for proper operation.
Electrical power and connections to the fire alarm panel and devices must be roughed-in and available before the system can be powered up and commissioned.
The fire alarm system must be commissioned and verified as operational before the local fire marshal or authority having jurisdiction can perform their final inspection and approval.
A commissioned and approved fire alarm system is a life-safety prerequisite for obtaining a certificate of occupancy and allowing building occupants to move in.

successor: Start Fire Alarm System Monitoring Service
rationale: The fire alarm system must be commissioned and verified to be functioning correctly before a third-party monitoring service can be connected and begin remote monitoring.
The building enclosure (walls, roof) must be weathertight so that exterior signage can be securely mounted and protected from weather damage during installation.
Local building and zoning codes require permits for exterior signage prior to installation to ensure compliance with size, placement, and safety regulations.
If the signage requires illumination, electrical conduit and wiring must be roughed-in to the sign location before the sign can be physically mounted and connected.
Exterior signage installation must be complete before final inspections and certificate of occupancy can be issued, as signage is often a code-required element.
While signage can be completed near the end, final touch-ups and closeout items typically follow its installation to ensure everything is in place for project handover.
The bus stop sign must be mounted on a stable foundation or slab; the foundation must be constructed first to provide a base for the sign post.
The sign identifying the stop location should be installed before the shelter is erected, so that the shelter is correctly positioned relative to the signage.
It is preferable to mark the signage position before painting pavement markings to ensure alignment, but markings can be adjusted afterward if needed.
Any underground utility work near the bus stop location must be completed before digging post holes or installing sign footings to avoid conflicts and rework.
Pedestrian access paths and curbs should be in place before installing the bus stop sign so that the sign location is referenced to the finished pedestrian infrastructure.

The real-time passenger information display requires electrical power to function, so the electrical power infrastructure (cabling, power supply units) must be installed and operational before the display can be installed and powered on.

Real-time information displays rely on network connectivity (fiber optic or wireless) to receive live data feeds. The communication network must be in place before the display can receive and show real-time information.
The physical mounting brackets, support frames, or poles must be securely installed on the building or station structure before the display unit can be attached and secured.

After the display is physically installed and connected to power and network, system integration testing can verify that the display correctly receives, processes, and shows real-time passenger information data.

While it is preferable to calibrate wayfinding and signage systems after the real-time displays are installed to ensure consistency of information, this is a soft preference as calibration could theoretically be done concurrently or adjusted later.
The bench must be anchored to or placed on a stable, level concrete pad; the pad must be cured and hardened before installing the bench.
The bus stop location and post marking the stop should be established first so the bench can be positioned correctly relative to the stop.
If a shelter is added, the bench must be in place first as the shelter structure is typically built around or after the bench to ensure proper positioning.
Soft preference: final grading and landscaping around the bench can be completed after the bench is installed to ensure clean edges and proper soil/sod placement.
The area must be cleared, leveled, and excavated for the foundation pad before any bench installation can take place.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and compacted before any foundation work can begin to ensure proper load-bearing capacity and drainage.
Underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid damaging existing gas, water, or electrical lines during excavation for the foundation.
Soil composition and bearing capacity must be assessed to determine the appropriate foundation depth and design before pouring concrete.
The foundation concrete must achieve sufficient structural strength before forms can be safely removed and further construction can proceed.
The foundation must be fully set and cured to provide a stable anchor point for the bus shelter frame, canopy, and seating structure.
Ticket vending machines require electrical power; conduit and wiring must be run to the machine location before the unit can be connected and powered on.
The ticket vending machine must be mounted on a stable, level concrete base or pedestal to ensure structural stability and proper operation.
Ticket vending machines require network connectivity for transaction processing and remote monitoring; data cabling must be installed and terminated before the machine can go online.

successor: Commissioning and testing of ticket vending machine
rationale: After physical installation and connection of power and data, the machine must be tested to verify coin/bill acceptance, ticket dispensing, touchscreen functionality, and network communication.

successor: Install protective bollards or barriers around machine
rationale: While bollards can be installed before or after, it is preferable to install them after the machine is in place to ensure proper positioning and clearance around the unit for user access and maintenance.
The ground must be leveled and cleared of debris before installing a trash receptacle to ensure a stable base.
The concrete pad or foundation for the bus stop area must be poured and cured before bolting or anchoring the trash receptacle in place.
It is preferable but not physically mandatory to install the shelter first so the trash receptacle can be positioned optimally relative to the shelter without having to move the receptacle later.

successor: Bus Stop Signage and Post Installation
rationale: The trash receptacle should be placed before installing signs or posts near it to avoid obstructions and ensure proper spacing.
It is preferred to install the receptacle before final landscaping so that any dirt or debris from installation can be cleaned up as part of final site finishing.
The bus stop pole requires a stable foundation or base slab to be installed first to ensure structural stability and safety.
Any underground conduits for power or communication lines needed for the bus stop (e.g., lighting, digital displays) must be laid before the pole is placed to avoid digging near the installed pole.

successor: Bus Stop Signage and Lighting Mounting
rationale: Signage (route maps, schedules) and lighting fixtures are physically attached to the pole; the pole must be in place first to serve as the mounting structure.

While final paving or sidewalk finishing around the pole base creates a cleaner finish, it is a soft preference as the pole can be installed before or after final paving; however, installing after paving avoids disturbing new pavement.
If the bus stop pole is part of a shelter structure, the pole must be erected first to provide the primary vertical support before attaching shelter roof or side panels.
Windbreak panels require a stable, level foundation or slab to be anchored to; without this structural base, panels cannot be securely installed.
Any cladding, coatings, or finishing applied to windbreak panels can only be done after the panels themselves are installed in their final position.

While it is physically possible to frame adjacent structures before panels are installed, sequencing panels first allows for proper alignment and reveals; however, this is a soft preference for construction efficiency and aesthetics.
Connecting windbreak panels to overhead beams or roofs requires the panels to be in place first so that connections can be accurately made.
Proper drainage and waterproofing at the base must be completed before windbreak panel installation to prevent water damage and ensure long-term durability of the panel anchorage.
The ground must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and obstacles, and graded to a level surface before shelters can be installed to ensure structural stability and proper foundation placement.
Concrete foundations, footings, or ground anchors must be fully cured and ready before shelters can be placed or assembled on them, as the shelter structure depends on a stable base.

Underground water, sewer, electrical, and data conduits must be laid and stubbed up before shelter installation, as placing the shelter beforehand would block access to run subsurface utilities beneath the shelter footprint.

Interior walls, flooring, electrical fixtures, and insulation cannot be installed until the shelter structure is erected and enclosed to protect interior work from weather and provide the structural frame to attach finishes to.

Final hookup of electrical panels, plumbing fixtures, and HVAC systems must occur after the shelter is installed because these components are housed within or attached to the shelter structure itself.
Signage must be mounted on finished surfaces (walls, ceilings, etc.); installing signage before finishing will require removal or damage when final finishes are applied.
Illuminated or powered signage requires electrical conduit and wiring behind walls/ceilings to be installed and roughed in before signage is mounted and connected.
Large or exterior signage often requires attachment to structural framing; the framing must be complete to provide a stable mounting surface.
Signage must be in place before the final walkthrough and inspection to verify correct installation, visibility, and compliance with codes.
Signage (directional, exit, building identification, room labels) must be installed before occupants or end-users can safely use and navigate the facility.
Electrical wiring, conduits, junction boxes, and switch leg runs must be installed in walls and ceilings before lighting fixtures can be physically mounted and connected.
In suspended ceiling systems, the ceiling grid or furring channels must be in place to support and attach lighting fixtures.
Wall framing and at least rough drywall installation provide the structural support and enclosed cavities for switch boxes, wiring paths, and fixture backing.
Lighting fixtures must be installed and their openings cut/masked before final ceiling finishing (mudding, taping, painting) to achieve flush, seamless integration.
Lighting fixtures must be mounted and wired before switches, dimmers, and wall plates are installed so that all circuits are complete and can be tested.

While lighting is often done before finished flooring to avoid damage, it is a soft preference; flooring can be installed first if fixtures are protected, but standard sequencing prefers lighting first.
Lighting fixtures must be installed prior to final painting so that cutouts are precise, fixtures can be masked off, and paint can be applied around them cleanly.
Ticket machines are physically located on platforms; platform surface must exist before machine can be anchored and installed.
Ticket machines require electrical power supply; conduit and wiring must be laid before machines can be connected and powered up.
Ticket machines need network connectivity for real-time ticketing operations and backend communication; data cabling must be in place before machine commissioning.
Machines must be physically installed and connected before they can be powered on and functionally tested for ticket dispensing, payment processing, and network integration.
Once ticket machines are placed, signage directing passengers to machine locations can be finalized; however, this is a soft preference as signage could be installed concurrently or adjusted later.
The subgrade must be properly graded, compacted, and prepared to support the kerb and channel, ensuring a stable foundation and proper drainage alignment.
Underground stormwater drainage pipes and pit connections must be installed before kerb and channel construction to allow proper connection and water flow into the drainage system.
Underground utility services such as water mains and sewers must be laid beneath the kerb alignment before the kerb and channel is formed, to avoid excavation after installation.
Kerb and channel acts as a formwork and edge restraint for the road pavement; asphalt or concrete pavement is laid directly against the finished kerb.
Footpaths are typically constructed adjacent to the kerb and channel and require the kerb to define the edge alignment and drainage line.
The food stand counter must be placed on a solid, level foundation to ensure stability and proper drainage.
The supporting frame for the food stand area must be erected before the counter can be securely mounted and fastened.
Plumbing and electrical lines for the food stand (e.g., sink supply, drain, power outlets) must be roughed-in behind the wall or under the counter before the counter is installed.
Final surface treatment such as sealing or applying a food-grade finish must be done after the counter is fully installed in its final position.
The sink must be dropped into the counter cutout and connected to plumbing after the counter is securely in place.

While typically done after the counter for proper alignment, upper cabinets can be installed before the counter if precise measurements are taken; however, best practice is to install after for fit and finish.
Display shelving is typically mounted on or attached to walls; wall framing and drywall must be complete to provide a structural surface for shelf mounting.
Flooring must be finished before installing display shelving to ensure the shelving sits on a stable, level finished surface and to avoid damaging flooring during shelving installation.
If display shelving includes integrated lighting or power outlets, electrical rough-in (wiring and boxes) must be completed before shelving installation to allow proper connection and avoid rework.
Products can only be placed on display shelving after the shelving unit is fully installed, secured, and ready to bear load.

It is preferable to install signage above or on shelving after shelving is in place to ensure proper alignment, though signage could theoretically be installed concurrently or beforehand with careful planning.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before any underground component like a grease interceptor can be placed.
The concrete slab or foundation must be poured and cured before setting the grease interceptor in place.
The inlet and outlet drainage pipes must be laid and connected before the grease interceptor is set and connected to the plumbing system.
After the grease interceptor is installed and connected, the excavation around it must be backfilled and compacted for stability and to allow subsequent surface work.
The grease interceptor must be in place before final connections to the kitchen plumbing fixtures can be completed and the system tested for leaks.
The sink must be mounted on or within a wall structure; framing and sheathing provide the necessary support structure.
Water supply lines and drainage pipes must be run within the walls and floor before the sink can be physically connected.
The sink often rests on or is supported by finished flooring; installing the sink before flooring can lead to water damage or improper fit.
The sink is typically set into the countertop cutout before the countertop is secured in place, so the sink must be installed first.
The sink body must be in its final position before the faucet, trap, and supply lines can be attached to it.
Cabinetry requires a level, stable base; the concrete slab foundation must be fully cured and hardened before any cabinetry installation can begin.
Countertops are installed on top of the base cabinets; the cabinetry must be in place and secured before countertops can be measured, cut, and fitted.
The sink cabinet must be in position before the plumber can rough-in and connect supply lines and drain pipes to the sink location.
Electrical outlets for food equipment are typically integrated into or mounted on the cabinetry back panels; cabinets must be placed before final wiring and outlet installation.
The structural frame and wall sheathing provide the enclosed space and backing for cabinets; cabinetry installation cannot proceed until the walls are framed and sheathed.
The cashier counter must be installed on a level, structurally sound floor. Floor slab preparation (including leveling and curing) must be completed first to provide a stable base.
Electrical wiring, outlet boxes, and data cabling for the POS system need to be run in the wall/floor area before the counter is placed, as they are difficult or impossible to access afterward.

successor: POS terminal setup and checkout system integration
rationale: The physical counter must be in place and secured before point-of-sale terminals, monitors, card readers, and other checkout equipment can be mounted and connected.

Finishing work such as sealing or applying a final countertop coating is a soft preference after installation rather than a hard constraint, as some installations allow pre-finished countertops, but doing it after avoids damage during handling.
The main counter structure must be in place before decorative fascia or front panels can be attached to it.
The base or frame must be ready to receive the menu board structure, otherwise the structure cannot be mounted or positioned.

successor: Connect electrical wiring for digital menu board
rationale: Electrical connections typically require the structure to be in place so wiring can be routed safely through it.
The structural frame must be installed to provide a mounting surface for the actual menu panels or digital displays.
Protective trims and covers are finished after the main structure is secured.
A stable foundation is required to anchor the menu board structure, especially if it is a freestanding unit.
The exact position must be marked on the ground or wall before installation to ensure correct placement and alignment.
The electrical receptacle strip must be mounted into or onto a secured electrical box that provides enclosure and support for wiring connections.
Electrical supply wiring and conduit must be in place before the receptacle strip can be connected and energized.
The receptacle strip installation must be complete and wired before circuits can be tested for continuity, grounding, and proper voltage.
While often done after trim to avoid damage, receptacle strips can be installed before final trim if carefully protected; this is a soft preference for sequencing.
Power must not be turned on until the receptacle strip is fully installed, wired, and inspected to ensure safety.

predecessor: Prepare food stand location / site preparation
rationale: The site must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any cabinetry can be installed on the floor surface.
Electrical wiring, outlets, and plumbing rough-ins behind the cabinetry must be completed before cabinets are placed against the wall.
Countertops must be mounted on top of the base cabinetry, so the cabinets need to be in place and secured first.

successor: Install food stand equipment (sinks, stoves, refrigeration)
rationale: Major equipment is often set into or against cabinetry; cabinets provide support and enclosures for built-in equipment.
Plumbing connections to sinks and other fixtures require the cabinetry framework to be in place for fixture mounting and pipe routing.
Countertops are installed on top of base cabinets, so cabinets must be in place first to support the countertop material.
Accurate measurements and templating must be completed before fabrication and installation of countertops to ensure proper fit.
The sink is typically mounted into or under the countertop, so the countertop must be installed first before the sink can be set and connected.
Drop-in cooktops and ranges are inserted into cutouts in the countertop, requiring the countertop to be in place first.
While the countertop supports the backsplash, some backsplash installation can be done alongside; however, full finishing typically follows countertop installation for a clean joint.
Electrical power supply must be available at the hood location before the hood unit can be wired and connected.
The ceiling structure must be in place to support and conceal exhaust ductwork runs before ducts can be installed.

successor: Connect ductwork to roof exhaust fan/termination
rationale: Exhaust duct must be installed from the hood up to the roof penetration before it can be connected to the roof-mounted exhaust fan or termination cap.

successor: Final electrical connection and hood commissioning
rationale: The hood unit and ductwork must be physically installed before the electrician can make final connections and test the hood operation.

successor: Install ceiling finishing (tiles, panels) around hood
rationale: Final ceiling finishing (e.g., installing tiles, trim) around the hood can only be done after the hood and ductwork are in place to ensure proper fit and alignment.
Electrical and data cabling is typically run through wall cavities and ceiling spaces, which require the structural framing to be in place to provide support and enclosure.
Plumbing rough-in must be completed before electrical work to avoid conflicts in wall cavities and to ensure proper routing of all MEP services.
Insulation must be installed after electrical and data cabling is in place so that it can enclose the wiring and avoid leaving gaps around cables.
Drywall cannot be installed until all rough electrical and data wiring is complete, as the walls must be open for access to run cables and install outlets.
Ceiling finishes must be installed after overhead electrical and data cabling is run, as the cables are placed in the ceiling plenum before it is enclosed.
A stable, level foundation must be prepared before the sleeping platform can be constructed to ensure structural integrity and prevent uneven settling.
The sleeping platform must be completed before the roof can be built above it, as the platform provides the primary support and anchoring for the roof structure.
The sleeping platform serves as the base floor; walls must be assembled on top of or around the completed platform to enclose the sleeping area.
While bedding can be placed anytime after the platform is built, it is a soft preference to place it after the platform is finished to avoid soiling or damaging the bedding during construction.
Insulation for the sleeping area must be installed after the platform is complete to properly seal and protect the space beneath or around the platform.
The privacy partition must be attached to framed walls; walls must be framed first to provide structural support.
Electrical wiring within or near the partition location must be roughed in before the partition is enclosed or installed to avoid rework.
The floor must be prepared and leveled to ensure the privacy partition is installed on a stable, even surface.
Once the partition framing is installed, drywall can be applied to enclose and finish the partition.
Final paint and finish work must occur after the partition is fully installed to achieve a uniform appearance.
The ventilation grille must be installed within or through the cubicle wall framing; the framing provides the structural support and mounting surface for the grille.
The ductwork that supplies air to the grille must be in place before the grille can be connected and secured to the duct system.
Although not physically required, completing electrical wiring before installing the grille avoids access issues and potential rework if wiring must be run behind the grille area.

successor: Sleep Cubicle Ceiling or Wall Finish
rationale: The grille must be installed prior to final finishes (drywall, painting, or ceiling tiles) so that the grille is properly integrated and finished surfaces can be cut and trimmed around it.
The grille must be in place for air balancing and system commissioning to measure airflow, adjust dampers, and verify proper ventilation performance.
The ground or foundation surface must be prepared and leveled before installing privacy enclosures (such as fences, walls, or screens) to ensure structural stability and proper alignment.
Foundation posts or footings must be set and cured to provide a stable anchor for privacy enclosure panels or fencing.
Any underground electrical, plumbing, or data lines in the enclosure area must be installed first to avoid excavation or disruption after the enclosure is built.
Final grading, planting, and landscaping around privacy enclosures should be done after installation to ensure proper drainage, aesthetics, and soil compaction against the enclosure base.
Gates or access doors are typically installed after the main privacy enclosure structure is in place to ensure proper fit, alignment, and hardware attachment.
The mattress base must have a supporting structure (bed frame or platform) installed first to provide a stable foundation.
The mattress base must be fully installed and secure before the mattress can be placed on top of it.
Rough carpentry and framing work (e.g., walls, alcoves) must be completed to define the space where the fixed mattress base will be installed.
Flooring should be installed first so the mattress base sits on the finished floor surface at the correct height.
While not physically blocking, it is preferable to complete electrical rough-in before installing a fixed base to avoid having to work around or remove the base later for outlet/switch placement.
The ventilation system must be physically installed and connected before it can be commissioned (tested, balanced, and verified for proper operation).

predecessor: Complete Electrical Rough-In for Sleep Pod
rationale: Electrical power supply must be in place to operate the ventilation system during commissioning tests.
The sleep pod cannot be deemed ready for occupancy until its ventilation system has been commissioned to ensure safe and adequate air quality.
While commissioning can occur before final finishes are complete, it is preferable to complete fit-out after commissioning to avoid dust and debris affecting the new system.
Air quality testing must follow commissioning to verify that the commissioned ventilation system achieves the required air exchange and quality standards.
The ground must be properly graded, compacted, and prepared before walkways can be laid to ensure stable subgrade and proper drainage.
All underground utilities (drainage, electrical conduits, water lines) must be installed before walkways to avoid cutting into or undermining the finished walkway.
Foundations of adjacent buildings must be completed so that walkways can tie into them properly and to prevent soil disturbance near finished walkways.
Landscaping, topsoil placement, and grass/shrub planting must occur after walkways are installed to avoid damaging finished landscaping during walkway construction.
Ideally, building exterior finishes are completed before walkways to prevent damage from scaffolding/material staging, but walkways can be installed first if access is needed.

Site preparation, including clearing, grading, and compaction, must be completed before utility connections can be installed, as the ground needs to be stable and accessible for trenching and laying utility lines.
Underground conduit, piping, and sleeves for electrical, water, sewer, and gas services must be roughed-in before making the final connections to the site utilities.
Foundation must be constructed with embedded sleeves and penetrations before site utilities can be connected to the building entry points.
After utility connections are made and inspected, trenches and excavations can be backfilled and final grading completed to protect the utility lines and prepare for paving or landscaping.
Paving and hardscape surfaces (roads, sidewalks, parking lots) should be installed after utility connections are complete to avoid cutting and repairing finished surfaces for utility access.
The canopy columns and supports require a structural foundation or slab to bear loads, so all foundation and slab work must be placed and cured before canopy erection can begin.

The drop-off canopy typically attaches to or abuts the main building's structural frame; thus, the adjacent building's steel framing must be in place to provide connection points and support for the canopy.
The canopy structure must be fully erected before roofing membranes and waterproofing layers can be applied to it.

successor: Electrical and Lighting Installation on Canopy
rationale: Electrical conduits, junction boxes, and light fixtures are mounted to the canopy frame or deck; the canopy must be in place before these MEP rough-in and finish activities can be performed.

The drop-off lane paving, curbs, and walkways directly beneath and adjacent to the canopy should be completed after the canopy is erected to ensure proper alignment and to avoid damaging finished paving during canopy installation.
The site must be cleared of all vegetation, debris, and existing structures before excavation can begin to provide unobstructed access to the ground surface and ensure safety.
Soil bearing capacity, groundwater levels, and soil classification must be determined to design proper excavation slopes, shoring systems, and dewatering methods.
Property boundaries, building footprints, and excavation limits must be clearly marked on-site to guide the excavation equipment and ensure accurate digging.
All underground utilities (gas, water, electric, telecom) must be located and marked to prevent damage, service interruptions, and safety hazards during excavation.
Excavation permits, environmental approvals, and sediment control permits must be obtained before any earth disturbance commences to comply with legal and regulatory requirements.
Excavation creates the cavity and leveled subgrade upon which concrete footings and foundation slabs are directly placed; foundation work cannot proceed without the earthwork being complete.
After excavation reaches design depth, temporary or permanent shoring, bracing, and underpinning systems are installed to support adjacent structures and maintain excavation wall stability.
Subsurface drainage systems (French drains, sump pits) and foundation waterproofing membranes are installed after excavation is complete and before backfill to manage groundwater.
After excavation and before subsequent work, the exposed subgrade must be inspected and compaction-tested to verify it meets bearing capacity and density specifications.
While backfill typically follows foundation and utility installation, minor initial backfill around foundation walls can begin after excavation; however, final grading is a later activity.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Site Preparation and Earthworks
successor: Construction Activity: Foundation and Substructure Construction
rationale: Site preparation, including clearing, grading, and compaction, must be completed before foundation construction to provide a stable and level working surface for excavation and concrete placement.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Geotechnical Investigation and Soil Testing
successor: Construction Activity: Foundation and Substructure Construction
rationale: Soil bearing capacity and ground conditions must be assessed before foundation design and construction to determine the appropriate foundation type and depth, ensuring structural safety.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Utility Relocation and Underground Service Diversion
successor: Construction Activity: Foundation and Substructure Construction
rationale: Existing underground utilities (water, gas, electrical, sewer) must be relocated or diverted prior to excavation and foundation work to prevent damage, service interruptions, and safety hazards.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Foundation and Substructure Construction
successor: Construction Activity: Superstructure Construction (Columns, Slabs, Beams)
rationale: Foundations must be fully cured and load-bearing before any vertical structural elements (columns, walls) and slabs are erected, as the superstructure transfers loads directly to the foundation system.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Foundation and Substructure Construction
successor: Construction Activity: Backfilling and Compaction Around Foundation
rationale: Backfilling of excavation pits around the foundation walls can only commence after the foundation concrete has achieved sufficient strength and waterproofing has been applied, to avoid damaging the structural element.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Foundation and Substructure Construction
rationale: The foundation and substructure must be completed to provide a stable load-bearing base for the structural frame. Without a cured, properly reinforced foundation, the frame cannot be safely erected as it would lack necessary support and anchorage.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Site Preparation and Earthworks
rationale: The site must be graded, excavated, and compacted before framing can begin to ensure a level and stable working surface for crane placement, material staging, and safe erection operations.

Underground utilities (drainage, water, electrical conduits) must be installed before the structural frame is erected, as access below the slab is effectively impossible once the frame and floor slabs are in place.

successor: Construction Activity: Roof Deck and Roofing Installation
rationale: The roof deck and roofing system require the structural frame to be in place to provide the supporting structure. The frame (columns, beams, trusses) must be erected to define the building envelope and support roof loads.

successor: Construction Activity: Exterior Wall Enclosure and Cladding
rationale: Exterior wall panels and cladding systems are installed onto the structural frame. The frame provides the attachment points and structural support for the building envelope, making it a physical prerequisite.

The building envelope (walls, roof, windows, doors) must be erected on a stable foundation and slab. The foundation provides the structural base and load-bearing surface required to support the walls and envelope system.

The structural frame (steel, concrete, or wood framing) must be in place before the building envelope can be installed, as the envelope components (exterior walls, cladding, roof deck) are attached to or supported by the structural frame.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Underfloor Rough-In (MEP Rough-In Below Slab)
rationale: Any underground or under-slab mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be completed before the slab is poured and before the envelope is installed, as these utilities are embedded in the foundation and cannot be accessed afterward.

successor: Construction Activity: Interior Wall and Partition Framing
rationale: Interior walls and partitions are built within the enclosed building envelope. The exterior shell must be weather-tight to protect interior framing materials from rain, moisture, and weather damage during construction.

The building envelope includes the roof structure and waterproof membrane installation. Once the envelope is substantially complete, final roofing, flashing, and weatherproofing layers are applied to seal the building from water intrusion.
Structural framing and the building enclosure must be complete to provide the physical space and support for MEP systems to be installed.

predecessor: Concrete Slab / Floor Deck Pour and Cure
rationale: Concrete slabs or floor decks must be poured and cured to provide the substrate for MEP rough-in work, especially for under-slab conduits and drain lines.

successor: Interior Wall Framing and Drywall Installation
rationale: MEP rough-in (piping, conduit, ductwork within walls and ceilings) must be completed before walls are closed with drywall to avoid costly rework and ensure code compliance.
MEP systems must be roughed in before insulation can be placed around them and before insulating exterior walls to ensure proper coverage and firestopping.
All MEP rough-in work must be installed and in place before the rough-in inspection can be performed by code enforcement authorities.

successor: Construction Activity: Interior Fit-Out and Finishing
rationale: The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) and core (stairs, elevator shafts, mechanical shafts) must be complete to provide the enclosed shell within which interior partitions, ceilings, and finishes can be installed. Installing finishes before the structure is complete would result in damage or require rework.

successor: Construction Activity: Interior Fit-Out and Finishing
rationale: The roof and exterior wall cladding must be watertight before interior finishing begins to protect moisture-sensitive materials such as drywall, insulation, paint, and flooring from weather damage.

successor: Construction Activity: Interior Fit-Out and Finishing
rationale: Conduits, ducts, piping, and wiring within walls and ceilings must be installed before they are enclosed by drywall, ceilings, and finishes. Retrofitting MEP systems after finishes are complete requires destructive demolition and rework.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Interior Fit-Out and Finishing
successor: Final MEP Trim-Out and Fixture Installation
rationale: Light fixtures, outlets, switches, plumbing fixtures, and HVAC diffusers are typically installed after or concurrently with ceiling and wall finishes but must follow the completion of finished surfaces to avoid damage to the fixtures during finishing work and to ensure proper alignment and fit.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Interior Fit-Out and Finishing
rationale: While some flooring (e.g., tile, hardwood) can be installed after wall painting, it is a soft preference to complete painting and wall finishes before final flooring to prevent paint drips, dust, and debris from damaging finished floors, and to allow for baseboard and trim installation.
The building's structural frame must be in place to provide the vertical shaft and support structure for elevator and escalator installation.
The building core (including elevator shafts and escalator openings) must be constructed to provide the physical pathways for elevator and escalator equipment.
Elevator and escalator equipment must be installed first so that electrical connections can be made to the specific equipment locations and control panels.
While not a hard physical constraint, it is preferred to install elevators and escalators before final interior finishes to avoid damage to finished surfaces from moving heavy equipment.
Elevator and escalator systems must be fully installed before they can be commissioned, tested, and certified for safe operation.

successor: Construction Activity: Site Paving and Landscaping
rationale: Rough grading and earthwork must be completed to establish the proper subgrade elevations, drainage slopes, and compacted base before any paving or landscaping can be installed. Without a properly graded and compacted surface, paving will not have adequate support and will fail.

successor: Construction Activity: Site Paving and Landscaping
rationale: All underground utilities (water, sewer, storm drainage, electrical conduits, gas lines) must be installed and backfilled before paving and landscaping to avoid cutting into finished pavement or disturbing newly planted areas for utility connections.

successor: Construction Activity: Site Paving and Landscaping
rationale: The main building structure must be substantially complete to allow coordination of final site grades, building perimeter drainage, and access points. Landscaping and paving around the building should be done after the building is enclosed to avoid damage from construction traffic and material storage.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Site Paving and Landscaping
successor: Construction Activity: Final Site Cleanup and Inspection
rationale: Paving and landscaping represent the final finishes of the site. After these are complete, the site can be cleaned up, any temporary protections removed, and final inspections performed for occupancy or project closeout.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Site Paving and Landscaping
successor: Construction Activity: Asphalt Seal Coating (if applicable)
rationale: While seal coating is typically applied after new asphalt paving has cured (usually 30-90 days), this is a recommended best practice for pavement longevity rather than a hard physical constraint. The paving can function without immediate seal coating.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Mechanical and Electrical Installation
successor: Construction Activity: Commissioning and Systems Integration Testing
rationale: All mechanical and electrical systems must be physically installed before they can be commissioned and tested for proper operation.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Plumbing and Piping Installation
successor: Construction Activity: Commissioning and Systems Integration Testing
rationale: Plumbing and piping systems must be installed so that they can be pressure-tested, flushed, and commissioned as part of the overall systems integration testing.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Fire Protection System Installation
successor: Construction Activity: Commissioning and Systems Integration Testing
rationale: Fire protection systems (sprinklers, alarms, etc.) must be in place to allow integrated testing with building management systems and life safety systems.

successor: Construction Activity: Commissioning and Systems Integration Testing
rationale: Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning equipment must be fully installed before commissioning can verify airflow, temperature control, and building automation integration.

successor: Construction Activity: Commissioning and Systems Integration Testing
rationale: All electrical rough-in work, wiring, and conduit must be completed to provide power to systems being commissioned and to allow electrical load testing.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Commissioning and Systems Integration Testing
successor: Construction Activity: Building Handover and Occupancy
rationale: Commissioning and systems integration testing must be successfully completed and signed off before the building can be handed over to the owner and occupied, ensuring all systems function safely and as designed.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Commissioning and Systems Integration Testing
successor: Construction Activity: Final Inspection and Punch List Close-Out
rationale: Commissioning results often feed into the final inspection process, and punch list items identified during commissioning must be resolved before final close-out.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Commissioning and Systems Integration Testing
successor: Construction Activity: Training of Owner's Operations Staff
rationale: It is preferred (soft preference) that commissioning is completed first so that training can cover the actual as-built system behavior and correct operating procedures, though some training could theoretically begin earlier.

Structural framing (columns, beams, slabs) and rough-in work (conduit, sleeves, openings) must be in place before fire protection systems (sprinkler pipes, standpipes) can be installed, as they attach to or run through the structure.

predecessor: Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP) Rough-In Coordination
rationale: Other MEP rough-ins (e.g., ductwork, electrical conduits) must be routed first to avoid conflicts and to allocate proper space for fire protection piping, especially overhead.
Fire protection sprinkler heads, piping, and valve boxes must be installed before ceilings are enclosed and walls are finished, to avoid cutting into finished surfaces and to allow proper inspection.
While fire alarm devices can be installed in parallel, final connection and commissioning of alarm/smoke detectors typically follows the sprinkler system installation to ensure integrated coverage.
After installation, the fire protection piping must be pressure-tested and the system commissioned before it can be certified and covered by finishes.
The site must be cleared and excavated to expose the subgrade before floor levels can be accurately marked and laid out.
The sub-base must be compacted and leveled to provide a stable reference surface for marking floor levels and layout lines.
Floor level markings and layout lines serve as the direct guide for pouring and screeding the concrete slab to the correct elevations and dimensions.
Formwork must be positioned according to the floor level and layout markings to ensure the slab is cast at the correct height and alignment.
Reinforcement steel must be placed within the area defined by the floor layout markings to ensure proper coverage and positioning.
Space planning defines the functional requirements and room heights needed, which directly inform the minimum floor-to-floor height required for the building.
The type of structural system (e.g., flat slab, beam-slab, post-tensioned) must be chosen first as it dictates the structural depth and thus the floor-to-floor height.

The space required for HVAC ducts, piping, and electrical conduits within the ceiling plenum must be known to determine the minimum floor-to-floor height that accommodates both structure and services.
Foundation depths and ground conditions influence the lowest floor elevation, which forms the reference point for floor-to-floor height calculations.
Once floor-to-floor height is set, individual structural member depths, beam/girder sizes, and slab thicknesses can be designed to fit within the allocated vertical space.
Stair riser heights, number of steps, and elevator travel distances depend directly on the floor-to-floor height.
Facade panel heights and mullion spacing are determined by the floor-to-floor height to align with spandrel panels and slab edges.
Floor-to-floor height affects smoke control zones, fire-rated vertical separation, and egress stair geometry requirements.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and prepared to provide a stable subsurface foundation before the barrier system can be installed.
Concrete foundations or mounting pads must be poured and fully cured to achieve necessary load-bearing strength before the barrier system can be anchored.
Any electrical conduits, control cables, or drainage pipes that need to run beneath the barrier must be laid and backfilled prior to barrier installation to avoid rework.
The barrier system must be physically installed and mechanically secured before electricians can connect power, control wiring, and perform functional tests.
The barrier system is set into the ground or on a foundation; final paving or surface finishing around the barrier must occur after installation to achieve a flush, finished grade.
A stable concrete foundation must be in place to support the weight and anchoring of the hardened parking entry portal structure.

Electrical, data, and any security cabling for the portal (e.g., gate operators, card readers, cameras) must be laid underground before the portal footing is poured and the structure erected, to avoid re-excavation.

successor: Gate Operator and Security Equipment Mounting
rationale: The portal structure (columns, lintel, barriers) provides the physical framework to which gate arms, sliding gates, card readers, intercoms, and cameras are attached.

successor: Paving and Asphalt Completion around Portal
rationale: The portal structure defines the entry lane geometry; paving must be placed flush against the portal base and curb stops to ensure proper vehicle alignment and drainage.
All portal-mounted equipment (gate motors, sensors, lights) must be physically installed before they can be connected, programmed, and tested in the commissioning phase.
Blast ventilation dampers must be installed within or connected to the ventilation ductwork system; the ductwork provides the structural support and airflow path into which the dampers are mounted.
The HVAC rough-in establishes the housing, sleeves, and penetration openings through walls/floors that receive blast dampers; dampers cannot be placed until these rough openings exist.
Blast dampers are typically mounted in structural walls or floors; the structural element must be built and cured before damper frames can be anchored and sealed into the opening.
Blast dampers form part of the sealed ductwork system; pressure testing cannot be performed accurately until all dampers are installed and closed, ensuring the duct system is complete and leak-tight.

Blast dampers are typically actuated devices that require electrical connection and control interlocks; the control system wiring and programming must follow damper installation so sensors and actuators are physically available for connection and calibration.
The foundation must be constructed first to provide a stable base for the shielded parking structural slab.
The slab provides the working platform and base for vertical structural elements to be erected upon.
The structural slab must be in place before any additional radiation shielding layers can be installed on top or integrated.
Waterproofing membranes and coatings are applied after the concrete slab has cured to protect the structure from moisture ingress.
While some rough-in can occur concurrently, major MEP rough-in work typically follows slab completion to embed conduits and pipes in or below the slab.
The ground must be leveled, cleared, and compacted before any structural wall can be erected to ensure proper foundation support and alignment.
Reinforced concrete footings or continuous foundations are required to anchor the blast walls and transfer loads to the ground; walls cannot be placed on unprepared subgrade.

Any drainage, electrical conduit, or other buried services that would pass under or near the wall line must be installed before the foundation and wall are constructed to avoid later excavation and structural compromise.
Earth or crushed stone backfill against the wall faces can only be placed after the walls have been cast and sufficiently cured to resist lateral soil pressures.

successor: Installation of Vehicle Barrier Systems / Bollards
rationale: Although bollards or active vehicle barriers are often coordinated with blast walls, they could theoretically be installed concurrently; however, sequential placement after the walls ensures proper alignment of the total perimeter security system and avoids rework.
The parking entry door frame and structure require a stable, level foundation and finished concrete slab to be set upon before the doors can be installed.
The structural framing around the parking entry (walls, headers, and supports) must be completed to provide the rough opening into which the blast-resistant door assembly is fitted.

Any power, access control, or interlock wiring serving the door must be roughed in from below or within walls before the door is installed, as retrofitting conduits after door placement is extremely difficult.

successor: Final Electrical and Access Control Trim-Out
rationale: The door must be physically in place before final wiring of card readers, intercoms, electric strikes, and magnetic locks can be completed and connected to the door assembly.

successor: Blast Door Certification and Pressure Testing
rationale: The fully installed door assembly must be in place and sealed before blast-pressure testing and certification can be performed to verify the door meets required blast-resistance standards.
The steel reinforcement cage must be installed before concrete encasement can be poured around the column.
Formwork must be set up to contain the concrete pour for the column encasement.
The column encasement must be supported on a completed footing or foundation that has achieved sufficient strength.
Formwork can only be removed after the concrete encasement has cured to sufficient strength.
Curing and any surface finishing (e.g., grinding, coating) must follow after the concrete encasement is poured and initially set.
The structural steel frame must be erected to provide the supporting structure onto which the blast glazing system is installed.
Concrete slabs must be placed and cured to provide the floor and mounting surfaces for the glazing system installation.
The blast glazing panels must be installed first before sealant and weatherproofing can be applied to ensure a watertight and blast-resistant envelope.
The glazing system must be in place to enclose the parking structure before interior finishes are applied to protect them from weather and to provide the completed building envelope.
The complete glazing system installation must be finished before blast testing can verify the system meets performance specifications.
The parking lot surface and base must be prepared before lighting poles can be installed and anchored properly.
Underground electrical conduits and wiring must be laid in the parking lot before lighting poles and fixtures can be connected to the power supply.
Lighting poles and fixtures are installed before the final asphalt or concrete layer is poured to avoid cutting into the finished surface for conduit connections.

While striping can technically be done before lighting, it is preferable to install lighting first to ensure adequate illumination for accurate line painting and to avoid damaging new markings during pole installation.

successor: Parking Lot Functional Testing and Inspection
rationale: Lighting must be fully installed and operational before final testing and inspection of the parking lot system can be completed.
The foundation areas must be excavated and prepared to receive the blast barriers and bollards, ensuring proper embedment and structural stability against blast loads.

Any underground utilities (e.g., electrical, water, data lines) in the installation zone must be rerouted or protected before bollard/pavement foundation work to avoid damage and ensure service continuity.
Concrete footings or anchor slabs must be poured and cured to the specified strength to provide a solid base for bolting or embedding blast barriers and bollards.
After installation, the barriers and bollards must be tested (e.g., pull-out tests, structural checks) to verify they meet the specified blast resistance requirements before being placed in service.
Surrounding pavement, sidewalks, or landscaping disturbed during installation should be restored after the bollards and barriers are securely in place to achieve a finished, safe surface.
Foundation walls must be in place to provide structural support and anchoring points for the hardened entry gates.
The structural rough framing around the entry opening must be completed to define the opening dimensions and provide attachment points for the gate frame.

predecessor: Install Electrical Conduit and Wiring for Entry
rationale: Electrical rough-in for access control systems, intercoms, and gate operators must be completed before gate installation to allow wiring connections within the gate framework.

successor: Install Access Control Electronics and Intercom
rationale: Access control devices, card readers, and intercom systems are mounted directly onto or adjacent to the hardened gates after they are in place.

successor: Test Gate Operation and Security Integration
rationale: Functional testing of gate movement, locking mechanisms, and integration with the building security system can only be performed after the gates are physically installed.
The dampers are installed within the ductwork system, so the ductwork must be in place first to provide the physical support and connection points for the dampers.
Blast dampers are typically mounted in wall or roof openings; the structural envelope must be complete to provide the mounting surfaces and openings for damper installation.

successor: Test and Balance Blast Ventilation System
rationale: System testing and air balancing cannot be performed until all dampers are installed and in place to ensure proper airflow and blast protection functionality.
Commissioning of the blast protection system requires all dampers to be installed so that functional tests (opening/closing, blast response) can be verified.

successor: Install Blast Ventilation Control Wiring and Actuators
rationale: Although wiring and actuators can be partially pre-installed, final connection and calibration should occur after damper installation to align actuators with damper positions.

predecessor: Install Formwork for Shielded Parking Slab
rationale: Formwork must be erected and secured to contain and shape the wet concrete before pouring can occur.

predecessor: Place Rebar / Reinforcement for Shielded Parking Slab
rationale: Steel reinforcement must be positioned and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity and proper cover.
Any embedded items (conduits, sleeves, anchor bolts) must be placed in the formwork prior to concrete placement so they become cast-in-place.
Concrete must be poured first and then undergo a curing period to achieve design strength before any loads or additional work can be applied.

successor: Strip Formwork from Shielded Parking Slab
rationale: Concrete must be poured and gain sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed without damaging the slab.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the required depth and footprint before concrete foundations or wall footings can be poured and blast walls erected.

Blast containment walls require a reinforced concrete foundation or base slab to transfer dynamic loads (blast overpressure, debris impact) safely to the ground. Walls cannot be erected on unprepared ground.

Underground drainage, electrical conduit, and process piping that pass beneath the containment area must be placed and embedded in the slab before the walls are erected; otherwise, retrofitting would require breaking through the completed structure.

The blast walls must be fully erected, aligned, and cured to their design height before any roof, lid, or top diaphragm can be placed, as the roof bears on the walls and completes the containment envelope.
