Inner linings (e.g., steel plate, fiber-reinforced panels) that provide additional spall resistance are installed after the structural walls are in place, as they are attached to the wall interior face.

predecessor: Pour Concrete Foundation for Vehicle Entrance
rationale: Vehicle access control systems (such as barriers, gates, bollards, or card readers) require a stable, level foundation or mounting surface. The concrete foundation and any embedded conduits must be poured and cured before the control hardware can be securely installed.

Access control systems require electrical power and low-voltage control wiring (for sensors, loops, card readers, etc.). The electrical rough-in (conduits, junction boxes, pull wires) must be completed and inspected before connecting the access control equipment.

predecessor: Install Network/Data Cabling to Control Panel Location
rationale: Modern vehicle access control systems typically require network connectivity (Ethernet or fiber) for communication with the central management system. Data cabling must be run and terminated before the controller panel is installed and configured.

successor: Commission and Test Access Control System
rationale: The physical hardware (barriers, gates, card readers, loop detectors, control panels) must be fully installed and wired before the system can be powered on, programmed, and functionally tested.

successor: Pave/Finish Asphalt or Concrete at Vehicle Entrance
rationale: It is preferable to install in-ground loops, bollards, and mount barriers before the final paving layer is placed, to avoid cutting into fresh pavement. However, if surface-mounted equipment is used, paving could be done first with careful planning. This is a soft preference based on construction efficiency and finish quality.
Column formwork must be in place to provide a surface and structure for applying blast-resistant wrapping materials.
Reinforcement steel must be installed before wrapping so that the structural integrity of the column is established and the wrapping can be applied over the completed reinforcement.
Concrete must be poured and fully cured to achieve the required strength before blast wrapping is applied; wrapping over wet or uncured concrete would compromise adhesion and performance.

successor: Install Cladding or Finishes on Columns
rationale: Blast wrapping must be completed before any final cladding or architectural finishes are installed, as the wrapping is a protective layer that needs to be directly against the structural element and unencumbered by other materials.

While testing is ideally performed after wrapping is complete to verify performance, it could potentially be done in phases; however, standard practice places testing after installation to confirm the complete system's effectiveness.

The building's structural frame and exterior shell must be in place before blast-resistant glazing can be installed, as the glazing units are fitted into the structural openings and require a stable, load-bearing framework for proper anchorage and support.

predecessor: Fabricate or procure blast-resistant glazing units
rationale: The glazing units must be manufactured, delivered, and available on site before installation can commence; installation cannot start without the physical components.

predecessor: Complete rough openings / window openings preparation
rationale: Rough openings must be framed, measured, and prepared (including proper shimming, anchoring surfaces, and weatherproofing substrates) to receive the blast-resistant glazing units.

successor: Apply sealants and test blast resistance
rationale: After glazing units are mechanically installed, perimeter sealants, gaskets, and caulking must be applied to ensure air/water tightness, and blast resistance performance verification tests can only be performed once the units are fully installed.

successor: Complete interior finishes (drywall, trim, etc.) around windows
rationale: Interior finishing work around window frames (e.g., drywall returns, window sills, trim) is typically done after glazing installation to avoid damage to finishes and to achieve proper fit and seal, though in some sequences interior furring could precede glazing.

Corridor partitions are typically non-structural elements that require the main structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) to be in place to define the overall building geometry and provide support/walls for partitions.

It is generally preferable to complete rough MEP work (conduit, piping, ducts) in ceiling spaces and walls before enclosing with partitions, though not an absolute physical necessity if access can be provided later.
Partition framing and drywall installation must be completed before applying any surface finishes such as painting, tiling, or floor coverings.
Door frames are installed within the partition walls, so the partition framing must be in place before doors and their hardware can be fitted.

successor: Final MEP Trim-Out and Fixture Installation
rationale: After partitions are erected, final installation of switches, outlets, light fixtures, and diffusers can occur; it is a logical sequence though some trim-out could theoretically happen concurrently.
The subfloor must be properly leveled, cleaned, and prepared before any floor finishing material can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and a smooth final surface.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work beneath the floor slab must be completed and inspected before the floor finish is installed, as accessing underfloor services afterward would require demolition of the finished floor.

A self-leveling underlayment or screed must be applied and fully cured to achieve the required flatness tolerance before the final floor finish (e.g., tile, vinyl, terrazzo, polished concrete) can be installed.
Wall base or skirting is installed after floor finishing to cover the expansion gap at the perimeter and to provide a clean transition between the finished floor and the wall.
Once the floor finish is fully installed and cured, a final cleaning and removal of protective coverings can take place without risk of damaging the fresh floor surface.
The staircase system is typically installed after the main structural frame (beams, columns, slabs) is in place to provide support and attachment points.
Interior finishes such as painting, flooring, and wall cladding should be done after staircase installation to avoid damage and ensure proper integration.
Handrails and balustrades are mounted directly onto the staircase structure, so the staircase must be in place first.
Applying fireproofing coatings to the staircase is often done after installation, but could be pre-applied if logistics allow; typically follows installation for site-applied systems.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs, stairs) must be in place to provide the physical support structure to which railings and guard systems are attached.
Floor slabs or deck surfaces must be completed to establish the walking/work surfaces adjacent to where railings and guards are installed, ensuring proper alignment and anchorage.

It is preferable to complete railing and guard installation before final finishes and paint to avoid damage to finished surfaces during installation, but this is a soft preference as touch-ups can be performed.

Railings and guard systems must be fully installed and secure before safety inspections can be conducted and before the area can be handed over for occupancy, as they are critical life-safety components.

If mechanical, electrical, or plumbing work is planned at heights near railings, the railing installation may provide fall protection for workers, making it a safety preference to install rails first, though not a strict physical dependency.
Wayfinding signage is typically mounted on finished walls, floors, or ceilings. Interior finishes must be complete to provide the proper surface and aesthetic backdrop for signage installation.

Many wayfinding signs require electrical power for illumination (backlit signs, digital displays). Electrical rough-in and lighting circuits must be in place before powered signage can be connected and commissioned.
Floor-mounted wayfinding elements (directional floor decals, tactile guidance strips, floor-standing signs) require the finished flooring material to be installed first as the substrate.

successor: Final Cleaning and Punch List Completion
rationale: Signage and wayfinding elements are delicate, finished components that must be protected from construction dust, debris, and damage. Final cleaning should occur after signage installation to avoid soiling newly installed signs.

Wayfinding signage is a critical component for building usability and occupant safety (egress signage, directional signs). Building cannot be occupied or handed over until all required wayfinding and signage elements are installed and verified.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to proper bearing capacity before any structural foundations or building frame can be erected.
A foundation (footings, slab, or pile caps) must be poured and cured to provide a stable load-bearing base for the building structure (columns, walls, frames).
Drainage, water supply, electrical conduits, and sewer lines below the slab or grade must be placed before the structure is built, as access is impossible afterward.
The roof relies on the completed structural frame (walls, columns, trusses) for support; it cannot be installed before the structure is erected.
Interior non-load-bearing walls and partitions are built within the completed primary structural frame and depend on it for attachment and alignment.
The exterior envelope (curtain wall, brick veneer, siding) must be attached to the completed structural frame to enclose the building.

Electrical, plumbing, and mechanical rough-ins must be completed within walls and structural spaces before built-in furniture and equipment (such as millwork, cabinets, and fixed shelving) can be installed, as these utilities would be inaccessible or would require damaging the finished built-in elements.

predecessor: Flooring and Wall Finishes (Paint, Wall Coverings)
rationale: Floor finishes and wall finishes should be completed before installing built-in furniture and equipment to ensure a clean substrate and to avoid damaging the built-in elements during finishing work. Additionally, built-in furniture often sits on and abuts finished floors and walls.

After built-in furniture and equipment are installed, any final touch-up painting, caulking, or trim work around the edges of the built-ins can be completed to achieve a seamless finish. This is a soft preference for aesthetic quality rather than a physical necessity.

The installation of built-in furniture and equipment must be completed before final cleaning and occupancy, as these elements provide essential functional and storage space and their installation generates dust and debris that must be cleaned before the space is used.

predecessor: Overhead and Ceiling Work (Ceiling Grid, Lighting, HVAC Diffusers)
rationale: Overhead ceiling work, including the installation of ceiling grid, lighting fixtures, and HVAC diffusers, must be completed before tall built-in furniture and equipment (e.g., tall cabinets, shelving) are brought in, as these elements can obstruct access to the ceiling and would be difficult to install around existing built-ins.
Partition walls require a completed floor slab or deck structure to provide a stable base for wall construction and load distribution.

The main structural frame (columns, beams, primary walls) must be in place before partition walls can be built, as partition walls are non-structural infill elements that fit within the structural grid.
Underslab conduits, piping, and rough-in utilities that run below the slab must be installed before partition walls are built to avoid cutting through finished walls and slab.

Electrical wiring, outlets, switches, plumbing pipes, and HVAC ducts that run inside or through partition walls require the wall framing to be complete so that chases, stud cavities, and blocking are accessible for installation.
Gypsum board or other wall cladding is applied directly onto the partition wall framing; the studs/tracks must be fully erected and inspected before boarding can commence.

The structural slab (typically a ground floor slab or suspended slab) requires a stable load-bearing base such as foundations, footings, or ground beams to support it; the slab cannot be constructed before the substructure is complete.
For ground-bearing slabs, the soil must be excavated, leveled, and compacted to provide a uniform subgrade; constructing a slab on unprepared ground would cause differential settlement and cracking.

A blinding layer of lean concrete is poured over the compacted subgrade to provide a clean, level working surface and to prevent contamination of the slab reinforcement from soil; the structural slab is placed on top of the blinding.
For below-grade or ground-bearing slabs, a damp-proof membrane or waterproofing layer is installed over the blinding before reinforcement and concrete pour to prevent moisture ingress into the slab.

Steel reinforcement bars or mesh must be laid and tied into position (including chairs, spacers, and cover blocks) before the concrete is poured; the placement of rebar is part of the slab construction sequence and must precede the pouring/concreting activity.

Vertical structural elements such as walls and columns on upper floors rely on the completed slab for their load-bearing support and working platform; they cannot be erected before the slab has cured.

After concrete placement, the slab must undergo a curing period to achieve sufficient strength before any construction loads (formwork, materials, equipment) are applied; cracking or failure would occur if loads are placed too early.

While not always physically required, in typical sequences a final floor screed, topping, or additional waterproofing layer is applied after the structural slab has cured to provide the finished floor surface – this is a conventional sequence preference.
The structural framing (roof/floor structure) must be in place to provide support for the ceiling system installation.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work above the ceiling must be completed before the ceiling is enclosed, as the ceiling system conceals these services.
Ceiling installation typically precedes final wall and floor finishes to allow for clean transitions and to avoid damaging finished surfaces during overhead work.
Ceiling system provides the mounting surface and integration for recessed or surface-mounted lighting fixtures.
Ceiling grid or panels must be in place before final installation and alignment of fire safety devices that penetrate or mount to the ceiling.
Structural columns must be supported by a stable foundation to transfer loads properly to the ground.
Column bases require footings to distribute the concentrated load from the column to the soil.
Steel reinforcement cages must be assembled and placed in position before concrete is poured to form the structural columns.
Formwork molds must be erected to contain and shape the wet concrete for column construction.
Floor slabs and decks rest on and are supported by the columns, so columns must be completed first.
Beams span between columns and transfer loads to them; thus columns must be in place before beams can be erected.
Shear walls often interconnect with columns for lateral stability; while typically columns come first, in some integrated systems they can proceed simultaneously.
Masonry infill walls are built between structural columns, requiring the columns to be in place as the bounding elements.
Structural beams require a stable foundation to bear their load and transfer forces to the ground; beams cannot be placed without an existing foundation system.
Structural beams typically rest on or connect to columns; columns must be erected first to provide vertical support and connection points for beams.
For cast-in-place concrete beams, formwork and temporary shoring must be constructed beforehand to mold and support the wet concrete until it cures.
Floor slabs or decks are typically supported by beams; beams must be in place to provide the structural framework before slabs can be poured or installed.
While not a physical necessity, it is more efficient to route mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems after beams are installed, as beams define the available space and supports for hangers.
Structural and framing work must be complete to provide support and pathways for ductwork, and rough-in inspections must be passed before concealing ducts in walls/ceilings.
Walls, ceilings, and roof structure must be in place to support and enclose the ductwork runs before installation can proceed.
The building envelope must be weathertight to prevent water damage to ductwork and insulation during installation.
Ductwork must be in place and leak-tested before insulation can be installed around ducts or before wall/ceiling insulation covers the ductwork.
Ductwork must be fully installed, sealed, and inspected before drywall can enclose the ducts within walls and ceilings.
Plumbing pipes must be laid within or beneath the slab/foundation before concrete is poured, making this a hard physical sequencing requirement.
While coordination is needed, electrical rough-in can often happen in parallel; however, some trades prefer electrical before plumbing to avoid conflicts in tight spaces.
Underground plumbing pipes (drain, waste, vent lines) require excavated trenches before they can be laid and connected.
Underslab plumbing must be fully installed, inspected, and pressure-tested before concrete can be poured to avoid costly rework.
Plumbing pipes within walls must be installed before walls are closed up with insulation, drywall, or other finishes.
Rough-in piping must be in place and connected to supply and drain lines before any fixtures can be mounted and connected.
After pipes are installed, they must be tested for leaks and inspected before being covered by walls, slabs, or backfill.
Electrical conduits and wiring are typically embedded in or run beneath concrete slabs, so the foundation must be poured before electrical rough-in work can begin.
Electrical cables are run through wall cavities, ceiling spaces, and stud bays, which require the structural framing to be erected first.
Wiring must be completely installed, terminated, and inspected before walls and ceilings are closed up with drywall, as access to wiring is needed during installation and inspection.
Terminated wiring connections must be in place before fixtures, switches, and outlets can be connected and mounted.
While insulation can sometimes be installed after wiring, best practice is to complete wiring first to avoid interference and allow easy access for routing cables through cavities.
The concrete slab must be poured and fully cured to provide a stable, dry, and level substrate for floor finishing materials such as tiles, hardwood, or polished concrete.
All underground conduits, pipes, and rough-in work must be completed before floor finishing so that no subsequent cutting or chipping of the finished floor is required.
Moisture barriers, soundproofing mats, or leveling compounds must be placed prior to the final floor finish to ensure proper performance and longevity.
Baseboards and trim are installed after flooring is complete so that they sit on top of and cover the edge of the finished floor material.

Typically painting is done before floor finishing to avoid drips on the new floor, but floor finishing can be completed first if careful masking and protection is used; thus it is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.

Structural framing and rough-in work (e.g., electrical, plumbing, HVAC in walls) must be completed before wall finishing (e.g., drywall, plaster) because once the walls are closed up, access to the internal cavities is lost without destructive removal.
Insulation must be placed within wall cavities before the finishing layer (drywall, plasterboard) is applied to seal it in place.
Wall finishing (e.g., taping, mudding, sanding drywall or applying plaster) must be completed before primer and paint are applied to achieve a smooth, continuous surface.
Wall tiles are typically installed over a finished wall surface (e.g., cement board or drywall that has been finished and prepared) to provide a flat substrate.
Baseboards and trim are usually installed after wall finishing for a clean aesthetic appearance, though this can sometimes be done concurrently; it is a soft sequencing preference for quality.
The structural framing (roof trusses or floor joists above) must be in place to provide a support structure for the ceiling system to attach to.
Ductwork, piping, and HVAC equipment must be installed in the ceiling plenum space before the ceiling is closed up, as accessing them afterwards would require removing or damaging the ceiling.
Electrical wiring, junction boxes, and conduit for ceiling-mounted lights and fixtures must be run in the ceiling cavity before the ceiling finish is applied.
Plumbing pipes, sprinkler lines, and drain pipes running through the ceiling space must be fully installed and pressure-tested before the ceiling enclosure is placed.
The ceiling boards or panels must be installed first before any finishing work such as taping, mudding, sanding, and painting can be applied to the ceiling surface.
Built-in furniture often sits directly on the finished floor. Installing flooring first ensures a level base and prevents damage to the furniture during floor installation.
Paint or wallpaper must be complete behind and around built-in furniture before assembly, as reaching these areas afterward would be impossible or require removing the furniture.
Ceiling work must be finished before tall built-in units are installed, as dust and debris from ceiling finishing would contaminate the furniture, and access for scaffolding may be blocked.
Any wiring for integrated lighting, outlets, or appliances within the built-in furniture must be roughed in before the cabinetry is assembled in place.
If the built-in includes base cabinets, countertops are installed on top of the assembled cabinet boxes to ensure proper fit and support.
Final touch-up painting around trim and built-ins is typically done after assembly to cover nail holes and gaps, but this is a practical sequencing preference rather than a physical impossibility.
Baseboards and shoe molding are installed against the built-in furniture after it is in place to create clean transitions between the furniture and the wall.
Door frames require rough openings created by framing to be in place before doors can be installed.
Electrical wiring in walls must be completed before door installation to avoid interference and rework.
Plumbing rough-ins in walls need to be completed before doors are installed to prevent obstruction.
HVAC ductwork and vents in walls must be in place before doors are hung to avoid rework.
Walls must be finished and painted before door casing and trim are installed for a clean finish.
While doors can be installed before flooring, it is preferable to install flooring first so door clearance and undercut can be properly set.
Touch-up painting around door frames and casings is typically done after door installation.
Door casing and trim are installed after the door is hung to cover gaps and complete the finish.
Doors and hardware must be fully installed for final inspection and punch list walkthrough.
The structural steel frame must be erected to provide the load-bearing support and attachment points for exterior cladding panels.
The roof structure and its waterproof membrane must be completed to protect the building envelope before cladding is installed from top down, ensuring weathertight sequencing.
Wall sheathing (e.g., plywood or gypsum board) must be applied to the exterior walls to provide a flat substrate and structural diaphragm before cladding can be attached.
Windows and doors are typically installed after the cladding system is in place so that cladding flashings and weather seals overlap the window frames for proper water management.

Final exterior paint or finish coatings are usually applied after cladding installation to achieve uniform color and coverage, though this is a logical sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
Steel columns and frames require a stable, level foundation (concrete footings, piers, or slab) to transfer loads safely. Erection cannot begin without completed foundations.

predecessor: Anchor Bolt Installation and Concrete Curing
rationale: Anchor bolts must be embedded and concrete must reach sufficient strength to hold bolts before steel columns can be bolted down.
The steel frame must be erected and stabilized before roof decking or floor decking can be placed on top of the structural steel.
The structural steel frame provides the support system for exterior wall panels, curtain walls, or cladding systems; they cannot be installed without the frame in place.

While some MEP work can begin in parallel, the majority of overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing runs are installed after the steel frame is complete to allow access and support from the steel structure.
The subgrade must be properly graded and compacted to provide a stable, load-bearing foundation for the pavement layers above, preventing settlement or deformation.
Underground utility lines and drainage systems must be laid and backfilled before pavement construction to avoid future excavation and patching of the finished pavement surface.
The aggregate base or sub-base layer must be placed and compacted to distribute loads from the pavement to the subgrade and provide a uniform working platform.

successor: Street Furniture & Amenities Installation (Benches, Lighting, Bollards)
rationale: Street furniture and amenities are typically anchored into or placed upon the finished paved surface; installing them before paving would damage or cover the pavement work.

successor: Line Marking & Surface Finishing (Tactile paving, striping)
rationale: Surface markings, tactile paving indicators, and final surface treatments must be applied after the pavement is fully laid and cured to ensure proper adhesion and alignment.
The sub-base must be properly prepared and compacted to provide a stable foundation for the pedestrian street deck/base slab, preventing future settlement or structural failure.
Underground utilities must be installed and covered before the base slab is poured, as placing them afterward would require breaking the slab.
The base slab must cure and achieve sufficient strength before any surface finishing, paving, or decorative topping can be applied.

successor: Street Furniture & Amenities Installation (Benches, Lighting, Bollards)
rationale: Street furniture typically requires anchor bolts or embedments set into the cured base slab, so the slab must be complete and cured first.
Joint sealing and waterproofing are applied after the slab has cured to protect the concrete and ensure long-term durability.
A stable, compacted subgrade is required to support the foundation and anchoring of street furniture such as benches, bollards, bike racks, and planters.
Underground utility lines must be laid before street furniture is installed to avoid digging up or relocating furniture for utility access.
The pedestrian street surface (pavers, concrete, or tiles) must be fully laid and cured before furniture is placed on top to ensure a level, finished surface and proper anchoring.
Installing street furniture first allows planters and green areas to be arranged around benches, waste bins, and other fixtures for functional and aesthetic integration.

Pedestrian-scale lighting poles and fixtures are often integrated with or placed adjacent to street furniture; furniture placement must be defined so lighting can be positioned effectively without obstruction.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any structural components like canopies can be installed, as the canopy supports require stable ground and proper foundation work.
Canopy columns/posts require concrete footings or foundations to anchor the structure securely; these must be poured and cured before the canopy framework can be erected.
Any electrical wiring for integrated canopy lighting must be run after the canopy structure is in place, but before final cladding/trim to allow access for wiring.
The structural frame of the canopy/awning must be erected first so that cladding panels, roofing sheets, or fabric covering can be attached to the frame.
It is preferable to install the canopy before laying final pedestrian paving to avoid damaging new paving with scaffolding and heavy equipment, though not strictly physically required.
The subgrade must be prepared, graded, and compacted to provide a stable foundation before any hardscape planter structures can be installed.
Underground utility lines such as drainage pipes and electrical conduits must be installed and inspected before planter construction to avoid excavation after planters are built.
The planter walls/structure must be fully constructed and cured before soil can be placed and plants installed inside the planters.
Pavers or concrete surfaces adjacent to planters should be installed after planter walls are in place to create clean abutting edges and proper alignment.
It is preferred but not physically required to install planters before lighting poles to avoid damaging new plantings; coordination can be managed either way with careful sequencing.
The site must be cleared, graded, and excavated before retaining walls can be constructed, as the walls require a stable, prepared subgrade and footing trench.

Underground utilities (water, drainage, electrical conduits) must be installed or relocated before retaining walls are built, otherwise the walls would need to be demolished or undermined to access utilities later.

predecessor: Foundation / Footing Construction for Retaining Walls
rationale: The concrete strip footing or foundation base for the retaining wall must be poured and cured before the wall masonry or precast panels can be erected on top.
Backfill material (gravel, soil) behind the wall can only be placed after the wall structure is complete and cured, to provide lateral support without displacing the unfinished wall.

The retaining walls define the edge boundaries of the pedestrian street; paving, surfacing, and final grading of the pedestrian area can only proceed once the walls are in place to contain the pavement structure.

successor: Installation of Street Furniture and Railings
rationale: While it is preferable to install railings, benches, and lighting after the walls are complete to avoid damage, some elements could theoretically be installed concurrently with careful coordination (soft preference).
The street subgrade and base layers must be compacted and prepared before bollard foundations can be excavated and poured to ensure proper load-bearing support.
Any underground utilities (electrical, water, or data conduits) must be trenched and installed before bollard footings are placed to avoid conflicts and rework.
Concrete curbs define the edge of the pedestrian zone and provide a fixed reference line for accurate bollard placement along the street edge.
Bollards must be installed and their footings cured before the final paving layer or surface finish is applied around them, ensuring a clean interface and preventing damage to fresh pavement.
While bollards can be installed before or after planting, it is preferred to install bollards first to protect newly planted areas from vehicle traffic during the landscaping phase.
The ground surface must be properly graded, leveled, and compacted before installing any pedestrian furniture such as benches, bollards, or trash receptacles to ensure stable and level placement.

Any underground electrical, water, or data lines that may be needed for street furniture (e.g., lighting within furniture, water fountains) must be roughed in before furniture is anchored or installed to avoid digging up completed work.
Concrete or paved surfaces must be finished and cured before street furniture can be bolted, anchored, or placed upon them to maintain integrity of both the surface and the furniture.
Curbs define the pedestrian zone edge and must be in place to correctly position street furniture relative to the roadway and to prevent vehicles from encroaching on the furniture zone.

Landscaping, planting, and decorative finishes around street furniture must be completed after the furniture is installed to avoid damaging plants or finished surfaces during the furniture installation process.
The subgrade must be properly graded, compacted, and stable to provide a uniform load-bearing foundation for the paving installation, preventing settlement or uneven surfaces.
All underground utilities and drainage systems must be laid and backfilled before paving, as installing them after would require cutting or tearing up the newly installed pavement.
Curbs and gutters define the edges and boundaries of the pedestrian street, providing lateral restraint and containing the paving materials within the designated area.

After pavers or concrete slabs are installed, control joints must be cut (for concrete) or joint sand swept in (for pavers) to manage cracking, and sufficient curing time is needed before traffic loading.

While it is physically possible to install furniture before paving, it is preferred to complete paving first to ensure a clean, level base and avoid damaging the finished pavement during heavy furniture placement.
The road base and subbase must be compacted and stable before lighting poles can be erected and foundations poured to ensure structural integrity.
Electrical conduits and cables for the lighting system must be laid underground before poles are installed to avoid digging up finished work.
Curbs and gutters define the pedestrian walkway edge and must be in place to correctly position lighting poles at the proper setback distance.
Concrete or asphalt around the base of each lighting pole must be poured after pole installation to achieve a flush, finished surface without gaps.
The physical lighting fixtures and poles must be fully installed and secured before making final electrical connections and conducting functional tests.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and prepared before any drainage pipes or structures can be installed.
Existing underground utilities (water, gas, electricity) must be relocated or protected before drainage work begins to avoid damage and ensure safe installation.
Trenches and excavations for drainage pipes must be backfilled and properly compacted only after all drainage components are in place and inspected.
The final pedestrian surface (concrete, asphalt, pavers) must be laid after drainage systems are installed to ensure proper grading, drainage inlets, and surface water management.

successor: Inspection and Testing of Drainage System
rationale: The drainage system must be fully installed before it can be inspected, tested for flow and leakage, and approved for coverage.
The ground surface must be properly prepared, leveled, and compacted before bollards can be installed to ensure stable foundations.
Bollards are typically anchored into the paved surface or sidewalk base; the base layer must be in place to provide a solid substrate for drilling and mounting.

Any buried utilities (water, gas, electrical, telecom) in the bollard footprint must be identified, relocated or protected before excavation or drilling for bollard footings to avoid damage and ensure safety.
Final paving or surface finishing around the bollards must be completed after installation to create a seamless, finished appearance and properly seal the base of the bollards.

It is logistically preferable to install bollards first so that the precise pedestrian-vehicle separation zones are established, helping to correctly position other street furniture without obstruction; however, this is a soft preference, not a strict physical requirement.
The road base and subbase must be properly prepared and compacted before installing pedestrian signage, as signage posts require stable, level ground for proper anchoring and alignment.
Curbs and gutters define the pedestrian pathway boundaries, and signage placement is often coordinated with curb locations to ensure proper setback and visibility.
Sidewalk surfaces must be fully poured and cured before signage posts can be anchored into or adjacent to the sidewalk, preventing damage to fresh concrete and ensuring stable post installation.
It is preferable to install pedestrian signage before lighting to coordinate pole locations and avoid conflicts, though lighting may proceed first with careful planning.
Signage indicating crosswalks, pedestrian zones, and wayfinding must be in place before final striping to ensure markings align correctly with sign locations and regulatory requirements.
Signage posts should be installed before final landscaping to avoid damaging newly planted vegetation and to ensure signs are visible above landscaping features.
The structural steel frame must be erected before any ceiling elements can be suspended or attached to provide structural support.
MEP systems such as ductwork, piping, and conduit must be installed above the ceiling before the ceiling is closed in, as they are concealed within the ceiling plenum.
The ceiling panels or surface must be installed before any final finishes like paint or protective coatings can be applied.
Ceiling-mounted lighting fixtures require the ceiling to be in place for proper mounting and alignment.
Fire safety devices such as sprinkler heads and smoke detectors that penetrate the ceiling must be installed after the ceiling is in place to ensure correct positioning and sealing.

The road base or pavement surface must be completed before installing thoroughfare signage to ensure the signs are properly anchored and positioned at the correct height relative to the finished road surface.
Underground utility lines (water, gas, electric, communications) must be installed before sign post footings are dug and concrete foundations are poured, to avoid conflicts and damage to utilities.
Final site grading and drainage must be completed to establish proper road levels and sight lines, ensuring signs are placed at correct elevations and visibility is maintained.
Road markings and lane striping are applied after signage is installed so that sign locations can be coordinated with markings, and to avoid damaging fresh paint during sign installation.

Thoroughfare signs should be installed before the final wearing course of asphalt or seal coat is applied, so that sign posts can be set at the correct final grade and the surface can be finished flush around them.
Handrails are attached to the structural frame (columns, walls, or beams) of the thoroughfare; the frame must be in place to provide a mounting surface.
The walking surface (deck or slab) must be completed to define the edge where handrails are installed and to provide access for installation crews.
Handrails must be fully installed and secure before the thoroughfare can be formally inspected for safety compliance.
While it is physically possible to paint before handrail installation, it is standard practice to install handrails first to avoid paint touch-ups and ensure consistent finish application.
Handrails and guardrails often share mounting brackets or posts; the handrail should be in place as the lower element before the guardrail above is installed for proper alignment.
Thoroughfare doors require framed and sheathed wall openings to be installed into; without the rough opening framed, the door has no structural support or defined aperture.
The rough opening must be measured, shimmed, and prepared with proper clearance and sill/header before the door unit can be placed and secured.
Hardware such as locks, hinges, door closers, and panic bars must be mounted on the installed door slab and frame; installation cannot proceed until the door is physically in place.
Weatherstripping, thresholds, and perimeter seals must be applied after the door is hung and aligned to ensure proper fit and seal against the frame.

While floor finishing can sometimes be done before door installation, it is preferred to install the door first to set the finished floor height relative to the threshold and avoid damaging new flooring during door installation.
The structural framing (walls, header, and rough opening) must be in place to provide the supporting structure and frame into which the fire door assembly is installed.

successor: Thoroughfare Fire Door Inspection and Testing
rationale: After installation, the fire door must be inspected and tested to verify proper operation, latching, clearance, and fire-rating compliance before the space can be considered finished.
Hardware such as closers, hinges, locks, and panic bars are mounted on or after the door is hung; the door leaf must be in place before final hardware can be fitted and adjusted.

Finishing work such as drywall taping, painting, and trim can be done after the door is installed, but it is a soft preference because finishing could also be done before if careful masking is used; however, post-installation finishing avoids damage to the door.
The fire door must be fully installed, inspected, and operational before the thoroughfare area can be occupied and used for egress and fire compartmentation purposes.
The smoke control damper is installed within the ductwork system; ductwork must be in place and tested to ensure proper fit and sealing.

successor: Damper Actuator Wiring and Control Integration
rationale: The damper must be physically installed before electrical actuators can be wired and integrated with the building management system (BMS) or smoke control panel.

successor: Smoke Control System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: System-level testing (e.g., smoke mode activation, damper position verification) requires dampers to be installed and actuators connected before functional testing can commence.

predecessor: Structural Framing and Fire-Rated Wall Construction
rationale: Dampers are mounted within fire-rated walls or partitions; structural framing and fire-rated assemblies must be complete to provide the mounting substrate and maintain fire compartmentation.
After damper installation, access hatches or ceilings can be closed and finished, as the damper must remain accessible for future inspection but is concealed behind finished surfaces.
The structural frame must be in place to provide the mounting surface and structural support for the ventilation grille.
The thoroughfare deck or floor slab must be installed so that the ventilation grille can be set into the designated opening.
Ductwork, electrical conduits, and other mechanical rough-ins serving the grille location must be completed before the grille is installed, as the grille covers and connects to these systems.
Ceiling finishing (e.g., drywall, painting, or suspended ceiling installation) around the grille must occur after the grille is in place to ensure proper fit, sealing, and aesthetic integration.
Airflow testing, system balancing, and commissioning of the HVAC system require all terminal devices (including ventilation grilles) to be installed to measure and adjust airflow correctly.

The fire extinguisher cabinet must be mounted on or within the structural framework (walls/columns) of the thoroughfare, so the structural framing must be complete to provide a stable mounting surface.
The cabinet is typically recessed into or surface-mounted onto finished wall surfaces; wall sheathing or cladding provides the finished surface for proper installation.
If the cabinet includes an alarm or status light, electrical rough-in must precede cabinet installation to provide power connections behind the wall.

successor: Thoroughfare Fire Extinguisher Inspection and Tagging
rationale: After the cabinet is installed, the fire extinguisher unit must be placed inside, inspected, and tagged to confirm it is operational and compliant with fire codes.

It is preferable to complete final touch-up painting and finishing after cabinet installation to blend paint around the cabinet edges, though this is a soft preference as painting could be done beforehand.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before the junction box can be placed into position.
Cables can only be pulled into and terminated at the junction box after it has been installed and secured in place.
Backfilling around the junction box can only occur after the box is installed and properly aligned to avoid displacement.
Testing and commissioning of the junction box connections can only begin after installation and cable terminations are complete.
Underground conduits or ducts leading to the junction box must be laid before the box is installed to ensure proper alignment and connection.
The subgrade must be graded and compacted to proper slope before floor drains can be positioned, ensuring positive drainage and preventing settlement.
A gravel or crushed stone base layer provides a stable setting bed and permits drainage around the drain body; the drain is placed on top of or embedded in this bedding.
The vapor retarder (polyethylene sheeting) is placed over the prepared base and under the slab; the floor drain penetrates this barrier and must be installed after the barrier is laid.
The floor drain body must be set, leveled, and secured with its flange at the correct elevation before concrete is poured around it, so the drain becomes integrally cast into the slab.

The drain outlet must be connected to the downstream drainage piping (hub or spigot connection) before concrete placement to avoid digging up the slab later; this connection is made after the drain is set but before the pour.
The ground must be prepared, graded, and excavated to the correct levels before any baseboard installation can begin, as the baseboard sits on the prepared substrate.
Underground utilities such as drainage pipes and water lines must be laid and inspected before the baseboard is installed, otherwise they would be buried beneath the baseboard and inaccessible.
A compacted aggregate sub-base layer is required to provide a stable, load-bearing foundation for the thoroughfare baseboard, ensuring it does not settle or shift.
The thoroughfare baseboard serves as the edge form and lateral support for the paving layer; the paving material is placed and finished against the installed baseboard.
After the baseboard and paving are in place, backfill material is placed and final grading is completed to match the finished surface level against the baseboard.
The road base must be properly compacted and prepared before expansion joints can be installed, as expansion joints need a stable, level foundation to function correctly.
The subgrade must be excavated, graded, and prepared to the required specifications before any expansion joint installation can begin.
Expansion joints must be installed in position before concrete is poured, as they are embedded or placed as formwork to create controlled gaps in the concrete pavement.
After the expansion joint is installed and concrete has cured, the joint must be sealed with filler material to prevent debris and water infiltration while allowing thermal movement.
Surface finishing operations such as brooming or troweling must occur after the expansion joint is in place and concrete is poured, as the joint defines the boundary for finishing sections.
A stable foundation is required structurally before any wall guard or barrier elements can be installed, as the wall guard must be anchored to a completed base.
The wall guard is mounted onto or along a wall surface; therefore the wall structure must be erected and finished before guard installation can begin.

Wall guards are typically installed before final wall finishes to protect the wall during subsequent work, but if the guard is a permanent fixture, final painting or coating around it must occur after installation to ensure proper sealing and appearance.

In some sequences, flooring is laid before wall guards; however, if the wall guard extends to the floor line, it may be preferable to install flooring first for a clean transition. This is a soft preference depending on design details.
Trim and molding often abut wall guards; installing the guard first ensures accurate fit and alignment of adjacent trim pieces.
A stable foundation is required to anchor the corner guard securely; the guard cannot be installed without a prepared base.
The corner guard must be set in place before the final paving or surfacing is applied so that the guard is properly embedded and aligned with the finished road level.
Corner guards often serve as impact protection; adjacent safety barriers are typically installed after to tie in with the guard's positioning, though sequencing could be adjusted.
The reception counter must be installed on a finished floor surface; the foundation and slab provide the structural base required to support the counter's weight and positioning.

Electrical outlets, data ports, and communication lines needed for the reception desk (computers, phones, lighting) must be roughed in behind the walls and floor before the counter is built or placed, as access becomes difficult afterward.
After the counter is installed, final connections, outlet covers, and device plug-ins can be completed at the reception area.

It is preferable to install the reception counter before final painting and wall finishing around it to ensure seamless caulking and trim integration, though paint touch-ups can be done later if needed.

successor: Reception Area Signage and Branding Installation
rationale: The counter serves as the focal point for branding elements such as welcome signs and logos, which must be mounted on or above the counter only after it is securely in place.
Gates and turnstiles require a stable, level foundation and proper site preparation to ensure structural integrity and correct alignment.

predecessor: Overhead utility rough-in (electrical and data cabling)
rationale: Underground or concealed electrical power and data/control cables must be run to the gate location before the gate structure is installed, to avoid later trenching or demolition.
Final paving or surface finishing around the gate area must occur after the gate is installed to ensure a flush, seamless transition and proper anchoring.
The physical gate/turnstile must be in place to mount card readers, biometric scanners, lock mechanisms, and to run final connections to the control system.
Functional testing of gate operation, access control logic, and safety sensors requires the gate to be fully installed before commissioning can proceed.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the door can be installed. The door cannot be placed without an existing opening.
The door must be installed and secured in the opening before any casing, trim or framing around it can be added.
Weatherstripping, caulking, and sealing must happen after the door is in place to ensure proper fit and protection against the elements.
Hardware such as locks, handles, and hinges are mounted onto the installed door leaf and frame; the door must be in position first.
The subfloor or finished flooring must be in place to establish the correct threshold height and clearance for the door to swing and close properly.
The entrance canopy structure requires a stable foundation and concrete slab to support its columns and load-bearing elements.
The entrance canopy often connects to or is supported by the main building's structural frame, so the main steel frame must be erected first.

successor: Exterior Finishing & Cladding Adjacent to Canopy
rationale: The canopy structure must be fully erected before any cladding, soffit, or ceiling finishes can be applied to its underside and exterior surfaces.
The canopy provides weather protection overhead; doors below should be installed after the canopy is in place to ensure proper alignment and protection during installation.
While wiring can be pre-run, final installation of light fixtures under/on the canopy is best done after the structure is complete to ensure correct placement and avoid damage.
The door frame must be installed and in place before any door hardware (hinges, locks, handles) can be attached, as the hardware is mounted onto the frame.

predecessor: Wall Framing and Rough Opening Preparation
rationale: The rough opening in the wall must be framed and prepared to receive the door frame, which then supports the hardware.
The door slab must be hung on hinges (or ready for hardware attachment) before locksets, handles, and other trim hardware can be installed onto the door itself.
After all hardware is installed, the door operation (latching, locking, closing) must be adjusted and inspected to ensure proper function.

Hardware installation is typically completed before final painting or touch-up work to protect the hardware from paint splatter, though this is a preferred sequence rather than a physical impossibility.
The entrance mat/grid needs a stable, level concrete slab or floor base to be installed upon. The substrate must be fully cured and prepared before the mat/grid can be set.
The entrance mat/grid must be in place so that adjacent floor finishes (e.g., tile, stone, carpet) can be fitted flush against its edges, ensuring a clean transition.

successor: Final Cleaning and Protection of Entry Area
rationale: Once the mat/grid is installed, the entry area can be cleaned and protected. This is a soft preference as cleaning could theoretically be done before, but it is more efficient to do it after installation.
If the entrance mat/grid is a recessed drainage type, any required underfloor plumbing or drainage must be completed and tested before the mat/grid is installed.

predecessor: Rough-In Electrical Work (if mat has heated or sensor elements)
rationale: If the entrance mat includes electrical components (e.g., heated mats, motion sensors), rough-in electrical wiring must be completed and terminated before the mat/grid is permanently placed.
The ground area where entrance signage will be installed must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any signage foundation or mounting can begin.
Concrete footings or slabs for entrance signage posts or monuments must be poured and cured before signage can be mounted or installed.
Any electrical conduits, data cables, or other underground utilities serving illuminated or electronic signage must be laid before the signage is installed to avoid re-excavation.
Landscaping, paving, and decorative finishes around the entrance should be completed after signage is in place to ensure proper alignment, access for installation equipment, and clean integration.
Final inspections for signage compliance, visibility, and illumination cannot be performed until the entrance signage is fully installed.
Door hardware such as handles, locks, and hinges must be fitted onto installed doors, so doors must be in place first.
Window hardware like locks, stays, and hinges require the windows to be installed before they can be attached.
Cabinet hardware such as handles, knobs, and drawer slides must be fitted after cabinets are installed.
Final trim and molding work typically follows hardware fitting to avoid damage to hardware and ensure clean finishing.
Hardware must be fully fitted before the final inspection to verify all components are properly installed and functional.
Power and low-voltage wiring for the intercom must be run in walls before the device can be physically installed and connected.
Conduit or raceway for intercom/data cables must be placed within walls/ceilings before pulling cables and mounting the unit.
The intercom unit is a finished-surface-mounted device; walls must be closed and painted before final mounting to avoid damage and ensure a clean finish.
The intercom must be physically installed and connected before system-level testing, programming, and commissioning can take place.

successor: Final security system integration and programming
rationale: The entry phone must be in place and wired so that it can be integrated with the building's access control and security system.
The foundation provides the structural base and support for the entrance threshold, so the foundation must be poured and cured before the threshold can be installed.
The rough framing defines the doorway opening dimensions and provides the structural framework to which the threshold will be attached, so framing must be completed first.
The entrance threshold serves as the bottom component of the door opening; the door frame is typically installed on top of and aligned with the threshold.

While floor finishing can technically begin before threshold installation, it is preferable to install the threshold first to ensure proper alignment and height transition between the floor and the doorway.
The entrance threshold must be in place before weatherproofing and sealing can be applied around the doorway bottom to prevent water infiltration and air leakage.
The ground must be properly graded and compacted to provide a stable, uniform subgrade before any paving surface can be applied. Paving on unprepared earth would lead to settlement and cracking.

A compacted aggregate sub-base layer is required to provide structural support, drainage, and a level surface for the paving material. Without the sub-base, the pavement would lack load-bearing capacity.

All underground utilities, drainage pipes, and conduits must be installed and covered before paving, as tearing up completed pavement to access underground services is extremely costly and destructive.
Asphalt or concrete paving requires a curing or cooling period after placement to achieve the necessary strength and durability before it can bear traffic loads.
Line striping, lane markings, and traffic paint must be applied only after the paving surface has fully cured/set, as painting on wet or uncured pavement results in poor adhesion and durability.
The parking area must be properly graded, compacted, and prepared before any striping can be applied to ensure a smooth, stable surface.
The aggregate base layer must be placed and compacted to provide a stable foundation for the asphalt or paving surface that will receive striping.
The paved surface (asphalt or concrete) must be fully installed, cured, and finished before any paint or thermoplastic markings can be applied.
Curbs and gutters define the parking area boundaries and must be in place so that stall lines can be accurately laid out relative to the edges.
Signage (e.g., handicap parking signs, no parking signs, directional signs) is typically installed after striping is complete to ensure signs align correctly with marked stalls and aisles.
The wheel stop must be mounted on a stable, level foundation or paved surface to function correctly and withstand vehicle impact.
Wheel stops define the stopping position for vehicles; parking space markings should align with the installed wheel stops to ensure proper vehicle positioning.
Wheel stops are typically anchored into the pavement; the pavement must be fully cured before drilling and anchoring to avoid compromising the surface integrity.

successor: Parking lot opening for vehicle use
rationale: Wheel stops must be securely installed before vehicles are allowed to park to prevent vehicles from overrunning the parking space boundaries.
Proper drainage must be established before installing wheel stops so that water flows away from the stops and does not pool around them, preventing deterioration or displacement.
The ground must be graded and excavated to the proper elevation and alignment before curb and gutter forms can be set and concrete poured.
A compacted aggregate base or subbase provides a stable, uniform foundation for the curb and gutter structure; pouring concrete directly on unprepared soil would lead to settlement and failure.

Any underground drainage pipes, catch basins, or utility conduits that pass under or adjacent to the curb line must be installed and backfilled before curb and gutter is placed to avoid digging up completed concrete.
Curb and gutter defines the edge of the roadway and acts as a form for asphalt; paving cannot proceed until the curb is in place to contain and shape the pavement.
Sidewalks often abut the back of the curb and gutter; the curb must be in place to establish the grade and alignment for adjacent sidewalk pours.
The parking lot surface must be fully installed and cured before any signage can be installed, as signs are mounted on or adjacent to the paved surface.
Parking lot striping defines the parking spaces, directional lanes, and ADA accessible routes; signage placement must align with the striped layout.
Soft preference: lighting poles and fixtures should ideally be installed after signage to avoid interference and ensure proper illumination of signs, but not physically required.
Signage must be in place before the final inspection can verify all parking lot elements (striping, signs, accessibility compliance) are complete.
The parking lot surface must be properly graded and compacted before landscaping can begin, as landscaping (trees, shrubs, planters) is installed around and within the finished parking lot layout.
The paved parking lot surface, curbs, and striping must be complete so that landscaped islands, medians, and perimeter planting areas are properly positioned and aligned with the parking layout.
Underground drainage systems, catch basins, and drain inlets must be installed before landscaping to ensure proper water management and to avoid disturbing newly planted vegetation.
All underground utilities (water, electrical, lighting conduits, irrigation lines) must be placed before planting to avoid digging up or damaging new landscaping.
Landscaping is typically a finishing activity; once planting, mulching, and sod/seed are completed, the site can be cleaned up and final inspections performed.
The parking barrier or gate requires a stable and level foundation or base slab to be mounted upon. Without the structural base completed, the barrier/gate cannot be securely anchored.
Electrical power and control cables for automatic parking barriers/gates must be routed in conduits beneath the surface before the barrier posts are installed, to avoid damaging finished work.

successor: Electrical Connection and Control System Configuration
rationale: The physical mounting of the barrier/gate mechanism must be complete before electricians can terminate wiring, connect motors/sensors, and configure the control system.

It is a soft preference to install pavement markings and signage after the barrier is in place so that lane positioning, stop lines, and signage align precisely with the barrier location, but markings could be done prior with careful measurement.
The barrier/gate must be fully installed and connected before integrated testing of opening/closing cycles, sensor activation, and safety systems can be performed.
A stable, level foundation or concrete slab must be in place to support the weight and anchoring of the pay station / ticket kiosk, ensuring structural stability and proper alignment.

predecessor: Underground Electrical and Data Conduit Installation
rationale: Power supply and data communication lines (conduits) must be run to the kiosk location before the unit can be connected and activated.
The pay station must be physically installed and positioned before electricians can make final connections to power and data lines and perform functional testing.

successor: Payment System Calibration and Software Configuration
rationale: After the kiosk is installed, technicians must configure the payment software, calibrate the ticket dispenser / card reader, and integrate with the central parking management system.

Directional signage indicating the location of the pay station should ideally be installed after the kiosk is in place to ensure accurate placement and visibility, though this is a logical preference rather than a physical necessity.
The parking lot base (asphalt/concrete) must be finished and cured before the bicycle rack can be anchored or placed on it.
Bicycle rack placement zone must be clearly marked and designated during striping before the rack can be installed.
Soft preference: installing the bike rack before lighting allows lighting to be positioned to properly illuminate the rack area, but lighting can also be adjusted around an existing rack.
Hard constraint: the bicycle rack must be installed before final landscaping and curbing around it, so that the rack is properly integrated and landscaping can be finished neatly around its base.

predecessor: Electrical infrastructure installation (trenching, conduit, and cabling)
rationale: EV charging stations require dedicated electrical supply lines, conduit, and cabling to be installed before the charging unit can be connected and energized.
The charging station pedestal or bollard needs a stable, level concrete base for mounting and anchoring, which must be poured and cured first.
The area must be properly graded and drained to prevent water pooling around electrical equipment, ensuring safety and longevity.

successor: Testing and commissioning of charging unit
rationale: After physical installation, the charging station must be tested for electrical safety, communication connectivity, and proper operation before being placed into service.

successor: Pavement marking / striping of EV parking space
rationale: It is easier to install the charging unit first and then mark the designated parking stall around it, though markings could theoretically be done before installation if exact placement is known.
Signs indicating the charging station location and usage rules are typically placed after the unit is installed to ensure correct positioning.
The ground must be graded and excavated to the proper elevations and cross-slopes before concrete forms can be set and concrete placed for curbs and gutters.
A stable, compacted subgrade is required to support the concrete curb and gutter structure and prevent differential settlement.
Underground utility lines beneath the curb and gutter area must be installed and backfilled before concrete is placed to avoid the need to cut or remove the finished concrete.
Curbs and gutters act as the edge form and containment for asphalt pavement; paving cannot proceed until the curbs are installed and cured.
Sidewalks and driveways typically tie into curbs and gutters; the curb alignment and height defines the transition point for these adjacent flatwork elements.
The subgrade must be properly graded, compacted, and leveled to provide a stable, uniform base for the asphalt layer. Asphalt cannot be placed directly on uneven or unprepared soil.
An aggregate base course provides structural support, drainage, and a stable platform for the asphalt. Asphalt paving requires a compacted granular base to prevent cracking and deformation.

predecessor: Installation of Drainage Systems (subsurface drains, culverts)
rationale: Subsurface drainage components must be in place before paving to ensure water is properly diverted away from the pavement structure, preventing future water damage and undermining.

predecessor: Utility Work and Underground Conduit Installation
rationale: All underground utilities (water, sewer, gas, electrical, telecommunications) must be installed and backfilled before paving to avoid cutting into or disturbing the finished asphalt surface later.
Traffic markings, lane lines, and crosswalks must be applied onto the cured asphalt surface. Striping cannot be done before the asphalt is laid and compacted.

While curbs are often placed before paving to act as forms, in some sequences asphalt is laid first and curbs are installed adjacent afterward. This is a soft preference depending on the construction method.

successor: Final Site Cleanup and Curing Period
rationale: After asphalt is placed and compacted, the area must be allowed to cool and cure before traffic is allowed, and cleanup of excess material must occur after paving is complete.

The parking lot surface must be fully constructed, including the base course and pavement, before striping can be applied. Striping requires a finished, smooth asphalt or concrete surface to adhere properly and provide accurate markings.

Striping paint and thermoplastic markings must be applied to a fully cured, clean pavement surface. If applied before paving is complete or before the surface has cured, markings will be damaged or deformed.

While striping can conceptually be done before or after lighting, it is generally preferred to complete striping before installing lighting poles to avoid construction traffic damaging fresh markings and to simplify layout verification using the unobstructed pavement surface.

It is preferred to complete striping before final landscaping and curbs are installed to ensure striping equipment has full access to the lot surface without obstructions. However, this is a soft preference as some sequencing flexibility exists.

Signage (stop signs, directional signs, handicap parking signs) must be installed after striping is complete because sign placement locations depend on the final marked stall layout, aisle widths, and traffic flow patterns as defined by the striping plan.
The parking lot surface must be graded and prepared before lighting poles can be properly installed and anchored.
Conduit and electrical supply lines for the parking lot lights must be installed underground before pole bases and foundations are poured.
Concrete bases and foundations for the lighting poles must be cured in place before the poles and luminaires can be mounted.
Lighting poles and fixtures must be installed before the final paved surface is laid to avoid damaging new pavement and to properly set pole heights relative to the finished grade.

It is preferred to have lighting operational before striping so that the illuminated conditions can guide proper line placement and visibility, but striping can technically be done in daylight without lights.

The pavement surface must be clean and free of debris, dirt, and loose materials before marking removal can begin. Removing markings on a dirty surface would be ineffective as debris can interfere with removal equipment and obscure the existing markings.

Any pavement repairs or patching must be completed before marking removal because the removal process can be performed on a uniform, stable surface. If repairs are done after marking removal, the newly patched areas may need remarking anyway, creating rework.

successor: Parking Lot Surface Preparation (for new markings)
rationale: After old markings are removed, the pavement surface needs to be prepared (cleaned, primed, or otherwise treated) to accept new pavement markings. New markings cannot be applied over residual debris or rough surfaces left from removal.

successor: Parking Lot New Pavement Marking Application
rationale: New pavement markings can only be applied after old markings have been completely removed. Applying new markings over existing ones would create confusion, non-compliance with striping standards, and poor adhesion.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil before any base or sub-base materials can be placed and compacted for the parking lot.
Rough grading establishes the proper subgrade elevations and drainage slopes, which must be in place before the aggregate base and sub-base layers are installed.
Underground utilities must be installed and backfilled before placing base materials to avoid excavating through completed base layers and causing settlement.
The base and sub-base layers provide a stable, well-drained foundation that must be completed before the final paving surface can be placed on top.
Parking lot striping is applied to the finished paved surface; the base layers must be complete and the paving laid before markings can be applied.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before earthmoving can begin, as obstacles would interfere with grading operations.
Topsoil must be stripped and stockpiled separately before cut/fill operations begin, as it is fertile material that should not be mixed with subsoils during grading.
The site must be surveyed and graded contours staked out to guide the equipment operators on where to cut and where to fill to achieve the designed elevations.
After earthmoving is complete, the rough grade must be verified and soil compaction tests performed before any further construction layers are placed.
The overall site grading must be completed to establish the building pad elevation before excavations for individual footings and foundations can be accurately executed.
Site access roads, temporary facilities, and equipment staging areas must be established before topsoil stripping can commence to enable equipment mobilization and material handling.
All trees, shrubs, and surface vegetation must be cleared and removed before topsoil stripping can begin to expose the topsoil layer and prevent organic debris from mixing with stockpiled topsoil.

predecessor: Environmental and Erosion Control Measures Installation
rationale: Sediment fences, silt basins, and other erosion control measures must be installed prior to stripping to contain sediment runoff from exposed areas and stockpiles.
Topsoil must be completely stripped and stockpiled before bulk earthworks (cut/fill operations) can begin, as the subgrade layers need to be exposed for excavation and compaction.
Subsurface drainage pipes, culverts, and stormwater systems are installed after topsoil removal because they require excavation into the subgrade which must be free of topsoil.
Vegetation and debris must be removed from the site before erosion control measures (such as silt fences, sediment basins, and straw wattles) can be installed effectively.
Accurate staking of property lines, grading limits, and drainage patterns is necessary to correctly position erosion and sediment control devices.
Erosion and sediment control measures must be in place before any soil-disturbing activities (cut, fill, grading) begin, to capture sediment runoff as required by environmental regulations.
Demolition generates debris and exposes soil; sediment controls must be installed beforehand to contain runoff.
Trenching disturbs large areas of soil; erosion controls must be operational prior to any underground utility installation.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before drainage and grading can begin, as the earth needs to be exposed and accessible for earthmoving equipment.

Erosion and sediment control measures (e.g., silt fences, sediment basins) must be installed before any earth-disturbing activities like grading commence, to comply with environmental regulations and prevent sediment runoff.
The site must be surveyed and staked to establish proposed grades, drainage patterns, and benchmark elevations before cut and fill operations can be accurately performed.

While not always critical before grading, knowing soil conditions (e.g., bearing capacity, shrink-swell potential) helps determine cut/fill suitability and drainage design; however, grading can begin with preliminary data if needed.

successor: Underground Utility Installation (water, sewer, electrical, gas)
rationale: Grading establishes the final subgrade elevations and drainage slopes; underground utilities should be installed after rough grading to avoid conflicts with planned grades and to ensure proper utility cover depths.

The site must be rough-graded to final subgrade elevations before building foundation excavation begins, so that footing elevations and building pad elevations are correctly referenced from the finished grade.
Paved areas require a stable, graded subgrade with proper drainage slopes before aggregate base and pavement layers can be placed.
Final grading establishes the contours for planting areas, swales, and finished surfaces; landscaping follows after all heavy earthwork and utility work is complete.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before subgrade work can begin, as any obstructions would prevent proper grading and compaction of the subgrade layer.
Accurate survey stakes and grade references must be established to guide the subgrade excavation, filling, and compaction to the correct elevations and alignments.

Rough grading through cut and fill operations must be completed to bring the area to approximate grade before the final subgrade preparation and compaction can achieve the specified density and smoothness.
The compacted subgrade provides a stable, uniform foundation for the base course layer; placing base material on unprepared subgrade would result in differential settlement and pavement failure.
Subgrade compaction must be completed before installing subsurface drainage systems such as underdrains or French drains, as these are placed within or directly on top of the prepared subgrade.
The site must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and existing structures before soil amendment can begin, as foreign materials would contaminate or obstruct the soil treatment process.
Excavation to final subgrade levels and rough grading must be completed so that the soil mass to be treated is exposed and accessible for amendment additives to be mixed in.

Laboratory tests of soil properties (e.g., compaction characteristics, plasticity index, organic content) must be performed first to determine the correct type and dosage of stabilizers such as lime, cement, or fly ash.
After amendment materials are mixed into the soil, fine grading and compaction must follow to achieve the specified density and surface tolerance before placing pavement, slabs, or foundations.

successor: Placement of Base Course or Subbase
rationale: The stabilized soil layer must be completed and properly cured before any subsequent base course materials are placed, as the subgrade must provide a stable platform for the base layer.
Concrete must reach sufficient strength before backfill forces are applied against the foundation walls to prevent structural damage.
Waterproofing membranes and coatings must be fully applied and cured before backfill to protect the foundation from moisture ingress.

predecessor: Foundation Drainage System Installation (e.g., drain tiles, gravel)
rationale: Drainage systems around the foundation must be in place before backfill so they can function properly and be properly protected.
Backfill must be compacted to proper density before interior floor slabs are poured to provide stable subgrade support and prevent settlement.
Rough backfill is completed before final grading and landscaping can shape the topsoil and plant vegetation, though this is a logical sequence preference rather than a physical necessity.
A stable foundation is required to support the weight and structural integrity of the sun shade structure before it can be erected.
The main building structural frame must be in place to provide attachment points and support for the sun shade structure.
The sun shade structure must be installed first as it may integrate with or be covered by the exterior cladding system.
