Sun shade elements often project over or attach adjacent to window openings, so the shade structure must be in place before glazing is installed to ensure proper fit and weather sealing.

Commissioning activities like solar heat gain testing benefit from having the sun shade already installed to measure its actual performance, but this is a preference for accurate testing rather than a physical construction necessity.

The ground must be graded to final contours, topsoil replaced, and the seedbed prepared (tilled, fertilized) before any seeding and mulching can take place, as seeding onto unprepared or uncompacted soil leads to poor germination and erosion.

successor: Erosion Control Installation (if not already complete)
rationale: Mulching is itself a critical erosion control measure; if additional erosion control blankets, netting, or hydroseed tackifiers are needed, they are typically applied immediately after or concurrently with seeding to protect the seedbed.

All construction debris, rocks, and waste materials must be removed from the restoration area before seeding and mulching to ensure a clean seedbed and prevent contamination or obstruction of germination.

Trenching, pipe laying, conduit installation, and backfill compaction must be completed before final grading and seeding, because re-excavation after seeding would destroy the newly established vegetation and mulch layer.

After seeding and mulching, the area enters a maintenance phase (irrigation, weed control, mowing, fertilization, and monitoring) to ensure successful germination and establishment of the vegetative cover.
The structural frame must be in place to provide the load-bearing support onto which the South-Facing Glazed Screen can be mounted and fixed.

predecessor: Floor Slab Completion at Screen Level
rationale: The floor slab at the relevant level must be finished to provide a stable working platform and base for installing the glazed screen unit.

successor: Weatherproofing and Sealing of Glazed Joints
rationale: After the glazed screen is installed, all joints between the screen frame and surrounding structure must be sealed to ensure the building envelope is watertight and airtight.
Interior finishing work such as drywall, flooring, and painting near the glazed screen should follow screen installation to avoid damaging the finished surfaces or the glass during subsequent work.

successor: Testing and Commissioning of Solar Control Systems
rationale: The glazed screen must be fully installed before any integrated solar shading or smart glass control systems can be tested and commissioned, as they rely on the installed screen assembly.
The steel frame provides the primary structural support and mounting surface for the railing system. The railing cannot be installed until the main structural frame is in place.
The deck or floor slab provides the base surface upon which the railing system will be anchored or mounted. The concrete slab must be cured and ready to accept railing anchors.

The railing system defines the outer perimeter and edge protection. Cladding or glazing panels adjacent to the railing should typically be installed after the railing is in place to ensure proper alignment and secure attachment.
While final finishing coats can be done after installation, it is often preferred to pre-finish components to avoid overspray or damage to adjacent finished surfaces.

successor: Connect South-Facing Outdoor Lighting to Power Source
rationale: The lighting fixtures must be physically installed in their proper locations before electrical wiring can be connected to them.

predecessor: Rough Electrical Work for Outdoor Areas
rationale: Conduit and junction boxes must be in place before fixtures can be mounted and wired.
The lighting system must be fully installed and connected before it can be tested for functionality.
While not physically required, completing lighting installation before final landscaping prevents damage to finished landscaping and reduces rework.
Ground disturbance and excavation work must be completed before installing any lighting components that are mounted on or near footings.
The ground must be prepared, cleared, and leveled before any construction of a terrace structure can begin to ensure a stable foundation.
A proper foundation or substructure must be in place to support the terrace, preventing settling or structural failure.
The terrace surface and structure must be built first so that drainage components (e.g., drains, gutters) can be properly integrated and aligned with the finished surface.
Safety railings or balustrades are attached to the finished terrace structure and must be installed after the terrace deck or slab is complete.

Waterproofing and sealing are typically applied after the terrace structure is built, though this could be done concurrently in some cases; it is a strong preference for durability but not an absolute physical necessity.
The building's structural frame must be fully erected and stable to provide the load-bearing support required for the balcony installation.
The floor slab at the balcony level must be poured and fully cured to provide a solid base for anchoring the balcony structure.
Waterproofing at the balcony junction must be in place before installation to prevent moisture ingress behind the balcony structure.

successor: Balcony Railing and Glass Balustrade Installation
rationale: The main balcony structure must be fully installed to provide the mounting surface and support framework for railings and glass balustrades.
The balcony structure must be in place before final drainage connections and waterproofing sealants can be applied to ensure proper water runoff.
The building structural frame must be complete to provide a stable mounting surface and structural support for sun shading devices.
Roof must be installed before exterior shading devices that attach to or integrate with the roof structure can be mounted.
Exterior walls must be constructed to provide anchorage points and support for sun shading devices, which are typically mounted on or integrated with the facade.
Ideally, exterior finishing would be completed after shading devices are installed to avoid damage to finishes, but shading devices can be installed after if scaffolding is already in place.

Sun shading devices (especially external shades, louvers, or overhangs) are typically mounted on the facade structure before or simultaneously with window installation to ensure proper alignment and integration.
Electrical conduits must be installed underground before outdoor lighting fixtures can be connected to the power supply.

predecessor: Foundation / Base Preparation for Light Poles
rationale: Concrete footings or base foundations for light poles must be poured and cured before mounting the lighting fixtures.
Final grading and landscaping should be completed to ensure proper positioning and elevation of outdoor lighting relative to finished grade.
While not a strict physical constraint, it is preferable to complete outdoor lighting before final commissioning and punch-list walks to verify illumination coverage and operation.
Lighting fixtures should be installed before adjacent planting and hardscape finishes to avoid damage to new plantings or paved surfaces during installation work.
The concrete slab or deck provides the structural base onto which railings and balustrades are anchored or fixed.
Railings and balustrades are often mounted against or adjacent to completed walls for support and alignment.
Railings and balustrades must be installed before the building can be handed over, as they are critical safety components providing fall protection.
It is preferable to complete painting and finishing after railing installation to avoid damaging newly painted surfaces during railing installation.
Where railings are attached to a steel structure, the steel frame must be erected first to provide the attachment points.
The rough framing (studs, support structure) must be in place before the built-in bench can be attached to the wall
A stable subfloor is needed as the base for the bench structure
The bench must be installed before surrounding trim and casing can be fitted around it
The bench needs to be in place so walls can be finished up to and behind the bench for a clean look
Soft preference for flooring after bench to avoid damaging new floors, but flooring can be cut around bench if needed
The trellis or pergola requires a stable, level foundation or concrete slab to anchor its posts and ensure structural integrity.
Proper drainage and grading must be completed before construction to prevent water accumulation around the pergola footings.
Any buried electrical, plumbing, or irrigation lines must be installed or rerouted before digging post holes to avoid damage and safety hazards.
Although often preferred after structure is up to allow for proper routing along beams, it is a soft preference as conduit could theoretically be attached afterward.
Planting around the pergola is typically done after the structure is complete to avoid damage to plants during construction, but this is a sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded before any deck construction can begin to ensure a stable base and proper drainage.
Concrete footings or foundation piers must be poured and cured to support the deck structure before deck framing can commence.
Underground gas, electric, water, and sewer lines must be located and marked before digging post holes to avoid damage and ensure safety.
The deck structure must be fully assembled before sealants, stains, or waterproofing membranes can be applied to protect the wood from moisture and UV damage.
Railings and balusters are attached to the completed deck frame, so the main deck structure must be built first to provide the attachment points and ensure proper alignment.

The fixed canopy must be mounted on or anchored to its foundation or supporting structure (e.g., columns, roof frame). Without the support structure in place, the canopy cannot be physically installed.
If the canopy is steel-framed or attached to a steel structure, the primary steel must be erected first to provide the attachment points and load-bearing framework for the canopy.
The fixed canopy frame must be in place before applying its cladding, roofing membrane, or weatherproof covering, as the cladding is installed onto the canopy structure.

Electrical, lighting, or drainage work directly attached to or located under the canopy must wait until the canopy is installed to ensure correct positioning, though this is a logical sequence rather than a strict physical impossibility if alternative access is available.

successor: Final Finishing and Waterproofing Sealant Application
rationale: All joints, edges, and penetrations of the fixed canopy must be sealed and finished after the canopy is fully installed to ensure weather-tightness and aesthetic continuity.
Underground utility conduits (including electrical conduits for outdoor lighting) must be installed before outdoor lighting can be connected to power sources.
The site must be graded and drainage systems installed to ensure that the foundation and mounting locations for light poles and fixtures are properly prepared and stable.
Concrete bases or footings for light poles and bollards must be poured and cured before the lighting fixtures can be mounted.
Outdoor lighting conduits and fixtures are typically installed before final paving and hardscape surfaces to avoid cutting and repairing finished pavement.
While lighting is often installed before final landscaping to avoid damaging plants, it is a soft preference as planting can be done around existing fixtures with care.

The ground must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded to provide a stable, well-draining base for paving materials. Paving on ungraded or unprepared ground will lead to settlement, cracking, and drainage failures.
A compacted aggregate sub-base (crushed stone, gravel) is required beneath paving to distribute loads and prevent frost heave or shifting. Paving cannot be laid directly on unprepared soil.

Any underground pipes, conduits, or drainage systems beneath the paved area must be installed and tested before paving, as tearing up finished paving to access utilities is extremely costly and destructive.

Edge restraints (concrete curbs, metal edging, or plastic borders) are typically installed after the paving is laid to lock the outer edges in place and prevent lateral movement, though in some methods they may be placed before. Sequential relationship depends on method but typically paving is placed first and edges finished after.
After paving units (e.g., pavers, slabs) are set, joints must be filled with polymeric sand or sealant and compacted to lock the surface, prevent weed growth, and stabilize the paving system.
A level and stable ground surface is physically required to support the pergola structure and ensure proper alignment of posts and beams.
Concrete footings or foundation piers must be cured and in place to anchor the pergola posts securely; without them the structure would lack stability.
Underground utilities (gas, electric, water) must be identified and marked before digging holes for posts to avoid service strikes and ensure safety.
Running wiring for integrated lights or fans is easier before the roof slats and decorative elements are fully installed, allowing access to the top beams.
The pergola structure must be fully erected and stable before any final inspections, staining, sealing, or decorative additions can be applied.
The structural wing canopy requires a stable base from foundation and slab works to support its load and ensure structural integrity.
The wing canopy typically attaches to or is supported by the main structural steel frame, which must be erected first to provide the anchoring structure.
The canopy structure must be in place before roofing and weatherproofing can be applied to ensure enclosure and protection from weather.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work in the wing area ideally follows canopy installation to avoid rework, though some preliminary work could proceed if carefully coordinated.
The canopy framework must be complete before external cladding or facade panels can be installed on the wing, as the canopy provides the structural support for these elements.
The building structural frame must be in place to provide mounting support for the integrated daylight control louver system.
Exterior walls must be built to define the openings and provide the structural substrate into which the daylight control louvers are installed.
Rough openings for windows and doors must be framed to accommodate the louver system that integrates with these openings for daylight control.
The louver framework and support system must be in place before windows or glazing are installed, as the louvers are integrated into the window assembly or positioned adjacent to glazed areas.
The louver installation must be completed and sealed before interior finishes are applied to avoid damage to finishes and to ensure proper integration with the building envelope.
The structural steel frame must be erected before light shelf assembly can begin, as light shelves are typically mounted to or supported by the building's structural framework.
The roof deck must be in place to provide overhead protection and structural support before interior light shelf assembly work can proceed.
Exterior walls must be framed to provide the vertical surfaces and support structure onto which light shelves are attached or integrated.

It is preferable to install light shelves before final interior finishing so that any gaps or junctions between the shelf and the wall finish can be properly sealed and trimmed for a clean appearance.

Light shelves are often installed adjacent to or integrated with window systems; the light shelf must be in place before the final glazing and window frames are set to ensure proper alignment and sealing.

successor: Wings of Light Steel Support Framework
rationale: The steel support framework requires a stable, level foundation to bear its load and ensure proper alignment.

successor: Wings of Light Steel Support Framework
rationale: The wings of the light steel support framework often attach to or integrate with the main structural steel frame, so the main frame must be erected first.

predecessor: Wings of Light Steel Support Framework
rationale: The cladding and building envelope (roofing, wall panels, glazing) are installed onto or supported by the steel framework, so the framework must be in place first.

predecessor: Wings of Light Steel Support Framework
rationale: While some MEP work can run in parallel, final routing and installation of services through/along the steel framework is ideally done after the framework is complete to avoid rework and ensure proper fit.

predecessor: Wings of Light Steel Support Framework
rationale: Fireproofing spray and insulation are applied to the steel members after the framework is fully erected, as the coatings must cover the completed structure.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the required profile before drainage channels can be installed, ensuring proper slope and alignment for water flow.
A stable, compacted sub-base or foundation is required to support the drainage channel structure and prevent differential settlement.
Existing underground utilities must be identified and relocated if necessary to avoid conflicts with the drainage channel excavation and installation.
Once the channel is installed, the excavated sides must be backfilled and compacted to provide lateral support and restore surface levels.

successor: Connection to Stormwater Outfall / Drainage Network
rationale: The channel must be fully installed before it can be connected to the downstream stormwater system or outfall pipes.
Grates, covers, or inlet structures are placed after the channel body is fixed in position to ensure proper fit and alignment.

successor: Surface Paving or Finishing (e.g., road pavement, landscaping)
rationale: Final paving or surface finishes should be applied after the channel is installed to achieve a flush finish and avoid damage to the channel during paving works.
The light-transmitting wing roof requires a structural steel frame as its load-bearing support system; the roof panels cannot be installed without the underlying frame being in place.
A continuous decking or substrate surface is needed to provide a stable base for installing the light-transmitting roof panels or glazing units.
The waterproofing layer must be applied to the substrate before the final light-transmitting roof covering to ensure weather-tightness of the assembly.
Flashing and edge trim components are installed after the main roof panels are in place to seal joints, edges, and penetrations against water ingress.
Water testing of the roof assembly can only be performed after all roof panels, seals, and flashings are installed to verify the integrity of the completed waterproofing system.
Structural framing provides the supporting framework onto which the daylight louvers are mounted, so it must be in place before louver installation can begin.
The building envelope must be weather-tight before installing louvers to prevent water damage and ensure proper integration with the facade.
Electrical rough-in work behind the wall surfaces must be completed before louver installation, as louvers may incorporate automated controls or motors that require concealed wiring.
Interior finishes should be installed after louver integration to avoid damaging finished surfaces during louver mounting and to ensure proper sealing around louver penetrations.
The automated daylighting control system (sensors, actuators, control logic) can only be calibrated and commissioned after the louvers are physically installed and connected.
The shading system must be physically installed before it can be commissioned, tested, and verified for proper operation.
Electrical power and control wiring must be roughed-in and connected to the shading system before it can be powered on and commissioned.
Low voltage control cables for motorized shades must be terminated and tested before the commissioning process can verify communication and control sequences.
The automated shading system must be fully commissioned before testing occupant override controls, as overrides are a subset feature of the fully commissioned system.
The shading system commissioning must be complete before it can be integrated into the Building Management System (BMS) for centralized monitoring and control.
Structural steel framing must be in place to provide the supporting structure for light shelf assemblies, which attach to the building's structural framework.
Exterior walls must be completed to provide the vertical surface onto which light shelves are mounted, typically above windows or glazing areas.
Windows or glazing must be installed before light shelves can be mounted, as light shelves are positioned above or adjacent to windows to reflect daylight deeper into the interior.
While not physically mandatory, it is preferable to complete light shelf installation before ceiling finishes to allow access for mounting hardware and adjustments without damaging finished ceilings.

Light shelf assemblies must be installed before daylight harvesting controls and sensors can be calibrated and commissioned, as the shelves affect light distribution patterns that the control system must accommodate.
The surface must be clean, dry, and free of debris or contaminants for the weatherproof sealant to properly adhere.
Flashing provides the primary water barrier at edges; weatherproof edge sealing is applied over or in conjunction with flashing to ensure continuous waterproofing.
Any cracks, gaps, or damage must be repaired before sealing to ensure the edge sealing can form a continuous weatherproof barrier.
Weatherproof edge sealing must be completed before final cladding or finish materials are installed, as the seal is often behind or beneath the finish layer.
A water test after edge sealing validates the weatherproof integrity before enclosing the area, though some projects test earlier stages as well.
The skybridge requires stable support from the building structures it connects; foundations and substructures must be complete to provide the necessary load-bearing capacity.

predecessor: Main Building Structural Framing (both connected towers)
rationale: The skybridge is typically installed between two completed building towers; the structural steel or concrete frames of both connected buildings must be erected to provide connection points and support.
Structural installation of the skybridge must be complete before applying finishes, cladding, flooring, or glazing to ensure a stable working platform.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the skybridge can only begin after the primary structure is in place to route services safely.
All finishing work must be completed before final inspection and load testing to ensure the skybridge meets safety and quality standards.
Expansion joints are typically placed where slabs meet walls, columns, or other slabs, so the supporting concrete structure must exist first.
The expansion joint material (backer rod, filler board) must be in place before applying sealant or joint filler on top.
Expansion joints accommodate movement in the substrate; finishes like tiles or toppings are placed after the joint system is installed to allow proper movement gaps.
Expansion joints in walls and frames require the structural elements to be erected first so the joint can be placed at the intended separation point.
It is preferable to inspect expansion joints after all surrounding work is complete to verify proper alignment, coverage, and performance, though inspection can sometimes occur earlier.
Structural tie beams connect columns and require columns to be in place to provide support and connection points.
Tie beams provide lateral support and a base for slab construction; slabs are typically cast after tie beams are in place.
Tie beams serve as horizontal bracing elements and a level base for subsequent wall construction above them.

predecessor: Formwork and Reinforcement for Tie Beam
rationale: Formwork and rebar placement must be completed prior to concrete pouring/curing of the tie beam.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded to provide a stable and uniform surface for pouring the foundation mat slab.
The subgrade soil must be compacted to the required density and tested to ensure it can support the load of the mat slab without excessive settlement.
Soil bearing capacity and subsurface conditions must be assessed to design the mat slab thickness and reinforcement appropriately.

predecessor: Placement of Vapor Barrier / Moisture Barrier
rationale: A vapor barrier must be laid over the prepared subgrade to prevent moisture migration from the soil into the concrete slab.
After pouring the mat slab, the concrete must be cured properly to achieve design strength and prevent cracking.
Waterproofing membrane or coating is applied to the cured mat slab to protect the foundation from groundwater intrusion.
Foundation walls are built atop the completed mat slab, which serves as the base structural element for the walls.

Underslab plumbing and drainage pipes must be embedded in or laid before the mat slab is poured, but if the slab is already in place, plumbing rough-in must occur by core-drilling or sleeving through the completed slab.
Expansion joints must be installed into freshly poured concrete before it sets, or cut into cured concrete; in either case, the concrete slab must exist first.
The subgrade and base layers must be compacted and leveled before concrete is placed and expansion joints are installed, as the joints serve the slab which rests on the base.

Expansion joint material is placed while concrete is still plastic, and surface finishing operations (troweling, edging) must be completed after joint installation to achieve proper surface texture and joint detailing.
Curing cannot begin until the concrete slab is placed and finished, including the installation of expansion joints, as curing follows final finishing.
Concrete forms must be set up to define the slab perimeter and joint locations before concrete is poured and expansion joints are installed within the pour.
Must understand ground conditions, soil/rock types, groundwater levels, and identify potential hazards before tunnel design and construction can proceed.
Detailed tunnel alignment, cross-section, support systems, and construction methodology must be finalized before physical construction begins.
Legal and regulatory approvals including environmental impact assessments, land access rights, and construction permits are required before any tunneling work can commence.
Existing underground utilities (cables, pipes, sewers) must be identified and relocated, and the surface site must be prepared (access roads, laydown areas) before tunneling starts.

After excavation of the tunnel bore, the permanent lining (concrete segments or cast-in-place lining) and waterproofing system must be installed to ensure structural integrity and prevent water ingress.
Systems such as ventilation, lighting, drainage, fire safety, and communication networks are installed after the tunnel structure is completed.
For tunnels constructed by cut-and-cover method, the excavated trench must be backfilled and the surface restored only after tunnel construction and waterproofing are complete.
Functional testing, safety inspections, and commissioning of all tunnel systems occur after construction and fit-out are finished before the tunnel can be opened for use.
The skybridge structure requires stable foundation support to bear its load; foundations must be fully cured and load-tested before erection can begin.
Skybridge spans are supported by columns or piers at each end (and possibly intermediate points); these vertical supports must be in place before the bridge deck or truss can be erected.
The primary structural frame (steel or concrete) of the skybridge must be erected to provide the framework onto which floor decking is placed.
The load-bearing structure must be fully erected before any roofing or weatherproof membranes can be applied to enclose the bridge.
Exterior cladding and glazing panels are attached to the erected structural frame; the frame must be in its final position for accurate fitment.
The shared MEP riser must be physically installed before connections to it can be made, as it provides the vertical distribution path for mechanical, electrical, and plumbing services.
The structural frame must be complete to provide support for MEP risers and to define the building geometry within which shared services will be routed.
Commissioning involves testing and verifying proper operation of MEP systems, which can only occur after all connections have been physically made.
Tenant branch connections take off from the shared MEP services, so the main shared services must be connected and operational first before branch connections can be made.

successor: Install Fire Stopping at MEP Penetrations
rationale: Fire stopping must be applied around MEP penetrations after the services are installed and connected, to properly seal gaps and maintain fire compartmentation.
The structural steel frame must be erected to provide the supporting framework onto which the end wall glazing panels are installed.
The roof structure must be in place to provide overhead protection and to ensure the building envelope is watertight before installing end wall glazing.
The end wall framing (girts, jambs, headers) must be installed to provide the structural support and attachment points for the glazing system.
Interior finishes such as drywall, insulation, and trim cannot be completed until the glazing is installed and the end wall is fully enclosed and weathertight.

successor: End Wall Flashing and Trim Installation
rationale: Perimeter flashing, capping, and trim details around the glazing must be installed after the glazing panels are in place to seal and finish the edges of the glazing system.
The continuous ridge beam sits atop and connects the roof trusses, providing longitudinal stability. Trusses must be in place first to support the ridge beam.
Wall framing and top plates must be completed to provide bearing support for the trusses and ridge beam system.
Roof sheathing panels are fastened to the ridge beam and trusses; the ridge beam must be in place to provide nailing surface and structural continuity at the roof ridge.
Ridge vents are typically installed after the ridge beam is in place and roofing is underway, but this is a sequencing preference to ensure proper alignment and sealing.
Ceiling drywall or finishes at the ridge cannot be completed until the ridge beam and roof structure are fully installed and stable.
The linear roof form requires a completed structural frame to provide support and attachment points before it can be installed.
The roof covering (such as panels, membranes, or shingles) must be installed after the linear roof form is in place, as the roof form provides the underlying structure and shape for the covering.
Gutters, downspouts, and other drainage components are typically installed after the roof form is in place to ensure proper alignment and attachment.
The foundation must be prepared and cured before any wall construction can begin to provide a stable base and prevent structural settlement or cracking.
The main structural frame (columns, beams, and load-bearing elements) must be in place to support the long window wall and provide attachment points.

Rough-in work for electrical conduits and plumbing lines that run through or adjacent to the wall area must be completed before the wall is installed to avoid rework and wall penetrations after installation.
Interior wall finishes, drywall, and painting should follow the window wall installation to ensure seamless integration and avoid damage to finished surfaces during window placement.
The window wall must be installed first so that exterior cladding, flashing, and weather seals can be properly integrated around the window wall assembly to ensure watertightness.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded to provide a stable and uniform subgrade before pouring any slab-on-grade.
The subgrade soil must be compacted to the required density to prevent differential settlement and ensure structural support for the thermally massive slab.

A vapor barrier (e.g., polyethylene sheeting) must be placed over the prepared subgrade to prevent moisture migration from the ground into the thermally massive slab, which could cause degradation or thermal performance issues.

Rigid insulation (e.g., extruded polystyrene) must be installed beneath and/or along the perimeter of the slab to reduce thermal bridging and heat loss to the ground, which is critical for the thermal mass performance.

Steel reinforcement (rebar or welded wire mesh) and any embedded utilities (conduits, piping for radiant heating) must be placed and tied in position before the concrete pour, as they cannot be added after the slab is cast.

After pouring and finishing the slab, a controlled curing period is required to allow the concrete to gain sufficient strength and to minimize cracking before any subsequent loads or finishes are applied.
Vertical structural elements such as walls must be built on top of the completed and cured slab, as the slab serves as the foundation bearing surface and working platform for framing.

Floor finishes (e.g., tile, polished concrete, or flooring underlayment) are typically applied after the slab has fully cured and dried to ensure proper adhesion and prevent moisture trapping, though some finishes can be applied earlier with special treatments.
The sliding partition wall requires a level and finished floor surface to slide smoothly along its bottom track. Any unevenness would prevent proper operation.

The top track or rail for the sliding partition wall must be securely anchored to the overhead structural slab or ceiling framework. The ceiling or overhead structure must be in place to support the top guide rail.
The surrounding wall framing defines the pocket or opening into which the sliding partition slides. The rough opening must be framed before the partition can be installed.

successor: Floor Covering Installation (e.g., tiles, wood, vinyl)
rationale: The sliding partition's bottom track must be installed directly on the structural floor, and finish flooring is typically laid up to or around the track. Installing floor covering first would block or interfere with the track placement.

While painting can be done after installation, it is often easier to paint the surrounding walls before installing the partition to avoid masking and overspray. However, this is a preference, not a physical necessity.
The main roof structure must be framed and sheathed to provide a substrate and support for the continuous soffit and canopy framing.
Exterior wall sheathing and air barrier must be installed so that the soffit/canopy interface with the wall is properly sealed and supported.
While not a strict physical dependency, coordinating fascia/gutter placement before soffit can simplify flashing integration and improve continuity.
The continuous soffit/canopy provides the overhang substrate; roofing material at the eave edge is applied over or integrated with the soffit assembly.
Soffit/canopy installation defines the transition line for exterior cladding; siding is typically installed up to the underside of the soffit or over a ledger.
The ground must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil, and graded to the proper elevation before excavation can begin for the foundation trench.
The exact alignment, width, and depth of the trench must be marked on the ground (staking/layout) before excavation equipment can cut the trench.
Soil bearing capacity, groundwater conditions, and soil type must be assessed before trench excavation to determine required depth and shoring needs.

successor: Placement of Foundation Drainage / Gravel Base
rationale: After the trench is excavated to the correct depth and width, a gravel or crushed stone base must be placed and compacted to provide a stable bearing surface and drainage layer before any reinforcing steel or concrete is placed.

successor: Installation of Reinforcement Steel (Rebar) for Strip Footing
rationale: The excavated trench must be completed before reinforcing steel can be placed within it to the correct cover and positioning for the strip footing or foundation wall.

successor: Pouring Concrete for Strip Footing / Foundation
rationale: Concrete placement for the foundation can only occur after the trench has been excavated, inspected, and any required reinforcement placed.
Long span joists require steel columns or supporting beams to be in place to bear the load and provide structural support.
Foundations must be cured and ready to support the columns that will hold the long span joists.
Temporary supports may be needed to stabilize joists during installation before permanent connections are made.
Metal decking is placed on top of and supported by the long span joists, so joists must be installed first.
Insulation is typically applied after the structural framing (including joists) is in place, though some sequences might allow partial parallel work.
Formwork provides the mold and structural support for the concrete slab; pouring cannot commence without the formwork in place.
Steel reinforcement must be positioned and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity.
Any electrical conduits, plumbing pipes, or sleeves embedded in the slab must be laid out and secured before concrete is poured, as they cannot be placed afterwards.
Concrete must be poured before the curing process (moisture retention, temperature control) can begin to achieve design strength.
Formwork cannot be removed until the concrete has been poured and has gained sufficient strength to be self-supporting.
Bearing walls require a solid foundation to transfer vertical loads to the ground; the foundation concrete must be cured and sufficiently strong before wall construction can begin.
Foundation rebar must be in place and tied before concrete is poured; the foundation itself must be complete before bearing walls can be erected on it.
Floor slabs typically bear on or are supported by the bearing walls; the walls must be in place to provide vertical support for the floor structure.
The roof structure rests on top of the bearing walls; walls must be erected to the full height to support roof beams, trusses, or decking.
Temporary bracing is often required immediately after wall erection to ensure stability before permanent lateral support systems (floors, diaphragms) are installed.

predecessor: Install Window Frame or Rough Opening
rationale: The continuous glazing track must be installed after the window frame or rough opening is in place, as the track is typically fastened to the frame or supporting structure to receive the glazing panels.

predecessor: Apply Sealant or Gaskets to Track
rationale: Sealants or gaskets are often applied to the track before glazing installation, but if the track itself is being installed, this may be a step within the glazing process rather than a separate predecessor.

successor: Place Glass or Glazing Panels into Track
rationale: The glazing panels must be inserted into the track after the track is securely installed, as the track serves as the channel or support for the panels.

successor: Secure Glazing with Retaining Clips or Beads
rationale: Retaining clips or beads are installed after the glazing panels are placed in the track, but they logically follow the track installation since the panels cannot be secured without the track being in place.
Final weatherproofing is typically applied after glazing panels are installed and secured, which depends on the track being in place first.
The linear HVAC run must be fully installed and physically in place before it can be commissioned, as commissioning involves testing and verifying the installed system.
Electrical power supply must be connected to the linear HVAC unit before it can be energized and tested during commissioning.
All control sensors, actuators, and BMS connections must be wired and terminated before the control system can be tested and commissioned.
Commissioning validates that the linear HVAC system operates correctly and safely, which is a prerequisite for building occupancy and handover to the owner.
After commissioning verifies individual component function, air balancing adjusts airflow to design specifications and logically follows commissioning.
The entrance frame requires a stable base to bear on; the foundation provides the structural support needed for the frame.
The entrance frame is typically installed within the main structural opening; the surrounding structural frame must be in place to define the rough opening and provide lateral support.
The entrance frame forms the structural surround into which doors or gates are hung; the frame must be fixed and aligned before doors can be installed.
Weather seals, gaskets, and flashings around the entrance opening can only be properly applied once the frame is in position.
While finishing can follow the frame installation for a clean aesthetic, it is a soft preference because the frame can be installed after finishes if necessary (though it may cause damage).
The rough opening for the entrance must be prepared, framed, and measured before the glazing unit can be installed.
The building's structural frame must be complete to provide the supporting structure for the entrance glazing system.
Weather barriers and flashing around the entrance opening must be in place before installing glazing to prevent moisture intrusion behind the frame.
Interior wall finishes, trim, and sealants around the entrance can only be completed after the glazing unit is installed and sealed.
Door handles, locks, closers, and other entrance hardware must be installed after the glazed door and frame are in place to ensure proper fit and alignment.
The door frame must be installed first to provide the structure and mounting surface for the locking hardware.
The door leaf must be hung in the frame before the locking hardware can be installed on it, as the hardware is mounted to the door slab.
Electrical wiring for powered locks (e.g., maglocks, electric strikes) must be roughed in before the hardware is installed, as wiring needs to be run through frame/door.
The locking hardware must be physically installed before it can be tested for proper operation, alignment, and security function.
It is preferable to install and adjust the locking hardware before final door trim and finishing work to avoid damage to finished surfaces during hardware installation and adjustment.
The entrance matting system requires a stable, cured concrete slab or subfloor as its base. The slab must be poured, cured, and finished to the correct level before matting can be installed.
If the entrance matting system includes integrated lighting or heating elements, any subsurface electrical conduit must be roughed-in and inspected before the matting is placed over it.

successor: Final Floor Finishing/Sealing Adjacent to Matting
rationale: The entrance matting system defines the threshold area; adjacent finished flooring (tile, vinyl, etc.) should be installed up to the matting edge after the matting is in place to ensure a clean transition.

successor: Interior Fit-Out and Wall Finishing (adjacent walls)
rationale: It is preferable to install entrance matting after adjacent wall finishes are complete to avoid damaging freshly painted or finished walls during matting installation, but this is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.

The door frame and door must be installed first to establish the exact threshold height and reveal, ensuring the entrance matting fits correctly within the door swing zone and provides proper clearance.
The building foundation must be in place before any above-ground structures and their electrical components, including entrance lighting, can be installed.
Electrical conduit and rough-in wiring to the entrance area must be completed before the entrance lighting fixtures can be connected and installed.
The entrance door and frame structure must be built to provide a mounting surface and proper positioning for the entrance lighting fixture.
After the entrance lighting fixture is physically installed, the final electrical connections must be made and the system tested to ensure proper operation.
While not physically required, it is preferred to install entrance lighting before interior finishing so that workers have adequate illumination during final trim and paint work.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared before constructing the entrance ramp to ensure proper drainage and stable foundation.
A compacted base layer or subbase is required to support the ramp structure and prevent settling or cracking.
The ramp structure must be in place before applying the final wearing surface (asphalt or concrete) to achieve proper bonding and thickness.
Guardrails and safety barriers must be installed after the ramp is constructed to ensure proper alignment and anchoring to the ramp structure.
Entrance steps require a stable, level foundation or slab to rest upon and tie into; the steps cannot be installed on unprepared ground.
The ground around the entrance must be rough-graded to the proper elevation before steps are built so that the steps align with the finished floor level and site drainage.
The entrance steps typically abut the exterior wall or stoop; the wall framing and sheathing must be in place to establish the interface point and support any landing or threshold connections.
Final grading and landscaping around the entrance should follow step installation to ensure proper drainage away from the steps and to blend the finished landscape with the step structure.
Handrails are anchored into or adjacent to the finished steps; the steps must be complete to provide the correct mounting surface and alignment for railings.
The entrance handrail requires a stable base or foundation to be anchored to; without a completed base slab or foundation, the handrail cannot be securely mounted.
Handrails are installed alongside or on top of stairs, ramps, or entrance platforms; those structures must exist before the handrail can be attached.
It is preferable but not physically required that the entrance handrail is complete before the final building inspection, since the handrail is a safety feature that inspectors typically check.
Finishing trades such as floor polishing near the entrance are easier without the handrail obstructing access, but the handrail can be installed after floors are finished as well.
If the handrail is wall-mounted, the supporting wall must be fully constructed and cured to provide a solid substrate for the handrail brackets.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before bollard bases can be poured or set.
Any underground pipes, cables, or conduits in the bollard area must be laid before bollard footings are installed to avoid digging around finished bollards.
Bollards require concrete footings or foundations to be cured and ready before the bollard posts can be anchored or set in place.
Bollards must be installed before the final paving or surface finish is applied so that the paving can be worked neatly around the bollard bases.
Landscaping and curbing around the entrance is typically completed after bollards are in place to ensure proper alignment and avoid damage to new plantings.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared (with proper dimensions, headers, and cripple studs) before the door frame can be installed.
Exterior wall sheathing must be in place to provide structural support and proper depth for the door frame installation.
The weather-resistant barrier (e.g., house wrap) should be installed and properly flashed around the rough opening before the door frame is set to ensure water tightness.

successor: Exterior Trim and Siding Completion Around Door
rationale: Exterior siding and trim around the entrance door cannot be finished until the door and frame are permanently installed and secured.
Interior drywall around the door opening must be installed after the door frame is in place to ensure proper alignment and gap management.
Hardware such as hinges, lockset, and handle can only be installed after the door is hung in the frame.
Weatherstripping and final adjustments to door fit and operation must occur after the door frame is fully installed and secured.
The automatic door operator requires electrical power to function; rough-in electrical wiring must be completed before installation to provide the necessary power connection.
The door operator must be installed before it can be tested for proper functionality, including opening, closing, and safety sensor operation.
The automatic door operator is mounted onto the door frame or header; the door frame and door leaf must be in place to provide the structural support for the operator.
While it is generally preferred to complete door operator installation before final trim and finishes to avoid damage, trim work can sometimes be done around the operator if carefully coordinated.

Any overhead work such as ceiling grids, ductwork, or conduit above the door area should be completed before installing the operator to avoid interference and to ensure safe access for mounting the operator.
The structural frame must be fully erected and stable before any canopy installation can begin, as the canopy attaches to the main structure.
Overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be completed before canopy installation, as the canopy will obstruct access to these systems.
Canopy-mounted lighting and fixtures can only be installed after the canopy structure is in place.
While not physically mandatory, it is preferable to complete exterior cladding work below the canopy after the canopy is installed to ensure proper weatherproofing and alignment at the interface.
The ground surface must be properly prepared, graded, and compacted before matting can be installed to ensure a stable and level base.
A proper subgrade or base course (e.g., aggregate or sand layer) must be placed and compacted to provide a uniform support layer for the matting system.
Subsurface drainage (e.g., underdrains or French drains) must be installed before matting to prevent water accumulation beneath the mats, which could cause instability or heaving.

successor: Surface Paving or Final Wearing Surface
rationale: If the matting serves as a base or reinforcement layer, it must be placed before the final paving or wearing surface is applied over it.

Once matting is fully installed and secured, surface markings, sealants, or decorative finishes can be applied; this is a soft preference as markings could theoretically be placed afterward with adjustments.
Entrance security equipment (e.g., card readers, biometric scanners, turnstiles, CCTV cameras) must be physically installed before they can be commissioned and tested for proper functionality.

predecessor: Complete Electrical Rough-In for Security Systems
rationale: Power and low-voltage wiring for security devices must be run and rough-in completed before commissioning can verify power connectivity and system operation.
The entrance security commissioning must verify that all hardware and software are functioning correctly before the overall access control system can be activated for operational use.
Entrance security commissioning is a prerequisite for life-safety and security compliance checks required before the building can receive its occupancy permit.
Commissioning of entrance security systems must be completed and signed off before the building can be formally handed over to the client/owner for operational use.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to proper depth before any wall foundation can be laid.
Concrete footings or strip foundations must be poured and cured to provide a stable load-bearing base for the wall.
Any underground electrical, irrigation, or drainage lines that will pass under or through the wall footprint must be laid before the wall is built to avoid later excavation damage.
After the wall is constructed (mortar/ concrete placed), it must be allowed to cure and then be waterproofed/ sealed before backfilling or finishing.
Earth must be backfilled against the wall only after the wall structure is fully built and cured to prevent shifting or collapse.

A stable and level foundation (e.g., concrete slab, paved area, or compacted ground) must be prepared before the garden canopy can be erected, as the canopy structure requires a solid base for anchoring and load distribution.

The main support posts, beams, and rafters of the canopy must be assembled and erected before any roofing or cladding can be installed, as the canopy's roof and side panels rely on the frame for support.
The canopy frame must be fully erected and secured before the roof covering (e.g., polycarbonate sheets, fabric, shingles) can be installed, as the covering attaches directly to the frame.
Side panels, screens, or lattice work are attached to the completed canopy frame and thus can only be installed after the main canopy structure is in place.

While gutters and downpipes are typically installed after the canopy roof is complete to manage rainwater, this ordering is a practical preference rather than a hard physical requirement, as drainage components could theoretically be retrofitted.
A stable, compacted sub-base is required to support the garden floor pavement and prevent uneven settling or cracking.
Proper drainage must be in place beneath the pavement to prevent water accumulation that could damage the pavement structure.
Any underground pipes, cables, or conduits must be laid before the pavement is poured or laid to avoid digging up the completed pavement.
After the pavement is installed, surface sealing or curing must be applied to protect it from weather and wear.
Adjacent landscaping, edging, and planting can only be completed after the pavement is in place to ensure proper alignment and finish against the pavement edge.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded before a planting bed can be established to ensure proper drainage and a stable soil base.

Any underground utilities (e.g., irrigation lines, drainage pipes, electrical conduits) must be installed before the planting bed is created to avoid disturbing the soil and root zone after the bed is finished.
The planting bed must be fully prepared (soil amended, edges defined) before any plants, shrubs, or trees can be placed into the bed.
Mulch is applied after the bed is shaped and plants are installed; the bed itself must exist as the receiving surface for mulch application.

While hardscape elements like paths or patios can technically be built before or after planting beds, it is often preferred to complete hardscape first to avoid soil compaction and damage to new plants from construction traffic.
The integrated seat wall requires a stable and level concrete foundation or slab to be in place before installation, as it bears directly on the concrete.
Surface finishing and waterproofing must be applied after the seat wall is installed to protect the material and achieve the final appearance.
Landscaping around the seat wall is typically done after installation to avoid damaging plants or disturbing the wall's position, though some planting can be done concurrently.
The top cap or seat surface must be installed after the main wall structure is in place to ensure proper alignment and support.
The site must be excavated and graded to the proper elevation before the seat wall foundation can be formed and poured.
A stable foundation or base must be in place before garden lighting fixtures can be fixed and secured.
Electrical conduit and wiring must be laid underground before lighting fixtures are installed to provide power to the lights.
After garden lights are fixed in position, final landscaping, soil backfill, and grading can be completed without disturbing the lighting installation.
The lighting fixtures must be installed and fixed before the full system can be tested for functionality and proper illumination.
While decorative elements can be placed before or after lighting, it is generally preferred to install lighting first to avoid damaging decorations during electrical work.
The exterior wall framing must be complete to provide the structural opening and support for the garden window assembly.
The rough opening must be framed, sized, and prepared to accommodate the garden window unit before installation can begin.
Exterior sheathing and weather-resistant barrier must be installed around the rough opening to protect against moisture intrusion before the window is set.
Interior wall finishes around the window area cannot be completed until the garden window wall assembly is fully installed to allow for proper integration and sealing.
While trim is typically installed after the window unit is in place, it is a soft preference as trim could theoretically be installed later during finish work.
The rough opening for the garden entry door must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the door assembly can be installed.
The door frame (jambs, head, and sill) must be installed and properly aligned before the door slab or assembly can be mounted.
Flashing, weather-resistant barrier, and sill pan must be installed around the rough opening to prevent water intrusion before the door assembly is placed.
Locks, handles, hinges, and other hardware can only be installed after the door assembly is in place and properly aligned.
Exterior trim, brickmold, or casing around the garden door must be installed after the door assembly is positioned to cover the gap between the door frame and the wall.
Interior finishing around the door opening is typically completed after door installation to ensure clean edges, though some prefer finishing before to avoid damaging the door.
A stable foundation and level site are physically required to support the structural loads of the trellis system.

Utilities such as drainage, electrical, or irrigation conduits must be laid beneath the trellis footprint before the structure is erected, as it would be impractical or impossible to excavate afterwards.
The structural trellis framework provides the supporting frame for any cladding, shading, or panel elements; they cannot be attached without the primary structure in place.
While soft preference may allow sequential finishing, completing hardscape/landscape after the trellis avoids damage to finished surfaces during installation.
Any integrated lighting, cabling, or electrical fixtures mounted on or within the trellis structure require the structure to be fully installed as a mounting surface.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before earthwork can begin to allow for unobstructed grading, excavation, and soil manipulation.
Proper survey and staking of the garden layout is required to mark boundaries, grades, and elevations so that earthwork operations follow the designed contours and levels.
All underground utilities must be located and marked prior to earthwork to avoid damage to existing services and ensure worker safety during excavation and grading.
Earthwork must be completed to establish the final grades and contours before drainage systems (French drains, catch basins, drain pipes) can be installed at the correct elevations and slopes.
Compacted earth and finished subgrade from earthwork are necessary before laying aggregate base layers for pathways, patios, or other hardscape elements.
The site must be properly graded, cleared of debris, and leveled before planting can begin to ensure proper drainage, soil stability, and a suitable growing environment for plants.

Hardscape elements such as walkways, patios, retaining walls, and other structural features must be completed before planting to avoid damage to new plantings from construction equipment, foot traffic, and material deliveries, and to ensure proper alignment and access.

predecessor: Underground Utility Installation (Irrigation, Drainage, Lighting Conduits)
rationale: Underground utilities like irrigation pipes, drainage systems, and electrical conduits for landscape lighting must be installed and tested before planting to avoid digging up or damaging newly installed plants and root systems.
Soil must be tested, amended with organic matter, fertilizer, and pH adjustments as needed before planting to provide optimal growing conditions for the selected plants.

After planting is complete, mulch must be applied around the new plantings to retain moisture, suppress weeds, and regulate soil temperature, followed by final fine grading to achieve a clean, finished appearance.
Newly installed plants require immediate watering and ongoing establishment care (deep watering, staking if needed, fertilization) to ensure successful root development and survival.

Earthworks and grading must be completed first to establish the proper ground levels, slopes, and drainage before any hardscape elements like paving, walls, or steps are installed. Hardscape requires a stable, leveled base.

Underground utilities such as drainage pipes, irrigation lines, and electrical conduits must be installed before hardscape is finished, as these are laid beneath paved surfaces and would be inaccessible or require destructive removal of hardscape afterward.

The sub-base (compacted aggregate, gravel base, or concrete foundation) must be prepared and compacted prior to laying the finished hardscape surface such as pavers, stone, or concrete topping, ensuring structural stability and proper load-bearing capacity.

Hardscape finishing such as paving, walls, and steps must be completed before planting and softscape installation to avoid damage to plants from construction traffic, material spills, and heavy equipment, and to ensure proper alignment of planting beds relative to finished hardscape edges.

successor: Garden Construction - Final Cleanup & Finishing Touches
rationale: Final cleanup and finishing touches such as sealing, sweeping, and detailing are typically performed after hardscape finishing to protect the completed surfaces and present a clean final product, though this is more of a logical sequence preference than a physical constraint.
Weather stripping must be applied to fully installed and framed door and window openings. The frames provide the surface onto which the seals are attached.
The wall assembly must be enclosed and the cladding installed before weather stripping can be fitted around the perimeter openings to create a continuous air/weather seal.
While not physically required, it is standard practice to complete sealing before interior finishing to avoid damaging finished surfaces during the installation of seals.

successor: Final commissioning and air leakage testing
rationale: Weather stripping must be in place to effectively test the building envelope for air tightness and to commission the HVAC system.
The entry canopy/porte-cochère requires a stable structural base; foundations and slab must be completed to support the canopy columns and structure.
The porte-cochère often connects to or is supported by the main building's structural steel frame; the main frame must be erected first to provide anchorage and lateral support.
The canopy structure must be in place before its roofing and waterproofing membrane can be installed.

successor: Exterior Finishing & Cladding Adjacent to Canopy
rationale: The structural frame of the canopy must be complete before applying exterior cladding, soffits, and decorative finishes.

successor: Electrical and Lighting Installation on Canopy
rationale: Electrical rough-in and lighting fixtures can only be installed after the canopy structure is erected and secured.

predecessor: Entry Floor Framing and Subfloor Preparation
rationale: The floor grille/mat must be installed onto a prepared subfloor or framed opening. Without the structural floor framing and subfloor in place, there is no substrate to attach or set the grille/mat onto.

successor: Finishing and Trim Installation at Entry
rationale: Finish trim, thresholds, and edge treatments around the entry floor grille/mat must be installed after the grille/mat is in place to achieve a clean, flush transition and properly cover the edges.

Any final sealing, coating, or waterproofing of the surrounding floor area must be done after the grille/mat is installed to ensure continuity of the finish and to avoid contaminating or damaging the grille/mat surface.

predecessor: Underfloor Drainage or Utility Rough-In (if applicable)
rationale: If the grille/mat is over a drainage point or utility access, those underground or underfloor systems must be roughed in before installing the grille/mat, as the grille/mat would block access afterward.

The entry area can only be opened to regular foot traffic or commissioned for use after the grille/mat is securely installed to prevent tripping hazards and ensure proper function of the mat/grille system.
The ramp must be built on a stable, compacted foundation to ensure structural integrity and prevent settling or cracking.
The ground at the entry point must be graded to the correct slope and elevation before the ramp can be constructed to ensure proper alignment and drainage.
The ramp provides the access platform and base level required for installing the entry door, ensuring the door threshold aligns with the ramp surface.
Handrails must be installed on the completed ramp structure to provide safety compliance and accessibility requirements.
The ramp structure must be fully constructed before applying non-slip surface treatments, coatings, or finishes to the ramp surface.
Entry stairs require a stable, level base; the foundation slab or footings must be poured and cured before any structural components like stairs are installed.
The building's structural frame and walls adjacent to the entry must be in place so that the stairs can be properly anchored and aligned to the structure.
Handrails and guardrails are safety features that attach to the stairs; stairs must be structurally complete before railings can be installed on them.
Final surface finishes such as treads, risers, tiles, or non-slip coatings are applied after the stair structure is fully built and stable.

While often the door frame is installed earlier, final door fit and weatherproofing is easier once the stair landing height is confirmed; however, this is a soft preference rather than a strict physical necessity.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical wiring for automatic door opener
rationale: Power supply wiring and low-voltage control cabling must be installed before the door operator unit can be connected and mounted.

predecessor: Install door frame and hang door slab
rationale: The door assembly (frame and door slab) must be in place to provide the structural support and mounting surface for the automatic door operator hardware.

successor: Connect and test automatic door controls
rationale: Final wiring, sensor adjustments, and functional testing of the operator electronics can only proceed after the operator unit is physically installed.

successor: Install push plates, signage, and activation devices
rationale: Wall-mounted push plates, touchless sensors, and accessibility signage must align precisely with the operator's activation system, which requires the operator to already be in place.
Final calibration of opening speed, closing force, and safety sensors is physically dependent on the operator being fully installed and connected.
Power and signal wiring must be run to the doorbell/intercom/keypad location before the device can be installed and connected.

predecessor: Wall Framing and Rough Opening Preparation
rationale: Walls must be framed to provide a mounting surface for the doorbell/intercom/keypad, and any required rough openings must be prepared.
After the device is physically mounted, final electrical connections and trim plates can be installed.
The device must be installed before it can be programmed, configured, and tested for proper operation.
While the doorbell can be installed before the door, final positioning relative to the door is best done after the door is hung to ensure proper alignment and aesthetics.
Handrails and guardrails are anchored into or mounted onto the concrete stair structure. The concrete must be poured, cured, and provide a stable substrate for railing installation.
The floor slab at the entry provides the base support for the guardrail posts at grade level; the slab must be in place and cured before post anchors can be embedded or bolted.
Where handrails attach to wall structures (e.g., entry walls adjacent to stairs), the wall framing must be complete to provide a secure mounting surface for railing brackets.
Handrails must be installed before final finishes so that finishing trades can work around the railings, and to avoid damaging finished surfaces during railing installation.

Though often installed concurrently, installing the handrail first allows easier access and alignment verification; it is a soft preference because doors can also be hung before railings without structural conflict.
The foundation or substrate must be prepared and leveled before a threshold plate can be installed, as the plate rests on the finished floor or foundation surface.
The door opening must be framed and roughed in so that the threshold plate has a defined opening and supporting structure to be placed within.
The subfloor or underlayment must be in place to provide a stable, level surface for the threshold plate to sit upon and be fastened to.
The threshold plate is typically installed first as the base component; the door frame (jambs and head) then sits on or attaches to the installed threshold plate.
The door leaf can only be hung after the threshold plate and door frame are in place, as the door swings over the threshold and its bottom edge seals against it.
The door frame or rough opening must be prepared and structurally complete before the entrance door assembly can be installed, as the door assembly is mounted into the prepared opening.
The entrance door assembly must be hung and in place before door hardware such as locks, handles, and hinges can be installed onto the door.
Weatherstripping and sealing around the door perimeter must be applied after the door assembly is installed to ensure a proper seal between the door and frame.
Rough electrical work and framing must be completed prior to door installation to ensure the opening is properly sized, framed, and free of obstructions.

Interior trim, casing, and finish work around the door typically follows door installation, though in some cases it can be considered a soft preference for sequencing efficiency rather than a strict physical necessity.
Weather seals and thresholds are installed onto prepared door and window openings; rough openings must be framed and ready before seal installation can begin.
Weather seals are typically mounted directly onto or within door and window frames; frames must be in place before seals can be attached.
Thresholds require a stable subfloor surface for proper anchoring and sealing at the bottom of door openings.
Thresholds are typically installed before finished flooring so that flooring materials (tile, hardwood, etc.) can be cut to fit snugly against the threshold.
Interior trim around doors is installed after weather seals and thresholds are in place to cover the gap between the frame and the seal, ensuring a finished appearance.
Electrical and data cabling must be roughed-in beneath the floor before grilles are installed, as the grilles cover and restrict access to underfloor systems.
The subfloor must be clean, level, and finished to receive entry floor grilles; installing on an unprepared surface would cause misalignment or damage.
Entry floor grilles are set into the finished floor and should be installed before the surrounding floor finish is applied to achieve a flush, seamless integration.
While not physically mandatory, it is preferable to install grilles before entry doors to avoid damaging door leafs and to coordinate floor-to-door clearances.
Painting overhead and walls should be completed before grille installation to prevent dust and paint drips from contaminating the grille finish.
The rough opening and structural frame must be in place to support and attach the entry canopy.

successor: Install Final Roofing / Flashing at Canopy
rationale: The canopy must be installed before roof flashing and final roofing materials can be integrated and sealed around it.

successor: Exterior Cladding / Siding at Canopy Area
rationale: The canopy attachment points and perimeter may need to be covered or flashed by exterior cladding/siding for a finished, weather-tight appearance.
Electrical wiring must be installed in the walls, ceiling, and junction boxes before light fixtures can be mounted and connected to the power supply.
Ceiling drywall must be in place so that the lighting fixture box is properly finished and supported, and so the fixture mounting surface is complete.

It is a soft preference to finish wall painting before installing lighting fixtures to avoid dust and debris from drywall sanding and painting settling on the new fixtures, and to achieve a cleaner finished look.

successor: Install Light Bulbs and Test Fixtures
rationale: The fixture housing must be physically mounted and wired before bulbs can be inserted and the circuit can be energized for testing.
It is a soft preference to install entry lighting first so that the work area is well lit for flooring installation, though flooring could technically be installed before or after lighting.

Access control devices (card readers, keypads, electric strikes, magnetic locks) require electrical power and data cabling connections to function. The rough-in wiring must be completed and tested before devices can be physically mounted, wired, and terminated.

Access control hardware such as electric strikes, magnetic locks, door position sensors, and request-to-exit devices are installed on or within door frames and doors. These must be in place and properly aligned before mounting access control devices.

Cabling for access control systems is often routed above ceilings. Ceiling installation must be complete or at least accessible pathways closed to prevent damage to cables and to allow for proper cable management before device installation.

successor: Configure and Program Access Control System
rationale: Access control devices must be physically installed, wired, and terminated before the central controller/software can be configured, programmed, and tested with those specific devices (assigning readers to doors, setting access levels, etc.).

successor: Commission and Test Access Control System
rationale: All access control devices must be physically installed and connected before end-to-end testing, credential validation, lock/unlock cycling, and commissioning can be performed to verify the system operates correctly.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the proper elevation before any concrete forms can be set and concrete poured for the entry landing/stoop.
The foundation walls and footings supporting the entry area must be in place before the landing/stoop concrete is poured against them or adjacent to them.
Any underground drainage, conduit, or plumbing that passes beneath the entry landing/stoop area must be installed before concrete is poured.
The concrete landing/stoop provides the finished walking surface and threshold height, which defines the exact elevation and position for the entry door frame and door installation.
Railing posts are typically anchored into or adjacent to the cured concrete stoop, so the concrete must be poured and cured first to provide a stable base.
The ground must be cleared, graded, and compacted before any ramp construction can begin to ensure a stable foundation and proper drainage.
The ramp's load-bearing base and any necessary retaining walls must be in place before building the ramp surface to ensure structural integrity.
Underground drainage pipes and stormwater systems below or adjacent to the ramp must be installed first to avoid excavating through the completed ramp later.

The entry ramp provides the transition and connection from the main road to the site's internal roads or parking lot, so the ramp must be built first to establish the proper grade and alignment for subsequent paving.

While the gate can be installed before the ramp in some designs, it is typically more efficient to complete the ramp first to provide a stable surface for gate installation equipment and to align the gate with the final ramp grade.
The entry stairs require a stable load-bearing base; the concrete foundation must be fully cured to support the stair structure.
The building's rough framing defines the doorway location and height that the entry stairs must align with.
The main floor deck provides the top landing reference and structural connection point for the top of the stairs.
The entry door must be installed after the stairs are built so that the door threshold and stair landing heights are coordinated.
Railings and balusters mount onto the completed stair structure and cannot be installed before the stairs exist.
Handrails and guardrails are typically attached to the structural frame or deck; the structural support must be in place to provide a substrate for mounting.

predecessor: Concrete Slab / Floor Deck Pour and Cure
rationale: Handrails are often anchored into concrete slabs or decks; the concrete must be poured and sufficiently cured to achieve required strength for anchoring.
Handrails and guardrails are safety-critical items that must be installed before final inspections can verify compliance with safety codes.
While painting can sometimes be done post-installation, it is a soft preference to install rails first and then apply finish coating to protect the installed product.
Vestibule partitions are typically framed and attached to door frames or the surrounding structure; rough door frames must be in place to define the vestibule opening and provide a mounting surface.
The partition sits on the finished floor or subfloor; a stable, level base surface must exist before erecting the partition wall.
Vestibule doors are hung within the partition framing; the partition frame and rough opening must be complete before doors can be installed.
Electrical boxes, switches, and wiring within the vestibule partition wall must be roughed in before the partition is closed up with drywall or finish panels.
The structural partition frame must be erected before applying drywall, paneling, or other surface finishes to the partition.
The vehicle restraint system (e.g., guardrails, barriers) requires a stable, compacted road base or subgrade to be properly anchored and achieve its design strength and impact resistance.
