Proper drainage must be in place before installing vehicle restraint systems to prevent water accumulation that could undermine the foundation or cause corrosion of the restraint system components.

Vehicle restraint systems (guardrails/barriers) must be installed before applying final pavement markings and signage, as the system's location influences lane marking placement and warning sign positioning.
The vehicle restraint system installation should be completed before final paving of adjacent lanes to ensure proper integration and avoid damage to the freshly paved surface during installation.
After installation, the vehicle restraint system must undergo safety inspection and impact testing to verify it meets structural and safety specifications before the road is opened to traffic.
The rough opening (structural framing, header, jambs, and sill) must be built and dimensionally complete to provide the structural support and correct opening size for the roller door installation.
The door tracks, brackets, springs, and mounting hardware must be installed first so that the door panels or curtain can be mounted onto the track system.
The floor slab at the door opening must be poured and cured to provide the finished floor level that the door seals against and to anchor the bottom track or sill.
The door itself must be fully assembled and hanging on its tracks before the automatic opener mechanism can be attached and aligned with the door.
Weatherstripping, seals, and insulation around the door perimeter must be applied after the door is installed to ensure proper fit and sealing against air and water infiltration.
A stable load-bearing foundation must be in place before the courtyard enclosure walls can be erected, as the walls require a solid base to transfer their weight and resist lateral forces.
The ground surface must be graded and leveled to the correct elevation and drainage slope before wall construction begins, ensuring proper alignment and water management around the base of the walls.

Underground utilities such as drainage pipes, electrical conduits, and water lines that pass beneath or through the wall footprint must be installed prior to wall construction to avoid later excavation and disruption of the completed walls.
If the courtyard walls support a roof, canopy, or pergola structure, the walls must be fully completed and cured to provide the necessary load-bearing support before overhead elements are installed.
The enclosure walls must be complete to define the courtyard perimeter before the interior floor or base surface is poured or laid, ensuring proper containment and edge detailing.
Structural wall construction must be finished before any exterior cladding, plastering, painting, or other surface finishes are applied to the walls.
Rough openings in the courtyard walls must be framed and the structural walls completed before doors, windows, and frames can be installed within those openings.
A stable, compacted sub-base is physically required before any paving or floor finish can be laid to prevent uneven settlement and structural failure.
Underground drainage pipes and gullies must be placed and backfilled before paving to avoid excavating through the finished paving and to ensure proper drainage falls.
Any electrical, water, or data conduits running under the courtyard must be installed prior to paving to eliminate the need for future disruptive trenching through the finished surface.

Walls that sit on or abutt the courtyard paving typically require the paving base or slab to be completed first to provide a stable footing and to ensure proper alignment and waterproofing detailing at the base.

It is a soft preference to complete hard paving before soft landscaping and planting to avoid soil compaction from construction traffic and to prevent damage to new plants, though it is not physically impossible to do some planting beforehand.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and graded to the proper drainage slopes before any planting beds can be constructed, as the beds sit on top of the prepared subgrade.
Any underground drainage, irrigation, or electrical conduits serving the courtyard must be installed and backfilled before the planting beds are built, to avoid digging up finished beds.
Concrete curbs, pathway edges, or retaining walls that border the planting beds need their foundations poured first, so the bed walls can abut or tie into these hardscape elements.
The physical bed structure (edging, walls, bottom liner) must be complete before clean topsoil, compost, and amendments are placed, and before any plants go into the beds.
Final fine grading and decorative mulch application are the finishing steps that occur after beds are constructed and planted, as the bed rims define the mulch area.

The courtyard water feature requires a stable, level base and proper drainage connections. Foundation and slab works must be completed first to provide the structural support and subsurface drainage infrastructure needed for the water feature.

Water supply lines, circulation pipes, drainage pipes, and electrical conduits for pumps and lighting must be roughed-in underground before the water feature basin and structure can be installed over them.

Hardscape surfaces around the water feature (pavers, tiles, decking) should be installed after the water feature basin is in place to ensure proper fit, alignment, and waterproofing transitions at the edges.

It is preferable to complete planting and soft landscaping after the water feature is installed to avoid damage to plants from construction debris and to allow precise grading around the feature, though some planting could theoretically be done earlier.

successor: Water Feature Finishing (Tiling, Liner, Decorative Stone)
rationale: The structural basin and shell must be completed before applying the final waterproof liner, tilework, or decorative stone cladding to the interior and exterior surfaces of the water feature.
The ground surface must be leveled and prepared before any structure can be erected to ensure a stable foundation.
The canopy or shade structure requires anchor points or footings to be set in concrete before the framework can be installed.
Any electrical, water, or drainage lines that will pass beneath or through the canopy location must be installed before the structure is built to avoid rework.
The canopy provides overhead cover; finishing the floor surface underneath after the structure is complete protects the finished pavement from damage during overhead installation.
Light fixtures, fans, or electrical outlets mounted on or under the canopy must be installed after the structure is fully framed to ensure safe and accurate attachment.
The ground must be leveled, compacted, and properly graded before any courtyard seating elements can be installed to ensure a stable and level foundation.

predecessor: Concrete Slab or Paver Base Installation
rationale: A hardscape base (concrete pad or paver sub-base) must be in place to anchor seating elements securely and prevent settling or movement.
Any underground electrical, drainage, or irrigation lines serving the courtyard must be installed before seating is placed, to avoid digging up finished seating later.
Final upholstery, cushions, or surface finishes must be applied after the main seating structure is fully assembled and fixed in place.
While landscaping can be done concurrently, it is preferable to complete seating installation first to avoid damaging newly planted areas during seating assembly.
The foundation and slab must be completed to provide a stable base for installing courtyard doors/gates.
The framed rough openings for doors/gates must be in place before the door/gate units can be installed.
Exterior wall finishes around the door frame must be applied after the door/gate is installed to ensure proper integration and weather sealing.
Locks, handles, and other hardware can only be fitted after the door/gate unit itself is securely in place.
While grading can start before, the final finish paving adjacent to the threshold is best completed after door/gate installation to ensure proper alignment and drainage.
The partition walls require a solid foundation or slab on grade to bear their load and provide a stable base for construction.
Underground and in-slab utility rough-ins must be placed before partition walls are built, as walls would block access to the slab for trenching and conduit placement.
Interior partition walls that define an enclosed courtyard space must be erected so that the main structural wall framing can tie into, abut, or interface with those partitions.
Wiring, piping, and ductwork that run inside or through the partition walls can only be installed after the wall framing is in place to provide the chase space.
Sheathing or exterior cladding on the courtyard side of the enclosed partition walls must be applied after the wall assembly is framed and structurally complete.

The foundation of the building must be completed before courtyard construction can begin, as the courtyard is often built around or adjacent to the main structure, and heavy machinery needed for foundation work would damage any pre-built courtyard features.

All underground utilities such as drainage, water lines, electrical conduits, and gas lines serving the courtyard must be installed and covered before courtyard surfaces, paving, or landscaping are constructed.
The building's exterior walls, roof, and structural elements adjacent to the courtyard must be completed to define the courtyard boundaries and prevent damage from ongoing construction activities.

Hardscape elements of the courtyard such as paving, walls, steps, and water features must be constructed first before any soft landscaping, planting, or grass seeding is done to avoid damage to plants.

While it is preferred to complete courtyard construction before installing decorative elements like furniture, lighting fixtures, and art pieces, this is a soft constraint as some decoration elements could potentially be added concurrently or in a different order if carefully managed.

The building foundation must be completed before courtyard installation because the courtyard system is typically constructed around or adjacent to the building, requiring a stable foundation to define the building footprint and ensure proper drainage and grading away from the structure.

Site grading must be completed first to establish proper drainage slopes, subgrade preparation, and elevation levels for the courtyard area, ensuring water flows away from buildings and prevents ponding.

All underground utilities such as drainage pipes, irrigation lines, electrical conduits, and water supply lines must be installed before courtyard construction to avoid trenching and disruption of the finished courtyard surfaces.

The courtyard system structure (including sub-base and drainage layers) must be installed before the final paving and hardscape finishes can be applied, as the system provides the foundational support for surface materials.

Courtyard system installation including drainage layers, root barriers, and soil preparation must be completed before any landscaping and planting can take place, as these components are necessary to support healthy plant growth and proper water management.
Wall framing must be completed to provide vertical support and attachment points for the roof step structure.
Roof trusses form the primary roof framework; the step structure is built onto or integrated with this framework.
Roof sheathing provides the underlying deck onto which the step structure components are installed.
Flashing must be installed after the step structure is in place to seal joints and prevent water infiltration around the step transitions.
Final roofing materials (shingles, tiles, etc.) are applied over and around the completed step structure for weatherproofing and finish.
The foundation must be cured and load-bearing before vertical risers can be installed to provide a stable base.
Horizontal reinforcement must be in place to tie into vertical riser reinforcement for structural continuity.
Vertical risers form the vertical face of each step; the stair slab concrete cannot be poured until risers are positioned and secured.
Treads (horizontal step surfaces) are installed on top of or between risers; risers must be in place first to define step geometry.
While finishing can typically only occur after risers are installed, this is a soft preference if access is still possible from one side.
The roof deck provides the structural base onto which step flashing is integrated; step flashing is installed along the edges of the roof deck where it meets walls.
Roof underlayment (e.g., felt or synthetic) must be laid over the roof deck before step flashing is placed, as the flashing overlaps the underlayment to ensure water tightness.

Step flashing is interwoven with roofing shingles; each piece of step flashing is installed before the shingle course above it, so shingle installation proceeds concurrently with and after the flashing placement.
Step flashing is typically installed against vertical walls; the siding is installed after the flashing to overlap and cover the vertical leg of the flashing, creating a water-resistant seal.
The roof deck must be in place before scupper openings can be properly positioned and integrated into the roof structure.
The structural roof framing must be completed to support and anchor the scupper system before it can be installed.
The waterproofing membrane must be installed first to ensure proper flashing integration and water-tight seal around the scupper opening.
Downspouts connect directly to the scupper outlet; the scupper must be in place to define the connection point and slope for drainage conductors.

successor: Exterior Wall Cladding / Finish (in scupper area)
rationale: The scupper penetration and flashing must be completed before final wall cladding is applied around the opening to achieve a weather-tight seal.
The structural frame (columns, beams, primary roof structure) must be in place to provide the load-bearing support onto which the cascading roof overhang is attached.
The main roof deck or sheathing must be installed to establish the base roof plane from which the cascading overhang extends and to which it connects.
Flashing and waterproofing at the overhang joints and transitions must be applied after the overhang structure is in place to ensure a continuous water barrier.
The soffit and fascia (underside and edge trim of the overhang) are finish elements that must be installed after the overhang framing and sheathing are complete.
Gutters and downspouts are mounted onto or below the finished overhang edge and must be attached after the overhang structure and fascia are in place.
The thermal break must be applied to clean, prepared concrete step surfaces; concrete must be cured and ready before applying the break system.
The thermal break must be in place before finishing materials (treads, tiles, or coatings) are applied over the steps to ensure thermal separation.

successor: Apply sealant or waterproofing over thermal break
rationale: Although not physically mandatory, it is best practice to seal/protect the thermal break shortly after installation to prevent damage before final stair finishing.
Steel columns must be in place to support the roof framing structure and transfer loads to the foundation.
Primary steel beams and girders must be installed to provide the base framework onto which the cascade roof framing system is attached.
The foundation must be fully cured and the slab completed to provide a stable base for column erection and subsequent roof framing loads.
Roof decking and sheathing materials are applied directly onto the completed roof framing structure.
Waterproofing is applied on top of the roof sheathing/decking, which itself requires the roof framing to be complete.
The step roof decking must be installed on top of the step framing, which provides the structural support. Without the framing in place, there is no structure to attach the decking to.
The step roof decking typically connects to or abuts the main roof decking, which must be installed first to ensure proper water shedding and structural continuity at the intersection.
Underlayment is installed over the decking to provide a water-resistant barrier; the decking must be in place first to serve as the substrate.
Flashing details at transitions and edges are installed after the decking is in place to properly integrate with the decking surface and provide weatherproofing.
While roofing felt is typically applied after decking, some sequences allow for alternative scheduling; however, the decking must be complete before any roofing membrane is laid.
The substrate must be clean, dry, and smooth to ensure proper adhesion of the waterproofing membrane.
The structural roof deck must be in place to provide a solid base for waterproofing application.
Underlayment provides a secondary weather barrier and prevents direct contact between waterproofing and deck.
Final roofing materials (tiles, slates, shingles) must be installed over the waterproofing to protect it from UV and mechanical damage.
Waterproofing must be completed and cured before inspection and flood testing can be performed to verify integrity.
Cascade flashing and trim are installed on top of the roof underlayment to provide water tightness at roof edges and valleys.
The roof decking provides the structural substrate to which flashing and trim components are attached.
The roof structure and any dormer/valley framing must be complete to provide support and attachment points for flashing.

successor: Install Roofing Shingles or Final Roof Covering
rationale: Cascade flashing is typically installed at valleys and edges before the primary roof covering to ensure proper overlap and water shedding.
Gutters are typically installed after trim and flashing to integrate with the finished roof edge, though this is a practical preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The drainage system must be fully installed and in place before it can be commissioned, as commissioning involves testing and verifying the installed system's functionality.
The system must be commissioned (tested and verified) before it can be put into normal operation, to ensure it meets design and safety requirements.

predecessor: Connect Cascade Drainage System to Main Outfall
rationale: All connections to the main drainage outfall must be completed before commissioning can proceed, as the commissioning tests require the full flow path to be operational.

predecessor: Install Cascade Drainage Pumps and Valves
rationale: Pumps and valves must be installed and ready before commissioning, as they are critical components that need to be tested during the commissioning process.

successor: Hand Over Cascade Drainage System to Client
rationale: The system must be successfully commissioned and verified as operational before it can be formally handed over to the client.
The structural roof framing (beams, trusses, or rafters) must be in place to provide the load-bearing support onto which the roof deck / substrate is installed.
The roof deck / substrate forms the solid base surface; underlayment or roofing felt is laid directly over it to provide secondary weather protection before the final roofing material is installed.
Roof insulation boards or layers are typically placed atop the roof deck / substrate to provide thermal performance, requiring the deck to be complete first.
Flashing at roof edges, valleys, and penetrations is installed after the deck is in place to seal transitions and prevent water intrusion.
The final weatherproof roof covering is applied over the substrate and underlayment; the deck must be fully installed as the base layer.
The roof sheathing or decking provides the structural base onto which the roof edge and fascia are mounted; fascia typically attaches to the ends of rafters and roof decking edges.
Underlayment is installed over the roof deck before edge metal/fascia is placed, ensuring water-tightness and proper flashing integration at the roof edge.
Drip edge is typically installed over or integrated with the fascia board to direct water away from the fascia and into the gutters.
Gutters are mounted directly onto the fascia board along the roof edge; fascia must be in place to provide the attachment surface for gutter hangers.
Roof edge metal and fascia are installed before the final roofing materials (shingles or tiles) to allow proper overlapping and water shedding at the eaves and rakes.
The roof deck provides the structural base onto which flashing components are mounted and sealed.
Underlayment must be in place to provide a water-resistive barrier before cutting and sealing around penetrations.
The pipes, vents, or ducts must be in place so that flashing can be formed and sealed around the actual penetration.
Flashing must be installed first so that the primary roofing material can overlap and seal over the top of the flashing to shed water properly.
It is advisable to complete all flashing work before final inspection so the inspector can verify water-tightness of all penetrations at once.
Roof overhang/eaves are built as an extension of the roof structure; the main roof framing or trusses must be in place to support and provide the framework for the eaves.
Wall sheathing provides the backing and lateral support for the roof structure and eave assembly; eaves typically tie into the wall top plates and sheathing.
Eaves form the edge of the roof; roof decking is installed after the eave framing is in place to create a continuous roof surface.
Fascia boards and soffits are attached directly to the eave ends and underside; the eave structure must exist before these finish components can be installed.
Gutters are mounted onto the fascia board at the eaves; both the eave framing and fascia must be complete before gutters can be attached.
The roof hatch must be installed within the roof framing and deck opening; the structural support must be in place before the hatch can be set.
The roof deck provides the surface and opening into which the hatch is mounted; it must be installed beforehand.
Flashing and waterproof membrane around the hatch must be applied after the hatch is in place to ensure a watertight seal.
Insulation around the hatch curb is typically installed after the hatch is set to properly fit and seal around the assembly.
Interior finishes below the hatch opening should be completed after the hatch is installed to allow for proper integration and trim work.
Snow guards/rails are mounted onto the roof surface or through the roofing material; roof sheathing provides the structural substrate needed to anchor the snow retention system.
The waterproof underlayment must be in place before any component that penetrates or attaches to the roof deck to maintain the building envelope's weathertightness.
Snow guards are typically installed concurrently with or immediately after the final roof covering, as they attach through or onto the finished roofing surface.

While snow guard installation often precedes final trim work so that trim can be fitted around or integrated with the snow retention system, this is more of a logical sequencing preference than a physical necessity.

Snow guards are typically installed from the roof edge or using roof access equipment; once installed, the scaffolding or access systems used for roof work can be safely dismantled, as no further roof-edge work is needed.
The roof deck must be structurally complete and load-bearing before any equipment supports can be installed on it.
Waterproofing must be applied first to protect the building envelope; equipment supports are then installed on top of or through the membrane with proper flashing.

successor: Roof-mounted Equipment Installation (HVAC units, solar panels, antennas)
rationale: Supports/curbs/mounting frames must be in place before the actual mechanical or electrical equipment can be set and fastened onto them.
After the support structure (e.g., curb) is installed, flashings and seals around it must be completed to maintain weatherproofing integrity.

successor: Roof Insulation and Final Roof Covering (near supports)
rationale: Ideally, supports are installed before the final roof covering in their immediate area to allow proper integration, though some sequencing flexibility exists depending on the system design.
The roof deck provides the structural surface that flashing is applied to; without a completed deck, there is no substrate for flashing installation.
Underlayment serves as a water-resistant barrier beneath the flashing; flashing must be installed over the underlayment to ensure proper drainage and waterproofing.

Flashing is integrated with the primary roofing material to seal joints and transitions; roofing material is installed after or concurrently with base flashing, but counter-flashing is typically installed after the roofing material is placed.
Counter-flashing is often embedded into or overlaps wall cladding to prevent water intrusion at the roof-wall intersection; wall cladding must follow to complete the weather seal.
All structural framing (roof trusses, rafters, and sheathing) must be in place to provide the rigid support needed for flashing installation.

A clean, dry, smooth, and structurally sound roof deck or substrate (e.g., concrete, wood, or metal deck) must be prepared and completed before any membrane roofing can be installed, as the membrane requires a stable base for adhesion or mechanical fastening.

Thermal insulation boards must be laid out and secured on the roof deck prior to membrane installation because the membrane is typically applied over the insulation layer to provide thermal performance and a uniform surface.

A vapor retarder or air barrier must be installed on the deck before the insulation and membrane to prevent moisture migration into the roofing assembly, which would otherwise cause blistering or delamination of the membrane.

Roof drains, scuppers, gutters, and any equipment curbs or parapet flashing bases must be in place before membrane installation so the membrane can be properly flashed and sealed around these penetrations and terminations.

After the membrane is installed, metal flashings, copings, edge trims, and counter-flashings must be placed to protect the membrane edges and provide watertight terminations at walls, parapets, and penetrations.
Roof covering (shingles, tiles, membrane) must be installed over a solid roof deck or sheathing for structural support and proper attachment.
Roof underlayment (felt paper, synthetic underlayment) must be laid down as a moisture barrier before the final roof covering is installed.
Flashing around roof penetrations and valleys must be installed before the final roof covering to ensure proper water tightness.
Gutters are typically installed after roof covering to allow proper alignment with the roof edge and drip edge flashing.
Final roof inspection occurs after the roof covering is complete to verify quality and compliance with building codes.
The structural framing (roof deck, joists, beams) must be in place to provide a surface to mount roof drains, gutters, and downspouts.
Roof sheathing or decking must be installed to create the base on which drain components (gutters, drains, flashing) are attached.
A waterproof membrane or underlayment must be laid before drainage components are installed to ensure water is directed properly and to prevent leaks.
Downspouts and gutter outlets are often integrated with or concealed behind exterior wall finishes; cladding should be installed after drainage components to allow proper integration and sealing.

Downspout extensions and drainage outlets should be in place before final grading and landscaping to direct water away from the foundation, though this is a strong preference rather than a strict physical constraint.
The roof must be structurally framed to provide the opening and support structure for the skylight to be installed.
The roof deck must be sheathed to create the finished surface through which the skylight opening is cut and the unit is mounted.
Weatherproofing underlayment must be laid before skylight installation to ensure proper flashing integration and moisture protection around the skylight curb.
The ceiling structure and shaft framing from the roof to the ceiling below must be completed to accommodate the skylight well and finished opening.
Final roofing materials (shingles, tiles, or membrane) around the skylight must be installed after the skylight curb and flashing are in place to ensure watertight integration.
The skylight unit must be in place before the interior ceiling drywall is installed and finished around the skylight shaft to create a clean, sealed interior opening.

Trusses and rafters bear directly on the load-bearing walls and top plates. Wall framing must be complete and sheathing installed to provide the necessary structural support, alignment, and load transfer path for the roof system.

The double top plate on the wall framing provides the bearing surface and tying mechanism for trusses and rafters. Without the top plates installed and tied at corners and intersections, there is no adequate surface or connection for truss/rafter placement.

Roof sheathing is installed directly onto the top chord of trusses or rafters. Trusses/rafters must be erected and properly braced before any sheathing or decking can be applied to the roof structure.

Temporary and permanent bracing (lateral, longitudinal, and cross-bracing) is installed as part of or immediately after truss erection to ensure stability. However, the trusses/rafters must first be placed and aligned before bracing can be fully installed.

Soffit and fascia boards are attached to the rafter tails or truss ends to enclose the roof edge. While typically done after truss erection, this is a logical sequencing preference rather than a strict structural necessity, as temporary supports could theoretically allow earlier installation.
The roof parapet is built on top of and anchored to the roof slab or deck; thus the structural base must be completely finished to provide a stable surface and attachment point for parapet walls.

The waterproofing membrane must be installed before parapet walls are constructed because the membrane typically extends up the vertical face of the parapet or must be flashed into the parapet. Building the parapet first would make proper membrane installation impossible or would require complex retrofitting.
Coping (capping) and flashing are installed over the top of the completed parapet wall to seal the top edge and divert water; they cannot be placed until the parapet structure itself exists.

While scuppers and gutters are often integrated with or penetrate through the parapet wall, some drainage provisions can be installed concurrently; however, final connection and sealing of through-wall scuppers should follow parapet completion to ensure proper integration and watertightness. This is a soft preference where sequencing can vary.

The parapet forms the top edge of the building's exterior walls; cladding and façade finishes that abut or cap off against the parapet cannot be completed until the parapet structure is in place to receive those finishes.
A waterproof membrane must be installed before any planting to prevent water damage and leaks into the building structure.
The structural roof deck must be fully completed and cured to support the weight of the planting medium, plants, and drainage layers.
Proper drainage layers (e.g., gravel, drainage mats) must be in place before planting to prevent waterlogging and root rot.
Irrigation systems should be tested after planting to ensure proper coverage and function around the newly installed plants.
Final surface treatments like mulch, decorative stone, and pathway finishes are applied after planting to protect the soil and complete the aesthetic.
The roof structural slab must be constructed to provide a stable base for the edge restraint/curb to be built upon.
Waterproofing must be installed before the curb is built to ensure continuous waterproofing beneath and up the curb, preventing water ingress.
The edge restraint/curb defines the perimeter boundary, so the drainage layer must be installed within the contained area after the curb is in place.

successor: Roof Garden Soil / Growing Medium Placement
rationale: The curb acts as a containment barrier for the growing medium; soil must be placed after the curb is complete to prevent spillage and ensure proper retention.
The edge restraint defines the planting area boundary and protects the waterproofing; planting must occur after the curb is installed to keep the growing medium contained.
The structural roof slab must be in place to provide a load-bearing surface for the roof garden pavers to be installed upon.
Waterproofing must be fully installed and tested before pavers are laid to protect the building structure from water intrusion.
Thermal insulation must be placed below the paver surface to provide energy efficiency and thermal comfort for the spaces below.
Drainage mat and filter fabric must be installed before pavers to ensure proper water collection and filtration away from the paver assembly.

While furnishings such as planters, seating, and lighting can be installed after paver completion for convenience, they could theoretically be placed simultaneously; however, standard sequencing prefers a completed walking surface before installing loose furnishings.
The roof garden pedestal system must be installed on a stable, load-bearing structural slab or deck that provides the foundational support for the entire assembly.
Waterproofing must be applied to the structural slab before installing the pedestal system to prevent water ingress and protect the building structure below the garden.
Thermal insulation over the waterproofing layer should be placed before the pedestal system to ensure proper thermal performance of the roof assembly.
Once the pedestal system is installed in its rough position, the individual pedestals must be adjusted and leveled to create a uniform plane for the paving or decking above.
The pedestal system provides the support structure; paving stones or deck tiles can only be laid after the pedestals are in place and properly leveled.
The roof structure or deck must be in place to provide a surface and structural support for installing the roof hatch.
The hatch opening and frame must be installed first so that the waterproofing membrane can be properly flashed and sealed around the hatch to prevent leaks.

successor: Roof Garden Soil / Growing Medium Placement
rationale: The hatch must be in place before soil is brought onto the roof to avoid blocking access and to ensure the hatch is fully operational and sealed.
Plants and vegetation should be placed after the hatch is installed to allow unobstructed access for installation and to avoid damaging plants.
Safety guardrails around the roof perimeter and hatch area should be installed after the hatch to ensure safe access and compliance with fall protection requirements.

successor: Roof Garden Substrate Retention Grid Installation
rationale: The roof deck must be structurally complete and waterproofed before any load from the substrate retention grid can be placed upon it. The grid sits directly on the roof membrane/protection layer.

successor: Roof Garden Substrate Retention Grid Installation
rationale: The waterproof membrane must be installed and tested before the retention grid is placed, as the grid and subsequent substrate would otherwise trap moisture against the structure and prevent access for repairs.

predecessor: Roof Garden Substrate Retention Grid Installation
rationale: If a separate drainage layer is placed above the retention grid (depending on system design), the grid must be in place first to contain the substrate while allowing water to pass through to drains below.

predecessor: Roof Garden Substrate Retention Grid Installation
rationale: The retention grid physically contains and stabilizes the growing substrate; substrate cannot be placed without the grid in position, otherwise it would slide or erode.

predecessor: Roof Garden Substrate Retention Grid Installation
rationale: Plants require the substrate medium to be in place for rooting; the grid supports the substrate depth, so both grid and substrate must precede planting.

successor: Roof Garden Installation – Layering and Waterproofing
rationale: The roof garden requires a solid structural base (the roof slab) to support the weight of soil, plants, and waterproofing layers. Without the structural slab, there is nothing to build upon.

successor: Roof Garden Installation – Layering and Waterproofing
rationale: Proper drainage must be in place before waterproofing and garden layers are applied, so that water can be directed away from the building structure. Installing drainage after would require disturbing the waterproofing membrane.

predecessor: Roof Garden Installation – Layering and Waterproofing
rationale: The waterproofing and protective layers must be fully installed and tested before any growing medium (substrate/soil) can be placed, as soil would trap moisture against the structure and conceal any defects in the waterproofing.

predecessor: Roof Garden Installation – Layering and Waterproofing
rationale: Plants require the completed waterproofing, drainage, filter fabric, and substrate layers to be in place before they can be planted, otherwise the root systems could damage exposed membranes or the structure would lack the necessary growing media.

predecessor: Roof Garden Installation – Layering and Waterproofing
rationale: The waterproofing membrane and protective layers must be completed before installing irrigation lines to avoid penetrating or compromising the waterproofing layer and to ensure the irrigation system rests on the finished substrate surface.
The roof structure must be verified to support the additional weight of soil, plants, water retention systems, and saturated growing medium before any planting begins.
A waterproof membrane is essential to prevent water damage to the building structure from irrigation and rainwater; planting cannot start until the roof is sealed.
Root barriers must be in place to protect the waterproofing membrane and structural deck from root penetration before any plants are installed.
Proper drainage systems and filter fabrics must be laid to prevent waterlogging and soil erosion; planting cannot proceed without these layers.
The engineered soil or growing medium must be spread and leveled on the roof as the substrate into which plants will be installed.
Irrigation pipes, drip lines, and emitters must be laid and tested for leaks and coverage before planting to avoid disturbing root systems later.

successor: Mulching and Erosion Control Blanket Installation
rationale: Once plants are installed, mulch and erosion control blankets are applied to protect soil, retain moisture, and suppress weeds.
After planting, a regular watering and fertilization regimen must begin immediately to support root establishment and plant health.
The planted roof garden is inspected for compliance with specifications before project closeout; this is a quality assurance preference rather than a strict physical necessity.

The roof structure must be complete and waterproofed before any irrigation system can be installed, as the irrigation pipes and components need a stable, leak-free base to mount on and the structure must be able to support the weight of water-filled pipes.
Proper roof drainage must be in place before irrigation installation to ensure excess water from the irrigation system can be properly drained away, preventing water pooling and structural damage.
The waterproofing membrane and root barrier must be installed before irrigation to protect the roof structure from water damage and root penetration when the irrigation system is operational.

successor: Roof Garden Soil / Growing Medium Placement
rationale: Irrigation pipes and drip lines must be laid out on top of the drainage layer and membrane before soil is placed, so that the irrigation infrastructure is correctly positioned beneath and within the growing medium to water plant roots effectively.

Plants cannot be placed until the irrigation system is installed and operational, as plants require immediate watering upon planting and the irrigation layout must be finalized to avoid disturbing root systems.

successor: Roof Garden Paver and Deck Assembly
rationale: The structural deck and waterproofing membrane must be fully installed and tested before any roofing or garden assembly can be placed atop it, as the deck provides the load-bearing surface and the waterproofing prevents water damage to the structure below.

successor: Roof Garden Paver and Deck Assembly
rationale: Proper drainage (roof drains, scuppers, or drainage mats) must be in place before installing pavers or deck assemblies, otherwise water could become trapped beneath the finished surface, leading to ponding, leakage, and structural damage.

successor: Roof Garden Paver and Deck Assembly
rationale: Insulation boards are typically laid over the waterproofing membrane and beneath the paver supports or deck substructure to meet thermal performance requirements; installing pavers before insulation would trap the insulation incorrectly or cause it to shift.

predecessor: Roof Garden Paver and Deck Assembly
rationale: Guardrails, handrails, or safety barriers must be installed after the deck surface is complete so they can be properly anchored into the finished deck structure and to ensure the walking surface is safe for workers during railing installation.

predecessor: Roof Garden Paver and Deck Assembly
successor: Landscaping and Planting in Green Roof Areas
rationale: The paver and deck system provides the access and support surface; any intensive green roof planting, planter boxes, or landscape features are placed after the deck/pavers are installed so that the structural base is stable and accessible.

successor: Roof Garden Guardrail and Safety Installation
rationale: The guardrail system must be anchored to the finished roof deck or floor slab. Installing the guardrail requires a stable, completed structural surface to attach to, and safety regulations typically require guardrails before work proceeds near roof edges.

successor: Roof Garden Guardrail and Safety Installation
rationale: The waterproof membrane must be installed before guardrails to ensure continuous sealing around any anchor points or penetrations. Installing guardrail posts after waterproofing prevents water intrusion at attachment points.

predecessor: Roof Garden Guardrail and Safety Installation
successor: Roof Garden Soil / Growing Medium Placement
rationale: Guardrails must be in place before soil and planting medium are brought onto the roof to ensure worker safety during material handling near roof edges and to define the perimeter boundary for garden installation.

predecessor: Roof Garden Guardrail and Safety Installation
rationale: All safety guardrails must be installed before workers begin planting activities near roof edges to provide fall protection and establish a safe working perimeter around the roof garden area.

predecessor: Structural Reinforcement or Parapet Wall Completion
successor: Roof Garden Guardrail and Safety Installation
rationale: Guardrail posts are often anchored to the parapet wall or structurally reinforced edges. The supporting structure must be fully cured and completed to bear the loads imposed by the guardrail system.
A solid foundation is required to bear the load of the arcade colonnade columns and arches.
The ground must be properly graded and compacted before any structural elements are erected.
The arcade colonnade provides vertical support for the roof or upper structure, so roof installation cannot proceed until the colonnade is complete.
Colonnade columns must be in place before the arches spanning between them can be constructed.

successor: Decorative cladding and finishing of columns
rationale: Final aesthetic treatments like carving, painting, or cladding are typically done after the structural colonnade is erected, though it could theoretically be done piecemeal.
Arcade vaulted ceilings require structural support from walls, columns, or arches beneath them to bear the load.
Temporary formwork or centering is required to support the masonry or concrete of the vaulted ceiling during construction.
The formwork or centering can only be safely removed after the vaulted ceiling has cured or set sufficiently to be self-supporting.

successor: Apply ceiling finishes (plaster, paint, decorative elements)
rationale: Finishing work such as plastering, painting, or adding decorative ribs/ornamentation typically follows the structural completion of the vault.

successor: Install roof or upper floor structure above
rationale: The vaulted ceiling must be completed to provide the structural base and load-bearing capacity for any roofing or upper-level construction above the arcade.
Arcade spandrel panels sit between and are supported by arcade columns, so columns must be erected first to provide structural support.
A stable foundation is required to support the arcade structure including the columns that carry the spandrel panels.
Spandrel panels form part of the arcade's vertical enclosure and support, so they must be in place before the roof or upper levels are added above them.

successor: Arch or vault construction above arcade
rationale: Arches or vaults often spring from the spandrel level or are supported by the spandrel panels, requiring the panels to be installed first.

predecessor: Arcade spandrel panel fabrication/sizing on site
rationale: Panels must be fabricated, delivered, and prepared before they can be lifted into position and installed.
The arcade keystone is the central top stone of an arch, which requires the supporting arch columns or piers to be in place before the arch can be assembled and the keystone set.

The keystone is the final stone inserted at the apex of an arch; all voussoirs (the wedge-shaped arch stones) must be placed from the springing points upward before the keystone can be inserted to lock the arch.
A temporary wooden centering or formwork must be built to support the arch stones during construction; the keystone is placed last on this support before the centering can be removed.
The temporary centering cannot be struck/dismantled until the keystone is in place and the arch is self-supporting, as removal earlier would cause the arch to collapse.
Any structural loads (walls, floors, roof) above the arcade can only be applied after the keystone locks the arch, ensuring the arch can transfer compressive forces properly.
The arcade entablature rests directly on top of the arcade columns. Columns must be in place to provide structural support for the entablature.
The entablature serves as the horizontal beam or lintel spanning the columns, forming the base upon which the roof or any upper superstructure is built.

successor: Apply decorative frieze/sculptural elements on entablature
rationale: While decorative elements could theoretically be carved in place later, it is far more practical to apply or finish them after the entablature is installed, as carving on the ground before lifting risks damage. However, some prefabrication may occur off-site.
Foundations and pedestals must be finished to support the columns, which in turn support the entablature.

successor: Install arcade balustrade or parapet above
rationale: Any balustrade, parapet, or attic story above the arcade is typically built on top of the entablature, requiring the entablature to be in place first.
The column base requires a stable, load-bearing foundation to transfer vertical loads safely to the ground; without proper foundation preparation, the column base would lack structural support.
The ground must be excavated and leveled to provide a flat, stable surface for placing the arcade column base accurately.
The column base serves as the bottom support for the column shaft; the shaft must be erected on top of the completed base to ensure proper load transfer and structural alignment.
The column capital sits atop the column shaft, which in turn rests on the column base; the structural sequence requires base → shaft → capital.
The arcade arches span between columns; the column bases and columns must be fully installed to provide the vertical supports that the arches will bear upon.
The impost block sits atop the arcade pier, so the pier must be completed first to provide structural support.
The impost block serves as the springing point for the arch; arches and their voussoirs rely on the impost block as their base support.

predecessor: Stone cutting / dressing of impost block
rationale: The stone block must be cut, shaped, and dressed to its final dimensions before it can be lifted and placed into position.
The underlying foundation and stylobate (or upper surface of the pier) must be level and stable before the impost block is set.
If a mortar or leveling bed is used, it must be prepared and applied to the bearing surface prior to placing the block.
Arcade machines need a level, finished floor surface to be placed on; installing flooring first ensures stability and protects the machines from dust/debris.
Arcade machines require electrical power outlets and connections; electrical work must be completed before machines can be plugged in and tested.
Arcade machines are heavy and difficult to move; walls should be finished and painted before machines are brought in to avoid rework and damage.
Machines must be physically installed and powered on before game software can be loaded, configured, and tested.
All arcade units must be in place and connected before a final quality check, safety inspection, and operational testing can be performed.
A solid foundation is structurally required before any masonry wall construction can begin to ensure stability and load transfer.
Columns supporting the arcade arches must be built before the arcade masonry can be laid between them.
Scaffolding is required to provide access for masons to construct elevated arcade masonry safely.
The arcade arches and masonry must be completed and sufficiently cured before supporting formwork or centering can be struck and removed.
Arcade masonry provides the vertical support for any roof structure or upper floor above the arcade level.
The arcade structural frame must be complete to provide a substrate for waterproofing membrane installation.
Roof sheathing or deck must be in place before waterproofing can be applied to protect the structure from water ingress.
Waterproofing must be installed before drainage components (gutters, downspouts) are placed to ensure proper water shedding and integration with the waterproof membrane.
Ideal to apply waterproofing behind cladding as a weatherproof barrier, though some sequences allow concurrent work if detailing permits.
Waterproofing must be fully cured and tested for leaks before subsequent covering layers are applied to avoid costly remedial work.
The pier arcade requires a stable structural base; foundations and piles must be in place to support the arcade structure before construction can commence.
Concrete substructure works including ground beams and slabs must be completed to provide the load-bearing platform upon which the pier arcade is built.
The arcade structure must be erected first before architectural cladding, decorative finishes, and facade elements can be applied to it.
The pier arcade structural frame must be in place to support roof trusses and roofing materials; roof installation cannot proceed without the underlying arcade structure.

While retail fit-out could theoretically begin once the arcade is structurally complete, it is a soft preference to sequence it after the arcade to avoid conflicts between structural and finishing trades.
The arcade cornice sits atop the arcade vaults and arches, so the vaulted structure must be complete to provide support for the cornice.
Columns or piers that form the arcade must be erected before the cornice can be placed, as the cornice rests on or is supported by the arcade columns.
The cornice often serves as a transition or bearing point for roof elements, so roof framing typically follows cornice installation.

Final decorative details, carving, or painting of the cornice are often done after the main cornice blocks are set in place, though this is a logical construction sequence preference rather than a physical necessity.
If the cornice includes a projecting ledge, gutters or drip edges are installed after the cornice is in place to manage water runoff.
Guardrails are typically mounted to the edge of the deck structure, so the deck must be in place to provide the structural base for guardrail attachment.
Overhang brackets support the edge of the deck where guardrails are installed, so they must be set before guardrails can be placed.
If guardrails are cast into or anchored to the concrete deck, the concrete must be cured sufficiently to bear loads before guardrail installation.
Guardrails define the edge of the roadway; paving should be completed after guardrails are in place to ensure clean transitions and proper alignment.
Safety testing and final inspection of guardrail systems must occur after installation to verify compliance with crash-testing standards and proper anchorage.
Step nosing must be installed after the concrete stair treads have been poured and cured, as the nosing is embedded into or mounted onto the finished concrete surface.
The stair structure (stringers, risers, treads) must be framed before any step nosing can be attached to the finished stair assembly.

Step nosing is often installed as a finished edge or underlayment; rubber stair treads or other finished tread coverings must be installed after nosing to overlap or align properly with the nosing edge.

While stair railing can often be done independently, it is typical to complete step nosing first to ensure consistent walking surface before railing layout and fit-up, though not a strict physical dependency.

If the nosing requires painting or sealing, final finishes should be applied after installation to protect and match the nosing material. However, some nosing is pre-finished, making this a soft constraint.
The rough opening (framed and sized) must be prepared and ready before the egress door can be installed, as the door frame requires a structurally complete opening.
Wall framing must be completed to create the structural opening into which the egress door is placed.
Door hardware such as hinges, locks, handles, and panic bars can only be installed after the door is hung in its frame.
Weatherstripping and exterior caulking around the door frame must be applied after the door is installed to ensure a proper seal.
Building code inspection for egress compliance (clear width, swing direction, and hardware function) can only be performed once the door is fully installed.

predecessor: Framing and Structural Support for Stairs
rationale: The stair stringers and rough stair framing must be structurally complete to provide the load-bearing support onto which treads and risers are fastened.
Stair stringers form the angled structural sides of the staircase; treads and risers cannot be installed until stringers are in place and secured.
Handrails and balusters are typically mounted onto or adjacent to the finished treads; the treads must be installed first to provide the walking surface and attachment points for railing posts.

While it is physically possible to install adjacent flooring after treads and risers, doing so before may damage stair finishes; this ordering is a standard sequencing preference to achieve clean transitions and avoid rework.
The exposed surfaces of treads and risers must be installed before final finishing coats can be applied to them, as the finishing process cannot begin until the material is in place.
Wayfinding and egress signage is typically suspended from or mounted to the ceiling grid; the ceiling structure must be in place to provide the physical mounting support for signage.
Most illuminated or electronic wayfinding/egress signs require electrical power; conduit and wiring must be roughed in and ready before signs can be connected and installed.
Wall-mounted signage requires finished wall surfaces to ensure proper adhesion, alignment, and a clean final appearance; installing signs before finishes would damage or necessitate rework.
While not strictly required, installing egress signage over finished flooring allows for accurate height placement and avoids later damage/disruption from floor work.
All signage must be in place and visible before final inspection and commissioning can verify that egress paths are properly marked and wayfinding meets code requirements.

The concrete subfloor must be clean, dry, and properly prepared (e.g., patched, leveled, and cured) to ensure adhesion of the slip-resistant finish. Applying finish to an unprepared surface will result in delamination or failure.

A primer or sealer may be required by the manufacturer to seal the concrete and promote proper bonding of the slip-resistant coating. Skipping this step can compromise finish durability and slip resistance.

predecessor: Complete Overhead Work (e.g., ceiling, lighting, ductwork)
rationale: All overhead work that could generate dust, debris, or drips onto the wet floor finish must be finished before applying the floor coating to avoid contamination and surface defects.

successor: Allow Slip-Resistant Floor Finish to Cure
rationale: The applied finish must be left undisturbed for a specified curing/drying period (typically 24–72 hours depending on product) to achieve full hardness, adhesion, and slip-resistance before any foot traffic or subsequent work.

successor: Install Floor-Mounted Equipment (e.g., toilet partitions, lockers, heavy fixtures)
rationale: Heavy equipment or fixtures should be installed after the slip-resistant floor finish is fully cured to prevent damage to the coating and to ensure the finish is continuous under the equipment.
A stable foundation is required to support the front structural frame; without it, the frame cannot be properly anchored.

predecessor: Base Slab or Floor Deck Installation
rationale: The front structural frame must be erected on a solid base surface to ensure alignment and load distribution.
The front structural frame provides vertical support and attachment points for the roof structure.
The exterior wall cladding attaches to the front structural frame; the frame must be in place for cladding installation.
Windows and doors are installed within the openings of the front structural frame, requiring the frame to be completed first.
The structural frame must be erected to provide the supporting structure and openings into which glazing and window systems are installed.
Rough openings must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before windows and glazing can be fitted.
Air and water barrier systems around openings should be installed before windows to ensure proper sealing and prevent moisture intrusion.
Windows must be installed and sealed before interior finishes are applied to protect them from weather and to allow for proper trimming and sealing around openings.
Windows and glazing are typically installed before the final exterior cladding or siding around them so that flashings and trim can integrate properly with the cladding system.
The front canopy/marquee is typically supported by the main structural steel frame. The steel frame must be erected to provide the structural support and attachment points for the canopy.
The roof decking and waterproofing must be completed to ensure the canopy/marquee integrates properly with the building envelope and prevents water ingress at the junction.

The marquee/canopy is a prominent architectural feature that must be installed before the final front facade cladding and finishes, as the canopy often penetrates or attaches to the facade and the cladding must be detailed around it.

While canopy lighting can be roughed-in after installation, it is more efficient to coordinate electrical work with the canopy installation to avoid rework. This is a soft preference for workflow optimization.
Scaffolding at the front entrance area cannot be fully dismantled until the canopy/marquee is installed, as the scaffolding may be needed for access during canopy installation.
The building must be fully enclosed (walls, roof, doors, windows) to protect signage materials from weather damage and provide a stable substrate for mounting.
Exterior cladding, paint, or finished surfaces must be in place so that signage can be properly mounted, aligned, and adhered to the final surface.
Interior walls must be painted and finished before applying interior lettering and signage to ensure proper adhesion and a clean final appearance.
Signage installation generates debris and dust; it is preferable to complete all signage before final cleaning to avoid re-cleaning, though not a physical necessity.
Required life-safety signage (exits, addresses, occupancy signs) must be installed before municipal inspection and issuance of the certificate of occupancy.
Electrical rough-in work, including wiring and junction boxes, must be completed before front lighting fixtures can be installed, as the fixtures need to connect to the electrical supply.
The front structural framework must be in place to provide mounting surfaces and support for the lighting fixtures.
The main lighting fixture bodies must be installed before trim pieces, lenses, or final electrical connections can be completed.
While it is preferable to install lighting before finishing work to conceal wiring, it is not a strict physical requirement as long as access is maintained.
Fixtures must be physically installed before they can be tested, commissioned, and verified for proper operation.
The facade (curtain wall, cladding, or exterior panels) requires the primary structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) to be in place to provide a stable mounting surface and load-bearing support.
Floor slabs are needed at each level to provide a working platform and to transfer facade loads into the structure; facade panels are typically installed floor-by-floor after slabs are cured.
The building envelope must be closed in (watertight) before interior finishes such as drywall, painting, and flooring are installed to protect them from weather damage.
Facade support systems (rails, brackets, frames) must be in place before windows and glazing units can be inserted and sealed into the facade openings.

Scaffolding erected for facade work can be partially removed as facade installation progresses upward, but complete dismantling typically occurs after facade installation is finished to allow access for sealing and adjustments.
The structural frame must be fully erected and stable to provide a secure mounting surface and support for the front glazing system.
Rough openings must be framed, measured, and prepared to the correct dimensions to accommodate the glazing panels or curtain wall system.
Waterproofing and air barriers must be applied around openings to prevent moisture intrusion and air leakage before the glazing is installed, as these are inaccessible afterward.
Once the glazing is physically installed, all perimeter joints and interfaces must be sealed with weatherproof sealants to ensure watertightness and thermal performance.

Soft preference: interior finishes such as drywall, trim, and paint near the front glazing are typically done after glazing to avoid damaging the glass, but could theoretically be sequenced otherwise with protection measures.
The building entrance must be structurally prepared and leveled before the entrance system (doors, frames, thresholds) can be installed.
The wall openings for the entrance must be framed and structurally complete to provide a proper mounting surface for the entrance system.
Electrical wiring for automatic door operators, access control systems, and doorbell/intercom must be run before the entrance system covers the wall cavities.
Drywall and interior finishes around the entrance should be completed after the door frame is installed to ensure proper alignment and seamless trim work.
Automatic door operators, sensors, and access control hardware can only be connected and tested after the entrance system is physically mounted.
The front canopy is typically supported by or attached to the main structural steel frame, so the steel frame must be erected first to provide structural support for the canopy.
Foundations for the building and canopy columns must be completed to provide stable load-bearing support before the canopy structure is built.
The canopy structure must be in place before exterior cladding and finishing works can be completed around the entrance area, ensuring weatherproofing and aesthetic continuity.
Canopy installation should precede window and glazing work at the front facade to provide overhead protection and ensure proper integration of the entrance assembly.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work near the entrance is more efficiently done after the canopy is in place, though coordination could allow some parallel work with proper sequencing.
The structural framing and glass panels must be installed to provide a stable mounting surface and structural support for the front signage.

The facade finishing (e.g., ACM panels, stone cladding, or render) must be completed so signage brackets can be anchored to the finished surface without requiring rework or damage to unfinished cladding.
Conduit, junction boxes, and power supply wiring must be roughed-in behind the facade before signage is mounted to enable concealed electrical connections.
After the signage is physically mounted, the final electrical connections, trimming, and testing of illuminated signage can be completed.
Signage mounting is typically one of the last exterior tasks on a facade; once it is done, scaffolding or mast climbers can be dismantled since no further exterior work is needed.
The cornice and parapet are typically installed atop the roof deck or structural frame, so the supporting structure must be in place first.

Parapets and cornices often integrate with or cap the roofing system; the roofing membrane is usually installed after the parapet framing is complete to ensure proper flashing and watertight detailing.

Cornices and parapets form the top edge of the façade; exterior cladding and finish work at the upper roof level are typically sequenced after these elements are in place to achieve a clean transition.

Once cornice and parapet are completed, the scaffolding or edge protection at the roof perimeter can be removed and roof access closed off, though this is more of a logical sequence than a physical necessity.
If the cornice and parapet are masonry or concrete, the supporting bearing walls below must be completed to provide a base for the cornice/parapet construction.
The front stoop and steps rest on or against the foundation; the foundation must be in place to provide structural support and proper alignment.
The ground must be excavated and leveled to the correct elevation before the stoop and steps can be formed and poured or assembled.
The stoop and steps provide the access platform and threshold height reference for installing the front door at the correct elevation.
If the stoop has a porch above, the steps and stoop surface must be in place before railings or balustrades can be anchored to them.
It is preferable to complete the stoop and steps before final grading and landscaping around the entrance to avoid rework and ensure proper drainage against the structure.
The awning or sunshade device is typically mounted onto or anchored to the structural frame or roof structure, which must be in place to provide structural support.
Awnings and sunshade devices are often attached to exterior walls; the wall finish must be complete to provide a secure mounting surface and to avoid rework or damage to finished surfaces.
Although not always strictly required, it is best practice to install windows and doors first so that the awning can be accurately positioned relative to openings for proper shading and clearance.

Final touch-up painting or coating around the awning mounting locations is best done after installation to cover any holes, cuts, or scuffs, though this is a cosmetic preference rather than a physical necessity.

The awning/sunshade must be fully installed before the final building inspection and commissioning can verify that all exterior elements, including shading devices, are correctly in place and functional.

Security grilles and shutters are typically mounted onto or anchored to the building's structural frame (walls, columns, or lintels). The structural support must be in place before the grilles/shutters can be installed.

If the shutters are motorized, electrical wiring and conduit connections to the shutter housing must be completed after the shutter unit is physically installed, as wiring terminates at the motor location within the shutter assembly.
It is a soft preference to complete security shutter installation before adjacent interior finishing to avoid damage to finished surfaces during shutter installation work.

predecessor: Masonry / Concrete Work at Entrance Area
rationale: Any masonry or concrete work (e.g., door sills, entrance slab, or frame surrounds) must be cured and complete to provide a stable mounting surface for the grille/shutter frame.

successor: Final Testing & Commissioning of Security Systems
rationale: The grilles/shutters must be fully installed before final testing (e.g., opening/closing cycles, interlock with access control) can be performed to verify proper operation.
The foundation must be excavated before any column or pilaster can be erected, as the column requires a stable base and footing.
Concrete footings or foundation pads must be poured and cured to provide structural support for the column/pilaster.
Reinforcing steel in the foundation must be placed and tied before the column's starter bars or anchor bolts can be set.
The column/pilaster must be in place to support beams, lintels, or arches that rest on top of it.
The column provides vertical support for the roof structure, so it must be completed before roof framing can be installed above it.
The building must pass final inspection to ensure it meets life safety codes and is habitable before occupants can enter.
Legal occupancy requires a certificate of occupancy from the authority having jurisdiction, certifying the building complies with regulations.

predecessor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: Fire alarm and life safety systems must be fully operational and tested to protect occupants before they occupy the building.

predecessor: Means of Egress Completion (Doors, Stairs, Exit Signs, Emergency Lighting)
rationale: All exit paths, doors, stairways, exit signage, and emergency lighting must be complete and functional to allow safe occupant evacuation.

While not a life-safety requirement, interior finishes, flooring, and furnishings are typically completed before occupants move in for practical and contractual reasons, though temporary occupancy could occur without full finishes.
The building's structural elements (floors, walls, columns) must be in place before crowd flow analysis can be meaningful, as crowd movement depends on the physical layout and available pathways.
Emergency exits, stairwells, and corridor widths must be physically installed before accurate crowd flow rates and evacuation capacities can be computed or measured.
Interior walls, doors, and permanent partitions define circulation paths and bottlenecks; crowd flow analysis requires these spatial divisions to be finalized.
Regulatory authorities require demonstrated crowd flow capacities and egress compliance (derived from crowd flow analysis) before issuing an occupancy permit.

successor: Final Safety Signage and Wayfinding Installation
rationale: While not physically required, it is best practice to finalize crowd flow analysis first so that signage placement (e.g., exit signs, directional markers) can be optimized based on predicted movement patterns and bottleneck locations.
The building must be physically complete and safe for occupancy before occupants can move in.
Interior finishes such as flooring, walls, ceilings, and paint must be completed before occupants can be distributed into the spaces.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems must be tested and operational to support occupant needs before distribution.
Although often furniture is installed before occupants arrive, occupant distribution can guide final placement; this is a soft preference as furniture could be pre-installed.
After occupants are distributed, a final inspection ensures the building is safe and ready for full occupancy use.
Structural framing (columns, beams, floors) must be in place before egress components like stair cores and exit corridors can be installed, as these require support from the primary structure.
Exit staircases are critical egress components that must be built before the overall egress capacity of the building can be realized and verified.
Exit access corridors and passageways need to be framed and enclosed to provide the physical paths of egress before egress capacity can be functionally achieved.
Fire-rated doors serving exit enclosures and corridors must be installed after egress pathways are established to ensure proper integration and compliance with rated separation requirements.
Exit signs and emergency egress lighting must be installed after the egress paths and exit components are in place, so that they can be properly positioned along the completed routes.
The acoustic treatment must be applied inside the pocket frame cavity; the frame provides the structural enclosure and mounting surface for the acoustic material.
All wiring, conduit, and mechanical services should be roughed-in before acoustic insulation is installed to avoid later disturbance or damage to the treatment.
The acoustic treatment must be fully in place before the wall is enclosed with cladding or finish materials; otherwise the treatment becomes inaccessible.
It is preferred to install the acoustic treatment before fitting the pocket door to ensure unobstructed access, but the door could theoretically be installed afterward if carefully handled.
The acoustic treatment must be fully installed for the acoustic performance tests to be valid and representative of the completed condition.
Pocket partitions/enclosures need a framed opening to be installed into; rough carpentry creates the structural cavity that houses the sliding/folding partition system.

Any mechanical, electrical, or plumbing lines that would run through or behind the pocket partition area must be roughed in before the enclosure is built, to avoid needing to cut into or remove the finished enclosure later.
The pocket partition enclosure must be fully installed before drywall can be applied over it, so that the enclosure is flush with the finished wall surface and properly integrated.

While painting can technically occur after installation, it is standard practice to prime and paint after the enclosure is installed to achieve a uniform finish; this is a soft preference for aesthetics rather than a physical necessity.
The enclosure (pocket/framed cavity) must be complete before the sliding or folding door panels can be hung or inserted into the track system within the pocket.
A stable, level concrete slab or structural deck must be in place to support the integrated seating, as the seating is typically anchored or set onto the slab.
Electrical and data conduits for power outlets, USB ports, or data connections integrated into the seating pockets must be roughed in before the seating is installed and concealed.

Finish flooring (e.g., carpet, tile, LVT) around and up to the integrated seating pockets is completed after the seating units are positioned, so that flooring edges can be trimmed neatly against the seating bases.
Any surrounding millwork, baseboards, or trim pieces that abut the seating must be installed after the seating is in place to ensure proper fit and finish.

successor: Final painting and finishing of adjacent walls
rationale: While painting could be done beforehand, it is preferable to paint adjacent walls before seating installation to avoid overspray or damage to the finished seating, though this is a soft preference and can be reversed if needed.
The pocket work surface needs to be mounted to or within the pocket door frame, so the frame must be installed first to provide structural support.

predecessor: Frame Wall Opening for Pocket Door
rationale: The wall opening must be framed to create the pocket cavity before any pocket door components, including the work surface, can be installed.
The work surface may obstruct or be integrated with the door panel installation; the surface must be in place before the door panels are hung to ensure proper alignment and clearance.

successor: Finish Trim and Casing Around Pocket Door
rationale: Trim work should be done after the work surface is installed so that the casing fits neatly around both the door opening and the integrated surface.

If the work surface includes lighting or power outlets, rough-in wiring should be completed before the surface is installed to allow for concealed connections, though this is a design preference rather than a physical necessity.
Pocket storage units are typically installed within wall cavities; the stud wall framing must be in place to provide the structural support and recess space for the unit.
Any electrical wiring that runs through or behind the pocket storage area must be completed before the unit is installed to avoid blocking access or requiring removal of the unit later.

The pocket storage unit must be fully installed and secured before drywall or sheathing is applied, as the unit is recessed into the wall and would be inaccessible or damaged if drywall was installed first.
Interior finishes such as painting and trim work must follow pocket storage installation to ensure clean edges, proper fit around the unit, and to avoid paint drips or damage to the finished unit.
Internal shelving, dividers, or organizational components within the pocket storage unit can only be installed after the main unit shell is securely in place within the wall.
Electrical wiring must be roughed-in behind walls before power and data outlets can be installed, as the outlet boxes need to connect to the wiring system.
Walls must be framed to provide a surface and cavity for mounting pocket power and data outlet boxes.
Power and data outlets must be installed and their boxes positioned before drywall is cut and installed around them, as the outlets are mounted within the wall assembly.

successor: Final Trim and Finish Electrical Work
rationale: The pocket power and data outlet units must be in place before final trim-out, faceplate installation, and finishing electrical connections can be completed.

While painting can sometimes be done before outlet installation, installing pocket outlets after painting reduces touch-up work; typically outlets are installed after painting to avoid paint on fixtures.
