Wall framing provides the structural support required to mount the pocket display/tack surface.
Electrical rough-in must be completed behind the wall before the pocket display is installed, as it would be inaccessible afterwards.
Drywall provides a finished surface onto which the pocket display/tack surface can be mounted or recessed.
Trim work around the pocket display should be installed after the unit is in place to ensure proper fit and finish.
While touch-up painting can be done after installation, it is often preferred to paint the wall before mounting the display to avoid getting paint on the unit.

predecessor: Rough-in Electrical and Data Floor Box Conduit
rationale: Conduit and wiring for the floor box must be roughed-in before the floor box itself can be installed, as the floor box encloses and connects to these services.
The pocket floor box must be set in place before the concrete slab is poured, so that it is flush with the finished floor surface and properly embedded.
Floor coverings are cut and finished around the pocket floor box opening; therefore the floor box must be permanently installed first.

successor: Snap-in Power and Data Modules / Device Installation
rationale: The pocket floor box must be physically in place and the concrete cured before power/data devices can be snapped in and terminated.
After the concrete slab has cured, the pocket floor box trim/adjustment ring can be set to final grade to match the finished floor surface.
The pocket door or gateway frame must be installed within the wall cavity, requiring the rough framing and wall structure to be complete to provide the necessary support and opening.

Any electrical wiring, outlets, or plumbing that will run through or adjacent to the pocket door wall cavity must be roughed in before the pocket door frame is installed to avoid obstructions and rework.
Drywall must be installed after the pocket door frame and track are in place so that the drywall can be cut and finished around the pocket door opening and track housing.
The pocket door or gateway frame must be fully installed and secured before any interior trim, casing, or the door slab itself is hung and fitted.

While flooring can be installed after pocket door installation, it is often preferred to complete flooring first to allow the door to slide smoothly over the finished floor surface, though this is a sequencing preference rather than a hard physical constraint.

predecessor: Rough-in of electrical and mechanical systems
rationale: Electrical wiring, conduit, ductwork, and plumbing lines must be installed in the ceiling plenum before the pocket ceiling system is installed, as the pocket ceiling will enclose and conceal these systems, making post-installation access difficult and requiring costly rework.
The supporting ceiling grid or tracks (e.g., T-bar grid, furring channels) must be in place to provide the structural support and attachment points for the pocket ceiling system panels.
The pocket ceiling panels must be fully installed before final finishing coats (paint, acoustic spray, or texture) can be applied to the ceiling surface.
Although not a hard physical constraint, it is preferred to complete the ceiling work before flooring and trim to avoid dust and debris falling onto finished floors.
The building's structural framing (walls, roof/floor above) must be complete to define the ceiling cavity and provide the substrate for attaching the ceiling system.
Ductwork must be installed first to provide the pathway for conditioned air to reach the terminal unit.
The ceiling grid provides the structural support and pocket recess into which the terminal unit is placed.
Power supply wiring must be roughed-in to the location before the terminal unit can be connected and powered.
Control wiring and thermostat connections must be made after the terminal unit is physically installed.
Ceiling finishing work must occur after the pocket terminal unit is in place to ensure proper fit and alignment around the unit.
Pocket partitions require the wall framing to be in place as they are installed within the framed opening.
Electrical wiring within the wall cavity must be completed before installing the pocket partition to avoid interference and rework.
Drywall cannot be hung until the pocket partition frame and hardware are fully installed within the wall opening.
Finish trim work around the pocket door opening must wait until the partition is in place to ensure proper alignment and fit.
Painting of the wall surface requires the pocket partition to be installed and prepared, as the partition surface becomes part of the finished wall.
The structural floor slab must be poured and fully cured to provide a stable, load-bearing substrate for the pocket floor finish installation.

predecessor: Construction Activity: Underfloor Rough-In (MEP Rough-In Below Slab)
rationale: All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the slab or below-floor zone must be completed before the finish flooring is installed to avoid future demolition or rework.
A waterproof membrane or vapor barrier must be laid over the substrate to protect the floor finish from moisture migration before the pocket flooring system is installed.
Wall finishes such as baseboards, skirting, or wall cladding are typically installed after the floor finish is complete to allow the wall finish to overlap or abut the finished floor cleanly.
The pocket floor finish must be fully installed and protected before the space is turned over for occupancy, but this is a soft preference as temporary protection can allow early access.
Materials must be procured and available on-site before installation can commence.
The wall cavity or pocket structure must be framed and ready to receive the acoustic treatment materials.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins within the wall cavity must be completed before enclosing the space with acoustic treatment, to avoid rework.
Acoustic treatment must be installed inside the pocket before the wall surface is closed with drywall and finished.
The pocket acoustic treatment must be fully installed in order to conduct valid acoustic performance tests of the completed assembly.
The pocket wall framing provides the structural support and enclosure within which the integrated furniture must be installed, so framing must be completed first.
Electrical wiring and outlets needed for integrated furniture (e.g., lighting, power) must be roughed in behind the wall before furniture is installed, as access will be blocked afterward.
Any plumbing lines serving the integrated furniture (e.g., for sinks or water features) must be installed within the wall cavity before furniture placement, as they will be inaccessible afterward.
Once the integrated furniture is installed in the pocket, the surrounding wall surfaces can be finished and painted to seamlessly blend with the furniture, creating a flush, built-in appearance.

While flooring can be installed before integrated furniture in some cases, it is preferred to install flooring after to ensure the furniture sits perfectly on top of the finished floor and to avoid damaging the flooring during furniture installation.

The building structure must be complete (walls, slabs, columns) before any electrical fit-out can commence, as the electrical conduits, back boxes, and wiring are embedded in or run along structural elements.

Primary electrical rough-in work (main cables, distribution boards, sub-mains) must be installed first to provide the source feeds that the pocket lighting and final electrical fit-out will connect to.
Lighting fixtures, switches, sockets, and electrical fit-out must be installed before ceilings are closed up and final finishes (paint, wall coverings) are applied, to avoid rework and damage.
All electrical fit-out work including pocket lighting must be fully installed before the system can be tested and commissioned for safety and functionality.
The electrical fit-out including lighting must be complete and operational before the building can be handed over to the client or occupants.
The pocket must be excavated before any commissioning activities can take place within it.
Formwork must be installed and secured before commissioning the pocket to ensure structural readiness.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied before commissioning to verify structural integrity.
Concrete must be poured and fully cured to achieve required strength before pocket commissioning can proceed.
Backfilling around the pocket can only commence after commissioning verifies that the pocket is properly constructed and safe.
The MEP rough-in (electrical, plumbing, mechanical) must be installed within the wall cavity, which is only accessible after the pocket framing is complete but before the wall is closed up.
Insulation must be installed after MEP rough-in work is complete so that the insulation does not block access to MEP components and to avoid damaging insulation during MEP installation.
Drywall installation closes the wall cavity; all MEP rough-in work must be finished and inspected before the wall is enclosed with drywall.
While the door frame can theoretically be installed before MEP rough-in, it is preferred to complete MEP work first to avoid interference and rework around the door frame elements.
The structural slab or floor deck provides the base surface and support for the pocket wall system and its MEP rough-in; work cannot start without the structural base in place.
The stair seat (the horizontal seating portion) must be installed first so that the riser (the vertical face below the seat) can be fitted against and aligned with the seat bottom.
Stair stringers provide the structural framework for the staircase; risers are attached to stringers and cannot be installed until stringers are in place.
Final trim, caulking, or finishing work on the riser surface can only be applied after the riser itself is fully installed and secured.
If treads are located below the stair seat riser, the riser must be installed before the tread below to establish the vertical back face of the step.
General framing and subflooring must be completed before any stair components, including risers, are installed to provide a stable base and proper alignment.
Stair stringers provide the structural support framework that carries treads; seat treads cannot be installed without the stringers in place to rest upon.
Risers are typically installed first to define the vertical spacing and backing for treads; seat treads are then placed on top of or against the risers.
Handrails and balusters are often anchored to or aligned with the treads; the treads must be in place to provide the walking surface and mounting points for rail posts.

Stair nosing (if used as a separate piece) is typically applied after treads are installed to finish the front edge; however, some treads come pre-finished with integral nosing, making this a soft preference.

Final protective coatings, sealants, or paint should be applied after all treads are installed to avoid damaging the finish during subsequent work; however, pre-finished treads may eliminate this need.
The stair rough framing, including the stringers and tread support structure, must be built first to provide the structural framework onto which the stair seat stringer is attached.
The landing or platform at the top and/or bottom of the stairs must be constructed to provide a bearing surface and anchorage point for the stair seat stringer.
The adjacent wall framing must be complete to provide lateral support and attachment points for the stair seat stringer.
Stair treads are installed directly onto or supported by the stair seat stringer; therefore, the seat stringer must be in place and secured before treads can be placed.
Stair risers are typically attached to the stringer or to the tread-riser assembly; the seat stringer must be installed first to provide the vertical support structure for the risers.
The stair structure must be physically in place to provide a mounting surface for the stair seat handrail.
If the stairs are concrete, the concrete must be poured and sufficiently cured to support the handrail anchors and structural loads.
Finishing work like painting or sealing can be done after installation, but it is a soft preference to do finishing after to avoid damaging the finish during installation.
The handrail must be fully installed before it can be inspected for compliance with building codes and safety standards.
Final cleaning is typically performed after all installation work is completed to remove debris and dust, but this is a preference rather than a physical necessity.
The stair structure must be framed and roughed-in to provide a substrate for the seat nosing to be installed onto.
Stair treads are typically installed before seat nosing, as the nosing sits at the edge of the tread/riser intersection.

successor: Stair Finishing / Carpet or Hard Surfacing
rationale: The nosing must be in place before final floor or stair surface finishes are applied, as the finish material abuts or wraps the nosing.
While often done after nosing for alignment, handrails can technically be installed before nosing if layout is predetermined; this is a soft preference for coordination.
If the nosing is set into concrete or over a subfloor, the base surface must be prepared and cured before nosing installation.
The guardrail/balustrade is mounted onto or adjacent to the stair seat structure; the supporting frame must be in place first to provide anchorage for the guardrail.
Guardrails/balustrades are typically anchored into the stair treads or adjacent concrete; the concrete must be cured to sufficient strength to support the anchorage loads.
Though often integrated, a separate handrail is typically installed after or concurrently with the balustrade to align with the same anchoring points and ensure consistent height and spacing.

successor: Final Inspection / Safety Certification of Stair Seating
rationale: Guardrails and balustrades serve critical life-safety functions; they must be fully installed before the seating area can be certified as safe for occupancy or use.

Finishing work such as painting, caulking, or cosmetic trim around the stair seat is typically done after the guardrail is in place to achieve a clean, integrated appearance and to seal attachment points.
The stair structure must be fully installed to provide a stable surface for mounting the handrail and seat lighting components.
Electrical wiring for the lighting components must be run and roughed in before the handrail and seat lighting fixtures can be connected and installed.
The seat frame must be assembled and in place so that the handrail and integrated lighting can be aligned and attached to the seat structure.
After the handrail lighting is installed, the lighting system must be tested and adjusted to ensure proper illumination and functionality.

Finish carpentry such as trim and molding around the handrail and seat area is typically done after lighting installation to avoid damage, though it is a soft preference rather than a strict physical requirement.
The stair seat structure must be installed to provide the physical framework onto which the lighting tread components will be mounted.

predecessor: Electrical Rough-In for Stair Seat Area
rationale: Electrical wiring and junction boxes must be roughed-in before installing the lighting tread, as the tread integrates lighting fixtures that need power supply connections behind or within the structure.
The lighting tread is a foundational or embedded component; finish coverings or surface treatments over the tread area can only be applied after the lighting tread unit is fully installed and tested.

successor: Stair Seat Lighting Testing and Commissioning
rationale: Testing and commissioning of the integrated lighting system must occur after the lighting tread is installed to verify proper illumination, electrical connections, and safety compliance.
Final inspections typically occur after all components including the lighting tread are in place, though this is a logical sequence preference rather than a physical necessity.
Reinforcement steel (rebar) must be installed and tied in place before concrete can be poured to form the stair seat concrete structure.
Formwork (mould) must be erected and secured to contain the wet concrete and shape the stair seat before the concrete pour can take place.
Concrete must be poured and gain sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed (struck) from the stair seat.
Once the concrete is poured, it must undergo a curing period to achieve the required strength and durability before any subsequent loads are applied.
The cured concrete stair seat provides the substrate onto which waterproofing membrane can be applied to protect the structure from moisture ingress.

predecessor: Steel Structure Foundation / Base Plate Installation
rationale: The stair seat steel structure must be anchored to a prepared steel foundation or base plate. Without the base/foundation in place, there is no structural support to attach the stair seat.

predecessor: Main Steel Structure Erection (Primary Columns & Beams)
rationale: The stair seat is a secondary steel component that connects to the main steel frame. The primary columns and beams must be erected first to provide the connection points and supporting framework for the stair seat.
Stair stringers (the inclined beams supporting the stair treads) are typically welded or bolted to the stair seat. The seat must be in place to receive and support the stringers.

Stair treads and risers are supported by the stair stringers which connect to the stair seat. The seat (and subsequently the stringers) must be installed before any tread/riser components can be placed.
The stair seat must be installed first to provide the physical mounting surface and structure for the convection heater to be attached to.
Electrical wiring and conduit must be roughed in to the stair seat location before the heater can be connected and installed.
The heater must be physically mounted before final electrical connections and trim-out can be completed to ensure safe and code-compliant wiring termination.
Testing of the heater operation can only occur after the heater is fully installed and electrically connected.

Final trim and finish work around the stair seat area is typically done after heater installation to avoid damaging finishes, though some finish work could potentially be done in parallel with careful sequencing.
The stair seat (landing or platform) must be structurally supported by the building's structural frame before the fire-rated enclosure walls can be built around it.
The floor slab or deck at each stair level must be in place to provide the base surface upon which the stair seat and its fire-rated enclosure will sit.

predecessor: Stair Structural Support / Stair Stringers Installation
rationale: The stair flight structural supports (stringers and treads) must be installed to define the stair geometry before the fire-rated enclosure can be framed around the stair opening.

successor: Fire-Rated Door Installation at Stair Enclosure
rationale: Fire-rated doors that provide access into the enclosed stair must be installed after the enclosure framing is complete to ensure proper fit, sealing, and fire-rating continuity.

successor: Firestopping and Sealant Application at Enclosure Penetrations
rationale: Firestopping and sealants are applied after the enclosure is fully built to seal all joints, gaps, and penetrations, maintaining the fire-resistance rating of the assembly.
Rough electrical work including conduit and wiring must be installed in the stair structure before the power/data outlet can be connected and mounted.
The stair structure and seating frame must be built and in place to provide a mounting surface and backing for the power/data outlet box.

successor: Outlet Trim and Cover Plate Installation
rationale: The outlet must be fully installed and wired before the trim-out phase where cover plates and final finishes are applied.
The power/data outlet must be complete and connected to allow for final electrical testing, verification of continuity, and safety inspection.
The power/data outlet must be installed before adjacent finish materials such as upholstery, cushions, or seat covers are applied, to avoid damage to finishes and allow access for wiring connections.
Stair stringers provide the primary structural support framework for the stairs; the seat structure must be mounted onto or supported by the stringers, so stringers must be in place first.

predecessor: Complete Rough Framing of Staircase Area
rationale: The rough framing defines the overall stair opening and structural support system, which is necessary before any stair components like the seat structure can be installed.
The seat structure supports the treads and risers; treads and risers must be placed onto or secured to the seat structure after it is installed.
Handrails and guardrails are often installed after the seat structure is in place so they can be aligned and secured to the completed stair assembly, though sometimes they are installed concurrently.

successor: Apply Finish Materials to Stair Structure
rationale: Finishes such as paint, stain, or sealant are applied after the structural components including the seat structure are fully installed to avoid damaging finishes during construction.
Stair seat railings must be attached to the stair framing structure, which provides the underlying support.
The stair seat railings are mounted onto the completed stair treads and risers, providing the finished walking surface and structural base.
The final inspection must occur after all stair components, including seat railings, are installed to verify compliance and safety.

successor: Apply Finish or Paint to Railings
rationale: While finishing can be done after installation, it is a soft preference as touch-ups may be needed post-installation but could also be done before.
Seat railings are typically installed before balusters as the railings form the top structure that balusters connect to.
The stair seat (the structural framing that supports the stair finish) must be built and in place before any finish material can be applied to it.
A smooth, stable subfloor or underlayment is required as the base for the stair seat finish material (e.g., treads, risers, carpet, or tile).
Any rough-in work within or near the stair structure must be finished before the finish surface is installed to avoid rework or damage to the finish.
Railings and balusters are typically mounted on or after the finished stair treads and risers are in place, as they often anchor into the finished surface.
Final trim, scotia, or quarter-round molding is installed after the main finish material to cover gaps and provide a clean transition.
The stair seat lighting is integrated into or mounted onto the stair structure itself; the physical stair frame must be in place to provide a mounting surface for the seat lights.

predecessor: Run Electrical Rough-In for Stair Area
rationale: Electrical wiring, conduit, and junction boxes must be installed in the stair area before the seat lighting fixtures can be connected and energized.

The seat lighting fixtures are typically recessed or mounted flush with the finished stair surface; finishing materials should not be installed until lighting placement is finalized to avoid damage or misalignment.
The lighting fixtures must be physically installed before final electrical connections, switch installation, and system testing can be completed.

predecessor: Complete Structural Framing of Stair Area
rationale: The structural frame must be in place to provide a stable mounting surface and support for the stair seat integrated equipment.

predecessor: Rough-in Electrical and Low-Voltage Wiring to Stair Location
rationale: Electrical and low-voltage wiring must be roughed in behind or within the stair area before the seat equipment is installed, as access will be blocked afterward.

predecessor: Complete Floor Slab/Subfloor at Stair Base
rationale: The floor/subfloor provides the foundational surface on which the stair seat equipment sits and must be fully cured and level.

successor: Finish Flooring and Wall Finishes Adjacent to Stair Seat
rationale: The seat equipment must be installed first so that finish materials (tile, carpet, wallboard) can be cut, trimmed, and fitted tightly around the installed unit for a clean appearance.
Final connections and testing of the seat's electrical features (e.g., lighting, controls) can only be performed after the equipment is physically mounted in its permanent position.
Bleacher seating requires a level, stable base surface (typically a concrete slab or foundation) to be installed upon, ensuring proper load distribution and structural stability.
Structural steel supports often form the primary framework that bleacher seating is attached to or rests upon; the steel structure must be in place first.
Handrails and guardrails are typically installed after bleacher seating to ensure proper alignment with seat rows and to meet safety codes for egress.
While it is easier to finish floors before installing bleachers, if access allows, finishing can be done after; however, it is a soft preference to do it beforehand to avoid difficult access.
Bleacher seating must be fully installed and secure before final safety inspections and occupancy approvals can be completed for the facility.
The monolithic stair bench requires a stable, level foundation or subfloor to bear its weight and integrate structurally. Without proper subfloor preparation, the bench cannot be securely placed.
The stair bench is often cast or built against or between walls; rough framing provides the necessary support structure and alignment reference for the bench installation.
Finish flooring (tile, hardwood, etc.) is typically laid after the bench is in place so that flooring can be cut or fitted neatly around or up to the bench base.
Drywall and wall finishes should follow bench installation so that the bench can be properly integrated with the wall surface, avoiding gaps or misalignment.

If the bench is made of concrete or masonry, sealing or waterproofing is recommended after curing; however, this is a protective/preventive preference rather than a physical necessity for construction sequencing.
The central structural core requires a solid foundation to transfer its loads to the ground; without the foundation, the core would have no stable base.
The site must be excavated and prepared before any structural elements, including the central core, can be constructed.
Floor slabs typically connect to or are supported by the central core; the core must be in place to provide lateral stability and support for floor systems.
The central core often provides the primary lateral load-resisting system; exterior walls and framing rely on the core for stability during construction.
Elevator shafts are typically housed within the central structural core; the core must be completed before elevator rails, cars, and mechanical systems can be installed.
The central staircase requires a solid foundation to support its structural load; the foundation must be completed before any vertical structural elements like staircases are installed.
The central staircase is typically housed within or adjacent to the building's core walls; these walls must be erected first to provide structural support and enclosure for the staircase.
The staircase originates from the ground floor level; the ground floor slab must be poured and cured to provide a level base and landing for the staircase installation.

The central staircase provides access to upper floors, but the upper floor slabs cannot be fully completed until the staircase structure is in place to support formwork and access for workers and materials.
Railings and handrails are installed onto the completed staircase structure; the staircase structure must be fully erected before safety railings can be attached.
The steel frame provides the structural support for the atrium; the floor slab opening must be framed and supported by the steel structure before concrete can be placed.

Any mechanical, electrical, or plumbing lines that run beneath the atrium slab must be installed before the slab is poured, as access will be blocked once the opening is formed and concrete is placed.

predecessor: Formwork and Shoring Installation for Atrium Opening
rationale: Formwork and temporary shoring must be erected to define the edges of the opening and support the wet concrete during the pour.

successor: Atrium Glazing and Curtain Wall Installation
rationale: The floor slab opening creates the vertical atrium space; the curtain wall or glazing system that encloses the atrium can only be installed after the slab-edge structure is permanent and the opening is fully formed.

successor: Interior Finishes and Railings Around Atrium Opening
rationale: Finish work such as floor toppings, waterproofing, and safety railings at the edge of the atrium opening depend on the concrete slab being poured, cured, and stripped of formwork first.
The central service core must be built on a stable foundation; foundation work must be completed before any superstructure elements like the service core can be erected.
MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) services entering the building from below must be laid in the ground before the core, which houses vertical risers for these services, is constructed.

The central service core provides lateral stability and vertical circulation; floor slabs typically frame into or are supported by the core, so the core must be in place before floor slabs can be installed.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing risers run within the central service core; rough-in installation can only proceed after the core structure is complete.
Elevator shafts are typically housed within the central service core; the core structure must be completed before elevator rails, cabs, and equipment can be installed.

successor: Atrium Glazing and Curtain Wall Installation
rationale: The structural steel frame must be in place to provide the supporting framework onto which the curtain wall and glazing system is attached and anchored.

successor: Atrium Glazing and Curtain Wall Installation
rationale: The atrium floor slabs must be completed to provide the base support and working platform for installing the curtain wall and glazing panels.

successor: Atrium Glazing and Curtain Wall Installation
rationale: Overhead roof structure must be in place to provide top anchorage points and to allow curtain wall mullions to be secured at both bottom and top.

predecessor: Atrium Glazing and Curtain Wall Installation
rationale: The curtain wall must be fully installed and weathertight before interior finishes such as drywall, painting, and flooring can proceed to avoid water damage and to establish the building envelope.

predecessor: Atrium Glazing and Curtain Wall Installation
rationale: While some MEP rough-in can begin earlier, final tie-ins and ductwork routing adjacent to the glazing should be completed after the curtain wall is in place to ensure proper fit and coordination with the glazing system.

The central vertical MEP risers run through structural shafts and chases within the building core. The core and shell structure (including slabs, walls, and shaft openings) must be fully constructed and cured before any riser installation can begin, as the risers physically depend on the structural enclosure for support and routing.

Central vertical risers are the main trunks that supply MEP services (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) to each floor. Horizontal branch distribution on each floor cannot commence until the vertical risers are installed and connected, as the horizontal runs take off from the riser connections.

After MEP risers are installed within vertical shafts, fire-stopping materials and shaft enclosures must be applied around the penetrations and throughout the shaft to restore fire-resistance ratings. This sealing cannot be completed before the risers are in place.

While some preliminary testing of individual components can occur earlier, full integrated system testing and commissioning of MEP systems requires the vertical risers to be installed and connected so that the systems can be pressurized, energized, and verified end-to-end.

predecessor: Rough-in of Floor Penetrations and Sleeves
rationale: Prior to installing vertical risers, all floor and wall penetrations/sleeves must be set and rough-in work completed. The riser pipes, ducts, and conduits pass through these pre-formed openings; the sleeves must be in place to guide and support the riser runs.

successor: Central Corridor Ceiling and Lighting Installation
rationale: All mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and data rough-in work must be completed in the central corridor before the ceiling can be enclosed and lighting installed. This is a hard physical constraint because once the ceiling is installed, access to overhead rough-in elements is blocked.

successor: Central Corridor Ceiling and Lighting Installation
rationale: The ceiling grid and lighting fixtures require the corridor walls and bulkheads to be framed and boarded so that the ceiling system has proper support structure and the finished wall heights are established.

predecessor: Central Corridor Ceiling and Lighting Installation
successor: Central Corridor Painting and Finish Work
rationale: Ceiling installation must precede final painting and finishing because paint and surface treatments are applied after the ceiling grid, tiles, and lighting fixtures are in place to ensure clean finish lines and avoid damaging newly painted surfaces.

predecessor: Central Corridor Ceiling and Lighting Installation
rationale: Flooring work (such as tile, VCT, or carpet) is typically installed after the ceiling and lighting are complete to protect the finished floor from dust, debris, and potential damage from overhead work like ceiling tile cutting and fixture installation.

predecessor: Central Corridor Ceiling and Lighting Installation
successor: Central Corridor Final Electrical Trim and Light Switch Installation
rationale: Final trim-out of electrical devices such as light switches and wall plates on the corridor walls typically follows completion of the ceiling and lighting installation, as the lighting circuit connections must be fully installed and tested before switch plates are finalized.
The structural frame of the central staircase must be fully erected and cured before precast treads can be installed, as the treads rest on and are supported by the structural frame.

predecessor: Central Staircase Landing Slab Pour & Cure
rationale: Landing slabs must be cast and cured to provide bearing surfaces for the precast treads at each floor level.
Handrails and balustrades are anchored to or mounted on the installed treads; the treads must be in place to provide the substrate and alignment reference.
Grouting of tread joints, pointing, and final surface finishing cannot commence until all precast treads are placed and aligned.

successor: Central Staircase Nosing & Anti-Slip Strip Installation
rationale: While nosing and anti-slip strips are typically installed after tread placement, minor adjustments could theoretically allow earlier installation off-site; however, standard practice places them after installation for alignment with the completed staircase geometry.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any wall foundation can be laid to ensure proper structural support.
A concrete footing or foundation must be poured and cured to provide a stable base for the privacy screen wall to bear its load and resist overturning.
Underground utilities in the wall's footprint must be located and moved to prevent damage and ensure safety during excavation and construction.
Any stucco, paint, stain, sealant, or other surface finish can only be applied after the wall structure is fully erected and cured.

successor: Landscaping and Planting Adjacent to Wall
rationale: While landscaping can begin after the wall is built to avoid damage to plants during construction, some planting could theoretically be done beforehand, so this is a soft preference for sequencing efficiency.
The structural steel frame provides the primary support and attachment points for the louver system. Without the completed frame, there is no structure to mount the louver onto.

The louver is typically integrated into the building envelope wall assembly. The wall framing and sheathing must be in place to define the opening and provide the surrounding structure for proper louver installation.

The louver must be installed before final exterior cladding or finishes are applied around it, as the louver is often embedded within or adjacent to the finished facade. Installing cladding first would block access.
The louver often extends through the ceiling plane or soffit area. Ceiling finishes cannot be completed until the louver housing and trim are in place to ensure a clean transition and seal.

If the louver is part of an air intake/exhaust system, mechanical balancing should occur after the louver is installed to account for actual airflow resistance. However, some balancing can be adjusted later.
The structural frame and exterior sheathing must be in place to define the opening and provide structural support for the recessed entry alcove.
The floor surface at the entry must be installed before the alcove can be framed and finished to ensure proper alignment and elevation.
The recessed alcove framing and rough opening must be completed before doors or windows can be installed into that opening.
The alcove assembly must be in place to properly apply weather-resistant cladding, flashing, and sealing around the recessed area.
Interior finishes around the entry alcove cannot be completed until the alcove framing and any backing are installed.
The door frame must be installed and properly aligned before the layered door assembly can be hung or fitted into the opening.

predecessor: Wall Framing and Rough Opening Preparation
rationale: The wall structure and rough opening must be framed and completed to provide the correct dimensions and support for the door assembly.
Door hardware such as hinges, locks, and handles must be installed after the layered door assembly is in place to ensure proper fit and alignment.
Weatherstripping and perimeter sealing can only be applied after the door assembly is installed to ensure continuous sealing around the door edges.

successor: Final Finishing and Painting of Door Assembly
rationale: Final finishing coats and painting of the door assembly should be performed after installation to avoid damage during handling and to achieve a seamless finish.
Electrical and data rough-in work must be completed before installing partitions, as the partitions would block access to walls and conceal the rough-in locations.
Plumbing rough-in for any nearby fixtures (e.g., water lines, drains) must be finished before partitions are installed, as partitions restrict access to plumbing chases.

predecessor: Complete Ceiling Grid and Overhead Work
rationale: Overhead ceiling grid, sprinklers, and lighting must be completed before partitions are installed so that the partitions align correctly with the ceiling layout and overhead work is not obstructed.
Flooring is typically installed after partitions to allow for continuous flooring without cuts around partition bases, and partitions must be in place to define floor zones.
Partition surfaces must be installed before they can be painted or finished, as painting is a final surface treatment applied after the partition structure is in place.
The access control system must be physically installed (hardware, controllers, readers, locks) before it can be commissioned, tested, and programmed.
Power and data cabling must be run to all door access control panels and devices before the system can be powered on and commissioned.
Commissioning (programming, configuring, initial testing) must be completed before formal integrated testing of the system can occur.

successor: Train End Users on Access Control System
rationale: It is preferable but not physically mandatory that commissioning is complete before user training, so that training reflects the final configured system.

successor: Hand Over Door Access Control System to Owner
rationale: The system must be fully commissioned and verified operational before it can be formally handed over to the building owner or facility management.
Window frames must be in place before applying film to the glazing, as the film is applied to the glass surface installed within the frame.
The glass surface must be thoroughly cleaned and free of dust, debris, or oils to ensure proper adhesion of the fritted glazing film.

predecessor: Deliver and Store Fritted Glazing Film On-Site
rationale: The film material must be delivered to the site and properly acclimated/stored before application can commence.
After the film is applied, an inspection must be performed to verify correct installation, adhesion, and absence of bubbles or defects before any subsequent work.

successor: Install Interior Finishes (if adjacent to glazing)
rationale: It is generally easier and preferable to apply window film before interior finishes are installed adjacent to windows, to avoid damaging finished surfaces, but this is often a soft preference rather than a strict physical requirement.
The structural frame (walls, headers, sills) must be in place and the rough openings framed to the correct dimensions before windows can be installed.

predecessor: Rough-In Waterproofing / Flashing at Rough Openings
rationale: Weather-resistive barriers, sill pans, and flashing must be applied to the rough openings prior to window installation to ensure proper water management and prevent moisture intrusion behind the window frame.
Exterior cladding is installed up to and integrated with the window frames after windows are in place, allowing proper flashing integration, trim, and a weathertight seal around the window perimeter.
Windows must be installed and sealed before interior finishes are applied adjacent to windows, to avoid damage to finishes and to allow proper installation of window trim and sill work.
Window casings, sills, and interior trim around windows can only be installed after the window units are permanently fixed and sealed in the rough openings.
The structural roof deck and steel framing must be in place to provide the support structure onto which skylights and roof glazing are installed.
Rough framing around roof openings must be completed to define the curbs and openings where skylight units will be set.
Roof membrane must be installed after skylights so it can be properly flashed and integrated around the skylight curbs to ensure watertightness.
Interior ceiling finishes are often completed after skylight installation to avoid damage from glazing work above, though some sequences may allow parallel work with protection.
Flashings and waterproofing details around skylight penetrations must be applied immediately after the skylight is set to seal the roof penetration before any subsequent work.
Light tubes and solar tunnels are installed through the roof structure; the structural framing and roof deck must be in place to provide the penetration points and support for the tube assemblies.
Coordination of ducting and electrical pathways near roof penetrations is easier if rough-in MEP work is completed first to avoid clashes with light tube routing.
Light tubes terminate at the ceiling level; interior ceiling finish work (drywall, taping, painting) cannot proceed until the tube diffuser assembly is installed and the opening is trimmed out.
Final electrical trim-out and lighting fixture installation is preferably sequenced after light tubes are in place to coordinate diffuser placement and avoid rework.
The structural framework and building envelope (walls, roof, slab edges) must be in place to provide the physical mounting points and support structure for sunshades and solar control devices.
Sunshades and solar control devices are typically mounted adjacent to or above windows and glazed areas; windows must be installed first to ensure correct alignment, clearance, and sealing details.
The exterior cladding or finish around mounting locations must be completed so that sunshade brackets and anchors can be properly attached to the finished surface without later rework.

While not a hard physical constraint, it is preferable to complete final painting and aesthetic finishes after sunshade installation to avoid damaging the devices or needing touch-ups around newly installed brackets.

Commissioning of solar control and shading systems (e.g., automated louver testing, sensor calibration) should occur after the physical devices are installed, though this is a logical sequence rather than a strict physical dependency.
The structural framing and roof deck must be in place to provide the supporting structure onto which light shelves and reflectors are mounted.
Interior walls define the occupied spaces and fenestration locations; light shelves must align with windows and interior partitions so these need to be framed first.
Light shelves are typically installed adjacent to or above windows to redirect daylight; the window frames and glazing must be in place to set proper alignment and sealing.

Light shelves affect the light distribution pattern on walls and ceilings; final paint and ceiling finishes should be applied after the reflectors are installed to avoid damage and ensure correct visual appearance.

While not physically required, it is preferable to install light shelves and reflectors before finalizing electric lighting fixtures so that daylighting performance can be assessed and electric lighting controls can be calibrated accordingly.

predecessor: Structural Framing and Ceiling Grid Installation
rationale: Structural framing and ceiling grids must be installed first to provide the supporting structure and overhead attachments for interior glazed partition systems.
MEP rough-in work including ductwork, piping, and electrical conduits must be completed before enclosing walls with glazed partitions to avoid rework and access issues.
Floor preparation and subfloor work must be done before glazed partitions are installed since the partition tracks are anchored to the finished floor surface.

successor: Overhead Doors and Architectural Millwork Installation
rationale: While not a strict physical dependency, installing overhead doors and architectural millwork after glazed partitions is preferred to avoid damaging the glass panels during heavy material handling.

Final painting and wall finishes should follow glazed partition installation because the partition frames integrate with surrounding walls, and painting after installation ensures a clean, continuous finish without masking or touch-ups.
The structural frame and roof must be in place to provide the load-bearing support and mounting surface for photovoltaic glazing and building-integrated photovoltaic (BIPV) panels.
Basic weatherproofing (e.g., roof underlayment, air/vapor barriers) must be installed before BIPV components to prevent moisture ingress behind the panels and ensure a continuous building envelope.
Conduits, junction boxes, and rough wiring for the PV system must be in place before the panels are installed so that connections can be made directly during panel mounting.
The BIPV panels and photovoltaic glazing must be physically installed before the final electrical connections to inverters and the building's electrical system can be completed.
System commissioning, performance testing, and grid connection testing can only occur after all BIPV panels are installed and electrically connected.
Building structural frame and roof must be in place to provide mounting points and support for sun-control systems such as louvers, shades, or overhangs.

predecessor: Completion of Building Envelope (Walls and Windows)
rationale: Exterior walls and windows define the surfaces adjacent to which sun-control devices are installed; the envelope must be finished to anchor and fit the systems properly.

Sun-control systems (e.g., external blinds, shading screens) must be mounted before interior finishes to allow access and avoid damage, and before final sealing of windows to integrate shading components.
Motorized sun-control systems require power and control wiring that must be run after the devices are installed and accessible.

successor: Final Commissioning and Testing of Shading Systems
rationale: Commissioning and testing of automated sun-control devices must occur after physical installation to verify operation.

Structural framing, roof deck installation, and rough-in work (MEP rough-ins) must be completed to provide the mounting surfaces and clear openings for daylight redirecting devices such as light shelves, tubular daylight devices (TDDs), or prismatic panels.

A watertight roof and proper flashing must be in place before installing roof-penetrating daylight devices (e.g., tubular daylight devices or skylight-integrated redirecting systems) to prevent water intrusion and damage to interior work.

Daylight redirecting devices are often mounted within or integrated with ceiling systems or upper wall assemblies; completing their installation before final ceiling grid, drywall, and painting avoids rework and ensures proper alignment and sealing.

Daylight redirecting devices impact the daylight-responsive lighting control zones; photosensors and dimming ballasts must be commissioned after the devices are in place to calibrate the lighting control system to the actual daylight distribution.

The performance of daylight redirecting devices must be verified during building commissioning to confirm that daylight penetration, glare control, and energy savings meet design specifications; this can only occur after full installation.
The structural frame and rough openings (window/door openings) must be built and prepared before glazing units can be physically placed and secured within them.
The weather-resistive barrier and flashing systems around openings should be in place prior to installing windows and glazing to ensure proper integration and prevent moisture intrusion.
Windows and glazing must be installed and sealed before interior wall finishes (e.g., drywall, trim, painting) can be completed around the openings to avoid damage and allow proper detailing.

While windows are often installed as the exterior cladding progresses, ideally glazing installation precedes final exterior finishes to ensure proper flashing integration and a weathertight seal; however, sequencing can vary.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins that connect through or around fenestration (e.g., weep holes, sensors, or power for motorized blinds) must be completed after the glazing is installed for accurate fit and integration.
The reception seating needs a stable, level floor base to be built upon; if installed before floor prep, the seating would be uneven or unstable.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical wiring for reception area
rationale: Electrical wiring for lighting, power outlets, and any integrated charging ports must be run in the walls and floor before the seating structure is built, as it would be inaccessible or very costly to retrofit afterward.

The reception counter is typically positioned adjacent to or integrated with the seating; constructing the seating first provides the spatial reference and clearance needed to properly align and install the counter.
It is preferable to complete painting and wall finishing before installing seating to avoid damaging finished surfaces, but if seating is built first, touch-up painting can still be done afterwards.
The seating structure often sits on top of or abuts the finished flooring; installing flooring after the seating avoids cutting around the built-in unit and ensures a seamless, professional finish.
Interior finishes provide the background surfaces and visual environment where signage will be mounted; signage cannot be installed before walls, floors, and ceilings are finished.
Signage, especially illuminated or backlit wayfinding signs, requires electrical power connections; electrical rough-in must be completed to provide power to signage locations.
Signage is typically mounted on walls, columns, or structural elements; these surfaces must be framed and enclosed before signage can be attached.

successor: Final Punch List and Commissioning / Occupancy
rationale: Wayfinding signage is essential for occupant navigation and egress; it must be in place before the building can be occupied or commissioned for use, as it supports safety and orientation.
While furniture can be installed concurrently, placing furniture after signage helps avoid blocking signs and ensures clear sightlines and accessibility for wayfinding elements.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared before any door assembly can be installed, as the doorset requires a structural opening to be set into.
The surrounding walls must be built to provide the rated assembly that the fire-rated doorset will be mounted within, ensuring proper fire containment.

successor: Fire sealant and gap filling application
rationale: Fire-rated doorsets require intumescent sealants and gap-filling materials to be applied around the frame after installation to maintain the fire integrity rating.

successor: Final inspection and fire rating certification
rationale: Once installed, the doorset must be inspected to verify correct installation, latching, clearances, and fire-rating compliance before the assembly can be certified.
Painting and final hardware adjustments are typically performed after installation to avoid damage during construction, though this is a sequencing preference rather than a physical requirement.

The stair handrail is installed on the staircase structure; the staircase framing (stringers, treads, risers) must be built first to provide the structural support and attachment surface for the handrail.
Wall framing provides the backing and attachment points for handrail brackets at the landing or wall side; handrails are often anchored to walls, so framing must be in place.

After installing the handrail, sanding and applying paint/stain/finish is typically done to protect the surface and achieve the desired appearance; finishing before installation would risk damage during installation.

Handrails are typically installed first to establish the top rail line, and balusters are then fitted between the tread/stringer and the handrail; the handrail provides the upper attachment point for balusters.

Installing the handrail is a prerequisite for the final inspection of the staircase for code compliance and safety; while not physically required in all cases, it is a practical sequence step in construction closeout.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work in the corridor must be completed before the ceiling system is installed, as the ceiling will cover and block access to these systems.
Corridor walls must be framed and finished before ceiling installation to provide the supporting structure and perimeter attachment points for the ceiling grid.

predecessor: Corridor Ceiling Grid / Suspension System Installation
rationale: The suspension grid or framing for the ceiling must be installed before the ceiling panels or finish material can be placed.
Ceiling-mounted lighting fixtures are typically installed after the ceiling grid is in place, as the ceiling provides the mounting surface and alignment reference.

While flooring can be done before or after ceilings, completing the ceiling first prevents dust and debris from falling onto newly installed flooring; this is a soft preference for cleanliness and sequence efficiency.
The ceiling grid provides the structural framework to which ceiling tiles or finish panels are attached.
Ceiling grid must be in place to support and provide attachment points for recessed or surface-mounted light fixtures.
The grid provides the framework for supporting and integrating HVAC diffusers into the ceiling system.

predecessor: Rough-in Electrical and Low-Voltage Wiring in Ceiling
rationale: Wiring and conduit must be run above the ceiling before the grid is installed, otherwise access for rough-in would be blocked or require grid removal.

predecessor: Rough-in HVAC Ductwork in Ceiling Plenum
rationale: Ductwork and mechanical runs above the ceiling must be completed before the grid is hung, as the grid would obstruct access.
Any sprinkler lines, drain pipes, or other overhead plumbing must be roughed-in before the ceiling grid is installed to allow access.

successor: Install Fire Alarm and Smoke Detection Devices in Ceiling
rationale: Fire alarm components such as smoke detectors and speakers are typically mounted to or within the ceiling grid system after the grid is in place.
While walls can be painted before the grid, painting after grid installation avoids damaging the grid and allows for a cleaner finish at the ceiling-wall intersection.
The wall openings must be framed before doorsets can be installed as doorsets require an existing framed opening to be fitted into.

predecessor: Complete Rough-in for MEP Services in Corridor Walls
rationale: Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the corridor walls must be completed before doorsets are installed to avoid rework or damage to the installed doorsets.
Fire doorsets must be installed prior to floor finishes to allow the doors to swing freely and to coordinate the finished floor height with the door bottom clearance.
Doorsets should be installed before ceiling work to provide access for lifting and positioning doors and frames, and to avoid damaging finished ceilings.

successor: Final Fire Caulking and Smoke Seal Inspection
rationale: Fire doorsets must be in place before fire caulking and smoke seal inspections can be performed, as the doors and frames form part of the fire-rated assembly being inspected.
The stair handrails must be attached to a fully framed stair structure. Without the stair frame in place, there is no physical substrate to mount the handrails onto.

Stringers and rough stair framing provide the structural support and geometry that define where handrails must be installed. Handrails cannot be positioned correctly without the stair profile established.
Handrail heights and bracket locations are measured from the finished tread surface. Treads and risers must be in place to determine proper handrail clearance and mounting height per building code.

Handrails must be installed before final inspections can verify compliance with safety codes and before adjacent finish work (e.g., drywall patching, painting, trim) is completed, as handrail installation may damage nearby finishes.

While painting/staining can be done before installation (pre-finishing), site-applied finish coats typically follow installation to touch up fastener holes and achieve a uniform appearance. This is a workflow preference, not a physical necessity.

Elevator lobby finishes (ceilings, walls, floors) must be fully installed before commissioning the lobby systems (lighting, HVAC, fire alarms, elevators) to ensure systems are tested in their final configuration and to avoid damage to finishes during commissioning work.

All electrical wiring, conduit, outlets, and switchgear serving the elevator lobby must be installed and energized before commissioning can verify proper operation of lighting, controls, and elevator functions.

Mechanical systems such as HVAC ducts, diffusers, and fire suppression must be installed prior to commissioning so that airflow, temperature control, and fire safety systems can be tested and balanced.

predecessor: Install Elevator Lobby Fire Alarm and Life Safety Systems
rationale: Fire alarm devices, smoke detectors, and emergency communication systems must be installed before commissioning to enable functional testing of life safety sequences and elevator recall functions.

Commissioning of elevator lobby systems must be completed and signed off before the building can receive final inspection approval and certificate of occupancy, as the elevator lobby is a critical egress and life safety area.
The entrance canopy/portico requires a stable foundation to support its structural loads; foundation work must be completed before any above-grade construction begins.

predecessor: Structural Steel / Frame Installation at Entry
rationale: The canopy/portico structure often connects to or rests upon the building's main structural frame; the supporting steel or concrete frame must be in place first.
The canopy/portico structure must be erected before its roofing and waterproofing membrane can be applied.

The portico provides overhead shelter and structural support for the entrance area; doors and glazing below the canopy are installed after the canopy structure is in place to ensure proper alignment and weather protection.

successor: Exterior Finishes and Cladding at Entry
rationale: The canopy/portico must be fully erected before its exterior cladding, soffit, and decorative finishes can be applied to achieve the final architectural appearance.
The reception desk/counter must be installed on a stable, level floor surface. The floor slab or subfloor must be completed and cured to provide a solid base for the desk.

Electrical power, data, and communication lines that will serve the reception desk must be roughed into the floor or wall before the desk is installed, as access to these conduits is impossible after placement.
The wall behind the reception desk must be framed, insulated, and drywalled (or at least backed) so that the desk can be anchored or abutted against a finished wall surface.
If the countertop is fabricated separately from the base, the base of the reception desk must be in position before the countertop can be installed on top of it.
Final connections of power outlets, data jacks, and cable management systems that are integrated into or mounted on the reception desk must be performed after the desk is set in its final location.

successor: Reception Area Flooring (finish flooring near desk)
rationale: While finish flooring like tile, carpet, or vinyl can be installed before the desk, it is often preferred to install the desk first and then finish flooring around it for a cleaner look, or vice versa depending on design; this is a soft preference based on installation sequence strategy.

Other furnishings such as chairs, signage, lighting fixtures, and decorative elements are typically placed after the reception desk is in position to coordinate with the desk layout, but this is a soft scheduling preference rather than a physical necessity.
Signage and directory boards are typically mounted on finished walls; wall finishes must be completed to provide a clean, stable surface and avoid damage to signage during finishing work.
Suspended or mounted signage often attaches to ceiling structures or uses ceiling-referenced alignment; ceiling installation must be complete to establish final mounting points and clearances.
Flooring is needed to establish final floor levels, which are referenced for signage height placement, and to avoid damaging new signage during floor finishing work.
If signage requires electrical power (e.g., illuminated directory boards), electrical rough-in wiring and conduit must be completed and concealed before final signage installation.

predecessor: Frame Rough Opening for Entrance Door
rationale: The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the door unit can be installed.
The subfloor or threshold area must be level and prepared to provide a stable base for the door frame and sill.
Weatherproofing and flashing around the door frame must be applied after the door is installed to seal gaps and prevent water infiltration.
Interior door casing and trim are installed after the door unit is in place to cover the gap between the frame and the wall.
Final adjustment of door operation, lockset, and weatherstripping can only be performed after the door and hardware are fully installed.
The subfloor must be clean, level, dry, and properly prepared before installing floor mats/grilles to ensure proper adhesion, fit, and long-term performance.
Any underlayment, vapor barrier, or subfloor repair work must be completed first before the floor mat/grille system is placed on top.

Overhead work such as ceiling installation and mechanical/electrical/plumbing rough-in generates dust and debris and requires overhead access; floor mats/grilles should be installed after to avoid damage and contamination.

successor: Install Final Flooring / Finish Flooring Over Mats
rationale: Floor mats/grilles are typically embedded into or installed beneath the final finished flooring; the final flooring layer is placed over or around the mat/grille system afterwards.
While it is possible to install baseboards before floor mats in some cases, it is generally a soft preference to install trim after floor mats to allow for proper fit and coverage of edges.

predecessor: Install Rough Wiring & Conduit for Access Control
rationale: Conduit and rough wiring must be in place before access control devices can be physically mounted and connected to the building's electrical system.

Access control components are typically surface-mounted on finished walls; installing before drywall would require removal and reinstallation, and finished surfaces provide the proper backing for device mounting.
The hardware must be physically installed before it can be powered on, programmed, and tested for functionality.
Access control panels and readers must be in place to coordinate with electric locking devices; the intercom and reader wiring connects to door strikes and magnetic locks.
While not physically required, completing ceilings first avoids dust and debris settling on sensitive electronic equipment and minimizes disruption from overhead work.
The directory signage must be physically fabricated before it can be mounted in its designated location.
Structural supports, brackets, or frames must be in place to securely attach the directory signage.
After mounting, the signage must be checked for correct positioning, level alignment, and clear visibility.
Final touch-ups such as painting, caulking, or cleaning around the mounted signage are typically done after installation to ensure a clean appearance.
The subfloor or base layer must be prepared, leveled, and cured before any finish flooring can be installed to ensure proper adhesion and a level surface.
Any required underlayment (moisture barrier, soundproofing, or cushion) must be in place prior to laying the final floor finish to protect the finish and meet manufacturer specifications.

predecessor: Complete Rough-In Services (Electrical/Plumbing/HVAC) in Adjacent Walls
rationale: Rough-in work in walls near the entry must be finished before flooring is laid to avoid damaging the finished floor during subsequent wall work.

predecessor: Complete Overhead Ceiling Work in Entry Area
rationale: Overhead work such as ceiling installation, painting, or overhead MEP rough-in should be completed before floor finishing to prevent debris, drips, or falling objects from damaging the new floor.
Baseboards and trim are installed after the floor finish is laid so that the trim covers the expansion gap and sits on top of the finished flooring for a clean, professional appearance.

While painting can be done before flooring, final touch-ups are often done after flooring is laid to fix any marks; however, the bulk painting typically precedes flooring to avoid paint drips on the new floor.
The threshold is typically installed after the floor finish is complete so that the flooring butts up to or runs under the threshold, ensuring proper transition and weather sealing.

successor: Move In Furniture/Fixtures to Entry Area
rationale: Heavy furniture, fixtures, or equipment should only be moved onto the floor after the finish is fully installed and cured to prevent damage, scratches, or indentations.
The building's structural frame must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the entrance canopy structure.

predecessor: Pour and Cure Foundation / Slab at Entrance Area
rationale: A stable foundation or slab is required to anchor the canopy columns and support the dead and live loads of the canopy structure.

successor: Install Final Roofing / Flashing at Canopy
rationale: The primary canopy structural frame must be erected before the roofing and flashing materials can be applied to seal and weatherproof the canopy.
Canopy electrical components are typically mounted to or routed through the canopy frame, so the structure must be in place before electrical rough-in work begins.

While doors can be installed before the canopy, best practice is to install the canopy first to provide weather protection during door installation and to ensure proper alignment of the entrance system.
Partition walls require a completed floor slab to provide a stable base and load-bearing surface for wall construction.
The main structural frame (columns, beams, primary walls) must be in place before non-load-bearing partition walls are installed, as partitions are infill elements within the structural grid.
Electrical conduit runs that go through or under the partition wall location should be placed in the slab before walls are erected, though some rough-in can happen after.
Plastering or drywall cladding cannot begin until the partition wall framing is complete and properly aligned.
Door and window frames are installed within partition wall openings after the wall framing is in place.
Electrical boxes and wiring within partition walls must be installed after the wall framing is complete but before final wall finishing.
Painting and final surface treatments occur after partition walls are fully constructed, finished, and cured.

Baseboards are installed over the finished flooring material, covering the gap between the wall and floor. Flooring must be in place first so that baseboards sit properly on top of the finished floor surface.
Baseboards are nailed or adhered to the finished drywall at the bottom of the wall. Drywall must be hung, taped, mudded, and sanded smooth before baseboard trim can be applied.

While baseboard can in some sequences be installed before painting and painted alongside walls, the preferred high-quality approach is to paint walls first then install baseboard, or to paint walls then install pre-primed/painted baseboard to avoid paint bleed and achieve crisp edges.

Quarter round or shoe molding is often installed against the baseboard at the floor line to cover expansion gaps; this molding butts against the baseboard and must be installed after the baseboard is in place.
Any final caulking, painting touch-ups, and inspection of the flooring/baseboard interface occur after the baseboard is fully installed to ensure a clean finished appearance.
Wiring and conduit must be in place within walls before outlets and switches can be mounted and connected.
Outlets and switches are mounted into wall boxes that are attached to studs and finished with drywall; the wall structure must be complete before devices can be installed.
While devices are often installed before final painting for convenience, it is a soft preference to protect finished surfaces from damage during installation.
Outlets and switches must be physically installed before they can be tested for proper voltage, polarity, grounding, and switch operation.
The device body must be mounted in the box before the decorative cover plate can be attached.
Ductwork must be in place to ensure the HVAC system can deliver conditioned air, which the thermostat controls.
Electrical and control wiring must be run from the HVAC unit to the thermostat location before the thermostat can be physically connected and mounted.
The thermostat must be installed and connected before the HVAC system can be tested, calibrated, and commissioned to ensure proper operation.
Programming and configuration of the thermostat's operational parameters can only occur after the device is physically installed and powered on.

predecessor: Complete interior wall finishing and painting
rationale: While not physically required, it is standard practice to finish walls first to avoid damage to the thermostat and to ensure a clean installation; this is a soft preference for workflow efficiency.
The rough opening for the door must be framed, inspected, and approved before any door hardware can be installed.
The door slab itself must be hung in place before hardware such as handles, locks, hinges (final adjustment), and strikes can be mounted.
Walls must be finished and painted before installing door hardware to avoid paint overspray or damage to hardware finishes.

Door bottoms and thresholds must be set relative to finished flooring; however in many sequences hardware is installed after flooring is complete to avoid damaging hardware during flooring work. Actually, typically flooring is done before door hanging, but if hardware includes bottom sweeps or threshold adjustments, flooring must precede final hardware adjustments.
Built-in cabinets need to be attached to and supported by framed walls; walls must be framed to provide the structural support and cavity space for cabinets.

Electrical wiring and outlet boxes must be roughed in behind or within the walls before cabinets are installed, as cabinets often cover or integrate with electrical components and accessing them afterward would require removing cabinets.
Drywall finishing creates the finished wall surface behind cabinets; installing cabinets before drywall would trap unfinished wallboard behind them and cause issues with fit and finish.

While painting can be completed before cabinet installation, it is often preferable to paint or finish walls after cabinets are installed to avoid damage to paint and to achieve a clean transition between cabinets and walls, though this is a sequencing preference rather than a strict physical requirement.

Cabinets are typically installed before finished flooring (especially if cabinets sit on the subfloor) to avoid damaging expensive flooring materials and to allow flooring to be installed flush against the cabinet toe kicks, though in some cases flooring can be installed first.
Room signage must be mounted on completed wall framing; without the wall structure in place, there is no surface to attach signage.
Signage is typically affixed to finished drywall surfaces; installing signage before drywall would require later removal and reinstallation.
Walls must be painted and finished before signage is mounted to avoid paint overspray on signs and to ensure clean final appearance.
Room signage must be installed prior to final inspections so that inspectors can verify room identification matches construction documents and occupancy requirements.
While not physically required, installing signage before furniture placement avoids obstructions and makes installation easier without moving furniture around.
The threshold or saddle sits directly on the subfloor or deck structure, requiring a level and stable base before installation.
The door opening must be framed to the correct dimensions and height to accommodate the threshold/saddle, as it spans the bottom of the door opening.
A moisture barrier or underlayment is typically installed beneath the threshold to prevent water intrusion and wicking.
Door jambs and frames are installed on top of the threshold/saddle, with the threshold serving as the base support for the side jambs.
The door slab hangs within the frame above the threshold, and the threshold must be in place to establish the bottom clearance and sweep interface.
The wall must be framed before sleeves can be installed, as sleeves are placed through the stud cavity to allow passage of pipes, conduits, or ducts.
The locations of pipe, conduit, and duct runs must be marked on the framed walls to determine where sleeves need to be positioned.
Firestopping must be applied around sleeves after they are installed and the penetrating item (pipe/duct) is in place to maintain fire-rated assembly integrity.
The sleeve creates the opening pathway; pipes, conduits, or ducts need the sleeve in place before they can be routed through the wall.
All sleeves must be installed and services pulled through before the wall is closed up with gypsum board or cladding, as access to the cavity is no longer possible afterward.

Structural framing (walls, columns, beams) must be completed before interior partitions can be installed, as partitions are non-load-bearing and require the building's primary structure for support and alignment reference.

predecessor: Complete rough-in of MEP services (electrical, HVAC, plumbing)
rationale: Rough-in work for mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems (conduits, pipes, ducts) within walls must be completed before partitions are closed up; otherwise, significant rework and demolition would be required to access these systems.
Interior partitions form the substrate or backing for wall finishes; drywall, paneling, or other finishes cannot be applied until the partition framework is fully erected and secured.
Door and window frames are typically installed within the partition openings and require the partition framework to be in place for proper fit and anchoring.

successor: Run Final MEP Trim-Out and Rough-In Inspection
rationale: After partitions are in place, final routing of electrical outlets, switches, and plumbing fixtures to partition locations can be completed, and inspections can verify that all rough-in work aligns with the partition layout.
Door frames must be installed and rough openings completed before doors can be hung and fitted properly.
Structural framing, including wall framing, must be complete to provide the supporting structure for door frames and doors.
Doors must be installed before finish flooring to allow proper clearance and undercutting of doors to match finished floor height.
Door casing and trim are installed after the door is hung to ensure proper fit and alignment around the door frame.
Final painting and touch-up work is typically performed after door installation, though some pre-finishing may occur off-site; this is a logical workflow preference.

The subfloor or underlayment must be installed and properly prepared before floor finishes can be applied, as floor finishes require a clean, level, and stable base to adhere to and avoid future damage.

All rough-in work for electrical, plumbing, and mechanical systems that run beneath the floor must be completed before flooring is installed; otherwise, accessing these systems would require tearing up the finished floor.

Cabinets and heavy millwork are typically installed after floor finishes to avoid damaging the flooring during cabinet installation and to ensure the floor runs continuously underneath for a professional appearance.

While final painting can be done before or after flooring, it is often preferred to complete floor finishes before final touch-up painting to avoid paint drips on the new floor and allow painters to work from the finished floor surface.
