Wall finishes such as drywall, paneling, or plaster require a structural framework to be attached to. Framing provides the necessary support structure for wall finishes.
Electrical wiring, outlet boxes, and switch boxes must be installed within the wall cavities before the walls are enclosed with finishes.
Plumbing pipes and supply lines running inside walls must be installed before wall finishes are applied, as accessing them afterward would require demolition.
HVAC ducts and vents that run through wall cavities must be installed and tested before the walls are closed up with finishes.
Insulation must be placed inside wall cavities before wall finishes are installed to ensure thermal and acoustic performance and to prevent trapping moisture.
Paint, texture, or wall covering applications can only be applied after wall surfaces (drywall, plaster, etc.) are fully installed, taped, and prepared.
Baseboards, crown molding, window casings, and other trim work are installed after wall finishes are in place to create clean finished edges and transitions.
Ideally flooring is installed after wall finishes to avoid damaging floors, though in some sequences flooring may be installed first with the wall finish overlapping it.

successor: Final electrical and lighting fixture installation
rationale: Light fixtures, switches, and outlet covers are installed after wall finishes are complete so that they sit flush against the finished wall surface.

All mechanical ducts, electrical wiring, conduit, and plumbing pipes that will be hidden above the ceiling must be installed before ceiling finishes can be applied, as these systems are roughed-in above the ceiling plane.
Wall framing and drywall must be completed to define room boundaries and allow ceiling finishes to abut walls properly; ceiling grid or drywall installation typically follows wall completion.
For suspended ceilings, the support grid (T-bar or furring channels) must be hung before ceiling tiles or panels can be placed or fastened.
Ceiling finishes are typically installed before flooring to avoid damaging finished floors with ladders, scaffolding, and debris from overhead work.
While final painting can occur after ceiling installation, it is a soft preference to complete ceiling work before final painting to avoid overspray and rework on fresh paint.
Baseboards are installed after flooring to cover the expansion gap between the floor and the wall, and to ensure a clean finish over the flooring edge.
Baseboards and trim are installed over finished drywall to create a seamless look; unfinished drywall would result in gaps and an improper fit.

Painting is done before trim installation because it is easier to cut in paint along the wall edge without trim in the way, and painting after trim risks getting paint on the trim or requiring additional masking.
After trim is installed, gaps between trim and walls are caulked and nail holes are filled, followed by touch-up painting on the trim itself for a finished appearance.

successor: Install Interior Doors and Door Casings
rationale: Door casings (trim around doors) are often installed in conjunction with or after baseboards to ensure consistent alignment and seamless transitions between door trim and wall baseboards.
Electrical rough-in (wiring, conduits, junction boxes) must be completed before any lighting fixtures can be installed, as the wiring must be in place and terminated at the fixture locations.
Ceiling surfaces must be finished and painted before installing lighting fixtures to avoid damage to fixtures during ceiling work and to ensure proper mounting surface.

While flooring can technically be installed before lighting, it is a soft preference to install lighting first so the room is well-lit for flooring work and to avoid dust/debris from floor work settling on new light fixtures.
Light switches and dimmer controls are typically wired to the lighting fixtures, so the fixtures must be installed and connected first to ensure proper switch wiring and functionality testing.

Soft preference: installing lighting before final touch-ups allows electricians to work without worrying about damaging fresh paint, and any minor wall/ceiling damage from installation can be repaired during final finishing.
Rough-in electrical wiring (running cables through walls/ceilings) must be completed before installing outlets, as outlets connect to the wiring and need to be wired into the rough-in system.
Walls must be enclosed with drywall/sheathing and cut openings prepared before outlets can be physically mounted and trimmed out.
Wall framing must be in place to provide the structural support and cavity for running wiring and mounting outlet boxes.

successor: Install Switch Plates and Cover Plates
rationale: Cover plates and trim can only be installed after the outlet devices themselves are mounted and wired.
Electrical testing (checking voltage, continuity, ground) must occur after outlets are installed to verify proper installation before walls are painted or final finishes are applied.
Ductwork must be installed and routed to the terminal locations before terminals (diffusers, grilles, VAV boxes) can be physically connected and installed.
Many HVAC terminals (e.g., diffusers, grilles) are mounted in or supported by the ceiling grid; the grid or support system must be in place first.

predecessor: Complete Overhead Rough-In Work (Electrical, Plumbing, Fire Protection)
rationale: All overhead MEP rough-in work should be completed before installing terminals to avoid conflicts, damage, and the need for rework in congested ceiling spaces.
Control wiring connections to VAV boxes, fan-powered boxes, and terminal units cannot be finalized until the terminals are physically installed and positioned.
Ceiling tiles are installed after terminals (diffusers, grilles) are mounted, as the terminals must be accessible for adjustment and the tiles fit around them.
Room systems must be physically installed before they can be commissioned and tested for proper operation.
Electrical power must be roughed in and available to room systems before commissioning can verify system functionality.
Low voltage control and building management system wiring must be complete for commissioning to test control sequences and communications.
Commissioning should be completed before final finishes and fit-out to avoid damage and ensure systems are operational behind finished surfaces.
It is preferred but not strictly required that room systems be commissioned before handover to ensure the room is fully functional for the occupant.

Fire safety devices such as smoke detectors and fire alarm panels require electrical power to function. Electrical wiring must be installed and energized (or at least rough-in complete) before these devices can be connected and tested.

predecessor: Complete Rough-In for Plumbing and HVAC
rationale: Fire sprinkler systems rely on the plumbing rough-in to supply water. Additionally, HVAC ductwork must be in place so that smoke detectors can be positioned correctly within ducts and the overall fire protection layout is coordinated.

Fire safety devices like smoke detectors, sprinkler heads, and alarm notification devices are often mounted within ceilings and walls. These devices must be installed prior to enclosing them with finished surfaces to avoid costly rework and ensure proper access for installation and inspection.

successor: Conduct Fire Alarm and Sprinkler System Testing
rationale: All fire safety devices must be physically installed, connected, and in place before any commissioning or testing of the fire alarm and sprinkler systems can begin, as testing verifies the functionality of the installed devices.

Structural framing (walls, floors, ceilings) provides the mounting surfaces and support for fire safety devices. The framing must be complete to allow proper installation of device brackets, conduit, and piping.

Acoustic penetrations (gaps around pipes, ducts, conduits) must be sealed after the acoustic insulation is installed, as the insulation provides the soundproofing barrier and penetrations through it need to be sealed to maintain acoustical integrity.

Penetrations through ceiling assemblies (e.g., for lighting, HVAC diffusers) must be coordinated with the ceiling grid layout; sealing can only happen once the ceiling system is in place to accurately locate and seal all penetrations.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing lines that penetrate acoustic barriers must be roughed-in first so that gaps around them can be properly sealed to prevent sound leakage.

successor: Install Acoustic Caulking / Sealant at Perimeter Joints
rationale: While perimeter joint sealing is often done concurrently or after penetration sealing, it is a soft preference that penetration sealing precede full perimeter sealing to ensure the acoustic envelope is fully addressed before finishing touches.
All acoustic sealing including penetrations must be completed before the final acoustic inspection can be performed to verify the integrity of the soundproofing system.

successor: Finish Flooring / Wall Finishes (Painted Walls, Trim)
rationale: Any sealing around penetrations in walls or floors must be completed before final finishes are applied, as the sealant application can affect finished surfaces and access to gaps would be blocked by finishes.
Room signage must be mounted on finished walls; installing signage before wall finishing is complete would require removal and reinstallation.
Ceiling work must be finished to ensure signage placement is not obstructed and to avoid damage from overhead work.
Flooring must be completed to establish final room layouts and to avoid damaging finished floors during sign installation.
Room signage installation may scuff or mark walls, so any final paint touch-ups should be done after signs are mounted.
Room signage is required for wayfinding and room identification before occupants can move in and use the space.

Rough framing defines the structural openings and support framework where built-in millwork (cabinetry, shelving, etc.) will be installed. Without completed framing, there is no structural surface to attach millwork to.
Rough electrical wiring for outlets, switches, and lighting within or behind millwork must be installed before millwork is placed, as access to wall cavities is blocked once millwork is installed.

Plumbing rough-ins for sinks, dishwashers, or other fixtures that will be housed within or adjacent to built-in millwork must be completed before millwork installation to ensure proper alignment and avoid rework.
HVAC ductwork, vents, and returns that will be concealed by or adjacent to millwork must be installed and tested beforehand, as millwork would block access.

Built-in millwork (such as base cabinets and toe kicks) is typically installed before finish flooring so that the flooring can be run up to or slightly under the millwork for a clean finished appearance, and to avoid damaging finished floors during millwork installation.

While drywall is typically finished before millwork, any touch-up taping, mudding, or painting adjacent to the millwork should be completed after millwork is installed to seal gaps. This is a soft preference as the primary drywall finish usually precedes millwork.
Countertops are installed on top of base cabinets (a type of built-in millwork); therefore, the millwork must be in place to support the countertops.

Final painting and touch-up work around the millwork is typically done after installation to ensure a seamless finish where millwork meets walls and ceilings. This is a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
Corridor walls must be installed before the ceiling can be attached, as the ceiling typically rests on or is supported by the wall framing.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be completed in the ceiling cavity before the ceiling is enclosed, to avoid costly rework and access issues.
The ceiling must be installed before finishing work such as painting or texturing can be applied.
Flooring installation typically follows ceiling installation to avoid damaging finished floors with overhead work and debris.
Lighting fixtures are mounted to or recessed into the ceiling, so the ceiling structure must be in place before fixtures can be installed.
Power supply cables, junction boxes, and switch wiring must be installed and routed through walls/ceilings before passage lighting fixtures can be connected and mounted.
Ceiling surfaces must be in place (or at least the ceiling framing) to provide a mounting substrate for recessed or surface-mounted passage light fixtures.
Walls and ceilings should be painted and finished before installing lighting fixtures to avoid damaging the fixtures with paint overspray or dust.
Lighting fixtures provide essential illumination for safe and accurate installation of flooring materials; also avoids the need to work around lighting equipment during flooring work.
Installed lighting is checked for proper operation, alignment, and aesthetics as part of the final walk-through; this is a quality control step rather than a physical constraint.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared before any door can be installed, as the door requires a prepared structural opening to fit into.
The fire-rated door frame must be installed and secured in the rough opening before the fire door itself can be hung, as the door hinges attach to the frame.

successor: Final inspection and fire rating certification
rationale: The door assembly must be fully installed before a fire rating inspection can verify the assembly meets code requirements.
Finishing work such as painting, trim, and caulking around the door is typically done after the door is installed for a clean appearance and proper sealing.
Passage signage must be mounted onto finished structural surfaces such as walls, ceilings, or soffits. Without the structural frame in place, there is no supporting substrate for the signage.

predecessor: Wall and Ceiling Finishes (Drywall, Plaster, Cladding)
rationale: Signage is typically applied onto finished wall and ceiling surfaces. Rough or unfinished surfaces would prevent proper adhesion, mounting, and alignment of passage signs.
Passage signage (including exit signs, directional signs) is a life-safety and code-compliance requirement. Building inspectors must verify signage is installed before issuing occupancy approval.

While it is physically possible to install furniture before signage, it is best practice to install signage first to ensure clear sightlines, correct placement above doors and corridors, and avoid obstruction by furniture.
Illuminated passage signs (e.g., exit signs) require electrical supply. Conduit and wiring must be roughed in behind finished surfaces prior to mounting the signage and connecting power.
Structural framing must be in place to provide support and attachment points for ductwork, and to define the spaces through which ducts will pass.

Electrical rough-in wiring and boxes must be installed before ductwork to avoid interference and to ensure proper clearances, as ductwork often occupies ceiling and wall cavities that would be inaccessible later.
Ductwork must be fully installed and tested before insulation is applied to ensure all joints and connections are accessible for sealing and inspection.
Passage ductwork must be in place before fire dampers can be installed, as dampers are mounted within or at the penetration points of the duct system through fire-rated walls.
While not strictly physically required, it is standard sequencing to complete ductwork before installing ceiling grids to avoid rework and provide easy access for duct adjustments and connections.
Under-slab plumbing must be completed before corridor framing can begin because the plumbing pipes are embedded in the concrete slab that supports the corridor walls and framing.
The concrete slab on grade must be fully poured and cured before corridor framing can start, as the slab provides the structural base and anchorage for the corridor walls and framing components.
Corridor framing must be complete before electrical rough-in can begin because the electrical conduits, boxes, and wiring are installed within the framed walls and ceiling cavities.
Corridor framing must be in place before mechanical ductwork and piping rough-in can proceed, as the framing defines the spaces where ducts and pipes are routed and supported.
Corridor framing must be fully erected and inspected before drywall can be installed, since drywall is directly attached to the studs and framing members.
The ceiling framing (joists, supports) must be in place before any ceiling material (drywall, tiles, etc.) can be installed.
Electrical wiring, boxes, and cables must be roughed-in above the ceiling before the ceiling is closed up, as accessing them afterward would require demolition.
Ductwork and HVAC components in the ceiling space must be installed before the ceiling is enclosed.
While painting typically follows ceiling installation, it is a soft preference as painting could theoretically be done before installation in some cases, though standard practice is to paint after.
Ceiling installation should be completed before flooring is installed to prevent debris and dust from falling on and damaging the new floor surface.
The ceiling grid provides the structural support and mounting surface for passage lighting fixtures, so it must be installed first.
Electrical conduit, junction boxes, and wiring must be roughed in to provide power to the lighting locations before fixtures can be installed.
Ceiling tiles are installed after passage lighting to allow access for wiring connections and to avoid damaging finished tiles when handling lighting fixtures.
After mounting the lighting fixtures, final connections, trim installation, and functional testing of the lights must occur to complete the electrical scope.
While it is preferable to paint before installing lights to avoid getting paint on fixtures, passage lighting may be installed early if protected; this is a soft preference for finish quality.
Rough-in work for mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems must be completed before flooring installation to avoid damaging the finished floor and to allow access to subfloor areas.
The subfloor must be clean, level, dry, and properly prepared with underlayment as needed before any finished flooring can be installed to ensure proper adhesion and a smooth final surface.
Baseboards and trim are typically installed after flooring is laid so that the flooring can run underneath or flush against the trim, providing a clean finished edge.
While doors can be hung before flooring, final installation and undercutting of doors to match floor height is ideally done after flooring is installed for proper clearance and appearance.
Final painting and touch-ups are often performed after flooring is installed to avoid paint drips on the new floor and to address any wall damage caused during flooring installation.
The door frame must be installed and secured in the wall opening before the door assembly can be hung, as the door hinges attach directly to the frame.
The wall opening must be framed (studs, header, rough opening) to provide the structural support and dimensions needed for the door frame and assembly.
The door assembly must be hung in the frame before hardware such as locks, closers, and final hinges can be installed and adjusted on the door leaf.
Fire-rated sealant and intumescent strips are applied around the installed door assembly to maintain the fire-resistance rating of the assembly.

successor: Final Inspection / Testing of Fire Door Assembly
rationale: The door must be fully installed before a fire door inspection can verify proper clearance, closing, latching, and overall compliance with fire codes.
Handrails are typically anchored into or mounted onto concrete stairs/landings; the concrete must be cured and structurally complete to provide a stable mounting surface.
Handrails often attach to walls or structural columns; wall framing must be in place to provide backing support and mounting locations.
Handrails must be installed before final safety inspection so inspector can verify proper height, graspability, load compliance, and guardrail requirements per building code.

While handrails can be installed after finished flooring, it's a soft preference to install handrails first to avoid damaging finished surfaces during drilling/anchoring; but flooring can also be completed first if care is taken.
Handrails are often installed before final painting and trim touch-ups so that any caulking, filling, and painting around the handrail brackets can be completed seamlessly for a clean finish.
Structural work (walls, ceilings, framing) must be finished before signage can be mounted, as signage needs stable surfaces and the structural integrity of the passage to be verified.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be completed before installing signage, so that signage does not interfere with or block access to MEP components and to avoid damage to signage during subsequent MEP work.

Wall and ceiling finishes (drywall, taping, painting) must be completed before signage installation to ensure a clean finished appearance and to prevent signage from being damaged or having to be removed/replaced during finishing work.
Signage must be in place before final inspections and commissioning, as inspectors need to verify that all required passage signage is correctly installed for safe egress and wayfinding.
All signage including passage signage must be installed before the building can be considered complete and turned over for occupancy, as signage is a life-safety and code-compliance requirement.
Wall framing provides the structural support substrate that the wall finish (e.g., drywall, plaster, or paneling) is applied to; the finish cannot be attached without framing in place.
Insulation must be placed inside wall cavities before the wall finish is sealed over it, otherwise it cannot be installed without later demolition of the finish.

All rough-in wiring, outlets, switches, and plumbing pipes that run inside the wall must be installed and inspected before the wall finish is applied, as accessing them afterward would require cutting or removing the finish.
Window and door frames must be set and secured in the rough openings before the wall finish is applied so the finish can be trimmed flush to the frames.
Painting, wallpapering, or other decorative coatings typically follow the wall finish application, but this is a soft preference because the wall could be left unfinished in some cases.
Baseboards and trim are installed over the finished wall surface; the wall finish must be in place to act as the backing surface against which trim is fitted and nailed.
Typically walls are finished before finished flooring is installed to avoid damaging the wall finish during floor work, though some sequences reverse this; thus it is a soft preference.
The tiered seating risers require a level, structurally sound concrete slab or foundation base to bear the load and provide a stable installation surface.

Any electrical conduits or plumbing lines that pass beneath the seating area must be roughed in and inspected before the slab is poured and the risers are built, to avoid cutting into the finished structure.
If the risers are supported by a structural frame, the primary steel or concrete structure must be erected first to provide the supporting framework.
Fixed seating is mechanically fastened to the finished riser structure; the risers must be fully built and cured (if concrete) before seats can be attached.
Guardrails and handrails for stepped aisles are anchored into the riser structure and must be installed after the risers are complete to ensure proper alignment and safety.
The stage structure/frame must be erected to provide the supporting framework onto which the handrail/balustrade is mounted.
The stage decking provides the walking surface and defines the edge where the handrail/balustrade is installed for safety.
The handrail/balustrade must be fully installed before final inspection can verify safety compliance and guardrail requirements.
While painting can be done before or after, it is preferable to paint after handrail installation to avoid damaging the finish during installation work.
Stage lighting may be installed before or after, but installing after handrails prevents risk of damaging lighting fixtures during handrail work.
The building foundation and substructure must be completed to provide structural support and a stable base for installing the stage trap door mechanism.
The space beneath the stage (understage area) must be excavated and prepared to accommodate the trap door's mechanical components, clearance, and access.
The trap door frame and mechanism must be installed first so that the surrounding stage decking can be laid flush and integrated around it.
The trap door must be physically installed before its opening/closing mechanisms can be tested and calibrated for proper operation.

While finishing (painting, sealing, surface treatment) is typically done after installation to ensure a seamless appearance, it could technically be done before or after depending on access and protection measures.

Concealed rigging points are typically installed within or attached to the building's structural frame (e.g., steel beams or concrete slabs). The structural framing must be in place to provide a secure anchoring surface before rigging points can be fixed.

MEP rough-in work above ceilings (ductwork, conduit, piping) should be completed before concealing rigging points within ceiling cavities, so that rigging points are not obstructed and MEP systems can be routed around them if necessary; however this is a soft preference as sequencing can be adjusted.

Concealed rigging points must be fully installed, tested, and load-rated before ceilings or drywall are closed in, because once the ceiling is sealed, access to install or verify these hidden structural supports would require demolition.

Concealed rigging points must be installed and load-tested before they can be used as anchor points for hoisting or suspending equipment, scenery, or other loads during construction or later building use.

It is preferable to install concealed rigging points before applying final architectural finishes to avoid damaging finished surfaces, though this is a soft preference as touch-ups can be performed if needed.
Curtain tracks need to be mounted on finished walls or ceilings. Wall framing and finishing must be completed to provide a solid mounting surface for the curtain track brackets and supports.
For ceiling-mounted curtain tracks, the ceiling structure (or structural overhead support) must be in place to safely anchor the track system.
Any electrical wiring for motorized curtain tracks or nearby lighting must be roughed-in before the track is installed to avoid interference and rework.
Curtains and drapes cannot be hung until the track system is securely installed, aligned, and tested to ensure smooth operation.

successor: Final Finishing and Touch-Up Painting (Last Coat)
rationale: While track installation can happen after final painting, it is often preferred to complete touch-up painting after track mounting to cover any marks made during installation, though not physically required.
The foundation must be fully completed and cured to provide a stable load-bearing base for the stage platform decking.
The structural steel framework that supports the stage platform must be erected and secured before decking can be installed on top of it.

predecessor: Complete Concrete Slab for Stage Area
rationale: A concrete slab or subfloor must be poured and cured to provide a level surface for the stage decking installation.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work beneath the stage area must be completed before the decking is installed, as access will be permanently blocked or severely restricted afterward.
Final floor finishes such as timber flooring, vinyl, or other stage surface materials must be applied after the structural decking is in place.
Stage lighting fixtures, rigging points, and associated equipment are installed after the decking provides a working platform for access and safe installation.
Any walls or partitions on the stage area are built after the decking is installed to ensure proper alignment and anchoring to the platform.
Seating installation on the stage is preferably done after decking is complete to avoid damaging decking materials, though it may be possible to sequence differently in some cases.
Structural framing provides the mounting surfaces and support structure (ceilings, walls) needed for integrated lighting fixtures.
Rough electrical wiring must be in place behind walls and ceilings to provide power feeds to integrated lighting fixtures before they can be connected and installed.
HVAC ductwork runs above ceilings and must be installed before ceiling-mounted integrated lighting to avoid conflicts and rework.
Integrated lighting fixtures are mounted to the ceiling structure and must be installed before the final ceiling finish is applied to allow proper access and integration.
The integrated lighting hardware must be physically installed before the control system can be programmed, tested, and commissioned.
Rigging hardware must be fabricated and available on site before installation can begin, as installation requires the physical components.
Mounting surfaces (e.g., steel beams, concrete anchors) must be prepared, cleaned, and inspected before rigging hardware can be securely attached.
The primary structural framework must be in place to provide the support points for rigging hardware attachment.
Rigging hardware must be installed before rigging lines can be connected and load testing can commence, as the hardware serves as the anchor points.
Suspended equipment (e.g., lighting, speakers, HVAC units) can only be hung after rigging hardware is installed and verified, as they depend on the rigging points for support.
Window or door frame must be in place to provide a mounting surface for the curtain track
Ceiling or wall framing above windows must be complete to provide structural support for curtain track mounting
While not strictly required, finishing the ceiling (or at least the area above windows) is typically done first to avoid damaging finished surfaces when mounting the track
Walls are typically painted or finished before installing curtain tracks to avoid getting paint on the hardware and to allow for clean edges
Curtains or drapes cannot be hung until the track or rod they attach to is securely installed
The stage floor must be fully installed before acoustic commissioning can begin, as the floor is a primary reflective and absorptive surface that affects acoustic measurements.
The walls and ceiling define the acoustic envelope of the stage space; acoustic commissioning requires the full enclosure to be in place to measure reverberation, sound reflection, and isolation.
HVAC must be operational to control temperature and humidity during acoustic testing, and to measure background noise levels from mechanical systems.
Electrical systems including lighting and sound system power must be roughed in so that acoustic testing equipment can be powered and any electrical noise sources can be assessed.
Seating installation must wait until acoustic commissioning is complete because seating can alter the acoustic characteristics of the space and may need to be adjusted based on acoustic test results.

predecessor: Rough Opening Framing for Stage Proscenium
rationale: The fire-rated stage curtain requires a framed proscenium opening to be in place to provide the structural support and attachment points for the curtain track and housing.
The curtain's support tracks, cables, and rigging must be anchored to the overhead steel or roof structure, which must be fully erected and stable before any curtain components can be installed.

The fire-rated curtain is a critical life-safety component; its deployment and operation must be integrated with and verified by the fire alarm system before the overall fire safety system can be commissioned.

successor: Final Interior Finishes (Painting, Plastering) Near Proscenium
rationale: It is preferred to install the curtain after final finishes to protect the curtain fabric from dust and debris, though the finishes could be touched up later if needed.

successor: Stage Lighting and Rigging Final Trim and Focus
rationale: The fire-rated curtain must be in place before final lighting focus so that lighting designers can work around the actual curtain position, and so that the curtain does not obstruct lighting after it is installed.
The structural framing (e.g., studs, joists, or rafters) must be in place to define and support the rough opening for the view-framing window or door.
The rough opening must be framed, measured, and squared before the view-framing component (window or door frame) can be installed into it.

After the view-framing opening unit is set in place, flashing and weatherproofing membranes must be applied around its perimeter to seal against water infiltration before any exterior cladding or interior finishes are applied.
The view-framing opening must be fully installed and sealed so that interior wall finishes can be applied flush around the opening, ensuring a clean finished appearance.
Exterior cladding (siding, brick, panels) must be installed after the view-framing opening is in place and properly flashed to create a continuous weather-resistant envelope around the opening.
The ground must be leveled, cleared, and have proper foundation/footing in place before any seating structure can be installed to ensure stability and safety.
If the seating includes concrete bases, piers, or masonry supports, these must cure and set before the seating components can be mounted or attached.

Any underground electrical conduits, drainage pipes, or irrigation lines needed near the seating area must be installed and buried before permanent seating is placed, to avoid excavation after installation.
Final landscaping, planting, mulch, decorative stone, or paving around the seating area should be completed after the seating is in place to ensure proper alignment and integration.

Informational or directional signs near the contemplation seating are best positioned after the seating is installed so they can be placed at the correct distance and orientation relative to the seating.
The concrete substructure and foundation must be completed to provide a stable base for the view-skirting wall to be built upon.
Waterproofing must be applied to the substructure before the view-skirting wall is erected to protect against moisture ingress.
The view-skirting wall must be fully constructed and cured before backfilling can occur against it to avoid damaging the wall.
The structural installation of the view-skirting wall must be completed before any finishes or cladding can be applied to its surface.
Although drainage can be installed concurrently in some cases, it is typically preferred to install the drainage layer against the completed wall to ensure proper placement and function.
The foundation must be in place to provide structural support for the overhang/canopy structure.
The main structural frame (columns and beams) must be erected to provide attachment points and load-bearing support for the overhang/canopy.
The overhang/canopy structure must be in place before roofing or waterproofing above it can be completed, as the canopy forms part of the roof assembly.

It is preferable to install the canopy before adjacent exterior cladding finishes so that cladding can be trimmed and sealed neatly around the canopy, though cladding could be done first with careful detailing.
Gutters and downspouts must be installed after the canopy is in place to collect rainwater from the canopy surface.
The structural frame (typically wood or aluminum) must be built and secured in place before the shoji screen can be mounted, as the screen is a panel that fits within or attaches to the frame.
The shoji screen frame/panel must first be installed in its opening before the translucent washi paper can be applied to the frame, as the paper is stretched over the completed panel structure.

The shoji screen is typically one of the final aesthetic elements; interior finishing like painting or wall treatments should come after the screen is placed to avoid damage and allow precise trim work.
The wall opening or alcove where the shoji screen will be placed must be fully framed and the surrounding structure completed before the screen can be installed.
Rough-in work must be completed before installing the shoji screen to avoid needing to disturb the screen later for access to wiring or pipes behind the wall opening.
The Zen View structure requires stable foundation and leveled ground, so site preparation and foundation work must be completed before any superstructure construction can begin.
All underground pipes, cables, and drainage systems must be laid before building construction to avoid later excavation and structural conflicts.
The main structural shell and framing of the Zen View must be completed before any interior finishing such as drywall, flooring, or painting can proceed.
The building structure must be fully erected to provide support for the roof system before roofing installation can commence.
External finishes and cladding depend on the completed structural frame of the Zen View building to be properly attached and aligned.
The structural steel frame must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the view-seat installations, which are typically mounted onto the steel structure.
The concrete floor slab must be cured and ready to provide a level foundation for seating supports and anchorages before seat installation can begin.
Electrical conduit and rough-in wiring must be completed in the seating area before seats are installed, as access to the floor and walls for electrical work would be blocked by the seating.
Final finishes and painting should be done after seat installation to avoid damaging the seats during finishing work, and to allow for touch-ups around the installed seating.
Functional testing and quality inspection of the installed seats can only proceed after all seats are fully installed and secured in place.
The foundation or piles must be installed and cured before deck/platform construction can begin, as the deck/platform rests on the foundation for structural support.
Columns or substructure elements must be completed to provide vertical support for the deck/platform before it can be constructed.
The deck/platform provides the base or working surface for erecting the superstructure or frame above it.
While MEP rough-in can sometimes be done concurrently, it is typically sequenced after the deck/platform is in place to allow access for routing mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems.
Waterproofing and finishing applications must be applied after the deck/platform structure is fully constructed to protect it from moisture and wear.
The ceiling grid provides the primary support structure onto which the membrane is stretched or clipped. The membrane cannot be installed without a secured framework in place.

predecessor: Complete Rough Electrical and HVAC Rough-In above Ceiling
rationale: All wiring, conduits, ductwork and other mechanical/electrical services must be installed and inspected above the ceiling before the membrane is placed, as the membrane will conceal and block access to these systems.
If lights are mounted below or integrated into the membrane system, the membrane must be in place first to define the mounting plane and support arrangement.

While not physically required, it is a soft preference to install the membrane after painting to avoid dust and dirt settling on the delicate membrane surface, and to protect it from damage during other finishing trades.

successor: Final Clean and Commissioning of Lighting System
rationale: The lighting system's diffusing effect can only be tested and commissioned once the membrane is fully installed, ensuring even light distribution and confirming proper performance.

The brise-soleil is a heavy external shading device that must be anchored to the building's primary structural frame (columns, slabs, or beams). The structural frame must be complete to provide load-bearing support before the brise-soleil can be installed.

Brise-soleil brackets and supports typically attach to or penetrate through the exterior wall sheathing or backing layer. The wall assembly behind the brise-soleil must be in place to provide a secure mounting surface and proper waterproofing continuity.
After the brise-soleil is mounted, the interface between its support brackets and the wall must be sealed and finished to prevent water intrusion and ensure aesthetic continuity of the façade.

While not a physical necessity, completing the brise-soleil before interior finishes near the façade is preferred to avoid damaging finished surfaces during the heavy installation work and to allow for any needed adjustments to window/door integration with the shading device.

successor: Scaffolding Dismantling / Final Façade Access Removal
rationale: The brise-soleil installation typically requires exterior scaffolding or lifts. Scaffolding cannot be fully dismantled until the brise-soleil and all associated façade work is complete, as the scaffold provides necessary access for installation.
The partition wall must be erected on a finished or prepared floor slab to ensure a level, stable foundation and proper load distribution.
MEP roughing-in in the floor zone beneath the wall must be completed before the wall is built, as access to those areas would be blocked once the partition is installed.
The structural or core panels of the light-sculpting wall must be fully erected before any surface finishes are applied to them.
The light-sculpting elements, fixtures, and control wiring are embedded into or mounted onto the completed wall structure; the wall must be in place before these systems are installed.

Floor finishes adjacent to the partition are typically laid after the wall is built to achieve a clean abutment without cutting materials, though some sequences allow pre-finishing with careful detailing.
The reflective ceiling trough requires a completed structural slab or deck overhead to which it can be mounted or suspended.

predecessor: Overhead MEP Rough-In (Ductwork, Piping, Electrical Conduit)
rationale: Major mechanical, electrical, and plumbing runs above the ceiling must be installed before the trough is placed, as the trough would obstruct access to the overhead MEP systems.
After the trough structure is in place, the electrical wiring, lighting fixtures, and reflective inserts can be installed within the trough.
The reflective trough is typically integrated into the ceiling system, so it must be installed before the surrounding ceiling grid and tiles are placed around it.

Although the trough does not structurally require painting to be done after, it is standard practice to complete all ceiling fixture installations before final touch-up painting to avoid rework and protect finishes.
The main building structure and roof shell must be complete to provide the supporting framework and enclosure for the tensile membrane ceiling system to be installed.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (ductwork, piping, conduit) that runs above the ceiling must be completed before the tensile membrane is installed, as the membrane will cover and block access to these systems.
To avoid damaging finished wall surfaces during membrane installation, it is preferable to complete the ceiling before final wall finishing, though not a physical necessity.
Tensile membrane ceilings often incorporate integrated lighting pockets or back-lighting; lighting fixtures must be installed after the membrane is in place to ensure correct alignment and sealing.
Installing the ceiling before flooring prevents dust, debris, and potential damage from overhead work to the finished floor surface.
The LED luminaires must be physically installed before they can be commissioned, as commissioning involves testing and verifying the installed fixtures and their network connectivity.

predecessor: Installation of Lighting Control System Infrastructure
rationale: The control system (gateways, controllers, wiring, network backbone) must be in place and operational before the color-tuning LED network can be commissioned, since commissioning tests the integrated control of the luminaires.

predecessor: Electrical Power Supply and Wiring Completion
rationale: Power must be supplied to all LED fixtures and control devices before any commissioning activities such as addressing, programming, and functional testing can begin.

After commissioning verifies that the network is operational, fine-tuning of color temperatures, dimming curves, and scene programming can proceed based on the functional baseline established during commissioning.
Commissioning must be successfully completed to demonstrate that the system performs as intended before end-users are trained and the system is formally handed over for occupancy or use.
Plumbing rough-in must be completed before the dual vanity can be installed, as the vanity will cover and restrict access to plumbing connections.
Wall surfaces must be finished before mounting the vanity so that the vanity can be properly secured against a finished surface and to avoid damage to finished walls.
The vanity cabinet must be installed and secured in place before the sink, faucet, and drain plumbing components can be connected to it.
The vanity base cabinet must be in place and leveled before the countertop can be set on top of it.
While it is possible to install mirrors and lighting before the vanity, it is standard practice to install them after the vanity is in place to ensure proper alignment and height positioning.
Plumbing supply and drain lines must be roughed-in to the tub location before the tub can be set in place and connected.
The floor area must be properly prepared and leveled to support the weight of a filled soaking tub before installation.
Waterproof membrane or backing must be installed around the tub area to prevent moisture damage before the tub is set.
Faucets, drains, overflow covers, and trim pieces cannot be installed until the tub body is permanently in place.
Finish tile, stone, or paneling around the tub deck must be installed after the tub is set to achieve proper alignment and sealing.

predecessor: Plumbing rough-in for bathroom supply lines
rationale: Bidet requires water supply connections; rough-in plumbing (hot/cold water lines) must be in place before the bidet can be connected and installed.
Bidet requires a drain connection; the waste pipe rough-in must be completed before the bidet fixture can be installed.
Wall and floor waterproofing should be completed before installing fixtures to prevent moisture damage behind and under the bidet.

successor: Bidet connection to supply lines and testing
rationale: After the bidet is physically mounted, the supply lines can be connected and the system tested for leaks.

successor: Tiling/finishing of adjacent walls and floors
rationale: While bidet can be installed after tiling, it is often preferred to install the bidet before finishing work to allow for precise cutouts and a cleaner finished appearance around the fixture.
The wardrobe system is typically installed against finished walls; wall plastering and painting must be completed first to avoid damage to the wardrobe and ensure proper fit and sealing.

Flooring (tiles, wood, or laminate) must be laid before the wardrobe is installed so that the wardrobe sits on top of the finished floor, ensuring level placement and avoiding the need to cut flooring around the base.
Any electrical wiring, outlets, or lighting points behind or inside the wardrobe area must be roughed in before the wardrobe is built, as access is impossible afterward.

Final touch-up painting may be needed after wardrobe installation to cover any gaps, nail holes, or scuffs caused during installation, but this is a cosmetic preference rather than a physical necessity.

successor: Final electrical and lighting fixture installation
rationale: If the wardrobe includes integrated lighting, the final connection of light fixtures or switches can only be completed after the wardrobe carcass is in place.
Power supply must be roughed in before the safe can be installed and connected.
Any electronic locking or communication systems require data cabling to be in place before safe installation.
The safe is typically set on the finished floor to ensure proper height and alignment, and to avoid damaging finished surfaces later.
Cabinetry, paneling, or millwork that encloses or surrounds the safe must be built after the safe is in place to ensure proper fit.
Final wiring connections to the safe (lighting, alarm, power) must occur after the safe is set in its final position.
The floor must be finished and leveled before installing a makeup vanity station to ensure stable placement and proper alignment.
Wall surfaces must be finished and painted before the vanity is mounted or placed against them to avoid damage and allow for clean finishes.
Electrical wiring and outlet boxes must be roughed in behind the wall before the vanity is installed, as access is difficult or impossible afterward.
The vanity station must be in place to correctly position and mount the mirror above it at the proper height and alignment.
Vanity-mounted or overhead lighting fixtures are typically installed after the vanity is positioned to ensure correct spacing and alignment.
The rough door frame (buck or jamb studs) must be in place before any finished door can be hung, as the door is physically attached to the frame.
The finished floor must be laid before the door is hung to establish the correct undercut clearance and ensure the door swings freely over the flooring.
The door must be hung in place before door knobs, locks, and final hinge adjustments can be installed, as these components attach directly to the door slab and frame.
Door casing (architrave) is installed around the door frame after the door slab is hung to allow proper alignment and reveal gaps.

successor: Painting and finishing of door and frame
rationale: Final painting or staining of the door and trim is performed after the door is hung and fitted, ensuring coverage of all surfaces including edges exposed during installation.
The structural frame (columns, beams, and roof structure) must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the exhaust ventilation ductwork.
The roof deck must be completed to allow roof-mounted exhaust fans and duct penetrations through the roof to be properly installed and sealed.
Fireproofing materials (e.g., fire-resistant wrap or spray-on coating) are applied over ducts to meet fire code requirements; ducts must be in place before they can be fireproofed.
The exhaust ducts must be fully installed before the system can be tested, balanced, and commissioned to verify proper airflow and performance.
Suspended ceilings or drywall ceilings are installed after ductwork is complete, as the ducts would otherwise be inaccessible for connection, sealing, and inspection.
Structural framing must be inspected and approved before window installation can begin to ensure load-bearing capacity and structural integrity.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed, measured, and prepared to the correct dimensions before the window unit can be set in place.
The window must be installed in the opening before flashing, waterproofing, and sealing can be applied around its perimeter to prevent moisture intrusion.
The window must be in place before drywall, trim, and interior wall finishes can be installed around the window opening.
Exterior siding must be installed after the window is in place to properly integrate with and seal against the window frame.
Electrical power is required for motorized blackout curtain tracks, so rough-in wiring must be completed before installing the track.
Mounting brackets or support structure must be in place before the curtain track can be attached.
Ceiling or soffit where the track mounts must be finished to allow secure and clean installation of the track.
Curtains must be hung on the track, so the track must be fully installed before curtains can be placed.
Curtain track installation should be completed before final touch-ups to avoid damage to curtains during other work.

The hook rail must be mounted on a finished wall surface. Any wall prep, patching, sanding, and painting must be completed before the hook rail is installed, as installing it first would interfere with wall finishing and risk damaging the rail.

successor: Hang Coats and Accessories on Hooks
rationale: The hook rail must be securely mounted to the wall before any items can be hung from it. The hooks require the rail to be fixed in place to bear weight.
The wall framing, drywall installation, and any rough-in work must be completed to provide the structural backing needed to securely fasten the hook rail to the wall.

While it is logically preferable to install the hook rail before decorating the room with final accessories (to avoid interference), this is a soft sequencing preference since decorative items could be rearranged around the rail if needed.
Water supply and drain lines must be in place before the towel warming rack can be connected to the plumbing system.
Electrical wiring and outlet boxes must be installed before the towel warming rack can be hardwired or plugged in.
The wall surface must be finished and smooth before the towel warming rack can be mounted to avoid damaging finished surfaces or having to work around the rack.
The rack must be physically mounted before its plumbing supply and return lines can be connected and pressure-tested.

It is often easier to install tile or backsplash before mounting the rack, but if the rack is surface-mounted with brackets, tile can be completed after; this is a sequencing preference rather than a strict physical requirement.
Interior wall framing provides the structural surface and support for mounting the vanity unit securely.
Rough-in plumbing (water supply lines and drain pipes) must be installed inside the wall before the vanity can be placed, as the vanity conceals and connects to these utility lines.
Drywall must be installed and finished behind the vanity area so that the wall surface is ready for vanity attachment and to avoid rework.
The vanity base cabinet must be in place and leveled before the countertop can be cut, fitted, and secured on top of it.
Rough-in plumbing (piping, waste lines, vent lines) must be installed in the walls and floors before any fixtures (toilet, sink, shower) can be connected and secured in place.
Electrical wiring, junction boxes, and rough-in for lighting/ventilation must be run in the walls and ceiling before fixtures like vanity lights, exhaust fans, or heated towel rails are installed.
Tiling around the shower, bath, and floor must be installed after the fixtures are in place so that tile work can be cut and fitted precisely around the installed fixtures for a watertight seal.
The vanity unit and mirror are typically installed after the sink and tap fixtures are in place to ensure proper alignment and connection to the plumbing.

predecessor: Framing and Wall Preparation for En-suite
rationale: Wall framing, backing boards, and any blocking must be completed to provide structural support for mounting fixtures such as the toilet, grab bars, and shower fittings.
Wall furring provides a level and stable surface for wardrobe installation. Without furring, the wardrobe cannot be securely mounted to the wall.
The wardrobe system requires a level floor to sit on. Floor levelling ensures the wardrobe base is stable and aligned.
Plastering and painting must be completed before wardrobe fitting to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to allow the wardrobe to be fitted flush against finished walls.
Skirting boards are typically cut and fitted around the wardrobe after it is in place, allowing a neat finish between the wardrobe and the wall.
If integrated lighting is planned inside the wardrobe, it is preferable to install it after the wardrobe is fitted so wiring can be routed correctly, though this is a soft preference if pre-wired.
Conduit and boxes provide the pathways and enclosures for wiring; they must be in place before any wire pulling.
The lighting fixtures must be mounted before control wiring can be connected to them; otherwise wires would have no termination points.
Rough-in electrical work (running main feeders, installing subpanels) is a prerequisite to distributing branch circuits for lighting controls.
Control panels and switches can only be connected after the wiring that feeds them has been run.
Commissioning and testing require the wires to be fully installed and connected to their endpoints.
Acoustic insulation is installed within wall or partition cavities; the framing must be in place to provide the cavity and support for the insulation material.
Services should be roughed in before insulation to avoid damaging the insulation later and to ensure proper sealing around penetrations for acoustic performance.
Insulation must be fully installed and inspected before enclosing walls or ceilings, as it cannot be placed after the surface is closed.

successor: Final MEP Trim-Out and Fixture Installation
rationale: While trim-out can partially proceed before insulation in some areas, it is generally preferred to complete insulation first to avoid debris and to allow proper sealing around final penetrations.
Acoustic performance testing must occur after insulation is installed to verify that the installed material meets design specifications.

A level, clean, and dry subfloor or screed base is physically required to provide a stable surface for laying underfloor heating pipes or mats, ensuring uniform heat distribution and preventing damage.

Insulation must be placed beneath underfloor heating to prevent downward heat loss, improve energy efficiency, and meet building regulations; heating cannot be laid directly on an uninsulated subfloor.
Underfloor heating pipes or cables must be fully laid and pressure-tested before being covered with a screed or self-levelling compound to encapsulate them and protect the system.
A pressure test must be performed immediately after laying the underfloor heating to verify the integrity of the pipes or cables before they are concealed by screed or flooring.
The final floor covering can only be installed after the underfloor heating system is laid, tested, and covered with screed, ensuring the heating system is fully operational and protected.
Wall framing provides the structural backing and substrate onto which childproof wall protection materials (such as protective panels, corner guards, or padding) are mounted or affixed.
Electrical wiring and outlet boxes must be installed within the wall before installing protective coverings to avoid damaging or covering access to electrical components.
Plumbing pipes and fittings within walls need to be installed and inspected before wall protection is applied, preventing the need to cut through protective materials later.
Drywall must be hung, taped, mudded, and sanded smooth to provide a clean, finished surface for childproof wall protection products to adhere or attach properly.

It is generally preferred to install childproof wall protection before final painting or finishing of adjacent wall areas so that paint lines end cleanly at the protection edges, though not a strict physical requirement.

Standard-height worktops must be installed first to establish the base level; child-height worktops are typically installed at a lower level alongside or after the main countertops to ensure proper alignment and support structure.
The wall and cabinet framing must be complete to provide a structural surface for mounting child-height worktops.
Plumbing rough-in must be completed before installing any worktops to avoid cutting or modifying countertops after installation.
A child-height sink can only be installed after the child-height worktop is in place, as the sink mounts into the cutout of the worktop.
Backsplash tiles or panels are installed after the worktops are fixed in place to create a seamless joint between the countertop and the wall.
The window guard must be attached to a structurally sound window frame; the frame must be installed first to provide a mounting surface.
Window guards are typically installed over or around the window glass; the glass must be in place so the guard can be properly fitted and secured.
Installing the window guard may affect or require adjustments to the surrounding trim; finishing work should be done after the guard is in place to ensure proper fit and appearance.
While painting can technically be done before guard installation, it is preferable to paint first to avoid getting paint on the guard and to achieve a cleaner finish behind and around the guard.
A final safety inspection must verify that the window guard is correctly installed, securely fastened, and meets child safety standards before the space is considered safe for occupancy.

The climbing structure must be anchored to a completed, load-bearing floor slab and subfloor that can support its weight and withstand dynamic loads from climbers. The floor must be fully cured and prepared before installation.

Many indoor climbing structures (especially taller walls) require top anchors and structural supports tied to the overhead structure or roof deck, which must be in place before the climbing frame can be erected and secured.

The climbing structure's support framing may need to integrate with or be independent from the building's interior wall framing; all MEP rough-in work behind walls must be complete to avoid interference with the climbing wall installation.

successor: Climbing Surface Panel Installation & T-Hold Mounting
rationale: The structural frame and support system of the climbing structure must be fully erected and stable before climbing panels can be attached and climbing holds can be mounted onto them.

successor: Safety Padding / Crash Pad & Floor Protection Installation
rationale: The climbing structure must be in place and structurally complete before the surrounding fall-protection safety padding and impact-absorbing floor mats can be fitted around its base and beneath climbing zones.

successor: Final Inspection & Load Testing of Climbing Wall
rationale: The complete climbing structure must be installed and all components secured before the final structural inspection and load testing can be conducted to verify safety and compliance.
The door frame and rough opening must be constructed and prepared before any hardware can be installed, as hardware attaches to the frame and door slab.

predecessor: Deliver and store Child-Sized Door Hardware
rationale: Hardware must be on-site and available before installation can begin.

successor: Adjust and test door operation (including child-sized hardware)
rationale: After hardware is installed, the door must be tested to ensure proper function, including latch alignment, handle operation, and closure.

successor: Final inspection of child-sized door assembly
rationale: Inspection of the completed door assembly can only occur after all hardware components are installed.

predecessor: Install plumbing rough-in for nappy changing station
rationale: Plumbing supply and drain lines must be in place behind the wall before the nappy changing station unit can be mounted and connected.

predecessor: Frame and finish wall at nappy changing station location
rationale: The wall structure (studs, backing) and finished surface must be complete to provide a solid mounting surface for the station.

successor: Connect water supply and drain to nappy changing station
rationale: The station unit must be physically mounted before the final plumbing connections to the fixture can be made.

successor: Inspect and test nappy changing station
rationale: The station must be fully installed before it can be inspected for proper function, stability, and compliance with safety codes.
While not physically required, it is logical to position the diaper disposal adjacent to the changing station after the station is placed to ensure proper spacing and workflow in the changing area.

Childproof electrical covers are designed to fit over standard electrical outlets and switches. The outlets and switches must be fully installed and wired before the childproof covers can be mounted or snapped into place.
All electrical wiring, boxes, and rough-in work must be completed and inspected before outlets and their safety covers can be installed.
The childproof covers are part of the final safety and childproofing measures; the final electrical safety inspection should verify that all covers are properly installed and functional.
Once electrical covers are in place, remaining childproofing tasks (e.g., cabinet locks, corner guards) can be completed as part of the overall childproofing scope.
Walls must be finished (drywall mudded, taped, sanded, and painted) before outlet covers are installed to avoid damage to covers from dust, debris, or paint.
The floor must be finished and level before installing fixed cubbies to ensure stability and proper alignment.
Walls must be framed to provide a structural surface for attaching and securing the fixed cubby system.
Electrical wiring and outlets must be roughed in behind the wall before the cubby system is installed, as access will be blocked afterward.
The cubby system must be installed before final painting and trim work so that trim can be fitted and painted around the installed unit for a finished appearance.
Baseboards and floor trim should be installed after the cubby system is in place to create clean transitions and cover gaps at the base.
The wall framing provides the structural support needed to attach the Art and Craft Activity Wall surface.
Electrical wiring behind the wall must be installed before closing the wall with the activity surface.
Any plumbing lines within the wall must be roughed in before the wall surface is installed.
The art and craft activity wall surface must be fully installed before applying final finishes like paint or wallpaper.

successor: Installation of Wall-Mounted Fixtures (e.g., shelves, hooks)
rationale: Wall-mounted fixtures should be attached after the activity wall surface is complete to ensure secure anchoring.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide the supporting structure around which the supervision window is installed.
Exterior walls must be built to define the openings and provide the rough opening framing for the supervision window.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to receive the supervision window unit.
After the supervision window is installed, the gaps around it must be sealed and waterproofed to prevent air and water infiltration.
Interior finishes around the window, such as drywall, trim, and painting, can only be completed after the window is installed.

predecessor: Measure and document radiator dimensions and location
rationale: Accurate measurements of the radiator's size, shape, and location are required to design or select a cover that fits properly and safely.

predecessor: Select or fabricate suitable child-safe cover material (e.g., rounded-edge wood, metal, or plastic)
rationale: The material must be chosen and prepared before the cover can be assembled or installed.

successor: Inspect cover for sharp edges, stability, and secure attachment
rationale: After the cover is installed, a safety inspection is required to ensure it is child-safe, properly secured, and free of hazards.

successor: Test clearance and airflow around radiator
rationale: Once the cover is in place, testing must confirm that adequate airflow is maintained to prevent overheating and that the cover does not obstruct heat distribution.

predecessor: Ensure radiator is turned off and cooled completely
rationale: The radiator must be cold and turned off to prevent burns during installation and to allow safe handling of the cover.
Excavation must be completed to expose the ground surface and create a level area for anchor installation.
Concrete footing/foundation must be poured and cured to provide a stable base to embed or attach the climbing structure anchors.
The anchors must be securely installed in the foundation before the climbing structure frame can be mounted and bolted to them.

Safety surfacing (e.g., rubber mulch or poured-in-place rubber) can be installed after anchors are in place, though this is a soft preference since surfacing could be done concurrently or after frame assembly in some cases.
Final coatings or sealants around the anchor points are best applied after the anchors are set, but this is a soft preference as it could be done later.

predecessor: Complete Structural Framing and Wall Rough-Ins
rationale: Wall framing, backing, and rough-in electrical/plumbing work must be completed before fixtures can be mounted, as the fixtures require attachment to structural framing and connections to utilities behind the wall.
Drywall, wainscoting, or other wall finishes must be installed and finished before mounting fixtures, as the fixtures mount onto the finished wall surface.
Flooring should be installed before child-height fixtures are mounted to ensure proper height measurement from the finished floor and to avoid damaging new flooring during fixture installation.

While not a hard physical constraint, mounting fixtures before final painting allows any minor patching or caulking around the fixture mounting points to be incorporated into the final paint finish for a seamless appearance.

In child-height bathroom or kitchen areas, child-height sinks and counters must be mounted on their supporting fixtures/cabinets, so the mounting of those fixtures precedes the countertop/sink installation.
Window guards must be installed into framed window openings; the frame provides the structural support and attachment points for the guards.
Electrical wiring near windows must be completed before window guards are installed to avoid interference and ensure safe access to the work area.
Window guards are typically mounted to the frame before the operating sashes or fixed glass are installed, allowing easier access for fastening and alignment.
While not a strict physical dependency, it is preferable to install window guards before finishing walls to avoid damaging finished surfaces during guard installation.
Window guards are a safety feature that must be in place before the final inspection can verify compliance with building codes and safety regulations.
Electrical wiring must be installed and tested before covering sockets with childproof plates, as the covers are the final protective layer over the electrical installation.
Childproof electrical covers are fitted over standard sockets and switches; thus the sockets/switches must be mounted first.
Electrical circuits must be tested for safety and correct wiring before applying childproof covers, which would hinder access for testing.
While covers can be removed for painting, it is preferred to install covers after painting to avoid damage from paint splatters, though this is a soft preference.
Childproof covers must be in place before the final safety inspection to verify that all electrical outlets are properly protected according to safety standards.
The structural framing system must be installed to provide the physical support structure onto which supervision glazing panels can be mounted and secured.
Overhead protection or deck above must be completed to provide weather protection and a safe working platform before installing glazing below.
The substrate must be properly prepared, cleaned, and primed to ensure proper adhesion and sealing of glazing materials.
Weatherproofing sealants must be applied after glazing installation to seal edges and joints against moisture ingress.
Interior trim and finishes adjacent to glazing are typically installed after glazing to avoid damage and achieve proper fit and alignment.
Windows must be placed within framed openings; structural walls and rough openings must be complete to receive windows.
Roof structure provides weather protection and structural stability; windows should not be placed before the building is enclosed from above.
After windows are placed, they must be sealed, flashed, and weatherproofed to prevent water and air infiltration.
Exterior cladding is installed around windows; window placement must precede final cladding work to allow proper integration and flashing.
Windows must be installed before interior finishes so that walls can be properly finished around the window frames.
The roller shade must be mounted onto or within the window frame, so the frame must be in place first.
The automated shade requires electrical wiring/power source at the east wall, which must be roughed-in before the shade can be connected and installed.

successor: Test and Commission East Automated Shade
rationale: The shade must be physically installed before it can be tested, programmed, and commissioned for operation.

It is preferred but not strictly required to install the shade before finishing the wall, as finishing after could cause damage to the shade; however, the wall could be finished first if carefully masked.
The shade installation is a prerequisite item that must be completed before the final inspection of the east side of the room can be conducted and signed off.
The structural steel frame provides the primary support and attachment points for the shading louvers, so the frame must be fully erected before louver installation can begin.
The roof deck serves as the overhead structural base; shading louvers are often mounted to or supported by the roof framing, requiring the deck to be in place first.
Shading louvers are integrated with the exterior envelope; installing louvers before cladding allows for proper alignment, flashing integration, and weatherproofing continuity.

While not physically required, completing louver installation before interior finishes prevents potential damage to interior surfaces from overhead work and allows for natural lighting conditions to be established early.
Shading louvers affect solar heat gain and daylighting performance; their installation should be complete before commissioning tests to ensure building systems operate under design conditions.
The structural frame of the east elevation must be fully erected and stable to provide a load-bearing support framework for the glazing panels to be attached.
Rough openings must be framed, squared, and properly sized to receive the glazing units; the assembly cannot proceed without prepared openings.
A weather-resistant barrier must be installed behind the glazing area to prevent moisture intrusion before the glazing assembly seals the exterior envelope.
After the glazing units are installed in their frames, sealants and gaskets must be applied to create an airtight/watertight seal; this finishing step cannot occur prior to placement.

successor: Interior Finishes Adjacent to East Glazing
rationale: Interior wall finishes, trim, and drywall near the east-facing windows are typically done after glazing to avoid damage to finishes during glass installation, though scheduling could be reordered with protection.
The foundation must be completed before any wall construction can begin, as walls require a solid base for structural support.
The floor slab must be in place before the thermal mass partition wall can be erected, as the wall rests on and is anchored to the floor slab.
Underfloor electrical, plumbing, or HVAC rough-in work must be completed before wall construction to avoid conflicts and the need to cut into or work around the wall footing.
The thermal mass partition must be fully constructed before any finishing layers like plaster or cladding can be applied to its surface.
The partition wall must be in place to provide lateral and vertical support before the roof or upper deck structure is installed above it.
The Morning Light Shelf is mounted onto or supported by the wall frame, so the wall must be framed first to provide a structural surface.
If the shelf integrates lighting or power features, electrical rough-in wiring must be completed behind the wall before the shelf is installed.
Flooring is typically installed after wall-mounted shelving to avoid damaging the shelf during floor installation, but it is not a physical necessity if protection is used.
Painting is often completed before shelves are mounted to allow painting behind the shelf, but if desired the shelf can be installed first and painting performed around it.
Decorative items are placed on the shelf after it is fully installed and stable, though this is a logical preference rather than a hard constraint.
The headboard must be mounted onto a completed frame structure; the frame provides the structural support needed to attach the headboard unit.
The electrical and control wiring for east-facing controls must be pulled and roughed in before the headboard is installed, as access to wall cavities is no longer available after headboard mounting.
Final upholstery and aesthetic finishing must be applied after the integrated headboard unit is fully installed and secured in place.

successor: East-Facing Control Panel Connection and Testing
rationale: The control panel's final connections and functional testing can only be performed once the headboard with the integrated controls is mounted and positioned.
The bed frame assembly and mattress placement must follow headboard installation because the headboard serves as the anchor point for the bed structure.
Scaffolding must be erected to provide safe working access to the eastern facade at height before insulation work can begin.
The existing facade surface must be cleaned and repaired to ensure proper adhesion of the insulation materials.
Insulation must be installed before the final cladding or render layer is applied to protect and finish the facade.
Scaffolding cannot be dismantled until all facade work including insulation installation is complete, as access is still required.
The final quality inspection of the facade should follow insulation installation, though this is a quality control preference rather than a physical necessity.

predecessor: Mount alarm clock base on nightstand
rationale: The alarm clock base must be physically mounted and secured before the integration kit can be installed onto or connected to it.

predecessor: Run power cable to nightstand location
rationale: Power must be available at the installation location before the integration kit can be powered on and tested during installation.

successor: Configure alarm time and sunrise simulation settings
rationale: The hardware must be fully installed before software configuration and testing can be performed.
Functional testing of the sunrise light simulation can only occur after the integration kit is physically installed and powered.

predecessor: Rough Opening Preparation for East Wall
