rationale: The rough opening in the east wall must be framed, sized, and prepared before the window sash can be installed into it.
The outer window frame or buck must be set and secured in the rough opening before the operating sash can be placed into the frame.
Flashing and weather-resistive barrier around the east window opening must be applied prior to sash installation to prevent water intrusion.
Interior casing, trim, and drywall finishing around the east window can only commence after the sash is installed and properly aligned.

successor: Exterior Sealant and Caulking (East Window Perimeter)
rationale: Final exterior sealant and caulking around the east window sash must be applied after the sash is fully installed to ensure a continuous weathertight seal.
The trickle vent is integrated into the window frame assembly; the frame must be installed first to provide the structural mounting point for the vent.

predecessor: East Wall Sheathing and Rough Opening Preparation
rationale: The rough opening in the east wall must be framed and sheathed to accept the window assembly that carries the trickle vent.

successor: Sealing and Weatherproofing of East Window Assembly
rationale: The vent must be installed before the window assembly can be fully sealed and weatherstripped to ensure continuity of the air barrier.

successor: Night-Cooling Duct Connection to East Window Vent
rationale: The vent must be in place to serve as the termination point for the night-cooling ductwork; duct connections cannot be finalized without the installed vent.

While the vent should ideally be installed before finishing work to avoid damage to finished surfaces, some finishing can proceed concurrently if the vent opening is protected; this is a soft sequencing preference to minimize rework.
The east wall must be framed first to provide the structural backing and attachment points for the bed niche framing.
Electrical wiring for outlets or lighting within or near the niche must be roughed in before the niche is framed to avoid rewiring through completed framing.
Drywall cannot be installed until the niche framing is complete, as the framing defines the shape and support surface for drywall.
Interior finishing of the niche must follow framing and drywall installation in sequence.
While not strictly physically required, trim work is conventionally done after framing and drywall to create clean edges around the niche opening.

predecessor: Structural Framing for East Sleeping Zone
successor: AC Installation for East Sleeping Zone
rationale: The structural framing must be completed before AC units can be mounted and supported within the structure.

predecessor: Roofing Installation for East Sleeping Zone
successor: AC Installation for East Sleeping Zone
rationale: Roofing must be in place to provide weather protection before installing sensitive AC equipment that could be damaged by exposure.

predecessor: Electrical Rough-In for East Sleeping Zone
successor: AC Installation for East Sleeping Zone
rationale: Electrical wiring, conduits, and power supply points must be roughed in to provide power connections for the AC units.

predecessor: AC Installation for East Sleeping Zone
successor: AC Ductwork Connection for East Sleeping Zone
rationale: AC units must be installed first before ductwork can be physically connected to the units.

predecessor: AC Installation for East Sleeping Zone
successor: Interior Finishing for East Sleeping Zone
rationale: While AC installation should ideally precede interior finishing to avoid rework, it is a soft preference as finishing can sometimes be done around AC components if necessary.
The bench must be built on a stable, level foundation or slab. Without the slab or foundation in place, the bench has no structural base to rest upon.
The storage bench is built into the wall structure. The wall framing must be complete so the bench can be properly anchored and integrated.
If the bench design includes electrical outlets or lighting, the rough electrical wiring must be run inside the wall cavity before enclosing it with the bench structure.
The bench structure must be fully installed before applying final trim, baseboards, or decorative finishes around it.

successor: Flooring Installation (if bench sits on finished floor)
rationale: Typically flooring is installed first and the bench is built on top; however, if the bench is built first, flooring can be cut around it. This is a soft preference for best finish quality.

predecessor: Framing and rough-in of kitchen walls
rationale: The kitchen walls must be framed and the rough-in for plumbing completed before the sink can be installed, as the sink needs a physical structure and drain/waste lines.
Water supply and drain lines must be roughed in and stubbed out to the sink location before the sink can be physically connected and mounted.

The farmhouse sink is typically a drop-in or undermount style, so the countertop must be cut and installed after the sink is positioned; however, for an apron-front farmhouse sink, the cabinet and countertop are often fitted around the sink, making sink placement a prerequisite.

successor: Connecting sink drain and water supply fixtures
rationale: The sink itself must be physically in place before the faucet, drain assembly, and water supply lines can be permanently connected to it.

successor: Tiling or backsplash around sink area
rationale: While backsplash can be installed after the sink, it is easier and cleaner to tile up to the sink edge after the sink is installed; however, tiling could also precede sink installation with careful planning.
The range/cooker is a heavy appliance that must be placed on the finished floor surface. Installing flooring first prevents damage to the floor and allows the range to sit level.
Wall finishes, especially backsplash tiling behind the range, must be completed before the range is installed, as the range would block access to the wall and create a difficult tiling situation.
The gas supply line must be roughed-in and terminated at the range location before the range can be connected and placed.
The dedicated electrical circuit, outlet, or hardwiring connection for the range/cooker must be installed prior to positioning and connecting the appliance.

Adjacent base cabinets are typically installed before the range so they can be aligned, but if the range is a slide-in type, the countertop and cabinetry on either side are fitted after the range is positioned to ensure precise fit and alignment.
The range hood must be installed above the range, and its position is determined by the range's final placement. The range must be in position to correctly align the hood above it.

While countertops are often templated and fabricated before the range arrives, final installation of countertops (especially for slide-in ranges) may be sequenced after the range is in place to ensure a perfect fit against the unit.
Rough framing establishes the structural walls and support framework that cabinets are mounted to; without completed framing, cabinetry cannot be properly installed or secured.
The roof must be installed to provide weather protection before installing finished kitchen cabinetry to prevent water damage to the wood and finishes.
Electrical rough-in (wiring for outlets, switches, and appliance connections) must be completed behind walls before cabinetry is installed, as cabinets would block access to wall cavities.
Plumbing rough-in for kitchen sink, dishwasher, and other fixtures must be run through walls and floors before cabinets are placed, since cabinets would obstruct access to plumbing lines.
Countertops are fabricated and installed directly on top of and supported by the base cabinets; cabinets must be in place and leveled before countertops can be measured, templated, and installed.
Drop-in sinks, cooktops, and built-in appliances (dishwasher, range) are installed into or adjacent to the cabinetry; cabinets must be in place to receive and support these fixtures.
Electrical outlets, wiring for under-cabinet lighting, and any plumbing rough-ins for a sink must be completed before the island framework is built and closed up.
The island must be built on a stable, level subfloor to ensure structural integrity and proper alignment of cabinetry and countertops.
The island base cabinet/frame must be fully assembled and secured in place before the countertop can be measured, fabricated, and installed on top.
The island structure must be in place before any drop-in sink, cooktop, or other integrated appliances can be mounted into the countertop and connected.

Although flooring can go under the island, it is often preferred to install flooring first for a seamless look; however, if the island is built first, flooring can be trimmed to fit as a soft preference.
Electrical wiring must be roughed in before the hood/exhaust unit can be installed, as the hood requires power for its fan and lights.
The exhaust ductwork must be in place before the hood can be mounted and connected, as the hood needs to be physically attached to the duct system to vent air outside.

While it is often easier to install the hood before upper cabinets to ensure proper alignment and fit, it is not a strict physical requirement; cabinets could be installed first and the hood fitted underneath.
It is preferable to paint walls and ceiling before mounting the hood to avoid paint splatter on the appliance, but this is a preference for finish quality rather than a physical necessity.
The final electrical connection and trim-out work (switches, cover plates) must occur after the hood is mounted so that it can be permanently wired and tested.
The electrical wiring and junction boxes must be installed and roughed-in within the ceiling and walls before any lighting fixtures can be physically mounted and connected to the power supply.
The ceiling drywall must be installed, taped, mudded, and finished so that there is a complete surface to mount the lighting fixtures and so that the electrical boxes are properly enclosed.

While not strictly required, painting the ceiling and walls before installing light fixtures prevents paint splatter on the fixtures and allows for easier, cleaner painting without working around the fixtures.

successor: Final Electrical Trim-out / Switch Plate Installation
rationale: The light fixtures must be installed and wired before the final trim plates, switch plates, and any decorative covers can be fitted over the junction boxes and switches.

Installing lighting fixtures is typically one of the finishing steps before the final inspection or walkthrough, as the fixtures need to be in place to verify function, aesthetics, and completeness of the kitchen space.
The wall and floor framing must be complete to provide the structural support for the built-in bench.
The subfloor/underlayment must be in place so the bench has a level, stable base to sit on.
Any wiring for outlets or lighting near the bench area must be roughed in before the bench is built, as the bench would block access to walls and floors.
Finish flooring should be installed after the bench is built so that the flooring can be cut and fitted neatly around the base of the bench for a finished appearance.
Baseboards and trim should be installed after the bench is in place so they can be cut to butt against the bench sides for a seamless finish.
Structural walls and framing must be in place to support cabinetry installation.
Electrical wiring must be roughed in behind walls before cabinets are installed, as cabinets cover wall surfaces and would block access.
Plumbing supply lines and drain pipes must be roughed in within walls before cabinetry is placed, since cabinets would obstruct access to these systems.
Drywall must be installed and finished behind the cabinets to provide a proper finished surface; cabinets are mounted to finished walls.
Countertops are installed on top of base cabinets; the cabinets must be in place to support and align the countertops.
Backsplash tiling typically meets the top of the countertops and runs behind the sink area; cabinets and countertops must be installed first to establish the finished surface for tiling.

successor: Install Kitchen Sink and Plumbing Fixtures
rationale: The sink is installed into the countertop or cabinet base; cabinets must be in place to support the sink and connect plumbing.
While some electrical trim can be done before, it is often easier to install outlet covers and light fixtures after cabinetry is in place to ensure proper alignment and fit around cabinets.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical and plumbing for kitchen
rationale: Electrical outlets, switches, and plumbing lines for the sink must be roughed-in behind the walls before countertops are installed, as countertops cover wall surfaces and cannot be easily removed for later rough-in work.
Countertops are installed directly on top of base cabinets; therefore, all base cabinets must be fully installed, leveled, and secured in place before countertop installation can proceed.

Drywall installation, taping, mudding, and painting behind the countertop area must be finished first since countertops abut walls; attempting wall finishing afterward would be difficult and could damage the finished counters.
The farmhouse sink is typically undermounted or integrated with the countertop; the countertop must be in place to set the sink and connect the faucet and plumbing fixtures.

Backsplash tile is installed above and against the countertop surface; the countertop must be in place to establish a clean horizontal reference line for tiling and to seal the joint between backsplash and countertop.
The wall must be cleaned, patched, and primed to ensure the backsplash tiles or panels adhere properly and the surface is level.
The backsplash typically sits on top of the countertop, so the countertop must be installed first to establish the bottom edge and reveal for the backsplash.
Any electrical boxes, wiring, or outlet relocations behind the backsplash area must be completed before tile/backsplash is installed to avoid cutting into finished work.

successor: Install Kitchen Cabinets (if not already done)
rationale: While cabinets are typically installed before backsplash, if cabinets are being installed after, the backsplash may need to be completed first in certain layouts to allow proper fit behind cabinets.
Grouting must follow tile installation once the thin-set mortar has cured to fill joints and seal the backsplash; sealing is also required after grouting to protect the finish.

successor: Install Kitchen Range Hood or Ventilation
rationale: The backsplash behind the range is typically installed before the range hood is mounted so the hood covers the top edge of the backsplash and the tile can be cut around the duct.
The subfloor must be clean, level, and structurally sound before any flooring can be installed to ensure proper adhesion and a finished surface.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical and plumbing for kitchen
rationale: Rough-in work for plumbing and electrical lines must be completed before flooring is laid, as these are run beneath the subfloor or within walls and would be inaccessible after flooring installation.
Drywall dust and debris from sanding can damage or soil flooring; therefore drywall finishing should be done prior to flooring installation.
Cabinets are typically installed on top of finished flooring to provide a clean look and to allow for future flooring replacement without cabinet removal.
The kitchen island is generally placed on top of the finished flooring for a seamless appearance and to ensure the flooring runs continuously under the island.
Base shoe molding and trim are installed after flooring to cover the expansion gap and create a finished edge where the floor meets walls and cabinets.
Electrical wiring must be run inside the wall cavities, which requires the wall framing to be complete.
The structure must be enclosed and weathertight before running electrical lines to protect wiring from weather damage.
Insulation must be installed after electrical rough-in so that wiring is not buried behind insulation, and electrical boxes remain accessible for inspection and finishing.
Drywall installation directly over the electrical rough-in encases the wiring; electrical must be inspected and approved before drywall closes up the walls.
Electrical rough-in is typically completed before plumbing rough-in to avoid conflicts with pipe placement and to ensure electrical safety clearances from water lines.

Foundation excavation must be completed before rough-in plumbing can begin, as the plumbing lines need to be placed in the ground beneath the foundation slab or within the foundation walls before they are covered.

While some rough-in plumbing occurs before the slab pour (underground lines), the final rough-in of kitchen plumbing for above-slab work typically occurs after the foundation is in place and the floor system is framed, allowing access for drain and supply lines.

Kitchen cabinets cannot be installed until the rough-in plumbing for the sink and other fixtures is complete, because the plumbing pipes must be in place within the walls and floor before cabinetry is mounted over them.

Countertops cannot be installed until all rough-in plumbing lines (supply and drain) are in place within the walls and the sink base cabinet area, as the plumbing must be roughed in prior to countertop templating and installation.

The farmhouse sink installation typically occurs after rough-in plumbing is complete, because the rough-in establishes the drain and supply stub-outs that connect to the sink; however, the sink itself is often installed during cabinet/countertop installation, but the rough-in must precede it.
Structural columns and framing must be erected to provide vertical support before the terrace slab/deck can be placed.
Formwork must be installed to create the mold and temporary support system before concrete for the terrace slab can be poured.

predecessor: Reinforcement Steel (Rebar) Placement for Terrace Slab
rationale: Reinforcement steel must be tied and placed within the formwork to provide tensile strength before the concrete slab can be cast.
The terrace slab must be cured and fully set before waterproofing can be applied to protect the slab from moisture ingress.
The structural terrace slab must be completed and waterproofed before any decorative floor finishes or tiles can be installed on top.
Electrical power must be roughed-in and wiring run to the hood location before the hood can be physically installed and connected.
The ductwork path from the hood to exterior must be framed and roughed-in before the hood and ductwork can be installed.

predecessor: Complete Ceiling/Wall Drywall (or at least substrate)
rationale: The ceiling and surrounding walls need to be finished (or at least have the substrate in place) so that the hood can be mounted securely and the ductwork can be connected through finished surfaces.
The hood must be physically mounted and in place before final electrical connections (hardwiring or plug-in) and circuit breaker termination can be completed.

successor: Install Kitchen Cabinetry (upper cabinets adjacent to hood)
rationale: While it is physically possible to install cabinets before the hood, it is far easier and preferred to install the hood/ductwork first to ensure proper alignment and access to duct connections, then fit cabinets around it.
The parapet wall is typically built on top of or at the edge of the roof slab; the roof slab must be completed first to provide a base for the parapet wall.
Waterproofing must be installed beneath or integrated with the parapet wall to ensure water-tightness at the roof edge; the membrane is typically laid before the parapet is built up.
Coping stones or metal coping caps are installed on top of the completed parapet wall to protect it from water ingress and weather damage.
Flashing details that seal the parapet wall to the roofing system are installed after the parapet wall is complete.

successor: Exterior Wall Finishing / Cladding Completion at Roof Level
rationale: Exterior cladding or finishes at the roof edge are finalized after the parapet wall is in place to ensure a clean termination and weather seal.
The terrace slab or deck provides the structural base upon which the balustrade/railing is anchored. The balustrade cannot be installed until the supporting slab/deck is completed and cured.
Balustrade/railing installation includes penetrations through the waterproofing membrane; thus waterproofing details at posts must be finalized after railing installation to ensure watertight seals.
Finishing materials (tiles, paving, etc.) should be laid after the railing posts are fixed to avoid cutting finishes around posts and to ensure a clean, continuous finish.
Permanent balustrade provides fall protection; temporary safety barriers can only be removed after the permanent railing is in place and certified.
The structural frame supports the terrace and provides the lateral stability needed before installing non-structural components like balustrades.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and cavity for the terrace door/access door installation.
Wall sheathing is typically installed before doors to provide structural bracing and a substrate for weather-resistive barriers.
The weather-resistive barrier must be applied to the wall before the door is installed to ensure proper water management and flashing integration.
Flashing and trim details are installed after the door is set to seal and finish the perimeter against weather intrusion.

While interior finishes like drywall can be done before door installation, it is typical and more efficient to install doors first to allow for proper clearances, though this is a soft preference depending on sequencing.
Exterior siding or cladding is installed after the door and its flashing are in place to maintain a continuous weather-tight envelope.
The structural steel frame must be in place to provide the supporting structure onto which the glass terrace balustrade can be mounted and fixed.

predecessor: Concrete Terrace Slab Pouring and Curing
rationale: The concrete terrace slab must be fully poured and cured to provide a stable level base for the balustrade base shoe or anchoring system.

successor: Waterproofing Membrane Application at Balustrade Base
rationale: The balustrade must be installed first so that waterproofing can be detailed around the base shoe and connection points to ensure a watertight seal.

successor: Handrail Installation (if separate from glass panels)
rationale: The glass panels must be in place to serve as the substrate or anchor point for the handrail that sits atop or alongside the glass balustrade.

successor: Final Terrace Floor Finishing (tiling/paving around base)
rationale: While it is preferable to complete the floor finish after the balustrade for a clean detail, in some sequences the floor can be finished first with the balustrade installed on top; this is a soft preference for better aesthetics and weather sealing.
The fixed planter requires a stable concrete slab or foundation base to be built upon; the slab must be poured and cured before any above-grade planter construction can begin.
Subsurface drainage and proper rough grading must be completed to ensure water does not accumulate under or around the planter, preventing future structural or drainage issues.
After the planter shell is built, waterproofing membranes and liners must be installed to protect the structure from moisture damage and contain soil within the planter.
The planter structure must be fully constructed, cured, and waterproofed before soil can be placed and plants installed; filling the planter before it is complete would damage the structure.
Caps, copings, or decorative finishes around the top edge of the planter must be installed after the main planter body is complete to achieve a clean finished appearance and protect the wall edges.
The bench/seating must be built on a stable, level foundation. The terrace slab provides the base support for the bench structure.
The underlying structural framing of the terrace must be complete to provide support and attachment points for the built-in bench/seating.

The bench/seating is a fixed structural element. Surface finishes like tiles or decking around the bench are installed after the bench frame is in place to create seamless edges and proper transitions.
While cushions are typically installed after the bench structure is complete, this is a soft preference because cushions could be placed later without impacting structural integrity.

predecessor: Rough Electrical (if applicable for lighting near seating)
rationale: Any electrical rough-ins for lighting or outlets near the bench area must be completed before the bench is built, as the bench structure would block access to wiring.
The terrace area must be excavated to the required depth and shape to provide space for drainage pipes, gravel layers, and proper slope before drainage installation can begin.
The foundation forms and base preparation must be completed to establish the structural base and ensure proper drainage positioning within the terrace layers.

Drainage pipes and gravel layers must be fully installed and inspected before the concrete slab is poured, as the drainage system will be embedded within or directly beneath the slab and inaccessible afterward.
After drainage installation, backfilling with gravel or soil around the drainage system is required to protect pipes, provide filtration, and stabilize the area before final surface finishing.

A stable, level, and compacted sub-base (e.g., hardcore, sand, or screed) is physically required to support the paving or decking material. Without proper sub-base preparation, the finished surface will settle, crack, or become uneven.

Any below-ground drainage pipes, drainage channels, or falls must be installed and tested before paving is laid, as it is physically impossible to install drainage after the paving surface is in place without breaking it up.

Sealants, stains, or protective finishes can only be applied after the paving or decking is fully installed, as they are surface treatments that would be damaged or rendered ineffective if applied beforehand.

It is logical to install furniture, planters, and decorative elements after the finished surface is complete to avoid damaging the new surface and to ensure proper placement, though this is a soft preference as furniture could be placed temporarily.

Adjacent soft landscaping, planting, and topsoiling should be completed after paving is laid to avoid soiling or damaging the finished paving surface and to achieve a clean edge detail where paving meets planting.
Balustrades and railings require a solid structural base (concrete slab or deck) to be anchored to; without the slab/deck in place, there is no substrate for installation.
Waterproofing membranes must be applied to the slab/deck prior to railing installation to ensure the waterproofing is continuous and not compromised by post-installed railing base plates.
The primary structure (columns, beams, walls) must be in place to provide lateral support and attachment points for railing systems, especially for wall-mounted handrails.
While painting can be done before railing installation, final touch-ups and finishing around railing connections are typically done after installation to cover scratches and bolt heads.

Balustrades are critical life-safety components (fall protection); a formal inspection for load compliance, guard height, and baluster spacing must occur after installation and before the area is opened for use.
The door frame and rough opening must be constructed before the door can be physically installed.
The terrace floor level must be established to ensure proper door threshold height and clearance.
Weatherproofing and sealing around the installed door must be done after the door is in place to prevent water intrusion.
Interior trim and casing work around the door can only be completed after the door unit is fully installed.
Hardware installation requires the door to be hung and properly aligned first.
A stable, level foundation or concrete slab must be in place to support the weight of the built-in terrace seating and prevent settling or cracking.
Any underground drainage or plumbing lines for the terrace/seating area must be installed before the seating structure is built to avoid costly retrofitting or demolition.
The seating structure defines the layout and boundaries of the terrace; flooring material around or adjacent to the seating can be installed only after the seating frame is complete.
Cushions, upholstery, or finishing surfaces are added last to protect them from construction debris and to ensure they are fitted precisely to the completed seating frame.
Paint, stain, or sealant is applied after the seating structure is fully built and any adjacent finishes are in place, ensuring a uniform, protected final surface.
The structural frame (columns, beams, or walls) must be in place to provide support for the canopy/awning structure and its attachments.
The terrace roof deck and waterproofing membrane must be completed to ensure proper drainage and prevent water damage before installing the canopy/awning above.
It is preferable to complete the canopy/awning first to protect the terrace floor finishing work from weather exposure, but this is not a hard physical constraint.
Installing the canopy/awning first provides covered access and mounting points for exterior lighting fixtures, but lighting can technically be installed before or after.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (Electrical conduits for awning controls/motors)
rationale: Electrical conduits, wiring, and motor controls for retractable or motorized awnings must be roughed-in before the canopy structure is installed to avoid rework and ensure concealed wiring.
Privacy screens and louvers require a structural frame or mounting system (e.g., brackets, mullions, or subframe) to be in place to attach to.
While finishing can sometimes be done before installation, it is generally preferred to install first to avoid damaging the finish during handling, then apply touch-ups or final sealant.
The exterior wall or façade surface must be sheathed and prepared before a privacy screen or louver can be mounted against or integrated with it.
Final inspections and commissioning of the building envelope or shading system must occur after all privacy screens and louvers are fully installed to verify correct operation and compliance.
Any mechanical, electrical, or plumbing rough-in that passes behind or through the screen area must be completed before covering with privacy screens/louvers to avoid rework.
Electrical wiring must be installed and run to outlet locations before outlets can be mounted and connected.
Wall framing provides the structural support and cavities for running wiring and mounting electrical boxes for outlets.
Electrical boxes must be installed and secured in walls before outlet receptacles can be mounted into them.
While outlets are often installed after drywall is hung but before final finishing, ideally the outlet installation should be completed so that drywall cutouts can be precisely made around boxes.
Outlet cover plates are typically installed after painting and trim work to keep them clean, but the outlet receptacles themselves can be installed before.
All outlet installations must be complete before the final electrical inspection can verify proper installation and code compliance.
Ductwork must be installed and in place before diffusers or registers can be attached, as they connect directly to the duct system.
Diffusers and registers are typically mounted into ceilings or walls, so the ceiling grid or wall framing must be completed to provide a mounting surface.
If the diffuser or register includes motorized dampers or sensors, electrical rough-in must be completed beforehand to allow connections.

Diffusers and registers must be installed before final interior finishing (painting, texturing) so that they can be blended or painted over and masked properly, and to avoid damaging finished surfaces during installation.
Diffusers and registers must be in place to allow for proper airflow measurement, adjustment, and balancing of the HVAC system.

Built-in storage units (e.g., wardrobes, cabinets) are typically attached to walls or built into structural openings, requiring rough framing, wall sheathing, and structural support to be in place first.
Any in-wall or behind-cabinet electrical outlets, switches, or data cables must be roughed in before built-in storage encloses wall cavities, avoiding costly rework.
If built-in storage includes or abuts plumbing (e.g., a built-in vanity or kitchen cabinet with sink rough-in), the plumbing pipes must be roughed in before the storage structure is installed.

Built-in storage is generally installed against framed walls; however, if it is a recessed or built-in design that sits flush with finished walls, the wall finishing must occur after to create seamless edges. In many sequences, the storage frame goes in, then drywall is butted up to it, or the storage is installed after drywall. Typically, for fully built-in units, the framing of the unit is done before drywall, but the final finishing and painting of surrounding walls happen after the storage frame is in place.

Flooring (hardwood, tile, carpet) should be installed up to or under built-in storage components. Typically, built-in storage is installed on top of subfloor, and finished flooring is installed around or up to the storage base, ensuring a clean trim line and avoiding damage to the storage during flooring work.
Flooring must be completed before built-in desk installation to ensure the desk sits evenly on the finished floor and to avoid damaging floor materials during desk assembly.
Wall framing must be complete to provide the structural support for attaching the built-in desk to the wall.
Wall surfaces behind and adjacent to the built-in desk must be finished before installation, as it is difficult or impossible to paint or finish walls once the desk is permanently installed.
Electrical wiring for outlets, data ports, and lighting needed at or near the desk must be roughed in before the desk is built, as it would be inaccessible or require destructive work to add later.

successor: Built-in Electrical Outlet / Data Port Trim-Out
rationale: After the desk frame is built, the final electrical outlets, data ports, and any desk-integrated power strips can be trimmed out and installed into the desk structure.
Final trim and touch-up painting around the desk edges must occur after the desk is installed to cover any gaps or fastener holes created during installation.
Walls require a solid foundation to bear the load and provide a stable base. Without a cured foundation, walls cannot be properly anchored or supported.
The floor slab provides the surface upon which walls are erected. Walls must be built on a completed floor to ensure proper alignment and structural integrity.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied within the foundation or slab before walls are installed to ensure continuity of structural reinforcement between foundation and walls.
Roof structures require completed load-bearing walls to rest upon and transfer loads to the foundation. Walls must be fully erected, aligned, and secured before roof framing can begin.

Electrical wiring within walls must be run after wall framing is complete but before wall cladding. However, the wall structure itself must first be fully installed to provide the cavities and support for conduit and wiring.

Built-in furniture (e.g., kitchen cabinets, wardrobes, shelving) must be installed on top of finished flooring to ensure proper leveling, fit, and finish. Installing flooring first also prevents damage to furniture during floor installation.
Walls need to be finished (painted or plastered) before built-in furniture is installed against them, as it would be difficult or impossible to finish walls behind or around the furniture afterward.

Electrical wiring, outlets, and switch boxes must be roughed-in before built-in furniture (like kitchen cabinets or built-in shelving) is placed, as the furniture may cover or require access to these elements.
Plumbing rough-in for sinks, dishwashers, or other fixtures must be completed before installing built-in cabinetry that will house or conceal these connections.
Countertops must be installed on top of the base cabinets or built-in furniture units after they are securely placed and leveled.
Built-in appliances (e.g., dishwashers, ovens, cooktops) are typically installed into or after the built-in cabinetry is in place to ensure proper fit and integration.

The structural frame of the building must be completed before any personalized room features can be installed, as the room enclosures and load-bearing elements provide the physical substrate for interior finishes and custom features.

All rough-in utility work (wiring, piping, ductwork) within walls and ceilings must be completed before personalized features such as custom cabinetry, wall paneling, or smart home systems are installed, to avoid covering inaccessible infrastructure.
Walls must be framed, insulated, and closed with drywall (at least base layer) before personalized finishes like paint, wallpaper, tile, or built-in shelving can be applied to them.

Personalized room features such as custom cabinetry, wall installations, and built-in furniture should be completed before final flooring (e.g., hardwood, tile, carpet) is laid, to avoid damaging finished floors during installation of heavy or fixed features.

While minor touch-ups can be done later, it is generally preferred to complete major personalized features before final painting to ensure a seamless finish without needing to repaint around newly installed elements.

predecessor: Room Electrical Wiring and Conduit Installation
rationale: Security system components (sensors, cameras, control panels) require power and network connectivity; electrical wiring and conduits must be in place before devices can be mounted and connected.
Security cameras, motion detectors, and other surface-mounted components are installed on finished walls and ceilings to ensure proper alignment, aesthetics, and secure mounting surfaces.

successor: Room Security System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: Testing and commissioning of the security system (verifying sensor operation, camera feeds, alarm triggers) can only occur after all security components are physically installed and wired.

It is preferred but not strictly required to complete painting before installing security components to avoid dust and debris affecting sensitive electronics; however, touch-ups can be done after installation if needed.
The security system must be fully installed, operational, and tested before the room is occupied to ensure safety and security of occupants and assets.
Electrical rough-in must be completed to provide power infrastructure and conduit pathways for network and data outlet installation.
Walls must be framed and drywall installed to provide the surfaces and cavities into which network and data outlets can be mounted and wired.
Network and data outlet faceplates and connections must be installed before final wall finishing so that they can be properly trimmed out and painted around.
Network and data outlets must be physically installed and terminated before IT systems can be tested for connectivity and performance.
Although not strictly required, it is preferable to install network/data outlets before workstations and furniture to avoid obstructions and rework when connecting equipment.
The fixed auditorium seating must be anchored to a structurally finished and level concrete slab or subfloor; installation cannot commence until the floor substrate is prepared and cured.
Electrical conduits for seat-mounted lighting or power outlets must be embedded in the floor or run in the slab before seating is installed, as access is impossible afterward.

After seating is bolted down, final floor finishes (e.g., carpet tiles trimmed around seat pedestals, or epoxy sealing around baseplates) must be completed to provide a clean, finished appearance and prevent trip hazards.

The auditorium seating defines the listening and viewing positions; optimal speaker placement and projector alignment are adjusted relative to the fixed seat locations, though rough A/V installation can occur earlier.
Permanent seat numbers, row markers, or aisle signage must be affixed after the seats are installed to ensure accurate alignment with actual seat positions.
The structural steel frame must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the bleacher/retractable seating system.
The concrete slab or finished floor must be installed to provide a level, stable base surface for the bleacher seating to rest upon and be anchored to.

Any required electrical rough-ins for power supply to motorized retractable seating, lighting controls, or power outlets near seating must be completed before the seating structure is installed and blocks access.
Once the main bleacher structure is installed, final seating components such as seat chairs, bench seats, railings, and trim can be attached to complete the assembly.
It is preferable to complete major bleacher installation before applying final floor coatings or performing touch-up painting around the seating area to avoid damage during installation.
The floor must be prepared and leveled before installing built-in bench seating to ensure the bench sits evenly and is properly anchored.
Wall framing must be completed to provide backing and support for built-in bench seating that attaches to or aligns with walls.
Rough-in work for electrical outlets, switches, or plumbing must be completed before bench installation to avoid having to remove or cut into the bench later.
If flooring runs up to or under the bench, the bench should be installed before the final floor finish to allow seamless integration or proper edge detailing.
The area behind and around the bench should be painted and finished after installation to avoid paint lines and to ensure clean finished edges where the bench meets the wall.
The seating must be placed on a finished floor slab to provide a stable, level base. Without the floor slab, there is no structural surface on which to install or anchor the seating.

Wall finishing (plastering and painting) should be completed before seating installation to avoid dust, debris, and paint splatter damaging the installed seats, and to allow easy access for wall work without obstacles.

Seating must be fully installed before the final inspection of the waiting area can be completed, as the seating is a key component that must be checked for proper installation, alignment, and safety.

It is a soft preference to install wayfinding signage after seating is in place so that signage positions can be adjusted relative to actual seating layout for optimal visibility, but signage could technically be installed beforehand.

Electrical outlets and conduit must be roughed in and completed behind or near seating areas before seats are installed; otherwise, accessing wall/floor outlets would require removing or working around the seats.

predecessor: Site preparation and floor slab completion
successor: Queue Management Rail & Stanchion System installation
rationale: The queue management system must be anchored to or installed on a finished, level floor surface. The floor slab must be poured, cured, and finished before stanchion bases can be fixed in place.

successor: Queue Management Rail & Stanchion System installation
rationale: If the queue stanchions require in-floor power or data connections (e.g., for electronic queue displays or integrated ticket dispensers), conduit must be embedded in the slab before the floor is poured and before stanchions are installed.

predecessor: Queue Management Rail & Stanchion System installation
rationale: While not physically mandatory, it is logical to install the queue stanchions and rails first so that overhead or wall-mounted signage can be aligned accurately with the actual queue lanes and pathways.

predecessor: Queue Management Rail & Stanchion System installation
successor: Final flooring finishes (e.g., tile, carpet, polished concrete)
rationale: It is preferable to install the stanchion system first so that flooring can be laid up to or around the baseplates cleanly, rather than cutting flooring pieces to fit around pre-placed stanchions. However, this is a sequencing preference for ease of installation and aesthetic finish rather than a physical necessity.

predecessor: Queue Management Rail & Stanchion System installation
successor: Occupancy / operational setup (queue signage, stanchion belt/rope installation, public opening)
rationale: The physical rail and stanchion structure must be fully assembled and secured before adding retractable belts, ropes, or electronic queue management components. The queue system cannot be functionally used for crowd control until the complete assembly is in place.
The seating row walkway and step structures must be fully constructed and cured before lighting can be installed on or within them.
The physical seating rows and steps must exist as a substrate before lighting fixtures can be mounted, embedded, or attached to them.
Electrical conduit and wiring pathways must be roughed in before lighting fixtures can be connected to power.
The lighting fixture installation must be completed before trim plates, covers, and aesthetic finishing can be applied.
All lighting fixtures must be installed before the system can be energized and tested for proper operation.
A stable foundation or base must be prepared before any sitting space (such as benches, seating areas, or platforms) can be constructed on top of it.
The ground must be graded and leveled to ensure a flat, stable surface for constructing sitting areas.
Once sitting spaces are built, surrounding landscaping (plants, pathways, decorative elements) can be installed without damaging the newly constructed sitting areas.
Shade structures (umbrellas, pergolas, awnings) are typically installed after sitting spaces are built so they can be properly aligned and anchored relative to the seating.
Final cleanup and inspection must occur after all construction including sitting spaces is complete to ensure safety and quality.
A stable foundation must be prepared before the bed platform can be installed to ensure structural support and level surface.
Plumbing lines beneath the floor must be laid before the bed platform is built over them, as access would be blocked afterward.
The bed platform provides the base structure; the frame components are assembled on top of or attached to the platform.
The mattress requires a completed platform to rest upon; placing the mattress before the platform is structurally impossible.
While the headboard can technically be installed independently, attaching it to the bed platform is easier and more secure if the platform is already in place.
The wall framing must be in place to provide a structural surface to which the headboard can be attached and integrated.
Any wiring for bedside lighting, outlets, or switches behind or within the headboard area must be installed before enclosing the wall with the headboard assembly.
The headboard must be fully installed so that surrounding trim, crown molding, and baseboards can be cut and fitted flush against it for a finished appearance.
The headboard installation must be complete so that wall finishing can be applied up to its edges without needing to mask or cut around it later.
Although the headboard should be in place before the bed is made up, this is a logical sequence preference rather than a structural requirement.

The personal storage unit (e.g., closet, cabinet, or shelving system) must be installed on a stable, level floor surface. Without the foundation and floor slab completed, there is no structural base to support the unit.
Personal storage units are typically attached to or enclosed by walls. The wall framing must be in place to provide anchoring points and define the spatial boundaries for the storage unit.
If the storage unit is located near or incorporates plumbing (e.g., a laundry room cabinet or sink base), the plumbing rough-in must be completed first to avoid rework or interference with the unit.

Electrical wiring for outlets or lighting behind or within the storage unit must be roughed-in before installing the unit, as accessing wiring after installation would require removal or destruction of the unit.

While it is often easier to install storage units before final flooring and trim for a clean finish, this is a soft preference. Some contractors install storage after flooring to avoid scratching surfaces; however, the more common sequence is storage first, then finish work around it.
Curtain tracks are typically mounted on or adjacent to window frames. Windows must be installed and glazed first to provide the structural support and finished surface for curtain track attachment.

Curtain tracks are often fixed to the ceiling or the wall-ceiling junction. Ceiling finishing must be completed to ensure a clean, finished surface for track mounting and to avoid damaging finished ceilings during track installation.

Curtain tracks are mounted on walls above windows. Wall finishing provides the final surface for secure track anchoring and prevents damage to unfinished walls during the curtain installation process.

If motorized curtains or curtain track lighting is planned, electrical wiring for the track motor or nearby outlets must be roughed-in before the tracks are installed to avoid having to re-open walls or ceilings.

While curtains can be installed before furniture placement, it is a soft preference to have curtains hung first so that window treatments are in place before arranging furniture and decorative items, allowing for a coordinated interior finish.
The over-bed shelf must be attached to the wall framing; therefore wall framing must be completed first to provide structural support.
Any electrical wiring for bed-area lighting or outlets behind or near the shelf must be completed before the shelf is installed to avoid interference or rework.
It is convenient to install the over-bed shelf before positioning the bed underneath, as the bed may obstruct access to the shelf installation area.

If the shelf is installed before final painting, the wall behind the shelf may not be painted; typically painting is done first, then shelf installed. However, if the shelf itself needs painting/finishing, it may be done before installation. Reversing the order is also common.
Headwall panels are structural wall components that must be installed after the main wall framing is in place to provide a backing structure for attachment.
MEP rough-in work behind the headwall area must be completed before headwall panels are installed, as the panels would block access to the wall cavity.
Surface finishing and painting must occur after the headwall panels are securely installed to ensure a uniform and continuous finish.

successor: Final MEP Trim-Out and Fixture Installation
rationale: Final installation of outlets, switches, medical gas outlets, and other fixtures mounted on or through the headwall must be done after the panels are in place.
Inspection of the installed headwall assembly (including fit, anchorage, and alignment) must follow installation before closing up adjacent work.
Electrical wiring for outlets, lighting, and switches near the bed area must be roughed in before bed platform installation to allow access to wall cavities and avoid interference.
Plumbing rough-in for any adjacent bathroom or wet areas must be completed before bed platforms are installed to avoid having to move or work around the frames.
Mattresses and bedding cannot be placed until the bed platforms and frames that support them are fully installed and stable.

If flooring is to be installed under the bed area, it should ideally be completed before the bed frame is installed, but access for final touch-ups or future maintenance may require the bed to be temporarily moved.
Wall finishing, including drywall, taping, mudding, and painting, must be completed before bed platforms are installed to avoid damage to finished walls and to allow full access for wall work.
The bed frame must be installed first to provide the structural base and mounting surface for the bed cluster lighting fixtures.
Electrical rough-in (conduit, junction boxes, wiring) must be completed before the lighting fixtures can be connected and installed.
The lighting fixtures must be physically installed before they can be tested for proper operation.
It is preferred to finish and test the lighting before installing decorative elements like bed skirts or valances to avoid rework, though not a physical necessity.
Lighting installation is best completed before final touch-ups to avoid damage to finished surfaces during fixture installation.
Personal storage units need a finished, level floor surface for proper installation and stability.
Wall finishing (painting, drywall) must be completed before installing storage units to avoid damage to finished walls and to allow proper anchoring/mounting.
Personal storage units must be installed and in place before the final inspection and handover of the space to the occupant or user.
Storage units must be installed before occupants can move in and begin using them for personal storage.
Plumbing supply and drain lines must be roughed into the floor and walls before the bathtub is set in place, as access to these connections is impossible once the tub is installed.
The subfloor must be properly leveled, reinforced, and waterproofed to support the bathtub load and prevent future water damage before the tub is placed.
Walls and studs around the tub alcove must be framed and adjusted to the exact dimensions of the tub so that the tub can be slid into place and attached securely.
Wall finishes, especially tile, must be installed after the tub is in place so that they overlap the tub flange for waterproofing and a clean aesthetic finish.
Faucets, handles, showerheads, and drain trim can only be connected and finalized after the tub is set and secured in its permanent position.

predecessor: Complete Rough-In Electrical and Low-Voltage Wiring
successor: Install Curtain Track and Privacy Curtains
rationale: Electrical and low-voltage wiring must be completed before curtain track installation to avoid interference with wiring runs and to ensure safe access to walls and ceilings without obstruction from curtain hardware.

successor: Install Curtain Track and Privacy Curtains
rationale: HVAC ductwork must be roughed in before curtain track installation to ensure clearance for duct runs and to avoid having to work around or remove curtains/tracks for duct access.

successor: Install Curtain Track and Privacy Curtains
rationale: Plumbing rough-in must be finished prior to installing curtain tracks to avoid conflicts with pipe locations and to ensure wall and ceiling openings are closed before track mounting.

successor: Install Curtain Track and Privacy Curtains
rationale: The ceiling structure or finish must be in place to provide a secure mounting surface for curtain tracks; tracks are typically attached to the ceiling or ceiling grid.

successor: Install Curtain Track and Privacy Curtains
rationale: All overhead rough-in work must be inspected and approved before closing in with curtain tracks, as tracks can obstruct access to MEP components that may need correction.

predecessor: Install Curtain Track and Privacy Curtains
successor: Install Finish Flooring and Wall Finishes
rationale: Curtains are typically installed before final flooring and delicate wall finishes to allow adjustment and to prevent damage to finished surfaces, though it can be reversed with careful protection.

predecessor: Install Curtain Track and Privacy Curtains
rationale: Installing curtains before final painting allows paint touch-ups around the track mounting points, though painting can also be done first if the track areas are masked.

predecessor: Install Curtain Track and Privacy Curtains
rationale: Privacy curtains must be installed before placing furniture and equipment beneath or adjacent to the curtain zones to ensure proper clearance and access for installation.
The subfloor must be level, clean, and structurally sound to properly support the shower tray and prevent cracking or uneven installation.
The drain pipe and waste plumbing must be roughed in and positioned correctly before the shower tray can be placed, as the tray sits over the drain connection.
The shower area floor and walls must be waterproofed/tanked before tray installation to ensure no moisture penetrates the substrate beneath the tray.
Tiles on the shower walls typically overlap the shower tray flange or sit flush against it, so the tray must be installed first to establish the finished profile and drainage slope.
The shower screen or glass enclosure is mounted onto or around the shower tray; the tray must be in place to provide the base for the screen frame and to seal against water leakage.
The plumbing supply lines and drain pipe must be installed before the shower enclosure can be placed, as the enclosure must connect to these fixtures.
A waterproof membrane or shower pan must be installed and tested to prevent water damage before the shower enclosure walls and door are installed.
Cement backer board or equivalent wall substrate must be in place to provide a solid mounting surface for the shower enclosure panels, tracks, and hardware.

If tile is used as the wall finish, the shower enclosure frame or track is often installed first, and tile is then cut to fit around the enclosure edges. However, if the enclosure is a prefabricated unit, it is typically installed after tiling. This ordering reflects a common sequence where enclosure installation precedes final finish touch-ups.
Shower head, faucet handles, and other trim fixtures should be installed after the shower enclosure is in place to ensure proper alignment and sealing against the enclosure walls.
Washbasin needs to be mounted on or attached to a framed wall structure; wall framing provides the structural support for the washbasin.
The water supply pipes and drain/waste pipes must be roughed into the wall before the washbasin can be connected to them.
The wall surface behind and around the washbasin (e.g., tile backer board or waterproofing) must be finished to provide a proper backing and waterproof seal before mounting the basin.
The washbasin (sink) must be placed and secured before the countertop is installed over/around it.
The basin must be in place before the faucet and drain components can be mechanically connected to it.
Plumbing pipes, drainage, and supply lines must be installed in walls and floors before the toilet fixture can be connected and mounted.
The floor must be prepared, leveled, and finished (e.g., tile or vinyl laid) before the toilet can be set on top to ensure proper fit and sealing.
Wall surfaces around the toilet area should be completed (e.g., drywall, tile, painting) before the toilet is installed to avoid damage and allow for proper flange positioning.
Once the toilet is installed, final plumbing connections can be completed, water supply turned on, and the system tested for leaks and proper flushing operation.
Installing the toilet is often done before adding accessories like toilet paper holders or towel racks, though this order can be swapped with minor inconvenience.
The towel rail/radiator must be mounted on finished tiled walls or at least waterproofed surfaces to ensure proper sealing and prevent water damage behind the fixture.
The water supply pipes or electric cables for the towel rail/radiator need to be in place within the wall before the unit can be physically connected and mounted.

While painting can be done before mounting, it is often preferred to install the towel rail first and then do touch-up painting around it for a cleaner finish, or alternatively paint behind it before installation.
The radiator must be physically installed and connected to the heating system before the entire system can be filled, bled, and tested for proper operation.

successor: Final plumbing connection and leak testing
rationale: The towel rail/radiator must be mounted and connected before final leak testing of the hot water or central heating circuits can be completed.

Plumbing supply lines and drain pipes for the sink must be roughed into the wall and floor before the vanity cabinet is placed, as the vanity covers these connections and they cannot be accessed after installation.
The wall structure must be completed to provide a mounting surface and backing for the vanity cabinet.
Flooring is installed before the vanity so that the vanity sits on top of the finished floor, allowing for proper sealing and preventing water damage to subfloor.
The vanity cabinet base must be installed and leveled first to provide support for the countertop/sink top that is placed on top of it.
The vanity cabinet must be in place before the sink basin and faucet can be mounted to the countertop or vanity top.
Grab bars must be installed on a finished wall surface with proper backing. Tile, backer board, or other wall finish provides the structural substrate needed for secure grab bar mounting.

Wood blocking or metal reinforcement must be installed within the wall cavity before wall finishing to provide a solid anchoring point for grab bars; otherwise the grab bar cannot support required loads.
Grab bars near toilets or showers should be installed before the final fixture placement to ensure proper alignment and accessibility without damaging the fixtures.

It is preferable to complete grab bar installation before final painting and touch-ups so that any sealant gaps or screw covers can be finished over, though this is a soft preference for aesthetic finish.
The wall framing must be in place to install the blocking/reinforcement that grab bars anchor into; grab bars cannot be attached to open framing without the studs and blocking being present.
The wall surface must be prepared and plastered before the recess unit can be set into the wall cavity.
The recess must be installed first so that tiles can be cut and fitted around it for a flush, waterproof finish.
Waterproofing membrane must be applied behind the recess to prevent moisture ingress; the recess is then installed over the waterproofed substrate.
Plumbing rough-in must be completed and inspected before the recess can be positioned, as pipes may run through or behind the recess area.
After the recess is installed and tiled around, grout and caulk must seal the edges to ensure waterproofing and a finished appearance.
The bathroom door frame and rough opening must be framed before the door can be installed.
Wall surfaces (e.g., cement board for tile backer or drywall) need to be in place around the door opening so the door casing can be properly attached and finished.

predecessor: Rough-In Electrical and Plumbing in Bathroom Walls
rationale: Electrical wiring and plumbing pipes routed through wall cavities must be installed before the door is hung, as access to the wall interior is needed and finishing the door would block that access.
Flooring should be laid after the door is installed to allow a clean transition and proper gap at the bottom of the door; if flooring is installed first, the door may need to be cut or planed to fit.
The door slab must be hung and operational before the decorative casing and trim can be applied around the frame.
Wall framing must be complete to provide a structural cavity and support for installing sauna/steam room inserts such as benches, heaters, and paneling.
Electrical wiring for sauna heaters, controls, and lighting must be roughed in before enclosing walls with sauna inserts.
Steam generator supply and drain lines must be roughed in before installing steam room inserts and finishes.
A vapor barrier must be installed behind sauna wall finishes to protect the structure from moisture; sauna inserts are installed over it.
Sauna/steam room inserts (benches, wall panels, ceiling) must be in place before the heater can be mounted and connected.
Flooring such as tile or moisture-resistant material is often installed after sauna inserts are complete to ensure a clean finish and proper waterproofing integration.
The sauna door must be installed after the wall inserts are complete to ensure proper fit and sealing against moisture and heat loss.
Rough openings for any sauna doors, vents, or windows must be framed before inserts and paneling can be applied.
Bathroom wall framing must be complete to provide a structural substrate for waterproofing membrane installation.
All plumbing pipes, drains, and fittings must be roughed in behind walls before waterproofing is applied so that penetrations are properly sealed within the membrane.
Electrical wiring, boxes, and conduits must be roughed in before waterproofing to ensure all penetrations through the membrane are correctly sealed at the backing material.
Floor tiles must be installed over a fully cured waterproofing membrane to prevent water ingress through the tile substrate and into the building structure.
The drainage and waste piping must be laid within the excavated area and below the slab; excavation and subgrade preparation must be completed before any piping can be placed.
A compacted gravel or crushed stone base is required as a stable bearing surface and for drainage beneath the slab before piping is installed.

successor: Pressure Test / Hydrostatic Test of Drainage Piping
rationale: The installed piping must be pressure-tested to verify water-tightness before it is covered or embedded in concrete.
Drainage piping is embedded in or runs beneath the slab; the slab can only be poured after all under-slab piping is installed and inspected.
After piping is laid and inspected, the trench around the pipes must be backfilled and compacted to provide support and protection before any surface construction continues.
Drainage and waste piping must be installed before water supply lines to ensure proper routing and avoid conflicts in wall cavities and under floors.
General rough-in work, including plumbing rough-in, provides the necessary preparatory framework and stub-out locations for water supply lines.
Water supply lines must be in place and connected to stub-outs before fixtures such as sinks, toilets, and showers can be physically connected to the system.
Once water supply lines are installed, pressure testing must be performed to verify there are no leaks before walls are closed up and fixtures are permanently connected.
Water supply pipes must be fully installed, inspected, and tested before walls are closed with drywall to allow access for any necessary repairs or adjustments.
Rough-in plumbing (piping, waste lines, vents) must be installed inside walls and floors before sanitary fixtures (toilets, sinks, basins) can be mounted onto those connections.
Electrical backboxes and cables for lighting/ventilation near sanitary fixtures must be roughed in before fixtures are placed; otherwise walls/ceilings would need rework.
Waterproof membranes in bathrooms, toilets, and kitchens must be applied and cured before installing sanitary fixtures to ensure a watertight seal beneath and around the fixtures.

predecessor: Complete Wall & Floor Tiling (or Finish Surfaces)
rationale: Tiling behind and under fixtures should ideally be completed before fixture installation to achieve a clean finish and proper sealing, though it is a quality preference rather than a physical impossibility to retile later.
The fixtures must be physically set in place and fixed before their flexible supply hoses and trap/drain connections can be made to the building's plumbing system.

A smooth, clean, and structurally sound subfloor or underlayment is physically required to receive tile. Tiling over an unprepared or uneven surface would result in cracked tiles and adhesive failure.
In wet areas like bathrooms or showers, waterproof membrane must be installed before tiling to prevent moisture damage to the substrate and structure.
All rough-in work for electrical, plumbing, and drainage must be completed before tiling, as accessing these systems afterward would require tile removal.
Baseboards, casings, and other trim pieces are installed after tiling to overlap and cover the edges of the finished tile work, creating a clean finished look.

Typically painting is done before tiling, but if painting is done after, care must be taken to protect the tile. Generally painting before tiling is the preferred sequence to avoid paint drips on new tile.
Waterproofing must be completed before installing joinery to prevent moisture damage to cabinets and vanities, and to ensure waterproof membrane continuity behind fixtures.
Plumbing rough-in (drainage and supply pipes) must be in place within walls and floor before vanity and joinery installation to allow proper connection of sink plumbing.
Electrical rough-in wiring and boxes must be installed before joinery to ensure power and lighting can be integrated behind or within cabinets.

While joinery is typically installed before wall tiling to allow tiles to overlap vanity edges for a clean finish, some sequences install tiles first. This is a common preference but not a physical necessity.
The sink and tapware are mounted onto or into the vanity/joinery, so the vanity must be installed first to provide the supporting structure.

successor: Connect Plumbing Fixtures to Supply & Waste
rationale: The supply and waste piping (rough-in) must be installed before fixtures can be physically connected to them, as the fixtures attach to the stub-outs of the already-placed pipes.

successor: Connect Plumbing Fixtures to Supply & Waste
rationale: The water heater must be in place and connected to the hot water supply line to provide hot water to fixtures; fixtures cannot be fully connected without a hot water source.

successor: Connect Plumbing Fixtures to Supply & Waste
rationale: Walls and floors must be framed and sheathed so that fixture mounting surfaces and backing are available for installation and support of sinks, toilets, and other fixtures.

predecessor: Connect Plumbing Fixtures to Supply & Waste
successor: Install Trim & Finish Plumbing (Faucets, Escutcheons, Trap Assemblies)
rationale: After fixtures are connected to supply and waste lines, the final trim items such as faucets, escutcheon plates, and visible trap assemblies are installed to complete the fixture appearance and function.

predecessor: Connect Plumbing Fixtures to Supply & Waste
rationale: Once all fixtures are connected, the entire plumbing system can be pressure-tested and commissioned to verify leak-free operation before walls and finishes are closed.
Electrical rough-in (wiring and junction box installation) must be completed before the exhaust fan unit can be wired and connected to power.
The ceiling structure must be framed and boarded to provide a mounting surface for the exhaust fan housing and to allow ducting to be routed through the ceiling cavity.
Exhaust ducting must be installed first so that insulation and sealing materials can be applied around the ductwork to prevent condensation and air leakage.
Final ceiling finishing should be done after the fan and ducting are installed to cover any cutouts or gaps around the fan housing and duct penetrations.
After the fan unit is physically mounted and ducting is in place, the final electrical connections (e.g., connecting fan to switch and breaker) can be completed.
Electrical rough-in wiring must be run through walls and ceilings before lighting fixtures and switches can be connected and mounted.
Ceiling must be installed to provide a mounting surface for ceiling-mounted light fixtures and to allow wiring to be concealed.
Wallboard must be installed to mount wall switches and to conceal wiring, and to provide finished surfaces for flush-mount lighting.
Switches must be wired and complete before final light fixture trim, bulbs, and covers can be installed, as power must be controlled.
If the exhaust fan is on the same switch circuit as lighting, the switch installation must precede the fan connection and testing.
Grab bars need to be anchored into wall studs or blocking within framed walls to support weight loads.
Sheathing or backer board provides the substrate and structural support needed for grab bar mounting.
Plumbing rough-in must be complete to ensure grab bars are not installed where they would interfere with pipes or fixtures.
Grab bars are typically installed before the final wall finish is applied so that flanges can be properly sealed and integrated into the finish surface.
Grab bars must be in place before installing final fixtures (e.g., toilets, shower controls) to allow for proper positioning and clearance.
Plumbing must be fully installed (rough-in) before it can be commissioned and tested, as testing requires the system to be complete and pressurized.
All fixtures must be installed before commissioning to ensure the entire system is operational and can be tested as a whole.
The plumbing system must be connected to the main water supply and drainage before any commissioning or pressure testing can be performed.
Walls and ceilings must remain open during plumbing testing to allow access for inspection and repair of any leaks; only after successful testing can they be closed.
While insulation can be partially installed before, final insulation around plumbing should often wait until after testing to allow access for leak detection and repair.

successor: Bulk Storage Bin or Silo Installation
rationale: A stable, level concrete foundation is structurally required to support the heavy weight of a bulk storage bin or silo before installation can begin.

successor: Bulk Storage Bin or Silo Installation
rationale: Proper site grading and drainage systems must be in place to prevent water accumulation and soil erosion around the silo foundation.

successor: Bulk Storage Bin or Silo Installation
rationale: Electrical conduits and any plumbing for the silo must be laid underground before the silo is placed to avoid excavation under the structure later.

predecessor: Bulk Storage Bin or Silo Installation
successor: Conveyor or Material Handling System Installation
rationale: Conveyors, augers, and material handling equipment that feed into or out of the silo must be installed after the silo is in its final position to ensure proper alignment and connections.

predecessor: Bulk Storage Bin or Silo Installation
rationale: If the silo is located indoors, the roof and building enclosure are typically completed after the silo is erected to allow crane access and assembly; however, in some designs the building may be built first, so this is a soft preference.

The bulk storage tank requires a stable, load-bearing foundation and base slab to distribute its weight and prevent settling or tilting. The foundation must be completed and cured before the tank can be erected on top.
The ground must be cleared, graded, and compacted to provide a stable surface for foundation construction and subsequent tank placement.
Piping for fill/draw connections, vent lines, and any underground electrical or instrumentation conduits that connect to the tank bottom must be laid before the tank is placed over them.
After the tank is erected and welded, it must be filled with water (or another test medium) to verify weld integrity, shell strength, and absence of leaks before it can be placed into service.

successor: Installation of Tank Insulation and Cladding
rationale: Insulation and weatherproof cladding are applied after the tank shell is fully erected and tested to protect the tank from thermal losses and environmental corrosion.

successor: Piping Connection and Tie-In to Tank Nozzles
rationale: Aboveground piping runs must be connected to the tank's nozzles after the tank is set in its final position to ensure proper alignment and avoid stresses on the tank shell.
Level transmitters, temperature sensors, pressure gauges, and safety interlocks are mounted on the tank after it is erected to avoid damage during tank construction.

successor: Commissioning and Fill with Stored Product
rationale: The tank must be fully constructed, tested, insulated, and instrumented before it can be commissioned and filled with the final product (e.g., fuel, oil, chemical) for operational use.

A stable concrete foundation is physically required to support the weight and operational loads of the bulk storage hopper. Without a properly cured foundation, the hopper cannot be safely placed or anchored.
The bulk storage hopper is typically suspended from or supported by the structural steel frame. The steel framework must be in place before the hopper can be lifted into position and secured.

The conveyor system that feeds material into or receives material from the hopper must be aligned and connected after the hopper is fixed in its final position to ensure proper material flow and belt alignment.

Dust collection ductwork and ventilation systems need to connect directly to the hopper's outlet/vent ports. These connections can only be accurately fitted once the hopper is in its permanent location.

successor: Electrical & Instrumentation Wiring for Level Sensors
rationale: Level sensors, load cells, and other instrumentation mounted on the hopper require wiring connections that are run after the hopper is set in place to avoid damage during installation and to ensure accurate sensor positioning.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the correct bearing level and compaction before any slab or pad can be poured to ensure structural stability.
A properly compacted sub-base layer is required to provide a uniform, load-bearing surface for the concrete slab, preventing differential settlement.
A damp-proof membrane must be laid beneath the slab to prevent moisture ingress from the ground into the bulk storage area.
After pouring the slab, sufficient curing time is physically required to allow the concrete to gain strength before any loads are applied or further work proceeds.

successor: Steel Erection / Structural Steelwork (for building superstructure)
rationale: The floor slab provides the working platform and base for erecting structural steel columns and frames; these cannot be safely installed without a hardened slab in place.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before any wall construction can begin, as the wall requires a stable, prepared foundation.
A reinforced concrete foundation or footing must be poured and fully cured to bear the load of the massive bulk storage/bunker wall before wall erection can start.

Steel reinforcement cages or rebar mats must be placed and tied within the foundation and along the wall alignment prior to pouring the wall concrete, as the wall's structural integrity depends on embedded reinforcement.

After the bunker wall is fully cured, waterproofing membranes or coatings must be applied to the exterior faces to protect against moisture ingress and groundwater, which cannot be done before the wall exists.
