Backfill against the exterior of the bunker wall can only commence once the wall has reached sufficient strength to resist lateral earth pressures.
The bulk storage partition/divider wall must be built on top of a finished floor slab or foundation. The slab provides the base support and bearing surface for the wall.

Any underground or in-slab utility rough-ins (conduit, piping, fire protection lines) that will serve the bulk storage area must be placed and embedded in the slab before the partition wall is erected, to avoid cutting or coring through the completed wall and slab.

The partition wall defines the boundary of the bulk storage bay and the opening for the overhead door. The door frame and door are installed after the wall structure is in place so they can be properly anchored.

It is standard practice to paint and apply wall finishes after the partition is erected, but this is a logical work sequence preference rather than a hard physical necessity—finishes could theoretically be applied earlier if protected.

Storage racking and shelving systems are typically installed after the partition walls are complete because the walls define the bay dimensions and provide reference lines for rack layout and anchoring.

successor: Bulk Storage Access Door / Hatch Installation
rationale: The access door/hatch requires the surrounding wall structure to be in place for proper mounting and framing.

predecessor: Bulk Storage Access Door / Hatch Installation
rationale: Interior finishing work should occur after the door/hatch is installed to ensure proper alignment and sealing around the opening.

predecessor: Bulk Storage Access Door / Hatch Installation
rationale: Weatherproofing seals around the door/hatch perimeter must be applied after the unit is installed to ensure a watertight and airtight fit.

successor: Bulk Storage Access Door / Hatch Installation
rationale: The floor slab and foundation must be completed to provide a stable base and proper threshold for the door/hatch installation.

predecessor: Bulk Storage Framework / Rough Opening Preparation
successor: Bulk Storage Access Door / Hatch Installation
rationale: The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the exact dimensions before the door/hatch can be set in place.

successor: Bulk Storage Level Sensor / Measurement Device
rationale: The level sensor must be installed on or into the bulk storage tank, so the tank structure must be in place first.

successor: Bulk Storage Level Sensor / Measurement Device
rationale: The bulk storage tank and its support structure require a stable foundation before the tank and sensor can be installed.

predecessor: Bulk Storage Level Sensor / Measurement Device
rationale: The level sensor must be physically installed before the overall bulk storage system can be calibrated and commissioned to ensure accurate readings.

predecessor: Bulk Storage Level Sensor / Measurement Device
rationale: The sensor must be mounted before its electrical and signal cables can be connected to it.

predecessor: Bulk Storage Level Sensor / Measurement Device
rationale: The sensor must be installed and wired before it can be integrated into the control system for monitoring and data acquisition.
Bulk storage equipment requires a stable, level concrete foundation to bear its weight and maintain structural integrity during installation and operation.

Underground utilities such as piping, drainage, and electrical conduits serving the bulk storage area must be installed before the above-ground storage equipment is placed to avoid conflicts and rework.
If the bulk storage is located within a building, the structural steel frame and overhead supports must be in place before tanks or vessels can be lifted and set into position.
Process piping, valves, and manifolds connect to the bulk storage vessels and must be installed after the tanks are in their final position to ensure proper alignment and fit-up.
Level instruments, pressure gauges, temperature sensors, and electrical connections for pumps and controls are mounted on or near the bulk storage vessels after they are installed and secured.
Fireproofing material is applied to structural steel members; the steel structure must be erected and in place before fireproofing can be applied.
Steel surfaces must be cleaned, primed, and prepared (e.g., abrasive blasting or cleaning) to ensure proper adhesion of fireproofing materials.
Fireproofing provides the base fire-resistance layer; any subsequent insulation or cladding over fireproofed surfaces must be installed after the fireproofing has cured.

While it is physically possible to install some MEP elements concurrently, it is a soft preference to complete fireproofing first to avoid damage to fireproofing from subsequent installation work and to maintain a clean, uninterrupted fireproofing layer.
Inspection and testing of fireproofing thickness, adhesion, and coverage must occur after the fireproofing has been fully applied and cured to verify compliance with fire-resistance specifications.

successor: Bulk Storage Dust Sealing and Weatherproofing
rationale: The bulk storage structure (e.g., silos, bins, hoppers) must be erected and in place before dust sealing and weatherproofing can be applied to it.

successor: Bulk Storage Dust Sealing and Weatherproofing
rationale: The supporting structural framework for the bulk storage must be complete and stable to provide a substrate for sealing and weatherproofing works.

predecessor: Bulk Storage Dust Sealing and Weatherproofing
rationale: Dust sealing and weatherproofing must be completed before installing cladding panels to ensure the sealant and weatherproofing layers are properly applied and protected.

predecessor: Bulk Storage Dust Sealing and Weatherproofing
rationale: Weatherproofing and dust sealing must be finished before applying interior linings to prevent moisture ingress compromising the lining system.

predecessor: Bulk Storage Dust Sealing and Weatherproofing
rationale: Dust sealing and weatherproofing must be complete to create a clean, dry, and sealed environment before installing sensitive mechanical and electrical equipment inside the storage facility.
Floor boxes and grommets are typically embedded in or mounted onto concrete slabs; the slab must be poured and cured first to provide the structural base for installation.
Electrical conduits that feed into floor boxes must be run beneath the slab before the box can be positioned and connected.
Floor boxes and grommets must be installed and adjusted to final height before the finished floor surface is applied so that the cover plate is flush with the finished floor.
Power and data connections to the floor box can only be completed after the box is physically installed and the floor finish is complete.
Mobile/demountable furniture systems require a finished, level floor surface to ensure stability and proper installation. Floor coverings must be completed before furniture placement.
Walls must be finished and painted before demountable furniture is brought in to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to allow for proper alignment of furniture against walls.
Ceiling installation, lighting, and overhead MEP work must be completed before furniture systems are installed to prevent contamination and access issues.
The building must be weathertight with all windows, doors, and roof sealed to protect demountable furniture systems from water damage and environmental exposure.
Furniture installation must be completed before final cleaning and commissioning activities can proceed, as furniture placement generates debris and must be in place for final space sign-off.
Structural walls and framing must be in place to define the opening and provide support for the door system.
A reinforced header or lintel is required above the opening to bear the weight of the sliding/folding door panels and track system.
Any power or data cabling for automated door operation must be roughed-in before the door is installed to avoid rework.
The door track and bottom guides must be installed before final flooring to allow proper integration and flush finishing around the track.

successor: Final Wall and Ceiling Finishes (paint, trim)
rationale: It is preferred to complete wall/ceiling finishes after door installation to avoid damaging finishes during the heavy door assembly process, though patching is possible if done carefully.
The floor slab must be fully cured and structurally complete to provide a stable, level surface for partition fixing and to avoid cracking or settlement.
Overhead MEP services (ductwork, piping, cable trays) and ceiling grid support must be installed before partitions to avoid interference and rework, as partitions terminate at the ceiling.
Partition panels must be in place to mount and route electrical sockets, data jacks, and low-voltage wiring within the partition cavities.
Demountable partition frames must be erected to allow correct alignment, hanging, and adjustment of doors, frames, and associated hardware.
All conduits, cabling, and plumbing that run beneath the raised floor must be installed before the floor panels are laid, as access to the subfloor space is blocked once panels are installed.
The concrete slab or subfloor must be clean, dry, and level to provide a stable base for the pedestals and support system of the raised floor.
The adjustable pedestals and understructure stringers must be installed and leveled first to support the individual floor panels.
Any final floor covering (carpet tiles, vinyl, or anti-static flooring) intended on top of the raised panels must be applied after the panels are securely in place.
Workstations, server racks, or heavy equipment should only be moved onto the raised floor after all panels are fully installed and load-rated, to avoid damaging or misaligning incomplete sections.
Structural steel framework must be in place to provide support points and attachment surfaces for overhead cable trays and grids.
Overhead lighting rough-in must be completed first to avoid conflicts and rework, and to ensure cable trays do not block light fixture locations.
Large HVAC ductwork should be installed before cable trays to ensure adequate clearance and access, as ducts are bulkier and less flexible to route around trays.
Cables can only be pulled or laid into cable trays after the tray support system is fully installed and secured.

While sprinkler piping can sometimes be routed around trays, it is generally preferred to install sprinkler drops and heads after trays to avoid obstruction and to coordinate final head placement for coverage.
Modular furniture must be placed on finished flooring to ensure stability, proper alignment, and to avoid damaging the flooring material after installation.

Wall finishes must be completed before modular furniture is assembled against walls to avoid dust, paint splatter, or damage to finished surfaces, and to allow full access to walls for painting or wallpapering.

Ceiling work (including MEP services above) must be completed before modular furniture is installed to prevent contamination from overhead dust/debris and to avoid having to work around furniture when accessing ceilings.

Electrical outlets, data ports, and cabling must be roughed-in and terminated at wall/floor locations before modular furniture is positioned, as access to these points would be blocked once furniture is assembled.
Final cleaning, polishing, and touch-up work must occur after all furniture is fully assembled and installed to ensure the space is clean and ready for occupancy without furniture obstructions.
Existing partitions must be removed or stripped out before new relocation or reconfiguration can begin, as the new layout cannot be built over the old structure.

The building's primary structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be complete to provide the supporting framework onto which new partition walls will be anchored or within which they will be placed.

Overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (ductwork, conduit, piping) should be installed before partition walls are framed to avoid conflicts and to allow services to pass through or above the new walls.
Partition walls must be fully framed and in their final position before any finishing work such as drywall installation, taping, mudding, and painting can be applied.
After partitions are reconfigured, electrical outlets, switches, plumbing lines, and data cabling can be run inside the newly framed wall cavities before they are closed up with drywall.
The floor area where the bench will be installed must be prepared and leveled before the bench can be built or installed on top of it.
The wall that the bench will attach to or sit against must be framed and in place before the bench can be constructed or secured to the wall.
The bench structure must be installed first so that finished flooring can be cut and fitted neatly around the bench base for a clean, integrated appearance.
The walls behind and beside the bench need to be finished after the bench is in place to achieve seamless joints and proper paint/trim transitions.
While rough electrical should be in place earlier, final outlet placement adjacent to the bench is easier after the bench is installed to ensure proper positioning and accessibility.

The cafeteria servery line requires a completed floor slab for structural support, and underfloor utilities (drainage, water, electrical) must be roughed-in before the servey equipment can be installed above.

predecessor: Structural Wall Framing and Partition Rough-In
rationale: The servery line must be installed within defined spatial boundaries; wall framing, backing, and partition rough-ins (e.g., for plumbing and electrical within walls) must be completed before installing the servery counter and equipment.

Mechanical ducts, electrical conduits, and plumbing lines that run in the ceiling above the servery must be roughed-in before the servery equipment is placed, to avoid removal or obstruction of equipment for overhead work.
After the servery base units and counters are installed in position, the final plumbing, electrical, and mechanical connections (trim-out) to the equipment can be made.
The servery base cabinets and equipment chassis must be in place before countertops and backsplash surfaces can be measured, cut, and installed on top of them.
The dining table must be installed on a finished floor surface to ensure stability and proper alignment.
Wall finishing should be completed before installing fixed dining tables to avoid damage to finished walls and allow easy access for painting or wallpapering.
Electrical work above the dining area (e.g., ceiling lights, wiring for pendant lights) must be completed before the table is in place to avoid obstruction and rework.
Seating (chairs or benches) around the fixed table can only be properly positioned and installed after the table is fixed in place to ensure correct spacing and alignment.
Final cleaning and polishing of the floor around the table is best done after table installation to address any dust or debris from the installation process, though it is a soft preference.
The Walk-in Cooler/Freezer must be installed on a level, cured concrete slab or foundation that provides structural support and a stable base for the unit.
Electrical conduit and wiring for the cooler/freezer's condenser, evaporator, lighting, and controls must be roughed-in before the unit is installed so connections can be made.
Floor drains and condensate drain lines must be roughed-in prior to cooler/freezer placement to ensure proper drainage from the unit.
The cooler/freezer panels, door, refrigeration system, and controls must be fully installed before commissioning, leak testing, temperature verification, and calibration can be performed.

Final flooring (e.g., tile, VCT, sealed concrete) around the exterior of the cooler is typically completed after the unit is set to avoid damaging the flooring during installation, though this is a preference for sequencing efficiency rather than a physical necessity.
The dishwashing station requires a properly waterproofed floor with drainage system to handle water spillage and wastewater from washing operations.

predecessor: Plumbing rough-in for hot and cold water supply
rationale: Dishwashing stations need hot and cold water supply lines roughed in before the station can be installed and connected.
Commercial dishwashers and associated equipment require electrical supply, which must be roughed in (conduit, wiring) before station installation.
Countertops and backsplashes adjacent to the dishwashing station must be installed after the station is in place to ensure proper alignment and sealing against water.

successor: Final Plumbing Connections and Fixture Trim-Out
rationale: Final connections of faucets, sprayers, and drain lines to the dishwashing station can only be completed after the station is physically installed and positioned.
The tray return conveyor must be mounted on or anchored to the finished concrete floor slab, which must be cured and ready to bear the load.
Foundations and sub-base must be completed to provide stable support for the conveyor system and its supports.
Overhead structural steel (where conveyor is suspended or supported) must be in place before the conveyor can be installed.
The conveyor must be fully installed and mechanically connected before any testing, alignment, and commissioning activities can begin.

successor: Electrical Wiring & Connection to Tray Return Conveyor
rationale: Electrical supply wiring and control connections to the conveyor motor and sensors can only be run after the conveyor is physically in place and its electrical termination points are accessible.
The serving counter must be installed on a completed floor slab to provide a stable, level base.
Electrical supply for heating/chilling units and plumbing for drainage must be roughed-in before the counter can be placed and connected.
The counter structure must be in place before countertops, heating/chilling equipment, and serving accessories can be installed on or within it.
Final wiring, plumbing hookups, and testing for the heated/chilled units must be performed after the counter is positioned and secured.
It is typical to complete surrounding wall finishes and tiling after the counter is installed to ensure a clean transition and fit; however, some sequencing may allow pre-finishing.

predecessor: Structural framing and floor slab installation
rationale: The waste compactor must be placed on a structurally completed floor slab and within the building's structural frame to provide adequate support and enclosure.
Power supply conduits, plumbing drains, and water lines must be roughed in to the compactor location before the unit can be installed and connected.
After the compactor is set in place, final hookups to power, water supply, and drainage can be completed.
The compactor unit must be in position before the waste chute and loading hopper can be aligned and connected to it.

successor: Testing and commissioning of waste handling system
rationale: The compactor must be fully installed and connected before operational testing and commissioning can be performed.

predecessor: Install Rough-in Plumbing for Cleaner's Sink
rationale: Plumbing rough-in (hot/cold water supply lines and drain/waste/vent piping) must be installed and pressure tested before the sink and mop basin can be set in place and connected.
The concrete floor slab or subfloor must be prepared and waterproofed in the janitorial area to provide a stable, water-resistant base before the mop basin is installed.

successor: Connect Faucet & Trim for Cleaner's Sink
rationale: The sink and basin must be physically set in place before faucets, trap, and supply stops can be connected to the fixture.

While not physically mandatory, it is best practice to install ceramic tile or other floor finishes after the mop basin is set so that the basin can be properly integrated and the floor can be sloped to drain.

successor: Final Connection to Drainage System & Commissioning
rationale: The mop basin's drain outlet must be connected to the sanitary drainage piping after the basin is placed, and the entire assembly must be water tested before service.
Acoustic panels are typically mounted onto finished ceiling or wall surfaces; the framing and drywall must be complete to provide a stable substrate for panel attachment.
Electrical work behind finished surfaces must be completed before panels are installed to avoid rework and to allow access for wiring without removing panels.
HVAC ducts and diffusers should be in place before acoustic panel installation, as panel placement is often coordinated with air distribution and to avoid interference.
Acoustic panels are usually installed before the final paint coat or wall finish so that edges can be caulked or trimmed for a clean appearance without damaging paint.
It is preferable to install acoustic panels before bringing in furniture and decorative fixtures to avoid dust/debris settling on finished items and to provide unobstructed access for panel mounting.
The drink dispensing station requires a connection to the main water supply lines for its water input; without water supply, the unit cannot be installed or tested.
The drink dispensing station requires electrical power for refrigeration, dispensing mechanisms, and control systems; electrical wiring must be in place before connecting the unit.
The area around the drink dispensing station must have proper floor drainage to handle spills and waste water; drainage must be completed before positioning the unit.

successor: Test and Commission Drink Dispensing Station
rationale: The station must be physically installed and connected to utilities before it can be tested for proper operation, water flow, temperature control, and dispensing accuracy.
Final countertop sealing, cabinetry trim work, and aesthetic finishing around the drink dispensing station can only be completed after the unit is installed and its exact position is confirmed.
The vertical conveyor requires a level, cured concrete floor slab or foundation to support its base and anchor bolts. Without a stable foundation, the conveyor cannot be safely installed or aligned.
The vertical conveyor often needs to be anchored to or supported by the building's structural steel frame. The frame must be erected and stable before the conveyor can be mounted.
Electrical power supply conduits and wiring for the conveyor motor and controls must be roughed-in to the installation location before the conveyor unit is placed, as access may be blocked afterward.
Once the conveyor is physically installed and secured, the final electrical connections to the motor and control panel can be made, and startup testing can begin.

successor: Conveyor Belt / Track Alignment and Tensioning
rationale: After the conveyor frame is installed, belts or chains must be fitted, aligned, and tensioned to ensure proper operation. This cannot be completed before the conveyor is in place.

The conveyor's control system (PLCs, sensors, safety interlocks) must be integrated and programmed after the conveyor is physically installed and wired, so that the actual device can be tested and calibrated.
The roof must be in place to provide the structural support and weatherproof penetration for the exhaust duct that will run through the roof and terminate at a roof cap.
If the exhaust duct exits through an exterior wall, the wall sheathing must be installed to provide a surface for the duct termination and weatherproofing.
Electrical power must be roughed-in to the location of the kitchen exhaust hood to provide the necessary electrical connection for the fan, lights, and controls.

While the exhaust hood is typically installed after upper cabinets are in place, if the hood is a separate unit it is easier to install it before cabinets to avoid interference; however, this is often sequenced after cabinets for fit and finish.
The exhaust ductwork must be installed before the ceiling is closed up so that the duct connections can be made, sealed, and inspected prior to being concealed behind drywall.
Grease waste plumbing connects to the sanitary drainage system to carry away wastewater, so the main drainage system must be installed first.
Trenches must be excavated and prepared before any underground plumbing pipes can be laid.

Underground grease waste pipes are typically embedded in or run beneath the concrete slab; the slab/foundation must be prepared or poured after rough-in, but for under-slab runs, rough-in plumbing precedes slab pour.
The grease trap/interceptor must be connected to the grease waste plumbing lines; the supply and discharge piping must be in place before the trap unit is set and connected.
All underground grease waste piping must be installed, inspected, and tested before the final concrete slab is poured to avoid future rework.
Plumbing and electrical rough-in work must be completed before installing servery counters, as the counters will cover and connect to these service lines.

predecessor: Floor Prep & Underlayment in Servery Area
rationale: The floor must be prepared and leveled before heavy servery counters are set in place to ensure stability and proper alignment.

successor: Connect Plumbing Fixtures & Equipment to Servery
rationale: Plumbing fixtures such as sinks and drains can only be connected after the counters are installed, as the counters support these fixtures.

successor: Install Servery Equipment (Steam Tables, Refrigeration Units)
rationale: Servery equipment like steam tables and drop-in refrigeration units are typically set into or on top of the counters after the counters are in place.

successor: Final Finishing & Trim in Servery Area
rationale: Final finishes such as backsplashes, edge trims, and caulking around counters must be completed after the counters are installed to achieve a finished appearance.

Electrical and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before the walk-in cooler/freezer is installed, as the unit needs connections for power, drains, and water lines that are run through the slab or walls before the cooler panels and equipment are in place.
The walk-in cooler/freezer must be placed on a level, cured concrete slab or finished floor that can support its weight. The slab must be poured and cured before installation begins.
Final electrical wiring, plumbing connections, and drain hookups to the walk-in unit can only be completed after the unit is physically installed in its final position.
The walk-in cooler/freezer must be fully assembled and installed before it can be tested for proper operation, temperature control, and refrigeration performance.

successor: Install Interior Finishes (walls, ceilings, flooring adjacent to cooler)
rationale: While not physically required, it is best practice to install the walk-in unit before completing adjacent interior finishes to avoid damage to finished surfaces during the bulky cooler installation and to allow for proper sealing and transitions.
Food service equipment must be installed before the ventilation system can be commissioned, as the ventilation system must be tested and balanced with all cooking equipment in place and operational.
The ductwork rough-in must be completed before commissioning so that the ventilation system is fully connected and can be properly tested and balanced.
The fire suppression system must be installed prior to commissioning the ventilation system, as kitchen hood commissioning includes testing of integrated fire suppression interfaces and interlocks.

predecessor: Complete Electrical Supply to Hoods and Fans
rationale: Electrical power must be available to hoods, exhaust fans, and make-up air units before the ventilation system can be commissioned and tested.

successor: Final Inspection and Acceptance of Food Service Area
rationale: The ventilation system must be fully commissioned and verified operational before the final inspection and acceptance of the food service area can take place.
Stage lighting must be installed and functional to properly illuminate the group presentation display area for visibility.
The stage or presentation platform must be fully set up and configured to provide a stable base for the group presentation display.
Audio system must be installed and tested to ensure presenters can be heard during group presentations.
Once the display is set up, presenters can rehearse with the actual equipment and layout to ensure smooth delivery.
Seating should be arranged after the presentation display is in place so that sightlines and audience positioning can be optimized relative to the display location.
The frame must be fabricated first to provide structural support for the whiteboard surface.
The whiteboard surface must be attached to the frame before the entire assembly can be mounted onto the mobile stand.
The frame must be mounted to the base before casters can be attached to make the whiteboard mobile.
Casters must be fully installed before the final quality check to ensure mobility and stability.
The shared storage unit requires a stable and level foundation to be placed upon, as it cannot be installed on unprepared ground.
Electrical and plumbing connections to the shared storage unit must be roughed in before the unit is placed, as accessing these after installation would be extremely difficult.
Interior finishing work such as shelving, lighting fixtures, and wall finishes cannot be completed until the storage unit structure is fully installed and enclosed.
Final connections of utilities to the shared storage unit (e.g., connecting supply lines, installing outlets) must happen after the unit is permanently positioned.
While it is preferable to complete landscaping after the storage unit is in place to avoid rework, some preliminary grading could be done beforehand if needed.
Electrical rough-in (conduit, junction boxes, and wiring) must be installed before task lighting fixtures can be mounted and connected to the power supply.
Task lighting fixtures are often recessed or surface-mounted to the ceiling; the ceiling grid or structure must be in place to support the fixture.

successor: Lighting Fixture Trim and Diffuser Installation
rationale: After the main fixture body is installed, trims, lenses, or diffusers are added to complete the assembly and provide proper light distribution.
Once the fixture is physically mounted, final wiring connections, grounding, and functional testing must be completed to ensure safe operation.
While finishing can be done before or after, installing fixtures before final ceiling finishing allows for precise cutting and fit, reducing touch-up work.
Structural framing provides the load-bearing framework and support structure that modular partitions attach to; partitions cannot be installed without a completed frame.
Rough electrical wiring, conduit, and outlet boxes must be placed within wall cavities before partition panels are installed, as access becomes impossible after.
Plumbing pipes and drain lines running through partition walls must be roughed in prior to partition installation, as they will be enclosed within the modular system.
HVAC ductwork, vents, and returns that pass through or are located in partition walls must be installed before the partition system encloses these spaces.
The modular partition system provides the substrate or mounting surface for wall finishes; finishes cannot be applied until the partition structure is fully installed and stable.
Trim elements such as baseboards, door casings, and corner beads are attached to the completed partition system and require its full installation for proper alignment and fastening.

successor: Final Fixture Installation (Lighting, Electrical Covers, Switches)
rationale: Electrical devices, cover plates, and trim are mounted onto or through the finished partition surface, so the partition must be installed first.
Group junction boxes collect and distribute power and data from the main infrastructure; they must be installed after the main power/data lines are in place to ensure proper connectivity.
Pre-commissioning activities such as continuity testing and insulation resistance checks require the power/data infrastructure to be fully installed before testing can begin.
String cables connect individual modules to the group-level power infrastructure; the group infrastructure must be in place to serve as the termination point for string cables.
Group power/data infrastructure is often mounted on or routed along the racking system; the racking must be installed first to provide support and routing pathways.
DC combiners aggregate outputs from multiple strings and connect to the group-level power infrastructure; they must be in place to define the upstream connection points for the group infrastructure.
The wall or support structure must be in place to provide a stable mounting surface for the presentation display.
Electrical wiring for power and data (HDMI, etc.) must be routed behind the wall before mounting the display to avoid having to remove or work around the mounted unit.
Cables (power, HDMI, network) must be connected to the display after it is mounted in its final position.
Functional testing of the presentation display can only be performed once the display is mounted and connected.

successor: Install Trim / Finish Work Around Display
rationale: Finishing work such as trim, bezels, or wall plates around the display is typically done after mounting for a clean appearance, though it could be done in reverse order with extra care.
Structural framing must be complete to provide the load-bearing support and enclosed spaces where built-in storage units are installed.
Electrical rough-in (wiring, outlet boxes) must be completed before built-in storage is installed to avoid having to cut into or remove the storage units for electrical access.
Wall surfaces must be finished and smooth before built-in cabinets or shelving are attached, ensuring proper fit and finish.

While flooring is often installed before built-ins to allow a seamless look, if storage units are floor-mounted with toe kicks, flooring can be installed after. Typically flooring is preferred before but can be soft.
Built-in storage must be in place before final painting and touch-up around the units to ensure clean edges and proper paint coverage around the integrated storage.
The building foundation must be completed to provide a stable load-bearing surface for the visitor waiting seating area.
The concrete floor slab must be poured and cured before seating can be anchored or placed on the floor.
The structural frame (columns, beams, roof) must be in place to define the enclosed space where seating will be located.
It is preferable to install seating before final wall finishes to avoid damaging finished surfaces during seating installation.
Seating installation must be complete before the area can be cleaned and handed over for visitor use.
The structural framing must be in place to provide the supporting framework onto which the backdrop/feature wall can be attached or built.
Any electrical wiring, outlets, or lighting that will be within or behind the feature wall must be roughed in before the wall is closed up with finish materials.
Any plumbing lines that run within or behind the feature wall must be installed before the wall surface is completed.
The backdrop/feature wall must be fully constructed and installed before it can be painted or receive final wall finishes.
Trim and molding details (e.g., baseboards, crown molding) are installed after the feature wall is built to create a clean transition and finished appearance.

The reception desk must be physically installed before its dedicated lighting can be positioned, mounted, or wired, as the lighting fixtures are typically attached to or aligned with the desk structure.
Electrical rough-in work (conduit, cabling, junction boxes) for the reception desk area must be completed before lighting fixtures can be connected and energized.
If recessed or surface-mounted ceiling lights are used above the reception desk, the lighting fixtures must be installed before ceiling finishes are applied, to allow access for mounting and wiring.
While the lighting can be installed before final trim-out, it is generally preferred to complete all fixture mounting before final connection and testing to avoid multiple electrical callbacks.
If any floor-mounted lighting or low-voltage wiring for desk lighting runs beneath the floor, the lighting must be installed before final flooring is laid to avoid damage or rework.
Wall framing must be completed before ceiling treatment can begin because the ceiling often ties into wall framing, and walls define the perimeter of the ceiling area.
All electrical wiring, conduit, ductwork, and plumbing rough-ins must be installed in the ceiling cavity before the ceiling treatment is closed up, to avoid costly rework.
Insulation must be placed above the ceiling before the final ceiling material (e.g., drywall, acoustic tiles) is installed.
The ceiling surface must be fully installed (e.g., drywall hung and taped) before any painting or decorative finishing can be applied.
While flooring can technically be done before or after ceiling work, performing ceiling work first avoids dust and debris falling on finished flooring, reducing cleanup and risk of damage.

predecessor: Rough-in Electrical and Data Cabling for Lobby Area
rationale: Electrical and data cabling must be roughed-in within the wall cavities and floor boxes before the partition framing and screen are installed, as they would be inaccessible afterward.

predecessor: Rough-in Mechanical/HVAC Ductwork in Lobby Ceiling
rationale: HVAC ductwork and diffuser rough-in within or adjacent to the partition must be completed before the partition framing closes off access.

predecessor: Concrete Floor Slab / Underlayment Preparation in Lobby
rationale: The floor slab or underlayment must be finished and cured to provide a stable base for anchoring the partition and screen components.

successor: Finish Wall Cladding / Painting on Lobby Partition
rationale: Wall cladding, drywall finishing, and painting cannot be applied until the partition framing and privacy screen structure are in place.
While flooring can technically be installed before the partition, it is standard practice to complete the partition first to allow for cleaner transitions and avoid damage to finished flooring.
Signage posts, poles, or mounting frames need to be physically installed and secured before signage panels can be attached to them.
If signage requires concrete footings or bases (e.g., for monument signs), these must be poured and cured before the sign structure is mounted.
The area around signage must be roughly graded and stable to allow safe access for installation equipment and proper placement of signage.
If the sign is illuminated or has electronic features, underground conduits and power supply must be run before the sign base is installed to connect electrical service.
Final grading, planting, and decorative landscaping around the sign should be done after the sign is in place to ensure proper alignment and finish around the sign base.
The concrete base or slab must be poured and fully cured before any seating components can be installed on it, as the seating requires a stable, level, and load-bearing foundation.
The structural frame (walls, columns, or supports) must be in place to provide anchoring points or enclosure for the waiting seating area.
Rough-in work for electrical outlets, lighting, or any plumbing near the seating area must be completed before installing seating to avoid rework and provide clear access.

Installation of waiting seating must be completed before final finishing touches such as baseboards, wall trim, or adjacent flooring can be completed, as the seating defines the layout of the finished space.

While occupancy can technically begin after seating is installed, it is a soft preference to stage furniture placement after the waiting seating is in place to ensure proper spacing and layout coordination.
The information display board must be mounted on or attached to a completed wall surface, so wall construction must be finished first to provide a stable mounting surface.
If the display board requires electrical power for lighting or digital display, electrical wiring must be roughed in and accessible before the board is installed.
Any printed signage, decals, or informational stickers applied to the board must be placed after the board itself is securely installed.

It is preferable to complete final inspection after the display board is installed so that it can be verified for compliance and accuracy, but inspection could theoretically be done earlier in some cases.
Functional testing of display content, lighting elements, or digital features can only be performed once the board is fully installed and connected.
The reception counter must be placed on a finished, stable floor slab. The concrete floor must be poured and fully cured to support the weight of the counter and provide a level base.

Electrical outlets, data ports, and conduit for the reception counter must be roughed-in within the floor and walls before the counter is installed, as access behind the counter becomes difficult or impossible afterward.
The base cabinetry/structural frame of the reception counter must be in place before the finished countertop surface (e.g., laminate, granite, solid surface) can be installed on top.
While not physically required, it is a logical sequence preference to position the reception counter first to then align adjacent workstations and guest seating relative to the front desk layout.

Once the reception counter is installed, final connection of power outlets, data jacks, and any built-in lighting fixtures can be completed, as the counter provides the mounting surface and access points for these finishes.
A stable foundation or base must be prepared before the ticket kiosk can be placed and anchored.
Electrical supply lines and conduit must be run to the kiosk location before the kiosk is installed so that it can be connected to power.
Network and data cables must be laid to the kiosk location before installation so the kiosk can be connected to the ticketing system.
After the kiosk is physically installed in its final position, the electrical and data connections can be completed and tested to verify power and system functionality.
The kiosk hardware must be in place and powered on before the ticketing software can be loaded, configured, and commissioned for public use.
Water supply and drain lines must be roughed into the wall or floor before the drinking fountain can be connected and mounted.
The wall must be framed to provide structural support and a mounting surface for the drinking fountain.
Drywall must be installed and finished behind the drinking fountain location so that the fountain can be mounted flush against a finished wall surface.
After the drinking fountain is physically mounted, the final plumbing connections (supply line and drain) can be made and tested for leaks.

It is preferable to install the drinking fountain before adjacent flooring and trim to avoid damaging these finishes during fountain installation, but this is a soft preference, not a physical necessity.

predecessor: Structural Wall Framing and Partition Rough-In
rationale: The coat rack/locker unit must be mounted on or against finished walls; rough-in framing and partition walls must be in place to provide structural support and proper anchoring.
The locker unit rests on the finished floor; installing flooring first ensures the unit sits at the correct height and prevents damage to the unit during floor work.

While some painting can be done before, the areas behind and around the locker unit should be painted and finished before the unit is installed to avoid difficult touch-up work. However, if the unit is wall-mounted, the wall behind must be fully painted/finished first, so this ordering can be reversed. Typical sequence: paint walls, install locker, then do trim/touch-up.

successor: Electrical and low-voltage outlet installation (if adjacent)
rationale: If lockers are placed near electrical outlets or data ports, those outlets should be roughed-in before locker installation, but final cover plates and trim can be installed after. This is a soft preference as wiring can be routed around lockers.

The locker unit must be fully installed and secure before the space can be used for coat/locker storage, and final cleaning should occur after installation to remove construction debris from the unit.
HVAC ductwork must be installed before diffusers can be attached, as diffusers connect directly to the duct system to deliver conditioned air.
The ceiling grid (or ceiling framing) must be in place to provide structural support and a mounting surface for the HVAC diffuser.
Ceiling tiles are installed after diffusers are mounted so that the diffuser face can be properly positioned flush with or slightly below the finished ceiling plane.

successor: Waiting Area Air Balancing and System Commissioning
rationale: All diffusers must be installed before the HVAC system can be balanced and commissioned to ensure proper airflow measurement and adjustment at each terminal device.

successor: Waiting Area Final Painting and Finishing
rationale: While not a physical necessity, installing diffusers before final painting allows the paint crew to cut in neatly around the diffuser frames, resulting in a cleaner finish.
Fixed seating requires a stable, level concrete floor base for proper anchoring and structural support.
Electrical conduits and junction boxes for seat-mounted lighting or power must be roughed in before seating is installed, as access beneath seats is blocked afterward.
Underfloor HVAC ductwork and ventilation must be completed before seating is installed, as permanent seating restricts access to floor systems.

successor: Final Floor Finishing (e.g., Epoxy, Tile, Carpet)
rationale: Fixed seating must be in place before final floor finishes around and under the seating rows can be applied to ensure seamless integration and avoid damage to finishes.
Fixed seating provides the structural support and mounting points for integrated A/V equipment such as seat-back screens, speakers, or translation systems.
Electrical power must be available to the display locations before information displays can be mounted and connected.
The structural framework (walls, columns, or support structures) must be in place to provide a mounting surface for information displays.
Data/network cables must be routed to display locations before displays are mounted so they can be connected for content delivery.
Displays must be physically mounted before they can be powered on, configured, and tested for proper operation.
While displays can be mounted after painting, it is often preferred to mount them before final trim work so that trim can be fitted neatly around the display frames.
A stable, level foundation or mounting surface is physically required before any queue system components (stanchions, rails, posts) can be securely installed.
Electrical wiring for any powered queue components (digital displays, ticket dispensers) must be roughed in before the queue system is physically mounted to avoid rework and safety hazards.
Flooring (tile, carpet, or similar) must be fully installed before placing queue stanchions and posts to ensure proper alignment, prevent damage to finished floors, and allow accurate layout marking.

Overhead or wall-mounted queue signage and digital display boards must be positioned based on the exact layout of the installed queue system, ensuring correct sight lines and queue direction indicators.

While software configuration can begin in parallel or after installation, final calibration and testing of the queue management system (ticket printers, displays, sensors) requires the physical queue hardware to be in place to validate real-world positioning and user flow.
A stable foundation or concrete pad must be in place to support the kiosk weight and ensure proper alignment before installation can proceed.

predecessor: Run Electrical Conduit / Wiring to Kiosk Location
rationale: Electrical power supply conduits must be installed in the ground or wall before the kiosk is placed, as the kiosk requires a power connection that is typically fed from below or behind.

predecessor: Run Data / Network Cabling to Kiosk Location
rationale: Network cables for transaction processing and connectivity must be laid and terminated before the kiosk is positioned and connected.
The kiosk must be physically installed and connected to power and network before it can be powered on, configured, and tested for functionality.
While it is preferred to complete final flooring and finishes after kiosk placement to avoid damage, the kiosk can sometimes be set on finished surfaces if adequately protected.

Final cleaning and touch-up work is preferably done after the floor finish is applied to avoid disturbing the wet finish, though this is a soft preference as some cleanup can occur concurrently with care.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work above the ceiling (e.g., ductwork, wiring, piping) must be finished before acoustic panels are installed, as panels would block access to these systems.
Any acoustic or thermal insulation placed in the ceiling cavity must be installed before the panels are mounted, as the panels will conceal and enclose the cavity.
Lighting fixtures are often integrated into the ceiling or wall panels; in many systems, panels are placed first and then cutouts or fixtures are installed after panel mounting.

successor: Paint and Finish Walls and Ceilings
rationale: Though not a strict physical dependency, painting and finishing work is typically done before installing acoustic panels to avoid damaging panels with paint splatter; in some sequences panels are installed after finishing for a cleaner look.
Electrical and data cabling must be roughed-in before installing coat storage units to avoid interference and allow access to wall cavities.
Coat storage units need to be mounted on or against finished wall framing; walls must be framed first.
While it's preferable to paint before installing storage to get a clean finish, coat storage can be installed first and painted around; a soft preference for painting first exists for quality.
Coat storage units should be installed before final flooring so that flooring can be laid up to or under the units for a finished look and to avoid cutting around them.
Coat storage installation must be complete before the final clean and inspection to ensure all fixtures are in place and the area is ready for turnover.
The floor slab must be installed and cured to provide a stable, level surface for placing conference chairs.
Conference room walls and partitions must be defined to know the layout and arrangement for chair placement.
Electrical outlets and data cabling in the floor must be completed before chairs are positioned to avoid obstruction or rework.
Chairs should be placed after flooring is complete to avoid damaging finished surfaces; however, if chairs are temporary or protected, this could be soft sequenced.
Once chairs are placed, audio-visual equipment can be positioned and calibrated relative to seating layout, though this can be done concurrently if layout is known.
The table must be ordered and delivered before it can be installed in the meeting room.
The floor surface needs to be finished and level before placing the meeting table to ensure stability and avoid damage.
Painting should be completed before furniture is brought in to avoid paint splatters on the table and to allow easy access to walls.
Lighting installation may generate dust and debris; it is preferred to install lighting before placing the table to keep it clean, though not strictly required.
Chairs cannot be properly positioned around the meeting table until the table itself is placed in its final location.
It is easier to install projectors, screens, and speakers before the table is in place to access ceiling and wall mounts, but AV setup can be done around the table if needed.
Installing floor outlets or desk-level power strips is more convenient before the table is placed, but can be done afterward with some difficulty.
After the table is installed, a final cleaning and polishing of the table and the surrounding area should be performed to remove any dust or debris.
Electrical wiring and conduit must be run to the switch box locations before the dimmer switch can be physically installed and connected.
The electrical box (junction box or switch box) must be mounted in the wall and securely fastened before the dimmer switch can be fitted into it.

Although dimmer switches are typically installed after drywall and painting are complete for aesthetic protection, rough-in can occur beforehand; however, to avoid damage to the finished switch, it is common practice to install the trim/cover plate after painting. This is a soft preference rather than a strict physical constraint.
The dimmer switch must be wired and functional before the lighting fixtures it controls can be tested and fully connected to the dimmer circuit.
All dimmer switches must be installed and wired before the electrical system can be energized, tested, and commissioned for safe operation.
The ceiling grid (or suspended ceiling framework) must be in place to provide the structural support and mounting points for recessed ceiling lights.
Electrical cables, junction boxes, and rough-in wiring for the light circuits must be run before the recessed lights can be connected and installed.
HVAC ducts in the ceiling plenum must be completed first to avoid interference and to allow proper positioning of recessed light housings around ductwork.

successor: Ceiling Drywall or Ceiling Panel Finish
rationale: Recessed light housings must be installed and their positions set before finishing the ceiling surface (drywall or drop ceiling panels) so that the trim rings/flanges can be properly seated and gaps closed.
The recessed light housings and wiring connections must be in place before trims, bulbs, and wall switches are installed and energized during the electrical trim-out phase.
Whiteboards must be mounted on finished walls; wall framing and drywall provide the necessary structural surface for mounting.
Electrical wiring behind walls must be completed before whiteboards are installed to avoid rework or damage to the board.
Wall surfaces must be painted and finished before mounting whiteboards to ensure a clean, finished appearance and to prevent paint splatter on the board.
Whiteboards must be installed before the room is furnished and occupied to allow clear access for mounting and to avoid interference with furniture or occupants.
Whiteboard installation should be completed prior to final inspections to ensure the room is fully finished and ready for use.
The rough window opening must be framed and prepared before any window covering can be installed, including motorized blinds.
Windows must be installed in the openings before motorized blinds can be mounted, as the blinds attach to the window frame or adjacent structure.
Interior walls must be finished (drywalled, mudded, taped, and painted) before mounting blinds, to avoid damaging finished surfaces and to ensure proper fit and aesthetics.
Motorized blinds require electrical wiring (low-voltage or line-voltage) for power and/or control; this rough-in must be completed before the blinds are installed.

It is often easier to install trim and casings around windows after blinds are in place to ensure proper clearances, though this is a soft preference and can be done in the reverse order with careful planning.

successor: Power and Data Floor Box Installation
rationale: Floor boxes are embedded in or mounted on the concrete slab; the slab must be poured and cured to provide a stable substrate.

successor: Power and Data Floor Box Installation
rationale: Electrical and data conduits must be run beneath the slab and stubbed up to the floor box location before the box can be installed and connected.

predecessor: Power and Data Floor Box Installation
rationale: Floor boxes are typically set to finished floor height; final flooring is installed around or up to the box after it is placed and adjusted.

predecessor: Power and Data Floor Box Installation
rationale: The floor box must be physically installed before final wiring connections, device insertion, and cover plate attachment can be completed.

predecessor: Power and Data Floor Box Installation
rationale: Data cables are pulled into the installed floor box and terminated on jacks or connectors after the box is in place.

Cable management trays are typically supported by and attached to the structural steel framework of the building. The steel structure must be in place to provide the physical support and anchorage points for the trays.
Overhead piping (e.g., sprinkler mains, drain lines) must be installed before cable trays so that the cable trays can be routed to avoid interference and to maintain required clearances.
Cables are placed into, on, or within the cable management tray; the tray must be fully installed, secured, and accessible before any cables can be laid or pulled into it.

successor: Firestop / Penetration Sealing at Tray Locations
rationale: After cable trays are installed and cable is placed, any penetrations through fire-rated walls or floors where the tray passes must be sealed with firestop materials to maintain the building's fire-resistance rating.
Ductwork must be installed and routed to the intended locations before diffusers and grilles can be attached to the duct terminations.
Diffusers and grilles are typically mounted into or supported by the ceiling grid; the grid must be in place to provide the structural support and opening.
Any ceiling-mounted sensors, actuators, or lighting near diffuser locations should be roughed-in first to avoid interference during diffuser placement.
Ceiling tiles are often cut to fit around diffusers and grilles; placing tiles first would require rework to cut openings, so diffusers/grilles should be installed before final tiles are placed.
Diffusers and grilles must be in place for the HVAC system to be balanced and airflow measured at each terminal device; balancing cannot occur without the terminal devices installed.
Electrical outlets, switches, and plumbing lines within or near the glass wall must be roughed-in before the glass partition is installed, as access behind the wall will be blocked.
The overhead support structure and ceiling grid must be in place to anchor the glass partition; glass walls often require top track support from the ceiling structure.
The floor must be prepared and leveled to receive the bottom track/channel of the glass partition system, ensuring proper alignment and stability.
Once glass partitions are installed, adjacent walls can be painted and finished up to the glass edges, avoiding damage to the glass from paint splatter during painting.

successor: Floor Covering Installation (e.g., carpet, tile, hardwood)
rationale: It is preferred to install floor coverings after glass walls to allow precise cutting and fitting of flooring materials around the partition base; however, flooring can sometimes be installed first if carefully cut later.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide support and attachment points for interior wall partitions.
The floor slab must be finished and cured to provide a level substrate for the wall partition to be built upon.
Electrical conduit, plumbing pipes, and other MEP rough-ins that run within or behind walls must be installed before the wall is closed up with solid partitions.
The solid wall partition must be fully erected to provide a substrate for plaster, drywall compound, or other surface finishes.
Wall painting and decorative finishes can only be applied after the solid wall partition is built and its surface finishing is complete.

successor: Meeting Room Door with Glass Lite
rationale: The rough opening framing must be completed to provide the structural support and defined space for the door installation.

successor: Meeting Room Door with Glass Lite
rationale: Wall sheathing around the door opening must be in place to ensure the door frame has proper backing and alignment.

predecessor: Meeting Room Door with Glass Lite
rationale: The door must be hung in place before hardware such as locks, handles, and hinges can be attached to it.

predecessor: Meeting Room Door with Glass Lite
rationale: The door frame must be installed before the glass lite panel can be glazed or set into the door's cutout.

predecessor: Meeting Room Door with Glass Lite
successor: Interior Painting and Finishing (door trim and surrounds)
rationale: While painting can often be done after installation, it is a soft preference to install the door first so that trim and casing can be finished properly around the installed door.
Structural framing (load-bearing walls, columns, beams) must be completed to provide the supporting structure against which interior non-load-bearing partitions are installed.
Electrical wiring must be run within wall cavities before the wall partitions are enclosed. Installing partitions first would require cutting or removing them to route wiring.
Plumbing pipes and drain lines that run inside interior walls must be installed before the wall partitions are closed up, as they cannot be retrofitted without demolition.
HVAC ducts, vents, and returns that pass through interior wall spaces must be positioned before the partitions are installed and enclosed.
Drywall or wallboard is fastened directly to the installed partition framing; the partition studs and tracks must be fully erected before sheathing can begin.
Insulation (soundproofing or thermal) is placed within the cavities of the partition framing after the studs are installed but before the wall is closed with drywall.
Doors are hung within door openings framed as part of the partitions, and trim is applied after the partition framing is complete and walls are finished.

HVAC ductwork and diffusers must be installed above the ceiling before the ceiling grid and tiles are placed; otherwise, the ducts would be inaccessible or would require removal of finished ceiling work.

Electrical cables, junction boxes, and low-voltage wiring (e.g., for lighting, data, speakers) that run above the ceiling must be roughed-in before the ceiling grid is hung, as access becomes severely limited afterward.

predecessor: Install Fire Sprinkler Piping and Heads
rationale: Fire sprinkler piping and head placement above the ceiling must be completed and inspected before the ceiling grid is installed to avoid cutting or retrofitting through finished tiles.
The structural overhead support (steel deck, concrete slab, or roof trusses) must be in place to provide anchorage for ceiling grid hanger wires and support.
Ceiling-mounted lighting fixtures are often integrated into or supported by the ceiling grid; the grid must be in place before fixtures are installed or trimmed out.

While not a strict physical necessity, final trim-out of MEP components (e.g., diffuser grilles, sprinkler escutcheons, light fixture trims) is typically sequenced after ceiling installation to achieve a clean finished appearance and avoid damage.
Final wall painting and touch-up is often done after ceiling installation to ensure clean lines at the wall-to-ceiling intersection and to avoid overspray on finished tiles.
The subfloor must be clean, level, dry, and structurally sound before any floor covering can be installed; otherwise the finished floor will be uneven, damaged, or fail prematurely.

Underlayment (e.g., moisture barrier, soundproofing, or cushioning layer) must be placed over the subfloor before the final floor covering is installed to protect the flooring and meet manufacturer specifications.

All MEP rough-in work in walls, ceilings, and below the floor must be finished before floor covering is laid, as accessing these systems afterward would require removing or damaging the finished floor.
Baseboards and trim are installed after the floor covering to cover the expansion gap at the perimeter and to sit on top of the finished flooring material.

While often done before floor covering to avoid drips on new flooring, if the floor is installed first, painting and touch-up must happen afterward with careful protection; this is a soft preference based on sequencing logistics.
The door frame (rough opening) must be built and ready before the door can be installed.
Wiring in walls adjacent to the door opening must be completed before the door is installed to avoid obstruction and rework.
Wall finishing around the door opening must be completed to provide a clean, finished surface for door casing and trim installation.
The door must be hung and clearances set before flooring is installed to ensure proper gap between the door bottom and finished floor.
Door installation must be complete before final painting to allow for caulking, filling nail holes, and painting the door and frame as part of the finish work.
Rough electrical wiring (cables, conduits, junction boxes) must be in place before fixtures can be physically connected to power sources.
Ceiling and wall surfaces must be framed and prepared (drywall, mounting points) before lighting fixtures can be mounted and secured.
Fixture housings and sockets must be installed before lamps/bulbs can be inserted into them.
All fixtures and controls must be physically installed before the system can be powered on, tested, and commissioned.

While painting can sometimes be done before fixtures are installed (with protective covering), it is generally preferred to install fixtures after ceiling finish to avoid damage to fixtures from paint and to achieve a cleaner aesthetic.
Window coverings (e.g., blinds, shades, curtains) require completed window frames and rough openings to be installed so they have a structure to mount to.
Windows must be physically installed in their frames before any interior or exterior coverings (blinds, shutters, curtains) can be mounted onto or around them.
If window coverings are motorized or automated, rough-in electrical wiring must be completed prior to covering installation so that power connections can be made behind the finished surfaces.

Generally, painting and wall finishing is done before installing window coverings to avoid getting paint on them, though in some sequences coverings are installed after painting; this is a soft preference.
Flooring is typically installed after window coverings are in place to allow installers to work without obstruction, but this is a sequencing preference rather than a strict physical requirement.

Electrical power and low-voltage cabling (e.g., HDMI, audio, control cables) must be pulled and terminated in the walls, ceilings, and conduits before AV equipment racks can be positioned and connected. This ensures cables are routed behind walls and above ceilings before equipment blocks access.

Ceilings and drywall must be finished so that projector mounts, speaker brackets, and cable pathways are fully enclosed and supported. Installing AV equipment before ceiling completion risks damage and rework.

While not strictly required, flooring and final finishes should be completed beforehand to avoid dust and debris contaminating sensitive AV equipment. This is a strong preference for protection and cleanliness.

All AV hardware (projectors, screens, speakers, microphones, control processors) must be physically installed and powered before software configuration, network setup, and control system programming can begin.

Calibration of audio levels, video alignment, and room tuning requires all AV components to be installed and operational. This cannot be performed until equipment mounting and rack installation is complete.
The room must have power, networking, and structural mounting points (walls, ceiling) prepared before any AV equipment can be installed.
Electrical and data cabling rough-in must be completed before AV system components can be connected and commissioned.
The AV system must be fully installed and wired before any testing or commissioning can begin.

successor: Commission Room AV Calibration and Tuning
rationale: Calibration and tuning are typically performed after installation, though some pre-calibration can happen in parallel; this is a strong preference for quality assurance.
Furniture installation can technically happen before or after AV installation, but it is preferable to install AV equipment first to avoid moving or damaging furniture.

The room scheduling system requires network connectivity to communicate with central servers, user devices, and other building systems. Network infrastructure must be installed first to provide the necessary communication backbone.

Rooms must be physically complete (walls, ceilings, flooring, doors) before installing scheduling hardware such as wall-mounted tablets, digital displays, or room panels. Installation on unfinished surfaces would be premature and potentially require rework.
Room scheduling devices (digital displays, tablets, sensors) require power. Electrical wiring, outlets, and circuits must be in place to provide power to these devices.

Software configuration (setting up room calendars, user permissions, integration with email systems) depends on the hardware being physically installed and operational. The hardware platform must exist before software can be configured and tested on it.

Commissioning and testing (verifying booking functionality, display accuracy, integration testing) can only occur after the complete system hardware is installed. This ensures end-to-end system verification.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slab edges) must be in place to provide the supporting framework for the glass storefront wall system.
The rough opening must be framed, squared, and properly sized to receive the storefront framing and glass panels.
Waterproof membranes and flashing at the sill and jambs must be installed before the storefront to prevent water intrusion behind the wall system.
Interior drywall, trim, and finishes around the storefront require the glass wall to be in place for proper alignment and gap sealing.
After the storefront frame and glass are installed, final weatherproof sealants and perimeter caulking must be applied to complete the enclosure.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical wiring for desk area
successor: Install Built-in Desk with Cable Management
rationale: Electrical wiring for outlets, data ports, and cable routing must be installed in the wall/floor before the desk is built in place, as access behind the desk would be blocked after installation.

successor: Install Built-in Desk with Cable Management
rationale: The desk is typically built against a finished wall; the wall surface (drywall) must be complete to provide the final backing and finished appearance before attaching the desk structure.

successor: Install Built-in Desk with Cable Management
rationale: Flooring (hardwood, tile, or LVP) should be laid down before the desk is installed so that the desk sits on top of the finished floor, and to avoid the need to cut flooring around the desk legs/base.

predecessor: Install Built-in Desk with Cable Management
rationale: While paint can be done before desk installation, final touch-ups around the desk edges and any caulking/sealing are typically done after the desk is in place for a clean, finished look.

predecessor: Install Built-in Desk with Cable Management
successor: Install desktop outlets and cable management accessories
rationale: Cable management trays, grommets, and final outlet covers/faceplates on the desk surface are installed after the desk structure is securely in place and all cables are routed.
The window or door opening must be framed and structurally complete to provide a mounting surface and support for the blinds or shades.
Windows and doors must be installed before blinds or shades can be mounted, as the blinds attach to the window frame, header, or adjacent wall surface.
Interior walls must be finished, painted, and fully cured before mounting blinds to avoid damaging finished surfaces and to ensure clean final installation.
It is often preferable to install blinds after window casing and trim are in place for proper fit and aesthetic integration, though blinds can be installed before trim in some cases.
Blinds and shades must be installed before the space can be considered finished and ready for occupancy, as they provide necessary privacy and light control.

predecessor: Rough-in Electrical and Data Conduit Routing
successor: Install Integrated Power and Data Floor Box
rationale: Conduit and wiring pathways must be roughed into the slab or subfloor before the floor box can be positioned and connected.

predecessor: Pour and Cure Concrete Slab (or Complete Subfloor)
successor: Install Integrated Power and Data Floor Box
rationale: The floor box is installed into the finished slab or subfloor; the structural substrate must be in place and cured to allow cutting/embedding of the box.

predecessor: Install Integrated Power and Data Floor Box
successor: Wire and Terminate Power/Data Connections to Floor Box
rationale: The physical box must be mounted and secured before electricians can pull wires into it and terminate connectors.

predecessor: Install Integrated Power and Data Floor Box
successor: Floor Covering Installation (e.g., carpet, tile, hardwood)
rationale: If the floor box is flush-mount, the floor covering should be installed up to the box or after box installation; this is a soft sequence preference to avoid damaging the box or requiring re-cutting of the covering.

predecessor: Install Integrated Power and Data Floor Box
successor: Commissioning and Testing of Floor Box Outlets
rationale: All power and data connections must be terminated and the box installed before functional testing of outlets and data ports can be performed.
Acoustic treatment materials (e.g., panels, insulation, baffles) are typically mounted on or within wall assemblies. Walls must be framed and closed-in before acoustic treatments can be installed.
Many acoustic treatments (e.g., ceiling clouds, baffles, acoustic tiles) are suspended from or attached to the ceiling structure. The ceiling grid must be in place to provide a mounting surface.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before acoustic treatments are installed to avoid damaging finished acoustic surfaces and to ensure access for MEP work.
Acoustic treatments such as wall panels and base treatments should be installed before finish flooring to allow proper alignment and to prevent damage to finished floors from ladders and scaffolding.

While it is physically possible to paint after acoustic treatment, it is standard practice to complete painting first to avoid overspray or drips on acoustic panels. However, this is a soft preference as touch-ups can be done later.
Integrated workstations require electrical power to function and be tested; building power distribution must be in place before workstation installation can commence.
Workstations need network connectivity; data cabling must be run and terminated at workstation locations before the workstations can be physically installed and connected.

Workstations are sensitive, precision equipment that require a clean, finished environment; dust and debris from finishing work would damage equipment, so finishes must be complete before installation.
Workstation systems (hardware, software, network) can only be tested and commissioned after the physical workstations are installed and connected to power and network.
Personnel can only occupy workspaces and begin operations after workstations are fully installed, tested, and ready for use.
The signage is applied to the physical office structure, which must be built first.
Signage should be installed before occupants move in to clearly designate the space and avoid disruption after furnishing.
The cabinet frame must be installed to provide the structural support and enclosure for the shared storage cabinet.
Flooring must be completed before installing the cabinet to ensure the cabinet sits on a finished, level surface and to avoid damaging the flooring.
Walls must be framed and finished to provide attachment surfaces and proper alignment for the cabinet installation.
Hardware must be mounted on the cabinet after the cabinet itself is in place to ensure proper fit and alignment.
Interior shelving and dividers are installed inside the cabinet after the main cabinet structure is secured in its final position.
Partition walls require a completed floor slab to provide a stable base for wall placement and load distribution.
Overhead structural elements (beams, slabs above) must be in place so that partition walls can be aligned to structural grids and any top-track anchoring can be installed.
Electrical and data rough-in work within the wall cavities (outlet boxes, conduit) must be completed before walls are closed up with drywall or panels.
Surface finishing such as painting or applying wallcoverings can only occur after partition walls are fully erected and stable.
Doors and their frames are installed into the wall openings after the partition walls are built and squared.
Final electrical trim-out (switches, receptacles, covers) and mechanical grilles are installed after partition walls are complete and finished.

predecessor: Overhead MEP Rough-In (Ductwork, Piping, Electrical Conduit)
rationale: Overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in must be completed first to avoid conflicts and to allow partitions to be placed under the installed services.
The rough opening framing must be completed before any door can be installed, as the door frame and slab require a structurally prepared opening.
The door frame (jambs, head, and sill) must be set and secured in the rough opening before the door leaf can be hung.
Door hardware such as hinges, locksets, and door closers must be installed after the door is hung in its frame to ensure proper fit and alignment.

While painting and finishing can be done before or after door installation, it is common practice to complete painting and trim work after doors are hung to avoid damage and achieve precise fit around the door.
Doors must be fully installed and operational before the final inspection can verify proper function, fire rating compliance, and accessibility requirements.
Electrical power and low-voltage wiring for access control devices (magnetic locks, card readers, electric strikes) must be roughed-in before the hardware can be physically installed and connected.
The door and frame must be in place to provide the substrate for mounting locks, strikes, hinges with electric transfer, and related hardware.
Cable pathways above ceilings or through walls need to be installed to route access control cables to door locations before hardware is mounted.

successor: Trim Out and Finish Hardware Adjustments
rationale: Once locking hardware is installed, final adjustments, strike plate alignment, and trim-out of interior finishes around hardware must occur to ensure proper operation.

successor: Access Control System Programming and Testing
