rationale: Physical hardware must be in place and wired before the electronic access control system can be programmed, addresses assigned, and end-to-end testing performed.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be complete to provide the load-bearing support and defined spatial boundaries for partition wall installation.
A finished floor surface is required as the base onto which the bottom track or channel of the demountable partition is fixed.

Overhead services (ductwork, piping, cable trays) and ceiling suspension components must be in place above the partition line before walls are installed, otherwise access for these services would be blocked.
Partition wall panels must be fully installed and aligned before final decorative finishes are applied to the wall surfaces.

Typically floor finishes like carpet or tiles are installed before partitions, but if partitions are installed first, floor finishing can be done afterward with careful edge detailing; this is a soft preference based on sequencing efficiency.
The structural frame must be complete to provide the supporting structure into which windows are installed.
Windows must be installed before interior finishes to ensure the building envelope is sealed against weather during interior work.
Once windows are glazed, the building envelope is sealed which allows for proper HVAC balancing and testing of the heating/cooling loads.
Window frames must be installed and secured in the structural openings before the glass glazing can be placed into the frames.
After glazing is installed, weatherproofing seals and caulking must be applied around the glass-to-frame interface to prevent air and water infiltration.

predecessor: Install Electrical Panels and Distribution Boards
rationale: Sub-metering equipment typically connects to and draws power from the main electrical distribution panels; the panels must be installed first to provide the physical connection point and power source for the sub-meters.

The conduit and wiring pathways that will connect the sub-meters to the circuits they monitor must be roughed in before the sub-metering devices can be physically mounted and wired into those pathways.

The primary utility meter serves as the master reference point; sub-meters are installed downstream of the main meter to disaggregate usage, so the main meter must be in place to establish the overall service boundary.
The sub-metering hardware must be physically installed and wired before it can be powered on, configured, calibrated, and tested to verify accurate readings and communication.

successor: Install Drywall and Finish Walls (if meters are in-wall enclosures)
rationale: If sub-meter enclosures are recessed or surface-mounted on walls, the electrical rough-in and meter installation must be completed prior to enclosing walls with drywall to avoid rework and ensure access for terminations.
Lighting fixtures require the room partition walls to be framed so that fixture locations and mounting points are established.
Electrical wiring, junction boxes, and conduit must be installed in the ceiling/floor prior to mounting lighting fixtures so that power connections are available.
Lighting fixtures are typically mounted into or supported by the ceiling grid; the grid must be in place before fixtures can be installed.

successor: Light Fixture Trim and Lens Installation
rationale: The main fixture housing must be mounted before trims, lenses, or diffusers are installed to avoid damage and ensure proper alignment.
After fixtures are physically mounted, final wiring connections, grounding, and functional testing can be performed to verify operation.
HVAC ductwork must be in place to supply conditioned air to the terminal unit; the terminal unit connects to the ductwork system.

predecessor: Structural Framing and Ceiling Grid Installation
rationale: The structural ceiling and support grid must be installed to provide a mounting surface and support for the terminal unit.
Electrical power supply wiring must be run to the terminal unit location before the unit can be connected and energized.
The terminal unit must be installed and connected before the HVAC system can be balanced and commissioned to verify proper airflow and performance.
The terminal unit is typically installed above the ceiling; ceiling tiles and finish work should follow to allow access for installation and adjustment.

Room numbering and signage must be applied onto finished wall surfaces; installing signage before wall finishes are complete would result in damage or removal of signage during painting and finishing work.
Flooring must be installed to establish final room boundaries and layouts; signage placement depends on confirmed room dimensions and floor levels.
Ceiling work must be completed before signage installation to avoid interference with overhead work and to ensure signage mounting points are clear.
Though safety systems can be installed beforehand, signage placement should consider fire exit signage and safety equipment locations for coordinated wayfinding.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any foundation work can begin to ensure a stable base.
Accurate site survey and layout marking are required to define the exact location and dimensions before foundation excavation and pouring.
Underground utility lines (water, sewer, electrical conduits) must be laid before the foundation is poured to avoid cutting into the concrete later.
After pouring, the foundation concrete must cure to achieve sufficient strength before waterproofing and backfilling can proceed.
The foundation provides the structural base and anchor points; wall framing and subsequent roof structure cannot start until the foundation is fully complete and cured.

The exterior walls must be built on a stable foundation. The foundation provides the base structural support and anchoring for the wall framing, and walls cannot be constructed without a completed foundation.
Floor framing (subfloor) must be installed before exterior walls so that the walls have a level working platform to be erected upon and the floor system provides lateral bracing for wall placement.
The roof structure (trusses/rafters) rests directly on top of the exterior walls and cannot be installed until the wall framing is complete and properly anchored.
Wall sheathing (OSB/plywood) is applied directly to the exterior wall framing and provides structural rigidity; it cannot be installed before the framing is erected and secured.
Windows and doors are installed into the rough openings framed within the exterior walls, so the wall framing must be complete before these openings exist to receive windows and doors.

The ground must be properly excavated, leveled, and the foundation (e.g., concrete slab, strip footings, or piers) must be poured and cured before any floor framing or subfloor can be installed, as the floor structure relies on a stable, load-bearing base.

Plumbing drainage pipes, water supply lines, and electrical conduits that run beneath the floor slab or within the subfloor space must be laid and inspected before the floor structure is built over them, to avoid costly rework.
The floor platform provides the working surface and lateral restraint needed to erect wall frames; walls are built on top of the completed floor structure.
Once the floor joists or beams are in place, the structural subfloor (e.g., plywood or OSB sheathing) is installed to create a continuous diaphragm and walking surface for subsequent trades.
Interior non-load-bearing partitions are typically laid out and framed after the main floor platform is complete, as their positions are marked on the subfloor surface.
The roof structure must be supported by completed wall framing to bear load and provide proper attachment points for roof trusses and sheathing.
The entire structure, including the roof, depends on a completed foundation and wall system; the foundation must be finished before any superstructure work proceeds.

successor: Teenager's Cottage Roof Sheathing and Underlayment
rationale: Roof sheathing and underlayment are installed directly onto the completed roof truss/rafter assembly, forming the deck for roofing materials.
The finished roofing material (shingles, metal panels, etc.) is applied after the roof structure and sheathing are fully in place to provide weatherproofing.
Interior ceilings are typically installed after the roof structure is complete to allow access for roof framing, insulation, and electrical/mechanical rough-ins.

predecessor: Teenager's Cottage Slab on Ground / Foundation
rationale: The interior partition walls must be built on top of the completed foundation slab to provide structural support and a level base.
If the cottage has timber floor framing, partition walls must be erected after the floor structure is in place to bear on and align with the floor system.
The main structural frame and roof must be completed first to provide overhead protection and stability before interior non-load-bearing partitions are installed.
Electrical wiring and outlet boxes must be installed within the partition wall cavities after the wall framing is up but before cladding is applied.
Plumbing pipes for any bathroom or wet areas within the cottage must be run inside the partition walls after they are framed.
The building shell (walls and roof structure) must be completed before windows can be installed, as windows are fitted into the wall openings of the completed shell structure.
Window rough openings and framing must be prepared and sized correctly before the actual windows can be fitted and installed into those openings.

successor: Teenager's Cottage Window Sealing and Weatherproofing
rationale: Windows must be installed and secured in their openings before they can be sealed, caulked, and weatherproofed to prevent air and water infiltration.

Window installation must be completed before interior wall finishes (drywall, trim) can be applied around the window openings, as the windows need to be in place for proper trim and casing installation.
Windows must be installed before the final exterior cladding or siding around the windows can be completed, as the cladding needs to integrate with and flash around the installed window frames.

predecessor: Install Teenager's Cottage Exterior Door Frames
rationale: The door frames must be installed and secured in the rough openings before the exterior doors can be hung, as the doors attach directly to the frames.
The exterior walls must be fully sheathed and the weather-resistant barrier installed to ensure the door openings are properly prepared and weather-tight before door installation.

successor: Install Teenager's Cottage Exterior Door Hardware (Locks, Handles, Closers)
rationale: Exterior doors must be hung and positioned before door hardware such as locksets, handles, and closers can be installed, as these components attach directly to the door and frame.

successor: Install Teenager's Cottage Exterior Door Trim and Weatherstripping
rationale: The doors must be in place and operable so that trim can be fitted around them and weatherstripping can be properly sealed to the door edges and frame to prevent air and water infiltration.

successor: Complete Teenager's Cottage Interior Finishes (Painting, Flooring, etc.)
rationale: While interior finishes can technically begin before exterior doors are installed, it is strongly preferable to have exterior doors installed to secure the building envelope, control dust, and protect interior work from weather and unauthorized access.
Interior doors require framed wall openings to be installed into, so wall framing must be completed before door installation.

Rough electrical and plumbing work within walls must be completed before interior doors are installed, as accessing these systems after door installation would be difficult and could damage the doors.
Drywall must be installed and finished around door openings before doors are hung, as the drywall work creates dust and debris that would damage finished doors.

successor: Interior Door Hardware Installation (handles, locks, hinges)
rationale: The door itself must be hung in the frame before door hardware such as handles, locks, and hinges can be installed on it.

Interior doors should be installed before final painting and trim work so that the doors can be painted or finished along with the rest of the interior, and trim can be fitted precisely around the door frames.
The desk is a built-in unit that attaches to the wall structure; wall framing must be complete to provide a mounting surface and structural support.
Any electrical outlets, lighting, or wiring intended for or behind the desk area must be roughed in before the desk is installed, as the desk would block wall access.
Wall surfaces behind and around the built-in desk must be finished and primed before the desk is attached, as the desk will be permanently mounted and would prevent later finishing.

While trim and built-ins are often painted before installation, final touch-up painting around the desk can be done after installation; this is a soft preference for sequencing paint work efficiently.

Flooring (e.g., hardwood, LVP, or carpet) must be installed after the desk if the desk sits on top of the flooring, or before the desk if the flooring butts up to the desk. Typically built-in furniture is installed after flooring is complete to avoid damaging floors, but if the desk has legs or a base that sits on the subfloor, flooring must be installed first. Most commonly, built-in desks are installed on top of finished flooring.
The wardrobe/closet structure requires the wall framing to be in place as a surface to attach to and define the space.
Electrical wiring for any lighting or outlets inside or near the wardrobe must be run before enclosing the space with the built-in structure.
Wall surfaces must be finished before installing built-in cabinetry so that the wardrobe sits against clean, finished walls.

While painting can be done before installation, it is often easier to install the wardrobe first so that painting and trim work can be completed around it for a seamless finish, though this is a soft preference based on construction workflow.
The wardrobe is typically installed over subfloor, and finished flooring can be laid up to it; however, some builders prefer flooring first, so this is a soft ordering preference.

The built-in bed/loft is a component that attaches to the structure of the cottage; the framing and walls must be erected to provide the structural support and enclosure for the bed/loft installation.
The flooring must be completed to provide a level, stable base for the bed/loft framework and to ensure the bed/loft is built on the finished floor surface at the correct elevation.
Any electrical wiring that will run inside or behind the built-in bed/loft must be roughed in before the bed/loft is constructed, as it would be inaccessible or difficult to run afterward.

successor: Teenager's Cottage Interior Painting and Finishing
rationale: The bed/loft structure must be in place before the final painting and finishing of the walls and trim around it, to ensure a seamless finished appearance and to avoid painting behind the bed/loft where it would be wasted.

successor: Teenager's Cottage Interior Trim and Molding Installation
rationale: Trim and molding that abuts or integrates with the bed/loft must be installed after the bed/loft is built to achieve proper fit, alignment, and a finished look at the junction points.
The foundation must be completed to provide structural support for the building, including interior stairs.
Floor framing must be in place to anchor and support the interior stairs.
Interior stairs provide access to the upper floor, so they must be installed before upper floor finishing work can begin.

successor: Teenager's Cottage Interior Wall Framing (Upper Level)
rationale: Stairs must be installed to allow workers and materials to access the upper level for wall framing.
The staircase structure must be complete before railings can be attached for safety and proper alignment.
The fireplace/heat source requires a stable foundation to bear its weight and prevent settling or fire hazards.
The fireplace and chimney structure must be integrated with the building's frame, requiring walls and roof framing to be in place before installation.
The heat source must be installed first so the flue system can be connected directly to it for proper exhaust venting.
Masonry, tiling, or other aesthetic finishing around the fireplace cannot be completed until the core fireplace unit or heat source is installed.
It is generally more convenient to complete wall finishing after the heat source is installed to avoid damage to finished surfaces, though it is not a physical necessity.

The main structural shell of the Teenager's Cottage must be completed before the deck/terrace can be attached, as the deck typically connects to the main building's framework and requires a stable structure to anchor against.
Proper ground preparation, grading, and footings/foundations for the deck area must be completed before deck construction begins to ensure structural stability and drainage.
Any underground electrical, plumbing, or gas lines that will run beneath or through the deck area must be roughed in prior to deck construction to avoid costly rework.
After the deck structure is built, waterproofing membranes, sealants, and weatherproof coatings must be applied to protect the materials from moisture and weathering.

Railings and balustrades are safety elements that must be installed after the deck platform is complete, as they attach directly to the deck structure and require the finished surface for proper alignment.
Smoke/CO detectors require electrical power to operate; electrical wiring must be completed first to supply power to the detector.
Smoke/CO detectors are typically mounted on ceilings; the ceiling structure must be in place before the detector can be installed.
While detectors are often installed before final finishing to avoid damage, it is a soft preference as finishing could be done around the detector.
Smoke/CO detectors must be installed and operational before final inspection can certify the building as safe for occupancy.
Building codes require functioning smoke/CO detectors before occupants can move in, as detectors are life-safety devices.

Electrical wiring must be run through walls, ceilings, and junction boxes before any light fixtures can be physically mounted and connected to the power supply. Without rough-in wiring in place, there is no electrical circuit to connect the fixture to.

Light fixtures (especially ceiling-mounted ones) must be installed after drywall is in place because the fixture mounts to the finished ceiling surface and the electrical box must be flush with the finished drywall. Installing fixtures before drywall would require removal and reinstallation.

successor: Lighting Fixture Trim and Bulb Installation
rationale: The main body/housing of the light fixture must be securely mounted and wired before any decorative trim, shades, lenses, or bulbs are added, as the trim attaches to the installed fixture base.

While not strictly required, it is standard practice to complete final painting before installing decorative light fixtures to avoid paint splatter on the fixtures. However, fixtures can be installed first and then carefully painted around.
Light fixtures must be fully installed and operational before the teenager can occupy the cottage, as lighting is essential for safe and functional living space.

Site mobilization (bringing equipment, materials, and establishing site access) must be completed before excavation can begin, as excavation requires heavy machinery, personnel, and a prepared worksite.

Accurate site survey and staking of the building footprint must be completed before excavation to ensure the excavation is performed in the correct location, alignment, and depth according to the design drawings.
Vegetation, trees, and surface obstructions must be cleared from the building footprint area before excavation can proceed, as they would physically obstruct digging operations.
Foundation excavation must be completed before footing construction can begin, as the footings are poured and formed within the excavated trench to provide structural support.

After excavation, the exposed subgrade at the bottom of the excavation must be compacted and tested for bearing capacity before any concrete is placed, to ensure adequate soil support for the foundation.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and prepared with proper compaction and formwork before any concrete can be poured to ensure structural integrity and proper foundation dimensions.
Steel reinforcement (rebar) must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured, as the rebar provides tensile strength within the concrete slab/foundation.
Any underground plumbing, conduit, or electrical lines that run beneath the concrete slab must be installed and inspected before concrete is poured, as they cannot be placed after the slab is cured.

The concrete foundation/slab must be fully poured and cured to sufficient strength before any vertical framing or wall construction can begin, as the walls depend on the concrete for a stable load-bearing base.
Once the concrete is cured, waterproofing membranes or coatings can be applied to the foundation walls/slab to protect against moisture ingress before backfilling or further construction.
The foundation must be fully cured and ready before any framing can begin, as the frame is anchored to and supported by the foundation.

While rough-ins can be installed after framing, it's generally more efficient to complete below-slab rough-ins before framing starts; however, this is a soft preference as most rough-in work happens after framing.
Roofing cannot begin until the roof framing and sheathing are complete, as the roof structure depends on the frame for support.
Windows and doors require framed and sheathed openings to be installed into the structure.
Exterior siding must be applied over the sheathing, which is installed during the framing and sheathing phase.
The foundation and slab must be completed to provide a stable base and structural support before walls and openings for windows and doors can be framed and installed.
Wall framing must be completed to create the rough openings and structural support needed to install windows and doors.
The roof structure should be completed to provide weather protection and structural integrity before installing windows and doors.
Windows and doors must be installed first to seal the building envelope before interior finishing work such as drywall or plaster can be applied around openings.
Windows and doors are installed before exterior cladding or siding so that the flashing and weatherproofing details can be properly integrated around the openings.
Foundations and slab must be poured and cured before any MEP rough-in work can begin, as MEP lines are embedded in or run beneath the slab.
Wall and ceiling framing must be complete to provide the cavities and structure through which MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) rough-in lines are run.
MEP rough-in must be completed and inspected before insulation is installed, as insulation would cover and block access to MEP lines.
All MEP rough-in work must be finished and approved before drywall is hung, otherwise walls would need to be opened up later for MEP work.

While interior finishes typically follow MEP rough-in, some finishes like painting can begin before all MEP is finalized; however, the standard sequence is to complete MEP rough-in before starting interior finishes to avoid rework.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (wiring, piping, ductwork) must be completed before interior finishes such as drywall, insulation, and trim are installed, as these finishes would cover and block access to rough-in components.

The structural shell (walls, roof, windows, doors) must be completed and the building enclosed to provide a weathertight environment before delicate interior finishes can be installed without risk of water or weather damage.

Interior finishes such as wall painting, trim installation, and ceiling work must be completed before flooring is installed to prevent damage to finished floors from paint drips, dust, and debris during wall and ceiling finishing.

successor: Teenager's Cottage Final Fixtures & Appliance Installation
rationale: Interior finishes (paint, trim, drywall) must be completed before installing final fixtures and appliances (light fixtures, switches, outlets, cabinets, countertops) to avoid damaging finished surfaces during the fixture installation process.

While cabinets and countertops are often installed before final painting or trim in some sequences, it is generally preferred to complete major interior finish work first to avoid dust and debris settling on new cabinets; however, this can vary by project and is a soft preference.
Rough carpentry (framing, sheathing, and structural elements) must be complete before built-in millwork can be installed, as millwork requires stable walls and structural support to be in place.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins must be completed behind walls and in ceilings before millwork is installed, as built-in millwork typically covers or integrates with these systems and would otherwise need to be removed or cut for access.

Drywall must be installed, taped, mudded, and sanded before millwork is installed, as millwork is typically attached to finished wall surfaces and would be damaged by drywall dust and finishing work if done afterwards.

successor: Teenager's Cottage Interior Painting and Finishing
rationale: Built-in millwork installation must be completed before final painting and wall finishing so that paint can be applied seamlessly to both walls and millwork, and so that trim and millwork joints can be caulked and painted as a unified finish.

Built-in millwork such as base cabinets, bookcases, and window seats must be installed prior to finished flooring so that flooring can be laid up to or around the millwork properly, or so that millwork sits on top of the subfloor before finished flooring is installed for a clean transition.
The ground must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil, and excavated to proper depth before any foundation work can begin.
Underground water, sewer, and electrical lines must be laid before pouring the foundation slab/footer to avoid breaking through the foundation later.
The foundation must be cured and load-bearing before any wall framing can be erected on top of it.
Floor joists and subflooring require a stable foundation as their base support.
Waterproofing membrane and drainage board must be applied to the cured foundation, and backfill placed against the foundation walls, before above-grade construction proceeds.
The internal wall lining (e.g., plasterboard or drywall) must be fixed to a completed wall frame or studwork structure. Without the framing, there is no substrate to attach the lining to.

All electrical cables, plumbing pipes, and HVAC ducts that run inside the walls must be installed, tested, and approved before the walls are closed up with lining. This is a hard physical constraint as the lining would otherwise need to be cut open or removed for access.
Any wall insulation (thermal or acoustic) must be placed inside the wall cavity before the lining is fixed, as the lining permanently encloses the cavity.
The process of finishing plasterboard joints (taping, joint compound application, sanding) and/or applying a plaster skim coat can only occur after the wall boards have been installed.
Decorative finishes such as paint or wallpaper require a completed and finished wall lining surface to be applied onto.
The roof structure must be in place to provide support and enclosure before ceiling lining can be installed.
Electrical wiring, cables, and junction boxes must be run in the ceiling cavity before it is closed off with ceiling lining.
Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning ducts must be installed in the ceiling void before it is enclosed by ceiling lining.
Any plumbing pipes or fire suppression sprinkler lines running through the ceiling space must be installed before the ceiling is closed in.
The ceiling lining boards must be fixed in place before any finishing work such as plastering, jointing, or painting can be applied.
Ceiling lining installation often secures the top of wall partitions, and walls may depend on the ceiling for lateral support and alignment.
Recessed lights, ceiling fans, and other ceiling-mounted fixtures can only be installed after the ceiling lining is in place to mount to.
It is generally preferred to paint ceilings before walls to avoid drips, but this is a soft sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
Ceiling work is typically completed before finished flooring to avoid damage to floors from falling debris or tools, but this is a protective preference rather than a hard constraint.
Internal doors require framed openings within walls to be installed; without wall framing, there is no structural support or rough opening for the door.
The rough opening must be framed and sized correctly to accommodate the door frame and door slab before installation can proceed.
The door must be hung and properly aligned before trim and casing can be applied around the door frame.

While painting can be done before door installation, it is often preferred to paint or finish the door after installation to ensure seamless integration and touch-up of any damage during installation.
Although doors can be installed before flooring, it is generally preferred to install flooring first so the door can be trimmed to the correct finished floor height, avoiding gaps or binding.
The door must be hung in place before door hardware such as locks, handles, and latch plates can be fitted and aligned with the strike plate in the frame.
Wall framing creates the cavities that will hold insulation; without the frame structure in place, there is no space to install insulation.
Electrical wiring must be run through wall cavities before insulation is installed, as insulation would block access to run wires afterwards.
Plumbing pipes routed through interior walls must be placed before insulation fills the cavities.
A vapor barrier (if required) is typically installed over the insulation to prevent moisture diffusion, so insulation must be in place first.
Drywall is installed directly over the insulated wall cavities, so all insulation must be complete before enclosing the walls.

Water supply pipes, drainage pipes, and vent stacks must be installed within the walls and floors before sanitary fixtures (toilets, sinks, showers) can be connected to them. The fixtures cannot be mounted until the rough plumbing connections are in place.

Floor and wall waterproofing, screeding, and tile installation must be completed before sanitary ware is installed, because fixtures are mounted onto finished surfaces. Installing fixtures before tiling would require removal and reinstallation, and waterproofing integrity would be compromised.

Electrical wiring, switch boxes, and outlet boxes must be roughed in behind walls before sanitary fixtures are installed. Once fixtures are mounted, access to install wiring behind them becomes difficult or impossible.
Sinks and countertop basins (sanitary ware) must be installed before the vanity cabinets can be fully fitted and sealed around them. The cabinet tops and cutouts are aligned to the installed sink.

The sanitary ware (toilet bowl, sink basin, shower tray) must be set in place and secured before the final trims like taps, mixers, flush mechanisms, and P-traps can be connected. These finishing pieces attach directly to the installed fixtures.
Roof decking provides the structural base upon which roof insulation is installed; insulation cannot be laid without a solid deck.
Underlayment (e.g., roofing felt or synthetic membrane) is installed directly on the deck to provide waterproofing and must be in place before insulation to protect against moisture ingress.

predecessor: Complete Rough-In of Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP) Services in Roof Cavity
rationale: Any wiring, ductwork, or piping that will run through or above the insulated space must be roughed in prior to insulation to avoid conflicts and rework.
A vapor barrier is typically placed on the warm side of insulation after installation; this is a design preference depending on climate, not a strict physical necessity.

successor: Install Roof Finish / Roofing Material (e.g., shingles, tiles, metal panels)
rationale: The final roofing material encloses and protects the insulation; the insulation must be fully installed before the roof finish is applied to ensure thermal continuity and protection.
The timber frame requires a solid, level load-bearing base. The concrete foundation must be fully cured and set before the timber frame can be erected to provide structural stability.
A damp proof course must be installed between the foundation and timber frame to prevent moisture rising from the ground into the timber, which could cause rot and structural failure.
Perimeter drainage around the foundation must be completed before the timber frame is erected, as access for drainage installation would be blocked or severely restricted once the frame is in place.
The roof structure relies on the timber frame walls for support. The frame must be fully erected and braced to provide the necessary load-bearing structure for roof installation.
Wall sheathing and cladding are applied directly to the exterior of the timber frame. The frame must be complete to serve as the substrate for these finishes.
The structural steel frame must be fully erected and stable to provide the supporting framework onto which cladding panels are attached.
The roof structure needs to be in place to provide top lateral support and weather protection; cladding typically ties into the roof perimeter.
Floor slabs provide the intermediate support ledges and anchorage points for cladding panels at each floor level.
Windows are typically installed after cladding is in place because cladding defines the rough openings and provides the weathertight envelope that window frames seal against.

Internal finishes can begin after cladding is installed because the building envelope is then weathertight, protecting interior work from the elements; however, this is a soft preference as temporary enclosures could be used.
The subfloor must be clean, level, and dry before any flooring material can be installed, otherwise the flooring will be uneven or damaged.
Underlayment provides moisture barrier, sound dampening, and a smooth surface required before laying most types of flooring.
All rough-in mechanical, electrical, and plumbing work below the floor must be finished before flooring is laid, as accessing these after flooring would require demolition.
Baseboards and trim are installed on top of or against the finished flooring to cover expansion gaps and create a finished appearance.
Transition strips between room edges and different flooring types must be installed after the main flooring is laid to bridge gaps and finish edges.
The rough opening (framed window opening) must be built and properly sized before a window can be physically installed into it.

predecessor: Install Flashing and Weather Barrier (House Wrap)
rationale: Weather-resistant barriers and flashing must be applied around the rough opening to prevent water infiltration before the window is set in place.
Exterior siding and trim are installed after windows are placed so that the siding can overlap the window flanges and trim can be fitted around the window frame.
Interior drywall installation around windows requires the window to be in place to properly tape, mud, and finish the edges where drywall meets the window frame.

successor: Install Window Sills and Interior Trim
rationale: Interior window sills, casing, and trim can only be measured, cut, and installed after the window unit itself is fixed in the opening.

Electrical rough-in (wiring, boxes, conduits) must be installed within wall cavities, ceiling spaces, and structural framing. Therefore, the framing and structural work must be complete to provide access to these spaces before electrical rough-in can begin.
Electrical rough-in work must be completed and fully visible before the inspection can be performed to verify compliance with code.

Insulation is typically installed after electrical rough-in because the wiring and boxes run through wall cavities that need to be insulated, and the insulation would block access to complete the electrical work if installed first.

Electrical boxes, wiring, and conduits must be roughed in behind walls before drywall is installed, as drywall closes off the wall cavities and makes it impossible to add electrical rough-in after without cutting openings.

While not always physically required, coordinating plumbing and electrical rough-in positions is best done with plumbing first to avoid conflicts in wall cavities, and electrical can work around plumbing. This is a soft preference for coordination efficiency.
Electrical wiring must be run through walls before cabinetry is installed, as cabinets would block access to wall cavities and make retrofitting electrical impossible without removing cabinets.
Plumbing supply lines and drain pipes must be roughed in within walls and floors before cabinets are installed, since cabinets cover these areas and would need to be removed for later plumbing work.
HVAC ducts and vents within walls or ceilings must be installed prior to cabinetry, as cabinets would obstruct access to these systems.
Countertops are fabricated and installed directly on top of base cabinets; the cabinets must be in place and level to support the countertops.

Backsplash tile or material is installed above countertops and against the wall behind cabinets; cabinets must be in place to define the backsplash boundary and to ensure a finished look at cabinet edges.
First fix plumbing must be completed to provide the pipework connections for sanitary ware such as toilets, basins, and baths.
Waterproofing of wet areas must be done before sanitary ware is fitted to avoid compromising the waterproof membrane and to ensure water-tightness.
Tiling and finished floor surfaces must be completed before sanitary ware installation so that fixtures sit on or against the finished surfaces for proper alignment and sealing.
Sanitary ware must be physically installed before final connection to water supply, waste pipes, and drainage systems can be made.
Electrical supply for shower pumps or heated towel rails is usually roughed in earlier, but final connection to sanitary-adjacent fittings occurs after the sanitary ware is in place.
All plumbing fixtures (pipes, valves, pumps, etc.) must be physically installed before the system can be tested, pressurized, and commissioned to ensure proper functionality.
Rough-in work (underground and in-wall piping) must be completed and inspected before the system can be turned on and commissioned.
Pressure testing must be performed to verify pipe integrity and leak-tightness before the system can be formally commissioned.

successor: Connect Plumbing System to Building Services
rationale: The plumbing system must be commissioned (tested and verified operational) before it can be tied into the main building water supply, sewer, and other building services.
Commissioning provides the operational verification needed before the final inspection can be conducted and the system signed off as complete.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before foundation work can begin to ensure a stable base.
Soil bearing capacity and composition must be analyzed to determine the foundation design and depth requirements before construction.
Building permits and foundation-specific approvals must be obtained from local authorities before any construction work can commence legally.
After the foundation is poured, sufficient curing time is required for the concrete to reach adequate strength before any load is placed on it.
Foundation waterproofing and damp-proofing membranes must be applied after the foundation has cured to protect against moisture ingress.
Backfilling around the foundation typically occurs after the foundation is complete and waterproofed, but in some sequences partial backfilling may occur earlier if needed for access.
The structural frame (columns, beams, walls) must be built on top of a completed and cured foundation to transfer loads safely to the ground.

Plumbing, electrical conduits, and other utilities that run beneath the slab must be laid after the foundation base is prepared but before the slab is poured, which is part of foundation construction.
All electrical components such as panels, switches, wiring, and fixtures must be physically installed before they can be tested and commissioned for proper operation.
The rough-in phase, including running conduits, cables, and mounting boxes, must be finished before commissioning can verify system integrity and connectivity.
The electrical system must be connected to the main power source to allow live testing, load balancing, and functional verification during commissioning.
Commissioning ensures the electrical system is safe and functional before other building systems (HVAC, lighting, elevators) can be energized and operated.
Commissioning must be completed to verify system performance before the final inspection by authorities can approve the installation for occupancy.
The roof framing (rafters, trusses, or joists) must be installed first to provide the structural support and slope for the skillion roof sheeting.
Wall framing must be completed to provide the bearing support for the skillion roof structure where the roof connects to the walls.
A vapour barrier or roof underlayment must be installed over the roof framing before the skillion roof cladding is applied to prevent moisture ingress.
Gutters and downpipes must be installed after the skillion roof sheeting is complete to collect water runoff from the roof edge.

Ceiling installation (particularly for a skillion roof where the ceiling follows the roof slope) must occur after the roof structure and cladding are complete to ensure weathertightness before interior work.
Wall framing must be completed to provide the structural support and bearing surface for the gable roof trusses or rafters.
Installing trusses or rafters is the primary structural activity that defines and creates the gable roof shape; the gable roof cannot exist without its framing members.
Roof sheathing (plywood/OSB) is installed directly onto the gable roof trusses/rafters, so the gable roof structural frame must be in place first.
The waterproof underlayment is applied over the roof sheathing, which itself is installed on the gable roof structure.
Final roofing materials (shingles, tiles, or metal panels) are installed on top of the underlayment and sheathing, all of which depend on the gable roof frame being complete.

A structural assessment must be completed before any retrofit work begins to determine the load-bearing capacity, existing conditions, and identify any structural deficiencies that could impact accessibility modifications.
Any necessary demolition, removal of existing barriers, and general site preparation must be completed before installing new accessibility features.
After completing accessibility retrofit installations, an inspection must be performed to verify compliance with accessibility codes and standards (e.g., ADA, local building codes).
Final finishing work and occupancy preparation (e.g., painting, cleaning, signage installation) must occur after the accessibility upgrades are installed to avoid damage or rework.
The project handover and commissioning to the facility owner/operator can only take place after all accessibility upgrades are verified complete and compliant.
The initial survey and setting out of reference points must be completed to establish the coordinate grid and baseline from which the Settled Work Indicator/Reference Mark is positioned.
The site must be cleared and prepared to expose stable ground or existing structures where the reference mark will be permanently fixed or embedded.
The reference mark serves as the fixed datum point; all subsequent excavation depths, alignments, and levels are measured relative to this established mark, so it must be in place beforehand.
Foundation layouts, depths, and vertical control depend on the settled reference mark to ensure correct positioning relative to the design coordinates.
The reference mark provides the fixed survey control point for plumbness, alignment, and elevation checks during frame erection, and therefore must be established first.

The settlement joint/accommodation strip must be placed at the interface between the foundation/pile cap and the superstructure to allow for differential settlement; thus foundation/pile cap construction must be completed first.
Ground conditions must be prepared and stabilized before installing settlement joints to ensure the joint functions correctly in accommodating expected differential movements.
The settlement joint/accommodation strip must be in place before pouring the adjacent superstructure concrete, as the strip forms the separation/interface and the concrete will be cast against it.
Waterproofing and sealing work can only be applied after the accommodation strip is installed, as the sealant needs to bond to the strip material and adjacent concrete surfaces.
Backfilling against a structure with a settlement joint must occur after the joint is fully installed to avoid damage and to ensure the joint can accommodate movement during backfilling.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to the required depth before any foundation slab can be placed.
Soil conditions must be assessed to determine the need for a compensated foundation and to verify bearing capacity before slab construction.
The foundation slab must be fully cured and structurally complete before waterproofing membranes can be applied to protect against moisture ingress.
Vertical structural elements (columns and walls) must be erected on top of the completed foundation slab, requiring the slab to be in place first.
While ideally drainage and plumbing are placed before the slab pour, if provisions (sleeves/pipes) are cast into the slab, further drainage connections can follow.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to expose the existing foundations before underpinning can be installed.

successor: Structural Load Transfer / Wall Construction Above
rationale: Underpinning must be completed and cured before vertical structural loads can be safely transferred or new walls built above to prevent settlement.
Underpinning must be set and stable prior to backfilling around the foundation and pouring ground floor slabs to avoid disturbing the new support.
Although waterproofing ideally follows underpinning to protect the interface, some waterproofing can be applied in stages during the underpinning sequence.
Soil conditions, foundation depth, and structural design must be assessed and finalized before underpinning work commences to determine pit dimensions and reinforcement.

The jacking pocket is typically located at the TBM launch shaft or within the tunnel alignment, so TBM launch must be completed first to establish the tunnel environment where the jacking pocket is needed.
The jacking pocket is constructed within or adjacent to the launch shaft; therefore the launch shaft must be excavated and prepared before the jacking pocket can be formed.
The jacking pocket provides the structural recess and reaction surface for the jacking frame; the frame must be installed into the completed pocket.
The thrust wall is often integrated with or built against the jacking pocket to transfer jacking forces; it must be constructed after or concurrently with the pocket.
The jacking pocket houses the jacks and serves as the launching point for pipe jacking; pipe jacking can only commence once the pocket is fully constructed and the jacking system is installed.
The foundation must be excavated and exposed before settlement cracks can be accessed and repaired.
Cracks must be identified, measured, and assessed for severity before the repair assembly can be planned and executed.
The underlying soil causing settlement must be stabilized to prevent further movement before cracks are repaired; otherwise, the repair would fail.
After the crack repair assembly (e.g., epoxy injection, stitching, or bracket installation) is completed, the surface can be finished, plastered, or painted over.
The repaired area must be inspected to verify the integrity of the repair before proceeding with subsequent works.

successor: On-Site Settlement Monitoring and Adjustment Activity
rationale: Settlement monitoring must begin after the foundation area is excavated and prepared, as the ground must be exposed and ready to install settlement monitoring instruments (e.g., settlement plates, tiltmeters, piezometers).

successor: On-Site Settlement Monitoring and Adjustment Activity
rationale: Monitoring instruments (settlement plates, optical targets, inclinometers, etc.) must be physically installed in the ground and on structural elements before any monitoring readings can be taken and adjustments made.

predecessor: On-Site Settlement Monitoring and Adjustment Activity
rationale: Raw monitoring data collected on-site must be processed and analyzed to determine if settlement thresholds are exceeded and if structural adjustments are needed.

predecessor: On-Site Settlement Monitoring and Adjustment Activity
rationale: On-site monitoring identifies excessive settlement, which triggers the need for remedial actions such as grouting, underpinning, or jacking. The corrective work cannot begin before monitoring data is collected and evaluated.

predecessor: On-Site Settlement Monitoring and Adjustment Activity
successor: Subsequent Construction Lifting Activities (e.g., Superstructure Erection)
rationale: It is a strong preference to confirm that settlement is within acceptable tolerances before proceeding with superstructure erection to avoid structural misalignment, though in some fast-track schedules these activities may overlap with careful monitoring.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to expose the existing foundation and provide working space before underpinning can begin.
Soil bearing capacity, groundwater conditions, and subsurface characteristics must be assessed to design the underpinning system appropriately.
The condition and load distribution of the existing foundation must be evaluated to determine the underpinning requirements and sequencing.
Temporary support structures must be installed to safely transfer loads while the existing foundation is being underpinned.
New underpinning elements (e.g., piles, needles, or slabs) must be fully installed before curing can commence to achieve design strength.
Underpinning installation must be complete before gradually transferring structural loads from the temporary shoring to the new foundation system.
Temporary propping and shoring can only be safely removed after the new underpinning system is in place and capable of carrying the load.
Excavated areas around the new underpinning must be backfilled only after installation is complete to avoid disturbing the fresh underpinning elements.
Waterproofing membranes and drainage systems are applied to the completed underpinning structure to protect it from groundwater ingress.

successor: Grout Injection for Settlement Remediation Activity
rationale: A structural and geotechnical survey must be conducted first to identify the extent of settlement, locate voids, and determine the required grout mix, injection pressure, and volume.

successor: Grout Injection for Settlement Remediation Activity
rationale: The work area must be cleared, safely accessed, and protected (e.g., shoring, exclusion zones) before any grouting equipment is mobilized and injection begins.

successor: Grout Injection for Settlement Remediation Activity
rationale: All buried utilities (water, gas, electric, telecom) must be located and marked to avoid damage during drilling and injection operations.

successor: Grout Injection for Settlement Remediation Activity
rationale: Injection holes must be drilled to the specified depth and pattern before grout can be pumped into the voids or soil.

predecessor: Grout Injection for Settlement Remediation Activity
rationale: After grouting is complete, settlement monitoring, load testing, or core sampling must be performed to verify that voids are filled and settlement is remediated.

predecessor: Grout Injection for Settlement Remediation Activity
rationale: Grout pumps, hoses, and mixing equipment must be flushed and demobilized immediately after injection before any restoration work begins.
A structural survey must be completed first to assess the current condition, settlement, and structural integrity of the building to determine if and how jacking can be safely performed.

predecessor: Design of Jacking Plan and Structural Calculations
rationale: Engineered drawings, jacking points, load calculations, and sequencing plan must be prepared and approved before any jacking operations commence.
The work area must be cleared, access for jacking equipment established, and ground conditions prepared to support the heavy loads during jacking.
After the building is releveled to the correct position, the voids beneath must be filled with grout and permanent underpinning installed to lock the structure in its new position.
After jacking is complete, a detailed inspection and ongoing monitoring must be conducted to verify that the structure is stable, level, and free from new cracks or distress.
The surface of the cracked area must be cleaned and prepared to expose sound substrate before crack stitching can be applied, ensuring proper adhesion and integrity of the repair.
Cracks must be assessed, measured, and mapped to determine the extent, pattern, and appropriate stitching locations before any repair work begins.
After crack stitching is installed, the stitched cracks must be grouted or sealed to fill voids, protect the stitching, and restore surface continuity.
Following the stitching and grouting, surface finishing (e.g., patching, smoothing) and curing of the repair material must occur to achieve the required surface quality and strength.

After completing the crack stitching repair, a structural load test or inspection is typically performed to verify the integrity of the repair, though it is a quality assurance step rather than a physical necessity for construction sequence.
A level and stable ground surface must be prepared before workbench installation to ensure proper support and alignment.
The concrete foundation must be cured and ready before placing the workbench to provide structural support.
Workbench must be in place before mounting equipment such as vises, grinders, or test fixtures onto its surface.
Electrical outlets and wiring for the workbench area are preferably run after the bench is positioned to optimize outlet placement, though pre-wiring is possible.
Organizing tools on shelves or pegboards above the workbench is best done after the bench is installed to ensure proper height and layout coordination.
The wall framing provides the structural support necessary for mounting the tool storage wall or pegboard.
Drywall must be installed and finished to provide a smooth, finished surface for attaching the pegboard or tool storage wall.
Any electrical wiring that will run behind the pegboard wall must be completed before the pegboard is mounted to avoid obstruction and safety issues.
Tools can only be hung or placed on the pegboard/storage wall after it has been securely installed on the wall.

While a workbench could theoretically be installed independently, it is often more efficient to install the pegboard first so that the workbench position can be aligned with the tool layout for optimal workflow.

predecessor: Workshop Sink Rough-In (Plumbing Supply Lines & Drain)
rationale: Plumbing supply lines and drain rough-in must be run inside the wall/floor before the sink basin and faucet can be physically connected.
The sink must be set in place before the countertop or surround can be cut around it and sealed permanently.
Final hookup of water supply lines and drain trap under the sink can only be completed after the sink is installed in its permanent position.
Walls must be framed and finished before the sink can be mounted or supported, and before plumbing rough-in is complete.

successor: Workshop Finish Trim & Electrical Outlet Installation (around sink area)
rationale: While not a physical necessity, it is preferable to complete the sink installation before finishing trim around the sink area to avoid damaging trim during sink handling.
The electrical subpanel must be mounted on a stable, finished surface. The foundation and slab must be completed to provide a proper mounting surface and to ensure grounding requirements are met.
Rough framing (walls, studs) must be in place so that the subpanel can be mounted to wall framing and wiring can be run through the walls to the subpanel location.
The subpanel must be installed and energized before branch circuit wiring can be routed from it to outlets, lights, and equipment throughout the workshop.
Electrical rough-in, including the subpanel installation, must be completed and inspected before walls are insulated and closed up with drywall, to avoid costly rework and ensure code compliance.

The main service panel must be installed and have available capacity to feed the workshop subpanel. The feeder cable from the main panel to the subpanel must also be routed before the subpanel can be connected.
Concrete foundation must be fully poured, set, and cured to provide a solid, level base capable of supporting the machinery loads and allowing proper anchor bolt installation.

Rebar cage and any embedment plates or anchor bolt templates must be positioned within the foundation before concrete is placed, as they become part of the monolithic foundation that anchors the machinery.
The machine must first be anchored and isolated from vibration sources before rough alignment and leveling can be performed, as anchoring sets the machine's initial position.
Anchoring and isolation elements must be in place before grout is poured under the baseplate, so the machine is secured and the grout fills the intended gap around anchors.
After anchoring and installing vibration isolation mounts, the final precision alignment and leveling can be performed, as the machine is now fixed in position and isolated from external vibrations.
The door frame must be structurally supported by the surrounding wall framing before the door can be installed.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed and sized correctly to accommodate the workshop door before installation can begin.
Hardware such as hinges, handles, and locks can only be installed after the door itself is mounted and properly aligned.
Weather stripping and sealants around the door perimeter must be applied after the door is installed to ensure a proper seal.
The finished floor level must be established so the door sill and bottom clearance can be set correctly, preventing binding or gaps.
The ground or slab must be properly leveled and compacted before installing racking systems to ensure stability, alignment, and load distribution.
Racking systems require a cured concrete slab to anchor and bear heavy loads; racking cannot be mounted on uncured or unpoured concrete.

predecessor: Site Layout & Marking of Rack Positions
rationale: Precise layout and marking must be completed before rack assembly to ensure correct spacing, alignment with warehouse columns, and compatibility with material handling equipment paths.
After racking is fully assembled, load testing and safety inspections must verify stability before any materials are stored.
Materials can only be placed on racking after the racking structure is fully installed, bolted, and inspected to prevent collapse or damage.
Rough framing establishes the structural walls and spaces where built-in cabinetry will be installed; cabinets cannot be placed without defined wall openings and support structures.
Interior wall surfaces must be finished before installing cabinetry, as cabinets are mounted against finished walls and installation would damage unfinished drywall or require rework.
Floor underlayment must be completed before cabinets are installed to ensure a level base and to avoid having to cut or work around cabinets later.
Countertops are fabricated and installed on top of the cabinet boxes; cabinets must be in place and leveled before countertops can be templated and mounted.

While some flooring can go under cabinets, if hardwood or tile is laid wall-to-wall after cabinets it provides a cleaner finish; this is typically a preference/sequencing choice depending on the flooring type.

successor: Install Clamp Rack and Tool Hangers
rationale: The support structure (e.g., mounting bracket, wall anchor, or overhead beam attachment) must be in place to physically hold the clamp rack and tool hangers.

successor: Install Clamp Rack and Tool Hangers
rationale: Electrical rough-in should be completed before installing rack and hangers to avoid interference and to ensure clear access for wiring.

predecessor: Install Clamp Rack and Tool Hangers
successor: Organize and Store Tools on Rack
rationale: Tools and clamps cannot be stored or organized until the rack and hangers are physically installed and secured.

predecessor: Install Clamp Rack and Tool Hangers
rationale: It is preferred to complete the final inspection after all fixtures, including clamp racks, are installed to ensure everything is properly secured and accessible.
Electrical conduit and wiring must be roughed-in within walls and ceilings before outlet strips can be installed and connected to the power source.
Outlet strips are typically mounted on finished walls; wall framing and drywall must be completed to provide a mounting surface.

predecessor: Overhead Cable Trays and Raceways Installation
rationale: Coordinating overhead power and data pathways before workstation power strips avoids conflicts and ensures clean power routing, though it is a coordination preference rather than a physical necessity.
Workstation power outlet strips must be installed and energized before workstations/furniture are assembled in place to allow proper integration and accessibility.
After outlet strips are installed, final electrical connections, trim-out, and testing (including polarity and grounding checks) must be performed to verify safe operation.
Flooring must be installed first as workbenches and cabinets are heavy and would damage unfinished flooring; also, flooring installation requires clear floorspace unobstructed by cabinetry.
Electrical rough-in must be completed before workbenches and cabinets are installed to allow wiring to be run behind walls where cabinets will be mounted.
Plumbing rough-in (e.g., for sinks in workbench areas) must be completed before cabinetry installation as pipes need to be in place behind walls and under floors before cabinets are set.
Countertops are installed on top of base cabinets and workbenches, so the cabinet bodies and workbench frames must be in place first.
Sinks and fixtures are mounted into/onto workbenches and cabinets, so the cabinetry and workbench structure must be installed first.

predecessor: Install Dust Collection System Equipment (Cyclone, Filter, Fan)
rationale: The primary dust collection equipment (cyclone separator, filter system, and fan) must be in place and connected to serve as the source of negative pressure and collection point before the ductwork network can be designed, routed, and physically connected to these components.
Electrical conduits, control wiring, and sensor mounting points must be roughed in before ductwork is installed to avoid conflicts and the need to work around or cut through completed duct runs.

successor: Ductwork pressure testing and leak check
rationale: The ductwork must be fully assembled and sealed before a pressure test or leak check can be performed to verify the integrity of all joints and connections.

successor: Install Blast Gates & Dampers at Pickup Points
rationale: Blast gates and dampers are typically installed as inline components of the ductwork; the main duct runs must be in place so that these control devices can be accurately positioned and connected at each branch or drop.

successor: Connect Drop Downs to Machine Dust Ports
rationale: The main ductwork system must be completed before final flexible or rigid drop-down connections can be made from the branch lines to each machine's dust port.
Structural steel provides the support framework and attachment points for hanging and supporting compressed air piping systems; piping cannot be installed without structural support in place.
A finished floor slab provides the base elevation reference and working platform for pipe routing, and some piping may be embedded in or supported from the slab.

successor: Pressure Test / Leak Test Compressed Air System
rationale: Pressure testing must be performed after the piping is fully assembled to verify integrity and detect leaks before the system is placed into service.

successor: Install Compressed Air Equipment (Compressors, Dryers, Filters)
rationale: While equipment can be set in place before piping, final connection and alignment of equipment to the piping network is typically performed after the main piping runs are installed to ensure proper fit-up and avoid rework.

Insulation application is performed after piping installation to prevent moisture condensation and reduce heat gain/loss; however, it is a soft preference because uninsulated piping can still function temporarily.
The floor slab must be poured and cured before electrical conduit can be embedded or electrical panels mounted, as the slab provides the base for workshop flooring and underground conduit runs.
Structural framing (walls, roof) must be complete to provide support for electrical wiring, conduits, junction boxes, and panels mounted on walls or ceilings.
Rough-in plumbing must be installed first to avoid conflicts with electrical conduit routing and to ensure proper separation between plumbing and electrical systems as per building codes.
Electrical wiring and boxes must be installed and inspected before insulation and drywall can be applied, as they will be enclosed within wall cavities.

successor: Install Workshop Lighting Fixtures and Equipment
rationale: Circuit wiring must be completed and energized before lighting fixtures, outlets, switches, and heavy equipment can be connected and tested.

predecessor: Rough-in Electrical and Conduit for Exhaust Fan
rationale: Electrical power and conduit connections must be roughed-in before the exhaust fan can be physically mounted and wired.

predecessor: Frame Ceiling/Wall Opening for Exhaust Fan
rationale: The structural opening and framing must be completed to provide a mounting location for the exhaust fan assembly.
Exterior sheathing must be in place to provide a substrate for mounting louvers and to ensure weather-tight installation.
It is preferable to complete the exhaust fan installation before finishing the surrounding ceiling/wall surfaces to avoid damaging finished work during fan installation.

successor: Install Ductwork Connecting Fan to Louvers
rationale: The fan and louver assemblies must be in place before ductwork can be connected between them to ensure proper alignment and sealing.
The subfloor must be clean, dry, level, and structurally sound before any flooring or coating can be applied. Any debris, moisture, or unevenness would compromise adhesion and final quality.
An underlayment (e.g., moisture barrier, soundproofing, or leveling compound) must be in place prior to installing the final floor finish to protect it and ensure proper performance.

It is common practice to install flooring before baseboards or wall trim so that the trim sits on top of the finished floor, creating a clean appearance; however, trim can be installed later with undercutting, so this is a soft preference.
Flooring should be installed after painting is complete to avoid damaging fresh paint with dust, debris, or adhesive, and to prevent paint drips from ruining the new floor surface.

While some trades install cabinets before flooring to save material costs under cabinets, it is more common and generally preferred to install flooring first to ensure a continuous finished surface and easier future replacement.

Stationary power tools (e.g., table saws, drill presses, band saws) must be anchored to a stable, level foundation or concrete floor slab to ensure safety, vibration control, and accurate operation. The floor must be fully cured and prepared first.

Stationary power tools typically require dedicated electrical circuits, outlets, and possibly 220V connections. Rough electrical work (conduit, wiring, breaker panels) must be completed before tools are anchored in their permanent locations.
The building or shop space must be enclosed (walls, roof, doors) to protect stationary power tools and their electrical connections from weather damage before they are installed and anchored.

After anchoring, stationary power tools must be precisely aligned (e.g., saw blade alignment, table flatness) and calibrated for safety and accuracy. Anchoring must be completed first as alignment can shift during the anchoring process.

Dust collection ductwork and hoses must be connected to the tool's dust ports after the tool is anchored in its final position, as the port locations and access depend on the tool's exact placement and orientation.

predecessor: Complete Fire Alarm and Suppression System Installation
rationale: Fire extinguisher stations are part of the overall fire suppression strategy; piping, sprinkler, and suppression infrastructure must be in place to properly locate and integrate extinguisher stations.
Electrical rough-in (conduit, wiring, junction boxes) must be completed before mounting fire extinguisher cabinets or stations, as these may house alarm or inspection systems that require power.
Fire extinguisher stations are typically mounted on finished walls. Drywall, taping, and painting must be done to provide a proper mounting surface and to meet code for wall assembly fire ratings.
Building cannot be occupied or handed over until all fire extinguisher stations are properly installed, tagged, sealed, and inspected per local fire safety regulations.
The dust collection system must be physically installed and connected before it can be commissioned, tested, and verified for proper operation.

predecessor: Connect Electrical Supply to Dust Collection System
rationale: Electrical power must be supplied to the dust collection system before it can be started up and commissioned.
All ductwork connecting collection points to the dust collector must be installed before the system can be tested and commissioned as a whole.
Production operations that rely on dust collection (e.g., woodworking, material handling) cannot commence until the dust collection system has been commissioned and verified safe.
The stringers provide the structural support framework for the stairs, so they must be installed before treads can be attached.
Handrails are typically installed after treads are in place to ensure proper alignment and spacing relative to the walking surface.
In closed stair construction, risers are installed first to create the vertical face, providing support and backing for the treads above them.
Risers are typically installed on top of finished slabs or foundations; they require a stable, level base to attach to.
Plumbing stubs and conduits that will enter through the riser must be roughed in beneath the slab before the riser is placed over them.
Risers serve as vertical chases for utilities; walls are framed after risers are in place to properly enclose and integrate them.
Electrical conduits and wiring that run through the riser must be pulled after the riser is installed, and the riser provides the vertical pathway.
Vertical plumbing pipes (risers for water supply or drainage) must be installed within the riser chase before walls are closed up.
Stringers require a stable, level foundation to bear the load and ensure proper alignment. Without prepared foundations, stringers cannot be securely placed.
Deck boards are fastened to the stringers for support. Stringers must be in place to provide the structural framework onto which decking is installed.
Stringers must be cut to precise dimensions (including tread rises and runs) before they can be positioned and secured on the foundation.
Accurate layout and marking of tread/riser patterns on the stringer material is required before cutting to ensure proper stair geometry.
Handrails are typically anchored to or supported by the stringers. Stringers must be installed first to provide the structural attachment points for the handrail system.
The deck or floor surface provides the base platform onto which the balustrade is mounted. Without a completed deck or floor, the balustrade has no structural support or attachment surface.

predecessor: Structural Framing of Staircase or Balcony
rationale: The structural frame (joists, beams, or slab edge) must be in place to provide anchorage points for balustrade posts or brackets.
The handrail is typically the topmost component mounted onto the assembled balustrade structure (posts and infill panels). The balustrade frame must be erected first to support the handrail.
The balustrade system must be fully assembled before safety inspections can verify guardrail compliance with building codes (height, load resistance, infill spacing).

Waterproofing can be performed before or after balustrade installation depending on design, but it is often preferred to seal the deck membrane after posts are installed to ensure proper integration of post base flashings.
The monolithic concrete open stair must be supported on a structurally sound foundation or slab; the stair cannot be built without the base structural support in place.
Any utility lines that pass under or through the stair location must be roughed-in before the concrete is poured, as access would be impossible afterward.
Finish materials such as stair treads, railings, and handrails are installed on top of or attached to the completed concrete stair structure.

successor: Interior Wall Finishing (Drywall/Paint) Adjacent to Stair
rationale: While it is practical to finish walls after the stair is in place to avoid damage, it is not a strict physical necessity; sequencing could be adjusted.

successor: Floor Covering Installation on Adjacent Floors
rationale: Floor coverings adjacent to the stair are best installed after the stair concrete work to avoid debris and damage, but the order can be swapped if protected.
The steel open stair is typically supported by or connected to the main structural steel frame; the frame must be in place to provide anchorage and support for the stair.
The stair's base or landing points require a stable foundation or slab to bear the load; foundations must cure before stair installation.
It is preferable to install the stair first so that finishing can be completed around it without requiring later cutting or rework, though it is not physically mandatory.
The stair structure must be fully erected before guardrails and handrails can be attached to it for safety compliance.
Floor slabs at each landing level need to be poured and cured to provide the bearing surface and level access for the stair installation.
The structural framing (floors, walls) must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the timber open stair structure.
The rough opening in the floor must be framed and prepared to receive the stair stringers and treads.
Handrails and balusters are attached to the completed stair structure and cannot be installed before the stair is in place.
Final floor finishes such as hardwood, tile, or carpet around the stair opening should be installed after the stair framing is complete to achieve a clean transition.
Finishing coats (stain, varnish, or paint) are applied to the timber after the stair components are fully installed and secured.
Cantilevered stairs are anchored into and supported by the structural wall or framing system; the supporting structure must be in place before stair installation can begin.
The base upon which the stair lands or terminates requires a completed foundation or slab to provide bearing and anchorage for the lowest point of the stair.
Handrails and guardrails are physically attached to or aligned with the stair structure; the stair must be in its final position for proper fit and attachment of railings.

successor: Floor Finishing / Tiling Adjacent to Stair
rationale: Floor finishes around the stair opening are typically installed after the stair is in place to ensure a clean transition and to avoid damaging finishes during stair installation.

Drywall or cladding around the stair opening must be completed after the stair is installed to allow for proper trimming, sealing, and fire-stopping at the interface between the stair and the wall opening.

The structural support framework, including stringers, landings, and rough openings, must be built before glass tread stairs can be installed, as the stairs depend on these supports for load transfer and proper positioning.
Subfloor or landing surfaces supporting the stair must be completed to provide a stable base for the stair structure and to avoid damaging the glass treads during subsequent work.
Handrails and guardrails are typically installed after the stair treads are in place to ensure proper alignment, attachment, and height relative to the finished tread surface.

To protect the glass treads from damage during painting or finishing work, it is preferable to complete painting and finishing before stair installation, but if needed, touch-up can follow; however, final finishing is generally sequenced after to avoid debris and scratches on the glass.

Step or under-tread lighting fixtures are often integrated with or positioned relative to the glass treads; it is a soft preference to install lighting after treads are in place to fine-tune positioning, though some rough-in work must happen before.

predecessor: Stair Substructure/Landing Slab Pouring and Curing
rationale: The stair nosing profile must be installed on a fully set and cured concrete or structural stair base. Attempting installation before the slab is poured and cured would leave no stable substrate to attach the nosing profile to.
The nosing profile anchors into the stair tread construction; the tread formwork and rebar must be in place before the nosing profile can be positioned and cast into the concrete.

successor: Stair Finishing / Tiling or Carpet Installation
rationale: The nosing profile serves as the edge trim and transition for the finished stair surface. Floor finishes (tiles, carpet, hardwood) must be installed after the nosing profile is in place so they can abut or overlap the nosing correctly.

successor: Final Grouting / Caulking and Touch-Up Painting
