rationale: Once the nosing profile is installed, any gaps around edges are grouted or caulked, and adjacent painted surfaces are touched up. This is a soft preference because the sealing can theoretically be done later, but it's best practice to complete finishing promptly to protect the installation.

Handrails are typically installed after the stair nosing is in place to ensure consistent alignment and clearance above the finished nosing edge. This is a soft preference because railings could be installed earlier and later adjusted, but standard sequence places them after the nosing.

Handrails and balustrades are safety barriers installed alongside stairs, landings, and elevated walkways. The staircase or step structure must be fully built and structurally stable before handrails can be fitted to it.
Balustrades are mounted onto floor slabs, balcony decks, or roof edges. These substrates must be cast and cured to provide a solid anchoring surface for the handrail posts and base plates.
Where balustrades attach to steel columns or beams, the structural steel frame must be erected and aligned to provide the proper support and connection points.

It is preferred to complete handrail installation before final painting and finishing of adjacent walls to avoid damaging fresh paint during the mounting process and to allow for any patching around anchors.

Installing handrails and balustrades before final floor finishes near edges prevents damage to the finished flooring and allows for precise fit of base plates; however, this is a preference for quality and ease rather than a strict physical necessity.
Stair stringers must be anchored to or supported by the concrete slab or deck; the slab must be poured and cured to provide a stable base for stringer installation.
The rough opening for the stairwell must be framed and in place so that stringers can be properly positioned and secured within the designated stairwell area.

predecessor: Layout and Marking of Stringer Locations
rationale: Accurate layout and marking of stringer positions on the landing and slab must be completed before erection to ensure correct alignment and fit.
Treads and risers are attached directly to the stringers; stringers must be erected first to provide the supporting framework.
Handrails are typically mounted to the stringers or adjacent structure; stringers must be in place to define the stair geometry and provide attachment points.

Stringers are the structural supports that run diagonally along the staircase. Treads and risers are fastened directly onto the stringers, so the stringers must be in place first to provide the mounting surface.

Landings provide the intermediate platform and structural support at the top and bottom of a stair flight. Treads and risers must be installed up to and from the landing, requiring the landing to be complete.
The overall structural frame and floor slabs must be in place before any stair components can be installed, as the stairs connect different floor levels.
Handrails and balustrades are typically anchored to or mounted on the treads. The treads must be securely installed to provide the base for railing posts and supports.

While finishing can sometimes occur off-site on pre-finished treads, when on-site finishing is required, the treads and risers must be fully installed first. This is a soft preference because pre-finished components could reverse this order.
The concrete surface must be clean, dry, and free of contaminants before anti-slip coating can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and bond strength.
Any cracks, spalls, or surface defects must be repaired prior to coating application to create a uniform substrate and prevent coating failure.
A primer coat must be applied and fully cured before the anti-slip coating is applied to enhance adhesion and seal the substrate.
After application, the anti-slip coating requires a specified curing and drying time before any traffic or subsequent work can occur on the surface to avoid damaging the coating.

Striping and marking paint should be applied after the anti-slip coating has fully cured to ensure clean lines and proper adhesion of markings, though this is a soft preference as markings could theoretically be applied beforehand in some sequences.
Perimeter glazing requires a stable structural frame to support the glass panels and transfer loads to the building structure.
The slab edges must be finished and prepared to receive the perimeter glazing system anchors and framing.
Interior finishes adjacent to perimeter glazing cannot be completed until the glazing is installed, as the glazing provides the finished surface and weather seal at the building envelope.
Weatherproofing sealants and flashings at the perimeter glazing joints can only be applied after the glazing panels are in place to form a continuous weather barrier.

successor: Final Commissioning of HVAC Zones near Perimeter
rationale: HVAC commissioning near perimeter zones is preferably done after glazing is complete to account for the actual thermal performance and air infiltration rates of the installed glazing system.
Structural framing provides the primary support structure and load-bearing capacity required before any non-structural components like light shelves can be attached.
Roof or upper deck must be in place to define the overhead conditions and to support any overhead attachments or brackets needed for light shelf installation.
Exterior wall sheathing provides the base surface onto which light shelves are mounted; they cannot be installed directly onto an open stud wall.
Windows must be installed first so that light shelves can be positioned relative to the window openings, typically mounted above or between windows to optimize daylight redirection.

Light shelves often affect the ceiling plane and adjacent wall finishes; interior finishes should be completed after light shelves are installed to allow proper integration and seamless finishing around the shelf brackets.
The rough opening must be framed, sized, and prepared before sidelights can be installed, as sidelights require a structurally sound and properly dimensioned opening.
The sidelight opening must be created and prepared before the sidelight unit itself can be physically placed and secured into the opening.
Sidelight openings must be in place before weatherproofing and flashing can be applied around them to ensure a watertight seal.
Interior trim work around sidelights typically follows opening preparation, but this may be considered a soft preference if trim installation is done after the sidelight unit is installed.
Exterior cladding around the sidelight area must be installed after the sidelight opening is ready to ensure proper integration and alignment.
The structural frame must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the window wall system.
Window openings must be framed, squared, and prepared to proper dimensions before window wall units can be installed.
Weather barriers, flashings, and sill pans must be installed at openings before window wall installation to ensure proper water drainage and prevent moisture intrusion behind the window system.
Interior drywall, trim, and finishes around window openings cannot be completed until the window wall units are installed and sealed.
Final glazing installation, perimeter sealants, and weatherstripping must be applied after the window wall frames are assembled and anchored in place to complete the weather-tight seal.

Automatic shading devices require a stable structural frame (e.g., window frames, curtain wall system, or building facade supports) to be mounted onto. The structural support must be in place before the shading devices can be attached.

The exterior wall or facade cladding must be completed to provide a finished surface and proper attachment points for the automatic shading devices. Installing shading before cladding would require rework or cause interface issues.

Automatic shading devices require electrical power for motors, sensors, and controls. The electrical rough-in (conduit, wiring, junction boxes) must be installed and roughed in behind the walls/facade before the shading devices themselves are mounted and connected.

successor: Building Management System (BMS) Integration and Programming
rationale: The automatic shading devices must be physically installed and connected to allow for system-level integration, control wiring termination, and programming/commissioning of the building management system to coordinate shading operation with lighting and HVAC.

While interior finishes can sometimes proceed concurrently, it is preferable to complete automatic shading installation before adjacent interior finishes (e.g., drywall finishing, painting near windows) to avoid damage to finished surfaces during shading device installation and to allow access for mounting brackets.
Structural steel framing provides the primary support structure onto which glare control louvers are mounted; louvers cannot be installed without a stable structural frame.
Glare control louvers are typically integrated into or mounted onto the exterior wall system. The wall enclosure must be in place to provide the substrate and proper interfaces for louver attachment.
If louvers are shading adjacent windows, it is preferable but not physically required to install louvers before glazing to allow access; however, sequence can be reversed with careful coordination.
Perimeter sealants, flashings, and weatherproofing around louver penetrations must be applied after louvers are secured to ensure a continuous weather-tight seal.
While not a strict physical constraint, completing louver installation before interior finishes prevents damage to finished surfaces and allows for any required access from the interior side.
The structural frame must be in place to support the window openings and provide the rough openings for window installation.
Rough openings must be framed, measured, and inspected to ensure they are square, level, and correctly sized before windows can be installed.

Exterior sheathing (such as plywood or OSB) is typically installed on the exterior walls before windows to provide structural diaphragm and a substrate for weather resistive barrier and window flashing.

predecessor: Install Weather Resistive Barrier (WRB) / House Wrap
rationale: The weather resistive barrier must be applied to the exterior walls before windows are installed so that window flashing can properly integrate with the WRB to prevent water intrusion.

Perimeter windows must be installed, flashed, and sealed before exterior siding or cladding is applied, as the cladding typically overlaps the window flanges and trim to create a watertight exterior envelope.
Rough framing must be complete to provide the structural support and defined openings where interior glass walls will be installed.

MEP rough-in work must be completed before installing glass walls to avoid having to cut through or work around glass panels, and to ensure that utilities are routed within the walls before they are enclosed.
Interior glass walls must be installed before ceiling work so that the walls can extend fully to the structure above and the ceiling grid can abut or integrate with the glass wall partitions.

Glass walls should be installed before final flooring to allow the flooring material to be laid up to or under the glass partition base channel, ensuring a clean finish without cutting around the glass.

While not a strict physical constraint, it is preferable to complete painting and wall finishing after glass installation to avoid damaging freshly painted surfaces during the delicate glass handling and installation process.
Daylight sensors must be physically installed before they can be commissioned and calibrated.
Lighting control panels must be installed and wired before commissioning can verify proper operation of daylight harvesting controls.
All electrical rough-in work including conduit, wiring, and backboxes must be completed before commissioning can take place.
Commissioning of daylight controls must be completed before performance verification testing can occur to validate system operation.

Training occupants on daylight control operation is best done after commissioning to cover how the system actually functions, though training could theoretically occur before final commissioning in some cases.
The reflective coating must be applied onto a stable, installed roof deck surface as its substrate.
The roof surface must be clean, dry, and free of debris/dirt for the reflective coating to properly adhere.
Some reflective coating systems require a primer coat to be applied and cured first to ensure proper bonding.
After applying the reflective coating, it must be allowed to cure and then be inspected for uniform coverage, thickness, and defects.
Roof-mounted equipment (e.g., HVAC units, solar panels) should be installed after coatings to avoid damaging the finished reflective surface.
Roofing must be completed to ensure the building is watertight and the interior is protected from weather before installing light shelves, which are interior architectural elements.
Rough framing establishes the structural walls and openings where light shelves will be mounted; the framing must be in place to provide support.
Light shelves are typically installed above or adjacent to windows to reflect daylight; windows must be installed first to define the opening and provide the reference surface.
Light shelves must be mounted before finishing interior walls, as they are anchored to the structure and need to be integrated with the finished wall surface.

While not physically mandatory, installing light shelves first allows lighting fixtures and sensors to be positioned optimally relative to the daylight-redirecting shelves for integrated daylighting design.
The ground must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and uneven terrain before any foundation work can begin to ensure a stable and properly prepared base.
Accurate surveying and stakeout of building corners and edge lines are required to position the edge foundation correctly on the site.
Trenches or excavations must be dug along the building perimeter to the required depth and width before placing the edge foundation materials.
The edge foundation provides the perimeter support and formwork boundary necessary before pouring or installing the interior floor slab.
Exterior load-bearing walls require the completed edge foundation as their base support and anchoring surface.
Edge formwork must be installed to define the shape and boundaries before the soffit concrete can be poured.
Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured for the soffit.
Any embedded conduits, pipes, or sleeves that pass through the soffit must be installed prior to concrete placement.
Concrete must be poured and initially set before the curing process can begin to ensure proper strength development.
Soffit concrete must achieve sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed to avoid structural damage.
Fascia is typically installed at the edge of the roof, and the roof decking/sheathing provides the underlying surface and structural support to which the fascia board is attached.
Roof trusses or rafters form the structural framework; roof decking is fastened to them, so trusses must be in place before decking.

The underlayment (felt or synthetic) is laid over the roof deck before fascia is installed to ensure proper water-shedding and to allow the fascia to be positioned correctly relative to the drip edge.
Gutters are attached directly to the fascia board. The fascia must be in place to provide a mounting surface for gutter brackets.
The fascia often forms the outer trim edge of the roof overhang, and the soffit (underside of the eave) typically meets the fascia, so the fascia must be installed first to define the edge.
The drip edge is a metal flashing that extends beyond the fascia to direct water away; it is installed over or integrated with the fascia, so fascia must be in place.

While the fascia is at the roof edge, having exterior wall sheathing in place provides a continuous backing and alignment reference; however, this is a soft preference because fascia can be installed without wall sheathing in some sequences.
Drip edge is installed on the edges of the roof deck; the roof deck must be in place to provide a mounting surface.
Drip edge is typically installed over the roof underlayment to direct water away from the fascia and into the gutter; underlayment must be laid first.
Drip edge is installed along roof edges before shingles or roofing material is applied to provide a clean edge and prevent water infiltration underneath.

While drip edge can be installed before final fascia and gutters for water diversion, gutter installation typically follows; however, this is a soft preference as sequence can vary depending on the system.
The slab must first be poured and cured to create a physical edge that can be formed or finished as 'Edge of Slab'.
Formwork for the slab edge must be installed before the edge of the slab can be defined or finished.
Waterproofing at the slab edge requires the edge to be fully formed and finished before application.
Cladding is typically installed after the slab edge is complete, but may be sequenced differently depending on design; this is a soft preference for a clean installation.
Insulation at the slab edge must be applied after the slab edge is fully formed and finished to ensure proper fit and thermal performance.

Copings and parapet caps serve as the top closure/protection for masonry walls, brick veneers, or parapet walls. The wall structure must be completed first so the coping can be properly anchored and sealed.
Parapet caps are installed at the top of parapet walls which are part of the roof edge system. The roof deck and parapet framing must be in place before caps are installed.
Waterproofing or flashing must be applied to the top of parapet walls before copings/caps are installed to ensure water is directed away from the wall assembly.
Copings and caps are the topmost protective elements; final counter-flashings, reglets, and trim details that integrate with the coping must be completed after caps are set.

successor: Scaffolding Dismantling / Final Exterior Finish Inspection
rationale: Once caps are installed, the parapet top is complete, and scaffolding can be removed and final inspections performed. This is a soft preference because work could theoretically be inspected earlier, but logically the cap finish is needed before sign-off.
Perimeter flashing is installed at roof edges and requires the roof deck to be in place as a structural base and substrate.
Perimeter flashing often integrates with wall surfaces; wall sheathing provides the backing and alignment surface for flashing installation at building corners and edges.
Roof underlayment is typically laid before perimeter flashing so that flashing can be installed over the underlayment to ensure proper water shedding and drainage direction.

Perimeter flashing must be in place before exterior cladding or siding is installed because the cladding laps over the flashing to create a weather-tight seal and direct water away from the wall assembly.

Roofing materials such as shingles or membrane are installed after perimeter flashing so that they overlap the flashing's top edge, ensuring continuous water runoff and preventing leaks at eaves and rakes.
The structural frame (e.g., steel or wood stud walls) must be fully erected, braced, and approved to provide a stable substrate and load-bearing surface for attaching the exterior cladding system.

Sheathing (e.g., plywood or OSB) is typically fastened to the framing to create a continuous substrate that supports the cladding and provides lateral bracing; cladding cannot be attached directly to open framing without sheathing.

predecessor: Install Weather-Resistive Barrier (WRB) and Air Barrier
rationale: The WRB (e.g., building wrap or fluid-applied membrane) and air barrier must be installed over the sheathing to prevent moisture intrusion and air leakage before the cladding is placed over it.

Though windows and doors are often installed before cladding for proper flashing integration, in some sequences cladding is installed up to rough openings first. However, final window/door installation and their associated flashings typically occur before the cladding is finished around those openings, or after the cladding is installed depending on the system. This ordering is often a soft preference based on detailing sequence.

successor: Install Exterior Trim, Soffits, and Fascia
rationale: The main cladding panels must be in place before trim elements (corner boards, soffits, fascia, and other finish details) are installed, as trim covers the edges and transitions of the cladding system and provides a finished appearance.
Window and door frames must be in place to define the perimeter where sealant is applied; sealant fills gaps between the frame and the wall opening.
Rough-in services should be completed before sealing the perimeter to avoid cutting through or damaging the newly applied sealant.
Exterior sheathing and weather barrier must be installed so perimeter sealant can create a continuous air and water seal at joints and transitions.
Perimeter sealant must be applied before cladding or siding is installed to ensure the sealant is accessible and properly placed at all perimeter joints.

successor: Perform Air and Water Tightness Testing
rationale: Sealant should be applied prior to air/water testing so the building envelope is complete; however, testing could be deferred if needed, making this a soft preference.
Edge flashing is installed on top of the roof sheathing to provide a weather-resistant barrier at the edges; sheathing must be in place first.
Underlayment (e.g., felt or synthetic) is laid over the sheathing before edge flashing is installed, as the flashing often overlaps the underlayment for proper water shedding.

Edge flashing is installed along eaves and rakes before the primary roofing material (e.g., shingles or metal panels) is applied, so that the roofing material can overlap the flashing for proper water diversion.

In many roof assemblies, a drip edge is a type of edge flashing itself, but if considered separately, edge flashing is typically placed before the final drip edge trim for continuity; however, this can vary by system and is sometimes considered part of the same step.

Gutters are installed after edge flashing is in place so that the flashing directs water properly into the gutter system; however, this is a soft preference as gutters could theoretically be added later.
Perimeter drainage requires proper site grading and earthwork to establish the final ground contours and slope directions, ensuring water flows away from the structure effectively.

Perimeter drainage is typically installed around the foundation base (footing level) after the foundation walls are constructed and waterproofed, as it must be positioned at the correct elevation relative to the footing.
Underground utilities (water, sewer, electrical conduits) running near the foundation must be roughed in before perimeter drainage installation to avoid conflicts and ensure proper depth placement.

Backfilling around the foundation walls must occur after the perimeter drainage system (perforated pipe, gravel, filter fabric) is fully installed and inspected, as the drainage system is covered by the backfill material.

While waterproofing is typically applied before drainage installation, some sequences allow drainage installation first if waterproofing extends down to the footing; however, standard practice applies waterproofing before drainage to protect the foundation wall.
The structural frame (load-bearing walls, columns, or curtain wall framing) must be erected to provide the support structure onto which the glazing panels are mounted.
A weatherproofing or air barrier behind the glazing zone must be installed to prevent moisture ingress and air leakage before the glazing assembly is sealed.
Window openings must be framed, blocked, and squared to receive the glazing units or curtain wall panels.
After the glass panels are set into their frames, perimeter sealants, gaskets, and weatherstripping are applied to create an airtight and watertight seal.

Interior wall finishes, window trim, and partition walls adjacent to glazing are typically completed after the glazing assembly is in place to allow for proper fit and sealing, though some overlapping work may be possible.
The building's structural frame must be in place to provide support and attachment points for exterior solar shading devices such as louvers, fins, or screens.

predecessor: Exterior Wall Cladding / Curtain Wall Installation
rationale: The exterior wall or curtain wall system must be installed to serve as the substrate or mounting surface for the solar shading devices, ensuring proper alignment and anchorage.
Solar shading devices are often installed before or concurrently with windows to protect glazing during construction and to ensure proper integration with the building envelope.
Final exterior finishes should be applied after shading devices are installed to avoid damage to finishes during device installation and to ensure seamless weather sealing.
Scaffolding used during installation of the shading devices must remain in place until installation is complete; dismantling can only occur after all devices are securely attached.

Electrical power and lighting controls must be roughed-in before the solar shading device can be installed, as the shading device may require motorized operation and integration with lighting controls.
Interior walls need to be finished before mounting shading hardware to ensure clean installation and avoid damaging finished surfaces.
The ceiling grid must be in place as the shading device brackets or tracks may attach to the ceiling structure.
The shading device is typically installed after windows are in place but before interior trim and glazing are fully completed, to allow for proper alignment and integration with the window assembly.
While trim can be installed before shades, it is preferable to install shades first to ensure proper fit and alignment of window casings around the shade hardware.

The Trombe wall requires a stable, level foundation to support its weight and ensure proper structural alignment. Without a completed foundation, the wall assembly cannot be safely or accurately installed.
The Trombe wall typically rests on or integrates with the concrete floor slab. The floor must be poured and cured before the wall can be assembled on top of it.

predecessor: Rough-In Electrical Work for Adjacent Zones
rationale: Any electrical conduits or wiring that will run behind or through the Trombe wall area must be installed before the wall is erected, as access will be blocked afterward.

successor: Glazing / Window Installation on Trombe Wall
rationale: The glass or glazing panels that form the outer layer of the Trombe wall system must be installed after the main wall mass (e.g., masonry or concrete) is assembled, as the glazing is attached to or supported by the wall structure.

It is preferable to complete the Trombe wall before finishing interior surfaces (e.g., drywall, painting) in adjacent occupied spaces to avoid dust, debris, and access issues, but it is not a strict physical necessity if careful sequencing is managed.
Ductwork must be in place to provide the physical conduit into which zone dampers are installed.
The main HVAC air handler and control system must be installed to provide airflow and power that the zone damper will regulate.

successor: Zone Damper Control Wiring and Commissioning
rationale: Control wiring, sensor integration, and system balancing for the solar-responsive damper can only be performed after the damper is physically mounted in the duct.
Final air balancing and testing of zone pressures and solar-responsive control logic requires the damper to be installed and operational.
The structural frame must be in place to provide the load-bearing support and openings for glazing installation.
Windows and glazing must be installed and sealed before interior finishes are applied to prevent weather damage and to ensure a proper building envelope.
Glazing installation affects the building's thermal envelope, so HVAC load calculations and commissioning are more accurate after windows are in place, though HVAC rough-in can precede glazing.
Rough openings must be properly framed, sized, and weatherproofed to receive glazing units correctly.
Glazing is a critical component of the building envelope, so envelope testing should be performed after glazing is fully installed and sealed.

Interior finishing work (e.g., drywall, painting, ceiling installation) must be completed before exterior shading is installed because exterior shading devices often attach to the building's structural frame or facade, and interior work can cause dust, debris, and vibrations that could damage delicate shading components or their mounting systems.

predecessor: Exterior Wall Cladding / Curtain Wall Installation
rationale: The exterior wall cladding or curtain wall system provides the primary mounting surface and structural attachment points for exterior shading devices (such as louvers, fins, or brise-soleil). Shading cannot be installed until the facade substrate is in place and fully secured.

Windows and glazing must be installed before exterior shading is mounted because many shading systems (e.g., external blinds, overhangs, or vertical fins) are positioned relative to window openings. Installing shading first would block access for window installation and glass handling.

Final exterior painting or coating should follow shading installation because shading devices are often mounted on or adjacent to finished surfaces, and touch-up painting or sealing is needed around mounting brackets and anchor points where the shading attaches.

Scaffolding used for facade work must remain in place to provide safe working access for installing exterior shading. Shading installation typically requires elevated access, and dismantling scaffolding prematurely would prevent workers from reaching upper-level mounting points.
Solar collectors require a stable, level foundation and support structure to be installed first, as the collectors must be mounted on this substructure.
The roof or ground surface must be prepared and structurally ready before mounting solar collectors to ensure safe installation and load bearing.
Pipes that connect to the solar collectors can only be installed after the collectors are mounted in their final position and aligned.
Pressure testing can only commence after the collectors are mounted and all collector-side connections are made.
Electrical connections to collector sensors, actuators, and monitoring devices must follow after the collectors are physically mounted and secured in place.
The north-facing wall assembly must be built atop a finished, cured foundation slab that provides structural support and a level base for wall framing.
Underground utilities running beneath the north wall footprint must be placed before the wall is erected; otherwise, access would be blocked by the wall assembly.
The north wall serves as a load-bearing support for roof trusses or ceiling joists; these structural elements cannot be installed until the wall is framed and secured in place.

successor: Exterior cladding and weatherproofing on north elevation
rationale: Exterior cladding, house wrap, and weather barrier are applied directly onto the completed north wall sheathing; the wall frame must be fully assembled to accept these finishes.

successor: Rough-in electrical and plumbing within north wall cavity
rationale: Electrical wiring, outlet boxes, and any plumbing lines that run inside the north wall must be installed after the wall is framed but before insulation and drywall; the open stud cavity provides access.
The foundation and slab must be completed and cured before any wall construction can begin, as walls require a stable, level base for load transfer and structural integrity.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied within the wall forms before pouring or assembling the PCM-enhanced wall system to ensure structural reinforcement is properly embedded.
Underground electrical, plumbing, and mechanical conduits that pass through the slab or into wall locations must be roughed in prior to wall construction to avoid cutting or coring finished walls.
Load-bearing walls must be erected and sufficiently cured/cured before roof trusses or ceiling structures can be placed, as the roof loads transfer through the walls to the foundation.
Electrical outlets, switches, plumbing stub-outs, and fixture backing within walls can only be installed after the walls are erected, as these are embedded or mounted within the wall assembly.
Exterior insulation layers, weather barriers, and cladding systems are applied over the completed PCM wall assembly to protect it from moisture and thermal bridging.
Interior finishes such as drywall, paneling, or plaster are applied after the PCM wall structure is complete, as they are surface finishes that conceal and protect the wall system.
Window and door frames are installed within the rough openings of completed walls, requiring the wall structure to be in place first for proper fit and anchorage.
The structural frame must be in place to provide the load-bearing support and attachment points for the glazing system.
Rough openings for windows and curtain walls must be framed and prepared before the glazing units can be installed.
Waterproof membranes and air barriers around openings must be installed prior to glazing to ensure a proper weather seal.
Interior wall finishes, trim, and sealants around the glazing system must be completed after the glazing is installed to achieve a finished appearance and proper air sealing.
The glazing system must be installed and sealed before exterior cladding or panels that abut the glazing can be completed, to maintain continuity and waterproofing.
The structural frame must be complete to provide a mounting surface and support for the shading devices.
Shading devices are typically installed as part of the facade system before final cladding to integrate with the building envelope and ensure proper sealing.
Shading devices are often mounted adjacent to or above windows; windows must be in place to align shading correctly for solar control and to avoid interfering with window installation.
While not a strict physical constraint, completing exterior shading before interior work avoids debris damage and allows for proper daylighting assessment during finishing.
Upper structure is needed to anchor top-mounted shading elements (e.g., overhangs, louvers) and to provide overhead structural support.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before any foundation work can begin, as footings require a stable, cleared base to bear structural loads.
Accurate surveying and layout marking must be completed first to ensure the north face footing is positioned correctly according to design drawings.

successor: Formwork installation for north face footing
rationale: The footing concrete must be placed and cured before formwork removal or subsequent vertical formwork can be installed above.
Footings provide the structural base; vertical wall reinforcement typically ties into the footing dowels, requiring the footing to be complete first.
After the footing concrete is poured, adequate curing time is a hard physical requirement to achieve design strength before any load is applied.
The roof edge and parapet must be installed after the roof substructure or deck is in place to provide a stable mounting surface and structural support.
The parapet and roof edge flashing must be installed before the roof membrane to allow proper integration, lapping, and sealing of the waterproofing layer at the edge details.
The parapet edge provides the structural base for attaching fascia and trim elements, so it must be completed first.
The structural framing must be erected to support the parapet walls and roof edge components.
Gutters and downspouts are often integrated with or mounted to the parapet and roof edge, so the edge must be in place for proper attachment and drainage alignment.

predecessor: North face structural framing and sheathing
successor: North face exterior insulation and finish system (EIFS)
rationale: Structural framing and sheathing provide the rigid substrate required to support the EIFS installation; EIFS cannot be applied without a complete backing.

predecessor: North face weather barrier / building wrap installation
successor: North face exterior insulation and finish system (EIFS)
rationale: A weather-resistant barrier (WRB) must be installed over the sheathing before EIFS to protect the structure from moisture infiltration.

predecessor: North face window and door installation (rough openings)
successor: North face exterior insulation and finish system (EIFS)
rationale: Windows and doors must be installed and flashed before EIFS is applied so that the EIFS can terminate properly against the frames and integrate with flashing.

predecessor: North face exterior insulation and finish system (EIFS)
successor: North face exterior paint/finish coating application
rationale: Typically EIFS includes its own finish coat, but if a separate paint or protective coating is specified, it must be applied after the EIFS base and reinforcement layers have cured.

predecessor: North face exterior insulation and finish system (EIFS)
successor: North face scaffold dismantling and site cleanup
rationale: Scaffolding must remain in place until EIFS installation is complete to provide access; dismantling can only start after all EIFS work is finished.
The north face must be fully installed before commissioning can begin, as commissioning tests the installed system for functionality and performance.
Structural steel must be erected to provide the supporting framework for the north face before it can be installed and commissioned.
Foundations must be completed to support the structural steel and north face elements before commissioning can occur.
Commissioning of the north face must be completed to ensure the building envelope is weather-tight before interior finishing works proceed.
Commissioning is a prerequisite step that must be completed and verified before the overall building can be handed over to the client.
The air barrier system requires a continuous substrate to attach to; structural framing provides the backing surface and structural support needed for air barrier membrane installation.
Sheathing provides the rigid substrate over the framing onto which the air barrier is applied; the air barrier cannot be installed directly on open framing.

successor: North face window/door rough openings sealed
rationale: Air barrier continuity must be established before rough openings are cut and sealed; otherwise, the air barrier surrounding openings would be disrupted.
The air barrier must be fully installed and continuous before exterior insulation is placed over it, as the insulation covers and hides the air barrier layer.
The air barrier is the innermost weather-resistive layer; cladding and rainscreen systems are installed over the air barrier to protect it and provide the final exterior finish.
Scaffolding provides the necessary access and working platform for installers to safely reach and work on the north face elevation for cladding installation.
The structural frame must be fully erected and stable to provide the supporting structure onto which the cladding panels are attached.
The underlying weather-resistant barrier and sheathing must be installed before cladding to protect the building envelope from moisture ingress.
Once cladding is installed, it must be inspected for proper installation, sealant integrity, and compliance with specifications before any subsequent finishing work.
Scaffolding cannot be removed until the cladding installation is complete, as the scaffolding is still needed for access during the cladding work.
Outdoor stairs require a stable load-bearing base; the foundation or slab provides the structural support for the stair landing and lowest tread.
Outdoor stairs often abut exterior walls; it is easier to install stair stringers and treads before applying final wall finishes to avoid rework or damage.
Handrails are mounted onto or adjacent to the stair structure; the stair frame and treads must be in place to properly anchor handrails.
Final grading and planting around the stair base should follow stair installation to achieve proper drainage and aesthetic integration.
The ground area where the stair will be placed must be excavated and roughly graded to the correct elevation and slope before any stair components are installed.
Proper grading, compaction and excavation of the ramp footprint area must be completed before the ramp structure can be built to ensure stable soil conditions and correct slope alignment.
Concrete footings or foundation walls that support the ramp must be poured and cured before ramp framing or slab placement begins.
Any drainage pipes, conduit, or utilities that will run beneath the ramp must be installed before the ramp slab or structure is placed to avoid rework.
The ramp structural base (concrete or framing) must be complete before applying non-slip coatings, sealants, or surface finishes.
Ramp structure must be in place before handrails and guardrails can be anchored to it for safety compliance.
The structural frame must be in place to provide a supporting surface for the balustrade to be anchored to.
The deck or floor slab must be completed so the balustrade has a base surface to mount to and to establish the finished floor level.
Balustrade posts and infill panels must be in place before handrails and top rails can be attached to them.
The balustrade must be fully installed before sealing joints against water ingress to prevent corrosion and leaks.
Typically finishing and painting is done after installation to avoid damage, though pre-finished components could allow reversal.
The handrail is typically anchored to or installed on top of the deck or patio surface; the surface must be complete to provide a stable base for handrail posts.
Handrails for stairs must be installed after the stair structure is built so that the handrail follows the correct slope and profile of the stairs.

While handrails can be painted before or after installation, it is often preferred to complete final finish work after installation to touch up scratches or fasteners, but this is a soft preference not a physical requirement.

successor: Outdoor Lighting Installation (if attached to handrail)
rationale: If lighting fixtures are to be mounted on or routed through the handrail, the handrail must be installed first to provide the mounting surface.
Handrail installation must be complete before final inspection to verify height, spacing, and structural requirements, though this is a sequential preference in the inspection process.
A solid foundation (e.g., concrete footings or a slab) must be completed before the pergola structure can be anchored and erected to ensure stability and load-bearing capacity.
Proper site grading and drainage systems must be in place before pergola construction begins to prevent water pooling around the footings and long-term structural damage.
Any electrical, gas, or water lines that will run beneath the pergola area must be installed before footings and posts are set to avoid future excavation or service conflicts.

The pergola's structural posts and framework serve as a reference point; deck boards or patio pavers are typically installed or fitted around the posts after the pergola is erected for proper alignment and finishing.

While wiring can be roughed in before, final installation of light fixtures, ceiling fans, and switches on or integrated with the pergola is done after the structure is complete; this is a logical/sequential preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The structural frame or roofing structure must be in place to provide support for the outdoor ceiling installation.
Outdoor ceiling lights and fixtures are typically mounted on or recessed into the ceiling surface, so the ceiling must be in place first.
Finishing work such as painting or staining is done after the ceiling material is installed to avoid damaging the finish during installation.
Soffit and fascia trim often abut the outdoor ceiling and are installed after the ceiling substrate is in place for proper alignment and sealing.
Ceiling fans for outdoor patios/porches must be mounted to a secured ceiling structure; the ceiling must be complete to provide the mounting surface and electrical box support.
The exterior wall must be framed to provide a mounting structure for the weatherproof electrical outlet.
Exterior sheathing provides the backing surface needed to mount and secure the weatherproof outlet box.
Electrical wiring must be run to the outlet location before the outlet can be connected and installed.
The weatherproof outlet must be installed and flashed before siding is applied to ensure proper waterproofing integration and to avoid having to cut into finished siding.
The outlet must be physically installed before the circuit can be tested for proper operation and ground fault protection.
Electrical conduits must be in place underground before lighting fixtures can be connected to the power supply.
Concrete slabs or foundations where lighting poles or bases are mounted must be cured and ready before fixtures can be installed.
Final grading and landscaping should be completed to avoid rework or damage to fixtures, though fixtures can be installed before final landscaping if needed.
Wall-mounted outdoor lighting fixtures are typically installed after exterior wall surfaces are finished to ensure proper mounting and weather sealing.
Lighting fixtures must be physically installed before they can be connected, tested, and commissioned as part of the electrical system.
The exterior ceiling fan mounts to the wall structure, so the sheathing and weather barrier must be in place to provide a mounting surface and prevent moisture intrusion.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical wiring for ceiling fan
rationale: Electrical power supply wiring must be roughed-in to the junction box location before the fan unit can be connected and installed.

successor: Complete electrical connection and test fan operation
rationale: Final electrical hookup and testing of the fan must occur after the fan is physically mounted in place.

successor: Install exterior trim and siding around fan
rationale: Exterior trim and siding around the fan location must be installed after the fan is in place to ensure proper fit, sealing, and a finished appearance.
The installed ceiling fan must be in place and connected before the final inspection can verify its correct installation and operation.
The mounting bracket must be installed first to provide a secure structural attachment point for the heater unit.
Electrical wiring and conduit must be run to the mounting location before the heater can be physically mounted and connected.
The heater must be mounted in its final position before electrical connections can be completed and terminated.
The heater unit must be mounted before any decorative trim, covers, or aesthetic finishes can be installed around it.
The heater must be fully mounted and secured before it can be tested for proper operation and safety.
The ground must be excavated and graded to proper slopes before drainage channels can be formed or installed to ensure proper water flow.
The subgrade must be compacted and prepared to provide a stable base for the drainage channel structure.
Underground utilities (water, sewer, electrical, gas) must be laid before drainage channels to avoid conflicts and the need to cut through or relocate the channel.
After the drainage channel is installed, the surrounding areas must be backfilled and compacted to secure the channel in place and restore grade.
Final paving, concrete slabs, or surface finishes should be applied after drainage channels are in place to ensure proper integration and drainage flow into the channel system.
The outdoor room enclosure wall requires a stable, load-bearing substrate. The foundation or slab must be poured, cured, and leveled before the wall can be constructed on it.
Any underground drains, conduits, or plumbing that will pass beneath the wall's footprint must be installed and inspected before the wall is built, to avoid later demolition or rework.
Flashing, sealants, and weather barriers are applied directly to the completed wall structure to prevent moisture intrusion before any cladding or finishes are added.
If the outdoor room has a roof or pergola, the enclosure walls must be built first to support the overhead structure and establish the correct bearing points.
While electrical boxes can be installed after the wall is framed, it is a soft preference to run wiring before the wall is fully enclosed to avoid fishing wires through finished surfaces.
The privacy screen requires a stable foundation or footings to support its structure, especially if it is a standalone wall or fence.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared before installing the privacy screen to ensure proper drainage and a level installation surface.

Once the privacy screen is installed, it typically requires finishing work such as staining or sealing for weather protection; this is a logical sequence preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
Planting or landscaping around the privacy screen is best done after installation to avoid damaging plants during construction and to ensure proper alignment with the screen.
Underground utilities must be located and avoided before digging post holes or footings for the privacy screen to prevent damage and ensure safety.
The structural steel frame provides the primary support structure onto which the outdoor shade louver system is mounted. The louvers cannot be installed without a stable underlying frame.

Shade louvers are often integrated into or abutting metal panel systems; the louver framework must be in place before adjacent cladding can be finished around it to ensure proper weatherproofing and alignment.
Exterior wall sheathing provides the weather-resistant barrier and backing behind the louver assembly; louvers are typically anchored through or onto the sheathed wall surface.

Although painting can often proceed before louver installation, if the louvers are integrated into a finished facade system, some final coating touch-ups may be preferred after louver installation to ensure continuity and coverage around mounting points.

predecessor: Roofing and Flashing Installation (above louver area)
rationale: Overhead roofing and flashing must be completed first to prevent water ingress behind and above the louver assembly; louvers are typically installed below finished roof edges and flashings to maintain proper water shedding.
The shade sail mount typically requires structural poles (wood, metal, or concrete footings) to be anchored in the ground or to a building structure before the sail can be attached.
The vertical support poles (e.g., steel or timber posts) must be set and secured in their foundations or footings before the shade sail mounting hardware can be installed onto them.

predecessor: Building Wall or Fascia Preparation (if wall-mounted)
rationale: If the sail mount attaches to an existing building wall or fascia, the wall structure must be completed/waterproofed and mounting brackets must be securely fastened before the sail hardware can be installed.

The mounting hardware (D-rings, turnbuckles, carabiners, anchor plates) must be fully installed and secured to the poles or wall before the shade sail fabric can be attached, stretched, and tensioned.

successor: Final Site Cleanup and Landscaping (adjacent areas)
rationale: While ideally landscaping is completed after mounting to avoid damage, some finishing work may be done concurrently; however, heavy landscaping near poles is best performed before final sail tensioning to prevent soiling or interference.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any outdoor bench can be placed to ensure stability and proper positioning.
If the bench requires a concrete pad, footing, or gravel base (for heavy or permanent benches), that substructure must be completed first to provide a stable foundation.

It is often easier to install landscaping, mulch, or decorative gravel around the bench after the bench is in place to achieve a clean finished look, though this can be done beforehand with careful planning.
Once the bench is installed, the work area can be cleaned up, debris removed, and final touches applied to the surrounding environment.
The planter wall must be built on a stable, level foundation. Any slab or footing work needs to be completed first to support the weight and structure of the masonry wall.

Proper drainage behind and beneath the planter wall is essential to prevent water buildup and hydrostatic pressure. The gravel base and drainage system should be installed before the wall is constructed.
Soil and planting medium can only be placed behind the wall after the wall structure is complete and cured, as the wall retains the soil.
Waterproofing membrane or sealant must be applied to the finished wall surface to protect it from moisture penetration and freeze-thaw damage.

While plants can be installed after the wall is complete, it is a soft preference since some planting could theoretically be done concurrently, but best practice is to complete the wall structure first to avoid soil disturbance.
The ground must be leveled and cleared before any heavy construction of a fireplace structure can begin to ensure a stable foundation.
The fireplace requires a reinforced concrete slab or footing to bear its weight and prevent settling; this must cure before masonry begins.
If the fireplace uses gas lines or includes electrical components (ignition, lighting), those underground utilities must be run and inspected before the fireplace structure is built over them.
The chimney structure must be fully constructed before a cap and flashing can be installed to seal the top and prevent water intrusion.

successor: Finish Stone/Veneer and Mortar Joint Tooling
rationale: The structural core (e.g., concrete block or firebrick) of the fireplace must be built first; the decorative stone or veneer is applied as a finish layer after the structural walls are complete.
The ground must be properly graded and excavated to create a stable, level base for the fire pit structure.
All underground utilities (gas, electric, data) must be located and marked before digging to avoid damage and ensure safe installation of any gas lines to the fire pit.

successor: Fire Pit Gas Line Connection & Testing
rationale: The fire pit structure must be fully assembled and in place before gas lines can be connected and pressure-tested.
The core structural shell of the fire pit must be completed before applying decorative stone or paver veneer around its exterior.
Ideally the fire pit is built before pouring the surrounding patio so that pavers or concrete can be laid flush against the pit, though it can also be added after with proper cutting.
The outdoor kitchen counter requires a stable and level foundation or concrete slab to be installed upon, as the counter structure cannot be placed directly on unfinished ground.
Plumbing and gas lines for the sink, grill, and other appliances must be run in the walls or through the slab before the counter is installed, as the counter would block access to these utilities.

predecessor: Outdoor Kitchen Base Cabinets / Frame Construction
rationale: The base cabinets or structural frame that supports the countertop must be fully built and secured in place before the counter can be mounted on top.
Drop-in appliances such as the grill, sink, and refrigerator are typically installed after the countertop is in place, as the counter provides the supporting surface and cutouts for these appliances.

While backsplash can technically be done before the counter, it is standard practice and easier to achieve a clean finish by installing the backsplash after the counter is set, to seal the joint between them.
Plumbing rough-in (water supply lines and drain pipes) must be installed and stubbed out before the sink can be positioned and connected.

predecessor: Pour Outdoor Kitchen Countertop Slab or Install Countertop Frame
rationale: The sink sits into (or under) the countertop, so the countertop base or slab must be in place to support the sink.
The sink must be physically set in place before the water supply lines, faucet, and drain can be connected to it.
Edge sealing and caulking against the countertop can only be done after the sink is installed in its final position.

successor: Final Outdoor Kitchen Finishes and Trim
rationale: It is preferable (but not strictly required) to complete final trim and finishing work after the sink is installed to avoid damaging finishes during sink installation.
A level, stable, and properly graded surface is required before constructing any permanent outdoor structure like a kitchen island to ensure proper drainage and structural integrity.
A concrete pad or foundation must be poured and fully cured to provide a solid, load-bearing base for the kitchen island structure.
Gas lines, water supply lines, and electrical conduit must be buried and roughed in beneath the planned island location before the island structure is built, as they will be inaccessible afterward.
The island base/frame structure must be fully assembled and in place before countertops can be measured, cut, and installed on top of it.
The island cabinetry and framework must be complete to provide the support structure and cutouts needed for built-in outdoor kitchen appliances.
Outdoor shower requires a stable, level base (concrete slab or deck structure) for proper drainage, mounting, and structural support.
Water supply lines must be roughed-in below ground or within the wall/floor before the shower fixture can be connected.
Drainage pipe must be installed and graded before the shower base is placed to ensure proper wastewater removal.

successor: Wall Cladding / Siding (if adjacent to a wall)
rationale: If the shower is mounted on an exterior wall, cladding should ideally be finished before mounting to avoid damage, but it can be done around the fixture if needed.
Final grading, gravel, or decking around the shower area must be completed after the shower is installed to ensure proper integration and drainage around the base.
The wall framing and rough opening must be complete to provide the structural support and mounting surface for the retractable awning.
Weather-resistant barrier and sheathing must be in place to prevent moisture intrusion behind the awning mounting brackets.
If the awning is motorized, conduit and wiring must be roughed in to the mounting location before the awning is installed to allow for proper electrical connection.

successor: Final electrical connection and motor testing
rationale: The awning must be physically mounted before the motor can be connected and tested for operation.

successor: Exterior finish and trim work around awning
rationale: It is preferred to install trim and finish around the awning brackets after mounting to achieve a clean appearance, but finishing could conceptually be done before if precise measurements are taken.
The mounting bracket must be securely attached to the wall or ceiling before the speaker mount can be installed onto it.
The outdoor speaker mount must be fully installed and secured before the speaker itself can be attached to the mount.
The speaker mount must be in place to support and position the speaker before connecting wiring to the speaker unit.
The surface area where the mount will be attached must be properly sealed and weatherproofed to prevent moisture infiltration behind the mount.
While typically the grille is installed after mounting, it could technically be pre-attached; however, standard practice is to mount first to avoid damage.
The ground must be excavated and leveled to create the proper foundation and footprint for the water feature basin.
A concrete slab or structural base must be cured in place to support the weight of the water feature basin before it can be installed.
Water supply lines, drain lines, and electrical conduit for pumps/lights must be run underground before the basin is placed over them.
Once the basin is positioned and secured, waterproofing membranes or liners must be applied to prevent leaks.
The pump and plumbing fixtures can only be connected after the basin is in its final position.

successor: Water Feature Finishing (Tiling, Liner, Decorative Stone)
rationale: Decorative finishes around the basin edge and interior cannot be completed until the basin structure is fully installed.

Soft preference: it is easier and cleaner to complete final landscaping and grading after the basin is installed to avoid disturbing the basin's position, though it could be done simultaneously with care.
The window head/lintel is a structural component that spans the opening above a window, requiring the surrounding wall framing or masonry to be in place to provide support and define the opening.
The rough opening for the window must be framed or created in the wall before the lintel can be installed to bridge the top of the opening.
The lintel provides structural support above the window opening; the window frame and sash are installed after the lintel is in place to ensure the opening is properly supported.

successor: Weep Hole / Flashing Installation at Window Head
rationale: Flashing and weep holes at the window head are installed after the lintel is placed to manage water drainage and prevent moisture intrusion above the window.
Exterior cladding or finishing above the window is applied after the lintel is in place, as the lintel defines the top of the window zone and provides a bearing surface for cladding.

The window frame and glass must be installed in the rough opening before the gasket or glazing bead can be applied, as the gasket/bead serves to seal and secure the glazing within the installed frame.
The gasket/glazing bead must be in place to provide a proper surface and seal before final weatherstripping or perimeter sealing can be applied around the window unit.

Interior trim such as architraves or drywall finishes should only be installed after the glazing bead is in place, as the bead secures the glass and completes the window assembly before cosmetic finishes are applied.

The glazing bead/gasket helps secure the window unit and seal against moisture; exterior cladding or siding that abuts the window should be installed after the bead is in place to ensure a continuous weather-resistant barrier.

The glazing bead or gasket is the component that holds the glass in place within the frame; therefore, the glass panel must first be positioned in the frame before the bead can be installed to retain it.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and cavity into which the window mullion is installed.
The mullion serves as a vertical or horizontal divider between window units; window frames must be installed after the mullion is in place to attach and align properly.
Glass panes (glazing) are installed after the mullion and frame assembly is complete because the mullion provides structural separation between panes.
Weather seals and caulking around the mullion and adjacent window units can only be applied after the mullion is fully installed to ensure a continuous waterproof barrier.
The structural wall sheathing provides the backing surface and opening within which the mullion is mounted; sheathing must precede mullion installation.
The rough opening framing creates the structural opening in the wall that physically supports and houses the window transom; the transom cannot be installed without a framed opening.
The window sill provides the bottom support and drainage surface that the transom rests upon; the transom requires a completed sill below it.
The weather barrier must be installed around the rough opening before the transom is placed to ensure proper flashing and water management integration.
After the transom is set in place, flashing and sealant must be applied around its perimeter to create a watertight installation; this cannot be done before the transom is positioned.
Interior trim and casing around the transom can only be installed after the transom unit is fully fixed in place, as the trim is fitted to the edges of the installed unit.
The window frame must be installed to provide a structural enclosure and mounting surface for the built-in window shading device.
Rough openings must be prepared and framed to accommodate the window assembly and built-in shading components.
The glass panels must be in place before built-in shading devices (e.g., blinds between glass or integrated shades) can be installed or adjusted within the window assembly.
Built-in shading devices should be enclosed and trimmed after installation to provide a finished appearance and protect the mechanism.
For motorized built-in shading devices, electrical wiring and connections must be completed after the device is mounted to ensure proper integration and power supply.
The wall structure must be in place to provide the rough opening and structural support for the window frame.
The rough opening must be cut, framed, and sized correctly to accommodate the window unit.
Flashings and weather-resistant barriers around the rough opening must be installed before the window to ensure water penetration is directed away from the building envelope.
Once the window is physically set in place, the perimeter gaps must be sealed with caulk or foam to ensure air and water tightness.
Drywall, trim, and interior finishes around the window can only be applied after the window unit is installed and secured.
Exterior siding or cladding that abuts the window frame must be installed after the window is in place to properly overlap and seal against the window flange.
The window frame must be installed first to provide a structural surface for the weather barrier to be applied around and sealed to.
The rough opening must be properly prepared (cleaned, primed, and have necessary sealants) before the weather barrier can be installed around the window.
The weather barrier (typically a membrane or flexible seal) is installed first, followed by window flashing which goes over the weather barrier to direct water away from the assembly.

The weather barrier must be fully installed and sealed around the window before exterior cladding or siding can be applied, as the weather barrier protects the building envelope from moisture infiltration behind the cladding.

While not a strict physical requirement, completing the weather barrier installation ensures the building envelope is sealed against moisture before interior finishes are applied, preventing potential water damage.
The entry canopy requires a stable foundation to support its structural load.
The entry canopy is typically attached to or supported by the main structural steel framework of the building.
Doors beneath the canopy should be installed after the canopy is in place to ensure proper alignment and weather protection.

successor: Exterior Finishes and Cladding at Entry
rationale: Finishing work around the entry area, such as siding or masonry, should follow canopy installation to ensure proper flashing and waterproofing integration.
While possible to pre-wire, installing light fixtures under the canopy is more efficient after the canopy structure is in place for precise placement.
The storefront requires a complete building shell with structural framing to provide an opening for the storefront system to be installed into.
The storefront base must rest on a finished floor slab or prepared substrate to ensure proper leveling and structural support.
While storefront can be installed before electrical rough-in, it is preferable to complete rough electrical to avoid rework or damage to the storefront framing later.
The storefront frame must be fully installed and anchored before glass panels or glazing can be placed into the frame.
Finishing work around the storefront is preferably done after installation to allow proper sealing and trim, but is not a strict physical necessity.
Signage must be mounted onto the completed storefront structure; the supporting frame and glazing must be in place first.
The storefront must be in place so that perimeter seals, caulking, and weather barriers can be applied to prevent water and air infiltration.
The structural frame (columns, beams, floor slabs) must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the window wall system.
The rough opening must be framed, squared, and reinforced to receive the window wall unit.
The building envelope weather barrier must be installed behind the window wall to prevent air and water infiltration.
After the window wall frame is installed, glass panels must be glazed and perimeter seals applied to complete the envelope.
Interior drywall and finishes around the window wall cannot be completed until the window wall is installed and weather-tight.
The display window must be installed within a framed wall opening; the wall frame provides structural support and defines the rough opening dimensions
Electrical wiring for window lighting or power must be roughed in behind the wall before the window is placed and sealed
Interior and exterior trim, casing, and sill installation requires the window unit to be securely in place first
Drywall or wall finish around the display window must abut the installed window frame for a clean finished edge
Flashing, caulking, and weatherproofing around the window frame can only be applied after the window is installed in the opening
The entry threshold is set on a prepared substrate; the foundation and slab must be completed to provide a stable, level base for the threshold.
The door opening frame and rough structure must be in place to receive and anchor the entry threshold assembly.
Sub-slab drainage and waterproofing membranes must be installed before the threshold to prevent moisture ingress at the entry point.
The threshold is the base upon which the door frame and door rest; the door assembly cannot be properly installed without the threshold in place.

successor: Floor Finishing (e.g., tiling, hardwood around threshold)
rationale: Although finishing can be done carefully after the threshold, it is preferable to install the threshold after final floor levelling to achieve a flush transition; considered a soft sequencing preference for best aesthetic and functional outcome.

successor: Weather Sealing and Caulking at Entry
rationale: The threshold acts as part of the weather barrier; sealing/caulking around the threshold and door frame must follow threshold installation to ensure water tightness.
The access ramp requires a stable foundation or base to rest upon; without proper foundation work, the ramp cannot be structurally supported.
The ground must be graded and excavated to the correct slope and elevation before the access ramp can be formed and poured.
Handrails are typically mounted onto the ramp surface or edges, so the ramp structure must be in place before handrails can be installed.
Anti-slip coatings or surface finishes must be applied after the ramp concrete or material has cured and the ramp structure is complete.

Signage indicating the accessible route is typically placed after the ramp is built, but this is a soft preference as signage could theoretically be installed nearby before the ramp is fully completed.
The frame structure must be erected to provide the supporting framework onto which the fixed canopy is attached.
The fixed canopy structure must be in place before glazing or panel infill can be installed onto it.
Weatherproofing and sealing can only be applied after the canopy is fully fixed in position to ensure continuous sealing around joints.
Gutters and drainage components are typically attached to the canopy structure, so the canopy must be fixed first.
Once the canopy is fixed, a final quality and safety inspection can be conducted to verify compliance.
The door closer and panic hardware must be mounted on a fully installed and secured door frame. Without the frame in place, there is no structural support for the hardware.
Door closer and panic hardware are installed onto the door leaf itself, so the door must be hung and aligned within the frame before the hardware can be attached and adjusted.
The walls surrounding the door opening must be built to provide anchorage for the door frame, which in turn supports the door and its hardware.
After installing the closer and panic hardware, the door must be tested for proper opening, closing, latching, and self-closing function before the area can be considered finished.
While not a physical necessity, it is common practice to perform final paint touch-ups and finish work after hardware installation to cover any scratches or marks made during hardware mounting.
The site must be cleared, graded, and excavated to proper elevation before the entry mat/grid system can be placed, as it serves as the base foundation layer.
The subgrade soil must be compacted and proof-rolled to ensure adequate bearing capacity before installing the entry mat/grid system to prevent differential settlement.
Geotextile separation fabric must be placed over the prepared subgrade before the mat/grid system is installed to prevent soil mixing and improve load distribution.

successor: Surface Paving or Gravel Wearing Course
rationale: The mat/grid system acts as a stabilization base; the final wearing surface (asphalt, concrete, or gravel) must be placed on top after the mat/grid is fully installed.
Edge restraints or curbs are typically installed after the mat/grid system to contain the wearing course material, though this can sometimes be done concurrently with soft preference for sequencing.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed, sized, and prepared before the door can be installed into it.
Structural framing including king studs, jack studs, and header must be in place to support the door.
Exterior wall sheathing and weather-resistive barrier must be installed before the door to ensure proper flashing integration and weatherproofing.
The finished floor surface or subfloor must be in place to establish the correct threshold height and door clearance.
After the door is set, flashing must be applied around the frame to seal against water intrusion.
Interior door casing and trim cannot be installed until the door unit is securely in place.

successor: Exterior Siding or Cladding Completion Around Door
rationale: Siding or cladding around the door opening is finished after the door is installed to ensure proper overlapping and sealing.
Door hardware such as handles, locks, and hinges are installed after the door is hung.
Electrical and data rough-ins must be completed before storefront installation to allow wiring and conduit to be placed within walls and framing that will be enclosed by the storefront system.
The structural framing and support system must be in place to provide the load-bearing framework onto which the storefront system will be mounted and secured.
Rough openings in the building envelope must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the storefront system can be installed.
After the storefront system is installed, waterproofing membranes and sealants must be applied around the perimeter and joints to ensure weather-tightness and prevent moisture intrusion.

Interior finishes typically follow storefront installation to avoid damage to finishes and to allow the storefront to serve as a reference point for interior wall placement, though some adjacent finishes could proceed in parallel with careful sequencing.
The subfloor or base surface must be properly prepared (clean, level, and dry) before installing thresholds and mat systems to ensure proper adhesion and fit.
Rough flooring or underlayment must be in place before thresholds and mats are installed as they serve as the final layer.
Doors and their frames must be installed first so that thresholds can be measured and fitted accurately to the door opening and clearance.
Thresholds and mat systems are typically installed before or alongside final flooring to provide a seamless transition and edge finishing.
After the threshold and mat system is installed, final inspections can verify proper installation, but this is a workflow preference rather than a physical necessity.
Automatic doors must be physically installed before they can be commissioned, as commissioning involves testing and verifying the installed system's operation.

predecessor: Provide Electrical Supply to Automatic Doors
rationale: Electrical power must be connected to the automatic doors before commissioning can proceed, as the doors need power for testing activation, sensors, and safety functions.
Automatic doors must be commissioned and verified to operate safely before they can be used for normal building access by occupants.
The vertical steelwork (columns and structural frame) for the gallery surround must be installed first to provide support and attachment points for the floor slab.
Foundations and base preparation must be completed to provide a stable and level substrate before pouring or placing the floor slab.

successor: Waterproofing / Membrane Application on Gallery Surround Slab
rationale: Waterproofing membranes must be applied after the slab has been poured and cured to protect the structure from moisture ingress.

successor: Gallery Surround Floor Finishes (tiling, screed, or coating)
rationale: Final floor finishes are applied after the structural slab is complete and properly cured to ensure a smooth, durable surface.

successor: Installation of Gallery Surround Balustrades / Glass Panels
rationale: Balustrades and glass panels are fixed into or onto the floor slab, requiring the slab to be in place before installation can proceed.
The gallery surround structure must be installed to provide the physical framework onto which the balustrade is mounted.
Structural steel framing provides the main support for the gallery surround before the balustrade can be attached.

successor: Balustrade Glass or Infill Panel Installation
rationale: The balustrade frame must be in place before glass panels or infill materials can be installed within it.
The balustrade structure must be completed to provide support for handrail attachment.
The balustrade must be fully installed before it can undergo final inspection and safety certification for compliance.
The structural frame of the gallery surround must be in place to provide the supporting framework onto which glazing panels are mounted.
Glazing panels must be installed before sealing and weatherproofing can be applied to the joints and edges.
Once glazing panels are in place, interior spaces become enclosed, allowing interior finishing works to proceed without exposure to weather.
The handrail must be attached to a stable gallery surround structure/frame; the frame provides the physical support for the handrail.
