Finishing work (paint, stain, sealant) must be applied after the handrail is fully installed to ensure complete coverage and a smooth finish without damaging underlying surfaces.
The handrail must be fully installed before it can be inspected for structural integrity, code compliance, and safety.
Any supporting posts or base plates for the gallery surround and handrail require a stable foundation or floor slab to be in place.
It is generally preferred to install the handrail before final cleaning and occupancy to avoid damage to finished surfaces, though it is not a strict physical necessity.
The cantilever bracket must be supported by the main structural steel frame; the frame provides the primary load path and anchorage points for the bracket.
Concrete cores and columns provide vertical support and lateral stability; the bracket attaches to or bears upon these structural elements.
The cantilever bracket supports the gallery floor deck; the deck cannot be placed until the bracket is in position to carry the load.
Handrails and guardrails for the gallery surround are typically mounted onto or adjacent to the cantilever bracket structure, requiring the bracket to be in place first.
Architectural cladding and finish materials (e.g., panels, facia) around the gallery surround are applied after the cantilever bracket is installed to achieve proper fit and alignment.
The gallery surround structural beam requires a stable foundation to support its load; foundation preparation must be completed before beam installation.
Columns provide vertical support for the gallery surround structural beam; beams typically rest on or connect to columns, requiring column completion first.
Formwork must be built and positioned to shape and support the concrete while the gallery surround structural beam is poured and cured.
Rebar or steel reinforcement must be installed within the formwork before concrete is poured for the structural beam to achieve required tensile strength.
The gallery surround structural beam provides edge support and containment for adjacent floor slabs or decks; slab pouring must wait until the beam is in place and cured.
Waterproofing is typically applied after the beam is fully cured to protect the structural element from moisture; this is a recommended sequencing but may have some flexibility depending on schedule.
Exterior cladding or façade elements around the gallery area attach to or cover the structural beam; the beam must be in place first to provide the structural backing.
The upstand wall sits on top of or against the gallery surround base; the base must be installed first to provide structural support and a reference surface.
The coping or cap (top finish) is typically installed after the upstand wall is complete to seal and finish the top edge of the wall.
Waterproofing membranes are applied over the completed upstand wall surface to ensure watertightness; the wall must be fully constructed first.
Backfilling against the upstand wall can only occur after the wall is fully constructed and cured to prevent displacement or damage.
The substrate or structural slab must be prepared and leveled before any upstand wall construction to ensure proper bonding and alignment.

The gallery surround soffit is a component attached to or supported by the structural steel frame. The steel frame must be erected first to provide the structural support and attachment points for the soffit.

predecessor: Deck/Pour Concrete Slab at Gallery Level
rationale: The gallery level slab must be in place as the soffit will be fitted underneath or adjacent to the gallery slab. The soffit finishing depends on the completed structural deck.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work in the ceiling space above the soffit area must be completed before the soffit is enclosed, to avoid costly rework and to provide access for MEP installations.
The soffit must be installed first before any surface finishing such as plastering, taping, or painting can be applied to it.
Once the soffit is in place and finished, final MEP trims, lighting fixtures, and ceiling-mounted devices can be installed through or onto the soffit surface.
The nosing profile is the finishing edge trim for the gallery surround, so the main gallery surround structure must be in place first to provide the surface to attach the nosing profile to.

The nosing profile forms the final edge detail; painting or final finishing should occur after the nosing profile is installed to ensure a continuous, uniform finish across both the surround surface and the nosing trim.
If the nosing profile abuts a handrail post or balustrade, it is preferable but not strictly required to install the balustrade first, so the nosing can be cut and fitted accurately around the post.

successor: Final Quality Inspection of Gallery Area
rationale: The final inspection should include checking the nosing profile for alignment, security, and finish; therefore it is logically done after installation of the nosing profile.

The gallery surround step is a secondary steel or architectural element that attaches to the main concrete columns. Therefore, the concrete columns must be erected and cured first to provide the structural support for the gallery surround step installation.

The gallery surround step typically connects to or is supported by the main structural steel frame. The primary steel frame must be in place before installing secondary components like the gallery surround step to ensure proper alignment and load transfer.

The gallery surround step forms part of the building's architectural envelope/finish. Once installed, it provides the substrate or alignment reference for subsequent cladding, paneling, or façade systems that cover or abut the gallery area.

successor: MEP Rough-In Works in Gallery Area
rationale: While not a physical necessity, it is highly preferred to complete the gallery surround step before running mechanical, electrical, and plumbing services in the adjacent gallery zone, as the surround defines the finished boundaries and access paths, reducing rework and ensuring a clean installation.

The gallery surround access hatch is a component of the gallery surround structure, so the main gallery surround must be installed first to provide the support frame and surrounding structure for the access hatch.

The access hatch provides entry to service spaces behind the gallery surround; electrical rough-in work behind the surround typically requires access through the hatch, so the hatch must be installed before workers can access those spaces for electrical work.

Similar to electrical rough-in, mechanical services (ductwork, piping) located behind or within the gallery surround area require the access hatch to be in place for service access, so the hatch installation must precede mechanical rough-in work requiring that access.
While it is typical to complete finishing work after the hatch is installed for a uniform appearance, this is a soft preference as finishes could be applied in stages around the hatch area if needed.
The structural wall or substrate that the gallery surround and its access hatch mount to must be framed and in place before the hatch assembly can be installed.
The floor slab must be prepared and poured before any floor-mounted boxes can be installed.
Floor boxes must be positioned, leveled, and secured in place before the final floor finish (screed, tiles, etc.) is applied around them.
The physical box must be in place before electrical conduits and wiring can be connected to it.
Underground or underfloor conduits and cabling routes must be laid before the floor box can be installed and connected to them.
The floor box body must be installed first, then after floor finishing the covers and trims can be fitted flush with the finished floor level.
The structural frame must be complete to provide the supporting structure onto which balustrades are attached.
Balustrades are typically mounted onto or adjacent to floor slabs or decks, so these surfaces must exist first.
Stair balustrades require the staircase structure to be in place for proper alignment and attachment.
Safety inspections of balustrades can only occur after they are installed, though this is a procedural rather than physical constraint.
The gallery surround baseboard must be installed onto a framed wall structure; wall framing provides the necessary structural support.
Electrical wiring must be roughed in before baseboard installation to avoid having to remove or cut through the baseboard for access.
Drywall must be installed and finished before baseboard can be attached, as baseboard covers the joint between drywall and flooring.

Baseboard is typically installed before finished flooring to allow the flooring to be fitted tightly against the baseboard, or alternatively after flooring; in standard sequence, baseboard goes on after drywall but before final flooring trim work.
Baseboards are typically painted or finished after installation to ensure a smooth, continuous finish without paint on surrounding surfaces.
The structural framing must be in place to support the soffit framing, as soffits are typically attached to the underside of roof overhangs or structural elements.
Electrical wiring that runs through soffit spaces must be roughed in before soffits are enclosed, as access is impossible after finishing.
Soffit finishing provides a clean, finished edge against which exterior siding and painting can be completed, ensuring weatherproofing and aesthetic continuity.

Gutters are often mounted to the fascia board which is part of the soffit/roof edge assembly; however, gutters can sometimes be installed after soffits are complete as a soft preference for work sequencing efficiency.
Exterior finishing including soffits must be completed before final exterior inspections can be conducted to verify code compliance.
Concrete foundations must be fully cured and ready to bear loads before any structural support elements (columns, beams, walls) are placed on them.
The building site must be cleared, excavated, and leveled before any structural supports can be installed to ensure stable ground conditions.

Underground plumbing, electrical conduits, and drainage must be placed before structural supports (especially footings and columns) are installed, as it is impractical to dig under completed supports.
Floor slabs, decks, or elevated platforms rely directly on the installed columns, beams, or walls for load transfer, so the structural support skeleton must be complete beforehand.
Roof and wall framing require the primary vertical and lateral structural supports to be in place to anchor and stabilize the building envelope.
The structural frame and columns must be erected first to provide the vertical support and load-bearing structure onto which the balcony slab is poured or fixed.
Formwork must be set up to shape and hold the wet concrete before the balcony slab can be cast.
Steel reinforcement bars must be positioned within the formwork to provide tensile strength before concrete pouring for the balcony slab.
Balcony slab must be fully cured and structurally complete before applying waterproofing to protect the slab from moisture ingress.
The balcony slab must be in place to provide a base and anchoring surface for installing railings or balustrades.
The structural frame (including columns, beams, and slabs) must be completed to provide the load-bearing support and openings into which glazing panels are installed.
Window and curtain wall openings must be framed, measured, and prepared (including setting sills, headers, and weatherproofing membranes) before glazing can be placed.
Air barriers and waterproofing around openings must be applied before glazing to ensure the building envelope is properly sealed and to prevent moisture intrusion.

While interior finishing can progress concurrently with glazing in some cases, it is a soft preference to complete glazing first to prevent damage to finished surfaces and to control the building environment (temperature/humidity) before delicate interior work.
Air and water infiltration testing of the building envelope can only be performed after glazing is fully installed and sealed to verify the curtain wall system performs as designed.
Balcony balusters are installed on top of or anchored into the balcony slab/deck. The structural deck must be fully cured and load-bearing before baluster installation can begin.
Waterproofing membrane must be applied on the balcony deck before balusters are installed, as the baluster base connections can compromise the waterproofing if done in reverse order.
Adjacent structural columns or wall framing provide lateral support and alignment reference for balcony balusters; ideally these are in place first for proper alignment.
Handrails are typically mounted onto or between balusters; the balusters must be fixed in position to serve as the supporting posts for the handrail.
Glass panels or infill elements between balusters are inserted after the balusters are fixed in place, as the balusters form the vertical supports that frame the infill.

The guardrail/handrail must be anchored into or mounted onto the structural balcony slab/deck. The concrete must be poured and fully cured to achieve sufficient strength to support the guardrail loads.

predecessor: Structural Steel/Masonry Wall Rough-In (at balcony perimeter)
rationale: Embedded anchors, sleeves, or brackets required for guardrail attachment must be installed within the structure before the guardrail itself can be fastened.
The main handrail structure or top rail must be in place to act as the supporting framework before individual balusters or pickets (if separate) are installed.
Final decorative caps, end covers, or cosmetic trims are applied after the primary guardrail assembly is stable and aligned.

successor: Balcony Waterproofing & Sealant Application (at rail penetrations)
rationale: Waterproofing sealants around guardrail anchor points and penetrations through the balcony membrane must be completed after the guardrail is installed to ensure water-tight sealing at all connection points.
The door frame must be installed first to provide the structural opening and mounting surface for the balcony door assembly.
The rough opening must be properly sized, squared, and prepared before the door assembly can be installed.
Weatherproofing membranes around the opening must be applied prior to door installation to ensure proper water tightness and sealing.
After the door assembly is in place, gaps must be sealed and insulated to ensure thermal and moisture protection.
Interior trim work around the door is typically done after the door is installed, but could theoretically be sequenced differently if needed, though standard practice follows this order.
The balcony soffit is attached to the underside of the balcony slab; the concrete slab must be poured and cured to provide the structural substrate for soffit installation.
Any formwork or falsework supporting the slab must be stripped before soffit work can proceed in the same area.
Waterproofing above the slab must be completed before enclosing the underside to avoid trapping moisture and to allow membrane inspection.
Vents, downlights, or other fixtures mounted in the soffit require the soffit surface to be in place for cutting, mounting, and trim finishing.

While often sequenced independently, installing the soffit before railing avoids working around railing posts and allows cleaner soffit edges against the building face; a soft preference for workflow efficiency.
The balcony structure must be in place to provide a mounting surface and support for lighting fixtures.
Electrical wiring, conduits, and junction boxes must be installed before lighting fixtures can be connected and mounted.
Waterproofing membrane and sealing must be completed to prevent water damage and electrical hazards before installing lighting.
Lighting fixtures are often integrated with or mounted near railings; installing lighting first allows proper alignment and access.
After lighting fixtures are mounted, final connections to power source and electrical testing must be performed to verify functionality.
The foundation must be completed to provide a stable structural base for the balcony anchorage system to be installed.
The main building structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be erected to provide the structural elements to which the balcony structure will be anchored.
The balcony anchorage system must be in place before the balcony deck panels or slabs can be installed and secured to the structure.
The balcony structure must be fully anchored and in its final position before waterproofing membranes can be applied to protect the structure from moisture intrusion.
The balcony structure must be securely anchored before safety railings or balustrades can be mounted on the balcony edge.

The balcony structural slab must be fully cured and sound before any waterproofing membrane can be applied, as the membrane requires a stable, crack-free substrate to adhere properly and prevent future leaks.
Parapet walls and upstands must be built first so that the waterproofing membrane can be turned up the walls to the required height, ensuring a continuous watertight seal at all vertical transitions.

Drain outlets and pipework are typically set into or connected through the waterproofing layer; however, the waterproofing must be installed first to ensure drains are properly flashed and sealed into the membrane system.

A protective screed or cementitious topping must be placed over the cured waterproofing membrane to shield it from physical damage during subsequent trades and from UV degradation if the balcony is exposed.

Tiles and finished floor coverings are laid on top of the protected waterproofing layer; the waterproofing must be complete and tested before any finish is applied to avoid trapping moisture and to allow for leak testing prior to covering.
Guardrails are mounted onto or alongside the bridge deck; the deck must be in place to provide the structural surface and anchorage for guardrail posts and connections.
If guardrails are anchored into concrete curbs or decks, the concrete must be fully cured to achieve design strength before drilling anchors or setting posts.

Paving can proceed after guardrails are installed to achieve a clean finished edge, but is a soft preference as paving can sometimes be done before guardrail installation if careful alignment is used.
Guardrail systems often form part of a continuous roadside safety system; other barrier types connect to or terminate at guardrail sections, requiring the guardrail to be in place first.
Guardrail installation must be complete before final safety inspections and punch-list walkthroughs can verify roadside protection compliance.
The earthing electrode must be installed in the ground, so the site must be cleared and excavated to the required depth before installation.
Foundation trenches and excavations are typically completed first to allow access for earthing electrode placement at the base of the foundation or nearby.
The earthing electrode must be installed first so that the earthing conductor can be physically connected to it.
If the earthing electrode is embedded in the foundation, it must be placed and secured before concrete is poured to encase it properly.
The earthing electrode must be installed and connected before the excavation can be backfilled.
The earth continuity conductor must be installed after the foundation is in place because it connects to the building's grounding system embedded in the foundation.
The main earthing terminal must be installed before the earth continuity conductor can be connected to it.
Electrical equipment must be bonded to the earth continuity conductor, which must first be in place to provide the grounding path.

successor: Testing and Commissioning of Grounding System
rationale: The continuity and resistance testing of the grounding system can only be performed after the earth continuity conductor is fully installed and connected.
Final inspection of the electrical grounding system requires the earth continuity conductor to be installed and properly connected.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to the required depth before any earth pit or inspection pit can be constructed.
The pit must be completed and inspected before backfilling around it can commence to avoid damaging the structure.
Earth/inspection pits serve as access points for cables and conduits; cables/conduits must be laid through or into the pit after it is constructed.
A stable concrete base or foundation is typically required to support the earth pit or inspection pit structure.
Surveying and marking the exact location of the pit ensures proper positioning but may sometimes be done concurrently.

The earth termination bar must be installed in a prepared location, typically within an equipment room or building foundation area. Excavation and foundation work must be completed first to provide a stable, accessible installation surface and to allow for proper grounding electrode connections.

Grounding electrodes (such as ground rods, ground plates, or ufer grounds) must be installed and connected to the building foundation before the earth termination bar can be terminated. The bar serves as a central point to bond all grounding electrodes together.

Any underground conduits or cables that will connect to the earth termination bar must be routed and laid in place before the bar is installed, to ensure proper connection paths are available without rework.

successor: Installation of Main Bonding Jumper and System Bonding
rationale: The earth termination bar provides the central grounding reference point. The main bonding jumper and system bonding conductors must be connected after the bar is in place to establish the grounding electrode system connection to the service equipment.

Equipment grounding conductors for downstream electrical panels, equipment, and metallic enclosures are terminated at the earth termination bar. This connection can only occur once the bar itself is securely installed and bonded to the grounding electrodes.
The earth electrode is installed within the foundation excavation, so excavation must be completed first to provide access and space for electrode placement.
A blinding layer of lean concrete is typically required at the base of the excavation to provide a clean, level working surface before installing the earth electrode.
The earth electrode must be placed and connected before reinforcement is fixed, as the electrode is often tied to or laid beneath the rebar cage and would be inaccessible afterward.
The earth electrode must be fully installed and connected before concrete is poured, as it is embedded within the foundation concrete and cannot be placed after.
Backfilling can only proceed after the electrode is installed, since the electrode is located within the foundation zone and backfilling would cover and prevent access to it.
The roof structure must be completed to provide a mounting surface and support for the lightning protection system components, including the air terminals and conductor pathways.
Foundation work is required to install the grounding electrodes and Earth termination system that the down conductor connects to, ensuring proper grounding path.
Structural steel provides the building frame that supports the routing of down conductors; conductors are typically fastened to or run alongside structural members.
While not a hard physical constraint, it is a best practice to coordinate down conductor routing with electrical system installation to avoid interference and ensure proper bonding.
Down conductors must be installed before exterior cladding (e.g., siding, brick, curtain wall) is applied, as the conductors are often concealed behind or integrated into the building envelope.
The earth electrodes must be installed and connected to provide a path to ground before the Main Earth Busbar can serve as a central bonding point.
The Main Earth Busbar is typically mounted on a wall or structure within the building; the foundation and slab must be complete to provide a stable mounting surface.
The Main Earth Busbar must be in place before the main earthing conductor (from the transformer/generator) can be terminated to it.
All equipment grounding conductors and bonding jumpers must be connected to the Main Earth Busbar after it is installed, as it is the central grounding reference point.
Electrical panels require a bonding connection to the Main Earth Busbar for system grounding, which can only be performed after the busbar is in place.

The bonding conductor connects to the electrical service entrance equipment (such as the main panel or meter) to create a low-impedance path to ground, so the service entrance must be installed first.

The bonding conductor must be connected to the grounding electrode system (e.g., ground rods, concrete-encased electrode) to provide an effective ground path; the electrode system must be in place first.

successor: Bonding of Metal Building Components (e.g., metal water pipes, structural steel)
rationale: The bonding conductor serves as the backbone or main bonding jumper that ties together all metallic components; other building components are bonded after the main bonding conductor is installed.
Continuity and resistance testing of the bonding conductor path must occur after installation to verify proper bonding before the system is energized.
While not a physical requirement, it is standard practice to complete rough-in wiring before installing bonding conductors to avoid interference and ensure neat, code-compliant installation.
The earth pit must be excavated to provide a physical space for installing the earth electrode before it can be placed.
After the earth electrode is installed in the pit, the excavated earth must be backfilled to cover and secure the electrode.

successor: Earth Electrode Connection to Main Earthing Busbar
rationale: The earth electrode must be physically in place before it can be electrically connected to the main earthing busbar.
The earth electrode must be installed and in the ground before its resistance can be measured to verify compliance with design specifications.
Foundation work must be completed to allow trenching and pit excavation adjacent to the building footprint before installing the earth electrode.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil, and rough grading completed to expose native soil for accurate resistivity measurements.
Existing underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid damage during test probe insertion and to select test locations clear of buried services.
Soil resistivity measurements directly determine the design parameters for the grounding electrode system, including rod depth, spacing, and conductor sizing.

Resistivity test results inform the location and depth requirements for grounding electrodes before foundation construction begins, and testing must be completed before excavation disturbs the soil strata.
Utility companies may need resistivity data to finalize service connection points and transformer grounding designs, though this is a coordination preference rather than a physical necessity.
Earth electrodes must be installed and connected to the grounding system before continuity can be verified across the entire earthing network.
The main earthing conductors and bonding conductors must be run and connected to all metallic parts before continuity testing can be performed.
Continuity of the earthing conductors must be confirmed first before measuring the overall earth resistance value, as broken conductors would give erroneous resistance readings.
Earth continuity must be verified to be within acceptable limits before any electrical system can be safely energized and commissioned.
The ground ring sits on the foundation; excavation must be completed to create space and prepare the base for the ground ring installation.
The concrete foundation must be poured and cured to provide a stable, level base for mounting the ground ring.
The ground ring serves as the anchor base for the wind turbine tower; the tower sections can only be erected after the ground ring is securely installed.
Backfilling is performed after the ground ring and foundation are in place to cover and protect the embedded components.
The tower flange bolts connect the tower base to the ground ring; this bolting operation can only proceed once the ground ring is fixed in position.

The earthing system is typically installed within or around the building foundation. Foundation construction must be completed first to provide the physical substrate for earthing electrodes, conductors, and ground loops before commissioning can test continuity and resistance.

Earthing grid conductors, rods, and tapes must be laid in excavated trenches. The earthing system cannot be physically installed or tested until excavation and trenching for the earthing grid are complete.

Commissioning (testing, verification, and certification) of the earthing system can only occur after the complete physical installation of all earthing conductors, electrodes, bonding conductors, and grounding rods has been finished.

The main electrical switchboard must be connected to a verified and tested earthing system for safety. Commissioning verifies that earth fault loop impedance and continuity meet standards, which is a prerequisite before energizing and installing the switchboard.

Power and control cables require a properly tested earthing system for their screen/armour earthing and safety bonding. Commissioning must confirm earth integrity before cables are laid and terminated to avoid rework and ensure safety.

While not a strict physical dependency, it is good practice to complete earthing system commissioning before broader building services commissioning (HVAC, lighting, fire alarms) to ensure all systems have a verified earth reference point, avoiding potential troubleshooting conflicts later.
The earthing system must be commissioned and verified to meet regulatory standards before the final inspection and handover of the building can take place, as it is a critical safety system.
The slope must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and graded to the proper profile before any terracing structures can be constructed.
Soil and slope stability analysis must be completed first to determine the appropriate design and anchoring requirements for the terraced structure.
Subsurface drainage (e.g., French drains, perforated pipes) must be placed behind or beneath the terrace to prevent hydrostatic pressure buildup that could destabilize the structure.
Backfill material behind the retaining wall or terrace face can only be placed and compacted after the structure is erected to provide lateral support.
Surface drainage channels, soil capping, and vegetative cover on the terrace should be installed after the structural elements are complete to prevent erosion and manage runoff.
The stepped seating risers must be built on a stable, level subfloor or concrete base slab to ensure structural integrity and proper alignment.
In multi-story venues, the supporting structural frame must be in place before the risers can be installed, as the risers bear on the frame.
Any electrical conduits, plumbing lines, or data cabling that run under or within the stepped riser structure must be roughed in before the riser formwork and concrete/steel are placed.
Individual seats or chair units are physically mounted onto the finished riser steps; the riser structure must be complete to provide the mounting surface.
The top surface of each riser step receives its final finish (e.g., carpet, terrazzo, non-slip coating) after the structural riser is built and cured.
The ground must be excavated and leveled to the required foundation depth before any tiered tread structure can be installed.
A stable sub-base or concrete foundation must be in place to support the weight and load distribution of tiered treads.
Proper drainage must be installed before tiered treads to prevent water accumulation and erosion beneath the treads.
Handrails and guardrails are safety features that are installed after the treads are in place to ensure proper alignment and attachment to the tread structure.
While sealing can be done immediately after installation, it is a finishing task that logically follows tread placement to protect the surface.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the appropriate foundation depth before any retaining wall construction can begin, as the wall requires a stable, prepared base.
A proper concrete footing or foundation (grade beam) must be poured and cured before the retaining wall blocks or masonry are placed on top, ensuring structural stability and load distribution.
Sub-surface drainage pipes and gravel backfill behind the wall must be installed at foundation level before wall construction proceeds, to manage hydrostatic pressure behind the structure.

The space behind the completed retaining wall can only be backfilled with soil/granular material and compacted after the wall is built and sufficiently cured, to avoid displacing or damaging an unfinished structure.

While landscaping can proceed after the wall is complete, there is a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint — topsoil and planting could theoretically be done beforehand near the wall zone, but it is best practice to finish the wall first to avoid soil disturbance and damage to plants.
The bench seating requires a stable, level foundation or base slab to be cast and cured before the seating structure can be installed or built upon it.
Proper grading and drainage of the terrace area must be completed to ensure water flows away from the bench seating area, preventing积水 and structural damage.
Bench seating is often integrated with or built into the terrace flooring, so the seating structure must be in place before surrounding decking or flooring is laid around it for a seamless finish.
Final landscaping and planting near the bench area is typically done after seating is installed to avoid damage to plants and to allow precise placement of greenery around the fixed benches.
If the bench seating is on an elevated terrace, handrails or barriers may need to be installed after the bench to ensure proper alignment and spacing relative to the seating area.

Handrails and guardrails are typically attached to the structural frame (e.g., concrete slabs, steel beams, stair stringers). The supporting structure must be in place before railings can be installed.
Handrails are mounted on or alongside stairs and ramps; those stairs/ramps must be built first to provide the mounting surface and define the railing alignment.
If the handrail system incorporates lighting or electrical components, rough-in wiring should be completed before installing the railings to avoid rework.
Guardrails and handrails are often anchored into walls or columns; wall finishes (drywall, plaster) must be installed after railing brackets are secured to avoid damaging finished surfaces.
While railings may come pre-finished, touch-up painting or final coating is typically done after installation to cover scratches and anchor points, making this a logical follow-up activity.
Vegetation, debris, and existing structures must be removed to provide unobstructed access for excavation equipment and to define the working area before earthmoving can begin.
Fertile topsoil must be stripped and stockpiled prior to bulk earthworks to preserve it from mixing with subsoil and to expose the underlying material that needs to be excavated and graded.

predecessor: Survey and Staking of Slope Geometry
rationale: The horizontal and vertical alignment of terrace benches, cut/fill limits, and drainage gradients must be surveyed and staked in the field to guide excavation equipment accurately.

After the terraced slopes have been rough-graded to design elevations, the fill and cut surfaces must be compacted and tested to verify they meet specified density and stability requirements before further work proceeds.
Surface drainage channels, interceptor ditches, and berms are installed after slope grading is complete to direct runoff away from the terraced faces and prevent erosion of the finished slopes.
The foundation must be completed and cured to provide a stable structural base before any tier-level formwork and concrete can be placed.
Steel reinforcement bars must be installed and tied in place before formwork is closed and concrete is poured, as the rebar is embedded within the concrete structural element.
Concrete must be placed and allowed to gain sufficient strength before the formwork can be safely stripped without damaging the structural element.
Immediately after concrete placement, the curing process must begin to maintain moisture and temperature conditions for proper hydration and strength development.

successor: Vertical Structural Elements (Columns/Walls on Next Tier)
rationale: The current tier's slab and beams must be completed and load-bearing before constructing vertical elements of the next level above them.
Excavation and levelling must be completed first to create the terrace area that will receive the backfill soil.
Drainage systems (e.g., gravel layer, perforated pipes) must be placed before backfilling to ensure proper water management within the terrace.
Any underground utilities (irrigation, drainage pipes, electrical conduits) running through the terrace must be laid before soil can be placed and compacted over them.
Backfill and compaction form the stable sub-base; the final topsoil layer and grading for landscape finishing can only be applied after the base is compacted.
Any paving stones, concrete slabs, or other hardscape elements on the terrace must be installed after the underlying fill soil is placed and properly compacted to provide a stable foundation.
Electrical wiring and junction boxes must be installed in the ceiling/soffit before terrace light fixtures can be connected and mounted.
The structural support (ceiling or soffit) must be framed in place to provide a mounting surface for the built-in lighting fixtures.
If lights are recessed or surface-mounted through the ceiling finish, the fixture mounting and wiring must be completed before drywall or cladding is installed around them.
Final connection of switches, dimmers, and trim (light covers/bezels) must occur after the light fixtures are physically installed and the ceiling finish is ready.
Painting or staining is best performed after lighting installation to avoid damaging finished surfaces, but it is a soft preference as fixtures can be protected with masking.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded before installing root barriers to ensure a stable and properly aligned installation.
A trench must be dug along the planned path of the root barrier before the barrier material can be placed into the ground.
After the root barrier is installed in the trench, the trench must be backfilled with soil and compacted to secure the barrier in place and restore the ground surface.
The root barrier must be installed prior to planting the fruit tree to ensure the tree's roots are contained and directed away from sensitive structures from the start.
All underground utilities must be located and marked before any trench excavation begins to avoid damaging existing services and ensure safety.
Fruit trees must be planted in the ground before protective cages can be installed around them, as the cage is placed to enclose the tree after it is in its final position.
Soil preparation at the planting site must be completed before caging is installed, as the cage location is determined by the tree's planting hole, and soil work would be obstructed by the cage.
Although mulch could technically be placed before caging, it is more practical to install the cage first and then spread mulch inside and around the cage base to avoid disturbing the cage placement.
Drip lines can be placed before or after caging, but running irrigation lines after caging may be easier to route around the cage supports without interference.
Initial pruning and training of young branches should be done after caging to ensure the tree growth is directed within the cage structure and to protect pruned branches from pests.
The tree pit must be excavated before the grate can be installed, as the grate sits over the excavated pit.
The tree must be planted in the pit before the grate is placed around the tree trunk to protect the root zone.
The grate must be in place before surrounding paving or surfacing is installed, as the grate defines the edge of the pit and adjacent paving is laid flush against it.
It is preferable to complete final soil top-up and fine grading after grate installation to ensure proper fit, but it could be done beforehand if necessary.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before the soakaway drain can be installed. The drain needs a prepared trench and stable subgrade.
All existing underground services must be identified and marked before any excavation for the soakaway drain to avoid damaging utilities.
The soakaway drain system must be fully installed and operational before fruit trees are planted, so that the trees immediately have proper drainage in the root zone.
Final grading and topsoil placement around the soakaway should occur after the drain is installed to ensure proper soil coverage and surface water flow to the drain.
The soakaway drain must be in place before irrigation lines are installed near the fruit trees to prevent damage to the drain and ensure drainage is considered in the irrigation layout.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before any tree pit structure can be installed.
Proper drainage must be in place before placing the tree pit structure to prevent waterlogging.
The tree pit container/structure must be completed before a tree can be planted inside it.
The tree pit must be fully constructed before surrounding paving and hardscape finishes can be laid up to the pit edge.
Irrigation lines connected to the tree pit should ideally be installed after the pit is in place, though this depends on system design.
The ground must be graded and excavated to the proper elevation before a tree grate can be installed, as the grate sits flush with the finished grade.
The tree must be planted and its root ball placed in the ground before the tree grate can be positioned around the tree trunk.

predecessor: Concrete or Paver Sidewalk / Plaza Installation
rationale: The surrounding hardscape (concrete sidewalks, pavers, or plaza surfaces) must be in place so the tree grate can be set flush with or within the finished paving surface.

All underground utilities and conduits serving the tree pit (e.g., irrigation lines, drainage pipes, tree lighting) must be installed and backfilled before the tree grate is placed to avoid excavation after installation.
Once the tree grate is in place, final surface treatments such as decorative mulch, soil amendments, or topdressing within or around the grate can be completed to finish the tree pit area.
Excavation must be completed to create the trench or space along foundations where the root barrier will be installed.
Root barriers are typically installed against foundation walls, so the walls must be in place first for the barrier to be attached or placed adjacent.
Backfilling around foundations should only occur after the root barrier is installed to protect the barrier and ensure it functions correctly.

Root barrier installation must precede waterproofing if the barrier is placed on the exterior side of the foundation, or follow waterproofing if the barrier is a separate layer; typically root barrier goes over waterproofing so waterproofing must be done first.
Landscaping and planting near foundations must occur after the root barrier is in place to prevent roots from damaging the foundation.
The tree must be physically installed and in place before integrated lighting can be applied or connected to it.
Electrical wiring and outlets need to be roughed in near the tree location before integrated lighting can be connected to a power source.
Trenching for underground lighting cables must be completed before running power to the integrated tree lighting.
The integrated lighting system must be fully installed before testing and commissioning can verify its functionality.
It is preferable to finish surrounding landscape elements like mulch or ground cover after tree lighting installation to avoid disturbing them, but it is not a strict physical necessity.
The tree pit must be excavated, prepared, and the tree planted before permanent seating can be installed around it, as the bench integrates with or wraps around the tree pit.
A concrete footing or base must be poured and cured to provide a stable structural foundation for the bench before the bench components can be assembled or installed.
Final paving, decorative aggregates, or ground surfacing adjacent to the bench should be completed after bench installation to ensure a tight fit and clean finish around the base.

Soft landscaping such as shrubs or groundcover around the bench area can be installed after the bench is in place without damaging the structure, though it could also be done concurrently or slightly before with care.

Any underground pipes, conduits, or drainage lines serving the tree pit or nearby area must be installed before the bench is placed to avoid the need for later excavation and disturbance of the seating structure.
The tree must already be installed/planted in its final location before a temporary guying system can be set up to support it.
The temporary guying system must be in place to stabilize the tree during the initial rooting period while it establishes its root system.
The temporary guying system must be installed first before it can be removed later once the tree is sufficiently established.
The soil must be graded and prepared properly to ensure the sensor is placed in stable, undisturbed soil that accurately represents field conditions.
All buried utilities must be identified before digging or inserting sensors to avoid damage to existing infrastructure and ensure worker safety.
After the sensor is placed at the correct depth, the excavation or insertion hole must be backfilled and compacted to restore soil structure and ensure good soil-sensor contact.
The sensor must be physically installed in the soil before it can be calibrated, powered on, and tested for accurate readings in its final position.

While sensors are commonly used to control irrigation, the irrigation system could technically be activated beforehand; however, optimal water management depends on sensor feedback, making sequencing preferable.
Rough grading and drainage systems must be installed before tree pits to ensure proper water management and prevent soil erosion or water accumulation in the planting area.
Concrete flatwork such as sidewalks and plazas must be poured before tree pit installation, as tree pits are often framed within or adjacent to these hardscape elements.
While trees can be planted before final paving, it is preferable to complete tree pit installation first to avoid damaging new paving during excavation and planting.
Tree planting must be completed before final grading and landscape finishing to integrate the trees into the overall landscape design and allow for proper soil placement around the root ball.
Irrigation lines can be laid before or after planting, but it is often preferred to install irrigation after planting to route lines directly to each tree without interfering with the root zone.
Excavation must be completed to reach the required subgrade level before the root barrier and drainage system can be installed on the prepared surface.
The subgrade must be properly prepared and compacted to provide a stable, uniform base for the root barrier and drainage layer.
The root barrier and drainage system must be in place before aggregate base course is placed over it to protect the barrier and allow proper drainage function.
Root barrier and drainage must be installed before any concrete slab or base is poured, as it lies beneath the structural slab.
The root barrier and drainage system must be fully installed before final surface finishes like pavers are placed on top.
The irrigation and monitoring system must be fully installed and physically in place before it can be commissioned, tested, and verified for operation.

predecessor: Connect Electrical Supply to Irrigation System
rationale: Electrical power must be supplied to the irrigation system components before commissioning can proceed to test control panels, pumps, and sensors.

predecessor: Connect Water Supply to Irrigation System
rationale: A water source connection is required before commissioning can test water flow, pressure, and distribution functionality.
The monitoring and control software must be installed and configured on the control system before integrated commissioning and testing of the complete system.
The system must be successfully commissioned and verified as operational before actual irrigation operations can commence.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared to ensure proper drainage and a stable base before any planting beds can be established.
All underground utilities and trenching must be completed before planting beds are installed to avoid disturbing newly planted areas and to prevent damage to buried lines.
Subsurface drainage systems and rough grading must be in place to prevent water pooling and soil erosion in planting bed areas.

While fine grading and topsoil can be done before planting, if planting beds are wild-maintained they may be planted directly into prepared soil, making fine grading a soft preference rather than a hard requirement.
Wild-maintained planting beds may require irrigation lines to be laid after planting to accommodate the specific layout of plants and avoid damaging root systems during trenching.

successor: Mulching and Erosion Control Blanket Installation
rationale: Mulching and erosion control measures must follow planting to protect the soil surface and newly planted vegetation from runoff and weed competition.

Protective fencing or signage around wild-maintained areas is typically installed after planting to define boundaries, but this is a soft preference as fencing could be installed beforehand in some cases.
A site survey must be completed to identify existing hedge rows, assess their condition, and determine which areas will retain untrimmed hedge rows before any landscaping or planting work begins.
The ground must be prepared, cleared of debris, and soil conditions improved to support the establishment of new hedge rows or to protect existing ones during construction.
Drainage systems must be installed first to prevent waterlogging and ensure proper soil moisture conditions for hedge row establishment and growth.
Hedge rows should be established or preserved before boundary fencing is installed to ensure fence posts do not damage root systems and to integrate the hedge row into the boundary design.

successor: Landscaping and Planting of Other Vegetation
rationale: Other planting and landscaping around hedge rows should ideally occur after hedge rows are established to ensure proper spacing and to avoid disturbing the hedge roots, though this is a preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The overall site grading must be established to define the topographic contours and drainage patterns before excavating and forming the pond or wetland depression.
Any underground utilities that would cross the pond area must be installed and backfilled prior to excavation to avoid disturbing the completed pond liner or wetland soils.
Topsoil must be stripped from the pond footprint area before excavation to preserve this resource and expose the subgrade for proper pond shaping and compaction.

successor: Planting of Aquatic and Marginal Vegetation
rationale: The pond basin and wetland soil zones must be fully formed, lined if needed, and filled with water or saturated before installing aquatic plants and marginal vegetation that require the aquatic environment.
The pond/wetland area must be completed before surrounding finish grading and topsoiling can be brought up to the final edge contours of the water feature.
The trellis or pergola structure must be anchored to a stable foundation or base (e.g., concrete footings, posts set in the ground) to ensure structural stability and load-bearing capacity.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before erecting the trellis/pergola to ensure proper drainage and a level installation surface.

The trellis/pergola structure must be fully erected and stable before climbing plants (vines, ivy, etc.) are planted or trained onto it, as the structure provides the necessary support for the overgrown effect.

successor: Weatherproofing / Sealing of Wood or Metal
rationale: Applying sealant, stain, or weatherproof coating is often easier before plants obscure the structure, but it can also be done after; however, doing it before is strongly preferred to avoid damaging plants.

successor: Lighting Installation (e.g., string lights, integrated LEDs)
rationale: Attaching lights to the pergola/trellis is easier and safer to accomplish before dense foliage grows, but lighting can also be added later as a retrofit.
The ground must be graded and leveled to provide a stable, properly sloped subgrade before placing the stone or gravel path surface.

predecessor: Base Layer Installation (Crushed Stone or Aggregate Base)
rationale: A compacted aggregate base layer is required beneath the surfacing stone or gravel to provide drainage and load distribution, preventing the path from sinking or becoming muddy.
Edging or border restraints (metal, plastic, or stone), if used, should typically be installed before placing the surface stone/gravel to contain the material and maintain the path shape.

Surrounding landscaping, including turf, plants, and mulch, should be installed after the path is completed to avoid soiling or damaging the new path surface and to achieve a clean edge between the path and planted areas.

successor: Installation of Pathway Lighting or Utilities
rationale: While underground conduit for lighting can be installed earlier, above-ground lighting fixtures and final connections are typically placed after the path surface is finished to avoid disturbing the gravel or stone during trenching.
Raw timber must be harvested and milled into usable lumber before any bench construction can begin, as the wooden components are the primary material.
Green lumber must be properly seasoned and dried to prevent warping, cracking, or structural failure before being cut and assembled into the bench.
Wood must be treated with preservatives, sealants, or weatherproofing agents before assembly to protect the finished bench from moisture, rot, and insect damage.
The bench must first be fully assembled (frame, slats, legs joined) before final sanding and surface finishing can be applied to ensure smooth edges and even coating.

Sanding and applying protective finishes (varnish, stain, or paint) must be completed before the bench is placed in its outdoor location to avoid damaging the finish during transport or soiling the work area.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before the cistern can be installed or constructed in place.
A stable concrete base or pad must be poured and cured to support the weight of the filled cistern before installation.
The cistern must be in place before downspouts and gutters can be connected to route rainwater into it.
Overflow and drain lines must be installed after the cistern is positioned to ensure proper alignment and connection.
Pumps and filters that draw from or treat cistern water must be installed after the cistern is in place for correct plumbing connections.
The ground must be excavated and leveled to provide a stable, compacted base for the retaining wall foundation.
A trench must be dug below frost line to accommodate the base course of large stones, ensuring wall stability against frost heave and lateral pressure.
The bottom row of the largest stones must be placed in the trench to form the foundation before subsequent courses can be stacked.
After the wall is built to full height, the space behind it must be backfilled with gravel and compacted soil to provide drainage and lateral support.
The final top row of flat capstones is placed after all lower courses are complete to finish the wall and provide a clean appearance.
The ground must be properly graded, cleared of debris, and prepared before any planting beds can be installed to ensure proper drainage and a stable base.
Any required subsurface drainage (e.g., French drains or perforated pipe systems) must be in place before planting beds are established to prevent waterlogging and root rot.
The subgrade elevation and slope must be established to match the finished planting bed design before soil and plants are placed.
While wild-maintained beds typically require minimal irrigation, any drip or supplemental irrigation should be installed after planting to avoid damaging lines during planting work.
Mulch should be applied after planting to retain moisture, suppress weeds, and protect the root zone of newly installed plants.
Rough grading establishes the overall site topography and drainage patterns, which must be in place before excavating and shaping a naturalistic water feature.
Subsurface drainage must be in place to manage groundwater and surface runoff before installing a water feature that will hold and circulate water.
Water supply lines and electrical conduits for pumps, filtration, and lighting must be run underground before the water feature excavation and liner installation.

The water feature structure (pond, stream, waterfall) must be fully constructed and water-tested before surrounding planting and soft landscaping are installed to avoid damage to plants and disruption of soils.

successor: Install Hardscape Finishes and Decorative Elements
rationale: Hardscape finishes such as stone coping, decking, or pathways around the water feature must be installed after the water feature structure is complete to ensure proper alignment and integration.
A stable, graded, and compacted subgrade is physically required to support the stone path and prevent settling or shifting.

predecessor: Install Base Layer (e.g., crushed stone or sand)
rationale: A base layer of crushed stone or sand provides drainage and a level bedding surface for the stones to sit on.

successor: Fill Joints/Gaps (with sand, gravel, or ground cover)
rationale: Joint filling material must be applied after stones are placed to lock them in position and stabilize the surface.
Compaction or tamping of the stones must occur after they are laid to ensure they are firmly seated in the base.
Edging or border installation is typically done after the path is laid to neatly define the edge, though it can sometimes be installed beforehand as a guide.

The ground must be cleared, leveled, and any concrete footings or anchor points must be set and cured before the trellis structure can be erected, as the trellis needs a stable, prepared base to be secured to.
All wooden posts, beams, crosspieces, and fastening hardware must be acquired, cut to length, and pre-assembled or treated prior to erection, otherwise there would be no components to build with.

While plants can be placed nearby, the trellis structure must be fully erected to provide the support framework for vines to climb; however, planting could theoretically be done concurrently or slightly before with temporary supports, making this a soft ordering preference.

The assembled trellis must be fully erected and in place before applying wood stain, sealant, or protective coating, as coating after erection ensures full coverage and avoids damage to the finish during assembly.
Final landscaping and inspection tasks logically follow the erection of the trellis structure, but this is more of a project workflow preference than a physical necessity.
Site grading and excavation must be completed to prepare the ground and trenches for rainwater harvesting system components such as cisterns, piping, and infiltration areas.
Foundation and slab work must be finished to provide a stable base for rainwater harvesting tanks and to allow for underground piping connections before tank placement.
Rough-in plumbing for the building's water system must be in place to allow proper connection of the rainwater harvesting system to the building's supply lines.

successor: Connect Rainwater Harvesting to Building Plumbing
rationale: The rainwater harvesting system must be physically installed before final connections can be made between the system and the building's internal plumbing infrastructure.
Gutters and downspouts must connect to the installed rainwater harvesting system's inlet, so the system must be in place before finalizing gutter and downspout connections.
A stable foundation trench must be excavated and leveled to provide a solid base for the stone wall, preventing settling or collapse.
Stones must be collected, sorted by size and shape, and delivered to the site before construction can begin.
A gravel drainage layer beneath the wall prevents water accumulation and frost heave, which would destabilize the dry-laid structure.
The wall structure must be fully erected before backfilling can safely occur, as backfill provides lateral support and would displace unfinished stones.
Coping stones are placed on top of the completed wall to provide a finished appearance and protect the wall from weather damage.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the proper depth before any foundation can be laid, as the foundation requires a prepared subgrade to bear on.
The exact wall alignment, corners, and foundation footprint must be marked on the ground before excavation and forming can begin to ensure the foundation is placed in the correct position.
Underground utilities (gas, water, electric, irrigation) in the foundation area must be located, marked, and either rerouted or protected before excavation to prevent damage and ensure safety.
After the foundation concrete is poured, it must be allowed to cure to sufficient strength before forms can be stripped and subsequent wall construction can proceed.
The wall structure (brick, block, or stone) must be built on top of the cured foundation; the foundation provides the load-bearing base and cannot be bypassed.

Applying waterproofing coating and installing drainage pipe or gravel along the foundation base is best done immediately after curing and before backfilling, but some drainage work could theoretically be retrofitted if necessary.
Soil cannot be placed back against the foundation until the concrete has cured and any waterproofing has been applied; fills rely on the finished foundation in place.
The wall structure must be fully built and stable before coping stones or capping can be installed on top of the wall.
Mortar used in the wall construction needs sufficient time to cure and gain strength before the weight of coping stones is applied, preventing displacement or collapse.
While pointing can be done before coping, it is often easier to complete final finishing and pointing of the coping joints after coping installation for a neat appearance.

successor: Garden Wall Damp Proof Course (DPC) Inspection
rationale: Coping acts as the top cover protecting the wall from water ingress; the DPC and coping integrity must be verified after coping installation to ensure weatherproofing.
Final landscaping and soil grading adjacent to the wall should be done after coping is installed to avoid damaging the top of the wall and to ensure proper drainage away from the wall.
Excavation must be completed to provide a stable base for the pier/pilaster footing.
The concrete footing must be poured and cured to support the masonry pier/pilaster above.
The pier/pilaster provides structural support and anchorage for the adjacent wall panels or infill sections.

successor: Coping / Capping Installation on Garden Wall
rationale: The pier/pilaster must be fully built to its finished height before the coping or capping can be installed on top.
Backfilling is typically done after the pier/pilaster and wall structure are complete and cured, but may be a soft constraint if partial backfill is possible.

The garden wall's foundation and concrete base must be completed and cured before the damp-proof course (DPC) can be installed, as DPC is typically laid on top of the finished foundation/base to prevent rising damp from below.

predecessor: Garden Wall Brickwork (First Few Courses Below DPC Level)
rationale: The first few courses of brickwork or blockwork up to the DPC level must be built so that the DPC material can be laid directly on top of this masonry layer, creating a continuous barrier against moisture rising from the ground.

successor: Garden Wall Brickwork (First Few Courses Below DPC Level)
rationale: The DPC must be installed first to form a waterproof barrier; the brickwork above the DPC level can only be built after the DPC is in place to ensure the barrier is continuous and unbroken, preventing moisture bridging.

successor: Coping / Capping Installation on Garden Wall
rationale: The DPC must be complete before the wall coping or capping is installed above it, as the entire wall structure from DPC level upward must be built to maintain the correct alignment and waterproofing sequence.

Backfilling against the garden wall should only occur after the DPC is fully installed and the wall is constructed to its full height, to prevent damage to the DPC and ensure the waterproof barrier remains effective against ground moisture.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to provide a stable foundation for the garden wall expansion before any wall construction or movement joint installation can begin.
The concrete foundation for the garden wall must be poured and fully cured to sufficient strength before the wall blocks/stones and movement joint can be installed on top.

The movement joint must be incorporated into the wall structure during construction; any external cladding or veneer applied to the wall surface must be installed after the movement joint is in place to ensure proper alignment and function.

Backfilling against the completed wall and final grading of adjacent ground must occur after the wall structure including movement joints is fully constructed to avoid damaging the wall or compromising the joint.

The final inspection of the garden wall assembly should be performed after all wall components, including the movement joint, are installed to verify compliance with specifications and proper joint function.
The wall base or foundation must be constructed first to provide the structural substrate into which weepholes and drainage paths are integrated.

successor: Wall Cladding / Finishing (e.g., stone, brick, render)
rationale: Weepholes and drainage provisions must be installed before the final wall cladding or finish is applied, as they are concealed within or at the base of the finished wall surface.
Weepholes must be in place before backfilling so that proper drainage paths exist to relieve hydrostatic pressure behind the wall.
The permeable aggregate or gravel backfill that feeds water to the weepholes must be placed prior to or concurrently with weephole installation to ensure continuous drainage paths.
Final pointing or finishing of the weephole openings must be done after the weephole pipes or channels are properly positioned, to ensure clean, unobstructed drainage outlets.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before excavation can begin to ensure unobstructed access and a safe working area.
All underground utilities must be located and marked before excavation to prevent damage to services and ensure worker safety.
The exact location and boundaries of the garden wall must be surveyed and staked out before excavation can proceed to ensure accurate positioning.
Excavation must be completed to the required depth and dimensions before the foundation base can be prepared and leveled for the wall construction.
The excavated trench or footing area must be ready before concrete or foundation material can be poured for the garden wall base.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before concrete can be poured into the foundation trench.
Formwork (shuttering) must be in place to shape and contain the wet concrete during pouring.
Steel reinforcement bars must be positioned within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity.
Freshly poured concrete must undergo a curing period to achieve sufficient strength before any subsequent loads are applied.
Formwork cannot be removed until the concrete has set and gained enough strength to support itself.
The foundation concrete must be fully cured and set before masonry or block walls can be built upon it.
Strip footings provide the load-bearing base for masonry walls; block laying cannot begin without a cured concrete foundation in place.
The ground slab or base provides a level, stable surface upon which the garden wall blocks are laid.
Subsoil drainage must be installed before wall construction to prevent water accumulation that could undermine the wall foundation.

successor: Garden Wall Waterproofing / Damp Proof Course
rationale: Damp proofing is applied to the completed masonry surface to prevent moisture ingress; masonry must be in place first.
Mortar joints are finished (pointed) after the blocks are laid and the mortar has initially set, to ensure weathertight joints and uniform appearance.

The coping is the cap or top piece of a garden wall. The wall structure including its foundation must be fully built and stable before the coping can be installed on top, as the coping sits on top of the wall and has no structural support without the underlying wall.
The main wall body (masonry, brickwork, or blockwork) must be completed to its full height before coping stones or units can be installed on top. Coping serves as the finishing top course.

While waterproofing the coping joints is typically done immediately after installation, it is a best practice (soft preference) rather than a physical necessity; however, applying sealant promptly after coping installation prevents water ingress during ongoing construction.

If the garden wall is a retaining wall, backfilling against the wall should only occur after the coping is installed to ensure the wall's top is finished and protected from soil and debris entering the wall core.

Final landscaping, grading, and planting around the base of the wall are typically done after coping installation to avoid damaging the newly installed coping with soil, equipment, or plant material, but this is a logical sequencing preference rather than a hard physical constraint.

The wall substrate (blockwork or brickwork) must be fully constructed and cured to provide a stable base for the render or finish application. Render cannot be applied to an incomplete or uncured wall.
Foundations must be complete and cured to support the wall structure before any finishing work such as rendering can be applied to the wall.

predecessor: Garden Wall Damp Proof Course (DPC) Installation
rationale: The damp proof course must be installed within the wall structure before rendering, as the render finish would otherwise cover and prevent access for DPC installation.

While it is typical practice to allow the render to cure before painting, it is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity as some paints can be applied to partially cured render with appropriate products.

successor: Coping / Capping Installation on Garden Wall
rationale: Wall coping or capping is typically installed after rendering to protect the top of the rendered wall and provide a clean finish, though in some sequences coping may be installed before render for weather protection.

The bricks or blocks must be laid and the mortar in the joints must be partially set (but not fully cured) before joint pointing and tooling can be performed. Pointing is done after the wall is built to compact and finish the mortar joints.

Fresh mortar must be prepared and used for the joint pointing/tooling process. The pointing mortar is typically a slightly different consistency or mix than the bedding mortar and must be available before pointing begins.
After joint pointing and tooling is completed, the mortar requires sufficient time to cure and dry before any further loads or weatherproofing treatments are applied.
Excess mortar smears on the brick faces must be cleaned off after pointing is finished but before the mortar hardens completely, making cleaning much more difficult.

successor: Garden Wall Damp Proof Course (DPC) Inspection
rationale: While DPC is usually installed during wall construction, a final inspection after joint pointing ensures that the pointing has not bridged the damp-proof course, which would compromise its effectiveness.
A structural foundation or footing must be prepared and cured before the garden wall can be erected to provide a stable base and prevent settling or tilting.
The ground must be graded and drainage provisions made prior to wall construction to ensure water flows away from the wall base, preventing hydrostatic pressure and erosion.
Any buried pipes, conduits, or cables in the wall's footprint must be laid before the wall is built to avoid excavation and disruption after construction.
The wall structure with the opening must be fully constructed and cured before the gate, hinges, latch, and frame can be installed into the prepared opening.

successor: Landscaping and Planting Adjacent to Wall
rationale: It is preferable to complete wall construction before final grading, mulching, and planting around the wall to avoid soil disturbance and damage to new plants.
The wall foundation/footing must be poured and cured before the garden wall (including the integrated planter/seat) can be built upon it, as the wall requires structural support.
The lower wall courses must be constructed to the appropriate height before the integrated planter/seat can be formed or installed within the wall.

successor: Coping / Capping Installation on Garden Wall
rationale: The integrated planter/seat structure must be fully built before the wall coping/capping is applied, as the coping finishes the top of the wall assembly.
The planter structure must be completed before soil and plants are added, as the planter must be watertight and structurally sound to contain the planting medium.
The wall and its integrated planter/seat must be fully constructed before final backfill and grading work is performed adjacent to the wall, to avoid disturbing or damaging the completed assembly.
The lighting niche is recessed into or mounted onto the garden wall; the wall structure must be built first to provide the supporting surface and cavity space for the niche.

predecessor: Rough Electrical Wiring to Wall Location
rationale: Electrical supply cables and junction boxes must be run to the niche location before the niche is enclosed or finished, as access to rough-in wiring behind the wall becomes difficult or impossible after niche installation.
After the niche structure is in place, waterproof membranes and sealants must be applied to protect the recessed area and electrical components from moisture ingress.
The physical niche enclosure must be complete before the lighting fixture can be mounted, wired, and secured within it.

The niche insert must be installed prior to applying final wall finishes (e.g., stone veneer, stucco, or tile) so that the finishes can be worked tightly around the niche opening for a seamless appearance.

successor: Garden Wall with Pier Cap / Ball Finial
rationale: The garden wall requires a structural foundation to bear its weight and ensure stability. Without proper footings, the wall would settle unevenly or collapse.

successor: Garden Wall with Pier Cap / Ball Finial
rationale: The ground must be leveled and prepared before the wall can be laid to ensure a stable base and proper alignment.

successor: Garden Wall with Pier Cap / Ball Finial
rationale: Installing drainage behind or under the wall is easier before construction; however, it can sometimes be retrofitted if needed.

predecessor: Garden Wall with Pier Cap / Ball Finial
rationale: Backfilling against the finished wall can only occur after the wall is fully constructed and cured, to avoid disturbing or damaging the fresh masonry.

predecessor: Garden Wall with Pier Cap / Ball Finial
successor: Landscaping and Planting Adjacent to Wall
rationale: Planting beds and decorative landscaping next to the wall are typically finished after the wall is complete to avoid damage to plants during construction.

The Trellis Framework requires a stable, level base. Foundation preparation (excavation, concrete footings/pad) must be completed first to provide structural support and prevent settling or instability.
If the Trellis Framework is integrated with or attaches to primary structural steel members, those steel columns/beams must be erected first to provide mounting points and load-bearing support.

Solar panels, cladding panels, or other modular components are typically mounted onto or supported by the Trellis Framework, so the framework must be fully erected and secured before these can be installed.

successor: Cable Tray and Electrical Conduit Routing
rationale: While some cable routing can occur in parallel, running final cable trays and conduits is more efficient after the framework is in place to avoid rework and to utilize framework attachment points; this is a strong preference but not an absolute physical requirement.

The Trellis Framework serves as the structural substrate for exterior cladding or weatherproofing layers. These finishes must be applied after the framework is complete to ensure continuity and proper sealing.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to reach undisturbed soil or load-bearing strata before support posts can be placed and anchored.
Concrete footings or pier foundations must be poured and fully cured to provide a stable, load-bearing base before trellis support posts are installed and secured.
Support posts must be erected and secured first to provide vertical support before horizontal beams or cross-members can be attached.
Temporary or permanent bracing and anchoring of posts must follow immediately after post placement to ensure stability before any load is applied.
The vertical support posts must be fully installed and secured before any lattice framework, cross-arms, or vine-support wires can be attached to the structure.
The foundation/footings must be set and cured before any structural framing (including the roof/canopy) can be erected to provide a stable load-bearing base.
Vertical support posts must be installed and secured before placing the roof/canopy structure on top of them, as the roof bears directly on these posts.
The structural roof/canopy frame must be in place before any roofing or decking materials (e.g., slats, panels, shade cloth) can be applied to it.
While not physically mandatory, it is best practice to complete the main roof/canopy structure before adding decorative trim, fascias, or soffits for a clean finished appearance.
