The roof/canopy installation should be substantially complete before final cleanup and inspection to avoid damaging finished work during remaining construction activities.
The subgrade must be prepared and compacted before any floor surface can be installed to ensure a stable base.
Drainage systems must be in place beneath the walk floor surface to prevent water accumulation and damage.
After the trellis walk floor surface is laid, curing time is required to achieve proper strength and durability before further use or loading.
Railings and safety barriers must be installed after the walk floor surface is complete to ensure safe access and secure mounting.
The final surface finishing and sealing treatments can only be applied after the trellis walk floor surface has been fully installed and cured.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded to provide a stable and properly sloped foundation before any trellis base or substrate can be installed.

Any underground electrical, water, or drainage lines that would run beneath the trellis walk must be trenched and installed before the base/substrate is placed to avoid future excavation and damage to the completed walkway.

The base/substrate layer provides the structural support and drainage platform; the final walking surface (e.g., pavers, concrete, gravel) cannot be laid until the base is compacted and properly formed.
Trellis support posts or columns must be anchored into or onto the completed base/substrate to ensure proper alignment, load distribution, and structural stability.

While edge restraints are often placed after the base is shaped to contain the surface material, some flexible systems can be installed simultaneously; this is a standard sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
The subgrade must be properly graded and compacted to provide a stable foundation before edge curbing can be installed, preventing settling or uneven alignment.
A trench or form must be excavated along the walk edge to receive the concrete or stone curbing material before the curbing can be placed.
The base course of the walkway must be completed so the edge curbing can align with the finished walk surface elevation and provide lateral restraint.
Freshly placed concrete or mortar for edge curbing must be allowed to cure and gain strength before any subsequent work can proceed.

successor: Walk Surface Finishing (e.g., paving stones, topping)
rationale: Edge curbing acts as a permanent form and boundary for the walk surface material, so it must be installed before the interior walk surface finish is laid.
A stable foundation and prepared site are necessary to anchor and support the climbing plant structure securely

predecessor: Structural Framework Installation (e.g., pergola, trellis frame)
rationale: The main load-bearing framework must be in place before the climbing plant support components (wires, mesh, or netting) can be attached
Plants need the support structure in place to be trained and guided as they grow; planting before the support is installed would disturb roots and make training impossible

successor: Tensioning and Final Adjustment of Support Wires/Nets
rationale: The support system must be installed first so it can be tensioned and adjusted to the correct tautness for plant growth

successor: Irrigation/Drip Line Installation (if attached to support)
rationale: While irrigation lines can be installed independently, attaching them to the support structure is easier once the support system is in place
The ground must be excavated and graded to the proper slope before any drainage system can be installed, as the drainage pipes and components require a stable, properly contoured bed.
After the drainage system (pipes, catch basins, and gravel) is laid and connected, the trench must be backfilled and compacted to protect and embed the drainage infrastructure.
The drainage system must be fully installed and covered before the walking surface (pavers, concrete, or decking) is placed on top, ensuring water capture and runoff paths are in place.

While the trellis structure could technically be erected before drainage, it is preferable to complete drainage first to avoid soil disruption and access restrictions that may damage the trellis footings.
If utilities must cross the same area, it is preferable to trench and lay utilities first to avoid digging up the newly installed drainage system, though it is not a strict physical necessity.
The trellis walk integrated seating requires stable, prepared ground and foundations to be installed on, so site preparation must be completed first.
Landscaping and planting around the integrated seating can only be done after the seating structure is fully installed to ensure proper alignment and to avoid damage to new plants.

successor: Installation of shading or canopy elements
rationale: If the trellis walk integrated seating includes a trellis or overhead structure, any shading or canopy components should logically follow the seating installation, though it may be possible to prefabricate these separately.
Any underground utilities (e.g., drainage, electrical for lighting) must be routed before the seating structure is installed to avoid digging up the completed seating area.

successor: Final surface finishing and paving around seating
rationale: The surrounding paving or surface finishing must be completed after the seating is installed to ensure proper fit and integration with the structure.
The trellis panels require a stable, level foundation or base structure to be installed upon, ensuring structural integrity and proper alignment.
The main structural frame of the trellis walk must be erected first to provide the supporting framework onto which the side panels/screens are attached.
The foundation must be prepared and cured to provide a stable and level base for the framework to be erected upon.

predecessor: Trellis Walk Construction - Material Procurement & Delivery
rationale: All framework materials (timber, steel, connectors, etc.) must be procured and delivered to site before erection can commence.

predecessor: Trellis Walk Construction - Site Survey & Layout
rationale: Accurate marking of post locations and alignment lines from the survey is required to position the framework correctly.

successor: Trellis Walk Construction - Cladding & Roof Installation
rationale: The structural framework must be fully erected and stable before any cladding, roofing, or overhead cover can be attached.

successor: Trellis Walk Construction - Bracing & Stability Check
rationale: After the framework is erected, temporary or permanent bracing must be installed and stability verified to ensure safety before further work proceeds.

The sub-base (e.g., compacted stone, gravel, or concrete base) must be prepared, leveled, and cured to provide a stable foundation before any surface paving material (e.g., concrete, asphalt, pavers) can be laid.
Formwork or edge restraints must be in place to define the shape, boundaries, and thickness of the paved surface before paving materials are poured or placed.

Subsurface drainage systems (e.g., French drains, perforated pipes) must be installed and tested before paving to ensure water does not accumulate beneath the paved surface, which could cause instability or frost heave.

After paving is complete, the surface must undergo proper curing (for concrete) or sealing (for pavers/asphalt) to achieve strength, durability, and weather resistance before the walk is opened to use.
Final finishing work such as joint cutting, edge detailing, texturing, or applying anti-slip treatments can only be performed after the main paving surface has been installed and is partially set.

successor: Trellis Walk Construction - Planting Support Installation
rationale: The ground must be properly graded and prepared to provide a stable, level base for the trellis structure and planting supports.

successor: Trellis Walk Construction - Planting Support Installation
rationale: Concrete footings or foundation piers must be poured and cured before the trellis posts and support structures can be erected on top of them.

successor: Trellis Walk Construction - Planting Support Installation
rationale: Any underground electrical, irrigation, or drainage lines must be installed before vertical construction to avoid digging conflicts and structural damage.

predecessor: Trellis Walk Construction - Planting Support Installation
rationale: The trellis and planting support framework must be in place before vines, climbers, or other vegetation can be planted and trained onto the supports.

predecessor: Trellis Walk Construction - Planting Support Installation
rationale: The trellis walk structure provides overhead and side support; the walking surface below (pavers, concrete, gravel) should be finished after the structure is erected to ensure proper alignment and access.
The structural framework of the trellis walk must be fully erected before lighting can be installed, as the lighting fixtures need to be mounted onto or within the existing structure.
Electrical wiring, conduit, and junction boxes must be roughed in before lighting fixtures can be connected and installed.

successor: Trellis Walk Construction - Lighting Testing & Commissioning
rationale: Lighting fixtures must be installed before they can be tested, commissioned, and verified for proper operation.

successor: Trellis Walk Construction - Finish Work & Trim
rationale: While some finish work can proceed concurrently, installing final trim and aesthetic covers after lighting installation helps avoid damage to fixtures and allows for proper alignment.

predecessor: Trellis Walk Construction - Conduit & Cable Tray Installation
rationale: Conduit and cable trays must be in place to route the electrical supply cables to the lighting fixture locations before installation can proceed.
The ground must be prepared, cleared, and excavated to the required levels before any drainage pipes or structures can be installed below or at grade.
Existing underground utilities must be identified and marked to avoid damaging them during excavation and drainage installation.
Drainage pipes and structures must be fully installed, inspected, and covered before backfilling trenches to protect the drainage system and ensure proper compaction.
Drainage installation must be completed first to allow water to be properly channeled away before the sub-base layer (e.g., crushed stone or aggregate) is placed for the walkway.
Drainage systems must be in place and operational before the final walkway surface is installed to ensure water does not pool on or undermine the finished surface.
The glazing system requires a stable, level base to be installed on. The foundation must be fully cured and load-bearing before any glazing work begins.
The structural frame (aluminum/steel rafters, purlins, and gutters) must be fully erected and secured to support and anchor the glazing panels.
Doors and vents are typically fitted into the glazed openings; the glazing panels define the openings into which doors and ventilation units are installed.

While it is possible to start some interior work before glazing is fully complete, it is strongly preferred to finish glazing first to protect interior components from weather and to provide a clean, enclosed environment.

The climate control system (heating, cooling, shading) depends on an enclosed building envelope created by the glazing to operate effectively and to be properly calibrated to the actual interior volume.
The greenhouse frame structure requires a stable, level foundation (concrete slab or base) to anchor upon. Without the prepared foundation, the frame cannot be properly positioned or secured.
Proper site grading and drainage systems must be in place before erecting the frame to prevent water accumulation and ensure long-term structural stability.
Underground electrical conduits, water supply lines, and drainage pipes must be installed before the frame is erected to avoid digging or trenching around completed structural elements.
The frame structure must be fully erected and secured before glass, polycarbonate panels, or film coverings can be attached to it, as the frame serves as the supporting skeleton.
Bracing and cross-members are installed onto the erected frame to provide lateral stability; these cannot be added before the main frame columns and beams are in place.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the proper depth and dimensions before any foundation work can begin, as the foundation requires a stable, prepared subgrade.
Accurate site surveying and staking out the foundation footprint must be completed before pouring or placing the foundation, to ensure correct positioning and alignment.

Any underground plumbing, drainage, electrical conduit, or irrigation lines that will pass beneath the foundation slab must be installed and inspected before the foundation is poured, as they cannot be placed afterward.

The foundation provides the structural base and anchorage for the greenhouse frame; walls, columns, and structural supports cannot be erected until the foundation has cured and achieved sufficient strength.

Interior floor systems (concrete slab, gravel base, or flooring material) are typically poured or installed on top of or within the foundation perimeter and must wait until foundation walls and footings are complete.
Benching and shelving systems require a stable, level floor surface for proper installation and load distribution, so the concrete floor slab must be completed first.
The greenhouse envelope (frame, walls, roof) must be in place to protect the benching system from weather and to define the interior layout before benching components are brought in and installed.
Overhead utility lines and ductwork must be installed before benching/shelving to avoid conflicts, as benching occupies floor space and can block access to ceiling work.

Workstations are often integrated with or placed adjacent to the benching system and rely on the benching layout for positioning, so they should be installed after the main benching system is in place.
Irrigation lines are typically routed onto or through the benching system to water plants, and must be laid out after the benching is installed to ensure correct fit and coverage.
The foundation must be completed and fully cured to provide a stable, level base for the greenhouse structure before glazing panels can be installed.

The structural frame (aluminum, steel, or wood) must be fully assembled and secured to support the glazing panels, as the glass or polycarbonate sheets are mounted directly onto or within the frame members.
Doors and ventilation openings are typically fitted into the glazed envelope; installing them after glazing allows proper sealing and alignment with the glazing panels.

Interior components such as shelving, irrigation systems, and benches should be installed after glazing to avoid damage to the glass or polycarbonate panels and to allow access for cleaning and sealing the glazing from inside.
All glazing panels must be in place before final weatherproofing sealant is applied around edges, joints, and flashings to ensure a continuous watertight and airtight envelope.
A stable level foundation is physically required to support and anchor the greenhouse frame; without it, the frame cannot be erected.
Concrete foundation must cure to sufficient strength before bearing the load of the frame; starting frame erection too early could cause structural failure.
Water lines, drainage pipes, and electrical conduits must be placed in the ground before the frame is erected, as access to the foundation area becomes restricted afterward.
Glass or polycarbonate panels (glazing) and sidewall cladding are attached directly to the frame; the frame structure must be fully erected to provide the mounting surface.
Roof purlins, ridge caps, and gutter systems are mounted onto the completed frame; the structural skeleton must be in place before roof components can be installed.
The ground or foundation must be level, compacted, and stable before benching can be installed to ensure structural integrity and prevent settling or uneven benching.

The main greenhouse structural frame (including roof supports) must be in place to provide enclosure and overhead structure; benching is typically installed after the frame is erected to avoid damage and to allow proper positioning relative to the frame.

While not strictly required in all cases, installing glazing or covering before benching protects benches and materials from weather; however, benching can sometimes proceed before full glazing is complete.
Under-bench irrigation lines and drip systems are typically laid out and secured after benches are in place so that the piping aligns precisely with bench locations and plant spacing.
Plants and pots cannot be placed on benches until the benching system is fully assembled, leveled, and load-tested for safety and functionality.
The greenhouse foundation must be in place to provide a stable base for the irrigation system pipes and components that run through or attach to the structure.
The structural frame of the greenhouse must be erected to support overhead irrigation lines, drip system hangers, and to define the layout for the irrigation network.
The main water supply line must be run to the greenhouse site to provide the water source that the irrigation system connects to.

successor: Greenhouse Flooring or Ground Cover Installation
rationale: Irrigation pipes and drip lines must be laid and connected before flooring or ground cover is installed, to avoid having to lift or cut through finished flooring.
The irrigation system must be fully operational to provide water to plants immediately upon planting; planting before irrigation is complete risks crop loss.
The greenhouse structure must be built and stable before environmental systems can be installed and commissioned.
The frame and glazing must be in place to enclose the space before HVAC, lighting, and environmental control systems can be commissioned.
Electrical power must be available to run pumps, fans, controllers, and sensors during commissioning.
Water supply and drainage infrastructure must be installed before the environmental control systems (e.g., misting, irrigation, humidity control) can be tested and commissioned.
The environmental systems (temperature, humidity, lighting, irrigation) must be verified and operational before introducing plants to ensure proper growing conditions.
While calibration can begin after commissioning, it is a soft preference because some fine-tuning may occur concurrently with early plant growth.
The bench needs a stable, level base (e.g., concrete slab or compacted gravel pad) to sit on; building the bench first would leave no solid foundation.
Proper drainage and grading must be established so water does not pool under or erode the bench's foundation area.
The bench must be fully assembled before a protective stain or sealant can be applied to its surface.
Soft preference: planting around the bench is easier and neater after the bench is in place, but could be done beforehand with careful layout.
All construction debris from building the bench must be cleared as part of final cleanup; doing cleanup first would be pointless.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared before any permanent landscape feature like a planter seat can be installed, ensuring stable foundation and proper drainage.
A concrete or masonry base/footing for the planter structure must be poured and cured before the integrated seat component can be placed on top to ensure structural stability.
Plants and soil should be added to the planter after the seat structure is in place, as the planter box itself must be installed first to contain the soil and plantings.
Any final grading, mulch, paving, or surface treatments around the seat should be completed after the seat is installed to avoid damaging finished surfaces and to ensure proper fit and alignment.
Any underground utilities, irrigation lines, or drainage pipes that will pass beneath or near the planter must be laid before the planter seat is installed to avoid excavation after installation.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the required depth to provide a stable foundation base before the retaining wall can be constructed.
A concrete footing or compacted base must be poured and cured to support the weight and lateral pressure of the retaining wall structure.
Drainage pipes and gravel backfill behind the wall must be installed prior to wall construction to prevent hydrostatic pressure buildup.
The wall must be fully constructed and cured before backfill material can be placed behind it to avoid displacing or damaging the wall.
The retaining wall structure must be complete to provide the supporting surface and anchor points for mounting the garden seat on top or against the wall.
The seat cushion base must be fabricated first to provide the structural platform onto which the weatherproofing and storage components are applied.
The cushion must be weatherproofed before it can be integrated into a storage assembly to prevent moisture damage during subsequent assembly steps.

The weatherproof seat cushion storage unit must be in place before the interior storage compartment lining is installed, as the lining is fitted into the storage cavity created by the cushion assembly.
Final sealing of the storage compartment lid must occur after the weatherproof cushion storage assembly is complete to ensure a watertight closure around the integrated cushion.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded before any foundation work can begin to ensure stable support and proper drainage for the garden seat foundation.
Underground utilities must be identified and marked before excavation for the foundation to avoid damage to existing services and ensure worker safety.
The concrete or masonry foundation must be poured and fully cured before any subsequent construction steps can proceed to ensure structural integrity.
The foundation provides the load-bearing base; the seat frame or superstructure elements cannot be erected without a completed foundation to anchor to.
After the foundation is set and cured, the excavated areas around it must be backfilled and compacted to restore ground level and provide lateral soil support.

predecessor: Assemble and Install Garden Seat Frame
rationale: The backrest must be attached to a stable frame; the seat frame assembly provides the structural support needed to hold the backrest in place.
The backrest components (slats, rails, etc.) must be cut, shaped, and finished before they can be assembled onto the seat frame.
Once the backrest is installed, the entire seat unit can be finished uniformly to ensure color consistency and protection.
A full inspection including backrest alignment, structural integrity, and finish quality is best performed after the backrest is installed.
The seat frame must be securely anchored on a level foundation before the backrest is added to avoid misalignment or instability.

predecessor: Assemble and Install Garden Seat Frame
rationale: The armrest must be attached to the seat frame; the frame must be assembled first to provide a stable base for armrest installation.
The armrest structure must be in place before any cushion, padding, or upholstery can be applied to it.
While finishing can sometimes be done on individual components before assembly, it is often preferred to mount the armrest first to ensure uniform coating and avoid handling damage.
The ground must be leveled and a stable foundation laid before the garden seat structure can be built upon it.
The seat structure must be in place before soil and landscaping elements can be added around or against it.
The complete seat assembly must be finished before protective sealants or waterproof coatings can be applied to its surfaces.
For cast-in-place concrete or similar, the curved formwork must be built and secured before the seat material (e.g., concrete) can be poured or placed.
The seat must be fully constructed and cured (if applicable) before any final surface finishing such as polishing, texturing, or painting is performed.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before any fire pit components can be installed to ensure a stable foundation.
A concrete base or footing must be poured and cured to provide a solid, level platform for the fire pit seat ring to rest upon.
The seat ring structure must be in place before inserting the fire pit liner or inner fire bowl, as the liner sits within or against the ring.
Backfilling soil or gravel around the exterior of the fire pit can only be done after the seat ring is positioned to avoid shifting or misalignment.

successor: Install Capstones/Top Trim on Seat Ring
rationale: Capstones or decorative top trim must be placed after the main seat ring structure is fully assembled and secured.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before any foundation can be installed to ensure proper bearing capacity and level surface.
The sub-base material must be compacted to provide a stable, load-bearing surface before pouring or placing the foundation.

predecessor: Set Out and Mark Garden Seat Location
rationale: The exact location and dimensions of the garden seat must be marked out on site to guide foundation placement.
Freshly placed concrete foundation requires sufficient curing time to gain strength before any loads are applied.
The foundation must be fully set and stable before any masonry or superstructure is built on top of it.
A stable and level foundation must be prepared before any framing can be erected to ensure structural integrity and proper alignment of the garden seat.
Support posts must be installed and secured first to provide the vertical structural anchors to which the seat frame members can be attached.
The frame must be fully assembled and braced before any deck boards or seat surface planks are fastened to it, as the frame provides the underlying support structure.
The main seat frame must be completed first to establish the base geometry and attachment points for installing the backrest components.

While it is generally preferable to apply finish after framing is complete to protect the wood, some pre-finishing of frame members can occur before assembly; however, the final coat is typically applied after the frame is erected.

predecessor: Prepare Foundation for Garden Seat Area
successor: Assemble and Install Garden Seat Frame
rationale: The foundation must be prepared and cured to provide a stable, level base for the garden seat frame assembly.

successor: Assemble and Install Garden Seat Frame
rationale: All frame components (lumber, fasteners, hardware) must be on-site before assembly can begin.

successor: Assemble and Install Garden Seat Frame
rationale: Individual frame pieces must be cut to size and pre-drilled for joinery prior to final assembly and installation.

predecessor: Assemble and Install Garden Seat Frame
rationale: The seat frame structure must be fully assembled and secured in place before seat slats can be fastened to it.

predecessor: Assemble and Install Garden Seat Frame
successor: Apply Primer and Paint/Sealer to Seat Frame
rationale: While painting could theoretically be done pre-assembly, it is standard practice and more efficient to paint after assembly to ensure complete coverage of joints and to avoid damage to the finish during installation.
The concrete seating risers or structural support must be fully cured and in place to provide a stable base for attaching seat decking, treads, and finish materials.

Any electrical conduit, junction boxes, or plumbing rough-ins that run beneath or through the seating areas must be completed and inspected before the decking is installed, as access will be blocked afterward.
The main decking provides the substrate to which anti-slip treads, nosing strips, or edge trims are applied; treads cannot be secured without the decking in place.
The decking and finish surfaces (e.g., wood, composite, or metal) must be fully installed before a sealant or waterproof coating can be applied to protect the material from moisture and wear.
Cushions, upholstered seat pads, or removable seat inserts are mounted onto the finished decking; the rigid deck must be complete to provide the attachment points or support surface.
The seat track system must be in place to provide the mounting structure and power/data routing pathways for integrated seat lighting components.
Ceiling and flooring work must be finished before seat lighting installation to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to ensure proper alignment references.
Seat upholstery and trim must be installed after lighting to allow access to wiring connections and to prevent damage to finished upholstery during lighting installation.
Lighting must be fully installed before electrical testing and commissioning can verify proper function, brightness levels, and control system integration.
Although possible to install entertainment systems concurrently, it is preferable to complete lighting first to avoid interference and to ensure clean cable management routing for both systems.
Concrete slabs and structural elements must be fully cured and prepared before any waterproofing membrane can be applied; otherwise, the membrane will not bond properly and may fail.
The site must be excavated and rough-graded to the proper elevations so that drainage pipes, gravel layers, and waterproofing systems can be installed on stable subgrade.
Underground utilities (e.g., sewer, water, electrical conduits) must be placed before drainage layers and waterproofing coverings are installed, as these systems go below the waterproofing plane.
Backfill against foundation walls can only proceed after waterproofing membranes and drainage boards have been fully installed and inspected to avoid damaging the waterproofing system.

Rigid insulation boards are typically placed over the waterproofing layer; while it is preferable to insulate after waterproofing, it is a soft preference because insulation could theoretically be applied later if access is maintained.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before constructing raised beds to ensure proper drainage, stability, and alignment.
Underground utilities must be identified and marked before excavation or construction of raised beds to avoid damage and ensure safety.
Subsurface drainage or French drains must be installed before placing raised beds to prevent water pooling and ensure proper drainage away from the bed area.
The raised bed frame structure must be fully assembled and in place before it can be filled with planting soil mix.

Drip irrigation lines are often laid on top of or within the raised bed after construction, but could theoretically be run underneath before filling; however, standard practice is to install after the bed frame is built.
Plants or seeds can only be placed into the raised bed after the bed structure is complete and filled with growing medium.
Mulch is applied after planting, but the raised bed must be constructed first as the physical container for the garden area.
The ground must be graded and rough earthwork completed to establish the proper topography, drainage patterns, and soil volumes before planting beds can be formed.
All underground utilities (irrigation lines, drainage pipes, conduit) must be installed before excavation for planting beds to avoid disturbing or damaging buried services.
Poor or contaminated soil must be removed, amended, or replaced to create a viable growing medium before any planting bed construction can commence.
The physical planting bed structure (excavation, edging, soil fill) must be fully complete and contained before any plants, shrubs, or trees are placed into it.

Mulch is typically spread after the planting bed is formed and plants are installed, but in some sequences mulch could be applied before planting and then plants placed through it; however, standard practice is to apply mulch after planting.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before any pathway construction can begin to ensure a stable and properly sloped base.
Any underground pipes, cables, or drainage systems that will run beneath or near the pathway must be installed first to avoid digging up the completed path.

Plants, mulch, and decorative features bordering the pathway should be installed after the path is laid to ensure proper alignment and to avoid soil or debris being placed on the finished path surface.

It is preferable to do the final cleanup after the pathway is complete so that any construction debris from the pathway work is removed, but this is a soft preference rather than a strict physical requirement.

Pathway lighting fixtures are typically installed after the path base and pavers are in place to ensure proper positioning along the finished walking surface and to avoid damaging the path during electrical work.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before edging materials can be installed to ensure a stable foundation.
The soil base must be compacted to prevent settling and shifting of the edging materials after installation.
Any underground irrigation, drainage, or electrical lines should be placed before edging to avoid disturbing the edging later.
After edging is installed, soil can be backfilled against the edging to secure it and achieve final grading.
Garden edging defines the boundary of planting beds, so planting and mulching activities occur after edging is in place.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded before any structure like a compost bin enclosure can be built on it to ensure stability and proper drainage.
A solid foundation or concrete base must be in place to support the compost bin enclosure structure and prevent settling or movement.
Underground utilities must be identified and marked before any excavation or digging for the enclosure to avoid damaging gas, water, or electrical lines.
The enclosure must be fully constructed before organic materials can be introduced and the composting process can begin.
While landscaping can be done after the enclosure is built, it is a soft preference because aesthetics and screening can be completed at any time after construction.
Fence posts provide the structural support base that the garden trellis attaches to or is integrated with; the trellis cannot be erected without the posts in place.
Soil preparation and any underground utility work must be completed before installing the trellis to avoid disturbing the trellis structure or roots of climbing plants.
Climbing plants need the trellis structure in place to be planted at the base and trained to grow up it; planting before the trellis is installed would damage plants or require replanting.

While a pre-finished trellis can be installed, if field painting or staining is desired, it is easier and more complete to apply finish before or immediately after installation, but this is a soft preference for quality.

Garden lighting is often positioned to illuminate or highlight the trellis and climbing plants, so the trellis should be in place first to guide optimal light placement, though this is a design preference.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before a cold frame can be built to ensure a stable, level foundation.

A cold frame typically requires a base frame or foundation (e.g., pressure-treated lumber or concrete blocks) to sit on, which must be constructed first to define the footprint and provide structural support.
The glazing or transparent lid (glass, polycarbonate, or plastic sheeting) must be installed after the frame is built, as it attaches directly to the completed frame structure.
The cold frame structure must be in place before soil, compost, or growing medium is added inside, as the frame contains and defines the planting area.
Hinges, automatic vent openers, or prop sticks for the lid must be installed after the main box structure is complete and the lid is ready to be mounted.

successor: Garden Hose Bib / Water Spigot Installation
rationale: The wall sheathing provides the structural surface onto which the hose bib can be mounted and penetrates through.

successor: Garden Hose Bib / Water Spigot Installation
rationale: The water supply line must be roughed in to the exterior wall location before the hose bib can be connected.

predecessor: Install Exterior Insulation and Weather Barrier
successor: Garden Hose Bib / Water Spigot Installation
rationale: Installing the weather barrier first allows proper flashing integration, though it can be cut and flashed around the spigot afterward if needed.

predecessor: Garden Hose Bib / Water Spigot Installation
rationale: The hose bib must be installed before the final siding/cladding so that the siding can be cut and fit around the spigot for a weathertight finish.

predecessor: Garden Hose Bib / Water Spigot Installation
successor: Interior Drywall Installation (on opposite side of wall)
rationale: While the hose bib can be installed after drywall, it is easier to access the mounting bracket and sealant from the interior before drywall is closed up.

predecessor: Garden Hose Bib / Water Spigot Installation
successor: Pressure Testing of Exterior Water Supply
rationale: The hose bib must be installed and connected to allow full pressure testing of the exterior branch of the water supply system.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before fence posts can be set or footing trenches dug.
Accurate boundary lines and property limits must be surveyed and marked before fence installation to ensure correct positioning.

predecessor: Underground Drainage / Utility Services (if crossing boundary)
rationale: Any drainage pipes, water lines, or electrical cables that need to run under or across the fence line must be laid before fence posts are installed to avoid digging up the completed fence.
Final soil grading, planting, and decorative landscaping around the fence should be done after the fence is in place so the landscape finish abuts the fence properly.
While not physically required, it is typical practice to complete boundary enclosures before the final inspection so the property perimeter is fully defined and secure.
Gate posts provide the structural support and hinge mounting points; the gate cannot be hung without posts being securely in place.
The gate must be hung and properly aligned on its hinges before the latch, handle, and closing hardware can be fitted and adjusted.

It is much easier to align the gate to the finished ground level and ensure proper clearance if the adjacent paving is already in place, though the gate can be installed before paving with careful measurement.
The gate must fit within the fence or wall opening; the surrounding structure defines the rough opening dimensions and attachment points.
Finishing landscaping and garden beds after gate installation prevents damage to new plants and allows heavy equipment and materials to pass through the opening before the gate is in place.
A level, stable base is required before any structure can be erected to ensure structural integrity and proper drainage.
The foundation (e.g., concrete base, ground anchors, or base rails) must be in place to secure the greenhouse/polytunnel frame and prevent movement or collapse.
The structural frame (hoops, trusses, etc.) must be fully erected before the glazing material (glass, polycarbonate, or polythene sheeting) can be attached.
It is practical but not physically mandatory to install benching after the structure is up; benching could theoretically be assembled inside after the frame is complete.
The enclosed structure must be complete before installing internal irrigation lines to protect equipment from weather and to properly route pipes within the defined space.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and graded before planter beds can be installed to ensure a stable and level foundation.
Any underground electrical, irrigation, or drainage lines must be installed before placing raised planter beds to avoid digging up or disturbing the beds later.
If a concrete base or pad is required for the planter beds, it must be poured and cured before the beds are installed on top.
The planter bed structures must be fully installed and secured before they can be filled with soil mix.
Irrigation components are typically laid out and connected after the beds are in place to ensure proper coverage within each bed.
The site must be excavated and graded to the final elevation before irrigation pipes and components can be laid, ensuring proper drainage and coverage.
Underground utilities such as water supply lines and electrical conduits must be in place before irrigation system installation to provide the necessary water source and power connections.
Irrigation system (sprinklers, drip lines, valves) must be installed and tested before planting to ensure coverage zones are functional and to avoid disturbing new plantings.
Irrigation piping and heads should be placed before concrete work so that pipe runs and pop-up sprinkler locations can be coordinated and embedded where needed.
While final grading can be done after irrigation, it is preferable to complete irrigation placement first to avoid re-digging and to allow precise pipe depth coverage.
The ground must be properly prepared, leveled, and cleared of debris before garden edging can be installed to ensure a stable, even base and proper alignment.
The garden bed layout and edging boundaries must be marked on the ground to guide accurate placement and alignment of the edging materials.
A trench of appropriate depth must be excavated along the marked layout to accommodate the edging material (e.g., stone, brick, metal, or plastic edging) securely.
After the edging is installed and secured in place, soil or fill material must be compacted around both sides to lock the edging in position and finish the transition.

While it is preferred to plant after edging is complete to avoid disturbing newly installed edging, planting could theoretically be done simultaneously or in a different order; this is a soft preference for sequencing efficiency and aesthetics.
The garden area must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any trellis installation can begin to ensure stable footing and proper layout.
If the trellis requires concrete footings or post anchors, these must be poured and cured before the trellis posts can be set and secured.
Climbing plants or vines intended to grow on the trellis should be planted after the trellis is installed so they can be trained onto the structure immediately.
If the trellis is made of wood, it is typically easier to apply stain or sealant before installation, but if done afterward it is a soft preference for aesthetics and protection.
Landscape lighting near the trellis area is often installed after the trellis is in place to ensure proper positioning relative to the structure.

The site must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and existing structures before soil preparation can begin, as these obstructions would prevent access to the soil surface and contaminate the soil zone.

Rough grading establishes the general topography and drainage patterns of the site; soil preparation and amendment must follow this to ensure the amended soil layer conforms to the final designed grades.

Underground utility trenches and conduits must be placed and backfilled before soil amendment to avoid disturbing the amended soil layer and to ensure utility lines are properly located below the root zone.
The irrigation system should be installed after soil is amended to avoid damaging newly conditioned soil layers and to ensure proper depth placement relative to the finished soil grade.
Plants and turf require properly prepared and amended soil for root establishment; soil must be tilled, amended with nutrients, and brought to final grade before any planting can occur.
The ground must be properly leveled, cleared of debris, and graded to ensure a stable base for garden pathways, preventing future settling or uneven surfaces.
Any underground pipes, cables, or drainage systems that will run under or near the pathways must be installed first to avoid having to dig up and disrupt the finished pathways later.

While pathway lighting can sometimes be installed concurrently, it is generally preferred to complete pathways first to establish the final walking surface and alignment before placing light fixtures along the edges.

Garden pathways define the borders for planting areas; turf, ground cover, or garden beds should be installed after pathways are laid to avoid damaging new plants during pathway construction and to ensure clean edges.

Edging elements such as bricks, stones, or metal strips that sit flush against the pathway must be installed after the pathway surface is complete to secure the perimeter and define the boundary between the path and adjacent landscaping.
The garden area must be cleared, leveled, and marked before fence installation can begin to ensure proper alignment and stability.
All underground utility lines must be located and marked before digging post holes to avoid damage to utilities and ensure safety.
Required building permits and approvals must be secured before fence construction to comply with local regulations and avoid legal issues.

It is preferable to apply protective stain or paint after fence installation so the finish is applied to the fully assembled structure, though it could technically be applied to components beforehand.
Garden beds and planting should be done after the fence is installed to protect plants from construction damage and to allow accurate placement relative to the fence boundary.
Excavation must be completed before any underground cabling or conduit for garden lighting can be laid, as the trenches need to be dug first for cable runs.
Underground electrical conduits and cabling must be in place before light fixtures can be installed and connected to the power supply.
Trenches dug for cabling can only be backfilled after all lighting cables and connections are laid and checked, to avoid burying incomplete or faulty wiring.
The lighting system must be fully installed before it can be powered on and tested for correct operation and waterproofing.

Soft preference: Final landscaping and decorative elements are typically placed after lighting installation to avoid damaging lights or disturbing the ground where cables run, though they could theoretically be done before with careful planning.
The greenhouse frame must be anchored to a stable foundation; the foundation must be poured and cured before any above-ground assembly can begin.
The structural frame members (aluminum or steel) must be cut, welded, and prepared prior to on-site assembly and glazing installation.
All frame components, glazing panels, sealants, and hardware must be onsite before assembly work can commence.
Benching and shelving are installed after the enclosed structure is complete to ensure proper fit and to avoid damaging the benching during the glazing process.
Irrigation piping and misting lines are run inside the completed glazed structure; installing them beforehand would risk damage during assembly and glazing.
Electrical wiring, lighting, fans, and thermostat controls are installed after the greenhouse is enclosed to protect equipment from weather and to follow proper construction sequencing.
The completed, glazed greenhouse must be inspected for structural integrity, seal quality, and safety before being put into operational use.
The site must be excavated and prepared before installing the rainwater collection system to ensure a stable foundation and proper drainage for storage tanks and components.
A concrete foundation is required to support the weight of rainwater storage tanks and structural components before installation can begin.
Underground or rough-in plumbing for supply lines and overflow drainage must be completed before the rainwater system is installed to ensure proper connectivity.

successor: Connect Rainwater System to Building Plumbing
rationale: The rainwater collection system must be fully installed before it can be connected to the building's plumbing system for water distribution.
Filtration and treatment components are typically installed after the main collection and storage system is in place to ensure proper integration and flow.
The system must be fully installed before testing and commissioning can verify its functionality and performance.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any cold frame structure can be built on it.
A stable base or foundation (e.g., concrete block, treated wood frame, or gravel bed) must be in place to support the cold frame structure.
All necessary materials such as lumber, glass/polycarbonate panels, hinges, and fasteners must be acquired before construction can begin.
The frame structure must be fully assembled before the transparent lid or glazing panels can be securely attached to it.
After the cold frame structure is built, sealing gaps and adding insulation around the edges ensures temperature control and prevents heat loss.
The ground surface must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstacles and brought to proper grade before a soil berm can be placed, as the berm requires a stable, prepared subgrade.
Underground utilities must be located and either protected or relocated before earthwork begins to prevent damage during berm construction.
After placing the berm material, compaction testing must be performed to verify the berm meets density specifications before any loads are placed on it.
Erosion control measures such as silt fences, matting, or hydroseeding are applied after the berm is shaped and placed to stabilize the soil surface and prevent erosion.

Planting grass, shrubs, or other vegetation on top of the berm is typically done after the berm is fully constructed to provide long-term stabilization and aesthetic integration, though this is a design preference rather than a hard physical requirement.
A level, stable foundation (e.g., concrete slab or gravel base) must be prepared before any shed construction can begin, as the shed structure requires a solid, load-bearing base.

successor: Landscaping and Final Grading Around Shed
rationale: Once the shed is erected, final landscaping, grading, and decorative elements can be installed around it for proper drainage and aesthetics, though this is a logical sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.

Interior fit-out such as shelving, hooks, and tool racks cannot be installed until the shed structure (walls, floor, roof) is fully complete, as these elements attach to the finished interior surfaces.
If electrical power or lighting is planned for the shed, underground conduit and wiring must be laid before the shed floor/foundation is poured to avoid later excavation under the structure.

While painting can be done after assembly, it is often preferred to apply a protective finish after the shed is fully assembled to protect the wood; however, pre-finished components could reverse this order.
The compost storage bin requires a level, stable, and well-drained surface. Site preparation and grading must be completed first to ensure the bin does not shift or become unstable.

A concrete base or compacted gravel foundation is needed to support the compost storage bin and prevent ground moisture from affecting the stored material. The foundation must be cured before bin assembly.
Underground utilities (water, gas, electric) must be located and marked before any excavation or ground penetration for the bin foundation to prevent damage and ensure safety.
The bin structure must be fully assembled and secure before it can be filled with compost materials to prevent structural failure or spillage.

successor: Final site cleanup and landscaping around bin
rationale: While not physically required, it is good practice to complete the bin installation first before finishing landscaping details around it to avoid damaging new plantings or grading work.
A stable foundation is required to support the compost chute structure and prevent settling or misalignment.
The compost chute typically passes through floor levels, so floor framing must be in place to create the necessary opening and support.
Walls must be framed to accommodate the chute path and provide structural attachment points.
The chute must be enclosed within the wall before drywall or other finishes are applied.
The exterior termination of the chute must be installed before final siding or cladding is completed to ensure proper flashing and weatherproofing.
The foundation or base for the compost area must be prepared before installing the access door, as the door frame needs a stable, level surface to be anchored to.
The main compost bin structure/frame must be assembled first so that the access door can be properly fitted into the designated opening.
Sealing and weatherproofing around the door should be done after the door is installed to ensure proper sealing against the elements.
Testing the door operation (opening/closing, latch function) naturally follows installation, though in some cases testing could occur simultaneously with final adjustments.
The compost chute must be installed before cleaning access can be provided, as the cleaning access is an integrated component of the chute system.
Cleaning access must be in place before any actual cleaning or maintenance activities can be performed on the chute.
Access to the chute interior is required before an inspection can be conducted to verify cleanliness and structural condition.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth and slope before any drainage infrastructure can be installed.
A stable, compacted base is needed to support the floor drain pipes and prevent settling or damage after installation.

successor: Slab / Concrete Pour for Compost Area Floor
rationale: The floor drain piping and catch basin must be placed and connected before the concrete slab is poured, so the drain is embedded in the slab with proper slope and drainage outlet.
The floor drain outlet pipe must be connected to the main drainage line after the drain is positioned, but before backfilling or final grading.
Waterproofing around the drain penetration is best applied after drain installation to ensure a watertight seal, though sequencing may vary depending on design.
The compost chute must be installed before the fire damper can be fitted, as the damper is mounted within or at the opening of the chute itself.
The fire damper must be physically installed before it can be tested and commissioned to ensure proper operation and fire safety compliance.
The fire damper installation must be completed before the surrounding chute enclosure is sealed and fireproofed, to allow access for proper fitting and inspection.
Structural supports and framing must be in place to provide a secure mounting point for the fire damper assembly.
After the damper is installed, any penetrations through floors or ceilings around the chute must be fire-sealed to maintain fire compartmentation integrity.

The compost chute system needs to be installed within the wall cavities and structural framing. Rough openings for the chute doors and the chute shaft must be framed before the chute system can be physically installed.
Ventilation ducts for the compost chute system (to manage odors) and any necessary drainage must be roughed in prior to installing the chute system itself, as they will connect to the chute assembly.

successor: Install Drywall and Finish Wall Surfaces
rationale: The compost chute doors, access panels, and chute shaft must be fully installed so that drywall can be cut and finished around them, creating a seamless finished wall surface.

It is preferable to install the compost chute system before final floor finishes to avoid damaging finished floors during chute installation and to allow for any floor-level chute access doors to be properly positioned.

successor: Install Compost Collection Bins and Final Connections
rationale: The chute system must be physically installed and secured before the collection bins can be positioned at the termination point of the chute and final connections (such as sealing and odor-control fittings) can be completed.
Rough-in work for plumbing and electrical must be completed before finishes are installed, as finishes would cover and block access to rough-ins.
The floor slab must be cured and in place before any wall or ceiling finishes can be applied.
Wall and ceiling framing must be complete to provide a substrate for finishes such as drywall, tile, or paneling.
Finished walls, floors, and ceilings must be in place before heavy equipment is brought in to avoid damage to finishes and to allow proper equipment mounting.
Final painting and sealing are the last steps in finishing and protect the underlying finish materials; they must follow the installation of finishes.
The ground must be leveled and cleared of debris before the compost bin enclosure can be placed and installed.
The enclosure must be fully installed and stable before any compost materials can be added to it.

successor: Connect Bin to Irrigation or Drainage (if applicable)
rationale: Drainage or irrigation connections should be made after the enclosure is in place to ensure proper positioning.
The ventilation system must be fully installed and connected before it can be commissioned and tested for proper operation.

predecessor: Complete Electrical Work for Compost Room
rationale: Electrical power supply and controls must be completed and available to run the ventilation equipment during commissioning.

predecessor: Install Compost Room Odor Control System
rationale: Odor control components are typically integrated with the ventilation system and must be in place before commissioning the integrated system.
The ventilation system must be verified to function correctly to maintain proper air quality, temperature, and odor control before active composting operations can begin.

successor: Finalize Compost Room Environmental Monitoring Setup
rationale: While monitoring setup can begin earlier, final calibration and integration of environmental sensors with the ventilation system is best completed after commissioning ensures stable system performance.

The alcove walls and framing must be built and finished (including drywall, plastering, and painting) before shelving can be installed, as shelving requires a solid, level, and finished supporting structure.

Any electrical wiring, outlets, or lighting intended for the alcove must be roughed in before shelving is installed; otherwise, accessing the walls for wiring afterward would require removing the shelving.
Shelving must be fully installed, secured, and load-tested before any items can be placed on it for storage or display.

successor: Final trim and molding around shelving (if integrated)
rationale: If the shelving is designed with integrated trim or molding that covers the joint between shelf and wall, that finishing work must occur after the shelves are installed to achieve a seamless appearance.

Soft preference: While styling and accessorizing (e.g., adding decorative objects, books, or bins) logically comes after the shelving is installed, it is a design preference rather than a physical necessity.
The alcove walls must be constructed first to provide the structural support and opening into which the architrave/frame is installed.
The architrave/frame must be installed in place before final surface finishing can be applied to ensure seamless integration with surrounding surfaces.
While the architrave defines the opening, interior finishes often proceed after framing to protect the architrave from damage during interior work; this is a preferred sequence to avoid rework.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the architrave/frame can be fitted.

successor: Door or decorative panel installation (if applicable)
rationale: Any door or panel that hinges or fits within the alcove opening must be installed after the architrave/frame is in place, as the frame provides the mounting surface and alignment reference.
The back wall finishing (e.g., tile, paneling, or paint) cannot be applied until the framing structure is in place to support the wall surface.
Backer board or substrate must be installed on the alcove back wall before any finishing material such as tile, stone, or stucco can be applied.
Waterproofing must be completed behind the finished surface to protect the wall structure, especially in wet areas.

successor: Alcove trim and edge profile installation
rationale: Trim pieces and edge profiles (e.g., tile edging, corner beads, or molding) are installed over or adjacent to the finished wall surface to provide clean edges and transitions.
If shelves or recessed niches are being installed within the alcove, the back wall finish must be completed first so that shelves can be attached to or set against the finished surface.
The subfloor must be leveled, cleaned, and structurally sound before any flooring or step installation can begin, as flooring requires a stable base.
Wall framing defines the alcove boundaries and ensures the flooring and step dimensions fit correctly within the alcove space.
Any plumbing lines that run beneath the alcove floor must be installed before the flooring is laid to avoid cutting into or damaging the finished floor later.
The base flooring or step structure must be in place before applying the finished surface material (tile, vinyl, etc.) as the finish is installed on top of the substrate.
Trim pieces and cove molding are installed after the flooring is laid to cover the gap between the floor and walls, providing a finished appearance.
The curtain track/blind must be fixed to a finished surface; the alcove lining provides the structural base for mounting the track.

predecessor: Complete ceiling and wall painting in alcove
rationale: Painting should be completed before installing the curtain track to avoid paint splatter on the track and to allow clean edges around the fixing brackets.
The track/blind mechanism must be securely in place before the curtain fabric, blinds slats or drapes can be hung or attached to it.
After the curtain/blind is installed, a final quality check of all alcove components can be completed, though this is a soft sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
Lighting fixtures should ideally be installed after the curtain track to allow precise positioning relative to the curtain line and avoid obstruction, though some lighting can be done in parallel.
The foundation or slab must be completed before any framing or drywall work can begin, as framing is built upon the foundation and requires a stable, level base.
Rough electrical wiring must be installed within the walls before drywall is placed, as drywall covers the wiring and cannot be easily accessed afterward.
Rough plumbing pipes must be installed in the walls before drywall is hung, as drywall would otherwise block access to the plumbing.
Drywall finishing, including taping and mudding, can only begin after the drywall sheets are installed and the framing for the alcove is complete.
Painting and priming must be done after drywall is installed and finished, as paint is applied to the finished drywall surface.
The alcove must be framed (studs, headers, etc.) in place to provide a structural substrate to which trim can be attached.
Trim is installed over finished drywall; drywall must be hung, taped, mudded, and sanded smooth before trim can be nailed or glued to the wall surface.
Trim is typically installed before final painting so that paint or stain can be applied to the trim and the adjacent wall can be cut in neatly against the trim edges.

After trim is in place, gaps between trim and drywall are caulked for a finished appearance; this is a finishing step that logically follows trim installation, though in some sequences caulking could be done slightly later.
The alcove must be measured and marked accurately before shelves can be fitted, as the shelf positions and dimensions depend on these measurements.
Wall surfaces within the alcove must be finished (plastered and painted) before shelf fitting to avoid damaging finished shelving or requiring rework.
Flooring should be installed before alcove shelving to ensure the shelf unit sits on the finished floor level and to avoid having to fit around shelving legs or supports.
Minor touch-up painting around the fitted shelves is often done after installation to cover any marks or gaps, but this is a soft preference rather than a strict physical constraint.
Items can only be placed on the shelves after the shelf fitting is complete and secure, as loading the shelves before installation would be unsafe and impractical.
The window seat must be built around or against the window frame; the frame must be in place to properly align and secure the seat.
The structural framing of the wall and window opening must be completed to provide support for the window seat.
Any electrical outlets or wiring planned near or within the window seat area must be roughed in before the seat is built, to avoid needing to cut into the finished seat later.
Trim around the window seat, such as baseboards or decorative molding, must be applied after the seat structure is in place to ensure proper fit and finish.
Final painting or staining of the window seat and surrounding wall area should occur after installation to achieve a seamless, finished appearance.

The window lintel is typically installed directly above the window frame to support the masonry above. The window frame must be in place first to ensure the lintel is positioned at the correct height and alignment.
The wall construction up to the window sill level must be completed before the lintel can be placed, as the lintel sits above the window opening and requires the lower wall to be built.
The lintel must be installed and set (with proper bearing) before masonry above can be built, as the lintel provides the structural support for the wall above the window opening.
The lintel creates the structural opening header; the window unit can only be installed after the lintel is in place and the opening is fully formed with structural support at the top.
The lintel must be installed and any associated mortar/structural work completed before interior finishing can be applied around the window opening.
The window arch is a structural component within a wall; the wall must be built up to the window level to provide support and an opening for the arch.
The rough opening for the window must be framed before the arch can be constructed or installed above or around the window opening.
The window arch forms part of the structural or decorative surround for the window; the window unit itself is typically installed after the arch is in place to ensure proper fit and support.
Finishing work such as plastering or applying decorative coatings to the arch must occur after the arch is fully constructed and set.
Painting of the arch and surrounding wall area typically follows arch completion, though this is a workflow preference rather than a strict structural necessity.
Windows must be installed first so that backing/blocking can be placed around them to secure and insulate the window frames.
The rough frame openings for windows must be constructed before any backing or blocking material can be added around the window perimeters.
Backing/blocking provides a nailing surface and structural support; exterior sheathing is installed over the backing to close the wall assembly.
Backing/blocking around windows must be in place before interior drywall can be installed, as the drywall butts against the window framing and requires a solid backing surface.
Insulation around windows is installed after backing/blocking is complete, as the blocking creates the cavity and support for insulation material.
The window frame provides the structural support and mounting surface for the drip edge; the drip edge must be installed on or around the frame to direct water away.
The drip edge must be in place before siding is installed so that the siding can overlap the drip edge, ensuring water is directed away from the window and preventing moisture intrusion.

Drip edge installation is part of the window waterproofing system; final flashing and sealant work around the window typically occurs after the drip edge is in place to create a continuous water barrier.
Interior trim can proceed once the window unit and exterior weatherproofing (including drip edge) are complete, though this is a logical sequence rather than a strict physical constraint.
The weather barrier and sheathing behind the window area must be installed before the drip edge to provide the underlying waterproof layer that the drip edge integrates with.
The window frame must be installed first to provide a fixed structural opening and anchor points for securing the security bar or grille.
The wall structure surrounding the window must be in place to define the opening and provide support for mounting the security bar/grille.
Access to the window area for welding, bolting, or fastening the security bar/grille must be completed before interior finishes are applied to avoid damage and allow proper installation.

While typically the glass is installed before the grille for exterior-mounted grilles, if the grille is interior-mounted, the glass should be installed first. However, as a soft preference, the grille is often installed after glazing to avoid obstructing glass placement.

successor: Final Inspection and Security System Testing
rationale: The security bar/grille must be fully installed and secured before final inspection and testing of security measures can be completed.
Power and control wiring must be run to the window location before the control device can be connected and terminated.
The device must be in place before final sealing and weatherproofing around the window to ensure a continuous air and water barrier.
The control device must be installed to enable functional testing of window opening/closing operations and integration with building management systems.
Installing the control device before interior trim and finishes allows access for adjustment, though it could be done after with careful planning; considered a soft preference for convenience.
The wall framing must be completed to provide a structural surface to which the window blind/shutter housing is attached.
Windows must be installed to define the opening and provide reference points for mounting blind/shutter hardware around the window frame.
Blind/shutter housing must be in place before wall finishing so that the housing can be integrated into the finished wall surface and trimmed properly.
If motorized blinds or electrical connections are required, the housing must be installed to allow routing of wiring before final wall closure.
It is preferred to install the blind/shutter housing before trim so that trim can be cut and fitted around the housing for a clean finish.
Window Boxing/Pelmet is fitted around the window frame, so the window must first be installed and in place for the boxing/pelmet to be properly measured, built, and attached.
The wall structure and framing must be complete to provide a substrate for attaching the window boxing/pelmet, which mounts to the wall surrounding the window.
If the pelmet is designed to house concealed lighting, electrical wiring should be roughed-in before the pelmet is installed to avoid having to retrofit wiring behind it.
The window boxing/pelmet must be installed and jointed/stopped before final painting or wall finishing can be applied, so that the boxing/pelmet is painted as part of the overall finish.
The pelmet provides a housing or mounting surface for curtains or blinds, so it must be fully installed before curtain tracks, rods, or blinds can be fitted.
The window frame must be installed first to provide the structural support and mounting surface for the fanlight component.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the fanlight can be installed.
Weatherproofing around the window opening must be applied prior to fanlight installation to ensure proper sealing and moisture protection.
The fanlight frame must be in place before glass panels can be installed into it.
Interior trim work around the fanlight is typically done after installation for aesthetic finish, though it can be done concurrently in some cases.
The structural steel frame must be erected to provide the supporting structure onto which the window deflection / spandrel panels are installed.
Concrete slabs provide the floor-to-floor separation and structural support needed before spandrel panels can be mounted between floors.
Spandrel panels are installed first as they form the opaque infill between vision glass; window/glazing units are then installed adjacent to or on top of the spandrel framing.
After spandrel panels are in place, all perimeter joints and interfaces require sealant application to ensure the building envelope is watertight and air-sealed.

successor: Interior Finishes (drywall/plaster adjacent to window openings)
rationale: Interior finishes near window openings are typically completed after spandrel panels and windows are installed to ensure proper alignment and to avoid damage to finished surfaces.
Dormer windows are structural components that are integrated into the roof framing. The roof structure must be framed and opened up to accept the dormer before the dormer window can be installed.
The roof decking provides the structural base and opening for the dormer. The dormer window sits within or on top of the roof deck, so sheathing must be in place first.
Flashing is installed around the dormer window to seal the joint between the window and the roof. It must be applied after the dormer window is in place to ensure a watertight seal.
The exterior siding and trim that integrates the dormer into the roof finish must be applied after the dormer window is installed to cover the edges and provide a finished appearance.

successor: Interior Drywall & Finishing of Dormer Walls
rationale: The interior surfaces of the dormer, including drywall, insulation, and finishing, can only be completed after the dormer window structure and glazing are in place to enclose the space.

A structural assessment must be completed before cutting into walls to enlarge or resize a window opening, to determine if the wall is load-bearing and identify required lintels or structural supports.
Interior finishes, drywall, and any obstructions must be removed from the area around the window opening before the structural modification can begin.
Exterior cladding, siding, or finishes around the existing window must be removed to expose the wall structure before enlarging the opening.
After the opening is enlarged, a new lintel or structural header must be installed above the opening to support the load above and ensure structural integrity.

successor: Window Framing and Rough Opening Adjustment
rationale: The rough opening framing (studs, sill, king studs, cripples) must be constructed to the new dimensions after the opening is cut and before the new window is installed.
The new window of the enlarged size can only be installed after the opening has been cut to the correct dimensions and the rough framing is complete.
After the rough opening is created, weatherproofing membranes, flashing, and sealing must be applied to protect the building envelope before the final window is placed.
The window operator/actuator must be mounted onto or within the window frame; the frame provides the structural support and attachment points for the operator mechanism.
The actuator mechanism often connects to and operates the window sash or glass panel; the glass must be in place to align and secure the operator.
The actuator must be physically installed so that electrical connections (power and control cables) can be terminated at its terminals.
Testing of opening/closing or automated operation cannot be performed until the actuator is installed and connected.
Integration with the BMS for automated control is typically done after the actuator hardware is in place, though this could be considered a soft preference if BMS setup can be parallelized.

The window sunshade/brise-soleil is typically mounted on or anchored to the structural framework (columns, slabs, or beams). The structure must be in place to provide a stable mounting surface and load path.

predecessor: Exterior wall cladding / Facade system installed
rationale: The brise-soleil is often integrated with or attached to the exterior wall/facade system. The wall cladding must be installed to provide the correct alignment and anchoring points for the sunshade brackets or supports.

The brise-soleil is positioned in relation to window openings to provide shading. Windows must be installed so that the sunshade can be correctly aligned relative to the glazing for optimal solar control and to avoid interference.
It is a soft preference to complete painting after sunshade installation to avoid painting around the brise-soleil elements, though painting could be done beforehand with careful masking.

Scaffolding is often used to access the facade for brise-soleil installation. The sunshade elements must be fully installed and secured before scaffolding can be dismantled, as re-erecting scaffolding would be costly and unsafe.
Fire barriers (such as fire-rated walls, floors, or partitions) rely on the structural framework to be in place to be supported and anchored properly.
Fire barriers must be installed before MEP rough-in work because penetrations for pipes, ducts, and conduits must be fire-stopped and sealed properly through the fire-rated assembly.
Firestopping is applied around penetrations through fire barriers; the barrier must be in place before the sealing can be performed.
While insulation can sometimes be placed concurrently, typically fire barriers in walls are finished before cavity insulation is installed to ensure continuity and fire rating integrity.
Fire barrier assemblies (e.g., fire-rated walls) must be fully erected before final interior finishes such as cladding, paint, or wall coverings are applied.
Fire dampers are installed within HVAC ductwork to seal off ducts in case of fire; ductwork must be in place before dampers can be mounted inside.
Fire dampers must be installed and properly seated before the ductwork system can be tested for air leakage and damper operation.
Fire dampers are critical fire-rated assemblies; their proper installation must be verified before the fire resistance rating of the compartment can be inspected and approved.
Fire dampers need to be accessible for inspection and testing before ceilings are closed up; finishing work can only proceed after damper installation and sign-off.
Fire dampers are installed in walls and floor-ceiling assemblies that must first be framed and constructed to provide the mounting structure and fire-rated barrier.
Structural steel provides the framework for hanging sprinkler pipes; piping cannot be installed without the overhead support structure in place.
Although sprinkler piping is often installed before ceiling grids are fully closed, having the grid layout helps coordinate sprinkler head locations; this is a soft preference for better alignment.
