The piping system must be fully installed before it can be pressure-tested to check for leaks.
Sprinkler piping is typically installed above the ceiling; finished ceilings cannot be closed until piping is in place.

Fire alarm devices (smoke detectors, pull stations, notification appliances) require electrical power and control wiring; commissioning cannot proceed without the infrastructure being installed and energized.
The fire alarm control panel (FACP) is the central brain of the system and must be physically installed, powered, and connected to initiate testing and commissioning.
Authorities having jurisdiction (AHJ) require a successfully commissioned and tested fire alarm system before issuing a certificate of occupancy or final building approval.
The fire alarm system must be commissioned and operational before it can be integrated and tested with other life safety systems (e.g., elevator recall, smoke control, sprinkler monitoring).
While not a strict physical constraint, commissioning is typically performed before final ceiling tile installation to allow access to ceiling-mounted devices for adjustment and troubleshooting.
The rough opening dimensions and condition must be verified to ensure they meet fire-rated assembly requirements before the fire door can be fitted.

predecessor: Masonry or drywall work around opening
rationale: Wall construction surrounding the door opening must be completed so that the fire door assembly can be properly sealed and integrated into the fire-rated barrier.

successor: Fire door hardware installation (closers, latches, hinges)
rationale: Fire-rated hardware must be mounted on the door itself after the door is hung in the frame; installing hardware on an uninstalled door is not practical.
Intumescent seals and smoke gaskets are applied around the perimeter of the installed door to maintain the fire rating integrity of the assembly.
Firestop sealing must be applied after all mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins are completed and approved, as firestops seal penetrations made by these trades.
Firestop must be applied before walls and ceilings are closed/ finished, as firestops seal penetrations that would become inaccessible after drywall is installed.
Firestop application must be complete and visible for inspection before the fire safety inspection can verify code compliance.
While painting is typically done after firestopping, this is a logical sequence preference to avoid contaminating fresh firestop or requiring touch-ups, but not a physical necessity.
The banquette must sit on a level, finished floor to ensure stability, proper alignment, and to avoid rocking or uneven seating surfaces.
Wall framing must be complete so the banquette can be securely anchored to the wall studs for structural support.
Any wiring for integrated lighting or outlets behind or within the banquette must be roughed in before enclosing with the banquette structure.
Baseboard, crown molding, and trim around the banquette must be installed after the banquette is in place to create clean transitions and a finished look.
Custom seat cushions and backrest upholstery are measured and fitted to the actual installed banquette frame to ensure precise fit and proper coverage.
The fixed dining table must be anchored to the finished floor; flooring must be completed to provide a level, stable surface and to avoid damaging the floor during installation.
Walls must be framed, finished, and painted before installing a fixed dining table that may be attached to or positioned against walls.
Any electrical outlets, junction boxes, or wiring for lighting above the dining area must be roughed in before the table is permanently installed, as the table may obstruct access.
Once the fixed dining table is installed, any final touch-up painting, trim work, or sealing around the table base can be completed to ensure a clean finish.
Overhead lighting fixtures (e.g., chandeliers or pendants) should be hung after the table is positioned to ensure proper alignment and centering above the table.
The floor must be installed and finished before placing any fixed furniture such as dining chairs or stools, as the chairs need a stable, completed surface to be positioned and secured on.
Walls should be finished to avoid dust, paint splatters, or damage to the furniture during wall work, and to allow proper positioning of chairs relative to finished wall surfaces.
Fixed dining chairs or stools are typically placed first to establish exact positioning and spacing, before installing or positioning the dining table to ensure proper alignment and clearance.
While it is easier to place a rug before chairs, if the chairs are fixed in place, the rug can be worked around them; this is a soft preference for cleaner installation.

Electrical wiring and outlet installation must be completed before any fixed furniture is placed, to avoid blocking access to outlets and to ensure all electrical work is done before furniture obstructs the workspace.
The sneeze guard/food shield is typically mounted onto or attached to the countertop, so the countertop must be in place first to provide a stable mounting surface.
The sneeze guard must be installed before placing food items underneath it to ensure proper coverage and hygiene protection.
Health and safety inspections require the sneeze guard to be fully installed to verify compliance with food safety regulations before the serving area can be approved for use.
Wall mounting brackets for some sneeze guards require finished walls (framing and drywall) for proper attachment and support.
The sneeze guard is a required food safety barrier; food service cannot commence without it being in place per health codes.
The tray slide or tray rail must be installed onto the assembled frame or drawer frame; the frame structure provides the mounting surface and structural support for the slide/rail component.
The tray or drawer bottom sits on or is guided by the tray slide/rail; the slide/rail must be in place to support and allow movement of the tray/drawer bottom.

The drawer front or face is attached to the drawer box which rides on the tray slide/rail; the slide/rail system must be installed first to ensure proper alignment and sliding function of the drawer front.
The cabinet body provides the structural enclosure and side panels onto which tray slides/rails are mounted; the cabinet must be assembled before internal components like slides can be installed.

After installing the tray slide/rail, fine-tuning and alignment of the sliding mechanism may be performed to ensure smooth operation; this is a soft preference as adjustment can be done later but is best performed immediately after installation to avoid rework.
Ductwork must be installed to deliver conditioned air before diffusers/vents can be attached to the duct system.
The ceiling grid or structure that supports the diffuser/vent must be in place before the diffuser can be mounted.
Diffusers/vents should be installed before ceiling finish is applied so that the finish can be cut and trimmed around the diffuser for a clean appearance.

successor: Dining Area HVAC System Balancing & Commissioning
rationale: All diffusers must be installed and in place before the HVAC system can be balanced and commissioned to ensure proper airflow measurement and adjustment.
While diffusers are typically installed before painting for a clean finish, this is a soft preference as painting could be done around installed diffusers with careful masking.
Wall framing must be completed to provide the structural backing onto which the wainscot and chair rail are installed.
Electrical wiring and outlet boxes must be in place behind the wall before wainscot is installed to avoid damaging finished woodwork.
Insulation must be placed inside wall cavities before enclosing them with wainscot or other wall finishes.
Wainscot and chair rail installation must be complete before final paint or wallcovering is applied to adjacent wall surfaces.
Chair rail and wainscot are installed before base molding so that base trim can meet the completed wainscot paneling seamlessly.
The floor must be finished and leveled before placing a heavy service station to ensure stability and proper alignment.
Wall finishes (tiling, painting, or paneling) behind the service station must be completed as the station will be placed against or near walls, making access difficult afterwards.
Electrical wiring and outlets for the service station's power needs must be roughed-in before the station is installed, as the station will cover or block access to wall electrical points.
Water supply and drainage lines for the service station's sink or plumbing fixtures must be roughed-in before the station is positioned and connected.
After the service station is set in place, any adjacent countertops or surfaces that abut or integrate with the station must be installed to complete the continuous work surface.
Once the station is in its final position, the sink and plumbing fixtures can be connected to the roughed-in supply and drain lines.
After the station is installed, final electrical connections (e.g., power for refrigeration, dispensers, or lighting within the station) can be completed.
The service station should be fully installed and connected before the final inspection and commissioning of the food service area to verify all systems are operational.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical wiring for dining area
rationale: The electrical and data cables must be routed and in place before the outlet can be installed and connected.
If the outlet is floor-mounted, the floor surface or at least the subfloor must be ready to receive and secure the outlet box and cover.

successor: Wall/floor finishing (paint, trim, or final floor covering)
rationale: The outlet must be installed so that finishes can be cut neatly around it and the outlet cover can be flush-mounted without damaging finished surfaces.

successor: Electrical trim-out and connection to breaker panel
rationale: The outlet box must be mounted and the wiring pulled before final connections to the branch circuit are made at the panel.

successor: Furniture placement and dining table setup
rationale: It is convenient but not strictly required to have the outlet installed before the dining table is positioned, as the outlet location is planned to serve the table.

Electrical wiring and junction boxes must be installed before ceiling treatment is applied, as the acoustic ceiling will cover and conceal these elements, making access difficult or impossible after installation.
HVAC ductwork, diffusers, and grilles must be roughed-in before ceiling treatment to ensure proper integration and avoid cutting or damaging acoustic panels after installation.
Any plumbing pipes, sprinkler heads, or fire suppression lines in the ceiling plenum must be installed and tested before acoustic ceiling work begins.
Wall framing must be complete to establish the perimeter support and enclosure for the ceiling system, ensuring proper alignment and attachment of acoustic ceiling components.

Acoustic ceiling panels must be installed before final finishes such as painting, trim work, and cleanup can occur, as the ceiling is considered a 'top-down' element that should precede floor and wall finishes.
While not a strict physical requirement, installing the ceiling before flooring is a best practice to prevent dust, debris, and accidental damage to finished flooring from overhead work.
The subfloor or underlayment provides a level, stable base for the banquette framing. Framing cannot be installed directly on open joists or an uneven surface.
Electrical wiring that will run within or behind the banquette must be roughed in before the framing is installed, as the framing will enclose and block access to the wall/floor cavities.

predecessor: Complete Rough-In Plumbing (if applicable for banquette area)
rationale: Any plumbing lines that need to pass through the banquette area must be installed before the framing covers them up.

The plywood or paneling substrate is attached directly onto the framing to create the solid surface for the banquette. The framing must be fully built to provide the structure to receive the substrate.

successor: Install Dining Banquette Seat Cushion/Seat Base
rationale: The seat base or cushion support platform is installed on top of the completed framing. The framing must be in place to support the seat structure.
Fixed dining tables must be installed on top of finished flooring, not before it, to ensure proper alignment and stability.
Electrical rough-in (wiring, conduit, outlets) must be completed before fixed dining tables are installed because tables may block access to walls and floors for electrical work.
Plumbing rough-in must be completed before fixed dining tables are installed because tables may obstruct access to plumbing lines in floors or walls.
Painting and wall finishing must be completed before installing fixed dining tables to avoid paint splatter, dust, or damage to the tables, and because tables would obstruct wall access.

While some lighting can be installed before tables, final placement of pendant lights or chandeliers above dining tables is often best aligned after tables are in place to ensure proper centering and spacing.
The subfloor must be clean, level, and dry before any flooring can be installed to ensure proper adhesion and a finished surface.
Underlayment (e.g., moisture barrier, soundproofing, or padding) must be laid down prior to the final flooring material to protect the floor and meet manufacturer requirements.

Any rough-in work behind walls or beneath the floor (e.g., wiring, pipes, ductwork) must be finished before flooring is installed to avoid damaging the finished floor or requiring costly removal later.
Baseboards and trim are installed after flooring to cover the expansion gap and create a finished look, as well as to avoid damaging trim during floor installation.
While painting is ideally done before flooring to avoid drips, final touch-up painting on walls is often performed after flooring is laid to fix any marks made during installation.
Electrical rough-in (running wires, installing junction boxes, and switches) must be completed before any lighting fixtures are installed, as the fixtures need to connect to the existing wiring.
The ceiling surface or grid must be in place to provide a mounting surface and support for the lighting fixtures.
Ceiling finishing should be done before installing lighting fixtures to avoid damaging finished fixtures during painting and to allow for clean paint lines around fixtures.

successor: Install Light Bulbs and Test Fixtures
rationale: The fixture housing and wiring connections must be installed and secured before bulbs can be placed and the system tested for functionality.
While not a strict physical requirement, installing lighting first provides better illumination for the floor finishing work, and prevents dust/debris from floor work from settling on new fixtures.
Electrical and data rough-in work must be completed in walls or counters before sneeze guards and service counters are installed, as the latter would cover or block access to those wall/floor areas.
Plumbing rough-ins for sinks or service areas must be completed before counters are installed, since the countertops will cover plumbing lines and cannot be easily removed later.
While flooring can be installed before counters, it is preferable to finish flooring after counter installation to avoid damaging finished floors during heavy counter placement.
Sneeze guards and service counters are part of the millwork package; adjacent millwork and trim pieces are installed after the main counter units are set in place to ensure proper fit and alignment.

Final connections to fixtures (e.g., lighting for sneeze guards, plumbing for service counters) must occur after the counters are physically installed, as the fixtures are mounted on or through the counters.
The tray slide/rail system must be physically attached to mounting brackets or rough-in hardware that is already secured to the structure; otherwise there is no support for the rails.
Overhead structural elements (e.g., ceiling grid, framing) must be in place before rail systems are installed, because the rails are mounted to or suspended from the structure.
While not physically mandatory, it is best practice to finish major above-ceiling rough-ins (ductwork, piping, conduit) before installing tray slides to avoid conflicts and rework.

successor: Install Cable Trays / Wire Management on Rails
rationale: Cable trays or wire management components physically rest on or attach to the slide/rail system, so the rails must be in place first.

successor: Pull and Route Cables Through Trays
rationale: Cables are laid into the tray system after the tray slides/rails are installed; installing cables beforehand would prevent proper tray assembly and securing.
The area where the workstation will be placed must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any workstation components can be brought in or assembled.
A solid, cured floor or foundation is required to support the workstation's weight and provide a stable base for anchoring.
Electrical conduits, data cabling, and compressed air lines must be roughed in and available at the workstation location before final connection and installation.
The workstation must be fully installed and connected before it can be powered on, tested, and commissioned for operation.
Final hookups of electrical power, network cables, and other utilities must occur after the workstation is physically positioned and secured.

predecessor: Pour and Cure Concrete Floor Slab
rationale: The concrete slab foundation must be poured, leveled, and cured before any framing can begin, as the framing for the dining nook rests directly on the slab.
Rough-in electrical wiring, outlets, and any plumbing lines that will run through the dining nook walls or floor must be installed before the framing is closed up, to avoid costly rework.

Flooring installation typically occurs after framing and finishing is complete, as the subfloor must be fully framed and the walls built before finished flooring can be installed up to the base of the walls.

successor: Prime and Paint Walls in Dining Nook
rationale: Painting must follow drywall finishing (which follows framing), as paint requires a finished, taped, and mudded drywall surface to adhere properly.
HVAC diffusers are the terminal units of ductwork; the duct system must be in place to supply conditioned air to the diffuser.
The ceiling grid or support structure must be installed to provide a mounting point for the diffuser and to establish its location within the finished ceiling.
Ceiling tiles and finishes are installed after the diffuser is mounted so that the diffuser can be properly integrated and aligned with the ceiling plane.
Diffusers must be in place and connected to the duct system before air balancing and commissioning can measure and adjust airflow at each terminal.
While not a physical necessity, final inspections typically occur after diffusers are installed to ensure proper finish and integration with ceiling systems.
The rough opening (window frame and structural support) must be built and squared before any window unit can be installed, as the window sits within this opening.

predecessor: Install Weather Resistive Barrier (WRB) / House Wrap
rationale: The weather-resistive barrier must be in place behind and around the window opening to provide waterproofing and drainage before the window is set, preventing moisture intrusion behind the unit.
Flashing and exterior trim are applied after the window is set to seal the joint between the window frame and the weather-resistive barrier, ensuring water tightness.
Interior drywall and finishes around the window are installed after the window is in place so that the drywall can be cut to fit snugly against the window frame and properly taped and finished.
Interior casing and trim are installed after the window unit is set and secured, as they cover the gap between the window frame and the interior wall finish.
The door frame provides the structural support and mounting surface for the door; the door cannot be hung without the frame in place.
Walls define the doorway opening and must be finished to the correct dimensions before the door unit can be installed.
Flooring must be completed so the door clearance and bottom gap are correctly measured from the finished floor level.
Hardware components are attached directly onto the installed door slab and cannot be properly fitted before the door is hung.
It is easier to paint walls and install trim without the door in the way, but it is a soft preference as painting can be done around the door if needed.
Wall framing provides the structural support and cavity within which electrical and data outlet boxes are mounted.
Electrical and data cables must be run through the walls before the outlet boxes and receptacles can be installed and terminated.
The junction boxes or low-voltage brackets must be secured to the studs before the actual outlet receptacle, switch, or data jack can be inserted and wired.

While outlet boxes are installed before drywall, the final outlet receptacles, cover plates, and data jacks are typically installed after drywall and painting are complete to avoid damage from finishing work.
Installing the outlet devices (receptacles, switches, data jacks) and cover plates is part of the final electrical trim-out which must happen after rough-in and wall finishing.
Built-in storage units typically rest on finished flooring; installing flooring first ensures the unit sits on a level, complete surface and avoids damaging the floor with heavy cabinetry.
Built-in storage units need to be anchored to stable, finished walls; wall framing and drywall must be completed to provide a proper backing and finished appearance.
Wiring for outlets or lighting that will be inside or behind the storage unit must be roughed in before the unit is built in place, to avoid having to cut into or move the completed unit later.

While painting can be done before installation, typically painting the walls behind and around the unit is completed after the built-in is installed to ensure seamless trim and color matching without drips on the unit.
If the built-in unit includes or supports a countertop (e.g., a built-in desk or cabinet), the countertop cannot be installed until the base unit is securely in place.
The desk seating must be placed on a finished floor slab to provide a stable, level foundation.
Electrical wiring and outlets for the integrated desk system must be roughed in before the desks are installed to avoid rework.
Data and communication cabling for the desks must be run beneath the floor before desk placement.
Once desks are installed, final floor finishing, wall touch-ups, and clean-up can be completed around the fixed seating.
It is preferable to complete desk installation before final adjustments to overhead lighting diffusers and HVAC diffuser placement to ensure alignment with workstations.
Privacy booths need a finished, level floor slab to be installed on, as they are standalone structures placed on the floor.
Power outlets and data cabling needed for the booth's ventilation, lighting, and electronics must be roughed in before the booth is placed to allow proper connection.
While painting can be done around the booth, it's preferred to install the booth first to avoid damage to finished surfaces and ensure proper fit against walls.
The booth's electrical components (lights, fans, USB ports) must be physically installed before electricians can make final connections and energize the system.

Electrical wiring, outlets, switches, and plumbing pipes must be roughed-in within wall cavities before partition framing and drywall are installed, as accessing these systems after partition installation would require destructive demolition.

Ceiling grids and overhead structural elements are typically installed before partitions so that partitions can be aligned with and terminated at the ceiling, and to avoid working around completed partitions when installing overhead systems.
The floor surface must be level, cured, and properly prepared (including any floor markings or track layout) before partition tracks can be anchored to the slab.

After partition framing is installed, MEP trades can run their final connections (e.g., wiring to switches/outlets in walls, plumbing to fixtures mounted on partitions) through the open stud cavities before drywall is applied.
The partition framing (studs, tracks, headers) must be fully erected and inspected before drywall sheets can be hung, taped, and finished to enclose the wall system.

Electrical wiring, conduit, and junction boxes must be installed in the ceiling plenum before the ceiling grid and tiles are installed, as they would be inaccessible or require removal of the finished ceiling.

HVAC ductwork, diffusers, and mechanical systems in the ceiling plenum must be installed and tested before the suspended ceiling is placed, as the ceiling conceals these systems and would block access.
Plumbing pipes, fire sprinkler lines, and drain lines routed above the ceiling must be installed and pressure-tested before ceiling installation to avoid costly demolition and rework.

Suspended ceiling grid provides the structural support and positioning framework for recessed or surface-mounted lighting fixtures; the grid must be in place before fixtures can be securely installed and wired.
The suspended ceiling grid system (main tees, cross tees, and hanger wires) must be fully installed and leveled before ceiling tiles or finish panels can be laid into the grid.
Lighting fixtures must be physically installed before lighting controls can be commissioned, as commissioning involves testing and verifying the controls operate the installed fixtures.
All lighting control hardware (sensors, dimmers, switches, control panels) must be installed and wired before commissioning can test their functionality and programming.
Electrical power and control wiring must be fully run, terminated, and energized before commissioning can verify control sequences and communication.
Base commissioning of installed controls must be completed before final programming adjustments and integration with BMS or building automation systems can be fully verified.

Commissioning of lighting controls must be completed before occupancy or functional testing, because the control system needs to be verified as operational to properly test lighting performance under real conditions.
The kitchen island must be installed on top of finished flooring to ensure proper fit and alignment.
Electrical wiring for island outlets or appliances must be run through the floor before the island is placed and secured.
If the island includes a sink or dishwasher, water supply and drain lines must be roughed in beneath the floor before the island is installed.
The island base must be fully installed and secured before the countertop can be fabricated and placed on top.
It is easier to install drawer pulls and handles after the island is in place, though this could technically be done before if preferred.
A stable foundation is required before any counter preparation can begin to ensure structural integrity and proper alignment.
The building's structural frame must be in place to support the walls and areas where the preparation counter will be installed.
Electrical wiring for outlets and appliances near the counter must be roughed in before counter installation to allow proper access and avoid rework.
Plumbing rough-ins for sinks and fixtures must be completed before counter installation to ensure proper connections and avoid damaging the counter.
While not physically mandatory, finishing walls before counter installation prevents damage to the counter from dust, debris, and construction activities.
The preparation counter base must be fully assembled and installed before the countertop can be placed on top of it.
Sinks and fixtures are typically mounted into or onto the preparation counter, requiring the counter to be in place first.
Final painting and touch-ups around the counter area are best done after counter installation to ensure clean edges and seamless finishes.
The ventilation hood must connect to ductwork to exhaust air, so ductwork must be installed first.
The hood requires electrical power for the fan and lights; electrical wiring must be in place before final connection.
The hood is mounted to the wall or ceiling structure; framing and drywall must be completed to provide a mounting surface.
After the hood is physically installed, the duct connection to the exterior vent can be finalized and sealed.
The hood must be in place before the electrician can make final wiring connections and test fan/lights operation.
Wall framing provides the structural support and mounting surface for kitchen cabinets.
Plumbing pipes for sink and water lines must be in place before cabinets are installed, as cabinets may conceal or need to be fitted around these pipes.
Electrical wiring, outlets, and switch boxes must be roughed in before cabinets are mounted, as cabinets will cover wall areas and wiring needs to be accessible.
Countertops are installed on top of and supported by the base cabinets; cabinets must be in place and leveled before countertops can be measured, cut, and set.
Cabinetry defines the layout and openings for built-in appliances (e.g., range, refrigerator, dishwasher); appliances are fitted into or adjacent to cabinets after they are installed.
Electrical wiring must be roughed in behind walls before cabinets are installed, as cabinets would block access to walls and wiring.
Plumbing rough-ins (water supply and drain lines) must be completed before cabinets are installed, as cabinets would block wall access for plumbing work.
Range hood ventilation ductwork must be roughed in the ceiling/walls before cabinets are installed, since cabinets would obstruct access.
Countertops are installed directly on top of base cabinets, so the cabinets must be in place first to support and align the countertops.
The cooktop or range is typically installed into or adjacent to the cabinetry, so cabinets must be in place first to provide support and proper fit.
Countertops must be installed on top of and supported by the base cabinets. The cabinets provide the structural foundation and mounting surface for the countertops.
Plumbing rough-ins for sinks and fixtures must be in place before countertops are installed, as the countertop will be cut to accommodate sink openings and plumbing access.
Electrical wiring for outlets, lighting, and appliances that will be mounted in or above the countertop must be roughed in before the countertop is placed, as access behind/underneath may be blocked.
The sink and faucet are mounted into or onto the countertop after it is secured in place. The countertop provides the supporting surface and cutout for sink installation.
The backsplash is installed after the countertop because the backsplash sits on top of or abuts the countertop surface, and the countertop edge provides the reference line for backsplash placement.
Gas and water supply lines must be roughed in and terminated at the appliance locations before stoves, ovens, and dishwashers can be installed.
Electrical circuits, outlets, and switch boxes must be wired and ready to connect to cooking appliances such as ranges, ovens, and cooktops.
Range hood ductwork must be installed and routed to the exterior before the hood or downdraft system can be mounted and connected.
After appliances are positioned, final connections of gas lines, water lines (e.g., for ovens with steam functions or pot fillers), and drain lines can be made.

Cooktops and drop-in ranges must be set into countertop cutouts, so the countertop must be installed first; however, in some sequences the appliance is installed after the countertop cutout is prepared. Typically, cooktops are installed after countertops are in place, but standalone ranges and ovens can be slid into place before or after counters.
The ventilation hood must be mounted to a finished ceiling structure; framing provides the necessary support and enclosure for ductwork.
The hood requires electrical power; wiring must be run and outlet boxes installed before the hood can be connected.
The hood must be connected to exhaust ducting; ducts must be in place before the hood is mounted and attached.
Ventilation hoods are typically installed before upper cabinets to allow access for mounting, duct connection, and wiring.
While the hood can be installed after drywall, it is preferable to complete surface finishes before mounting fixtures to avoid damage and rework.
Electrical rough-in wiring must be completed before lighting fixtures can be installed, as the wiring provides the power source and must be run behind walls and ceilings first.
Ceiling finishing must be done before installing recessed or surface-mounted lighting fixtures to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to allow proper mounting.

successor: Install Light Bulbs and Test Fixtures
rationale: Light bulbs and final testing can only occur after the lighting fixtures are physically installed and connected.

While lighting can be installed before final painting, it is often preferred to complete painting first to avoid getting paint on fixtures, but this is a sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
Lighting is typically installed after cabinets and countertops to ensure proper alignment and positioning of task lighting over cooking areas.
The side/end tables need to be integrated into the frame structure, so the main frame must be assembled first to provide the structural support and attachment points.
The side/end tables are integrated into the furniture frame; upholstery and cushions are installed after the tables are in place to avoid interference and ensure proper fit.
Final assembly and finishing touches occur after all major components including the integrated tables are installed to complete the product.
The structural steel framing must be in place to provide the primary support structure onto which fixed auditorium seating platforms and terraces are mounted.
A level concrete slab or subfloor is required as the base substrate for installing fixed seating rows and anchoring systems.
Underslab or in-wall conduit for seat lighting, power outlets, or accessibility devices must be roughed in before seating is installed to avoid costly rework.
Final flooring around and between seating rows must be completed after seating is fixed in place to ensure proper alignment and seamless transitions.
While painting can be done before seating is installed, final touch-up painting and wall finishes near seating are typically performed after installation to avoid damage during seating placement.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical and data cabling at reception area
rationale: Electrical outlets, data ports, and cabling for computer systems and lighting must be roughed in behind the wall before the desk structure is installed to avoid rework.

successor: Finish electrical and data connections at desk
rationale: Final wiring terminations, outlet covers, and device connections can only be completed after the desk framework is in place.
Flooring (tile, carpet, or other finish) must be installed before placing the heavy desk to allow seamless installation and avoid damage.

successor: Paint and finish walls at reception
rationale: It is easier to paint the wall behind the desk before the desk is installed, but if needed, touch-ups can be done after; thus a soft preference.

successor: Install decorative countertop and front panels
rationale: The base frame of the desk must be securely in place before adding the final decorative countertop and aesthetic panels that sit on top.
The Modular Platform/Deck Base requires a stable, load-bearing foundation or substructure to be completed first. Without a prepared foundation, the platform cannot be placed or leveled correctly.
Proper site grading and drainage systems must be installed before the deck base to prevent water accumulation and ensure long-term stability of the platform.
Utility rough-ins can be done before or after, but pre-running below-deck utilities before placing the deck base avoids costly overhead work and improves access.
The modular superstructure/frame must be erected on top of a completed deck base, as the deck provides the reference surface and load distribution for the frame.
Waterproofing and sealing cannot be applied until the deck base is fully installed and cured, as it must be applied to the completed surface.
Electrical rough-in wiring must be completed within walls/ceilings before outlet boxes and devices can be installed, as the wiring needs to be in place to connect to the outlets.
Wall surfaces (drywall, paneling, etc.) must be installed and finished before outlets can be mounted flush into the wall.
Outlets must be physically installed before they can be connected to branch circuits and tested for power and data continuity.
Outlet installation must be complete to allow final cover plates and aesthetic trim to be fitted over the outlet openings.
All power and data outlets must be in place before the final inspection and commissioning of the electrical and data systems can be performed.
The structural frame must be in place to provide the physical support and attachment points for railing and guardrail systems.
Railing and guardrails are typically mounted onto finished decks, slabs, or floor edges, so these surfaces must be installed first.
Guardrails and railings are critical safety components that must be in place and verified before the area can be certified as safe for occupancy or use.
While it is easier to paint walls before railings are installed, touch-up painting and finishing near railing attachments can also be done after installation, so this is a soft preference.
Guardrails along stairs and ramps are safety requirements that must be installed before those circulation elements are considered complete and usable.
Stringers provide the structural support and angle for stairs; treads must be installed onto already-positioned stringers.
The rough opening and stairwell framing must be complete to define the space where steps/treads are installed.
Handrails are mounted after treads are in place to ensure proper alignment and code-compliant height relative to the finished walking surface.
Finish trim, nosing, and aesthetic treatments are applied after the structural treads are securely installed.
A completed subfloor provides the level base and support structure needed to frame and install stair stringers and treads.

Wall framing must be completed to provide the structural support system for mounting acoustic panels. Rough-in utilities (electrical, data) must be in place before panels are installed as they would be inaccessible behind the finished acoustic surface.

successor: Painting and Finishing of Adjacent Surfaces
rationale: Typically painting of adjacent walls/ceilings is done before acoustic panel installation to avoid overspray on the specialized acoustic fabric/finish. However, if panels are pre-finished, touch-up painting can be done after, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.

Acoustic backdrop panels are often installed behind stage/performance areas where seating rows are placed. Seating installation must wait until acoustic panel work is complete to allow unobstructed access for panel installation and to prevent damage to installed panels from scaffolding or equipment used during seating setup.

Acoustic testing and commissioning must occur after all acoustic panels are fully installed and sealed, as the testing measures the complete acoustic environment. Any gaps or missing panels would produce inaccurate test results.

While typically acoustic ceilings are installed before wall panels to allow for continuous finishes at the wall-ceiling junction, this is often a soft preference as both trades can sequence their work if proper coordination is maintained.
The concrete slab provides the structural base and level surface needed to support and anchor the seating platforms. The platforms cannot be installed without a solid foundation.

Electrical conduit and wiring for lighting, power outlets, or any integrated seating features must be run before platforms are installed, as access to the floor slab is blocked once platforms are in place.
The seating platforms must be fully installed and secured before individual seats or chairs can be mounted onto them.

Floor finishing (e.g., painting, sealing, or polishing) is often done after platform installation to avoid damaging finishes during heavy platform work, though this can be phased if platforms are pre-finished.
The seating installation must be complete before final inspection and commissioning of the space can occur.
Fixed seating units require a level, stable structural floor to be installed upon; they must be anchored to the finished subfloor or slab.

predecessor: Complete Rough Electrical and Data Rough-Ins
rationale: Any in-floor electrical, data, or power outlets required for fixed seating (e.g., accessible charging ports) must be roughed in before the seating is installed over them.

successor: Install Final Floor Finishes (e.g., carpet, tile, epoxy)
rationale: Fixed seating is typically installed before final floor finishes because the seating anchors through or beneath the finished flooring; installing finished flooring first would require cutting around anchors later.
While some painting can be done before seating, final touch-ups and finish coats are often completed after installation to repair any scuffs or gaps caused during installation.

predecessor: Complete Overhead Structure and Ceiling Work
rationale: Overhead work such as ceiling installation, lighting, and sprinklers above the seating area should be completed before fixed seating is installed to avoid damage to the seats and to provide unobstructed access for overhead trades.
Circle lighting fixtures must be mounted to or supported by the ceiling grid or structure; the support system must be in place before any lighting can be installed.
Electrical cables, junction boxes, and conduits for the circle lighting must be run before the fixtures can be wired and mounted.
Ceiling tiles or finish panels should be installed after the lighting fixture is in place to allow for proper fit, alignment, and access to wiring.
The permanent electrical connections, switch installation, and testing of the lighting circuit must happen after the fixture is physically installed.
While painting can often be done before installation, final touch-up painting around the fixture is best done after the lighting is in place to ensure clean edges and coverage.
The subfloor must be properly prepared (cleaned, leveled, and primed) before any floor finish can be applied; otherwise, the finish will not adhere properly or will result in an uneven surface.

predecessor: Install Floor Base Layer for Circle
rationale: Any base flooring layer (such as underlayment or subflooring panels) must be installed prior to applying the final finish layer to ensure structural integrity and a proper surface for finishing.

successor: Allow Floor Finish to Cure/Dry for Circle
rationale: After applying the floor finish, a mandatory curing or drying period is required for the finish to harden, off-gas, and reach full durability before any foot traffic or subsequent work can occur.

While baseboards can be installed before floor finishing, it is often preferred to install them after the floor finish to avoid damaging the finish during trim installation and to allow a cleaner edge between the floor and trim.
Furniture and heavy equipment must only be placed on the floor after the finish has fully cured to prevent indentations, scratches, or adhesion of debris to the wet finish.
The locker unit must be placed on a level, cured concrete slab or finished floor. Without a stable foundation, the locker structure cannot be safely anchored or aligned.

If the locker unit requires integrated lighting, power outlets, or access control, the underlying conduit and wiring must be run in the floor or wall before the locker is set in place, as access behind or beneath the unit will be blocked.

Once the locker unit is physically installed, electricians can complete the final connections, install outlets, and trim out any integrated lighting or access control hardware that is housed within or on the locker unit.

The locker unit acts as a built-in fixture; adjacent wall painting, floor finishing, and baseboard installation should be completed after the locker is in place so that finishes abut the locker cleanly and no gaps or unfinished edges remain.

It is common practice to install lockers before final inspections so that all built-in fixtures are present for review, though this is a scheduling preference rather than a physical constructability constraint.
The sleeping partition wall must be built on top of a finished floor slab to provide a stable base and proper load distribution.
The main structural walls must be in place to define the room boundaries and provide lateral support for the partition wall connections.
Electrical wiring and outlets for the sleeping area must be routed after the partition wall framing is complete, as the wall cavities provide the conduit pathways.
Finish materials such as drywall or plaster cannot be applied until the partition wall frame is fully erected and secured.
Painting must occur after the partition wall is fully built and finished to ensure a continuous, smooth painted surface.
HVAC ductwork must be installed before ventilation zone partitions can be placed, as the partitions define and separate zones based on the ductwork layout and air distribution requirements.
Electrical rough-in work for zone sensors, dampers, and controls must be completed before enclosing spaces with ventilation zone partitions.
Structural framing (walls, ceilings, floor decks) must be complete to provide the physical support structure onto which ventilation zone partitions are mounted or attached.
Fire dampers are installed at partition penetrations where ductwork crosses zone boundaries; these can only be installed after the zone partitions defining those boundaries are in place.

successor: Insulation and Air Sealing of Zones
rationale: Insulation and air sealing work is performed after partitions are erected to ensure each ventilation zone is properly sealed and thermally separated from adjacent zones.

The structural frame must be complete to provide the pathways (corridors, stairwells, doors) that will serve as emergency egress routes, ensuring the building's load-bearing system is stable before clearing egress paths.

Fire protection systems such as sprinklers and fire alarms are critical safety elements that must be installed and operational before egress routes are cleared, so that the egress paths are safe in the event of an emergency during subsequent construction phases.
Interior walls and partitions define the egress corridors and pathways; they must be built and finished so that the exact egress routes are established before they can be cleared and marked.
Egress doors with panic hardware, exit devices, and door frames must be installed so that the actual exit points are functional before the egress paths can be deemed clear and usable.

Emergency egress routes must be cleared and unobstructed before the occupancy permit inspection can take place, as the inspector will verify that all means of egress are clear, properly marked, and fully functional.
The foundation slab must be fully cured and provide a stable base before any bunk frame can be installed upon it.
Reinforcement steel for the bunker slab must be placed before the bunk frame is installed, as the frame may tie into or sit on the reinforced slab.
The bunk frame defines the perimeter and structural datum for the walls; wall reinforcement cannot be accurately placed until the frame is set.
The frame must first be placed and aligned before it can be permanently bolted and anchored into position.
Concrete for bunker walls can only be poured after the frame (which serves as formwork or structural support) is fully installed and secured.
The structural framing and building enclosure (walls, roof, floor) must be complete to provide the substrate for acoustic treatment installation.
Interior walls must be framed and covered with drywall before acoustic panels, insulation, or treatments can be applied to those surfaces.
Electrical wiring, outlets, and junction boxes must be installed behind walls before acoustic treatments are placed, to avoid rework or damage.
HVAC ducts and vents must be installed in walls and ceilings before acoustic treatments are applied, as they would otherwise block access.

Acoustic treatments such as panels, bass traps, and soundproofing materials are typically installed before final paint and finish touches, as they are considered part of the wall/ceiling finish layer.
Flooring installation can be done before or after acoustic wall treatments, but typically acoustic wall panels are installed after flooring to avoid damage to the flooring from ladders and tools.
All acoustic treatments must be fully installed and in place before final inspection to verify acoustic performance and code compliance.
The railings are installed on the sleeping platform itself, so the platform structure must be complete to provide the base for railing attachment.
After railing installation, a safety inspection must be performed to verify that the railings are secure and meet safety standards before the platform can be used.
Though not strictly required, it is preferable to install railings before placing mattresses to avoid having to work around the mattresses and to ensure the railing provides safety from the start.

Mosquito net mounting systems (frames, tracks, or adhesive strips) must be attached to the finished window or door frame. The frame provides the structural surface required for proper alignment and secure mounting.

Wall surfaces around windows and doors must be fully finished before mounting mosquito net systems because the mounting brackets or tracks are often fixed to the finished wall surface, and installing before finishing would damage the net or require removal during painting/plastering.

While mosquito net mounting is typically done before final trim installation for a clean finish, it is a soft preference because the trim can also be installed first and the net system fitted with minor adjustments.

Mosquito net mounting must be completed before final cleaning and handover because the nets are a finished component that can collect dust during other construction activities and should be one of the last installed items to remain clean and undamaged.
The bed frame must be placed on a stable, level surface. Floor preparation (e.g., concrete slab, wooden subfloor) must be completed to provide a solid base.
The bed frame is positioned within the room; the walls must first be framed to define the room boundaries and support any headboard attachment.
Although not strictly required, it is preferable to run electrical wiring for bedside outlets and lighting before placing a large bed frame that could obstruct wall access.
The mattress rests on top of the bed frame slats or platform; therefore, the bed frame must be fully assembled and positioned before the mattress can be placed.
The headboard is typically bolted or attached to the bed frame; thus, the frame must be in place to mount the headboard securely.
The frame must be fully assembled to provide structure for the mattress support base.
The mattress support base must be installed before the mattress or comfort layer can be placed on top.
Slats or springs (if used) need to be installed before the mattress support base is placed.
Testing weight distribution may be more convenient after the support base is in place, though not physically required.
The headboard must be mounted to the bed frame; the frame needs to be fully assembled first to provide the structural support and attachment points for the headboard.
The headboard itself must be fully constructed (cut, shaped, upholstered, finished) before it can be installed onto the bed frame.

If the headboard is wall-mounted rather than frame-mounted, the wall must be prepared (patched, painted) before installation to avoid rework, though this is a soft preference if the headboard covers the wall area.
The headboard must be installed before the mattress is placed to allow clear access for mounting hardware and to avoid having to move the heavy mattress out of the way.
Final decorative elements such as bedding arrangement, pillows, and headboard accessories should be placed after the headboard is installed for proper alignment and visual consistency.
The footboard needs a stable and level base to be installed upon; without a fully cured foundation, the footboard cannot be properly anchored or aligned.
Footboards (also known as baseboards or skirting boards) are installed at the bottom of walls; the wall framing must be complete to provide a surface to which the footboard is attached.

The subfloor provides the walking surface and the substrate that meets the bottom of the wall; footboards are installed along the junction between the wall and the floor, requiring the subfloor to be in place.

Footboards are typically installed before the final finish flooring (e.g., hardwood, tile, carpet) so that the flooring material can be cut to fit snugly against the footboard, or so the footboard covers the expansion gap left around the perimeter of the flooring.

While often footboards are installed after painting to avoid getting paint on them, if the footboard is pre-finished, it can go before painting; however, typically painting the walls first is preferred (soft constraint) to avoid needing to cut in tape perfectly along the footboard edge.
The wall framing must be in place to provide the structural support and cavity needed for built-in bedside tables to be anchored securely.

Electrical wiring and outlet boxes must be installed within the wall cavity before the built-in bedside tables are constructed, as the tables often incorporate lighting, USB ports, or power outlets that require hidden wiring.
The built-in bedside tables must be installed before the surrounding drywall can be finished flush against them, ensuring clean edges and a seamless integration.

While it is physically possible to install flooring first, it is standard practice to install bedside tables after rough flooring but before finishing flooring or baseboards to ensure a tight fit and avoid damaging finished floors.

successor: Painting / Final Finishing (of tables and adjacent walls)
rationale: The built-in bedside tables must be fully installed and secured before the final paint and finish coats are applied to both the tables and the adjacent wall surfaces, as painting before installation would result in unfinished edges and touch-ups.
The bed canopy structure is mounted on or attached to the bed frame, so the bed frame must be installed first to provide a stable base and structural support for the canopy.
If the canopy requires wall or ceiling anchors, the wall framing and structural rough-in must be completed beforehand to ensure proper load-bearing support for the canopy mounting points.
Any electrical wiring for integrated canopy lighting must be roughed in before the canopy structure is installed, as accessing wiring after installation would be difficult and may damage the canopy.
The structural frame or posts of the bed canopy must be fully erected before any fabric, drapes, or soft panels can be hung or attached to the frame.
Final decorative trims, crown moldings, or ornamental elements on the canopy must be applied after the main structural canopy frame is in place to ensure proper alignment and fit.
The bed frame must be fully assembled to provide the structural support and cavity into which under-bed storage drawers are installed.
The floor surface must be finished before placing storage drawers underneath the bed to ensure smooth operation and to avoid damaging unfinished flooring.
The under-bed drawers must be installed before the mattress is placed on the bed frame, as accessing and installing drawers would be difficult or impossible with the mattress in place.

It is preferable to complete storage drawer installation before final decorative touches (e.g., bed skirt, dust ruffle, or decorative bins) to ensure proper fit and alignment, though this is a soft preference for work sequencing.
Wall paneling requires a completed wall frame and stud structure to attach the panels to.
Electrical wiring must be run inside the wall cavity before the wall is enclosed with paneling.
Insulation must be placed in wall cavities before paneling covers and seals the wall.
Paneling must be installed before any painting, staining, or sealing of the panel surface can be applied.
The bed and headboard cannot be properly positioned against the wall until the wall paneling is fully installed and finished.
Raw materials such as timber, adhesives, and hardware must be procured and available before fabrication can begin.
Detailed joinery shop drawings and design specifications must be finalized and approved before fabrication commences to ensure accuracy.
CNC machines, saws, routers, and assembly jigs must be calibrated and ready prior to starting fabrication.
Fabricated joinery pieces must be fully assembled and glued before any sanding, staining, or finishing can be applied.
Fabrication must be complete before dimensional and fitment inspection can be performed.
Joinery components need to be fabricated before they can be transported, though logistics may allow some flexibility in staging.
A stable foundation (e.g., concrete slab, piers, or ground-level base) must be completed before any deck or platform structure can be placed, as the deck requires a load-bearing surface to rest upon.
Support posts, beams, or a subframe must be erected to carry the sleeping platform/deck, as it cannot be self-supporting without underlying structural elements.
The platform/deck structure must be fully installed before applying any protective finishes (sealants, stains, or paints) to ensure complete coverage and curing.
Railings or guardrails must be attached to a completed platform/deck structure for safety, as they depend on the deck edge for anchoring.

While physically the mattress can be placed at any time, it is logically placed after deck completion to avoid damaging bedding during construction—this is a soft preference, not a structural necessity.
Wall surfaces must be finished (painted/papered) before bed frames are anchored to walls to avoid damaging finished surfaces and to ensure proper alignment with finished wall heights.
Flooring must be completed before bed frame installation to ensure the frame sits level on the finished floor surface and to avoid damaging the flooring material during installation.
Electrical outlets, wiring, and any bed-mounted lighting connections must be roughed-in and accessible before the bed frame is permanently anchored, as access behind the frame becomes restricted.
The bed frame must be securely fixed and anchored before placing the mattress and bedding, as the mattress requires a stable, fully assembled base.
The bed frame must be anchored first to establish the correct position and alignment before installing the headboard or placing bedside furniture, ensuring proper spacing and fit.
The integrated mattress requires a stable, level foundation surface to be installed upon; without proper foundation preparation, the mattress cannot be properly placed or supported.
The floor structure must be completed to provide the supporting surface and cavity where the integrated mattress will be installed.
The integrated mattress must be installed before final floor finishes (such as trim, molding, or adjacent flooring) can be completed around or against it.
While the bed frame can be partially assembled beforehand, final assembly and fitting around the integrated mattress is easier and more precise after the mattress is in place.
The integrated mattress must be fully installed before the overall sleep system can be inspected for proper fit, alignment, and function.
Electrical wiring must be run through wall cavities and studs, which are only accessible after the wall framing is complete.
Electrical conduits and boxes for overhead fixtures require the structural slab/ceiling to be in place before rough-in wiring can be installed.
Insulation must be installed after electrical wiring is in place so that wiring runs behind and within the insulation, and to avoid fire hazards of covering uncertified wiring.
Drywall cannot be installed until electrical boxes, wiring, and rough-in work are complete, as they must be accessible for inspection and are enclosed once walls are closed up.
Inspection of rough electrical work must occur before any covering (insulation, drywall) is installed to ensure code compliance and safety.

A stable foundation or base (e.g., concrete footings, slab, or ground anchors) must be prepared and cured before the canopy structure can be installed to ensure structural stability and load-bearing capacity.
The primary steel frame or support columns that will carry the canopy must be erected and properly anchored before the canopy structure itself can be mounted.
Any underground electrical, plumbing, or data lines that will serve the canopy area must be roughed in before the canopy is installed to avoid excavation conflicts and rework.
After the canopy structure frame is in place, the roofing membrane, weatherproofing layer, or canopy cover must be applied to provide weather protection and complete the assembly.
Overhead lighting, wiring, and electrical fixtures attached to the canopy must be installed after the canopy structure is securely in place to ensure safe and proper mounting.
The ceiling structure requires the underlying framing to be in place to support it.
Ceiling must be installed before electrical wiring can be run through it.
Insulation is installed after the ceiling structure is in place to enclose the space.

successor: Drywall Installation on Bed Alcove Ceiling
rationale: Drywall or finish material is applied over the structural ceiling after it is installed.
Any MEP rough-in work that needs to run above the ceiling must be completed before the ceiling is closed in.
A stable foundation or floor slab must be in place before constructing the bed alcove to ensure structural support and levelness.
The main walls of the room must be framed to define the space and provide attachment points before the alcove framing can be integrated.
Electrical wiring for outlets, switches, or lighting in the alcove can only be installed after the alcove structure is built so that wires can be run through the stud cavities.
Any plumbing lines intended for features near the alcove must be roughed in after the structural framing is complete to properly locate pipes within the wall cavities.
Drywall or wallboard can only be applied after the alcove frame is fully erected to provide a surface for attachment and finishing.
The electrical outlets must be installed within the framed walls of the bed alcove; framing provides the structural cavity for running wiring and mounting outlet boxes.
Rough-in wiring must be pulled to the outlet locations before the outlet boxes and receptacles can be installed and connected.
Insulation should be installed after electrical outlets and boxes are in place to avoid covering unfinished electrical work and to allow proper fitting around outlet boxes.
Drywall cannot be installed until outlet boxes are mounted and wires are terminated, as the drywall must be cut around the outlet boxes.
Cover plates are installed after drywall and painting are complete; this is a finish sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
The structural walls enclosing the bed alcove must be framed before the floor can be installed, as the floor typically sits within the alcove and requires the wall framing for reference and support.
A level subfloor must be in place before any finished flooring in the bed alcove can be laid to ensure proper support and a stable base.
Any electrical wiring, outlets, or plumbing lines that will run beneath or within the bed alcove floor must be roughed-in prior to floor installation to avoid costly rework.

Wall finishes (e.g., drywall, paneling, or tile) in the bed alcove should be installed after the floor to allow the wall material to overlap and cover the floor edge for a clean finished appearance and to prevent damage to the floor.
Baseboard and trim installation must follow the finished floor so that the trim sits flush on top of the floor surface, concealing the expansion gap and providing a finished look.
The bed platform requires a level and structurally sound floor base to be built upon; the subfloor must be complete before any platform framing begins.

Electrical wiring for any outlets or lighting near or under the bed platform must be roughed in before the platform is constructed; otherwise, wiring would be inaccessible or require destructive rework.
The bed platform is typically built against a wall; the adjacent walls must be framed and sheathed to provide a stable attachment surface and to establish the correct room dimensions.

Finish flooring (such as hardwood, carpet, or tile) should be installed after the platform is framed, as the platform sits on top of or against the flooring, and the flooring should run continuously or transition cleanly at the platform edge.
Trim work around the bed platform (such as baseboards or fascia) must be installed after the platform is completed so that all joints, gaps, and transitions are properly covered and finished.
The storage units within the bed alcove require the alcove's structural frame to be built first as the storage components are installed into or against the framing.
Finishing work such as painting or applying cladding must occur after storage installation to ensure seamless integration and coverage of all surfaces including storage elements.
Any electrical wiring for lighting or outlets behind or within storage areas must be roughed-in before enclosing those spaces with storage units.
Doors, drawer fronts, and hardware for storage compartments can only be installed after the storage boxes/carcasses are in place.

While it's often preferable to install flooring before built-in storage to avoid having to cut around the units, it can be done in reverse order; thus this is a soft preference for better finish quality.
The bed alcove opening must be framed and sheetrocked to provide a mounting surface for the curtain track.
The curtain track must be installed and secured before any curtain can be hung from it.
Electrical rough-in should be completed before ceiling-mounted track installation to avoid interference, though it's a soft preference if track is wall-mounted.

predecessor: Complete Ceiling Finishes in Bed Alcove
rationale: Ceiling finishes (paint/texture) must be completed before mounting a ceiling track to avoid damaging finished surfaces.
It is easier to paint walls before installing the track, but if the track is installed first, touch-up painting can be done afterward.
The headboard wall framing must be built before the headboard wall can be installed or finished.
Electrical wiring, outlets, and switches must be roughed in behind the wall before the headboard wall is closed up.

predecessor: Plumbing Rough-In for Bed Alcove (if applicable)
rationale: Any plumbing lines serving the bed alcove area must be installed before the wall is completed.
The headboard wall structure must be in place before applying drywall, paneling, or other finish materials.

successor: Bed Alcove Trim and Molding Installation
rationale: Trim and moldings are applied to the completed wall surface and cannot be installed before the wall is built.
The alcove bed needs a framed rough opening in the wall to be installed into, so the framing must be completed first.

successor: Finish drywall and trim around alcove
rationale: Drywall and trim work around the alcove bed must happen after the bed unit is in place to ensure proper fit and seamless finishing.
While electrical can be roughed in before, final outlet installation near the alcove is easier after the bed is positioned to ensure precise placement.
Painting the interior of the alcove should be done after the bed is installed to avoid damage to painted surfaces during bed installation.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical wiring in alcove area
rationale: Electrical wiring must be roughed in behind the wall before the alcove bed is permanently installed, as access to wall cavities will be blocked.
The framing of the bed alcove must be complete to provide a structural support surface for attaching the privacy screen.
Electrical wiring and junction boxes must be roughed in before the privacy screen is installed, as accessing the wall cavity behind the screen would be difficult or impossible afterward.
The privacy screen must be installed before final painting and finishing can be applied around it, ensuring a seamless finish and avoiding damage to the screen.
While lighting fixtures can technically be installed before the screen, it is preferred to install the screen first to position lighting correctly relative to the screen's location and avoid rework.

predecessor: Flooring Installation in Bed Alcove Area
rationale: Flooring should be completed before the privacy screen is installed to allow the screen to sit on top of the finished floor and to avoid the need for precise cuts around the screen's base.
The bed alcove must be physically constructed before the smoke detector can be installed within it, as the detector mounts to the alcove structure.
Electrical wiring for the smoke detector must be run to the bed alcove location before the detector unit can be connected and mounted.

successor: Bed Alcove Smoke Detector Testing and Commissioning
rationale: The smoke detector must be physically installed before it can be tested, verified, and commissioned for operation.
Finishing work around the detector (e.g., painting, trim) should only be done after the detector is installed to ensure proper fit and sealing.
The individual bed alcove smoke detector must be installed and connected before the entire fire alarm system can be integrated and tested as a whole.
The HVAC register requires the bed alcove framed cavity to be built before the register can be installed into the wall or ceiling.
The ductwork serving the bed alcove must be roughed in and terminated at the register location before the register (diffuser/grille) can be attached.
Drywall must be cut and finished around the register; if the register is not in place, the drywall opening cannot be properly finished and trimmed.
While painting can often proceed with the register masked off, it is preferable to install the register after painting to avoid getting paint on the register fins and to achieve a cleaner finish.
The register must be installed so that airflow can be measured and dampers adjusted during the system balancing and commissioning phase.

predecessor: Frame rough opening for bed alcove egress window
successor: Install Bed Alcove Emergency Egress Window
rationale: The rough opening must be framed before the window unit can be installed into the wall.

predecessor: Install Bed Alcove Emergency Egress Window
rationale: The window must be fully installed before flashing and weatherproofing can be applied around its perimeter to prevent water intrusion.

predecessor: Install Bed Alcove Emergency Egress Window
successor: Install interior drywall and finish around window
rationale: The window must be in place before interior wall finishes (drywall, trim) can be installed around the window opening.

predecessor: Install Bed Alcove Emergency Egress Window
rationale: The window must be set and flashed before exterior cladding is installed up to the window frame.

predecessor: Verify egress window rough opening dimensions meet building code
successor: Install Bed Alcove Emergency Egress Window
rationale: The rough opening must be verified to meet egress size requirements before the window is installed, as emergency escape and rescue windows have strict code-minimum clear opening dimensions.
The bed alcove structure requires framed walls to define its boundaries and support its structure, so wall framing must be completed first.
A level and prepared floor substrate is needed to build the alcove's base platform and ensure structural stability.
Any electrical outlets, switches, or lighting rough-ins intended for the alcove area must be run behind the walls before the alcove framing and finishes enclose them.
The bed alcove framework must be fully constructed before drywall can be applied to its surfaces and integrated with adjacent walls.
Trim work such as baseboards, crown molding, or alcove shelving details can only be installed after the alcove structure is built, though the sequencing could be adjusted with some rework.
The framing of the bed alcove must be completed before any mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) rough-in work can begin, as the MEP systems are installed within the framed walls and cavities.

MEP rough-in must be completed before insulation is installed, as insulation is placed after all wiring, piping, and ductwork are in place, and covering them up before inspection/rough-in would violate code.
All MEP rough-in work must be completed and inspected before drywall can be installed, as drywall encloses the walls and would block access to MEP systems.
The floor slab or subfloor must be prepared and cured before any MEP rough-in that runs through or along the floor can begin.

successor: Final MEP Trim-Out and Fixture Installation
rationale: Rough-in of MEP systems (running wires, pipes, and ducts) must be completed before trim-out and final fixture installation can occur, as fixtures connect to the rough-in terminations.
The bed alcove must be framed before any finish materials (such as drywall, paneling, or trim) can be applied to the alcove surfaces.
Electrical wiring for outlets, switches, or lighting within the bed alcove must be roughed in behind the walls before the finish surfaces are installed.
Final painting or wall finishing should occur after the alcove finish materials (e.g., drywall, trim) are installed to ensure a smooth, continuous finish surface.
Lighting fixtures mounted to finished surfaces or trim within the alcove must be installed after the finish materials are in place to allow proper mounting and alignment.

successor: Bed Alcove Trim and Molding Installation
rationale: Finish-grade trim and molding around the bed alcove must be installed after the primary finish surfaces (e.g., drywall, paneling) are in place to cover joints and provide a finished appearance.
The frame components must be manufactured before they can be assembled into the dressing table's main structure.
The mirror is mounted onto the completed frame, so the frame assembly must be finished first.
Drawers and their slides need to be installed into the assembled frame cavity.
Finishing should be done after mirror attachment to ensure a seamless, uniform coating and to avoid masking issues.
Drawers and the frame should be finished together to ensure color/stain consistency, and finishing after installation prevents hardware from being painted shut.
Wardrobe/closet enclosures require surrounding wall framing to define the space and provide backing for closet components.
Electrical wiring for lighting or outlets within or near the closet must be roughed in before closet interior components are installed to avoid obstruction.
The floor base must be prepared to provide a level surface for wardrobe/closet installation.
While painting can be done before, it is preferable to install closet components first to allow for seamless finishing around the wardrobe framing and avoid touch-ups.
The wardrobe/closet box or frame must be in place before internal shelving, hanging rods, and drawer systems can be mounted inside.
The drawer components must be cut to size before they can be assembled into the drawer bank structure.
The drawer bank must be assembled first so that drawer slides can be properly aligned and attached to the drawer box and cabinet frame.
Drawer fronts cannot be mounted until the slides are installed, as the fronts attach to the slide mechanism and must be aligned with the slides.

successor: Install drawer bank into cabinet carcass
rationale: The drawer bank must be fully assembled before it can be positioned and secured within the cabinet carcass.

predecessor: Install drawer bank into cabinet carcass
rationale: Drawer pulls/handles are typically installed after the drawer bank is in place and the fronts are mounted, though this could be done earlier as a soft preference for workflow convenience.
Built-in shelving requires the wall framing to be in place as a structural substrate for attachment and support.

Drywall must be installed and finished before built-in shelving can be mounted, as the shelving is typically attached to finished wall surfaces and would otherwise require drywall work to be done around or behind it.
Walls behind and around the built-in shelving must be painted or finished before installation, as access to those surfaces will be blocked or made difficult once shelving is installed.
Flooring should be installed after built-in shelving is in place so that the flooring can be cut and fitted precisely around the base of the shelving unit, ensuring a clean finished appearance.
Baseboards and trim should be installed after built-in shelving so that the trim can be cut to fit snugly against the shelving unit for a finished look.
The seating must be anchored to or placed against finished walls; walls provide structural support and the backing for seating installation.
Flooring must be completed before seating is installed so that seating can be placed on the finished floor surface without interference or need for later lifting.
Mirrors are typically positioned above or adjacent to seating; seating provides the reference height and location for optimal mirror placement.
It is preferable to complete seating installation before final styling and dressing of the room to ensure the layout is set; however, some decorative elements can be adjusted afterwards.
Electrical rough-in (wiring for nearby lighting or outlets) must be completed before seating is installed to avoid blocking access to walls and electrical boxes.
The mirror must be mounted on a framed wall surface; wall framing provides the structural support needed for secure attachment.
The mirror requires a smooth, finished wall surface for proper adhesion and aesthetic mounting; installing on unfinished drywall would cause alignment issues and potential damage.
Wall painting or final wall finishing must be completed before mirror installation to avoid paint splatter on the mirror surface and to ensure a clean finished look around the mirror edges.

While it is possible to install baseboard after the mirror, installing baseboard first may interfere with mirror placement; however, this is a workflow preference to achieve clean trim abutting the mirror rather than a physical necessity.
