The mirror is a finishing touch; final inspection or staging should occur after the mirror is installed to present the completed room, but this is an aesthetic/procedural preference rather than a structural requirement.
The jewelry/valet organizer must be attached to or installed within a fully assembled frame structure to ensure proper alignment and support.
The organizer is typically built as or integrated into a drawer component; the drawer box must be constructed first to provide the cavity and mounting surface.
Finishing must be completed before installing the organizer to avoid overspray or finish drips on the delicate interior compartments and to ensure the raw wood is sealed properly.
Hardware such as knobs or pulls is attached to the drawer front or organizer face, which requires the organizer to be in its final position first.
The final inspection must verify that the organizer is correctly installed, all compartments are functional, and no damage occurred during installation.
The valet rod/tie rack must be mounted to a finished or roughed-in wall structure; the supporting wall must be framed and ready before any rack can be attached.

The rod/rack must be installed before final paint or wall finish is applied behind/around it, or the installation would damage finished surfaces; however touch-ups can be done after. Typically the rack is mounted to bare or primed walls, then final paint is done around it.
While not a strict physical necessity, it is standard practice to install primary closet shelving and rods before adding accessory racks so that clearances and alignments can be verified.
The valet rod/tie rack should be installed before loading it with clothing/ties/accessories, as the empty rack is easier to mount and adjust.
The shoe rack sits on the floor; flooring must be complete to provide a stable, level surface and to avoid damaging the floor during rack installation.
Wall finishing should be done before mounting any shoe rack to avoid paint splatters or wallpaper damage and to allow access for finishing behind the rack.
It is convenient to place decorative items and organize the entryway only after the shoe storage is in place, but it is a soft preference as decor can be rearranged anytime.
Installing the shoe rack creates dust and debris; final cleaning must follow to ensure a tidy finished space.
Baseboards should be installed before a shoe rack that abuts the wall to ensure continuous trim and prevent gaps that are hard to address after the rack is in place.
The island dressing table is built on top of or integrated with the island base cabinetry; the base must be in place first to provide structural support.
Electrical wiring for outlets or lighting in the island area must be run before the dressing table is installed to avoid blocking access to walls or subfloor.
The dressing table must be fully installed and secured before the countertop can be placed on top of it.
While painting can be done before installation, finishing work is often easier after installation to touch up any marks; however, this is a soft preference rather than a strict physical requirement.
If the island includes a sink, the dressing table (cabinet) must be in place first to support the sink basin and connect plumbing.
Partition walls require a level, load-bearing subfloor or slab to anchor the bottom plate and ensure structural stability.

predecessor: Rough-In Electrical / Plumbing for Dressing Room
rationale: Electrical wires, outlets, switches, and any plumbing lines that will run inside or through the partition wall must be installed before the wall framing is erected; otherwise, retrofitting would require cutting into finished framing.
Drywall cannot be installed until the partition wall framing is fully built, braced, and secured in place.
The door frame and door require the partition wall to be in place to provide the rough opening and structural support.
Finishing work such as painting, baseboards, and trim can only commence after the wall framing is complete and any drywall or sheathing has been applied.
The door frame must be installed and structurally complete before the door can be hung, as the door requires the frame for support and alignment.
Walls must be built to define the dressing room opening where the door will be installed; without the surrounding wall structure, there is no location to mount the door.
Door hardware such as hinges, handles, and locks can only be properly installed after the door is hung and aligned in its frame.
While painting can be done before door installation, it is often preferred to install doors first so that painting can be done continuously across walls and door surfaces for a uniform finish.
Flooring should be completed after door installation to ensure proper clearance between the bottom of the door and the finished floor surface.
Electrical wiring must be roughed-in behind walls before mirrors are installed, as mirrors cover walls and accessing wiring afterward would require mirror removal.

predecessor: Complete Wall Finishing (Drywall, Taping, Mudding, Priming)
rationale: Mirrors are mounted on finished wall surfaces. Wall finishing (including drywall, taping, mudding, and priming) must be completed to provide a smooth, clean substrate for mirror adhesion and attachment.
Painting behind mirrors should be completed first because once mirrors are installed, the wall area behind them is inaccessible for painting touch-ups or finishing.
After mirrors are installed, edges must be trimmed and caulked to provide a finished appearance and seal edges against moisture.
Mirror installation produces debris and leaves fingerprints/ smudges; final cleaning must occur after mirrors are in place to ensure a pristine, streak-free finish.

The dressing room joinery (cabinetry, wardrobes, shelving) must be installed against finished wall surfaces. Framing and drywall provide the structural backing and flat surface required for secure attachment of joinery.
Joinery units must sit on a level, stable floor to ensure proper alignment, door operation, and structural integrity. Uneven subfloors would cause joinery to be misaligned or unstable.

Electrical cables and outlet boxes must be routed and placed within the walls before joinery is installed, as the joinery would block access to the wall cavities and make retrofitting electrical work extremely difficult or impossible.
Any plumbing supply or drain lines that will be hidden behind or within joinery must be completed before installation to avoid having to dismantle the joinery for future plumbing access.

Joinery must be installed before final painting and wall finishing so that paint edges can be cut in neatly against the joinery, and to avoid damaging freshly painted walls during joinery installation.

It is common practice to install floor coverings after joinery so that the joinery sits on top of the finished floor, providing a clean transition. However, this is a soft preference as some sequences install flooring first and then fit joinery on top.
Electrical wiring, conduit, and junction boxes must be roughed in before any lighting fixtures can be installed to provide power connections.
The ceiling structure must be framed and drywalled (or otherwise finished) before light fixtures can be mounted, as fixtures attach to the finished ceiling surface or its supports.
Light fixtures must be physically mounted before the final electrical connections, switch installation, and trim-out can be completed.
While painting can be done before lighting, final touch-up painting is typically done after fixtures are installed to cover any marks or gaps around the mounted fixtures.

Proper lighting placement relative to mirrors is important for dressing rooms; however mirrors can technically be installed before or after, though installing after lighting allows for optimal alignment.
The ceiling grid provides the structural support and framework onto which the transition trim is attached; trim cannot be installed without the grid in place.

predecessor: Complete Overhead MEP Rough-In (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing)
rationale: MEP rough-in work above the ceiling must be completed before trim installation to avoid interference and rework, and so that the trim can properly align with the finished ceiling plane.
The transition trim defines the edge or transition point between different ceiling heights; ceiling tiles or panels are then cut and fitted up to the trim for a clean finish.
Painting after trim installation allows for a seamless finish, though it is a soft preference as trim can be masked off if painted beforehand.

successor: Install light fixtures and diffusers adjacent to transition
rationale: The transition trim establishes the final ceiling plane geometry; light fixtures and diffusers must be positioned relative to the finished trim to ensure proper alignment and fit.
The ceiling height measurement point must be established on the finished slab or deck surface; formwork installation creates the structural surface from which ceiling heights are measured.
Concrete must be poured and cured to achieve the final slab elevation; measuring ceiling height before the slab is set would yield inaccurate results.
Overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in must be installed at the correct elevation relative to the established ceiling height benchmark to ensure proper clearances.
The suspended ceiling grid must be installed at the exact ceiling height as indicated by the measurement benchmarks to maintain consistent finished ceiling elevation.
Partition wall heights and top track placement depend on the established ceiling height reference point to ensure walls extend to the correct elevation.
The structural framing must be fully installed and inspected to provide the support framework and load-bearing capacity required for hanging variable height ceiling systems.

All mechanical ducts, electrical conduits, plumbing pipes, and other MEP rough-in work must be completed before ceiling installation, as these services run above the ceiling and would be inaccessible afterward.
Overhead conduits and cable trays must be routed and installed prior to ceiling grids to ensure proper clearance and accessibility for future maintenance.
Fire sprinkler piping and heads must be installed and pressure-tested before ceiling installation, as sprinkler heads must penetrate the ceiling in precise locations.
The ceiling panels, tiles, and support grid must be fully installed before any finishing work such as painting, texturing, or applying acoustic treatments can be applied to the ceiling surface.
Recessed lighting fixtures, troffers, and other ceiling-mounted lights must be installed after the ceiling grid is in place to ensure proper alignment and integration with the ceiling system.

successor: Final MEP Trim-Out and Fixture Installation
rationale: Final installation of registers, diffusers, grilles, and other MEP trim items that penetrate the ceiling surface must occur after ceiling installation to achieve proper fit and finish.

While walls can be partially built beforehand, final full-height partitions that connect to the ceiling are best installed after ceiling work to ensure tight sealing and proper alignment at the ceiling-wall interface.
The ceiling grid must be installed to establish the actual finished ceiling height that needs to be verified against design specifications.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work above the ceiling must be completed so that the ceiling height survey can confirm adequate clearance and access are maintained.
Ceiling tiles must not be installed until the ceiling height has been verified and approved, as tiles would conceal the structure and prevent accurate measurement.

successor: Final MEP trim-out and device installation
rationale: MEP devices such as sprinklers, lights, and diffusers must be installed at the verified ceiling height to ensure proper alignment and code compliance.

The ceiling height verification survey serves as a quality checkpoint; final inspections and punch list items for ceiling-related work can only proceed once the survey confirms compliance with specifications.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide support and attachment points for enclosure surfaces such as walls and exterior cladding.
Foundations must be completed to support the structural frame and subsequently the enclosure surfaces that rest on or attach to the structure.
The roof structure must be in place before interior wall and ceiling enclosure surfaces are installed to provide weather protection during construction.
Interior finishes such as drywall, plaster, and paint are applied onto the enclosure surfaces (walls and ceilings) after they are installed.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within walls and ceilings must occur after enclosure surfaces are framed and closed up, but before final finishes. Note: Rough-in is typically done before the final layer of enclosure (e.g., drywall) is fully installed.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to define the vertical space and establish the reference elevations before floor-to-floor height clearance can be measured or verified.

predecessor: Foundation and Ground Floor Slab Completion
rationale: The base slab or floor deck must be completed to provide a stable starting point from which vertical floor-to-floor heights are measured.
MEP rough-in work (ductwork, piping, conduits) must not encroach into the required clearance zone; therefore the target floor-to-floor height must be established first to guide vertical routing.
Partition wall heights are determined by the floor-to-floor clearance; walls cannot be framed correctly until the vertical space between floors is confirmed.
Suspended ceiling systems are installed based on the available floor-to-floor height; the clearance must be established to set ceiling suspension heights and ensure adequate headroom.
The subfloor must be prepared, leveled, and cured before any floor finish can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and a flat surface.
All electrical, plumbing, and mechanical rough-ins that run beneath or within the floor slab must be completed before the floor finish is installed to avoid cutting or damaging the finished surface.
Floor finishes are typically installed before baseboards and lower wall finishes so that wall materials can overlap and cover the edge of the flooring for a clean transition.
Baseboards, shoe molding, and other trim must be installed after the floor finish is complete to sit flush against the finished floor surface and hide expansion gaps.

While painting can be done before or after flooring, it is common practice to paint walls first and then install flooring to avoid drips on the finished floor; however this is a soft preference not a physical necessity.
The structural ceiling (beams, slabs, or decking) must be installed first as the ceiling finish is applied to or suspended from the structural substrate.
All ductwork, piping, conduit, and wiring that will run above the ceiling must be installed before the ceiling is closed up to avoid costly rework.
Sprinkler piping and heads above the ceiling must be roughed-in and tested before ceiling installation.
Wall finishing is typically completed after the ceiling is installed to ensure clean junctions and avoid damage to finished walls during ceiling work.
Flooring is often installed after the ceiling to prevent debris from ceiling work damaging the finished floor, though sequencing can vary.
Recessed lighting fixtures and ceiling-mounted light fixtures are installed as part of or immediately after the ceiling grid/finish is completed.
Ceiling completion is one of the last major finish trades, after which final inspections, touch-ups, and close-out activities can proceed.
Wall framing must be in place to provide the structural substrate onto which wall finishes (e.g., drywall, plaster, panels) are applied.
All concealed MEP services within walls must be installed and inspected before wall surfaces are closed up with finish materials.
Insulation is placed inside wall cavities and must be in position before the finish layer seals the wall.
The wall surface must be fully finished (e.g., drywall taped, mudded, and sanded) before any paint, wallcovering, or final coating can be applied.

Typically wall finishing is completed before floor finishes to avoid damaging floors; however, in some sequences floor finishing may start after wall framing but before final wall trim, making this a soft preference.
Structural columns must be supported by adequate foundations or footings to transfer loads safely to the ground; columns cannot be erected without a stable base.
Columns often require a prepared slab or base surface for accurate positioning, plumb alignment, and anchorage; the slab provides a working platform and structural interface.
Steel reinforcement must be pre-positioned, tied, and inspected before concrete is poured for cast-in-place columns; the reinforcement cage defines the column's structural integrity.
Beams and girders typically bear on or connect to columns; columns must be in place and cured to sufficient strength before beams can be supported or bolted/welded.
Floor slabs are typically supported by beams that rest on columns, or are directly supported by columns; columns must be erected and stable before slab formwork and pouring can proceed.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be completed and inspected before interior partitions are installed, as partitions would cover and block access to these systems.
A finished and cured concrete slab or subfloor is required as the base for framing and installing interior partition walls.
Overhead mechanical ducts, electrical conduit, and plumbing runs must be in place before partitions are framed, as they may need to connect into walls or be routed around them.
After interior partitions are installed, a framing inspection is typically required before closing up walls with drywall.
Interior partitions must be fully framed, braced, and stable before drywall can be applied to the studs.
The structural slab or subfloor provides the base surface that requires leveling and finishing; without it there is nothing to finish.
All buried conduits, pipes, and wiring must be installed and inspected before the floor leveling compound is poured to avoid cutting into the finished floor.

predecessor: Concrete Curing / Moisture Vapor Retarder Installation
rationale: Concrete must be fully cured and any vapor barrier must be in place before applying self-leveling underlayment or finish coatings to prevent moisture damage.

successor: Final Floor Covering Installation (Tile, Wood, Vinyl, Carpet)
rationale: The leveled and finished subfloor provides the smooth, uniform surface required for installing final floor coverings; coverings cannot be laid on an uneven base.
Wall base and trim are installed after the finished floor is in place so that the trim sits on top of the flooring and covers the expansion gap.

The structural frame and building shell must be complete to provide a stable, enclosed environment in which spatial measurements and tolerances can be meaningfully checked against design specifications.

Major MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) rough-in work must be installed before spatial commissioning to verify that clearances, pathways, and tolerances are maintained with all services in place.

Interior finishes (drywall, ceilings, flooring, cladding) must not proceed until spatial tolerance checks confirm that substrates and framing are within acceptable dimensional limits, as finishes would conceal and make corrections difficult or impossible.

successor: Final MEP trim-out and device installation
rationale: Final installation of MEP trim items (diffusers, registers, fixtures, devices) must be deferred until spatial tolerances are verified to ensure proper alignment, clearance, and fit within the completed spaces.
Full equipment and system commissioning depends on spaces being certified within tolerance, as equipment placement, access, and clearance are prerequisites for safe and reliable start-up and testing.
The plant shelf is designed to sit on or attach to the window sill, so the sill must be in place first to provide structural support.
The window frame and sill assembly must be completed before any add-on components like a plant shelf can be installed.
Wall finishing around the window area should be completed before attaching a plant shelf to avoid damaging finished surfaces or needing to work around the shelf.
After the shelf is installed, gaps between the shelf and sill/wall need to be sealed to prevent water damage and ensure stability.

successor: Decorative trim or molding installation around shelf
rationale: Adding decorative trim around the shelf is a cosmetic preference that can only be done after the shelf itself is in place.
The planter box must be supported on a stable foundation or base slab to ensure structural integrity and proper load distribution.
The planter box structure must be fully built and cured before soil and plants are added to prevent damage to the structure.
If the planter box is integrated into a building structure, waterproofing must be applied after the planter box is built but before soil is added, to seal against moisture penetration.
The wall surface must be prepared (e.g., cleaned, leveled, or repaired) before the support bracket can be securely attached to ensure proper load distribution and adhesion.
The support bracket must be securely fastened to the wall before the window box can be placed onto it, as the bracket serves as the structural mounting component.
After installing the bracket, a load test or inspection should be performed to verify the bracket can safely support the window box weight before final use.
The building's structural frame must be in place to provide the load-bearing support for the internal green wall frame.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) rough-in work within the wall cavity must be completed before enclosing it with the green wall frame system.
The green wall frame provides the structural attachment points and support for the irrigation lines and emitters that water the plants.
The frame must be fully installed and secured before the planting panels, growing medium, or live plants can be mounted onto or within it.

While not a strict physical dependency, it is best practice to inspect the moisture barrier behind the green wall frame before fully loading it with plants and irrigation, as access becomes difficult afterward.
A stable, level base and proper foundation are required to anchor the trellis or climbing support frame securely.
Any underground pipes, conduits, or electrical lines that would pass beneath the trellis area must be installed before digging post holes or setting footings for the support frame.
Plants need the completed support structure to be trained and attached onto; the frame must be fully erected before planting or training climbing vegetation.

It is easier to perform final grading, soil placement, and mulching around the trellis base after the frame is installed to achieve a clean finish, though this could be done beforehand with careful work.

successor: Decorative Cladding or Shade Fabric Attachment
rationale: Any additional cladding, shading mesh, or decorative panels that mount onto the trellis frame require the frame to be structurally complete as a mounting substrate.
The base structure must be assembled first to provide a stable platform for the reservoir tray.
The reservoir tray must be in place before adding the growing medium to prevent spillage and ensure proper containment.
The reservoir tray must be installed before the water level indicator can be placed, as the indicator measures the water within the tray.
The drainage layer (e.g., gravel or perlite) must be placed on top of or within the reservoir tray to separate it from the growing medium.
Any waterproofing or sealant on the base or tray contact surfaces must be applied and cured before installing the tray to prevent leaks.

successor: Window Overhang / Shading Louvres for Plants
rationale: The structural frame must be erected first to provide the load-bearing support onto which the window overhang and shading louvres can be attached or mounted.

successor: Window Overhang / Shading Louvres for Plants
rationale: The exterior walls or cladding must be in place so that the window overhang and shading louvres can be properly integrated and sealed against the building envelope.

successor: Window Overhang / Shading Louvres for Plants
rationale: Windows must be installed before shading louvres and overhangs are added, as the louvres/overhangs are positioned relative to window openings to provide proper shading.

predecessor: Window Overhang / Shading Louvres for Plants
rationale: It is preferable to complete final exterior finishes and painting after shading elements are installed to avoid touch-ups or damage, though this is a soft preference rather than a strict physical requirement.

predecessor: Window Overhang / Shading Louvres for Plants
rationale: The shading louvres are specifically designed for plants; thus, any climbing plants or green wall elements intended to use the louvres must be planted after the louvre structure is in place to allow them to grow onto/over it.
The window frame must be installed and secured before any transition seal can be applied, as the seal interfaces directly with the window frame.
The greenwall's structural support must be in place so that the transition seal can bridge between the window frame and the greenwall assembly.

successor: Air and Moisture Barrier Application Over Seal
rationale: Continuity of the building envelope requires that the transition seal be installed first, then the air and moisture barrier can be lapped over and sealed to the transition member.

While it is physically possible to install planting media before the seal is fully finished, doing so risks damaging the seal. Best practice (soft preference) is to complete the seal first to protect the planting area from leaks and to ensure a clean substrate.
Exposed transition seals must be covered by flashing or trim to protect them from UV and mechanical damage; thus, finishing the seal is a prerequisite for installing the protective covering elements.

successor: Operable Casement with Plant Access Hatch
rationale: The structural opening (rough opening) must be framed, sized, and prepared to receive the casement unit before the casement can be installed.

predecessor: Operable Casement with Plant Access Hatch
rationale: After the casement is installed, gaps around the frame must be sealed and weatherproofed to prevent air and water infiltration.

predecessor: Operable Casement with Plant Access Hatch
rationale: Interior trim work (e.g., architraves, sills) is completed after the window unit is in place to cover the gap between frame and wall.

predecessor: Operable Casement with Plant Access Hatch
rationale: While it is physically possible to adjust hardware later, it is best practice to test and fine-tune the casement operation and plant access hatch mechanism immediately after installation to ensure proper function before other finishes cover access points.

successor: Operable Casement with Plant Access Hatch
rationale: The main structural elements supporting the casement must be in place before the casement component can be fixed into position.
The window opening must be framed before any window-mounted fixture like a planter box can be installed, as the planter box attaches to or sits on the sill of the framed opening.
The window itself must be installed to provide the sill surface or support structure onto which the planter box is mounted or attached.
Weatherproofing and flashing around the window must be completed to prevent moisture intrusion behind the planter box, as accessing those areas after installation would be difficult or impossible.

Final landscaping or exterior trim work near the planter box is typically completed after the planter box is in place to ensure proper fit and aesthetic integration, though this is a soft preference for sequencing rather than a strict physical requirement.

successor: Install Drip Irrigation / Water Supply (if applicable)
rationale: If the planter box includes integrated irrigation, the water supply line connection must be made after the box is in its final position to accurately connect and test the system.
The window opening must be framed and roughed in before any window-integrated system can be installed, as the physical opening and structural support must exist to accommodate the window unit.

predecessor: Run Supply Plumbing to Window Location
rationale: Water supply lines must be brought to the rough location of the window before connecting the integrated irrigation supply to ensure the plumbing connection point is available and properly aligned.

predecessor: Complete Rough Electrical Work at Window Location
rationale: Any electrical rough-in needed for controls, valves, or pumps associated with the irrigation supply must be completed before the window unit is installed to avoid rework or inaccessible wiring.
Final trim, sealing, and finishing around the window-integrated irrigation system must occur after the unit is installed to ensure proper fit, weather sealing, and aesthetic finish.
Functional testing of the integrated irrigation system and verification of window seals can only be performed after the window unit with its irrigation supply is fully installed.

predecessor: Install Ceiling or Wall-Mounted Support Structure
rationale: The curtain track system must be physically attached to a ceiling or wall support structure; this structure must be in place before the track can be mounted.

predecessor: Complete Rough-In Electrical Work (if motorized track)
rationale: If the curtain track is motorized, electrical wiring and outlet boxes must be roughed-in and available at the installation location before the track can be wired and installed.
Finishing work such as painting and drywall should be completed before installing the curtain track to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to ensure the track is mounted on the final surface.
Curtain panels physically attach to or hang from the installed track; the track must be securely in place before curtains can be hung.

successor: Install Curtain Track Covers / Fascia (if applicable)
rationale: Decorative covers or fascia for the track are installed after the track itself is mounted, as they conceal the track hardware.
The irrigation system must be physically installed before it can be commissioned and tested for proper operation.

predecessor: Connect Water Supply to Green Wall
rationale: A water supply connection must be established to the green wall system before commissioning can verify water flow and pressure.
Planting containers or growing medium must be in place before the watering system can be commissioned to ensure the system delivers water to the correct locations.
The watering system must be verified as operational before plants are installed, to ensure they receive adequate water immediately after planting.

It is preferable but not strictly required that the watering system is commissioned before the final inspection, as inspection can occur in stages and commissioning issues can be addressed during inspection.
The window-planter structure must be physically installed before any waterproof membrane can be applied to its surfaces.
Surfaces must be clean, dry, and free of debris before applying waterproof membrane to ensure proper adhesion and sealing.
Primer must be applied and cured before the waterproof membrane to ensure proper bonding of the membrane to the substrate.
The drainage layer must be installed on top of the waterproof membrane to protect the membrane and allow water to flow away from the planter.
Growing medium must only be added after the waterproof membrane is fully sealed and cured to prevent moisture damage to the building envelope.
The half-open wall frame must be built on top of a completed floor slab or foundation system to provide a stable level base for wall layout and anchoring.
The bottom plate (or sole plate) must be anchored to the floor slab before the wall frame studs can be erected and nailed/bolted into place.
Wall locations including door and window openings must be marked on the floor slab/plate to guide precise placement of the half-open wall frame.
The top plate is installed on top of the wall studs after the frame is erected and plumbed, tying the studs together at their upper ends.
Structural sheathing (plywood/OSB) or exterior finish is applied over the completed wall frame to provide lateral bracing and enclosure.
The wall frame provides the structural support and enclosure needed to install glazing panels or windows.
Rough openings must be framed, squared, and weatherproofed before glazing units can be placed and secured.
Glazing must be installed and sealed before interior finishes are applied to avoid damage and to allow for proper sealing around the window frames.
The glazing installation must be complete to integrate with the exterior weather barrier and cladding system, ensuring a watertight seal.
While MEP work can be done before glazing in some areas, completing glazing first allows for better coordination of penetrations and avoids conflicts with window placement.
The half-open wall must be framed first to provide the structural support and cavity into which the built-in bench is installed.
Any electrical outlets, switches, or plumbing that will be within or behind the bench must be roughed in before the bench is built, as access would be blocked afterward.
The bench structure and any exposed wall surfaces behind/around the bench must be in place before finishing work like drywall, mudding, and taping can be completed around it.
The primary bench structure must be built before adding decorative trim, molding, or finish carpentry details to the bench face and edges.
It is preferable but not strictly required to install flooring before the bench; however, often the bench sits on top of finished flooring for a clean look, so sequencing can vary.
The half-open wall must be framed and structurally complete before the counter/desk top can be attached to it.
Any electrical outlets, data ports, or plumbing for the counter area must be roughed in within the wall before the counter top is installed.
The counter/desk top must be fully installed before final surface finishing, sealing, or coating can be applied.
Installing surrounding trim, edge banding, or decorative millwork is typically done after the counter top is in place for proper alignment and fit.
Final paint touch-ups and wall finishes near the counter are best completed after the counter is installed to ensure seamless edges and avoid damaging the counter surface during painting.
The half-open wall sill is installed onto the framed wall opening. The wall frame must be constructed first to provide the structural support and rough opening into which the sill will be placed.
The rough opening dimensions and substrate must be prepared and verified before the half-open wall sill can be installed to ensure proper fit and alignment.
The half-open wall sill serves as the bottom support and mounting surface for a window or door unit. The window or door frame rests on and is secured to the sill, so the sill must be in place first.

Weatherproofing and flashing details are applied over and around the installed sill to seal it against moisture intrusion. The sill must be fixed in place before these protective layers can be applied.

Trim work (e.g., stool, apron, or casing) is typically installed after the sill is in place for a finished appearance. This is a preference based on standard finishing sequence, but in some cases trim can be fitted before the sill is fully secured.
The wall must be constructed first to provide the supporting structure on which the half-open wall head beam rests.
The head beam must be installed to provide a bearing point and support for roof elements above the half-open wall section.
The head beam serves as a load-bearing element; upper floor framing or subsequent vertical loads cannot be placed until the beam is in position.
If the beam is cast-in-place, formwork must be erected and aligned before concrete placement and curing can begin for the beam.
Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured for the beam.
The foundation must be completed to provide a stable base and load-bearing support for the half-open walls.
The slab on grade must be prepared and cured to serve as the floor substrate upon which the half-open walls will be installed.
Primary steel columns and beams must be erected to define the structural grid and provide connection points for half-open wall panels.
Half-open walls provide vertical support and bearing for roof structural elements, so they must be installed before the roof can be placed.
The half-open wall framework must be erected before external cladding, insulation, and interior finishes can be applied to the walls.
Wall framing provides the structural support and opening into which the half-open wall glazing system is installed. Without the framed opening, there is no physical location to mount the glazing.

The rough opening must be prepared (sized correctly, headers installed, and load-bearing checks completed) to receive the glazing unit. Glazing installation cannot proceed without a properly prepared opening.
The primary building structure (steel frame or concrete slab) must be complete to support any wall framing activities.
After the glazing panels are installed, weatherproofing seals and perimeter sealants must be applied to ensure water tightness and air barrier continuity around the half-open wall system.
Interior finishes adjacent to the half-open wall glazing, such as drywall returns or plaster trims, are applied after the glazing is in place to create clean transitions and cover fixings.
The wall frame provides the structural support and defining boundary for the half-open wall, so furniture cannot be installed until the wall frame is built.

Electrical wiring, outlets, and any plumbing lines that will run within or behind the built-in furniture must be roughed in before the furniture is installed to avoid needing to dismantle or cut into the finished furniture.
It is generally easier to finish the ceiling before tall built-in furniture is placed against the wall, avoiding the need to work around or over the installed furniture.
If the built-in furniture includes a countertop surface, the furniture body must be fully installed first so the countertop can be accurately measured, cut, and placed on top of the unit.
Installing the furniture first allows trim pieces, baseboards, and decorative moldings to be fitted precisely against the furniture for a clean, finished appearance.
The structural framing elements (studs, joists, rafters) must be in place to provide the substrate and support for the wall finishing materials such as drywall, plaster, or paneling.
Electrical cables, outlets, and switch boxes must be installed inside the wall cavities before they are enclosed by wall finishing, as it is impossible or extremely costly to add them afterwards.
Plumbing pipes and drain lines running within walls must be installed before the walls are finished, since the finishing covers access to these elements.
Insulation batts or foam must be placed within wall cavities prior to finishing to achieve thermal and acoustic performance, and cannot be effectively added after the wall surface is in place.

The finished wall surface (e.g., drywall taped, mudded, and sanded, or plastered) must be completely dry and smooth before paint or wall coatings can be applied for proper adhesion and finish quality.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared (including header, sill, and cripple studs) before the interior window frame can be installed, as the frame fits into this prepared opening.
The exterior window unit or glass pane must be installed first so that the interior window frame can be aligned and attached to it, ensuring a proper seal and fit from the interior side.
The interior window frame must be in place before casing and trim can be applied around it, as the trim is fastened to the frame and the surrounding wall.

While interior window frames are often installed before drywall and painting for a clean finish, this is a soft preference as some sequences install frames after rough drywall to protect the frame from damage, then finish trim later.

It is generally preferred to complete rough electrical work (e.g., wiring near windows for lighting or outlets) before installing window frames to avoid interference, but it is not a strict physical necessity.
The window frame must be installed and properly sealed before the interior window sill can be attached, as the sill typically rests on or against the frame and integrates with the window opening.
The rough opening for the window must be framed in the wall to provide the structural support and cavity into which the window and sill are installed.

Exterior wall sheathing, weather-resistant barrier, and air sealing must be completed before interior finishes like the window sill are installed to protect the building envelope from moisture ingress.
The interior window sill provides a base surface; window casing and trim pieces are typically installed after and around the sill to create finished edges and hide gaps.

While wall finishing can be done before sill installation in some sequences, it is generally preferred to install the sill first so that drywall and paint can be fitted neatly around it, avoiding caulking gaps. However, this is a soft preference as the order can vary.
The window header/transom is installed within the framed wall opening; framing must be complete to provide the structural support and rough opening dimensions.
The rough sill at the bottom of the window opening must be in place before the header/transom can be installed as part of the complete rough opening assembly.
The header/transom provides the top structural support for the window or door unit; the unit cannot be placed until the header is installed.

While sheathing can technically proceed without the header fully finished, best practice is to complete all rough openings including headers before closing up walls to avoid rework and ensure proper alignment.
The window header/transom forms part of the rough opening structure; interior trim/casing around the window cannot be installed until the header and window unit are in place.
Interior walls must be framed to create the opening and structural support for the fixed interior window.
The rough opening must be prepared (sized and framed) before the fixed window unit can be installed.
The window must be installed before drywall can be applied around it to ensure proper fit and sealing.
Trim and casing around the window can only be installed after the window unit is fixed in place.
Painting is typically done after window installation to avoid damaging the window finish, though it could be done before if the window is carefully masked off.
The rough opening framing must be complete to provide the structural support and defined opening into which the interior window mullion will be installed.
The primary window frame must be installed first so that the interior mullion can be properly positioned and attached to the existing frame structure.
Interior wall surfaces around the window opening need to be in place to establish the finished plane and reveal that the mullion will align with.
Interior trim and casing around the mullion must be installed after the mullion is in place to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance.
Painting and final finishing of the window area should occur after the mullion is installed so that the mullion and adjacent surfaces are painted uniformly in the correct sequence.
The rough opening (stud framing, header, sill, and cripples) must be framed and in place to provide the structural support and defined opening for the window unit to be installed.
Building code requires inspection of the rough opening dimensions, squareness, and structural adequacy before any window installation can proceed.

predecessor: Interior Wall Sheathing / Drywall (Rough Openings Cut)
rationale: It is more efficient to install interior operable windows after wall sheathing or drywall is hung and the rough openings are cut, though window can technically be installed before drywall if necessary.
Interior window trim and casing boards are nailed onto the window frame and jambs; the window unit must be fully installed and shimmed level/plumb before trim can be applied.

While painting can occur before window installation, final touch-ups and painting of the window frame and surrounding wall area are typically completed after the window is set to achieve a clean finish without overspray on glass.
The window frame must be installed to provide a structural mounting surface for interior window hardware such as handles, locks, and hinges.
Glass panes must be set into the window frame before hardware (like locking mechanisms and sash hardware) can be attached, as the hardware often secures and operates the glazed sash.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared before any window components, including hardware, can be installed.

Interior window casing and trim are installed after the window hardware is in place because the trim must fit around the hardware components, and access to the hardware is needed during trim installation.
It is a soft preference to complete painting before installing hardware to avoid getting paint on hardware; however, if hardware is installed first, it can be masked off, but this is less efficient.
Windows must be installed and in place before interior trim/casing can be applied around them, as the casing covers the gap between the window frame and the wall.
Wall framing must be complete to provide the structure that supports the window and the surrounding wall surface to which the trim attaches.
Exterior sheathing and weatherproofing must be finished to protect the wall assembly before interior finishes like trim are installed.
Drywall must be hung, taped, mudded, and sanded smooth around the window opening before trim/casing can be installed, as the casing covers the drywall edge.

While trim can be painted before or after installation, typically the casing is installed first and then painted along with the walls, but some painters prefer to paint the wall surface first and then install pre-finished trim. This is a soft preference depending on the finishing strategy.

Typically flooring is installed before baseboards but after window casing; however, this order can vary. Often the casing is installed before flooring to allow flooring to run up to the casing neatly, but this is a workflow preference rather than a physical necessity.
The rough opening for the window must be framed in the wall before the borrowed light window can be installed, as the window requires an opening to be placed into.
The wall structure must be prepared to receive the window; any necessary weather barrier or sheathing must be cut to accommodate the window frame.
After the borrowed light window unit is set and secured in the opening, interior trim and casing can be installed around it to cover the gap between the window frame and the wall finish.
The window frame must be in place before the glass panels or glazing units are inserted and sealed.

successor: Interior Wall Finishing (taping/mudding/painting adjacent to window)
rationale: Final wall finishes around the window, such as drywall finishing and painting, should be completed after the window is installed to ensure proper integration and sealing.
Exterior wall sheathing provides the structural backing and rough opening into which the window frame is set; windows cannot be installed before the sheathing is in place.
The rough opening for the window must be framed to the correct dimensions to accommodate the window unit.

The exterior (outer) window unit is typically installed first from the outside; interior trim, casing, and finish work can only proceed after the exterior window is securely placed and weather-sealed.
Interior window installation includes setting the window frame and trim; drywall or plaster is then applied around the installed window to create a finished wall surface.
The window unit must be set in place before decorative casing and interior trim can be applied around it.
Exterior windows must be installed and framed before interior glazing work can begin, as the window frame and glass must be in place from the outside first.
The window frame must be roughed in and structurally prepared to receive the interior glazing components.
Exterior weatherproofing and flashing must be completed to prevent moisture intrusion before interior glazing is installed.
Interior trim and casing around windows is typically installed after glazing is complete for a finished appearance, though this is a logical sequence rather than a strict physical necessity.
Final painting and finishing around windows is typically done after glazing is installed to avoid damaging paint or getting paint on the glass.
Window and door frames must be installed first to provide the structural opening and rough framing that the interior trim and sealing will attach to and seal against.

Exterior cladding and weatherproofing around windows must be completed to ensure the building envelope is watertight before interior sealing and trim work begins; otherwise moisture could damage the interior finishes.

Drywall must be installed and finished around window openings so that the interior trim (e.g., casing, architraves) has a smooth finished wall surface to be installed against and to cover the gap between drywall and window frame.

While painting can be done before trim (back-painting), typically trim is installed before final wall painting so that the paint on walls can be cut in neatly against the trim without taping; however this is a preference for quality finish rather than a physical necessity.

Typically flooring (especially hardwood or tile) is installed before window trim so that the trim can sit flush on top of the finished floor; but with proper planning, flooring can also be installed after trim. This is a soft sequencing preference for best fit and finish.
Pass-through windows are installed within interior walls; the wall framing must be in place to provide the structural opening and support for the window unit.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (Electrical, Plumbing, and Mechanical rough-in within the wall)
rationale: MEP rough-in work inside the wall cavity (e.g., electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, or ductwork) must be completed before the window is installed, as the window will occupy and enclose a portion of the wall opening, making later access difficult or impossible.
Drywall must be installed after the window is placed so that it can be fitted and taped around the window frame, ensuring a seamless finished appearance around the opening.

Trim work around the pass-through window (such as casing, sill, and apron) cannot be properly installed until the window unit itself is secured in place, as the trim is fitted directly to the window frame.

While painting can often be done before window installation in some cases, the typical sequence is to install the window, apply primer and paint to adjacent walls and the window frame area last for the best finish. However, this is a soft preference because some trades may pre-paint and touch up later.
The window frame must be installed and positioned in the rough opening before anchors or fasteners can be applied to secure it to the surrounding structure.
The rough opening must be framed, squared, and properly sized to receive the window frame before it can be anchored and fastened into place.

The window frame must be securely anchored and fastened before any sealing or weatherproofing materials (such as caulk, foam, or flashing) are applied, as the fasteners provide structural stability needed before sealing.
Anchoring and fastening the window frame must be completed before interior wall finishes such as drywall, trim, or casing can be installed, as these finishes cover and conceal the fastening area.

While not a hard physical necessity, it is preferred that the window frame is fully anchored and secured before exterior siding or cladding is installed around the window to ensure proper integration and alignment.
A stable foundation is physically required before any intermediate landing structure can be installed to ensure load-bearing capacity and structural integrity.
The main structural framework (beams, columns) must be in place to provide the supporting structure onto which the intermediate landing is attached.
Staircases or ramps physically connect to the intermediate landing; the landing must be installed first to serve as the anchoring point.
Handrails and guardrails are mounted onto the landing structure for safety; they cannot be installed before the landing exists.

While surface finishing can be done after the landing is installed, it is a soft preference because finishing could theoretically be done beforehand if prefabricated; however, in practice, installation precedes finishing to avoid damage.
Stringers provide the structural support framework for the staircase; the half-landing must be seated on or attached to the stringers.

predecessor: Form and Pour Concrete for Half-Landing
rationale: If the half-landing is cast in-situ, the concrete must be poured and cured before it can support any subsequent loading or connections.
Stair flights typically bear on or connect to the half-landing at the change of direction; the landing must be in place to support the flight ends.
Handrails and balustrades are mounted on or adjacent to the half-landing; the landing structural element must be fixed before safety barriers can be attached.

Floor finishes such as tiles, timber, or non-slip coating are applied after the structural landing is installed, but this is a soft preference because it could be done later without affecting structural sequence.
The stair enclosure wall must be built on a solid foundation or slab to provide a stable base and bearing surface.
Structural framing inspections often need to be approved before enclosing walls are constructed.

successor: Rough-in Electrical / MEP for Stair Area
rationale: MEP rough-ins within or adjacent to the stair enclosure wall must wait until the wall framing is in place to run conduit, piping, or wiring through the wall cavities.
Drywall and interior finish cannot be applied until the stair enclosure wall is fully framed and in place.
The stair structure often depends on the enclosure wall for lateral support, attachment, or alignment, so the wall should be erected before the stair stringers or treads are installed.
The stair enclosure door frame requires the structural frame to be in place to provide proper support and attachment points.

The stair enclosure door must align with the finished stair slabs and landings for proper egress and access; without the stair slab in place, the door location and threshold height cannot be established.
The door is installed within the stair enclosure walls; rough opening framing must be completed before the door unit can be set.
Firestopping and sealant around the door frame can only be applied after the door is installed and the gaps between frame and wall are exposed.
While painting and trim can technically proceed before the door, it is generally preferred to install the door early so that finishes can be cut in neatly around the door frame, avoiding rework.
The monumental stair requires a stable foundation to bear its structural load; without foundation work completed, the stair cannot be safely or durably constructed.
The monumental stair typically connects to or is supported by the main building frame; the structural frame must be in place to provide anchorage and support for the stair.
Once the monumental stair structure is complete, finishing works such as balustrades, handrails, cladding, painting, and flooring can proceed.
Lighting, electrical, and other services can be installed after the stair structure is in place, but they may partially be done in parallel with careful coordination.
The area where the monumental stair will be built must be excavated, leveled, and prepared before any stair construction can commence.
The scissor stair must be supported by the building's structural steel frame; the stair cannot be installed without the main structural framework in place to attach to.
The vertical shaft or opening where the scissor stair will be placed must be roughed in and prepared before the stair components can be installed.
Guardrails and handrails are attached to the installed stair structure; they cannot be placed until the stair itself is in position.
Fireproofing spray or board application must be applied after the stair is erected to ensure full coverage of all exposed structural surfaces.

While stair finishing typically follows installation, some finishes may be pre-applied in a controlled factory environment; however, on-site finishing work such as paint touch-ups and tread installation conventionally occur after the stair is set in place.
Stairs require a stable load-bearing base. The foundation must be completed to support the structural load of the stair system.
The main structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to define the floor-to-floor heights and provide the structural supports onto which stairs will be anchored.
Stairs connect different floor levels; the floor slabs at both the lower and upper levels must be cast and cured to provide the landing surfaces and support points for the stair flights.

While some MEP rough-in can proceed in parallel, final routing of electrical conduits, plumbing, or fire protection near stair enclosures is easier and avoids rework if performed after stair structure is in place to verify clearances.

Final finishes such as handrail installation, painting, tile or tread covering, and wall finishes adjacent to stairs must occur after the stair structure is complete to ensure proper fit and alignment.
The concrete stairs must be poured and fully cured to provide a stable structural base for finishing activities such as grinding, coating, or tiling.
Electrical, plumbing, and mechanical rough-ins that pass through or near stair areas must be completed before finishing to avoid cutting into finished surfaces.
The structural framing (steel or concrete) of the stair must be complete and inspected before any finishing work can be applied.
Handrails and guardrails are typically installed after stair surfaces are finished to ensure proper alignment and secure attachment without damaging finished surfaces.
While final paint touch-ups can be done after stair finishing, it is a soft preference to complete painting after finishing to protect freshly finished stair surfaces from paint drips and overspray.
Handrails must be anchored into a solid, cured concrete structure. Installing before the concrete has fully cured would compromise structural integrity and safety.
The structural framework (e.g., stairs, balconies, ramps) must be in place to provide the supporting structure onto which handrails are mounted.
Safety inspections and load testing of handrails can only be performed once the handrails are fully installed and secured.

successor: Wall Cladding / Railing Panel Installation (if adjacent)
rationale: While it is often easier to install handrails after adjacent wall cladding, the cladding can sometimes be worked around. This is a soft preference to prevent damage to finished surfaces.

successor: Painting and Finishing of Adjacent Surfaces
rationale: Touch-up painting and finishing of areas around handrails is typically done after installation to cover anchors and scratches, but painting can also be completed beforehand with careful masking.
Fireproofing material must be applied to the structural frame; the stair/stairwell frame must be fully erected and secured before fireproofing can be applied to it.
Any concrete landings or structural slabs must be poured and cured before fireproofing is applied to adjacent steel or structural elements.
Fireproofing must be fully cured and inspected before applying final finishes (paint, drywall, handrails, etc.) to avoid damaging the fireproofing layer.
Fireproofing must be completed before permanent mechanical, electrical, or plumbing installations to ensure fire-rated assemblies are not compromised by later cutting or drilling.
While inspections often follow fireproofing application, if staging is needed for access it is a soft preference to schedule inspection after fireproofing is fully dry and inspected itself.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before a corner door frame can be installed, as the frame fits into the prepared opening.
A level and structurally sound floor or foundation is required to support and anchor the corner door frame properly.
The adjacent wall studs and corner framing must be in place to receive and secure the corner door frame assembly.
The door frame must be securely installed before the door leaf can be hung and aligned within the frame.
The door frame must be fully installed and secured before decorative casing and trim can be applied around it.
The door leaf must be assembled within or attached to the frame; the frame provides structural support and alignment for the door leaf.
The corner door leaf must be fully fabricated before it can be installed in the opening.
Hardware components like hinges and handles must be mounted onto the installed door leaf.
Sealing and weatherproofing around the corner door leaf can only be applied after the leaf is properly positioned and fixed.
Inspection and testing of the door leaf operation (swing, clearance, latch) typically follows installation, though some checks can be done prior.
The corner pivot hinge set must be attached to the frame assembly; the frame must be assembled first to provide the structural member to which the hinge is mounted.
The hinge set must be installed on the frame before the door or panel can be hung onto it, as the hinge provides the pivot point for the door/panel.
The hinge set must be fabricated or procured (i.e., made available on-site) before installation can begin.
The door frame must be installed to provide a mounting surface for the weatherseal.
Weatherseal must be applied to the frame corners before the door leaf is hung to ensure proper sealing alignment.
Applying the weatherseal before final adjustments allows the door fit to be checked and fine-tuned for optimal sealing.
Corner door hardware (hinges, locks, handles) must be mounted onto the door frame. Without the frame in place, there is no structural substrate to attach the hardware to.

predecessor: Wall Framing and Rough Opening Preparation
rationale: The rough opening for the corner door must be framed and prepared before any door components, including hardware, can be installed, as the hardware is part of the door assembly that fits into the opening.
Once hardware is installed, the door must be tested for proper swing, latch engagement, and clearance. This cannot occur until the hardware is physically mounted.

While finishing can sometimes be done in part before hardware installation, typically final painting and trim work around the corner door hardware is performed after installation to ensure clean edges and proper fit around the hardware components.
The door slab itself must be prepared (cut to size, routed for hinges and lockset) before the hardware can be installed onto it. Hardware cannot be mounted on an unprepared door.

successor: Corner Door Fixed Glazing Panel Installation
rationale: The rough opening and structural framing must be in place to provide the supporting framework into which the fixed glazing panel will be installed.

successor: Corner Door Fixed Glazing Panel Installation
rationale: Weatherproofing the surrounding wall prevents moisture ingress that could damage the panel or its seals during and after installation.

predecessor: Corner Door Fixed Glazing Panel Installation
rationale: Installing the fixed glazing panel before interior finishes allows clean edges, but interior finishing can be partially done before; typically the panel goes in before final trim and paint to avoid damage to finishes.

predecessor: Corner Door Fixed Glazing Panel Installation
rationale: Exterior sealants and caulking around the panel must be applied after the panel is fixed in place to ensure a watertight seal around its perimeter.

predecessor: Corner Door Fixed Glazing Panel Installation
rationale: Final exterior cladding around the corner door area should be completed after the glazing panel is installed to properly integrate and flash the panel into the building envelope.
The corner door must have a framed rough opening to be installed into; the framing defines the structural space and support for the door unit.
Trim and casing cannot be applied until the door unit is physically installed and secured in the rough opening.
Exterior weatherproofing and flashing around the door frame must be applied after the door is installed to ensure a proper seal against moisture.
Drywall finishing around the door opening should be completed after the door is in place to allow for proper taping and mudding against the door frame.
The door must be hung before hardware such as locks, handles, and hinges can be fully installed and aligned on the door and jamb.
The door frame must be installed before hardware can be adjusted and commissioned on it.
The door must be hung on its hinges before hardware such as locks, handles, and closers can be adjusted and commissioned.
Rough-in wiring, blocking, and backing for hardware must be completed before final hardware adjustment and commissioning can proceed.
Hardware adjustment and commissioning must be completed before the final door inspection and testing can be performed.
Weatherstripping and sealing should be applied after hardware is adjusted to ensure proper alignment and clearance of seals around the adjusted hardware components.
Thick walls require a stable foundation to bear their significant weight and load; foundation must be fully cured and ready before wall construction begins.
The building site must be excavated, leveled, and prepared before any structural wall construction can commence.
Thick walls provide the vertical load-bearing support for roof structures; the roof cannot be installed until the walls are built and have achieved sufficient strength.
Window and door openings are formed within the thick walls as they are constructed; frames must be installed after the wall structure is in place.
Interior wall finishes typically begin after the thick wall structural work is complete, though some finishing can be parallel in certain cases.

Loadbearing thick walls require a stable foundation to transfer vertical loads safely to the ground. Without completed foundations, the wall would lack proper support and could settle unevenly or collapse.
The wall base often sits on or ties into the ground floor slab, which must be cast and cured before the wall is erected to provide a level working platform and structural tie-in.
The roof framing and decking bear directly on top of loadbearing walls. The walls must be fully constructed, aligned, and cured to support roof loads and provide the correct bearing points.
Upper floor joists or slabs typically rest on or are supported by loadbearing walls below. The wall must be in place to transfer vertical loads from upper floors down to the foundation.

Exterior cladding, insulation, or interior finishes are applied after the structural wall is complete. This is a logical sequence (rough structure before finish), though in some cases partial finishes could start before full wall completion.
The non-loadbearing thick wall requires a stable, level base such as a foundation or slab on grade to support its weight and provide a substrate for construction.

The main structural frame (columns, beams, loadbearing walls) must be erected first because the non-loadbearing thick wall is an infill or partition element that does not carry structural loads and is placed within or against the already established structural grid.

Any electrical conduits, plumbing pipes, or ductwork that will be embedded within or pass through the thick wall must be installed before the wall is built to avoid costly retrofitting and damage to the finished wall.
The thick wall substrate must be fully constructed and cured before applying finishes such as plaster, render, cladding, or paint to ensure a sound base and avoid cracking or adhesion failure.
Finishing adjacent floors or ceilings is often sequenced after wall construction to achieve clean junctions, but can sometimes be done before; this is a soft preference for quality of workmanship.
Thick wall reinforcement must be built upon a stable foundation; without it, the reinforcement cannot be properly anchored and the structural integrity would be compromised.
Thick wall reinforcement (rebar and steel mesh) must be fully placed and tied before concrete can be poured, as the reinforcement provides the tensile strength within the concrete structure.
Formwork is assembled around the placed reinforcement to shape the concrete pour, so reinforcement must be in position first before formwork can be closed.
The site must be excavated and leveled before any reinforcement work can begin, as the reinforcement requires a prepared subgrade and proper working surface.
Backfilling around reinforced walls can only occur after the wall reinforcement and concrete have cured sufficiently, to avoid damaging the reinforced structure.
The foundation or plinth provides the stable base upon which walls are built, and thick wall ties/connectors are installed within or between wall elements that sit on this foundation.

predecessor: Hollow Block / Brick Wall Masonry (First Leaf)
rationale: Thick wall ties are embedded into the mortar joints of masonry walls during construction; at least the first leaf of the wall must be laid to receive the tie.
After placing the wall tie into the first leaf, the second leaf or opposite wythe is built up, embedding the other end of the tie to structurally connect the two leaves.
While insulation can be installed as the cavity progresses, it is typically placed after ties are positioned to avoid displacing the ties, though some sequencing flexibility exists.
DPCs are often installed concurrently with or after wall ties, but ties should be in place before completing the upper wall sections to ensure structural continuity.
The thick wall must be in place before an opening can be created and a lintel installed to support the structure above the opening.
After the lintel is placed, it requires time to cure and gain strength before any load is applied above it.
Typically finishing work occurs after lintel installation, though this is a soft preference as some finishing could be done around the opening beforehand.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth and shape before any foundation can be poured or laid, as the foundation sits within the excavated area.
The soil subgrade must be compacted and stable to provide adequate load-bearing capacity before placing the foundation, otherwise differential settlement could occur.
The precise location, alignment, and levels of the thick wall must be marked on site before foundation construction begins to ensure dimensional accuracy.
Waterproofing membranes or coatings are applied to the cured foundation surface to prevent moisture ingress; the foundation must be complete and cured before waterproofing can be installed.

The thick wall foundation provides the structural base and load transfer surface upon which the wall itself is built; wall construction cannot start until the foundation is in place and has achieved sufficient strength.
The wall or parapet structure must be constructed first to provide a stable substrate onto which the thick wall coping/parapet can be installed.
The coping/parapet must be in place before any waterproofing membrane can be applied over it to ensure continuous weather protection.
Flashing details tie into the coping/parapet; the coping must be installed first to serve as a secure anchoring point for flashing.
Railings are often anchored into the parapet/coping; the coping must be fully cured and in place to provide a secure base for railing posts.
Although inspections often follow completion of the coping, the order is a procedural preference rather than a physical necessity.
Thick walls require a solid, load-bearing foundation to support their weight and transfer loads to the ground. The foundation must be fully cured and set before any wall construction begins.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the required depth for the foundation before any wall construction can proceed.
Roof structures depend on the load-bearing walls for support. The thick walls must be completed, cured, and able to bear loads before roof framing or trusses can be installed.

While it is possible to chase or core through thick walls later, it is more efficient and structurally advisable to install conduits, pipes, and sleeves within the wall formwork before pouring or laying the wall. However, this is a soft preference as retrofitting is possible but disruptive.
Interior finishes such as plastering, drywall, or cladding can only be applied after the wall is fully constructed, cured, and stable. Finishing before wall completion is physically impossible.
The structural wall must be built and fully cured before insulation can be installed against it, as insulation requires a stable substrate to attach to.
The cavity or wall assembly must be weatherproofed (e.g., external cladding or membrane installed) to protect insulation materials from moisture ingress before installation.
Electrical wiring, conduits, and plumbing pipes must be routed within the wall cavity before insulation is installed, as insulating after would block access to these services.
Insulation must be in place before the internal lining (e.g., plasterboard or drywall) is fixed, to enclose the insulation and complete the wall assembly.
A continuous vapor barrier or air seal is typically applied over the insulation surface on the warm side of the wall, so insulation must be installed first to provide a backing surface.
The thick wall must be fully constructed and cured before any waterproofing membrane or coating can be applied to its surface.
The wall surface must be clean, dry, and free of debris or protrusions to ensure proper adhesion of the waterproofing material.
The waterproofing layer must be allowed to cure or dry fully before any subsequent work that could damage it.
Waterproofing must be fully applied and cured before backfilling soil or gravel against the wall to avoid damage and ensure a continuous water barrier.
Insulation boards or drainage panels are typically installed over the cured waterproofing membrane, so waterproofing must be completed first.

The foundation slab must be fully poured and cured to provide a stable, level base for installing thick wall reinforcement. Without a finished foundation, the reinforcement cannot be properly anchored or positioned.

Accurate survey markings and layout lines are needed to define the exact position, alignment, and dimensions of the thick walls so that reinforcement can be placed correctly within the designated footprint.
Reinforcement (rebar cages/mats) must be fully installed, tied, and inspected before formwork can be erected around it. Formwork encloses the reinforcement to shape the concrete pour.

While some embedded items can be placed concurrently with reinforcement, critical conduits, sleeves, and anchor bolts are best positioned after the main reinforcement is in place to avoid interference. This is a soft preference for sequencing efficiency.
Concrete cannot be poured until all reinforcement is installed and inspected. The reinforcement must be fully in place to provide structural integrity within the poured concrete.
The wall frame or studs provide the structural backing and substrate necessary for applying any thick wall finish, ensuring the finish adheres properly and has a stable surface.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing services within the wall must be roughed-in before the wall finish is applied, as accessing these systems after the finish is in place would be destructive and costly.
Insulation must be placed within the wall cavity before the wall finish is applied, as the finish would seal off the cavity and prevent installation of insulation later.
Thick wall finishes (such as stucco, plaster, or textured coatings) require a drying or curing period before any final paint or decorative coating can be applied over them.
Typically wall finishes are completed before flooring to avoid damaging finished floors, but this is a soft preference as some sequences do flooring first with proper protection.
The damp-proof course (DPC) must be installed above ground level and after the foundation walls are built to provide a continuous barrier against rising damp.
The DPC must be installed in the wall at the correct height before the walls above are built, as it is built into the mortar joint and cannot be added later.

successor: Floor Slab / Ground Bearing Slab Installation
rationale: The DPC in thick walls typically ties into the floor damp-proof membrane, so the wall DPC should be installed before or simultaneously with the floor slab to ensure continuity of the damp-proofing.
The site must be excavated and prepared before any wall construction and DPC installation can commence.
A level concrete blinding or footing is required to build the thick wall upon before the DPC can be installed at the correct height.
The closet partition walls must be built on top of a completed floor slab or underlayment to provide a stable, level base.
The locations for closet partition walls must be marked out on the floor based on the architectural plans before framing can begin.
Partition walls must be fully framed before sheathing or drywall can be applied to them.
Electrical wiring for closet lights or outlets must be run through the framed wall cavities before the walls are enclosed with drywall.
The closet partition walls must be fully built, sheathed, and taped/mudded before painting or final finishing can occur.
The closet door requires the closet framing to be completed first, as the door frame needs to be installed within the rough opening created by the framing.
The rough opening for the closet door must be properly sized, shimmed, and prepared before the door unit can be installed.
Drywall around the closet opening should be installed and finished before the door casing and door are hung to allow for proper trim installation and gap coverage.
The closet door must be hung and properly aligned before casing and trim can be installed around the door opening.
The door must be in place before handles, hinges, and other hardware can be attached to the door.
While painting can be done before installation, final touch-up painting and finishing of the door and trim is typically performed after installation for best aesthetic results.
