Closet shelving requires a framed wall to attach to; without wall framing there is no structural support for shelving brackets or supports.
Drywall must be installed and finished before closet shelving can be mounted, as shelving is attached to finished wall surfaces.
Flooring must be completed before closet shelving is installed to ensure shelving is measured and leveled from the finished floor height.

While not a hard physical constraint, it is a soft preference to install shelving before painting so that shelving area can be painted behind and around, or alternatively painting is often done before shelving; but typically shelving goes in after painting to avoid damaging finished paint.
Closet doors must be installed after shelving is in place to ensure proper clearance and to avoid interference with shelving during door hanging and adjustment.

predecessor: Rough-in Electrical and Plumbing for Closet Area
rationale: Electrical and plumbing rough-ins must be completed in the walls before closet rod brackets and supports are installed to avoid interference and rework.
Closet walls must be framed to provide the structural support for mounting the closet rod brackets or flanges.
Wall surfaces need to be finished before installing closet rods so that brackets can be securely attached to finished walls and the rod is correctly positioned.

successor: Final Painting and Touch-up of Closet Interior
rationale: While painting can be done before rod installation, final touch-up painting is often performed after rod installation to cover any marks from installation; this is a soft preference for cosmetic finish.

successor: Installation of Closet Shelving and Storage Systems
rationale: Hanging rod provides the primary hanging storage; additional shelving is typically positioned relative to the rod height and must be installed after the rod to ensure proper spacing and clearance.
Electrical wiring and junction box must be installed and roughed-in at the closet location before the light fixture can be mounted and connected.
The ceiling surface (drywall) must be in place so the light fixture can be mounted securely and the electrical box can be properly finished flush with the ceiling.
It is a soft preference to install the light fixture before painting so that the painter can cut in around the fixture; however the fixture can also be installed after painting if care is taken.
The light fixture installation should be completed before closet shelving and rods are installed to allow unobstructed access and avoid damage to shelving when working overhead.
The closet framing must be built on a completed, cured concrete slab or foundation to provide a stable base and proper anchoring.
The subfloor or underlayment must be in place before framing walls or closet partitions to ensure proper alignment and load distribution.

predecessor: Rough Electrical / Wiring for Closet Area
rationale: While electrical rough-in can be done before or after framing, it is often preferred to run wiring in open wall cavities before framing is completed in tight closet spaces for easier access.
Drywall cannot be installed until the closet wall framing is fully constructed, secured, and inspected, as the framing provides the structural support for the drywall.
The door frame requires the closet framing to be in place to define the opening dimensions and provide structural support for hanging the door.
The closet door frame provides the structural opening and support needed to hang the door; without the framed opening, the door has no structure to attach to.

Drywall must be installed and finished around the closet opening to create smooth, finished surfaces that the door casing and jambs will abut against. Installing the door before drywall would require rework or damage.
It is easier and cleaner to paint the walls adjacent to the closet opening before the door casing and door are installed, avoiding paint drips on the door and hard-to-reach areas behind the casing.
Door knobs, hinges, and latches are physically attached to the door and jamb, so the door must first be hung in place before these components can be installed and aligned.
The door casing and trim are installed around the door frame to cover the gap between the jamb and drywall; the door must be in place to properly set reveals and clearances around the casing.
Shelving and rods are typically mounted onto or attached to wall framing. The wall framing provides the structural support needed to securely install closet systems.
Drywall provides the finished surface onto which shelving tracks, brackets, and rod flanges are mounted. Installing shelving before drywall would require rework or result in unfinished appearance.
Painting must be completed before shelving is installed because it is difficult to paint behind installed shelving and rods, and to avoid damaging or getting paint on the closet components.

While shelving can technically be installed before flooring, it is standard practice to complete flooring first to avoid cutting shelving/rods around flooring or damaging flooring during shelving installation. This is a soft preference for quality and workflow efficiency.

After all closet components are installed, final cleaning and inspection must occur to ensure the shelving and rods are properly secured, level, and free of debris before the space is considered complete.

Closet doors are typically installed after shelving to prevent interference and damage. However, in some cases doors can be installed first if clearance allows, making this a soft preference for installation convenience.
The wall framing must be complete to provide the structural support and enclosed space for the closet installation.
Electrical wiring for any closet lighting or outlets must be run within the walls before the closet is built and finished to avoid destructive rework.
The interior walls of the closet area must be drywalled, taped, and finished before closet components are installed to provide a clean finished surface.
Wall-to-wall closets are typically painted or finished as part of the room, so closet installation must precede final painting to achieve a seamless appearance.
The closet base and floor area should be accessible for flooring installation; however, in many sequences the closet is installed before final flooring to ensure proper fit and transitions.
The closet framing must be in place to provide the structural opening and support for installing the ventilation grille.
Drywall must be installed and finished around the closet opening before the grille can be mounted, as the grille attaches to the finished wall surface.

While painting can be done before or after grille installation, it is often preferred to install the grille after painting to avoid getting paint on the grille, but this is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
The ventilation grille must be installed before the HVAC system can be fully inspected and balanced, as the grille is a visible and functional component of the ventilation system.

The counter base/cabinet must be placed on a level, prepared subfloor. Floor rough-ins (e.g., plumbing, electrical) need to be completed before the cabinet is installed so that connections are accessible and the cabinet can be properly positioned.

Walls must be framed and finished (including any backing/blocking) before cabinets are hung or aligned against them, as the cabinets attach to the wall structure and require a completed wall surface for proper fit and anchoring.

If the counter includes a sink, the base cabinet must be installed first so that the sink can be mounted into the countertop and plumbing connections (supply lines, drain) can be made to the fixture within the cabinet.
The backsplash is typically installed after the counter base/cabinet and countertop are in place to create a continuous finished surface and cover the gap between wall and counter.
Countertops must be installed on top of a stable base cabinet structure for support and alignment.
Base cabinets need a level, prepared subfloor to sit on before countertops can be installed.
Plumbing supply and drain lines must be roughed in behind the base cabinets before countertops are placed, as the countertop would block access.
Sink must be mounted into the cutout in the completed countertop surface.
While backsplash is typically installed after countertop to overlap the seam, it could be done before in some cases; this is a soft preference for proper sequencing.
The countertop base cabinets provide the structural foundation upon which the counters and backsplash are mounted. Without installed cabinets, the backsplash has no supporting structure.
Plumbing rough-in work (pipes, drain lines) must be completed behind the wall before the backsplash is installed, as the backsplash will cover the wall surface and make access difficult.
Electrical wiring and outlet boxes must be roughed-in before backsplash installation, otherwise wiring would need to be run over or through the finished backsplash.

The backsplash is typically installed after the countertop is in place to ensure proper alignment and sealing at the counter-to-wall junction. However, in some sequences backsplash goes after countertop. Assuming typical residential construction: countertop is installed first, then backsplash.

After the backsplash tiles or panels are installed, the joint between countertop and backsplash must be sealed/caulked to prevent water damage. This final finishing step must occur after backsplash installation.
The integrated sink is part of the countertop assembly; the countertop must be fabricated and installed before the sink can be integrated into it.
Water supply and drain lines must be roughed in before the sink is physically installed and connected.

successor: Sink Fixture Connection (Faucet, Trap, Drain Assembly)
rationale: The sink body must be in place before faucets, drains, and traps can be connected to it.
The integrated sink is part of the countertop surface; sealing and finishing must occur after the sink is fully installed to ensure a continuous watertight surface.
Installing the backsplash after the sink allows for a clean interface between the countertop/sink and wall, but it can sometimes be done beforehand if the sink area is left accessible.
The Sunny Counter Edge Profile is an edge treatment applied to the countertop; the base countertop must be installed first to provide the substrate for the edge profile.
The countertop material must be cut, shaped, and fabricated to size before the edge profile detailing can be applied.
The edge profile must be fully applied before final sealing or finishing coats are applied to ensure a continuous, uniform surface treatment.
It is typical to complete edge profiling before cutting openings for sinks or cooktops to avoid damaging the finished edge, though in some sequences this order can be reversed.
The counter edge profile should be completed before backsplash installation to ensure the backsplash butts cleanly against the finished counter edge.
The counter overhang/seating extension requires a stable concrete slab or foundation base to be built upon, so foundation/slab work must be completed first.
The main building structural framing provides the support structure to which the counter overhang and seating extension attach, so it must be in place first.

Any underground or in-slab rough-in utilities needed for the counter area (e.g., electrical outlets, water for sink if applicable) must be installed before the counter/seating structure is built over them.
After the counter overhang structural frame and substrate are built, the finished countertop surface (e.g., stone, concrete, tile) can be installed on top.
The overhang and seating structure must be fully constructed before final finishing work such as painting, caulking, and sealing can be applied to the assembly.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical wiring for counter area
rationale: Electrical rough-in must be completed before installing the drawer system to avoid interference and allow access for wiring behind and under the counter.
The base cabinets or supporting structure for the counter must be in place before the drawer system can be mounted or installed upon them.

predecessor: Plumbing rough-in for sink area (if applicable)
rationale: Any plumbing supply or drain lines that will run behind or beneath the counter must be roughed in before the drawer system blocks access.

successor: Countertop surface installation (e.g., granite, quartz, laminate)
rationale: The drawer system frame must be fully installed and secured before the countertop surface is placed on top, as the countertop covers and rests upon the drawer/cabinet structure.
All drawer hardware and alignment adjustments should be completed before final sealing/caulking to avoid contaminating surfaces or needing to rework finished edges.
The under-counter lighting must be mounted underneath the countertop, so the countertop must be installed first to provide the mounting surface and support structure.
Electrical power supply wiring and junction boxes must be roughed in before the under-counter lighting can be connected and mounted.
After the lighting fixture is mounted, the final electrical connections, switch plate installation, and trim-out work can be completed.
It is preferable to install the under-counter lighting before the backsplash to conceal wiring and avoid damaging the backsplash material, though it could be done after with additional effort.
Final cabinet trim around the lighting area is typically completed after lighting installation to ensure a clean fit and conceal any mounting brackets or wiring channels.
Electrical wiring must be run through walls and floors before outlets can be installed on the counter.
The counter surface must be in place before outlets can be mounted into or onto it.
Walls and backsplashes must be finished before outlets are installed to avoid damage to finished surfaces.

successor: Outlet Trim and Cover Plate Installation
rationale: Outlet boxes and receptacles must be installed and wired before cover plates can be attached for safety and aesthetics.
Outlets must be physically installed and connected before they can be tested for continuity, grounding, and safe operation.
The splash apron is attached to the countertop, so the countertop must be installed first to provide the structural base for the apron.
If the sink is undermounted, it is typically installed before the splash apron to ensure proper sealing and alignment with the countertop edge.
The splash apron forms the lower border of the backsplash area; the backsplash tiles are installed after the apron to abut it properly and create a clean seam.
Final sealing or finishing of the countertop edge near the apron should occur after the apron is installed to ensure continuous protection and a seamless appearance.
Base cabinets must be installed and leveled before the countertop (and hence the splash apron) can be placed and secured.
Base cabinets require a level, cured concrete slab foundation to sit on. Installing cabinets before the slab is poured and cured would result in an unstable and unlevel installation.
Electrical outlets and wiring for countertop appliances must be roughed in behind the cabinet locations before cabinets are installed, as they would be inaccessible afterwards.
Plumbing supply lines and drain pipes for the sink must be roughed in within the cabinet footprint before the cabinets are placed.
Countertops are measured, fabricated, and installed directly on top of the base cabinets. Base cabinets must be in place and leveled to support the countertop.
The sink is mounted into the countertop or sits on the base cabinet; base cabinets must be installed first to provide the structural support and enclosure for the sink.
Plumbing and electrical rough-ins must be complete before countertop installation to avoid damaging the countertop and ensure proper fit around fixtures.
Base cabinets provide the structural support for the countertop, so they must be installed and level before the countertop can be placed.
The countertop must be installed first so that the sink and fixtures can be properly mounted into or onto the countertop surface.
The countertop provides the bottom edge reference for the backsplash; backsplash tiles or panels must be installed after the countertop is in place to ensure a seamless joint.
Final connections of the sink drain and faucet supply lines can only be made after the countertop and sink are installed.
The counter surface must be fully prepared (cleaned, leveled, and ready) before any backsplash can be installed on top of or behind it.
The base cabinets supporting the counter must be in place to provide a stable foundation for the counter and backsplash installation.
Grout application can only occur after the backsplash tiles or panels are firmly installed in their final positions.

successor: Install Countertop Trim and Edge Molding
rationale: Trim and edge molding are finished details that should be applied after the backsplash is installed to ensure proper alignment and a seamless appearance.
Caulking along the seams between the counter and backsplash must be done after the backsplash is fully installed to seal gaps and provide a waterproof finish.

predecessor: Install Sunny Counter Sink and Plumbing
successor: Connect Water Supply Lines to Sunny Counter Sink
rationale: The sink and its plumbing must be physically installed before water supply lines can be connected to it.

predecessor: Install Sunny Counter Sink and Plumbing
successor: Install Drain Pipe for Sunny Counter Sink
rationale: The sink and its plumbing must be in place before the drain pipe can be properly aligned and connected.

predecessor: Install Sunny Counter Sink and Plumbing
successor: Test Faucet and Sink for Leaks
rationale: The sink and plumbing system must be fully installed before any leak testing can be performed.

predecessor: Frame and Rough-In Plumbing for Sunny Counter
successor: Install Sunny Counter Sink and Plumbing
rationale: Rough-in plumbing (including drain and supply stub-outs) must be completed prior to installing the sink and its final plumbing connections.

successor: Install Sunny Counter Sink and Plumbing
rationale: The countertop must be installed first so that the sink can be mounted into/onto it and plumbing connections can be made through the counter.

successor: Seal Sunny Counter Seams and Edges
rationale: The counter must be installed before its seams and edges can be sealed, as sealing is a finishing step applied to the installed counter surface.

successor: Seal Sunny Counter Seams and Edges
rationale: The counter surface must be clean and free of debris, dust, and residues before applying sealant to ensure proper adhesion and a smooth finish.

predecessor: Seal Sunny Counter Seams and Edges
rationale: After applying the sealant to seams and edges, sufficient curing/drying time is required before any further work or use of the counter can proceed.

predecessor: Seal Sunny Counter Seams and Edges
rationale: Once sealing is complete, a quality inspection should follow to verify that the sealant has been applied uniformly and that seams and edges are properly protected.
The junction box must be installed before wiring can begin, as it provides the enclosure and connection point for electrical components.

predecessor: Rough-in Electrical Conduit to Sunny Counter
rationale: Conduit must be routed to the counter location before wires can be pulled through it.
Wiring must be completed and in place before outlets and switches can be connected and mounted.
Wiring must be fully installed before electrical testing and verification can be performed.
Electrical wiring must be completed before the countertop or face coverings are installed, to avoid covering unfinished electrical work.
Countertop rough-in (including plumbing and electrical rough-ins for the wet bar) must be completed before the wet bar extension can be installed.
The base cabinets for the wet bar must be installed to provide support and a mounting surface for the countertop extension.
The wet bar countertop extension must be installed before the final sealing and finishing of the countertop surface can be applied.
The countertop extension must be in place before the sink and faucet can be mounted, as they are installed into/through the countertop.
Typically the countertop is installed before the backsplash, but this can be a soft constraint if the backsplash is a separate piece.
The reception desk variant must be installed on a prepared, level floor surface to ensure stability and proper alignment.
Any required electrical outlets, data ports, or wiring for the reception desk must be roughed in before the desk is placed to avoid needing to move or work around the installed unit.

While walls can be painted before desk installation for easier access, it is often preferred to install the desk first so that surrounding finishes can be completed up to the desk edges for a clean, custom fit.
Final connection of power and data cabling to the desk's integrated outlets and workstations can only be completed after the desk is in its final position.
Any signage, monitor mounts, or accessory items that attach to or sit on the desk require the desk to be fully installed and secured first.
The open shelf bracket must be mounted to a framed wall. Wall framing provides the structural support needed to securely attach the bracket.
Electrical wiring within the wall must be completed and inspected before installing brackets to avoid interference or damage to wiring.
The bracket must be securely installed on the wall before any shelf board can be placed onto it for support.
Aesthetic finishing touches like painting or trim work around the shelf are typically done after the bracket is installed to ensure a clean look, though not physically mandatory.

The base shelf standard/rail provides the bottom support and structural foundation upon which the open shelf standard/rail is mounted. Without the base shelf standard in place, there is no stable anchor for the open shelf component.
Wall anchors or structural supports must be installed first to provide load-bearing capacity for the open shelf standard/rail, ensuring it can safely support shelf loads.
The open shelf standard/rail must be in place before shelf panels can be placed onto it, as the standard/rail serves as the supporting track or bracket system for the shelves.
Brackets that attach to the open shelf standard/rail cannot be installed until the standard/rail itself is securely mounted, as brackets require the rail as their mounting surface.
Layout markings and measurements must be completed first to ensure the open shelf standard/rail is positioned at the correct height, level, and alignment for the shelving system.
Shelf pins/clips are inserted into or mounted onto shelf brackets, which must be installed first to provide the support structure.
Shelf pins/clips must be installed first to create the supports on which the shelf board rests.
The wall must be prepared with anchors or the bracket locations marked at studs before shelf pins/clips can be positioned relative to those supports.
Clipping or pin placement should be complete before placing items on the shelf to ensure stability, though minor adjustments could theoretically be made after.
Wall cleats require a framed wall structure to be in place as they are mounted onto or within the wall framing.
Wall cleats serve as structural supports for cabinets, shelves, or other wall-mounted fixtures, so they must be installed first.

While often cleats are installed over finished walls, if the cleat is to be concealed behind wall finish, it must be installed before finishing; otherwise, this is a soft preference based on design intent.
Framing must be inspected and approved before cleats are installed to ensure the wall structure meets load-bearing requirements.
Wall cleats provide the anchoring point for mounting heavy equipment (e.g., HVAC units, water heaters, or workshop tools); mounting cannot proceed until cleats are secured.
Corbels are structural projections from a wall; the wall must be built first to provide the vertical support surface onto which the corbel can be anchored or projected from.
If the corbel is cast-in-place concrete, formwork must be erected and aligned before the corbel concrete can be poured and shaped.
Steel reinforcing bars (rebar) designed for the corbel must be positioned and tied within the wall/formwork prior to concrete placement to provide structural integrity.
Corbels are specifically designed to support beams, roof trusses, or other structural elements; those elements can only be placed after the corbel is fully cured and capable of bearing the load.
If the corbel projects from a masonry wall, masonry units placed above the corbel must wait until the corbel is complete, as it acts as a stepped offset or shelf for the wall above.
Floating shelves are mounted on finished walls; drywall must be installed, taped, and mudded before shelf attachment.
Walls should be painted or finished before mounting the shelf to avoid paint work around the installed shelf.
Items can be placed on the shelf once it is securely installed, but this is a soft preference as decorating can be done anytime after installation.
The floating shelf installation must be completed before the room can be signed off as finished.
The corner shelf needs a framed wall structure to be attached to; framing provides the necessary structural support.
Corner shelves are typically mounted on finished drywall surfaces; drywall must be in place before the shelf can be attached.
It is preferable to paint walls before installing shelves to avoid painting around the shelf and achieve a cleaner finish.
Once the corner shelf is installed, items can be placed or arranged on it; this is a logical sequence but not a hard physical requirement.
Inspectors may need to verify that shelves are securely installed before signing off on interior finishes, but this is a procedural preference rather than a physical necessity.
Drywall mudding, taping, and sanding must be complete to avoid dust and debris contaminating the shelf and to ensure a clean finished surface for mounting.
The wall behind the shelf should be painted before the shelf is mounted to avoid the need to paint around the brackets or remove the shelf for painting.
Items can only be placed on the bracket shelf after the shelf brackets and shelf board have been securely installed and fastened to the wall.
Wall framing provides the structural support needed to anchor floating shelves securely.
Drywall must be in place to provide a finished surface for mounting the shelf; the shelf attaches to the wall through the drywall into studs.
Electrical wiring and boxes must be routed before shelves are installed, as shelves may obstruct access to walls and rerouting afterward would require removing the shelf.
The wall behind the floating shelf must be painted or finished before installation, as accessing the wall surface after the shelf is mounted would be impossible without removal.
Decorating and placing items on the shelf is typically done after installation, but this is a soft preference as items could theoretically be placed on the shelf during installation.
Final inspection of the room should occur after all fixtures including floating shelves are installed to verify proper mounting and load capacity.
Floor finishing must be completed before open shelving framing to avoid damage to finished floors from construction debris and work activities.
Wall finishing behind and around the shelving must be completed before framing to ensure access for finishing work and to prevent damage to finished walls from shelving installation.
Any electrical rough-in that needs to run within or behind the shelving walls must be completed before framing encloses those areas.
The support framing structure must be built first to provide the framework onto which the actual shelves and brackets are installed.
Final trim, molding, and touch-up painting around the shelving unit must occur after the framing is constructed to ensure a clean, finished appearance.
Shelf brackets must be attached to wall studs or wall framing; walls must be framed before brackets can be securely mounted.
Drywall provides the finished surface that shelf brackets are mounted against; drywall must be in place so brackets can be anchored to the wall material.
Bracket positions need to be measured and marked on the wall before the actual installation fastening can begin.
Shelf brackets must be securely fastened to the wall before the shelf board can be placed on top of them.
After brackets are installed, the shelf boards can be placed and then leveled/adjusted for proper alignment.
The shelf board must be cut to the correct dimensions before it can be installed in the shelving unit.
Edges must be sanded smooth to ensure proper fit and safety before installation.
Finishing protects the wood and must be done prior to installation to ensure even coverage and proper drying.
The shelf board must be securely installed in place before any weight or items are placed on it.

Brackets may be installed before or after the shelf board is placed, but typically the board is set onto brackets already in place; if brackets are installed after, the board needs to be temporarily supported.
Shelf trim/nosing is applied to the front edge of installed shelves, so the shelves must first be in place.
Final quality checks typically occur after trim/nosing is applied to ensure a complete and finished appearance.
Trim/nosing installation can produce dust or debris, so final cleaning should follow after completion.
Shelf support cleats must be attached to wall framing; without the wall frame in place, there is no structural backing to anchor the cleat.
Cleats must be screwed into studs for load-bearing support; marking stud locations ensures fasteners hit solid framing.
The shelf cleat provides the physical support ledge for the shelf board to rest on; the board cannot be placed before its support is installed.
It is often easier to finish or stain the cleat before installing it, but finishing can also be done after installation as a soft preference.
The cleat must be installed level and at the correct height; layout markings and level lines must be established beforehand to ensure proper shelf alignment.
Shelf supports must be anchored to the structural wall sheathing or framing; without sheathing, there is no solid surface to attach supports.
Framing and sheathing must pass inspection before any non-structural elements like shelf supports are installed.
Shelf panels rest directly on the installed supports; supports are the immediate substrate for the shelf surface.
The shelf structure must be fully installed before any load or storage items are placed on it to prevent damage or collapse.
While painting can often precede shelving, if the shelf supports are exposed or require paint integration, finishing after installation yields a cleaner appearance.
The wall structure must be in place to provide a mounting surface for shelf boards
Electrical wiring must be completed and inspected before shelves are installed, as shelves may obstruct access to walls
Plumbing must be roughed in and inspected before shelves block wall access
Wall surface (e.g., drywall, plywood) must be installed to provide a finished surface to attach shelf brackets or supports
Wall finishing should be completed before shelves are fixed to avoid needing to paint or finish around installed shelves, which is difficult and results in poor finish quality
Shelves must be securely installed before any items can be placed on them to ensure safety and structural integrity
It is preferable to inspect fixed shelving after installation but before loading, though inspections can also be done after loading in some cases
A stable and level foundation or base structure must be in place before shelf levelling and alignment can commence, as the shelves need a solid, even substrate to be aligned upon.
The vertical structural supports (columns or frames) that will hold the shelves must be erected first, as the shelves are mounted to or aligned with these structural elements.
Brackets, cantilevers, or other shelf support hardware must be installed prior to levelling and aligning the shelves themselves, as the shelves rest on these supports.
Shelves must be properly levelled and aligned before any load is applied or weight testing conducted, to ensure even load distribution and prevent instability or collapse.
While not physically mandatory, it is best practice to complete levelling and alignment before the final inspection so the inspector can verify proper installation and adjust if needed.
The shelves must be installed and assembled in place before edge trim can be applied, as the trim is attached directly to the shelf edges.
Edge trim application must be completed before the final quality inspection to ensure all shelf finishing details are in place.
Trim application should be finished before shelves are loaded with product to prevent damage to the trim and ensure clean installation.
The backing wall must be constructed and fully cured before the shelf-to-backing-wall interface can be installed, as the interface requires a stable, load-bearing vertical surface to attach to.
The shelf component must be fabricated, sized, and prepared before it can be interfaced with the backing wall, ensuring proper fit and alignment at the connection point.

The interface connection must be fully installed and secured before any loads are applied to the shelf or final finishes (e.g., sealing, painting) are completed, to avoid damaging an incomplete connection.
The interface installation must be complete before a quality inspection can verify the structural integrity, alignment, and fastening of the shelf-to-wall connection.

successor: Subsequent Wall or Shelf Installations (if tiered)
rationale: If the shelf system is tiered or modular, upper or adjacent shelf interfaces typically wait until lower/critical interfaces are established to maintain consistent alignment and load transfer path.

predecessor: Cut Shelf Underside Panel to Size
rationale: The panel must be cut to the correct dimensions before it can be installed in the shelf frame.
Rough edges and surfaces must be sanded smooth before installation to ensure proper fit and finish.

predecessor: Apply Primer or Sealant to Panel
rationale: Priming or sealing the panel before installation protects the material and ensures a uniform finish.
The underside panel provides the bottom support structure; the top panel is installed after the underside framing is in place.
Side panels are typically attached after the underside base panel is positioned and secured to form the shelf box.

successor: Apply Final Finish/Paint to Shelf Assembly
rationale: Applying final finishing (paint, stain, or varnish) is typically done after all panels are installed and assembled for a cohesive look.
The foundation and concrete slab must be fully cured and prepared before any bleacher structure can be installed, as bleachers require a stable, level load-bearing surface to anchor securely.
Any primary structural steel supports for the bleacher tiers must be erected and fixed in place before bleacher seating components can be attached or mounted to them.
Safety railings are installed onto or adjacent to the bleacher structure after the bleacher frames are in place, ensuring proper alignment and attachment points exist.

Seat numbering and directional signage is typically applied after bleacher assembly is complete so that markings align correctly with the installed seating layout, though it could theoretically be done concurrently with careful planning.
Load testing and safety inspection of the bleacher system must occur after full installation to verify structural integrity before public use is permitted.
A stable foundation or subgrade is required to support the seating/terraced step structure; without proper ground preparation, the step would lack structural support.
Retaining walls or backfill must be in place to create the terraced slope or stepped platform that the seating step is built upon.
Handrails or guardrails depend on the completed step structure for anchoring and alignment; they cannot be installed before the step is in place.
Subsurface drainage must be installed before the terraced step is built to prevent water accumulation behind or under the step structure.
A stable foundation must be prepared before any fixed seating can be installed to ensure structural integrity and level placement.
The concrete floor slab must be poured and fully cured to provide a solid mounting surface for bolting down fixed waiting area seats.
Underground or in-slab conduits for electrical or data outlets serving the waiting area must be roughed in before seats are installed over those locations.
Fixed seats must be installed before final floor finishes so that flooring can be laid up to or around the seat bases for a clean, finished appearance.

While signage can be installed after seating, it is a soft preference to place signs first to guide seat layout, but seats are typically installed before overhead or wall signage to ensure proper alignment and spacing.
The storage seat integrates into the bicycle frame structure; the frame must be assembled first to provide the mounting points and structural support for the seat.
The integrated storage seat is a key component that must be installed before the final quality inspection can verify overall assembly completeness and function.

The integrated storage seat requires the seat post (or the seat tube area of the frame) to be prepared and ready; the seat post or mounting interface must exist before the storage seat can be attached.
The base plate must be fabricated before it can be anchored to the floor, as the anchored base assembly requires the fabricated plate component.
The floor must be prepared (cleaned, leveled, and marked) before the anchored base can be installed to ensure proper adhesion and alignment.
The anchored base must be secured to the floor before the stool frame can be attached, as the frame depends on the base for structural support.
The anchored base must be positioned and aligned before permanent floor anchors are drilled and set, as anchor placement depends on base orientation.

Electrical outlets and data ports for the bench area (including judge's workstation, clerk, and court reporter positions) must be roughed-in before the bench is installed to avoid needing to run wiring after the bench is in place.

The finished floor surface under and around the bench area must be completed before the heavy bench is set in place, as installing the bench over unfinished flooring would require future lifting or moving of the bench.
Wall surfaces behind and around the bench should be painted and finished before installation to avoid the need to work around the fixed bench during painting.
The bench base and supporting framework must be fully installed before the finished countertop/bench top surface can be placed and secured.
Final electrical connections, outlet covers, and data port terminations at the bench can only be installed after the bench is in its final position to ensure proper alignment and accessibility.
The seat mounting bracket must be attached to the floor panel; therefore the floor panel must be installed first to provide a secure mounting surface.
The seat mounting bracket serves as the anchor point for the seat; the seat cannot be installed until its mounting bracket is securely in place.
Seat rails/tracks are typically mounted onto the seat mounting brackets, so the brackets must be installed first.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to provide a stable, level foundation before the cave structure frame can be erected.
Concrete foundations must be poured and fully cured to support the structural loads of the cave frame before any frame erection begins.
Utilities such as drainage, electrical conduits, and water lines must be placed beneath the footprint before the frame is installed to avoid rework after the structure is in place.
The frame must be fully erected and structurally stable before exterior cladding and weatherproof membranes can be applied to enclose the structure.
Interior partitions, ceilings, and finishes cannot be installed until the primary structural frame is in place to provide support and attachment points.
The cave must first be excavated and its basic structural form established before any ventilation grille can be fitted, as the grille is mounted within the cave opening or wall.
The main ventilation ductwork and air pathways must be installed to the point where the grille connects, ensuring a sealed and functional air pathway before the grille is attached.
After the grille is installed, the complete ventilation system including the grille must be tested for proper airflow, pressure balance, and leak-free operation.

It is preferable to install the grille before applying final finishes around it so that the finishing work can be neatly trimmed to the grille edges, though it could be done in reverse with careful measurement.

Electrical supply for any powered ventilation fan that connects to the grille must be roughed in before the grille is installed, as the fan unit is typically mounted behind or integrated with the grille assembly.
The structural wall or cave face must be built/formed before any window opening can be framed and glazed into it.
The building envelope must be weather-sealed to provide a proper substrate and flashing integration for window installation.
The rough opening must be framed, measured, and prepared to the correct dimensions before the window unit can be placed.
The window must be installed and sealed before interior finishes can be applied around the window frame.
The window unit must be positioned and secured before glazing sealants can be applied and allowed to cure.
The wall surface must be prepared and ready before attaching or constructing a built-in bench/shelf against it.
A level floor is required to provide a stable base for the bench/shelf structure.
The underlying framing and structural supports for the bench/shelf must be in place before the bench/shelf itself is installed.
Sealing and waterproofing around the bench/shelf should be done after installation to ensure a watertight finish.
Final interior finishing such as painting or trim work around the bench/shelf must be completed after the bench/shelf is installed.
The site must be excavated and leveled to provide a stable foundation and clear access area for installing the cave access hatch/door.

predecessor: Cave Entrance Framing / Rough Opening Preparation
rationale: The rough opening or frame for the hatch/door must be constructed and prepared before the hatch/door unit itself can be installed into it.
After the hatch/door is installed, sealing and weatherproofing around its perimeter must be completed to ensure water tightness and insulation.

Interior finishing work inside the cave can begin after the access hatch/door is installed, providing secure and controlled entry, though this is a logical sequence preference rather than a strict physical requirement.

successor: Exterior Landscaping and Concealment Around Entrance
rationale: Exterior finishing, backfilling, and landscaping around the hatch/door area must be done after installation to blend the entrance with the surrounding terrain and provide proper drainage.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any cave construction can begin to ensure a stable foundation and safe working area.
The cave structure must be fully constructed before interior finishing work (such as insulation, lighting, flooring) and safety inspections can be performed.
While furnishing typically follows construction, some elements could be prepared in parallel; however, it is strongly preferred to complete the structure first to avoid damage or rework.
External landscaping and restoration around the cave must wait until the cave structure is complete to avoid disturbing construction work and to allow final grading around the entrance.
The main cave structure must be built first to provide the physical space and structural support for lighting fixtures to be installed.
Electrical wiring and conduit must be run before lighting fixtures can be connected and installed.
Flooring is typically installed before lighting to avoid damage to finished floors from ladder work, though not physically required.

successor: Lighting Trim and Switch Plate Installation
rationale: Main lighting fixtures must be installed before trim pieces, covers, and switch plates can be fitted.
All lighting fixtures must be installed before the electrical system can be fully tested and inspected for safety and functionality.
Hidden doors require structural wall framing to be in place so the door frame can be properly installed and integrated into the wall cavity.
Electrical wiring must be routed through the wall before the hidden door is installed, as access to the wall cavity will be blocked once the door is in place.
Drywall must be installed after the hidden door assembly so that it can be finished flush with the door surface, creating the seamless hidden appearance.
Flooring can be installed after the hidden door to ensure the door swing clearance and floor gap are properly aligned, though it could be done before with careful planning.
Trim and molding must be applied after the hidden door is assembled and drywall is finished to conceal the door edges and blend with the surrounding wall.
The wall framing provides the structural support onto which the disguised wall panel must be attached.
Electrical wiring and outlets must be installed behind the wall before the panel conceals access to them.
Any plumbing running within the wall must be completed before the panel is placed to avoid requiring removal of the panel for later access.
While painting or wallpapering can occur before installation, it is generally preferred to finish the disguised panel as part of the overall wall finish to ensure a seamless appearance.
The disguised wall panel must be installed and closed before the final inspection can verify that hidden elements (e.g., safe room, secret compartment) are properly concealed.
The concealed hinge and hardware set must be mounted onto the door and frame; the rough door frame must be installed and properly squared before hinges can be aligned and fastened.
The door slab must have hinge mortises cut (or prepped) at the correct locations before the concealed hinge cups and leafs can be installed onto the door.
After hinges are installed on both the door and frame, the door can be hung (lifted into place and pinned) and then aligned/adjusted using the set screws on the concealed hinges.

The latch and strike plate are part of the concealed hardware set; the latch mechanism is typically inserted into the door edge after the hinge set is installed, and the strike plate is mounted on the frame after the door is aligned.
The secret latch mechanism must be installed within the wall framework; the framing provides the structural cavity and support needed to house the latch assembly.

If the magnetic release requires wiring (e.g., for an electromagnet or electronic release), the electrical rough-in must be completed first to run cables behind the wall before the latch unit is installed.
The latch/release mechanism must be installed in the wall/frame before the secret door is hung, so that the door can be aligned and adjusted to properly engage with the latch.
The latch components must be fully installed and tested before the wall surface is closed up with drywall or paneling, as access is needed for mounting and adjustment.
It is a soft preference to install trim after the latch is in place so that the trim can be cut or adjusted to conceal the latch mechanism seamlessly, but trim could also be retrofitted if needed.
Ventilation ducts must be installed before the grill can be concealed, as the grill covers the duct opening and provides the finished appearance.
The concealed grill must be in place before final ceiling finishing is applied, so that the finish can be applied around the grill for a seamless appearance.
While not physically required, completing electrical rough-in before grill concealment avoids having to remove or work around the finished grill.
The concealed grill must be in its final position for inspection of airflow, alignment, and finish quality.
The rough opening frame must be built to structurally support and define the space for the one-way mirror/observation window installation.
Wall sheathing provides the structural backing and cavity needed to mount the observation window assembly.
Any electrical wiring for lighting near the observation window must be roughed in behind the wall before the mirror assembly is installed, to avoid damaging the glass.
Interior finishes around the window frame must follow after the observation window is fully installed to allow proper sealing, trimming, and seamless finishing.
Trim and glazing beads are applied after the mirror/window is set to secure it in place and provide a finished appearance.
Electrical power supply and wiring must be run to the fixture location before the hidden light fixture can be physically installed and connected.
The ceiling structure must be framed to provide a mounting surface and cavity for the recessed hidden light fixture.
For hidden/recessed light fixtures, the drywall is typically installed first, then the fixture is mounted or the trim is installed, so the fixture sits flush with the finished ceiling surface.

It is preferable (though not strictly required) to paint and finish the ceiling after the hidden light fixture is installed so that paint edges and trim can be neatly blended around the fixture opening.

successor: Lighting Fixture Trim and Bulb Installation
rationale: The hidden light fixture housing must be mounted in place before the decorative trim and bulbs can be added to complete the fixture.
The floor framing must be in place to provide structural support and a cavity for the trapdoor mechanism.
The subfloor sheathing provides the base surface in which the trapdoor opening will be cut and framed.
The supporting frame for the trapdoor must be built before the trapdoor itself can be mounted and hinged.
The final floor finish (e.g., carpet, tile, hardwood) must be installed after the trapdoor is in place so that the finish can be cut flush around the trapdoor edges for a seamless hidden appearance.
The latch and hinge hardware can only be fully aligned and tested once the trapdoor is physically installed in its frame.
The bookshelf door system requires a framed opening to be installed into, as the frame provides the structural support and mounting surface for the door system.
The wall sheathing or backing behind the bookshelf must be in place before the bookshelf door system is installed, as the door hinges and pivot mechanism attach to the solid backing structure.

If the bookshelf door conceals a hidden room, electrical wiring for lights or security in that room must be routed after the door frame is in place to avoid interference with the door swing and pivot mechanism.
It is preferred to install interior trim and molding after the bookshelf door system is operational to ensure the door swings freely and the trim aligns properly with the door edges.
Flooring should be installed after the bookshelf door system is in place because the door sweeps over the floor surface and the floor must accommodate the swing path without obstruction.
The wall safe must be installed within the wall cavity, which requires the stud frame to be erected first to define the wall thickness and provide structure to attach the safe to.
Electrical wiring may need to be routed around or behind the safe location, and must be completed before the safe is installed to avoid obstruction or safety hazards.
The safe must be fully installed and secured within the wall cavity before the wall surface is enclosed with drywall or plaster to conceal and finish the wall.
Final wall finishes like painting or tiling should only be applied after the safe is installed and the wall surface is prepared, to ensure a seamless concealed appearance.
Trim work around the safe area (baseboards, door casings) is typically done after the safe is in place for a finished look, but could be partially done before if carefully planned.
Walls require a solid foundation to bear load and ensure structural stability.
Walls must be constructed on top of a completed floor slab to provide a level base.
Excavation is necessary to expose the building footprint and prepare the ground before any foundation or wall work.
Electrical work within walls must be done after walls are framed but before they are closed up with drywall.
Plumbing pipes inside walls require the wall framing to be in place for installation.
Insulation is installed into the wall cavities after framing is complete.
Drywall is attached directly to the wall framing; walls must be fully constructed first.
The rough framing establishes the wall structure and opening dimensions required for the hidden door framing to be integrated properly.
Inspection must confirm framing is correct before the hidden door unit can be installed, as modifications after installation would be difficult.
The hidden door must be installed and shimmed in place before drywall can be applied, as the drywall needs to be continuous over the door surface to maintain concealment.
Trim and casing around the hidden door can only be installed after the door unit is in place and leveled, to ensure proper fit and alignment.
The hidden door must be installed and functional before any painting or finishing can occur, so that paint coats are continuous across the seam for concealment.
Acoustic seals are typically applied to gaps and joints in finished wall assemblies; drywall must be installed first to create the surfaces and joints that require sealing.
The structural framing must be in place to support the wall assembly and define gaps before acoustic sealing can be applied.
Penetrations for MEP systems must be completed before acoustic sealing, as seals are applied around and after penetrations to maintain the acoustic barrier.
While acoustic sealants are often paintable, it is preferred to apply seals before final finishes to ensure continuity; however, painting can sometimes be done prior if sealant is applied over paint.
Acoustic door frames and seals integrate with the surrounding wall seals; the wall acoustic sealing should be completed first to ensure a continuous acoustic boundary before doors are installed.
Electrical wiring runs through stud cavities, joists, and other structural framing members. The framing must be complete to provide the pathways and support for electrical cables and boxes.
Window and door rough openings must be framed so that electrical boxes and wiring can be properly positioned adjacent to them before interior finishes.
It is a soft preference/coordination practice to sequence plumbing before electrical in walls to avoid conflicts, but this can be reversed if carefully managed.
Insulation must be installed after electrical rough-in because wiring and boxes are placed within wall and ceiling cavities first; insulation then fills around them.
The rough-in inspection must occur after all concealed electrical work is complete to verify code compliance before any covering (insulation, drywall) closes the cavities.
The secret latch mechanism must be installed within the wall cavity, so wall framing must be completed first to provide the structural space and support for the mechanism.
Any electrical wiring for the release mechanism (e.g., button, sensor) must be routed before the latch mechanism is mounted, as the mechanism encloses access to the wiring paths.
Once the latch mechanism is installed and tested, the wall covering (drywall or sheathing) must be applied to conceal it; the mechanism cannot be covered before it is in place.
The latch mechanism must be installed on the frame before the concealed door is hung, as the door must align with and engage the latch for proper operation.
The mechanism must be fully installed before testing can be performed to verify that the latch releases correctly and opens the hidden access point.
The frame must be installed first to provide a secure mounting surface and structural support for the one-way glass panels.
The wall opening must be properly framed, sized, and finished to accommodate the one-way glass unit before installation can begin.
Any electrical wiring for lighting or power near the glass installation area must be completed beforehand to avoid damage to the glass or rework.
The one-way glass must be fully installed before inspections can verify proper visibility, privacy performance, and security of the installation.
The wall framing and structural sheathing must be complete to provide a backing surface and structural support for the bench/window seat.
Any electrical wiring or outlet boxes that will be within or behind the bench/window seat must be roughed in before the seat structure encloses the wall cavity.
If the bench/seat is beneath a window, the window must be installed first so that the bench can be framed and finished relative to the window's exact position and trim.
The bench/seat base is typically built on top of the subfloor; finish flooring is installed up to or under the bench, so the seat structure must be in place first.
Casework, crown molding, and other finish trim around the window seat must be installed after the bench/seat box is fully built and in place.
A stable, level floor surface must be completed before the reception desk can be placed and secured.
Power outlets, data cabling, and any underfloor wiring must be roughed in before the desk is installed to avoid costly rework.

predecessor: Rough-in plumbing (if reception includes a sink/wet bar)
rationale: Any water supply and drain lines for a reception sink or coffee station must be roughed in before the desk cabinetry is placed.

successor: Final electrical and data connections (outlets, switches, data ports)
rationale: Once the desk is in its final position, power and data outlets integrated into the desk can be trimmed out and connected.
The desk base/frame must be installed first so that the countertop can be properly fitted, leveled, and sealed on top.

While painting can be done before desk placement, it is often preferred to install the desk first to ensure paint edges align perfectly with the desk; however, this is a soft preference as painting can be done before with careful masking.
The seating/benches must be installed on a stable, load-bearing structural floor. The slab or deck provides the necessary substrate.

predecessor: Auditorium Raked Floor / Tiered Sub-Frame Construction
rationale: The stepped or raked floor structure that creates the tiered levels must be built before seating can be fitted onto those tiers.
Electrical conduits, data cabling, and HVAC ductwork that run beneath the seating area must be installed and tested before the seating is fixed in place, as access becomes impossible afterward.
Soft preference: floor finishes in areas under and between seating rows may be installed after seating for a cleaner edge finish, but could also be done before if seating is installed afterward.

Large seating units and tiered benches can obstruct access to walls; acoustic wall panels are typically installed before seating is put in place. If seating is installed first, it will need protection from subsequent wall work.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical and MEP services (conduits, wiring, ductwork, piping) in ceiling plenum
successor: Install acoustic ceiling cloud / baffle framing and suspension system
rationale: All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) rough-in work within the ceiling cavity must be completed before cloud/baffle framing is installed; otherwise, access to run services above the acoustic elements would be blocked.

predecessor: Install acoustic ceiling cloud / baffle framing and suspension system
successor: Install acoustic ceiling cloud / baffle panels
rationale: The suspension grid, hanger wires, and support structure must be in place before the acoustic panels or baffle components can be attached or hung.

predecessor: Complete overhead rough-in inspections (MEP, fire protection)
successor: Install acoustic ceiling cloud / baffle framing and suspension system
rationale: Inspections of all concealed rough-in work above the ceiling must be passed before enclosing the space with cloud/baffle framing, to avoid costly rework.

predecessor: Install acoustic ceiling cloud / baffle panels
successor: Paint and finish walls and final floor finishes
rationale: Soft preference: completing the acoustic cloud first allows wall/floor finishers to work without risk of damaging the ceiling elements, though not physically mandatory.

predecessor: Install acoustic ceiling cloud / baffle panels
successor: Install ceiling-mounted lighting fixtures and ceiling-mounted audio/visual equipment
rationale: Many cloud/baffle systems integrate or conceal lighting and AV equipment; the panels must be installed to properly align fixture cutouts and support hardware.
The structural floor slab and framing must be in place to provide a load-bearing surface and support for the glazed screen system.
Any mechanical, electrical, or plumbing rough-in work that will run above the screen area must be completed before the screen is installed, to avoid obstruction and rework.

While it is preferable to complete finishes before installing the screen to avoid damage, the screen can be installed first with careful protection; a soft preference is to finish walls before screen installation.
Flooring should be completed before the glazed screen is installed so that the screen sits on top of the finished floor surface, ensuring proper alignment and avoiding trapping the flooring edge.
Lighting fixtures and trim-out elements adjacent to or integrated with the glazed screen require the screen to be in place for accurate positioning and connection.
The structural wall surface must exist to provide a mounting substrate for the built-in display or pin-up wall system.
Any electrical wiring for lighting, screens, or outlets within or behind the display wall must be roughed in before the built-in assembly is installed.
Paint or wall finishes adjacent to the built-in unit are typically completed after the unit is installed to ensure seamless transitions and avoid damaging finished surfaces.

successor: Installation of display items / pin-up content
rationale: The display or pin-up surface must be fully installed before any items are mounted or pinned onto it, though this is a functional preference rather than a physical necessity.
Trim pieces, frames, and fit adjustments around the built-in display must occur after the main unit is in place to achieve proper alignment and finish.
The ground surface must be properly prepared, graded, and leveled before installing seating and benches to ensure they are placed on a stable, even foundation.

predecessor: Pour and Cure Concrete Slab or Foundation
rationale: If benches are to be anchored to a concrete base or slab, the concrete must be poured and fully cured to achieve sufficient strength before bench installation.
Any underground utility installations (drainage, electrical, water) in the area must be completed before placing permanent seating to avoid digging up or moving the benches later.
Final landscaping touches such as planting, mulching, or decorative gravel are often done after seating is installed to work around the fixtures and achieve a finished look.
Site inspection and project handover can only occur after all seating and benches are fully installed and secured, as these are part of the deliverable scope.

predecessor: Prepare / inspect glazing panel installation surfaces
rationale: The installation surfaces must be prepared, clean, and ready to receive the glazed social screens before the screens themselves can be installed.

successor: Seal and weatherproof glazed screen edges
rationale: Weatherproofing and sealing of the glazed screen edges can only be applied after the screens are in place and properly positioned.

successor: Inspect and test glazed screen stability and safety
rationale: Inspection and testing of the installed screens for stability and safety compliance must occur after installation is complete.
Lighting fixtures must be physically installed and connected before they can be commissioned and tested for proper operation.

predecessor: Run Power Supply Cables to Social Zone
rationale: Electrical power supply infrastructure must be in place and energized before commissioning tests can be performed on the lighting system.
Control system (switches, dimmers, sensors, controllers) must be installed to allow full functional testing during commissioning.

successor: Occupancy / Final Handover of Social Zone
rationale: Commissioning verifies that the lighting system operates correctly and safely; the area cannot be handed over for occupancy until all systems are commissioned and accepted.
Formal acceptance testing and sign-off by the client/engineer typically follows successful commissioning of the lighting system.
The subfloor must be properly prepared (cleaned, leveled, and dried) before any flooring installation to ensure proper adhesion and a level finished surface.
All rough-in work such as electrical, plumbing, and HVAC must be completed before flooring installation to avoid damaging the finished floor and to allow access to subfloor areas.
Baseboards and trim are installed after flooring to cover the expansion gap around the perimeter and to sit on top of the finished flooring.
In some construction sequences, floor installation precedes non-load-bearing wall partitions so that the walls sit on top of the finished floor, providing a clean interface.
It is preferred to complete painting and touch-ups after flooring to avoid paint drips on the new floor, though touch-ups can be done carefully before if needed.

successor: Install Social Stair Structure and Seating
rationale: The social stair structure requires a stable, level concrete foundation and slab to bear its weight and provide a secure mounting surface.

successor: Install Social Stair Structure and Seating
rationale: Underground or in-slab utilities must be roughed in before the stair foundation is poured and the structure is installed, as access would be blocked afterward.

predecessor: Install Social Stair Structure and Seating
rationale: Railings and guardrails must be installed after the stair structure is in place so they can be properly aligned and anchored to the stair stringers and platforms.

predecessor: Install Social Stair Structure and Seating
successor: Apply Final Finishes (Staining/Sealing to Stair Surfaces)
rationale: Final surface finishes like staining and sealing must be applied after the structure is fully installed to ensure even coverage and protection of all exposed surfaces.

predecessor: Install Social Stair Structure and Seating
successor: Install Lighting Fixtures (Stair Tread or Accent Lighting)
rationale: While lighting can be installed concurrently or after, it is preferable to install fixtures after the stair structure is complete to avoid damage during stair assembly and to ensure proper wire routing.
Structural walls require a stable load-bearing base. The foundation must be completed and cured to support the weight and transfer loads from the wall to the ground.
Steel reinforcement bars must be placed and secured within the formwork before concrete is poured for the structural wall to achieve required tensile strength and structural integrity.
Formwork molds must be erected and braced in the correct position and alignment to shape and contain the wet concrete until it cures and forms the structural wall.
Upper floor slabs or decks require completed load-bearing walls below to support their weight and transfer vertical loads through the structure.

Finishing applications such as plastering, rendering, or painting must wait until the structural wall concrete has fully cured and achieved sufficient strength to avoid damage and ensure proper adhesion.
The structural connection relies on a stable base provided by completed foundations to ensure load transfer and alignment.
Steel frame members must be erected and positioned before they can be connected to each other via structural connections (bolting or welding).
Concrete slabs and decks require the structural steel frame to be interconnected and stable before concrete can be placed on top.
While some MEP work can start in parallel, full MEP rough-in is typically sequenced after structural connections are complete to avoid conflicts and allow open access.
The structural frame must be fully connected and stable before exterior cladding or curtain wall systems can be attached to the building envelope.
The foundation must be properly prepared and leveled before precast concrete elements can be placed, as they require a stable, level base for installation.
Precast concrete elements must be manufactured, cured, and transported to the site before they can be installed or erected in their final position.
Cranes and lifting equipment must be mobilized and set up on site before precast elements can be lifted and placed into position.
After precast elements are placed, connections between elements and grouting of joints must be completed to ensure structural integrity.
Once precast elements are installed and connections are made, inspection and quality control testing (e.g., for alignment and connection strength) must occur before further work proceeds.
Formwork and falsework must be erected on a stable, completed foundation or substructure to ensure proper load transfer and alignment.

Reinforcement steel is typically placed within the formwork; however, formwork erection often precedes or is concurrent with rebar installation. In many sequences, formwork is set first, then rebar is placed inside. But structurally, the foundation or slab must be ready before formwork goes up.
Accurate surveying and layout marking are required to position formwork correctly according to design coordinates and elevations.
Formwork and falsework create the mold and temporary support structure that contains and shapes wet concrete until it cures; concrete cannot be poured without the formwork in place.
In some sequences, rebar is placed after formwork is erected, but this is a construction preference rather than a strict physical constraint—rebar can also be pre-assembled before formwork.
After concrete has cured to sufficient strength, the formwork and falsework can be stripped and removed; this must follow concrete placement and curing.
Formwork provides the mold or framework into which reinforcement bars are placed; reinforcement cannot be installed without first having the formwork in place to support and position it.
The load-bearing base or slab must be completed (or at least prepared) before reinforcement can be placed, as reinforcement needs a stable surface and proper cover tolerances.
Concrete must be poured immediately after reinforcement is installed and inspected; reinforcement must be in place before concrete can be placed around it to ensure structural integrity.
All reinforcement placement work must be completed before the inspection of rebar positioning, spacing, cover, and tie connections is performed to verify compliance with engineering drawings.

While it is physically possible to install some conduits after reinforcement, it is standard practice and more efficient to place embedded services (electrical conduits, plumbing sleeves) after rebar is in place but before concrete, to coordinate positioning.
Formwork provides the mold or containment structure that shapes and supports wet concrete until it cures; concrete cannot be placed without formwork in place.
Steel reinforcement (rebar) must be positioned and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide tensile strength to the cured concrete element.
The ground or sub-base must be properly compacted, leveled, and prepared to receive concrete, ensuring proper load distribution and preventing settlement or failure.
Concrete must be placed and cured to sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed; stripping too early can cause structural failure or surface damage.
Post-tensioning of tendons can only be performed after the concrete has reached a specified minimum compressive strength through proper curing.

Post-tensioning involves tensioning steel tendons after the concrete has been placed and has reached sufficient strength. The tendons are embedded in the concrete, so the concrete must first be poured and cured to an initial strength before tensioning can begin.
The tendons (strands or bars) must be installed within their ducts/sheathing before tensioning can occur. Tensioning cannot start if the tendons are not yet placed in the concrete member.

After the tendons have been tensioned and locked off, the ducts must be filled with grout to bond the tendons to the concrete and protect them from corrosion. Grouting can only occur after tensioning is complete.

In post-tensioned structures, the concrete member gains significant pre-compression from tensioning. Forms can often be removed only after post-tensioning has transferred load into the member, ensuring the structure can support itself without formwork.

The foundation provides the stable base and load-bearing surface upon which structural connections are installed; without a completed foundation, there is no secure anchoring point for structural connections.
Structural connections (e.g., bolting, welding) join individual steel members together; the steel frame members must first be positioned and erected before their connections can be installed.

If structural connections involve embedments in concrete (e.g., anchor bolts, base plates), the concrete must be sufficiently cured to achieve design strength before connections can be tightened or loaded.
Welded connections must be installed before they can be inspected for quality and compliance with welding codes and specifications.

Temporary or permanent bracing and stabilization systems connect to the structural connections; the primary connections must be in place before bracing can be attached to complete the lateral load path.
Material specifications and sourcing requirements must be defined in the project plans and design before verification can commence, as the verification checks against these predefined criteria.
Suppliers must be identified and contracts must be in place before their sourcing documentation and material certifications can be verified for sustainability compliance.
Verification must confirm that a supplier meets sustainability criteria before procurement orders are placed with that supplier to avoid non-compliant material purchases.
Sourcing verification must be completed before materials are delivered to site; otherwise, non-sustainable materials could be received and potentially used.

While it is strongly preferred that verification is complete before construction to ensure only approved sustainable materials are used, in some cases construction can begin with provisional approval pending final documentation review.

The site must be cleared, levelled, and prepared before installing material waste sorting and recycling equipment, as a stable, prepared ground surface is physically necessary for foundations and equipment placement.
Concrete foundations and floor slabs must be completed and cured to provide a stable structural base to support the sorting lines, bins, crushers, and other recycling equipment.

The building or shelter structure enclosing the waste sorting area must be erected before installing the sorting and recycling equipment to provide weather protection and overhead support for conveyor systems or crane rails.

Electrical power, water supply, and compressed air connections to the sorting and recycling equipment can only be finalized after the equipment is positioned and installed, as the connection points depend on actual equipment locations.

successor: Commissioning & Testing of Waste Sorting System
rationale: The system must be fully installed and mechanically complete before it can be commissioned, tested, and calibrated to ensure proper sorting and recycling functionality.
The site must be properly graded and prepared to provide a stable, level base before low-impact materials (such as permeable pavers, recycled aggregates, or stabilized earth) can be installed.
Underground utility lines (water, sewer, electrical) must be laid and buried before low-impact surface materials are placed, to avoid cutting into or disturbing the installed materials.
A compacted sub-base or aggregate base layer is often required to support low-impact materials (e.g., permeable pavers, crushed stone) and ensure proper drainage and load distribution.

Surrounding landscape finish grades, topsoil placement, and soft landscaping should be completed after the low-impact materials are in place to avoid disturbing or contaminating the installed surface.
Some low-impact materials (e.g., stabilized earth, permeable pavers with joint stabilization) may require a curing period or application of sealant after installation to achieve final performance.
Materials must be procured and delivered to the site before they can be conditioned or cured.
Materials need to be properly stored and handled before conditioning and curing processes can begin.
While not always physically dependent, site preparation is typically completed before material conditioning to ensure a coordinated workflow.
Materials must be properly conditioned and cured before they can be tested or inspected for quality compliance.
Conditioned and cured materials (e.g., cured concrete, treated lumber) are required before they can be placed or installed in their final position.
The structural deck or canopy must be installed to provide the load-bearing surface upon which the green roof growing medium is placed.
A waterproof membrane must be installed over the structural deck before placing growing medium to protect the building structure from moisture damage.
A root barrier must be placed above the waterproof membrane to prevent plant roots from penetrating and damaging the waterproofing system.
A drainage layer must be installed beneath the growing medium to allow excess water to drain away, preventing waterlogging and ensuring proper roof drainage.
A filter fabric (geotextile) must be placed over the drainage layer to prevent fine particles of growing medium from washing into and clogging the drainage system.
Plants or vegetation (e.g., sedum, grasses, or pre-vegetated mats) can only be installed after the growing medium has been placed and prepared to provide the root substrate.

Irrigation components are often laid on or within the growing medium and so can only be installed after the medium is in place, though this is a design preference rather than a strict physical necessity in all cases.
Rammed earth walls require a solid, level, and well-drained foundation to bear their weight and prevent moisture wicking; the foundation must be cured and set before wall construction begins.
