The building site must be cleared, leveled, and graded to provide a stable working platform and proper drainage before rammed earth walls can be erected.
Underground plumbing, electrical conduit, and drainage pipes must be laid in the slab/foundation before walls are built, as it is extremely difficult to trench through cured rammed earth walls later.
The roof structure bears directly on the rammed earth walls; walls must be complete, cured, and at full strength to support roof loads and provide a bearing surface for roof framing.
Window and door openings are formed during rammed earth construction; frames and glazing are installed after the walls are complete, cured, and the openings are stable.
A stable foundation is required to support the load of straw bale walls; walls cannot be built without a completed foundation.
The floor platform provides the working surface and base upon which straw bale walls are erected; walls must be assembled on top of the finished floor structure.
The roof structure typically bears on or is supported by the walls; straw bale walls must be complete and stable before the roof can be installed.
Rough openings for windows and doors are cut and framed within the straw bale walls after the walls are assembled; bales must be in place to lay out and form openings.
Straw bale walls require a protective plaster or render coating on both sides; this finish layer cannot be applied until the bale wall assembly is complete and any settling has occurred.
Cob walls require a solid, load-bearing foundation to prevent moisture wicking and structural settling. The foundation must be cured and leveled before cob can be applied.
Proper drainage and grading must be established before building cob walls to prevent water pooling at the base, which can weaken or erode the cob material.

predecessor: Cob Material Preparation (Soil Mixing and Puddling)
rationale: The cob mix (clay, sand, straw, and water) must be prepared and properly puddled to the right consistency before it can be applied to form walls.
After building, cob walls must be allowed to dry and cure slowly to achieve structural strength and prevent cracking. This is a physically required sequence.
A roof or protective covering must be installed after cob walls are built to shield the vulnerable cob material from rain and weather exposure during and after curing.
Reclaimed materials must be sourced, salvaged, and collected from donor sites before they can be integrated into the new construction.
Reclaimed materials must be inspected, cleaned, and tested for structural integrity and safety compliance before being incorporated into the building.
Architectural and engineering designs specifying where and how reclaimed materials will be used must be completed and approved before integration begins.
After reclaimed materials are integrated, the completed work must be inspected and verified to meet building codes, structural standards, and sustainability certifications.
Once reclaimed materials are installed, any needed finishing work (sealing, coating, matching adjacent surfaces) can proceed over the newly integrated elements.
Surfaces must be properly prepared (cleaned, sanded, primed) before applying low-VOC paints, coatings, or adhesives to ensure proper adhesion and finish quality.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and mudded before painting or coating with low-VOC materials, as these finishes are applied over the finished drywall surface.
Electrical, plumbing, and mechanical rough-in inspections must be completed before finishing work like painting, as access to walls and ceilings is needed for any corrections.
Painting and wall finishing should be completed before flooring is installed to avoid drips, spills, and overspray damaging finished floors, and to allow for easier cleanup.

While trim is often installed before painting for a seamless look, low-VOC wall finishes can be applied before final trim installation to allow for easier cutting-in and to avoid paint buildup on trim surfaces.
The site must be properly graded and prepared to create a stable, well-drained surface for storing green materials, preventing water pooling and contamination.
Green materials must be procured and delivered before they can be stored and protected on site; storage planning is contingent on material availability.
Materials must be properly stored and protected from weather, moisture, and damage before they can be used in installation or application to ensure quality and performance.
Stored materials should be inspected for damage, moisture content, and other quality parameters before being released for installation to verify they meet specifications.
The reinforcement cage must be in place before stiffening can be applied to the stepped column
Formwork provides the mold and support for the column shape, and must be erected before stiffening elements are installed
The concrete must be poured and achieve initial set so that the column has structural integrity before stiffening components (such as steel plates, brackets, or external stiffeners) are attached
Stiffening must be complete before the final curing and finishing process can commence to ensure all stiffening elements are properly integrated
Stiffening must be fully completed and set before any structural loads are applied to the column to prevent deformation or failure
The foundation must be built first to provide structural support and load transfer for the shear walls before any wall thickening can begin.
Vertical rebar must be placed in the existing wall section before concrete is added for thickening, as the reinforcement must be embedded within the thickened section for structural continuity.
Horizontal reinforcement (e.g., dowels or ties) is installed after the thickened wall is cast to connect the new concrete to adjacent structural elements.
The newly poured concrete for the wall thickening must gain sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed and curing processes are completed.
Diaphragm connections to the thickened shear wall require the wall concrete to be fully cured and achieve design strength to transfer lateral loads effectively.
The floor diaphragm requires a completed foundation to transfer loads to the ground and provide a stable base.
The floor diaphragm bears on or connects to vertical structural elements (columns or shear walls) which must be in place to support the diaphragm.

successor: Floor Finishing and MEP Rough-In Above
rationale: MEP rough-in and floor finishes on the level above cannot be installed until the structural diaphragm providing the working platform and support is complete.

successor: Vertical Enclosure (Curtain Wall/Façade) on That Floor
rationale: While not physically mandatory, it is standard sequencing to enclose the building floor after the structural slab is in place to protect subsequent interior work.
The diaphragm provides lateral stability and a working platform; upper-level columns/walls cannot be erected until the floor below is complete.

successor: Placement of Progressive-Stiffness Shear Wall Reinforcement
rationale: The foundation must be excavated and prepared before any shear wall reinforcement can be placed, as the reinforcement needs to be anchored into the foundation.

successor: Placement of Progressive-Stiffness Shear Wall Reinforcement
rationale: Formwork must be in place to define the shape and position of the shear wall before reinforcement bars can be placed within the formwork cavity.

predecessor: Placement of Progressive-Stiffness Shear Wall Reinforcement
rationale: Reinforcement must be fully placed, tied, and inspected before concrete can be poured to ensure the reinforcement is correctly positioned within the wall.

predecessor: Placement of Progressive-Stiffness Shear Wall Reinforcement
rationale: Embedded conduits and sleeves are typically placed after reinforcement to avoid interference with rebar placement, but must be completed before concrete pouring.

predecessor: Placement of Progressive-Stiffness Shear Wall Reinforcement
rationale: After reinforcement placement, inspection must be performed to verify bar sizes, spacing, laps, and ties before concrete placement is permitted.
The main steel columns must be erected first to provide the vertical structural framework to which the outriggers will connect and transfer lateral loads.

predecessor: Completion of Core Wall Construction (up to outrigger level)
rationale: The concrete or steel core wall must be built up to the level where the outriggers will be installed, as outriggers typically connect the core to perimeter columns to resist overturning moments.

successor: Continuation of Upper Floor Steel Framing
rationale: Upper floor steel framing above the outrigger level depends on the outriggers being in place to maintain structural stability and load transfer during construction.

successor: Placement of Outrigger Level Concrete Deck/Slab
rationale: While it is physically possible to place the slab after outrigger installation, it is preferred to complete the slab to provide a working platform and to integrate the diaphragm action with the outrigger system.

successor: Cladding and Facade Installation at Outrigger Zone
rationale: Cladding work should typically follow outrigger installation to avoid interference and to ensure the structural steel is fully erected and connected before enclosing it.
Column zones require a stable foundation to transfer loads; columns cannot be erected without completed foundation works.
Reinforcement cages must be in place before concrete is poured to form the graded stiffness column zones.
Formwork molds are required to shape the column zones and contain the concrete during construction.
Freshly constructed column zones must undergo curing to achieve design strength before any loading.

successor: Installation of Floor Slabs on Constructed Columns
rationale: Floor slabs and beams rely on completed columns as vertical support elements; columns must be fully constructed and cured before slab placement.

The transfer plate/podium slab must be supported by the foundation elements (pile caps and footings) which transfer loads to the ground. Without completed foundations, the transfer plate has no structural support.
Basement retaining walls and core walls provide lateral stability and form the enclosure below the transfer plate. The transfer plate typically bears on or connects to these walls.

predecessor: Column / Wall Reinforcement up to Transfer Level
rationale: Vertical reinforcing bars from columns and walls below must extend into the transfer plate for continuity of load transfer. These elements must be cast to the underside of the transfer plate before the transfer plate itself is constructed.

The columns above the transfer plate must bear directly onto the completed transfer plate, which redistributes loads from the upper structure to the lower supports. The transfer plate must be cured and strong enough to support the vertical elements above.

successor: Upper Floor Slab Construction (typical floors above podium)
rationale: Floor slabs above the podium level are supported by columns that rise from the transfer plate. The transfer plate serves as the structural base for the entire superstructure above, so it must be complete before any upper-level floor construction begins.
Eaves and soffits are attached to the roof structure and trusses, which must be fully erected and secured first to provide the supporting framework.
Roof decking provides the substrate and structural base against which eaves and soffit installation occurs; soffits are typically fitted under the roof overhang which requires decking to be in place.
Fascia boards are installed along the roof edge before soffits, as the soffit fits between the fascia and the building wall, creating the enclosed overhang.
Gutters and downpipes are mounted on top of or against the fascia board, which is part of the eaves assembly. The eaves/soffit must be complete to provide the mounting surface for gutter systems.

While not strictly physically required, it is a construction sequencing preference to complete eaves/soffit before finishing upper cladding/siding so that the soffit trims can be properly integrated and flashed against the wall finish.
Structural steel and deck must be in place to provide the substrate onto which roof penetrations and curbs are mounted.
The roof substrate (e.g., plywood, metal deck) must be installed to provide a surface for curbs and penetration flashings to be properly attached and sealed.
MEP rough-ins that will penetrate the roof (e.g., exhaust ducts, plumbing vents, electrical conduits) must be brought up to roof level before curbs and sleeves are installed around them.
The roof membrane must be applied after curbs and penetrations are in place so that it can be flashed and sealed up the sides of each penetration/curb to maintain a watertight envelope.
HVAC units and other rooftop equipment are set onto the curbs only after the curbs are installed and flashed, as the curb serves as the mounting base.
Load-bearing walls or vertical supports must be built before roof trusses can be placed, as the trusses rest directly on the walls and require a stable support structure.
Roof sheathing (e.g. plywood or OSB) is installed on top of the trusses, so the truss framework must be fully erected first.
The waterproof membrane and final roofing materials are applied over the sheathing, which itself requires completed trusses.
Ceiling drywall is attached to the underside of the roof trusses; trusses must be in place to provide the nailing surface.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work in the attic or roof cavity can begin after trusses are installed, though in practice some MEP work may be coordinated in parallel; this is a logical sequencing preference for efficiency.
Gutters are attached to the fascia board, which is installed after roof sheathing. The roof structure must be complete to provide a surface for gutter attachment.
Gutters are directly mounted onto fascia boards. Fascia must be installed first to provide the structural support and attachment point for gutters.
The roof underlayment must be in place before gutters are installed to ensure proper water shedding and to prevent water damage behind the gutter system.
Downspouts connect directly to the gutter system to channel water from gutters to the ground or drainage system; gutters must first be in place.

While soffits are often installed before gutters for easier access, in some sequences gutters are installed first to allow soffits to be fitted neatly against the gutter edge; this is a soft preference depending on construction staging.
Walls must be structurally complete to support the roof structure and provide bearing surfaces for roof framing.
The building's structural frame (columns, beams, load-bearing walls) must be in place to provide support for roof trusses or rafters.
It is preferable to complete rough mechanical, electrical, and plumbing work within walls before the roof is enclosed, as access is easier and weather protection is not yet needed for interior work.
Ceiling assemblies (drywall, suspended ceilings) are installed after the roof structure is complete to have a finished overhead surface to attach to and to protect interior work from weather.
Interior finishes such as drywall, painting, and flooring must be protected from weather; therefore the roof (and building envelope) must be closed in before interior finishing begins.
The structural framing of the roof must be complete to support both the deck and the insulation layers.
A vapor barrier (if specified) must be laid down before insulation to prevent moisture migration into the insulation layer.
The waterproof membrane is installed over the insulation to protect it and the building from water ingress; insulation must be in place first.
The final roof covering (e.g., tiles, metal sheets, or built-up roofing) is laid on top of the insulation layer.
The skylight must be installed onto a completed roof deck structure that provides the necessary support and opening for the skylight.
The roof framing must be complete to create the rough opening and structural support required for skylight placement.
Roof sheathing provides the surface onto which the skylight is mounted and flashed; without sheathing the skylight cannot be properly secured.
Flashing around the skylight must be installed immediately after the skylight is placed to ensure waterproofing and prevent leaks.
Roofing materials such as shingles or membrane are installed after the skylight and its flashing are in place to integrate the skylight into the continuous roof covering.

Gutters and downspouts are attached to the roof edge/fascia and collect water from the roof surface. The roof must be installed first to provide the structural surface and edge from which gutters hang and to which downspouts connect.
Gutters are mounted directly onto the fascia board. The fascia must be in place to provide the structural backing and nailing surface for the gutter system.

Downspouts run along the exterior walls and are attached to the siding or wall surface. The exterior cladding must be completed so downspout brackets can be properly secured and the downspouts can be routed to ground level.

Soft preference: Downspout extensions and drainage outlets should be positioned before final grading and landscaping to ensure proper water runoff away from the foundation. However, landscaping can be completed first with later adjustments.
The gutter and downspout system must be fully installed to pass the exterior final inspection, as it is a critical component of the building envelope's water management system.

The ceiling membrane is typically attached to or supported by the structural framing. The structural framing must be complete to provide a substrate or support structure for the ceiling membrane system.

All mechanical ducts, electrical conduits, and plumbing pipes that run above the ceiling must be installed before the ceiling membrane is closed in. Installing the ceiling membrane first would block access and require costly removal and rework.
Fire sprinkler piping and heads that are concealed above the ceiling must be roughed in and tested before ceiling membrane installation. Access is needed for connections and pressure testing.

successor: Final MEP Trim-Out and Fixture Installation
rationale: Ceiling-mounted fixtures such as lights, speakers, sprinkler heads, and diffusers are installed after the ceiling membrane is in place, as they penetrate through or attach to the finished ceiling surface.

Final wall and ceiling finishes, particularly painting near the ceiling line, are performed after the ceiling membrane is installed to ensure clean edges, avoid damage to the membrane, and achieve a uniform finish where walls meet the ceiling.
The structural frame (steel columns/beams or concrete slabs) must be in place to provide the primary vertical and lateral support system before decking can be installed.

Structural decking (e.g., metal deck, precast planks, or wood decking) serves as the formwork or substrate; the concrete topping or slab cannot be poured until the deck is fully installed and secured.

While some MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) rough-in may occur in parallel, final routing of conduit, ductwork, and piping directly below the deck is best done after decking is in place to allow precise attachment and hanger installation.
Waterproofing or roof membrane application requires a stable, clean structural deck surface as the substrate; the membrane cannot be installed before the deck is complete.

All finishes applied to or above the deck (e.g., floor coverings, suspended ceilings, drywall) require the structural deck to be in place and cured to provide structural support and a level working surface.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the proper slope before trench drains can be installed, as the drain relies on gravity flow and proper subgrade preparation.
The main drain lines and sewer connections must be roughed-in beneath the slab before floor drains can be tied into the plumbing system.
A properly compacted gravel or stone base must be placed and leveled to support the trench drain body and prevent settling.
The floor drain and trench body must be set in position and secured before the concrete slab is poured, so that the drain is cast integrally with the slab.
After trench drains are installed, waterproofing membranes must be applied around the drain penetrations and up the walls to ensure a watertight seal before finishing.
Expansion joint covers are installed where structural frames meet; the structural frame must be complete to define the joint locations and widths accurately.
Expansion joints in slabs/ decks must be formed and concrete cured before covers can be installed over them.
Waterproofing at expansion joints is typically applied before the cover is placed to seal the joint.
Expansion joint covers are embedded in or abut floor finishes; final floor toppings or finishes are placed after the cover is set to achieve a flush transition.
Wall expansion joint covers must be installed before adjacent wall finishes and paint are applied to allow for clean edges and proper detailing.
The ceiling suspension hanger system must be attached to the overhead structural deck or framing above. Therefore structural framing must be in place to provide a secure anchoring surface.

Major ductwork, piping, conduit and electrical cabling that runs above the ceiling must be installed before the ceiling hanger grid is suspended, as access becomes restricted or impossible once hangers are in place.
The suspension hangers provide the vertical support from which the main ceiling grid runners (tees or tracks) are hung. The grid cannot be installed until the hangers are attached to the structure.
Suspension hangers must first be in place to carry the grid system, which in turn supports the ceiling tiles or panels. Tiles cannot be placed without the hanger-supported grid.

While it is preferred to install fireproofing and acoustic insulation before enclosing the ceiling with tiles, insulation can sometimes be placed after hanger installation but before grid closure. However, best practice is to apply these materials after hangers are hung but before final ceiling finish.
Cove base requires a clean, smooth, and properly prepared subfloor surface to adhere correctly; any debris, moisture, or unevenness would compromise adhesion and final appearance.

Cove base is typically installed after the main floor covering (e.g., vinyl, tile, carpet) is laid, as it covers the joint between the floor and wall, providing a finished transition and protecting the flooring edge.

Wall surfaces should be finished (painted or wallpapered) before cove base is installed because the cove base seals the wall-floor junction, and any painting or wallpapering afterward would risk damaging the cove base or leaving uneven edges.

While not physically required, it is standard practice to complete cove base installation before final cleaning and punch list walkthroughs to avoid soiling or damaging the newly installed cove base and to allow inspection of all finished edges.

Cove base should be installed before corner guards because corner guards are applied over the cove base at internal and external corners to provide protection and a clean finish; attempting to install corner guards first would leave gaps behind the cove base.
Electrical rough-in including conduit and wiring must be completed before floor boxes can be installed and connected to the power source.
The concrete slab or structural floor must be poured and cured before floor boxes can be set in place or mounted.
Floor boxes must be installed before final floor finishes (tile, carpet, vinyl, etc.) are laid so that the box is flush with the finished floor surface.
Once the floor box is physically installed, the electrical devices (plugs, connectors) can be trimmed out and connected to the branch circuits.
After floor boxes are installed and connected, electrical inspection and commissioning of outlets typically follows as a verification step.

The foundation or slab provides the structural base and support upon which the floor framing system (joists and beams) must be placed. Without a cured foundation or slab, there is no stable surface to anchor or support the floor framing.

Plumbing and drainage lines that run beneath the floor must be installed before the floor joists and beams are placed, as access to the sub-grade area would be blocked or severely restricted once the floor framing is in place.
Soil termite treatment/prevention must be applied to the ground area before the floor structure is built over it, as the treatment cannot be effectively applied after the framing is installed.

The subfloor sheathing (plywood or OSB decking) is installed directly on top of the floor joists and beams to create the walking surface and structural diaphragm. The framing must be complete to provide the supporting structure for the sheathing.
Floor underlayment materials are applied over the subfloor decking, which itself rests on the joists and beams. The structural framing must be in place first to support all layers above.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical and mechanical work above ceiling
rationale: Electrical wiring, conduit, ductwork, and other mechanical systems that will be hidden above the ceiling must be installed before the ceiling-mounted track can be secured, as the track would block access to the plenum space.
The ceiling structure (e.g., suspended ceiling grid, drywall ceiling) must be in place to have a mounting surface for the track system.
The track must be installed before final finish coats are applied to the ceiling so that the track flanges or brackets can be painted to match, and so painting does not damage the installed curtain.

successor: Installation of curtain fabric or panels
rationale: The track or curtain rail must be mounted and securely fixed to the ceiling before the curtain material itself can be hung from the carriers or gliders.
It is preferable to install the track and curtain before floor finishes to avoid moving heavy ladders over new flooring, but this is a soft preference for protection rather than a physical necessity.
The T-bar grid framework must be fully installed to provide the structural support onto which splines and clips are attached.
Splines and clips are used to secure and align ceiling tiles; tiles cannot be installed until the spline and clip attachments are in place.
All electrical, HVAC, and other MEP rough-in work above the ceiling must be completed before the spline and clip components are installed to avoid interference and rework.
Although final trim adjustments often follow spline and clip installation, minor realignment may be done later, so this is a soft sequencing preference rather than a strict physical constraint.
The thickened structural wythe requires a stable load-bearing base to transfer vertical loads; the foundation/footing must be completed first to provide this support.
Reinforcement steel must be positioned within the formwork before concrete for the thickened wythe is placed, as the steel is embedded within the pour.
Formwork must be assembled and braced to contain and shape the wet concrete of the thickened structural wythe before pouring can begin.
After concrete is placed in the thickened wythe formwork, it must undergo a curing period to reach sufficient strength before any subsequent loads are applied.

successor: Vertical / Lateral Structural Wall Construction Above
rationale: The thickened wythe acts as a bearing or starter element for the wall above; the upper wall construction depends on the completed thickened wythe for support and alignment.
The rough stair framing (stringers, supports) must be in place structurally before treads and landings can be installed, as treads and landings are mounted onto or supported by the rough framing.

Treads and landings provide the walking surface; railings and balusters are typically installed after the treads are placed because the railing posts often attach to the treads/stringers, and the railing height is referenced from the finished walking surface.

While treads and landings can be pre-finished, if final touch-up painting or staining is done on site, it typically occurs after installation. However, this is a soft preference as pre-finished materials are common.
The subfloor or floor sheathing at the top and bottom of the stair opening must be in place to establish finished floor elevations and provide a level surface for landing support and transition.

Transition moldings at the edges of landings are typically installed after the treads and landings are secured, but this is often a soft preference as it depends on the finishing sequence and material choices.
The building's structural frame (steel) must be fully erected and stable to provide the supporting framework onto which exterior cladding panels or curtain wall systems are attached.
The roof structure and waterproofing should be substantially complete to protect the building interior and cladding materials from weather damage during cladding installation.

Exterior cladding defines the final building envelope openings; windows and doors are typically installed after or integrated with the cladding system to ensure proper flashing, sealing, and integration with the weather barrier.
The building envelope must be closed and watertight before interior work (e.g., drywall, insulation, electrical rough-in) begins to prevent moisture damage to interior materials.

Once cladding is complete, access scaffolding can be removed; however, some punch-list or touch-up work may keep scaffolding in place temporarily, so this is a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
The thickened connection is cast integrally with or onto the foundation slab; the slab must be prepared and poured first to provide the base for the connection.

predecessor: Rebar cage / reinforcement placement for wall base
rationale: Reinforcing steel for the thickened connection must be placed and tied before concrete is poured for the connection.
Forms must be erected to shape the thickened connection before concrete can be placed.

successor: Wall vertical reinforcement placement and formwork
rationale: The thickened connection provides the load-bearing interface and anchorage for the wall above; wall construction can only proceed after the connection is cured and capable of transferring loads.

While the connection is often poured monolithically with the floor slab, if done separately the adjacent slab should follow to ensure continuity and minimize cold joints, but sequencing can be adjusted.
The window frame must be installed first to provide the structural boundary and reference surface for the expanded window reveal installation.
The rough opening must be framed, sized, and prepared to accommodate the expanded window reveal assembly before installation can begin.
The expanded window reveal must be fully installed before interior trim can be applied, as the reveal provides the backing and alignment surface for trim.
Drywall finishing and taping around the window opening must follow the reveal installation to ensure a seamless transition between the reveal and the surrounding wall surface.
Final caulking and sealing around the window reveal edges can only be performed after the reveal is fully installed to ensure a continuous weather seal and finished appearance.
Thermal breaks are typically installed at the interface between foundation walls and superstructure to prevent thermal bridging; the foundation wall must be in place first.
Thermal breaks at slab edges require the slab edge to be formed and prepared before the break material can be placed.
Concrete must reach sufficient strength before thermal break components can be installed against or onto it to avoid damage and ensure proper bonding.
Thermal breaks must be in place at structural interfaces before the superstructure elements are erected to avoid thermal bridging through the connection.
While not a hard physical constraint, it is best practice to install the air barrier system after thermal breaks are placed to ensure continuity of the building envelope.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the required bearing level before any foundation bearing element can be placed; otherwise the bearing would have no stable substrate.

A blinding layer of lean concrete is typically required to provide a clean, level working surface and to protect the reinforcement from ground moisture before placing the reinforced foundation bearing.

The steel reinforcement cage must be assembled and positioned within the formwork before the concrete for the foundation bearing is poured, as the rebar provides the tensile strength required for the reinforced component.

After the reinforced foundation bearing concrete is poured and has achieved sufficient initial set, the formwork can be stripped and the curing process begins to develop the required concrete strength.
Waterproofing membranes or coatings are applied to the cured foundation bearing surface to protect the reinforced concrete from groundwater ingress and chemical attack.
A structural survey must be completed to assess the condition of the existing walls and determine suitability for insulation, ensuring the substrate is sound enough to support the insulation system.
Safe working access to all elevations of the building is required before installers can begin applying insulation boards and render to the external walls.

predecessor: Preparation and Cleaning of Existing Wall Surface
rationale: Existing wall surfaces must be cleaned, repaired, and any loose material removed to ensure proper adhesion of the insulation system.

successor: Application of Base Coat and Reinforcement Mesh
rationale: Once insulation boards are fixed to the wall, a base coat with embedded reinforcement mesh must be applied to provide mechanical strength and a stable substrate for the finishing layers.
The installation of the insulation layer must be completed before the decorative and protective finish (render, cladding, or brick slip finish) can be applied to seal and weatherproof the system.
Safe access to elevated wall areas is physically required before any wall enlargement or repointing work can be performed.
The existing cavity wall must be inspected and assessed for structural integrity, cracks, or defects before enlargement and repointing can proceed safely.
Old, deteriorated pointing and finishes must be removed to expose the brick/masonry surface before new repointing and wall enlargement can be carried out.
Any cavity insulation installation must logically follow after the cavity has been enlarged and the wall repointed, as the wall structure needs to be complete and weathertight first.
A final inspection to verify the quality of repointing and that the enlarged cavity meets specifications can only occur after the work is completed.
A stable foundation must be prepared before any column, including corner columns, can be installed to support the structural load.
Corner columns must be in place before beams can be connected to them, as the column provides the vertical support and connection point for beams.
Corner columns support the structural framework, and slabs are poured after the column framework is erected to ensure proper load transfer.
The reinforcement cage for the column must be assembled and placed before the column concrete is poured or the column element is installed.
Corner columns define the building envelope corners and must be erected before exterior cladding can be applied to those corner regions.
The ground surface must be graded and excavated to the proper elevation and bearing capacity before any foundation work can begin.
The exact position of the corner column must be staked out on site before excavation and forming can proceed for the foundation.
Engineered foundation design requires confirmation that the soil at the corner location can support the loads; this test must be completed before placing concrete.
The column foundation must be cured and achieve sufficient strength to support the steel column before the column can be erected on it.

Anchor bolts are typically set into the wet concrete of the foundation; however, if considered as a separate activity, they must be placed before the concrete cures. More commonly, anchor bolts are part of the foundation pour itself, meaning the foundation must be complete for the bolts to be in place for column erection.
The corner column capital sits atop the column, so the column must be erected first to provide structural support for the capital.
The capital must be fabricated or cast before it can be lifted and installed into position.
Arches or beams often rest on the capital, so the capital must be in place to receive and support these upper structural elements.
If there is an upper column or pilaster above the capital, it must be installed after the capital is in place as it bears onto the capital.
In classical orders, the cornice is part of the entablature which sits above the capital; thus the capital must be installed before the cornice can be placed.
The base plate requires a stable, level concrete foundation or slab to be cast and cured to the specified compressive strength before any steel column components can be placed and anchored.

predecessor: Layout and Marking of Column Centers
rationale: The exact position of the corner column must be surveyed, marked, and verified on the foundation to ensure the base plate is placed in the correct location and alignment.
The base plate must be installed, leveled, and grouted (or shimmed) before the corner column can be set onto it and welded or bolted in place.

successor: Anchor Rod / Bolt Installation and Torqueing
rationale: The base plate is typically placed onto protruding anchor rods cast into the foundation; final tightening and torqueing of nuts onto the anchor rods occurs after plate placement.
After the base plate is set and leveled, non-shrink grout must be injected beneath the plate to provide full bearing and load transfer to the foundation.

The column reinforcement cage must be anchored into the footing foundation, which provides the structural base and load transfer. Without completed footings, the reinforcement cage cannot be placed or secured.
Starter bars or dowels from the foundation/pedestal need to be in place before the column cage can be assembled and tied to them for continuity.
The reinforcement cage must be fully assembled, tied, and in position before formwork can be erected around it to encase the steel.
All reinforcement steel must be in place and inspected before concrete can be poured. The cage provides the tensile strength embedded in the concrete.

While column cage completion is often preferred before beam steel integration (to allow proper lapping and continuity), in some sequences beam reinforcement can be partially prepared in parallel. However, for proper structural connection, the column cage should be complete first.
The structural steel frame, including corner columns, must be erected and stable before any cladding can be applied to the columns.
The corner column itself must be fabricated and delivered to site before cladding installation can begin on it.
Safe working access at height must be established before workers can perform cladding installation on the corner column.
Cladding panels must be installed first so that sealants and waterproofing can be applied to the joints and edges to prevent water ingress.

successor: Final Quality Inspection of Column Cladding
rationale: Cladding must be fully installed before a final quality check can be performed to verify alignment, fastening, and finish.
The foundation must be prepared and cured before any structural components like corner column brackets can be installed to provide a stable base.
The column must be erected in place before the corner column bracket can be attached to it, as the bracket connects to the column.
The corner column bracket must be installed first to provide the support seat for beams that rest on it.
The bracket must be in position before welding can secure the corner joint connections.
Structural load testing is typically performed after all brackets are installed to verify stability, though it is a quality assurance step rather than a strict physical dependency.
The column must be erected and positioned before the corner column connection joint can be installed, as the joint connects the column to other structural elements.
The foundation or base supporting the column must be complete before the column and its connection joint can be installed.
The column itself must be fabricated and delivered to the site before the connection joint can be attached to it.
Beams that connect into the corner column require the connection joint to be in place to provide the attachment point.
Structural bracing that ties into the corner column connection joint can only be installed after the joint is fixed in position.
A stable, level foundation is physically required before any column can be erected; the column base plate or anchor bolts must be set into the cured foundation.
Anchor bolts must be accurately positioned and checked in the foundation to align with the column base plate; the column cannot be placed without these embedded connections.
The foundation concrete must reach sufficient strength before it can safely support the column load and withstand bolt tightening forces.
Once erected, the corner column must be temporarily braced and plumbed (vertically aligned) before it can safely stand alone or before subsequent members are attached.
Corner beams or girders that frame into the column can only be connected after the column is set in its final position and temporarily secured.

predecessor: Rebar Cage Installation for Corner Column
rationale: The rebar cage must be installed and tied in place before concrete can be poured, as the reinforcement provides structural integrity to the column.
Formwork must be erected and secured to contain the wet concrete and shape the column before pouring can commence.
Concrete must be poured and allowed to gain sufficient strength before the formwork can be safely removed.
Curing begins immediately after concrete placement to maintain moisture and temperature conditions for proper hydration and strength development.

successor: Vertical Load Application on Corner Column
rationale: Structural loads from beams or slabs above should only be applied after the concrete has cured to sufficient strength, but this is a soft constraint depending on construction sequencing and load timing.
Corner columns require a cured, level foundation to bear the load and maintain alignment; placing columns before the foundation is set would compromise structural integrity.
The base plates must be accurately positioned and grouted to provide a stable mounting point for the corner columns before they can be installed and aligned.
Survey marks and layout lines defining column centerlines and grid positions are needed to set the corner columns in the correct location and orientation.
Once columns are installed and aligned, they must be grouted and permanently fixed into position to secure them before any further structural elements are attached.
Beams and girders spanning between columns rely on the columns being installed, aligned, and secured to provide the correct support points and elevations.
The column must be installed and in place before fireproofing can be applied to it, as fireproofing is a coating applied to the structural element.
The fireproofing must be fully applied before it can be inspected and tested for thickness, adhesion, and compliance with fire-resistance ratings.
Fireproofing is a base layer that must be applied before any decorative or architectural finishes can be installed over it.
The structural column must be in place to provide the load-bearing support and substrate for the architectural wrap.
The architectural wrap must be installed before final exterior cladding to ensure proper integration and sealing around the column.
It is preferable to complete the wrap before adding decorative trim so that the trim can be fitted neatly against the wrap surface.

predecessor: Masonry or Concrete Work at Column Base
rationale: Base masonry or concrete must be finished and cured to provide a stable foundation and anchor point for the wrap.
Painting is typically done after the wrap is installed to achieve a uniform finish, though it is a soft constraint as the wrap could be pre-finished.
Structural analysis determines the loads and forces on columns, which directly dictates the required column size, reinforcement, and cross-section dimensions.
Architectural layout defines column grid positions and spatial constraints, which must be known before finalizing column sizes and sections.
Column loads calculated from column sizing are required for foundation design, so column size must be determined before foundation design can proceed.
The column cross-section dimensions and reinforcement details must be finalized before the rebar cage can be fabricated and placed into the column formwork.
Formwork must be built to match the precise column dimensions and cross-sectional shape determined during column sizing.
Rebar cage must be in place before formwork can be erected around it; formwork encloses the reinforcement.
The exact column location and centerline must be marked on the deck/slab before formwork panels can be positioned accurately.
Formwork creates the mould into which wet concrete is poured; pouring cannot start until the formwork is fully erected, aligned, and secured.
The installed formwork must be checked for plumbness, alignment, and tightness before concrete placement to ensure dimensional accuracy and prevent blowouts.
Columns must be built on a stable foundation; without completed foundations, column reinforcement cannot be properly anchored or supported.
Column formwork (shuttering) must be erected first to define the shape and position of the column before reinforcement bars (rebar) can be placed inside.
Reinforcement steel must be fully placed, tied, and inspected inside the column formwork before concrete can be poured; the rebar provides tensile strength and must be embedded in the concrete.
The reinforcement cage must be completed and positioned before inspectors can verify correct cover, spacing, and tying of rebar within the formwork.

While slab/beam reinforcement is typically done after column concreting, in some sequences column cage assembly can proceed independently; this is a soft sequencing preference depending on the construction method.
Rebar reinforcement must be in place before concrete is poured to provide structural reinforcement within the column.
Formwork must be assembled and secured to contain the wet concrete and shape the column during pouring.
Concrete must be poured and allowed to cure sufficiently before formwork can be safely removed to avoid collapse or deformation.
Curing must begin immediately after pouring to maintain proper moisture and temperature conditions for concrete strength development.

successor: Vertical Structural Load Application (e.g., Beams/Slabs above)
rationale: Concrete must be poured and reach sufficient strength before any structural loads from beams or slabs above can be applied to the column.
Formwork provides the mold and support structure needed to hold the rebar cage in place during assembly and subsequent concreting.
The column rebar cage must be anchored into the foundation or pedestal; the foundation must be cured and ready to receive starter bars.
Longitudinal bars, ties, and stirrups must be cut and bent to the specified dimensions before they can be assembled into the cage.
The assembled rebar cage must be in position and tied before the formwork can be fully closed and secured around it.
Concrete cannot be poured until the rebar cage is fully assembled, tied, and inspected within the formwork.

Steel columns require a solid, cured foundation (typically reinforced concrete footings or pad foundations) to transfer the vertical load and provide a level bearing surface. Without the foundation in place, columns cannot be set.

Anchor bolts (or base plates) must be embedded and aligned in the foundation to receive and secure the steel column base. The column cannot be positioned or bolted down until the anchor bolt assembly is installed.

The foundation concrete must reach sufficient compressive strength (typically 75% of design strength) to withstand the concentrated load from the steel column and the stresses from bolting/grouting. Erection on uncured concrete risks foundation failure.
Beams and girders span between columns. Columns must be erected and plumbed before the primary horizontal framing members can be connected to them.
Temporary or permanent bracing (cross-bracing, knee braces) must be installed once columns are in place to provide lateral stability to the frame before additional loads are applied.
The foundation concrete must be poured and cured to sufficient strength to support the base plate and anchorage system, providing a stable load-bearing surface.
Column centerlines and anchor bolt locations must be accurately surveyed and marked out before base plates and anchorages can be positioned.
The ground must be excavated and sub-base prepared and compacted before foundation work and subsequent base plate installation can occur.
Column base plates must be installed, leveled, and grouted before steel columns can be erected and welded/bolted to them.
After base plate installation, anchor bolts must be properly torqued and the base plate grouted to ensure load transfer and stability.
The column must first be erected and positioned in place before the splice connection can be made between column sections.
After splicing the column sections together, the connected column must be checked and adjusted for plumbness and alignment before proceeding to the next level.
Beams and girders framing into the column at the splice location typically require the column splice to be completed first to provide a continuous load path and stability.
The column's base must be anchored to a completed foundation before upper column sections can be spliced in place.
Permanent or temporary bracing installation often follows column splicing to ensure the frame's lateral stability during construction.
The reinforcement cage must be in place to position and fix the void/sleeve accurately within the column, ensuring it does not displace during concreting.
The column formwork provides the enclosure and reference surfaces needed to locate and secure the embedded sleeve at the correct elevation and orientation before concrete is placed.
The void/sleeve must be fully positioned, secured, and inspected before concrete is placed; otherwise the embedment would be buried and impossible to install later.

While it is physically possible to run MEP lines later, it is standard practice to rough-in through the sleeve soon after concrete cures to avoid rework, though this is a preferential sequencing dependency.

successor: Inspection / Quality Check of Embedded Items
rationale: Embedded sleeves must be inspected for position, alignment, and security before concrete pour; if inspection fails, the pour must be delayed for corrective action.
The column must be erected and in place before the tie beam can be connected to it, as the tie beam spans between columns and relies on the columns for support.
The tie beam connection provides lateral support and load transfer; floor slabs are typically poured after the tie beam frame is connected and stable.
The column must be anchored to a completed foundation before tie beam connections can be made to ensure structural stability and alignment.
If columns are cast-in-place, the concrete must reach sufficient strength before connecting tie beams to avoid damage to the column.
Temporary bracing or shoring used during column erection can be removed only after tie beam connections are complete and the frame is laterally stable.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstacles before any footing construction can begin to provide a clean working area and ensure proper load-bearing conditions.
Surveying and setting out the precise locations and levels for the pad footings must be completed before excavation or concreting to ensure accurate positioning of the footings.
Excavation to the required depth and dimensions must precede pad footing construction as the footing concrete is placed into the excavated pit.
Pad footings must be cast and cured before ground beams can be constructed, as ground beams typically bear onto or are cast integrally with the pad footings.
Pad footings provide the foundation base and hold-down bolts for steel columns; columns can only be erected after the footings have been cast and achieved sufficient strength.
The ground must be cleared, excavated, and leveled before any foundation work can begin.
Soil bearing capacity and ground conditions must be assessed to design the raft foundation thickness and reinforcement.
A level working surface of lean concrete or compacted hardcore is required to place reinforcement and pour the raft slab upon.
Waterproofing membranes are applied directly onto the cured raft slab to protect against ground moisture before superstructure continues.
The raft foundation provides the structural base upon which load-bearing walls and columns are erected.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil before excavation and foundation work can begin, as mat foundations require undisturbed or properly prepared subgrade.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth and subgrade level before placing the mat foundation, as the concrete slab is cast directly on the prepared subgrade.
The subgrade soil must be properly graded, leveled, and compacted to provide uniform bearing capacity before the mat foundation is placed, preventing differential settlement.

predecessor: Installation of Blinding Layer / Lean Concrete
rationale: A thin layer of lean concrete (blinding) is typically placed over the compacted subgrade to provide a clean, level working surface and prevent soil contamination of the reinforcement and fresh concrete of the mat foundation.
While waterproofing is often applied after mat foundation curing, in some designs a waterproof membrane is placed beneath the mat before concrete placement to protect against groundwater ingress.
After the mat foundation concrete is placed, it must undergo a specified curing period to achieve design strength before any subsequent loads or construction activities can be applied.
The mat foundation concrete must be placed and reach initial set before any side forms can be stripped.
Typically, waterproofing on the top and sides of the mat foundation is applied after the concrete has cured sufficiently to bond with the membrane or coating.
The mat foundation must be fully placed, cured, and achieve adequate strength before vertical structural elements like columns, shear walls, or core walls can be constructed on top of it.

Backfilling against the mat foundation edges is typically done after waterproofing is applied and the concrete has achieved sufficient strength, but can sometimes proceed sooner in staged construction.
The ground surface must be cleared, stripped of vegetation, and graded to provide a stable, level working platform for drilling equipment and for layout of pier locations.
Accurate surveying and staking of pier locations is required before drilling can commence to ensure piers are placed in correct positions per structural drawings.
Soil borings and geotechnical analysis must be completed to determine bearing capacity, soil strata, and depth requirements for the drilled piers before design and installation can proceed.
Drilled piers must be installed and concrete cured before pile caps can be formed and poured atop the piers to distribute loads from columns.
Caissons/drilled piers form the deep foundation elements; vertical columns or superstructure elements cannot be erected until the piers are installed and have achieved sufficient concrete strength.
The drilled shaft must be excavated first before the reinforcing steel cage can be placed and concrete poured into the excavation.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before subgrade preparation can begin, as these obstructions would interfere with grading and compaction operations.
Accurate survey stakes and grade markers are needed to guide the excavation, filling, and grading work during subgrade preparation to achieve the correct elevations and slopes.
Erosion and sediment control measures (e.g., silt fences, sediment basins) must be installed before disturbing the ground to comply with environmental regulations and prevent off-site sedimentation.

The subgrade must be properly graded, compacted, and proof-rolled to provide a stable, uniform foundation before placing the base course material; placing base on unprepared subgrade would lead to differential settlement and pavement failure.

After subgrade preparation is complete, underground utilities (e.g., storm drains, water lines, conduits) can be trenched and laid on a prepared surface, while the subgrade must be ready to support trenching and backfill operations.
Formwork must be installed first to create the mold and support structure into which the reinforcement steel will be placed and tied.
The surface where rebar will be placed must be clean and prepared to ensure proper bonding and positioning of steel reinforcement.
Reinforcement steel must be fully placed, tied, and inspected before concrete can be poured, as the steel provides tensile strength within the concrete element.

Post-tensioning tendons or ducts are often placed after or concurrently with rebar, and tensioning occurs after concrete cures; but the placement of reinforcement steel must precede post-tensioning duct installation and concrete pour.
Inspection of the placed reinforcement steel must occur after placement but before concrete pouring to verify spacing, cover, ties, and compliance with engineering drawings.
Excavation must be completed to expose the foundation walls and provide working space for waterproofing application.
Concrete foundation must be fully placed and cured to provide a stable, clean substrate for waterproofing membrane adhesion.
Formwork must be stripped to expose the foundation wall surface for waterproofing application.
Drainage boards and/or rigid insulation are typically installed directly over the cured waterproofing membrane to protect it and provide drainage pathways.
Backfilling against the foundation must only occur after waterproofing is fully applied and cured to avoid damaging the membrane.
The foundation sub-base must be excavated, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable load-bearing surface before seismic isolation bearings can be placed.
A reinforced concrete footing or pad must be cast and cured to support the seismic isolation bearings. The bearings sit directly on this foundation element.

The isolation bearings must be bolted or grouted in place on the foundation first, then the superstructure columns or piers are erected on top of the bearings to allow the isolation system to function correctly.

The entire superstructure (bridge deck or building frame) is supported through the isolation bearings; therefore, the bearings must be installed prior to starting superstructure erection to transfer loads properly.

After the bearings are positioned and the superstructure load begins to bear, final grouting under the bearing base plates and installation of protective cover plates must be completed to secure and protect the bearings.
The excavation must be completed to expose the foundation area where the anchor bolts and base plate will be placed.
Concrete foundation must be poured and sufficiently cured to provide a solid base for embedding or mounting anchor bolts and the base plate.
Accurate surveying and layout marking are needed to position the anchor bolts precisely before assembly.
The anchor bolts and base plate must be in place and secured to provide the connection point for the steel column.
After the base plate is positioned and leveled on the anchor bolts, grout is applied beneath it to fill voids and ensure full load transfer to the foundation.
Formwork provides the mold and support structure for wet concrete; slab cannot be poured without formwork in place
Steel reinforcement bars must be positioned within the formwork prior to concrete pouring to ensure structural integrity
Freshly poured concrete requires a specified curing period to gain strength before any loads can be applied
Waterproofing membrane or coating is applied on top of the cured structural slab to protect against moisture ingress
Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied before concrete cover/topping is poured, as the concrete encases the reinforcement to create composite structural action.
Formwork must be erected to contain and shape the wet concrete before the concrete cover/topping can be poured.

predecessor: Concrete slab / deck preparation (cleaning and wetting)
rationale: The substrate must be clean, free of debris, and properly moistened to ensure adequate bond between the existing slab and the new concrete topping.
After placement, the concrete topping must undergo a controlled curing period to achieve design strength and prevent cracking from premature drying.

successor: Surface finishing / tiling or flooring installation
rationale: The concrete topping must be fully cured and sufficiently hardened before any final floor finishes (tiles, screed, flooring) can be applied over it.
Vapor barrier must be applied to the interior side of exterior wall framing; framing provides the structural surface for the vapor barrier to be attached to.
Exterior sheathing must be in place before vapor barrier is installed, as the vapor barrier goes between the sheathing and interior finishes.
In many climate zones, the vapor barrier is installed before insulation to control moisture migration; the vapor barrier must be continuous behind the insulation layer.
Vapor barrier must be fully installed and sealed before interior finishes like drywall are applied, as the vapor barrier sits behind the drywall.

While rough-ins are typically done before vapor barrier to avoid puncturing it, this can be done after with careful sealing; preference is to complete rough-ins first to minimize penetrations through the vapor barrier.

predecessor: Install vapor barrier / air barrier membrane
rationale: A vapor barrier or air barrier membrane must be installed before rigid insulation to prevent moisture diffusion and condensation within the wall assembly; rigid insulation is placed directly over this membrane.
Rigid insulation must be fully installed before exterior cladding or siding is applied, as the insulation provides a continuous thermal barrier and substrate for the cladding attachment system.

successor: Install weather-resistive barrier (if applied over insulation)
rationale: If a weather-resistive barrier is placed over the rigid insulation (e.g., in a drained cavity system), the insulation must be in place to serve as the backing layer.
Rigid insulation is typically installed over exterior structural sheathing, which provides a flat, load-bearing surface for the insulation to be mechanically fastened or adhesively attached.

Furring strips or vertical strapping for cladding attachment are installed over the rigid insulation to create a ventilation cavity; the insulation must be in place first to support and align the strapping.
The ground must be excavated to the correct formation level before placing blinding concrete, as blinding provides a clean, level working platform over the exposed soil or rock.
The subgrade must be properly compacted and prepared to ensure uniform support before the lean concrete is poured.
Blinding concrete provides a clean, level, and stable working surface for placing and tying reinforcement bars for the foundation.
The blinding layer serves as a smooth substrate for applying waterproofing membranes (e.g., on raft foundations) before the main pour.
Once the blinding concrete has been placed and has cured sufficiently, surveyors can accurately mark out column positions and wall lines on the clean, level surface.
The structural frame must be in place before expansion/contraction joints can be installed, as these joints are typically placed between structural elements to accommodate thermal movement.
Expansion/contraction joints in concrete slabs are typically cut or formed after the concrete has been poured and partially cured to control cracking from thermal and moisture movement.

Floor finishes and toppings must be applied after expansion joints are installed so that the joints can be properly detailed, filled with sealant, or carried through the finish layer to maintain their function.
Wall cladding or paneling is installed after expansion joints are in place so that the joints align with structural movement gaps and the cladding can be detailed to accommodate movement.
Sealants are applied into the formed or cut joint gaps after the expansion/contraction joint itself is in place, to allow for movement while preventing debris and moisture ingress.
Edge/perimeter insulation is installed against the foundation walls. The foundation must be poured and cured before insulation can be applied to its exterior surface.
Waterproofing membrane or coating must be applied to the foundation wall before rigid insulation boards are placed, as the insulation is typically installed over the waterproofed surface.
Perimeter insulation boards must be in place on the exterior of the foundation before soil can be backfilled against them; otherwise the insulation would be buried and inaccessible.

successor: Slab-on-grade / floor slab pouring (if interior edge insulation)
rationale: If perimeter insulation is placed along the interior edge of a slab (vertical or horizontal), it must be positioned before the concrete slab is poured so the insulation becomes embedded or butted against the slab edge.

While it is good practice to have perimeter insulation in place before finishing the exterior wall cladding to ensure continuous thermal protection, the cladding could theoretically be installed later if the insulation is protected temporarily. This is a soft preference for continuity of the building envelope.
The ground must be excavated and graded to create a level base before the radon vent mat can be laid.
A gravel base course providing a capillary break must be placed first to support the radon vent mat and allow proper gas flow beneath it.
The radon vent mat is installed on top of the gravel bed and under the concrete slab; the slab is poured directly over the mat, embedding it.
The vent mat must be in place so that the vent pipe can be connected to the collection mat system before the slab is poured.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before any drainage layer can be placed, as the drainage layer requires a stable, prepared subgrade.
The subgrade soil must be compacted and graded to the correct slopes to ensure proper drainage away from the structure before placing the drainage layer.
The vapor barrier or moisture membrane is typically laid directly on top of the drainage layer to prevent moisture migration into the slab, so the drainage layer must be in place first.
Steel reinforcement for the concrete slab is placed on supports above the drainage layer and vapor barrier, requiring the drainage layer to be completed first.
The concrete slab is poured over the prepared base consisting of the drainage layer, vapor barrier, and reinforcement, all of which depend on the drainage layer being in place first.
Formwork must be installed and secured before concrete can be poured into it; the formwork provides the mold that shapes the slab.
Steel reinforcement bars must be placed and tied in position within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity of the slab.
Any electrical conduits, plumbing pipes, or other embedded services must be installed and inspected before concrete pouring, as they cannot be added after the slab hardens.
After pouring and finishing, the concrete slab must undergo proper curing to achieve design strength before any loads are placed on it.

Waterproofing is typically applied after the slab has cured sufficiently, but in some sequences it may be deferred; however, best practice is to waterproof after finishing and initial curing to protect the slab.
Joints are cut into hardened concrete after it has been poured and sufficiently cured to achieve initial set and strength, preventing damage to the fresh concrete.
The positions and patterns of joints must be planned and marked on the concrete surface before cutting begins to ensure proper joint alignment and spacing.

Often curing compounds are applied after joint sealing to protect the entire slab surface; however some sequences apply curing before joint cutting, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.

Final surface finishing and texturing operations (e.g., brooming or troweling) are typically completed before joint cutting to avoid damaging the finished surface texture; joint sealing then follows after cutting and cleaning.
Traffic or heavy loads must not be applied to the slab until joints have been cut and sealed to control cracking and allow sealant to cure, preventing joint raveling and uncontrolled cracking.

Vapor barrier is installed after the structural framing (walls, roof, floor) is in place, as the barrier is typically applied to the interior side of exterior walls and requires a stable frame to attach to.
Rough framing (studs, joists, rafters) must be complete to create the cavities where insulation will be placed.
The roof must be in place to protect insulation materials from moisture before installation in attic or ceiling cavities.
Windows and exterior doors must be installed and sealed to create a weather-tight envelope before insulation is placed.
Electrical wiring, outlet boxes, and plumbing pipes must be routed through the wall cavities before insulation fills the space.
Vapor barrier or vapor retarder is typically placed over the insulation (on the warm side of the wall) to control moisture diffusion.
Drywall (interior wallboard) cannot be hung until insulation is fully placed inside the wall cavities.
All painting, texturing, and wall coverings must follow after drywall, which requires insulation to be installed first.
Formwork provides the mold and support structure for concrete; reinforcement bars must be placed inside the formwork before concrete pouring.
Reinforcement must be fully fixed and in position before concrete is poured, so that the steel is embedded within the concrete to provide tensile strength.
Reinforcement bars must be cut and bent to specified shapes before they can be placed and tied into position.
After fixing, the reinforcement must be inspected for correct positioning, spacing, and cover before concrete is poured (inspection typically occurs between fixing and pouring).
Concrete pouring and subsequent curing can only occur after reinforcement fixing is complete and inspected.
A stable, clean, and level structural base is required to support and protect the underfloor heating pipes before they are laid out and fixed in position.
Thermal insulation must be placed beneath underfloor heating pipes to prevent downward heat loss and ensure efficient operation; pipes are laid directly onto the insulation.

successor: Pipework Pressure Testing and Leak Testing
rationale: After pipes are installed, they must be pressure-tested before being covered to verify there are no leaks; this can only be done once the pipe network is complete.

successor: Screed / floor covering pour (cement or anhydrite screed)
rationale: A protective screed layer is poured over the underfloor heating pipes to encase them and provide a flat finished floor surface; pipes must be fully laid and tested before encasement.

successor: Final floor finish (tiles, wood, vinyl) installation
rationale: Final floor finishes are applied only after the screed has cured and the heating pipes are fully covered; the pipe installation is a prerequisite for all subsequent floor layers.

Slab void formers are placed within the reinforcement cage of the slab. The bottom layer of reinforcement must be installed first to provide support and positioning for void formers, which are then tied or fixed in place before the top reinforcement is placed.

The slab formwork (soffit formwork) must be fully erected and leveled to create the surface upon which slab void formers are placed. Void formers cannot be positioned without a supporting formwork deck.

After slab void formers are positioned and secured, the top layer of slab reinforcement must be placed over them. The top reinforcement cannot be installed before void formers are in place as the void formers occupy the mid-depth zone of the slab.

Concrete cannot be poured over slab void formers until all void formers have been correctly positioned, secured against flotation, and inspected. Pouring concrete is the final step after all reinforcement and void formers are in place.

While electrical or mechanical conduits can sometimes be laid before void formers, it is typically preferable to install services after void formers to avoid displacing them. This is a soft preference as it can vary by design and trade sequencing.
The ground moisture sensor must be embedded in or placed on a stable foundation or slab; the foundation must be prepared and poured first to provide a solid base for sensor placement.
Any underground cabling or conduit for the sensor must be trenched and laid before the sensor is placed to avoid digging up the sensor after installation.
After the sensor is installed in its correct position, final landscaping, soil backfill, and grading can proceed to cover and protect the sensor.

Calibrating the irrigation controller using sensor readings is logically dependent on having the sensor in place and operational, though if a temporary sensor is used calibration could start earlier (soft preference).
The sensor must be physically installed before its electrical connections can be tested and the monitoring system commissioned.
Structural screed is typically applied over a concrete slab or structural deck to provide a level surface or topping; the substrate must be in place and cured before the screed can be applied.

successor: Floor finishing (e.g., tiling, flooring, or final topping)
rationale: The structural screed must be fully cured and prepared before any final floor finishes can be applied over it to ensure a stable and level base.

successor: Underfloor heating installation (if embedded in screed)
rationale: Underfloor heating pipes or cables are often embedded within the structural screed, so the screed is placed after the heating elements; however, if the heating is installed on top of the screed this order may differ, making it a soft preference.
Where a damp-proof membrane or waterproofing layer is required beneath the screed, it must be installed and inspected before the screed is poured to prevent moisture ingress.

successor: Heavy equipment or partition wall installation (on screed surface)
rationale: Heavy partitions, machinery bases, or other structural loads should only be placed after the screed has achieved sufficient strength to avoid cracking or deformation.
The solid box column requires a stable load-bearing base or foundation to transfer its loads. Without completed foundation/pile cap, the column cannot be erected as it would lack structural support.

For a reinforced concrete solid box column, the steel reinforcement cage must be assembled and positioned within the formwork before concrete can be poured. This is a physically required sequence in reinforced concrete construction.
The formwork (molds) for the solid box column must be erected and secured before concrete placement. The wet concrete requires containment to achieve the designed box shape and dimensions.

After the concrete for the solid box column is poured, it must undergo a curing period to gain sufficient strength before the formwork can be safely removed. This is a hard physical/chemical constraint.

The solid box column acts as a vertical load-bearing element that supports beams, slabs, or other superstructure components above. Those elements can only be constructed after the column has been completed and achieved adequate strength to bear the loads.
The steel reinforcement cage provides the internal tensile reinforcement for the hollow box column and must be fabricated and placed before concrete can be poured to form the column.

predecessor: Erect Formwork for Hollow Box Column
rationale: Formwork creates the mold that shapes the hollow box column; it must be assembled and secured in position before the concrete is cast.
The hollow box column typically rests on a foundation or base slab which must be cured and load-bearing prior to erecting the column to provide structural support.

successor: Cure Concrete of Hollow Box Column
rationale: After casting the hollow box column, the concrete must be allowed to cure and gain strength before any further loads or construction activities can be applied to it.

predecessor: Cure Concrete of Hollow Box Column
rationale: Formwork can only be removed after the concrete has gained sufficient strength through curing to support its own weight and prevent deformation or collapse.
Steel box columns must be fabricated in the factory and transported to site before they can be installed.
The foundation or pile cap for the column must be completed and cured to provide a stable base before the steel box column can be erected.
Precise surveying and marking of column locations are required before placing the column to ensure correct alignment and positioning.

successor: Steel Box Column Grouting & Base Plate Fixing
rationale: After installing the steel box column on its base plate, the gap must be grouted and anchor bolts tightened to secure the column permanently.
Steel beams and girders connecting into the column can only be erected after the column is in place and stabilized, as the column provides vertical support and connection points.
The concrete box column must be built on a stable foundation; footings must be poured and cured before any column construction can begin to ensure structural integrity and load transfer.
Reinforcement steel cages must be assembled, positioned, and tied inside the formwork before concrete is placed for the box column; the rebar gives the column its tensile strength.
Formwork (molds for the box shape) must be erected, aligned, and braced before pouring concrete to contain and shape the wet concrete until it cures.
After concreting the box column, sufficient curing time is required before formwork can be removed, and the column must gain adequate strength before any further loads are applied.

Beams, slabs, or other structural elements that bear on or connect into the box column can only be constructed after the column has been cast and cured to design strength, as these elements transfer loads into the column.
A stable foundation is required to support the load-bearing timber box column before it can be erected.
