The site must be cleared, leveled, and the column locations marked out before column installation can begin.
Timber components must be sourced, cut to size, and treated (e.g., with preservatives or fire retardants) before assembly and erection of the box column.
Primary beams rest on or connect to the timber box columns, so columns must be in place to support the beams.
After the column is erected, temporary bracing must be added to ensure stability until permanent connections and lateral support are installed.
The steel reinforcement cage provides the internal tensile strength and must be fabricated and placed before concrete can be poured around it to form the composite box column.
Formwork defines the outer shape of the box column and must be erected and secured before concrete casting to contain the wet concrete.
After casting the concrete in the formwork, sufficient curing time is required for the concrete to gain design strength before any structural loads are applied.
The formwork cannot be removed until the concrete column has hardened to a sufficient strength to be self-supporting.
Steel beams framing into the composite column require the column to be fully cured and in place to provide the connection point and support.
The box column base plate must be placed on a cured concrete foundation pour to provide stable support and load distribution.
Reinforcing steel cage must be in place within the foundation before the base plate can be positioned and anchored.
The base plate must be installed, leveled, and anchored first to provide the mounting surface and connection point for the box column above.
After the base plate is positioned and leveled, high-strength grout is pumped underneath to fill voids and ensure full bearing.
Survey control points, centerlines, and bolt locations must be laid out and verified before setting the base plate to ensure correct positioning and alignment.
The box column cap/head sits on top of the column, so the column must be erected and secured before the cap/head can be placed.
The column cap/head provides the bearing surface and connection points for beams or girders; beams can only be placed after the cap is installed.
The cap/head component must be fabricated, delivered, and prepared on site before it can be lifted and installed onto the column.
The foundation or base supporting the column must be completed before the column (and subsequently its cap) can be erected.
The column reinforcement cage must be in place before the box column diaphragm can be installed, as the diaphragm sits within or around the reinforced column section.
The formwork for the box column must be erected and aligned before the diaphragm can be placed inside or integrated with the column form.
The diaphragm must be fully installed and positioned before concrete is poured into the column, as the diaphragm becomes embedded in the concrete.
After the diaphragm is placed, it must be welded or mechanically connected to the column steel or reinforcement to ensure structural continuity.
The column base or foundation must be in place and cured before any column component can be spliced onto it, providing structural support.
The lower segment of the box column must already be erected and stabilized before the splice connection to the upper segment can be performed.
The lower column section must be fully secured (welded or bolted) at its base before it can receive the splice connection for the next tier.
The splice connection must be completed before the next upper column section can be placed and aligned on top of it.

Although inspection can be done after further work, best practice requires non-destructive testing of the splice weld/bolts before significant load is applied, so it is a soft preference for quality assurance.
The Engaged Box Column requires a stable foundation to bear its load; foundation must be prepared and cured before column erection.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied before concrete can be poured into the box column formwork.

predecessor: Formwork Setup for Engaged Box Column
rationale: The formwork molds must be erected and braced before concrete placement can begin.

successor: Concrete Curing for Engaged Box Column
rationale: Concrete must be placed in the column before the curing process can commence.
The column must be erected and cured to support beams or slabs that bear on it.
The steel column must be erected first to provide the structural support and framing onto which the box column cladding/casing can be applied.
Any protective coating or primer on the steel column must be applied before enclosing it with cladding/casing to ensure corrosion protection is in place.
If fireproofing is to be applied to the column assembly, the cladding/casing must be installed first so that fireproofing material can be applied over the completed assembly.

Final architectural finishes (e.g., paint, decorative wraps) around the column casing typically follow cladding installation for aesthetic continuity, though in some sequences finishes could be pre-applied.

Adjacent wall systems often abut the column cladding; completing the column cladding first allows for clean detailing and alignment, though this is a logical preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The free-standing box column requires a stable, level foundation to bear its load and maintain vertical alignment. The foundation or base slab must be completed and cured before column installation.

predecessor: Column Base Plate / Anchor Bolt Setting
rationale: Anchor bolts or base plates must be embedded in the foundation to provide a secure connection point for the box column. The column cannot be placed until these are in position.
Once the box column is erected and plumbed, it serves as a vertical support for connecting horizontal beams, girders, or other structural steel elements.
If the box column is multi-story or multi-segment, additional column sections can only be spliced and connected after the lower section is installed and secured.
Fireproofing spray or encasement is applied after the steel column is fully erected to protect it without interfering with hoisting or alignment operations.
Reinforcement bars must be placed and tied inside the column before formwork can be erected around them, as formwork encloses the reinforcement cage.
The exact column position and alignment must be marked on the slab/deck to accurately place the formwork panels.
Formwork creates the mold into which concrete is poured; concrete placement cannot commence until the formwork is fully erected, aligned, and braced.
Before concrete is poured, the erected formwork must be inspected for alignment, plumbness, stability, and tightness to ensure safety and quality.
Concrete must be poured and gain sufficient strength before formwork can be removed; thus striking (dismantling) occurs only after the pour and curing period.
The reinforcement cage must be anchored into or placed upon a completed foundation or footing to provide structural support and load transfer.
Individual reinforcing bars must be cut, bent, and prepared to specified dimensions before they can be assembled into a cage.
Formwork is placed around the completed reinforcement cage to contain the concrete pour and shape the column.
Concrete cannot be poured until the reinforcement cage is fully assembled, tied, and inspected in its final position.
While inspection is typically done after cage completion and before concrete pour, it is a quality control step rather than a physical necessity, though strongly recommended.
A stable foundation or base must be prepared and cured before box columns can be erected, as the columns require a solid load-bearing surface for anchorage and alignment.
Accurate survey marks and grid lines must be established to ensure the box columns are positioned correctly within the structural layout.
Box column materials must be delivered to site and inspected for quality and dimensions before erection can proceed.

successor: Box Column Alignment and Plumb Checking
rationale: After placing the box column, it must be immediately aligned, plumbed, and temporarily braced before any further connections are made.
Beams and girders can only be connected after the box columns are erected and secured, as the columns serve as vertical supports for horizontal structural members.
Reinforcement steel must be in place before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity of the box column.
Formwork must be erected and secured to provide the mold and support for the wet concrete during pouring and initial curing.
Concrete must be poured and allowed to gain sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed.
Concrete curing (moisture retention and temperature control) must commence immediately after concrete placement to ensure proper hydration and strength development.
Post-pour inspections such as slump tests, compressive strength tests, and visual checks must be performed after concreting to verify compliance with specifications.
Steel plates and welding consumables must be procured and delivered to the fabrication yard before any welding operations can commence.
Steel plates must be cut to size, edge-prepared, and beveled as required before they can be assembled and welded into box column sections.
After welding is complete, all welds must be inspected via ultrasonic or radiographic testing to verify weld integrity before the column can proceed to the next stage.
Welding must be finished and inspected before the column surface can be blast-cleaned and coated with primer/finish paint to prevent corrosion.
The box column must be fully welded, inspected, and completed before it can be loaded and transported to the construction site for installation.
Box columns must first be physically constructed (cast) before their survey and alignment can be performed.
Accurate box column alignment is required to ensure steel beams or trusses can be properly seated and connected to the columns.
If survey reveals misalignment, grouting or corrective works to plumb and position the column must follow before further vertical construction.
The column base must be set, levelled, and grouted to a stable finished elevation before accurate column survey and alignment can be conducted.
Floor slabs and upper-level works depend on column positions being verified and aligned to maintain structural geometry and load paths.
The ring beam requires a stable foundation to transfer loads; without foundation, the ring beam would have no structural support.
Ring beams are typically cast or installed atop columns or vertical supports to tie them together; columns must be in place to receive the ring beam.
Formwork must be erected and aligned before concrete can be poured or steel placed for the ring beam.
The ring beam provides lateral support and a bearing surface for the roof or upper floor slab; roof construction depends on the completed ring beam.
Walls above the ring beam level (e.g., parapet walls or upper story walls) require the ring beam as a base or tie element.
Wall starter beams require a stable, level foundation to bear on; the foundation slab or ground beams must be cured and load-bearing before the starter beam is placed.
Accurate positioning of the wall starter beam depends on completed surveying and layout marking of wall lines on the foundation.
Wall starter beams serve as the base registration for subsequent blockwork or brickwork; walls cannot commence without the starter beam in place.
The damp-proof course is typically laid on top of the starter beam before the first course of masonry begins, so the starter beam must be installed first.
Starter beams often incorporate starter bars or dowels for vertical reinforcement; the beam must be placed before vertical rebar can be tied or positioned above it.
Reinforcement bars (rebar) must be placed and tied within the parapet formwork before concrete can be poured to form the parapet beam.
Formwork or shuttering must be erected and aligned to shape and contain the wet concrete for the parapet beam.
After the concrete is poured, sufficient curing time is required to allow the concrete to gain strength before any loads are applied.
The formwork cannot be removed until the concrete parapet beam has achieved sufficient strength to support itself.
Waterproofing membrane or coating is applied to the cured parapet beam surface to protect the concrete from water ingress and weathering.
A bond beam must be placed on a stable foundation or wall structure; the foundation must be completed to provide support.
Bond beams are typically cast into or on top of masonry or CMU walls; the wall must be built first to receive the bond beam reinforcement and concrete.
Reinforcing steel must be placed and tied within the bond beam block or formwork before concrete can be poured.
The bond beam provides a continuous bearing surface and anchorage for roof trusses or floor joists; the diaphragm cannot be installed until the bond beam has cured.
In some sequences, bond beam placement may precede vertical grouting to confine the grout, but this can vary; typically a preference to avoid segregation of grout.
The ground must be excavated and leveled to the required bearing depth before any foundation beam can be poured or placed.
A clean, level blinding concrete layer must be placed over the excavation to provide a stable working surface and prevent soil contamination of the reinforcement and concrete.
The steel reinforcement cage for the beam must be assembled, positioned, and tied in place before concrete can be poured into the formwork.
Formwork (shuttering) must be erected and secured to define the shape and dimensions of the beam before concrete is placed.
After the beam is poured, the concrete must be allowed to cure to sufficient strength before the formwork can be safely removed.
Waterproofing layers are applied to the cured foundation beam to protect against moisture ingress before backfilling or subsequent wall construction.
The perimeter foundation beam provides the continuous bearing surface and structural support upon which load-bearing walls or the superstructure can be erected.
Backfilling against the foundation beam can only commence after the concrete has fully cured and waterproofing has been applied to avoid damage.
Perimeter beams rest on and transfer loads to columns, so columns must be installed first to provide structural support.
Formwork or falsework must be erected to support the wet concrete of the perimeter beams before they can be cast.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured for the perimeter beams.
Perimeter beams provide edge support and formwork for floor slabs; the slab pour typically follows beam installation.
After the perimeter beam is cast, sufficient curing time is required before any loads (e.g., from subsequent floors) can be applied.
Columns and vertical supports must be cast and cured before beam formwork can be erected, as beams are supported by columns.
Adjacent slab formwork provides the working platform and lateral support needed to safely place and secure perimeter beam forms.
Formwork must be fully erected before reinforcement steel can be placed inside the beam forms.
Concrete for perimeter beams can only be poured after the formwork is complete and reinforcement is in place.
Perimeter beam formwork installation typically precedes or is concurrent with slab formwork to ensure proper alignment and load transfer at the beam-slab interface.
Formwork must be installed and secured to create the mold that shapes the concrete for the perimeter beams before concrete can be poured.

predecessor: Rebar/Steel Reinforcement Placement for Perimeter Beams
rationale: Steel reinforcement cage must be placed and tied within the formwork to provide structural tensile strength before concrete is poured.
After concrete is poured, a designated curing period is required to allow the concrete to achieve sufficient strength before any subsequent loads are applied or formwork is removed.
Concrete must be poured and sufficiently cured before formwork can be safely removed to avoid collapse or damage to the beam.

Columns and walls provide the vertical support and structural anchorage for perimeter beams. The beam reinforcement cannot be placed and tied until the vertical reinforcement of columns/walls is completed as beams bear on or are monolithic with these vertical elements.
The bottom formwork (soffit) and side forms for the beam must be erected before reinforcement bars can be placed inside the formwork. Reinforcement is laid on the formwork and then tied in position.

Adequate shoring and falsework must be installed to support the weight of the wet concrete, formwork, and reinforcement before any reinforcement work proceeds. Safety and structural stability during construction depend on this.

All reinforcement bars must be fully placed, tied, and inspected before concrete can be poured. Concrete covers and encases the steel reinforcement; thus pouring must follow completion of reinforcement.

successor: Electrical and Mechanical Conduit Installation in Beam
rationale: Although MEP conduits embedded in the beam are often placed after reinforcement is tied but before concrete pour, this is a soft preference as conduits can also be placed concurrently with some minor rebar work. However, typically minimum rebar clearance is checked after full reinforcement for MEP routing.
The perimeter beams must be erected and in place before fireproofing can be applied to them.
All steel connections must be fully secured before fireproofing is applied to ensure structural stability and to avoid damaging the fireproofing material during connection work.
Fireproofing must be completed before enclosing the perimeter beams with exterior cladding, as the cladding would block access to apply the fireproofing material.
It is easier to install ceilings after fireproofing is done to avoid rework or damage, though in some sequences ceilings could be partially installed beforehand.

successor: Final Inspection of Structural Fire Protection
rationale: The fireproofing application must be complete and cured before it can be inspected for compliance with fire codes.
The column must be erected and in place before any beam-to-column connection can be made, as the column serves as the vertical structural support that the beam connects to.

predecessor: Beam Delivery and Lifting to Position
rationale: The perimeter beam must be lifted and positioned adjacent to the column before the physical connection (bolting or welding) between beam and column can be executed.

successor: Connection Inspection and Bolt Torqueing/Welding Quality Check
rationale: After the connection is made, it must be inspected and tightened (bolts) or tested (welds) to verify structural integrity before any further loading or subsequent steel erection proceeds.

successor: Decking / Slab Placement on Connected Beams
rationale: Metal decking or concrete slab formwork is placed on top of the beams only after the beams are securely connected to columns at both ends, providing the necessary support structure.

While sequential bay erection is common for crane efficiency and stability, adjacent beams could theoretically be erected concurrently if multiple cranes and crews are available; however, completing one connection before moving to the next bay is standard practice to ensure progressive structural stability.
The substrate (e.g., sheathing, framing, or existing wall surface) must be clean, dry, and sound before membrane flashing can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and performance.
Membrane flashing is typically integrated with or applied over the water-resistive barrier to manage water drainage and continuity at penetrations and transitions.
Membrane flashing at rough openings must be installed before windows or doors are set to provide proper water management behind and beneath the units.

All membrane flashing components (e.g., at windows, doors, roof-to-wall intersections) must be fully installed and integrated before the final cladding or siding is applied to ensure a continuous drainage plane and avoid trapping moisture.
Step flashing or base flashing at roof-to-wall intersections must be completed before the roofing underlayment and finished roofing are installed to create a watertight seal at the transition.

The weather-resistive barrier (WRB) is installed directly over the structural sheathing (e.g., OSB or plywood) to provide a drainage plane and air barrier; sheathing must be in place to provide a continuous substrate for the WRB.
Rough framing (walls, roof, etc.) must be fully erected and braced so that sheathing can be attached and the WRB applied in a continuous, weathertight manner.
Window and door frames are typically installed, flashed, and sealed before the WRB is applied so that the WRB can lap over the flanges and integrated flashing, creating a continuous waterproof seal.

successor: Install Exterior Cladding (Siding, Brick, Stucco, etc.)
rationale: The WRB serves as the water-resistive layer behind the exterior cladding; cladding is installed over the WRB to protect it from UV and physical damage and to provide the finished facade.

While exterior insulation can be installed over the WRB (with appropriate drainage), some sequences may place insulation before the WRB in certain wall assemblies; however, the most common best practice is to install WRB first then insulation or directly to cladding.
Excavation must be completed to expose the below-grade surfaces that require waterproofing.
The subgrade must be prepared and leveled to provide a proper working surface for waterproofing installation.
Concrete foundation walls must be poured, set, and cured before waterproofing can be applied to their exterior surfaces.

successor: Installation of Drainage Board / Protection Board
rationale: Drainage board or protection board is installed directly over the waterproofing membrane to protect it and facilitate water drainage.
Backfilling must only occur after waterproofing is fully installed and cured to avoid damaging the membrane or disrupting the application.
The air and vapor barrier is typically installed on the exterior side of the structural framing (e.g., stud walls). The framing must be in place to provide a substrate for the barrier material.
Sheathing (such as plywood or OSB) is usually installed over the framing and provides the continuous surface onto which the air and vapor barrier is applied.
The air and vapor barrier must be in place as a weather-resistant layer before exterior cladding or siding can be installed over it.
Flashing around window and door openings is integrated with the air and vapor barrier to ensure continuous water and air sealing, so the barrier must be installed first to lap properly.

If exterior insulation is specified, it is typically installed over the air and vapor barrier to avoid trapping moisture; however, this order may vary by design, so it is a strong preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
A structural roof deck or substrate (e.g., concrete, plywood, or metal) must be in place to provide a stable surface for the fluid-applied membrane to bond to.
Any thermal insulation layers must be installed before the membrane is applied so that the membrane can be placed over the insulation per the roofing assembly design.
The substrate must be clean, dry, free of contaminants, and properly primed to ensure adequate adhesion of the fluid-applied membrane.
A protective top coat, ballast, or traffic coating must be applied after the fluid-applied membrane has cured to protect the membrane from UV, physical damage, and foot traffic.
Water testing or flood testing of the membrane is often performed after full cure to verify watertightness before covering the membrane with subsequent layers.
The vault structural frame requires a stable foundation to support its load, making foundation completion a physical necessity before any frame erection can begin.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the required levels and compaction before foundation work and subsequent frame construction can proceed.
The structural frame must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the vault enclosure, roof cladding, or waterproofing membrane.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in within the vault space cannot commence until the structural frame is erected, as the frame defines the spatial boundaries and provides mounting points for services.
Any masonry infill panels or brickwork between frame members must wait until the main structural frame is complete and stable to ensure proper alignment and load transfer.
The vault's structural shell must be erected first to provide the substrate onto which the soffit/intrados finish is applied. Without the underlying vault structure, there is no surface to finish.
Formwork or falsework supporting the vault must be in place before the soffit finish is applied, as the soffit is the underside surface that follows the formwork shape.

Waterproofing (if required) is typically applied over the completed soffit/intrados surface to protect the vault interior from moisture ingress; the soffit finish must be cured and sound before membrane application.
Final decorative finishes or plaster are applied onto the completed soffit/intrados surface; the soffit must be stable and clean before finish work begins.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the vault void should ideally follow soffit completion to avoid damaging the finished surface; however, coordination may allow concurrent work, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.

The vault extrados waterproofing and backing layer can only be applied after the vault's structural formwork, reinforcement, and concrete have been completed and cured, as it is a finish/protective layer applied to the outer surface of the vault shell.

The extrados waterproofing and backing must be fully installed and cured before any backfill or earth cover is placed against the vault, to protect the waterproof membrane from damage during backfilling operations.

While intrados finishes can technically proceed independently, it is preferable to complete extrados waterproofing first to avoid weather exposure damaging interior work if the vault is not yet sealed from above.
After the extrades backing is installed, it must be inspected and tested (e.g., flood test, electrical continuity test) to verify waterproof integrity before being covered.

The base slab and subgrade preparation are necessary predecessors to any vault construction, though the extrades backing specifically depends on the vault structure itself rather than the base slab directly.
The vault foundation or base slab must be completed before the vault web/panel can be erected, as the web/panel requires a stable, level base to bear upon and be anchored to.
Reinforcement steel for the vault walls must be fixed and in place before the vault web/panel formwork is installed and concrete is poured.
The vault web/panel (walls) must be completed before the roof or top slab can be constructed, as the top slab sits on and is supported by the walls.
Waterproofing membranes or coatings can only be applied after the vault web/panel concrete has cured and the surface is prepared.
Backfilling operations around the vault must wait until the vault web/panel is complete and waterproofed, to avoid damaging the structure and to ensure proper load transfer.
The vault springing point/haunch requires a stable foundation to bear the lateral and vertical loads transferred from the vault, so foundations must be completed first.

The vault springing point/haunch is typically positioned at the top of vertical supports (columns or walls) that carry the vault's thrust; these supports must be built before the springing point can be installed.
Temporary scaffolding or centering must be erected to support the haunch and vault during construction before the springing point can be placed.
The vault ribs or arches spring from the haunch/springing point, so the springing point must be in place to serve as the launch point for the ribs.
The vault web (the infill between ribs) rests on or between the ribs that originate at the springing point; therefore the springing point must be complete before vault web construction can proceed.

The keystone is the final piece placed at the apex of a vault; the supporting arch structure must be fully erected (including voussoirs and centering) before the keystone can be inserted to lock the arch together.
Temporary formwork (centering) must be in place to support the arch during construction; the keystone is placed last on this support system.
All other arch stones (voussoirs) must be positioned symmetrically from the springing points upward before the keystone can be inserted at the crown.
The temporary centering can only be removed after the keystone is in place and the arch is fully self-supporting; removing it earlier would cause collapse.
The vault structure must be completed (with keystone locked in) before waterproofing membranes and backfill material can be applied to the extrados of the vault.

successor: Vault Tie Rod / Lateral Restraint Installation
rationale: The vault masonry must be partially or fully constructed before tie rods can be installed, as tie rods provide lateral restraint to the completed masonry vault and are anchored into or through the masonry.

successor: Vault Tie Rod / Lateral Restraint Installation
rationale: The abutments or bearing walls that resist the thrust from the vault must be in place to provide the end anchorage and structural support for the tie rods.

predecessor: Vault Tie Rod / Lateral Restraint Installation
successor: Vault Arch Backfilling or Crown Finishing
rationale: Tie rods must be tensioned and in place before backfilling or finishing above the vault crown to ensure lateral forces are properly restrained during subsequent load applications.

predecessor: Vault Tie Rod / Lateral Restraint Installation
successor: Removal of Temporary Formwork or Centering
rationale: Permanent lateral restraint systems (tie rods) must be installed and active before temporary centering is removed, to prevent the vault from spreading or collapsing under its own thrust.

predecessor: Vault Tie Rod / Lateral Restraint Installation
rationale: It is preferred to install and tension tie rods before final plastering or surface finishing to conceal or integrate the tie rod anchorages cleanly, though not physically required.
The gantry/tower provides the lifting and positioning capability needed to place the groin/intersection rib components at height.
The groin/intersection rib is the diagonal rib that crosses and connects the main arch ribs at the intersection point; the main arch ribs must be in place to define the intersection location.

predecessor: Complete Foundation / Abutment Work on both sides
rationale: The arch ribs (including groin/intersection ribs) bear on the foundations/abutments; these must be finished and cured to support the loads.

successor: Install Secondary Bracing / Cross Beams at Intersection
rationale: Cross beams and secondary bracing at the intersection node depend on the groin rib being in its final position to connect to it.

successor: Erect Vault / Roof Decking (if rib is part of vaulted structure)
rationale: The groin/intersection rib acts as a primary structural support for the vault or roof cladding; decking cannot be placed until the supporting rib is installed.
Columns and walls provide the vertical support structure that the vault formwork rests upon; they must be built first to carry the loads.
Foundations must be completed to provide a stable base for columns/walls that support the vault, ensuring structural integrity.
Formwork/centering provides the mold and temporary support structure; rebar must be placed inside the formwork before concrete can be poured.
The formwork/centering must be fully erected and stable before concrete is poured, as it defines the shape and supports the wet concrete.
After concrete is poured and cured, the formwork/centering can be stripped; this is the final step in the vault construction sequence.
The structural steel framing must be erected to provide the supporting structure and load-bearing framework onto which the Vault Skylight / Oculus can be mounted.
The roof deck must be installed to create the opening and substrate into which the skylight/oculus is integrated.
The skylight/oculus must be fully installed and sealed before the continuous waterproofing membrane can be applied around it to ensure a watertight integration and prevent leaks.

Interior finishes around the oculus area are typically completed after the skylight is installed to ensure proper alignment, trim work, and aesthetic continuity, though some finishes could proceed in parallel with care.
The vault skylight frame and structure must be in place before the glass/glazing panels can be installed into the oculus opening.

The vault structure must be fully built and enclosed before acoustic treatment can be installed, as acoustic panels, baffles, or sound-absorbing materials are typically mounted onto or within the finished structural shell.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins (conduit, ductwork, piping) must be completed before acoustic treatment is applied, because these services run within walls and ceilings that will be covered by acoustic finishes. Installing them after acoustic treatment would damage or require removal of the installed acoustic materials.

Acoustic treatment installation must precede final interior finishes such as painting and decorative wall/ceiling coverings, because acoustic panels or treatments are part of the finished surface layer and any painting or final coating should be done after the acoustic substrate is in place to ensure a seamless appearance.

Acoustic treatment must be fully installed before acoustic testing and commissioning can be performed, as the tests are intended to verify that the installed acoustic system meets design specifications and performance criteria.

successor: Installation of Sensitive Equipment (e.g., Recording, Monitoring)
rationale: It is strongly preferred (soft constraint) to install acoustic treatment before bringing in sensitive electronic equipment, because the construction dust and debris from acoustic work could damage sensitive equipment. However, in some cases equipment could be protected and installed earlier.
The vault surface must be properly prepared (clean, leveled, primed) before any mosaic or decorative finish can be applied to ensure adhesion and a smooth final surface.
The structural vault must be fully constructed and cured before decorative finishes are applied, as the finish is non-structural and would be damaged if structural work occurred afterward.
Any waterproofing or membrane layers must be installed before decorative finishes, as these protect the substrate and must be continuous behind the finish layer.
A protective sealant or coating must be applied after the mosaic/decorative finish is complete to protect the finish from moisture, staining, and wear.
Final inspection and any touch-up work typically occur after the decorative finish is installed, though this is a quality-control preference rather than a physical necessity.

Reinforcement bars (rebar) must be placed and tied before formwork assembly, as the formwork is erected around and over the reinforcement cage. Attempting to place rebar after formwork is assembled would be extremely difficult or impossible, and would not allow proper cover and positioning.

Formwork provides the mold into which concrete is poured. Therefore, the formwork structure must be fully assembled, aligned, and secured before any concrete can be placed. Pouring concrete without formwork in place would result in uncontrolled flow and loss of shape.

After the concrete is poured into the formwork and has gained sufficient strength, the formwork can be stripped (removed). The curing and striking process inherently follows formwork assembly and concrete pouring.

Formwork for vault construction typically requires a supporting falsework or scaffolding system to hold the form panels at the correct elevation and curvature. This support structure must be erected first to provide a stable platform and support for the formwork assembly.

Accurate survey and setting out of the vault geometry, alignment, and levels must be completed before formwork assembly begins, to ensure the formwork is positioned correctly according to design specifications and to achieve the required vault curvature.
The vault foundation must be prepared and set to provide a stable base for the rib placement, as ribs require a solid foundation to anchor into.
Temporary falsework or centering must be installed to support the ribs during placement before the vault is self-supporting.
Ribs must be placed and secured first to create the structural framework before infill panels can be installed between them.
Rib placement defines the structural skeleton; subsequent concrete pouring or cladding can only occur after the ribs are in position.
Ribs must be fully placed, connected, and load-bearing before temporary supports can be safely dismantled.
Formwork must be installed and secured before concrete can be poured into it to shape the vault.
Steel reinforcement bars must be positioned within the formwork prior to concrete casting to provide structural integrity to the vault.
The supporting foundation or substructure must be fully cured and load-bearing ready before the vault concrete can be cast on top.
Freshly cast concrete must undergo a controlled curing process to achieve design strength before any subsequent loads or finishing work can be applied.
Concrete must be cast and sufficiently cured before formwork can be safely stripped without damaging the vault structure.

The vault masonry must be laid on a stable foundation and footings that can bear the load; without proper foundation preparation, the vault structure would lack structural support and could settle or collapse.

Vault masonry requires a temporary supporting structure (centering or formwork) to shape the arch/curvature of the vault and support the masonry until the mortar sets and the vault becomes self-supporting.
Workers need safe access at height to lay masonry for the vault; scaffolding must be erected before masonry work can begin at the vault elevation.
The masonry mortar and vault structure must be fully set and hardened before the temporary centering/formwork can be safely removed; removing centering prematurely could cause the vault to collapse.

Waterproofing membranes, sealants, and final finishes (plaster, pointing) can only be applied after the vault masonry is complete and the mortar has cured, as they are surface treatments over the finished masonry.
Tie rods are installed through the formwork to hold the form panels together and resist concrete pressure; thus formwork must be assembled first.
Tie rods must be in place to secure and brace the formwork before concrete can be poured, as they resist the lateral pressure exerted by wet concrete.
Rebar and reinforcement mesh are typically placed within the formwork before tie rods are tightened, allowing the tie rods to pass through and secure both the formwork and reinforcement cage.
Tie rods must be removed (cut or released) before formwork panels can be stripped away from the hardened concrete structure.
The vault geometry must be surveyed and marked out first to ensure the formwork and tie rod positions align with the designed arch curvature and dimensions.

Concrete must be fully cured before waterproofing can be applied, as waterproofing membranes require a dry, stable surface to bond properly and to avoid moisture entrapment that could cause delamination or blistering.
The concrete surface must be cleaned of debris, dust, and laitance, and any rough spots smoothed prior to waterproofing to ensure proper adhesion and uniform coverage of the waterproofing membrane.

successor: Vault Construction - Protection Layer / Drainage Board Installation
rationale: A protection layer or drainage board must be placed over the cured waterproofing membrane to shield it from mechanical damage during subsequent backfilling or construction activities, and to facilitate water drainage away from the vault.

Backfilling around the vault can only proceed after waterproofing is fully applied and cured, as the waterproofing system must be intact to prevent groundwater ingress; backfilling without waterproofing would expose the structure to moisture damage.

successor: Vault Construction - Quality Control / Leak Testing
rationale: Leak testing or quality inspection of the waterproofing system must be performed after application to verify continuity and adhesion before any covering or backfilling operations commence, ensuring the waterproofing is defect-free.
The excavation and site preparation must be completed before any vault construction can begin, as it provides the stable substrate and workspace necessary for the insulation and finish layup.
The foundation and base slab must be fully cured and in place before insulation and finish layup can be applied, as the layup is installed on top of the slab.

The structural frame or shell of the vault must be erected before interior insulation and finish layers can be installed, as the finishes are applied to the interior surfaces of the completed structure.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work typically follows the insulation and finish layup because these services are installed within or through the finished surfaces, and the insulation must be in place to enclose them.

Final sealing and waterproofing inspection can only occur after the insulation and finish layup is complete, as the layup forms part of the vapor barrier and finish system that must be verified for integrity.

The structural shell of the vault must be fully constructed and cured before any decorative finishing (such as plastering, painting, or ornamental work) can begin, as the finishing is applied onto the completed structural surface.
Waterproofing and membrane layers must be installed over the structural shell before decorative finishes are applied, to protect the finishes from moisture damage and ensure durability.

Decorative finishing (e.g., ornamental plaster, paint, or cladding) must be completed before lighting fixtures are installed, so that fixtures can be mounted on or integrated into the finished surface without damaging the decorative work.

Scaffolding and temporary access structures should remain in place to support workers during decorative finishing, and can only be dismantled after the finishing is complete to avoid rework or damage.

While not a strict physical necessity, it is standard practice to complete all decorative finishes before the final inspection and commissioning of the vault interior, to present a complete and finished product for review.
The vault must be excavated to expose the walls before any drainage or weep system can be installed against or within the vault structure.
The concrete slab or base must be poured and cured to provide a stable base against which the drainage system can be installed and to ensure proper water collection and drainage flow.
Backfilling must occur after the drainage/weep system is installed to prevent damage to the drainage components and ensure the system functions correctly for water evacuation.
Waterproofing membrane is typically applied over or integrated with the drainage/weep system to protect the vault structure from moisture infiltration, so the drainage system must be in place first.
Interior finishes should ideally be completed after drainage is installed to avoid moisture damage to finishes, but some finishing work could proceed in parallel if waterproofing is already in place.
The vault structure must be built first to provide the framework onto which the ribbing is applied.
Ribbing must be in place before any finishing layers (such as plaster, cladding, or decorative covering) can be applied to the vault.
Temporary support structures (falsework or centering) must be erected to support the vault ribs during construction before ribbing can begin.
The ribbing must be completed and structurally self-supporting before temporary falsework can be safely removed.
All rib components (stone, timber, or metal segments) must be cut, shaped, and prepared prior to assembly and installation on the vault.
The vault foundation must be fully cured and load-bearing before web panels can be installed, as the panels rely on the foundation for structural support.
The steel frame provides the structural skeleton to which the web panels are attached; panels cannot be mounted without the frame in place.
Web panels form the underlying structural support and substrate for roof cladding; cladding cannot be installed until the web panels are secured.
Weatherproofing membranes and sealants are applied over the installed web panels to ensure water tightness; this can only proceed after panels are in place.

successor: Electrical and Mechanical Rough-In within Vault
rationale: While some rough-in work can be done before panels are installed, final routing and fixing of conduits and ducts to the web panels is most efficiently completed after the panels are mounted.
The vault springing points must be supported on stable foundations that can bear the lateral thrust and vertical loads transmitted by the vault.

Vault springing points are typically located at the top of piers or columns; these supporting vertical elements must be fully built and cured to provide the necessary support before springing points can be set.
The centering or formwork that defines the vault's curvature must be positioned and aligned to the correct springing level before the springing points can be established.
Vault ribs or arches emanate from the springing points; the springing points must be fixed to provide the exact start positions for rib masonry or construction.
The vault web or shell surface is constructed between the springing points and the crown; the springing points define the lower boundary and must be complete before infill can proceed.

The vault haunch is part of the vault structure and can only be formed or installed after the main vault construction is underway or complete, as it provides transitional support between the vault and its supporting elements.

Finishing work on the vault (such as plastering or decorative treatments) must follow after the haunch is in place, as the haunch is a structural component that supports the vault's base and must be completed before surface finishes are applied.

The haunch transfers lateral thrust from the vault to the abutments or buttresses; therefore, the haunch must be in place before the final loading and completion of the supporting abutment or buttress system.
Temporary formwork and falsework must be erected to support the vault and haunch during construction before the haunch itself can be cast or assembled.

successor: Roof or Floor Loading Above Vault
rationale: The vault haunch must be fully cured and structurally capable before any superimposed loads from roofs or floors above the vault can be applied.
The vault crown is the topmost stone or concrete segment of an arch or vault; formwork must be erected first to provide the necessary support and shape for the crown to be placed.

The vault crown sits at the apex of the arch; the lower voussoirs and haunch sections must be installed progressively from the springing points upward before the keystone or crown can be inserted to complete the arch.
The crown is the final structural element that locks the arch; temporary formwork cannot be safely removed until the crown is in place and the arch is self-supporting.

Waterproofing is typically applied over the completed vault structure to protect against moisture; although it is possible to waterproof in stages, it is standard practice to complete the vault structure including the crown before final waterproofing.
Backfilling over a vault can only commence once the crown is fully placed and cured, as the backfill loads the vault structure; placing backfill before the crown would risk collapse or misalignment.
The vault must be excavated and structurally supported before any penetrations or openings can be created through its walls or slab.
The vault walls and slab must be poured and sufficiently cured to achieve structural strength before core drilling or cutting openings through them.
All existing underground utilities must be located and marked before creating any penetrations to avoid utility strikes and ensure safe excavation around the vault.
All penetrations and openings must be completed before waterproofing is applied, so that waterproofing can seal around the finished openings and prevent leaks.

successor: Electrical and Mechanical Rough-In within Vault
rationale: The penetration holes must be cut and available before any conduit, piping, or cabling can be routed through them into the vault.
The vault edge/wall connections are embedded or cast into the vault wall/abutment concrete, so the concrete must be placed first to provide the substrate for the connection elements.
The connections between the vault edge and walls must be completed to secure and integrate the vault structure before the roof/slab concrete is placed above.
Waterproofing is applied after the vault edge/wall connections are finished to ensure a continuous, sealed surface without gaps at connection points.
Formwork must be installed and aligned to define the vault wall geometry before connection elements can be positioned and secured.
Reinforcement steel must be in place to tie into and anchor the vault edge/wall connection hardware, ensuring structural continuity.
The vault structure requires a stable and completed foundation and substructure to bear its load and provide a level base for erection.
Reinforcement must be placed and tied in the supporting elements before the vault components can be erected onto them.
Formwork for beams, columns, or walls that support the vault must be complete before vault erection can begin.
The vault must be fully assembled (including formwork and reinforcement) before concrete can be placed and cured.
Waterproofing and finishing works can only commence after the vault structure is fully erected and stable.

The vault concrete must be fully poured and cured before any waterproofing can be applied, as waterproofing membranes require a stable, dry, and cured concrete substrate to bond properly and prevent adhesion failure or trapped moisture.
The vault surfaces must be cleaned, smoothed, and free of debris, laitance, or protrusions before waterproofing installation to ensure proper adhesion and continuity of the waterproofing system.

successor: Vault Construction - Protection Layer / Drainage Board Installation
rationale: Drainage boards and protection layers are installed directly over the finished waterproofing membrane to protect it from damage during backfilling and to provide a drainage path; they cannot be placed before the waterproofing is complete.

Backfilling against the vault walls can only commence after the waterproofing system and its protective/drainage layers are fully installed and inspected, to avoid damaging the waterproofing membrane during soil placement and compaction.

While a post-waterproofing leak test is strongly recommended to verify the integrity of the installation before covering, it is a quality control preference rather than a physical necessity; however, it is typically required by specification to confirm watertightness before backfilling.
The vault structure and waterstop must be fully installed and cured before insulation can be applied and backfill can commence, as the insulation is placed against the completed vault walls.

Waterproofing must be applied to the vault exterior before installing insulation and backfilling, as the insulation and backfill would permanently cover and prevent access to the waterproofing membrane.

After insulation is placed and initial backfill is completed, compaction testing must be performed to verify that the backfill meets specified density requirements before further construction proceeds.

Final grading and surface restoration typically follows backfill operations, though this is often a soft preference as grading can be staged and may not require backfill to be fully complete everywhere.

Utility connections that penetrate the vault wall must be completed before insulation and backfill, as those connections would be buried and inaccessible after backfill. However, overhead or trenchless utility connections might follow.
The window frame provides the structural support and rough opening into which the operable window is installed. Without the frame in place, there is nothing to securely mount the operable window.
The rough opening (including header, sill, and jambs) must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the operable window can be fitted and secured.
Weather-resistant barriers, sill pans, and flashing must be installed around the rough opening to prevent water intrusion before the operable window is placed.
Once the operable window is installed, all perimeter gaps must be sealed with caulk or backer rod and the exterior trim must be applied to ensure an airtight and watertight enclosure.
Interior drywall, trim, and paint around the window are typically completed after the window is installed, though this is a logical sequencing preference rather than a physical requirement.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and dimensions for the French door unit to be installed.
Weatherproofing membranes (house wrap, flashing) must be applied around the rough opening to protect against moisture infiltration before the door is set in place.
Once the door is installed, gaps between the door frame and rough opening must be insulated and sealed to prevent air and water leakage.

Interior trim and casing around the French door is typically installed after the door is hung and functioning to provide a finished appearance, but this is a preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
Exterior siding or finish material must be installed around the French door after the door is in place to ensure proper integration, flashing, and weatherproofing.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before a bi-fold door can be installed.
The surrounding walls must be framed to create the opening and provide structural support for the door frame.
Trim and casing around the door are installed after the door is mounted to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance.

While painting can be done before door installation, it is often preferred to install the door first so that paint can be touched up around the trim, or alternatively the door can be painted off-site beforehand.
Flooring is typically installed after the door to ensure proper clearance and to allow the door to swing or slide freely above the finished floor surface.
The rough opening must be framed, sized, and prepared before a pivot door can be installed, as the door leaf and frame require a structurally sound and correctly dimensioned opening.

predecessor: Floor Finishing (e.g., Tiling, Polishing, Floor Coverings)
rationale: Pivot doors have a bottom pivot that is often mounted into the finished floor, and the floor finish must be in place to set the correct height and bearing surface for the pivot mechanism.
The pivot door leaf must be hung and properly aligned in its frame before handles, locks, and closing mechanisms can be fitted and adjusted to function correctly.
Once the pivot door is installed and operational, gaps around the frame can be sealed with weatherstripping or caulk, and any finishing trim can be applied to complete the assembly.
The rough opening frame (studs, header, and sill) must be built to provide the structural support and correct dimensions for the acoustic door to be installed.
The door frame (including jambs and stops) must be installed and properly aligned before the acoustic door leaf can be hung.
Drop seals or automatic door bottoms at the threshold are often installed or prepared before the door is hung to ensure proper acoustic sealing once the door is in place.
Hardware such as hinges, handles, locks, and closers can only be mounted after the acoustic door leaf is positioned and hung in its frame.
Final acoustic performance testing (e.g., STC rating verification) can only be performed once the door is fully installed, sealed, and all components are in place.
Door frames are installed within wall openings; walls must be built first to define the rough opening and provide structural support for the frame.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed and sized correctly before the door frame can be positioned and secured within it.
The floor slab or subfloor provides the finished surface level from which the door frame height and plumbness are referenced; it must be in place for accurate installation.
Door leaves (doors) are hung onto the installed door frame; the frame and lining must be fixed in place and plumb before the door can be attached to its hinges.
Hardware such as locks, handles, and strike plates are mounted onto the door and frame; the frame must be installed first to mark and drill the correct positions.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed, sized, and prepared (including headers, sills, and cripple studs) before the window frame and sash can be installed into the opening.
The weather-resistive barrier (e.g., house wrap) must be installed over the sheathing before window installation to ensure proper flashing integration and water tightness.
After the window frame and sash are set in place, flashing tapes and sealants must be applied around the perimeter to prevent water intrusion.
The window unit must be installed and sealed before interior wall insulation and drywall can be installed up to and around the window opening.
Exterior siding or cladding is installed after the window is in place so that siding can be fitted around the window frame and properly flashed.
Door frames must be installed and properly aligned before hinges can be attached to the frame and door leaf.
Walls must be framed and drywalled to provide the structural support for door frames and hinges.
The door leaf must be hung on hinges before locks, handles, and other hardware can be installed on it.
Final paint touch-ups are often done after hardware installation to cover any scratches or marks, though painting can also be completed beforehand if hardware is masked.
All door hardware must be fully installed and functional before the final walkthrough and inspection can verify proper operation, security, and accessibility.
The window frame must be installed first so that the sill and surround can be fitted around it, ensuring proper alignment and sealing.
The rough opening for the window must be framed and prepared before the window sill and surround can be installed.
Wall sheathing provides the structural backing and weather-resistant surface that the window sill and surround need to be mounted against.
The window sill and surround must be in place before interior finishes such as drywall, plaster, or paint are applied around the window opening to achieve clean edges and proper trim integration.
The window sill and surround should be installed before exterior cladding or siding is applied to ensure proper flashing, weatherproofing, and a finished appearance around the window.
The window frame must be installed first to provide the structural mounting surface for catches, stays, and hinges.
The glass must be glazed into the window frame before hardware such as stays and hinges can be attached, as the hardware often mounts to both the frame and the sash holding the glass.
Hardware must be fully installed before the window's opening, closing, and locking mechanisms can be functionally tested.
Weather seals and gaskets should be installed after hinges and stays are in place to ensure proper alignment and compression around the closed window.
Interior trim work is typically done after hardware installation to allow access for adjustment, though trim could be pre-fitted with careful sequencing.
The supporting wall must be constructed up to the height of the opening to provide bearing surfaces for the lintel ends.
The lintel must be installed to carry the load of the wall above the opening before that upper wall section can be built.
If the lintel is cast in place, formwork must be erected and secured before concrete placement can begin.
The opening structure including the lintel must be complete and cured before the door or window frame can be fitted into the opening.

Finishing work above the opening is typically done after the lintel is in place, though this is a preferred sequencing to avoid rework rather than a strict physical necessity if access can be arranged otherwise.
Window frames must be installed to provide a mounting structure for window shading and sunscreen systems.
Glass panels must be in place before shading devices can be attached or mounted to the window assembly.
The building's structural frame must be complete to support the loads transferred from shading devices and to provide secure attachment points.
It is preferable to complete shading installation before interior finishes around windows to avoid damage or rework, but some interior work can proceed if access is maintained.
Shading devices are often integrated with or mounted onto the exterior cladding system, so they must be installed before the façade is fully sealed and finished.
The rough opening must be framed, sized, and prepared to receive windows; windows cannot be installed without a properly sized structural opening.
Weather-resistant barrier and flashing must be applied around the opening before window installation to prevent water infiltration behind the window frame.
Exterior wall sheathing (e.g., plywood or OSB) must be in place to provide structural support and a mounting surface for window flanges.
After the window is physically set in the opening, the gaps around the frame must be insulated and sealed with caulk or spray foam to ensure thermal efficiency and air/water tightness.
Interior drywall installation and finishing around the window area must occur after the window is in place so that the window frame is accessible for trim and the drywall can be cut neatly to fit.
Doors require framed openings (rough openings) with properly sized headers and supports; without the wall frame, there is no structure to mount the door into.
The door frame or jamb must be installed and properly aligned before hanging the door slab to ensure correct fit and operation.
Electrical wiring, outlets, switches, and ductwork that pass near or through door openings must be roughed in before door frames are installed to avoid interference and rework.
The door slab must be hung in the frame before hardware such as locks, handles, hinges (or final hinge adjustment) and strike plates can be installed onto it.

While doors are often installed before final painting and trim for a seamless finish, this is a soft preference in some sequences where doors can be installed after painting in certain modular approaches; however, conventional sequencing installs doors first to allow casing/trim to be fitted tightly against the door frame.
Structural framing must be complete to provide a stable substrate for weather sealing materials such as membranes, sealants, or cladding.
The roof deck provides the base upon which weather sealing (roofing membrane, flashing) is applied; without the deck there is no surface to seal.
Exterior wall sheathing (e.g., plywood or OSB) must be installed to create a continuous surface for the weather-resistant barrier and sealant application.
Windows and doors must be in place so that weather sealing can integrate with their frames, flashing, and perimeter seals to prevent water intrusion.
Weather sealing (e.g., weather-resistant barrier, flashing, sealants) must be completed before cladding is installed to provide a continuous waterproof layer behind the finished exterior finish.

While interior work can technically begin in parallel, best practice recommends completing weather sealing first to avoid moisture damage to drywall if leaks occur; this is a soft preference for quality assurance.

MEP rough-in can be done before weather sealing, but final inspection is often sequenced after weather sealing to ensure envelope integrity before enclosing interiors; this is a soft preference based on project phasing.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth and shape before any low sill concrete or masonry can be placed, as the sill sits directly on the foundation soils or prepared subgrade.
The soil or rock subgrade must be leveled, compacted, and approved to provide uniform bearing support for the low sill structure, preventing differential settlement.
Waterproofing is applied to the finished low sill concrete/masonry surfaces to protect against moisture ingress; the sill structure must be fully cured and clean before membrane installation.
Backfill material can only be placed against the low sill after the structure is fully cured and has achieved sufficient strength to resist lateral earth pressures.

Mechanical or structural components (e.g., gate guides, stop logs, machinery) are anchored into the low sill; the concrete or masonry must be in place, cured, and drilled/grouted before anchors are set.
Low sill flashing must be installed over the rough framing and sheathing, which provide the structural substrate and backing surface for the flashing membrane.
The rough opening for windows or doors must be framed and prepared before low sill flashing can be applied at the sill, as the flashing integrates with the opening.
Low sill flashing is applied before the window or door unit is installed, so that the flashing can lap over the sill and be integrated behind or under the unit to provide a watertight seal.
The low sill flashing must be in place before the weather-resistive barrier is taped and lapped over it, ensuring continuous drainage and waterproofing at the sill area.
Siding or exterior finishes are installed after sill flashing to cover and protect the flashing, though careful sequencing can sometimes allow later integration if prefabricated details exist.

Low sill framing (typically a wood sill plate or bottom track) must be anchored to and bear directly on top of the completed foundation or slab. The concrete must be fully cured and the foundation layout set before sill placement can begin.
Anchor bolts (or other hold‑down anchors) must be embedded in the foundation concrete so that the low sill plate can be drilled and bolted down to resist overturning and lateral forces.

While not a strict physical requirement, waterproofing the foundation wall below grade should be completed before the sill is placed to avoid later access difficulties and to prevent moisture intrusion behind the sill.
Floor joists or trusses bear on or are framed into the low sill plate; the sill provides the level bearing surface and load transfer path from the floor structure to the foundation.
Exterior and interior bearing walls sit on top of the low sill plate. The sill must be anchored and leveled before wall panels are erected and fastened to it.

successor: Low Sill Cill / Sill Board Installation
rationale: The low sill cill/sill board is installed below or against the window/door frame, so the frame must be in place first to establish the correct position and alignment.

successor: Low Sill Cill / Sill Board Installation
rationale: A damp proof course or waterproof membrane must be installed beneath the sill to prevent moisture ingress from the wall or structure below.

successor: Low Sill Cill / Sill Board Installation
rationale: The supporting masonry or brickwork must be built up to the sill level height before the cill/sill board can be bedded and fixed in place.

predecessor: Low Sill Cill / Sill Board Installation
rationale: Plastering and rendering around the window/door opening must be completed after the sill is installed, as the sill provides the finished edge and prevents plaster from bridging the damp-proof course.

predecessor: Low Sill Cill / Sill Board Installation
successor: Window/Door Installation (if unit sits on sill)
rationale: If the window/door unit is designed to sit directly on or against the low sill cill, the sill must be installed first to provide the bearing surface and weather seal.
The rough opening and framing of the sill must be built first to provide the structural support and substrate onto which the drip edge or drip groove can be installed.
The window or door frame must be positioned and secured so that the low sill drip edge/groove can be properly aligned and integrated into the finished opening for water drainage.
The drip edge or groove directs water away from the sill; finishing and trim work must follow to avoid trapping moisture behind finished surfaces.
After the drip edge/groove is in place, sealant must be applied to joints and penetrations to ensure watertight performance of the sill assembly.
The drip edge/groove must be installed before the surrounding siding or cladding is applied so that the weather-resistant detailing is continuous and properly layered.
Weep holes are installed within or at the base of masonry walls; the wall structure must exist first to accommodate the weep hole placement.
Flashing is typically installed over or integrated with weep holes to direct water outward; weep holes must be in place before flashing is completed around them.

Weep holes must be accessible and unobstructed during backfilling to ensure proper drainage; backfilling after installation prevents clogging, though it is a soft preference as adjustments can be made later.
A stable, level foundation or base slab must be prepared before low sills can be installed, as the sill rests directly on the foundation.
The building's structural shell and rough framing must be in place to define the openings where low sills will be installed.
Windows and doors are typically installed onto or into the low sill, so the sill must be in place first to provide a mounting surface and weatherproofing interface.
Flashing, sealants, and weatherproof membranes are applied around the sill after installation to ensure watertightness before adjacent finishes are applied.
Interior drywall and finishes can proceed after sill installation, though it is a soft preference as they could be completed in parallel with careful sequencing.
The low sill must be installed and set in place before any waterproofing can be applied to its surfaces, as waterproofing is a coating/sealing step applied to the installed component.
Waterproofing of the low sill must be completed before the window or door frame is installed above/around it, to ensure a continuous water barrier behind and beneath the frame.
Any flashing, trim, or cover over the sill must be applied after the waterproofing membrane/caulk is in place to protect the waterproofing and direct water away.
The sill surface must be clean, dry, and properly primed for the waterproofing material to adhere correctly; preparation is a prerequisite for any coating application.

Although cladding can often proceed after waterproofing, it is a soft preference because some cladding details may overlap the sill; best practice is to have waterproofing complete first to ensure the water barrier is continuous behind cladding.
The sill plate must be installed to provide a mounting surface against which the low sill insulation can be placed and secured.
Low sill insulation is placed before the subfloor or floor sheathing goes down so that the insulation sits between the sill and the floor assembly, providing a thermal break and air seal.
The foundation walls must be fully cured and complete to provide a stable substrate where the sill plate and sill insulation can be installed.
Low sill insulation must be in place before the rough-in framing inspection, as the insulation is part of the inspected envelope components.
Termite treatment or a physical pest shield must be applied before insulating, so that the insulation does not block access or interfere with the treatment/shield.
The window frame must be installed first to establish the rough opening dimensions and provide the structural support onto which the low sill will interface.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed, squared, and prepared before the low sill component can be positioned and secured at the base of the window opening.
A sill pan or waterproof membrane must be installed at the base of the rough opening before the low sill is placed, to ensure proper drainage and prevent water ingress.
The low sill must be fully installed and secured before the window glazing or glass unit is placed, as the sill provides the bottom support and bearing surface for the window.

successor: Exterior Cladding / Siding Installation (at sill area)
rationale: Exterior cladding or siding around the window opening must follow sill installation to allow proper overlapping, sealing, and flashing integration at the sill-to-wall interface.
The wall must be framed and the rough opening prepared before the low sill component can be installed against or within the wall assembly.
Any required structural header or support above the opening must be in place before the low sill is positioned, as the sill sits below the opening and relies on the framed rough opening dimensions.

predecessor: Waterproofing / weather barrier (membrane or flashing) at sill area
rationale: A weather-resistant barrier and any pan flashing must be installed at the sill rough opening before the low sill component is placed, to ensure proper drainage and prevent water intrusion behind the sill.
The low sill forms the bottom bearing surface for the window or door frame; the fenestration unit cannot be installed until the sill is in place and leveled.

successor: Interior wall finish (drywall/plaster) at sill area
rationale: While not a strict physical dependency, it is standard sequencing to complete the sill and its interface before finishing interior wall surfaces around the opening to avoid damage to finishes during sill installation.
The window frame must be installed first to provide the structural opening and reference surface around which the reveal lining is fitted.
Glazing should generally be in place before reveal lining so that the lining can be fitted tightly against the glass edge for a neat finish and weather seal.

predecessor: Wall Waterproofing / Damp Proof Membrane (if applicable)
rationale: Any waterproofing or damp-proof membranes in the wall opening must be completed before the reveal lining is installed to avoid trapping moisture behind the lining.
Architraves and decorative trims around the window are fixed over the edges of the reveal lining, so lining must be in place first.
Final paint or decorative finish to the window reveal area is applied after the lining is installed to achieve a uniform, clean appearance.
The rough opening (framed and sized) must be prepared before any reveal lining can be installed, as the lining is fitted into the prepared opening.
Wall framing must be complete to provide the structural support and opening into which the door reveal lining is installed.
The reveal lining forms the finished surround of the opening; the door leaf or frame is installed into the lined opening.
Architraves and decorative trim are fixed around the reveal lining to cover the joint between lining and wall, so lining must be in place first.

While reveal lining is typically installed before final plastering or finishing around the opening for a neat edge, in some sequences plastering can be done before lining if carefully detailed; thus it is a soft preference for quality and ease.
The rough framing and sheathing of the wall opening must be completed first to provide the structural support and cavity into which the deep reveal sill is installed.
The rough opening dimensions and framing must be established before the deep reveal sill can be placed, as the sill sits within and is supported by the rough opening.
The deep reveal sill must be in place before the window or door frame is installed, because the frame typically rests on or is anchored to the sill.
The sill must be installed first so that air and weather sealing can be applied continuously around the perimeter of the opening, including at the sill-to-frame interface.

The deep reveal sill is typically finished with trim or cladding after installation; this is a soft preference because in some sequences the sill can be finished before being set in place, but most commonly trim follows installation for a clean fit.
The concrete soffit/lintel must be formed and poured before the finish (e.g., formwork removal, patching, coating) can be applied to the revealed surface.
Formwork must be stripped to expose the concrete soffit/lintel surface before any finishing work (grinding, patching, painting) can be performed on that surface.
Concrete must achieve sufficient curing strength before finishing operations (e.g., surface grinding, coating application) can begin to avoid damage.

successor: Install MEP Rough-In at Soffit/Lintel Area
rationale: While not always a hard physical constraint, it is preferred to complete the finish reveal before mechanical/electrical/plumbing rough-ins in the soffit area to avoid damaging finished surfaces during MEP installation.
The soffit/lintel finish must be completed (including any patching, coating, or paint) before adjacent ceiling finishes are applied to ensure a clean transition and avoid damaging the soffit finish.
The reveal (e.g., window or door reveal framing) must be installed first so that the thermal break material has a substrate to be applied to.
The thermal break must be in place before any finishing or cladding over the reveal is applied, to ensure thermal separation is complete.
The reveal thermal break should be installed prior to window or door unit installation to ensure proper thermal isolation at the interface.
The reveal angle bead is installed around the perimeter of a framed opening (such as a window or door), so the frame must be in place to provide the substrate and reference edge for bead placement.
The reveal angle bead is typically attached to the wall sheathing or substrate around the opening; the sheathing must be installed to give a stable surface for fastening the bead.

The reveal angle bead creates a clean edge and helps integrate the flashing; the WRB is applied over the sheathing and must be properly detailed around the bead to ensure water tightness, so the bead must be in place before the WRB is fully installed over the opening.

The reveal angle bead defines the crisp edge where exterior cladding (e.g., siding, stucco, brick veneer) terminates at the opening; the cladding is installed up to the bead, so the bead must be fixed first to provide the finished reveal line.

The reveal angle bead is often installed before the window or door unit is placed, serving as a guide and providing a clean reveal; the unit is then set against or within the bead to achieve proper alignment and finished appearance.
The deep reveal requires the structural formwork and reinforcement to be in place to provide a stable substrate for installation.
