The concrete structure must be poured and fully cured before deep reveals can be installed, as they integrate with or attach to the cured concrete surface.
Waterproofing must be applied over the installed deep reveal to ensure continuous watertight integrity of the building envelope.
The deep reveal forms part of the façade system and must be installed before the final cladding or finishing layers are applied.
Interior finishes such as drywall or plastering can proceed after the deep reveal is installed to ensure clean transitions and proper alignment around openings.
The surface must be properly cleaned, dried, and prepared to ensure proper adhesion of the reveal sealant.
Dust, debris, and contaminants must be removed from the reveal joint to allow the sealant to bond correctly.
Masking tape is often applied along the edges of the reveal to create clean, sharp lines before sealant application, though it is a best practice rather than a physical necessity.
After the sealant is applied, it must be tooled and smoothed to ensure proper adhesion, uniform profile, and aesthetic finish before it cures.
Masking tape must be removed shortly after sealant application and tooling, before the sealant sets, to avoid tearing or damaging the sealant bead.
The low doorway frame is installed within the wall opening. Wall framing must be completed first to define the rough opening dimensions and provide the structural support for the door frame.
The rough opening must be properly sized, leveled, and prepared before the low doorway frame can be set in place and secured.
The door frame must be installed and securely anchored before the door slab can be hung on hinges within that frame.
Casing and trim are applied around the installed frame to cover the gap between frame and wall. The frame must be in place first to establish the reference for trim.
While it is good practice to seal around the installed frame promptly, some sealing can be done later during final finishing. This is a soft preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The door frame must be in place to provide structural support and hinge mounting points for the low door leaf.
The door leaf must be hung before hardware such as handles, locks, and latch plates can be fitted to it.
Weatherstripping is typically applied after the door is hung to ensure proper fit and seal around the edges.
Floor finishing should be completed before hanging the door leaf to ensure the correct undercut clearance and avoid damaging finished flooring during installation.

predecessor: Rough Opening Preparation / Masonry or Stud Wall Construction
rationale: The supporting wall structure and rough opening must be fully built and stable before any door components can be installed.
The rough opening framing must be in place to define the dimensions and support structure for the header/lintel installation.
The header/lintel must be installed to provide structural support and a secure anchor for the door frame above the opening.
The header/lintel must be in place to ensure the wall sheathing can be properly attached and aligned over the structural opening.
If applicable, masonry or veneer work above the opening should wait until the lintel is installed to support the weight, though temporary supports may allow flexibility.
Foundation or slab must be completed to provide a stable base before any wall framing and header installation can proceed.
Clearance height markers are typically mounted on walls, columns, or structural supports, so the supporting structure must be in place first.
Clearance height markers indicate the actual clear height available, which depends on the finished ceiling or overhead structure height.
The clearance height marker must be installed so that verification of actual clearance heights can be performed against it.
Inspectors and commissioning agents typically use clearance markers to verify that overhead pathways meet minimum height requirements.
Clearance height markers are usually installed on finished surfaces to ensure secure adhesion and proper visibility, avoiding damage during finishing work.
The door frame must be installed first to provide the structural surround and proper alignment for the threshold to fit against.
The subfloor must be level, clean, and prepared to provide a stable base for the threshold to be anchored and seated properly.
Underlayment or subflooring material must be in place so the threshold has a solid foundation and can be set at the correct height relative to the finished floor.
The threshold must be installed first to define the transition point; finished flooring on both sides is then laid up to or over the threshold for a clean, flush finish.
The threshold provides the bottom clearance reference; the door slab must be hung and adjusted after the threshold is in place to ensure proper clearance, sweep seal fit, and smooth operation.
A stable foundation is required before any structural component like a doorway arch can be erected, otherwise the arch would lack proper support and could settle unevenly.
The surrounding walls or structural openings must be framed to define the opening dimensions and provide bearing points before the arch can be installed or built in place.
The main arch structure must be completed before the keystone (if applicable) is placed, as the keystone locks the arch and cannot be installed mid-construction.
Finishing work such as plastering, cladding, or trim installation around the arch can only begin after the arch structure is fully constructed and stable.
The arch opening must be fully completed before a door can be hung within the opening, as the door frame and hardware require the finished arch dimensions.
Low doorway frame anchors must be set into or against a finished foundation wall or slab, so the foundation must exist before anchors can be installed.
Door frame anchors provide the structural connection points; the door frame cannot be placed and secured until the anchors are in position.
The anchors define the location and fastening points for the doorway framing; rough framing (studs, header, jambs) around the low doorway can only proceed after anchors are installed.
If anchors are embedded in concrete, the concrete pour or grouting step must occur after anchor placement to encase them securely.
The positions for the anchors must be measured and marked on the foundation before drilling or embedding the anchors themselves.
The wall frame provides the structural opening and support needed to install a low doorway; without the frame, there is no structure to mount the doorway into.
The rough opening must be cut and framed to the correct dimensions for the low doorway before the doorway unit can be installed and secured.
After the low doorway is installed, the surrounding framing and trim work can be completed to finish the edges and integrate the doorway with the wall surface.
Drywall finishing around the doorway must occur after the doorway is installed to ensure proper taping, mudding, and seamless integration with the wall.
Door handles, hinges, locks, and other hardware can only be mounted after the doorway unit itself is securely in place.

successor: Low Doorway Head Protection Pad Installation
rationale: The doorway frame must be installed first to provide the structural support and defined opening dimensions onto which the head protection pad can be mounted or fitted.

predecessor: Low Doorway Head Protection Pad Installation
rationale: The head protection pad must be installed before applying final trim, molding, or paint around the top of the doorway so that the pad is properly integrated and the finishes can be applied flush around it.

predecessor: Low Doorway Head Protection Pad Installation
rationale: It is preferred to install the head protection pad before finishing the wall surfaces around the door header so that the pad sits cleanly behind or integrated with the wall finish, avoiding rework.

The concrete slab must be poured and finished to provide the substrate surface against which the edge formwork will be placed and secured. Edge formwork cannot be installed before the slab is poured as it would have no structural support.

Once the edge formwork is in place, it defines and contains the concrete edges during curing. The curing process cannot properly commence until the formwork is installed to shape and support the edges.
Edge formwork must be completely installed and the concrete must set before any formwork can be stripped and removed. Edge formwork installation logically precedes its removal.
The site must be excavated, leveled, and prepared to receive concrete. Edge formwork requires a prepared sub-base and proper grading to be positioned correctly.
After the edge formwork is installed and concrete is poured, the exposed concrete surface (including edges) must be finished and sealed. Edge formwork defines the edge geometry for finishing work.
The base layer must be installed to provide a substrate onto which the edge tapering detail can be applied.
The edge tapering detail must be completed before any final surface finish or coating is applied to ensure a smooth transition and proper coverage.
The substrate must be cleaned, leveled, and prepared to ensure proper adhesion and geometry for the edge tapering detail.
Edge tapering detail provides the necessary slope and transition for effective drainage before waterproofing membrane is installed.

The foundation or base surface must be prepared, leveled, and cured before any load-bearing edge profile can be positioned and installed, as the profile rests on and transfers loads to the foundation.
The primary load-bearing structural frame (columns, beams, walls) must be erected to provide the supporting framework onto which the load-bearing edge profile is attached or aligned.

The load-bearing edge profile defines the perimeter edge and provides the bearing support for cladding panels or facade elements, so cladding installation must follow after the profile is fixed in place.
Edge profiles must be installed before weatherproofing seals and joint sealants are applied, as the seals bridge the gap between the profile and adjacent building elements.

While the edge profile often supports the edge of floor or roof decks, in some construction sequences the deck can be placed first and the profile added later as a trim or edge closure; however, for load-bearing function the profile is typically installed before the deck bears on it.
The drip edge is installed along the edges of the roof deck; the roof deck must be in place to provide a mounting surface.

Drip edge is typically installed over the underlayment on the eaves (or under it on the rakes depending on method), but generally the underlayment must be present before the drip edge can be properly integrated to direct water away.
The drip edge provides a finished edge and water diversion at the roof perimeter; roofing shingles or panels are installed over and overlapping the drip edge to ensure water runs off properly.

While not a strict physical necessity, it is best practice to have the drip edge in place before enclosing the fascia and soffit to ensure the water drainage path is correctly established and concealed.

Wall sheathing provides the vertical surface adjacent to the roof edge; the drip edge often tucks behind or interfaces with the wall sheathing and building paper, requiring the sheathing to be in place first.
The edge formwork must be installed to provide the mold and support structure before the reinforcement cage can be placed into position.
The reinforcement cage must be fully positioned and tied before concrete can be poured around it to create the composite reinforced concrete edge member.
The reinforcement cage must be fabricated and assembled (cutting, bending, tying rebar) off-site or on-site before it can be lifted/placed into the edge formwork.

successor: Edge Formwork Closure / Top Form Installation
rationale: The top form or closure panel can only be installed after the reinforcement cage is in place and inspected, though this is a logical preference for access rather than a physical impossibility.

While inspection of base reinforcement may occur before cage placement, the primary inspection of the completed cage is done after placement; this ordering reflects a soft preference for sequential workflow.
The edge anchor embedment and anchorage zone must be cast into the concrete. Therefore formwork and concrete placement for the edge beam must occur first.
Post-tensioning anchors are set into fresh or hardened concrete. The concrete must be placed and sufficiently cured to develop the required strength before stressing the anchor against it.
The edge anchor must be installed and embedded in the hardened concrete to provide a fixed end against which the post-tensioning jack can react during stressing of the tendon.
After the anchor is stressed and the tendon is locked off, the duct can be grouted to protect the tendon from corrosion. Grouting must follow stressing and anchoring.

Once the anchor has been stressed and the tendon locked, the anchor pocket (recess) must be filled with non-shrink grout or mortar and waterproofed to protect the anchor from corrosion and to complete the permanent works.
The edge formwork is installed after the main slab formwork is in place, as the edge formwork connects to and is supported by the main slab forms.

While reinforcement is typically placed before edge forms are fully closed, some partial edge formwork may be installed first to define the slab perimeter and support rebar placement, so this is a soft preference.
Edge formwork must be fully installed, aligned, and secured before concrete is poured to contain the concrete at the slab perimeter and achieve the correct edge profile.
The edge formwork defines the slab boundary and must be in place before concrete finishing operations can proceed at the edges.

predecessor: Surveying and Layout of Slab Edges
rationale: Accurate surveying and marking of slab edge lines must be completed first to position the edge formwork correctly to the required dimensions and alignment.
Formwork provides the mold and support structure into which edge reinforcement bars are placed; the formwork must be in position before reinforcement can be laid.
Reinforcement bars must be cut, bent, and prepared to the required dimensions before they can be placed and tied at the edge locations.
The positions for edge reinforcement must be marked on the formwork or structural slab to ensure accurate placement and cover.
Edge reinforcement must be fully placed, tied, and inspected before concrete can be poured, as the reinforcement is embedded within the concrete.
After placing edge reinforcement, a quality inspection must be performed to verify bar spacing, cover, and tying before subsequent work proceeds.
The subfloor or concrete slab must be prepared and cured before edge insulation can be installed, as edge insulation is placed along the perimeter of the slab/foundation.
Foundation walls must be built before edge insulation can be applied to them, as the insulation is installed directly against the foundation wall surface.
Waterproofing membranes must be applied to the foundation walls before edge insulation is installed, as the insulation is typically placed over the waterproofing layer.
Edge insulation must be in place along the perimeter before the concrete slab is poured, so that the insulation is embedded and forms a continuous thermal break at the slab edge.
It is preferable to complete edge insulation before interior walls are framed to avoid obstructions and ensure continuous insulation coverage, though some sequencing flexibility exists.

The subgrade must be excavated, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable, uniform base for the concrete pour. Without proper subgrade preparation, the thickened edge will not have adequate support and may settle or crack.
Forms must be set and secured to define the shape and dimensions of the thickened edge before concrete can be poured. The liquid concrete requires containing forms to achieve the designed geometry.
Steel reinforcement bars must be positioned and tied within the formwork prior to pouring concrete so that they become fully encased and bonded within the structural element for strength.
After pouring, the concrete must undergo a specified curing period to achieve sufficient strength and durability before any loads are applied or subsequent construction proceeds.
The forms cannot be removed until the poured concrete has set and gained enough strength to support its own weight and maintain the edge shape without deformation.
The concrete slab must be fully cured before waterproofing can be applied to the slab edge. Applying waterproofing to uncured concrete can cause adhesion failure and chemical incompatibility.
The slab edge surfaces must be cleaned, free of dust, debris, laitance, and contaminants to ensure proper bonding of the waterproofing membrane.
After applying the waterproofing material, it requires sufficient curing or drying time before subsequent work (e.g., backfilling, insulation, or protection board installation) can proceed.
A protection board or drainage layer must be installed over the cured waterproofing membrane to shield it from mechanical damage during backfilling or subsequent construction activities.
Backfilling against the slab edge can only commence after the waterproofing membrane has been fully applied and cured, and protection board installed, to prevent damage to the membrane.
The thermal break assembly must be installed on a fully cured concrete foundation to ensure structural stability and proper load transfer.
Underslab rough-in services must be completed before thermal break installation to avoid penetrating or damaging the thermal barrier.
The thermal break must be in place before the floor slab is poured to create a continuous thermal barrier and prevent thermal bridging at the foundation-to-wall interface.
Wall framing must be built on top of or against the completed thermal break assembly to maintain the thermal envelope and prevent direct conduction paths.
The air barrier membrane is typically installed after the thermal break to ensure a continuous seal over the thermal break layer and prevent air leakage at the junction.
The steel edge angle is typically attached to the steel frame, so the frame must be erected first to provide a mounting surface.
The steel edge angle serves as a support or attachment point for exterior cladding (e.g., brick veneer, metal panels), so cladding installation must follow.
Steel edge angles are often used as shelf angles to support masonry at floor lines; brick or masonry courses are laid on top of or after the angle is in place.
The precast edge beam must be supported by the building's structural columns and foundation; without these in place, the edge beam has no support.
Supporting columns must reach sufficient strength before accepting the load of the precast edge beam to prevent structural failure.

successor: Installation of Cladding or Façade Panels
rationale: The edge beam defines the building perimeter and provides the structural attachment point for exterior cladding panels.
The edge beam forms part of the building envelope; waterproofing must be applied over the installed beam to ensure weather tightness.

successor: Installation of Parapet or Roof Edge Details
rationale: Roof edge details and parapets are typically built on top of or integrated with the precast edge beam to complete the roof perimeter.
The structural column frame must be erected and stable before any cladding or enclosure can be applied to it, as the cladding is attached to the supporting structure.
Foundations must be completed to support the columns and the overall structure before cladding can be installed.
All structural steel connections must be fully welded, bolted, and inspected before cladding is applied to ensure structural integrity and to allow access for inspection.
Exterior cladding must be completed before interior partitions are installed to seal the building envelope and protect interior work from weather.
Cladding often forms the substrate around which windows and doors are fitted; the cladding system must be in place to properly integrate fenestration.

The composite deck edge closure is installed at the perimeter of the deck structure. The structural deck (typically concrete or metal) must be in place to provide a substrate and attachment points for the edge closure system.
Edge closures are often set into or against formwork or blockouts at slab edges. These must be installed first to define the edge geometry and provide containment for concrete placement.
Where the edge closure integrates with a waterproofing system, the membrane must be applied to the deck before the closure is fixed, to ensure continuous water tightness at the edge detail.

Composite edge closures often serve as permanent formwork or edge containment for a concrete topping slab or composite slab pour. The concrete cannot be poured until the edge closure is securely installed to prevent leakage and define the slab edge profile.

Finishing trades such as facade panels or cladding systems often abut or cover the edge closure. While not a strict structural necessity, sequencing the cladding after the edge closure ensures a neat interface and avoids rework.
The column base rests on the foundation/footing, so the foundation must be completed first to provide a stable load-bearing surface.
Formwork must be set up to shape and contain the concrete or material for the column base before it can be poured/constructed.
Steel reinforcement must be positioned within the formwork before concrete is placed to ensure structural integrity.
The column base provides the anchorage and support for the column shaft; the shaft cannot be installed until the base is cured and in place.
While waterproofing and finishing can often be done after the column base is complete, it is a soft preference as some finishing work could theoretically proceed in parallel with other works.
Columns must be erected and standing in place before any beam-to-column connections can be made, as the column provides the vertical support and attachment point for beams.
Beams must be lifted, positioned, and aligned adjacent to the column before the bolting or welding connection can be executed.
Columns must be verified as plumb and properly aligned before connections are made to ensure structural accuracy and load transfer.
Column-to-beam connections establish the primary structural node; subsequent beam-to-beam connections in adjacent spans typically follow after the column-to-beam node is secured.
Metal decking or concrete slab work on a given floor level requires the underlying beam framework (connected to columns) to be in place to provide support.
Columns must be erected and in place before they can be connected to slabs, as the connection physically joins the column to the slab.
The slab must be poured and sufficiently cured to provide a stable surface and anchorage for the column-to-slab connection.
Reinforcing steel (rebar) at the column-slab joint must be placed prior to making the connection to ensure structural integrity.
After the column-to-slab connection is made, any grouting, welding inspection, or finishing of the joint can proceed.

successor: Vertical Structural Frame Continuation (Next Floor Columns)
rationale: The column-to-slab connection at one level must be complete before erecting columns on the next level, as the upper columns rely on the completed connection for support and alignment.
Column formwork provides the mold and containment structure; reinforcement bars must be placed inside the formwork before concrete can be poured, so formwork must be erected first.
Reinforcement bars must be securely positioned and tied inside the formwork before concrete is poured to embed the steel within the concrete column.
Concrete pouring must occur after reinforcement installation, and curing follows pouring; reinforcement must be in place before any concrete is placed.
Base plates and anchorage systems must be installed and leveled prior to placing column reinforcement to ensure proper alignment and load transfer to the foundation.
Reinforcement bars must be cut, bent, and fabricated to the specified dimensions before they can be transported to the column location and installed within the formwork.
The structural steel frame must be erected to provide the supporting framework onto which column cladding panels are attached.
Concrete columns must be fully poured and cured to sufficient strength before cladding can be installed, as the cladding is mounted onto or against the column structure.

successor: Sealing and Weatherproofing of Column Joints
rationale: Weatherproof sealants and flashings must be applied after cladding panels are in place to seal joints and prevent water ingress.

successor: Final Inspection and Sign-off of Cladding Works
rationale: A quality and compliance inspection can only occur after all cladding panels are installed to verify alignment, fixings, and finish.
Scaffolding erected for access during cladding installation must remain in place until cladding work is complete; dismantling can only begin afterward for safety reasons.

The column must be constructed and the concrete must achieve sufficient strength before its plumbness (vertical alignment) can be surveyed. Surveying a freshly poured column is meaningless and physically impossible.
The formwork must be removed to expose the column surface so that survey instruments can take accurate measurements of the column's vertical alignment.
Survey results identify any out-of-plumb conditions; corrective action (e.g., grinding, shimming, or structural assessment) can only be determined and executed after the survey data is available.

successor: Follow-on Structural Work (e.g., beams, slabs, precast panels)
rationale: Columns must be verified as plumb before erecting beams, slabs, or other structural elements that bear on or connect to the columns, to ensure proper alignment and load transfer.

Although the survey should be completed before formal sign-off, this is a procedural/administrative preference rather than a physical necessity; the documentation step can theoretically proceed in parallel.
The foundation area must be excavated to expose the ground where the base plate will be placed and the concrete foundation poured.
The exact positions and elevations for the embedded base plates must be surveyed and marked before the plates can be set in place.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied in the foundation area before the base plate is embedded so that the plate can be integrated with the rebar cage.
The embedded base plate must be positioned, leveled, and secured in place before concrete is poured so that it becomes cast into the foundation.
Concrete must cure and develop sufficient strength before the steel column can be erected and bolted/welded to the embedded base plate.

Pedestal columns require a stable foundation to bear their load; foundation preparation (including excavation, compaction, and footing construction) must be completed before any vertical column element can be placed.
The reinforcing steel cage must be assembled and positioned within the foundation connection prior to pouring concrete for the pedestal column, as it provides the structural reinforcement.
Formwork must be erected and braced around the rebar cage to contain the wet concrete and shape the pedestal column before concrete placement can begin.

predecessor: Pedestal Column Concrete Pour and Cure
rationale: Concrete must be poured and allowed to cure to sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed without damaging the column.
The pedestal column must be fully constructed, cured, and inspected to provide a load-bearing support for any superstructure elements (e.g., steel beams or upper columns) that bear onto it.
The column must be erected and placed in position before its connection can be bolted.
The column must be properly aligned and plumbed before bolting the connection to ensure correct fit-up and structural integrity.
After the column connection is bolted, the bolts must be tightened and torqued to the specified tension.
The bolted connection must be completed before it can be inspected and tested for quality assurance.
Once the column connection is bolted, subsequent bracing activities can proceed, though this is a logical sequence preference rather than a strict physical requirement.
Steel columns must be erected and positioned in place before their connections can be welded.
Columns must be properly aligned, plumbed, and temporarily braced before permanent welded connections are made to ensure structural accuracy.
After welding the column connection, non-destructive testing (e.g., ultrasonic testing) must be performed to verify weld integrity before further loading.
Fireproofing material (e.g., intumescent coating or spray-applied fire resistive material) is applied only after welded connections are completed and inspected.
Beams and girders framing into the column require the column's welded connections to be complete so the column is fully stable and ready to receive loads from the beams.
The concrete foundation must be fully cured and achieved sufficient strength to support the load of the column before the base plate can be placed and anchored.
Anchor bolts must be embedded and set in the foundation concrete at precise locations to match the base plate holes before the column base plate can be positioned and fastened.
The exact column centerline and anchor bolt locations must be surveyed, marked, and verified on the foundation before the base plate can be set in the correct position.
The column base plate must be bolted down and leveled before the column shaft can be erected, aligned, and plumbed vertically.
The base plate must first be bolted into position so that the gap between the plate and the foundation can be filled with non-shrink grout for full bearing transfer.
The beam-to-column moment connection requires the column to already be in place and secured, as the beam is connected to the column.
The column must be properly aligned and plumb before beam connections are made to ensure correct fit-up, structural alignment, and load transfer.
The moment connection between beam and column is a critical structural link that must be completed before the overall moment frame bay can be considered structurally stable and self-supporting.
The welding of the moment connection must be completed before it can be inspected for quality, compliance, and structural integrity.

successor: Decking and Slab Placement on Supported Floor
rationale: The steel moment frame must be connected and stable before metal decking and concrete slab can be placed, as the decking bears on the beams that are part of the moment connection.
The beam-to-column shear connection requires the steel column to be erected and in place first, as the connection joins the beam to the column.
The beam must be positioned and aligned at the column location before the shear connection can be bolted or welded to secure it.
Once the shear connection is made (bolts inserted through the web and bracket), the bolts must be tightened to the specified torque to ensure the connection is secure.
If the design requires welding in addition to bolting, the welding must occur after the shear tab connection is established.
The shear connection must be completed before quality control inspection can verify bolt tightness, weld quality, and overall connection integrity.
The column must be cast and cured before the column cap or head connection can be installed, as the cap connects to the top of the column and requires the column to be structurally complete.
Column formwork must be in place for the column pour, and after casting and curing, the formwork is removed, but the column needs to exist before the cap connection.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied within the column before the column cap connection, as the cap often ties into the column rebar.
Column caps or heads provide bearing support for beams and slabs; beam and slab formwork is typically erected on or after column cap installation.
Beam reinforcement is placed after column caps are in position because beam rebar may rest on or integrate with the column cap connection.
Anchor bolts must be embedded in the concrete foundation. The foundation must be poured and cured to sufficient strength to support and hold the anchor bolts in place before assembly can begin.
The exact locations for the anchor bolts must be surveyed and marked on the foundation to ensure accurate positioning and alignment of the columns.

Columns are erected by placing their base plates over the installed anchor bolts and securing them with nuts. The anchor bolts must be assembled and in place before the column itself can be positioned and fastened.

After the column is placed and aligned on the anchor bolts, the space under the base plate is grouted for load transfer. The anchor bolt assembly must be complete (bolts installed, column positioned, nuts tightened) before grouting can proceed.

Final tightening or torquing of the anchor bolt nuts to the specified tension is performed after the column is erected and plumbed. This activity directly depends on the anchor bolt assembly being in place.
The column must be erected and in place before stiffener plates can be connected to it, as stiffener plates are welded/bolted to the column itself.
The stiffener plates must be fabricated, cut to size, and delivered to the site before they can be installed and connected to the column.

predecessor: Layout and Marking of Connection Points
rationale: The exact connection locations on the column need to be measured, marked, and laid out before stiffener plates can be positioned and attached.
After stiffener plates are installed (positioned and temporarily fastened), the welded or bolted connections must be completed and inspected for quality and structural integrity.
Column connection stiffener plates reinforce the column at beam connection points; beams can only be connected after the stiffener plates are in place to provide the necessary reinforcement.
The gusset plate connects to the column, so the steel column must be erected in place before the gusset plate can be installed at the connection point.
The gusset plate serves as the connecting element between beams and the column; beams are bolted to the gusset plate, so the plate must be in place before beam connections can be completed.
The gusset plate must be fabricated, inspected, and delivered to the site before it can be installed on the column.
After the gusset plate is installed and welded to the column, non-destructive testing and quality control inspections must be performed to verify weld integrity before further loading.

While the column must be supported on its foundation, the gusset plate installation is at the upper column connection point and does not physically depend on the foundation completion — this is a sequencing preference for logical construction flow.
The column must be erected and positioned in place before the base can be grouted to secure its final position and fill gaps between the base plate and foundation.

predecessor: Column Base Plate Alignment and Leveling
rationale: The base plate must be properly aligned, leveled, and shimmed before grouting to ensure the column is in its correct position and elevation.
After grouting is placed, sufficient curing time is required before any loads can be applied or subsequent structural connections can be made.

Full structural connections (beams, bracing) to the column should only be made after the base grout has achieved sufficient strength to resist overturning moments and transfer loads to the foundation.
The column must first be erected and placed in its correct position before any bolting-up of its connections can be performed.
The column must be properly aligned, plumbed, and temporarily secured before the connection bolts can be finally tightened (bolted-up).

predecessor: Placement of High-Strength Bolts in Connection
rationale: Bolts must first be inserted into the connection holes before they can be tightened/bolted-up using a torque wrench or impact wrench.
The crane holding the column can only be released once the column connection has been fully bolted-up and the connection is secure.
Subsequent structural steel elements that rely on the bolted-up column as a support or attachment point can only be erected after the column connection is fully tightened and stable.
The steel column must be erected and positioned before the column connection can be welded. Welding requires the column to be in place and properly aligned.
The column must be accurately aligned and plumbed before welding the connection to ensure structural integrity and proper fit-up.
Temporary bolts or clamps are used to hold the connection pieces together prior to welding to maintain alignment and gap control during the welding process.
After welding is complete, the weld must be inspected using non-destructive testing methods (e.g., ultrasonic, magnetic particle) to verify quality and identify any defects.

successor: Application of Protective Coating / Paint to Weld Area
rationale: Once welding is finished and inspected, protective coatings or paint can be applied to prevent corrosion. This is a soft preference as it could be deferred but is best practice to do promptly.
Columns must first be erected and positioned in their approximate locations before the connections between them can be installed and aligned.
Foundations and anchor bolts must be in place and cured to provide a stable base and connection points for the columns before column connection work can commence.

successor: Final Column Plumbness and Alignment Verification
rationale: After connections are installed and aligned, a final verification of plumbness and alignment must be performed to ensure the structure meets specifications.
Column connections must be completed and aligned to provide proper support and connection points for beams and girders that span between columns.
Once column connections are positioned and aligned, the permanent welding or bolting of those connections can be executed to finalize the structural joints.
Non-destructive testing can only be performed after the column connection (e.g., welding, bolting, or grouting) has been completed, as there is no joint to test before the connection is made.
The connection must pass non-destructive testing before it can be formally accepted or signed off as meeting quality standards.
The NDT results must verify the connection's integrity before erecting subsequent columns that will rely on the completed connection for structural stability.
Non-destructive testing must be completed before any grouting or encasement work that would obscure the connection and prevent access for testing.
Full design loads should not be applied to the connection until NDT has confirmed the integrity of the connection.

The column haunch connection is a structural connection at the base or mid-height of a steel column. The column must first be erected and positioned before the haunch connection can be installed to attach beams or braces to the column.
The haunch connection itself must be complete (bolted or welded to the column) before any beam can be connected to that haunch, as the haunch serves as the receiving bracket for the beam end.
The haunch bracket must be in place and secured to the column before steel beams can be lifted and set onto the haunch seat for connection.
If the column haunch connection is at the column base (connecting to a foundation), the concrete foundation or column cap must be cured and ready to receive the column and its base haunch connection.
After the haunch connection is welded to the column, non-destructive testing and inspection of the welds must be performed before proceeding with further loading of the connection.
The column must be erected and in place before shear tab connection components can be installed, as the shear tab connects to the erected column.
The shear tab must be installed on the column first to serve as the connection point for beams that will be attached to the column.
The column itself must be fabricated and delivered to the site before any shear tab connection hardware can be attached to it.

predecessor: Layout and Marking of Column Connection Points
rationale: The exact locations for shear tab connections must be laid out and marked on the column to ensure proper alignment and fit-up with connecting beams.

successor: Welding or Bolting of Beam-to-Column Connection
rationale: After the shear tab is installed on the column, the beam can be connected to the tab via bolting or welding to complete the moment or shear connection.
The column must be erected in place before the connection end plate can be installed, as the end plate connects to the column base.
The foundation must be prepared (poured and cured) to provide a stable base for the column connection end plate.
Anchor bolts must be set in the foundation before the end plate can be positioned and bolted down.
Grouting is performed after the end plate is in position to fill the gap between the plate and foundation.
Steel beams connect to the column at the end plate, so the end plate must be installed first to provide the connection point.
Column formwork must be installed to define the column shape and position before dowels can be placed and connected to the reinforcement.
The reinforcement cage must be assembled and placed inside the formwork before dowel bars can be tied or welded to the column reinforcement.
The foundation or footing must be completed and cured to provide a stable base for the column and to anchor the starter bars or dowels.
Dowel connections must be completed and inspected before the column concrete is poured to ensure the dowels are properly anchored and positioned.
Dowel connections must be finished before the formwork can be finally closed and secured for concrete pouring, as access is needed for dowel placement and tying.
The foundation must be excavated and prepared to create the socket base that receives the precast column.
The concrete socket footing must be cast and cured to provide a stable, hardened receptacle for inserting the precast column.
The socket concrete must reach sufficient strength before the column load is applied, otherwise the foundation may crack or fail.
After the column is inserted into the socket, the gap between column and socket walls must be filled with grout to lock the column in place and transfer loads.
Once the column is seated in the socket, its verticality and position must be checked before final grouting or connection of subsequent structural elements.
Beams and slabs supported by the precast column can only be installed after the column is securely connected and grouted in its socket.
Backfilling is preferably done after the column is socketed and grouted to avoid disturbing the foundation, though in some sequences it could be done earlier if designed.
The fire protection wrap is applied to the column connections, so the steel columns must be erected and connections completed first.

predecessor: Welding & Bolting Completion of Column Connections
rationale: The bolting or welding of the column connections must be finished before fire protection wrap can be applied to those connections.
Inspection of the fireproofing application must occur after the fire protection wrap is installed to verify proper coverage and adhesion.

successor: Subsequent Trade Work (e.g., MEP rough-in, drywall)
rationale: It is generally preferable but not physically required that fire protection wrap be installed before other trades work nearby to avoid difficult access later; however, some coordination can allow concurrent work.
The column connection surfaces must be clean and free of debris, grease, or loose rust to ensure proper adhesion of the fire protection wrap.
Columns must be installed and erected before their connections (bolts, welds, etc.) can be inspected and tested.
Column connections must be inspected and tested to confirm integrity before structural loads or concrete can be applied to the columns.
Inspections and testing of connections should be completed before applying protective coatings or fireproofing, which would cover and obscure the connection details.

The existing condition and capacity of the columns must be assessed to determine the required retrofitting scope, material specifications, and connection details before any strengthening work can proceed.

predecessor: Removal of Existing Fireproofing/Finishes at Connections
rationale: Fireproofing, paint, or other finishes must be removed from the connection area to expose the steel/concrete surface for welding, bolting, or other strengthening techniques.
Temporary shoring must be installed to relieve load from the existing column connections before any modification or strengthening work begins, ensuring structural safety during retrofitting.
After the strengthening work is completed, all fireproofing, intumescent coatings, or other protective finishes must be reinstated to restore the required fire resistance rating of the connection.

successor: Quality Control Inspection/Testing of Strengthened Connection
rationale: Nondestructive testing (e.g., ultrasonic testing of welds, torque verification of bolts) and visual inspection must be performed after the retrofitting work to verify that the connection meets design specifications.
The stair vault structure must be erected first to provide the framework or base onto which the enclosing walls are built.
Enclosing walls must be completed before any waterproofing or cladding can be applied to the exterior surfaces of the stair vault.
The enclosing walls must be fully in place before interior finishing work (such as plastering, painting, or tiling) can begin inside the stair vault.
A stable foundation or substructure is required to support the load of the stair vault enclosing walls.
The enclosing walls must be constructed before the roof or cover can be installed atop the stair vault.
The structural framing must be in place to provide support and a substrate for the ceiling/soffit installation.
Ceiling/soffit must be completed before installing light fixtures that are mounted on or recessed into the soffit surface.
The ceiling/soffit surface must be in place before any final finishing or painting can be applied.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the ceiling cavity must be completed before enclosing with the soffit/ceiling.
It is preferable but not physically required to complete the vault ceiling before installing railings, as railings are independent of the overhead soffit.

The stair core or shear walls must be constructed first to provide vertical load-bearing support and lateral stability for the stair vault floor slab, which typically bears onto or is cast integrally with these walls.
Reinforcing steel (rebar) must be placed and tied in position before the concrete slab is poured to ensure structural integrity as per engineering design.

predecessor: Formwork / Falsework Erection for Stair Vault
rationale: Formwork and falsework must be installed to create the mould and temporary support system for the wet concrete until it gains sufficient strength.

Stair flights (the steps/risers) typically bear onto or are cast monolithically with the vault slab; the floor slab must be in place to provide the landing or structural support for the flights above.

Waterproofing is often applied after the concrete slab has cured to prevent moisture ingress, but this is a preference for durability sequencing rather than a physical necessity (the slab could be waterproofed later if access is maintained).
The stair structure must be in place to provide the structural support and frame for the vault door installation.
The vault door frame must be fabricated and installed before the vault door can be mounted, as the door hinges and locking mechanism attach to the frame.
The floor area beneath the vault door must be finished and leveled to ensure proper door clearance, threshold sealing, and smooth operation.

After the vault door is installed, sealing (e.g., gaskets, weatherstripping) and functional testing (lock operation, closure alignment) must be performed to ensure security and environmental integrity.
Security sensors, alarms, and access control systems for the vault door can only be wired and calibrated after the door is physically installed and operational.
The stair vault structure must be built first to provide a surface for mounting signage.
Signage must be installed before the stair vault can be inspected for compliance with safety and wayfinding requirements.
Wall surfaces must be finished (painted, clad, etc.) before signage is applied to ensure proper adhesion and alignment.
It is preferable to install signage before final cleaning to avoid having to re-clean areas after installation, though signage could be installed after cleaning with additional protection measures.
Lighting must be in place to ensure signage is properly illuminated and visible upon installation, allowing for correct positioning relative to light sources.
The stair vault requires a stable load-bearing foundation to support its weight and structural loads before any vertical construction can begin.
The stair vault is typically built from the ground floor level upward, requiring the ground floor slab to be in place to provide a working platform and base support.
In steel-framed buildings, the main structural frame must be erected to provide attachment points and support for stair vault elements.
The structural stair vault must be fully constructed and cured before any finishing works such as tiling, plastering, or railing installation can be applied to the stair surfaces.

successor: Rough-in Electrical / MEP for Stair Area
rationale: Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work in the stairwell area can only be performed after the stair vault structure is in place to define the spatial envelope and mounting locations.
The structural steel frame for the stair vault must be erected first to provide the substrate onto which fireproofing material is applied.
Fireproofing must be completed before MEP rough-in to avoid damaging fireproofing material and to ensure fire-resistance ratings are not compromised by subsequent trades.
Interior finishes such as drywall, painting, and wall coverings must be installed after fireproofing is complete to avoid covering or damaging the fireproofing layer.
The concrete slab or deck that supports the stair vault must be fully cured to provide a stable working platform and to prevent moisture from interfering with fireproofing adhesion.
While typically fireproofing is done before installing permanent stairs to allow unrestricted access, it is a soft preference as scaffolding could be used if necessary.
The structural concrete or base framework of the stair vault must be fully cured and complete before any finishing work (plastering, painting, cladding) can be applied.
Electrical conduits, lighting rough-ins, or any plumbing that will be embedded within or behind the stair vault finishes must be installed prior to the application of finishes.
Formwork from the concrete pour must be stripped, and the vault surface properly cleaned and prepared, before any finishing coatings or cladding can be applied.
Handrails and balustrades are typically installed after the vault finish is complete to avoid damage to the finish and to ensure proper alignment and fixing into the finished surface.
Any final paint or decorative wall treatments adjacent to the stair vault should be applied after the vault finishing is done to prevent splatter, damage, or edge misalignment.
Structural steel or building frame must be in place to provide support and attachment points for ductwork.
Electrical conduits and plumbing pipes that may conflict with duct paths must be roughed in first to avoid clashes and rework.
Fireproofing materials (e.g., firestop sealants, wrap) are applied after ducts are installed to seal penetrations and protect ductwork as per fire code.
Ducts must be fully installed before the HVAC system can be balanced, tested, and commissioned for airflow performance.
Ductwork must be in place before ceilings are enclosed so that ducts can be inspected and any future maintenance can be accessed.
Duct dampers are installed within the ductwork system; the ductwork must be in place before dampers can be mounted inside the ducts.
The overall HVAC rough-in including duct routing and supports must be completed to provide the framework and location for damper placement.
Dampers must be installed and sealed before the duct system can be pressure-tested for leaks to ensure accurate test results.
Dampers control airflow; they must be in place before the system can be balanced and commissioned to regulate air distribution properly.
Fire-rated dampers must be installed prior to testing their fire/smoke closure operation to verify compliance with fire safety codes.
Duct hangers and supports must be attached to structural framing (beams, joists, or slabs). The structural frame must be in place to provide anchorage points for the hangers.
Coordination of overhead space is needed so duct hangers are not placed where other major MEP systems will conflict; this is a sequencing preference to avoid rework.
Duct sections are placed onto and secured to the installed hangers and supports. The support system must be in place before any ductwork can be hung from it.
Once duckwork is installed on the hangers, the system must be tested for leaks. The hanger installation is a prerequisite for duct installation, which in turn must be complete before testing.

Inspectors need to verify that duct hangers are properly installed per code (spacing, materials, fire stopping) before ceilings are enclosed. The hanger installation must be complete for this inspection.
The duct access door must be framed and installed into the ductwork; therefore the ductwork must be in place first to receive the access door.
Insulation is typically applied over the ductwork and access door assembly; the access door must be installed and sealed before insulation can be wrapped around it.
Leak testing requires all duct components including access doors to be fully installed and sealed to ensure an accurate test of system airtightness.
Commissioning and airflow balancing should occur after all duct components including access doors are in place so adjustments can be made and future maintenance access is available.
The duct's supporting hangers, brackets, or framing must be installed before the ductwork and access doors to provide structural support for the system.

Flexible duct connectors are used to connect rigid ductwork to diffusers, grilles, or equipment. The rigid ductwork must be in place first so the flexible connector can bridge the gap between the rigid system and the terminal device.

predecessor: HVAC Equipment Placement (Air Handling Unit / Fan Coil)
rationale: Flexible duct connectors often connect the main HVAC equipment (e.g., AHU, fan coil) to the branch ducts. The equipment must be set in its final position before flexible connections can be made.

Flexible duct connectors serve as the final link between the duct system and the diffuser or grille. The connector must be installed first so the diffuser can be attached to the end of the flexible duct.

Flexible duct connectors are typically routed within ceiling plenums and terminated at diffuser locations. The connectors must be in place before the ceiling is closed so that final connections to diffusers can be made and so that the ducts are not trapped behind finished surfaces.

While air balancing is typically performed after all ducts and terminals are installed, it is only a soft preference because some preliminary testing could theoretically begin before final flexible connections are made, but full system balancing requires all connectors to be in place for accurate airflow measurement.
The duct system layout and design must be approved to determine where turning vanes are needed for proper airflow direction changes.
The duct sections must be fabricated and assembled before turning vanes can be installed inside them at the duct bends.
Duct sections must be positioned and hung in place before turning vanes can be physically installed inside the ductwork at the bend locations.
Turning vanes must be installed before the duct system can be sealed and leak-tested, as access to the interior of the duct bends would otherwise be blocked.
Turning vanes should be installed before insulating the ductwork, as insulation would obstruct access to install the vanes at the bends.
Structural framing and rough-in work must be complete to provide the physical space and support structure for ductwork installation.
General HVAC rough-in planning and ductwork layout must be determined before actual duct space can be allocated and installed.
The designated duct space must be installed first to allow the actual duct runs and connections to be placed within that allocated space.
Duct space must be in place before insulation can be applied around or adjacent to the ductwork to ensure proper thermal and acoustic treatment.
Duct space installation must be completed before ceilings and walls are closed in, as access is required for installation and inspection.
Ductwork must be fully installed and in place before insulation can be applied to it. Insulation is applied directly onto the installed duct surfaces.
Leakage testing and any necessary sealing of duct joints must be completed prior to insulation, as access to duct joints for sealing would be blocked by insulation.
Ceilings, drywall, and mechanical room enclosures should be installed after duct insulation to allow full access for insulation work and inspection.

While system balancing can begin before insulation in some areas, final balancing and commissioning of insulated duct runs is preferably done after insulation to ensure accurate thermal performance readings.
Firestopping and sealing of penetrations through fire-rated assemblies should be completed after duct insulation is installed, as insulation can affect how penetrations are sealed.
Ducts must be fully installed and in place before they can be tested for leaks, as testing requires a complete duct system.
Leakage testing identifies leaks, which must then be sealed or repaired before the system can be finalized.
The duct system must be tested and proven airtight before the HVAC system can be commissioned and balanced.
Duct leakage testing should be performed before insulating ducts so that leaks can be detected and repaired without removing insulation.
Ducts must be tested for leaks before they are concealed behind walls, ceilings, or other finishes to allow access for repairs.
Hydronic piping must be roughed-in above the ceiling before radiant panels are installed, so the piping can connect to the panels.
Overhead electrical, ductwork, and other mechanical rough-ins must be completed before ceiling panels are installed to avoid rework and access issues.
The ceiling suspension system or support framing must be in place to provide a mounting structure for the radiant panels.
Radiant panels must be installed before final ceiling finishes and painting to ensure a seamless appearance and avoid damage to finished surfaces.

successor: Pressure Testing and Commissioning of Hydronic System
rationale: Radiant panels must be installed and connected to the hydronic system before the system can be pressure-tested and commissioned.
Radiant wall panels must be mounted onto or within framed wall cavities, so the wall framing structure must be complete to provide support and attachment points.
Electrical wiring and boxes must be installed behind or within walls before radiant panels are placed, as access to wall cavities is blocked after panel installation.
For hydronic radiant wall panels, the supply and return piping must be run within the wall assembly before the panels are installed.
Radiant wall panels are typically embedded within or mounted behind the finished wall surface, so they must be in place prior to drywall or plaster application.
The control system wiring for the radiant panels must be connected to the panels themselves after they are installed, but before the wall is closed up.
The Radiant Manifold must be mounted onto the primary load-bearing core structure; the core must exist first to provide physical support and alignment.
The thermal shield must be in place behind or around the manifold area to protect sensitive components from radiant heat before the manifold is installed.
All connections and seals must be verified under pressure after manifold installation to ensure no leaks before system activation.
Conduits carrying radiant energy to/from the manifold can only be attached after the manifold is securely positioned and fastened.
The control system must be calibrated using the manifold's actual position and response characteristics; this cannot occur until the manifold is physically installed.
The structural ceiling must be installed to provide a mounting surface and support for the radiant ceiling hydronic module.
The hydronic module must be installed before ceiling finishes (e.g., drywall, tiles, or plaster) are applied, as access to the module and its connections is required for installation and testing.
The supply and return hydronic piping must be roughed-in to the module location to allow connection of the radiant ceiling hydronic module to the hydronic system.
The module must be installed and connected to the piping before the complete hydronic system can be pressure tested for leaks.

While the module installation should precede control wiring to allow proper connection, electrical rough-in could partially proceed in parallel; however, final control wiring connections to the module require the module to be in place.
The subfloor must be clean, dry, and level to provide a stable base for the radiant tubing. Any debris or unevenness could damage the tubing or create air pockets that reduce thermal efficiency.
Rigid foam or reflective insulation must be laid down first to prevent heat loss downward, ensuring the radiant system operates efficiently and that heat is directed upward into the living space.

predecessor: Rough-In of Plumbing and Electrical (Slab or Subfloor)
rationale: Any plumbing drains, electrical conduits, or other embedded utilities that run through the floor slab must be installed and inspected before the radiant tubing is placed, to avoid conflicts and the need to disturb the tubing later.

successor: Slab Pouring or Self-Leveling Underlayment Application
rationale: Once the radiant tubing is laid out and secured in its pattern, a concrete slab or gypsum-based self-leveling underlayment must be poured over it to encase and protect the tubing, providing thermal mass and a flat surface for the final flooring.

Immediately after installation but before being covered, the tubing must be pressure-tested to verify there are no leaks or damage. Any leaks must be repaired before the slab or underlayment is poured.

Radiant heating loops must be physically installed (tubing, manifolds, and connections in place) before they can be commissioned, as commissioning involves pressure testing, flow balancing, and verifying system functionality.
Pressure testing (hydrostatic or pneumatic) must be completed prior to commissioning to ensure the integrity of the piping system and identify any leaks before the system is activated.

predecessor: Completion of Concrete Slab / Floor Pour (if embedded loops)
rationale: For embedded radiant loops, the concrete slab or floor screed must be cured before commissioning to allow system pressurization and testing without risk of damaging the uncured material.

successor: Connection to Central Boiler/Heat Pump System
rationale: The radiant loops must be individually commissioned (tested, flushed, and balanced) before being integrated and connected to the central heating plant to avoid contaminating or damaging the main system.

Control system integration and thermostat programming for each zone should follow commissioning so that the actual flow and temperature characteristics of each loop are known and can be programmed into the control logic.
The insulation layer must be placed and secured on the subfloor before any screed or radiant cables are installed, as the insulation provides thermal separation and a stable base for the screed.
Edge insulation strips must be installed around the perimeter of the room to allow for thermal expansion of the screed before the screed and cables are placed.

predecessor: Installing Radiant Cable Fixing System (e.g., Clips/Tracks)
rationale: The cable fixing system (clips, tracks, or mesh) must be fastened to the insulation layer to hold the radiant cables in position before the cables are laid and subsequently embedded in screed.

successor: Applying Floor Finish (e.g., Tiles, Wood, Vinyl)
rationale: The screed must be fully cured and dried after embedding the radiant cables before any final floor covering can be applied, to prevent damage to the screed and cables.
Pressure testing of the radiant pipes/cables should be conducted after the cables are embedded in screed and the screed has cured, to verify the integrity of the system before covering.
Electrical conduit, junction boxes, and mechanical ductwork must be installed above the ceiling before radiant panels are placed, as the panels would block access to overhead rough-in work.
The suspended ceiling grid (T-bar system) must be in place to provide the structural support and mounting framework for the radiant panels.
Radiant panels must be installed first so that the ceiling finish, painting, and touch-up work around the panel edges can be completed without damaging the panels.

successor: Hydronic Piping Connection and Pressure Testing
rationale: Once radiant panels are hung, the supply and return hydronic piping must be connected to each panel and the entire system pressure-tested to verify no leaks exist before ceiling closure.

successor: Final Electrical Trim-Out and Thermostat Wiring
rationale: Electrical connections to the radiant panel controls, zone valves, and thermostats must be completed after the panels are physically installed and their control wiring can be run.
The radiant floor tubing must be installed before the thermostat can be mounted and connected, as the thermostat controls the flow of heated water through the tubing.
The manifold distributing hot water to the radiant loops must be in place before the thermostat can be wired and commissioned to control the zone valves.
Low-voltage thermostat wiring must be run to the thermostat location before the device can be physically installed and connected.
The thermostat must be installed and operational before the HVAC system can be balanced and commissioned, as it provides the control input for zone temperature regulation.
It is preferred but not strictly required to install the thermostat after painting is complete to avoid damage and paint contamination on the device.

predecessor: Install radiant heating piping and manifolds
rationale: The control valve must be connected to the existing radiant heating piping system, so the piping and manifolds must be installed first to provide the physical connection points.

predecessor: Mount and secure valve bracket or support
rationale: The valve requires a structural bracket or support to be mounted on before it can be securely installed in place.

predecessor: Complete rough-in electrical work for valve actuator
rationale: If the control valve has an electric actuator, the electrical rough-in (wiring, conduit) must be completed to allow connection and power supply to the valve actuator.

successor: Connect and test valve actuator wiring
rationale: The valve must be physically installed before its actuator wiring can be connected and tested, as the wiring terminates at the valve location.

successor: Commission and balance radiant heating system
rationale: The control valve must be in place and operational before the overall radiant heating system can be commissioned and balanced to ensure proper flow control.
The dormer frame provides the structural support; sheathing or cladding cannot be applied until the frame is erected and secured.
The dormer must be framed onto the main roof structure; the main roof framing must be in place to tie the dormer into the main roof system.

predecessor: Rough Opening Preparation in Main Roof
rationale: The opening in the main roof deck must be cut and prepared before the dormer frame can be set into position and attached.
The dormer frame defines the window opening and provides structural support; windows must be installed after the frame is secure.
Roofing and flashing for the dormer rely on the completed frame to establish the correct slope and attachment points.
The dormer roof deck (sheathing/plywood) must be installed on top of the dormer framing members (rafters/trusses). Framing provides the structural support for the deck.
Underlayment (felt/synthetic) is laid directly on top of the roof deck sheathing to provide a water-resistant barrier before shingles are installed.
Flashing is installed around dormer edges and intersections with the main roof after the deck is in place to seal joints against water intrusion.
Roof shingles or finished roofing material must be applied over the deck and underlayment as the final roofing layer.
Siding on dormer cheeks/walls is typically completed after the roof deck is installed to ensure proper weatherproofing at the roof-to-wall interface, though some overlap may occur.
The dormer structure must be fully built before flashing can be installed, as flashing is applied to seal the joints and transitions around the dormer.
The roof deck around the dormer must be in place to provide a surface for the flashing to integrate with and properly shed water.
Roof underlayment should be installed before flashing to provide a waterproof barrier beneath the flashing material.
Flashing must be installed before the final shingles are laid so that shingles can overlap the flashing for proper water shedding.
Flashing around the dormer must be complete before siding or exterior finishes are applied to ensure a weather-tight seal behind the finishes.
The roof structure must be framed to provide the structural opening and support for the dormer window unit.
Roof sheathing must be in place to define the rough opening and provide a substrate around the dormer penetration.
The dormer window unit must be installed first so that flashing can be applied around it to seal against water intrusion.

successor: Exterior Siding or Cladding around Dormer
rationale: Siding or cladding is installed after the window unit to trim around and integrate the dormer into the finished exterior wall surface.

successor: Interior Drywall and Trim around Dormer
rationale: Interior finishing work around the dormer can only proceed once the window unit is in place to ensure proper alignment and sealing.
The dormer window trim must be attached to the framed dormer structure. The framing provides the structural support and nailing surface for the trim, so it must be completed first.
Sheathing (e.g., plywood or OSB) must be installed over the dormer framing before trim can be applied. Trim is fastened to or over the sheathing.
The window unit itself must be installed in the rough opening before the interior or exterior window trim can be applied around it.
Flashing is installed over the top and side trim pieces to shed water away, so trim must be in place first to receive the flashing.

Siding is typically installed up to or overlapping the window trim. The trim provides a finished edge and weather barrier transition, so it must be completed before siding is applied around the dormer.
The dormer roof framing and structure must be completed first to provide the structural support onto which the soffit and fascia can be attached.
Sheathing (e.g., plywood or OSB) must be installed on the dormer roof and walls to create a solid substrate before the soffit and fascia trim can be applied.
The underlayment (felt or synthetic membrane) protects the sheathing and must be in place before finishing the soffit and fascia for weatherproofing continuity.
Soffit and fascia trim are installed along the eaves and rake edges of the dormer roof; roofing materials are then installed over the underlayment and must terminate properly at the fascia edge.
The soffit under the dormer eaves must be in place before exterior siding can be fitted and trimmed tightly against it to ensure a clean, weathertight finish.
The exterior trim is installed onto the framed dormer structure; framing provides the structural substrate that trim attaches to.
Sheathing covers the dormer framing and provides a solid surface for trim attachment, and trim is installed over the sheathing.
Waterproofing and flashing protect the dormer against moisture intrusion; exterior trim is installed after these weather-resistive layers are in place.
Trim pieces (e.g., corner boards, fascia, window surrounds) are installed first to define edges and transitions, then siding butts against or overlaps the trim.
Final paint or stain is applied to the exterior trim after it is fully installed; coating seals and protects the trim material.
Dormer construction is built within or onto the existing roof structure. The roof framing must be complete to provide the structural support and opening needed for dormer installation.
After the dormer is framed and constructed, the roof sheathing can be installed around and up to the dormer structure to ensure a watertight and continuous roof deck.
Flashing around the dormer must be installed after the dormer is fully constructed to seal the joint between the dormer and the main roof, preventing water infiltration.
Siding, trim, and exterior finishing of the dormer walls can only begin after the dormer structure is fully framed and sheathed.
Dormer windows must be installed after the dormer frame is complete, as the rough opening for the window is prepared during dormer framing.
The dormer window frame must be fully constructed and structurally sound to provide a proper opening and support for the window unit to be installed into.
The roof sheathing around the dormer must be in place to define the rough opening and provide a weather-resistant surface before the window can be installed.
Window flashing must be installed after the window is placed to properly seal the joints between the window frame and the surrounding roof/dormer structure, preventing water infiltration.
Exterior siding and trim around the dormer window can only be installed after the window unit is in place, as the window defines the finish perimeter and trim details.

Interior drywall and finishing work around the dormer window area is typically done after window installation to ensure proper sealing and to avoid damaging finished surfaces during window placement, though it is a logical sequencing preference rather than a strict structural necessity.
The roof cap flashing is installed over and around the roof deck, so the deck must be in place to provide a surface for the flashing to be secured to.

The underlayment (e.g., felt paper or synthetic membrane) must be laid over the roof deck before cap flashing can be installed, as the flashing sits above the underlayment and helps seal the roof edges.
Roof cap flashing ties into the exterior wall assembly; therefore, the wall sheathing must be in place so the flashing can be properly integrated and flashed into the wall system.
Cap flashing is typically installed before the exterior wall cladding so that the cladding can overlap the flashing leg, ensuring water is directed away from the wall-roof intersection.

successor: Final Roofing Material Installation (e.g., shingles, tiles)
rationale: The cap flashing is often installed at the perimeter before the final roofing material is laid, allowing the roofing material to be properly trimmed and sealed against the flashing.
The roof cap substrate/deck requires structural support from the underlying framing and walls to bear the load before installation.
Roof insulation is typically installed before the roof cap substrate/deck to provide thermal performance and a base layer for the roofing system.
The roof cap substrate/deck provides the base surface upon which the waterproofing membrane is applied to ensure a watertight seal.
Flashing is installed after the substrate/deck is in place to seal joints and transitions around the roof perimeter and penetrations.
The final roof covering (e.g., shingles, tiles, metal panels) is installed on top of the completed substrate/deck to provide the weather-exposed surface.
The roof cap coping sits on top of and along the edges of the roof deck; the deck must be in place to support and anchor the coping.
The waterproofing membrane must be installed before the coping can be placed, as the coping often secures and covers the membrane edges (flashing) to prevent water intrusion.

The coping typically caps the parapet wall and flashing; however, the final flashing counterflashing is often completed after coping is set to ensure a watertight seal. More precisely, coping goes on first, then counterflashing is installed over it.
Installing coping after adjacent cladding ensures a clean aesthetic transition, but this is a soft preference for sequencing convenience rather than a physical necessity.
The coping is part of the roof edge termination system; final inspection and water testing of the roof assembly must occur after coping installation to verify weathertightness.
The roof cap gravel stop is installed at the edge of the roof deck; the deck must be in place to provide a structure for attachment.
Insulation is typically laid over the roof deck before edge flashing and gravel stop are installed to ensure proper thermal protection and edge height.
The gravel stop serves as a termination bar and edge detail; roofing plies or membrane are often lapped over the gravel stop flange to create a watertight seal.
In a built-up or ballasted roof system, the gravel stop contains the gravel layer; gravel is poured after the cap is in place.
Counterflashing is installed over or adjacent to the gravel stop to seal the roof edge against water infiltration, requiring the gravel stop to be in place first.
The structural steel frame provides the primary load-bearing support onto which the precast concrete roof cap is installed; the frame must be in place before roof components can be set.
The roof deck forms the base surface upon which the precast concrete roof cap is placed or secured; the deck must be completed before cap installation.
The precast concrete roof cap must be in place before waterproofing membranes can be applied over it to seal the roof assembly against water ingress.
Thermal insulation is typically laid over or around the roof cap components; the cap structure must be completed first to provide a substrate for insulation.

While it is common practice to install trims and flashings after the roof cap is set to cover joints and edges, some flashing work could be done concurrently; however, the cleanest sequence has the cap complete first.
