The metal roof cap is typically installed at the ridge or peak of the roof, which requires the roof deck (sheathing) to be fully in place to provide support and a nailing surface.
Waterproof underlayment (e.g., felt or synthetic) must be laid over the roof deck before the metal roof cap is installed to provide a moisture barrier beneath the cap.

predecessor: Standing Seam or Metal Roof Panel Installation
rationale: The metal roof cap (ridge cap) is installed after the main metal roof panels are in place, as it covers the seam where panels meet at the ridge and overlaps the top edges of the panels.
After the metal roof cap is installed, the ridge flashing and trim details are finalized to seal the cap ends and ensure watertight integration with adjacent roofing elements.
While not a hard physical constraint, it is standard practice to complete all roof cap installation before the final inspection to verify proper installation and weatherproofing.
The stone roof cap sits on top of the concrete roof slab, so the concrete slab must be fully cured and in place to provide the structural base for the stone cap.
The stone roof cap is installed over the waterproofing layer to protect it and provide drainage, so the waterproofing membrane must be applied first.
The roof inspection must verify the installed stone roof cap for proper fit, anchoring, and weather-tightness; the cap must be in place before the inspection can be performed.

While the stone roof cap is often installed as the final stone element, coordinating with wall cladding for aesthetics and waterproofing junctions is preferred, though not a strict physical necessity in all cases.
Scaffolding that provides access for stone roof cap installation cannot be dismantled until the cap is fully installed, anchored, and sealed.
The roof deck provides the structural base onto which cap sealant joints are applied; without a completed deck, there is no substrate for the sealant.
Insulation must be in place before cap sealant joints are applied, as the sealant covers and seals transitions between insulation boards or between insulation and other roof components.
The primary roof membrane must be installed first because cap sealant joints are applied at membrane seams, edges, and terminations to ensure watertight sealing.
Cap sealant joints must cure and be fully set before flashings are installed over or adjacent to them, to avoid disturbing the sealant bond and to ensure continuity of the waterproofing system.

Flood testing of the roof drainage system must occur after cap sealant joints are completed and cured, as these joints are critical to watertightness and must be verified as leak-free before drainage components are tested.
Roof cap fasteners and clips are installed onto the roof deck; the deck must be in place to provide a substrate for attachment.
Underlayment is typically laid over the roof deck before any roof cap or flashing components are fastened, to ensure waterproofing and a proper base.
Fasteners and clips are used to secure the roof cap; the cap cannot be attached until its fastening hardware is in place.
While trim and flashing can be partially installed beforehand, final alignment and securing often wait until roof cap fasteners are set to ensure proper fit and finish.
The roof deck provides the structural base and substrate onto which the roof cap flashing is installed; without a completed deck, there is nothing to attach the flashing to.
Underlayment is installed beneath the flashing to provide a waterproof barrier; flashing must be placed over the underlayment to ensure proper water shedding and prevent leaks.
Cap flashing is installed as the topmost layer of a flashing assembly, overlapping lower flashing components to create a complete watertight seal; base or step flashing must be in place first.
Sealant is applied to the exposed edges and joints of the cap flashing after installation to seal penetrations and ensure waterproofing; the flashing must be in place before it can be sealed.

Roof cap flashing is typically installed before final ridge caps and other finishing accessories to maintain the proper overlapping sequence (upper components over lower) and ensure water runs down and away from the structure.
The roof deck provides the structural base and working surface on which the roof cap coping is installed; without a completed roof deck, there is no substrate to attach the coping to.
Roof insulation is typically installed before the final coping to ensure proper thermal performance and to provide a continuous surface under the cap.
The waterproofing membrane must be in place and terminated properly at the edges before coping can be installed to secure and protect the membrane edges from uplift and water ingress.

successor: Apply Final Sealant / Caulking at Coping Joints
rationale: After the coping sections are installed, joints and seams must be sealed to prevent water penetration and ensure weathertightness.
Coping installation provides attachment points for lightning protection components; however, this can be coordinated concurrently or after, depending on design.
Roof insulation must be installed before the cap membrane is applied, as the membrane is the final waterproofing layer that goes over the insulation.
The roof deck provides the structural substrate; the cap membrane cannot be applied until the deck is in place and secure.
The base sheet or underlayment is installed as a preparatory layer; the cap membrane is the topmost layer and must be applied over the underlayment.

While gutters are often installed after the roof membrane to avoid damaging the membrane, this is a preferred sequence but not a strict physical necessity if careful installation procedures are followed.
Water testing and final inspection must occur after the cap membrane is fully installed to verify the waterproofing integrity of the completed roofing system.
The roof deck provides the structural substrate onto which the roof cap insulation is installed; insulation cannot be placed without a deck to support it.

Underlayment (e.g., felt or synthetic) is installed over the roof deck to provide a weather-resistant barrier; cap insulation is placed over this layer for thermal performance and must follow underlayment installation.
Cap insulation serves as a thermal layer beneath the final roofing membrane; the finished roofing material must be placed over the insulation to protect it from weather and secure it in place.
The substrate (deck and underlayment) must be inspected and approved before covering with cap insulation to ensure no defects or moisture issues are trapped.

While edge flashing can follow insulation, it is a soft preference because some sequencing flexibility exists; however, best practice often completes flashing after insulation to ensure proper thermal bridging and continuity at edges.
The roof cap must be installed in place before its joints can be sealed; sealing is a finishing step that cannot be performed on an uninstalled component.
Joint surfaces must be clean and free of debris, dust, or moisture to ensure proper adhesion of the sealant.
Some sealants require a primer for proper bonding; this is a manufacturer-specific soft preference depending on sealant type.
Inspection of the seal quality can only occur after the sealing work is completed.
Flashing or trim pieces often overlap sealed joints; installing them before the sealant cures could disturb the seal, so a soft preference is to seal first.
The structural slab or deck forms the load-bearing substrate onto which the screed is poured; without a cured structural slab, the screed has no support and would crack or fail.
A damp proof membrane must be laid over the structural slab before screeding to prevent moisture migration from the ground into the screed layer, which would cause damp issues and adhesion failure.
Underfloor heating pipes are embedded within or directly beneath the screed layer, so they must be laid and pressure-tested before the screed is poured to encase them.

After the screed is poured, it requires a minimum curing and drying period (typically 1 day per mm of thickness) before any subsequent floor finishes can be applied; this is a physical requirement for strength development and moisture reduction.

Final floor coverings such as tiles, wood flooring, or vinyl can only be installed after the screed has fully cured and dried, otherwise they would be laid on a wet/unstable base leading to delamination, cracking, or mold growth.
The ground must be graded and leveled before a vapor barrier can be laid over it, ensuring a smooth, uniform substrate that prevents puncture and allows proper drainage away from the foundation.

A granular base layer (usually 4–6 inches of compacted gravel) provides a capillary break and a stable, penetrating- resistant bed on which the vapor barrier is placed; the barrier cannot be laid directly on unprepared soil.

The vapor barrier is placed directly beneath the concrete slab to block soil moisture rising into the slab; once the barrier is installed, the concrete can be poured immediately over it so that the barrier is fully encapsulated and protected.

For basement or crawlspace applications, the damp-proof membrane is applied to the exterior of foundation walls; the wall must be cured and clean before coating, and after application the wall can be backfilled or insulated.

While typically insulation boards are placed on top of the vapor barrier before the slab pour, in some assemblies the insulation goes below the barrier; if insulation is above, it must be placed after the barrier but before the slab. This ordering is conventional but can vary by design.
The site must be excavated and graded to the proper elevations before floor drains can be installed, as the drain pipes need to be placed in the subgrade with proper slope.
Underground drain lines and connections to the main sewer or drainage system must be roughed in before the floor drain body and trap can be connected.
The subgrade or base course material must be compacted and leveled to provide a stable foundation for the floor drain assembly and prevent future settling.
Floor drains must be set in place, positioned, and secured at the correct elevation and slope before the concrete slab is poured, so the drain rim is flush with the finished floor surface.
While waterproofing is often done before slab pour, any post-install waterproofing around the drain flange should occur after the drain is set to ensure a watertight seal at the penetration point.
Expansion/control joints are typically installed after concrete slabs or foundations have been poured and partially cured, as the joints are cut or formed into the concrete to control cracking.
Concrete must reach initial set before control joints can be cut or tooled; otherwise the joint will not form properly or the concrete will be damaged.
Control joints must be completed and often sealed before floor coatings or finishes are applied, so that the joint functions properly and the finish does not bridge across the joint.
While not always physically required, it is best practice to complete control joints in the slab before building walls above to avoid cracking from settlement or movement.
After the joint is cut or formed, joint sealant (if specified) must be applied to the clean, prepared joint to prevent debris and moisture ingress.
The subfloor must be level, clean, and structurally sound before access floor panels can be installed to ensure proper support and alignment.

All electrical, data, and mechanical services that will run beneath the raised access floor must be laid out and roughed in before panels are placed, as they become inaccessible once panels are installed.
The adjustable pedestals and support grid that elevate the access floor must be installed, aligned, and leveled before any panels can be laid on top of them.
Final floor finishes (e.g., carpet tiles, vinyl, anti-static coating) can only be applied after the access floor panels are fully installed and secured in position.
Installing workstations, server racks, and heavy equipment is typically done after the access floor is complete to avoid damaging panels and to ensure a stable walking/working surface.
Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied before concrete can be poured to form the structural slab.
Formwork must be erected to contain and shape the wet concrete before slab pouring.
Freshly poured concrete slab must undergo a curing period to gain sufficient strength before any loads are applied.
Walls or columns above the slab can only be constructed after the slab concrete has cured to required strength.
Waterproofing is typically applied after the slab is cured but could be delayed; it is a soft preference to protect the slab from moisture ingress early.

The gutter and downspout system must be installed after the dormer structure is fully framed and sheathed, as the gutter attaches to the fascia board along the edges of the dormer roof, which requires the underlying structure to be complete.

Roofing and underlayment must be completed before gutter installation because the gutter mounts at the roof edge, and water drainage from the roof must be established. Additionally, the underlayment typically extends beneath the gutter flashing.

Step flashing and other counter-flashing around the dormer must be installed prior to gutters, as the gutter system typically integrates with or sits above the flashing at the roof edge to ensure proper water diversion.

Siding installation around the dormer should occur after the downspout is in place, as the siding typically needs to be cut and fitted around downspout brackets and the downspout itself for a clean finish and proper weatherproofing.

It is a soft preference to complete final trim and paint work after gutters and downspouts are installed, as the gutter attachment points and downspout brackets can be painted over or touched up for a uniform appearance, but this is not structurally required.
Stair stringers provide the structural support framework that stair treads and landings are mounted upon. Without stringers in place, there is no substrate to attach treads or landings to.
Risers form the vertical face of each step and are typically installed before treads to provide backing and proper step geometry for tread placement.
For landing surfaces, the subfloor or underlayment must be complete and level to provide a stable base for the landing material installation.

Stair railings and balustrades are typically anchored to the treads or landings themselves, or require treads to be in place to establish proper height and positioning relative to the finished walking surface.
Stair nosing is applied to the leading edge of treads after the tread surface is installed, as it serves as a finishing trim piece that covers the tread edge.
Floor sockets/boxes are typically cast into or mounted on the finished floor slab, so the concrete slab must be poured and cured first.
Electrical conduits or raceways that supply power/data to the floor box must be laid in the slab or underfloor before the floor box can be connected or set in place.
Rough electrical wiring and conduit stubs must be run to the location of the floor box before the box itself can be installed and terminated.

successor: Floor Finishing / Floor Covering (e.g., tiles, carpet)
rationale: Floor boxes must be set to the correct height and secured before the final floor finish is applied, so that the box cover or lid is flush with the finished floor surface.

After the floor box is physically installed, the final wiring connections, outlet inserts, and cover plates are completed during the electrical trim-out phase, which must happen after the box is fixed in place.
Floor grating is typically supported by the structural steel framework; the steel beams and support members must be in place before grating can be laid or bolted down.

successor: Electrical Conduit & Cable Tray Installation Below Grating
rationale: Once grating is installed, it provides a working platform and access for running electrical conduits, cable trays, or piping below the grating level.

successor: Final Surface Coating / Painting of Grating Area
rationale: Painters may prefer to apply final coatings after grating is in place to ensure uniform coverage, but this can sometimes be done beforehand with touch-ups.
Grating is installed over openings or as part of floor systems that require a stable, level concrete slab or foundation support.
Handrails and guardrails are typically attached to or around grating edges for safety; the grating must be in place to provide the mounting surface and edge alignment.
The floor mat must be placed on a finished, level subfloor or slab. The subfloor must be cleaned and prepared before installing any mat.
If an underlayment is specified beneath the mat, it must be laid down first before the entrance mat is placed on top.

predecessor: Rough-In Electrical (if mat has lighting/heated elements)
rationale: If the entrance mat includes integrated lighting, heating, or other powered features, the electrical rough-in and conduit must be completed before the mat is installed.
Any adjacent floor finishes (tile, vinyl, epoxy, etc.) that abut or overlap the entrance mat should be completed after the mat is placed to ensure proper transitions and alignment.
Doors that swing over or adjacent to the entrance mat must be installed or adjusted after the mat is in place to ensure proper clearance and to avoid catching on the mat.
A smooth, clean, cured subfloor (concrete slab or underlayment) is physically required to support tile and prevent cracking; tiling cannot start until the substrate is ready.
In bathrooms or wet areas, waterproof membrane must be applied and cured before tile installation to prevent moisture damage; this is a hard physical sequencing requirement.
Tiles must be set and the mortar must cure before grout can be applied between tiles; grouting cannot start until all floor tiles are firmly in place.
Baseboards and trim should be installed after tiling so that they overlap the tile edge cleanly and hide expansion gaps; installing before would leave a gap or require removal.
Cabinets, vanities, and heavy fixtures must be placed on top of finished tile flooring to avoid damaging uncured tile and to ensure proper fit and water sealing.
Screed is typically applied over a structural concrete slab. The concrete slab must be poured and sufficiently cured to provide a stable, rigid substrate for the screed layer.
Any underfloor pipes, conduits, or wiring must be laid and inspected before the screed is poured, as they will be embedded and inaccessible afterward.
A damp-proof membrane is laid over the subfloor before screeding to prevent moisture migration into the screed layer.
The finished floor covering (tiles, hardwood, vinyl, etc.) is applied directly on top of the leveled screed once it has fully cured.

Skirting boards and baseboards are typically installed after screeding to cover the gap between the floor and the wall. This is a practical sequence preference but not a strict physical impossibility if done otherwise.

The substrate must be clean, dry, structurally sound, and free of contaminants before self-leveling compound can be applied; otherwise, the compound will not bond properly and may crack or delaminate.
All cracks, spalls, and joints in the concrete slab must be repaired and sealed prior to self-leveling compound application to prevent reflective cracking and ensure a smooth, continuous surface.
A primer must be applied to the prepared substrate to seal it, control suction, and promote adhesion of the self-leveling compound; without priming, the compound may dry unevenly or debond.
The self-leveling compound must be allowed to cure and dry to its specified moisture content and compressive strength before any subsequent floor covering or traffic is applied.

successor: Final Floor Covering Installation (Tile, Wood, Vinyl, Carpet)
rationale: Floor finishes must only be installed after the self-leveling compound has fully cured to provide a flat, level, and stable base; premature installation can cause damage, unevenness, or failure of the finished flooring.
The floor substrate (e.g., concrete slab or screed) must be level, clean, and cured before laying any underfloor heating loops to ensure proper placement and prevent damage to the pipes.
Thermal insulation boards must be placed on the prepared subfloor before the heating loops to prevent heat loss downward and ensure efficient heating.
The manifold and supply/return pipework to the zone must be positioned and roughed-in prior to laying the individual loop circuits so they can be connected properly.
All installed underfloor heating loops must be pressure tested immediately after installation to verify there are no leaks before the screed or floor covering is applied.
A structural screed or self-leveling compound must be poured over the installed heating loops to encase and protect the pipes, and to provide a smooth finished floor surface.
Floor grating is typically installed on or supported by structural steel framework, so the steel structure must be in place before grating can be laid or secured.
Columns provide vertical support and attachment points for grating support beams; they must be erected before grating is placed.
Once grating sections are laid out, they must be welded, clipped, or otherwise permanently fastened to the supporting structure.

Handrails and guardrails are typically installed after grating is in place, as they are often mounted to the grating or the adjacent steel and are needed for fall protection on the completed walking surface.

While some conduit, piping, or cable tray work can be done before or after grating installation, it is often more convenient to complete rough-in work below the grating level before grating is installed to avoid working from below or through hatches.
The subfloor must be smooth, clean, and level before vinyl/linoleum sheets are laid and welded, otherwise the welded seams will fail due to uneven backing.
The vinyl/linoleum sheets must first be installed and positioned before the seams between them can be heat-welded or chemically welded.
After welding is complete, the welded seams need time to cool and cure before the floor can be walked on or subjected to heavy traffic.

successor: Final Cleaning & Buffing of Resilient Floor
rationale: Welding creates excess weld rod material that must be trimmed and the entire floor cleaned and buffed only after welding is finished.
Wall base and cove base are installed after the floor welding is complete so that the base covers the finished floor edge and the welded seams are undisturbed.
Wall sheathing provides the structural backing and flat surface onto which lapped wall flashing is applied; flashing cannot be installed on an open stud wall.
Lapped wall flashing overlaps and integrates with window and door rough openings to direct water away; windows/doors must be in place to properly integrate flashing.
House wrap is typically installed before lapped wall flashing, with the flashing lapped over the wrap to shed water; reversing this order would trap water behind the wrap.
Siding is installed over lapped wall flashing, with the flashing extending out from behind the siding to direct water away from the wall assembly.
Exterior trim pieces (corner boards, window casings) are typically installed after lapped wall flashing, as the flashing runs behind or integrates with these trim elements.
A solid substrate or sheathing (e.g., plywood, OSB, or existing wall surface) must be in place to provide a mounting surface for the battens or counter-battens to be fastened to the wall structure.
The load-bearing wall frame must be completed to support the sheathing and subsequent batten/counter-batten system; battens are attached through sheathing to the framing.

A weather-resistant barrier (e.g., house wrap or building paper) must be installed over the sheathing before adding battens, as the battens create a rainscreen cavity that requires the weather barrier to protect the underlying structure from moisture.

The lapped battens/counter-battens form the vertical furring or rainscreen framework onto which the final external wall cladding (e.g., timber siding, fiber cement, metal panels) is fastened; cladding cannot be installed without the batten support structure in place.

Once the batten cavity is created, ventilation openings or weep holes at the top and bottom of the wall assembly must be provided to allow airflow and drainage within the rainscreen cavity; these are integrated with or installed after the batten system is in place.
The wall sheathing and weather barrier (e.g., house wrap) must be installed first to provide a flat, protected substrate for the trim and corner boards to be attached against.
The wall framing must be complete to provide the structural backing required for mounting trim and corner boards.

While trim can be installed before or after adjacent siding in some sequences, it is often preferred to have siding laid up to the corners first so the lapped trim can cover the siding edges for a clean, weather-resistant finish.
After the trim and corner boards are fastened, all exposed joints, gaps, and penetrations must be caulked and sealed to prevent moisture infiltration and ensure weathertightness.
Trim and corner boards must be fully installed before the final exterior paint or stain finish is applied to protect the material and achieve a uniform appearance.
Wall panels must be in place before fasteners and fixings can be applied to secure them to the structure.
The load-bearing structural frame (studs, tracks, columns) must be fully erected to provide a substrate for lapped wall fasteners and fixings.
Lapped wall fasteners and fixings secure the wall panels; external cladding or finishing layers cannot be installed until the wall assembly is firmly fastened.
Weatherproofing membranes are applied over the fastened wall assembly; without the fasteners in place, the membrane cannot be properly anchored or supported.
Interior finishing work such as drywall or plaster can proceed only after the wall fastenings have been inspected and approved as secure.
The foundation must be prepared and cured to provide a stable base for the lapped wall installation.
The concrete slab must be poured and set before lapped walls can be installed on top of it.
Reinforcement bars must be placed and tied within the foundation or slab to properly integrate with and anchor the lapped wall system.
Inspection of the lapped wall installation must occur after completion to verify structural integrity before proceeding with subsequent work.
Exterior cladding or masonry finishing can only be applied after the lapped wall structure is fully installed and stable.

The wall sheathing provides the structural backing and surface onto which the lapped wall air seal membrane or tape is applied. Without the sheathing in place, there is no substrate to adhere the air seal to.
The wall framing must be complete and inspected before sheathing is installed, and the air seal goes over the sheathing. Framing provides the structural support system.

The lapped wall air seal serves as an air barrier that must be fully installed and continuous before exterior cladding (e.g., siding, brick veneer) is placed over it, as the air seal is designed to be behind the cladding and would be inaccessible afterwards.

While windows/doors are typically installed after the air barrier is in place to allow proper flashing integration with the air seal, in some sequences windows may be installed first with the air seal later lapped to the window flanges. However, best practice prefers air seal continuity first.

The lapped wall air seal must be complete to effectively test the building envelope airtightness. However, blower door testing typically occurs later after all air barriers are complete, not immediately after this single component.
Interior partition walls require a solid, level base for construction. The foundation or slab provides the structural support and bearing surface for the wall framing.

MEP rough-in work (conduit, piping, wiring) within the floor slab or below the wall location must be completed before partition walls are built, otherwise access to those areas would be permanently blocked.

The main structural frame and load-bearing walls must be erected first to define the building's primary grid, so that non-load-bearing interior partitions can be accurately located within the structural bays.
Drywall is directly attached to the partition wall framing. The wall studs and tracks must be fully installed and braced before any finishing layers can be applied.

Electrical wiring, data cables, and plumbing pipes that run inside the wall cavities must be installed after the wall framing is up but before the second side of drywall is closed, to allow access for placement and inspection.
The foundation or slab must be fully cured and in place to provide a stable base for load-bearing and non-load-bearing interior walls.
Underslab plumbing, electrical conduits, and mechanical chases that run beneath or within the floor must be installed before walls are framed over them.
On multi-story buildings, the floor deck or subfloor must be complete to provide a working surface and support for interior wall layout and erection.
Electrical cables, outlet boxes, plumbing pipes, and HVAC ducts that run inside wall cavities can only be installed after the wall framing is erected and open.
Drywall and interior wall finishes cannot be applied until the wall framing is complete, inspected, and all rough-ins are approved.

predecessor: Wall Surface Preparation (e.g., drywall taping and mudding)
rationale: Corner bead must be installed over prepared drywall, after taping and mudding have been applied to provide a smooth base for the bead.
Corner bead must be in place before final finishing and painting so that the bead creates a clean, crisp edge and is fully covered by paint.
The wall framing and drywall must be installed and finished before corner bead can be applied to the corners.
Drywall sheets must be hung and fastened to the framing before corner bead can be installed over the seams and corners.
Primer is applied over the corner bead and drywall finish to seal the surface before painting, so bead installation must come first.
Wall expansion joints must be installed within the framed wall cavity, requiring the framing structure to be in place first.

The expansion joint must be installed within the wall assembly before the interior finish surfaces (e.g., drywall or cladding) are applied, so the joint can properly interface with both sides of the wall.
While not strictly required, it is preferred to complete MEP rough-in before installing expansion joints to avoid cutting through or damaging the joint assembly later.
Paint and texture must be applied after the expansion joint is fully installed and properly integrated into the wall surface to ensure a clean finish and accommodate movement.

The structural frame of the building (including columns, beams, and slabs) must be erected to define the locations where expansion joints are needed, as these joints accommodate movement between adjacent structural elements.
The building's foundation must be fully completed and cured before any interior wall construction can begin, as interior walls require a stable, level base to build upon.
The main structural frame (columns, beams, roof) must be in place to provide the supporting structure that interior walls will tie into.
Floor slabs or decks must be completed to provide the walking surface and support for interior wall placement.
Electrical wiring and outlets are installed within the interior wall cavities after the wall framing is complete.
Plumbing pipes and fixtures must be run inside interior walls after the walls are framed but before wall cladding is applied.
Insulation is placed inside interior wall cavities after framing is complete to improve thermal and acoustic performance.
Drywall or wall finishing materials are applied over the framed interior walls after all rough-in work (electrical, plumbing, insulation) is completed.
The hopper window must be installed into a pre-existing window frame that provides structural support and the mounting surface.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed, measured, and prepared to the correct dimensions before the hopper window unit can be placed.
Weather-resistant barriers and flashing around the opening must be in place before installing the window to prevent water infiltration behind the unit.
After the hopper window is physically set in the opening, gaps must be sealed with foam or caulk and insulated to ensure thermal performance and airtightness.
Interior drywall, casing, and trim work around the window can only be completed after the window unit is fully installed and secured in place.
The rough framing must be complete to create the opening where the projection window will be installed.
The window must be installed before it can be sealed and waterproofed to prevent leaks.
Interior finishing around the window can only be completed after the projection window is installed to ensure proper fit and finish.
Exterior cladding must be installed around the projection window after it is in place to ensure proper integration and weatherproofing.
While not physically required, it is preferred to run electrical wiring after window installation to avoid damage to wiring during the window installation process.
The rough opening (frame) must be constructed, sized, and structurally prepared to receive the sliding window unit. The window cannot be installed without a properly framed opening.
Weather-resistant barrier, sill pan flashing, and window flashing tape must be applied to the rough opening before installing the window to prevent water infiltration and ensure proper drainage.
After the sliding window is set in place, gaps around the frame must be sealed with expanding foam or backer rod and caulked to provide air sealing and thermal insulation.
Interior window trim and casing are installed after the window unit is fully placed and secured to cover the gap between the window frame and the wall finish.
Exterior siding or cladding is installed or completed around the window after it is positioned to create a weathertight seal and a finished appearance.
The jalousie/louvre window slats are mounted within a supporting frame; the frame must be installed first to provide the structural support and mounting surface for the louvre mechanism.
After the jalousie window frame and operating hardware are in place, the individual glass or aluminum slats (louvers) are installed into the frame tracks.
Weatherstripping and sealing around the jalousie window assembly must be applied after the slats and hardware are fully installed to ensure proper fit and airtight closure.
The rough opening in the wall (sized and framed to accommodate the jalousie unit) must be prepared before the window assembly can be placed and secured.
Interior trim work and finishes around the window are typically done after the jalousie unit is installed, though this can sometimes be sequenced differently with careful planning.
The frame opening (rough opening) must be constructed and prepared before the pivot window can be installed, as the window unit fits into the opening.
Waterproof membrane and flashing must be applied around the opening to prevent water ingress before the window is set in place.
The wall structure must be framed to define the rough opening dimensions before the opening is prepared for window installation.
The pivot window frame must be installed first before the glass panels or glazing units are fitted into the frame.
Once the pivot window is installed, gaps around the frame must be sealed and insulated to ensure thermal efficiency and weather tightness.
Interior trim and architraves around the window are typically installed after the window is in place for aesthetic finish, though this is a logical preference rather than a physical necessity.
Exterior cladding around the window is typically completed after window installation for a clean interface, though in some sequences cladding can precede window fitting with careful detailing.
The rough opening must be framed, sized, and prepared to the correct dimensions before the bi-fold window can be installed, as the window fits into the opening.
Proper waterproofing and flashing around the opening must be in place to prevent water intrusion before the window unit is set.
After the window is placed and secured, gaps around the frame must be sealed and insulated for thermal performance and weather tightness.

Interior trim such as casing and drywall finishing around the window is typically done after the window is installed, but this is a soft preference as it could be done simultaneously in some sequences.
Exterior cladding or siding around the window area must be completed after the window is installed to properly integrate with the window frame and flashing.
The tilt-and-turn window must be installed into a prepared and framed opening; the frame provides the structural support and mounting interface for the window unit.
The rough opening must be sized, squared, and weatherproofed before the window can be placed and secured.
Weather-resistive barriers and flashing around the opening must be installed prior to the window to prevent water ingress behind the window frame.
Interior wall finishes, trim, and sealing around the window should be completed after the window is installed to achieve a clean, weathertight fit and proper integration with the wall assembly.
The final exterior perimeter sealant and caulking must be applied after the window is installed and secured to ensure a continuous weather seal.
Window rough openings must be framed and prepared to receive the window frame assembly; the frame cannot be installed without a prepared opening.
Wall sheathing provides structural backing and the rough opening needed for window frame installation; the frame cannot be placed before sheathing is complete.
Glass panes or glazing units are installed into the assembled window frame; the frame must be in place first to support the glass.
Weatherproofing seals, flashings, and caulking are applied around the installed window frame to prevent water intrusion; the frame must be installed first.
While interior wall finishing (drywall, trim) typically follows window installation for a clean finish, it is a soft preference because finishing could theoretically proceed before glazing if needed.
The operable glazing panel (sash) must be installed within a pre-installed frame that supports and guides its operation.
Weatherstripping and sealant application around the sash must occur after the sash is positioned in its frame to ensure proper sealing.
Operating hardware such as hinges, handles, and locks are attached directly to the sash and cannot be installed before the sash is in place.
Testing the smooth opening, closing, and locking of the operable sash can only be performed after the sash is fully installed.

predecessor: Rough Opening Preparation and Weather Barrier
rationale: The rough opening must be prepared with weather barriers and flashings before any window components, including the sash, are installed to prevent water intrusion.
The window frame must be installed first to provide the structural mounting surface for the hinge and hardware set to attach to.
The hinge and hardware set must be mounted to the frame before the window sash can be hung and secured onto the hinges.
The hinge and hardware must be fully installed before testing the window's opening, closing, and locking mechanisms.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to receive the window assembly, which includes the hinge and hardware installation.
While weatherstripping is typically applied after hardware is in place for proper sealing, it could technically be partially installed before, but best practice is after hardware is mounted.
The window crank mechanism must be installed into or onto a window frame that is already in place, as the frame provides the mounting structure and support for the operator.

The crank mechanism must be installed before the glass is set, as the operator hardware often needs access to the frame and sash tracks, and installing glass first would block access or risk damage to the glass during mechanism installation.
Interior and exterior trim around the window should be installed after the operator mechanism is in place to allow for proper alignment, clearance, and adjustment of the crank handle and hardware.
After installing the crank mechanism, it must be tested for smooth operation, proper engagement, and full open/close function before other finishing work closes off access.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed and prepared before any window components, including the crank mechanism, can be installed.
The window balance system is housed within or attached to the window frame; the frame must be installed first to provide structural support.
Window balances support the sash, so the balance system must be in place before the sash is installed to allow proper connection and weight support.
The window balance system must be installed before testing window operation, as the balance controls the smooth opening and closing of the window.
The window frame must be installed before adding any limit stop hardware that attaches to or interacts with the frame.
The window sash must be in place so the limit stop can be positioned correctly relative to the sash travel path.
The limit stop must be installed before testing the window's open range to ensure safe and proper operation.
The wide-open limit stop defines the maximum open position; weatherstripping should be installed after the limit stop is in place to avoid interference or damage.
While not physically required, it is strongly preferred to complete interior wall finishing before installing the limit stop to avoid damaging finished surfaces during limit stop installation work.
The rough opening for windows must be framed and prepared before any window can be set in place, as the window unit needs a structurally complete opening to be installed into.
Exterior wall sheathing must be installed prior to window installation to provide the structural backing and weather-resistant barrier that the window flange or frame attaches to.
The weather-resistant barrier or house wrap must be applied before windows are installed to ensure proper integration of window flashing and to prevent water intrusion behind the window.
Flashings and sealants are applied around the window frame after the window is set in place to create a watertight seal between the window and the surrounding wall assembly.

Interior wall finishes such as drywall or plaster are installed after windows are in place because the window trim and interior finishes need to butt against or wrap around the installed window frame.
The rough opening must be properly prepared (framed, sheathed, and clean) before window flashing can be applied, as flashing seals the gap between the window frame and the rough opening.
Flashing must be completed before exterior cladding (siding, brick, stucco) is applied, as the flashing is integrated into the weather-resistant barrier behind or integrated with the cladding.
The window must be fully sealed and weathertight before interior trim, drywall, or finishes are installed to prevent moisture damage behind finished surfaces.
The window perimeter must be sealed against air and water intrusion before insulation and air barrier materials are applied around the window assembly.
Windows must be physically installed before they can be commissioned and adjusted.
Window frames must be properly sealed and weatherproofed before commissioning to ensure the adjustment process works correctly and no weather infiltration occurs during testing.
Commissioning and adjustment must be completed before applying final finishes and trim, as adjustments may require access to the window frame and surrounding areas.
Window commissioning and adjustment must be complete and verified before the final quality inspection can assess the window's performance.
While interior wall finishing can occur before window commissioning, it is preferable to complete window adjustment first to avoid potential damage to finished surfaces during the adjustment process.

successor: Door Leaf (Solid Core with Glass Panel) Installation
rationale: The door frame must be installed and properly aligned before the door leaf can be hung, as the leaf is mounted onto the frame via hinges.

predecessor: Door Leaf (Solid Core with Glass Panel) Installation
rationale: Door hardware such as locks, handles, and door closers are mounted onto the door leaf itself, so the leaf must be in place before these can be fitted and adjusted.

successor: Door Leaf (Solid Core with Glass Panel) Installation
rationale: The wall rough opening must be fully framed and ready to receive the door assembly before the door leaf can be installed.

predecessor: Door Leaf (Solid Core with Glass Panel) Delivery & Inspection
successor: Door Leaf (Solid Core with Glass Panel) Installation
rationale: The door leaf must be delivered to site and inspected for damage or defects prior to installation.

predecessor: Door Leaf (Solid Core with Glass Panel) Installation
rationale: Once the door leaf is hung, final finishing work such as painting, staining, or touch-ups can be performed on the leaf surface. Installing before finishing avoids damage to finished surfaces.

predecessor: Wall Framing and Rough Opening Preparation
rationale: The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the door frame can be installed, as the frame fits into the opening.
The door frame must be fixed in place and plumb before the door leaf can be hung, as the hinges attach to the frame.
The glazing rebates in the door frame must be in place before glass panels can be installed into those rebates.
The finished floor level should be established before setting the door frame to ensure the correct clearance and alignment at the bottom of the frame.

Typically wall lining is installed after framing but can be done before or after door frame installation; however, it is often easier to install the door frame after the wall sheathing is complete to ensure proper fit and finishing.

The frame opening must be prepared (cleaned, measured, and fitted with necessary components) before the sidelight glazing panel can be installed, as the panel requires a structurally sound and properly dimensioned opening.
The sidelight glazing panel must be in place before sealant can be applied to create a weather-tight seal around its perimeter.
Typically, trim and finishing elements (like interior molding or exterior cladding) are installed after the glazing panel is secured, though this could sometimes be done concurrently.
The structural framing of the wall or door assembly must be completed to provide a stable support framework for the sidelight glazing panel.

Final inspection and performance testing (e.g., water penetration test) are typically conducted after the glazing panel is fully installed, though this is a quality assurance preference rather than a physical necessity.
The rough opening must be framed, sized, and prepared to receive the transom panel. Without a properly prepared opening, the panel cannot be installed.
The transom panel itself must be manufactured, assembled with the glass, and delivered to the site before it can be installed.
After the transom panel is installed, the perimeter must be sealed and weatherproofed to prevent air and water infiltration.
Interior casing, trim, and finishing work around the transom panel typically occur after the panel is securely installed, though this is a soft preference sequence.
Once the transom panel assembly is in place, the final glazing (if separate) and quality inspection must take place to verify proper installation and glass integrity.
The door closer must be mounted on or within the door frame and door leaf; the frame must be in place to provide the structural support and anchor points required for closer installation.
The door closer connects between the door frame and the door leaf; the door leaf must be hung and properly aligned before the closer can be attached and adjusted.
After the closer is installed, the door's closing speed, latch action, and overall hardware coordination must be fine-tuned to ensure proper door operation.

If the door closer is surface-mounted, it is often installed after final painting to avoid getting paint on the unit; however, concealed closers may be installed earlier with trim covers applied after finishing.
The closer must be installed and operational before the door assembly can be inspected, tested for fire/smoke compliance, and commissioned for use.
Hinges must be attached to structural framing or door frames, which require walls and rough framing to be in place first.
Hinges are mounted onto door frames; the frame must be installed and properly aligned before hinges can be attached.
Doors are hung onto hinges; hinges must be fastened to the frame first before the door can be attached.
Locks, latches, and other door hardware are typically installed after the door is hung on hinges, as the door's position affects alignment of these components.
While hinges are installed before final painting touch-ups, it is a soft preference to paint before hinge installation to avoid paint on hardware, but field adjustments may require painting after.

successor: Lock/Latch Set with Key Cylinder Installation
rationale: The lock/latch set cannot be installed on a door until the door itself is installed, hung, and properly aligned within its frame, as the lock requires precise positioning relative to the door edge and strike plate.

successor: Lock/Latch Set with Key Cylinder Installation
rationale: The door frame must be in place and square before the lock can be installed, because the strike plate is mounted on the frame and the lock mechanism must align with it.

successor: Lock/Latch Set with Key Cylinder Installation
rationale: Bored holes for the lockset (cross bore, edge bore, and latch bore) must be pre-drilled in the door before the lockset components can be inserted and fastened.

predecessor: Lock/Latch Set with Key Cylinder Installation
rationale: After the lock/latch set is installed, it must be tested to ensure proper latching, key operation, and alignment, with any necessary adjustments made before the door can be considered finished.

predecessor: Lock/Latch Set with Key Cylinder Installation
successor: Final Door Hardware Trim and Escutcheon Installation
rationale: Any decorative trim, escutcheon plates, or cover plates that go over or around the lockset can only be installed after the lockset mechanism is fully seated and secured in the door.
The door frame must be installed and secured in the opening before door hardware like handles and pulls can be mounted to it.
The door itself must be hung on its hinges before back-to-back handles/pulls can be mounted through both sides of the door slab.

successor: Final door hardware adjustment and testing
rationale: Once the back-to-back handle/pull is installed, the hardware must be adjusted and tested to ensure smooth operation, latch alignment, and proper function.

When the handle/pull integrates with a lockset, the handle/pull is typically installed first as the foundation, then the locking mechanism is added. This is a soft preference as some systems allow simultaneous installation.

Finishing work around the door is often completed before hardware installation to avoid damage, but touch-ups after hardware installation may be needed if the hardware installation mars the finish. This is a soft preference.
The kick plate is attached to the wall framing, so the framing must be in place before the kick plate can be installed.
The kick plate is typically mounted over finished drywall at the base of a wall; drywall must be complete to provide a finished surface for attachment.
The kick plate sits at the bottom of a wall where it meets the floor; the finished flooring must be installed first so the kick plate overlaps the joint properly.
Any touch-up painting or sealing around the kick plate is easier after it is installed, but this is a soft preference as painting could be done before with careful masking.
Corner guards and wall trims often abut or overlap kick plates, so installing kick plates first provides a clean base; however this is a soft preference as order can be swapped with careful fitment.
The intumescent glazing channel must be installed within or onto the glazing system frame; the frame provides the structural support and mounting surface for the channel.
The wall opening or structural rough opening must be framed and ready before the glazing channel can be placed, as the channel is mounted to the building structure.
Fire-resistant boards around the opening are typically installed first to ensure the intumescent channel integrates properly with the fire-rated assembly.
The intumescent channel must be in place to receive and support the glass panel; the channel provides the thermal expansion protection and edge retention for the glazing.
Fire-rated sealants are applied after the channel is installed to seal the perimeter and ensure continuity of the fire-resistive barrier.

successor: Install Solid Door with Glass Assembly
rationale: The door frame must be in place to provide the structural support and mounting surface for the door hinges and hardware.

successor: Install Solid Door with Glass Assembly
rationale: The rough opening must be framed, leveled, and properly sized to accommodate the door unit before installation can begin.

predecessor: Install Solid Door with Glass Assembly
rationale: Door hardware such as locksets, handles, and door closers must be mounted onto the installed door slab after it is hung in the frame.

predecessor: Install Solid Door with Glass Assembly
rationale: Weatherstripping must be applied after the door is hung to ensure proper alignment and sealing around the door edge and frame.

predecessor: Install Solid Door with Glass Assembly
rationale: While painting can be done before installation (pre-finishing), final touch-up painting is typically performed after the door is installed to cover any damage or adjustments.

successor: Install Glazing Panel into Door Leaf
rationale: The door leaf must be physically fabricated before a glazing panel can be installed into it.

successor: Install Glazing Panel into Door Leaf
rationale: The door leaf must be on-site and available before installation of the glazing panel can commence.

predecessor: Prepare Door Leaf Opening (Cut Out / Frame Glazing Rebate)
successor: Install Glazing Panel into Door Leaf
rationale: The door leaf must have the appropriate opening or rebate prepared to receive the glazing panel.

predecessor: Install Glazing Panel into Door Leaf
rationale: Sealing (e.g., glazing compound, gaskets, or silicone) can only be applied after the glazing panel is physically positioned in the opening.

predecessor: Install Glazing Panel into Door Leaf
rationale: The door leaf with the glazing panel installed must be assembled before it can be hung in the door frame.
The light shelf is typically mounted on the building structure (walls or roof) and requires the structural framing to be in place to support it.
Light shelves are often attached to or integrated with exterior walls, curtain walls, or window systems, so the wall/glazing system must be installed first.
Light shelves affect daylight distribution; interior finishes near windows or ceilings are best done after light shelf placement to ensure proper alignment and integration.

successor: Daylighting sensor and lighting control calibration
rationale: Light shelves redirect daylight; sensors and lighting controls must be calibrated after the shelf is installed to measure actual daylight levels correctly.

successor: Final commissioning of daylight harvesting system
rationale: The light shelf is a key component of the daylighting strategy; commissioning cannot be completed until it is in place to verify performance.
Door frames must be in place to provide the structural mounting surface for hinges, latch strike plates, and closers. Hardware cannot be installed without the frame present.

predecessor: Rough-in Electrical for Door Hardware (if electrified)
rationale: Any electrical wiring for powered locks, maglocks, or access control must be roughed-in before hardware installation to allow for proper connection and avoid damaging finished hardware.
Hinges must be installed on the door leaf and frame before the door can be hung. Hanging the door requires hinges to be already attached.

Painting is typically completed before door hardware installation to avoid getting paint on hardware, but if hardware is installed first, it must be masked or removed during painting. This is a soft preference for quality and efficiency.
All hardware (hinges, locks, closers) must be fully installed before the door can be tested for proper swing, latching, closing speed, and security function.
The structural frame must be in place to provide the mounting surface and load-bearing support for the light-directing louvers.
The roof deck (or roof structure) must be completed so that the louvers can be anchored and integrated with the roof system.

It is preferable to install light-directing louvers before interior finishes because the louvers affect the daylighting distribution and interior design layout; however, it is not a strict physical requirement.

The light-directing louvers must be in place before commissioning daylight-responsive lighting controls, as the louvers directly impact the daylight entering the space and the calibration of photosensors.
The structural frame must be in place to provide the load-bearing support onto which the prismatic skylight is mounted.
The roof must be watertight and structurally complete before cutting openings and installing the skylight to prevent water damage and ensure proper flashing integration.

The skylight must be installed and sealed before interior ceiling work begins so that the ceiling finishes can be trimmed neatly around the skylight shaft and any light wells can be properly constructed.
Daylight-harvesting sensors and controls are typically integrated with the skylight; they must be wired and positioned after the skylight is in place to properly sense the incoming light.
The skylight installation must be completed and sealed so that a quality-assurance inspection can verify watertightness, thermal performance, and structural integrity before the building is enclosed.

The lightshelf bracket and support assembly must be mounted to the structural steel framework of the building. The steel structure provides the load-bearing anchor points for the brackets and supports, so it must be erected and stabilized first.

predecessor: Exterior Wall Sheathing / Cladding (Rough Openings Prepared)
rationale: Lightshelves are typically installed at window or curtain-wall openings. The exterior wall sheathing must be complete and the rough openings framed out so the bracket supports have a defined mounting surface and alignment reference.
The brackets and support arms must be securely attached to the structure before the lightshelf panel itself can be placed onto them. The shelf panel relies on the brackets for structural support.

successor: Glazing / Window Frame Installation (around lightshelf zone)
rationale: The lightshelf bracket assembly defines the vertical and horizontal position of the shelf within the glazing opening. Window frames and glass are installed after the brackets are in place to ensure proper fit and sealing around the shelf supports.
Light shelves are typically mounted on exterior walls or above windows; the wall framing must be in place to provide structural support for the shelf brackets and mounting hardware.
Light shelves are positioned relative to windows to reflect daylight deeper into the space; windows/glazing must be installed first to establish the proper alignment and clearance for the shelf.
Rough electrical work (conduit, junction boxes) near windows or upper walls must be completed before light shelf installation to avoid interference and rework.
Light shelves are often integrated with the interior finish; painting and drywall should follow shelf installation to achieve clean edges and seamless integration.

While not a hard physical constraint, commissioning daylight-responsive lighting controls is best done after light shelves are in place so sensors can be calibrated to the actual daylight distribution created by the shelves.
The light tube system must be installed through the roof deck; therefore, the roof deck must be in place first to provide the structural surface for penetration and flashing.
Light tubes require clear shaft pathways through the framing; rough framing must be complete to define the spaces and openings through which the light tubes will pass.
The ceiling finish must be installed after the light tube is in place, as the light tube's diffuser and trim integrate into the finished ceiling surface.
After the light tube is installed through the roof, the roof flashing and waterproofing around the tube must be completed to prevent leaks.
While it is typical to paint after light tube installation so that the trim can be cut in neatly, this is a preference for finish quality rather than a physical necessity.
Glazing panels must be fabricated and delivered to site before they can be installed.
The structural frame must be in place to provide the supporting framework for glazing installation.
Mullions and frames must be installed to provide the physical mounting points for diffusing glazing panels.
Weather sealing can only be applied after the glazing panels are in place to ensure a proper seal around the installed panels.
Water tightness testing of the glazing assembly must occur after installation to verify performance, though in some sequences testing could be partially staged.

successor: Install Interior Finishes (if adjacent to glazing)
rationale: Interior finishes adjacent to glazing (e.g., drywall, trim) should be installed after glazing to avoid damage and ensure proper fit and alignment.

predecessor: Complete Structural Framing and Roof Deck
rationale: The structural framing and roof deck must be in place to provide a supporting substrate and opening for the skylight installation.
Roof waterproofing and underlayment must be applied around the rough opening to prevent water intrusion before the skylight unit is installed.
Flashing must be installed around the skylight after the unit is set in place to seal the penetration and direct water away from the opening.
Interior ceiling finishes around the skylight shaft should be completed after the skylight is installed to ensure proper alignment, sealing, and a clean finished edge.

successor: Complete Interior Electrical Rough-in for Skylight Area
rationale: While electrical rough-in can often be done in parallel, any wiring or fixtures integrated with or immediately adjacent to the skylight should ideally follow skylight placement to avoid interference and ensure accurate positioning.

successor: Window pane with small-divided lights installation
rationale: The window frame must be installed first to provide the structural support and casing into which the divided-light window pane can be fitted.

predecessor: Window pane with small-divided lights installation
rationale: The divided-light pane must be in place before glazing compound, putty, or sealant can be applied to secure it and make it weathertight.

predecessor: Window pane with small-divided lights installation
rationale: Interior window trim or casing is typically installed after the window pane is set, but this is a soft preference as it could in theory be done concurrently.

successor: Window pane with small-divided lights installation
rationale: The rough opening in the wall must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before any window assembly, including a divided-light pane, can be installed.

predecessor: Window pane with small-divided lights installation
rationale: Exterior weatherproofing details such as flashing, caulking, and trim must be completed after the window pane is installed to ensure a watertight seal around the assembly.
Muntin/grille bars are decorative or structural elements that sit within the window frame; the frame must be in place first to provide the structural boundary and support for the bars.
Muntin/grille bars are typically installed between or over glass panes to create divided-light appearances; the glass must be in place before adding the grille bars.
Final sealing and weatherproofing must be applied after the muntin/grille bars are installed to ensure the assembly is watertight and secure.

Interior finishes around the window are typically completed after the window components including grille bars are installed to ensure a clean, integrated appearance; this is a practical sequencing preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The completed window assembly including muntin/grille bars must be inspected before the window is considered fully installed and operational.
The rough opening frame must be installed and properly sized before the TDL sash can be fitted into it.
The window frame (including jambs and head) must be in place to receive the TDL sash.
Weatherproofing must be applied around the window opening before installing the sash to ensure proper sealing and moisture protection.
After the TDL sash is installed, individual glass panes (lights) must be set into the divided muntins and glazed with putty or sealant.
Interior trim and casing around the window can only be installed after the TDL sash is in place and properly aligned.
Exterior trim and flashing must be installed after the TDL sash to seal and finish the window assembly.
Final caulking and sealing around the sash edges can only be done after the sash is fully installed and secured.
Painting or finishing the sash and surrounding frame is typically done after installation, though in some cases pre-finishing may occur before installation.

The SDL sash components (mullions, muntins, spacers) must be integrated into the frame structure; the frame must be assembled first to provide the structural support and perimeter for the SDL grid installation.
Glass panes must be cut, cleaned, and prepared before they can be placed into the SDL sash, as the simulated dividers are applied onto or between the glass layers within the sash assembly process.
The simulated dividing bars (mullions and muntins) must be fabricated and cut to size before they can be installed into the sash during the assembly process.
After the SDL sash is fully assembled with glass and simulated dividers in place, sealants and glazing compounds must be applied to weatherproof the unit and secure the glass within the sash.
The completed SDL sash assembly must undergo quality control testing to verify proper sealing, divider alignment, and structural integrity before it can be approved for installation or shipment.

predecessor: Rough opening framing for transom window
rationale: The rough opening must be framed in the wall before the transom window unit can be installed into that opening.

successor: Interior trim and casing around transom window
rationale: Trim and casing are applied around the installed window to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance; the window must be in place first.
The window must be installed before any painting or finishing of its frame and surrounding surfaces can be completed, as painting after installation ensures seamless coverage.
The wall structure, including studs and sheathing, must be completed to provide the supporting framework into which the transom window is installed.
Drywall finishing around the window opening is done after the window is installed to ensure proper fit and seamless integration between drywall and window frame.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to provide the structural support and correct dimensions for installing the window assembly.
The window sill must be in place to provide a level base and support for the casement window assembly.
Weatherproofing must be applied around the rough opening to prevent moisture intrusion before the window is installed.
Interior and exterior trim/casing is installed after the window is in place to cover the gap between the window frame and the rough opening.
Flashing is applied over the window flanges after installation to direct water away and complete the weather-resistant barrier.
The window opening must be framed, sheathed, and weatherproofed to provide a structurally sound and weathertight cavity into which the window assembly can be installed.
The sill pan and flashing must be in place before setting the window to ensure proper water drainage and prevent moisture intrusion behind the window frame.
The weather-resistive barrier must be installed and properly integrated with window flashing details to create a continuous water shedding plane before the window is placed.
Interior and exterior trim, casing, and stop beads are applied after the window unit is secured in the opening to cover the gap between the window frame and the rough opening.
Interior wall finishes must be completed after the window is installed so that the wallboard or plaster can be fitted neatly against the window frame and jamb extensions.
The rough opening frame must be built and structurally ready to receive the window assembly before the window can be installed.
The weather-resistant barrier must be in place before window installation to ensure proper water management and flashing integration.
After the window assembly is placed, the perimeter must be flashed and sealed to prevent water infiltration.
Interior trim work is typically done after the window is in place, but this is a preference for finish sequencing rather than a physical necessity.
Exterior siding must terminate or be trimmed against the installed window frame to create a weathertight seal.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared before any window sash can be installed, as the sash needs a structural opening to be placed into.
The main window frame or buck must be installed first to provide the surrounding structure that the sash hinges or fits into.
Weather-resistant barriers and flashing must be applied before the sash is installed to prevent water intrusion behind the window assembly.

successor: Interior trim and casing around sash
rationale: Interior trim work around the window must follow sash installation because the trim covers the gap between sash/frame and the finished wall surface.

successor: Exterior glazing and putty / sealant application
rationale: Exterior glazing compound, putty, or sealant around the small panes is applied after the sash is in place to ensure the glass is properly bedded and sealed.

successor: Install cam lock/keeper for small-pane sash
rationale: The cam lock/keeper is a hardware component mounted onto the sash; the sash must be in place and assembled before the cam lock/keeper can be installed on it.

successor: Install cam lock/keeper for small-pane sash
rationale: The sash frame must be fully fabricated and assembled to provide the structural substrate for mounting the cam lock and keeper components.

predecessor: Install cam lock/keeper for small-pane sash
rationale: The locking mechanism cannot be tested or operated until the cam lock and keeper hardware are physically installed on the sash.

predecessor: Install cam lock/keeper for small-pane sash
rationale: The lock hardware must be attached to the sash before the sash is placed into its final frame/opening, as access for hardware installation is easier and safer with the sash out of the opening.

predecessor: Install cam lock/keeper for small-pane sash
rationale: After installation, the cam lock and keeper need final alignment and adjustment against the mating strike plate or keeper on the frame to ensure proper operation.
The wall structure must be in place to provide the rough opening and support for the window frame.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed and sized correctly before the window frame can be installed into it.
Flashing and weather-resistant barriers around the rough opening must be applied first to ensure water tightness behind and under the window frame.
The window frame must be securely installed in the opening before glass panes can be fitted into the frame.
Trim and casing are typically installed after the window frame is in place to cover the gap between frame and wall; this is standard practice but can be done concurrently in some cases.
The storm window must be mounted onto or within an existing window frame; the frame provides the structural support and attachment points.
Storm windows are typically installed over existing primary windows; the primary window must be in place first to provide the base and seal.
After the storm window is installed, the gaps around it must be sealed and weatherproofed to prevent air and water infiltration.
It is preferable to complete storm window installation before installing interior window trim to ensure proper fit and access for adjustments, though it is not physically impossible to do trim first.
The rough opening (window frame) must be built into the wall structure to provide a stable, dimensionally accurate opening for the window to be installed into.

The weather-resistant barrier must be applied to the exterior wall before window installation so that the window can be properly integrated with the WRB for water tightness and to prevent moisture intrusion behind the window.
Exterior wall sheathing provides structural rigidity and a substrate for the window flashing and trim; windows are typically installed after sheathing is in place.
Flashing and sealant must be applied around the window after it is set into the opening to waterproof the interface between the window and the wall assembly.
The window must be installed before interior finishes around the window (such as drywall returns, casing trim, and sill) can be completed, as these finishes abut the window frame.
The window frame must be in place to provide a structure to receive and support the small-pane glass units.
The rough opening must be prepared, framed, and weatherproofed before glazing can be installed.
The dividing bars (mullions and muntins) that create the small-pane grid must be installed first to define the openings for each small pane.
The small panes must be set in place before sealant can be applied to weatherproof the edges and secure the glass.
While trim can be installed after glazing for a cleaner finish, it is a soft preference as trim could theoretically be installed before if carefully coordinated.
Weatherstripping must be applied to installed window frames; the frame provides the surface and structure for the weatherstripping material to adhere to.
The window panes must be installed in the frame before weatherstripping can be applied around them to seal gaps.
Weatherstripping is typically applied before trim is installed, as trim often covers or abuts the weatherstripping edges.
It is practical to test window operation after weatherstripping is applied to ensure the seal does not interfere with opening and closing, though testing could theoretically be done earlier.
Weatherstripping should be in place before final interior finishing around the window to create clean sealed edges.
The window frame must be in place before any hardware (hinges, latches, locks, handles) can be attached to it.
Glass panes must be set and secured in the frame before installing hardware such as latches or locks that interface with the glass or sash.
Hardware must be fully installed before the window can be tested for proper operation (opening, closing, locking).
While weatherstripping can sometimes be done concurrently, it is typically easier to install after hardware is in place to ensure proper fit and sealing around operating hardware components.
Trim work should be completed after hardware installation to avoid damaging surrounding finishes and to ensure proper alignment of hardware with trim elements.
The old window must be removed from its frame before restoration and reglazing work can begin on the individual panes.
Scaffolding or access equipment must be erected to safely reach the windows before restoration work can start.
The restored panes must be completed and cured before the window unit can be reinstalled into its opening.

successor: Paint removal and surface preparation (window frames)
rationale: It is preferable to complete reglazing before painting the frames to avoid damaging fresh paint during glass installation, though not a physical necessity.
The restored windows must be fully installed and sealed before interior trim, moldings, and finishes are applied around the window opening.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and enclosure into which the mullion and window assembly will be installed.

successor: Install small-pane window units into mullion assembly
rationale: The mullion must be in place to define the vertical dividers between window panes before the individual window units can be set and secured against it.

successor: Apply exterior trim and flashing around mullion
rationale: Exterior weatherproofing details (trim, flashing) are installed after the mullion is fixed in place to seal the joints and prevent water intrusion around the mullion-to-frame interface.

Interior finishes can begin after the mullion and windows are installed, but this is a logical sequencing preference rather than a strict physical necessity, as some finishing could be done concurrently.

The exterior wall sheathing and weather resistant barrier must be in place before mullions are installed so that the mullion can be integrated into the building envelope with proper flashing and waterproofing.
Structural framing provides the underlying support system; trim fasteners cannot be attached until the main structural frame is in place to receive them.
Rough-in inspections for MEP systems must be completed before covering works with trim, as trim fasteners would obstruct access to rough-in components.
Sheathing or decking provides the substrate into which trim fasteners are driven; the substrate surface must exist before fasteners can be installed.
Trim fasteners secure trim pieces which serve as a mounting or finishing base for final cladding; cladding cannot be properly aligned and secured without the underlying trim being fastened.
Caulking and sealants are applied over and around installed and fastened trim to create watertight seals; trim must be securely fastened before sealants can be applied effectively.
The coped joint is cut into the web of a steel beam, so the beam must first be fabricated/installed before the coping cut can be made to fit around an adjacent beam.
Coped joints are formed at the ends of steel beams where they connect to other beams or girders, requiring the primary steel framing to be in place.
After the cope is cut, the beam end can be fitted and connected to the supporting beam or girder via bolting or welding.
The coped end of a beam is specifically prepared to facilitate connection to a girder, so the coping must precede the final connection assembly.
