Cope location, depth, and length must be specified in shop drawings before the cope can be fabricated in the beam web.
The angle must be measured and marked on the material before cutting to ensure accurate alignment.
The material (e.g., trim, molding, or baseboard) must be selected, cut to approximate length, and prepared before creating the mitered corner.
After cutting the mitered corner, the pieces must be dry-fitted together to verify the angle and alignment before final assembly.
The mitered joint must be cut and fit-checked before applying glue, nails, or screws to secure the corner permanently.
Any gaps or imperfections at the mitered corner must be filled with wood filler and sanded smooth only after the corner is assembled and fastened.
Crown molding is attached to walls and ceilings; wall framing and sheathing must be complete to provide a surface for installation.
Crown molding is installed where walls meet ceilings; the ceiling drywall must be in place to provide a finished surface and reference for molding placement.
Crown molding is mounted on walls; drywall must be installed, taped, and finished (mudded/sanded) before molding can be attached flush to the wall surface.

Painting must be done after crown molding installation because the molding joints and nail holes need to be caulked, filled, and painted along with the rest of the trim, and painting before installation would result in unfinished transitions.

While ideally flooring is installed before trim for a clean look, this is a soft preference; crown molding is on the ceiling/wall junction and does not physically interfere with flooring, so flooring could precede or follow without structural conflict.

Baseboard trim must be installed after wall finishing is complete because the trim is nailed to the finished wall surface. Drywall, taping, mudding, and sanding create dust and require unobstructed access to the wall surface, which would be blocked by installed trim.

Baseboard trim is typically installed after the finished flooring is laid, as the trim sits on top of the finished floor and covers the expansion gap between the floor and the wall. Installing baseboard first would make proper flooring installation difficult.

Walls should be painted before baseboard installation because painting after trim is installed requires careful taping and risks getting paint on the trim. Painting first allows for a clean edge and faster work.

successor: Carpet/Flooring Base Shoe or Quarter Round Installation
rationale: If a flexible base shoe or quarter round is used to cover the gap between the baseboard and the floor, it is installed after the baseboard. However, this is a soft preference depending on the flooring type — sometimes base shoe is installed after carpet for a cleaner look.
After baseboard trim is installed, nail holes need to be filled, caulk applied along the top edge where trim meets the wall, and touch-up painting performed to create a seamless finish.
Casing trim is attached to wall frames; framing provides the structural surface for trim installation.
Casing trim is typically installed around doors; doors must be in place to trim around them.
Casing trim is installed around windows; windows must be set before trim can be applied.
Drywall provides the finished wall surface to which casing trim is nailed or glued; trim cannot be installed on open studs.
While trim is often pre-primed, final painting or touch-up of casing trim typically occurs after installation.

In many sequences, flooring is installed before base and casing trim to allow for proper gaps, but if flooring is installed after, the casing trim may need to be undercut. This is a soft preference as sequence can vary.
Chair rail must be attached to a framed wall structure; without wall framing there is no surface to mount the chair rail.
Chair rail is typically installed over finished drywall; the drywall provides the finished surface that the chair rail is mounted to.
Drywall joints must be taped, mudded, and sanded smooth before installing trim and chair rail to ensure a flat, finished surface behind the chair rail.

The chair rail must be installed before final painting so that paint can be applied continuously over both the wall and the chair rail, or so the chair rail can be painted separately but still integrated with the wall finish.
Chair rails and baseboards are often installed in sequence from top to bottom; however, this is a soft preference for workflow efficiency rather than a strict physical necessity.
The picture rail needs to be mounted on the wall surface, so wall framing must be complete to provide the structural support for attaching the rail.
Picture rails are typically installed over finished drywall, so drywall must be hung and finished before the picture rail can be mounted.
While picture rails can be painted separately, it is often preferred to complete painting after installation so the rail can be painted to match the wall or trim, and paint lines are clean.

It is common to install picture rails before or alongside crown molding and baseboards, as the rail is often integrated with the trim scheme, but this is a sequencing preference rather than a hard constraint.
Shoe molding is typically installed after the main flooring (e.g., hardwood, laminate, or tile) is laid, as it covers the expansion gap between the flooring and the baseboard.
Shoe molding is installed at the bottom of the baseboard to cover the gap between the baseboard and the flooring, so baseboards must be in place first.

While touch-up painting is often done after shoe molding installation to cover nail holes and seams, this is a soft preference because painting can also be done before installation if pre-finished molding is used.
The final inspection of floor trim work can only be performed after all shoe molding has been fully installed and secured.
Corner guards are installed over drywall to protect corners; drywall must be in place first.

predecessor: Finish taping and mudding of drywall joints
rationale: Drywall finishing (taping, mudding, sanding) must be completed before corner guards are installed, as they would interfere with finishing work and be damaged by subsequent sanding.

While corner guards can be installed before or after priming, priming before installation provides a cleaner finish and protects the drywall; typically a preference for better adhesion and appearance.
Corner guards can be painted over along with walls, though some installers prefer painting before installation to avoid paint buildup on the guard. This is a soft preference.
Corner guards typically terminate at or above baseboard height, so baseboards can be installed before or after; but corner guards are often installed first to allow trim to butt against them cleanly.
Trim must be installed and in place before it can be primed and painted, as priming and painting are finishing applied to the installed material surface.
Rough carpentry (framing) must be completed before trim can be installed, as trim attaches to framed walls and openings.
Once trim is painted, final cleanup and touch-up work can proceed, as the painted surfaces are complete and need protection from further finishing work.
Trim painting should be completed before flooring installation to prevent paint drips, overspray, or damage to finished flooring surfaces.
Trim (e.g., baseboards, casings) is attached to framed walls and rough openings; framing provides the structural surface to which trim is fastened.
Sheathing encloses the frame and provides a flat substrate; trim is installed over sheathed walls.
Electrical wires must be run inside walls before trim can be installed, as trim like baseboards and casings would block access to wall cavities.
Plumbing pipes and drains must be roughed in within wall cavities before trim encloses those areas.
Insulation fills wall cavities before they are closed off by trim; trim cannot be removed easily to add insulation later.
Drywall must be hung, taped, mudded, and sanded before trim is applied, as trim covers the gaps and edges between drywall sheets and the floor/window/door frames.
It is common practice to paint or prime walls before installing trim so that paint lines are crisp and trim sits cleanly against finished walls; painting after trim requires careful taping.

Baseboard trim typically sits on top of finished flooring; installing flooring first ensures the baseboard covers the expansion gap and sits flush. However, some installers prefer to trim first and run flooring up to it.
Trim is often painted or stained after installation to avoid damaging pre-finished surfaces during handling and nailing.
In kitchens and bathrooms, cabinets may be installed before or after trim; however, installing cabinets first can simplify baseboard runs along cabinet toe kicks.
Trim (casing around doors/windows) creates the finished opening; outlet and switch cover plates are installed after trim is in place to fit properly.
Trim pieces must be fully installed and secured in place before caulking can be applied, as caulk seals the gaps between the trim and the wall or adjacent surfaces.

While not always strictly required, it is best practice to have the wall surfaces painted or primed before caulking to avoid painting over caulk later, but caulking can also be done before final paint if the trim itself is unfinished.
Caulking must be fully applied and allowed to cure/set before the trim can be painted or stained, as painting over uncured caulk will ruin the finish and caulk must seal gaps first.

After caulking, any final touch-up painting on the walls adjacent to the caulk line is typically done to ensure a clean finished look, but this is a sequencing preference rather than a strict physical requirement.
The concrete slab or foundation must be fully cured and load-bearing before bench seating can be installed to provide a stable, level base.
Bench seating must be in place before seat numbers or labels can be affixed to the individual seats.
All bench seating must be fully installed before the final quality inspection and commissioning of the seating area can be completed.
The scarf joint is a method of joining two pieces of timber end-to-end. The timber pieces must be selected, cut, and prepared before the scarf joint can be formed.
The angled or shaped faces of the scarf joint must be cut into the timber ends before the joint can be assembled.
After the scarf joint is fitted together, adhesive must be applied and the joint clamped to secure the connection.
Mechanical fasteners are typically added after the scarf joint is assembled to reinforce the connection.
The assembled scarf joint must be sanded smooth and finished to blend with the surrounding timber surface.
The seat row spacing tread must be set on a completed structural slab or deck that provides the stable base surface.
Layout lines for each seat row must be marked on the slab to define the exact positions before installing the tread components.
Seats must be bolted or anchored onto the tread components; the tread provides the mounting surface and correct spacing for seat attachment.
In stepped seating layouts, the riser (vertical face between rows) is typically installed after the tread to close the gap.
After tread placement, a verification of row alignment and spacing is recommended to confirm compliance with design before proceeding with seat installation.
Seats must be physically installed in their designated positions before numbering plates and wayfinding signage can be applied, as the numbering references the actual seat locations.

Floor finishes (e.g., tiling, carpeting, or concrete sealing) need to be completed before installing wayfinding plates, as plates are often affixed to the floor and would be damaged or covered during finishing work.

Seat numbering and wayfinding plates must be in place for the final inspection and commissioning to verify that all seating is correctly labeled and that wayfinding signage meets safety and navigation requirements.
The venue cannot be opened or handed over to the client/operator until all seat numbering and wayfinding plates are installed, as these are essential for visitor orientation and emergency egress.
The armrest and cup holder unit attaches to the seat frame structure, so the seat frame must be assembled first to provide a mounting base.
Installing the armrest/cup holder unit before upholstery and trim finishing ensures that the armrest structure is in place and can be properly covered or integrated with the final trim materials.

predecessor: Seat Track and Adjustment Mechanism Installation
rationale: The seat frame must be mounted on the tracks/adjustment mechanism before the armrest can be aligned correctly relative to the seat position.
If the armrest contains power adjustment switches or cup holder lighting, the electrical connections can be finalized after installation, though some pre-wiring may also be done beforehand.

predecessor: Structural Welding and Metal Framework Completion
rationale: The metal framework of the seat that supports the armrest must be fully welded and inspected before the armrest/cup holder component is attached.
The fold-down seat mechanism requires a stable frame structure to be installed first, as it will be mounted onto or within the frame assembly.
The seat mechanism (folding brackets, hinges, and structural support) must be in place before cushions and upholstery can be attached onto it.

predecessor: Floor Panel or Mounting Bracket Installation
rationale: The fold-down seat mechanism needs floor panels or dedicated mounting brackets to be installed as its base anchoring point before it can be secured.
Seatbelt anchors are often integrated with or mounted directly to the fold-down seat structure, so the seat mechanism must be in place before belts can be attached.

It is easier and more efficient to install trim panels and interior finishing after the seat mechanism is mounted, though in some cases trim could be pre-installed if designed for it; thus it is a soft preference for workflow efficiency.
The seating layout must be planned first to determine the location and spacing requirements for the accessible companion seat.
A level and stable floor surface must be in place to support the seat anchorage and provide proper wheelchair access.

predecessor: Accessibility Route / Path of Travel Construction
rationale: The accessible path leading to the companion seat must be built first to ensure wheelchair users can reach the seat location.
The companion seat frame and structure must be installed before applying final finishes or upholstery to the seat.
The companion seat installation must be complete before the final accessibility inspection can verify that the seat meets code requirements for clearances, positioning, and accessibility.
Underfloor heating pipes and components must be installed and tested before seats are placed to avoid damage to heating elements and ensure accessibility for maintenance.
Electrical outlets and floor boxes for seating areas must be roughed in and wired before seats are installed, as seats would block access to these elements.
The finished floor surface must be fully completed and cured before seats are installed to prevent damage to flooring and ensure the seats are mounted on the permanent finished surface.
The structural slab must be fully cured and load-bearing before any seat anchorage or installation can proceed.
Seats must be installed before final audio/visual system tuning and integration can occur, as seating positions affect sightlines and sound calibration.

The foundation and substructure must be completed to provide a stable load-bearing base for the riser and tier construction. Without a properly constructed foundation, the vertical riser elements and tiered seating cannot be safely supported.
The riser and tier structural framework must be fully constructed before seating can be installed, as seating platforms and chairs are mounted directly onto the tiered structure.
Handrails and safety barriers are attached to the completed riser and tier structure, and their installation requires the underlying tier geometry to be fully in place.

While it is more efficient to run utilities after the riser structure is built, some rough-in work could theoretically be coordinated concurrently. However, best practice places this after tier completion to avoid rework.

predecessor: Steel Reinforcement & Concrete Placement for Lower Levels
rationale: Lower level concrete and steel work must be completed to form the base upon which successive riser and tier elements are constructed, especially in cast-in-place stadium or amphitheater construction.
Concrete must be fully cured to provide sufficient strength and dimensional stability for anchoring seat anchor points.
The surface must be clean, level, and free of debris to ensure accurate placement and secure fixing of seat anchor points.
Embedded anchors or reinforcement for seat fixings must be in place before anchor point setting can proceed.
Anchor points must be fixed and set before the seat frames can be bolted or welded onto them.
After setting the anchor points, grout must be applied and cured to lock the anchors in place before any load is applied.
A stable foundation is required to support the bench seat structure; without foundation preparation, the bench seat cannot be securely placed.
The bench seat is typically installed on or anchored to a concrete slab or base which must be cured before installation.
The bench seat structure must be fully installed before applying any surface finishes such as sealing, painting, or coating to the seating surface.
While landscaping can be done simultaneously, it is preferred to install the bench seat first to avoid damaging newly planted areas and to ensure proper alignment with pathways and green spaces.
The bench frame requires a stable, level foundation to be placed on, so foundation preparation must be completed first.
The bench frame serves as the structural support for the bench surface; the surface cannot be installed until the frame is in place.
The backrest is typically mounted to the bench frame structure, so the frame must be assembled first.
The raw materials for the frame must be acquired before fabrication and assembly of the bench frame can begin.
The frame must be fully assembled and welded before surface finishing treatments can be applied.
The armrests must be attached to the bench frame, which requires the frame to be fully assembled first to provide a stable structure for mounting.
In many bench designs, the armrests must be installed before the seat cushions or seat panels to allow proper access for fastening hardware and alignment.
After armrests are installed, any final cosmetic trimming, edge finishing, or painting touch-ups can be done to ensure a seamless appearance.
The bench frame must be fully assembled and stable before the backrest can be attached, as the backrest mounts to and relies on the frame for structural support.
The backrest must be placed in position before it can be permanently fastened or secured with bolts/screws.
Typically the backrest should be installed before final painting or sealing to ensure seamless coating, though it could be repainted later if needed.
The ground surface or floor where the bench sits must be prepared and level before installing the backrest to ensure proper alignment and stability.
The backrest must be fully installed before load testing or safety inspections can verify its structural integrity and compliance.
Bench leg/base anchors require a cured concrete foundation or slab to be in place to provide structural support and a solid substrate for drilling or embedding anchor bolts.
Anchor positions must be accurately marked on the foundation according to the bench design drawings before anchors can be installed to ensure correct alignment and spacing.
The bench frame and seat assembly must be bolted or secured onto the installed anchors; therefore the anchors must be in place first as the attachment points.
Anchor bolts need to be initially set and embedded; final torqueing and tightening to specified values must occur after the bench legs are positioned on the anchors.

successor: Final Alignment and Leveling of Bench
rationale: The bench legs must be anchored before the full bench assembly can be aligned and leveled to final tolerances, as the anchors provide fixed reference points.
Ground must be excavated to proper depth and dimensions before the structural support wall can be poured or constructed
A footing or foundation base must be set and cured before the wall can be built upon it to ensure structural stability and load distribution

predecessor: Rebar / Reinforcement Installation for Support Wall
rationale: Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured for the structural wall
Formwork molds must be erected and secured before concrete can be poured to shape the structural support wall
The structural support wall must be fully cured and load-bearing before the bench seat or top slab can be installed or poured on top of it
The structural wall must be completed and cured before waterproofing membrane can be applied and backfill placed against it
The concrete slab must be cured and hardened to provide a stable, level base for assembling and anchoring the bench frame.
All frame components (lumber, hardware, fasteners) must be on-site before assembly can begin.
The bench frame provides the structural support onto which seat planks are fastened.
The frame should be fully assembled before finishing/sealing to ensure complete coverage of all joints and surfaces.
The bench must be fully assembled before it can be positioned and bolted/anchored to the concrete slab.
Concrete must be poured and cured to provide a solid, level base for bench anchor bolts or embedments.
Anchor bolts or embedments must be set in the foundation before the bench anchorage can be bolted or welded into place.
The anchorage must be installed first so that the bench frame or seat structure can be secured to it.
After anchorage is installed, final alignment and bolt tightening ensures the bench is properly positioned and secured.

If safety railings are adjacent to the bench area, they are typically installed after bench anchorage to avoid interference, though this is a preference for construction sequencing rather than a physical necessity.
The bench seat and backrest require a stable, level concrete slab as their supporting base. The slab must be fully cured and structurally ready before the bench can be anchored or installed onto it.
The steel frame substructure for the bench must be prefabricated and available on-site before the seat and backrest components can be installed.
The protective coating or sealant should be applied only after the bench seat and backrest are fully installed, so the coating covers all exterior surfaces and joints properly.

While safety bollards are often installed after the bench is in place to protect it, they could theoretically be placed before; however, sequencing installation after the bench ensures proper alignment and spacing relative to the actual bench location.
The bench must be installed and in its final position before the joint between the bench and the building can be sealed, as the sealant fills the gap created by the installed bench.
The surfaces at the joint interface must be cleaned, primed, and prepared before applying sealant to ensure proper adhesion.
Backfill material must not be placed against the bench until the joint seal is complete, as the seal protects the interface and backfill could displace or damage uncured sealant.
The sealed joint must be inspected for continuity and integrity before any subsequent work that could cover or obscure it.
Final finishes near the bench-to-building interface should be applied only after the sealant is installed and cured to avoid contaminating or damaging the seal.
The cushion is a finishing element; once installed, final touch-ups and inspections can proceed, though this ordering is a soft preference to avoid damaging the cushion during other work.

The sitting wall bench is typically a masonry or cast-in-place concrete element that requires a stable, level foundation. The concrete slab or footing must be poured and cured before any wall construction can begin.

predecessor: Rough-in MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing) Underground Work
rationale: Any underground conduits, drainage, or electrical lines that pass beneath or near the bench location must be installed and inspected prior to bench construction to avoid costly rework or damage.
The ground surface must be graded and compacted to the correct elevation and slope to provide a stable subgrade for the bench foundation.
After the bench structure (concrete block or poured concrete) is built and cured, final surface finishes such as plaster, tile, or stone veneer can be applied.
Landscaping, soil backfill, and planting adjacent to the bench can only proceed after the bench structure is fully completed and cured, to avoid disturbing or damaging the bench.

The foundation or base structure for the sitting wall must be prepared and cured before the backrest component can be installed, as the backrest requires a stable base for proper alignment and structural support.
The main body or base of the sitting wall must be constructed to the required height before the backrest can be added, ensuring correct positioning and structural integration.
The backrest must be fully installed and secured before any finishing treatments (such as sealing, painting, or applying surface coatings) can be applied to ensure complete coverage and protection.
While not physically required, it is standard practice to complete the backrest installation before conducting quality inspections to verify structural integrity and compliance with specifications.

Installing the backrest first prevents damage to finished landscaping or cleanup areas from construction activities, though final landscaping could theoretically be done simultaneously or before if carefully coordinated.
The wall must be built first to provide the structural support onto which the armrest can be attached or integrated.
The armrest must be installed before finishing work begins so that finishing materials can be applied seamlessly around or over the armrest, and to avoid damaging finished surfaces.
The armrest defines the boundary or side support for the seating area; the bench or seating element should be installed after the armrest is in place to ensure correct alignment and spacing.
Excavation must be completed to prepare the ground and achieve proper bearing capacity before any substructure work can begin.
A compacted and leveled sub-base is required to provide a stable foundation for the sitting wall substructure.
The substructure (footings/foundation) must be cured and set before any above-grade masonry or wall construction can commence.
Backfilling can only proceed after the substructure is complete and sufficiently cured to withstand lateral earth pressures.
Drainage installation is best sequenced after the substructure is built but before final grading; however, some drainage work can be done concurrently.
The sitting wall planter requires a stable base. The foundation or footing must be constructed and cured before any wall or planter structure can be built upon it.
Proper site grading and drainage must be established before the planter is built to prevent water accumulation, soil erosion, and structural issues.
Once the planter structure is complete, waterproofing membranes must be applied to the interior surfaces to protect the structure from moisture damage.
The planter walls must be fully constructed and cured before soil can be placed inside and plants installed, as the soil weight and planting activities could damage an incomplete structure.

Applying coping stones, caps, or sealants to the top of the sitting wall is typically done after the main wall planter is built, though sometimes caps are integrated as part of the construction process rather than a separate step.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before any foundation can be poured or laid to ensure proper bearing capacity and alignment.
Proper drainage and site grading must be completed before foundation work to prevent water pooling and ensure long-term stability of the sitting wall.
The foundation must be fully cured and set before the wall structure (brick, stone, or block) can be built on top of it to provide a stable load-bearing base.
Backfilling can only commence after the foundation is complete and cured to avoid disturbing or damaging the uncured foundation material.
Waterproofing membranes or damp-proof courses are applied after the foundation is finished and cured to protect the wall from moisture ingress.
The wall must be built to provide a mounting surface for the sitting wall lighting fixtures.
Electrical conduits, wiring, and junction boxes must be installed within the wall before lighting fixtures can be connected and mounted.
Lighting fixtures should be installed before final wall finishing to allow for seamless integration and covering of mounting plates or conduits.
The lighting system must be physically installed before it can be powered on, tested, and commissioned for proper operation.
The sitting wall storage niche is built into the wall structure, requiring the wall framing to be in place to define the opening and provide support.
Any electrical wiring intended to serve the niche area (e.g., outlets or lighting) must be roughed in behind the wall before the niche cavity is enclosed.
The niche must be built and framed before drywall can be installed around and inside the opening to finish the wall surface.
While not strictly required, it is best practice to complete the niche before installing adjacent cabinetry or trim to ensure proper alignment and fit.
The niche structure must be fully built and taped/mudded (if drywall) before painting and final finishing can be applied to the wall and niche surfaces.
The wall must be framed to provide a structural cavity and mounting surface for electrical outlet boxes before outlets can be installed.
Electrical cables must be run from the panel to the outlet location before the outlet device can be wired and mounted.
Outlet installation must be complete before insulation is placed, as the outlet box and wiring must be exposed for inspection and connection.
The electrical outlet must be installed and secured in its box before drywall can be hung, since drywall will be cut around the outlet box and the outlet needs to be accessible for later trim-out.

successor: Outlet Trim and Cover Plate Installation
rationale: The outlet device must be mounted and wired in its box before the cover plate and final trim can be installed.
The structural frame of the sitting wall must be in place before surface finishing can be applied.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the wall must be completed before the wall surface is finished and covered.
Insulation must be placed inside the wall cavity before the surface finishing layer is applied.
The surface finish (e.g., drywall or plaster) must be complete and cured before paint or final coatings can be applied.

successor: Installation of Wall-Mounted Fixtures (e.g., seating brackets, shelves)
rationale: Wall-mounted fixtures should be installed after the wall surface is finished to ensure proper alignment and to avoid damaging the finish.
The foundation or base for the sitting wall must be properly prepared (excavated, leveled, and compacted) before the wall can be installed to ensure structural stability and proper load distribution.
Concrete footings must be poured and cured to provide a solid, level base that supports the sitting wall's weight and prevents settling or shifting over time.
Proper drainage (e.g., gravel backfill, perforated pipe) must be in place behind the wall to prevent hydrostatic pressure buildup, which could cause wall failure.
Wall caps or coping stones can only be placed after the main wall body is fully constructed, as caps sit on top of the finished wall and provide a finished appearance and weather protection.
Backfilling behind the wall and final grading must be done after the wall is installed to lock the wall in place and direct drainage away from the structure.
The wall frame must be constructed first to provide the structural support onto which the sitting wall cushion will be installed.
The wall surface must be fully sheathed or clad to create a solid, finished backing before cushion installation can occur.
Insulation must be placed inside the wall cavity before enclosing it with the cushion to ensure thermal and acoustic performance.
The cushion installation must be completed before the final inspection can verify that all finish work, including cushions, meets specifications.
While cushions are typically installed before final styling, it is a soft preference because styling can proceed around the cushion installation if needed.
The sitting wall structure must be fully constructed to provide the planter cavity or bed area where plants will be placed.
If a planter box or liner is used within the sitting wall, it must be installed prior to adding soil and plants.
Proper drainage material (e.g., gravel or drainage mat) must be placed at the bottom of the planter cavity before soil and plants are added to prevent waterlogging.
Growing medium/soil must be filled into the planter area and prepared (leveled, fertilized if needed) before any planting can occur.
After planting, mulch is typically applied around the plants and final grading/tidying is done for aesthetic finish and moisture retention.
Wall framing must be completed to provide the structural cavity and support for running electrical wiring within the sitting wall.
General rough electrical work (such as running main supply lines and junction boxes) must be in place before the specific sitting wall lighting wiring can be connected.
Lighting wiring must be installed before insulation is placed, as insulation would cover and obstruct access to the wiring if done first.
Wiring must be completed and inspected before drywall is installed, since drywall encloses the wall cavity and hides the wiring permanently.
The rough wiring must be run and terminated at switch/outlet boxes before the actual lighting fixtures and switches can be connected and mounted.
The steel cable network requires a stable foundation to anchor against, as cables exert significant tensile forces that must be transferred to the ground.
Steel columns or masts serve as the primary support structures from which the cable network is suspended or anchored.
For cable-stayed or suspension structures, the cable network must be installed first to provide support for the deck sections that are lifted into place and connected to the cables.
After the cable network is physically installed, tensioning and fine-adjustment of cable forces must occur to achieve the designed load distribution and geometry.

While the cable network often serves as a support for cladding, in some designs the cladding can be installed concurrently; however, it is typically preferred to complete the cable structure first to provide a stable framework.
The mast or compression strut requires a stable foundation or base structure to be installed first to provide load-bearing support and stability.
Cables and stays are tensioned and attached to the mast or compression strut to provide lateral support and stability; the mast must be in place before cables can be connected.
Cross-arms, brackets, or other mounted components require the mast or strut to be erected first as they are physically attached to it.
The top cap, fitting, or head assembly must be installed after the mast is in place since it sits atop the mast or strut.
Site must be excavated and leveled, and any embedment hole prepared, before the mast or strut can be placed into position.
The catenary support structures (poles, masts, or brackets) must be in place before the edge catenary cable can be strung and secured along its path.
The track must be laid and aligned to establish the correct geometry and position reference for the catenary cable run, ensuring proper clearance and pantograph contact.
The catenary cable must be fully installed, tensioned, and terminated before it can be safely energized and undergo high-voltage testing.
Final commissioning and integration of the overhead catenary system (including pantograph clearance and current collection checks) can only proceed after the catenary cable is installed.
The ground must be excavated to create the space where the foundation anchors will be placed and embedded.
The site must be leveled and prepared to provide a stable working area for installing the foundation anchors.
Masts cannot be erected until their foundation anchors are securely in place to provide structural support and alignment.
If the anchors are embedded in concrete, the concrete must be poured after the anchors are positioned, and the anchors must be in place before concrete cures around them.
Guy wires supporting a mast are tensioned after the mast is installed, which requires the foundation anchors to already be fixed and load-bearing.
The compression ring or perimeter ridge must be supported on a stable foundation slab that distributes loads evenly before the ring structure can be erected.
The reinforcing steel cage must be prefabricated and positioned before concrete can be placed for the compression ring.
Formwork must be erected and braced to the correct geometry before any concrete placement for the ring.
The compression ring acts as the top support for the dome shell; the dome cannot be constructed without the ring in place to resist thrust.
Post-tensioning can only be applied after the concrete ring has achieved sufficient strength to withstand the compressive stresses.
Turnbuckles and plates must be physically installed and in place before they can be tensioned; tensioning is the act of applying force to already-positioned hardware.
Cables must be properly aligned and connected to the turnbuckles before tensioning can begin; otherwise the tensioning would be applied to misaligned or disconnected components.
After tensioning is complete, the connections must be inspected to verify that the correct tension has been achieved and that all components are secure.
Locking hardware (e.g., lock nuts or safety wires) can only be installed after tensioning is finalized, as they serve to lock the turnbuckle in its tensioned position.
Rainwater gutters and downpipes are attached to the roof edge/eaves; the roof structure must be in place to provide a mounting surface and proper alignment for gutter installation.

Downpipes are typically installed against external walls and their placement may need to be coordinated with or completed before final wall cladding or finishing to allow proper integration and sealing.
Downpipes must be installed before they can be connected to the underground stormwater drainage system to route water away from the building.
Gutters are typically mounted on the fascia board; fascia and soffits must be installed first to provide the structural support and proper positioning for gutter brackets.
Downpipes are fixed to exterior walls; any painting or final finish coating should be done after downpipe installation to ensure seamless coverage around the pipes and avoid staining or rework.
A stable and level foundation or substructure is physically required to provide the rigid support onto which the membrane can be anchored, stretched, and fixed.
The primary structural frame (steel arches, cables, or trusses) must be erected first to create the supporting skeleton that the membrane will be draped over or attached to.

For tensioned membrane structures, the cable network or catenary cables must be installed and pretensioned to define the membrane's support geometry before membrane panels can be placed and stretched.
After the membrane is laid out and tensioned, the edges must be secured with clamps, extrusions, or termination profiles to lock in the tension and finalize the attachment to the structure.
Once the membrane is installed and fully stretched to its design shape, all joints, seams, and membrane-to-structure interfaces must be sealed to ensure the envelope is weathertight and waterproof.
Towers or supporting structures must be fully erected and assembled before cables can be rigged and tensioned, as they provide the structural support and anchorage points for the cables.
Tower foundations must be completed and cured before tower erection, and thus before cable rigging, to ensure stable anchorage for the cables under tension.
Cables must first be rigged and tensioned to the specified sag before permanent anchoring and dead-ending can be performed at the termination points.

successor: Final Inspection and Load Testing of Cable System
rationale: After cables are rigged, tensioned, and anchored, a final inspection and load testing must be conducted to verify that tensions and sags meet design specifications.

While some hardware can be pre-installed on towers, final attachment of crossarms and supporting hardware to the tensioned cables is typically done after rigging, though this is a construction sequencing preference rather than a strict physical constraint.
The mast must be anchored to a properly installed foundation and anchor bolts to ensure structural stability and alignment.
Anchor bolts must be set in concrete and fully cured to provide a secure base for mast erection and prevent bolt pullout or movement during erection.
Cross-arms are mounted onto the mast after it is erected and plumbed, so the mast must be in place and vertical before cross-arms can be attached.
Conductors are strung between masts or towers; the mast must first be erected, plumbed, and cross-arms installed to support conductor attachment points.
Final bolting and torque checks on mast connections should be performed after the mast is erected and aligned to ensure all joints are properly secured.
The ground must be leveled and a stable foundation prepared before placing the planter box to ensure structural stability and proper drainage.
The planter box structure must be fully assembled and in its final position before adding soil and plants to prevent damage or displacement of the structure.
If the planter box connects to a drainage system, the drainage infrastructure must be in place before the planter box is installed to ensure proper water runoff.
The planter box components must be fabricated or pre-assembled before they can be positioned and installed on site.
Surrounding landscaping, decorative elements, and final finishes around the planter box should be completed after the planter box is in place to ensure proper alignment and integration.
Planter walls require a stable load-bearing base, typically a concrete footing or slab, to support their weight and prevent settlement or cracking.
The site must be excavated and graded to the correct elevations before planter walls can be laid out and constructed.
Any drainage pipes or irrigation lines that will run beneath or through the planter wall area must be installed prior to wall construction to avoid rework.
After the planter wall is built and cured, soil can be backfilled against it and finish grading completed to match the wall's height.
Plants, shrubs, and soil amendments cannot be placed until the planter wall structure is complete and any required waterproofing or drainage is in place.
The planter cap/finish trim is installed on top of the planter walls. The wall assembly must be complete to provide the structural base for the cap.
Waterproofing must be applied to the planter structure before the cap is installed, as the cap seals the top and access to the waterproofing layer would be blocked afterwards.
The cap/finish trim provides the finished edge of the planter; backfill and planting should occur after the cap is in place to avoid damaging the trim and to ensure a clean finish.
Final cleaning and inspection is typically done after all finish trims are installed to protect the finished surfaces, though it is a soft scheduling preference rather than a physical necessity.
The ground or surface area must be prepared, leveled, and cleared before placing planters to ensure stable placement and proper drainage.
If the planter requires a structural base or foundation (e.g., for large built-in planters), that base must be completed before setting the planter to provide adequate support.
Proper drainage provisions (drainage layers, weep holes, or connected drainage pipes) must be in place before the planter is filled with soil to prevent waterlogging and structural damage.
The planter container must be installed and in its final position before it can be filled with growing medium and planted with vegetation.
Planters intended for irrigation need the container in place before installing and connecting drip lines or irrigation emitters to the planter.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before any planter installation to ensure a stable base and proper drainage.
If the raised planters will sit on a concrete slab or foundation, that slab must be poured and cured before the planters are constructed or placed on top.
Any underground drainage pipes, irrigation lines, or electrical conduits that will serve the planters must be installed before the planters are built to avoid excavation damage later.
The planter structure must be fully constructed and cured before soil, gravel, and planting media can be placed inside it.
Plants must be installed only after the planter structure is complete and filled with soil to ensure proper root placement and structural integrity.
It is preferable to finish adjacent hardscape after planter installation to avoid damaging new pavers/edging, but it is not a physical necessity if careful sequencing is used.
A support structure (trellis, pergola, wall anchors, or wire system) must be installed before climbing plants can be trained onto it, as the plants need something physical to climb on.
The soil must be prepared, amended, and the planting bed or containers must be ready before installing climbing plants so that roots have appropriate growing medium.
It is strongly preferred to install drip irrigation or soaker hoses before planting to avoid disturbing the roots later, though watering by hand could be done after.
Mulch should be applied after planting to retain moisture and suppress weeds without smothering the new plants.
Once climbing plants are installed in the ground, they must be immediately trained and loosely tied to the support structure to guide their growth direction.
The green wall support structure requires a stable and level foundation to bear its load and ensure proper alignment; foundation work must be completed before any above-grade assembly begins.
Concrete footings or slab must be fully cured to reach sufficient strength to anchor the green wall support assembly; premature loading could cause structural failure.

The irrigation lines for the green wall are typically mounted on or integrated into the support framework; the support structure must be in place before the irrigation system can be attached and routed.

The panels or planting pots that hold the vegetation must be mounted onto the completed support framework; the support structure must be fully assembled before any cladding or planting modules can be attached.

Waterproofing behind the green wall is often applied after the support frame is installed to ensure continuous coverage around attachment points, though in some sequences waterproofing may precede assembly; this is a soft preference based on typical best practice.

successor: Irrigation System Installation for Green Facade
rationale: The structural support system for the green facade must be installed first to provide a mounting surface and load-bearing framework for the irrigation pipes, drippers, and related equipment.

successor: Irrigation System Installation for Green Facade
rationale: A dedicated water supply line with proper pressure and connections must be roughed-in to the facade location before the irrigation system components can be connected and installed.

predecessor: Irrigation System Installation for Green Facade
rationale: The irrigation system must be fully installed, tested, and operational before any plants are placed in the green facade, as the plants require immediate watering upon installation.

predecessor: Irrigation System Installation for Green Facade
successor: Green Facade Drainage and Waterproofing Testing
rationale: While not physically mandatory, it is a soft preference to verify drainage and waterproofing after irrigation installation to ensure no leaks exist before planting proceeds.

successor: Irrigation System Installation for Green Facade
rationale: The building envelope behind the green facade must be waterproofed before installing irrigation to prevent water intrusion and damage to the building structure from irrigation runoff or leaks.
Planter boxes are often attached to or supported by the building's structural frame or walls, which must be in place first to provide a secure mounting surface.
Installing the roof before planter boxes is a soft preference to avoid damage from falling debris or weather exposure during roofing work.
If the planter boxes are located on a balcony, roof, or podium, the underlying waterproofing membrane must be installed first to prevent water ingress and structural damage.
The planter box structure must be fully installed, sealed, and cured before it can be filled with soil or planting media.
Plants, shrubs, or trees can only be placed into the planter boxes after the boxes themselves are securely installed.

Edge restraints are typically placed at the perimeter of a slab on grade to contain the concrete pour; thus the slab sub-base and formwork must be in place before edge restraints can be positioned and secured.
Edge restraints act as formwork or containment borders that must be fully installed before concrete is poured, otherwise the wet concrete would spread beyond the intended slab edge.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the correct levels and compaction before any edge restraint system can be laid out and installed along the slab perimeter.
The aggregate base or sub-base layer must be placed and compacted to provide a stable foundation for the edge restraint to sit on and be anchored into.

While control joints are typically cut after concrete has cured, the edge restraint must be in place first to define the slab boundary; however this is a soft preference as joint cutting could theoretically be sequenced differently in some methods.
The site must be cleared and rough grading completed to expose the area where the drainage inlet will be installed and to ensure proper drainage slopes.
Trenches for stormwater pipes connecting to the inlet must be excavated before the inlet structure can be placed and connected to the pipe network.
The incoming and outgoing drainage pipes must be laid in the trench and positioned before the inlet structure is installed so that the inlet can be connected directly to the pipes.
The concrete or precast inlet structure must be fully set and cured before the metal grate and frame can be mounted on top.
The inlet must be in place before the surrounding trench and excavation can be backfilled with soil and compacted for stability.
The inlet with its grate installed must be completed before asphalt, concrete, or other surface finishes are applied to ensure proper elevation and fit with the finished surface.
A stable, level, and compacted base (typically crushed stone or gravel) is physically required to support the pavers and prevent settling or shifting after installation.
Edge restraints (such as concrete curbs or plastic edging) must be installed before paver laying to contain the pavers and prevent lateral movement or spreading under load.
Proper grading and drainage systems must be established before paver installation to ensure water runoff away from the paved surface, preventing water pooling and base erosion.
After pavers are laid, joint sand must be spread and compacted into the gaps between pavers to lock them together, provide load transfer, and prevent weed growth and ant infiltration.

A protective sealer is typically applied after paver installation to enhance color, provide stain resistance, and extend pavement life, though this is a recommended practice rather than a physical necessity.
Surfaces must be clean, dry, and free of debris, dust, or contaminants to ensure proper adhesion of joint filler material.
The joint grooves must be cut into the concrete or substrate before filler can be applied into them.
After filler is placed, it must be allowed to cure or dry to achieve its designed strength and performance before any loads are applied.

successor: Surface Finishing / Grinding (if flush finish required)
rationale: If a flush surface is specified, any excess filler can be ground or finished after the filler has set; this is a quality/preference step rather than a hard physical constraint.
Vehicular or pedestrian traffic and other loads must not be applied until the joint filler has fully cured to avoid deformation or failure of the filler.
The subgrade must be properly prepared and leveled before base compaction can begin to ensure a stable foundation for the base material.
The base material (e.g., aggregate, gravel) must be spread and placed to the required thickness before compaction equipment can densify it.
The base material must be at the optimal moisture content before compaction to achieve the required density; adding or removing moisture must occur prior to rolling.
The base layer must be compacted to the specified density and smoothness before the surface course (asphalt or concrete) can be placed on top.
After compaction is complete, field density tests (e.g., nuclear gauge, sand cone) must be performed to verify that compaction meets specifications before subsequent layers are applied.
Edge restraints must be installed after the concrete slab is placed because the slab provides a stable base and the correct elevation against which the edge restraint can be set.
Proper base preparation and grading must be completed before edge restraint installation to ensure a stable, well-drained foundation for the restraints.
Pavers or blocks cannot be installed until edge restraints are in place, as the restraints provide a fixed boundary and containment for the paving units.
Final compaction of pavers occurs after edge restraints are installed because the restraints hold the pavers in position during compaction.
Joint sanding and sealing follows edge restraint installation because the restraints define the perimeter and prevent sand loss at the edges.
A stable, properly graded and compacted base is physically required to support paver installation and prevent settling or shifting.
Geotextile fabric must be laid over the prepared base to separate subgrade from base material and prevent weed growth before paver pattern layout begins.
The aggregate base course must be installed and compacted to the required thickness to provide a load-bearing foundation for the pavers.
Edge restraints must be in place to contain the pavers laterally and prevent the pattern from spreading or shifting during installation.
A level, screeded bedding sand layer is the direct setting bed for pavers and must be in place before pavers can be laid in the intended pattern.
After pavers are arranged in the desired pattern, they must be compacted with a plate compactor to seat them into the bedding sand for stability.
Joint sand is swept into the gaps between pavers after they are laid to lock the pattern together; this cannot be done before the pavers are placed.
Final compaction and sealing is typically performed after the pattern is complete to set the pavers and protect the surface, but minor adjustments could be made after sealing if needed.

The brick mortar joint is formed as part of the brick laying process itself. Brick units must be placed first, and mortar is applied between them to form the joint. Without laying the bricks, there can be no mortar joint between them.
Fresh mortar must be prepared and mixed to the proper consistency before it can be applied to form brick mortar joints. The mortar joint cannot exist without mixed mortar being available.
A prepared foundation, base slab, or starting course is required before brick laying (and thus mortar joints) can begin. The structural support must be in place to bear the load of the brickwork.

After the mortar joint is formed between bricks, the mortar must be allowed to cure and gain strength before further construction loads are applied or before subsequent courses are added without disturbance.

The mortar joints must first be formed (filled with mortar between bricks) before they can be tooled, struck, or pointed to achieve the desired finish and weatherproofing shape. Tooling is done while the mortar is still semi-plastic.
The substrate (e.g., concrete slab or underlayment) must be clean, dry, and level before tiles can be laid; otherwise, tiles will crack or become uneven.
In wet areas (showers, bathrooms), waterproof membranes must be applied and cured before tile installation to prevent moisture damage behind tiles.
All electrical boxes, plumbing pipes, and drain lines must be roughed-in behind walls/floors before tiling, as tile work covers and is difficult to remove for access.
Tiles must be fully set and the thin-set mortar must cure before grout can be applied between the joints.

successor: Final Flooring or Wall Finishing (e.g., baseboards, trim)
rationale: While tile work is ideally completed before installing baseboards or trim so that trim covers the tile edges neatly, it is a soft preference as trim can sometimes be cut and fitted after tiling with extra effort.

The foundation must be fully poured, set, and cured to provide a stable, level load-bearing base for brick walls. Without a completed foundation, brick laying cannot commence as there is no structural support.
The ground-floor slab or floor deck must be in place so that bricklayers have a working platform and the brick walls have a solid bearing surface.
Bricks, mortar mix, and reinforcing materials must be delivered and staged on site, and mortar must be freshly mixed before bricklaying can start.
Brick openings (reveals) must be built to the correct dimensions before door and window frames can be fitted and secured into the masonry.
Conduits, junction boxes, and plumbing pipes that run through or are embedded in masonry walls must be installed after the brickwork is laid, as the walls are the structural substrate.
The masonry walls (brick or tile surfaces) must be fully constructed and cured before waterproofing can be applied, as waterproofing is a surface treatment applied to the finished substrate.
The tile/brick surface must be cleaned, free of dust, dirt, loose particles, and efflorescence before waterproofing agents can bond properly to the substrate.
Mortar joints between tiles and bricks must be fully cured (typically 7-14 days) before waterproofing is applied to prevent cracking or damage to the freshly pointed joints.
Waterproofing must be fully applied, cured, and inspected before backfilling occurs to avoid damaging unprotected masonry surfaces and to ensure the waterproof membrane is intact.
Exterior waterproofing must be completed before interior finishes are applied to prevent moisture ingress that would ruin interior plaster, paint, or drywall.
The surface must be prepared (cleaned, smoothed, primed) before any ornament can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and finish quality.
Ornamental elements must be attached in place before the final paint or protective coating is applied, so that the coating covers both the base surface and the ornament uniformly.
The main structural support (walls, columns, or frames) must be erected before decorative or non-structural ornaments can be installed, as the ornament depends on the structure for support.
Ornaments are typically installed before the final quality inspection and touch-up phase to allow inspectors to verify proper placement and alignment before project closeout.
Rough-in work such as wiring or piping must be completed behind walls or ceilings before ornamental surfaces are applied, to avoid damaging the ornament or requiring costly removal/rework.
Raw stone material must be selected and quarried before any carving can begin on the ornament.
The stone block must be cut to approximate size and shape before detailed carving work can start.
The ornamental design must be drawn or transferred onto the stone surface before carving can proceed.
Final surface polishing and finishing must occur after carving is complete to avoid damaging carved details.
The carved ornament must be fully completed before it can be installed or mounted at its intended location.
A physical mold must be designed and created before any ornament can be cast, as the casting process requires a mold to shape the material.
The mold material (e.g., sand, plaster, or metal) must be prepared and assembled before the casting pour can take place.
The casting material (e.g., concrete, plaster, or molten metal) must be mixed or melted and ready before pouring into the mold.
After casting, the material must be allowed to cure, set, or harden before further handling or finishing.
The ornament must be cast and sufficiently set before it can be safely removed from the mold without deformation.
Final finishing (grinding, sanding, painting) can only occur after the ornament has been cast and cured.
Inspection for defects must occur after casting is complete and the ornament has been removed from the mold.
The ornament must be fully cast, cured, finished, and inspected before it can be transported and installed at its final location.
The structural frame provides the load-bearing support that ornamental cladding attaches to; cladding cannot be installed without a stable structural frame in place.
Waterproofing must be applied to the building envelope before cladding is installed to ensure the building is protected from moisture ingress behind the cladding.
A sheathing or substrate layer is typically required as a backing surface for attaching ornamental cladding panels or materials.
Cladding must be completed to seal the building envelope before interior finishes are applied, to protect interior work from weather exposure.
Scaffolding used for cladding installation must remain in place until cladding is complete; dismantling can only begin after cladding installation is finished and inspected.
The structural framing must be in place to provide a secure mounting surface and support for ornamental glass panels.
Sealing and weatherproofing can only be applied after the ornamental glass is properly installed in its frame.
Although not physically mandatory, it is preferable to install ornamental glass before adjacent interior finishes to avoid damage to finished surfaces during glass handling.
The final inspection of glazing work must occur after ornamental glass is fully installed to verify correct placement, alignment, and security.

predecessor: Masonry or Wall Rough Opening Preparation
rationale: Rough openings (e.g., window openings in masonry or walls) must be prepared and cured before ornamental glass can be fitted into them.
The structural steel framing provides the primary load-bearing structure to which ornamental metalwork is often attached or supported by, making it a prerequisite.
Architectural metalwork such as railings, grilles, and brackets must be fabricated and installed prior to decorative ornamental metal components that integrate with or are supported by them.
Ornamental metalwork is often anchored into or mounted on masonry, concrete, or stone surfaces, which must be completed first to provide the substrate for installation.

While painting can sometimes be done before installation, it is preferred to paint or apply protective finishes after ornamental metalwork is installed to ensure full coverage and to avoid damage to the metal during construction.

Ornamental metalwork installation must be complete before final cleaning and punch list activities to avoid damaging the ornamental finishes during cleanup and to allow for final inspection and touch-up.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be completed before installing ornamental ceilings, as these systems are hidden above the ceiling and would be inaccessible or damaged if the ceiling is installed first.
The structural framing (roof or floor deck above) must be complete to provide a substrate and support structure for hanging or attaching the ornamental ceiling system.

Fireproofing and insulation applied to the structure above must be installed before enclosing with the ornamental ceiling, as these materials are part of the fire-resistance rating and thermal envelope requirements.

Ornamental ceiling installation should precede final wall and floor finishes to avoid damaging delicate finishes during overhead work, and to allow for proper alignment and seams at wall-ceiling junctions.

successor: Final electrical and lighting fixture installation
rationale: Decorative lighting fixtures, chandeliers, and other ceiling-mounted elements are installed after the ornamental ceiling is in place to ensure proper anchoring and alignment with the ceiling pattern or design.
The subfloor must be properly prepared (leveled, cleaned, and cured) to provide a stable and even base for ornamental flooring installation; otherwise the flooring will be uneven or damaged.
Underlayment (moisture barrier, acoustic layer, etc.) must be installed before ornamental flooring to protect the finished floor and ensure performance requirements are met.
All structural framing and rough carpentry must be completed to provide the load-bearing support and enclosure for the flooring system.
All rough-in work (electrical conduit, plumbing pipes) in or under the floor area must be finished before ornamental flooring is installed to avoid later destructive access.
Baseboards, trim, and wall finishes should be installed after ornamental flooring is complete to allow clean edges and proper fitting against the finished floor surface.

It is generally preferred to complete painting of lower walls and baseboards after flooring to avoid drips and damage on the finished floor, though this can be done before if careful protection is used.
Heavy furniture, fixtures, and equipment should only be placed after ornamental flooring is fully installed and cured to prevent damage to the floor surface.

Final inspection of the ornamental flooring should occur after installation is complete to verify quality and workmanship, though this is an administrative preference rather than a physical constraint.
Columns and pilasters require a stable load-bearing foundation and substructure to support their weight and transfer loads to the ground.
Ornamental columns and pilasters are typically non-structural or semi-structural cladding elements that are attached to or supported by the primary structural frame, which must be in place first.
In classical architectural sequencing, architraves and cornices rest directly on top of columns and pilasters, so the vertical supports must be installed before the horizontal entablature elements.

Ornamental columns and pilasters are part of the building envelope or decorative facade; adjacent wall cladding and finishing work must accommodate the column positions and thus proceed after column installation.

Decorative plasterwork and mouldings often integrate with or abut ornamental columns and pilasters, so finishing the column surfaces first provides a clean substrate; however, some parallel work may be possible with careful sequencing.
The arch and keystone must be supported on a stable foundation and base structure to bear the load and ensure stability.
The ornamental arch is typically set into or supported by flanking walls; the walls must be erected to provide the abutments for the arch.
Finishing work such as pointing, sealing, or decorative trim around the arch can only be done after the arch and keystone are in place.

successor: Roof/Upper Structure Installation (if arch is load-bearing)
rationale: If the arch is load-bearing, any structure above it (roof, upper floor) must be installed after the arch is complete to transfer loads through the arch.

Painting or surface treatment of the arch and keystone, along with surrounding areas, is typically done after the arch installation to achieve a uniform finish, though this could be considered a soft preference if finishing can be done in situ later.
The structural frame and columns must be erected first because the ornamental frieze and entablature are supported by the columns and bear on the structural frame.
The frieze and entablature typically sit atop masonry or load-bearing walls, so these walls must be built to the required height before the entablature can be placed.
The frieze and entablature provide the base onto which decorative cornices and additional moldings are attached; these fine ornamental details are applied after the main entablature is in place.

Scaffolding erected for installing the entablature cannot be fully dismantled until the entablature and any work immediately above it are complete, as the scaffold provides access and support for the entablature installation.
The balustrade and handrail system must be anchored to or supported by the structural floor slab; the slab must be installed and cured to provide a stable base.
Where balustrades are installed along staircases, the structural stair must be in place to provide support and establish the correct geometry for handrail alignment.
Any damage to surrounding finishes during balustrade installation must be repaired after installation is complete to ensure a uniform final appearance.
The balustrade must be fully installed and secured before safety inspections can verify that it meets code requirements for fall protection.

successor: Floor Tiling / Floor Finishing adjacent to Balustrade
rationale: While it is possible to install floor finishes before balustrades, it is preferred to install the balustrade first so that floor tiles or finishes can be cut and fitted neatly around the balustrade base, avoiding unsightly gaps or damage.
The structural steel frame must be in place to provide the primary load-bearing structure onto which the ornamental mullion and transom system can be attached.
The building envelope (sheathing/weather barrier) must be installed to create a sealed substrate before adding decorative mullion and transom elements that interface with the facade.
The ornamental mullion and transom framework must be in place to support and receive the glass panels or infill cladding material that fits within the mullion/transom grid.
All mullion and transom joints and interfaces must be fully installed before weather-sealing caulks and sealants can be applied to make the assembly watertight.

While scaffolding can be partially removed earlier, final dismantling of facade-access scaffolding is often deferred until the ornamental mullion/transom installation is complete to maintain safe working access; this is a soft preference because alternate access methods could allow earlier removal.
Roof sheathing provides the structural base and nailing surface for gutter attachment; gutters cannot be installed without a completed roof deck.
Underlayment protects the roof deck from moisture; gutters must be installed over the finished roof underlayment to ensure proper water shedding and waterproofing.
Eave flashing (drip edge) must be in place before gutters are hung, as the gutter hangers and back edge attach under or integrate with the drip edge for proper water diversion.

successor: Exterior Wall Siding (upper portions near roofline)
rationale: Gutters and downspouts must be installed before the final siding courses near the roofline so that siding can be trimmed and fitted around gutter hangers and downspout brackets, creating a clean finished appearance and preventing water intrusion behind siding.

successor: Downspout Drainage System / French Drain Connection
rationale: Connecting downspouts to underground drainage (e.g., French drains, dry wells) requires the downspouts to first be in place to align piping, though sometimes both can be coordinated; it is a strong practical preference for sequencing but can be adjusted with careful planning.
The cornice requires a completed structural frame to attach to; without the frame, there is no supporting structure for the cornice.
Cornice is typically installed at the roof edge/eave, so roof sheathing must be in place to establish the cornice line and provide a base for proper alignment.
The cornice is part of the exterior trim and is typically installed before the main siding so that siding can be fitted up to or tucked under the cornice for a watertight finish.
Painting is often done after all exterior trim is in place; this is a logical sequence but some painting may happen in stages.
Gutters are typically mounted to the fascia of the cornice; the cornice must be in place to provide the attachment surface and correct slope for gutters.
The arch barrel and centering must be in place to provide the structural support and geometry for placing the ornamental voussoirs and keystone at the crown.
The individual voussoirs must be cut, dressed, and bedded in mortar along the arch ring before the ornamental keystone can be inserted as the final locking piece.
The keystone is the last component placed in the arch; only after it is fully seated and the mortar has cured can the temporary centering be struck and removed.

successor: Final Pointing & Tooling of Arch Joints
rationale: Once the ornamental voussoirs and keystone are set, the joints can be pointed and tooled for a finished appearance; this is a finishing step but could theoretically be done concurrently in some workflows.
Waterproofing and backfilling behind the arch ring must wait until the keystone and voussoirs are fully placed and stable to avoid disturbing the masonry.
The pediment and gable are ornamental architectural elements installed onto the finished structural wall and roof framing; the structure must be in place to support the ornamental additions.
Exterior cladding and finishes often integrate with or abut the pediment/gable details, and installing them after ensures a clean transition and protects the ornamental work.

While painting can be done after installation, it is a soft preference because the pediment/gable may be pre-finished; however final touch-up painting typically follows installation to seal joints and match the overall facade.
The gable is part of the roof's triangular end section; the roof deck must be installed to define the gable shape and provide a base for the ornamental gable trim.
Scaffolding used for the pediment/gable installation must remain until the ornamental work is complete; dismantling cannot begin until installation is finished.
The niche and aedicule are typically set into or attached to a wall surface, so the supporting wall structure must be built first to provide a stable substrate.
The structural framing of the building must be complete to define the opening or recess where the ornamental niche/aedicule will be placed.
Any MEP services that would run behind or through the niche area must be roughed in before the ornamental element is installed, to avoid later destructive rework.

The niche and aedicule installation must be complete so that plaster/drywall can be finished flush up to the edges, providing a clean transition between the ornamental element and surrounding wall finish.
The ornamental niche and aedicule must be fully installed before final painting and decorative finishes are applied, to achieve a seamless, integrated aesthetic appearance.

The ornamental rosette and boss are decorative plaster elements that must be applied onto a smooth, prepared ceiling or wall surface. The underlying plaster base coat must be finished and cured before these ornamental pieces can be attached.
The ceiling substrate or framework must be fully installed and stable to provide a structural anchor for the rosette and boss, which are typically heavy decorative elements.

The rosette and boss are often primed and painted together with the ceiling, and painting must occur after they are installed to achieve a uniform finish. Alternatively, they are installed before final decorative paint coats.

Rosettes are commonly centered around light fixture mounting points. While the wiring can be roughed-in earlier, the final fixture is typically hung after the rosette is in place to align properly with the decorative centerpiece.

Cornice and trim work often interfaces with ceiling rosettes; however, in some sequences the cornice is installed first and the rosette overlaps it, or vice versa. A soft preference exists because of aesthetic alignment but is not physically mandatory.
The ornamental quoins are applied to the corners of a masonry wall; the wall structure must be built first to provide a substrate for the quoins.
A stable foundation is required before any wall construction, including quoin installation, can proceed.

predecessor: Mortar Bedding/Curing (for quoins set in mortar)
rationale: If quoins are installed using mortar, the mortar must be prepared and the previous course must have sufficiently cured to bear load.
Scaffolding erected at corners for quoin installation cannot be dismantled until the quoins are fully installed and secured.
Weatherproofing and pointing of joints around the quoins must be performed after the quoins are in place to seal gaps and ensure durability.
The parapet and balustrade are mounted on the roof edge; the structural roof slab must be in place to provide a load-bearing base.
Roof waterproofing is installed before parapet construction to ensure continuous membrane lapping and proper flashing details at the parapet base.
Parapet installation provides a finished edge datum, but facade work can be sequenced in parallel with careful coordination; typically parapet is completed first for clean junctions.
Parapet and balustrade must be fully installed and secured before roof-level scaffolding can be removed, as the balustrade serves as edge protection.
Gutters are fixed to or below the parapet; the parapet profile defines the gutter alignment and fixing points.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to receive the ornamental door surround and frame assembly.
The wall structure must be in place to provide support and attachment surface for the door surround and frame.
If the surround integrates with masonry or exterior cladding, that work should ideally precede to avoid damaging the ornamental piece.
The door frame and surround must be in place before the actual door leaf can be hung and fitted.
Finishing trim work around the door is typically done after the surround and frame are installed to achieve clean junctions.
Final painting or staining of the ornamental surround and frame is done after installation, but this may follow or precede other finishing trades depending on schedule.
The window frame must be installed first to provide the structural opening and reference points onto which the ornamental surround and hood are attached.
