The rough opening framing establishes the structural opening dimensions and support needed before any window components or decorative surrounds can be installed.
Exterior sheathing must be in place to provide a backing surface and weatherproof substrate against which the ornamental surround and hood can be mounted and sealed.

The ornamental surround and hood are typically applied before the final exterior cladding or siding so that the cladding can be cut and fitted neatly around the surround profile for a clean, weathertight finish.

Caulking and sealant is applied after the surround is installed to seal the joints between the surround and the adjacent wall/cladding; while highly recommended, some sequencing flexibility exists if access is maintained for later sealing.

Ornamental corbelling is a decorative masonry projection that requires the structural load-bearing wall to be built first, as the corbelling projects outward from the wall surface and relies on the wall for structural support.
The mortar in the structural wall must sufficiently cure to bear the additional load and projection forces of the corbelled masonry before corbelling can be added.

successor: Roof or Floor Slab Installation (above corbelling)
rationale: Corbelling often supports or visually transitions to upper roof/floor structures; if the corbelling is load-bearing or decorative at the eaves, it must be completed before the roof structure above is installed.
After corbelling is laid, the joints and mortar finish (pointing) are applied to seal and beautify the corbelled courses; this cannot be done before the corbelling stones/bricks are in place.
Ornamental corbelling is typically installed at higher wall elevations; scaffolding must be erected to provide safe access for masons to place and finish the corbelled courses.
The wall or ceiling surface must be smooth, level, and properly plastered before an ornamental medallion or cartouche can be applied or mounted securely.
The underlying structural support (e.g., ceiling joists, wall framing, or backing board) must be in place to provide a stable substrate for the medallion or cartouche.
The medallion or cartouche itself may be painted, gilded, or otherwise finished after it is installed or applied to the surface.
Any final aesthetic adjustments or touch-ups around the medallion/cartouche area are performed after its installation to ensure a seamless integration with surrounding finishes.

predecessor: Wall Masonry or Concrete Core Construction
rationale: The string course and belt course are ornamental projections that are cast or installed onto the main wall surface; the main wall structure must be completed first to provide a substrate.
Belt courses often wrap around columns or beams of the structural frame; the frame must be in place before ornamental bands can be applied.
String courses and belt courses create horizontal ledges that can trap water; waterproofing and sealants must be applied after installation to prevent moisture ingress.
It is preferable to complete ornamental banding before final wall finishes so that paint or plaster can be applied uniformly over the entire facade, though it could be touched up afterward.
Working at height to install ornamental courses requires scaffolding to be in place for safe access.
The spire and finial are ornamental components mounted atop the main structural framework; the structure must be fully erected to provide a stable support base.
The spire and finial are typically installed at the highest point of the roof; the roof must be completed to serve as the working platform and to ensure waterproofing continuity.
The spire is a prominent high point that requires integration with the lightning protection system; the air terminal and conductors are connected to or routed around the spire after its placement.
Scaffolding around the upper roof and spire area must remain in place until the spire and finial are installed; only after installation can the upper scaffolding be safely removed.

Although inspection can be done later, it is good practice to inspect the spire and finial immediately after installation to verify alignment, finish, and secure fastening before other finishing work closes access.
The ornamental cresting and ridge components are installed on top of the roof structure, so the roof structure must be completed first to provide a stable base.
Cresting and ridge elements are mounted along the ridge line of the finished roof surface, so the roof covering (slates, tiles, or decking) must be in place first.
Cresting and ridge installation is among the final finishing steps on a roof; the final inspection should occur after all ornamental elements are in place to verify completeness.
Scaffolding or access equipment at the roof level should remain until all ornamental ridge work is finished, as cresting installation requires roof access.

While gutters can technically be installed before cresting, it is preferable to install cresting first to avoid damaging gutters during ridge work, though this is a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
The rough-in of ductwork and framing must be inspected and approved before installing ornamental grilles and registers, as these cover the openings and prevent access for adjustments.
Grilles and registers are the visible terminals of the ductwork system; the ducts must be in place and properly connected before the decorative covers can be installed.
Grilles and registers are installed over finished wall or ceiling openings; the surrounding surface must be complete, taped, floated, and painted for proper fit and aesthetic finish.
While grilles and registers are typically among the last items installed, some final adjustments may be needed; however, this is a soft preference as punch work can still occur with grilles in place.

Ornamental grilles are themselves decorative trim; they can be installed concurrently or slightly before other millwork, but there is no strict physical dependency — this is a sequencing preference for aesthetic staging.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical work (conduit, junction boxes, wiring)
rationale: Electrical rough-in must be completed to provide the necessary power supply infrastructure (conduits, boxes, wires) before the fixture can be physically connected and mounted.

The lighting fixture must be installed first so that ceiling and wall finishing work can be completed flush around the fixture base, ensuring a clean aesthetic appearance and avoiding damage to finished surfaces during fixture installation.
The fixture housing must be securely mounted and wired before lamps can be inserted and energized, to protect bulbs from damage and ensure electrical safety.
The fixture must be fully installed before circuits can be tested for correct operation, voltage, and grounding under load conditions.
The fixture's structural mounting and wiring must be completed before attaching decorative elements that would obstruct access to mounting points or electrical connections.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and mudded before any wall finish can be applied to ensure a smooth substrate.
Primer must be applied to seal the drywall and provide a uniform base for the warm color paint to adhere properly.
Ceiling painting is typically completed before wall painting to avoid dripping paint onto finished walls.
Baseboards and trim are installed after wall painting to cover the bottom edge of the wall finish and achieve a clean transition.
Although flooring can be installed before wall painting, it is often done after to avoid paint drips on finished floors; this is a soft preference for quality control.
Electrical wiring and junction boxes must be installed in the ceiling cavity before the ceiling finish is applied, as the finish would cover access to these components.
HVAC ductwork and diffusers must be installed in the ceiling plenum before the ceiling finish is applied, as they would be inaccessible afterward.
The ceiling substrate or framing (e.g., drywall backing or grid system) must be in place before any finish coating can be applied.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and mudded to create a smooth surface before paint or other ceiling finish can be applied.
Ceiling finishing should be completed before final floor work to prevent paint drips, dust, or debris from damaging newly installed floor finishes.
The wall surface must be clean, smooth, and primed to ensure proper paint adhesion and an even finish for the accent color.
Applying a clear coat sealant after the accent wall paint has fully dried protects the finish and enhances durability, though it is a preference for longevity.
The underlying wall structure (studs, drywall, tape, and mud) must be in place before any painting can occur.
The building structure and rough framing must be complete to provide a substrate and support for architectural millwork installation.
Electrical wiring and boxes must be installed behind wall surfaces before millwork can be placed, as millwork would cover or interfere with access to these areas.
Plumbing lines within walls must be run before millwork is installed to avoid having to remove or cut through finished millwork for plumbing access.
HVAC ductwork and vents within walls/ceilings must be completed before millwork is installed to ensure proper airflow and avoid rework.
Millwork must be installed before final painting and finish coatings around it can be applied, as the millwork defines the final surfaces requiring paint or stain touch-up and adjacent wall finishes.

Electrical wiring for lighting fixtures must be completed and tested before any lighting finish or filter can be installed, as the fixtures need power to verify function and the filter is a final aesthetic layer.
Ceiling surfaces must be complete and finished to provide the mounting surface and ensure the lighting filter is installed against the final ceiling finish without risk of damage or rework.
The physical light fixtures must be mounted and operational before adding color filters or finish layers, as the filter is applied to the assembled fixture.

Once warm color lighting filters/finishes are in place, the final lighting commissioning and punch list activities can verify overall lighting quality, color temperature, and aesthetics as part of project closeout.

Although decorative finishes can often proceed in parallel, it is preferable to have the lighting filter/finish installed first so that interior paint and trim can be evaluated under the actual warm lighting conditions, ensuring color coordination.
Walls and surfaces must be properly prepared, cleaned, and primed before applying warm color paint to ensure proper adhesion and a uniform finish.
Drywall must be installed, taped, mudded, and sanded smooth before painting can begin, as paint cannot be applied to unfinished drywall.
Ceilings are typically painted before walls to avoid dripping onto finished wall surfaces and to maintain a logical top-down workflow.

Painting walls before installing trim and baseboards allows for easier cutting-in and avoids getting paint on finished millwork; however, if trim is pre-painted it may be installed after wall painting.

After painting is complete, the area should be cleaned and touch-ups performed to address any missed spots or drips, though this is a soft preference for workflow organization rather than a physical necessity.
Wallcovering requires a clean, smooth, and primed surface for proper adhesion; applying to unprepared surfaces will cause peeling and failure.
Drywall must be installed, taped, mudded, and sanded smooth before any wallcovering can be applied to ensure a flat substrate.
Electrical boxes and wiring must be in place behind the wall surface before wallcovering is installed; cutting into finished wallcovering to add boxes would damage it.
Baseboards and trim are typically installed after wallcovering to cover the bottom edge of the wallcovering and provide a clean finished look.

successor: Final Painting of Ceiling and Adjacent Surfaces
rationale: While it is physically possible to paint after wallcovering, it is a soft preference to complete painting of ceilings and trim first to avoid overspray or drips on the new wallcovering.
The subfloor must be clean, dry, level, and structurally sound before any flooring can be installed to ensure proper adhesion and a finished surface.
For concrete subfloors, the concrete must be fully cured to reduce moisture content to acceptable levels before installing flooring to prevent mold, warping, or adhesive failure.
A moisture barrier must be placed over the subfloor before flooring installation to protect the flooring material from moisture rising from the subfloor.

All plumbing, electrical, and HVAC rough-in work in walls and ceilings must be completed and inspected before flooring is installed because access to subfloor areas may be needed and flooring should not be damaged by subsequent overhead work.
Baseboards and trim are installed after flooring to cover the expansion gap at the wall edges and to sit on top of the finished flooring for a clean, finished look.

While painting can be done before flooring to avoid drips on the new floor, often the final wall painting is done after flooring to touch up any marks; this is a soft preference as sequencing can vary.
Furniture and occupancy should only be placed after flooring installation is complete and the flooring has been allowed to acclimate and set properly to avoid damage.
Surfaces must be properly sanded and prepared to ensure the stain or sealant adheres correctly and achieves a uniform finish.
A primer may be required on certain surfaces (e.g., raw wood, drywall) to ensure proper stain or sealant adhesion and color consistency.
All dust, debris, and contaminants must be removed from the surface before staining/sealing to prevent imperfections and poor adhesion.
After applying the stain or sealant, sufficient drying and curing time is required before any subsequent activities can take place.
A protective topcoat or finish must be applied after the stain/sealant has cured to protect the color and surface from wear and damage.
The concrete slab or foundation must be poured and cured before seating can be installed, as the seating structure requires a solid, level base to anchor to.
The building's structural steel frame must be erected to create the tiered superstructure that supports the seating rows and risers.
Rough electrical conduits and junction boxes for aisle lighting, seat numbering, and power outlets must be installed in the floor and risers before seating is placed over them.
Permanent flooring and carpet in aisles and around seating areas should be installed after seating is in place to ensure a seamless fit and avoid damaging flooring during seating installation.

Painting and wall finishes can be done before or after seating, but typically finishing is done first to avoid overspray or damage to seats; however, if seating is installed first, protective covering is needed.
The concrete floor slab must be poured and cured to provide a stable load-bearing surface for the reception desk seating area.
Electrical and data cabling must be roughed in beneath the floor before the desk seating area is constructed to avoid cutting into finished surfaces later.
The seating area must be defined and prepared before the actual reception counter can be installed, as the counter typically interfaces with the seating layout.
While seating can be placed after finishes are done, it is preferable to complete painting and flooring first to avoid damage to seating; however, this is a soft preference for work sequencing.

predecessor: Rough Framing / Partition Walls for Reception Area
rationale: The partition walls defining the reception zone must be framed before the seating area can be accurately positioned and constructed within that space.
The ground must be prepared and excavated before any fixed structures like benches can be installed to ensure a stable foundation.
Fixed public benches typically require a concrete base or footing to anchor them securely, so the concrete must be poured and cured first.
If benches are near or integrated with shelters requiring lighting or power, underground utility lines must be laid before bench installation to avoid digging up finished work.
Benches must be in place before surrounding paving, tiling, or landscaping is completed so that the ground finish can be flush with the bench base for a clean, finished appearance.
While structurally independent, it is preferable to install benches before an overhead shelter so that bench positioning can be precisely aligned with shelter columns and user access paths.
The floor slab must be completed to provide a stable, level surface for installing pews and chapel seating.
Wall finishing work such as plastering and painting should be complete to avoid dust, debris, and damage to the pews and seating during installation.
Electrical rough-in work for lighting and outlets in the chapel area must be done before pews are installed to allow access to walls and floors without obstruction.
If any final floor treatments like sealing, waxing, or carpet installation remain, they may be done after pews are in place, though it is preferable to complete flooring first as a soft preference.
Pews and seating must be installed before the chapel can be used for occupancy or final inspection for the seating areas.
The floor slab provides the structural base and support for the heavy desking systems in courtrooms and lecture halls, so the slab must be cured and ready before desking installation can begin.

Electrical outlets, data ports, and cabling for courtroom and lecture hall desks must be roughed-in within the slab or walls before desking can be placed, as accessing these services after desks are installed would be extremely difficult.

Wall framing and drywall define the room boundaries and provide mounting surfaces for any fixed desking components, so these must be completed to ensure proper alignment and attachment of desking units.
After desking is installed, final finishes such as painting touch-ups, trim work, and any adjustments to wall or floor finishes can be completed without risk of damaging the desking.
Seating in courtrooms and lecture halls is typically positioned relative to the desking layout, so desking must be installed first to establish the correct spacing and configuration for chairs.

Bleacher/telescopic seating systems require a structurally sound steel framework and support structure to be in place before they can be mounted or attached, ensuring load-bearing capacity and safety.
A level, cured concrete slab or floor surface is required to provide a stable base for the telescopic seating system to roll, extend, and retract properly without binding or misalignment.
Electrical conduit, junction boxes, and wiring for power and control systems (e.g., motorized seating controls, lighting) must be roughed in before seating is installed to avoid costly retrofitting.

The floor surfaces beneath and around the bleacher/telescopic seating must be finished and sealed after installation, as the seating covers large areas of the floor that would be inaccessible for finishing work once installed.

A formal inspection for compliance with accessibility codes (e.g., ADA), egress requirements, and seating safety standards can only occur after the bleacher/telescopic seating system is fully installed and operational.
Floor drains must be roughed-in and connected before chairs are mounted, as chairs are heavy and can block access to floor drains.
Chairs need to be anchored to a finished, cured concrete slab or subfloor to ensure stable and permanent installation.
Electrical wiring for outlets near the chairs must be roughed-in before mounting chairs so that power can be connected to the chairs or nearby receptacles.
While it's generally preferred to finish flooring before mounting heavy equipment, if chairs are mounted first, final floor finishing around the mounts may be needed to achieve a clean appearance.
Chairs must be mounted and positioned before installing wall-mounted mirrors and cabinetry so that spacing and alignment can be properly coordinated.
Stool mounts must be anchored to a finished floor surface to ensure stable installation and proper alignment.
Wall-mounted stool mounts require structural wall framing to be in place before they can be securely attached.

predecessor: Rough-in Plumbing for Medical Gas and Vacuum Lines
rationale: Any underfloor or in-wall medical gas, suction, or vacuum lines serving the stool must be roughed in before mounting the stool, as the stool often integrates or covers these service connections.

successor: Final Connection of Medical Gas/Vacuum Hoses to Stool
rationale: The stool mount must be physically installed before final hookup of flexible gas, suction, or water lines can be made to the stool's integrated connections.

successor: Commissioning and Testing of Dental/Medical Equipment
rationale: Functional testing of the procedural stool (e.g., height adjustment, locking casters, instrument tray stability) can only be performed after the mount is fully installed and secured.
The seating assemblies must be placed on a finished booth floor surface to ensure stability and proper alignment.
Wall panels and partitions define the booth boundaries and layout, providing the spatial context needed before seating can be positioned correctly.
Electrical wiring and outlet boxes need to be installed in floors or walls before seating assemblies are placed, as seating would block access to these areas.
Final decorative elements such as table tops, cushions, signage, and finishing touches should be applied after seating is in place to ensure proper fit and visual integration.
Seating must be fully assembled and secured before exhibitors or visitors can occupy the booth and use the seating.
Wall surfaces must be smooth, clean, and primed before installing chair rails and wall protection strips to ensure proper adhesion and a finished appearance.
Electrical and low voltage wiring in walls must be completed before installing wall protection strips to avoid damaging or covering accessible wiring paths.
Structural wall framing and sheathing must be in place to provide a secure substrate for mounting chair rails and protection strips.
Chair rails and wall protection strips are finished elements that should be installed before final paint coats so that painting can be completed over and around them for a seamless look.

While chair rails are typically installed after flooring is complete, wall protection strips at lower levels may be coordinated with base molding installation; typically chair rails go after flooring but can be done before base molding for a cleaner trim fit.
Fixed auditorium seating must be installed on a completed, stable floor slab to provide a level and structurally sound base for anchoring seats.

predecessor: Installation of MEP Rough-Ins (Electrical, Mechanical, Plumbing) in Floor/Slab
rationale: Any conduit, wiring, or piping that runs beneath or through the seating area floor must be roughed-in before seats are installed, as access is permanently blocked by fixed seating.

predecessor: Completion of Auditorium Floor Finish / Sealing
rationale: Floor finishes (e.g., concrete sealant, epoxy, or other permanent flooring) must be completed prior to seating installation, as fixed seats prevent access for finishing afterward.

successor: Installation of Auditorium Ceiling / Acoustic Panels (if over seating area)
rationale: Overhead ceiling work and acoustic panel installation above the seating area should be completed before seating is installed to avoid damage to seats and to provide clear access for lifts and scaffolding.

successor: Final Floor Cleaning and Commissioning of Auditorium
rationale: Once seating is installed, final cleaning and commissioning of the auditorium space can proceed, though this is a soft preference for project sequence rather than a strict physical requirement.
The bench seating requires a level, stable, and finished floor surface to be installed upon; the subfloor must be prepared and cured before bench installation can proceed.
Any power outlets, data ports, or lighting intended near or within the bench area must be roughed in behind the wall before the bench is installed, as the bench would block access to wiring.
Wall framing must be complete where the bench will be mounted or abutted against, providing the structural backing for secure attachment of the bench.

Flooring materials and base moldings should be installed after the bench is in place so that flooring can be cut to fit neatly against the bench's base and base moldings can terminate cleanly into the bench.

successor: Final painting and finishing of adjacent walls
rationale: While painting can be done before bench installation, it is typically preferred to complete final paint touch-ups after bench installation to cover any fastener holes or gaps created during the installation process.
The flooring must be fully installed and stable before mounting chairs that sit on or are anchored to the floor, to ensure a level and secure base.
Electrical wiring and outlets for the desk area must be roughed in before installing operator chairs to avoid interference and allow safe access for electrical work.

successor: Installation of Desk-Mounted Equipment (e.g., monitors, keyboards)
rationale: Chairs must be mounted and positioned first so that desks and associated equipment can be arranged ergonomically relative to the chair positions.
It is preferred to finish mounting chairs before final cleaning to avoid re-soiling floors, but not a physical necessity.
Wall painting and finishing should be completed before installing chairs to prevent paint splatter or dust from damaging the chairs and to allow unobstructed access to walls.
Recessed downlights are installed into the ceiling; the ceiling structure must be in place to receive and support the light fixtures.
Electrical cables and junction boxes need to be run to the downlight locations before the fixtures can be connected and installed.
Recessed downlights must be installed before the final ceiling finish is applied so that the trim/flange can be flush with the finished surface and holes can be neatly cut/taped around.
The recessed housing must be in place before trim, bulbs, and decorative covers can be installed.
After the downlight housing is mounted, final wiring connections and system testing can be performed.
Electrical wiring and junction boxes must be in place in the ceiling before pendant lights can be connected and mounted.
The ceiling surface must be finished and painted prior to mounting pendant lights to avoid damage to the finish and to ensure proper installation alignment.
Pendant lights must be physically installed before electricians can complete final connections, install bulbs, and test the lighting circuit.

It is preferable to complete pendant light installation before installing delicate floor finishes to avoid dust/debris from electrical work falling on new floors, though not a strict physical dependency.
Pendant light clusters must be fully installed and operational before the final project inspection and walkthrough can be completed.
Electrical conduits and wiring must be run to the floor locations before canisters can be mounted and connected.
The floor surface or slab must be in place and prepared to receive the canister embedment or mounting.
Finish flooring (e.g., tile, wood, carpet) is typically laid around or after the canisters are set so that the canisters are flush with the finished floor.

successor: Final Electrical Trim-Out / Light Fixture Connection
rationale: After canisters are physically installed in the floor, the final wiring connections and trim/light fixture installation can be completed.
The uplight fixtures must be in place and connected before they can be tested and commissioned for proper operation.
Electrical power supply and wiring infrastructure must be in place before lighting fixtures can be installed and connected.
Wall wash luminaires are typically mounted on or recessed into ceilings; the ceiling structure must be complete to provide a mounting surface.
Wall surfaces must be finished and painted before installing wall wash fixtures, as the fixtures are positioned to illuminate the walls and any subsequent finishing would be obstructed or damaged.
After luminaires are installed, the complete lighting system must be tested and commissioned to verify proper operation, aiming, and control.
Minor cosmetic touch-ups to ceilings and walls near the installed fixtures may be needed after installation, though this is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
The trim rings and baffles are finish/fascia components that go around the light pool opening; the light pool structure must exist before trim can be installed.
Electrical wiring to the light pool location must be roughed in before trim rings and baffles are installed, as they cover and conceal the wiring access.
Trim rings and baffles define the finished edge around the light pool; ceiling finishing/painting is completed up to and around these installed elements to ensure a clean, flush appearance.
Trim rings and baffles are installed first to create the housing/frame, then light fixtures/lamps are placed into the baffles.
Electrical power supply and wiring infrastructure must be installed before LED linear cove channels can be connected and energized.
The ceiling or wall structure where the cove channels are mounted must be framed and finished before the channels can be physically attached.
The cove channels must be mounted and wired before the dedicated LED drivers can be connected and commissioned.

successor: Lighting Fixture Trim and Diffuser Installation
rationale: The linear cove channels housing the LED strips must be in place before diffusers, lenses, or trim covers can be installed over them.
All fixture mounting and wiring must be complete before the system can be tested, commissioned, and final adjustments made.
Electrical wiring must be in place before trim installation to provide power connections to adjustable lighting trims.
The ceiling surface must be completed and finished before installing trim rings to ensure proper fitment and aesthetic finish.
The supporting ceiling structure or grid must be installed to provide a secure mounting point for the adjustable trims.
While painting can be done before trim installation, final touch-ups after trim installation ensure clean edges and a professional finish around the trim rings.

successor: Lighting fixture trim adjustment and aiming
rationale: The gimbal ring trims must be installed first before they can be adjusted and aimed to achieve the desired lighting direction.
Rough-in electrical wiring must be run to the ceiling locations before downlight housings can be physically installed and connected to the power supply.
The ceiling surface must be in place so that the downlight housings can be cut into and mounted within the finished ceiling assembly.
Ceiling joists and framing must be complete to provide structural support for attaching the downlight housings.
The housings must be in place before bulbs and decorative trims can be inserted and before final circuit connections can be made at the electrical panel.
Electrical rough-in (wiring, boxes, switches) must be complete before trim and lamp installation can begin, as trim covers the rough work and lamps require existing wiring connections.
Plumbing rough-in must be finished before trim work to ensure pipes and fixtures are in place behind walls before finish work covers them.
Insulation must be installed before trim and lamps are installed, as insulation is placed within wall cavities that are later enclosed by trim and finished surfaces.
Drywall must be hung, taped, mudded, and sanded before trim (baseboards, casing, crown molding) can be applied and lamps mounted, as trim is fastened to finished walls.
Trim installation (baseboards, casing, crown molding) must be completed before final painting and touch-up, as painters need to caulk and paint trim and touch up walls after trim is installed.
The pool shell must be physically complete to provide the structure where lighting fixtures, zones, and dimming systems are installed and commissioned.
Power and control wiring must be run to the pool area before lighting zone and dimming systems can be energized and commissioned.
All pool lighting fixtures must be physically installed before zoning and dimming commissioning can occur, as commissioning requires functional testing of each fixture and zone.
Commissioning of zoning and dimming must be completed before final acceptance testing can verify the entire pool lighting system operates correctly.

It is preferable to complete lighting commissioning before final finishes so that any access needed to fixtures or controls does not damage finished surfaces, though it is not a physical impossibility to do otherwise.
A stable concrete foundation must be fully poured and cured to provide a level, load-bearing surface for mounting track rails, ensuring structural integrity and alignment.
Precise layout marking and surveying must be completed to define the exact alignment, elevation, and spacing of the track rails before installation can begin.
Underground conduits and duct banks for wiring must be installed prior to track rail mounting to avoid excavation and disruption after rails are in place.
After the rails are mounted and wired, precise alignment, gauging, and tuning must be performed to ensure the track meets operational specifications.
Wiring must be fully installed along the track before electrical power connections can be made and circuit testing performed.
Personal storage units require a stable, level load-bearing floor surface. The concrete slab foundation must be poured, cured, and finished before any storage units can be erected or placed on top.
Proper drainage away from the storage unit area must be established to prevent water pooling under and around the units, which could cause rust, rot, or structural settling issues.
The outer shell and structural frame of the storage units define the boundaries within which interior partitions, if any, must be laid out and framed.
Electrical conduit, junction boxes, and wiring for unit lighting and power outlets cannot be installed until the storage unit walls and ceilings are in place to determine routing paths.
Roll-up or overhead doors must be installed after the storage unit structure is complete because the door frame and track system mount directly onto the finished unit opening.
Structural framing and ceiling must be installed to provide the overhead support structure from which gallery hanging systems (rails, rods, cables) are suspended.
Electrical wiring for track lighting and gallery outlets must be roughed-in behind walls and ceilings before hanging systems are mounted, as later access would be obstructed.

Walls must be finished and painted before installing picture rails and gallery hanging tracks, as these systems are surface-mounted and would need to be removed or protected if wall finishing were done afterward.
The gallery hanging system (rails, cables, hooks) must be fully installed and load-tested before any artwork can be hung, as it provides the physical support infrastructure for the art pieces.

While floor finishing can technically be done before hanging systems are installed, it is preferred to complete hanging systems first to avoid damage to finished floors from ladders, scaffolding, and dropped tools during installation.
The structural frame and floor slab must be in place to provide a stable load-bearing surface for the reception desks.
Underfloor electrical outlets, data ports, and cabling must be roughed in before desks are positioned over them.
Lobby partition walls define the spatial layout and boundaries where the reception desk will be located.
The desk framework must be fully assembled and anchored before countertop materials and final surface finishes can be applied.
While lighting can be roughed in earlier, final fixture placement and aiming above reception desks is best done after desks are in place to ensure proper alignment.
Rough framing and sheathing must be completed to define the structural walls and spaces where built-in workstations will be installed.
Electrical wiring must be run within walls before built-in workstations are constructed, as the workstations may conceal or require access to electrical outlets and cabling.
Any plumbing lines that will run behind or beneath built-in workstations must be roughed in prior to workstation installation to avoid costly rework.
Built-in workstations must be fully installed before final interior finishes like painting and trim are applied, so that finishes can be applied seamlessly around the workstations.
The base cabinets/framing of the built-in workstations must be in place before countertops are fitted and secured on top.
Flooring should be installed before cabinets to allow cabinets to sit on top of finished flooring and avoid damaging flooring during cabinet installation.
Rough plumbing for sinks must be completed before cabinet installation so that cabinets can be positioned around existing plumbing lines and connections.
Electrical wiring for outlets, lighting, and appliances must be roughed in before cabinets are installed, as cabinets may conceal or interfere with wiring paths.
Walls must be framed, insulated, and drywalled before cabinet installation so cabinets have a finished surface to mount against and can be properly anchored.
Countertops must be installed on top of base cabinets; cabinets must be in place to support and align countertops.
Sinks, cooktops, and other drop-in appliances are installed after cabinets are in place and countertops are fitted.
Backsplash is typically installed after cabinets and countertops for a seamless finish, though it could technically be done before if planned carefully.
Final touch-up painting and trim work around cabinets is often done after installation, but this is a soft preference as painting can be done before with careful masking.
Wall finishes must be completed before wardrobe installation to ensure walls are smooth and painted, preventing damage to finished surfaces and allowing proper fit of wardrobe units against walls.
Floor finishes must be laid before wardrobe installation so that wardrobes sit on the finished floor level, ensuring correct height alignment and avoiding the need to cut or adjust wardrobes later.
Ceiling finishing (including cornices and paint) must be completed before tall wardrobes are installed, as wardrobes often reach ceiling height and would obstruct access to ceiling work.
Electrical wiring and outlet boxes must be roughed in before wardrobe installation, as wardrobes may conceal or require integration with lighting, switches, and power points within closets.
It is preferable to install architraves and decorative trims after wardrobe installation so that trims can be fitted flush against the wardrobe frames, creating a clean finished appearance.
The mudroom and entry storage must be built on top of a finished foundation and slab; the structural base must be in place before any framing or flooring can commence.
Exterior walls and roof structure for the mudroom area must be framed before interior work like storage installation, benching, and cabinetry can proceed.
Any wiring for lighting/outlets and any plumbing for a mudroom sink or laundry area must be roughed in before walls are closed up with insulation and drywall.
After mudroom framing and rough-ins are complete, interior finishes like drywall installation, taping, painting, and trim work can proceed to create the finished space.
Flooring for the mudroom is typically installed after the space is dried in and finished, as it is a surface-level finish that must be protected until final stages.
Wall framing provides the structural support and cavity within which vanities are installed, and must be completed before any finish carpentry or cabinet installation can begin.
The water supply lines and drain pipes for the sink must be roughed-in within the wall before vanities are positioned, as installing them afterward would require removing or cutting into the vanity.

Electrical wiring for outlets, switches, and lighting above or beside the vanity must be roughed-in before the vanity is installed to avoid interference and allow proper placement of electrical boxes.
Wall surfaces (backer board or drywall) need to be installed prior to vanity installation because the vanity is typically mounted to or placed against the finished wall surface.

Flooring is typically installed before vanities to ensure a clean, finished look and to prevent the need for cutting flooring around the vanity base, though some installations place vanity over subfloor with flooring cut around it.
The vanity cabinet must be secured in place and leveled before the countertop can be measured, cut, and installed on top of it.
The vanity cabinet supports the sink; the sink and faucet are mounted into or onto the vanity/countertop assembly after the vanity is in place.
Mirrors are typically mounted above the vanity; the vanity's final position determines the exact height and centering of the mirror.
Finish trim and molding around the vanity base or top edge is installed after the vanity cabinet is fixed in place to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance.
Flooring must be installed before built-in bookcases and library systems are constructed, as the bookcases will sit on top of the finished floor.
Walls must be framed, drywalled, and finished before installing built-in bookcase systems, as bookcases attach to or are built into the walls.
Electrical wiring for lighting outlets or data ports in or near the bookcases must be roughed in before the bookcase system is installed, as walls need to be open for wiring.
Built-in bookcases and library systems are typically painted or stained and trimmed out as part of the final finishing, so they must be installed before final paint and trim work around them.

Any final touch-up or refinishing of flooring adjacent to the bookcases is best done after installation to address any scratches or gaps, though this is a soft preference rather than a strict requirement.
Display cases and vitrines must be placed on a finished, level floor to ensure stability and proper alignment.
Walls must be finished and painted before installing display cases to avoid dust, paint splatter, and damage to the cases.
Electrical wiring for lighting within or near display cases must be roughed-in before the cases are positioned.
Items to be displayed within the cases should be placed after the cases are installed, though this is a logical sequence preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
Final cleaning and commissioning of the space should occur after display cases are installed to ensure the entire space is clean and ready for use.
The bed frame provides the structural base onto which the headboard and bed platform are mounted; without a frame, the headboard and platform have no support.
Flooring must be completed before installing any bedroom furniture including bed components to avoid damaging the flooring and to ensure proper leveling of the bed.
Walls behind the headboard must be finished and painted before the headboard is attached, as installing the headboard first would block access to the wall surface.
The mattress is placed directly on top of the bed platform; the platform must be fully assembled and installed before the mattress can be set in place.
Although bedding can technically be placed anytime, it is logical and conventional to install the headboard and platform first so that the bed is fully assembled before making it with linens.
Wall framing provides the structural support and cavity needed to securely mount and house the media center units.
Electrical wiring must be completed within the walls before media centers are fitted, as they require power outlets and cable access that would be inaccessible afterward.
Drywall provides the finished wall surface to which media centers are attached or into which they are recessed.
Trim and molding around the media centers must be installed after the units are in place to achieve a finished appearance.
Final connection of media equipment to power and signal sources, along with testing, can only be performed once the media center units are fitted in their final position.
Electrical power and data cabling must be run behind walls and ceilings before display systems are mounted, as displays require power and signal connections that are inaccessible after mounting.
Display systems are typically mounted on finished walls; wall framing and drywall must be complete to provide a stable mounting surface and allow for proper anchoring.
For ceiling-mounted displays, the ceiling structure and finish must be in place to support the mounting brackets and hardware.
Display systems must be physically installed and connected before audiovisual system testing, calibration, and signal testing can be performed.

While not a hard physical constraint, it is preferred to perform final paint touch-ups after display installation to address any wall damage caused during mounting; however, displays can be installed after painting if care is taken.
Flooring must be completed first to provide a level, finished base surface for fitted storage units to sit upon securely.
Walls need to be finished (plastered and painted) before installing fitted storage so that cabinets and shelves can be fixed cleanly to finished walls without needing rework.
Electrical rough-in work must be completed and signed off before storage units are installed, as access to wall cavities for wiring would be blocked by the fitted storage.

successor: Final Electrical Fit-Off (switches, lighting, power points)
rationale: Fitted storage installation must be complete before electricians can install final faceplates, switches, and lighting fixtures that are integrated with or adjacent to the storage units.

successor: Final Finishing and Touch-Ups (caulking, painting touch-ups)
rationale: After fitted storage is installed, any gaps between units and walls can be caulked and paint touched up, but this is a soft preference as touch-ups can be deferred to final defects period.
